name: Satisfactory
detailed_description: Satisfactory is a first-person open-world factory building game with a dash of exploration and combat. Play alone or with friends, explore an alien planet, create multi-story factories, and enter conveyor belt heaven! Construct Conquer nature by building massive factories across the land. Expand wherever and however you want. The planet is filled with valuable natural resources just waiting to be utilized. As an employee of FICSIT it’s your duty to make sure they come to good use. Automate Construct your factories with gracious perfection or build intricate webs of conveyor belts to supply all your needs. Automate trucks and trains to reach your faraway outposts and be sure to handle liquids properly by transporting them in pipes. It’s all about minimizing manual labour! Explore & Exploit Venture on expeditions to search for new materials and be sure to put everything to good use. Nature is yours to harvest! You have vehicles, jetpacks, jump pads and more at your disposal to make the exploration easier. Equip the proper safety gear as well, just in case you run into the local wildlife. FEATURES • Open World: Explore the huge (30km2) alien planet that is Massage-2(AB)b with its unique fauna and creatures. • Co-Op: Build a factory yourself or share the joy with your friends. Up to you! • Factory Building: Experience building a huge factory from a first-person perspective. Automate and optimize it to perfection for your personal satisfaction. • Customization: Customize your factory to your own liking. Build at high altitudes or over wide plains, there is almost no limits in the making of your tailor-made factory. • Vehicles: Travel the world with class. Use jump pads, factory carts, jetpacks, hypertubes, trucks or trains. The choice is yours!

_childDocuments_.review: First thing I want to say: What a beautiful game!It is truly wonderful to look at with the new Unreal Engine 5 update.For a beginner, and I would count myself as one even with 60 hours in, there is just so much to do that at times it can become overwhelming. _childDocuments_.review: Having played it way back in early access and now after it's big release, the game has come far. While on one hand it was very easy to pick up and figure your way onwards during early access, I somehow got caught off guard with all the new features and tutorials the game brings with it's 1.0 release. Nonetheless I stumbled along trying to remember all the systems I had designed once before.It's definitely a game that takes a bit of time to get into. It isn't as rewarding for me at the start as I love maxxing and optimizing so there is a bit of a progression stage (which isn't inherently bad) during which you REALLY want the faster belts or miners but just.. can't. Once that little hurdle is passed, you're off to the races writing down notes to calculate your factory output and constantly improving every little detail.With a busy life it might not be the ideal game to pick up after a long day, should you want an "in and out, 20 minute adventure" but after progressing your way through, it's .

_childDocuments_.review: When I initially reviewed this, I was very sceptical.  How could it possibly match up to the complexity and depth of something like Factorio?I was so, so wrong.  The sheer depth and scale of projects that you can build is incredible. Its a massive open world with so much to explore and open space to utilise.  There are threats to encounter (although that is toggleable.  You cant turn them off altogether, but you can make them completely indifferent to you) and secrets to be found.The important part though, is the building.  The sheer scale of factories that can be built is incredible.  Even just building on a vertical plain, the sky really is the limit.  The game fully supports this as well, with conveyor belts, pipelines, power lines etc all capable of fully vertical transport, along with clever ways of hiding them, or passing through floors and walls.The range of transport for both you and your products is also extremely varied.  For yourself, this can be dirty buggies, tractors or even just humble factory carts (complete with flashing red beacon!) that can only be used effectively indoors.  For the more refined traveller, hypertubes are the answer, firing you across the map at high speeds to whatever destination you choose.  You can also turn these into super powered cannons that fire you through the air should you wish.  For products, there are tractors, huge heavy goods vehicles, trains and drones.  Setting up the pathing for trains and road vehicles is something I found very satisfying to do, although it can come with some issues when the networks become larger.This is still in early access and they are still changing some features (including to an updated game engine recently, as of time of writing) and adding new ones.  You WILL encounter bugs, especially if you choose to install the experimental builds.  That being said, Coffee Stain Studios have been very open and honest about where they are up to and what they are working on with this game.  This really is Early Access done right.I cannot recommend this game enough to anybody that enjoys the factory/automation genre.  Factorio is still being used as the standard bearer but I can see that changing once this game reaches full release.

_childDocuments_.review: If you’ve ever dreamed of building sprawling factories that stretch across the horizon while experimenting with complex production lines, Satisfactory is the game for you. _childDocuments_.review: I'd like to preface this review by saying that I am not a fan of factory games.  A friend of mine tried to get me into Factorio years ago and I just could not.  Even modded Minecraft that features tech mods in this style were just too much for me, but this game is different.  My husband asked me to play this with him knowing full well that I don't enjoy this genre of game, but I'm so glad he did.  We've had so much fun playing this together, working on the milestones and just trying to figure everything out.  I do much more of the exploration side and he prefers the actual base building, but that works out perfectly.  I don't find the new pieces of tech that we unlock along the way too difficult to understand and I love running around the world looking for power slugs (OOOH SHINY).  I'm so glad I gave this game a chance and you should too.
_childDocuments_.name: Satisfactory

_childDocuments_.review: Satisfactory 1.0 is out today... and I am probably back in for the next 250 hours.I have played this game a LOT in early access first on EGS, then on Steam. It is great.Beautiful world, stunning wildlife, great game mechanics that just scratch my brain itch in the right way, without the sense of urgency that other factory games tend to have.Thank you Coffee Stain for this amazing game.HIGHLY recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Satisfactory

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a game to play for those who liked Factorio or games which focus on optimisation and efficiency. The game mechanics are complex and unique yet are reasonably easy to understand for players who are new to the genre. Plenty of guides online which help with understanding game knowledge. Highly recommend a youtuber named "Scalti" as he has a lot of videos on early game builds and general knowledge on game mechanics which are easy to understand. Although the game is restricted to a set map, it has various areas which will benefit different players at different levels. In terms of difficulty, it's pretty chill as the game doesn't force you to progress with any questlines or storylines, which there aren't, so you can take it at your own pace. Has high replayability potential as the your first run would most likely be discovering the game and its map, whereas your future runs will be fully optimising your builds. There's also a large community that provide mods which I highly recommend trying out as well, maybe on your 3rd or 4th run as it'll make it just 100 times better. Be cautious though, as gameplay might be a bit physically nauseating for some people because of the player and camera movement. If you get nauseous playing Portal or Minecraft, maybe look at some gameplay and see how you feel. 10/10 definitely recommend for players who are interested in getting into factory building games.

_childDocuments_.review: Over a thousand hours in an early access game I think says it all.  The game's come a long way since it's beginnings and keeps adding more and more.  I'm eager for the final release and finding out what those mercer spheres and somersloops are all about -- plus what I can make with SAM!If you love building a factory on an alien planet, or petting lizard doggos (cute!), or doing a lot of math to finely tune your production chain, then play this game!  The game allows for a tutorial phase (or not) in the beginning and then advances stage by stage.  And unlocking alternate recipes to allow for more flexibility in all that math I mentioned.  Plus an AI that can at times be a bit pushy in harvesting "artifacts"... evidently there's some fine print in your character's contract.

_childDocuments_.review: To be honest after playing this game for about 50+ hours I have to say it is very well made. The graphics are really nice and good especially if you have a good PC.But there is one problem, once you start building bigger factories and expanding them like mad, then your Fps goes down and it starts lagging pretty bad so you will eventually have to turn the graphics down.The core game play and complexity of game makes it challenging.It never gets easier, with each step you take you have to go one back because there are so many factors you have to think about (for example efficiency , outputs , inputs , power , ratios,building space , looks , future expantion of your factory and many other factors).I recommend this game to the real engineers , industrialist , designers , problem solvers out there and for those who want a real challenge when it comes to gaming.But of course you can also play the game to just chill out and pass time , this game is so peaceful and relaxing that sometimes i would play 4 hours non stop because its just so well mad.The Soundtrack is limited but it works well with the atmosphere and overall i have nothing else to say to the music. The world is beautiful with many biomes and all kinds of vegetation not only that but it has friendly and hostile organic life like Lizard Doggos and Spiders ( dont worry there is an arachnophobia mode which you can turn on in the settings ).The world is massive but the different terrain makes each factory look different which in its own way it makes every factory unique.This game allows you to have mods which you can use to either make the game easier or harder it depends what you want. The Mods are reliable and work really well just dont use more then 20 mods or you will start crashing a lot.The work the people put in the mods is incredible which just shows how passionate the people in this community are.not only that but the community is one of a kind everybody is friendly and willing to help each other ( also lots of memes and fun to be had).The game gets small life improving updates and it sometimes gets Huge updates that make the game so much better. Of course you will always have bugs here and there but the Team tackles the problems very quick so you shouldnt be worried.Now we come to the downsides of this game. The game gets very hard which makes lots of people quit the game early like a couple of my friends and it doesnt have a proper tutorial which i would have liked but remember this is an early access version of the game and there is a lot of space for improvement . I would wish for the game to have like a planning mode where you could build and plan out your factory before actually building it with resources kind of like a creative mode. I would also like to have factory templates from other people so you can copy them in your world and study the design and learn how to make a good factory .Because sadly most youtube videos and websites wont help you that much when it comes to designing a really good and neat factory atleast from what i saw.(one little note yes you can play it with your friends.)I give this game a 8 out 10 just because its still needs some polishing and its not complete. I recommend this game a 100 percent .
_childDocuments_.name: Satisfactory

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Leaving negative because it no longer works as of the latest update with my latest-gen AMD GPUI am going to recommend this game, but I am conflicted as there are many things I really like and many things I strongly dislike about the game. All in all it's a very promising game, but it's obvious that the developers don't have experience with making something of this scope. It may be an Early Access game but it's obvious that many of my complaints will never be fixed even with a full release, and the developers already stated that they will not be adding certain strongly requested features into the game because even seemingly simple features would require extensive reworks and rewriting of existing code and systems just to avoid conflicts and more jank.Now, the good:+ Beautiful hand crafted world, with tons of special landmarks, secret caves, biomes and natural formations.+ Resource nodes are infinite because it's a finite world.+ Nearly unlimited verticality and plenty of empty space in the corners of the world to allow for massive production plants.+ Exploration feels rewarding as you not only find resource deposits, but also collectibles that may be used to enhance your factory, character or unlock alternate recipes. Meat from slain enemies can also be used to get cosmetic unlocks at a much faster rate than the alternative.+ Your structures do not get destroyed and enemies do not attack your base.+ There are a couple separate systems for unlocking recipes and upgrades which complement each other quite well, so there are plenty of different things to unlock while you wait for other things to be crafted+ Factory and logistics are varied, there are a lot of recipes, components, and alternative recipes to allow you a lot of variety when it comes to base design, logistics, and efficiencyHere are the negatives besides crashes and bugs you'd expect from an EA title:- Resources are mostly spread out far and wide which makes it difficult to get any production line going without bringing resources from different areas that are 1-2km away from each other. Some areas of the map have a lot of one resource, in other areas it's completely absent. There's a few resources that basically need the presence of 1 or 2 others to make even one basic product out of them (Sulfur + Coal + Oil | Iron | Copper OR Quartz + Copper + Iron), so you are forced to set up 2km long roads, trains or conveyor belt systems just to craft a simple recipe that requires 2 crafting steps.  It makes sense that certain parts of the map will have certain resources, but what I don't like is that one starter area puts you on the half of the map has every other resource except 2, a different starting zone has every resource in the game with twice the amount of nodes within 2km, and a third starting zone puts you so far away from any resources you will run a marathon to even get the bare essentials, until you can lay down a road or railway that goes halfway across the world. It also kills replay value, because even if you start in a different area you will have to trek halfway across the world just to get access to those.- Most buildings past Phase 2 are way too big, and they are so tall that using verticality is even harder. Once your factory expands, you will basically need a 5 minute trip from one end of a production line to the other. A normal Phase 3-4 building will be bigger than your entire starter base. It's especially bad with truck stops, train stations and power generators because they are so massive that it's really difficult to make a good-looking base around them. Do not be surprised if it takes you over a minute to run from one end of a mdoestly sized base to another.- Vehicles are terrible. Their AI is really bad and setting up vehicles to drive from a point to point is very time consuming and tedious. If you make even one mistake, you have to repeat an entire route, because the developers only let you delete steps, not move them. It's especially bad for long routes where your vehicle could take 10 minutes to complete the route.- There is almost no logic for items or storage containers in the game besides having some "Smart Splitters" that are not really all that smart. You have 1 input and 3 outputs with different filters, all in different directions. If you want your logistics to work perfectly you will only be able to filter for 1 item at a time with 1 side being configured for that item, 1 side for the overflow, and 1 side for any undefined items. Except overflow will still not work properly half the time and will send even filtered items through that side. Even setting up huge filter lines can't help you because your conveyor belts are capped at 780 items per minute, and a single machine will have an output of 1-60 per minute. You basically need a separate smart splitter for every single resource you want to filter, which will really blow up the size of your conveyor belt lanes and storage systems. The problems extend to trucks and trains too, because they are not smart, they can only either load OR unload from a stop, so if you want two-way transport you will need two stops. I have no idea why stops even have 2x input and 2x output holes if they can only do one at a time.- A lot of the convenient, helpful splitting/merging/sorting/switching functions are locked late into progression, but you'd want to have them as soon as humanly possible. Even automatic power generation is not available till 10+ hours into the game, so unless you skip to that stage, you will spend the entire early game hand feeding generators like some pleb.- Building is extremely frustrating and time consuming. Why? Mainly because of the way buildables snap to each other by using the shortest, most direct route. Even something as basic as laying down conveyor belts and sorters can be extremely time consuming because the game defaults to just directly connecting whatever you can, so if you want to use verticality and rectangular connections, you will need to move conveyor belt 1 meter, see if it'll snap in a rectangular fashion, disassemble the belt, disassemble the support, and then try placing it again. The way foundations, belts, supports and splitters stack on each other is way out of proportion to each other and makes it difficult to combine any of these without clipping. If you try placing one above the other, your entire factory will not align, and you will need to use some hacky way to make them have the correct height and length. Pretty much 90% of the Satisfactory building tips border on exploits because the base building system is absolute dogwater and the game has almost no restrictions on clipping and placement for most things, so if you want your base to not look like a spaghetti nightmare, you need to make sure to spend 1 hour placing things in the correct order with the correct layers underneath them unless you want a frankenstein abomination that you will have to tear down and try again.- Wood, mycelium and flowers are virtually non-renewable. None of the vegetation regrows, and the only way to get them afterwards is by taming a "lizard doggo" ( I thought this game was released in 2019, not 2014?). There's no way to make tamed lizard doggos stay in place or even on the same plane of existence, since if you put them in a box, you will discover they have all disappeared and you'll find them wandering the wilderness 1000m away from where your box was. Oh and they sometimes bring radioactive things that kill you and there's no legitimate way to get rid of that in the game.- Some trees, plants, foliage is indestructible. Best case it causes clipping and some nasty visuals, worst case there's invisible walls that your conveyor belts and vehicles can't go through.

_childDocuments_.review: Satisfactory is a mostly competent automation game overall, that gets brought down by completely flawed fundamentals. In a game about building massive factories they got the most important thing radically wrong - the building. It's annoying at best, and frustrating most of the time.It's really not clear what they were thinking. There is a sort of grid system for buildings of 1m, but it's not represented by anything visual in the game. There are foundations, but they are 8x8, and almost none of the buildings align with the foundations. This is the fundamental (pun intended) issue, and many of the others come as a result of it, but every single category of buildings is clunky and unintuitive to place. Comparing that to any other major automation game, and Satisfactory comes out way behind.Belts are obnoxious in this game. They have a minimal length, so connecting two buildings directly next to each other is  (sometimes) not possible. Except it's unreliable, because the grid is not actually a grid, so you are at the mercy of floating point calculations. That's not even a game design flaw, just a technical competency flaw at the very core of the game. Dragging long belts is extraordinarily tedious, as they have a maximum length, but there is nothing visualizing that maximum length, So you randomly run around, placing foundations until you hit the range by accident.Belt splitters and mergers are even worse. You can have belts that visually connect to a splitter slot, but don't *actually*, so nothing will come in or out. What's worse is that you can remove an existing splitter, replace it with a different one, and some of the belts will be connected, while others won't... Splitters also have an internal inventory, which is not visible in any way. This is particularly annoying for smart splitters, as if they get clogged by an unexpected item by accident, the only way to even notice the issue is to destroy the smart splitter. Which means you need to replace the 4 connecting belts as well due to the previous issue.Probably the worst aspect of building are the blueprints. Satisfactory has easily the weakest and most buggy blueprint system of any automation game I've played. The blueprint size is gated by game progression, so certain types of buildings are not possible to usefully blueprint until the late game, or never at all. For example railway intersections, a very obvious thing to blueprint, are way too large to fit even the largest blueprint, so enjoy building an identical intersection dozens of time in your playthrough.Pipes are a whole other story. They attempted some kind of fluid simulation, but it sucks. It doesn't make any sense, the game explains none of it, and the community has not figured out the rules. There is just a collection of tricks that usually work, but sometimes not, and nobody knows why. The devs even acknowledge that pipes are frustrating  , but for some reason think that they are not worth the time to fix because "players already use them". No ♥♥♥♥ players use them, you can't finish the game without using pipes, it's the most useless metric imaginable.Speaking of things that players don't use, hypertubes. The only meaningful way anybody uses them is by building "hypertube cannons". The problem with that is they appear to be unintentional - hypertube entrance acceleration stacks infinitely, so you can launch yourself at ridiculous speeds. However it's quite easy to go so fast as to crash the game...Meanwhile the "naive" and seemingly intended use of hypertubes is completely nonsensical. They are terrible at long and medium range transportation - they are just too slow, and you have many options which unlock earlier and move faster. They'd be perfect for short range movement, as a fancy stair of sorts - but for some reason hypertubes consume a significant amount of power at all times, so you are not going to spam them in your blueprints and small factories. You also have access to jump pads way earlier than hypertubes, which take less power, move you faster, and the only real cost is larger footprint, and you are never limited by space in Satisfactory, only by your own aversion to placing floating foundation in the sky.I could keep listing flawed systems of this game for a long time. Many people enjoy the decorative aspect of Satisfactory, and while you have lots of options there, the relevant systems are just as clunky and buggy to use as the rest.Overall it's a passable casual automation game, which is okay to play in coop, but I would not recommend it unless you are bored of the less janky automation games like Factorio, Oxygen not Included, Shapez (2), or what have you.

_childDocuments_.review: My friend and I just finished Tier 7 which is the current end of the game, and it took us 60ish hours and alone it might have been twice that, so that's how much content there is at this point. Satisfactory is pretty much what is advertised: you are hooking up resources into production lines and using the output to progress, so you pretty much know what you're getting into with this one from the promotional material.What I misinterpreted was the theme of the game... I thought Satisfactory was a portmanteau of "Satisfying" and "Factory" and the game would be really nice and give the player satisfaction from lining things up and getting production optimized... it is QUITE the opposite! The name fits into the gameplay when you struggle to find structure placement after calculating input and power ratios that will all be SATISFACTORY as in just enough to continue production and get you to the next checkpoint. Once I came to terms with that and adjusted my expectations I continued to enjoy the game.I had a very good time overall but I would recommend waiting until full release to play. There are many multiplayer bugs and WIP (work in progress) items that detract significantly from the experience. Also my processors heat up my whole room when playing this game, I'm not sure if it's the graphics or maybe it's keeping track of each single unit and tick of each machine or what but both my processor (i7-9700KF) and GPU (RTX 2070 Super) heat up to 80 degrees Celsius at times. I usually run Half Life Alyx and other demanding games in the mid 50s so that is very troubling to me. The graphics are almost worth it though, the visuals are unnecessarily impressive so much so that I turned everything to "low" settings which is a noticeable change but still fine to play on, and it brought the temp down to 75.... =(

_childDocuments_.review: I can't play this game. It has ruined me. The game is extremely well designed, executed and has a sense of humour. Your task is pretty simple, and the learning curve is created as part of this so the game is very easy to get into. It's set in First Person mode with some 3rd person elements and overall controls are simple enough and I found using a joy pad far easier than M&K. The game is extremely smooth, my rig is old and the game runs exceptionally well. Overall you're stranded on a dangerous planet tasked with collecting resources, you look for resources , run around and build equipment. You then create different buildings and these create resources that you store or use to create other resources. It's a FP Resource/Building game. It wont be for everyone, but for those gamers who are OCD, or like building and designing things, messing around this is potentially the best game there is for that. It's addictive, so addictive I dream about how I can make things even more efficient or overcome certain challenges and then I wake up and destroy 8 hours worth of buildings and make it "Better". I haven't even played it with friends, and wanted it on my XBox so badly (As my friends are on Live). I cannot fault the game, other than it will destroy your life, your waking hours as it is relentless and there are so many copy cats games around that are similar ...this is the king and it's compelling. _childDocuments_.review: Coffee Stain delivers yet again.Satisfactory is 5% survival 45% building and 50% cursing your previous self for building everything wrong.There is more than enough content in the vanilla game to keep you occupied for 100+ hours with ease.  Mods are supported which can bring the playtime up substantially with added milestones.Currently there are 3 maps to explore so replay-ability is there, however I do wish the maps were more procedural (some parts of the map are procedural it seems, or maybe they just have different set spawns.  However major nodes and encounters all seem to be pre-set).Multiplayer is a little bit wonky, some functionality doesn't seem to work for the non-server owner, however these issues are far and few between.  The game can easily be played solo or with friends without too much disruption.One thing I would like to see improved/implemented is to maybe have a journal or some sort of log where the player can see all the known recipes without having to be near and interact with an assembler for example.  It could help newer players be able to set goals and plan out layouts easier.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't understand why this game got so popular.I guess there are people in the world that believe "game" includes performing a trivial task repeatedly without any chance of failure or obstacle to overcome.For me, I want to fail, I want to be challenged, I want my neurons to fire. The only challenge in this game seems to be the calculation of fractions when you figure the output of one machine and the input of another. Hell, that is barely even there, since most people just use an online tool to do that calculation for them. At any rate, I mastered that skill in second grade, 36 years ago. Your mileage may vary depending on your education system.I suppose you could build things to be pleasing to the eye, and line it all up with right angles or multiple floors vertically, but why would you? No one is going to see it.Other than that, I found myself, simply building the same thing, as needed, over and over and over again, with no purpose, no obstacle, and no challenge. The game doesn't even let you save a blueprint, so once you spend three hours lining everything up for item X, you have to do it all over again in another spot when you need more of item X. It isn't possible to lose at all, and that's a huge turn off for me. It's an exercise of how many times I can do the same thing over hours until boredom prevents me from playing anymore.I enjoyed Factorio quite a bit more, simply because there was opposition and the possibility of losing. In Satisfactory, both resources and time are infinite. This truly is a game for people to turn off their brains. I want to exercise mine. I have a backyard full of grass I can watch grow if I want to.

_childDocuments_.review: Oddly addicting.You keep building, you don't know why, you don't really know what it all accomplishes in the end, but you keep going. I've played for 3 hours and have no idea what the end point of this game is. It seems like it's a game built specifically for people with OCD. I must keep building. Goodbye
_childDocuments_.name: Satisfactory

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Calm factory building gameplay with no threats and no limited resources. Build as quickly or slowly as you'd like with no threat of biters destroying your precious factory.Many options to make your factory look as beautiful or hideous as you'd like, with the 3D environment really adding something special to looking out over what you've built. Once you unlock the hoverpack, building in 3D is much easier as you can fly around your whole factory as long as you are near a power source.Cons:The much awaited story is almost nonexistent. The lack of story doesn't ruin the game, but it is a disappointment given how it was advertised as an important part of the 1.0 release.
_childDocuments_.name: Satisfactory

_childDocuments_.review: A shining star of the "engineering games" genre. Beautiful and runs well even on average hardware, it's essentially FarCry meets (some parts of) Factorio.No survival element apart from occasional exploration mobs that dont respawn is a relaxing experience, quite easy to just tab out with your machine/world ambience pleasantly humming in the background for days at a time. UI/UX puts many far bigger games to shame. Dedicated servers need some work,  worth every penny.
_childDocuments_.name: Satisfactory

_childDocuments_.review: Its a game that I keep coming back to over and over! I know what to expect and how to progress, but the updates that Coffee Stain constantly put out always go above and beyond my expectations. The games replay-ability is through the roof and it tickles that little OCD itch to make a perfect looking mega factory - until you play with that one friend who is just pure chaos, that makes you want to burn the factory to the ground and start again.Its a fantastic game and I Highly recommend it to anyone who is on the fence about it still or likes other factory/management games!
_childDocuments_.name: Satisfactory

_childDocuments_.review: Great game overall. If you're a fan of automation games (like me) then this is a must-have. Highlights for me are as follows:-Progression is well thought-out. Introduction of new stuff is well paced. Teaching of core mechanics is done right with how the milestones are laid out-User experience is fantastic. Update after update, the quality-of-life improvements demonstrate the care the devs have with their player base.-There aren't any penalties other than sub-optimal production, so gameplay can be quite zen. Other ppl might not like the lack of urgency, but it's perfect for me.-Graphics are lovely, but can be prohibitive with computers on the potato end. For the amount of detail the devs have made with the world and the environment, it's almost a shame to put factories on top of them.For a game called Satisfactory, the quality is leagues above satisfactory. A masterclass in game design, if I do say so myself.
_childDocuments_.name: Satisfactory

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing game, even though it's not even finished yet. Literally hours of fun and it constantly keeps you busy with something, willingly. You're not on a timer and there's nothing that's forcing you to continue until you feel that the time is right to do so. The in-game environment is downright stunning at times, so even outside of building factories, it's very much worth exploring the world just for the fun of it.The game is quite well optimized, even with a ton of machinery running, I'm still getting very playable framerates on a very average computer:i5 8400, RX 580 8GB, 16GB RAMBottom line: I don't understand this games ability to take away hours upon hours of my life, but gosh, I simply love it. Get it, it's amazing. It's a solid 9.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: INDUSTRIAL SOCIETY AND ITS FUTUREIntroduction1. The Industrial Revolution and its consequences have been a disaster for the human race. They have greatly increased the life-expectancy of those of us who live in “advanced” countries, but they have destabilized society, have made life unfulfilling, have subjected human beings to indignities, have led to widespread psychological suffering (in the Third World to physical suffering as well) and have inflicted severe damage on the natural world. The continued development of technology will worsen the situation. It will certainly subject human beings to greater indignities and inflict greater damage on the natural world, it will probably lead to greater social disruption and psychological suffering, and it may lead to increased physical suffering even in “advanced” countries.2. The industrial-technological system may survive or it may break down. If it survives, it MAY eventually achieve a low level of physical and psychological suffering, but only after passing through a long and very painful period of adjustment and only at the cost of permanently reducing human beings and many other living organisms to engineered products and mere cogs in the social machine. Furthermore, if the system survives, the consequences will be inevitable: There is no way of reforming or modifying the system so as to prevent it from depriving people of dignity and autonomy.3. If the system breaks down the consequences will still be very painful. But the bigger the system grows the more disastrous the results of its breakdown will be, so if it is to break down it had best break down sooner rather than later.4. We therefore advocate a revolution against the industrial system. This revolution may or may not make use of violence; it may be sudden or it may be a relatively gradual process spanning a few decades. We can’t predict any of that. But we do outline in a very general way the measures that those who hate the industrial system should take in order to prepare the way for a revolution against that form of society. This is not to be a POLITICAL revolution. Its object will be to overthrow not governments but the economic and technological basis of the present society.5. In this article we give attention to only some of the negative developments that have grown out of the industrial-technological system. Other such developments we mention only briefly or ignore altogether. This does not mean that we regard these other developments as unimportant. For practical reasons we have to confine our discussion to areas that have received insufficient public attention or in which we have something new to say. For example, since there are well-developed environmental and wilderness movements, we have written very little about environmental degradation or the destruction of wild nature, even though we consider these to be highly important.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a tough game to recommend at first, was going to give it a solid 'No'.  Main issues  I had were:-Insanely boring traversal across the map.  Once you hit Oil and realize the node is 2km from your base and how far you'll have to set up a line or transport becomes mind-numbingly repetitive.  This goes for other remote nodes you'll inevitably have to tap and run a very long belt or setup a long train run to it.-Needs some sort of builtin map or top down view.  I got sick of having to use 3rd party webapps to plan my expansion, this should be in the game.-Can't stress just how boring running long belts and pipes is, they reallllly need to figure out an easier/faster way to travel than slide-jumping for eons.-Needs a much better way of mass-building platforms.  They did implement a "zoop" feature, but it's barely good and still a boring task to build long runs of platforms even with "zoop"-Power poles should really not be limited to 4 in the beginning, and you should be able to set a default power line to run an updated MK pole instead of forcing you to place a bunch of mk1's that you're going to upgrade later anyways.-The monsters are incredibly annoying and boring to deal with.  Nothing challenging at all, just super annoying.So un-modded, I definitely do not recommend this game and suggest you go play Factorio or Dyson Project.However, modded, this game is amazing and super addicting!  I am usually anti-modding since mods are unreliable and break games and constantly have to be updated, but I can't recommend it enough for this game.  I highly recommend these mods:-Area Actions Mod-Smart!-Pak Utility ModArea Actions is the MAIN reason I love this game now.  It allows you to fly endlessly, so you can go way up in the sky and EASILY build large amounts of stuff.  Travelling is way more enjoyable and less boring, makes it so much easier to get to far away nodes.Smart! makes it even easier to build large amounts of platforms and building and align them with ease.Pak Utility Mod was solely used to increase the fly speed of Area Actions Mod.  Use "!fly fast" and start getting to those far away nodes in no time.So yeah, mod it and the game is great.I will say the graphics are super impressive and as your base grows it's cool to see all the machines chugging along, and when you get better at organizing and building, the nicer parts of your base look really cool.  I have a lot of fun planning power setups, adding more power to your base is a nice break from the resource chain building grind.

_childDocuments_.review: Updated when game updates come outPost 1.0Satisfactory: A Factory Builder’s DreamSatisfactory is a beautifully designed and thoroughly engaging factory-building game that effortlessly combines creativity, strategy, and exploration. From the moment you land on the alien planet, you’re immersed in a visually stunning and expansive world teeming with resources and potential.The gameplay is both challenging and rewarding, pushing you to optimize every conveyor belt, production line, and power grid. The sense of achievement you get when your factory runs smoothly is incredibly satisfying. The open-world exploration adds another layer of depth, making each discovery and biome feel fresh and exciting.One of the standout features is the cooperative multiplayer mode, which allows you to build and innovate with friends. The community is also fantastic, full of helpful and creative players who enhance the overall experience.Overall, Satisfactory is not just a game, but an endless journey of innovation and efficiency. Whether you’re a seasoned builder or a newcomer, it’s a must-play that will keep you hooked for hours on end.Update 1.0 is outSatisfactory 1.0 is nothing short of an engineering marvel, delivering a gaming experience that’s both deeply satisfying and endlessly creative. After years in early access, the full release of Satisfactory cements its place as one of the most captivating factory-building and open-world exploration games ever made.From the moment you land on the alien planet of Massage-2(A-B)b, you are instantly thrust into a visually stunning world, brimming with vast biomes, strange creatures, and natural resources waiting to be harnessed. Coffee Stain Studios has crafted a universe that not only begs to be explored but also feels alive, with dynamic weather systems, day-night cycles, and landscapes that are as treacherous as they are beautiful.The Core Gameplay – Addictive and SatisfyingAt its heart, Satisfactory is a factory-building and automation game, but it offers so much more than just putting machines together. The sense of progression is masterfully paced, as you start with basic machinery and slowly expand into sprawling, intricate factories that sprawl across mountains, deserts, and forests. The balance between exploration and automation is impeccable. You’re always torn between optimizing your production lines and venturing further into the unknown to uncover new resources and secrets.The level of customization and creativity in factory-building is where the game truly shines. Conveyor belts crisscross your landscape, efficient production lines hum in harmony, and massive structures rise from the ground like futuristic megacities. The modularity and flexibility of the systems allow players to create something truly unique, and there’s always room for refinement or expansion, making every moment feel productive and rewarding.Multiplayer – Cooperation at Its FinestMultiplayer in Satisfactory 1.0 takes the fun to a whole new level. Playing with friends opens up opportunities for collaboration, division of labor, and shared creativity. Tackling complex production problems together, or simply exploring the world, is a blast. The multiplayer performance has been fine-tuned, allowing for smooth, lag-free gameplay, even as your factory expands to epic proportions.Visuals and Audio – Immersive and PolishedThe graphics in Satisfactory 1.0 are nothing short of breathtaking. The vibrant and alien world feels meticulously detailed, from the lush green plains to the towering cliffs and deadly fauna. The seamlessness of transitioning from ground exploration to towering factory viewpoints is awe-inspiring. Every biome feels alive, with a unique personality that keeps exploration fresh and engaging.Accompanying the beautiful visuals is an ambient, futuristic soundtrack that complements the atmosphere perfectly. The subtle, electronic music ebbs and flows as you build, explore, and automate, enhancing both the serenity of your quieter moments and the intensity of high-energy situations.The Learning Curve – Complex Yet AccessibleSatisfactory 1.0 introduces a satisfying complexity without overwhelming new players. The tutorial system and milestones provide clear goals and guidance, while leaving enough room for experimentation. Whether you're a seasoned builder or completely new to the genre, the game scales its complexity in a way that feels manageable but also deep enough for hardcore fans of automation games.Endgame and Longevity – Infinite PotentialEven after you’ve reached the pinnacle of production, unlocked nuclear power, and constructed mind-bogglingly efficient factories, Satisfactory never runs out of surprises. The ability to continue refining your creations, push the boundaries of your designs, and pursue perfection ensures that Satisfactory offers near-infinite replayability. And let’s not forget the robust modding community, which adds endless customization options to extend the game’s lifespan even further.VerdictSatisfactory 1.0 is a monumental achievement in game design, blending exploration, creativity, and automation into an experience that is both deeply engaging and incredibly rewarding. Whether you’re laying out your first conveyor belt or overseeing a mega-factory with nuclear power, the game continues to deliver moments of joy, discovery, and wonder. It’s the perfect game for both casual builders and hardcore factory aficionados, with a balance of depth and accessibility that few games manage to achieve.In short, Satisfactory 1.0 is the ultimate sandbox for anyone who loves the thrill of creation, optimization, and exploration. Prepare to lose hours, days, even weeks as you dive into the endless possibilities this game offers. Simply put: it's an absolute must-play.Rating: ★★★★★ (5/5)

_childDocuments_.review: I initially avoided this game as a Factorio clone with the "but it's 3D!!" gimmick, and while that's true in a broad sense, there's a lot more to Satisfactory than you'd think.For one, it's surprisingly well-optimized, and runs surprisingly well on lower-end hardware, and for another, Satisfactory does atmosphere, exploration, and world 'feel' in a way that blows Factorio out of the water. While Satisfactory is less complex, it isn't done to the point of absurdity, and there's plenty to play around with. When you add in a bunch of interesting mechanics and some genuinely entertaining movement and transport elements, it really has a funny way of sucking you in for hours at a time.Putting it bluntly, this is what you want from a "clone" of another game. In a sense, Satisfactory is to Factorio what Terraria is to Minecraft, at least in a broad sense, and that's a very good thing indeed.

_childDocuments_.review: I've put almost 1000 hrs into this game and with the upcoming 1.0 release looking forward to adding a few hundred more to that number. To say this game is addictive is an understatement. It starts out simple enough - mine a few rocks, pick up a few leaves, build a few smelters. Then you're thinking, well it's time to automate some of the stuff, and I need belts to connect these machines, and that's when the belt spaghetti starts taking over, and then before you know it, you're up at 3am in the morning working on a spreadsheet to plan out your next mega factory so that it's all 100% efficient!This game has an ingenious leaning curve - you never feel overwhelmed with options, and always have a clear goal in mind. The genius part is that at first it's the game that's giving you the goals, but before you know it you are the one planning out this or that factory, and how to get the materials to it, and how to keep everything efficient, and how to make it look awesome, and it never ends - there's the next part of the factory, then there's the next factory, and the next and the next... :)

_childDocuments_.review: Satisfactory is an engaging construction and automation simulator by Coffee Stain Studios. Players find themselves on an alien planet, where they must gather resources and build factories. The storyline is secondary here, with the main focus on gameplay.The game impresses with its beauty and detailed worlds, built on the Unreal Engine 4. This requires powerful hardware: a GTX 760 graphics card with 2 GB of memory and an i5 processor. However, the visual component fully justifies the high system requirements.The main aspect of Satisfactory is construction and automation. The ability to build both horizontally and vertically allows for creativity. Despite some minor inconveniences with modular construction, the gameplay remains captivating.Exploration plays a crucial role. Players need to find rare resources and unlock new technologies, making the gameplay diverse and interesting. However, only one type of resource can be placed on a conveyor belt, limiting logistics.Multiplayer adds another dimension to the game. Playing with friends makes the process more enjoyable, although conflicts over development strategies are possible.Satisfactory is a beautiful and engaging game, perfect for fans of the construction and automation genre. Despite some gameplay inconveniences and limited replay variability, it offers a unique and immersive gaming experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Satisfactory is fantastic! I highly recommend it. Over the last year, I've spent over 800 hours playing the game on Epic. And still enjoying it. If you're the type that likes building, and crunching numbers, Along with exploring a large open world map that's hand made, You will love this game also.Though building your factory is the main objective it's not the only important thing you have to do. Exploring though not required is a fun side activity that really rewards you for time invested. You have tons of tools that you unlock to make things easier on your adventure but while you're out you can find crashed drop ships that are unlockable.Inside you'll find new recipes that can great affect how efficient your factory can become. Also you'll find power slugs which will also greatly improve your factory.Building your factory is the whole purpose. And it's a lot of fun! After you get some basic resources going and start producing your products you'll become addicted quickly. As you build basic items starting out, You'll have missions that you must complete, These are order fulfillments from upper management. Completing a order, You can then unlock a new tier of structures, Or better gear / building pieces to help your factory.Once you finish unlocking all 8 Tiers, The game isn't over. Building your factory in a way to make it most efficient is the end game goal.Coop is also here, Though it doesn't add to much for building, Unless everyone is planning out sections of a base to build, It is great when exploring the vast map. Having someone with you to kill off would be enemies or help reach a mountain top is fun in a small group.Really happy to see the game finally come to Steam, And Coffee Stain along with their Dev's are very friendly and support the game really well! I've since re-bought the game on Steam, And even a copy for a friend. Excited to see what comes next from the team as they push another year in Early Access.Highly recommend this game!Update 5 was another huge improvement to a great game!

The game can feel overwhelming at first, but it's okay, there is no time constraints, and there are plenty of pros at this game on youtube that can help get you started so you don't feel so helpless. It can be up in the air or down on the ground gravity does not seem to be an issue unless of course you jump off a high platform or a cliff then you die. _childDocuments_.review: In Satisfactory, the player is stranded on an alien planet and must gather resources, build factories, and create a supply chain to survive and thrive. The game's world is vast and filled with diverse biomes, each with its own set of resources and challenges.The gameplay in Satisfactory is focused on exploration and automation, with the player using machines and conveyors to move resources and products around their factory. The game's machinery is highly detailed and customizable, with a wide range of options for optimization and efficiency.The game's graphics are impressive, with highly detailed environments and machinery that are visually striking and immersive. The game's sound design is also notable, with a mix of ambient noise, machine sounds, and a calming soundtrack that enhances the player's sense of immersion.One of the game's strengths is its level of depth and complexity, which allows the player to optimize their factory and supply chain to an incredible degree. The game also offers a variety of challenges and goals, including resource scarcity, environmental hazards, and alien creatures that can attack the player's factory.The game's multiplayer mode is also a standout feature, allowing players to collaborate and work together to create even larger and more complex factories. However, the game's single-player mode is also highly engaging and satisfying.The game's learning curve can be somewhat steep, especially for players new to the factory-building genre. However, the game's tutorial and in-game encyclopedia are helpful resources that make it easier to learn the game's mechanics and systems.In conclusion, Satisfactory is a highly engaging and addictive factory-building simulation game that offers a deep and complex gameplay experience. The game's level of depth and customization, combined with its impressive graphics and sound design, make it a must-play for fans of the genre. If you enjoy games like Factorio or RimWorld, then Satisfactory is definitely worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is a great addition to the library alongside my favorite game, Factorio. This game shares a lot with Factorio but it differs in that it's more immersive and allows that sort of fun "build a cool base" vibe, and the other elements of exploring the beautiful map and collecting things is well thought out. The downside is that it's much more finnicky to build (on account of it being 3d mostly), it takes a long time to do things, and it has quite a few bugs and quality of life needs. The game does get a lot of love from the devs though so I see it only getting better from here. Don't decide between this and factorio, get them both.

_childDocuments_.review: The pinnacle of base builder crafting games, hands down. It's not a voxel miner, mind you, so if you're after that aspect maybe try Astroneer. But if turning "one workbench where you hammer out iron parts" into "a sprawling factory that extracts various ores and liquids and churns out quantum computers" is the kind of thing you look for in a crafting base builder, you'll have a good time with Satisfactory. The exploration aspect is also excellent, with a huge world that seems insurmountably large at first, but that you'll gradually reach the far corners of with the vehicles you unlock. You'll even be able to automate entire outposts' and bases' logistics with trains and drones.Speaking of which, Satisfactory has been an example of Early Access done right. The devs are clear about their intentions for each update, and provide general but reliable release windows. If you don't want to wait for new content, they have an experimental branch to beta test with. So far, they've already met and exceeded the original scope of the game, so I wouldn't be bothered if they took it out of Early Access, but, I guess they will once they feel like it's finished. I'm sure they'll continue to improve it after the last EA update though.

_childDocuments_.review: Update at bottom:This review is not based on the quality of the gameplay itself, but on serious technical issues I had when I bought it.I bought Satisfactory after hearing so many good things about it, and needless to say, it delivered from what little I saw. The visuals were good, the movement was smooth, the tutorial was easy to understand. I didn't play enough of it to give a full opinion on it, but if was able to play it more I would most likely be making a positive review.This review is negative because of a serious technical issue, one that i have not seen before, and is practically not mentioned online. When I first bought the game, loaded up a world, did the tutorial, and played on my own for a little bit. After awhile, I noticed my computer fans revving up, I put my hand on my computer and felt it was very hot. I looked at my performance metrics and saw that my computer was well over 80C, and some junctions even reached 100C!!! I immediately closed the game and let the computer cool. My computer has never run like that before or since, I looked around my PC to see if something else was the cause, trying my other intensive games too see if this was a issue with my computer. Nope it was Satisfactory, my factory wasn't even big, only about 6 buildings; I had no problems with framerate. Even when just opening the game and going to the main menu, my GPU starts to heat up. Soon after I had these issues I refunded the game, I will not put my computer in danger just to play this game, even though it is good.So devs, if you see this, please make some serious optimizations to your game, because it makes computers run dangerously hot.Update: It has been many months since I made this review and I am glad to say it no longer runs my GPU in the ground. It may have been the updates to the game, or my better monitoring software and increased knowledge, but it runs at an acceptable 80c now. Overall great game, I like it a bit more than Factorio.

Add to the fact that you can just buy the ingredients from the ticket shop before you even place a machine has made research and tier goals easy to fulfill. This is made worse by crash sites that has a lot of free stuff and a tamed doggo that will ♥♥♥♥ out late game stuff you can sink for beaucoop bucks. This is of course a major symptom of the real design flaw: Building factories, the core gameplay loop in this automation game, is a excruciatingly painful, tedious and frustrating process. I could barely tolerate it in 0.8, but since absolutely nothing has been done to make it better, 1.0 fails to meet my most basic expectations. I expect mods, once they come out, will alleviate some of these issues, but since the developers don't care enough to make the actual building and planning of a factory more accessible and fun I've lost the spirit to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Listen, I downloaded Satisfactory thinking I’d kill a few hours. Fast forward 90 hours later, I’m questioning if I even need sleep anymore. Time? Irrelevant. You start small, just a few belts, a miner or two… and before you know it, you’re restructuring your entire power grid at 3 AM because your new oil refinery needs 0.5% more efficiency. I’ve ripped down entire factories just to shave a few seconds off production. I’m an absolute maniac.And every time you unlock a new item or recipe? It’s like hitting the jackpot at a casino for nerds. Oh, you thought you were done? Surprise! Here’s a new shiny gadget to throw your entire operation into chaos. _childDocuments_.review: I love factory games when they get it right. Factorio gets a lot of things right, but one of the places it struggles is in some of the resource management stuff - to me, the finite-depth resource locations makes the game less fun, because at a certain point it becomes about pure outposting.With Satisfactory, the experience is much better from a logistics perspective. The resource nodes are infinite depth. Instead of being returned the explicit structure placed / removed like in Factorio, you're returned the parts that comprise that structure - I significantly prefer this system. Satisfactory's world is finite, but beautiful. I have a few gripes after playing almost 1300 hours (lots of AFK time in there for sure). With update 7 comes blueprints - in my opinion a necessary addition. However, creating blueprints requires a special building that you make the blueprints in. This is a 32x32x32 cube. Max, 3 refineries fit. You cannot connect anything to power that's not also inside the blueprint structure, meaning that if you want to test some transport functionality, like jump pads, no joy. If you want to do something slightly more mundane, like wanting to pre-configure street lights or otherwise, no joy. Going back to refineries / coal power generators, if you want to do your logistics underneath the structures, you can't. Not enough vertical clearance. Returning to more ordinary blueprinty things, if you do a belt highway blueprint and place 2 of them to connect, to turn a 4-foundation belt highway into an 8-foundation belt highway (or more), they will not in fact connect to one another. The parts will stop at the end of the first blueprint. The player then has to make sure there's space between one blueprint and the next, and fill in the gaps themselves. This is a very big deal. Very high friction experience. No overlapping, like one would see in Factorio to just add what's lacking, and keep that belt highway going.Insofar as I'm aware, the goal was to force greater levels of creativity, discourage large scale sharing of blueprints, and force users to find ways to integrate blueprints modularly inside their factories, and this is why there are the limitations that there are. While on the one hand I understand and respect that, it also creates several friction points that are challenging, immersion breaking, and problematic. I've developed a few of those ideas, but with a broader brush, I cannot set up refineries for "smelting" copper once, make a blueprint of that, and then copy / place the whole thing. I have to do it 1 or 2 or 3 refineries at a time from a blueprint. If I want to do something complex with my oil, residual resources into recycled resources, I don't want to have to duplicate that - I want to be able to place another one down. Given how central refineries are to resource processing mid-late game, and how frustrating they are to set up, especially before the hoverpack, one would think that the devs would give more consideration to cases like this in the creation of the tool. Last gripe re: blueprints - no "undo" capability. If I'm off by one tile, I could need to delete a plurality of structures. This is a high-friction experience. All this being said, I'm already completely dependent on blueprints, from belt highways to production structure layouts. They should have been in the game sooner and now that they are, there's room for refining (no pun intended) so as to remove some of these friction points.Another point to keep in mind, if you're anything like me, is the fact that as I move through the game's progression, I keep feeling like I need to dismantle my entire factory and start again, better organized, integrate the new parts into automated production, etc. This is a significant mental hurdle sometimes, as this is the game I come to when I'm tired of grinding in the games I grind in. :) There are things that would make this easier. The ability to remove all placed structures at or above a given y-level would be a major benefit. Obviously this intersects with some of my above blueprint gripes / suggestions as potentially a version of an "undo" button.To close this point up a little neater - its annoying that I don't feel like I can plan properly in advance for the level of part complexity / production from the get-go, and rely on ongoing cycles of creation / destruction after producing "enough" resources for that level of progression to afford going up a level.Final note - in my opinion, too many customization options are locked behind the awesome sink / awesome shop. While yes, awesome, and while I'm not the most creative of builders, etc, being able to get all the customization options unlocked is in my mind too expensive. I understand that a way around that is with alien DNA capsules, but that becomes prohibitive as well.I've been playing Satisfactory on and off since Update 3, and it's a wonderful game. I wouldn't have so much to say if I enjoyed the game less. As we're moving towards 1.0, seeing the team add so many QoL things into the game is really fun and encouraging. The world is a joy to play in. The new combat stuff is excellent. I'm a huge fan of the explosive rebar. I love the new-to-me foundation coatings. I really enjoy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Satisfactory

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, two major issues though. Nonrenewable items, especially healing items, are completely out of place in a game where all other resources are unlimited. _childDocuments_.review: This is the most addictive game I've ever played. Upgraded my computer just to play it.Update: OMG... another 700 hours down the tubes. Satisfactory Update 5 really changed the whole building aspect of the game. Now our factories aren't just floating platforms of untidy machines, they can be grand structures of epic proportions. The soft clipping of assets, combined with the implementation of a world grid and the ability to dynamically switch between three different building modes when laying foundations and walls, make building a factory take a fraction of the time it used to. I'm in my last semester of a CS degree as i write this update and the thought has crossed my mind more than once that I may need to uninstall Satisfactory until I graduate. _childDocuments_.review: Very well balanced game, very addictive. Always something to do. It can get grindy at times, but that usually means you are not doing things efficiently.The best part is that tearing structures down refunds the materials so when you make a mistake or just want to re-design your facility (part or whole), you can do that with no additional resources unless you add more parts. The building is also immediate unlike in something like Space Engineers where you have to put the components into the structure with a welder. I usually like hardcore elements like that, that punish for mistakes, but this game is designed around restructing. As you "level up", you unlock new components which allow you to do things differently, so sometimes reorganizing is a good thing. I actually tore down my entire plant last night and rebuilt it from the ground up,, for example.Great game if you like to organize, and take pride in your creations, and work efficiently. It also has a decent exploration element. The combat element is probably the weakest, and can mostly be ignored. You can easily outrun or jump over unfriendlies. I don't know how they've balanced the progression so perfectly -- it's a fantastic gradual process to go from your very first objectives to having a massive factory with numerous lines cranking out gizmos -- multiple power plants fueling all the activity --- I'm 90+ hours into the game and it feels like it was maybe only like 10-20 hrs because it's all flown by so fast (because of how immersive it is) and it's really a joy because you're basically only 'competing against' lack of imagination -- but you don't have to be 'imaginative' or creative to succeed -- you can be a very left-brain analytical type of have a great experience as well (for someone like me the game is like pure heroin in how it gets both my creative and logical sides working in unison!)Again, if you enjoy resource management type games at all -- I cannot recommend this game strongly enough!!

_childDocuments_.review: It's right in the name. It's a factory-building game, and is very peaceful and satisfying. There's not really any "story" yet, but theme is very interesting. It definitely has a strong element of: "chainsaw all this filthy vegetation away into pieces, good riddance to all the aggressive alien wildlife standing in the way, and make way for a beautiful landscape of smokestacks, pipelines, and artificial lighting. We've got to pillage all the resources we can get our hands on."And the really interesting thing is, you'll enjoy doing it. You'll look back on areas you've developed into a spaghetti knot of conveyor belts with pride, and when you go exploring new areas you'll instantly see all vegetation as nothing more than another useful resource you need that can't be automatically mined, at best; and at worst, it blocks your sightlines for planning the most efficient conveyor belt routes for this new area. So no matter what, it must go. (And there's always so much of it everywhere, you feel proud when you finally clear a large space to build in, and after a while it becomes tiring to have to move to an area with new resources and do it all over again.)The conveyor belt system is really powerful once you understand it's limits. It can make endlessly sprawling spaghetti reaching out across the entire planet, that's still fully-functional. (And be honest, is still beautiful, in it's own way) Or, they also snap to the foundation and wall pieces, if you want to get fancy and try your hand at designing a building for/around a section of your factory, and let your OCD run wild inside. But my favorite part right now is the trains. You can setup an automatic freight route for one type of resource, then if you plan your stations right, can easily add more trains with different frieght routes to the same rail. Add bypasses around stations to keep things flowing. Then expanding the rail network to far away locations is easy! Trains are fast, and can carry a lot. And c'mon: trains.Sad part is they obviously intended to add a story (or at least an ending), but there's still no word on it. You'll eventually find several glowing artifacts that call out to you in a weird voice, but they usually say WIP (Work in progress) in the name. There's even a type of mineable ore that currently doesn't do anything. It sucks because I really like the theme & style of the game, would love to see some kind of narrative ending twist.

_childDocuments_.review: Short review: Just buy Factorio instead. If you have never played an automation or factory building game, most people will point you in the direction of this game or Factorio. On the surface they might look very similar besides graphics and player perspective, however, when it comes to the gameplay, Factorio tops this game in any reasonable metric. I could give 100's of reasons but many of them would be lost on those who have never played either of these games. What it boils down to is: Factorio is deep, Satisfactory is tedious. What takes you 5 minutes in Factorio takes you 30 minutes in Satisfactory. It isn't that Satisfactory is more complicated (on the contrary it's much simpler) it's just that it hasn't figured out how to make building in 3D fast and efficient. Belts are wonky, connections between machines often don't work the first time, and managing power is frustrating. Gameplay time in Factorio is spent thinking up solutions to logistical problems and then quickly implementing them and moving on to the next thing. In Satisfactory a small portion is spent actually thinking critically and most of your time will be spent laboriously putting it together. You might think "Well isn't that the point of the game? To get good at building in 3D?" but that is also incorrect. Satisfactory gives you zero incentive to build machines close together, so your factory can be a jumbled gross mess and there's no penalty. In Factorio enemies and non-infinite resource deposits actually make you value space and your building materials. The other largest problem is the shift to late game. The late game in Factorio is incredibly complex, but you eventually unlock an army of robots to help build your incredibly complex and resource hungry factory. You might think this spoils the fun, but trust me, if you know in your head "I want to put a line of 300 furnaces here, each with their own power pole and each with their own belt going in and out" you can let the robots do the heavy lifting while your big brain is masterminding it all. In Satisfactory if you want to put down 300 furnaces, guess what you're going to be doing for the next two hours. Factorio gets harder and less tedious as the game goes on, whiles Satisfactory gets harder and FAR more tedious. I gave up 30 hrs in because even then it was more tedious than it was fun. This game has potential. Many issues I have can be fixed. Maybe someday this will become "3D Factorio" but as of right now it is far from that and feels more like a chore than a video game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome, played since version late version 5, introduced by 2 of my friends. Thats one of the ''recent'' games on the market who just what to drain your wallet with stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and no contents that are on top full of game breaking bugs. The Steam review system is somewhat biased by a lot by people who got literally scammed by those games and who tries to convince themselves that they have purchased a good game and end up with under 30 hours of playing with it before never touching it again. This one game right here cost under 20$CDN when you can grab a deal, often cheaper even on other platforms, aside the new unreal engine issues(see notes at the end), its seammingly bug free and very soon gonna be released in v1.0 (somewhere this year reffering to the official channels). Its a factory game with a lot of options for you to enjoy, basic straight conveyors, water pipes, or more complex transportation systems like factory carts, various trucks, train and drones. Your imagination and architectural prowess and comprehension of management of large scale production lines will be put to test, trust me. Electricity is very easy *maybe a lil bit easy for my taste even* to handle, liquids are pretty straightforward too : X+Y = Z up to the max numbers in their respective mean of transportation - use pumps and flow valves wisely. Anything else is pure +/- and ''X'' times as many as you want and up to your mines productions. Graphics are very good, even despite a super large factory (way over a 100 nuclear reactors, countless coal and fuel generators... im at almost 800GW energy production, mapwide) my game keeps it around 40fps in the large production area. Even after 1000 hours (my steam timer is broken due to several crash after the last update until I fixed the unreal engine) I kept coming back to it and still do. But the better they enhance this game, the bigger our project goes and we still will hit the hardware limitation somehow... So of course even now, im still building stuff, making more  production lines, sink more items per minutes, trying new impossible setups for my pure enjoyment... my fps might drop more... its bound to happen. But please, if you know one, do tell me if there is one factory game out there that do not push your machine to its limit after a while? Dyson sphere do it specially on systems with very large scale dyson spheres, Techtonica do it and very early unfortunately, Factorio does it too... even with potato graphics. Its often not a gpu issue, its a computational issue for so many items moving all over the place all at once. Added July 29 : Unfortunately, for me, this is the end of this game, for now at least. As mentioned by devs, they unleash the 1.0 official version of the game, accompagnied with several changes to the node dispositions. This will impact my game so much that I find it totally impossible for me to continue playing. The resource nodes changes, depsite having a total more available ressources, imply that some nodes change their output, some new one arises, but also, some of them will literally just vanish. In my actual game state, 1k hours, where I used all the said vanishing nodes to make my nuclear energy output and other nuclear pasta sinking, perfectly efffectives and balanced with my productions. Having those nodes disappear, it will result in a failscade of events, effectively ending in the whole map to turn offline... with no possibility to put it back online unless, estimated, an hundred of hours or so is spent making new distribution lines all over the map, isolate systems in isolated power sectors with switch and so on.  I know and you'll say : But start a new game... or... it was early access what did you expected? Im not the kind of player that likes to start fresh on the same game... especially not on sandbox games. *unless there is a different ending that requires a different approach during the gameplay session. Wich makes the game totally anew imo. These changes to nodes, with no possibility to avoid it, is in no way ''fun'' nor ''appealing'' and despite the new content, it is just making me abandon the game. Now lucky for anyone else having no problem starting fresh, or who waited to try satisfactory in its final version. Youll most certainly enjoy it as I enjoyed it. Having the whole of my 1k hrs invested into the game, pushed down the drain with this update, it is just too much to enjoy anymore for me. So before I get angry and/or mad, im shutting down the whole thing and will keep happy memories of the time invested into this game.Additional Note: For peoples, who like me, are having super large scale factories. Just be aware of the limitations of the new unreal engine, it will make your game crash if you have a very large factory in the same area of the loaded map around you as the new engine has something like 2.4m items loaded capacity. Its well documented on the internet however and very easy to fix in an .ini file of the game. Even I could do it... so yes... VERY easy! Its not a game related issue, but it would be great if the devs implement the engine limitation unlock to their game without anyone fixing it manually.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay initial knee jerk frustration review due to piles of stress is gone.1. Yes you do have to link your Steam ID and connect with multiplayer through Epic Online Services. 2. You are required to do this from the title screen once you click past the screen acknowledging that this game is early access. This is required of you even if you are not planning on playing multi-player at all but serves as essentially a way to verify you actually own a copy of the game as well.3. It should be noted that this is not requiring you to create an Epic Games Account. EOS and EGA are separate things, but one way of linking your Steam ID is also through linking it to an already existing EGA if you already have one.4. None of which is mentioned anywhere on the store as a requirement but is assumed as something you must do given this game first released on the Epic Games Store. That's a terrible assumption to make and should have been clarified so as to avoid all the negative fallout that has resulted from people stumbling into this fact without warning.This is clarification of what is going on, you need to tie your Steam ID to Epic Online Services by sending your Steam ID over through their servers. You are not required to make an Epic Games Account(even I in my initial knee-jerk did not conflate the two as the same).
