_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR. This feels like an unfinished game, because it literally is. The game is a buggy mess. I my disk filled up with 600 GB of errors from a single play session. As for gameplay, the core bones of the game are there, but it's definitely not finished. It lacks content, fixes, polish, and life. I can't recommend the game in its current state, and knowing Paradox they will make you buy a completed version of the game via DLC. I'd recommend just playing another economy-focused game (there's a ton of stellar ones!), and look at Victoria 3 again in a few years. The Good:* Several reviews have complained about the bad UI not giving information in favor of aesthetics. I'm guessing this is coming from a lack of familiarity with the drilldown system in the modern Paradox game engine. Just like CK3 you can 'drilldown' into tooltips to get more tooltips explaining keywords, showing places, people, etc. You have a tremendous amount of information available to you pretty easily. I put in thousands of hours in Victoria 2, and this system really, truly is much better. I imagine people are just ignorant and bashing the system without even trying to learn it. * The game looks and feels great. Little touches like steam coming off of the play/pause UI are great. The map looks and feels alive. * The base economic system is quite good. I found myself naturally doing things that real world countries did, like aggressively seeking our resources to the detriment of natives. * The base diplomacy system is pretty good. (Caveats later)* I found this the easiest Paradox title to role play in. I had a blast just picking a single concept and running with it. * I actually like the idea of abstracted wars; however, the current implementation is not good. * Surprisingly you can get achievements now without ironman. I don't savescum (I've 100%'d other Paradox titles on Ironman); however, I found that this made the whole experience low stress and made it easier to just relax and play the game.  The Bad:* The game is still really buggy. The 'Mobilize All' button consistently causes a crash, 100% of the time when I click it. There's integer overflows all over the place.* Certain sections of the game still feel really shallow, and I know Paradox knows this. They explicitly stated it on livestream. Given the Paradox DLC model I can't help but feel I'm being sold only a portion of the game. I want the full game Paradox. I don't want to have it dolled out to me slowly via DLC for 10-20 USD a pop over the next few years..  * The journal system is a good idea, but it's way too barebones. I commented on this above. I get the feeling I'm going to be sold the rest of the game at 10-20 USD a pop for the next few years. * The game is unplayable past the turn of the century, and it runs like molasses past 1890ish. I can play Cyberpunk on Ultra at 60FPS, but I can't run this game past the 1900s* The AI is absolutely awful at basically every aspect of the game. As long as you don't start as a major that's okay for the first half of the game, but after that it quickly turns into a dunkfest. * The AI doesn't know how to deal with a human player. Even with high infamy there was at most only one country ever joining a war.* I never had a great war, which is really disappointing. At most I only ever had 1 GP fighting a single other GP with their puppets. That's a tragedy. This was true even when I had the highest infamy the game would even allow. * The automatic front generation during wars is bad. It creates a large number of weird, tiny fronts that the AI routinely fails to deal with. This compounds the problem that the army system requires you mass group your units under generals. * There's a bizarre hard cap to generals and admirals that's not tied to anything. I managed to hit it before the 20th century even dawned. That's pretty weird, and it's in some sense game breaking for large, sprawling nations depending on conscription. * Possibly due to the above, I repeatedly saw AI countries not using generals. * Naval invasions are absolutely awful and need to be rethought from the ground up. There's way too many weird restrictions on how they work.* The convoy protection is bizarrely set up.* I never saw the AI convoy raiding or naval invading.

_childDocuments_.review: Temporarily swapping this to Not Recommended as the November 2024 update has (for now) introduced some rather aggravating bugs, gameplay issues, and user interface difficulties. It feels like it's undone a lot of the great progress the game has made since its rough launch. Hopefully things will be fixed promptly.--------This game is essentially an economy simulator, focused especially on growing your economy through construction, research, and expansion. The game had a rough start, but with the 1.5 update (November 2023) a lot of the more substantial issues have been resolved & the game finally looks to be on a positive path to the point that I've changed my Not Recommended to Recommended.That said, there's still a lot of work it needs, and my review is more "Recommended if you're really interested, but it still needs work". Some of the things I hope the design team takes on in the coming months: - Fixing bugs (including a few substantial ones) - Improve the user interface with quality of life improvements, hotkeys, shortcuts (especially the outliner, army management, everything involving navies, and setting default building types for each use) - Improve the economic modeling (or give better user feedback) as an economy can swing between death spiral & mega-powerhouse every other week - Improve AI for other nations (which to be fair feels adequate... just not great) - Add a resource availability check to Auto-Build - Either make individual characters & agitators more meaningful or trash the system entirely; it requires so much micromanaging to keep up with, but also feels like an almost totally ignorable system - Refine resource availabilities & especially more regional modifiers. And I probably shouldn't be able to develop my early 20th century economies to the point that they can use every drop of the oil in the world & still not have enough. - More laws, tech, and ways to customize your builds & empire - Fill out more nations with tailored events & other unique things.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games where I wish there was a "meh" button to the "Would you recommend this game to other players?" question.Summary of the below: It is an okay game, but it could be a lot better. It might not give you as much return of investment as other Paradox titles. I still recommend it to people who have time and money, but if you are on the fence I would recommend waitingOn one hand I have enjoyed the game a whole lot, from the "omg, I have no idea what's going on" stages, to the "Hey I sort of understand this game now" stages. But the game also feel lacking. It might be unfair to compare it to Crusader Kings 3, which has had a lot of post-game support, but that is the closest game in time and you'd think the latest game was at least as competent.Victoria 3 is a very convoluted supply chain management game, with some cool economics attached. Oh and there's combat too, but unless you start off as a major power you'll probably be busy getting your supply chains up and running, and won't have time to build a military.This is done through different menus, as expected from a Paradox game. The problem here is that the game operates with three different menu systems. First you can click on a region of the map, then flip through different tabs to get different information. The main one being the buildings tab because that's where the core of the gameplay happens. This let's you control the specific region. You can also construct using the "lens menu" at the bottom of the screen. Which lets you change your map view into different lenses, such as construction, diplomacy, and trade. All these lenses have construction related buttons in them, which makes finding what you want to build tedious at times. The good thing about this menu is that you get a good overview of what is available to you. All the resources and industries you can build is shown here. If that wasn't enough, you have a menu system on the left-hand side of the screen which allows you to also enter a buildings menu, which gives you an easy overview of all your buildings in your nation. From here you can also build new buildings, but it takes you over to the Lens view. I don't mind having several ways to do things, but the game does come out feeling very unpolished because of it. Like they did not know what style of game they wanted to make.Beyond building your economy, and fighting some wars, there's currently in 1.0.6 very little else to do. Some nations can form bigger nations. Like Germany. Some nations like Great Qing have events that happen, but overall, these tend to feel very little impactful. "Journal entries" are your small quests but compared to Crusader Kings 3's Decisions they feel quite demanding to achieve, for very little gameplay impact.I am not sure if this is because the game tries to simulate the setting, and thus don't want you to go "crazy" with decisions and options, but for now it feels shallow. Furthermore, as a Norwegian I'm very annoyed at how easy it is for Sweden to form the un-historical nation of Scandinavia. This straight up makes you game over as Norway. (And it usually happens long before 1905, which was when Norway and Sweden ended their Union). Despite all this I do have fun with the game. It's particularly fun in multi-player. It's an unpolished gem and could go on to becoming a great game... but right now I find myself still going back to Crusader Kings 3, as it allows for a lot more freedom in how you play the game. Victoria 3 right now feels like the slowest rush gameplay I have played. You are constantly trying to fix something in your economy and supply chain, but everything takes forever to get going even when you play at the highest level.

_childDocuments_.review: Against all odds this became my favorite paradox title. What always continues to impress me is the remarkable overwhelming depth this game offers - I think the entire playerbase, myself included, came in trying to play like other paradox titles and were somewhat disappointed at first. The learning curve is steep, and war has enormous and frustrating consequences for the unprepared. Where this game truly excels is the manipulation of the background simulation - beyond just transforming the political realities of your nation, you can shape the world around you through trade, politics, and diplomacy. No other game will give me the high of making the united states my dominion playing as Luxembourg, after I manipulated the power of the south with my exports to make the north succeed from the south, leaving them weak and the scraps of their expansion up for grabs. Nothing can top paying close attention to the UK to see when it's empire has stretched it too thin, and shredding their empire to pieces as an Ethiopian principality because they can't reinforce its troops in Kenya. Sometimes I'm in the mood to wreak some peaceful havoc as the Danish, watching Prussia collapse because I convinced a city state to join my market and splitt a great power in two. There's so many opportunities, and maybe the greatest weakness of this game is the lack of flavor for small fledgling nations - and the communities fear of trying out the few that do. I really do believe this is the most underrated paradox title out there, I pray the company continues to invest more into this game, and the community gives it a second chance. This game pushes the limits of how much it's players are willing to improve there skills - those willing to suffer through the learning curve will find a hidden gem unlike anything else out there.

_childDocuments_.review: Good economic simulator as long as you have more than one state. Too many times I've seen landlocked single state/ few province minor just starve their population to death because they are unable to handle their economy or the game is not set up for that. Nevermind all of Africa starving to death until Europeans colonize them. Forcing a new country to release from a great power: too bad, the new country is starving to death and they have sub 100% market access in their own capital. Diplomacy does not exist, you make a demand and you either win the demand or you lose the demand, there is no middle ground. Diplomacy options are very sparse anyway, basically just trade/ market related or things that result in war. War kinda stinks too. Does not take enough from Hearts of Iron for the fronts system to make sense and not enough control over individual army movements to compensate.Game does not give you much feedback and makes it very easy to dig yourself in a very big hole. You can easily build a few too many construction sectors and all of a sudden your balance is deep in the negative and need to raise taxes a bunch or crash the economy. Game chugs in late game too. Need a Ryzen x3d chip to make any meaningful progress in a reasonable amount of time.

_childDocuments_.review: For the TLDR: The game is Mediocre at best and I feel like paradox really dropped the balls with many of the design choices of this game. Theres a lot that I'm willing to forgive the game for such as the controversial war system that many are harking on right now and the AI being bad in general as thats some things that can be expected. but What can't be excused is the complete barebones nature of the game, Every country in this game has the exact same loop for the most part, the exact same gameplay. with barely little flavor. There is some if you look for it but there is no universal Historical events or things that impact the world, a lot of big no brainer countries that you expect people to try have very little content, the majors have some unique stuff but not enough for example the USA has maybe three events that just happen and you have to deal with, the first is the indian removal acts and then the very easily avoided civil war that you just pass a law to ban slavery for, and then prohibition. With a handful of decisions as well. Thats it.  Most nations aren't that lucky. Ottomans have a crisis at the start that resolves pretty early. Japan from the bit I had played seems to not really have anything other than the decision to overthrow the shogunate and all you need for that is to not have an interest group in the government. Sorry the TLDR ended up being a little long, but for a more detailed reason why please read on. Here are my list of Grievances:1.The Politics screen is pretty lackluster with the ability to just completely ignore elections and keep the party in control with seemingly no downside other than "Legitimacy" which ties into time to enact laws, with lower legitimacy taking longer to pass. Parties that the population votes for don't get added automatically to the government based on voter share or something similar. You can pick and choose however you want really as long as you don't care about law passage time.  It's just completely lackluster. Barely serviceable as a base game experience. 2. The Economy is very much a departure from Victoria 2 and that is not a good thing. Vicky 2 had its problems but the Economy fascinated me, with so many different ways to manage your country, all of this has been reduced in Vicky 3 to what is in the most basic terms possible, a "Command Economy" with private Investments. What I mean by this is that you the player. I.E. The "spirit" of the nation has complete control over what your little pops employ themselves into, what gets built and where. This is probably my biggest dislike of the game. It is hilariously tedious to click through and provide the goods needed and by late game it seems to take up a majority of my time checking the market and building like 20+ of whatever good is needed by the pops. There is no international trade like in Vicky 2 either you have to manually establish those trade routes for every good you need and even then there is a level cap that I for one cannot really figure out, some trade routes seem to just increase the amount of goods available from that nation with no rhyme or reason. I much prefer the Vicky 2 system of trade. The Population should be able to grow and expand factories as it pleases, and fail at those endeavors as much as succeed with government intervention when necessary. 3. The War system needs to be ironed out. Now I'm not one of those band-waggoning the new war system being ass. I think that the concept is very interesting but definitely poorly executed. I do understand the idea of Vicky being more of an economic sim than another paradox war sim, but there needs to be some input from the player other than what we have right now. You can have 500 battalions on a front to the enemies 100 and still have the AI auto gen you engagements where the enemy outnumbers you 3 to 1 for seemingly no reason other than the luck of the draw. You can win wars you should in theory lose and Lose wars you should have no way of losing just by the way the game handles the front for you which is kind of dumb imo.4. The Politics that I have already described to some extent, but to add on to it, All government types and laws feel fundamentally the same, The Economic laws as far as I can tell only really determine what you can subsidize and what your investment pool if you have one is used for with the most extreme command economy meaning you subsidize everything. Its kind of weird how most laws give you a new government institution but it seems like you don't really have to pay for it in any way, i.e. a dedicated police force doesn't cost money it costs bureaucracy, which while fundamentally might be the same thing since you have to spend money to build government centers, is kind of a weird choice, and same goes for most of the expenses other than The category for the pension laws which do cost money.  Sorry that wen't back into the economy for a little bit but it is all tied in the end. One of the biggest interesting things for me with the politics is the Interest groups and you being limited to picking three at the most usually for how many are in your government. Because in a democratic system if they garnored enough votes would they not have senators or MP's or whatever for that party? especially if we are looking at the US system where in Vicky 3 Every interest group is getting millions of votes, there seems to be no way that they don't get their own little stake in the government. All in all if I do get any feedback from this I expect it will be the same things I've heard for every other paradox game. "This game *Just* got released you can't expect a paradox game to be good on release"  or "Just wait for the DLC" or  "wait for mods" or something like that. But Don't you see how that is a completely unacceptable way of thinking? Why do we have to wait for the game to be fixed on a $50 dollar title from a studio with decades of experience and be okay with it? Are you really so beaten that YOU are okay with it? if it was any other studio many of you would refuse to purchase from them ever again. Its ridiculous the amount of hoops of logic I hear from fanboys of Paradox and don't get me wrong I'm one too I love paradox but I'm sick and tired of giving them excuses for the mediocre ♥♥♥♥ they shovel down our mouths every few months and we as a community are just supposed to take it because no matter what when that next DLC or expansion or game whatever comes out, people are going to buy it, ♥♥♥♥ I'm probably going to but all I'm saying is the Criticism is totally valid and you know it too. Thanks for reading my little tangent. Have a good day.

_childDocuments_.review: Still digging into the game but it's already clear that the fundamental gameplay loops with the economic and political subsystems are gripping and well-done. Based on that alone, this game is an unqualified success.The diplomatic systems probably need some more work, some of the numbers and game play balance things need to be adjusted here and there, and it would be nice to have additional historical content through the whole span of the game. It's not perfect. But I think all of those things are relatively easy to implement when the underlying structure is so strong. And also, the game as it exists now is already extremely fun and absorbing, and surprisingly easy to play and interact with given its complexity.Bottom line: already really good and only going to improve.

_childDocuments_.review: I would not currently recommend the game. I enjoyed Vicky 2 and was looking forwards to this game but it has been a disappointment. My biggest complaint is that the game feels like a bunch of poorly strung together mini-games instead of a cohesive product. Additionally I really dislike the way the game handles trade. The current system is unrealistic and unfun. It should not be on the player to be obsessively optimizing trade-routes. Instead the player should be focused on setting high level policy (tarrifs, quotas, ect) and then let the game play out the results. This would more accurately mirror real world dynamics and reduce tedious micro.The military system as everyone mentions is bad. It is not a huge issue but it does scream "we left this as a place for future mandatory DLC."

_childDocuments_.review: TBH I kind of like it, but as with all paradox games at the start, I think there is a lot of room for improvementThings I enjoyed:- Making the buildings actually, some people are complaining that its annoying that you have to build every single building, but it reminded me a lot of games like sim city almost, like leveling up the nation and slowly improving the tax revenue and handling population needs. Very tycoon. I'd reccomend for free market economies to have Investors build buildings in addition to us as the player in some cases, or that investors come forward with proposals that you can accept/deny. I think for bigger empires this can be even more annoying- Politics. I felt pretty satisfied when the Landowners who were originally 50% of my government were then only 2%- Trade, though I thought it was stupid that I had to find markets to export to, it would be much cooler if other nations traded freely with you according to your trade policy (asking if youre on mercantilism or protectionism or something, but freely buying on free trade)- Warfare, I liked the part of it where I could just watch the conquests happen. I initially was thrown off since I used to play HOI4 a lot, but its kind of nice and reflects the shows of power of the eraThings to be improved:- This game needs flavor. Lots and lots of flavor. I normally like playing smaller nations, and did a Shewa playthrough and even though I had a wargoal to unify ethiopia, there was no decision for me to become ethiopia, so in 1936 i was still Shewa. Flavor around historical events, like Russia occupying outer manchuria would be great too. This steak needs some spice- The AI. Most all of my games ended with the European powers looking like just how they started with some minor exceptions. A Russia that hasn't taken Manchuria, or central aisa, a Japan that is still a shogunate with a GDP of $20 million, A Germany that never unified, a Ottoman Empire that wasn't carved up, a china that is still Qing, or at peace with the Heavenly Kingdom...- The US. Most games, the US made the west coast look like garbage with some random mexican enclave. Bad.- Politics needs more diversity. I want to see nations go through facism and come out of it- Formable nations by decision- More types of "diplomatic incident". I was playing Korea, couldn't even do an independence war, so I just had to revolution myself, and it wasn't even because my pops wanted independence, it was because I angered the conservatives- Scramble for africa has TONS of border gore, and often times in 1936 there will be like 20 still uncolonized african nations- It would be cool to have some reincarnation of the newspaper from Vic2, but more optimized so you dont have a backlog of 40 newspapers but can read up on interesting things that have happened in the past 5 years or somethingOverall, 7/10 but needs a lot of work. Has the potential to be amazingEDIT: Just discovered that you manually have to change building production methods...really hard to manage in large countries

_childDocuments_.review: The game crashes to desktop constantly and reproducibly the larger your empire gets, especially during wars. It's not necessarily related to taking certain actions, sometimes you can abort all your builds or battles or change the time speed to get past the crash point, but a few minutes later you'll hit a new set of random/unknown conditions that consistently triggers another crash to desktop.I've tried setting graphics to potato quality including limiting fps, slowing down time to the slowest setting, randomly changing all my orders, underclocking my gpu/cpu/ram, updating drivers, clearing shader caches, rolling back to previous releases. This is the 3rd play through that, things have gotten completely unplayable on. I played once as denmark and kept my number of states small (7 total) and got through the whole 100 year campaign, so that's nice. If you want to expand and take over the world though... crash to desktop.

_childDocuments_.review: Can't recommend in its current state, the game is extremely tedious for little reward. Most mechanics in the game are tied around buildings, which means you stare at the building screen and click expand the whole time. I wouldn't mind the tedium if the result of building a large economy gave me anything to do besides look at GPD/SoL lines go up.  Diplomacy is extremely shallow, and nothing about your nation effects diplomacy aside from your military strength and the involved nation's opinion of you. This leads to Taiping China intervening in your Conquest of the Congo for no reason other than they have a similar prestige rating. Most unforgivable is the lack of flavor(unique plays?) for every country besides maybe the USA and Prussia. Every nation plays the same, even the economic laws only change what buildings you can and can't subsidize further compounding the tedious clicking minigame. It will probably be good after a couple $30 DLCs.

_childDocuments_.review: I actually purchased this opening day... only to find out the game wouldn't open. I tried to look for any potential problem, then realized it was due to this little note in the system requirements:"AVX support required"Alright, seriously, Paradox? You're running strategy games, not high-end first person shooters. I've never had to play a strategy or 4x game or anything similar that required a processor change like this. I also really don't see how limiting the amount of people who can at the very least boot up the game and give it a try is a good marketing strategy. I ended up refunding my game, and it was perhaps the first time I've ever done so on Steam, and all because of some really random specific system requirement.Well, their antics with DLC and other releases (see my review for "Imperator") over the years have been waning on my anyway. Paradox is losing a lot of die-hard fans, and seem to be intent on continuing down this road, sadly.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game.  The depth that paradox offers in it's games is practically unrivaled.  I do feel like this game offers great challenges with certain countries, or you can choose a country, like china, that is destined to be 1st to best learn the game. No two games are the same.  Different situations happen randomly in any part of the world, which makes each play unique and unlike the last.  It really makes the games replay value that much more.Update:Paradox did an update that makes this game ridiculous to play now.  First off is the new military changes.  They tried making it more interactive with evolving fronts that move and split during the battle, but it just makes it more of a hassle somehow to have to monitor and have several armies to use to cover all of the different fronts that emerge during a battle.  It's just not fun anymore.Secondly, and maybe this is just something that i haven't figured out how to resolve is resources.  Before if i had say Iron and wood in one of my states, and build a Tool factory in a different state, as long as i had enough in my market, the tool factory would find a way to get the resources to their factory.  Now, if the resources aren't in the same state as the factory, it shows that i have a shortage of wood and iron and the factory will not make enough tools to support the rest of my economy.  It's so annoying, i can't even play this game anymore.  So disappointing.I can not recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I have no idea what I'm doing, but I'm having fun doing it.Edit: Changed the review to negative:Nearly one year later I still don't know what I'm doing, but I did find out that it isn't my fault. _childDocuments_.review: This will be my 3rd edit. I will sum up the game from 1.0 to 1.3.Game released as a disaster. Constant crashes, AI failing to manage a country or causing any challenge, performance issues and MP stability.1.2 patch fixed a lot of things and I felt that only problems left were AI and MP stability.Then came the 1.3 patch. Which destroyed 1.2.Main problems;- AI can't manage economy- AI can't manage revolutions- AI is easly fooled while having war- Multiplayer hotjoin breaks down- Multiplayer desync issues can't be handled without a rehost, which takes tremendous amount of time.- Lack of content for major countries- Performance issues ( I have RTX 3070, Intel i7 10700K and 32 gb ram and I still can't manage to get more than 30 FPS)- Warfare is senseless. It's just numbers against numbers.- Technology seems unbalanced- No depth in economy- Minor QoL issuesI should explain more.The logic behind a great economy is Tax more > Construct more > Gain more tax(through production and wages). QoL issues are the easiest. There is no hold and drag to constructions or technologies. Having technologies added to queue was nice. But we should be changing the order.Warfare is dull because you have no interaction at all. You only put generals on the fronts. You can't change generals theatres. You can't somehow train generals or soldiers to be more efficient. However, you can research technology for difference. Which is also dull. No cavalary types, no ammunition types, no bayonet techs... Production methods for army are meaningless. You can research 3rd and 4th production methods in late game but there is nothing for early game. And those researches are too close to each other, you end up not using some of them. Peformance is a disaster due to population getting divided constantly by their culture, religion and class. Check out the performance mods, they are all using increased assimilation and conversion.Multiplayer is such a huge disappointment to me. I have played other Paradox titles for years. I still can't understand how it doesn't work. The best MP tech was in HOI 4. You could resync in-game and have hotjoin without problem. After 6 years, in Vic3, you can't seem to hotjoin without breaking the game or make a resync. This doesn't feel like a progress to me. For core players, it makes a lot of difference.Lack of content is a bummer but I can't say it's the main problem.I want to love this game. I do play this game. I loved Vic2. But the problems for the core game itself is too much. The progress of fixing those, ends up breaking other things. Which frustrates me even more. Use testers, use open beta as you did in 1.2. Let people help the process.1.2 was a success because warfare system was a failure. The new changes in law-change process is succesful too. But as 1.3 introduced, AI failed to manage economy. Which was fixed in 1.2. Devs can successfuly change things but other things ends up broken. My initial comment was that "there is a long way to go for this game". I still stand by it. I am sad to see this game trying to hold on to life.People tend to confused by the gameplay hours. I have played 2000+ hours of HOI4 just to see it got destroyed by some dlc. And let's be honest to each other, there are no games like these in the market. Not graphic wise or QoL wise.TL,DR;I can see Paradox is simplifying the games for new players. I am not against that. But DLC's and mechanics are getting simplified too. I want more complexity. More to discover. More to micro manage and a good performance while doing those. Also, for God's sake please fix the multiplayer.

_childDocuments_.review: I love a paradox grand strategy game. I’ve played most and must have sunk somewhere beyond a thousand hours into them because they’ve always triggered that part of my brain that refuses to be beaten by puzzles. Stellaris is good for new players as it’s relatively less complex and the blinky lights help push through that initially intimidating difficulty curve; Crusader Kings provides a more role-playing experience; Hearts of Iron is great for people weirdly obsessed with Warhammer and Victoria is for people sexually aroused by accounting.Victoria is a great big real time board game set during the industrial revolution that focuses on economic dominance and government and it really is as dreary as that description. It’s all about supply lines, production methods, resource availability and pacifying the population to balance the budget. I wouldn’t blame you for skipping over this one entirely but allow me to explain why it’s sucked up so much of my time.A large part of my enjoyment of Crusader Kings came from trying to master its complexities. It took me like fifteen attempts and then suddenly the enjoyment dropped off. I’d mastered it. It was too easy to dominate the world and I found myself cracking open the modding tools to chase that feeling. After 200 hours into Victoria I’m still getting my ass handed to me. It’s the sort of game that requires careful micro-management and where the slightest mistake will send you spiralling into debt and failure.Let me try and explain the core mechanics (bear with). You take control of a pre-industrial nation and attempt to force your rivals into submission with your sheer economic power. You do this by researching new productive ways of producing your goods to sell, boosting your income and allowing you to dominate the other nations either militarily or diplomatically. For instance, iron is an important resource for a developing nation and you have plenty to extract. That iron could be sold for profit but to extract it you require tools. A shortage of tools would drive up their price making the extraction of iron unprofitable and causing your economy to tank. You could import tools from a foreign nation but that takes up your bureaucratic resources and increasing those are incredibly expensive. Later you could use engines to extract greater amounts of iron but you’d require engines and coal, produced or imported.If your eyes are glazing over reading that last paragraph that is entirely understandable. It’s a complex and delicate web of production where the slightest change could bring the whole thing toppling down. It requires careful micro-management to make sure each building uses the resources available to it to maximise its production.This is the era when the nations of Europe was colonising Africa of course and that brings a whole bunch of new problems. Some nations can be conquered, while others have no government to force into submission and can only be gradually colonised. Doing so gives you access to new resources to feed into your factories but are a drain on your funds, adds another province to manage and might piss off some very powerful neighbours.The game does feature a very token combat system for conquering territory but the emphasis is on providing the equipment they need to keep going. There’s no equipment customisation or freedom to plan your strategy like you might get in Hearts of Iron, it’s just this army attacks that province. It always just comes down to who brought the biggest stick, which is a shame because it could be much deeper. It shouldn’t be difficult to transplant some of Heart of Iron’s mechanics.This game is Paradox’s final boss. The one to play if you’ve mastered the others and want a real challenge. It’s like juggling twelve spinning plates and I’d recommend it only if you’re mad. And apparently I am because I’ve sunk 200 hours into this game and it absolutely won’t beat me.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Wait for further improvements before purchasing.Ah... Where to start.The game itself is quite polished; as typical of grand strategy game from Paradox, it has A LOT of systems intertwined together, and the UI is quite a labyrinth to navigate through. There were some bugs here and there and I did encounter some CTDs, but nothing major. This is my first Victoria game, and it was fun for me.The main problem is the lack of depth in military and diplomacy, and the end game to a degree. The list can get long, so I just put my main sticking points:- No diplomacy when at war.- War is severely limited; no multiple war, can only conquer one region per war, etc.- You can't invest in your protectorates; if you want to develop their mines, you have to conquer them.- Lacking building for handling unemployment. It's almost impossible to be Egalitarian in a country with a lot of population; even with trade, you won't have enough raw resources to fuel your industries.- Tutorial could've been better.- The AI is dumb. An AI mod released within few days of the game release performs much better than vanilla!Edit #1 (Update 1.5): Most of my grievances have been fixed, but the new update massively changed how military works and army formation movement is still janky. In a war against a big country, I have to pause a lot and manually re-assign army formations to fronts because the automatic reassignment is useless right now. This micro-management is NOT fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I have given this game so many chances and I desperately want to enjoy it and love it but I seriously cannot overstate how frustrating and downright bad this game is. The choices you make are so depressingly insignificant and it is almost impossible to actually control or do anything you want to do in this game due to how it is designed. It takes decades upon decades in game and hours upon hours to actually try and achieve one thing. Want to declare a war of independence as the Dominion of Canada, have fun spending hours trying to increase you ever falling liberty desire while Great Britain continues to buy out your entire GDP without really being able to do anything to stop it. Paradox has ruined its potential by catering to the select few players that enjoy the mind-numbing extreme detail of a game like this and alienated casual gamer's who don't have the time or the interest to learn volumes of historical economic policy in order to succeed in this game. It is easy to just sit there and advance your tech tree, modernize your army, balance your budget, and then half the game goes by and you realize you haven't done anything to reform your laws or have done anything diplomatic yet. I would not be surprised if they release DLCs that are more focused on laws or certain ideas being researched (eg socialism) that will start the liberal global movement and force some action between countries. _childDocuments_.review: So Victoria III comes with ground breaking new design decisions in this genre of Paradox Grand Strategy Games. They are trying in this era of Victorianism to up the gameplay part of not moving armies around but take care of industrialization. You manage your market, infrastructure, and each factory and building, where you adjust production methods so that you get the most out of your economy and at the same time keep everything runing. You must keep an eye on the market, prices of stuff are affected by availability, so if your market lacks tools the prices spike - like in capitalistic markets they do because everybody tries to get the last tools available - and if you then happen to have a coal mine that is using tools for efficiency the prices of tools may cripple that mine, which will lower its output, people will get fired and loose work, those folks drop in their living standard and take their families down with them, the coal mine meanwhile will loose its stored money and go bankrupt eventually, if the laws allow that in your country and you have the cash you can jump in and subsidise to save that coal mine, otherwise you are looking at ♥♥♥♥ hitting the fan because spiking coal prices will put out a lot of other factories out of service as well, so in the end you have to build more tool factories, to solve this, but then you will find out there is not enough wood and iron to produce more tools, so the prices of that spike and now you have more issues. Meanwhile in the neighbourhood a country decides to attack your other neighbour and now you must ask yourself if you can allow that attacker to conquer that other state or will that other neighbour then become to powerfull? At the same time thousands of kilometers away from your capital your fleet is engaging in some local war and another thousands of kilometers you are to be dealing with a native uprising in your colony. And behind the scenes two major powers are preparing to ally against you because they want this fancy state you just colonized because of all the oil was just found there. Once you deal with all that an agitator spawns in your country and wants to force your majesty to enact a law and enable voting and change the basis of your power structure in your country, which will if he succeeds end your country up having elections every now and then, which will have the potential to change your countries politics and policies for the years to come. And then there is the hard decisions about what new crazy groundbreaking technologies would you want to pursuit and where to build those universities to boost that research. Now after all this you will have to deal with the revolution that suddenly happened in your country and there is a whole bunch of traiterous states that seceeded from you and want to attack you because they didnt like the new tax laws you enacted to push your financies... Well, your majesty, what should we do with them. I'd suggest to mobilize those armies, make sure they have enough food, ammo and weapons and bomb the hell out of those revolutionary marxists.That is about how Victoria III feels.I have to say that a lot of the changes felt good, and the first time i had really a feeling that there is something to do besides moving armies and doing wars and paint the map with your colors. They really nailed the peacetime gameplay this time around. And war is also dissinsentivized since it is so crazy expansive in a lot of aspects, so that it is recommended to make sure that its worth it. And, there is one more issue. The new diplomacy play system of declaring wars and stuff, makes it possible that your calculation of the upcoming war gets southways really fast if suddenly some major powers get swayed to join the enemies side, you can swiftly see yourself fighting a lot more enemies than you expected. But, there are some issues. For example the design of army commands causes some issues some times. Armies would return to the capital even though you had them stationed at some other place. In a small country thats not an issue, but if you have a colonial empire it is quite the issue if your army decides to run to the capital after the war ends and you wanted them to stay in the colonies. Also you can not simply upgrade ships. I do not understand this design decision. It makes upgrading ships so much unpleasent. If you have the rescources you dont care about rebuilding the naval bases, but it is not at all realistic and is void of any logic. Also I felt that something with the market is not working right. I could not understand how surpluses and lacks happen exactely. Because at one point I had like -40 tools. Lets pretend everything else was about okay. Now, i built a tool factory which lets say outputs 40 tools. I also made sure it had all the iron and wood available by adding those capacities too. I would then expect the market to have 0 available since -40 + 40 equals out at null. But somehow there are other factors which are at play and I ended up with +20 within a few months. So... I did not understand that at all. Also at one point my market was quite large, enharbouring a lot of smaller countries around my country. And my market was at about -1200 in tools. Yet the price is just +11% which sounds like not an issue at all. So that doesnt make any much sence to me either... _childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this game to other players?  Yes. ..But, understand what this game is, and is not.  This review comes at ~60 hrs and seeing one game to the time out.   In a quick summary this is the big 'Tycoon' game dressed as part industrial revolution, part colonialism, part trade and economy.  I modernized Persia when it comes to human rights and education.  I built a massive industry that could never keep up in many goods because my larger neighbours had bigger hungrier populations.  I dabbled in spreading out through the world chasing down good gold deposits.It is not a war simulation, nor a character or dynasty builder.   You are the economy, you tinker with many levers and options.  You are the problem solver who has to deal with the fact that one of your biggest trading partners just stopped shipping you a critical resource.I learned just how costly war really can be.  Thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is a good example of a grand strategy game set during the Industrial Revolution. Victoria is lighter on story and personality than other Paradox games like Crusader Kings or Stellaris. That's not to say I found it boring. Victoria 3 is one of the most extensively simulated economies perhaps in all of PC gaming. If that sounds daunting, managing that economy isn't the matrix-like spreadsheet of Wall Street stock drivel that it sounds like. Actually, managing it is more like budgeting for your family. Balance the books and you'll be fine. You will definitely want some idea of how supply and demand works though. Victoria 3 is my first foray into the Victoria series from Paradox. I held off on giving this game a review because my first impressions weren't positive and a dear friend purchased this for me as a gift knowing I like other Paradox games. Like all Paradox games, once you understand exactly what you're looking at on the screen the rest falls into place. Now I can dump countless hours into Victoria 3 and feel good recommending it. It's also worth noting that in just the few months the game has been out Paradox has pushed many fixes and a few absolutely monstrous patches. They clearly intend to heavily invest into making this game something to stick with. If it looks anything like the path that has been taken supporting Crusader Kings and Stellaris then I'm sure I'll get plenty of hours out of this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is a fun game. It is a complex and seemingly deep experience. However, if you spend time exploring the game, you realize that complexity and depth are not the same thing. Victoria 3 is very complex, but often this complexity offers frustration rather than a pleasant experience.    TLDR:   1.) Line go up. Seriously, watching your economy grow is extremely engaging. Its a lot of fun to change   production and see your country get stronger. This is probably the first game that gives a good feeling of   what industrialization is like. While other games can capture the feeling of growth or advancement, this is   the first game I've seen that really makes it feel as though you are taking a primitive society and emerging   an industrialized juggernaut.   2.) Focusing on the economy as the main driver of fun is not a bad game idea. As your economy grows, you   require more resource. This leads to development but also expansion, both colonial and through continental   wars.   3.) Trade and markets are actually important. Unlike other Paradox games, the world-wide nature of trade is   actually represented and makes a significant impact on your games.   4.) You can get achievements with mods. Enough said.   Unfortunately, the game has an almost never-ending amount of shortfalls. Every point in the "Good"   column above (except for #4) is limited by the implementation. Furthermore, this is a Paradox game. This   means that all the same issues that Paradox games have are present.   1.) The game is slow. No really, the games takes many more hours than any of Paradox's other titles like   HOI4. This is not bad per say, but it means you cannot get a good experience playing for only 2 hours. You   need to play for 10. Furthermore, this means that youtubers will interact with this content a lot less. Each   video they will make on Victoria 3 will require them to work much longer and harder and thusly will be   avoided.   2.) The game is slow. No really. Wait, don't look away. This isn't an an accidental copy and paste of the   above. In addition to the game experience itself being slow, the game itself is slow. Since wars are   automated, and micromanaging the economy comes in bursts, there is a lot of waiting. The game basically   looks like this:      First, look at your market.      Then build what you need. (This is added to your build queue)      Wait until everything is built.      Then repeat.   You don't have to be a genius to figure out that waiting will be a large part of the game. Unfortunately, this   really is catastrophic. This is because the fastest speed you can set the game too is just too slow. This is a   problem that plagues other Paradox titles as well.   3.) The game is slow. But it gets worse. When playing HOI4, the lategame gets extremely laggy. The   computer needs to do many calculations and it can't keep up. Victoria 3 is worse because lategame is the   whole point. In HOI4, you get done what you wanted in the early years of the game. In Victoria 3, many   countries (like Japan) only get good later during this time period. This means that playing the lategame is   kind of the whole point.     By 1880, my game could not keep up with 5x speed. So I was forced to play at 4x. By 1890, even that was     too much. Now I was at 3x speed. Let me tell you, playing the game at 3x speed is excruciatingly slow. Its     actually torture. Playing any faster speed has the game stutter like it was having a seizure.   4.) Crashes. They don't usually happen. However, often the computer does not have time to run all its   calculations at 5x speed and when a war breaks out it causes the whole game to crash. Over a gaming   session of around 15 hours I had somewhere around 6 crashes. Not great but not the worst. Still should be   fixed though.   5.) Remember how in HOI4 the game mechanics really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ you over sometimes? Yeah? Well, welcome    to Victoria 3! Its the same stuff all over again. If your state rebels, you enter into a war with it. However, if it    splinters internally (i.e. has a revolt of its own), that part just leaves.     Example: You own Oman. Oman rebels from you. You land your troops in Oman. Oman splits into Oman    and Revolutionary Oman. You subdue Oman. However, Revolutionary Oman is not Oman. Revolutionary    Oman is an independent country who doesn't need no overlord. Remember how Dobby was freed by Harry    Potter? Well yah, same thing here. Revolutionary Oman is free and there isn't anything you can do about it.     Note: You can attack them, but by now they have their own allies and you get a diplo penalty for taking    back your own territory. Great work Paradox!!!  6.) Yeah no. This is just #5 but again. Lets say you are defending Afghanistan (you own) from an Indian   invasion. Lets say Afghanistan rebels. Yeah, your troops are immediately teleported back to your home   country. Yeah, your entire army was in Afghanistan, but no one cares and you lost the entire territory.   Thanks Paradox.   7.) Navy still sucks. I mean, its really doesn't have a point. Ironclads should be immune to wooden ships but   aren't. You should be able to blackade a country but you can't. (You can raid a node, but not surround a   country). Naval battles have no meaning whatsoever. The fleets just regenerate and do it again. Since   everything in Victoria 3 is production and no storage, it means that the fleet has the same upkeep no   matter what. In other words, your fleet getting wiped out means nothing since it has no military value and   does nothing bad to your economy. Your fleet will be back in action in a few weeks without any impact at   all. There does not seem to be warscore associated with fleets either btw.   8.) War diplomacy sucks. I invade Korea (as Japan) and need to fight China. I win. I invade Vietnam, have to   fight China again. Big sigh, why can't we have something like in EUV where you can stop a country from   meddling in your affairs? If I beat you completely, you should not then challenge me 5 min later.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is a the newest entry to Paradox's Grand Strategy series of games. It takes place in the 1830's through the 1930s and is very different from CK3. I did not play Victoria 2 so I wasn't sure what to expect. The game is heavily focused on the economy and politics. You need to balance your resources and creating buildings to manage the inputs and outputs of your economy. It's a fairly simple concept that gets increasingly complex and can be absolutely addicting to try and perfect. There are some very deep and intricate systems - some that you need to know and some that you can get by with less. This game is not for everyone. It is fairly accessible compared to older Paradox games but takes a long time to master. Overall, I have enjoyed my time with the game and think it's worth checking out. If the idea of managing a country to make them an economical and military powerhouse seems interesting than give this game a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those times I wish Steam provided a "maybe" check box when recommending a game. That's not to say I hate this game. I certainly do not. But I also am not head over heels for it. I'm 50/50 as it were. I followed the dev diaries leading up to the release, albeit not religiously, just casually looking through and then going about my day. So I had a rough idea of what to expect.The CONS:- WARFARE SYSTEM: I've read both arguments, once you get passed the passive aggressive insults and inflammatory posts of course, some people have made valid for/against the combat. And they're all valid too. Personally, I do not care for it but I knew that going in. Admittedly, I do miss the unit models though. However, I like the idea of not being able to micromanage every army stack all the time. That was the most annoying aspect of Vic2 combat, especially late game in my opinion. Don't believe me? Play Germany and be surrounded on all sides by enemies. Good luck. - NATIONS: Aside from a few unique journal entries, there is no difference between countries. Depending on what nation you choose to begin with, but they all play the same. I just don't feel the uniqueness when it comes to playing in South America or Europe.- GOVERNMENTS: Again, I don't feel difference in any government system. In Vic2 you're ability to influence your economy depended on your government. You can micro your economy to perfection in this game with no regard to the ruling party. The difference between a capitalist system of government and a planned economy is nonexistent.- DLC(eventually): If you know, then you know. It's coming. My criticism stems from potential flavor packs and/or reworked systems under a price tag. This is nothing new though from any game developer, I just never agreed with it. But it is what it is.The PROS:- MAP: The map is beautiful. It feels alive and that is engaging to see. CK3 can take notes from what a map is supposed to convey. I'm sure some people may disagree, and they're not wrong, as a part of me does miss the "paper" look to the Vic2 map. Nostalgia hits hard at times.- THE GAME ITSELF: I gave my "thumbs down" due to the sole fact that the foundation for Vic3 to be an amazing game is absolutely there. I have no doubt about that at all. But in its current state I cannot recommend, sadly. However, I compare the current gameplay is like dating a beautiful woman only to find out she has very little personality. I would know as I've dated/banged a few of them over the years. But unlike them, I know this game will remain with me longer than they did. Thank God.

_childDocuments_.review: Beware, most people are disliking this game because they were coming in expecting it to be like other Paradox GSG's where it's mostly about using your units to conquer other countries and paint the map with your color, not realizing Paradox were trying to do something different here that was more focused on economics and political simulation and dealing with your country internally. A good example of this is people complaining about having to micro your trade routes... except if you get rid of microing your trade then what's the point of the economic system if you're having an AI do it all for you?There's definitely some issues with this game don't get me wrong, but most of them are just launch jitters regarding balance, the AI behaving weirdly, and general bugs. The main core issues with the game I've found so far come down to mainly that the UI can sometimes be a bit opaque in showing you the information you need, and that the war system in general does need to be fleshed out and fixed a bit. What they were going for in general with not having you micro individual units in war makes a lot of sense because they shifted that micro focus over to the economy and politics side of things where you're constantly building buildings and microing your marketplace, but they did go a bit too far and it wouldn't hurt to at least give your generals a sense of direction ala HOI4 battleplans, and on top of that there's some unrealistic intricacies like how despite having complete naval supremacy as Britain, France can still ship and supply their army halfway across the world and attack Britain's colonies. Needless to day though these issues can be ironed out with a few DLCS.Ultimately I'm very much enjoying my time with Victoria 3 so I can't help but give it a positive review. Your mileage may vary though. If you're someone coming in here for more of the combat and conquest side of things then this is not your game. In general I'd even say if you're coming here expecting a typical Paradox Grand Strategy game this may not be your game right at the moment, as Paradox usually focuses quite a lot on the military aspect of the economics, diplomacy and military systems of GSG, whereas this is more focused on economics and diplomacy, though with a few dlcs that might change somewhat. If you're someone who likes economics simulators like the Anno series or political simulators like Democracy, this is very much a game right up your alley and you will enjoy it. I'm that kind of player and I feel like I got my money's worth.

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen Paradox release multiple games in this genre before. Hoi4, Stellaris, CK3, and Imperator:Rome. Out of all of them, this has been the smoothest and most enjoyable release, both in terms of performance, but also in terms of mechanics.The great:Playing victoria 3 gives you the same sense of deep satisfaction in nation building as victoria 2. Seeing your interest groups slowly change from landowners and clergy to labour unions and industrialists, your economy transform from a subsistence agriculture dominated traditional economy into a booming industrial hub, and your rank skyrocket as your treaty ports and trade routes give you cheap imports and a market for your goods... It's incredibly satisfying. It really does scratch the same itch victoria 2 does, even if you don't spend your time doing anything remotely similar to what you do in victoria 2 (v3: trade and politics, v2: production, imo).The meh:Politics are predictable. Your interest groups do not react to world events, and they almost never react differently to your efforts from country to country. Each IG has a set of ideologies, and they do vary from country to country (clergy in China are very different from clergy elsewhere, some IGs can completely swap out their ideologies once socialism appears, etc), but it still feels static and predictable. But hey, it works, and it works very well for being an universal system. The kinda ♥♥♥♥:Parties are good, and I like them, but boy are they janky. I expect it'll be fixed, but right now, parties are very obscure. It's difficult to tell when they'll appear, it's difficult to tell what parties get votes and why, and interest groups joining and leaving parties cause issues with your government and clout distribution. It's janky. Overall, the "great" outweighs the "meh" and the "kinda ♥♥♥♥" by an order of magnitude. It's a wonderful game, and will be my go-to paradox game for the foreseeable future. I have 6100 hours combined in Paradox strategy games (of which 600 is in vicky 2). I don't mean to say that gives me any authority on the subject, but other reviews mention their playtime, so I guess I should too.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this review by saying that I've sunk a considerable amount of time into the various PDX 4X games.I think what Victoria 3 does best is how it represents the economy (as it should). It essentially boils down to building more factories in an endless loop to keep the price of raw resources down while simultaneously creating more demand for your manufactured goods, While there are some irritants, like bigger countries buying up all your steel or coal (even when they themselves have a good surplus), causing prices to skyrocket, I think it is represented quite well. As of right now, there is not much country flavour (likely to be remedied with a paid DLC, of course), and as per usual, the AI isn't very good at the game. In the four campaigns I have played so far, France and Austria seem a lot stronger than they would've been historically, while Britain and the U.S. are significantly weaker. The U.S., in particular, seems especially weak as they never start the Mexican-American war over Texas, they usually just let Mexico annex Texas. Lastly, the warfare. I personally disagree with the way Paradox decided to go about doing it. You simply don't have enough control over your own armies; they'll just inexplicably lose to a smaller power despite having numbers and better stats. If a system similar to HOI4's frontline system was in the game instead, I think there would be massive improvements.However, despite these shortcomings, I believe that Victoria 3 is a fun game with decent replay value. It is a little lacklustre at the moment, but this is sure to be improved through DLCs in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: So this is coming from a Veteran of Vic 2. I am fully up for Comments on this but I wanted to voice what I feel is right with the game, wrong with the game then give my honest opinion on what should change and if you should get this game.So first the goods:-I think the way the industry has been changed in this game from Vic2 is a bit better. It definitely adds more complexity to what is honestly a pretty big drive of the victorian era.-I like how streamlined politics has become with the game but I will touch on this in a bit.-And I like how the technology of the military has changedNow lets go into some things I feel are wrong with this title:-The game is definitely way too complicated for casual plays. The way you have to micromanage your industry definitely hurts your overall experience of the game. I come to a paradox game to enjoy my time in a certain era of history and make my name in the world not look at a menu for 90% of the game constructing stuff because the AI has no clue what I need constructed when.-The military is complete garbage. The AI is not programmed to make the best moves to get you closer to winning a war. I had naval invaded Bejing to take the capital Bejing and get a war with china done sooner but the AI decided, "Let me move north and in the opposite direction of Bejing, Split the front, and lose the whole frontline". This honestly needs changing in some way, if we are meant to put full faith in our armies AI to win a war.-Diplomatic plays are still stupid. "Why do I need to fight Austria to gain control of Mexico as the United States? What interest does Austria have in a continent it has never been to nor ever will be because its a Mediterranean naval power. Why do I need to fight France who I have great relations with to gain this one province it has no reason to be interested in". Seriously we gave great powers way too much power by removing the Sphere of Influence mechanic and replacing it with Diplomatic plays. Now any great power or minor power can just ruin your plans for your achievement by joining a diplomatic play.-Infamy is way too powerful. it should not cost me half my play through to conquer a central american country or to puppet a minor nation.-Political parties have too much power now. This was to solve the issue of the US avoiding Civil war but now I have the issue of one party winning an election and basically taking 20-30% of the government power and then just abusing that to hell. It makes it nearly impossible to make normal laws for a country and can screw your game in one simple move. -Radicals have way too much power. I cant describe the immense suffering when your capital of states have unrest. The tax modifier on that is way too strong for any reasonable person and even after patch the radicals increase just as fast as before patch. Its broken and definitely needs patching.Do I honestly recommend you buy this game post first update. No. Its still messy. The game has many issues paradox has not addressed and now new ones that I dont think paradox fully considered with this update. I have high hopes for victoria 3 its just in my honest opinion I dont know if paradox is up to the task of making this game better after the multiple failed launches of prior games, the abandonment of Imperator Rome, the obvious superiority of Vic 2 over this. and well the tendency to lock updates behind a pay wall. I would recommend waiting till the first DLC's launch to actually think about buying this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a good base for what is to come. Specific things that are missing that should be adjusted:It's nigh impossible to conquer colonies in the endgame. There is no "dismantle empire" CB like in vic2.Infamy for states is ridiculously high. Nobody should care if a random state in Africa is conquered from an insignificant power, but it inflicts 17-35 infamy.It's possible to fall into a welfare trap with institutions, where minimum wage is 100% and welfare is 100%, which causes everybody to quit their job. This is unintuitive.There are simply not enough of certain resources available, limiting growth absolutely. I own the entirety of the middle east and cannot supply my army with oil or rubber. Either make it easier to have split production types in nations or make it more viable to set an entire army to tanks.Only being able to have one diplomatic play is incredibly annoying. Why do OPMs count as a full diplo play in this case? Make it so that play time is dynamic on country size or something similar.The politics are still obtuse. You can have an entire country of loyalists and have the country completely flip-flop in one election.Secessions are confusing and ill defined. They start randomly and are nigh-impossible to slow down or stop. Especially confusing after you annex a state and then it starts to rebel. They just lost a war, they shouldn't be able to fight yet.There are plenty more, but these are what stand out after a full campaign. It'll be interesting to see what things they can adjust, as some of these feel baked into the game intrinsically. Maybe HPM2 can overhaul some of these, but the designs of the plays worry me. Overall, it is still enjoyable and hopefully fixable. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: The game is simply just too buggy and unpolished for me to recommend in this state.... one year after its already come out. I understand having an under-baked game on launch, as nowadays to keep up with the release schedule and market, you need to be pumping out games or updates to those games. But it's already been one year, how long are we supposed to wait until the game is playable enough to warrant the price? There have been many free updates, reworking and overhauling portions of the game, and while there have been some major improvements, each of those updates has brought with them countless bugs, even after a lengthy open beta period. I'm not blaming the developers on this, it's quite obvious to me that they're being overworked, but I just simply cant recommend the game. Come back in three years and it might be good enough to buy.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is the long-awaited sequel to Victoria 2, a 12 year old cult classic. Although it was a buggy, janky, fundamentally broken mess, the economy of Victoria 2 was unique among games. It featured a closed loop economy, where every good bought or pound spent by one entity is a good produced or a pound earned by a different entity. The entire thing operated and changed by itself. You could not control it, only influence it. It had many bugs and design flaws, but it was a truly unique economic system for a videogame. The surrounding systems like diplomacy and war were simple and lazy, in the old Paradox style, but just functional enough.In comes Victoria 3. Looking at it as a sequel to Victoria 2, it disappoints in most ways. The unique economic system is gone, and the economy more closely resembles Anno. Your goal is to grow your economy using your construction sector, and your main activity is fixing the economic impacts of the last thing you did. Supply, demand, and prices change instantly. Nothing in your country happens without your input, and you have absolute control over every production building in your country. Making new buildings and changing how they operate is your primary gameplay loop, making you feel more like a middle manager than a country. While balancing production methods in every backyard moonshine-still is fun once as a small country, it devolves into tedious micromanagement quickly when playing anything larger than Liechtenstein.The only thing that happens without your input is other countries setting up trade routes, but this is mostly just infuriating. Because everything is in short supply and the AI is incompetent at growing their own economy, these trade routes mostly just steal your resources and rarely if ever sell you anything of substance. Protecting particular goods could have been an interesting gameplay mechanic, but it isn’t. You can’t stop a good from being exported. You can only embargo entire countries. So trade boils down to you trying to steal resources you’re short on, the AI doing the same, and you embargoing the AI if it starts stealing too many of yours. Devolving into isolationism becomes an appealing prospect, if only to remove the micromanagement and instability.Speaking of the AI: In typical Paradox fashion, it's terrible. As a result, singleplayer is a bland, sterile experience. You are playing in a sandbox with other kids, but the other kids are just balloons with faces drawn on them. It would be nice to believe that the AI will get better with some patches, but this is unlikely given the reputation of Paradox and Victoria 3’s game director. The AI nations in Victoria 3 are slow to grow, constantly in turmoil due to mismanagement, and regularly destroy themselves over the tiniest diplomatic disputes.Those diplomatic disputes are probably the one aspect where Victoria 3 actually has some interesting innovation. Most hostile interactions are no longer just a button, but executed through a ‘Diplomatic play’ mechanic involving all major powers with an interest in the region. Diplomatic plays are a neat concept, but they are sadly underdeveloped, and let down further by the bad AI. There is no real distinction between a small colonial engagement and major war in Europe. Both become plays potentially involving every country with an interest committing their entire army. It’s impossible to ensure a nation’s neutrality beforehand. If you plan to simply befriend the other powers, or convince them to stay out once it’s started, good luck. Friendly nations will turn on you in a heartbeat during a play, and major AI powers will join a diplomatic play for the most insane reasons. The US will fight to the death to defend Danish Holstein in exchange for an IOU. China will sacrifice millions to keep an Indonesian province out of Dutch hands because they were promised war reparations. The East India Company will happily fight a war against its overlord over some border dispute between Indian nations, before magically returning to being an obedient dominion once the war ends.This entire experience is wrapped up in a UI more hostile to the end-user than a suicide vest. Tooltips can be helpful, but the endless recursion of tooltips on your tooltips on your tooltips, ad infinitum, invokes an Escherian feeling of endlessness that makes you feel more lost than before you started. This wouldn’t be as bad if these tooltips did not contain important information that can’t be found elsewhere. The game will only tell you the most important information at a glance, such as the number of radicals in your country, but make it impossibly difficult to find out exactly who is radical and what caused it.Critics have said the game looks like a mobile game, and while this is unfair to the gameplay, the UI does lean heavily towards modern mobile-friendly UI trends. Lists and tables are frowned upon, while grid layouts are preferred whenever possible. The amount of information allowed on the screen at any one point is extremely limited, forcing you to constantly swap between windows. Multiple lists simply can’t be sorted at all, and no list ever takes up more than a third of your screen width. A full screen table with all the information you could want is anathema. Buttons are large, and the UI scaling is very high by default, unless you have a widescreen monitor, in which case it defaults to unreadably tiny. The game defaults to tree maps instead of pie charts, suggesting that the UI designer had some very strong personal convictions about design without necessarily having the understanding of visual data comprehension to back them up.I have yet to mention the political system, because it hardly matters. Unless you are trying to change a particular law that’s affecting your gameplay, like isolationism, it’s possible to forget it exists entirely. The interest groups controlling your government do nothing to stop you from changing the economy and eroding their power, so the power of interest groups is just a result of what buildings you build rather than an interesting mechanic.Ultimately, the game is an exercise in making a line go up for the sake of the line going up. Every country plays exactly the same, and there is no real payoff at the end. Warfare could theoretically provide something to work towards, but the war system is so barebones, clunky, and dysfunctional that warfare is more frustrating than fun. There is no micromanagement of units, as that system has been replaced with automatic AI fronts, but fronts split, merge, and disappear so much that the micromanagement is somehow just as annoying. Since the fighting happens automatically, wars are heavily affected by arcane mechanics behind the scene that the player can’t see or interact with, such as the number of troops that participate in a battle, or the direction a general advances. The reward for dealing with this system is often lackluster, since wargoals are decided during the diplomatic play phase and cannot be altered during the war.Victoria 3 isn’t a terrible game per say. It is simply mediocre as a game, and bad as a Victoria sequel. If it had been an early-access indie game for 30 dollars under a different name, it would have been received very well, with praise for some of its innovative ideas and its potential. As a released full-price sequel to a cult classic developed by a major studio, it is disappointing. The arguments about its potential ring hollow in the context of a studio known for selling buggy, half-baked products that had potential but failed to deliver.If you are looking for a complex economic simulator, this isn’t it. If you are looking for a game focused on diplomacy and war, this also isn’t it. If you are looking for a cute Anno-style economy game that you can play with friends so you can bicker over who ate all the tools in the market, this is actually alright, though buggy and overpriced.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't buy this game. You could consider a purchase in a couple of years.
