_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Buggy. Streotype IGs and no historic research for individual countries. Things can and should sandbox as time goes on, but things go completely off the rails within <4 years. USA shows awful application of a generic template: people are all speedruning banning slavery pre 1840 and there are no consequences when it should cause an early civil war or a crisis of some sort. Generic template means coalition governments in the usa are easy when Jackson literally pioneered the spoils system that currently defines the US political system / cabinent. Andrew Jackson can't get re-elected, gets replaced with Calhoun who Jackson actively fought against in the nullifaction crisis - it should at least be Martin Van Buren or James K Polk. Slavers arent their own IG, so many northern states join the csa if you do try force get a civil war - everyone remembers how mass and ny are even remotely plausible bastions of the csa. Diplomacy is awful - being able to surrender the primary war goal for a truce should still require the other side to accept - if I want to escalate for the whole Mexican Cession, I can't - i can take 1 "state" and then wait an entire truce to take another. Because of the horrible set up, this really means the half of texas is a truce, and the tiny southern mexcian bit of Colorado is an entire truce - i dont even get a whole state.  Europe and Ottomans isn't much better. Egypt taking istanbul, northern greece, or izmir (e.g. Thessaly or Macedonia) instead of anything contiguous. Likewise, Russia attacks ottomans and takes... adana? Instead of Kars or the balkans, it goes for some random exclave?France has a bonapartist party, but there is no way to make Napoleon III the emperor.If you don't want it railroaded, there should be optional decisions or events or flavor. EU3 and EU4 are sandboxs, and no one was crying that the pick 1 of 3 missions was railroading even if that was guidance, like the old EU3 mssion conquer novgorod as muscovy [equal to conquer Mexican cession as the USA]. Even if the mission tree in later EU4 is a bit more guidance, people LIKED that even if it was semi railroads to even ahistoric outcomes. You dont have to do the missions, but they give the ai some guidance and noobs some guidance and teach people about history. Now we have a barren journal / decisions section by comparison.CK3 suffered from sims syndrome and slow, expensive dlc, but launch ck3 was still a decent game. Not great, but decent. CK3 is going in the right direction but still needs several more real dlcs to be great, and it has been out for a long while.Vicky 3 has launched in a state several cuts below launch CK3.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Paradox games for the last 20 years, and this is probably the worst release to date (considering how great Vic1 and 2 were). I feel I'm playing a glorified mobile game on this one, just watching progress bars. That's basically it. Build this, and that to produce X.Devs really ruined this game by "innovating" in the warfare system. They underestimated an essential element of fun in Paradox games, which is to grab your armies and put them to march, embark them into an overseas mission, etc. This is not just about giving the player agency, but creating stories.Sad to say, but Vic3 is a game that, after a couple of plays, you realize there's not much to do.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 released as a buggy, unintuitive mess that had a few mechanics that were fun to play with, but overall was just not fun. Paradox is known for supporting games for years after release with free patches alongside paid dlc. Many of us knew the game would take a few years of patches and it would become a great game on the same standing as other paradox games IE, Europa Universalis 4 or Hearts of Iron 4. One year since release and it is safe to say, this game will never be more than a 6-7/10 middling experience, and to even reach the higher end of that rating, it will take many years of patches which most of us will give up waiting for. Paradox reworks entire game mechanics every major patch, and this is a big sign that the game was built on a poor base. It will take them years to slowly replace every boring mechanic. Maybe get the game on sale to mess around with some of the fun mechanics, but it isn't a good game imo.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok so, here's the thing about this game. It has some issues. But it has some goods. Don't let my hours in other PDX games fool you, I play in offline mode most of the time. I have only been using my phone's hotspot data (about 15GB / month) to download patches and other things as I need them so I could save up to start a business (started that this past Monday yay!). Anyway on to the review. Very Good:- The economic system is really good. Being where the core of the game is focused you would hope so. It does a very good job simulating a market.- The pops is a really good system. - In general the different mechanics of the game all tie into each other very well. Better than in most games. You actually have a reason to do things (everything comes down to standard of living and the market)The Very Bad:- Warfare: It's not fun. I get it's not the focus of the game, but I'm sorry PDX, this feels more like y'all wanted to make an economic sim but knew no one would buy it without war during a period that covers WW1, so you threw something in and hoped it would satiate our warmongering thirst. It didn't. If you want to go with a more hands off approach than you need to be telling me exactly what is happening and why. I should be able to determine which states belong to which HQ, so I can better allocate Battalions to Generals. And I should be able to send troops for a temporary attachment. I should also be able to assign objectives to individual Generals beyond just "attack front" I should be able to tell 1 general to push the war objectives and 1 to push to the capital. or both to push the same objectives, or whatever. If you're not going to let me micro that's fine, I don't want to micro war I have enough going on and it's one of the things I hate doing in HOI4. But for mechanic that can so thoroughly destroy a playthrough, I need some way to make a real informed decision and to have some final control over *how* the war is prosecuted.Armies just teleport to places, uniforms were so nice during this time period and we don't even get to see our armies move across the map. On a map game. Where we stare at the map. And the first game they ever put life into the map. I don't want to see every Battalion like we do division in HOI4, I'm ok with it like CK3 where it is done by army. I'm going to assume you ran out of time and this is coming in the big patch a month or two after release. But the worst part is when they just randomly teleport back to their HQ and you have no idea why. Actually, I think the worst part about war is the fact my 20 battalion army can fight a 10 battalion army and then we go fight and only 6 of my battalions showed up. That should never happen.- It's very unintuitive to find what goods pops want. - No flavor among different countries really. I understand not wanting to pigeonhole people into playing a certain way but there is functionally no difference between the nations. Put the events in game, then when I play give me a journal entry that lays out the conditions I need to meet in order to cause the event to trigger. The only real difference is a production modifier for certain resources or whatever. At least with CK3 you have a different religion and different culture. OVERALL: It does what it does good...very good. And it does what it does bad, very bad. But the bads I don't think totally ruin the game play experience and it will be a good game to add into the Paradox rotation. Will it be your primary game? I don't know, for me, I don't even know. My primary game is CK3.If you're an econ sim fan you'll love it. If you're a PDX fan once you get the hang of things I think you'll enjoy it. It has some areas to improve but no one should expect it to be like a game like Victoria 2 - for one they will have a different vision and for two that game was years of post release development. You can't do everything or the game will never comeYou will find most of the "No" folks here are still playing it

A fascinating setting and mechanical concepts to explore ideas of the statecraft of the day are let down by absolutely piss-poor execution every step of the way. _childDocuments_.review: If all of this worked as intended, it would still be a faulty game. A lot of fidgeting that feels unnecessary and entirely on the UI's fault. I would still play it, but the game needs a lot of bug fixes AND reworking. I am at frustration of seeing a lot of simplified features and saying to myself: "oh no, they gonna sell the better version of this feature as an expansion". The game's most interesting feature - the macroeconomic game - lacks any notion of stockpiling, even for strategic resources such as Weapons, Ammunition or Oil. The war is delegated to generals, who you command one by one to move their armies to a front you pick and "do their thing". I like the idea, as all other games in this genre relied heavily on you micro-managing army compositions and tiny movements of units. But it doesn't work in the current state.The devs promised a patch before Christmas, I would give this game another try in 3 months.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: I personally enjoy this game, but I cannot give it a positive review. In short this game feels incredibly unfinished and low pop multiplayer is miserable. The economy system of this game seems solid although simplistic and nearly the same for every country. It has a very similar loop that rarely differs between nations: build iron, coal, and/or wood; build tools, always more tools; find silk, opium, and sugar; build luxury items. The nation you choose has nearly no effect on how the game plays. The above economic loop is nearly universal. Location also is not nearly as important as any other grand strategy games, the loop of England, France, and US intervening in squabbles between minor or insignificant powers anywhere in the world grows old quickly. The war system......Multiplayer is what makes or breaks a game for me. I have 1000+ hours of multiplayer on HOI4 and EU4 and it has been the main drive of replayability for me, in this regard VIC3 has fallen short. Large player count multiplayer lobbies are fairly fun, but are very unstable. They are getting more stable as updates are rolled out, but in some lobbies containing players with less than perfect internet you will likely spend as much time paused or rehosting as playing the game. Smaller player lobbies in the 2-5 player counts are fairly stable, but are simply not fun. The AIs in multiplayer ruin the experience, forcing players to choose only major nations or spend the entire game barely scraping by, fending them off. And frankly there are not enough players to pick up casual games, requiring a group of dedicated players to assemble a lobby.In summary, the game is very simple, the economy is simple and fairly easy to manage, the game has little variability and low amounts of replayability, the war system is terrible, and the multiplayer is not at a state that I believe will maintain a sizable player base as related games have.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: The Multiplayer experience and stability makes this one of my favorite paradox titles alone. Great Music, Great artwork. The world becomes alive as you industrialize. Playing with the market, I guess is not everyone's cup of tea but I have a ton of fun with the game. Yes, war needs to be flushed out but its honestly nice because I spend so much time microing my industry and diplo that I prefer that I don't have to move armies around and can focus on building up my country. _childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is an exceptionally designed game and the mechanics theoretically would achieve what the game sets out to do, which is to simulate the progression of economy and society from 1836-1936 in a fun and interesting way. The execution is only half way there, though. Some stuff feels awesome all the time, like the new market system - it manages to simulate the feel of a real economy and create interesting decisions better than Victoria II ever did, even if it takes some shortcuts. Those shortcuts allow it to be fun, rather than limit it.Other stuff feels awesome only some of the time, like diplomacy and diplomatic plays. When they work, the tension created in your decisions whether to begin a diplomatic play, how much to ask for, whether or not to back down, etc. is palpable. Often, however, they don't work, and it can be unclear what happened, or the AI makes some odd or nonsensical decisions. The AI definitely needs work in a lot of systems more generally.And finally there is also some stuff that feels bad most of the time, like warfare. I don't dislike the new warfare system, as I actually think it's a real and marked improvement on its predecessor. Instead of micromanaging the war, your decision-making before the war and during diplomacy has far more of an impact. You can't use exploits in the AI - No strategy AI right now will be able to beat humans in such a complex system - to get an artificial advantage. I think it speaks to the design philosophy of the game that they were willing and able to take the decision to sideline warfare in gameplay. That said, it feels terrible because the implementation is really not great. Teleporting units, janky frontlines, unclear information and peace deals. Warfare could be a smooth system that complements the economic and political play -  which is mostly excellent - but instead it is an unstable mess that takes away from those other elements. I think there is also some room to deepen warfare, definitely by playing with generals, tactics and doctrines.In terms of visuals, the game looks pretty. I don't really mind the 3D models, but I love the 2D art which is just breathtaking and the map is also very relaxing to look at and play with. It performs alright, though the game starts to chug a little past 1900 as the complexity mounts. I am using a Ryzen 5 3600 and 1660 Ti, I expect the prior is the bottleneck here.My biggest issue, however, is the  significant and sometimes crippling lack of content. I get the idea of not railroading and giving the player more freedom, but I think there is still tons of room for more content. You could create small things that don't impact the game that much, or give people freedom to choose between multiple options. Countries like the U.S, the Ottomans and Japan have plenty of content, which should be extended to other Major Powers.Overall, I recommend the game and give it a solid 7/10. It really is fun and I love some of the foundational concepts and mechanics, but it is unpolished and suffers from blandness. I think over time this will become a 9/10, with proper dev support, and it could eventually become one of the best, if not the best, games created by Paradox.P.S- For those saying capitalism doesn't exist in the game, yes it does. There is a whole system wherein the capitalists get the profits from buildings and give to an investment pool that is used for building, the player still does the building because they represent the Spirit of the Nation, not the state. I find it more fun like this.

_childDocuments_.review: I played Victoria 3 at launch, then put it aside because I found it boring. I returned to the game during the holidays and I found that in the meantime, successive patches and rebalancing had turned it into a fun game - with plenty of rough edges and room for improvement.At its core, Victoria 3 is an economic and political simulation. Your country's political and social make-up directly influences its economic performance and vice versa. By this point in the game's development, I find the ways in which the two systems interact fun, interesting, and believable. Other systems don't work so well, with the controversial new warfare mechanics and diplomacy merely serviceable at this stage. Victoria 3 is also short on country-specific flavor. Still, game's improved a lot in the last year or so, and the company seems committed to continued development.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR; At the time of writing this I currently have 2,444.5 hours played in Europa Universalis 4 and 1,134.1 hours in Crusader Kings 2. This is in all likelihood the last Paradox game that I will ever buy, as this game's release state and the release state of CK3 have turned me off of the company in it's entirety for several reasons. In both EU4 and CK2, I learned to expect less from the release state of Paradox games than how their marketing is portraying their games, but CK3 and now V3 are so far below my already low expectations for content that I can no longer support a company that releases unfinished games.1. Neither V3 or CK3 released with any content of note that made countries play differently from one another. In V3 there are journal entries for the US and the Ottoman Empire that affect the direction that you play the country. France? Prussia? Austria? Great Britain, in a game named after Queen Victoria? Nope. You play them all the same, and the ONLY journal entry that you get in all of them is a laughably dumb journal entry where a character in your country is a serial killer that causes "widespread panic" that gives debuffs to your country that you can safely ignore until the RNG roll you have little control over decides it's time for Abraham Lincoln to be caught red-handed after killing his 20th victim. There are an unacceptably small number of events in the game in my opinion, and next to no flavor events.The developers have defended this absence of content by stating that their goal was for each nation to develop and play differently based on the differences in starting positions and did not want to "railroad" the player; however, given the fact that they as the developers can make the journal entries ignorable by making them not give penalties to nations if they are ignored or unmet this excuse rings hollow in my ears. Taking the example of CK3, and taking the plenitude of mechanical problems that need fixing in V3's current state that CK3 did not have, I expect the earliest we will see any mechanics or flavor of note to be added to V3 2 years after release at the earliest, as the DLC that did so for CK3 was released about 1.5 years after that game's release.2. There are two very glaring mechanical problems that severely affect this game in a negative way. I personally find the trade system to be acceptable if annoying in it's current iteration. But the lacking AI and war system are completely unacceptable for not only the caliber of game that V3 was marketed as, but also what I expected from Paradox given what I experienced in EU4 and CK2.The AI is nonsensically bad. In vanilla V3, you can start as any nation in the game and become the highest GDP, largest military in the game by 1870s-1880s at the LATEST. There are plenty of examples available if you search for such things, one such that I am aware of is a player starting as Laos, a landlocked unrecognized nation in southeast asia that starts with a single state, who didn't expand by a single province for the entirety of the game and became the country with the highest GDP and largest military. The AI does not exist in vanilla, and given that this game is based entirely around singleplayer vs AI, to me this makes the game not exist. This is not to mention that larger countries are willing to lose tens of millions of their citizens to attrition defending the interests of *random unrecognized nation in Africa* so that when you try to play as a smaller country to give yourself a challenge, you just get blocked by a major power like France who loses 10 million men to attrition and contracts their GDP by 40% just to stop you from making a single diplomatic play for no discernible reason. This means you have to play with a mod, Anbeeld's Revision of AI, to even have an enjoyable experience playing this game. Paradox should consider contacting Anbeeld and negotiating to pay him ~20k euro just so they can copy and paste his mod into the base game files. That is how bad Vanilla AI is.The new war system is both laughably bad in its current iteration and laughably easy to fix, and it would have been fixed by a modder in a week or less if Paradox was willing to be embarrassed by having a random, singular modder in their community fix such a core mechanic in V3 in such a short amount of time. They must have decided they weren't willing to be embarrassed though, as that is the only reason I can think of for why MAX_NUM_BATTLES_PER_FRONT = 1 isn't in the modifiable DEFINES file for the game. In vanilla V3 you can only have one battle per front, and battles take approximately the same time from beginning to finish no matter what stage of the game you are in or what version of military building production method(line infantry, skirmish infantry, etc.) you are using. This makes warfare an incredibly tedious and boring affair, particularly in the late game as one thing that Paradox did is they made it so that the more advanced military building production method you are using the less provinces you take when you win a battle. Modders currently have the ability to change the time for a battle to start, the amount of provinces you take when you win a battle, the stats of the various military productions methods, and the amount of regiments that are in the front that participate in any given battle; however, as it is currently not possible to change the maximum number of battles per front it's generally not worthwhile assigning more than 100 regiments to a front. Modders are currently hamstrung from totally fixing the warfare system and so are forced to put out band-aid mods using what they can change to make it more bearable in its current state. How bad the current warfare system is, is compounded by the nonsensical AI as the AI rarely has the capacity to upgrade their military building production methods to a better form of infantry. So in the later stages of Vanilla V3 you are generally fighting against Line Infantry from the 1830s with Tanks and Airplanes, so Paradox fixed this by making it so that if one side of a battle is using a better military production method, then the other side gets to bring more regiments into the battle. So you get to watch as your tanks and planes slowly lose morale due to base morale loss (morale loss being the only reason you lose a battle) while they slaughter tens of thousands of line infantry per week.3. The UI was marketed as being streamlined and easy to follow, but is the most clumsy UI that I have yet to experience in a Paradox game. They replaced 30+ map modes with 5 Lenses, so instead of the 2 step process of 1. Find map mode 2. Click or hover on province to see information, you now have to go through an indeterminate step process of 1. Find lense that probably, MAYBE pertains to the information you seek, 2. Click or hover on province, 3. Hover over part of description that pops up that sounds like what you're looking for, 4. Repeat 3 for each nested description until you get to what you were looking for. Some information like Population Needs/Wants are a 6 step process to find, to the point that describing that information as hidden is apt. But don't worry, there are UI mods that you can download to fix the UI!!! ....... Notice how the modding community is fixing or trying to fix all the problems the game has? I very much believe that Paradox has become incredibly lazy in their game development, all the while telling themselves that they are "focusing on the core mechanics of the game" because each of their games has such an active modding community that any problem can and probably will be fixed by the modding community. No content or flavor? Don't worry there will be content or flavor mods for people that want it. ♥♥♥♥ AI? Don't worry there will be AI mods for people that want it. This might not be an openly stated opinion in their offices, but given the release states of their 2 latest titles, I can only assume this to be the case.

_childDocuments_.review: I could see myself changing my review in the future. It's a game with a lot of potential but godamn is it terrible as is. The game is unplayable past 1890 as the lag is so bad that the max you can play on is 3 speed and even then it has the worst frame drops I have ever seen. The game also a lot of the time just randomly resets stuff for example in the economy you choose the production methods and randomly you'll notice that your economy has collapsed and it's because every decision you've made has reset itself. Not only that but sometimes mid war your armies just decide they would like to go home and it doesn't even tell you. There are so many major issues I have encountered and these are just a few of the biggest ones. The biggest major complaint I have though is the clunkiness. The game simultaneously feels like it was made in 1990 and 2020 with the menus being impossibly long and annoying to navigate especially the army menu where late game you have to manually assign 20 generals which is a hassle because they made assigning generals annoying as possible. They need to add automatic general assignment or a hoi4 esque front line system where you can just press a button instead of navigating through 50 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ menus.

_childDocuments_.review: There appears to be an in dept system on how combat results are calculated, but the game does not communicate it in any way. As a result, the combat feels completely random: a random number of soldiers enters the battle, they ignore their attack and defense values and a random side wins. (Usually it is the player, since the AI does not know how to play the game)Economic information is deliberately spread over multiple menus, making the economic part of the game feel tedious. Otherwise, the economic part of the game is fun, so hopefully this issue will be patched.For most nations, there is very little flavor  in terms of unique events or decisions, so all nation feel very similar.Any non-war diplomacy with the AI is incredibly annoying, since the AI countries never agree to anything unless you have maxed out your relations with them.I also experienced the occasional crash and the game gets significantly slower when playing past 1880.Overall, this game would have needed a couple of months of additional tweaking and balancing before its release.

_childDocuments_.review: What Paradox Interactive brings is unique compared to other games in the genre.I expect this game to get deeper and better during its life cycle and in that regard I see my first few hours in the game as an introduction to what to come. This is a really good game and deserves better than the "Mixed" review label.

_childDocuments_.review: Before anyone notices my playtime, it doesn't register because i'm still using a device running on windows 7, had to do work a work around to play this game regardless if steam could detect playtime. I've invested at least 50hrs in this game. I'm kinda rambling a lot in this review, but that is a result of my extreme disappointment. Just scroll towards the bottom to get a slightly shorter version. I found this to be a gravely disappointing experience. The biggest mistake is expecting this game to be like Vicky 2, when in reality its basically a completely different game in its own right. That wouldn't be a problem, if these game mechanics were capable of being mastered by the player. But at least in my experience, it doesn't matter what strategies you try to use, if you don't take advantage of a window of opportunity you will perpetually fall behind the rest of the great powers and never achieve splendor and thus be forced to start a new game. Achieving greatness in this game requires a acceptable level of control, of which is completely lacking in this game. Many nations in the game start out autocratic or authoritarian, and that wouldn't be a problem if there were some actual rewards to being a absolute monarchy. But there really isn't in the long run, if you don't liberalize and allowing things like, voting rights, workers rights, culture rights, etc, your nation will forever remain an backwards society that falls behind the rest of the world. Want to colonize Africa and Asia and rise to splendor? Want to ease cultural acceptance to your potential colonies?Want to more efficiently assimilate and integrate your populations to your rule?Want to create a efficient police force to maintain order?Want to grant workers rights to improve working conditions and attract more laborers to expand your economy?Want to create a better tax code that generates more revenue?Want to increase education so your country isn't some illiterate backwater incapable of producing research and advancing technologically? The answer is simply this: You need your political parties to pass laws that approve it.The only viable strategy to achieving some advantage in your country is to pass laws that make your country stronger. But all the political parties, all of which you have virtually no control over,  all have different contradicting interests that make law passing, slow, inefficient, and capable of producign revolution taht coudl destroy your nation. At least in Vicky 2 you could help expand support for the party you want in your various pops.In this game it feels like you have no control of your own government. You want to pass a law you want? Make sure you have the party that supports it in power, but changing parties affects government legitimacy which can make law passing impossible while imposing penalties to your country. And thats another thing, if your political parties are not happy, they can someitmes cause crippling penalties to your country. Ugh, i'm rambling now.Long story short,The economy in this game, feels like a overglorified excell sheet. Your country politics are abysmal, and you have no real control over what laws you can pass.Diplomacy stinks, Alliances with the AI are unreliable and countries constantly flip flop, unless its against you. And every country that is capable of bullying you, will do it, even though the AI country will not achieve anything beyond making your game a terrible experience. Warfare is mediocre, theres no strategy, its just mass produce soldiers, send them to the front, and cross your fingers. You can't colonize anywhere unless you have permission from your political parties. So yeah, this game stinks, i dont' even have the energy to go into detail of how bad this game is.I feel that i am not powerful or in control of anything in this game. I feel that the time and money invested in this game was a waste. I am very disappointed in this game. Maybe someone could make a HPM for Vicky 3 just to make the game not stink but that's unlikely. The devs could flesh out the game more in a couple years, but no one has the patience for that. To be honest, i think this game is doomed, and was doomed from the start. Lets do a quick comparison.Ck3 was successful because CK2 was successful.Instead of reinventing the wheel, paradox basically rebuilt ck2 up again into ck3 with basically the same mechanics and features  but a WHOLE lot more content and flavor making a for a genuine worthy sequel to CK2.Like i said, my mistake was assuming this hot mess of a game was going to be like Vicky 2. Instead, they built a completely new game all together and slapped Vicky 3 on the box. And that's why i think this game is doomed. Everything in this game is hard coded now. They would have to rebuild the entire game from the ground up to achieve anything and correct all the mistakes this failure caused.So yeah i think this game is just un-salvageable and have uninstalled it from my library. Extremely disappointing experience, would not recommend, please do something better with your life, or at least give Vicky 2 a try. EDIT: Every time i try to give this stupid game another shot it just blows up in my face. So forget it, i'm done trying to master the constantly changing mechanics on this game. The final straw was dealing with AI that constantly co-operate against the player despite setting the AI aggression to lenient. And additionally, not being able to put down separatist rebellions because my armies refuse to move from one hq to the next, or reach a coastline that is accessible with the navy. I was in such a good mood today until i played this. This is how bad this game is, its a poison that brings out the worst in me while wasting my time. I'd get a refund if could.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never played a game for over a hundred hours before and felt so, so, so very disappointed. I cannot, in good conscience, recommend this game to any Victoria fan that was expecting a modernized update to the previous games. This is an entirely different game, only sharing the most superficial similarities to what came before, and honestly should not even be called a grand strategy game. I'll detail why here..well, I tried, but I ran out of rEconomy- There is no simulated historical economy in this. It's simply a matter of gathering enough resources, building new buildings to gather more resources, rinse and then repeat. An example of this is the bureaucracy resource. In past Victoria games, you had to research more advanced technologies and then adapt more advanced political systems to deal with high bureaucratic strain. In Victoria 3, you literally just build government buildings, which also double as tax collecting buildings. I could go on for hours about how they've dumbed this down into what is essentially a building simulator. Have too many radical pops? Build more buildings, creating jobs for them, in turn increasing the standard of living which then decreases the radical pops (the vast majority of which will come from decreases in standard of living levels). Are your input resources too expensive? Build more mines. Are your government or military resources too expensive? Build more factories. Need more workers? Build more universities, research technology advances, then apply those advances to your factories/mines/farms and voila, you now have more workers to staff more factories/mines/farms. There is no depth to the economy as in previous games. There are no mechanics for capitalists, where depending on the political system your country had in Victoria 2, very well could have been the main driver of your economy, investing in and then building both factories, railroads, etc in your states. In this, capitalists are simply another pop that happens to have a qualification (what the game calls a specialist job). There is an "investment bar" that slowly fills with what is essentially free money, which is this games way of trying to abstract that mechanic, but it, like so incredibly much of this game, is about as deep as a shallow puddle. For that matter, your political system has very little effect on your economy, barring your governments trade policy (whether its isolationist, mercantilist, etc). Whereas in Victoria 2 you were potentially heavily confined on what you could do as a government, depending on your political systems economic policies. In this game, no matter whether you're an unrecognized tribal government on the Great Plains of America or playing as the British Empire itself, you're free to build whatever building you please, provided you have the funds and the unemployed pops/peasants to work it.Warfare- God, where to even begin? For example, they've abstracted war so much so that they've gutted what came before and what could have been. You don't "fight" wars. You build barracks buildings, then "battalions" magically appear within a few weeks at the "regional HQ" of whatever province you built the barracks buildings in, and then you order a "general" (which they laughably call a character, even though it's literally just another resource with some perks, which you can't even move out of whatever regional HQ you first recruited them to) to either advance or defend on what they call a "front" (basically a line on the map, since apparently everything is World War 1 now). They've erased a hundred years worth of advances in warfare, abstracting it down to a few arbitrary choices in what either your arms factories, munitions factories, or shipyards build, and then selecting the infantry type, artillery type, cavalry type, and "specialist troop" type on the barracks building, or what your main line ship is (man o'war, ironclad, monitor, dreadnought, or battleship), then either a frigate, a destroyer (once you've researched the tech) or a carrier (for whatever godawful reason they decided carriers are now escort ships), and then whether you have torpedo boats or submarines on the naval base selection menu. God, the naval bases. Entire flotilla's worth of ships now magically appear a week or so once you've completed a new naval base building, since Paradox apparently thought that all of those ships all worked together in one "flotilla" and not at all separately. Once you've built your ships out of thin air and recruited "battalions" into your regional HQ's, you're now ready for the challenging part. You take your "general" (nothing of the sort but that's neither here nor there) and order him to the "front" (that magical line on the map, since all warfare over this 100 year period was just like World War 1 in Paradox's eyes). You now have the supremely challenging task of ordering your "general" to either attack on said front, defend on said front, or withdraw back to their regional HQ. There are no tactical moves, no drawing forces away (except when the AI stupidly abandons a "front", sending a hundred+ battalion army to attack or defend on a useless "front"), no sense of actually fighting a war, beyond a blue bar above each sides forces count filling up, with whomever's fills up faster attacking, which then pops up a pair of crossed swords where a seemingly random number of battalions (playing as the German's, I eventually went to war with France, where even though both countries had 200 or more battalions on the Al Sace/Lorraine front only around 12 from each side fought in each "battle") then engage in hostilities, where each side has either an offense or defense factor, which then effects which way a blue bar moves across the screen, simulating who is winning and losing the "battle". Yes, they literally turned warfare in Victoria 3, sequel to Victoria 2 which is probably the most grognardy of all of Paradoxes titles, into what is essentially the equivalent of shovelware mobile game trash. There is really no denying that, no matter what the developers say. Warfare was not simply about whose economy is strongest, nor who can field the most troops, especially in this time frame. It's frankly insulting that the developers just claimed they're "happy" with where what they call warfare is at in the game. I genuinely kick myself for stupidly preordering the Grand Edition, caught up in the excitement of having a more advanced Victoria 2. It certainly got "modernized", i.e. dumbed down to literally the most basic level, but it is nowhere near what Victoria 2 was. The warfare getting gutted honestly isn't even the most disappointing thing about this game. I'll get to that.Politics- Remember that time that the United States colonized huge chunks of West Africa in the 1830's and 1840's? No? Weird, because it has happened in every game I've played where the US is controlled by the AI. I loved how in Victoria 2, every country had a unique political system that tried to simulate where that country stood on major issues at the start of the game. You had an uphill battle if you wanted to differentiate from that political system. It was doable, but you had to plan out gradual changes to your countries political system. So, basically, strategize to get to where you wanted to go. Whether that was trying to change your populations political leanings or trying to change your governments political policies, it was something you actually had to plan for, something you had to try and navigate the complex political system to achieve. Anyone getting this far into the review probably won't be surprised but you don't have to do that in Victoria 3. Instead of being split into political ideology and then further split into political party, and then further split into opinions on specific policies, every pop is grouped into a group of major interests, landowners, armed forces, trade unions, intelligentsia, the church, industrialists, and then rural folk.

_childDocuments_.review: I should preface this review by saying I'm relatively new to paradox games, and almost all of my experience in them is from CK3, which as far as I'm aware is the easiest of any of them.I'm giving Victoria 3 a negative review because I don't think you should buy it right now. It's in a bit of a rough state at the moment and I think it needs some work. My primary sticking points are the UI, lack of flavor/immersion, and the confusing war system.1. UIThe UI overall looks quite nice. Everything is readable and and pretty. But the problem with the UI is that it's rather arcane and hard to glean information from. Trying to discover why your pops are angry requires you to navigate into the population menu to individual pops, and then mousing over their personal standard of living. You can get a general overview of radicalization in by mousing over your radicals and over the new radicals number, but it still won't give you a very clear, concise method for discovering why people are angry. Similarly, trying to find out why your population is growing or shrinking is headache inducing. You have to go to individual states and navigate to their pops to discern this information, and when you're playing a large nation like the US, this becomes incredibly time consuming. There are many more things that the UI should clearly communicate to you that are either difficult or impossible to access, and the pop-ups definitely need a rework.2. Flavor/ImmersionEvery country is on the exact same course at this point, the inevitable march towards European style imperialism. The major players have a couple unique decisions and events, but honestly after trying several different campaigns, I found that I was doing the same thing every time: developing my economy before colonizing Africa. There needs to be more to set different nations apart, because right now, I feel like I've already played every nation in the game.3. WarWar is baffling. Now, I should say that I think there's potential for this system. Leaving war to your commanders across large fronts is a cool idea. But there's several issues. Fronts can only support one battle at a time, no matter how big they are. As the US, I was fighting Mexico across the west, and France had decided to support them. There were about 1000 battalions across the front, but only anywhere from 20-40 of them would fight at anyone time. It was ridiculous.Fronts will often subdivide as you take more tiles as well. The AI will fail to rearrange your generals correctly, so this often leads to the enemy making unopposed pushes back into territory you had just taken. There is no way to define your own fronts or even reassign battalions to generals, so you have to rely on the AI to manage things, and the AI is abysmal.And tying in with the UI issue, its almost impossible to tell why you're losing a battle. I had a front with 22 advantage where I outnumbered the enemy and had better generals and more offense than they had defense and I kept losing battles. I tried mousing over everything to see if I could tell why, but to no avail. Apparently, there's also some code right now that causes conscripts to massacre professional soldiers, which means no matter your tech advantage, just having a lot of conscripts is the way to go.The bones of a great game are here, but wait to pick it up until they've fixed the damn thing.

_childDocuments_.review: Line goes up, brain makes the happy chemicals, repeat. Definitely has some flaws right now as you can read from many other reviews but if you've played most Paradox games on release then you shouldn't be surprised, and the devs have so far been good at communicating that they're aware of and working on the issues. But if that's a deal breaker to you then fair enough, check back in a couple of months or so.With that said the core of the game is a lot of fun, not many strategy games that I've played have scratched that itch of being able to play entirely peaceful and just focus on building up your own nation and economy without getting overly boring or feeling like you're missing out (if you're the kind of person who's into that sort of thing at least). With some general refinement and improvements to systems like warfare I think there's something really great here. But hey I also enjoyed Imperator:Rome so really what do I know? Though I will say that this game is a lot more solid than Imperator was on release so I don't think the comparisons being made by some are really warranted.TL;DR: Very rough in many places and needs a a good amount of TLC, but the core of the game is a lot of fun. If you're unsure then wait a bit and see how the game develops, I've certainly enjoyed my time with it so far.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really wanted Vic3 to be good. Unfortunately, it's a boring, incredibly buggy game with a line-go-up gameplay loop that is the exact same every time you play. No country feels different from any other, the devs refuse to listen to the community regarding the serious problems with the clunky and unsatisfying warfare system, and DLC gets rushed out with unfun mechanics that amount to "press a button to win." The AI can't even play their game properly so it's a joke to beat without mods, made by unpaid community members, that improve the AI apparently more than the paid devs are capable of. The game was clearly released unfinished. For their part, the devs are at least in regular communication with the community (as is standard for Paradox), and they do seem to be taking feedback to heart for many of the problem areas. With the state it's in now I can't recommend it, but in 2 years it'll probably be alright. Let's hope the game isn't abandoned before then.

So building your economy is important but the AI does the most of it for you.Warfare would be fun, if the AI didn't do all of it for you and if it showed animated figures fighting rather than just fire coming out of a bunker when zoomed in. _childDocuments_.review: I cannot, in good conscience, recommend this to other people. While some people complain about the war systems or the diplomacy and praise the economy simulator, I say: it's all kind of just boring. Often I would find myself just letting the game run while I went to go get some food or to the bathroom, because I was just waiting for a new building to finish. The economy system DOES have so much potential, but construction always takes so many weeks that you are always *reacting* to your economy, rather than taking proactive moves. And with the scarcity of events, I rarely found that I had much to do as I waited years for a law to pass and months to get through my construction queue. Events trigger rarely and tend to repeat a lot. In all, it is just boring. If you love Paradox games like I do and are thinking of sinking $60CAD into this, I recommend just watching a lets-play. It cuts out all the waiting and doing-nothing and adds some personality/narrative to an otherwise bland game.

_childDocuments_.review: The map is gorgeous, the music is great, and it has steam workshop integration, but gameplay-wise it's a downgrade from Vic2 in almost every way. Heck, even some HOI4 mods are doing more interesting things with economics systems currently.  And boy is this game a performance hog.As a modern Paradox game, of course we know it's going to be a dlc cash cow platform where the playerbase is milked for years to improve the base game. A few years and +$100 of dlc will probably make it a better game than Vic2.  Do you really want to spend all that time and money though?  I'd just get Vic2 on sale with its expansions (currently $20 total rn) and install HPM or another vanilla-enhanced mod. _childDocuments_.review: Like with almost every Paradox game, release is a bit of a mess.CTDs in the late game are commonplace (at least for me), but they might be connected to the autosave for the most part (since reloading basically puts me where it crashed).Balancing in general is an issue at this point. Endgame, the AI is just locked in constant revolutions, while you as a player have a very easy time keeping the internal peace. And if you keep an eye on your economy over the whole game, you can easily steamroll everyone else.Warfare is actually quite fun in theory, but has a lot of issues they still need to iron out. From weird automated behavior (especially when switching frontlines) to the way it presents vital information. (or hides it)UI/UX is its biggest weak point atm. I wouldn't say its far from great, but navigation between menus needs some TLC. Lots of information is hidden in menus 2-3 levels deep, and thats fine IMO, but finding the number you're looking for and actually being able to influence it are often are 2 completely different menu flows, you at best have the most basic sorting/filtering options and no custom tables in general. Context menus on pop-ups might also be worth experimenting with more.Doesn't help that you can absolutely lose yourself in micromanaging the economy, which makes this even more of an issue. (and makes little sense in most economic systems in the game) And finally, the nations need more unique content. I know Paradox has hired more narrative designers for Vicky3, so I'm expecting a lot more to come in terms of events, which is great. Nonetheless, this is an amazing first step for a new and very unique grand strategy game. I love watching my nation develop over a longer period of time, seeing cities grow, political changes take place and numbers go up. It seems like a very solid skeleton to build upon for the next couple of years. But yeah, maybe Paradox should start releasing their games as Early Access for the first year

_childDocuments_.review: To qualify my review, I've put around 30 hours into Victoria 2, over 1000 hours into eu4, and probably around 400 hours into the Crusader Kings games. I'd like to think of myself as well versed in PDX strategy games, and historical sims in general.with what said.Victoria 3 is a 4/10 at best, It feels like Eu4 Lite at the current point.Economics In Vic2, different economic systems were modelled and you had to play around them, dealing with the various levels of direct or indirect control you would have over your economy. In Victoria 3, you have a command economy. You need a factory? you build a factory.it honestly feels like a downgrade in terms of economic simulation, and the overall experience is worse for the lack of variety between political systems. Warfarein Vic2, you directly controlled your units, which was ahistorical, but allowed for warfare to actually be interesting.in Victoria 3, you click on an army, click on a front, and ignore it because you'll either win cause you're bigger, or get crushed because you're smaller. Compared to every other PDX strategy game, Victoria 3 is worse due to it just being incredibly shallow. You can't even watch battles unfold, its just two army camps shooting bullets at a front. Instead of seeing a little set of Napoleonic era block formations fighting or watching trenches be dug. Which makes the warfare, not only boring to play, but boring to watch,Diplomacythis is the only area I believe that Victoria 3 has improved over Vic2,  but even that is up to debate as the move from Spheres of influence to markets is seemingly a little controversial. Overall, if you want to buy this? I cannot suggest buying it until PDX has added more content to make the game worth playing or at least overhauled some of the issues there are.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's address the elephant in the room: this is VIC3, to VIC2.Is VIC3 perfect? Certainly not. But I find the game, overall, enjoyable.I have mix feelings about the war system, no shock there. Not necessarily because of the direction (close to no control); but more because when I loose, I do not understand why (and more or less the same when I win, but that's less frustrating...)My main critic is about the Trade system, which is lacking. It is either too restrictive in early game or becomes insignificant later on since trading for 10 units of something at a time has no impact whatsoever on a market dealing in thousands of units...Now that the bad is dealt with;I have a lot of fun and can be lost for hours trying to min-max my economy and see the result. Playing tall feel as rewarding as playing wide for the first time (a revamp of the trading will be necessary for it to be truly as viable thought).This is not your average paradox game. It is not as complex as it seems: it simply is not the same feeling as the other where everything lead to warfare. You can make it so if you wish; if so, then you will be displeased as the war system is but an extension of diplomacy; which serves toward your development. That's the real end-goal.Have fun and take the game as it is.

_childDocuments_.review: I've put in about 60 hours on Vic 3 as i'm writing this review.I've played the other pdx games and have put in 100+ hours on all but vic 2. Although I do have Vic 2, I specifically held off on playing it as I wanted to experience this one fresh.I love Vic 3. Coming from the perspective of someone who loves economy/production type games in general, I think Vic 3 is amazing.It combines their usual historical grand strategy simulator style game with pop & production management that is similar but also very different to games like anno. The economy and production simulation in Vic 3 is the best that I have seen in this type of game.The economy has A LOT of moving parts and resources. You want to build some ships, weapons or industry well you need resources first, either by producing yourself, trading or both. You may need to research the proper tech first which might require more educated workers which will require more schools. These all have side effects on things like population standard of living, nation relations, Rebel/Loyal pops and more.The economy is the foundation here, but there is so much depth in the other aspects of the game such as war, colonization, diplomacy, politics and more. Your economy is the engine that powers all of this and the game puts you in control of your economy. You can even use laws and decrees to further push your economy to match your vision. To pass these laws you need to balance your political parties appropriately. You want a free trade economy? Well you want to make sure the industrialist faction is gaining power so you can pass a law like that with ease. But watch our for the trade unions faction, they won't like that one bit.I think Vic 3 is going to be phenemonal for players that are new to the series. I understand seasoned players want to see some more in depth elements from other pdx titles, like more in depth war mechanics that is seen in HOI4. That would be cool too. Looking forward the next updates. For now, back to expanding my market across the globe!

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I've played Victoria 2 for well over 500 hours, and the sequel fails to have any of the charm of the original. Do not recommend at the moment, although it's certainly getting expansions in the future that'll make it better.After playing two full campaigns as GB and Japan (and a smattering of abandoned runs) in Victoria 3, I've come out of it with very mixed impressions about the game in general. The core gameplay is decently fun, in the model of Victoria 2: build factories, industrialise your nation, and generally watch the GDP line go up. The political system with interest groups (essentially different factions in government) is interesting, and the different goods represented in the game are a welcome change. However, the main issue I have with the game is the lack of replayability and lack of player action in the running of the nation. In Victoria 2, after the initial setup, there were a few things you generally did in every campaign: set your budgets, research tech, declare wars, do your sphere of influence, build/expand factories, and set your national foci. In Victoria 3 you do much of the same, except the satisfaction of doing so is completely gone: sliders for budget are removed, replaced with static tax levels, the varied techs of V2 are slimmed down, spheres and national focuses are gone, and (most importantly) building/expanding buildings has no immediate effect that you can look at and get feedback from. Oftentimes I found myself just spamming factories for goods that were expensive, but the UI didn't really give me any data on how that was impacting the price of the good. Another issue that's mainly QoL is that every time you research a new production method in Victoria 3, as well, you have to do a billion annoying and monotonous clicks to switch the method in every single one of your buildings, and this happens way too often: for instance, when I research fertilisers, I have to manually go into every single type of farm (rye, wheat, rice, etc) and do two clicks: one to select the production method, and one to select the new one. This may sound like a meaningless gripe, but the amount of things that you have to click for no reason in this game is way too large. The law system sounds interesting, and is interesting, but the different laws aren't really different enough to drive me to debate whether one is better than the other. This is an issue that Victoria 2 had as well, where laws are just progressively better, but considering how this is a sequel and much was made of the political aspect of the game, I expected something more nuanced. The way that you enact laws is absolutely awful as well, it's an RNG system reminiscent of Europa Universalis sieges, with ticks taking forever and it being a simple dice roll if something gets passed or not. I tried to pass a law for wage subsidies for like a decade and a half with a 25% chance just because I got bad luck, and I could do very little about it except shrug and try again. There's basically no flavour differences between nations as well. Japan actually has a lot of different events and such (using the Journal system, of which my thoughts are generally positive), but really, every country feels the same when you get down to actually playing the core loop of the game. When I played as the UK, there was basically nothing I could do that really showed how preeminent I was as a power. The events are all generic and shared across every nation, and aside from "Confederating Canada/Australia", the journal entries were the exact same as any other nations I played. Nothing interesting about it.And to keep it brief, the war system is an absolute unmitigated disaster. Each front can only have *one* battle at a time, making long fronts such as in China or the USA absolute slogs. The general system is intuitive but annoying, requiring lots of boring clicks every time you declare a war to throw them into battle. The amount of troops set to a front has basically no bearing on how many troops actually go into the battle: I had 2 million soldiers fighting in Russia against a similar amount of Russo-French soldiers, and every single battle that happens only has 8k or so engaged, with the front moving a miniscule amount every time I win or lose. In that war, I had 1.5 million dead and wounded, where 50,000 were from battles and the rest were all attrition due to the ridiculous lack of battles (especially big ones). This is absolutely outrageous: I know disease, starvation, etc were massive killers in the 18th and 19th centuries, but that proportion is just wrong.All in all, I did enjoy the game for the little time I played it. Was it worth the price? In my opinion, absolutely not, and I don't see myself playing it for more than 50 hours or so until there's a big change in the game. The fact Paradox will surely make me pay £30 per DLC or more pushes me even further away from trying it out in future updates, especially since I'm certain it'll be 3 or 4 DLCs until the game is better, and many of the new features will probably just be random mechanics taped onto a base game that just isn't that good (cf. CK3 Royal Court).Save your money and buy Victoria 2 with all expansions. The game is janky, buggy, unintuitive, but it's something that Victoria 3 is not: consistent fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: - In-depth economy building. (And the game description does not lie, this is what you will be doing mostly) - Interesting diplomatic mechanics (I would say the best among Paradox games) - Incredible and innovative graphics (for a strategy game) - The sound design is good too, but I am missing the Sabaton songs.Cons: - AI builds like ♥♥♥♥. No oil, no silk, no opium, no rubber, even when the demand is insane. Naturally this means you can not trade for them. You will have to conquer territories that have these resources no matter which country you play as. (Yup, better learn to fly with Luxemburg) Have fun with the naval invasions, they are a treat. - Bugs, there are so many I am opening a separate section for them. - There are naval battles. I think. Sometimes I see my ships with low morale when I check them. - Very lame warfare system. You create an army, equip it however you want/can, assign it to a frontline and that is it. Even if the frontline is the size of the Canadian-USA border at maximum there will be 1 battle happening. Even if one side outnumbers the other 50-1. The only difference you can achieve with a vastly larger army is that you will get most of the initiatives (which decides who attacks a territory and who defends it). Naturally the better equipped batallions usually win, because YOU CAN NOT CONTROL how many units you have in a battle. This makes games with Russia plain stupid. You will never have superior technology, your numbers mean nothing, and you can not even smash units in a battle, because it gets decided relatively randomly (I did not figure out how the game decides how much of your army will participate in a battle. Yet.) - As every Paradox game at the last third of the game, it is awfully laggy. In solo games too, where usually there is only 1 nation (yours) that gets massively ahead. In multiplayer it is a menace. I doubt anyone attempts to play it after 1890 in MP. (I believe I have a fairly good setup, considering games like Alyx, New world, etc. have absolutely no issues) Bugs: - Mobilizing with the "Mobilize all" button if you have over 300 units crashes the game. - Lategame build spamming crashes the game (unless you do it on 3/5 speed, I guess this has some connection to the speed issues) - And the most infuriating one, is the fact that it is impossible to naval invade anything. Why? Because if you manage to land your poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ units, THEY DECIDE TO TELEPORT HOME.     In more depth:     1. Set up naval invasion, travel time takes X days.     2. Arrive at destination, a battle breaks out, hoping for victory.     3. Won battle, secured a sweet landing, territory flipped to me.     4. Hold on, where the ♥♥♥♥ is my army?     5. THE MOMENT THEY LANDED, THEY TELEPORTED HOME BACK TO HQ.     6. Get annoyed, select the army and send it to the frontline since the territory is still flipped.     7. Travel time takes X days.     8. They start reconquering their territories, since nothing is there to stop them.     9. They reconquered all of them, order stops, try again.     And this happens 10/10 times. I do not understand how this got through playtesting.  - Expect some random crash every hour.Conclusion:If you like strategy games this is a must have. It only has bug and warfare issues, and since this is an economy simulator the latter can be forgiven. The bugs will probably be fixed in a few months. As for the warfare... This is Paradox, they will probably launch a few DLCs which will cost as much as the base game and those will make it liveable.8/10 without naval invasions. suicide attempt/10 with naval invasion.

_childDocuments_.review: I am going to recommend, tentatively, you keep an eye on this game. For sales, for updates, for its potential. If you buy and play, do so with the understanding this is a work in progress that, in Paradox style, WILL change for the better so long as people invest a little now and then. That said, I am not that patient of a patron, and I think this title has a long way to go before I invest any further.The good:- Looks great, sounds great, smells great. It does slow down quite a bit on some UIs and as the game nears the end, but that is the nature of a complex simulation.- The business-based economic model is sensible and intuitive. I have seen some people complain that this isn't the case, but they are likely missing understanding of how these businesses chain together; you should not, for example, change all buildings over to a production method that your supply cannot support, or demand does not need.- The political revolution is also modeled fairly intuitively, with several factions having different values and opposing agendas. Stagnation can be just as radicalizing as passing unpopular reform, and it is a clever puzzle to advance while avoiding civil war.The bad:- The tutorial explains some mechanics well, but it is cluttered with "journal entry" goals like "Central Archives" that will ruin your nation if you pursue them when prompted.- Most UIs are frustratingly linear and clunky, with either too many nested button presses or hundred-item lists, that make it slow to get anything done. Diplomatic mapmode, for example, should be better searchable by likelihood of acceptance, opinion, etc.- The diplomatic play mechanics seem too obscure. There should be an extra phase, or clarity on an existing early phase, that you can see who would support your play before either side has to lose something to "back down".- It is annoying to be notified that I have a goods shortage when my AI subjects change production to something nobody can produce. Straight up, they shouldn't be allowed to adopt a production method that is not supported by the market, and it would probably save on processing needs.- The combat system is either very buggy or completely decoupled from the graphical representation. I find myself stuck in wars where the AI wants white peace but can't accept, having one weird shared frontline straddle both sides of the Black Sea so my units bounce around, having too many tiny frontlines, having troops instantly teleport to HQ without explaining why. And again, I am pressing way too many buttons to move troops and generals around. I would recommend they clarify and simplify how combat is supposed to be, then add the visual complexity overtop.

_childDocuments_.review: Having reached 40+ hours in the game, I feel like I have a greater grasp of the game - and my opinion is still that I really enjoy it. I appreciate Vicky 3 for being a socio-economic sandbox in a sea of military sandbox games. I think that there's a lot of things that this game does better than Vicky 2, even ignoring obvious things like the graphics - but there are still things which this game can improve on.The thing which I will grant the nay-sayers is that the military system needs work. That said, I think it is a very good foundation. Ultimately, I think that making warfare into a system entirely dependent (and secondary) to the socio-economic game only strengthens the rest of the game. They managed to avoid the pitfall that so many similar economic games fall into, where adding a military system into the game ends up undercutting the intended "main" mechanics of the game. There is a legitimate concern that the player can render everything else meaningless simply by gaming the AI in warfare. You can say what you like about the system - but this is undeniably a solution to that problem. The only thing I would ask is for is for them to add more ways to interact with the military system through pops and the economy - maybe adding an officer corps or whatnot.Overall, I enjoy the game a lot - and I think it's well worth the money. If what you want is a deep victorian military simulator, then this is not it - but if what you want is a political, social, and economic sandbox - this may very well be it.

_childDocuments_.review: Half-decent, but half-baked.Politics are surface level and easily exploitable; interest groups are stagnant and don't evolve over time to meet changing circumstances and social movements. Laws can be enacted far too quickly (Slavery Banned ---> Multicultural US in the 1830s, or multicultural Germany by 1845 are both possible!). Interest groups, in general, rarely present a credible threat to enacting your agenda, and can easily be appeased by enacting laws in a certain order. Using the Suppress or Bolster authority actions often isn't even needed to marginalize a group completely. There's few downsides to heavily supporting/favoring groups like the Intelligentisa and Industrialists, and powerful bonuses are given for doing so. Lack of historical flavor. Several pivotal historical moments are absent, including the Mexican-American war, revolutions of 1848, etc. Failure to balance 'lack of railroading' with 'including actual historical content' by Paradox.Warfare is atrocious. Popups on the map during war are loud and noisy. Generals teleport around fronts arbitrarily, and fronts themselves appear and disappear for mysterious reasons. Wars involve huge amounts of RNG. Attrition numbers are monstrous; expect to lose literally tens of thousands of men in minor wars with few casualties in battle unless you have extremely advanced hospitals. A HOI4-like system with front management and commands that can be given at a high level would make sense. Current system is not engaging, lacks meaningful opportunities for player input and skill expression, and is a major part of the game anyway despite being so poorly implemented. Diplomatic behavior by the AI is strange and comes off as arbitrary (German minors viewing a 0 infamy Prussia with 'caution' at high relations, and refusing to defensive pact them - Which would alleviate the problem of 'this country may attack me'). Diplomatic plays and maneuvers are interesting in theory, but irritating in implementation. The ability to 'back down' as the defender and obtain a 5-year truce in return for giving up a single province, in a game that lasts only 100 years, is a serious problem. There's no way as an attacker to truly force a war against somebody. As an example in this system, Mexico could just give the United States a single province for every single diplomatic play demand, delaying America's conquest of the west despite being economically and militarily inferior by 40+ years simply utilizing the truce timer. Multiplayer becomes exponentially unstable with high numbers of players.Trade is tedious and micro-heavy. There are no stockpiles.Generic events are, for the most part, flavorful and well-made. There are some events which are far too punishing (For example, an event in Africa that gives tons of infamy).Infamy penalties do nothing to address or punish puppet spam.Economic management is probably one of the game's strong points, but fails to introduce compelling gameplay for different types of societies; the answer is always 'industrialize as fast as possible with tons of construction', maybe after fixing your country's intrinsic issues (Such as Austria or Qing's poor tax capacity). Tooltips and information given are inaccurate and do not properly account for all inputs and externalities. Buildings that the game insists will be 'unprofitable' if built are often some of the most profitable. Pops are overly detailed, such that migration and changing of culture late-game will cause crashes and extreme lag on many machines. The requirement to simulate the political and economic behavior of Catholic Mongolian English-Speaking Pops who work as a laborer in factories in New York does not add any particular value to the experience, but does result in catastrophic performance problems. While pop simulation is necessary, there needs to be a more pragmatic solution here. The AI has literally no clue what it is doing, and will absolutely fail to use its country to the fullest potential. France and even Austria involved themselves in a war to defend Mexico for no apparent gain. The AI will not structure its economy well, exploit goods with high market demand, etc. Puppets and Dominions are often a bad idea because the player cannot invest in them. Failures of AI makes peaceful playstyles less possible due to critical shortages of goods, forcing the player to conquer in order to fuel their economy instead of just trading. This causes engagement with the war system, which is currently horrible - See above. Tech tree feels a little short. Deceptively small due to knowledge spread.Minimum wage is straight up a trap and will destroy even the most developed of economies, leading to economic stagnation and mass unemployment. Game presents itself as a society simulator and for the most part does this well, but liberalizing is usually the right call for your society, but paradoxically removes a crucial gameplay tool you have to direct your nation (Authority), meaning less engagement and more automation. There's ultimately little incentive or disincentive to liberalizing as quick as possible; choosing to remain conservative will absolutely destroy your country in the long-run, and while this is accurate, the game doesn't do enough to force you to stay on these non-ideal systems. It's always a LARP-decision moreso than something that is mechanically enforced. That is to say - Choosing to stay agrarian is moreso a deliberate choice you'd make, rather than something the game tries to constrain you to due to the limitations of your country and the demographics within. Art direction and music are delightful, echoing the spirit of the era with beautiful illustrations and engaging tunes. Sound design in events is great, painting a picture with audio. The art direction and music are easily the best part of Victoria 3. Overall, Victoria 3 is a 6/10, perhaps a 5. Paradox has created a surface-level game that is somewhat engaging in what it does correctly, and absolutely horrible in what it doesn't. While the game is fun, the depth and system competency required to engage me over a long period of time just isn't present. Perfect title for people that just want to do quirky things with their country, like turning the USA into a monarchy by 1844 or something, but not a good title for strategically minded gamers who are looking for a challenge and engaging gameplay. Cannot recommend for people like me in good faith.
