_childDocuments_.review: I cant recommend this game. I have played like 2k hours on Vic2, 4k hours in EU4 and a few hundred in CK2 and HoI4 so I am by no means new to Paradox games and do enjoy myself a learning curve and intricate systems. The only thing this game has going for it its economic system whichas micromanagy as it is can be hella fun. Everything else more or less sucks. The Army and warfare system is, as has been pointed out since release, utter dogsch*t. The frontlines system just doesnt work. New frontlines just split off and ruin your war because suddenly you need an extra army in Africa because a 1 strength army can just exploit a new and undefended frontline while your 30 stack is compeltely occupied fighting 5 enemies on a somehow different front. Also, what exactly decides how many of your troops assigned to a frontline will engage in combat is compeltely unknown. It just sometimes happens that despite you having more troops on a frontline than the enemy the enemy gets to use all their troops in a battle and you only get a 1/4 of yours. If I am fighting a war in China and one of my armies "finishes" their frontline or is unassigned from a frontline, why exactly do they automatically travel back to Europe for 6 weeks where you have to assign them to a new frontline in China where they have to travel to for another 6 weeks from Europe? Apart from all that its just boring af. All you do is assign an army to a frontline and press "attack" or "defend" and the computer does the rest. I get it, warfare is not supposed to be the main event in this game BUT as its still part of it it should still be a fun experience and not just an endless rolercoaster of boredom and frustration. The 1.5 update has arguably made it a little better but you cant polish a turd. Enough has been said and critisized about the warfare system by plenty of people so I wont delve deeper. However, why not just keep the warfare system of armies as stacks of individual troops that can be moved around on provonces like in Vicky 2, EU4, CK 1,2,3 or virtually any other real time strategy game. How has nobody realised this during playtesting? Paradox has literally taken a wheel and said to themselves "We need to be more creative and innovative, lets invent a wheel with 4 corners, thats gonna be the next big thing"Next off, the politicial system. Unlike the utterly infuriating warfare and combat system there are actually interesting and good innovations here. Simulating a 19th century socio-political system with factions and lawns and so on is difficult and they have at least put a lot of thought into it. However who decided to then make all the passing of laws (ie the most important aspect of the whole political system from the players perspective) entirely RNG based eludes me. I am sitting here playing Morrocco trying to pass a law for the 5th time because RNGesus said no everytime i tried to pass this in the last 10 years (the whole campaign lasts 100 years btw), I finally get it to the last stage before adoption and wham, negative event -15% success chance, next event, -15%, next event +5%, next event -15% aaand its dead. I can try again in another 2 years  and I am ready to throw my PC out of the window. Especially because passing certain military, social and economic laws is VITAL for your campaign. If RNG says f*ck you often enough then you may aswell restart your campaign. First of all, how is it engaging gameplay to just constantly wait for a diceroll on which you have virtually no influence? Secondly, real world legislative decisions are not actually decided by diceroll (as surprising as this may seem) but are actually the result of negotiations and compromises between political actors. It just doesnt make sense that a law that has cleared the first 2 stages of assent and has a 60% chance of success gets 3 negative events in a row and is done for. There should be way more opportunity for the player to get involved through decisions and events. Maybe the player has to compromise too and give up something in order for the law to pass or he can proactively try to approach actors and try to "grease the wheels" a bit so to speak. But in the current system the player is relegated to sitting in the passenger seat and to occasioanlly clicking an event that gives you 0-3 options on how to handle the diceroll result. Here an example of the my latest (5th) attempt to pass Proffessional Army as Morrocco: Base chance 29%, +15%, -5%, -15%, +10%, -10%, +5%, -15%, -10% aand its done for, again. Can you get an appreciation of how frustrating this can be? At some point I just started tabbing out and waching youtube (with occasionall tab ins to click the 2 or so events I got in an in game year) because my building queue would basically manage itself and despite almost 2 years of ingame time the law that i tried to pass had moved from 29% base chance to 24% base chance. These are the moments where I wish this game wasnt capped at 5-speed but had a 10-speed option.The diplomacy in this game feels weirdly "absent". You are not really engaging with any other countries unless there is a crisis or you want something from them. The diplomatic options are quite limited and while the real 19th century diplomacy was generally characterized by highly complex alliance structures that would frequently change and the pursuit of the "balance of power" this just feels like all the countries would just do their own thing independent from each other. Diplomacy just feels sort of empty or flavourless.All in all I feel like the game devs took this idea of Victoria being the economy simulator too far and neglected everything else about this game. As much fun as micromangaing your economy can be, you just mostly find yourself checking the market what is needed and building those resources/industries in your state. The warfare system is tragic and the best thing Paradox could do is to just compeltely trash the frontline system and patch in a modified and improved version of the EU4 combat system. Politics is interesting but passing laws is a frustrating RNG fiesta and apart from the economy managment and "building up your nation" everything else has a tendency to be really boring and/or frustrating which sort of defeats the point of "what am I building my nation up for"?I was so hyped for Vicky 3 since I loved Vicky 2 and all I wanted was an upgraded, updated and better looking Vicky 2. I waited over 10 years for this and I am seroiously disappointed. Paradox, you seriously dropped the ball on this. And based on the relative lack of enthusiasm, interest, news and general engagement even from within the paradox community let alone the wider gaming world I suspect other people are similarilly disappointed. I hope you are learning your lesson here and when there is an EU5 (so god will) you can manage to deliver what people want instead of reinventing the wheel (terribly). Or as Einstein said: "Genius is making complex ideas simple, not making simple things complex".

The historical accuracy is nothing short of astounding, and the level of research that must have gone into recreating this era is truly commendable.The depth of gameplay mechanics in Victoria 3 is where it truly shines. The intricate political system allows for nuanced decision-making, and the diplomacy options add a layer of realism that is both challenging and rewarding. Managing the economy is a delicate balancing act, requiring strategic planning and foresight. The attention to the economic intricacies of the time period is evident, making every financial decision a crucial aspect of your nation's success.Warfare in Victoria 3 is a strategic masterpiece. The revamped military system introduces a level of tactical depth that strategy enthusiasts will relish. From mobilizing troops to managing supply lines, every aspect of warfare is a thoughtful process. The addition of the army composition and the importance of technology in military advancements add layers of complexity that keep the gameplay engaging and dynamic.The user interface in Victoria 3 deserves special mention. _childDocuments_.review: So far, this game is terribly flawed. Other people who are smarter than me have pointed them out better than I could, like the war system, the AI etc. etc.But what I find myself longing for, is the incredible realism Vic2 had. Sure some things were limited to make the game playable, but most of it is really realistic. If you wanted to expand a factory you either used the resources you had on hand or bought it from the market, if you wanted to defund your military in order to enhance your nation, you could do that, if you wanted to build buildings slower (but not less in numbers), you could do that, if you wanted to make the rich richer so that they can build your economy with you, you could do that. If you understand what I mean, it's that Vic3 has none of those aspects. Instead of realistic ways you can shape your nation, you have tiers for your taxes, tiers for your military and tiers for your building. Instead of it being your money and your funding how quickly you build up your economy, it's a number that goes up by building things, a limit instead of a slider. If you see, that you cannot afford all of those buildings to be finished so quickly, be it oyur taxes are already maxed out or your naton is too unstable, you can either pause it completely, or reduce the funding, where your buildings will take longer to complete and you can only build less buildings. This of course is not everything I dislike about the game, but it is what nags me the most. Overall this game will suffer the fate as other Paradox titles do, we will wait for a few months, get a DLC that improves something and then we wait for another. We repeat this until we've spent over 200 bucks on a singular game, just to make it playable, only because Paradox has a monopoly on grand strategy map games.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll change this review if my impressions change, but it's not looking too hot.The command the player has over the economy makes the game feel more like a city builder or playing EU4 tall as opposed to wrestling with a global economy, the warfare system has severe issues, and the diplomatic AI is bipolar, but my biggest problem that is being brought up less, and is probably never going to change, is the UI.I honestly want to know what kind of heavy doobies the UI team was smoking when they designed this abomination of an interface. There is no excuse for Victoria 2, a game which is mocked by outsiders for being an unreadable pie chart simulator, to have a more readable interface and legible map, with more crucial information close at hand. It takes the worst tendencies of CK3's UI (large buttons, lists that don't scale well), and adds new issues of its own (aesthetics are strongly favored over functionality, summaries of important information are not compact, the lens modes honestly feel like they shouldn't exist, no really for god's sake, why do we need lens modes).I'm once again finding myself rolling my eyes at the gRapHIcal iMpRoveMenTs. I don't play games in this series (or catalog, for that matter), for the visuals. I don't care that you perfectly animated a horse drawing a buggy, or that the pops have cute little 3D models that look much worse than stylized 2D art would likely look, or about water reflections or high resolution mountains. This obsession with visual polish bleeds over into the UI, which is so heavily stylized in places as to be painful to look at for extended periods. The veneer of *style* does little to hide the fact that most panels look like a choleric coal miner projectile vomited buttons of various sizes all over the screen. Commands that are in the same subject area and should be close together instead too often require you to go back and forth between the relevant lens mode and another summary panel to get feedback on changes. On large countries you'll be doing this A LOT with trade in particular. The whole thing just feels slick and fake, a lot of the art for buildings reminds me of a mobile game, and the game is stuttering quite a bit for me on a 2080ti, so I'm sure it's not brilliant for people on worse setups. The "feel" just isn't there. Victoria 2, which this game will be obsessively compared to until the end of time, feels chunky and utilitarian. When you get to grips with it, though, everything is a few clicks away, often in a small window. In Victoria 3, some menus unnecessarily take up the entire screen (the tech tree and laws are the biggest offenders here), while in other cases, like the trade routes map mode, you have to scroll through fifty different goods in a tiny panel crammed at the bottom of the screen. Information screens often feature text with five to six different combinations of colors, underlining, font size, and gradients, which is not only hard to parse, but fittingly evokes a circus clown motif.Maybe I just need more time with this interface or something. Maybe I'll get to that point where everything feels close at hand in V3. I am going to give it a fair chance. My first impression now that I have my hands on it, though, is that I hate it. And before someone tells me that I'm a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ idiot and that the UI progress was in Dev Diary #263 or something, just know that I don't actually give a ♥♥♥♥! I don't follow dev diaries! I simply don't have the time. If they don't want people to complain, maybe they shouldn't make it suck so bad!EDIT: I'd also like to add that the art for buildings and trade goods is some of the shoddiest art I've ever seen in a PDX game. They all have garish colors, are not easy to read at a glance, and generally look like they were pulled straight out of a mobile game (complete with rounded edges and drop shadows). Some of them, like furniture factories, look like Dali paintings. On the other hand, many icons are way too small and lack sufficient detail. Good luck recognizing general traits at a glance! You can't convince me that the art for trench rat trait isn't a shield with Gorbachev's birthmark on it. Compare this to V2, which had simple, consistent pixel art. The technical and financial limitations placed on development actually contributed to a more cohesive and readable end product.

_childDocuments_.review: After hundreds of hours playing Crusader Kings, Europa Universalis, Stellaris and Hearts of Iron, this is the first Paradox grand strategy game that really disappoints me. The base game feels unfinished and unpolished, with one of the worst user interface I've ever seen. It's cramped, unwieldy, and counter-intuitive. I constantly feel more like I'm fighting the interface rather than using it. Overwhelming notifications, badly designed menus, uncomplete tooltips... A total downgrade from previous Paradox games. The economic gameplay, based on intense micromanagement of your nation, is not uninteresting, but it quickly becomes a chore when playing a larger nation. The political gameplay requires the player to spend a lot of time in the aforementioned menus, which doesn't make for a pleasant experience. The warfare gameplay is frustrating because the player only has indirect control.And the game lacks flavour, it lacks soul. It lacks something to make it more than a game about watching your GDP grow. Perhaps this soul can be found in the additional content, but I'm not prepared to add a 30 € DLC to this full price game to see what the experience envisioned by Paradox was supposed to be.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3: Faustian Bargains.I have a rule with games, especially ones locked under the divine tutelage of Paradox Interactive. "Give it half a year and then bite". Nothing personal to popular games, I've just learned after the last decade of bad initial releases. Half a year gives a game time to burn through the initial shilling, fix some of the issues and ideally be in a functional state. Vic 3 was the same thing. I saw it on release, saw the videos on it and was hesitant, and so I decided to bide my time. Wait for it to go as cheap as possible and then see how it operates. Got lucky and managed to get it for a whole 15 bucks and man.I hate how I like it and I hate the issues WITH it as well.Victoria 3's root problem is the fact it's a perfect sequel on paper. This game knows the root issues that made people love and hate Victoria 2. Everyone loved industry and the economy system, while hating warfare and the AI. So it made overall improvements to everything and is now rife with what I will only describe as "Paradox Bargaining" as a result. Every single marked part of this game is an improvement on the original, and to an extent that it ends up neutering the game in some aspects. Your economy management is now upgraded with the ability to micro each industry's upgrades, and the improved tech system that allows you to just pre-plan out what tech you research is SO nice. It beats the constant red light/green light of Vic 2 or HoI's tech system, and it means no more searching for each port you need to upgrade. You have one menu. It's then kneecapped by the market system, which keeps certain nations tied to their own markets. On one hand, no more flooding the markets and causing an international stock market crash, but you also will now have to deal with the fact you can't really economically cause problems. The Army system makes sense on paper, no more accidentally nuking your economy with 934 dragoons nor having to micro every soldier. You have a front lines mechanic and the ability to just set a point and watch your men commit crimes against humanity prior to the Geneva Convention existing. Which is fine. The issue is the barracks system, tying individual armies to barracks you have to build. Sure it means you have to make sure you can afford an army, but it doesn't stop the AI from farting out 9 gorillion conscripts suddenly. Let alone the random modifiers that make naval invasions a gamble half of the time. Speaking of which.I whinged about Victoria 2's AI, calling it a trigger happy monster that didn't know how to manage itself while also barreling across the map causing problems. Clearly they knew that as well, but they overcooked it. Vic 3's AI is a dumbed down menace to fun, somehow barely managing their nations and yet still at the last second clinching any power play you try to make. It's been an absolute delight to watch in some aspects, seeing France go through Napoleon's and Louis's like a revolving door of monarchs but it's a constant problem in the game. Things just do not happen without you either kickstarting it or in some way inducing it. I've seen America's still not annexing Texas by 1890 or the Qing still being alive and not filled with opium. I think we can ratchet it up at least a smidge, although knowing Paradox, they'll overcook THAT as well.And no I will not be mentioning the DLC's, I didn't buy them. It's the real reason I didn't buy in until now because I know the first few DLC's for a Paradox game are basically tinsel before they actually nut up and give us something good. Vic 3's a good framework of a game, which is classically Paradox but don't fully uninstall Vic 2 yet. This game still has a lot of flab that they're going to iron out over time, the question being how much of that ironing out is going to have a price tag attached to it? Time will tell. Until then, I'm going back to beating up Paraguay.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played the leaked beta back in April/May, I feel like I am playing the same exact game with just a couple extra mechanics. The events are all boring, buggy and repetitive. The warfare mechanic is just as janky, the economy is just as broken, and overall the game is just as unfinished. What have they been doing in the last 6 months? In my opinion, this game shouldn't have been released for at least another year at this rate. It is a real shame because of how much fun Vic 2 was, and I get the feeling that it is going to be up to the modding community to do the job that the Paradox devs should have done to begin with.EDIT: After the release of 1.2, I am VERY happy with how things have changed in the game. It seems as if the devs actually took the advice of the community and added in fixes and improvements that we have all been asking for since before the release. I am quite eager to see how the game continues to improve of the next few months and years. I have high hopes for this game now and I am proud to say that it is actually quite fun now.

_childDocuments_.review: I never understood people who like Victoria 2. I see a lot of people here complaining that this game is a downgrade of some sorts. It isn't. It's just a different game. Some disagree with those differences. I prefer them. I enjoy the new economy, it makes more sense than 2's. I love the new warfare system. It really captures what geopolitics was like back then in the lead-up to war. There's so much less micro needed with your troops than in the previous iteration and other paradox grand strategy games (like EUIV). Speaking of micro, the economy can be super micro-heavy if you want it to be. I enjoy this, the economy is what I want to spend most of my time on in this game. However, if you don't want to, there are automation options available which make it easier. All this said, Paradox games are notorious for their learning curves, and while you can learn the game's core within a few hours, learning enough to make the perfect review takes longer. Maybe I'll change my mind.

_childDocuments_.review: i like this game, it's not a generic war game there is warefare in it but i barely went to war, was attacked by some largers members once of twice but managed to fight them off. the thing that drew me to this game was the economy, it's fairly simple to build up but it can be difficult to bring up standard of living and your national education. conquest is not the focus of this game the focus is to work through the research and build up your economy. you new research works really well into the economy aswell and if you ready your economy for the transition with your new technology you can really get your GDP skyrocketing. but if you fall behind on military you may just be attacked so you can ignore the military. there needs more work on the game but the basics are there. there are bugs but not game breaking. there are thing that could be done better though. just watch a vid first of the game and don't pay attention to this negatives reviews, it's a different approach to the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 ends just when the gameplay loop starts to feel satisfyingI stopped playing major powers for the most part because I realized the gameplay loop and decisions were the exact same for pretty much every country, you just start further or farther ahead on the path than others based on what country to choose. This lead me to start playing small countries but I ran into a problem and realization that makes me not want to play the game altogether.I feel like 90% of the game is waiting for the gameplay to become satisfying. This problem becomes so much worse for smaller nations. From the start of the game to about 1900 you are just sitting there waiting for things to happen. I'm waiting for technology to make my economy more efficient. I'm waiting for laws to pass to reform whatever backwater ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm playing. I'm waiting for the small chance that a neighbor gets tied up in a war and I can hopefully take a couple of provinces, but even THEN I'm just sitting there waiting for my army to capture provinces, I'm not doing anything.Just when I reform my country into something I'm proud of and want to lead into the future the game only has 10-20 years left. These last few years feel pointless to me. In hoi4 I can use those last few years and everything I have built up to to wage war and conquer an enemy. In eu4 you can do the same thing. In CK3 I can see how powerful my empire and vassals have become and see how my family tree has changed the course of history. In Victoria, I can use those last few years to.... build more power plants??Another problem I have is that when the game ends I don't feel like I've really accomplished anything. In the other games I have mentioned towards the end of the game I can feel how most decisions and choices I have made lead me to that point. I get satisfaction because I have made so many different and unique choices and I can see how they paid off. In victoria 3 I have waited 90% of the game for buildings to finish and I've made maybe a total of 5-10 decisions that actually affected my experience. I honestly think that I could turn almost any nation into an economic powerhouse without even worrying about laws too much even though some laws are just so clearly better than others that there is no point in choosing them.Sure, I've taken Greece or whatever nation and made them a top 10 power through my economy, but when the game ends I can't shake the feeling of "so what?". There is no payoff and the game ends too quickly without a vic3 to hoi4 conversion mod for any sort of late-game payoff feeling to exist.DO NOT BUY THIS GAME. It is sorely unfinished and lacking any flavor. Every single game you will feel like you're doing the same thing. You're waiting. In ever single game. You're just waiting.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly love this games concept and many choices that they took, but I am reluctant to recommend it in this state. I plan to keep playing and look forward to the free updates hoping the developers learn from this dumper fire of a DLC policy. I think the developers should look closer at the DLC policies for HOI4. I appreciate the changes that have come and I love that this game is still getting attention. I hope the developers learn that locking historic figures, movements, and mechanics behind DLC is a recipe to lose all good will from the fan base.I have tolerated the pre-order bonuses for HOI4, but that is limited to songs and background art insignificant to the game itself. Each DLC for HOI4 comes with alternate focus trees as DLC with the historic ones released in a free update. There should not be DLC that locks historical content for a HISTORICAL GAME behind a paywall. I suggest for DLC to focus on cosmetics or unique ahistorical content that makes new stories within the period. The game's base mechanics and gameplay makes the game a fun nation building simulation.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is will surely give you countless hours of fun, as long as you avoid any open conflict. The problem with this game is that, while you can develop a thriving society and its economy, your games will be destroyed by a ahistoric and probably ridiculous conflict. I can only guess they did not want anyone to go to war. If you go to war in this game, be it with North German Confederation and Bavaria, or the United States and Mexico, than a 'world war' of sorts will possibly, and probably, begin. Under the current "diplomatic play" and "sway" system, the game allows the two conflicting nations to recruit NON ALLIED major and minor nations as their allies just as the conflict erupts. In almost any war, there will be a long list of all of the major powers who may or may not decide to join your enemy on a whim, although they have no relevance to the conflict or with the enemy nation. My issue beyond what the "diplomatic play" system creates, is IF you are going to make a world war out every war, GIVE ME the ability to win it. If this game is going to unrealistically and non-historically tack on enemies to my ATTEMPT at historic conflicts, than GIVE ME a SYSTEM in which I CAN WIN against them. In my opinion, the entire war system should be reworked ALONG WITH a massive overhaul to the motivations of the AI in this game. This is a beautiful game and with a LOT of potential but for everything they got right, the way in which war is conducted is completely wrong.

_childDocuments_.review: Visual - 9/10 There's always room for improvements. I can't see how to improve visually on the game, other than optimization refinements for older GPUs.Performance - 7/10 Older CPUs and lower core counts will struggle with this game. Just because you're CPU meets the minimum doesn't mean it'll handle it no problem. You'll experience late game lag from time to time on the 3rd and 4th gen Intel CPUs. On newer CPUs, the performance isn't really an issue since patch 1.06.Gameplay - 9/10 Who doesn't like to replay their favorite historical moments, or to rewrite history? The options you have are wide and varied. Be warned that early game deviations from normal historical actions will see an alternate history world begin to unfold. There's a lot to enjoy and discover in the game. A few bugs here and there, but relatively little to nothing that is game breaking. I will note: warfare... don't just take every possible war goal, as if either side can't press the primary target you can get stuck in a stalemate war without the ability to white peace. Been rare for me since I don't take pick too many war goals in diplomatic plays.Thoughts and Opinions:Different enough from past PDX grand strategies that some of the warfare mechanics can be a shock. Warfare does work rather well, just there are a lot of smaller mechanics to pay attention. There's a learning curve to the game and it takes time to get the hang of it, and just when you think you have, you probably didn't and that's probably why you will lose a war or tank your economy. Don't get discouraged, try again but try something different and check out more of the UI and features of your nation.Mechanics are quite involved. Though there are some improvements to still be made, all in all, the vocal minority community with their complaints are exaggerating minor problems. Warfare isn't entirely broken. Pop management isn't broken. There's just a lot of little details to pay attention to, to turn even the smallest nation into the world's number 1 super power.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is Paradox' newest attempt at the Grand Strategy genre. Unfortunately, it can not build on the legacy the developers have left with their other famous titles like Hearts of Iron, Europa Universalis, Crusader Kings and Stellaris. First of all, the game itself is playable. Most of the functions it promises work as intented, especially the economic simulation is well implemented. Unfortunately, Victoria is supposed to be more than that. There are three major points which make enjoying the game difficult for me. These are: 1. The military management and war mechanics, which I will describe in detail below; 2. The politics system, which mainly is based of a randomly chosen AI stance (e.g. 'defending the borders' makes them hate you in all aspects); 3. The historical events which should take place between 1836 and 1936, which are just NOT happing (e.g. German and Italy don't form at all most games).To keep this somewhat short, I'll focus on the warfare for this review. The military aspects are so underdeveloped, it is plainly obvious there was no effort into them. Warfare works based on four very basic principles:1. You build barracks in a state, which each host exactly 1 battalion. 2. You then declare war by selecting a war goal via a diplomatic play and wait until everyone who has declared an interest in the affected region has picked a side or declared neutrality. 3. For the war itself, you need to assign a general to the region of states in which your barracks are based. You can NOT assign the battalions manually. Assigning multiple generals to a region redistributes the troops automatically. You can then assign a general to a front line - provide one exists. A frontline requires two states to border each other. Troops not assigned to a front will defend the region their barracks are based in. It is NOT possible to defend a specific postion, e.g. to prepare for a naval invasion. It is also NOT possible to move troops to another region until a frontline is established there. 4. A battle starts. The resuls of the battle are determined by your technology and the production method you barracks are working on - meaning if you choose line infantry, your troops will have the stats of line infantry. In practice, this is useless. You need to have a technological advantage if you want to attack, since the defensive stat is always about 1/3 higher than the attack stat.  Apart from the troop stats, the battle itself will roll a dice on what modifier you get on your stats. These rolls are random (yes, it's as bad as it sounds). The only somewhat reliable way to make a difference in warfare is to have a powerful general with an attack trait. But guess what - apart from the 'historical' (scripted) characters, the traits are also random. Naval warfare is even worse. 1. Naval units are produce the same way land units are - just build naval bases in some states. 2. Declare the war. 3. Assign a admiral to the region the naval bases are in. 4. You get to send you admiral on mission 4 different missions: Patrol coast, Convoi rading, Convoi escort and naval invasion. The problem with the first three are the naval regions. All battles are fought in one of several dozen area points. Patrolling engages enemies in the points next to the region they're stationed in. Convoi rading let's you raid one specific point. And convoi escort is SUPPOSED to protect your convois between two regions. The problem is, the AI can raid ANY of the points your trade is flowing through - which are dozenz of points. You can however only assign your fleet to cover a few of them - which means the AI will keep sinking convois on all the other routes. Since the game doesn't let you forbid any routes from being entered by your convois, your only coice is the cancel ALL of your naval trade routes or to suffer a steady decline in convois. 5. Naval invasions are stupid. You get two steep penalties for naval invading. The first one strictly technology based - you simply need to research Landing Crafts an it's gone. The second one occurs when you want to send a general with more battalions under your command to invade with an admiral with less naval units than battalions. E.g., if you want to invade with 50 Battalions, you need 50 war ships. Remember how you can't reassign battalions to balance these numbers? Yea, it's horrible. You can also ONLY use generals from coastal regions to a naval invasion. You can not order troops from depper in your own country to be send on naval invasion. You can also not re-assign general to another region. Once you assigned one, he stays with these units - so you better assign all the good attackers to coastal regions, or else you are doomed. For such an integral part of the game, these mechanics are terrible. There is no strategy involved in warfare at all - you can only assign troops to an order and hope for the best.

_childDocuments_.review: This game scratches every gaming itch I have. I had been watching it since the messy release and waiting for an opportunity to arrive where it was in a state where I felt I would enjoy the hell out of it. I've always enjoyed pretty much all of the Paradox suite of games, but I'd say this one has very quickly become my favorite. I love the simulation this game delivers, and the alt-history silliness that can happen. I've made an ultra-capitalistic Presidential Republic Spain, a militarist Sokoto Caliphate, and most recently I had a blast with Japan achieving the Meiji Restoration achievement.Normally, I hate randomly generated systems in games with almost no exceptions, however, V3 has somehow achieved a way to make it feel fair. The events that are purely bad don't linger for too long, or they are there to present a reasonable challenge. The difficulty varies all over, and I wholeheartedly appreciate it. The challenging starts that I've tried genuinely feel fun, for example: Egypt is a race against time to build up military to defend against an eventual Ottoman attack, and I'm not good enough yet to figure out how to do it without ruining my run. I actually enjoy playing all the way through to the end when in EU4 I've only ever done that once. The soundtrack is absolutely without a doubt my favorite soundtrack in all of the Paradox suite of games. I have had a lot of fun so far, and I think that especially if the development keeps going in the direction it has been I will continue to have more fun. I definitely feel good recommending this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: I saw a top review say a Monarchy can not force laws to pass. This is untrue. I played dozens of hours as Imperial Japan and you can indeed force laws to pass by choosing the "The will of the Emperor is absolute!" option that comes up while trying to pass the law. This will pass the law instantly. But you are NOT playing as the emperor, you are playing as the nation. You can't do this with every bill every time. I was hesitant to play this game because of negative reviews, but I think this is a very underrated game in its current state. It's the game to go to if your that Civilization player whose fun comes from staring at their cities, building buildings, and watching money numbers go up. There's a decent amount of political focus and diplomatic stuff, for sure. But the bulk of this game is doing things like building your industries and pushing new laws. Every time Russia declared war on me, I was like "I GUESS I'll put the fun stuff on hold to go fight a war."I have seen many people criticize the way the game runs in mid to late game. "It's unplayable!" they say. I'm sure it is for them, but I played as Japan from the start date to 1930, fighting a massive war and  a Great War, without ONCE running into any performance issues on max game speed at max settings. I have a 3060 CPU and a Ryzen 7600, the equivalent of the i5-14400, so if you have anything similar or better, you're good to go. I will say that when I tested this game on an i5-7400 CPU and a 1060 GPU it did indeed run very badly. But of course, those are not very powerful. I also think this is a great game for people who are not deep down the Paradox rabbit whole. In terms of difficulty, I found it to be the easiest game to learn after Crusader Kings 3. It seems a lot more daunting than it is. I coasted by, not knowing what I was doing at all, for quite a few hours without being too harshly punished. I would recommend turning Ai aggression down in the game rules for your first couple of games. If you start out as one of the "tutorial" countries the game does this automatically. Just remember that decrees are good and construction sectors are your country's backbone.I think the simulation of the economy balances fun and realism rather well. It's relatively deep. For instance, you can buy wood (import) or build up a domestic wood industry, which makes wood less expensive. Supply and demand. Easy to understand, hard to master.I feel I should comment on war because other people seem to hate it. It's okay. It's not really the focus of the game, but it's pretty fun. The only real issue I have is that units can "teleport" around the map. meaning if they get cornered they just kind of go away and come back somewhere else instead of getting wiped out. They can also be stationed somewhere and move to their home country freely and completely ignore things like naval blockades. Other than that, it's pretty fun. You're not directing troops yourself, you have generals who do it for you. There is some freedom you have here. You tell which generals to defend and which to attack, set up strategic objectives, and you can hire more generals which will cause many more battles to happen. You can promote them to be able to lead more soldiers in a single battle and command more overall. It's hands-off in the sense you're not telling each unit to move and when. You set up the situation and your general handles the actual fighting. I think for a game not about war, this is a very interesting way to handle not having to micro-manage battles. It could certainly use tuning, but it's very enjoyable for what it is.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, but a BIG caveat here before you buy:Lots of positives here. Gameplay is great, lots of depth and complexity and over 20 hours in I feel like I've only scratched the surface. Combat/war system is a bit frustrating, it doesn't really give you any insight into why you are winning/losing battles or why a won battle didn't result in gains, but combat systems have always been the weak point of Paradox games. The economic and political systems though,  which is what this series is about, are incredibly engaging and fun. You've got so many little levers to pull and can drive your nation in so many different directions. Overall I'm really enjoying it.BUTPart of the reason I have only scratched the surface is that I keep having to restart my runs due to bugs that render the run unplayable. The most common of which are: wars bugging out in a state where neither party can go below 0 and the war therefore can't end; your balance immediately diving into the negative inexplicably on loading a save; and getting stuck in a civil war because the rebels founded a colony before surrendering.If you've got the patience to be continually starting over again, you'll have a lot of fun playing this. If you're the type to get frustrated by that, I'd wait another 6 months, because based on recent history that's how long it's gonna take for paradox to fix any of the launch bugs.

_childDocuments_.review: Room for Improvement: - The Pops are very visually rough right now!- Increase visibility and agency over warfare.- More specifically use the language of development-urbanization in your explanations of what the state economic operations are. - Colonization system still the more facile and verging on problematic systems from earlier versions of the game, but I would like to see a different/more complex process of colonization with local resistance and negotiation 'from below' operate to change the colonial-imperialist powers. The Good: - I have seen people who come from Victoria 2 talk about private prod being automated as a "realistic" touch but nineteenth century economies operated on vast networks of state and private alliance - a Dictatorship of the Bourgeoisie - which the game's mechanics illustrate very well in a nineteenth-century way. - I have played both Mexico and Japan, similar powers and felt very different on both playthroughs in terms of republicanism vs the Shogunate. I will probably follow up with an African power to test the gameplay in the region and situation of those powers.- I like the density of choices about my urban centers and how they are organized as a way to operate productively and schedule municipal and national governmental choices.

_childDocuments_.review: Seven major patches in, Paradox has made some superficial improvements to the game so that it no longer plays like an open beta, but overall major problems remain with most of its important mechanics. Warfare has been improved but is still not good (and it could be! the system isn't inherently bad! Paradox just refuse to put the effort in), diplomatic interactions are still even more limited than they were in Vicky 2 despite the addition of the bloc system, playing as a subject nation trying to break free is actively hellish and means not playing most of the game for the majority of the campaign, and capitalists are barely more intelligent than they were in Vicky 2, causing major problems for your infrastructure continually with no recourse for the player. Several important aspects of the game relating to interest groups, political parties, and elections are outright broken. Maybe given time, they'll improve it, but for the moment it seems like they're content to focus on their DLC content rather than actually making the base game playable.I would like to add that what many people are saying in their reviews is incorrect: they are not locking game fixes behind DLCs. Paradox abandoned that strategy starting with Stellaris (because it worked very poorly in EU4) and now their DLCs all release alongside a free update that includes any improvements to the base game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is when a mixed yes or no would be good. Ultimately however I do recommend this game for the right type of person. The economic simulations are great while not perfect. In the economic game sphere it is very limited at the moment and I can easily recommend people who are interested in that. For business game players this is also something that I recommend. It is fun to find problems in your market and work out to fix it. However do remember that the population and your country will react to the choices you make. The next best tech is not always the best choice. For Paradox players you know what you are getting into. If you are not captured by the economic and pop features then wait this out. War is horrible to play at the moment. Think Hoi4 AI front breaking and then up that by triple the pain. For EU4 you will feel the pain of not being able to fight wars in a clear manner. If you require a good UI and clear guidance from tool tips this is not the game for you. That is not knocking players who want and need this and not saying this UI is acceptable. This game will lie to you about what is good to build and its own features do not capture why you would build different things. I got my moneys worth easily from just the economic simulations. I recommend a little bit of checking to see if it is good for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I was waiting for patch 1.5 mostly because they were going to change warfare a bit, because I didn't really like its state in previous versions.Well, what can I say... They managed to do that.They managed to make this unusable ♥♥♥♥ even worse.* Managing your armies/fleets is now an absolute pain in the ass, because you cannot just build barracks/naval bases and upgrade units via production methods in the building interface. You have to click through several menus for every damn army.* Vassals are not even useless, but undesireable, because they will successfully lose any battle for any peace of land you managed to conquer. And there is no way to forbid them joining into your wars or just order to defend the front.* Front system is ridiculous. In a war between Russia and Qing the lake Balkhash is big enough to make two fronts at the border between countries. But in a war between Russia and Ottomans Black Sea is apparently small enough to combine fronts in Caucasus and Romania together. So, my armies in Caucasus magically teleport into Romania to figth someone, and vice versa.* Sometimes, when you do a naval invasion, defeated enemy fleets return to the sea node again and again right after being defeated, trapping you in the invasion state, because you cannot even cancel the invasion order once it was started.* Sometimes countries are being trapped in infinite wars. Either because no one can achieve victory goals (in one of my campaings I had Great Britain fighting for some ports in Qing for decades). Or because these wars start again and again: for example, Prussia was declaring war on France for the unification of Germany, signing a white peace, because both sides couldn't do anything - and immediately declaring a new war.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fairly decent game that IMO is utterly ruined by the terrible AI and absolutely awful War system.  The AI is extremely placid and loves backing down from conflict.  As Russia, I grabbed Persia and Afghanistan without fighting a single battle - even though they had support of their neighbors!With regards to War: In theory, I like the idea of a streamlined 'Front' system where you don't have to keep marching dudes around obscure regions.  In practice, the system plays out exactly the same as before - it's just a glorified Whack-a-Mole, except the armies teleport around and you have very, very little control over who goes where.  An enemy ally has 2 divisions attacking your distant border?  Too bad!  You have no choice but to spread out your divisions evenly, so you're forced to assign about 30 divisions to take care of them.  The "flow" of war becomes utterly incomprehensible when there's more than 2 nations involved.  All you're doing when fighting a war is constantly re-assigning generals to empty fronts that the AI decided to sneakily open up.  If you don't pay close attention and micro-manage the war, you're going to get your ass handed to you because the general AI is basically nonexistent.In practice, this is exactly like the Whack-a-Mole system in previous games, except you have frustratingly little control over your units.  The economic part of the game is pretty fun, but what's the point if diplomacy is nonexistent and the game utterly falls apart the moment a war breaks out?

_childDocuments_.review: After playing the game as Germany, USA and Russia it's clear that the game needed more time in development.The game has a lot of potential - but it's either going to take mods or DLC to make it replayable. I'll list a couple of the larger issues.1) The AI is pretty bad at managing their nations and fighting wars. This is readily apparent in how Prussia has a hard time forming Germany and the USA more often than not can't beat Mexico in wars and form their traditional borders in North America. Its just deflating not seeing the AI be able to do the things that are easily done by a player - and are easily done in Victoria 2 most of the time. There is nothing wrong with their being ahistoric outcomes - but that shouldn't be most games - in V3 it is most games.On top of that - the American Civil War when it launches can include non-slave states - so the bordergore in this game is horrendous and seemingly random due to the way civil wars currently work.2) The second reason is that the way the game operates currently is you spend 80% of your time figuring out what economic buildings to build, balancing your budget with construction needs and prioritizing construction of buildings of in demand goods in your market. The diplomatic game is pretty devoid of choice and same goes with warfare, there are limited options with both of those sides of the game so you end up spending your entire time completing economic building chains and researching technologies to improve those same buildings. It's interesting to learn - but once you've played a few games it isn't entertaining.Overall - game needs more time - can definitely be good with mods or more DLC but its clear to say the game needed more time.

_childDocuments_.review: With over 2000 hours in EU4 and 20 hours of Victoria 2, I can say that Victoria 3 is a refreshing change from the constant warmongering of Europa. The game focuses very much on an Economic/political lens and turning your sub-optimised starting date country into an economic powerhouse able to rival the English is a very satisfying experience.To acknowledge the downsides, the game is littered with sub-systems that need improvement but I'm optimistic that it'll be improved with time (especially knowing I enjoy it in it's current state). In particular these systems are all focused around War and the AI. War is basically an "assign a general with troops to X front" and you can give them a "hold your ground" or "Go charge" order. It's nothing special and it really feels like they've pandered War to be fixed in a DLC system like EU4's Common Sense pack. AI is very flippant if you have good relations, sometimes they stab you in the back without any opportunity to really stop them (looking at you Russia).Good news? _childDocuments_.review: This game has the potential to be one of my favorites in Paradox's library, but after more than a year of post-release development, I've sadly given up on seeing it reach that level. The war system is genuinely broken; even after several updates specifically targeted at fixing it, I have seen armies abandon fronts for no reason, or two armies swap fronts on opposite sides of the country despite specific orders to stay on their sides, or get stuck in an infinite loop of advancing into an uncontested front, but failing to ever actually take ground due to being stuck in battles against phantom armies of zero soldiers. Enemy countries will completely ignore a new war declared on them, allowing other forces to entirely conquer their country uncontested because they're so focused on fighting the player.The politics are too random and swingy. resulting in some games where you easily pass radical laws that fundamentally transform your country, and some games where you spend 5 years failing to shift between different types of school system. The economic systems, the core of the game, are starting to be fleshed out over the course of all these updates, but everything surrounding them is too much of a slog to push through. Can't recommend this game as is, and I have no confidence it will be worth the time or money in the future at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is shaping up to be my favorite Paradox game. This is possibly the most complex game I've played, as all of this game's systems are so interconnected. It is, at its heart, an extremely interesting economic simulation. The game director is one of my favorite game developers, I think everything he has led is some of the best stuff Paradox has put out. In addition, Paradox supports their games for a long time after release, which means this game will be receiving content for a long time. Older Paradox titles would lock game systems behind paid DLCs, which meant the developers couldn't justify iterating on that system going forward. Having realized this, the developers begun including new systems with the free patch that accompanies every DLC they release and to put flavor in the paid DLC. What this means is that the game can continue to grow and old content can continue to be updated/kept relevant while still being tied into systems developed years later. Mechanically, this game is a strong foundation and I truly believe in the team behind it. I had an incredible time learning this game and look forward to putting many more hours in over the years.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is not really satisfyingNot much of V2's gameplay loop made it into this game. That's fine on it's own as long as what they replace it with is good. But that didn't really happen.The core gameplay loop is similar to the building and trade system from EU3/EU4 but with more focus on monitoring market prices. This is fine but not when it's 90% of the game. In V2 you needed to colonize or sphere territories so you could secure inputs for your factories and then the excess goods would be sold off on international markets. More developed countries have more access to these markets than less developed ones. In this it doesn't really seem to matter, there's a global market with an infinite supply, There's no strong incentive to colonize or sphere, only weak ones. All that will happen is your factories will be less efficient. This removes most of the asymmetry from the gameplay which means it's unlikely to produce an accurate simulation of the time period.Removing the military aspect of the game seems like a mistake to me (so far) as well because it removed asymmetrical aspects of warfare during the time period. Colonial wars that European powers used to open foreign ports did not rely on conscription, they used their overwhelming technological superiority. The warfare feels like an automated risk game where superior numbers usually win, which again was not the case during this time period.I don't know if it's just the countries I've played so far but the politics system seems to be broken or there's little not much policy progression available. Same for the diplomatic system. Can't really form alliances or trade deals, some countries have permanent -100 debuffs to relations for some reason.Overall the game is a conceptual failure because it fails to simulate the history of this period or provide the opportunity for interesting alternate histories.

_childDocuments_.review: This game released in late 2022 at a retail price of 50 US dollars. Then, nothing worked as intended and there barely were any features in the game. War was utterly broken, the economic simulation produced nonsensical results, diplomacy was absolute comedy. The best part : there wasn't even half the features that Victoria 2 launched with some decade ago. Two years on, they have not fixed much, since the game's systems are fundamentally flawed and, therefore, cannot be readily fixed. Now, these developpers have the absolute gall to release features that should have been in the game in a functional state at release, in a DLC priced at 30 US dollars. Some important points to note are that this DLC is not the only one: the store contains content locked behind some 20 US dollars' worth of DLC; as well, fundamental flaws within the game still are not fixed, neither by updates nor by DLCs. So here we are, with software priced at a total of 100 US dollars that barely works and still lacks many important features. We all know Paradox's reputation, but on this one, they've outdone themselves.

_childDocuments_.review: Try to ignore the negative reviewbombs since a lot of them are just there to be salty :/.Important to understand is that this game is an economy simulator over a map painter. Even though it is possible to go full mayhem and conquer the map, the game is designed in a way where wars are to be viewed as last resort options to conflicts of interest.I personally find it very enjoyable to manage my economy and steer my nation in a certain direction. I find the fact that laws are locked behind the need of support of your groups of interest very immersive and interesting to play with. It forces you to try to manage a gouvernment that has enough loyalty to not spawn any revolts but also allow you to enact the laws you want.War might be a bit hands off compared to other paradox games but I don't think it's that bad, war is not the focus of this game after all.I really enjoy how much more I feel involved with my population and how they live their lives compared to the other paradox games where I feel very unattached from the people I'm ruling except crushing a revolt every now and then.Flavor is a bit lacking for now and performance drops HEAVILY as the game goes on (around 1900's seems to be the start of the lag apocalypse) but I'm pretty sure the devs are aware of these issues and will fix them very soon.I think this game has a lot of potential and I look forward to seeing what it will become :)

_childDocuments_.review: I think it's a good place to start. There is definitely opportunity for fun, but it does have its fair share of problems.It feels bare-bones everywhere except the economy, and that gets tedious by the mid-game, when you have so much construction capacity that you have to queue up 50 building levels at a time over and over again, and lord help you if, in the monotony of it, you forget to build another level of railway alongside all those factories. There is an auto-expand feature, but it doesn't look at the detail of your economic situation (ex, building more levels of a factory, despite lacking enough input goods to sustain it).The diplomatic play system is annoying and too rigid. The number of tiny pops overwhelms weaker CPUs. War is boring. Probably the worst is that holy crap the UI sucks. For a company that is supposedly focused on approachability, they sure found a lot of annoying ways to hide important information. It has seriously taken me 100 hours to get a decent handle on where certain extremely vital pieces of information are, such information regarding my pops' dependent ratio and trend direction.I'm rambling now. It is fun, for the first hundred hours at least, so I got my money's worth, but it definitely needs more work.

_childDocuments_.review: I have really enjoyed Vicky 3. It is a good 19th century simulation game from 1836 to 1936 and I have been waiting for this game for years after sinking hundreds of hours into Vicky 2. I think large parts of this game are an improvement on Vicky 2: The interest group system is a more accurate representation of 19th century politics with parties often being formed from a coalition of the interest groups. The economy system isn't perfect, but still excellent in terms of demanding the player to become involved in managing the economy to a greater extent than in Vicky 2, where you could largely leave it on autopilot. I have also really enjoyed the addition of the private sector construction in v1.2.One improvement over vicky 2 is that I think it is much more fun to play a secondary or minor power in vicky 3.The biggest issue is obviously the war mechanics, where they seem to have gone in the opposite direction to add autopilot and decrease the amount of player involvement. I understand their reasons for this design choice such as making the game a simulation and adding balance by decreasing how the player can 'game' the AI in a war. But the reality is that it just isn't as fun. This does need to be revised at some point in the future. I am also desperate for some more flavour and events, but understand that will be added later, and there will be plenty of mods to add that, what is important at the moment is that it has a good base game.Despite that, this is a good base which makes me excitedly await the addition of lots of flavour and events in future patches, I was more mixed about the state of the game before v1.2, but since v1.2, I would recommend this game to anyone who loves 19th century history or paradox games.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very difficult review to write down, for different reasons. First off all I don't like negative reviews or negative feed-backs in general, and I prefer to always take the positives. Second I'm a Hobsbawm nerd, I've read The Age of Capital and  The Age of Empire for every year over the last four years. There has never ever been a grand strategy game that got me hyped more than Victoria 3, and don't get me wrong there were enjoyable moments, That's why I'm keeping this as a positive review. Now, this game unfortunately falls short and just flat on a lot of points. There is a primary issue with Victoria 3 in my point of view, and that is while the market is supposed to be very realistic, its just not. And in an age were political expansion, foreign offices, embassies, loans and political interventions need to be of utmost influence, they're just not. There are some paradox legacy mechanics which simply don't fit the kind of game that is being intended here. One of them is how infamy is calculated, and the AI just going insane trying to cut you down for ten times for no reason, even though they need your cheaper resources! And while these mechanics were really nice and fun to have in EU4 and made sense, they just simply don't make sense in a game that is coming to focus on completely different and more dynamic things. A game that is supposed to be about economic wars, trade routes and convoy safety wars, industrial struggles with your population, colonial resources, a great power enabling smaller economies, a growing middle class, secret police, regime change, spheres of influence, etc... What is infamy in its current form doing here? Also the effects of political legislative changes are so much very black and white in a way that yes is linear in progression, and in line with the very linear change of your pops if you're growing your economy, but they're just more of a mandate. This game and I will say it, clearly suffers from what I could think of as some sort of a lack of supremacy for one clear vision. This game has an identity crisis. It's a paradox game mechanically, the ins and outs are all paradox, but it wanted to be more in line with economic simulation games. It wanted to be an economic project simulator, but have flavor built into it. It wanted to have a war system, but more of a small system where you go to war for a small island in the ocean, to get a specific resource. Problem is these things aren't just working out together.And also all of us who have given the game decent time, just focus on conquest, because like any grand strategy game, dominance will always factor in with player psychology. No one will go into a game and say I wanna have the biggest shipping yards in the game, that's where I'll get my prestige from, and if it was so, then let me through that power have a significant impact upon the shipping industry! If I'm the biggest exporter of cotton for example, then let me control the textile industry completely, let me control the prices! How is it that a game that wanted to be about economic prowess, and dominance doesn't have a stockpile mechanic, and this was like one of the vital elements in Victoria 2! And that's where I keep asserting, there is an issue of identity here. Think of just having this element in effect with a mechanic such as infamy, and make it fit the Victorian playbook. And then France won't just decide I'm gonna go to war with this Russia because they're seeking GuanXi and Manchuria. If I control half the map, then prop one of the AI to control the other half, but don't let them just embargo me for no reason, when I have all the raw materials, and elements which can make them just as powerful. This and I haven't discussed the lack of flavor in this game, the only thing which provides me with flavor, and certainly a strategic element of difficulty in this game is a country's starting position and its economic situation. Which again shows how there was a lot of effort put in this game. But the Journal entries like really, I'm very sorry are lifeless. Compare them to the events in a game like CK, and I know that CK is primarily about your character's narrative, but even on a nation's macro level, they are boring. This system needs tons of add ons to introduce flavor, and beyond images of dissidents and influential characters, there needs to be further interactivity, and life. Interactive mechanics with those dissidents, interactive mechanics with your institutions. These things should have been there I would say, because we might probably be at a point beyond fixing these issues. This game wanted to be revolutionary, and you can tell, we all can, but something happened along the way, and I really hope that with the introduction of spheres of influence, maybe, maybe this could change something. Maybe there is hope to save this. I do believe that this game needed a different overhaul to all paradox mechanics and a fresher younger approach, and this could have been  the introduction of a newer version of these mechanics, because they are getting old, to be very frank. I Know I will still play it, and I recommend it for a specific type of modern history and political nerd. Especially if you can get it on sale, yeah it will help you kill your time, will give you an interesting outlook on the important economic shifts of the time, societal progression. But its very linear, and I'm very sorry to say this, ultra bland and just lacking. It clearly suffered from a lack of one primary vision, or maybe just got overwhelmed by the weight of its ambition. You can try world conquests with nations such France, make Russia a democracy, form The united states of the Americas, or Arabia, but that's basically it.There is something about the game that just keeps me coming back to play it again and again. It might be having to humiliate all the Big Boys before deciding I'll go and conqueror all of Qing or half of the US or half of Russia where I can get my hands on all their oil, but the game is more of a time killer, than something compelling.I'm still hoping I could have a different say in the future, hopefully with spheres of influence, interactivity with dissidents and institutions, and real market control.  Thanks!

_childDocuments_.review: After some SP and MP games, here's my review:If you don't like complex economy & market management and love old style paradox war... THIS GAME IS NOT FOR YOUVictoria 3 is a game where you play as the spirit of the government, not the spirit of the nation itself like in past games.I love the army system. You don't have control over each and every movement, and its up to the skill of your generals to triumph on the fronts, not generic micro skills. This game allows beginners to play against the pros in the context of war and actually stand a chance. A 250 Regiment Ottomans can stand their ground against a 350 regiment France long enough to ask the int'l community for assistance. War is slow and methodical, and becomes more violent as the years go by, much like in real life, how the Napoleonic style of warfare was phased out for a more brutal style in the latter years of the 19th century. Small skirmishes always take place before the big one, reflecting how in fact there weren't that many massive battles in the grand scheme of things.

_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot, and will not recommend this game in its current state.Warfare is broken.AI cannot manage the economy well, and struggles to build buildings for important resources like Oil.Lack of capitalists and an intense focus on tedious micromanagement.Lacklustre Interest Groups system.Lack of flavour for even the major nations of the era, forget about countries which could've been a fun campaign, like Cuba.Rather, wait for updates and maybe (sadly) a couple of DLCs to drop first before buying it.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: The game still has some problems that make it simply not fun to play for longer than a bit at a time every other patch. I have some hope this is eventually going to be solved by the devs and I am going to eventually change my review when it happens. Then again we are closing in on DLC #3. The game has been out for almost two years and some problems like frontlines or naval invasions continue to be a source of frustration although in different shapes and sizes every other patch. I won´t lie, I have had a lot of fun, too. Most of that can be attributed to my initial enthusiasm when V3 came out and to a great extent to some awesome friends I did play the game with largely in spite of all the issues like irrational AI, frontline bugs or out-of-synchs or relobbying-issues. I would love to play this game in a stable multiplayer lobby for once, but you simply can´t play a few hours and return to it on another free evening more than two times in 50% of the cases.In single player I have enjoyed industrializing some countries or reforming them, but there is only that many times I enjoy simply going through the building loops. Which is fine. I like this part of the game somewhat. More militarily focused campaigns are not fun to me yet. Too many bad experiences with frontlines, naval invasions or erratic AIs. Might get used to it and you can reload every time it happens, but that sure is killing the fun for me at least.Political reforms on the other hand often feel arbitrary especially in more traditional countries. Sure you can work on your odds, but at any point when passing reforms everything can turn against you for no other reason than being unlucky. There is no actual political progress or developement while passing laws. Percentage chances change, dice are rolled, but what was a 40% chance a minute ago being explained in debate-events can all turn around to failing completely. Those events don´t mean anthing but a change in chance. They are in detail not connected to parties or peoples stances. Sometimes they boost parties or politicians, but you never really interact with them as in offering them something for fixed support that is going to remain for the duration of the reform process. One debate-event I get opposition support and the next one somehow that is lost due to something that doesn´t make any sense in relation to the overall process and the previous events positive change. What could I have done? I guess nothing really and that makes it rather frustrating.All in all I have played the game a good bit and I am not mad at the money I have spend vs the fun I have gotten out of it. But I can imagine the overall experience being a lot better, if it wasn´t for the issues one could detect and solve. I could see past the frustrating gameplay aspects in the last paragraph, if that was the only issue. Thanks for reading.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: I love simulations, especially on abstract things such as society and markets. This game is ground-breaking in that regard. Setting up your economy, real social issues arise which still persist to this day. The influence Groups are amazing, mirroring abstract social groups that persist to this day. The game dynamically uses them and the economy to teach and show the players why and how things in history happened, how some bad ideas persisted throughout history, or popped up when things were rough. All this without forcing the players to engage with meaningless "mana points" or abstractions.  It's the players job to create and maintain the societal structure, or rip it down in glorious revolutions.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, so far this game is rather good for what I have come to expect from any franchise nowadays. Lets get the bad out of the way; this game literally drags ass in past 1890, its like the optimization stopped only for the demos. This was super unprofessional and rather annoying and seems to be a common symptom in the industry now: release half-baked game, then repair for 6 months to distract you from the fact that they will now charge you DLC for features in game made 12 years ago. I see where this is going and it is super disheartening to see Paradox continue this trend. Now for what I have liked; this game has super- potential, right now there are parts of the game where it will go off the deep end, however there are still many parts that are rather shallow. Take for instance the Economy, rather than having a stronger variety in economics as Vicky2, Vicky3's seems alot more stable however more gameified. It seems less of an economics simulator and more of a civilization gardener; nothing wrong with that, it's just not like the simulation in Victoria 2. I do have to complain about the lack of information layers, like where is a Demographic Pyramid, so I can see the true structure of my population and what I have to face down the line, what happened to the countless layers Victoria 2 had?? Otherwise this game is more of a beefed up EU4 visually. You build buildings, except this time you just have to watch your supply systems, but everything else is pretty similar. Yet whilst I'm on visuals I must say this is the prettiest Grand Strategy Game I have seen. I do love seeing industrialization effect the terrain and environment around it, plus, just how visually pleasing the little towns and farms can be and watching them change with time and wealth; it makes it so much more immersive visually. I still reccomend this game because it has huge potential and it is genuinely fun; however I will always recommend Vic2 over this until they add more depth and flavor to the economy in the game and shift war to be more playable.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game, but the biggest issue is while i do like the direction of a more decentralised warfare system the way they have it in game to this point is really bad. The warfare feels like I have no say in how things go, and pair that with the ai generals who attack in random directions or the stupidly hard naval invasions being stopped by 1 tribesmen. The way Mexico and Texas just... instant peace?, but the United States still get to use it as a pretext to invade?, why does the US colonise africa and invade Japan?. The whole ai needs, and war system need to be improved.the economy and politics section of the game is really good it just needs a lot more flavor, events, missions, choices. Because as it stands now, if i'm not trying to change a law after every law passing it really does feel like i'm wasting time, since the game only goes 100 years, give us more to do to make the game feel longer.Over all, the game is really good and a right direction for the Vic series but as it stands id say wait for a sale or wait for the game to update a bit more before deciding to buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: This game, above all else, focuses on the economy, and seemingly in order to do so throws everything else overboard, including war, diplomacy, accurate political instability, and most glaringly (in my opinion) FLAVOR.There is next to nothing to separate Russia from Austria beyond the color and location on the map, as there are next to ZERO events which are specific to Russia or Austria! This was unbelievable on my first playthrough, as anyone with knowledge of the time period will know that Russia is the nation which (arguably) experienced the greatest internal political strife among all of the great powers, and has ONE (1) nation-specific journal entry.This lack of flavor continues into the rest of the map (which looks like a mobile game zoomed out, by the way) and results in a thoroughly stable Qing, Ottomans (despite oftentimes losing Constantinople to Egypt in my games), and an alarmingly low danger level from insurrection. Additionally, the war system is terrible and makes ZERO sense. You have no control over when, where and how your generals maneuver themselves and engage the enemy. I understand that some were afraid of the micromanaging of units on a map, but it is honestly ridiculous how boring this system is. Seriously, with nearly everyone in the community raising concerns about the war system, the fact that they stuck to it up to and after release is unfortunate.This all culminates into a focus on economy. But, after any length of time, leaves you with the glaring question: WHY? Why am I working so hard to make the green number higher? To fund what? More boring wars? It funds nothing because in their quest to pursue the perfect economic simulator, they jettisoned everything else that makes the game's time period special.And when the honeymoon phase ends, people will finally see this.
