_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: The game has potential but I would not recommend it at this stage.So far it's a nice economic simulation with a fairly realistic portrayal of supply and demand. Unlike most, I do not mind the unusual war mechanics either. However, diplomacy feels very odd. Most powers are very happy to get involved in any wars all over the world, which leads to huge conflicts, which seems somewhat ahistorical for the 19th century. My biggest objection however is that the game feels somehow "empty". There are very few events that often repeat themselves and there are very few national differences. I've played as Prussia/Germany, Sicily/Italy, Persia and the US and they all played very similar. Unification of Germany or Italy was ridicously and ahistorally easy. Also, the characterstics of your rulers and political leaders are pretty much inconsequential. In my games there was also never really the danger of revolution, which made politics a bit boring (tbf though this could be because I never played into the 1900s).I am sure they will fix this with DLCs in the future, but I don't have the patience and mind to wait for that. The best thing that could happen to this game is that it gets the same treatment as Imperator: Rome, which became a really good game after several years and updates. But again, I don't think I have that much patience with Paradox.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: I find this game in many ways a fun and interesting experience, especially the economic aspects. Presently, however, the war system is so lacking that I can't  really recommend buying it, especially given the steep price. In my view, the war system needs to be changed to allow for more player control and interaction, as well as transparency. I found it hard to figure out what was winning or losing me battles. The lack of tactical control of your armies is extremely frustrating at times, for example in situations where your supposed allies just decide to sit back and let you fight the war on your own (yes Britain, I'm looking at you). Overall it's not very fun to sit and watch the computer make tactical decisions for you. This should be in the hands of the player. I would heartily recommend letting go of cherished design principles, and re-introduce some form of tactical war system. For the price tag, this game also seems very unpolished.

_childDocuments_.review: the base game was always released barebones, with not much to do expect waiting for the lines to go upthe direction of the DLC has been to provide features that should have been there from the start for a Victoria game (you know, diplomacy and investments, that kind of stuff) while making any country expect the GP unplayable. _childDocuments_.review: So, this game comes with a couple of caveats. It's a typical Paradox game, which means there is a lot of complexity, and an ambitious design. _childDocuments_.review: The learning curve is steep (worse, I bet, for anyone (like me) who hadn't played V2). The tutorials are poor – don't try the Sweden one first, because that's just useless. _childDocuments_.review: Economy mechanics are good. War mechanics are still student-created-project level of amateurism.Especially the continuous break-up of fronts into micro fronts. Like cells replicating themselves. If Paradox intended to make war more macro-centric through appointment of generals to their respective fronts, they have failed. Players are no longer moving individual units or armies, but instead they have to babysit these so called generals, reassigning them around the broken fronts they create.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is a great game for developing the economy and seeing changes in the society and politics. You can develop your country is many different directions and see how it shapes every aspect of your society. You can focus on warring all over the world and see how your soldiers gain an important place in your society and your economy becomes focusing around providing for your wars, meanwhile discontent grows as the rest of your economy suffers from the conflicts and the conquered people want to rebel. You can try to become the industrial hub of the world and see the political opposition between the capitalists and communists, both empowered by the rising capitalist and worker classes. You can focus on your farms and stay a traditional country controlled largely by aristocrats and the clergy, but maybe the farmers will unite and try to force a revolution on your society. You can have many entirely different games with the same country simply based on how your economy. This is what makes Victoria 3 such a good game. For the comparisons with Victoria 2, Vic3 is definitely an improvement largely thanks to its higher degree of details in the economy. It results in less static games, more different each time, more political dynamism, less railroading and societies actually evolving organically. The warfare is less detailed, but considering how much of a micro hell warfare was in Vic2, I say it is an improvement. Lastly, for the multiplayer, it is pretty good. It is far less focused on the meta as HoI4 and less messy and chaotic than CK3’s one. It’s overall a very enjoyable experience, both if you’re looking for something chill or serious. It feels also less gamey than most other Paradox games.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Fun for the first like 40 or so hours before you realize that everything is essentially the same and there's really no differences between countries etc. After that it's pretty boring. Looks like a lot of depth on the surface but it's actually really shallow. I'm sure in two years it will be a super deep game if you're willing to shell out like $200 for extra DLC.If you're looking for a game that will entertain you for a bit, sure buy it. If you're looking for a good grand strategy/socio economic simulation game with a lot of depth don't buy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: I conquered england with literally 2 units. (Ai is terrible)Not only the fact that everything is managed by some sort of mana and AI makes the game quite ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stupid.The Trade system is bugged out of his mindYour economy can also crash at random moments without telling you why (Even tho your income is higher than your expenses)You can be an Absolute Monarchy or a Republic and you control your country the same. (Though it's fun to pass laws and dealing with the other parties or reforming your government but I would like to see a difference between Absolute Monarchy and full on Socialists countries.) * Also you have to pin-point micro manage every single buildings to make efficient profit which isn't fun. *I don't understand the biased reviewers "this isn't a war game" but every time there's a single conflict, every major countries join in or your only way to interfere is through war or if you are making colonies, they'll attack you (putting you in a war) The war is fun at times but can be ridiculous. Your front will keep dividing itself against the same opponent and the Ai will push hard in those cracks so you have to pause and micro your army. (Which they didn't want players to do)Is the game fun to play? Yes and no.You can expand your country, boom your economy and interfere in other wars (That's cool)You have to micro every single building being built in your country with no automation whatsoever. (That's only cool when you are a small country, it feels rewarding. But when you can build over 80 buildings throughout literally 40 different regions, it's starting to get tedious and you then have to manually check every single regions to see if they are being properly managed)Is it worth the 60 + $ NoCan it be a good game in the future? Yes, absolutely. Will put negative because after so, so many years of developing this shouldn't be the final product.We shouldn't have to say "DLC'S or Mods" will save this.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Economic simulation is just great.Diplomacy system is pretty bland and seems hard to work with and I don't really understand how to sway the ai or get it to help you when playing a minor country, definitely rough but fine for multiplayer (I also have a skill issue).War system is bleh, the front system is kind of a neat idea but the execution is confusing and doesn't always work in a way that makes sense, building up your army and industrializing it is a fun process and I really do like it from that aspect, the front system and the player having literally no sway in it whatsoever apart from attack and defend is upsetting though, some will say that's the main point but in my opinion if the point is considered a flaw by many then that indicates a serious question with whether that design choice is good or not. I can see why they thought about implementing this war system but it just feels like there's so much left to improve about it, I don't have much constructive to say about it I just don't like it in general and It's something I can deal with.The colonization system is just awful, I don't even know what to say or what to suggest It's just insane how fast europeans will rush malaria prevention, france and britain (sometimes with the USA, Russia, etc.) will control a third or more of africa by 1865 which is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nuts, the mechanic itself isn't very nice to use nor does it feel very realistic.I also think in general the game could use more content in the form of journals with more events, rewards, etc. to make playing as different nations feel more distinct, this can include alt-history and history based ones, overall the system has a lot of potential and It's very good I just feel It's painfully underused and the fear of railroading the game is exaggerated. All in all, I think the game is pretty cool from the angle of it as game where you build up financially and progress your society (or whatever your self-set goal is in the domestic regard), but trying to do the other part of the game, imperialism (via war and diplomacy), is just upsetting, as well as minor countries in single player due to the issues I mentioned previously with the diplomatic system.I heavily recommend multiplayer over singleplayer despite the multiplayer having some issues like frequent desyncs, when you can use your "people skills" (removing ingame chat ♥♥♥♥♥ with this heavily btw) instead of the in-game diplomacy mechanics It's a lot more fun. I also dedicate most of this review to talking to my negatives rather than my praise because I feel knowing what to improve is more valuable than knowing what is already done for a developer, feel free to comment and ask about my points or anything.tldr economy good, play multiplayer, war system <mid but not ♥♥♥♥, diplomacy is rough, add more journals, and ottomans is the best country.7/10 please improve

_childDocuments_.review: After almost 400 hours of playing i have come to decide that i would not recommend anyone buy this game,  The economy is alright but the way system and how the AI loves to blob over the player is not a fun experience,  ive played as a great nation and started as the smallest one ive found and done alot of great things,  Sure you can become world power from any little nation you want but Paradox cant make challanging games without making the AI get alot of random buffs you cant explain happening.

_childDocuments_.review: The game, upon its release, was a buggy and incomplete mess. Many of the core mechanics were not fleshed out. 1.1 and 1.2 are, essentially, just the finishing touches on 1.0. 1.1 is a bugfix update and 1.2 expands the basegame mechanics to release expectations. The "finished basegame" Victoria 3 1.2 however will yet still be a barren game. Paradox is well known for releasing empty frameworks of great games and spicing them up over time with expansions that give the game a soul. I may recommend the game once it has received the sorely needed love and attention it deserves, but as of now it will only appeal to the most diehard of fans. There just is nothing to recommend except the basic idea of a Victorian-era grand strategy game which sounds like just what I've always wanted to play

_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is the most in-depth social-economic-political simulator currently available on steam. It allows you to play as any country during the Victorian era and build whatever economy you desire. You can carefully influence your country’s politics and ideology to your desired end-state, whilst building intricate supply chains. Or you can just build the largest military-industrial complex in the world and conquer the planet whilst watching your Green Line Go Up!
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely not Vicky 2 with better graphics. This is a full-blown 1800s politics and economics sim with lite combat mechanics - and I dig it. This time around you have far more control over your country and where it goes, but it's not as heavy on the historic routes (unify Germany, westernize Japan, get Russia out of the Stone Age, etc.), but you have the ability to do all those things, it's just not as narrative-driven as Vicky 2, which isn't necessarily a downside, though I do miss the flavor text.It's a solid reboot, but I groan thinking about the dlc that's gonna happen to spruce up the game, cause there's a lot that can be done, but mods should be able to help in that dept in the meantime. Overall, I would recommend if you're interested. I wasn't disappointed and was satisfied with gameplay and the freedom I was allowed to try weird combos and strategies that I couldn't pull off in Vicky 2. It's not perfect, but it's good. _childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is a fun and engaging Grand Strategy game.  It's strongest element is the economic simulation, which blows most other strategy games out of the water, and the "Just one more..." aspect is super strong here as you adjust and balance your economy throughout the entire campaign.The Diplomatic Play system feels like a solid improvement over Victoria II's crisis system, allowing much more engagement by nations below Great Power ranking, I look forward to seeing where this goes.The War System is currently the weakest element, but a lot of this has to do with a few key weaknesses rather than the system itself.  First, there are a number of bugs and mishaps, such as an army closing a front and returning home, rather than moving to the nearest front (but not always).  Some of the aspects of the system are unclear, as to why you lose or win some battles, especially when the Offense and Defense rolls don't match the way the battle goes.  Ultimately, I still enjoy the system and the deprioritization of war as a focus.At time of this review, there are some frustrating bugs, for example permanent revolter states, but the key parts of the game work well.  Watching your GDP number go up, and seeing the impacts of your decisions and reforms play out in your society is thoroughly satisfying.As someone who has worked on mod teams for EU4, HOI4 and Stellaris, I am eager to see the possibilities for mods in Victoria 3.  The systems as they are lend themselves heavily to Cold War and later scenarios in a way that other Paradox Titles don't quite nail.Victoria 3 is a great foundation for a Paradox Game.  Long-term fans of the developer know that the game receive extensive support after release, so I know the game will continue to develop and expand with critiques of the playerbase in mind.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has generated a surprising amount of controversy, so while I normally don't bother with reviewing games, I think it's worth sharing my thoughts here given the focus on it and the difficult nature of evaluating this game, which I would say overall is a flawed but still enjoyable game.For context, I am a huge fan of Victoria 2 and have played many hours of it outside of Steam in addition to what is listed on my Steam account. In that context, I do disagree with a couple of the decisions made in the development of Victoria 3, but that being said, the fundamental mechanics of this game in terms of economics, politics, and diplomacy are for the most part strong, even if the game is also flawed. As I see it, there are 4 main gameplay pillars to this game which are varying in their level of polish and engagement for the player: This is the strongest point of the game. The switch to market-based economies from the unrealistic (for the era) global economy of Vic2 is a big step forward and creates more interesting decision making regarding resource and goods production. If you don't have the potential to extract certain resources in your land and you aren't in a customs union with someone who does produce that resource, you are going to need to trade for it (which is limited by your bureacratic capacity so not an unlimited option), or go about securing land that produces that resource, either via war or diplomacy. There is an argument that some resources are too common relative to history, which can make the game a bit too easy for huge nations, but for small and medium-sized nations the struggle to procure the resources you need to build your industry is real and engaging. And TBF in Vic2 if you had enough prestige you could just access goods from the global market anyways, so big nations are always easier in this sort of game if you know what you're doing.The consumer and industrial good production chains are also far more complex than in Vic2, and provide a constant need to think about how to balance and expand your industries to supply your market with needed goods. For example, in Vic2 if I wanted steel I would build a steel mill which consumed coal and iron from RGOs that I couldn't really interact with. In Vic3 if I want steel I have to build a steel mill which consumes tools, coal, and iron, which to produce everything efficiently requires a tooling workshop, iron mine, coal mine, chemical plant (for explosives in the mines), sulfur mine (for the chemical plant), logging camp (for wood for tools), railroads (for transportation of goods to improve efficiency), motor industries (so the railroads have trains), etc. It's much more in depth and requires more thinking on the part of the player to set up a successful economy since so many industries are co-dependent on each other in some way. I can see an argument that it should still be possible for capitalists to build industries themselves, it would certainly make things a little easier in the late game. That said, I don't think the player should ever be locked out of building factories like in Vic2 laissez-faire as it is a key gameplay mechanic that should have player agency. The interest group system is at a baseline the most interactive internal politics gameplay mechanic Paradox has created. Pops organize into IGs based on their needs, profession, strata, beliefs, etc. and those IGs pressure or support you as you try to implement or remove laws and policies. Depending on the social and economic structure of your nation, an IG that only represents 2% of the population might hold 30% of the power, as is not uncommon with landowners in the early game in many nations. The issue that remains here is balance. The actual mechanics are solid, but powerful IGs as it stands are not dangerous enough. Powerful and angry IGs need to be much more willing to revolt, right now they are too willing to stand by as they lose laws and policies they like. Even happy powerful IGs should occasionally come to you with demands if they think they can force the issue. But these are balance tweaks that can be made and the mechanics themselves work well. Diplomatic plays are a great idea and are just the evolution of Vic2's crisis system. It feels accurate to the era that powers can choose to jump in alongside a smaller nation if it serves their larger geopolitical interests even if they don't have an official alliance or pact. However, there are balance issues at play here, where it seems like currently major powers are a little too eager to jump in to help minor nations, particularly in the early game. This should probably be looked at and toned down a bit so that huge wars aren't breaking out over minor colonial conquests. Similarly, it would be nice if minor colonial conquests across the globe were treated a bit differently in the system compared to a nation trying to conquer a minor that borders a major power.I also like the ability to diplomatically influence nations into your customs union, joining them with your market. However, it does feel like there needs to be a way to "defend" your customs union diplomatically, as it stands you just have to hope that if you maintain good enough relations with them that they won't agree to join another major's customs union. This is undeniably the weak point of the game and where a lot of the complaints come from. For one thing, warfare is buggy, I've had generals unassign themselves from fronts randomly and other bugs that make war unnecessarily frustrating.Fundamentally though, this is the one area of the game where I think the mechanics need an overhaul as opposed to just tweaking and balance. I understand the move away from army micro as it did not represent early 20th century warfare well, but the new system lacks player agency as the fronts are all auto-generated and the player cannot direct their generals much beyond basic attack, defend, and stand by commands. What I would suggest is more of a "HoI4 light" system where the player can draw their own fronts if they wish and can direct attacks along specific approaches (battle planning essentially), manually garrison areas, create fall back lines to defend, etc. I don't think the return of army stack micro is truly necessary, but a better frontline system with more player agency is needed.The final thought I would note is that there is a valid complaint regarding lack of historical flavor for many nations. That said, I've always felt that mods were primarily what added flavor for Vic2, so it isn't that surprising. And nations do feel different to play already if they have different resource potentials, interest group power dynamics, and laws. With tweaks to how impactful powerful interest groups are, they would feel even more different. But I would certainly welcome more historical flavor myself.If you played Vic2 or other strategy games primarily for the economic components and internal politics, I would recommend Vic3. If you are more focused on war, I wouldn't recommend it for you at this time. Fundamentally it's a game with a solid economic, political, and diplomatic base that needs some tweaking to resolve its flaws, plus a larger overhaul of warfare.

Nice to include the power blocs as a new mechanic, being able to invest in puppet nations and the like; but late in the game all my trade is broken - trade routes just disappear seconds after setting them up despite meeting all requirements (shipping, bureacracy, good relations...)The game continues to provide some enjoyable moments if you're familiar with the franchise, but PDX, you seriously need to up your game because a year after release and the game still has game-breaking bugs because you released way too early. Stop the cash-grabbing and DLC spanning and get it together!***UPDATE to v.1.6.2-Some serious rebalancing across the game which is good, but should've been done earlier or even before launch: harder to push for dramatic changes or install communist govts; key nations (Prussia, USA, Russia...) have had their pressure groups rebalanced to better reflect historical path-dependencies (ie: haven't had much luck passing multiculturalism since update, while it was a given in previous versions)-Have not encountered NULL_STATE bugs so far...-NPCs no longer overwhelm a single province with infrastructure, maybe some over-investment but not as ludicrous as previous version-Some tweaks to warfare but continues to be lacking imo: path-finding continues to be a problem with armies relocating haphazardly when advancing or between fronts and this may lead to micro-managing or else risk losing a close call. On the plus side, there has been some streamlining in terms of upgrading units, assigning units and generals etc.For a newcomer and if you find a good deal, it may be worth buying if you're into the genre; but honestly it feels like PDX is still fixing bugs and updating the UI/UX well after launch and that just poor planning on their part.***Playing version 1.5.13 and several hotfixes later and yet some fundamental mechanics are still buggy or broken:- private investors will build dozens of power generating plants in a single province, hogging infrastructure and this good being now local thus needed across provinces and not in a single one;- pandemic and promoting migration events as the US continues to be buggy, on both I have either had NULL_STATE as target state or no migration at all respectively (bad script for both?);- warfare has been improved but remains a mistery: weird pathfinding, sea-adjacent territories are unreachable sometimes despite having ports and whatnot, armies will relocate to their HQ after closing a front instead of going to the nearest active front, so you can easily win or loose wars if you (and AI) don't micromanage those movements.These problems continue months after release, very disappointed to see Paradox releasing an unpolished game; they are getting there but they launched way too early and without testing.With all that, yes, it can be fun, but it's ruined once the bugs start popping up.

_childDocuments_.review: Really loved Victoria II, but I don't like Victoria 3 in its current state. Many of the core features from the previous game are absent, most noticeably player commanded armies and navies. The exclusion of player input in warfare was a really bizarre and jarring move to make, however I was hopeful that it would not end up being implemented poorly. After playing the game, I can definitively say that this change was a disaster. In addition to the lack of player input and agency in warfare, the AI which takes control of warfare is very stupid. It's frustrating to watch repeatedly as a Field Marshal with command of 100 units repeatedly attacks with only 20 or thirty of them against a superior force. I would much rather have had micromanagement in the game, albeit tedious and time consuming, over what was presented in this game. I also find uninteresting the core gameplay loop itself. It is not fun to click the build factory/railroad/port button over and over again just to watch a green number go up. Another important aspect of the game, technology, westernization and literacy are either entirely absent or severely lacking. The technology tree is a huge downgrade from the previous game, being much smaller and removing the discovery feature from the previous game. The ability to westernize when playing as an Asian or African nation was removed, now they start with the ability to build factories and railroads upon the start of the game, which just makes no sense. I can't think of anything at all that is done better in Victoria 3 that wasn't done better in Victoria II. tl;dr : I hate libtards

_childDocuments_.review: You cannot control almost any aspect of warfare, no unit movement on the map. the economy is broken because capitalists do nothing but donate money to a govt controlled investment pool. you have to build everything yourself. You have to make trade agreements for all trades so no organic international economy. Pops can't be influenced directly. Do not buy, this is in my opinion the worst paradox title. The fanbase was ignored every step of the way. this is a DLC bait and switch pump and dump. they are going to nickle and dime you for the next decade to make basic features that worked in Vicky 2. If you want a better game get vicky 2 or a Vicky mod for HOI4. Vicky 3 takes the grand out of grand strategy.

_childDocuments_.review: There is some wild analysis from folks giving negatives that is clearly "I don't know how you know that because you couldn't have accomplished that in your hours." I simply don't believe you played a thorough Russian game to revolution by 20 hours with everything else you're mentioning in the same review.I've been waiting for this game for a decade. I was a fan of 2 and its mods. I even played the original Victoria. I think the economic and society aspect are the most fleshed out elements of this game and in fact an absolute upgrade from Victoria II. Interest groups, legitimacy, etc, is simply done better here as well as managing pops in relation to them. The pop system here too is a vast improvement and can be more directly handled. I build factories not so much for the production, but for preferred pops with my goals.I think the diplomatic plays are an incredibly new and interesting means of playing. It makes wars far more interesting and higher stakes. It feels like you wage war significantly less than compared to Vicky 2, but the war is a lot more meaningful. The combat itself is simplified and irrelevant, but the generals, the research, and the allies are that much more important. I successfully unified Scandinavia with three diplomatic plays, only one of which resulted in a war. I do think the AI needs to be better about standing its ground, but that's an easy improvement to expect from Paradox. I think the Radical V Loyalist aspect is interesting and that there could've been a better term to use than Radicals, especially considering with how that term is used in other parts of the game. It makes revolution and internal politics a lot more dynamic to which I've had a fun time. I ruined the legitimacy of my government by removing landlords and the church, but I provoked them into a civil war that decimated them and then decades later when I finally initiated party politics + killing the King, my legitimacy shot through the roof. It took about 20+ in game years and it was worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Lately, apart from HOI4, paradox has been kinda slow, even unpolished with the other 4X titles.I never played Vicky 2, but I had high hopes for this game and kept up with all the dev diaries.The promise of Victoria 3 was a deep economic and diplomatic game with some wars and rp on the side.Sadly, it only partially delivers on the economics front and absolutely blunders on all of the others.It doesn't feel like a 4X game very much and I'd rather compare it to some resource management heavy city builders.And that part is actually very fun and addicting for me, even if it doesn't really accomplish the feeling they were going for."Diplomatic plays" and "non-micromanaged frontlines" in wars have potential but are absolutely terrible currently. Unreasonable amount of rng, unclarity when it comes to mechanics and lack of control even when you do understand what's happening in them.I'm 100% convinced that the choice to give achievement in non-ironman mode was made because they knew the wars are nearly unplayable and it's unreasonable to ask you to go with it.The amount of country/region specific events is laughable, it has to be the worst one from paradox yet.Internal politics is mostly just waiting for 10-20% chance rolls to pass laws.Other reviews mention the upcoming DLCs and fixes but I'm worried that's not coming.Imperator had mixed reception like this, and it's just abandoned now.CK3 was good, but not a money maker like HOI4 is and therefore has gotten 1 real DLC and couple minor ones in 2 years.Sadly, I think Victoria 3 is now about as good as it's going to get.But still.. there just isn't much competition in the genre, and especially with the setting and gimmicks Victoria 3 has, and playing without warring is actually viable.And while others might disagree, I think Vicky 3 has the best looking 3d map so far.All in all, if you like games with "grain number go up - i build mill - pop happiness go up - i build workshop" -type gameplay and are willing to put up with or avoid cancer war mechanics, maybe get it at 50% off.I'll probably keep playing it on and off but for now especially for the price:2/5.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: To update this review, I feel the game has finally reached a point where bugs aren't interfering with the gameplay experience.---This was a hard one. I *really* like the concept of the Victoria franchise, going through one of the most rapid periods of advancement in human history and seeing the growth of living standards, the uplifting of the world out of starvation and poverty through forces of industry and productivity - empowering the people by moving the source of power away from landownership and to the labour of workers and proper management of capital.These same forces that brought about a scramble for resources, to fuel that very same industry - an era of empire.At the same time, every time I play issues pop up, usually not game breaking, but big enough to be both infuriating and put a damper on the gameplay. It's been 18 months since the release of the game, and some parts are still a bit buggy and unfinished. I want to like the game, and to a large extent I do, but it's hard to recommend it to others until it gets *a bit* more finished.Still, the game provides excellent gameplay, and for the strategically minded player you're bound to have lots of fun - just beware the bugs.Hopefully this review will become a recommendation at some point - hopefully.

_childDocuments_.review: Economy is a hassle to manage as you have to go through a horrible UI to manually build it up. Auto-expand your buildings? Get a hiccup as the system has to think every - single - week for your orders. So the only mechanic that this game has that approaches good is a chore to play through.War? No thanks. You're limited to making only diplomatic plays to declare war. When you're targeting an outmatched foe, you cannot press all claims or war, only the initial demand that started the incident. So if you're playing as America, buttered up the big boys interested in USA-Land so they don't interfere, and decide to try to instigate something similar to the Mexican-American war, prepare to be disappointed. Pay infamy for more demands from Mexico, get ready for war, and when they back down they only give you the initial province and not the enormous concession that I'm PAYING to declare war for. Very bad.If you're paying infamy for war (even against non-nation tribes that you're colonizing) then in order to mitigate infamy buildup you actively don't engage in diplomacy so you have influence to get your infamy to go down to reasonable levels. This has made me not engage in diplomacy at large, so I can't really say whether or not I like it. Improve relations, that's about it for me.The exploration events are repetitive and boring as well. Came across a bug that the military leaders that I sent on the trip died, he gets automatically replaced, and even when the exploration finished that general remains "busy". A busy military leader CANNOT DO WAR. You cannot mobilize his troops, you cannot command him, or even retire him. Since military leaders are tied to regions, this hamstrung my military and ended my run. Events and internal politics are a joke. It is EASY to end slavery in the US, 2 to 5 years into the game. Guaranteed liberties as a home interest, then slavery abolished, then multiculturism enabled in the 1840s. In the US. Yeah. Work needs to be done on this game, a lot of work.

_childDocuments_.review: Make no mistake I was looking forward to this game. I love the series. I love the genre. But Paradox here done really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ UP. I hope the Devs fix this crap before it ends up like Imperator Rome or March of the eagles.So starting off:-The game crashes. A LOT. Paradox games usually require you to play for a minimum of 2 hours and the game crashes about every hour.-The game is too expensive for the currently implemented features. The only meaningful features of the game are economy and trading. I'll get to the features later.-MANY features that we have come to enjoy from grand strategy series such as a diplomacy and warfare are COMPLETELY shoved into the trash can and pushed over to the zoo corner with the abacus monkeys to develop.-Diplomacy. Gone are the spheres of influence, most nations won't accept your proposals because the "base reluctance" is MINUS 100 which is ridiculous even for a trade agreement! Heck, sometimes allies won't even join your wars, obligations mean nothing in this game and what's worse the subject nation management is atrocious, yeah I'm talking to you all EU4 players that love subject interactions, there's none here for you.-Warfare. Warfare is completely automated and bought over by Elon Musk and sent to Mars. Litteraly can't even phrase this any better. The generals are 90% of the time retarded and get encircled, admirals never seem to be able to naval invade for players and are also unable to protect YOU from naval invasions, but hey bro, we need 100 ironclads so better pay up. By far warfare is the most guttered aspect of this game. No occupation laws, no micromanagement, just giving the AI guns to fight your wars which is the dumbest idea ever.-Economy. Economy management is probably one of the better aspects of the game, allowing you to tax different goods in order to control prices, as well as enact economic reforms through the politics menu for pensions etc. Overall good work here.-Trading. Trading is mediocre at best. The AI buys off most of your stock so you end up with an order book of MINUS two THOUSAND of cloth so prices get insanely high. Build more clothes factories..? Nope. Russian AI will buy off ALL of your clothes anyway! And what the hell is up with this bug where I get notifications that my ports need extra convoys for trade routes while having over two thousand convoys available? Seriously. Did nobody backtest this before release?-Politics. Politics is probably the last part this game shines, allowing you to interact with different classes within your country, enacting religious and discrimination laws as well as pensions with different buffs or debuffs, overall good work here, would have been much nicer if you could change primary culture or religion like EU4.-Population mechanic. Don't even get me started on this one. People within your market will flock to whichever province you have available jobs for, I'm speaking to you. Yue culture in Wales. Yeah you. And don't get me started on how it's impossible to assimilate people from their homelands completely, I get it, you don't want cultures to go extict, then add a debuff for assimilation, don't disable it completely Jeez...-Conclusion. Essentially this game offers nothing to expand or improve upon other titles, it doesn't offer the combat of HOI4, it doesn't include the diplomacy of EU4, and it barely simulates the economy of the previous Victoria title. Paradox has only itself to compete here on this genre of games and they know it by pushing out unfinished games one after another. I really loved you Paradox. I used to play your games since I was 12. I was really amazed on how you were the only ones who could feed me this niche gaming experience I was longing for. And now you're starting to become just another company that cuts corners in order to generate more profit. I remember the loading screens "This game is dedicated to our fans". You used to have passion for your games, and you've disappointed us all.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is the long-awaited sequel to Victoria 2, a 12 year old cult classic. Although it was a buggy, janky, fundamentally broken mess, the economy of Victoria 2 was unique among games. It featured a closed loop economy, where every good bought or pound spent by one entity is a good produced or a pound earned by a different entity. The entire thing operated and changed by itself. You could not control it, only influence it. It had many bugs and design flaws, but it was a truly unique economic system for a videogame. The surrounding systems like diplomacy and war were simple and lazy, in the old Paradox style, but just functional enough.In comes Victoria 3. Looking at it as a sequel to Victoria 2, it disappoints in most ways. The unique economic system is gone, and the economy more closely resembles Anno. Your goal is to grow your economy using your construction sector, and your main activity is fixing the economic impacts of the last thing you did. Supply, demand, and prices change instantly. Nothing in your country happens without your input, and you have absolute control over every production building in your country. Making new buildings and changing how they operate is your primary gameplay loop, making you feel more like a middle manager than a country. While balancing production methods in every backyard moonshine-still is fun once as a small country, it devolves into tedious micromanagement quickly when playing anything larger than Liechtenstein.The only thing that happens without your input is other countries setting up trade routes, but this is mostly just infuriating. Because everything is in short supply and the AI is incompetent at growing their own economy, these trade routes mostly just steal your resources and rarely if ever sell you anything of substance. Protecting particular goods could have been an interesting gameplay mechanic, but it isn’t. You can’t stop a good from being exported. You can only embargo entire countries. So trade boils down to you trying to steal resources you’re short on, the AI doing the same, and you embargoing the AI if it starts stealing too many of yours. Devolving into isolationism becomes an appealing prospect, if only to remove the micromanagement and instability.Speaking of the AI: In typical Paradox fashion, it's terrible. As a result, singleplayer is a bland, sterile experience. You are playing in a sandbox with other kids, but the other kids are just balloons with faces drawn on them. It would be nice to believe that the AI will get better with some patches, but this is unlikely given the reputation of Paradox and Victoria 3’s game director. The AI nations in Victoria 3 are slow to grow, constantly in turmoil due to mismanagement, and regularly destroy themselves over the tiniest diplomatic disputes.Those diplomatic disputes are probably the one aspect where Victoria 3 actually has some interesting innovation. Most hostile interactions are no longer just a button, but executed through a ‘Diplomatic play’ mechanic involving all major powers with an interest in the region. Diplomatic plays are a neat concept, but they are sadly underdeveloped, and let down further by the bad AI. There is no real distinction between a small colonial engagement and major war in Europe. Both become plays potentially involving every country with an interest committing their entire army. It’s impossible to ensure a nation’s neutrality beforehand. If you plan to simply befriend the other powers, or convince them to stay out once it’s started, good luck. Friendly nations will turn on you in a heartbeat during a play, and major AI powers will join a diplomatic play for the most insane reasons. The US will fight to the death to defend Danish Holstein in exchange for an IOU. China will sacrifice millions to keep an Indonesian province out of Dutch hands because they were promised war reparations. The East India Company will happily fight a war against its overlord over some border dispute between Indian nations, before magically returning to being an obedient dominion once the war ends.This entire experience is wrapped up in a UI more hostile to the end-user than a suicide vest. Tooltips can be helpful, but the endless recursion of tooltips on your tooltips on your tooltips, ad infinitum, invokes an Escherian feeling of endlessness that makes you feel more lost than before you started. This wouldn’t be as bad if these tooltips did not contain important information that can’t be found elsewhere. The game will only tell you the most important information at a glance, such as the number of radicals in your country, but make it impossibly difficult to find out exactly who is radical and what caused it.Critics have said the game looks like a mobile game, and while this is unfair to the gameplay, the UI does lean heavily towards modern mobile-friendly UI trends. Lists and tables are frowned upon, while grid layouts are preferred whenever possible. The amount of information allowed on the screen at any one point is extremely limited, forcing you to constantly swap between windows. Multiple lists simply can’t be sorted at all, and no list ever takes up more than a third of your screen width. A full screen table with all the information you could want is anathema. Buttons are large, and the UI scaling is very high by default, unless you have a widescreen monitor, in which case it defaults to unreadably tiny. The game defaults to tree maps instead of pie charts, suggesting that the UI designer had some very strong personal convictions about design without necessarily having the understanding of visual data comprehension to back them up.I have yet to mention the political system, because it hardly matters. Unless you are trying to change a particular law that’s affecting your gameplay, like isolationism, it’s possible to forget it exists entirely. The interest groups controlling your government do nothing to stop you from changing the economy and eroding their power, so the power of interest groups is just a result of what buildings you build rather than an interesting mechanic.Ultimately, the game is an exercise in making a line go up for the sake of the line going up. Every country plays exactly the same, and there is no real payoff at the end. Warfare could theoretically provide something to work towards, but the war system is so barebones, clunky, and dysfunctional that warfare is more frustrating than fun. There is no micromanagement of units, as that system has been replaced with automatic AI fronts, but fronts split, merge, and disappear so much that the micromanagement is somehow just as annoying. Since the fighting happens automatically, wars are heavily affected by arcane mechanics behind the scene that the player can’t see or interact with, such as the number of troops that participate in a battle, or the direction a general advances. The reward for dealing with this system is often lackluster, since wargoals are decided during the diplomatic play phase and cannot be altered during the war.Victoria 3 isn’t a terrible game per se. It is simply mediocre as a game, and bad as a Victoria sequel. If it had been an early-access indie game for 30 euros with a different name, it would have been received very well, with praise for some of its innovative ideas and its potential. As a released full-price sequel to a cult classic developed by a major studio, it is disappointing. The arguments about its potential ring hollow in the context of a studio known for selling buggy, half-baked products that had potential but failed to deliver.If you are looking for a complex economic simulator, this isn’t it. If you are looking for a game focused on diplomacy and war, this also isn’t it. If you are looking for a cute Anno-style economy game that you can play with friends so you can bicker over who ate all the tools in the market, this is actually alright, though buggy and overpriced.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Its a good game, but it has its issues.First of all, the way paradox does DLCs and the like: Keep content behind a paywall that should be in the base gameThe wars feel boring and very easy as soon as you have the slightest technological advantageEvery state eventually becomes a social democracy welfare state, with no bonusses for autocratic governments except for authority, something you wont even need if you raise SoL high enough and enact proportional taxes.The best way to raise SoL in impoverished states is to offer jobs. If your products become too cheap and their wages plummet, export that good to raise the price at home, the improvement in wages cancels out the extra domestic cost.This time period (1836 - 1936) was just an enormous hog measuring contest between all the european powers, so there are so much interesting possibilities, but the system isnt fleshed out (yet)These can all be fixed or improved, which will happen over time. Currently some mods are already fixing a lot of stuff, thanks to the great modding scene as is custom in all paradox gamesIt has a great foundation to start upon, and I look forward to what the game will be like in a couple of years.

_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Its a paradox game, it will have bugs and issues at release if that bugs you then wait but if that's not a issue for you then buy the game. _childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like all paradox games, with issues. I think that they have put forth a novel idea that they are willing to work on and improve over time and that's the bargain that you should understand going forth with this game. It's not completely mapped out and over time they will release dlc that will make the game feel more whole. If that's not for you then it's not. If you are ok with that then you will have fun with an interesting strategy game with a fun internal politics simulator and interesting class based fun. The game feels like you are running a society and trying to steer the forces within to shape what you want while battling with the outside world. I give this a recommendation but only if the above mentioned things interest you.

_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Before you play: This is a society-builder game, not a wargame. That is why Victoria 3 is unique.Please, consider feeding your pops and do not act quickly to wage war. It is bad in long-term. Because, just like in real life, war is bad, and war shouldn't be an option at all. War is just a result of a bad diplomacy. A successful diplomacy and economy is the most important factor for a prosperous nation.The rest? Well, you know what to do...
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: After pumping in nearly 60 hours I do enjoy the game and would recommend it to any paradox enjoyer. The first few hours were allot of fun, especially when playing with friends. Figuring out the economic system and the political system was a very entertaining process for me, like figuring out a puzzle and finally reaching the point where you can make the GREEN LINE GO UP was very satisfying. I love the economics system and how everything goes into impacting your population, every decision you make feels like it has a real impact on the state of your nation, and expasion while really good for economy can have some very negative long term effects if your not careful which I love. There is atention to nearly every aspect of what you do and each layer makes it a very thoughtfilled game. There are some negatives to the gameThe war system needs workThe UI and information tabs could do with not being as flipping through different pages The Ai's ability to reach historical borders and keep up with the playerREVOLUTIONARIES EVERYWHERE (Could be a skill issue)Give upgrading building a automatic button so I don't have to go through it every time I expand or incorporate new territory.We need a way to see what resources are where allot easier, at least I don't particularly like the map system they have in place. I do find myself going AFK while im not at war and just building up my industry, there needs to be more to do in the intermittent period. The war system is OK to me, it definitely needs some changes to make it more interactive and I don't fully understand how the game decides how many units are thrown into a battle and thats something that has really annoyed me so far. I do like the premise of a more hands off war system myself, but I don't want it to be on the level of Stelaris wars over planets as that is a very boring "send army, numbers go down, you won" I like that battles are not the main focal point of wars as much as a front line is, but even in Hoi4 you can interact and have a nice mix of Macro and Micro to keep yourself entertained. Theres also an issue of the diplomatic plays, its strange that it doesnt give you a better idea of whos going to join against you. It gives you a list of a bunch of majors (Depending on relations, infamy, etc) but it doesnt tell you the likelyhood of them actually joining and this had led to me being stuck in these draining wars over annexing my own puppets. Final ThoughtsThose are just some of the things I found but I really want to say, Its a paradox game, on release can always be rough, but unlike Imperator I do see this game being another amazing addition to paradox. Much like CK3 it has the base game to become really good it just needs more added to really flesh it out. I know how frustrating that is but thats the way these games have always been, there is no paradox game that is perfection on release, even HOI4 and EU4 were lacking on release but they are now some of the best grand strategy games out there if not THE BEST.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Lets be frank, you're either here because you've played paradox games before and wanted to see what Vicky 3 is all about (1) or you are a fan of the genre/era and wanted to dip your toes into a paradox game for the first time (2).1) If you've played paradox games before, then you know the formula. Paradox releases a game that is bland, bare-bones, and uninspiring. Mechanics are buggy, glitchy, or outright bad at launch. The game lacks content and we're left really wanting to like the game but ultimately being disappointed.- However, as paradox does, they add content, patch bugs, and put out a bunch of DLC that we later need to separate into "necessary to have a good time with the game" and "not really necessary but neat if you really want it". 1.5 added major updates and much needed fixes and new mechanics. 1.6 is promising much of the same. Eventually they'll start putting out DLC that I'll wait to buy on sale and it'll probably prove to be game changing and very enjoyable. It's just their MO, and it appears Vicky 3 is no different. For all it's worth- I personally enjoy the game in its current state, but I agree it is severely limited relative to its possibilities.2) If you've never played a grand strategy game and want to try a paradox game, Vicky 3 is a great place to start. It's one of their simpler games (for better or worse) and includes much of the UI quality of life that paradox has been nurturing over the years (such as nested tips). You'll probably enjoy this game a lot more than the average paradox fan (simply because you're not coming in with such expectations), and paradox is bound to add a lot more content in the future. Just be warned that paradox is known for gate-keeping a lot of instrumental content behind paid DLC. Do with that as you see fit. Overall: if you've read other reviews and you're still on the fence about it, just buy it. Clearly the current negatives haven't swayed your opinion, and they are bound to get addressed over time. If you're a paradox fan, this shouldn't be new to you. Don't let it stop you if you really wanna buy the game. Wait for a sale if you're not convinced. If you're new to paradox, know that these issues come with the territory of playing paradox games. The game is fun in its current state (opinion) and will probably only get better moving forward. If you're still not so sure, come back after 1.6 and see what's changed.**EDIT 02/07/2024For those new to paradox: I forgot to mention the incredible modding community paradox games usually encourage. The steam workshop typically has a lot of mods that improve certain aspects of the game until paradox gets around to dropping an official patch (many mods just add content to the game overall if that's what you're looking for)
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: The strategy gamer in me wants to tell you to look past all the crashes, all the bugs, the absolutely dreadful and arbitrary warfare mechanics, the totally railroaded cultural development mechanics, the random and poorly explained questlines that can completely ruin your game as the USA, the lack of a search feature or knowledge page for research. That part of me wants to tell you "It's a good 1800s economics and geopolitics simulator and that's what it should be".Unfortunately there is another part of me that has a sense of justice and a sense of right and wrong. There is a part of me that cares about abstract concepts like design and utility, and believes criticism is only helpful to others when it is objective. That part of me joined the "Victora 3 sucks" party, along with the software developer in me that knows when i have been given a late alpha build presented as a finished product, and the part of me that is sick and tired of screaming at the game for crashing when I do something as basic as "click the colonization option" and make a 6 hour save file unusable. Just like in Victoria 3's actually really good (if poorly explained) government system, I can't make those two sides of myself that love and hate this game work together. I have to kick the part of me that likes this game and wants it to be good out in order to write this review.Yes there are a lot of things in this game that work great. Yes there will be 4 expansions in 2 years over the course of which you will be paying extra money to make this game functional and fully featured (♥♥♥♥ that!). Yes I have played more than 50 hours. Yes, for a lot of this time I am having fun, especially when I'm playing Japan; a well-balanced country that's just begging to become an economic powerhouse and start slapping around european "majors". But, I just can't recommend this game to people who aren't passionate about this genre.The tutorial system that they have been hyping up is completely useless because it is mixed in with actual game mechanics that progress your story, politics, and economy; it's very hard to tell which of these are guidelines and which demand attention in order for you to do important things. The economics simulation is actually the least complicated thing about the game, it works decently and is engaging. The warfare is a mind numbing mess of micro, classic paradox "cat herding" that's even worse than HOI4 because at least in that game _sometimes_ units stay where you ask them to go.One last thing before I wrap up; the people online, ie. youtubers like iSorrowProductions and pontificators on le reddit, saying that they would rather play Factorio... They're entitled to their opinion (especially iSP who does this for a living basically), but I think that their criticism is not aimed well. Map games like this are there to help you construct a narrative around what you are doing. I just don't really enjoy straight up economics/production simulators like Factorio, and I should be able to enjoy this game (and I somewhat do). I really did enjoy beefing up Japan into a world power and then losing it all late in the game over a bad political gamble. That part works great, and is what shines in _all_ paradox games and separates them from games like dyson sphere simulator, factorio, etc. where it's just you and an economy waiting to happen. When those people criticize and lament this game in that way, it hurts both genres of games because it doesn't really address what's wrong with this game. Those games can't be what this game is, and vice versa, even if this game was perfect. What's wrong with this game is; it's crashy, the developers made poor choices with the tutorial system, the combat makes no sense and needs way too much micro for what it is, there are only 4 sound tracks in the game and you're forced to listen to "glory to the queen" while you fight a revolution to replace her, nonwhite people wear nothing but traditional clothes all the way through 1936 no matter how advanced your society is, etc etc etc. What's wrong with this game isn't that it's not Factorio, or hell it isn't even that it's not HoI4, Steallaris, or CK3, or even Vic2. What's wrong with this game is that it's a bad Vic3. That's it. Anyway, I preordered this game and it's a sunk cost, so i'm getting what enjoyment out of it that I can. But if you're on the fence and looking at reviews to help you make a decision on this game, I would say please don't buy it. Wait 2 years for the game to become playable and refined, and be sure to never pay full price. The developers who worked on it are nice, hard working nerds with metal band t-shirts, but their bosses and VPs and Execs and shareholders need to be punished for releasing this mess and the only way we can do that is through the market. How fitting!

_childDocuments_.review: Yesterday I played as Japan. Defensive pact with Russia. Civil war pops, the revolt is hilariously outgunned, Russia only sends one stack of 8 to help. Civil war lost. This time, same story. Defensive pact with Russia, Korea, Austria, and Spain. Spain won't join, Russia sends a stack of 8, Austria sends a stack of 16, Korea just doesn't send anyone at all, and landowners who are only at 30% support magically have 80% of our armed forces and plow through us. Civil wars are currently unwinnable and frankly after the direction Stellaris, EU4, and every other paradox product has taken, I'm considering just not supporting them as a company going forward. It isn't even a matter of bugfixing and balancing following a new patch, because they don't fix long-standing issues regardless of the game. Several years of a Stellaris bug which just makes your ships stop attacking for no reason is what I have to look forward to in this game in the future as well. Most people complain about the price of supporting them, with outrageous DLC prices, but to me it's not the DLC prices that are the problem, it's the amount of development time spent on trying to sell their products and the lack of time on basic quality control that's driven me away. Paradox has adopted the sales strategy of taking a big obnoxious flashing sign that looks like what's underneath it must be really fun, and then pointing it directly at a latrine. The more you understand how these games work on a technical level the more you should hate them.

The allure of virtual worlds and captivating narratives intertwines with my very existence, captivating my senses and transporting me to realms beyond imagination. The joy of grasping a controller, feeling its weight in my hands, is like a symphony playing in perfect harmony.From the pixelated wonders of retro classics to the breathtaking landscapes of modern masterpieces, video games have the power to ignite my passion and ignite my soul. They have become a canvas for creativity, where artists and storytellers weave intricate tales that can move me to tears or make my heart race with excitement.The immersive experiences they offer are unparalleled. The way a game envelopes me in its universe, allowing me to become someone else, to embark on grand adventures or solve intricate puzzles, is a feeling of pure bliss. name: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey
detailed_description: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey is a third-person open world survival game where you Explore, Expand, and Evolve to advance your clan to the next generation in this exhilarating new adventure from Panache Digital Games. Embark on the most incredible odyssey known to humankind: human evolution. Spanning from 10 million to 2 million years ago, begin your journey, before us, in Neogene period Africa. Explore a beautiful yet ruthless world, from swinging through tree branches in the jungle to stalking prey across the golden savannah grasslands. Decide what attributes to learn and hone in order to pass down knowledge to future generations, from crafting tools to enhancing evasive tactics against predators. Just like real life, make sure to eat, drink, and sleep to stay alive and have the energy to face any danger that may come your way. Grow your clan and find strength in numbers as you progress through critical evolutionary stages of human evolution. Your choices will write your clan’s story and determine if you can survive your evolution. Explore Ruthless Africa Explore the never-before-experienced world of Neogene Africa starting 10 million years ago at the dawn of humankind. From the tops of tree canopies overlooking lush jungles to the golden grasslands of the savannah, traverse a beautiful yet unforgiving landscape. For every breath-taking view, beware of the weather, predators, and other dangers that threaten your survival. Expand Your Territory and Grow Your Clan Increase your chances of survival by uniting new members of your species and giving birth to future generations. Control different clan members, form bonds to create families, and work together to intimidate predators during expeditions. Conquer fear as you explore unknown locations in order to expand your territory. Evolve Through Multiple Generations See the physical and intellectual evolution of the first hominids as you explore, learn, and survive. Spanning from 10 million to 2 million years ago, play as one of the first hominids and evolve over the course of millions of years during key stages in human evolution. Make crucial discoveries and hone physical abilities that will be passed down to future generations such as Ardipithecus ramidus and Australopithecus. Choose How You Survive Evolution was not written in stone. Your decisions shape how you will overcome obstacles, increase your species, and what knowledge will pass on to future generations. Focus on specific attributes or choose a more balanced approach to survival. Your clan’s ability to survive will be directly impacted by your choices, making each player’s experience unique.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most fun, but at the same time frustrating games I have ever played. I love the game for it's core idea of showing the evolution of the primates to the early stages of hominids and as your tribe of apes evolves and develops various new neurons, skills and mutations, so does the player discover and learn new techniques and tools to help yourself survive in Africa of the late Miocene and early Pleistocene. The graphics are gorgeous, all different terrains from the deepest jungles to savannahs and desert are a pleasure to behold and the different types of wildlife, predators and plants make the world feel alive.The main problem with the game is that a lot of times while exploring with your clan someone gets left behind, sometimes even the whole group (this happened when I climbed up to the Tree Father, all my apes kept on hanging in the treetop like, well, apes). I lost hours to backtracking and trying to find all individuals, especially when they are females carrying infants with mutations, but sometimes I never found them. This is beyond tedious and who knows what the developers were thinking, because this could have been easily fixed by making clanmates respawn in your camp. Sure, not a very realistic way of keeping your clan together, but way better than this buggy mess. The gameplay can also be a bit tedious at times and you will have to do a lot of things over and over again which at times feels like a chore. Also the gameplay mechanics of switching generations and evolving are far from self-explainatory and since the game doesn't hold your hand in any way, some of the functions are downright cryptic and you will probably mess up your first run in some way or another, so I highly recommend on reading into that matter to save yourself the loss of time and nerves. Overall a great game and I had a lot of fun, but boy could the gameplay have used some polish.
_childDocuments_.name: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey

_childDocuments_.review: This game offers an extremely unique experience like nothing I have ever played. It may not be for everyone but for those that love exploring and figuring things out on their own this is fantastic.  Some of the tutorials could do with way better descriptions as they can be extremely vague and sometimes just simply not helpful (thank god for google and the internet though).The tutorial/info based stuff aside I honestly don't understand how this game doesn't have a 90%+ rating or higher. I really don't. Truly a unique experience and it costs less than a lot of the crappy AAA garbage released.I don't fully know exactly how far this game goes or how much time it takes to beat it because of how little info in really gives you, like I said before with the tutorials the lack of specific info most of the time really adds to the experience of the game but some of the time it just makes you think.. okay.. this should have just been said.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little open-world survival game. I went in blind and only searched up things when I was utterly stumped once or twice, which was quite fun. But it was a bit hard in some cases, especially with the QTEs I really didn't get how to do the various versions for a long time, and my poor apes got hurt so often, lol. The in-game guides are hazy at best, but I suppose that was part of the difficulty "figure it out naturally" vibe the developers were going for. The gameplay loop became a little rote and boring by the second to last/last evolution because I had explored everything, so I was mostly just grinding out neurons just to change generations and evolve. One gripe I had used the Intelligence search so much that Scent (food was too plentiful to need to search this way) and Hearing (with a good eye and ear, it's easy to spot predators from far away) became almost useless, but that may be because I played on the easiest difficulty. A little sad that it ends so abruptly instead of letting me play infinitely as the last evolution (instead re-loading me to before I evolved), but it's understandable. Overall, a good 4/5 stars from me. Got 50+ hours out of me and I regret nothingmonke

_childDocuments_.review: I really really wanted to like this game, and I kind of do. Unfortunately it feels unfinished with limited a core gameplay loop, clunky mechanics, and a desire to hide all this behind an unforgiving, and unrewarding, progression system. Ancestors looks great and exploring the primitive jungle and the other various environments is definitely one of its strongest features. Swinging through the canopy and leaping across ravines as an angry ape with a sharp stick is one of the main reasons why I was interested in this game and oh boy does it deliver in this regard. The controls are a bit lack luster, especially if you happen to be using a mouse and keyboard, I frequently found myself jumping in the wrong direction or not at all resulting in a missed grab and a whole days delay as I patched up my hominid. However I still found the movement system to be fairly robust and one of the games stronger features.My main issue with this game is the lack of diversity in progression. Generally speaking you have to perform specific actions a certain number of times to strengthen the neuronal connections before spending neural energy to unlock the next locus. This presents a fairly significant grind, especially when your neurons are reset between generations or evolutions but is especially tedious when you consider the limited mechanics presented in your options. Every bit of crafting, called “altering”, in the game is composed of holding the correct two items in your hands and holing down a button until you receive a prompt. There are a few interesting options but this system is creatively limited by the sheer lack of recipes in the game. Most recipes are strictly linear. There is one type of of wood in the game, a dead branch, which can be turned into a stick and then sharpened. That’s it. The deepest recipe in the game with the exception of opening a coconut. This contributes to a general lack of progression. Within a half hour you can sharpen a stick and have the best “weapon” in the game no matter your current evolution. Access to food and other resources is similarly shallow. You might need a simple tool like a stem to get honey or termites but other than that there isn't much in the way of innovation or creativity here. The game tries very hard to hide this behind obfuscated mechanics and no instruction or tutorial but as a result the game just feels even more shallow. There just aren’t that many options for interaction so trying in vain to find what specific set of objects in which hand will result in the desired outcome just ends up undercutting whatever sense of achievement or discovery the devs were going for. Additionally clunky fear and path-finding mechanics mean trying to organize an expedition with a troop of your fellow hominids is more an exercise in frustration than cooperation.The concept is definitely here and they have strong bones to make an interesting and comprehensive game, but this isn't early access so what we have is what we get and unfortunately it just isn't worth the money. If you have a thing for beautiful handcrafted environments and vertical game play then you can definitely get some mileage out of this but if you are looking for a genuine survival experience you’d be better served somewhere else.
