_childDocuments_.review: A longtime interest in anthropology and having recently read Yuval Harari's  prompted my eager purchase of this when I noticed it on sale. I'm not disappointed; it's been an incredible imaginative vehicle against the informational backdrop of that book. My takeaway: whether you're a kid who grew up on a stack of s or you're just a hard-nosed open-world-survival-craft buff, this one's for you. On sale.  game mechanics, from genetics to teaching offspring, are thoughtfully and uniquely developed. The world is immersive, the risks are believable, and the evolutionary tree is an excellent motivator. I'm really blown away by the nutritional food system and the nuanced depiction of "unknown danger." And while I understand from other reviews that the narrative development (not that there really is one) can be slow and ultimately becomes open-ended, I've thoroughly enjoyed the experience so far. I don't need another .  In fact, I'm kind of looking forward to going nowhere with this. After all, it's nonfiction, and the ultimate conclusion of this human species drama is... exactly what I'm doing in this present moment.One critical note: Since the controls can be a little sticky and there's such a learning curve to survival, do yourself a favor: keep the tutorials with full HUD at the game's start.

_childDocuments_.review: Go back! I want to be Monke! This game defines this idea. If you're not ready to be a clueless ape fighting for your survival in a Jungle for 3 hours then you're not ready for this game. That being said, this game performs that function extremely well. You scavenge, climb, and fight your way through ancient Africa as a common ancestor. It does give tutorials for some things, but for the most part you're on your own to bang rocks together and lead your ape troop how you see fit. The one thing that I would add to this game that we probably won't see due to the construction of the game is a multiplayer setup. I would love to see an option to play co-op and play side by side with your friends. This would make certain aspects of the game easier, such as hunting. The ape AI is pretty lack luster and despite them having the ability to attack the enemy after certain evolutions, they rarely do. Having a friend would make this easier despite the fact that it's not too hard if you plan correctly. Still nothing would be beat being be able to do monkey stuff with a friend.

_childDocuments_.review: Rigid and slow. Many game mechanics wipe out 30 minutes or an hour of effort with nothing you can do to avoid it (evolution leap sent my clan back to the first settlment repeatedly). Repeatedly had a tiger pin a clan member, every time I got close enough to distract the tiger, my clan member just stood up and didn't move, just to get pounced on by the tiger again. I've had saves delete clan members, kept getting knocked back to 2 adults. Sooo many annoying features, everything about the reliance on and utilizing senses is just a boring grind. You have to be visiting the wiki to figure out the mostly nonsensical crafting (the dev apparently takes pride in not guiding you, leaving you to evolve and grow by yourself).It is pretty immersive. There's some pretty neat unorthodox story-telling going on here. If you're in the mood to sip tea and wander around an ancient, dangerous jungle, then this has some merit. Otherwise, don't be enticed by the pretty screenshots.

_childDocuments_.review: Terrible game. At least 3/4 of it is spent doing tedious tasks and chores. A better title for this game would be "Tedium: doing the same thing over and over while hoping something good happens!"The Good:well... I don't know. For about 10% of my play time I thought I knew what I was doing and it was mildly fun. That's all I can say for the good.The Bad:No tutorial whatsoever. There is a Tutorial option. I selected it. It said "we will not give you much help, explore the world for yourself!" ummm... thanks?I only reached the third "task" that you can receive in the game. Are there more? I have no idea, but I'll bore you with my extremely boring game play!Opening cutscene: you are an adult carrying an infant. A bird grabs you and your child falls. You are flown to the birds nest and fed to the babies. Camera switches to the infant you now control.First task: Find a hiding spot!I find the hiding spot without much trouble. A big rock. I approach big rock. Nothing happens. No tutorial tips, keep in mind I selected the tutorial option, no hints, nothing. That's not true, there is danger music and visuals implying you are scared. I stand right next to big rock, nothing happens. Maybe the hiding spot is on the other side? I circle the rock, nothing happens. I get on top of the rock. Nothing happens. Welp, sorry little ape, you will probably be eaten by the bird. Except you can't switch characters or do anything else. Great, so I keep circling and jumping on top of the rock while thinking this is a terrible start to the game. Eventually I somehow get the little idiot into the hiding spot. First ten minutes wasted traveling a few paces and trying to figure out how to get into the hiding spot. Great start ughSecond Task: Find the lost child!You are automatically switched to an adult of your tribe. With absolutely no help whatsoever even though the tutorial option was chosen, you are tasked with finding the idiot child that couldn't be bothered to just jump into the hiding spot. 15 minutes of wandering around with absolutely no help from the game, trying to figure out the controls and hoping to find some kind of clue to where I am supposed to go, I find the dead body of the adult in a nest. Soon after I find my way to the child and have to take it back to the tribe. Again no help on how to get back, but I soon find a way back. Immediate cutscene: I honestly don't know what was supposed to be happening. I guess a meteor flew overhead?Third Task: Inspect a meteor!Let's just say that after about 20 hours of gameplay, I never found the meteor. Terrible controls. You are *supposed* to be able to jump from one tree to another, but you do not jump in the direction you are looking. I lost at least a half dozen apes to falls and never figured out the nearly random direction you jump. Somewhere between wherever you look and directly away from the tree. I don't know.The point: even though I selected the tutorial option, I was given absolutely no help at all and the first hour of gameplay was spent trying to figure out the basic controls of the game. That could possibly be forgiven, after all I will spend at least 100 hours on a decent game, so who cares if the first hour is all learning curve?Let's get to the biggest problem: How is your time spent?1/4 - Tedious mating1/4 - Eating, drinking, sleeping1/4 - Playing what might as well be a minigame called "What's in your hand and why are you carrying that??"1/4 - Exploring / being eaten by catsTedious mating:Yes, good old fashioned baby making. Why would such an activity be considered tedious and take 25% of your game time? Because the developers thought it would be fun I guess. You will need to do this every other day on average. Let's break it down into steps.Step 1: Find a suitable mate. Doesn't sound hard, does it? Find out if you are controlling a male or female, then search out one of your tribe that is a similar age of the opposite gender. This *should* be easy but it's not. The tribe seems to know what your intention is and will scatter to the winds, making you hunt them down. In order to find out what gender and mating status a member is, you must "inspect" them. Getting all three of my couples mated usually takes 5-10 minutes of tedious hunting and inspecting.Step 2: Groom. For some reason you must "groom" your new mate to actually form a couple. Several times without mistakes. Each mistake will require an additional success, further increasing the time you must spend on the whole tedious affair. Why not skip step one and just groom anyone you ask? Because you can groom siblings and same sex partners. I once wasted 10-15 minutes because I thought I was controlling a female, hunted the single male, finally found him, groomed him, made a couple, took him to the sleeping area, told them to mate, and- nothing. Huh, so far the first mating always results in a pregnancy, have I just been lucky? Mate. Mate. Mate. No pregnancy. Check the ape I'm controlling, it's male. ♥♥♥♥. I never switched away from the second male after getting him mated to the second female, now he's mated to the third male instead, so I have to get him mated to a female again, then go back and find the third male to get him to *hopefully* mate the third female. There is no indication or symbol to help you find a suitable mate, so after the first two couples are mated, you could find out that the third set are brother and sister, and incest is not allowed, so you have to rework your mated pairs.Step 3: Go to bed. Easy enough, assuming there are not any tribe mates near your sleeping area. If there are, you could have trouble focusing on the bed and not the tribe member.Step 4: Call mate. Not a big deal. Hit a button and wait. Sometimes only 5 seconds, sometimes the mate apparently sprints in the opposite direction after you groomed them and it takes up to 15 seconds. Keep in mind, you will have to do this twice for every mated pair. Since I had 3 mated pairs for most of the game, this means 6 times. so 30 seconds to three minutes spent getting an ape to bed and calling a mate.Step 5: Mate. Simple, hit one button, the camera will pan away for 5-10 seconds, and your female is pregnant.Step 6: Give birth. I recommend you wait until you have all your females pregnant as it will speed up this whole tedious process just a little bit. You will be switched to a cutscene that is about a minute long. You *can* skip it once you know the right button to push. In the lower left hand side of the cutscene there is a strange symbol and the word skip. I have no clue what the symbol is supposed to be. It is not any of the standard playstation or xbox remote control symbols, and after pushing every button on both my controller and the keyboard, nothing would make it skip this minute long cutscene that you need to do at least twice a generation, one generation every other day. What. The. ♥♥♥♥???? FYI that symbol that looks like two browser tabs open at the same time means "hold the back key on your controller for a couple seconds."Step 7: Repeat steps 3-6. Each female can have two children. No more. so, unless you want your clan to shrink, which means you will have to go through this whole mating process more frequently (explained later) you should always have every female put out two children.Again, this will take about 1/4 of your time. I feel this entire process could (and should) be automated. But it's not.Eating, Drinking, Sleeping:Our basic needs. Before setting out to explore you will need to take care of these things. Straight forward enough, you can expect it to take anywhere from 5-15 real life minutes per in game day. Combined with the mating every other day, you are looking at half your play time already, just doing chores. Expect 15-30 minutes per game day spent on these first to sections.I guess I've reached my character cap for a review. Just don't buy!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, this is "return to monke", the game. And that is totally fine by me. I've sunk a bit more time into the game now than I had initially, so I'll have more to add about its flaws... It starts fast of learning, slow of movement.  It works its way up to fast of movement, slow of learning. Still a bit too slow on both counts though.Trying to progress some of the neurons is troublesome as the devs are REALLY cagey about information.  They arrogantly present their cagey crap as a feature, but it is just annoying.  I'd rather a detailed walkthrough than all this "we're not going to tell you anything" bullsh!t. The controls are janky as hell but I've mostly got used to them.  Having got used to them doesn't make them any less janky though.  My fingers are in quite a bit of pain from playing this game every day for the last week or so.   Seriously, the controls are THE worst thing about this game.  They could have been so much better.   Like setting Left and Right to toggle the moods instead of having them activated while holding the shoulder triggers, which could have been dedicated to running or something (not only because holding A to run is a huge pain, but to free up the running from the jumping, as they should NOT be together). I even wrote a movement guide precisely because the controls are so janky and the devs so cagey with info. I figure some people might benefit from what it took me many hours to figure out on my own and wished I'd known from the start.Also there are some areas of the game that are dangerous for the wrong reasons... i.e. poorly programmed game mechanics rather than actual features.  Losing my monkes because the game  them  rather than next to me, causing them to be ambushed by a certain venomous cave predator where I couldn't even reach them, is NOT my idea of good game design.That said, despite the various flaws, I am technically still enjoying this game.That is to say I'm mostly enjoying monkeying out all over the place and being a silly sod because I have a juvenile sense of humour. I also like murdering various animals and leaving their corpses all over the place just because it feels good to be the top predator. This game, while ostensibly serious, is actually very silly in all the best chest-beating, screeching, monkey magic ways.  Also lots of pretty vistas.  The game world is very pretty, assuming you're not viewing it through the annoying motion blur or temperature-triggered vignettes.
_childDocuments_.name: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey

_childDocuments_.review: This is surprisingly probably the absolute best game I have played.  I will go into further detail about it later, but I can say that if you need to zen and just find your pack...THIS is the game you want to find!  There might be a walkthrough, but I would recommend NOT using one ... your pack will change accordingly ... you will either find yourself in sync with your pack or you will find yourself as a single explorer.  Either way, it's a new adventure everytime you play. _childDocuments_.review: The game and it's concept are BEAUTIFUL and I just LOVE it. BUT. The implementation of the game mechanics is unfairly clumsy and I would've enjoyed this SO MUCH MORE if the experience was overall more polished.Anyway, just so I'm clear with my thumbs up, I really recommend this game to anyone that likes original, intriguing and immersive experiences and/or liked Desilets's Assassins Creeds far more than any others that came after them. Why? Because they where genuinely thought out out of passion and both artistic and intellectual ambition.SoI get why there is a lack of guidance for the player. I love the focus and I found the game really really enjoyable. Is ment to be immersive (as I understand) and it has been for me so far. The concept of the game itself I believe it is superb.NowThe AI of the NPCs is very clumsy and I personally found the control of the main character not as realiable as I think it should be, concerning the situations and dangers you are brought into... which they are, more often than not, too complex for the solutions to them that the game offers.As I understand, the game is supposed to be realistic. You know: a monkey in the jungle, among saber tooth tigers, pythons and crocodiles...!? That is dangerous. The game is trying to transmit that tension. That's why it is hard on the player. But a lot of the times I have felt ENRAGED, because the control you have over the monkey is very limited when you are being attacked and NPCs behave even worse in these situations. It feels like when Altair wouldn't jump in the direction you where pointing to. Ahh... those're some memories.There was one situation, after the first evolution process was done, I was in a new settlement and I had to guide some monkeys that where lost in the jungle. And then two tigers come. Is not just that the NPCs couldn't deffend themselves; they wouldn't even try to get away!! They would be eternaly struggling with the tiger until I came along.As far as I'm concerned, Desilets (main creative mind behind the game) tries to get away from mechanics that feel "gamey", like combat mechanics or maps full of icons and such. I wholeheartedly respect that, I love that focus of creating a "virtual experience" rather than "another" videogame. But I think, in this particular case, the character should have a bit more control options. I don't know. If you have a stone, you should be able to hit the beast, right? Or have more control on escaping or helping others.And yes, it is ment to be an "experience", but STILL, there ARE "gamey" features in Ancestors. You are supposed to find your own way, but in the same time, the game is giving you quests to accomplish. Some things don't work well either in this regard. Between "you're on your own" and "this is your mission" focuses, there are colissions.An exampleI found some monkeys and convinced them to join the clan before the quest that pushed me to "meet a stranger" for the "first" time was given to me. The game would not recognise that I already did that, so I'd have to find more strangers... but there where no more strangers nearby. So I started to explore further and further and further... like REEEALLY far (still didn't find any) until there was no more adults left in the clan (... because they where killed mercilessly by merciless beasts).Also, I don't get how the little ones grow up. Should I just play for years until they do? Because if I decide to evolve I just start with a completely different clan.So, anyway.That's a lot of complaining here, complaining that I still think is a bit justified BUT I still recommend the game to anyone that wants something different and likes immersive experiences......................................................................NEW NOTES / EDITED: I discovered how to counterattack. I found the mechanic very difficult to figure out at first... but now that I know, the game becomes much more rewarding. I still think the main problems are NPC's AI and clumsy playability... but man, overall, I really enjoyed the game......................................................................There are more situations where the game works than the ones that don't. I think that this game is actualy very interesting, very rewarding when it works and inspiring really. Making a game like this is risky and I very much respect the ambition of the developing team. In fact, this is the kind of game I like, really. I'm so f@#!g tired of the Triple A industry.The concept of ANCESTORS, The Humankind Odyssey and what I believe it is aiming for, WORK. It's original and ambitious and I LOVE that there are veteran developers making this kind of games. They just need to polish the idea. I'm eagerly looking forward for the next game.

_childDocuments_.review: 9.3/10Without a doubt the greatest experience I've ever gotten out of a game so far. A hidden, underappreciated, and underrated gem. I'm of course going to be biased here since paleoanthropology and primatology have always been personal interests of mine.Even the concept by itself is shamelessly unique, but Panache really pulled out all the stops with executing it as well. I honestly wish I could forget the experience to play it again entirely blind. The aesthetics, the unorthodox and challenging gameplay mechanics, the expansive and exceedingly detailed setting in Miocene Africa, the lack of guidance provided to the player, all of it has clearly been thoroughly thought out and near-flawlessly executed. Everything works in tandem and forces the player to think like their ancestors in order to survive. The player needs to explore, expand, adapt, and evolve, if they want their lineage to continue.My biggest piece of advice into anyone looking to play this masterpiece of a game is to look up as little as possible. Learn as much as you can through personal experimentation, observation, active thinking to solve the situation you find yourself in - and to some extent, trial and error. Potential downsides for some: Somewhat grindy (I don't mind this personally but many do); almost no direction given to the player, they are left to do their own exploring and learning of the sometimes unintuitive mechanics (this is a feature I actually adore, given how well it simulates the confusion and survival mentality of ancient Miocene apes, but I can certainly see why it might put off a lot of people); and very little replay value (this is the one that really stops it from being a 10/10 for me, playing the game a second time will never truly feel close to the first time I explored the map and learned new mechanics). All in all, a fantastic game. Look up as little as possible, and give this one a try, especially if you're into anthropology, human evolutionary history, and more science/history oriented games.Some suggestions for improvement:1. Randomly generated environments. While the map in this game is absolutely huge and by itself presents a challenge and visual spectacle for the player, it can become repetitive once you're already familiar with it. This is especially problematic for players who have explored the entire map and haven't yet finished the game - or players revisiting the game after having finished it before (this links back to what I said before about replay value). This game would 100% benefit from at least having an option for a randomly generated or semi-randomly generated environment. Even just adding this for the Survivor difficulty would be an amazing addition to the game without many downsides.2. Dynamic environments. Another minor issue I see with the game - although this is something that honestly didn't bother me while playing it, since the player is always moving through biomes which present new gameplay mechanics, challenges, and force the player to adapt in order to survive - is that while the player's clan evolves, the biomes do not. If at the end of the game, you choose to return to an older biome, nothing has changed, none of the animals have undergone any kind of evolutionary shift or counter-adaptation to the player, which might come off as unrealistic or a jarring waste of potential to some players. This is less of a problem and more of a missed opportunity, I suppose.3. Actual difficulty variation. The difficulty options when starting a game are rather shallow and deceiving, in that the only changes they actually offer are reduced UI (or no UI at all). There's no way to increase how deadly your adversaries are, or to increase the difficulty of accessing new skills/species. Ultimately this game would benefit from a more challenging mode wherein even experienced players will have a hard time surviving.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is phenomenal.  If you find prehistory / paleontology interesting and want to try a game where you explore a representation of what the world may have been like a few million years ago, this is by far the best example I've seen at actually doing it.  It's incredibly immersive, putting you in control of an early hominid in a gorgeous but dangerous world, giving you next to no guidance with threats everywhere.  You have to learn how to use anything & everything to survive; it's one of the few exploration-focused games that manages to make simple things like coming across a new type of fruit interesting because you have to figure out what to do with it - you might need to get a rock to break it open, or if you aren't familiar with how its color changes at different stages of its ripeness then you might get food poisoning by eating a rotten one.  And almost everything you do gives you progression - walking, using tools, healing injuries, dodging attacks, hearing predators, smelling food (yes, really), etc., all of them can unlock that next ability that then branches out to more potential abilities.  It's incredibly addicting just trying to figure out what the next ability unlock requires (as the game doesn't completely spell it out to you, instead giving hints that often make you wondering if you just need to do the action a few more times or if you're totally off track).I can't recommend this game enough if you have any interest in ancient life, enjoy exploration games, or just want to try something totally new and difficult to compare to almost any other game I've ever played.  It perfectly combines a very unique progression system with an exploration style that focuses on the minute details of figuring out how to use simple objects found throughout the world instead of relying solely on spectacle, and that gives it a truly distinct feel (though don't worry, there's still plenty of spectacle too, mostly from reaching new environments & finding new wildlife - there's nothing quite like journeying from the safety of the jungle trees to the open savannah and coming across a Miocene Elephant for the first time).

_childDocuments_.review: BLUF: Don't even bother. UI is bad, controls are clunky, game is not intuitive, graphics are dated.So many issues with this game that I have no idea where to start. I guess I'll just start with when you first start up the game.1. When you open the game for the first time it automatically assumes you're using a game controller, even if you've never had a controller within 50 yards of your computer, let alone installed.  You then have to reset everything before you even get past the start menu. Not a good omen.2. So, now you've sorted out the basic UI, you go to start your first game, and then have to wait a good 10-15 minutes through the unskippable opening credits. And i'm not talking about an even slightly interesting cut scene to get you into the mood of the game. No! it's a black screen with elevator music, with the names listed of everyone who delivered pizza to the developers while they made the game.  You know you're almost going to be able to play the game when the pretentious claim that it's a true story comes on the screen.3. Now that you've rolled your eyes into the back of your head, you might as well keep them there for a little bit longer.  The next cut scene highlights the finest graphics from 1995 as you watch a comically large eagle effortlessly lift two apes hundreds of meters into the air at once.  Didn't I just say this is based on a true story? oh well.4. Now you're finally into the game and able to control a character.  Your first job is to control a lost infant ape as you walk him 20 yards to hide under a log. But that's complicated by your screen going on a bad mushroom trip as  it bombards you with cartoonish lion's teeth all over the screen.5. Now that your baby ape is hidden, you take control of an adult who has to go rescue the baby. Despite what you'd think would be an urgent situation, you're going to spend at least one in-game day walking around the start point, figuring out how to pick up a rock.  Now that you've picked up the rock, you need to inspect it.  Upon inspection, you find out that it is, indeed, a rock.6. Now that you've made that scientific breakthrough, you proceed out of the starting area to find you have to climb and swing your way through the trees. You quickly discover that the controls are as awkward and clumsy as a 12 year old on their first date. As you climb trees, you'll get hung up on invisible obstacles, try to swing to branches you'll teleport through, and fall hundreds of feet to end up completely fine unless it's not a specific place the game's designers decided you  shouldn't, then you're dead.7. Controls are atrocious.  The developers decided that you only need four buttons for everything.  Climbing in trees? well hold space to jump to another branch. Grabbing the next branch? then hold the space bar also. What's that? you wanted to grab that branch? too bad, you were already holding the space bar.  You want to inspect that item the game prompts you to? Too bad, you just yelled out, alerting any predators in the area to your location. The game will give you an on screen list of things you can do with an item then randomly do a different action that's also tied to that key.

_childDocuments_.review: If it usually said, not game is made for everyone, this is even more the case. I would say the main point fo this game is survival strategy, is not a game to rush from a point to another. A rushed decision and you will regret it later. For me the most negative point were the controllers, not intuitive at all in the beginning it takes time to get used to it, but once you understand the mechanics it gets easy. The other less good thing is the IA of your clan, they most of the time do nothing by themselves, if they were a bit better the experience could have been much better.Another thing I enjoyed was the absence of a map, leading you to memorize specific places to understand how close or far you are from a specific point. I felt the "evolution" in game, you notice you are advancing as you go from I was easily interested and kept playing for hours(for some reason some of them were not counted, maybe a server bug, don't know)TL;DRIf you like to have your pace but with danger all around if you relax too much it is a really good game, if you enjoy to study the terrain and surroundings so you are not get by surprise than it is definitelly for you. There are moments of action mixed much other times of preparation for a lot of things.

_childDocuments_.review: ***might contain spoilers to the game mechanics***Unique game that throws you into the “shoes” of individuals in our ancestral lineage. The game mostly revolves around a small tribe of individuals and you get to play as one of them in a lone wolf type of gameplay, or as the leader of the tribe, leading the group to scavenge, hunt and explore. The game is a survival based game and similar to our ancestors, you are an easy pray, but as you gain experience, a neuronal energy, your character develops and learns new skills, even how to counter predators. In order to speed the development, you can carry up to two infants with you to gain more of the neuronal energy.Unlike other games, where your playable character is permanently improved, here everything gets lost, unless you pass the generation and eventually evolve. In order to evolve your species efficiently, you need to gather mutations and fyi you can load up 3 adults with 6 infants, when you mutate your offsprings.Additionally, the developers really did their job when going through anthropological facts. In this regard, the game gives you an introductory information about human evolution. Unfortunately, they get many things wrong and it is important to note some examples, such as the Australopithecus species is not our ancestor, rather a dead end branch in our ancestral tree. Another downside is that evolution is not linear and does not jump from species to species. On the other hand, the mechanics regarding omnivorous behaviour and bipedalism are well implemented and, as it was with our ancesters, greatly improve humans “game”.I bought at the discount for about 10 euro. It was one of the best games I have ever played. I enjoyed it even more, because it reminded me a lot from what I have studied in my majors. If there are any DLCs going forward, I am definitely in. Great job, developers!
_childDocuments_.name: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey

_childDocuments_.review: I ABSOLUTELY love this game. I love how hard and unforgiving this game can be. _childDocuments_.review: Took me a while to get into this, and with very little patience, the lack of assistance almost had me give up.Yet, I've now figured out the mechanics of the game, how it works, what you're meant to do, and I'm actually enjoying it.It's actually really smart how progression works in this game, and once you've figured it out, you realise the "skill tree" works on the same basics as any other game.Get a single male and a single female to form a couple (through grooming), have 2 kids (the max I think).Repeat that with other adults in the group.For every kid, you can lock in a skill for the next generation - so go out there with your kids to earn XP to unlock skills."Achievements" are called "Evolutions", and completing a set of Evolutions allows the unlock of a special skill that kids are randomly born with. Make sure they reach adulthood (by "changing generation") once you've unlocked the max number of skills you can (based on the number of kids you've got), then as long as their lineage are having kids in future generations, those special skills will be saved - since their inherited through the generations.Anyway... takes some getting used to, but now - fun game, in my opinion.Still need to figure out how to fight etc, and am not even out of the first zone - since I also don't know how to fight the fear of moving into a new area (but am fairly sure it involves unlocking the relevant skill).I think the game is fun overall, but you need patience.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really, wanted to like this game. I think that it has a fantastic and original premise, I also think that most of the gameplay mechanics are fine as they are. I loved the fact that there was very little hand holding in comparison to other games and I liked having to use my brain to figure things out. I genuinely believed that this game would become a fast favorite. It hasn’t. Here is the issue. A game about adaptation and evolution should have gameplay that adapts and evolves. This game doesn’t do that. I was excited by the gameplay initially, but after several hours of repeatedly clicking on boxes while an unending onslaught of tigers, snakes, and warthogs attacked me, it wore pretty thin. I was disappointed in my desire that the game would eventually allow me to actually defend myself without a gimmicky quick-time event. The other big issue is the neuronal energy system. Why is does it take several hours to fill the energy bar every single time? It takes so long that actually filling it became the the ONLY thing I was doing.Don’t buy this game unless you’re a masochist or you’re trying to find a reason to stop playing video games for a while. This is the only game that has ever made me rage quit.

_childDocuments_.review: Challenging but not in fun way. I've played other challenging games such as dark souls (100%'d all of them).Interaction other apes can be frustrating. Example, when trying to drink from water, sometimes the ape would walk by and you 'accidentally commanded them to stay' and then you move to other location and notice that ape has not followed you because of this silly interaction.Jumping between trees can be fun but when you miss, you get punished.... honestly, apes are supposed to be pro at this and the game makes it so clunky in this sense. I find myself falling to death too often than not. Climbing the trees are clunky as well, cannot climb when you get to specific section of the tree and force you to figure out where to go, like there's invisible wall? This is quite annoying. When you 'change the generation', you find yourself needing to find a mate in order to get offsprings... they're nowhere to found. Google says to go back to first area where you started out. Still nowhere to be found... frustrating to waste your time looking for a mate when it's unclear on why.Combat, well... I'm deaf and I could not figure out how to dodge for life of me for awhile... google says 'listen for audio cue'... really helpful until I figured out that I am supposed to dodge just as screen shows rainbow frame, whatever that is. _childDocuments_.review: It's an interesting idea but ends up pretty shallow and repetitive. In the first 2-3 hours you can learn most of the crafting recipes and a good amount of the "skills" so you saw most of the game beside the other evolutions that add very little. After that you repeat the same thing with the next generation and slowly evolve until you are done with the game. I wish there would be more things to craft and build.I don't see the problem people have with the UI or run and jump using the same button. Buttons prompt are sensitive to what you are doing but are always the same so you can press it before the prompt if you know what you are doing and if you don't want to jump you simply stop moving before releasing the button. I broke my legs twice jumping from trees to trees and climbing sometimes is a bit awkward but it's overall pretty responsive.Not worth the full price but at 50% I think it's a fair price if you plan to go all the way, explore, survive and don't mind the repetitiveness. It's very confusing at first because the game helps you very little but once you learn a couple things by trial and error it's not too hard.I'm giving it a thumbs up because of the pretty unique concept and some cool ideas but overall it falls short of what it could have been maybe with a bigger team or more time. I might update this review if going to the end of the game is suddenly mind blowing but from what I read it's more of the same with different skins.

I definitely developed a bond with my apes and loved to see them slowly change over millions of years. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent, very insightful game, stifled by an unimaginative endgame.Ancestors is not a game about humans; it is a game about the many species that, over 10 million years, would eventually evolve into humans. I feel like I should make this clear. You are not gonna make fire, or a cave painting, or learn how to talk. You will, however, slowly evolve from a scared, clueless ape into a master of your surroundings. The way the game models this is by growing neurons - doing new activities will grow new neurons, which will, in turn, unlock more new activities. It is ingenious game design: as you learn the game, your apes will also get smarter and gain abilities to help you make the most use of your newfound learning.The world does a great job feeling BIG. It is an awe-inspiring feeling to leap through the branches of enormous trees. It is divided in biomes, and I really like the way the game handles progressing between them up to a certain point. You start off in the Jungle, where you can easily escape predators by just climbing a tree, but there's little variety in food sources and traversal is difficult; predators also get an advantage in that it's easier for them to hide here. You'll then proceed to the Great Lake, a wide valley with more flat terrain and more types of animals - including otters which you can hunt, helping your species acclimate to eating meat. After that, it's on to the Savanna, which will present a huge new variety of plant and animal life. Encountering new things helps your species evolve. There is a sort of achievement system that controls the limits of what you can do - whenever you do something new, you will gain an "evolution feat". Each evolution feat gives you fuel for when you decide to do an "evolutionary leap" and advance millions of years.The problems come with the last two biomes, the Canyon and the Ocean (really just a beach, since swimming kills your energy). They are, for lack of a better phrase, utterly devoid of interesting content. They have barely any new fauna, being simply chock-full of the same tigers and snakes you've been fleeing from since the Jungle. They have barely any landmarks. They have barely any food and water sources. There is simply no incentive for you to move your clan into them, unlike the previous biomes. Even the game's main objective line ends when you get to the beach. And the only way to progress from this point is to achievement hunt: the chore of hitting each of the three kinds of tiger with each of the tree kinds of stone, finding each landmark and each item, witnessing each predator kill each prey, etc..If the devs ever release an update to the late stages, I'm sure to come back!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great, it really makes you think about what it would be have to discover everything for yourself. I did started playing with a keyboard, and I didn't mind it at all, but I would agree that it is better with a controller. One design aspect that I really enjoyed was that since you are allowed to move at your own pace, you can get more and more comfortable with everything and learn new mechanics as you discover them and not be forced to areas that you aren't ready for.
_childDocuments_.name: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting game. Tough to get a good grip of controls at first and how to play, essentialy, but fun and somewhat chilling when you learn it. The best thing, there's no hand-holding - you do everything yourself. Mind you, it's not your explosions full action game. This game is a bit slow in it's nature, a bit like Red Dead Redemption 2 is.Graphics, well, it's 6/10 at most. The worst thing is, you're forced to use the blurry mess of an AA, which is TAA, because otherwise, everything hair-like gets rendered very dotty. There's no proper AA like MSAA, so you are forced to have the game blurry, even if you have the rig to run it at 4K. You can also see quite often, that there had to be cuts here and there, because the budget would not allow better.Anyway, there's no other game like this and I definitely recommend you try it - if you have some patience and persistence.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was the one and only reason my depression was cured. I know this may seem a little weird but genuinely this game cured my depression, everything was going wrong until I bought this game, my life was in a state so bad I didn't think anything could fix it especially not a video game about the evolution of monkeys. Once I started playing this game I understood how hard life truly was for me to get where I am, all the lives sacrificed for me to be here, right now, writing this review, happy. I used this thought process when doing anything and it truly helped me pull through. Thank you to the developers of this game, truly I am forever in your debt.

Often resulting in frustrating situations of, "how do I do what I want to do", yet... the base philosophy of evolution via observation and practice hold true to this and strengthens the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game with an interesting concept and execution. I honestly had a blast and would love a sequel.the enemies are diverse and interesting and the biomes are extremely well down with a lot of detail. As you unlock more skills and master your environment the game becomes easier and easier and it feels so deserved. The way you interact with items in the game is well done and sometimes you are forced to improvise on the fly. The exploration always feels good and the unlockable skills are all fairly useful other than concentrate which seems bugged for its intended purpose. A few caveats though the skill tree  or neurons becomes so grindy late in the game, and at times you are as clueless as your apes on how to upgrade certain branches as it is not entirely made clear. Also you sometimes randomly just lose a hominid that has been following you and it is not clear why it stops following you. You have no way to track it down and if it is carrying infants you are handicapped for the rest of the game. I would like to see recruitable hominids play a bigger role. An ideal play though is literally just recruiting an additional female at the start then just having six offspring at all time so there is no need to recruit.
_childDocuments_.name: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey

_childDocuments_.review: Times are tight, and I had to wait on a sale to make it happen, but if money were no objective, this game is EASILY worth its asking price.You start out lost, alone, confused, and afraid. The way that the game steadily offers the player options governing your avatar, it really does feel like being an entity blossoming into situational awareness. I really don't want to blow any of the secrets or any of the moments that make you smile or take your breathe away, but this game is so intuitively designed, it is mind-blowing.Yes, it's hard. Yes, you have to make survival decisions on the fly, with the VERY SLIGHT help of a contextual pseudo-bullet time reaction mechanic. Yes, you will not know what the ♥♥♥♥ to do if you don't explore, if you don't inspect, if you don't try combinations of tools. Watch bushcrafting videos or something. It will come to you if you immerse yourself in the game!Easily worth a AAA experience, in my mind, only without the AAA price.
_childDocuments_.name: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey

_childDocuments_.review: Unique, beautiful, and complex. This is storytelling at its finest. The game tells the story of human origin by making you experience it. As long as you don't seek help online, you'll experience the journey that brought animals into technology. What's more, it's a constant challenge of mind, awareness, and skill. Each little problem becomes a puzzle to solve that seems obvious once you figure it out. Figure it out, don't cheat, and you'll be rewarded. Thank you for this work of art!
_childDocuments_.name: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey

_childDocuments_.review: Warning: this review sounds much more negative than it is. I love that game, but see lots of missed opportunities - hoping for a part 2The only thing I really don't like about this game are the controlls (with controller) - they are wonky at best and get frustrating quickly (who puts jump and sprint on the same button?! why?! and as if that's not annoying enough, the same button is to - partially - interact with the world... standing on a stick and trying to jump?! - no ... sprinting up a tree while escaping a predator?! you better not let go of that A button, or you uncontrollably jump down again). Also the UI is a bit weird - you shouldn't have to guess if you're hungry, thirsty, tired or anything else - those things should be apparent - you feel them in real life and never get unconsious suddenly because you forget to fulfill one of them for days, becasue you didn't know why your vision gets blurry. The visual effects are nice, but a bar for each need would be a lot more realistic - my vision doesn't get whobbly from not drinking enough - I just know how thirsty I am!Other than that, it's a lot of fun, unless you are a fan of quick games that point you in the right direction of your next goal with a huge quest marker, where a chest with loot, guarded by a leveled enemy awaits you. Then move along ^^It's a slow game and that's good. I love roaming around and exploring the environment - I just wish there were more things to discover - maybe I'm simply not far enough into the game (40h), but it feels like I have everything uncovered that there is. (and I really don't want to look it up - I want to find stuff myself) Tools for example - there's pretty much only Obsidian and Granite - out of which you can make a ... this fits the evolutionary timeframe the game is set in, but I still wish there was more - maybe a second part of the game that focusses more on (stone) technology and the possibilities they unlock in the world and less on trying not to die of dehydration would be in order. At least I'd buy it in a heartbeat!TL:DRGreat game if you enjoy taking it slow and exploring, and don't mind the horrible controlls

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most striking aspects of the game is its emphasis on exploration and learning. Instead of traditional objectives, you're encouraged to experiment and discover your surroundings. I loved how this approach made me feel connected to the environment, whether it was foraging for food, learning to use tools, or avoiding predators. The sense of accomplishment from mastering these skills was incredibly rewarding.The visuals are stunning, capturing the beauty and danger of the prehistoric world. I found myself often stopping just to take in the scenery. However, I did encounter some frustrating moments with the controls and navigation, which felt a bit clunky at times. This can be challenging, especially when you’re trying to escape danger or interact with the environment.The game also does an excellent job of highlighting the importance of community and lineage. As you progress, you can pass on knowledge and skills to future generations, which adds a meaningful layer to the gameplay. This aspect resonated with me, reflecting the real-world importance of family and learning.Cons: Clunky Controls: The controls can feel awkward and unresponsive at times, making navigation and interactions frustrating, especially in high-pressure situations.Slow Pacing: The game's emphasis on exploration and gradual evolution can lead to slow pacing, which may not appeal to players looking for more action-oriented gameplay.Limited Guidance: While the lack of hand-holding can enhance the experience, it may also leave some players feeling lost or unsure of their objectives, leading to moments of confusion.Permadeath Mechanics: The permadeath system can be punishing, as losing a character means losing progress and learned skills. This might discourage some players from taking risks or fully engaging with the game.Repetitive Gameplay: Some players may find that the core gameplay loop becomes repetitive over time, as the tasks and challenges can feel similar across different playthroughs.Technical Issues: There have been reports of bugs and performance issues, which can detract from the overall experience.Pros:Unique Concept: The game offers a fresh take on survival and exploration by focusing on early human evolution, providing a distinctive gaming experience.Immersive Environment: The stunning visuals and richly detailed prehistoric world create an immersive atmosphere that draws players in and makes exploration feel rewarding.Emphasis on Exploration: Players are encouraged to experiment and discover their surroundings without traditional objectives, promoting a sense of curiosity and adventure.Skill Progression: The ability to pass on knowledge and skills to future generations adds depth and strategy, enhancing the game's longevity.Realistic Survival Mechanics: The game incorporates survival elements that challenge players to gather food, avoid predators, and learn new skills, creating a sense of accomplishment.Community Building: The importance of lineage and community in gameplay fosters a deeper connection to the characters and their development.Diverse Gameplay Styles: Players can choose how to approach challenges, whether through stealth, exploration, or strategic planning, catering to different play styles.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm torn on this game because there's some really good stuff here. I think the idea of a crafting/survival game following our early hominid ancestors is really cool. I enjoyed exploring and finding new environments, and I actually did, for the most part, enjoy struggling to understand the different environmental interactions, the controls, etc. without much guidance from the developers. However, once you get through that struggle, the threats of the game become trivial, and there's nothing to do except grind. Unlocking new abilities requires repetition, so to learn to digest new foods you have to find them and eat them, to get better at dodging and fighting you have to dodge and fight, etc. That's cool except there are no real goals in the game except to develop the species, so instead of doing interesting things and developing your skills incidentally, you end up chasing snakes around to trigger the fight mechanics or eating your 500th mushroom in the hope it opens up your next set of unlocks. There is map exploration and there is satisfaction and enjoyment to be had by moving about the environment, climbing up cliff faces and jumping from tree to tree (once you figure out how to do this without dying), and discovering new landmarks, but even that gets stale after a while once predators are no longer a concern and there's nothing to do except from move from point A to point B while occasionally stabbing yet another machairodus that hasn't figured out it's no longer the most dangerous species on the planet. I think it's probably still worthwhile as a chill game to play every now and again if you like the general flow and vibe of the game, but for me it ran out of steam once the initial struggle is overcome.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is actually a lot of fun.  In short, you run around, as our ape ancestors, trying to "invent" and "discover" the various things that made us the way that we are -- be it walking on two legs, using sticks and other tools for defence and offence, or whatever else -- in a _very_ unguided way. It's up to you to figure out what to do with something that you see or find -- how to make it useful -- and the game does very little to help you in this regard on purpose, though if you turn up the HUD, that can give you a good sense in many cases. Honestly, I love the way that the game works and find it incredibly fun, but I will say that if you feel frustrated or lost, there are a lot of resources online that can help you figure out how to, for example, get a mate and produce offspring or whatever else you want or need to know. I like that it's fairly unguided because I like "discovering" that I need this or that to do something or that putting a bunch of these things in a pile lets me build "fences" and things like that, though I'm sure that some will find that either daunting or perhaps simply lost.

_childDocuments_.review: **Review of the Game Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey****Rating: 7/10****Introduction***Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey* is an ambitious and unique project from Panache Digital Games, led by Patrice Désilets, one of the creators of the Assassin’s Creed series. The game invites players to travel back in time and experience the evolution of humanity, starting with our distant ancestors who lived around 10 million years ago. It’s a captivating experiment that aims to recreate the process of survival and evolution of our early predecessors.**Gameplay**The core gameplay revolves around managing a small clan of primates that gradually evolves and adapts to the surrounding world. The game begins in the forests of Africa, where players must explore the environment, find food, avoid predators, and secure safe places to sleep. With each generation, your clan becomes more advanced, acquiring new skills and adapting to the environment.One of the main features of the gameplay is the lack of clear instructions and hints. The game throws you into a wild world and forces you to figure out the mechanics on your own, which adds to the authenticity of the evolutionary process. However, this aspect might deter less patient players, as the game can sometimes feel overwhelmingly difficult and confusing.**Graphics and Sound**The visual aspect of *Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey* is impressive. The developers have created a detailed and beautiful world, where the African jungles come to life thanks to high-quality textures, dynamic lighting, and realistic character animations. The sound is also well-executed: the environment is filled with the sounds of wildlife, helping you fully immerse yourself in the game’s atmosphere.**Pros**- **Unique Concept:** The game offers an original take on the process of evolution, which has no analogs in the gaming industry.- **Freedom of Exploration:** Players can choose their own path of development, experimenting with different approaches to survival and evolution.- **Atmosphere:** The graphics and sound create a deep immersion into the world of the wild.**Cons**- **High Difficulty:** The game provides almost no guidance, which can make it challenging for less experienced players.- **Repetitiveness:** Despite the richness of the mechanics, the gameplay can become monotonous and repetitive over time.- **Limited Interactions:** Interactions with the environment and other creatures sometimes feel limited and not always realistic.**Conclusion***Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey* is a bold and original game that offers a unique experience in the survival and evolution genre. It’s designed for those who are ready to face challenges and patiently explore the mechanics to uncover all its secrets. However, the game is not without its flaws, such as high difficulty and a certain degree of monotony. If you’re looking for something unusual and are up for a challenge, *Ancestors* could be an exciting adventure for you, but don’t expect an easy and intuitive gameplay experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly love this game. It's a combo of "Breath of the Wild" and "Upgrade Complete!" (Yes, the ancient ArmorGames one) You start off as a wimpy borderline useless ape that can only scare off snakes and moves like a sloth on a caffeine binge. You quickly start to develop new skills by doing certain things, such as discovering resources nearby with your senses and practicing standing up. You use "experience" you gain from doing various activities to unlock and activate your new skills as you unlock them. When you change generations, letting your babies mature, adults age, and elders pass on, you can lock in 1-12 of those skills permanently depending on how many babies you have (max 6) and how many of them were exposed to meteorite radiation (+1 per baby). Any skills you haven't locked in will remain unlocked, but you will have to reactivate them during the next generation. Babies also have a 50% chance to be born with a genetic mutation, and can be forcibly given one by exposing them to meteorite radiation. When you activate a generation leap after those babies have grown into adults and elders they'll be unlocked and locked in automatically for you.You quickly grow from a lame, slow, jankily moving ape that has to stay in the trees to avoid predators to an apex predator that can sprint along the ground without needing to worry about predators, because to you the predators you learned to fear in previous generations are now your prey. The seemingly endless, maze like jungle you started off in becomes a small corner of a massive hand crafted map you get to explore at your leisure, full of gorgeous scenery and resources you can experiment with and collect into a treasure trove.The game has a lot of negative reviews which I really haven't experienced the issues of myself. Here's my tips on how to get the most out of it.1: Use a controller. The game starts with an unskippable loading screen that states you should use one. If you don't have one, maybe just add it to your wishlist and forget about it til you can get one. It won't measure up without one.2: The movement starts off pretty bad. IMO, this isn't a game design flaw, it's a feature that helps make future evolutions that enhance your movement abilities all the more satisfying.3: The controls tend to be heavily context specific. For example, A is run and releasing A while you're moving is jump. It's never bothered me, but you should pay attention to the fact that you have control over these differences if you control the context of the input, even if they're admittedly not your traditional control setup.4: The community building/interaction with your clan is largely overstated, but it also gets better as you evolve further. For the most part you can ignore your clan mates completely, they'll teleport to you when you get too far from them as long as they're set to follow you. They're at their worst around other animals, even when you've unlocked the ability for them to dodge and attack automatically. Your best bet is to travel small or fast and use intimidation rather than engage when you've got more than 1 or 2 followers.5: The first 200-300 meters of your starting oasis downriver are perfectly safe. It's only once you're entered the swampy area that the sabre tooth tigers will spawn on you if you're travelling on the ground. They're terrifying at the start, but if you attack them or intimidate them they'll disappear for a while, and if you manage to kill them they won't spawn again in a wide area until you pass generations. Meaning you can clear a path if you take it slow, killing any threats you come across. It's slow, but safe.6: Your current settlement prevents sabre tooth tigers from spawning, and it can be abused to move safely if you feel the need to. It also means you don't have to worry about clan members if they're at your settlement. I HIGHLY recommend only placing your permanent settlement at one of the many discoverable oasis's, specifically centered where the white flowers are growing in circles. It guarantees your borders won't overlap with regular animals' territory and just generally optimizes the AI to work in a non-suicidal manner.7: After a generational leap, your settlement is moved randomly to a nearby oasis. If you feel you're not ready to deal with the new area and the threats that come with it, just travel back upstream and you'll reach your first oasis, and you can re-settle there without consequence.8: Clan members that aren't following you cannot be attacked if they're outside YOUR render distance, and will not die of starvation/dehydration/sleep deprivation, even if they're outside your settlement. Which means you can travel without worry!7: As long as you're near clan members when they're attacked, they won't be killed immediately, including yourself if you fail a dodge. Just approach the attacking animal with a weapon to wound it and make it run off, or use intimidation to make it run off. If you travel with at least 1 other ape, the only thing you have to worry about is a deadly fall.8: The only thing clan members can die from other than being left alone after a direct animal attack is if you leave them bleeding, which you can see at any time in the bottom right corner of the UI. If an ape is bleeding then there will be a dot with a flashing red background. Bleeding doesn't heal on it's own, so you'll have to treat it yourself, either by switching to them or handing them medicine.9: There is a "secret" fast travel method to return to your settlement instantly. Simply allow yourself to reach the hysteria stage of fear by hanging out near enemies such as in a tree above them or by sitting in an undiscovered zone for too long. Your dopamine meter will run out and turn red, then you'll be teleported back home with the message that you freaked out and ran home. *I admittedly do not know if this has a chance to result in death, I've only ever been teleported home safely.There's so much you can do and far more than 40 hours of gameplay available. It starts off as a slow burn that quickly ramps up with your evolution speed, and I highly recommend it to anyone who's curious about it. After just 2 generational leaps I went from a crawling sloth to a bipedal sprinting spear hunter ready to kill anything in my path, from snake to tiger to elephant. A few leaps later and nothing beat the feeling of discovering what lay beyond the desert.

_childDocuments_.review: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey is an incredibly unique and captivating game that takes players on a thrilling journey through human evolution. It skillfully combines elements of adventure, survival, and exploration, offering a truly immersive experience for gamers of all kinds.One of the standout features of Ancestors is its stunningly realistic graphics. The game developers paid meticulous attention to detail in recreating the prehistoric landscapes and flora/fauna, transporting players to a bygone era. The lush environments, complete with sprawling jungles and vast savannas, make exploration a truly awe-inspiring experience.The gameplay itself is a refreshing departure from traditional gaming experiences. As players control a clan of our earliest ancestors, they must survive in a harsh and dangerous environment. From hunting for food to defending against predators, every action must be carefully considered. The mechanics are skillfully crafted, striking a balance between challenging and rewarding.One of the game's strongest attributes is its unique take on character progression. Instead of leveling up your character through experience points, you must evolve your clan over generations. This innovative approach adds an extra layer of complexity and realism to the game, as the decisions you make in one generation can have a lasting impact on future lineages.Ancestors also excels in its educational value. The game encourages players to explore and learn about the behaviors and habits of early humans. It effectively blends entertainment with information, making it an excellent tool for sparking interest in anthropology and evolution.Furthermore, the game's open-world sandbox nature allows for endless possibilities. Whether you choose to traverse the wild landscapes to unlock new abilities or focus on expanding and fortifying your clan's territory, Ancestors provides a vast and enthralling playground for players to discover and create their own stories.In conclusion, Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey is an exceptional gaming experience that offers a fresh and innovative take on human evolution. Its breathtaking visuals, immersive gameplay, unique character progression, educational value, and open-world exploration combine to create an unforgettable adventure. Whether you are a fan of survival games or curious about our ancient beginnings, this game is a must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my GOTY.There is some early frustration learning the controls and mechanics, but once you get the hang of it the sense of exploration and accomishment is incredible. The game is trying to do something very different, and maybe it's not for everyone, but when you barely dodge the fangs of a sabertooth only to watch it stumble into the maw if a crocodile I don't think you'll regret it.Some things to keep in mind when starting out:- you'll die a lot from random falls/predators early on. This is fine. Keep going and pass generations then pop out 6 kids if your numbers thin out.- max tribe size is 18 (6 weak/expendable elders, 6 adults and 6 children who generate valuable neurons). You can only pop out 2 kids per female, so keep them safe. There is no point trying to find or breed more apes if you are maxed.- pass generations to lock in as many traits as you have kids- evolve when you have adults and elders with valuable mutations. You probably want to evolve after two generations, when the starting kid is an elder, to get his mutation that unlocks the omnivore branch.- the "missions" are 100% optional. You progress through the game naturally by finding and interacting with new stuff. Don't be afraid to go explore somewhere else if those swamp gators keep eating your apes.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this game is like watching a Discovery Channel documentary. You start out as a helpless monkey trying to figure out how to use a stick with nothing but your wits and a strong will to survive. But within minutes you've discovered the magic of the pointed stick and suddenly you're the jungle's alpha predator, killing everything in your path. It's like a real "Survivor" series. It's like real life, but with less paperwork and more animal blood.But the real highlight of this game is the sense of power and accomplishment you feel as you progress through the evolutionary stages. I stopped for months, then started again and wondered why I was doing this to myself again. But every time there's that "aha" moment and I break through on my own, it adds to that sense of personal accomplishment. You will feel like a god among beasts.This game is criticized by people who are used to having a glowing arrow with a path to every important location, piece of gear, mission, etc. This isn't that kind of game. This is a survival game designed to make you think. You have to put yourself in the monkey's shoes and think as if you were a real early hominid trying to discover everything around you. It's fun to do something as simple as take the cubs to a meteor location to get that extra boost for the next generation. However, every time your clan is decimated because you didn't do something right, you have to start over or face the consequences of failure later. This definitely adds to the replay factor, especially when you're trying to figure out almost everything on your own.Overall, this is a good game, but it's not for the faint of heart. If you are looking for a game where you can unleash your inner wild and take over the animal kingdom, then this is the game for you.Ancestors is not only an exciting gaming experience, but also educational. The game is based on real scientific research, and the developers have done an excellent job of incorporating this knowledge into the gameplay. As you progress through the game, you will learn more about human evolution and the various challenges our ancestors faced during their development. It's like taking a crash course in anthropology and archeology without having to sit through boring lectures.In addition, the game also provides players with a lot of information about the different species and ecosystems, so it's a great way to learn more about the different animals and plants of the prehistoric era, as well as the dynamics of the environment in which they lived.All in all, Ancestors: A Human Kind Odyssey is not only a fun, challenging, and enjoyable game, but also an excellent way to learn about the history of our species in an interactive and engaging way.One silly thing is, if you don't do it first, your tribe won't eat or drink even if it's important.

_childDocuments_.review: Great for 20 or so hours. The interesting content ran out after most of the ingame tips were applied. After that the game is repetitive and tedious. The programming for the AI monkeys to collect healing meds is hit-or-miss. It's frustrating because there are a ton of attacks that will then require healing and this collection is mostly done manually for the entire tribe. Exploring with the tribe was a pain until unlocking the counter-attack and group crafting perks and even after I had to do almost everything  while in combat because the AI is hit-or-miss.Before these traits were unlocked the monkeys would basically just get mauled over and over even if I climbed a tree and tried to regroup them into the tree. The AI was too stupid to climb the tree if my character was not past the programmed maximum distance threshhold, so if there aren't the tallest trees nearby to climb then the monkeys won't get to safety. This mechanic is worse the bigger the tribe gets and there was little point in climbing trees for safety when I had a maxed clan because there are usually a few monkey AI standing idle at the base of the tree seasoning themselves up for the tigers. Those monkeys then promptly get mauled and I have to scare away the predators or agro them to my character, bringing the monkeys back out of the tree and repeating the cycle. AI has the ability to switch hands when they're holding an object but they won't be able to eat or drink when they have something in their "active" hand. It requires telling them to switch hands or drop the item they're holding so they can grab and eat food. This overall feels lame, as I expected starving monkeys to decide to drop whatever they're holding to grab food on their own when the rest of the tribe is eating. That's what the whole game is supposed to be about, monkey see monkey do.There are a ton of unintuitive features in this game, but it was well worth what I paid for it on sale and the experience of discovering new things in this game was great. I could continue to evolve the tribe but I don't have plans to because it's a slog from here, and I'm convinced the best of the content has already been experienced at 26 hours in.

_childDocuments_.review: Possibly the greatest survival sandbox i have ever played and an amazing 3D platformer. The controls feel tight and fluid and do not do you the disservice of making navigation too easy. Sure you can traverse virtually any surface, but if the rock face has a fissure in it such that the rock above juts out above your head you will have to navigate a different way. The gameplay isnt like assasins creed where the points the character jumps to are always super precise and flawless in execution and require no more than the holding of a couple buttons; if you want to soar through the tree tops and leap from branch to branch in this game, you will need skill, timing, and the ability to make split second decisions that will either leave you swinging from the next limb or falling down through the canopy several dozen feet. And all that is just the core movement and navigation. This game is all about the joy of discovery and conquering the unknown, so i wont say much more about it other than it appears very well polished, highly functional and realistic, and suprisingly quite the thrill ride through and through. Honestly i was prepared for a more casual experience, but i was delightfully suprised by the amount of depth and inensity to be found. 10/10 would reccomend. Last note, there is a distinct lack of multiplayer support, and while this would be a great boon to the game i wouldnt want multiplayer support to sacrifice any of the  other amazing aspects of this game. Who knows what may happen when you wish upon a metiorite...

_childDocuments_.review: A masterpiece of survival gaming. In the beginning, you are a nearly helpless, quadrupedal herbivore who must hide in trees to elude danger. By the end, you are a bipedal omnivore that can confidently face down elephants and saber-tooths on open plains. The basic mechanics and available actions barely change over the course of the game's simulated 8 million years, but your ability to perform those actions and freely explore the world are like night and day when compared beginning to end.Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey can be frustrating at first for new players. Nearly all tasks are performed as quick-time actions (QTA), and initially take a ludicrous amount of precision with a very short window of opportunity. You will probably fail a lot at first. Do not be discouraged: this is by design. Your apes, in the beginning, do not have the precise muscular control needed for fine tool handling. Over time, the game's light RPG elements will make these QTAs easier, more forgiving, and less tedious. You'll also naturally learn to compensate for your apes' lack of precision, and the combination of your own growing skill and perk-tree progression will make the game feel exponentially easier as time goes on.The game is fairly hardcore as the survival genre goes. You have no inventory other than your own two hands. Stamina is directly tied to how well you're meeting your hunger, thirst, and sleep needs, and can never exceed your health. Important to note is that your health, called "lifespan" in this game, never regenerates. Ever. An ape that you allow to get excessively beaten and abused is an ape that is effectively crippled. Worse, your lifespan actually acts as a backup stamina meter should your actual stamina become depleted, so even excessive activity without rest can kill you eventually.On the flip side, the game is very forgiving with your NPC clan mates. Any ape you are not currently controlling, is not following you, and is within your settlement, will never have its three needs deplete. Infants' needs never deplete unless you play as them. Apes who are following you also only need their right hand free in order to drink or eat, removing some of the need for you to micro-manage their inventory. So as hardcore as the game's mechanics are, they mostly only apply to your current character.The game is not without its flaws. While most of the animals you encounter are indeed from the Miocene period, there are a few instances of modern animals like antelope and African rock pythons being present. Several animals are oversized, such as the aforementioned python being closer to the size of Titanoboa than to its real life counterpart, and a giant millipede far bigger than any arthropod that has existed since the Carboniferous period. Perhaps the most noticeable flaw in realism is that in the 8 million year time span of the game, only your apes evolve. All other animals remain the same from beginning to end.The gameplay itself also has some issues. If you're on the ground for too long, a tiger will spawn and attack you. If you defend yourself, it almost immediately despawns unless chased. This will continue to happen every five minutes that you're on the ground until you kill it; at which point you're given about a thirty minute reprieve before the tiger starts spawning again. This is in addition to the many hostile animals already present in the game (including more tigers), and there is no way to stop it. Unless you live in the trees, this "ghost cat" as players have come to call it will always appear and attack you. A similar issue is present at the treetops, where your presence eventually causes a giant eagle to spawn in and attack you. The developers clearly wanted players to always feel in danger, but I personally feel that the presence of these two attackers is a bit much.Gripes aside, this is a great game overall, and I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys hardcore survival, and doesn't mind being limited by mild RPG elements.
