_childDocuments_.review: It was a decent game, worth the $20 I spent but I'm glad I didn't spend more. It was pretty short. Good to waste a little time and get a small story out of it. I put about 12 hours into the game, and much of that was trying to get through some of the more difficult missions. The gameplay was a little unbalanced in one or two missions, but nothing too terrible.The gameplay wasn't great. Nothing really new is introduced you haven't seen in any other game, and other things you have are missing. You're a gravcycle pilot, but instead of racing around in the gravcycle tearing it up in a sort of motorcycle meets hover-gunship death machine, you're stuck mainly floating around the battlefield, dodging some gunfire and trying to return fire and not die because you're too slow to really fly around, and not as powerful as you'd like to be. No real cover system to speak of, since you typically are floating above most of your enemies. You don't even have the ability to use your boost to damage enemies or break any of the destructible stuff on the battlefield really. The attempt to integrate more strategy into an FPS could've been awesome. An RTS where you can still blast the heck out of enemies directly. But it instead lacked in both areas. You cannot direct your units individually just tell all of them to choose one enemy, or move to a different location. You can only directly select specific units when telling them to use their abilities. So some of the more tactical applications where you could've separated out your force, dealt with different threats at once, and generally done what you do in a strategy game, while still pitching in and blowing the hell out of some of the smarter or stronger enemies weren't available to you. It made it very bland and not something that would've added a whole new spin on 'shoot em ups'.No upgrades to speak of either, or ability to kit your own gravcycle out the way you want to for each mission. Not that there were huge differences between the frames of each gravycle, from what I could tell. The story was kind of fun, but too short. I don't know if it was just because the game was so short, but the story was missing a lot of what would've made it good. Backstory, more interactions, etc anything that really went beyond a very basic storyline wasn't there. I do think there should be a Disintegration 2, but it needs to have something new, something exciting that makes gameplay a thrill (c'mon you're in a hovering motorcycle with guns. add speed and courses rather than small mission areas, zipping around in the air... the whole concept should be self-explanatory and intuitive!) , and definitely more storyline. I really want to know more about the world of Disintegration.

_childDocuments_.review: So I read about this game only a few days before it's release and immediately decided that I want to buy it. Why? The RTS/FPS (two of the genres I play the most) sounded awesome. Therefore I was on board on day 1 and finished the campaign within around 12 hours. Afterwards I wanted to give the multiplayer a shot. This first impression revealed several pros/contras:Contra:- Missing base building. Could've known about that but imho this just belongs to an classical RTS game.- You can't control your team mates individually. This should've given more tactical freedom, but on the other side, it's also a pro (see below).- Small player base so it is hard to find mates for MP.- Few skins for your troops in multiplayer.Pro:- Very fluid gameplay! Disintegration made me dive deeper into the hybrid genre so I tried several other games like Eximius and Executive Assault 2. Even though both are great games as well, both are much more stressful as you switch from commander/RTS to FPS sight a lot if you want to really enjoy both. And every time you feel like you miss something. Disintegration reduces the hybrid idea to first person with the control of your squad via right click, so as easy as it can get. From this point of view it also makes sense that you can only control your squad as a whole and no single units.- Very committed player base and active devs. Check out the respective discord and you will see that there're multiplayergames almost every evening...you just have to know, when.- Most important: The game is just fun. You can always complain about individual aspects of a game but all this matters less, when the whole picture is entertaining! And Disintegration fully delivers on this part.- 9 teams in multiplayer with different attacks/specials so you can always chose a different play style. This aspect even reminds of a hero shooter, just with gravcycles and a team you can command. So you got tanks, healers, snipers a.s.o.- Lots of unlockables in multiplayer (except for the skins as mentioned above)So, is it a perfect game worth 50 bucks? No and this has already been addressed to the devs, but imho it is not by far too overpriced. Do I regret the buy? Absolutely not! It's just fun to jump on your gravcycle, shoot robots and learn some tactics.This game is one of it's kind that uses elements from other games and combines them to something unique. If you got the money buy it now and support the devs. Otherwise wait gor a price drop to 30-40 bucks. One way or the other: It's definitely worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: No one is going to argue that Disintegration is the next Destiny or even the next Halo. The game has heart, but there are always small problems reminding you of its limited scope. Despite that, Disintegration succeeds at presenting an AAA-style shooter the likes of which we haven't seen in a long while. It's got a meaty campaign and a unique gameplay hook that's worth digging into. Much like Titanfall before it, it's the type of solid foundation that cries out for a refined and robust sequel effort. Considering what they've done on their first time out, I'd say that V1 is up to the challenge.[Review was conducted primarily on Xbox]Want to know more? My full review is avialable over on .

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to really hate the game, you can see that the devs have put a lot of care in the thing.It looks good, it sounds good, the cinematics and overall photography is remarkably good.But where the game fail, and HARD at that, is the game play.You get an hybrid shooter/rts where both are very, very flawed.First before going into detail here's one baffling point : You CANNOT choose your load out or team before a mission. You are just served a random assortement of weapons and teamate which is incredibly frustrating and feels extremely arbitrary.You gather 2 ressources in the missions, one is scrap and the other is chips.Chips are basically level up that you can spend on you or your team to increase flat stats, its boring and it's heavily limited by the level of the characters, so you often have more points than slot to use them.And the scraps... I have no idea. It looks like something you'd spend in some kind of crafting system, right? So... what's the point exactly?It's a very weird choice on the devs part since letting the player manage that kind of stuff would not only have been easy, but felt way better than having good weapons given and taken at the whims of the game.Then comes the actual gameplay.The FPS side is extremely weak. You are flying so you are constantly exposed, you got a dash, but is has an incredibly long cooldown, your weapon range from interesting to frankly boring, and since you can't CHOOSE them it just frustrating. You'll soon learn that the only skill required here is to abuse the vertical movement since unlike the vertical one, it makes the ai almost unable to hit you.The shooting itself gets very repetitive since you don't really have to aim for weak points (outside of the pretty borring bigger enemy) and everything, even the standard troops, feel very bulletspongy.The comes the rts side, managing the team of ground troopers you have with you.Welp, that side is basically a lie. You'll learly quickly that it's impossible to mange them.You can't give them orders individually, you can't them any standard orders you'd expect of a tactical rts like getting behind that cover or stuff like that, and since they move very, VERY fast their positioning overall doesn't matter. You'll just end up using on CD their "skill" that feel mostly like if you were the one doing them... except with a delay, and some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tied to pathfinding and line of sight. Having them die don't matter at all beside forcing you to grab their corps (which should always be very close to you anyway) and they'll respawn in a handful of seconds.So in the end you'll just start to ignore them entierly, even not bottering to tell them to focus fire on something because if you are looking at it to tell them to shoot, it means that you too can just do that and will kill the thing faster than they'll do anyway.Probably the most anoying part is the mine/grenade the enemy some times drop on the ground. The only way to remove them is to shoot at them, but your soldiers by default move toward were you aim, thus making them jump right in the mines that will one shot them. It's probably the most frustrating thing in that game and shows how little understanding the gamedesigners had of their own game.Overall it feels like an incredible wast of opportunity, both on the shooting and the rts side.That dull gameplay coupled with the very limited, and frankly unintersting, pool of enemy makes the 12 missions (and around 10 hours) of gameplay a chore to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: Disintegration

_childDocuments_.review: After seeing the reviews here beforehand I went into this with low hopes for the game, but thanks to that I ended up not hyping up my expectations for this so I like to think I came into this with reasonable expectations. Saying that I've clocked in 1.4 hours of play time of the campaign for the first two missions and have some points to make about the gameplay first:Pros:+ controls are simple to fly around with and to command your units.+ the RTS (but more like an RTS-lite) element comes into play by choosing where your units move to and each have an individual ability that they can use with the hotkeys. simple and effective (but ends up having little variety but that's in the cons)+ is fairly easy to control and move your units and then moving on as yourself to lay down support fire on weaker groups of enemies + the FPS and RTSlite elements blend together nicely and is intuitive to play+ mission environments have a good variety in the missions that ive played. mainly a forest/farm area moving through open fields to narrow forest paths leading up to a wreckage of a crashed ship.cons:- There seems to be little variety with the abilities of the units being mortar, grenade, and slow time AOE ability(edit: there is also a fourth ability that i've noticed but never got to use). this is between the 4 story unit characters. hopefully in the future there can be a system that allow you to choose what abilities your units can have in the upgrade menu- The units only have one ability leaving no variety again. this could be forgiven if there was a second ability they could use similar to how mass effect handled it with a menu wheel popping up.- no way to individually move units to separate areas or to even make them take cover behind objects or walls. that would have been a good edition to the game.- there was an ability that was shown in the tutorial that i could preform in the game. it was to deploy a healing AOE. it worked in the tutorial but i was unable to do it in the campaign missions. i believe it was to hold Q while aiming at the ground.- sometimes it would seem like if i was too far away and shooting at the enemy then the first few seconds of connecting shots wouldn't _childDocuments_.review: Disintegration is a game for people who never got over the five Michael Bay Transformers movies.  Whether this is good or bad depends on your view of Bayformers.It has a fun ragtag group of robot* characters, some nice voice acting and character design, scenic and cinematic views, and mid-to-late 2000s humor.  It also has cliches abound, an assumption that players understand the backstory and lore and doesn't wait for them to catch up, a tough female love interest who is essentially there to be tough and female and a love interest, and mid-to-late 2000s humor.  Pulling away from the story for a bit (because in the spirit of Bayformers, this isn't really about the story and characters (although its a nice bonus); its about a blazing guns and the big explosions), there's an interesting combination of first-person shooting and real-time strategy; you're assigned guns and a squad at the beginning of each mission and have to adapt to what you have.  The gravcycle can feel very floaty (and not in the way it should, considering it does literally float), the guns need to reload way too much, and the squad AI can get confused sometimes...but in general the gameplay loop is very smooth.  The game scaffolds its difficulty, easing players in to the truly chaotic battles later on.  There's a lot of unseen potential, too; I would have loved to be able to pick and choose how to build my gravcycle or have more options for squad members (which might have been in multiplayer; I don't know, because by the time I got this game that mode had been removed completely).  But what we have is what we get.I, personally, love me some cool robot dudes.  I love me some cool robot dudes shooting other cool robot dudes.  I kinda wish this game had done better so that we could get a sequel that fixes up a lot of the janky bits (I personally choose to blame Epic and their exclusivity for the failure), but what is there is good.  It has that 2007 soulfulness.  It has unique ideas that could have used a bit more refining.  The overall product is fun and I would say the game is worth it if you like weird shooters. *yes I know they're human brains in robot bodies and that drives the lore and conflict, we could sit here all day and debate whether a human brain being the only organ in a mechanical body makes it robot or human, but for the sake of simplicity i'm going with "robot"(also i call dibs on doyle.)

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Tactical gameplay is the main draw of the game, with lovable characters coming in second place, and an interesting but ancillary scifi story in the background.I'll elaborate on a couple of issues I see other people raising and then list my own pros and cons.Issue #1 - limited variety in (a) character customization, (b) enemy type, and (c) gameplay. (a) Character customization is limited to using chips that you find in missions to upgrade your squad in health, damage, ability recharge, health regen, and seemingly one unique upgrade per class.(b) Almost every mission introduces new enemy types. There are support enemies, melee and ranged enemies, flying enemies. This is more than enough to make the levels feel varied.(c) There are a variety of combat arenas which, in combination with aerial movement and the ground squad, make for lots of tactical flexibility: for example, you can send your squad into a building and fly around the outside shooting through the windows, you can set up flanks, play high/low ground, etc. There is a great deal of room for creativity. Combine that with the different abilities and mission objectives and I don't think the accusation of repetitive gameplay sticks to this any more than it does to halo, destiny or any similar game.Issue #2 - dumb AI/bad controls for squad.I have only noticed one instance where the AI feels dumb and that is when an enemy throws a proximity grenade. Your squad will stand right on top of it and not move. You can command them to move away and they will (and their response is very fast). Otherwise the AI is good. It does require attention, but I think that is by design (at least on the higher difficulties); you are supposed to play the grav-cycle AND your squad. This isn't an FPS with an AI squad following you—and I think the RTS comparison is not apt, either. This is more like an FPS where you control two characters in unison (the gravcycle commander and your squad). I also haven't had any problems getting my squad to do what I want them to; no pathfinding issues or "I didn't tell you to go there!!" or "I told you to stay there!!" moments.This won't help you decide if the price is worth it, but keep in mind that the dev team is around 30 people. Okay, now my pros and cons.Pros+++ The tactical landscape. It is very fun to set up ability combos and execute combat plans—flying around the battlefield and directing the flow of combat. It's great fun to flush out a group of enemies with your squad straight into the double auto-shotguns on your gravcycle, or to set your squad up on high ground and then fly around the side and flush enemies out into the open. Controls are also polished and intuitive.+++ The difficulty. Outlaw (the highest difficulty) is awesome; rarely do I play a game and feel like I need to utilize everything available to me in order to win. I think to beat missions on outlaw, you really need to use your squad optimally: combo abilities, use good tactical placement of both your squad and your grav-cycle (must be able to multi-task!!), and have a high level of situational awareness. You get a scanner (which is basically like a toggleable Widowmaker's sight from Overwatch (it highlights enemies through walls), except that it highlights explosives, too) and it is key to mapping out the battlefield: more often than not on Outlaw, I scout with my scanner and then set up my squad in an ideal position to take advantage of the enemy's position.++ Voice acting and character design are top notch. Each member feels unique even though they are robots without facial expressions. + The world is not incredibly inventive, but it is full of cool scifi ideas and the general presentation is engaging.+ The backgrounds are beautiful and the models, textures and animations look AAA tier even though the dev team is small.Cons-- Invisible walls everywhere. Part of the game is exploring for caches (which can contain the chips to upgrade your units), but it is usually not clear what paths are actually available to go down. This is exacerbated by the lack of a minimap or map (but I actually enjoy not having a minimap that I'm constantly referencing). - Getting your grav-cycle stuck. This is related to the first con but, despite the controls feeling very fluid, it's pretty easy to get your grav-cycle stuck in a hallway or on a piece of the environment if you try to fly anywhere confined (e.g. around the pillars in mission 3).- There are some problems with narrative flow (there aren't always great transitions between story points). I think this is largely due to the hubs; it feels disjointed to have the cutscenes play on interaction with the console instead of in a fluid motion from point A to B. There is also a bit of "disorientation" in understanding where you are. It might help to have transition cutscenes showing how you get to the hub or leave the hub, or a "map" that shows the various mission positions compared to the hub (though I kind of like not having a world map and experiencing the world in a more natural way). Overall, if hours of challenging tactical combat with a unique FPS system sounds appealing to you, I highly recommend Disintegration. If you want to play primarily for the story, I think you will probably be disappointed with what the game has to offer, but—as an accompaniment to the great gameplay—the story, and especially the characters, are more than serviceable.

The minimal command controls are functional and a little lacking feedback, the gun-play is frustratingly broken up by limited ammo, weapon cool down, and no ability to select the weapons you use for a mission. Which combined with the floaty sluggish movement of your vehicle can be very frustrating, especially when rough terrain will make you constantly fall out of the air or bump into things while strafing. However, despite those problems with the core gameplay, I still found myself compelled to finish and do think it was time well spent. Once I got past the initial impressions I found the world of the game, and even the character writing fairly compelling. It's definately a world I would love to see more of, though in future I would prefer more front loaded exposition, working alongside a faction for 4+ missions before a mission challenge told me who they were was ridiculous). Over all I would give it a 6/10. A decent enough experience, a little above average, despite its flaws. Wait for a sale, but it is worth your time. Oh and an honourable 10/10 for not experiencing a single bug, or major glitch in an entire campaign playthrough. Not many games I can say that for, especially when its such a polished game from a small studio.

_childDocuments_.review: Picked up and played a little of this game during the free to play weekend, so I do not own this, nor did I pay for itFor clarity, I have only played the campaign, and I have not beaten the campaign (didn't really have enough time in my schedule to justify playing all the way through, nor did I want to confirm my suspicions on what the multiplayer would be like after playing some of the campaign), but I do believe I can give some information. Not as much as others, such as SecretAgent:KiiN, who appears to have a much more detailed review of this game for potential players out there, so I recommend reading their review if your looking to decide whether pick this up or not.This game is an interesting style. I enjoy the concept of having to play a FPS while also having to control more than that. You are given a small squad, one where you have to control their movement, and can direct firing. This is difficult on occasion, as your troops like to constantly move ahead of you, unless you specifically tell them where to wait. In addition, this leads to further difficulties in playing. For example, when you are getting shot at yourself, and trying also to coordinate your squad to most effectively take down the vast numbers you are faced with, while also healing them and yourself. This makes for a very interesting split in your mind, where you need to be both good at FPS games, and also still have the mental ability to coordinate your troops and use all of their abilities.Personally, I am a fan of the grav cycle, even keeping in mind the complaints that I  with a majority of reviewers. The grav cycle doesn't get too high off the ground and it isn't as fast as I would like. Abilities take longer to come back than I want. Boosting your speed takes a hair too long to reset cooldown so you can dip in and out (maybe a fix is 2+ boosts, or faster cooldown, unless grav cycle speed is bumped up, to maintain some balance). The grav cycle adds some verticality to the game in a different way from standard genres, and I do appreciate that, but it needs to be fine tuned still. In addition, I was not able to choose what weapons I wanted on the grav cycle. Every campaign mission I played just gave me whatever grav cycle the developers designed for that mission, and it was a little annoying for me. For example, you were able to heal troops from your grav cycle, but in one mission the way to do this is a direct fire on your allies (which does seem to follow them a little, so no real need to worry about being super precise), and another mission it was a press and hold to activate ability that set down a healing zone for me and teammates. Was the change-up more effective, as I can now heal everyone, including me at once? Yes. Was it nice to have my entire previous way of playing uprooted, without being given the choice, nor really knowing about it until I was in a bad situation, trying to heal and couldn't figure it out, because it was a push and hold, instead of a point and click? Not at all.I personally like the mix of FPS, real time strategy (in a weird way) and especially the verticality of the game! It is very different from the standard mix of genres currently available, so a little time will be needed to truly learn and enjoy the game, but it can be done easily and quickly. However, I believe that this game still needs more polishing. I currently love the idea of this game, more than I love the actual game. IF this game was to get some serious polishing up, I do believe it could become very popular and successful, but as it lies currently,

A first person shooter with real-time strategy mixed in and being extremely important at times.Instead of focusing on how much ammo you have you have to focus on how long it takes for your abilities to cool downHow long it takes for you weapons to rechargeAnd how much ammo you have in that specific shotWe're able to play this in three dimensions fighting things above below and in quite literally every direction of you. Well simultaneously controlling three to four troops who themselves have special abilities and health barsOn all hearing that at one point in time would sound.... Oppressive. IntimidatingBut once you get into the actual fray It almost becomes natural if you have a good idea of what you need to doOver the last 7 days I have spent about 8 to 12 hours straight playing this campaign. And in that time I have come up with good and bad about the game.Let's start with the bad parts.In the scenes in between missions the graphics are a little wonky. It looks almost as if each frame during movement was hand-painted. This results in an effect that if focused on even unintentionally. Can cause nausea and for me cause temporary motion sickness. during the same scenes if you focus on how the character moves between going left to right to left to right it's almost as if you are two steps ahead of the controller or the joystick or the keypad and going in a circle while being spun around. like you're stepping forward while on a disc that is spinning to the right left. For those who pay close attention to detail this can be rather distracting.Now let's talk about the good. In my opinion the storytelling was good. I went into this campaign knowing the bare bones having only seen one or two trailers and played the beta test for the multiplayer.I had absolutely no idea what I was getting myself into. Those some things I had to piece together myself for the most part seemed like the story would give you the information you needed when you needed it and let you figure the other stuff out. It was telling a story but still giving you the information you needed to understand the story. You weren't giving all the information up front that wouldn't have made it fun. You're given the information when it's relevant And I for one agree with that. It keeps you on your toes It keeps you paying attention to what people are saying. Banter between the characters during the gameplay and cutscenes and pre-mission gameplay gives small insights into what the story truly is and the backstories behind each character. In my opinion the gameplay was challenging and frustrating but at the same time on point. I couldn't afford to look away from the screen. I had to focus. I had to pay attention and keep an eye on every part of the screen at all points in time just to make sure that I had who I needed when I needed them.This created a minor panic but at the same time great exhilaration as I was rushing against the clock to heal my allies while at the same time telling them where to shoot and how to shoot.I would met at a first glance the final part of the campaign was lackluster however upon a second look I realized that it told the story just as it had to be told. There are of course things that I would change if I was in charge but those are things that I will leave feedback on in a later post. On all in my opinion this game is definitely worth playing. The campaign pulled me in and kept me guessing about some things while telling me upfront about others. there were parts of the story that I had to go searching for in order to understand what was going onI was able to get an idea of how the story should have gone without any guides I only played the game I never went to any other media about itAnd to be honest I'm glad I didn't look at any other media. It would have ruined the campaign for me. Even now the plot twists that take place still surprise me just looking back on themHowever due to the cons that I have already mentioned as well as a feeling of lacklusterness to the end of the campaign. I only feel comfortable getting the game currently a seven and a half out of 10 with room for improvement and a hope for improvement. This is a beautiful game and very clearly a work that came from the heart not necessarily the mind. I hope it stays that way

_childDocuments_.review: *BUY ON SALE* in my opnion, this game is probably worth $10-15, not $30. I tried this game out for the free weekend, so i didn't play the whole game. Pros:1. Interesting gameplay - It's a sci-fi FPS with RTS elements. you fly around in this thing called a Gravcycle and command your allies to do stuff (attack enemies, open stuff, use their special abilities, etc.) as well as shoot at things. 2. Decent story - you play as this guy named Romer, an integrated (brain in robot body) guy who escapes from a sky prison and joins a group of other integrated people to form a resistance against the bad guys, whose names I forget. It isn't something spectacular, but its alright. Cons: 1. Dead multiplayer - In my experience, i couldn't get into a single match of the multiplayer. I waited 7 minutes at most, but i couldn't get into a match. I was very let down by the multiplayer because there was no one online, 2. Gameplay can sometimes feel repetitive - sometimes the levels can drag on and feel repetitive gameplay wise because you do a lot of the same stuff. I also wish that you could take control of your ground troops and play as them in first-person, but also be able to switch back to Romer. 3. If you quit during a campaign mission, you loose all of your progress in that mission. 4. You don't get to pick your loadouts each mission - in each mission, you the game chooses who you go with and what equipment you use. Some of them have awesome abilities, and others have less-awesome abilities.  Final Verdict: I don't recommend buying this at full price, wait for it to be $10-15. Don't expect an amazing story on par with the first Halo, or The Last of us. Expect good gameplay that might feel repetitive. Don't expect a good multiplayer experience, or any multiplayer experience for that matter.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very unique combination of genres. I wish more gaming companies would be doing this. CONS:1. I had to modify some of the keybinds because the default settings didn't make much sense to me. A good example would be that pinging friendly attack zones is bound to *mouse right click, and zooming weapon is bound to *middle mouse click. This is a simple switch of the two but honestly should have defaulted the other way to start. 2. The base you start in is just kind of a vast empty space with nothing to do. I'm sure eventually this could change and it's simply a blank slate, but it feels a bit bland. 3. I qued "quickplay" multiplayer for over 10 minutes with no games. There just aren't enough people playing this game right now.Pros:1. Unique and exciting gameplay mechanics. 2. Challenging.3. Very cool cinematics and story progression in the single player.Overall I would absolutely recommend the game, although I think they needed to do a couple things on release to make this game more accessible. I mean... it only has 31 reviews in the first 24 hours. That's CRAZY low for the kind of game this is. Anyway I believe the multiplayer and campaign should have been sold separately with maybe even a free to play multiplayer option. I strongly believe if there was a free-to-play option for multiplayer there would be tens of thousands of game downloads already and a lower price point of $19.99 for the campaign mode would have sold thousands of copies already after people got a chance to play around with the game in multiplayer. This is just a way smarter business model. I have friends I play other games with who like the looks of this game but they just can't justify spending $49.99 on it when so many other free to play games are currently available to play. Obviously I know developers need to grow their businesses and make a profit, but a $49.99 price point to even dip your toes into a game seems like such an antiquated business model at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: [My recommendation at this point is WAIT TO BUY, not NO as recommendation]I played DISINTEGRATION for +18 hours and completed the campaign story mode at maverick difficulty. This review will be updated when I complete 25 of gameplay as PVP sessions weren't open till game release date.Gameplay OverviewDisintegration is a shooting game with some RTS gameplay mechanics. It has 12 campaign missions and 3 PVP game modes (5v5) with various cosmetics options. Most of the gameplay you will be shooting enemies, targeting crews' special attacks, and collecting loot boxes.You play as a GRAVCYCLE (flying hover motorcycle) PILOT that fights and commands a ground crew. The "FLYING" DEFINES a lot of the gameplay experience.It is required a good view distance to manage the crew, which reminds the viewing perspective of an RTS game. Being far away from combat, naturally makes it LESS INTENSE than an FPS game. And... as there is an FPS character and vehicle to control, crew mechanics can't be as complex as RTS games.Here are the review toplines:1. Disintegration is an FPS game with RTS elements. It is less intense than an FPS and not as complex as an RTS game. 		2. The gameplay consists of shooting, controlling the vehicle, commanding a crew, and collecting loot boxes.		3. The game is full of cutscenes, every mission has one scene at the beginning and end. 		4. After the first half of the campaign mode, the game lacks novelty and new challenges. 	5. The campaign mode (PVE) is short when compared to the price tag, so to get an honest value out of the game, playing PVP is almost a requirement. _childDocuments_.review: I really wish I could recommend this. I stuck with it longer than most people, and there was some fun to be had in small doses. But aside from the problems mentioned in other reviews, the OTHER issue is a lack of gameplay evolution. By the time you've played 2-3 missions, you've basically seen everything the game has to offer. I kept waiting for it to open up, such as letting me choose my own loadout and team, which would have added interest. Or even just making the levels more complex, with more opportunities for tactical positioning and choices in approach. But it just didn't happen.(Is it possible these get added even later in the game? Sure, but if so, they waited far too long.)So it turned into a situation where every mission felt fundamentally the same: Flying through linear corridors, fighting the same enemies in nearly-identical battlefields over and over, with the same aggravating spawn patterns... just with every mission adding more enemies, making battles go on for obnoxiously long, and with fewer and fewer opportunities to heal. So once it got to the point the missions were genuinely difficult, it felt like a pure grind, and there just wasn't enough good about the game to keep me going.

_childDocuments_.review: I was hesitant at first about this game due to its hybrid nature. Thankfully I got a free key to try it out.Initially the game was surprisingly refreshing in the way the controls and mechanics work. The tutorial was very helpful in setting you up for success and all controls are easy use. While you can deal damage yourself, your squad is your core. The graphics an great and the sound is solid. Even the writing is pretty good. However, what could have been a new take on Destiny or Mass Effect ultimately is ruined by the fact that game play is repetitive and your choices are forced. Essentially the game devolves into a go find this or destroy that. It is a linear path and the game guides you. Difficulty settings determine how much of a fight this is and in the long run again a plus for the game is the game will either give you the mission or make it damn near impossible to get past the first wave unless you got some Pro StarCraft 2 reflexes. Upgrades are based on the amount of scrap caches both in view and hidden. In a lot of cases there were caches hidden that forced replay of the level. In most cases this would be fine but when you have to literally replay the mission cut scenes and all this is a huge problem.With missions you are forced to take certain operatives leaving a huge desire in building a team that fits with your play style. While there were missions that specific operatives are necessary there were others where the forced choice didn't make much sense.Multiplayer is not apparently online at this point or if it is I wasn't willing to wait longer than 5 minutes to find a match.I hope that these things will be addressed as there is potential here for a very unique and good game, but this overall feels like a trial of capabilities to see if this studio can do bigger things. I hope to see a patch soon and give it another go.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy the core of this game; riding on the bike feels smooth and has a nice feel to it, ordering your units is definitely simplified but still gives you enough control that, especially in the higher difficulties, makes them a crucial aspect of the combat to learn and master while you're busy shooting as well, and as someone attempting to play on the highest difficulty, while I wish there were more checkpoints and in mission saves so that I could come back to a mission later if I leave, it is absolutely brutal sometimes but victory does end up being very satisfying for it, understanding your squad and the environment is key and it is just fantastic when everything is going well. I will say though that I'm still early in the campaign and especially the opening story elements feel pretty rushed so at least so far it's the gameplay that I think is going to be the selling point.Now the multiplayer....I love it, but there's already a population problem and while V1 and PD have said in the discord that they are looking into ways to fix this issue I do think that the buy in price along with the niche aspects of it are turning people away which means, as of this review, 4 days in, I'm struggling to find games; I won't downvote it for that though, because I know I love the multiplayer, and telling everyone "don't buy because dead" isn't exactly going to solve the issue, just know that I am enjoying the campaign so far and when I can play multiplayer I do genuinely adore it....It's the when that worries me, I truly wish perhaps more people felt like I currently do in regards to it or at least that there was some form of bot match with private match support because that would be amazing, until then though I have to make this positive review incredibly bittersweet; I genuinely hold this game is really fun, but I will say that if you're buying this just for its multiplayer that might be an awkward proposition right now, and I find that thoroughly heartbreaking.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: I did get this game for free. Getting the game for free doesn’t affect my review at all.---In today's day and age with titles only being online-only and featuring no campaign, it's nice to see a company making a game with both online capability and a decent campaign for their game even though the campaign is kinda corny.The Disintegration campaign consists of 12 missions, if played on Regular difficulty it will take you about 9 hours to complete. Give or take if you die at specific missions as I did. Disintegration has many cut-scenes some are very detailed and some even detailed to real-life locations. It's a cliche hero story, though it was fun to play going through its humor moments to its sad moments.I do though have to say, $50 seems like a steep price for this type of game with out-of-game currency. Out-of-game currency? Sadly, you can buy skins with currency that you can buy with real-world money ranging from $4.99, $9.99, $19.99 and $49.99.I do agree that the developers need some sort of income to help develop this game further with free DLC and content, though I feel like they could have done it a better way. Maybe a Battle Pass similar to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare with new weapons where you can earn new Gravcycles through this Pass. For those without the Pass or if the Pass has ended, the user can unlock this Gravcycle through in-game challenges.Multiplayer is fun just like the campaign where you can control a crew but instead of doing it all alone, you have teammates on your side this time. Hopefully, cross-play with console players gets hammered out soon so the player-base for multiplayer can stay active. On a disappointing note, if you beat the campaign, you don't get any exclusive banners, badges or emotes for multiplayer use. At the moment, Disintegration doesn't feature any private servers so you can't host your own games / tournaments.Based on that, the game is not worth $49.99, I would personally price it at $29.99 or $19.99 like the Surge titles.Like my reviews? Follow my  and get updated about my latest reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: i play this game during the free weekend, so that might clouded my judgement. That's my disclaimer.Gameplay is actually pretty interesting, the genre-mixing is actually working but not in the way it should be.If you boot this game up and expecting a good RTS gameplay and nice fps icing on top, you'll be disappointed.This game feels like FPS with RTS part as a crowd control abilites and side mini gameThe game feels like they compromise too many unique RTS gameplay mechanics such as micromanaging, positioning for the sake of good FPS gameplay flowMaybe the V1 think micromanaging might kill the fps pacing, who knows?On top of that, the game don't allow you to choose your setup for different mission. You just need to run with either 1 of 3 gravicycles the game had with 2-4 from 6 of the available crews, depend on where you are in the campaign.and by this way they can manage to introduce you different units and abilities without overwhelming the playerDespite very small numbers of enemy type, the game manage to challenge you with making you with different lineup or sometimes take out some mechanics to challenge you in either the RTS part or the FPS partDoes it make the game challenging? Definitely yes. Does it make the game interesting? I can hardly agreeFrom the devs interview, this game was actually developed to be a RTS game but due they mixed the fps part later on to make the game stand out. Which i might commend that they actually succeed.The production is actually decent, but not great. The visuals, musics, character designs, and abilities are decent with some gut weird quality drop, here and there.Sometimes they forgot to put in the music despite having really nice soundtrackSometimes they cut the cinematic very weird ways, the pacing feels off with so many good lines interspersed with long silence, or they change the mood too fast you don't know what to feel.This game has so many late 90s and 2000s influences all over it and it seems like they really not notice how out of touch they are with the gaming community todayI feels like this game might be working better if it was published in late 2000s, when player expectations were low and anything that is playable with console command is eaten up by the mass audienceThe game was developed by 30 developers without crunch, published for 3 platforms and tried to present itself as a AAA titles. I don't know how to feel about thatV1 actually tried so many things, many studio did't triedBut at the same time they really struggle to make this game stands on it own without getting it judged by the market's expectation, and i find the lack of polish and different encounter to be the game's weak pointThis game is actually worth playing just to experience it as a case study of genre blending.In the age where every developers seems to go for the safe bait, i find this game to be a great endeavor, despite not meeting the market expectation.Should you buy?at any price you want, set your expectation low and wait for a deep salesBig claps for Marcus Lehto and V1 interactive for this beautifully foolish endeavor, i take this game with more heart pour into it more than whatever bungie is doing now

_childDocuments_.review: Is this an early access? No?Hell it really feels like an early access, with many things not ironed straight.And it definitely does not worth the price tag. Personally, I will pay only $20 for this, at most, in it's current state.So one big feature about this game, as it advertised, is that you can command your troops on the ground. This is supposed to give you the feeling of fighting strategically with you supporting your troops (or your troops supporting you whatever).But the awful AI ruined it all, like entirely.You see those little troops act like toy soldier, not knowing where to go, not knowing how to use cover, mindlessly running into already deployed hazards, and doing all sort of stupid things. So in the end, the expected "strategic gameplay" eventually boils down to:1) Order your troops to focus on one single enemy unit2) See your troops rush into the face of that target, and hope that your troops could overwhelm the enemy instead of being overwhelmed by the enemy3) Heal your troops in the process to increase that chance4) Rinse, repeatThat is all the "strategy" or "tactics" that is available right now, due to the horrible AI in this game. (Also, if you don't overwhelm an enemy in a timely fashion, it will heal it self. So rush and overwhelm is the only "tactic")========================================================================Aside from the AI problem, the voice acting just doesn't sound right. It feels like some homemade voice acting, with some armatures using a microphone bought from Walmart, and it just doesn't feel right.========================================================================There are other problems, but I don't want to list them all.========================================================================The only good thing I can feel so far, is the graphic and optimization.Graphic is good, and FPS is stable, even though my rig isn't top notch at all.Also the shooting doesn't feel bad.So it's best played in easy difficulty, where you can just shoot all the enemies by yourself, without worrying about your brainless troops.Can't recommend it now.

The story is very Halo-ey and the cinematic cutscenes reminded me a lot of Halo.Character development within the plot feels so rushed. You spend way more time listening to what you have to do in the missions rather than seeing character development. They kinda just smudge it into the cutscenes, which makes sense but feel rushed cause you don't really spend time learning about the characters. Also in between missions just feels so bland how uneventful things are, it's a very sour point in between riding a damn Gravcycle destroying machines..to slowly jogging around to see what allies single sentences thoughts are (sometimes they are good conversations but 80% of the are single sentence).Again, it definitely needs refinement, but besides that I "quite enjoyed playing the game" rather than "loved playing it."

_childDocuments_.review: Unique game play that goes beyond just shooting everything in sight. Story is well thought out; although, some "transition" cutscenes would be nice to know how characters got from point A to point B. The AI are not as bad as others say they are. They are set to follow in front of you at a set distance and unless you tell them otherwise they will continue to do that so once combat starts you need to tell them to take cover or target an enemy. after a targeted enemy dies they will go back to following you at that set distance as well as after interacting with an object. Some say the commands telling all the AI to go there is annoying but in reality it would be difficult to tell each one to go to a specific spot WHILE still trying to be a support with your own weapons and healing. Enemy diversity is perfectly fine. Some are arguing that their isn't enough enemy diversity but I feel it is just right. So far I have encountered 4 grunt like units which include: the common solider, the healer, the melee swarm, and snipers. After that I have ran into 2 tank units: the tank, and the Rhino. then I have met 2 flying units: Drones, and wasps (I think they are called) and I'm going to run into another in my next mission going off of what one of my challenges is. Not every game needs dozens on dozens of different enemies. My one critic of the game is the lack of special abilities for the AI. As of where I am I have only seen 3 abilities: the concussion grenade, slow bolt, and mortar fire. All in all its a fun and entertaining game and I recommend trying it for yourself rather than basing you opinion purely on others opinions of the game.

name: Tiny Thor
detailed_description: Tiny Thor features 16-bit graphics and gameplay centered around using Mjölnir, leading our Norse hero through challenging levels filled with all kinds of obstacles. It offers tight controls, fast-paced action and an experience tinged with nostalgia. Mjölnir, Tool of the Gods “It’s your birthday Thor! Now take Mjölnir, the hammer that never misses its target!” —Odin Everything has been carefully designed around this premise. The hammer can be freely aimed and bounces off surfaces and enemies, enabling all kinds of trick shots. Old-School Platformer Tiny Thor will feel familiar to retro fans, but also unique in its own ways. It features true 16-bit pixel art from Henk Nieborg and an original soundtrack by Chris Hülsbeck. Starting as a relatively simple platformer, Tiny Thor unfolds along the way, as you unlock all kinds of abilities that you dreamed of having back in the day. Boss Fights Worthy of a Young Deity The platforming is punctuated with exhilarating boss battles which will test the son of Odin. Each realm features a set of almighty adversaries who want to stop Thor on his way to becoming a true god. You will need to make use of everything you learned along the way to beat them! Overview Master ricocheting hammer throws to overwhelm enemies Learn awesome special abilities Explore over 30 handcrafted levels across three distinct realms Challenging boss fights , each with unique mechanics Rattle your brain to solve tricky environmental puzzles Discover tons of secrets and collect hidden gems to unlock challenge levels Enjoy the story of a boy taking responsibility

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Rarely have I looked forward to the final product after playing a demo as much as I did with Tiny Thor. And I was not disappointed, the final product delivered everything the demo promised. Extremely well done pixel art graphics - on the level of Dead Cells. Plus tight controls - essential for a platformer. The game doesn't show any weaknesses here either - little Thor does exactly what you tell him to do with your gamepad. Nothing is more demotivating in a platformer than when the game mechanics absolutely don't change from level to level, and here too I can give the all-clear. Tiny Thor keeps coming up with new ideas (and abilities) that make roaming through the 30 different sections not bland anytime soon, but unfortunately not necessarily easier either. In addition to the dangers from the environment, such as water - the little one can't swim, or long spikes sticking out of the ground - the mortal enemy of every jump and run hero, a variety of different enemies also want to prevent you from finishing the levels. While I wouldn't necessarily call the enemies hyper-intelligent, they are graphically different and - and this is important - all have completely different attack patterns. The various bosses are also attractively designed and will give you a run for your money. The difficulty level really starts to pick up from the third boss, a huge worm with a big eye. Up until then it's still relatively leisurely, after that it's a bit reminiscent of the brilliant Celeste, extended by a few fights.You play as Thor, the 8-year-old son of the Viking god Odin, who is given a magic hammer called Mjölnir for his birthday and immediately tries it out. This is such a hammer that is thrown and returns like a boomerang, even if it makes a few detours in the process. You can also call it back to you ahead of time by pressing a button. It bounces off walls, which makes complex trick shots possible. Soon these will also be necessary to solve simple puzzles. Equipped with Mjölnir, we set off on a journey through Asgard, after a friendly young man (who was absolutely not suspicious, but eight-year-old boys are still quite naive...) encouraged us to do so. Along the way we encounter various dangerous mythical creatures (furiously fast and well-armored killer snails, snakes, bees,...) and some bosses at the end of some levels.We start the game without many special abilities, even our hammer we get only after meeting our father, although this happens very early in the game. At first we can just jump on enemies' heads to eliminate them. We can also slide down slopes quickly from the beginning. Skills like the double jump, however, we have to earn and steal from the first boss. We also learn to dash and other useful things only in later sections. In addition to the gems lying around everywhere, there are also three diamonds to find per level, which lie around more or less off the fastest path or even well hidden. With the collected gems we can buy improvements in the store of the thieving magpies. Runes also improve our character. If we lose a life, we just restart at the last save point, if we restart the game completely, the levels we have already played through remain unlocked. We can also restart already completed levels at any time. The game is also very suitable for speedrunners, the time is automatically stopped in each level.With the help of Amiga legends Chris Hülsbeck (sound) and Henk Nieborg (graphics), a game has been created that recaptures the gameplay feel of the great platforming classics. Nieborg's distinctive graphic style embellished some of my biggest favorites in the 90s - Lionheart and Ambermoon. Also Flink and Lomark, if anyone still remembers them. Chris Hülsbeck's music is memorable to me through Turrican, or through the intro music of the Amiga version of R-Type.If you're looking for just one classic platformer this year, this may be the one for you. Extremely well done pixel art graphics, tight controls, varied levels and bosses, fast-paced gameplay with challenging platforming passages - a clear thumbs up from me!

_childDocuments_.review: For anyone who played Flink on the Sega back in the 90's and enjoyed it, this game is a dream come true. The same pixel artist returned, and his style is so dinstinctive and unique, I just felt right back at that period in time. Music is also really good, I enjoyed every level music.Gameplay is  solid, I can't complain, everything is precise to me, the movement is slow but I think it was balanced for what they present. Speaking of which, the difficulty level was clearly the highlight of this game. I could not believe how brutally difficult some of the regular stage sections were. I consider myself a pretty good gamer, even at my old age, but I was restarting too much during the last dozen of levels, too much. The ice sections in particular, with those sequential ice portals that functions with the hammer to create a path, they were hell to get through. Not only it is needed to follow it quickly to scroll the screen, with no room for a tiny mistake, sometimes you barely have time to assess what you need to do before falling to your death. I was just in awe at this level of challenge because I think a huge portion of gamers will never be able to pass these sections - only after I cleared the game I got to know there is an assist mode available.Sometimes while playing this game I considered just quitting - that's something only a few games do to me - and I wondered if my old age is decreasing my gamer skills... But I would like to think I'd still suffer with these levels even at my prime. Maybe I'm just not that good, after all. 8/10, great game. But clearly not for everyone.
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Thor

_childDocuments_.review: I see some people complaining about the difficulty level of Tiny Thor. But in my experience the game is fair. It's challenging because it actually requires you to get better at the game, something many modern games don't do. +Thor's Hammer as a mechanic was a really unique feature that I never got bored with. Both when platforming and doing puzzles. + The game doesn't just excell at being a platformer but the boss fights are also something praise. + The game also has beautiful 16bit graphics that you don't see much these days.+The story is nothing crazy deep but it's interesting enough for this type of game. - On the other hand the levels' look get very repetitive. Once you enter a new world every level pretty much looks the same. - the music also is nothing to write home about. Its got some good and upbeat tracks but they overall come of as generic. +/- Something I'm not sure how to feel about is the lack of a health system. In traditional platformers you collect coins or fruit. When you reach a 100, the game rewards you with an extra life. In Tiny Thor however you use the gemstones you collect to buy certain upgrades such as "immediately call back the hammer" while this can be fun, I miss the intensity you get from games like Crash Bandicoot when your counting down each fruit you collect waiting for that extra life that might save your life.The reward feels more instant, as opposed to Tiny Thor where you might even forget to visit the reward tree. But I also understand the levels in Tiny Thor are much longer than other platformers, so I understand why the developer didn't want to include that type of health system. You would be in the same level for days! There's a health system, you collect hearts through out each level. However when you get hit by an enemy your heart essentially falls out and the longer it stays out, the more hearts you lose. If you lose them all one hit will kill you. Which was at the very least a decent attempt at giving the player some of that intensity of collecting health.Tiny Thor is a really great platformer that drops the ball in some areas but overall offers a unique platforming experience with their take on Thor's Hammer.                       I 100% recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Thor

_childDocuments_.review: I was very excited about the game until the middle of the third world unfortunately. The levels become frustrating for my average platform player skills. After hours of trying to overcome levels I got exasperated and decided to quit the game. Too bad because I was really loving it in the first 15 levels. I really appreciated the tricks to overcome the stages with the hammer and its old school level structure. But then, as I already said, I didn’t have the patience to stay behind too long at the levels and watch videos on youtube to see help. I’m really sorry. Obviously there will be other players who will appreciate the elements of difficulty that instead led me to leave it. Rating 7.
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Thor

_childDocuments_.review: It's a creative platformer game that constantly introduces new and fun challenges. The world, not enemies, is your biggest obstacle here. This one is closer to Celeste than Contra, though there are (excellent) bosses to battle. The controls are great, though there is some subtlety to them you need to learn. Wall jumps are a two-part input: jump, then push away from the wall rapidly. And a dash doesn't count as a jump, so you can dash off cliffs and still jump twice. The music isn't for me and seems repetitive—a significant difficulty spike near the end with maybe two or three frustrating parts. Checkpoints are generous but expect a challenge. Tiny Thor is a great platformer who drops the ball in some areas but offers a unique platforming experience with their take on Thor's Hammer. I highly recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Thor

_childDocuments_.review: Tiny Thor is a perfect precision platformer that throws combat into the mix and makes it work like a charm! Seriously, it is one of the best games I’ve ever played this year and I wasn’t expecting it to be this good! Its beautiful pixel art caught my attention in the first place and seeing the fluid gameplay in the trailer, I grabbed it the first chance I got and, boy oh, boy, if only I knew I was in for a very, very good time. It starts off with very simple stages to get you familiar with the mechanics and the difficulty gradually increases so that you don’t feel like it’s unfair in any way. Although it warns you about being a difficult game in the opening, it actually has a very sweet difficulty that seasoned platformer players will be satisfied with and the beginners will probably be able to enjoy the game with the Assist Mode. However, I can’t really give you information about the Assist Mode since I haven’t played the game with the Assist Mode activated, but I’m sure it will serve its purpose for the newcomers. It starts with our little god making his way to his birthday party and his father, Odin, gives him Mjölnir as a birthday present. He later runs off to play with his new toy, only to encounter a stranger who tricks him into doing something very bad which immediately puts him on a quest to fix the mess he caused to get things right. After navigating through carefully designed stages, solving cleverly put puzzles, and defeating the perfectly crafted bosses that have their own gimmicks, our little brave god gets a new ability after each encounter that helps him on his quest. You can also buy new abilities and unlock challenge stages with blue and red diamonds you find scattered across the stages. The soundtrack is also pretty good, and the achievements are quite fair. I personally had a lot of fun unlocking them. I also hardly needed to check any guides to find blue and red diamonds in stages and it shows how fair and accessible this game is to every kind of player out there. A perfect precision platformer that is mixed with combat. It has tight controls, fair, but tough difficulty, perfectly designed stages, puzzles, and bosses. If you’re into precision platformers, Tiny Thor will be one hell of an experience for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Thor

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful art, great level design and cool music. Easily the best platformer I played in years. Good job! Can't wait to see the rest of the game and unlock all abilities. I just finished the first challenge level after 1h trying and within 10 more minutes I managed to nearly half the time. 37 seconds, What's your time? :D
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Thor

_childDocuments_.review: Lot of blind falls/jumps on your first time in areas. Almost always if you mess up you cannot recover and die, leading you to do the entire section again. Really annoying that you have to keep track if you have an available dash/jump left because it doesn't show you. Sometimes while dashing through tight spots it will teleport you forward. The final boss was very lame, first phase repeat the same patterns twice (even the climbing section all the platforms were the exact same...). The 2nd phase was very janky too. Do not recommend in its current state. The first half was very fun and simple then the platforming difficulty really spikes up.
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Thor

_childDocuments_.review: I always thought this one was a tad pricey for a 16 bit platformer, so have been patiently waiting for a sale. At 24 AUD, I thought it was more reasonable, so took the plunge.After all that, this is really one of the tougher games for me to rate, as I love 16 bit action platformers and action platformers in general, but I don't really love Tiny Thor.So ultimately,  I can't recommend it, and will explain why in this review. In a nutshell though, for those who don't want to read everything, I didn't like it enough and didn't like the feel of the main weapon.There was also never a point where I LOVED the game. I am an old man who comes from the 8, 16 and 32 bit console era, not to mention arcade. So I know what I really like in a platformer, and control feel/weapon feel is always right there at the top of importance.First, let's get the good out of the way. The jumping mechanics feel 100% precise, and input lag is low. You can confidently make edge jumps.There's layers of parallax and overall it looks pretty, mostly. Even though I only played for an hour, I flicked through a long play video and noticed the basic brown building blocks are present throughout the ~6 hour game.The variety, visually, doesn't seem to really be there, so whilst somewhat striking, it all becomes a bit samey after a while.It has native 4K support in full screen mode or borderless, which is a great feature that every game should have. The actual bordered window options were very limited to 3 sizes though, all way too small for a 4K panel, so forget playing it in that mode. So borderless windowed it was. I am ok with that.What I am not ok with is the main weapon and soundtrack.Firstly, the hammer.Even after an hour, it felt completely alien to me and hence the main reason why I decided to uninstall and refund.Rather than feeling like a natural extension of the character, the hammer feels, well, kludgy. I am trying to find the word. Unwieldy perhaps?Rather than feeling precisely connected to a button, it feels more like a chore every single time you want to aim it.The game also heavily encourages use of the left analog stick, as for some reason d-p ad aiming is limited to up and down rather than the direction aiming of the stick. This I can not understand, as a precision platformer (IMHO) should be played with a digital arcade stick or d-pad. 30 minutes had gone by and I was still trying to aim the hammer by pointing it where I wanted it to go, and eventually I just succumbed and used the analog stick.Even a non aimed, straight ahead quick hammer attack feels wrong to me. Kludgy.The best action platformers have combat that feels entirely natural and never fighting the player. Tiny Thor does the opposite.Oh, a quick word about difficulty. If you can get used to the hammer mechanic, the rest of the level design feels fair and polished, form my limited time with the game in any case. It's again nothing bad, but I just didn't enjoy myself. I hope I am making sense. I mean I can see that real love and effort was put into this, and on paper it should be my type of game, but it just doesn't work for me.I did notice in a long-play video that you get some dash and hammer upgrades, and that would certainly be something to look forwards to for those who want to stick it out with Tiny Thor.Music, well, it's good, compositionally speaking - the problem is that out of the tracks I heard, none truly fit the gameplay! The first level was downright lethargic and sleep inducing, second picked it up and third again, and so on.. (boss music was the best bit for sure in the time I played but still not quite there). Music is SUCH a big part of a retro gaming experience for me, and Tiny Thor really let me down in that department. In an action game, I want action music. Something that excites me and helps drive the game along. A perfect example would be the two bloodstained curse of the moon games. Masterful music that goes with exactly what you are doing and what I expect in a $30 game.Man I will probably get hate for this, but if I had to sum it up, I'd honestly say it's the elevator music of the retro platform game genre. Nothing is ever unpleasant, but it's just "there".Some minor issues: The game refused to recognise my 144hz refresh rate, all the in game resolution options showing it as a 60hz panel (I double checked that the screen was set at 144 and not 60, and even went to 60 and back to 144 just in case that would trigger the game to realise it was a 144hz panel), so the unlock frame rate setting in the options screen did nothing, it always maxed at 60 FPS, even with v sync disabled. That said, I highly advise turning off v-sync as the game exhibited no tearing with it off (and if the frame rate works above 60 for you, obviously cap it at a couple blow your refresh rate with RTSS and this should maintain a tear free experience).As already mentioned, lag was very low like this. The thing is, according to pc gaming wiki and indication from the game's own settings, this game should support higher FPS. Had that worked on my system as it should have, the lag would have been improved even more, and who knows, may have helped the hammer throwing feel better. I can not say as I was stuck at 60 FPS no matter what I tried.I also didn't like how I could not change sound levels in game, and yes, you have to leave the level you are playing to do so! So, fine tuning the SFX/Music ratio was a chore. EVEN THAT! Lol.I mean this is something I want to do in game as I play, whilst I hear the sounds in real time. Ultimately, it took only about 8 goes to get the balance to my liking, but still, sound level should be accessible at any time in game. Actually I think this is the first game I have played on Steam where it's not!I just realised I used the word chore above. I think that sums it all up for me. Rather than having a blast, it more or less feels like I am working for no pay yet having a *little* fun here and there to break it up, but overall, I am just getting tired and more tired, bored even, and want to go home. And then I take another look at it and think, "hang on, it all looks like it should be the kind of thing I want to spend time on", so I try again, but then am reminded why I want to go home.I can't be the only one, since the reviews for this one are "mixed". I hate giving a negative review but at the same time, well, honesty is the best policy.
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Thor

_childDocuments_.review: I only narrowly recommend this one.  I got most of the way through the game.  It is quite short, though a bit longer if you collect all of the gems to unlock all of its harder, optional stages. I didn't love Tiny Thor.  It's not an immersive, straightforward platformer like Donkey Kong Country or Mario World. I don't outright hate precision platformers (Super Meat Boy, Aeterna Noctis <3) though I do tend to avoid puzzle platformers for the most part.  Every now and then you'll hit a section in a level where you might need to spend a few minutes just figuring out how to progress and then die a few times trying to execute the plan near-perfectly.Tiny Thor also doesn't have much diversity in biomes/areas which makes it easy not to get immersed or care about the world you are advancing in on the map screen.  The music was.. "fine" but didn't hook me in either.Tiny Thor isn't bad, in fact some things like the way the throwing hammer is used to solve problems can be quite creative, but ultimately I found the experience to be lackluster and unexceptional.
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Thor

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly going to have to say no to this one. I did finish it but reluctantly (and stubbornly) after about 7hrs. The longer the game went on the more I just wanted to be done with it. It's got a lot of neat ideas, every so often I'd come across a section that made me say "Oh that was really cool!" but then a lot of the level design decisions with trying to make the game "difficult" just got in the way of the fun that could and should have been had.I will say the game visually looks great and going back through some of the earlier levels after you have all the movement skills felt way smoother and more enjoyable like that's how it should have been to start lol. And props for the subtle hints early on in a stage showing you how do tricks you'll need later on in the level in more complicated sections, nice touch.As far as difficulty, really not bad. Found it a bit too slow paced with a lot of waiting around and trial and error. Once you get to Level 21 Tempest Towers, from then on it's kind of a sh*t show. It doesn't really get harder, it just becomes...questionable. A lot of time I just found myself damage boosting through sections rather than doing the intended method. After the first level, I had no desire to go out of my way to get any of the collectibles. Getting 300+ (and sometimes even 400+, 500+) blue crystals in each level??? Sometimes less is more, this is one of those times. I think the blue gems could have been used a bit more strategically to indicate more of the platforming sections that were unclear on how to proceed or secrets, instead of mostly just random placement and hiding them everywhere.Anyways the ideas for a great game were there and definitely felt like there was some influence from the OG DKCs and Yoshi's Island. It had some great moments (Challenge IV Floorless Frivolity felt really smooth except the middle part with the lowering columns which I just skipped lol) but it wasn't as fun as it could have been.PS I unintentionally beat the final boss hit-less and saw there was a hit-less achievement for each and all bosses so I felt compelled to go back to do that and a few more of the easier-to-get achievements XD
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Thor

_childDocuments_.review: Puts the "F" both in "Fun" and "Frustrating"! You might die a hundred times but don't you worry, you'll always come back cause  it must be possible to beat this level, you can't be  bad, right? That's to say, Tiny Thor is, as difficult as it might be (without being unfair), kind of addicting and honestly a lot of fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Whaouw, what a huge pain in the ass that was.It starts off ok-ish, your basic 16bit era platformer with lots of micro-issues that make it somewhat awkward to play but it could have deserved a 6/10.But soon the platforming starts getting quite hardcore and the gameplay issues make it a huge pain. Things are just not tight enough to build a precision platformer and the physics is quite questionable. I forced myself to finish it and started really resenting it more and more as i was getting closer to the end.Also there are only 3 environments, the levels are way too long and very little music variety.4/10

_childDocuments_.review: If I were to disregard the level design, then by all accounts this would be a wonderful game. Authentic sprites, music and sound effects that really appeal to me, with tight controls and really tight hitboxes/programming. I will solely recommend it based on that because I do think it deserves it. I also think the hammer is a fun gimmick, despite not being sure why aiming the hammer isn't just the same button as throwing the hammer, but I digress.However, the level design is straight out of hell. I actually thought this wasn't going to be as hard as some reviews made it out to be and it looked like a really cute platformer with just some harder passages, but the levels really have been made by satan himself. Up until around 25% of the game, it really is fun, enjoyable, well paced and whimsical at moments. Gives you plenty of time to adore the wonderful sprite work... then once the rest of the plot is revealed to you it will just continue being more and more difficult. There are moments of short peace whenever you are introduced to a new mechanic, but then it just continues shifting into higher gears. I actually think a lot of the puzzles and mechanical stuff you can pull off is quite clever and the level design is actually really good if you're looking for a challenge that doesn't get boring too fast. Like there's a ton of things I haven't seen in other hardcore platformers before and usually that type of level design gets repetitive really fast. I also don't think it ever is "unfair" in a sense of just throwing random stuff at you. The design is deliberate and fair, with decent checkpoints, so most of it really boils down to pressing movement keys in the right order... but it really is exhausting and draining at the butt clenching pace a lot of levels are going. There's an accessibility mode, but it doesn't really help you because the problem are not the enemies, it's the mechanical skill that's required. They would need to add something like a flying thor mode.I think it's worth the money because everything else is stellar and to be honest I should've just expected it to be really hard, so I'm not really the main demographic anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Thor

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic! I love pretty much everything about it! From the design to the awesome music to the incredible level design and the ideas that can be found in so many little things. I am simply blasted and no game managed to do that in a long time!! The later the game the more complex the levels became but they were always very thought through, a pure joy to play!
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Thor

_childDocuments_.review: I never liked precision platforming. I think i'm just not good at it. BUT this one really hooked me.It's just fun....i'd died a trillion of times and I almost gave up several times. But then there was an idea - and it worked.It is really challenging - but so far (50+% - 25hours playtime) not unfair.There is always a save point after an hard area.And you get better and better.When you've found a solution that works - it just works again and again (most times :)Some levels you have to play 2-3 times to find all the secrets and diamonds...There is also an included cheat mode.Which is nice - and i used it twice to train a part without instant death - to then play it in "real".Only the bonus levels are too stressful for my age (40+). So i leave them aside - so far...Thanks to the Devs for this gem.

_childDocuments_.review: Was really looking forward to this game after the demo.  It does not disappoint.  I love the art style.  The platforming and puzzle solving are top notch and make great use of the hammer bouncing around the environment.  The combat is good but not great, though, IMO.  It's definitely intended to be a challenge, but I just think it's got more issues than the platforming that lead to it becoming more frustrating than fun at times.But all in all a strong recommend!
