_childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is a racing game that explores rally's golden era with an unabashed fervor and tasteful minimalist (but not too much) graphical design. The game has such a passion for the sport and driving in general, that it resonates through the whole experience. Is there a plot? Not in a traditional sense. Every stage is a story, from popping your tire when you decided to cut on a hairpin or nailing that upcoming corner after hitting an incline flatout. A narrative isn't necessary, because the experience communicates to you what the era of driving is like, as you see the vehicle grow immensely in power, adapt all-wheel drivetrains, and feel in your own hands the exponential speed the technology was growing as you struggle to keep up with the extra power as many drivers at the time did, as it was at the end of the Group B era of fast but dangerous experimental race cars. It's perspective might not be standard, but is welcome in malaise of similar looking racing games, especially so since you will not be hearing from a co-driver. The cars are all here and you'll recognize them not just by how they look, but how they drive too, each feeling sublime in the hand but distinct as well. Evidently, the developers passion didn't end at just making the game itself as they continue to release updates since the games release. This is fantastic, especially considering the games relatively niche status. Don't let a $25 price tag scare you, it's completely worth asking price. It's the Alfa Romeo of racing games: not many people are going to own it, but it is nonetheless a treat for those who do and an absolute gem that bleeds passion. If Forza Horizon gets you down with shoddy online racing, if Need for Speed is too cheesy, if Assetto Corsa is too involved, if Wreckfest is too lacking in sportsmanship, and if Gran Turismo is too on Playstation, Art of Rally will be here to pick up the pieces, tell you everything is alright, and to focus on the one thing that matters: the drive. What beautiful drive it is.

_childDocuments_.review: This game actively punishes you for taking jumps, there is no co-driver and no driver cues, it promotes replaying courses over and over to get decent times. This goes against the spirit of rally entirely.  The gravel physics are also flaming garbage, the cars drive like it's ice and there is absolutely no nuance to control at all, weight transfer is incredibly unrealistic and all of the cars feel very floaty. I'm pretty sure the gravity is really low, it explains how you can spend over 5 seconds in the air on a blind jump that exceeds twice any jump you'd find in Finland in real life. These blind jumps are suicidal to get any airtime on because many go from being long fast straights to the jump, and then mid-jump it becomes a sharp corner. Imagine going from a long 6  right, 250, to big jump square right triple caution. Nowhere on earth is that realistic, and it's even worse not having any cues that warn of them especially at night since the view is more top-down than forwards-facing that could give you the opportunity to look ahead, but no you have to spend time staring at how awful your car drives since the camera is not completely locked and sways around with drag and your momentum instead of the car chassis itself. It's a recipe for an unplayable game that is the antithesis of rally, it has no redeeming characteristics that would make me ever recommend this game in the face of these issues. Do not play.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the simplicity of its graphics, the game performance is horrible. People who made the Unity Engine are not stupid, they created an industry standard game engine. It's up to the developers to utilize the engine in a smart way to optimize the performance. Devs of this game assume everyone can throw enough chip power at the game so it runs good no matter how bad the optimization is, but the reality is people who would buy this game are not really invested in gaming that much, they don't want to spend huge cash just to run this one.So, to cut it short, if you have a machine that can run, say, BF1 at full settings, this game will push it to its limits, not in terms of graphical fidelity though.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just extremely good. And I really didn't expect it to be. I usually don't play single player games anymore. I am not an enthusiast for minimalistic/stylized graphics or indie productions. I don't think I really would've ever bought the game if I hadn't been so annoyed by long loading times of other games (Forza) or would my friends have been online to play some multiplayer game. But damn am I happy I did.This game... it reminds you of better times. _childDocuments_.review: It's gonna be a maybe yes from me.To begin with the positives.The general graphical style is pleasant and easy to read.Car physics strike a good balance and cars definitely feel different from one another as do FF vs FR/RR vs AWD and different surface and conditionsAudio is great for the most part (with one major exception but I'll mention that latter)The campaign portion is nicely paced, though slightly lacking at the upper end (wouldn't mind a super expert one with all 12 stage rallies and free choice of vehicle)The car selection isn't perfect but it's so damn good I think it's easily the best I've seen in a rally game.Now the less good partFrom how the game is presented it would seem it's targeted at people not really that familiar with rally games and aims to introduce them to it in a slightly different way, while still retaining a certain level of interest for people familiar with rally games.However the game is actually really punishing to anyone not actually decent to good at rally games and by design makes some parts of that harder.First the camera, it's not nearly as bad as you might think even if you come from even a hood / bumper / cockpit camera hardliner perspective, takes a bit of tweaking and getting used to but definitely decent, except for one single thing, you cannot gauge with any reliability that your wheels have lifted off the ground, this leads to some crashes / rolling over not being really avoidable, coupled with the artstyle masking bumps on the side of the road it leads to you having to learn stages to a degree.Second is the auto transmission being absolute trash, it's the worst I've had to play with, literally losing seconds to the game deciding to not downshift when you're at a speed that would be fine two gears down is infuriating, lack of semi auto doesn't help here.Third is the AI being extremely inconsistent, you can have top 1% times, and come second, you can have top 50% times, and wipe away the competition by a decent margin, unless there's some sort of autotuned AI difficulty the normal AI should not be that extreme, it's unpleasant for me but I'd assume a less competent player might actually feel really bad to see he still got beaten when he drove the best he ever has.Fourth, the auto recovery when you go "too far" off track is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ absurd in some corner, as in it's way too close to the actual road, in some case you almost have a tire on the road and still can get reset.Fifth, Finland is disgustingly easy, yes I'm that upset about that, Finland in any other rally game I can think of is at least among the hardest rally in the game if not the hardest by far.Slightly more minor nitpicks include the turbo flutter on some car sounding like someone scratching paper with a pencil, some track, camera and conditions leading to you getting flasbanged by the sun in some part, the RWD cars in Group B are just there to make you feel miserable when you chose them over AWD cars and might deserve a category split just for that.In conclusion, if you're fine with getting a bit roughed up by the game and really like the different approach to rallying then go ahead and get the game, if you wanna get introduced to rally, do yourself a favor and wait for Sebastian Loeb Rally Evo to go on sale, nab the deluxe edition and 100% it, it's not flawless, but it does a far better job at easing you into rallying on top of being 3 bucks only, and you get the second best car roster of the rally subgenre on top (not counting modded games obviously).

_childDocuments_.review: What if Rally Racing never got bogged down by rules and regulations?That is a question this game answers. Starting out with classic Rally cars of the early 60s such as the iconic Renault Alpine A110, over icons of the sport from the 80s like the Lancia 037 all the way to fictional marvels and powerful AWD beasts, this game takes its players on a journey through the history of rally sport.The game has a learning curve as steep as the player wants, the AI is quite slow on the lowest and almost unbeatable on the highest - That said, the AI is just a bunch of times that appear on a board. But that doesn't matter. What matters is the driving, this is a racing game, after all. And it feels fantastic. Each car has its own character, they feel different enough for me to pick favorites even after trying each car only once. The handling feels realistic, the cars have palpable weight, and to handle that is the challenge. They sound amazing, and the visual of the game, albeit simple, do the job and the light effects through the trees of Norway as you blast through a Forest going 130 mph still look mesmerizing. That and the plethora of options, customizability of the camera angle, for example, make this game one of the true gems of 2020.If you like racing, you should consider buying it. If you love racing games, you should definitely buy it. If you love the history of rally, you must buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece. Yes, it may be a top down arcade game, something that could make sim fans look elsewhere, but its physic engine really puts many sims to shame (for me, it's the second best rally game after the great old Richard Burns Rally). Once you get the hang of the driving model, you will be hooked forever, AoR really is a work of love, and it shows it every moment you play. The only downside for me is that wheels are not officially supported, so they can work or not, but it's not a great problem in the end. It's a game meant to be played with a gamepad, but it's surprisingly good with a keyboard too. It has more than 50 cars (plus some "extras"), ranging from group 2 to group A, and 8 rallies (Finland, Sardinia, Japan, Norway, Germany, Kenya, Indonesia and, with the dlc, Australia), for a total of 84 (96 with the Australia dlc) stages, considering normal and reverse versions (complete with daylight, night, fog, rainy/snowy conditions). Graphics speaks for themselves: Its wonderful, minimalistic art style is simply beautiful to look at, it's like looking at a childhood dream come true, with little cars running in amazing dioramas. It has beautiful replays and an A-M-A-Z-I-N-G photo mode to make every virtual photographer happy, especially now that you can create and/or import custom made liveries. It also has an amazing soundtrack. If you love cars, rally, or simply a game that you can easily pick up and play for a few minutes (but remember, this is one of those games where you say "just five minutes more" and then you look at the clock and hours have passed :) ) there's really no reason for not buying Art Of Rally. Do it. You won't be disappointed.

Can't wait to dive more in the career modes!

_childDocuments_.review: art of rally is quite a unique game that follows hot on the footsteps of Absolute Drift and I think it improves upon it in virtually every way. Even though I find some parts of it rather frustrating, there's just something about it that makes me come back to it.The art style is very characteristic and clean, emulating the lower poly models of games like CMR 2 and SEGA Rally, which are obvious inspirations in my eyes. Other than that distinction, everything else presentation wise, like sounds and UI is solid but minimalistic. So far there's a small variety of locations which will be expanded (hopefully soon!). As of writing this, it includes: Norway, Germany, Italy, Finland, Japan. The stage variety is good, and the layouts can range from high speed wide gravel roads, to narrow tarmac paths with a lot of hazards. Every stage also has different weather conditions. Rain in particular can be quite interesting with the introduction of puddles that can throw your car off balance.Now, the meat of the topic: gameplay. I have to say that they've done an amazing job at making the cars drivable AND driftable with arrow keys. The system is so good that I'm comfortable enough to do 1% times on most stages with a lot of cars! The driving model is not perfect though; my main strife (which is thankfully slowly getting better it seems) is the weight of the car during jumps and while it is generally unstable seems to be negligible and on occassion it can even be thrown around by the poles on the sides of the road if you hit them in the wrong way. This is just minor though, and it doesn't take anything away from the solid dynamics that funselektor has produced!Normally, I'm mostly a Dirt Rally 2.0 guy and I also play some circuit sims and naturally that means that I will find some parts of the game frustrating and a little off in a pedantic, subconsciously elitist sort of way. But when I can't be arsed to bolt on my wheel and boot up a sim to slide around in a Group A car, I think I'll be hard-pressed to find a better alternative than this!

_childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is pure, gorgeous, authentic rally racing zen. Don't let its simple visuals fool you. There is beauty around every corner and an exhilarating sense of accomplishment for nailing them just right. You can tell this game comes from a place of passion for the sport, and this shows in the choice of detail on the courses, the cars, the sound design, and the physics. It captures the essence of rally in only the most important details. If you pick up this game, don't let the controls and perspective scare you off. If you're like me, you'll find yourself struggling to find a footing, but if you give it a few races, and as you unlock the newer, better handling cars, you'll find yourself at home, one with the car and whatever sits under the rubber of your wheels.If you like racing, rally, or history of the sport, don't miss out on this one. Even if you're new to it, give it a try. You might find yourself surprised.

_childDocuments_.review: Just before i start the review i'd like to say I'm not that well versed in this genre, but i still really like the driving games I have played.It's a great driving game, with somewhat strange driving physics. Where you have to be more aware of your speed and ability to turn in certain situations than games like Mario Kart 8, (which i've always felt as having a bit too uninteresting driving, especially compared to games like Sonic Robo Blast 2 Kart, and this game, so if you feel the same way about Mario Kart that i do, maybe check those games out?)  and Sonic Robo Blast 2 Kart.I haven't tried online yet, but i can give my opinion on the rest of the gamemodes. The racing mode in this game is more like a time trial, which may not sound as cool as playing head to head, but it still feels great to play.On that point, i'd recommend playing the free driving mode, to get the hang of the driving controls, since you can rocket off the track and still be fine, unless you get stuck upside down or fall into a lake. And it feels so cool  to successfully do a difficult turn with this game's physics, especially when going really fast. And the open worlds it has, all feel different from one another, while also being fun, and pretty.I've spent a fair bit of my time offroading in this game, trying to get as far away from the road before i get stuck, and get teleported back to the road. _childDocuments_.review: I definitely recommend this fun and somewhat casual rally game.  I don't consider myself a sim-racer but I have been playing game series like Forza, Dirt, Burnout and Flatout for years.  This game lies somewhere in-between arcade and sim with a less-than-serious aesthetic but surprisingly engaging driving.  The handling reminds me of the original Flatout in that it is not a full simulation yet demands reasonable driving input.  Be careful or you will crash, unlike something like Burnout where you just apply full left or right and scrape the wall.  A lot of people compare art of rally to Dirt Rally, but I feel that Dirt Rally is much more of a simulator than this game is.  The biggest downside to art of rally is the high camera angle which makes judging elevation changes or crests kind of hard.Anyway, if you wish the '80s and Group B never ended than buy this game!

_childDocuments_.review: I don't play many driving games, but I really enjoyed Absolute Drift a couple of years ago and despite rallying being the least interesting racing to me after F1, I decided to give this game a try. In brief: this is a driving game anyone can pick up if you are happy to spend a little time getting used to it, and I think that time investment is well worth it.The driving itself feels crisp and consistent, so much so that after a while you find yourself making instinctive changes to your speed/angle in the approach to a corner, without having a good explanation as to why, but when those instinctive changes are right and you slide through the corner perfectly...there's few experiences like it.You can play this a bit like Absolute Drift, where you explore the open areas and find collectibles/do challenges, or you can do what I did and absolutely laser through the career mode after you do your first race. There's something incredibly compelling about knocking out just one or two more stages, gambling with your restarts to try and get a better placement, trying out a new car and struggling with its nuances. I like the game a lot because it rarely makes you repeat stuff, you usually only repeat if _you_ want to do better. Really messing up a stage isn't that uncommon, but this is not a game where you make one or two mistakes and have to retry to proceed. It's not so much that it is forgiving, as that pretty much every driver is going to have screwups and slow stages across a rally. So if you come 5th in a stage, and you don't feel confident in a rerun, just let the cards fall where they may and you could have a huge time advantage after another stage or two. Get used to using the 'back to road' rescue button though, just because sometimes you'll waste far more than the 5-second penalty getting yourself back.*If you are struggling early on:* Try more cars! I found the initial group a bit of a struggle to get to grips with, possibly just because getting used to the control system, but I probably stuck to one of them for too long. I was afraid of failing badly in season mode with an unfamiliar car and being 'stuck' but you can always just try again. Worst case, quit the season and try another if it's feeling bad after two races. Or if you're better at preparing than me, try the car in single races instead of in a season!The music bears mentioning all on its own for being truly great, a serious contributor to the relaxed feeling I have when proceeding through a stage that isn't going terribly. Tatreal did an unreal job and I went directly to Bandcamp to buy the OST.Thank you Funselektor and especially thank you for the continued updates, I hopped on pretty late (only a couple of months ago) and there is a TON to see and do.

_childDocuments_.review: Without a doubt one of the greatest videogames I have ever had the privilege to play. The atmosphere, visuals, controls, sound, music, performance is all perfect and combine together to make an experience that is absolutely seamless and genuinely fulfils its name by going beyond being just a game and entering the realm of a work of art.I am a huge fan of rallying, both the present form of the sport and its entire historical lifetime, so the content of the game I can confidently say is made by people who are genuinely interested in, and genuinely dedicated to replicating, the historic feel of 1960s-1990s rallying. The wide range of cars and locations are beautifully accurate and encapsulate both the genuine articles as well as the popular fan conscience of what they should feel, look, and be like - it's a masterful balance that is no mean feat to pull off.The game is designed for keyboard or controller use, but I use a Logitech G29 steering wheel and the game handles it perfectly anyway - cars control very well and with sufficient time tweaking the controls to fit my needs I am very confident in throwing them sideways into corners or even using more advanced techniques like clutch kicking or stomping the accelerator entering a turn to throw the rear end out much like in the real-world equivalent.The soundtrack I love enough that I bought the album on Bandcamp from the game's musician's account directly, it's a brilliant homage to 80s synth and electronic music - the game's sounds outside of the music such as car noises are spot-on too, it properly feels like you have hundreds of horsepower at your beck and call.Performance-wise I have had zero issues - I run the game on a slightly older but still decent PC, with an i5-6600K CPU and an original GTX 1070, and I would comfortably say despite it no longer being particularly high-end, the game is not resource-demanding in the slightest and these two components easily run well above what the game requires.Overall, as I have reached the last two years of Group A in the game's career mode and polished off finding all the collectables in freeroam mode, I feel I can greatly recommend this game to anyone looking for a highly enjoyable racing / rallying game that recreates a golden era of motorsport, doesn't need simulator levels of expense and preparation, yet is also looking for something to enjoy putting a bit of work into to progress with. It has been a fabulous experience for me.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR;Recommended for: Players who has a controller, love rally and has a thing for grinding the same track over and over to get that 1 sec. off your track record.Not recommended for: Players with no controllers, want a casual pick-up & go game-play.I first thought this would be a relaxing casual top-down racer with beautiful minimal designed graphics.. boy was I wrong. This is a very sim-cadey race game where it requests full concentration while you race. I say sim-cadey because the game sort of simulates a realistic driving mechanics and physics but it's nothing like the real world and has it's own rules of physics that you need to get used to. First the control seemed very awkward and finicky but after getting used on how the vehicles react it just became finicky. I think it would have been more beginner friendly if they had a better tutorial and more guidelines on how and what matters to the physics of driving a car. This definitely isn't for everyone but if you find joy in figuring out things on yourself and get a dopamine boost when you shave that half of a second off after trying a track for tens of times in a row - this game is just right for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely game. Enough of a challenge without being massively rage inducing as rally games often are. Simplistic graphics work really well. It's a really pleasant place to spend some time.The steep camera angle shows enough of the road ahead to do away with the need for pace notes, which is nice. It took me a while to figure out why the camera angle needs getting used to.Typically in driving games, your eyeline is aligned with the direction of the car. It's therefore sufficient to look at the road ahead and let your peripheral vision take care of keeping track of the car's attitude.With the top down view, if you look at your car, you lose track of the road ahead. If you look at the road ahead, you lose track of the car's attitude.The solution seems to be to focus at a point halfway between the car and the edge of the screen. Your peripheral vision then takes care of both, with occasional glances back and forth to check on one or the other. Hope that helps someone :-)

_childDocuments_.review: Artistic, arcadey, but pretty good physics simulation. If you liked Absolute Drift, you'll most likely like the Art of Rally.It's not very challenging, the AI times and your position is rather arbitrary, more so that you can adjust the difficulty of AI and how fast your car breaks down. As the Buddha in the beginning said - "To finish first - first you must finish" - you only need to finish each and every race in career mode, to my knowledge you can finish at last place and you'll still unlock most stuff, and the only two limitations are the difficulty of tracks/car handling, amount of restarts you get and damaging your car makes progress harder since you can repair the car only at certain races and you have limited amount of time to do it.I would say that the game is at it's best when you find that car in the season that you really like and driving it is just pure Zen, and the challenge and progression is getting better at handling it and driving around tracks as perfect as possible.The visuals are simple but stunning. Cars handle incredible even on keyboard (except for the group b rotary, holy heck is it hard to control). Sound design is also nice. Tracks are varied and challenging in different ways, rain weather makes a drastic impact on handling.Linux-native, too!For me the only downsides are:- Some glitches on linux with AMD when using bloom at night (something similar happens in other games too tho), easily fixed.- Physics can get wonky sometimes - hitting a hay bale sometimes can pinball you away, slightly scratching your car with guardrail at 200km/h can result in terminal damage (have to restart)- AI times are not challenging but also not very consistent, you can potentially still get 1st place even though you finished 4-8 places in the season, purely because you still got more points than AI.- AI is arbitrary, you never see them, they just appear at race results in table as names, times, flags and car. Each race is essentially a time trial - there's no car behind you and no car ahead of you. It feels a bit tacked on because rally has to have some competition in some form.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is going to be my game of the year, and no I did not forget about games like "Cyberpunk 2077". I want to explain all of you why, and why this game is definetly worth its money  (I played the demo since release, so I have a bit more playtime then it displays on the main game.)"art of rally" is a arcade rally game, which uses some interesting graphics design and camera. The game currently has over 40 cars and 15 tracks, all of them are heavily based on real cars/locations. The games biggest selling point, at least in my opinion, would be the overall feeling of the game. As Kotaku said, "art of rally turns driving into meditation". The graphics stlye is unrivaled, and the photo mode can make some crazy pictures. The OST, the graphics, the sounds, the controls, the general driving feel - everything works together perfectly for this masterpiece of a game. You just plug in your controller, boot the game, and drive for hours on hours, which brings us to the next topic:The game itself has some assists like ABS and stability-control, but they are configurable from 100% down to 0% for purists. You can obviously switch between automatic or manual shifting, and if you choose manual then you even have to use the clutch in certain cars. The story can be challenging, at least you will have to get used to some tracks before you will master the art of rallying there. But of course you can also compete agains your friends:Currently, every track has its own worldwide leaderboard for you to compete in. But there are also daily and weekly challanges, so you have something new to master every day.The game currently has over 40 cars, which you unlock as you progress through the story (yes, there even is a story.) All of the cars are very very heavily inspired by realy world (rally) cars, for example you can drive a BMW 2002 Turbo, a BMW M1, a Ford Escord 1600, a Porsche 959 rally, a Lancia Delta, Lancia Stratos, I could go on like this forever. Basically there will be at least 2 or 3 cars everyone will like.The tracks are based of real tracks aswell, at least for the country / general location. There are tracks in Japan, Africa, Sweden, Poland, Marocco, even the german "Panzerplatte" - more then enough. There also is a freeroam map with some collectibles.Obviously, this game is an arcade game that was designed around using a controller. The game has mouse and keyboard support, but is definetly best enjoyed with a controller.This game was designed almost entirely by one dev (@funselektor on twitter.) "art of rally" is an incredible game, even for a 30 man dev team. But if you think about the fact that one guy did almost all of this by himself in over 5 years, it is even more impressive., and is a must have for every singe rally fan out there. The complete vibe and package you get with this game is incredible, I can guarantee that I will spend way too much time with this game. There is so much variety, daily challanges to compete in, leaderboards to climb, tracks to master and photos to shoot. If this review or any of the trailers made you interested in the game but you are still unsure, try the free demo in the steam store. Its free and 800mb, so why not?See you on the leaderboards, and watch out for the trees.I dont write that many steam reviews, and english is not my native language, so please ignore any spelling mistakes :)

_childDocuments_.review: A great game, although would only recommend it to people who enjoyed Dirt Rally or enjoy other at least semi simulator driving/rallying games. For people who enjoyed those games this is a great change of pace and a bit more casual and less punishing.The physics, although took me a few hours to get the hang of, are a good level of realism. The graphics speak for themselves and are amazing.If you don't enjoy driving mechanics and the art of perfecting them then you likely won't get too much longevity out of this game as there's not much to it other than driving down a road by yourself (as rallying is) trying to improve, riding that line of control and speed. There's no story, just a bunch of different classes of cars which all handle differently and you merely have to finish the rally to unlock the next one. The progression isn't gated on difficulty or placement (other than not using up all your restarts to unlock liveries), which is why I say if you don't enjoy rallying you probably won't enjoy the game.You are limited to a multitude of varying birds eye view, which takes a lot of the mental effort out as you're able to see all upcoming corners and prepare and position for them as opposed to listening to a co driver. It took me a few hours to get the hang of controlling the car (so don't despair if you're wiggling around all over the road, it does get better!) and it's very satisfying once you do.A minor complaint is that the different road textures don't feel particularly different from each other, the transition between road and gravel isn't noticeable but then rain feels way overtuned and closer to ice or driving with slicks in the wet.For me as someone who has a few hundred hours in other racing games and Dirt Rally, I have thoroughly enjoyed it and am amazed that no one has done a racing game before with great physics without super realistic graphics. Such a good niche has been filled with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Motorsport games have always been a mix of power, precision, and noise. There have certainly been plenty of titles that have managed to combine these 3 qualities into intriguing packages, but none have managed to pull this off with such stylish bravado. Developer Funselektor has put together an incredibly minimalist, yet stylish, package that deserves the attention of any keen Motorsport enthusiast.From the very first time you take to the tarmac, the game’s strict adherence to minimalism is at the forefront of every decision. Not only are the graphics absolutely gorgeous, but this minimalist approach stretches to every nook and cranny of the game. The menus here are simple and clean, with little fuss or hassle. Real brands have been replaced by sleek and simple slogans. Combine this with the lo-fi soundtrack and you have the recipe for what is a very calming and zen-like experience. Driving takes precedence in this game, and I’ll be damned if it doesn’t look good doing it. Fans of Funselektor’s previous game, Absolute Drift, will certainly feel right at home immediately.The game isn’t just pure eye candy either. Art of Rally contains a diverse roster of over 50 different cars. All your favorite vehicles from rally games old and new have made it, along with some fun vehicles I won’t spoil. None of the official likenesses have made it in the game, but this doesn’t really affect things in the long run as its very easy to spot your favorite rally car. I had particular fun sliding around corners in Funselektor’s version of the Ford Escort MK2. Whether you’re driving a 1960 classic or one of the modern competitors, each vehicle handles differently. Some of the antiques can be small and nimble, requiring good use of momentum to keep speed around corners. On the other hand, some of the more modern cars require more force as they surge to speeds that will leave you desperately fighting for control. I certainly didn’t expect this level of nuance in the gameplay. Don’t let the graphics fool you, the controls have more in common with a sim like Dirt Rally than Sega Rally.Art of Rally also comes packed with a handful of different modes to keep you entertained. There’s a free roam mode that initially chucks you into the lush forests of Finland, where, after a brief introduction with the “God of Motorsport”, you’re left to explore on your own whim. This exploration also includes some collectibles that have you search for letters around the map like a Tony Hawk game. This was a fun way to get to grips with the controls of the game.Once you’re feeling a bit more confident, you can tackle the more traditional career mode, which places you into the beautifully created stages around the world. This includes the gorgeous cherry-blossom trees of Japan or the sunny beaches of Sardinia. Every stage felt handcrafted with a beautiful backdrop that sometimes distracted me due to the sheer gorgeousness in the landscape. I now understand why the developers included a photo mode. It was hard not to stop and gawk at the visuals. Once you’re done being mesmerized by the visuals, you can get to the actual racing again. The career mode allows you to slowly unlock new vehicles and liveries depending on how well you do. This serves as a great place to try out all the different vehicle classes as you race through the decades, unlocking new vehicle groups.More traditional fans will no doubt spend most of their time in the time trial modes. The game features a robust set of challenges, from custom rallies to ever-rotating daily and weekly online time trials. I’ve already been addicted trying to set a high score in today’s daily time trial. None of these modes would matter if the driving wasn’t up to scratch. Thankfully, the robust handling and inertia meant every stage was a constant test of reflexes. The aforementioned car handling was smooth and there wasn’t a location or weather condition I did not enjoy driving in. One small mistake in a chicane or hairpin turn often spelled the end of a good run. This kept me on my toes for the entire run.The only issue I did have with this game is that the camera often became my own worst enemy. The dolly-tracking style used was sometimes a little bit too slow for a corner, however, this issue was rare and did not detract from my overall experience with this game.Overall, the minimalist approach has definitely paid off for Funselektor. What they’ve managed to pull off here is nothing short of marvelous. Motorsport enthusiasts will no doubt enjoy the smooth handling and abundance of modes to keep them occupied. From the soundtrack to the menu, every part of Art of Rally has been meticulously tailored to provide a zen-like experience that is unparalleled in top-down racers. Art of Rally is a stylized experience that is not to be missed.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun! It has a difficult learning curve, but in my opinion it's worth it anyways.The stage and environment selections are quite good for the genre, but where Art of Rally *shines* is its car roster. Every historical rally car you could want is here, including ones that never saw production, or ones that were only used sparingly. They all feel unique to drive, and you'll quickly find your favorites among the huge roster if you experiment.The physics feel *amazing*, drifting is an absolute dream, and going sideways is both fun and almost always optimal. RWD feels absolutely wonderful here, and while certainly harder to drive than AWD or the rare FWD, they're definitely worth learning. You'll find yourself sliding around like a pro after your first few hours, and enjoying the hell out of it all the while.But for those first few hours, the game is quite challenging. Learning the limits of the game and how to tell your speed from the unusual camera angle is no easy task, and the game's default assist settings don't help either. This is a lovely game, so if you want to get into it, here's my advice:1: Turn off stability assist as soon as you can. You want to be drifting, and this assist prevents you from doing so. If you're having trouble keeping your car from spinning out, turning up the counter steer factor is a much less intrusive and more useful way to help yourself out on those tough corners.2: Brake more and earlier than you think you need to. Whether going over jumps or heading into a corner, just apply a *bit* more braking than you think is necessary. Being a bit slow into a corner or not getting huge air might feel awkward, but it's a surefire way to stop the much more embarrassing feeling of flying off into a tree.

_childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is undoubtedly one of the best gaming experiences I have ever had. That being said, its philosophy is very idiosyncratic and if you approach it expecting a 'typical' racing game experience, you may be in for disappointment. Art of Rally is not a game about racing - it's a game about passion, about mastery, about expression, about nostalgia, about art, and above all else, about flow. The entire experience is  focused on simulating the joy and freedom that inspired generations of rally drivers and fans, while stripping away absolutely every possible distraction. It's the kind of game you sometimes catch yourself grinning like an idiot playing - as you're taking a corner perfectly at warp speed just inches away from the fence that wiped you out dozens of times before, with banging synthwave blasting over a gorgeous acid trip of colorful visuals.Every single part of Art of Rally's design is purpose built to get out of the way and distill rally down into as much of that brilliant fun per second as possible. The cars all have distinct personality - each era, manufacturer, even national origin has its own quirks and feeling, from extravagant but unruly earlier French sports cars to nimble and precise Japanese supercars to quirky and idiosyncratic Italian art cars - without getting bogged down in statistics and sliders. The tracks give a wide range of racing styles - from twisting Japanese mountains that require patience and technique, to German highways that test your consistency and offer high-risk, high-reward barrier patterns, to Kenyan mountains where you're free to go flat out for long stretches at a time - each with its own aesthetics.I have been playing this game for years and there is, simply put, nothing else like Art of Rally. It is the pure distilled joy of going fast and feeling cool. Break free from narrow ideas of what a racing game 'ought' to be and I promise you'll be in for a hell of a ride.

_childDocuments_.review: Beat Absolute Drift 100% and have been waiting for this game since it was announced. I love the simple art style. It reminds me of playing with micro machines and imitating races on TV with a large LSD dose boosting imagination. Most games are all photorealism which is cool but a lot of them have been coming out a buggy mess. I didn't notice any bugs during my first playthrough. This game requires fine motor control to handle the brake, accelerator and the steering. Want to hammer the gas on every corner to drift? Enjoy spinning out. Noticed complaints about jumping but I loved the floaty kind of feel to it. It's a game that made me feel like you had to be God Arm and God Foot from Initial D in order to successfully beat the track. Every bit of incremental pressure on the triggers and joystick meant something and gave instant feedback. Even down to feeling the rumble in different areas of my controller depending on where my tires were and what they were doing. The car selection is amazing and you can unlock every single one. Some are just hilarious like the vans and if I remember right a tricycle. Every car felt different. I don't know how the hell the Dev managed to do all this on his own but I felt the passion put into this game. That is something this game has that a lot of other games are missing. This isn't a simulator. It's not like most arcade style racers either. This game is a unique rally game which is why you have to buy it to experience it if you like racing games. It built so much on top of what Absolute Drift built that I played the hell out of this game in just a few short days, beat it and ready to try a harder difficulty as well as exploration mode.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is peaceful and meditative, while also somehow evoking rage quits :) If you're a fan of racers with other cars on the track, then probably won't enjoy this game. The challenges with those games come from having to drive fast and conquer the course, with cars behind you, pressuring you. This game is not like that. It is much more a "cross country runner" type of game: the race is against yourself. How well can you drive fast and conquer the course, driving entirely by yourself?If you played Absolute Drift, then you are already familiar with Art of Rally's style (and you're probably aware of how sneaky difficult Funselektor games can be). There's fun to be had with this game. It's not exactly a true-to-life sim, but it's also not arcade. It's sim-adjacent, which makes it challenging and rewarding. You'll need to finesse your way to success.I have an absurd number of games in my Steam library, but right now, I find myself coming back to Art of Rally, struggling to admit my budding addiction... (And it has a photo mode, which make replaying your races arguably as fun as, if not more fun than, actually driving the races).As with Absolute Drift, the environments are minimalistic (though, Art of Rally is much more scenic than Absolute Drift; but it retains a similar low-poly aesthetic). The music is zen. The color palette is relaxing. The game is good.  You'll need a controller though - gamepad at least (I play with a PS4 controller).I'll admit I'm biased :) I received the game for free -- I was a beta tester, and I learned that my beta key enabled me to receive the release for free. But also, I know the lead developer. Dune is awesome, and I tried to pay for the game anyway; he wouldn't let me. I am not bragging here; my point is that Funselektor is an awesome indie team, they put a lot of love into their titles, and they are also actually good peoples.In conclusion: Art of Rally is totally worth it.

Coming out of corners or when regaining control after a slide, the car pendulums back and forth without staying straight. Your car reacts wildly to camber and elevation changes on the road, but most of the time you can't even see those changes because of the graphics and camera angles. _childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is an interesting game; it’s a clear evolution from the dev’s previous game Absolute Drift and has been created with a clear love of rally racing and its history. The game looks great and the overall experience in the game is top notch.But…the driving model. It’s…not bad at all but very unique. There is a ton of momentum to all the cars and weight transfer forwards and back is very exaggerated. This is a double-edged sword: on one hand, finding that groove and being able to pull of a series of drifts around corners feels great! It’s not easy to do and there is a real level of mastery of the driving model to accomplish it. On the other hand, if you fall out of that rhythm or can’t quite give the game the level of attention and investment it wants, it can turn into a frustrating mess where you can barely even keep the car on the road.If you have a love for rally racing or really enjoyed their previous game, definitely check this one out. That said, it’s a cautions recommendation from me because I think some will simply find the driving model too unforgiving and give up on it before they can get a sense of how it all clicks together once you have a good feel for things.

_childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is a loveletter to Retro Rally games. Isometric racing with A hybrid simulator and arcade physics system makes difficult mountain roads feel incredibly satisfying and cinematic while you're challenging your car and yourself to chain your drifts together and get the fastest times. The Graphics are simple yet iconic, low-poly cars that look like toys are found to each have a different deep handling. Clear cute models of recognizable cars from your favorite eras are in place with names that reference the cars culture. With 4WD FWD RWD as well as front mid and rear engine cars the choice in car makes each map very re-playable trying to get gold in every career group and better times in the time trials. As you progress you unlock cars from further generations of rally, starting with group 2 in the late 60s ending with group A in the 90s, the unlocked cars are noticeably faster and harder to control but allow for faster times and better drifts. This is a racing game through and though, designed for DIRT fans who want a Sandbox made of beautiful polygons, smooth drifting and little square people standing in the middle of the road. _childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is a minimalist, conceptually simple game where you go throught the different ages of rally. It projects a very ZEN aura and along with the soundtrack poses a perfect relaxing game. At least in concept.If I could I would give this game a neutral rating. It is not a bad game. It runs just fine even on lower end PCs. However the gameplay is very flawed. For a game that presents itself as a casual, relaxing game, the controls of the cars are very fiddly, even inconsistent. This is made worse by the fact that you cannot turn of automatic compensation and oversteering, which often results in cars zig-zagging out of the track without you having any reasonable say on it. Not only that, the grip of the car onto the road changes from track to track with no discernible logic. Sometimes I have better control on snow than I do on gravel or even asphalt.It feels like you're driving on ice cream, is what I am saying, regardless of conditions.Do not get me wrong, I like the game. But it is very frustrating, very inconsistent and does not deliver the experience it advertises. I am sure I will get derided a lot for saying this, but it does not feel like driving skill (not mastery of mechanics, driving) has anything to do with how well you do in the game and for these reasons I cannot give it a positive review, even though it runs well.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably my favorite non-sim racing game out now. It has an enthusiast focus, so don't expect art of rally to deliver typical basic ♥♥♥♥♥ arcade racing and "gamey"  features. It's a "drivers' game" through and through. The physics aren't overbearingly realistic, but have enough realistic mechanics to feel natural and dynamic enough for a seasoned driver, a perfect match for the game's overall caricaturization of rallying. Cars handle more simplistically than they do in real life or sims, but with variables like drivetrain type, road camber, and weight transfer still affecting the way you drive, being quick in-game means you have to understand the principles behind driving real cars fast. One wrong move and your stage is pretty much over- but that's what makes the good runs rewarding. Historic liveries and humorous little blurbs for each car add to this game's charm as a love letter not only to rallying, but to car culture as a whole. Doesn't hurt that fresh content other devs would release as DLC is available to all players for free. Pair with a little Eurobeat and enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Pick up and play goodness.I play what I classify as casual driving games and simulations. I don't mean the difference between simcade driving games and so on, I mean the difference between actual rally sims of various kinds and a top-down racer like this one. I've seen some people say this is a rally sim, but I have this in my casual driving games. I don't class it as a sim personally, though there are some very nice rare cars in there, though unlicensed, you can obviously tell what they are. They don't really handle like their real versions, you get a selection of cars for each category, including some fantasy ones after Group B, but that's ok, as you probably know from the blurb, this game tries to capture the feel of Group B before it got banned and tries to continue that vibe on into the 1990s.But you won't wrap the car around a pole or kill any of the blocky bystanders, which is also not a bad thing in this game by me. This is because it's a relaxing game with the gorgeous colour palette and exotic rally settings. The previous game these developers made was a drifting game, and I would say that the drifting provenance shows through in this game.I don't really like drifting games and stages much in other games, but in this for me it's tolerable, because it's in the context of rally driving, often on loose surfaces using twisty-turny roads in places. Just find a car in the relevant class that you find easiest to drive, have a go, improve your times.I got the Australia DLC the other day, but because I've completed the game, could only use those on Free Roam to get the collectables or on custom rallies to get my stage score up to a Thousand and get the last achievement.I am personally not that disappointed by that, because I know it would play much better in the career mode when playing it through the first time. I do therefore recommend you getting it along with the game first time, if it's in your budget. If you've completed the main game, then there's that, which I personally did not mind, because of the price point and having a good impression of the developers.I've got gold and stars in all the classes and don't want to risk my scores in Career mode, but I'm sure the Australian stages will pop up there. There are set tracks, and I like that. There are so many of them by now, it's hard to just learn them all straight away. The rouguelike element that other reviews mention is the track generation for the stages. Well, they are not generated, the stages are set and you can practice them in the time attacks and time trials. The locations and which particular stages are generated randomly when you take a particular rally in career mode based on the group.You can terminate a rally year and start it again to get a different set of stages, but each time the locations and particular stages, time of stages and weather are all randomised again.Definitely a good candidate to keep on a Steamdeck too, IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: I love to play a nice rally game once in a while. Most games are either too realistic for me to enjoy (high difficulty and super lengthy in-depth career mode which doesn't work for a casual player like me) or too unrealistic to enjoy (I do like some realism and not the Mariokart style alternatives). This game hits the sweet spot. Don't let the cartoony style and top-down view distract you. The gameplay is serious and difficult enough for me to enjoy without getting too difficult/serious. _childDocuments_.review: Nice game. I don't think it's a  great game, but it's a nice one.First, art of rally is beautiful, it's simple but pretty; the choice of the low poly style is to thanked for that. There's some iconic cars to drive, there's a free roam mode if you just want to chill. The career mode is divided by group of cars and then by season: it's a normal career mode for a rally game, in which you have to compete against the AI's time to win a season. Although I find the game quite arcadey, all the cars behave differently, all the different surfaces have an impact on their grip, there's also damages and you might have to repair your car to continue a season. There's also some unlockables (cars, liveries). And your car will fly if you miss a corner.But there's one big flaw for me. Or you could say the flaw comes from me. I'll explain: art of rally is one of the rare games that gave me a slight nausea. Nothing too serious, but I can still feel it when I play it for a long time. Other games that made me suffer something similar: Descent, Fable, CrossCode and Sonic Robo Blast 2. I'm not sure what might be the cause, maybe it's the camera but for those who had a similar experience while playing video games, I think it's an important information to know before buying art of rally.And while I'm talking about flaws, I wish there were more environments (and especially a desertic, rocky one). Right now, there's only 5: Sardinia, Finland, Japan, Germany and Norway. While there's not a lot of different locations, the game is beautiful. And I have to add that Japan, with all its hairpin corners and the constant change in elevation, is my favorite location. And Germany might be the worst: too much "tombstones" (?) on the side of the road (and why though?).About the music: it's some kind of synthwave. To be honest, it's not for me but I guess fans of this genre might like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Got this to try out and have decided to hold onto it.  Well worth the price for the development work that has went into it by a small studio.  Plenty of vehicles inspired from real life counter parts and five distinct open worlds to explore which are sectioned off into the multiple rally stages.  This is a deceptively simple game due to its presentation and in that regard is somewhat reminiscent of the Trials series - a lot of momentum physics to master to really get good at it.At first it feels very twitchy with a controller (have seen people use a wheel on YouTube to play so that's an indicator of the depth this game can offer) but there are an abundance of options for sensitivity, deadzone etc.  Spending some time to adjust this to get the feel set up right for yourself is well worth it.   As a rally game fan, the lack of pace notes was off putting at first but the views are generally clear enough to plan ahead and after a while you don't notice.  This is 100% a 'rally' game, but a very different one than Dirt or this years excellent WRC 9. Oh - and the synthwave soundtrack is absolutely sublime.

The art is simple yet effective, and the music just brings everything together. No licenced cars, but come on, we all know every single one of the legends they've put in. Campaign seems very good so far with a great variety of tracks and an abundance of cars to choose from. Daily and weekly challenges is a great addition as well. The freeroam with objectives are great for when you really want to just shut off your brain for an hour and grab some collectibles. I would say this is a must buy for anyone who appreciates good driving physics in a more simple setting than most of the sims out there. _childDocuments_.review: Art of rally plays in an alternate universe where the legendary "Group B" never ended the greed for more horsepower and lighter cars in the rally sport. Due to multiple accidents in the Group B series including multiple deaths (of spectators and drivers) the series had to get canceled. Cars going 0-60 mp/h in less than 3 seconds on gravel that could keep up with F1 cars of the era might've been a bit too much to pilot on narrow technical roads, even for the best drivers. However, in this game the series continued and the planned "Group S" is a reality, with actual prototype cars that were in development before the series got canceled.Despite it's innocent look and low-poly art style, this game is still to be taken seriously. The physics are incredibly well optimized for controller gameplay and dare I say - realistic. All the real life rally techniques can be applied in this game: clutch kicking, scandinavian flicks, weight transfers, anything you can think of, can be done in this game and the best thing about it, it gains you time. Heck, the developers visited rally schools and it shows in the physics. It's obviously not a simulation, but this is as good as it gets for a game that isn't meant to be driven with a wheel and pedals.Due to the game playing in an alternate universe, you won't find any licensed cars. However, this is actually a brilliant way to bypass licensing fees. All the cars seen in the game are basically real life cars as they exist, but with a slight change in the name, as you would imagine, since it is an alternate universe after all. Regardless of that, the vehicle descriptions are hilarious and filled with references. Any enthusiast that knows the cars and the history of rallying is going to love it, especially since all the iconic cars are featured. On top of it, every car has very distinctive handling, mimicking their real life counterparts.Unfortunately this is where the game falls a bit short. You can't change the car setups, solely the paint. You can unlock new paints by finishing stages and most of them are also references to the real world counterparts, but that's about it. Not a big deal for me since I don't fiddle all that much with setups, but still worth mentioning.Why would I talk about the music in a racing game, when all you want to hear is the car sounds? Simple answer: the music is absolutely brilliant. Synthwave isn't necessarily a genre I was familiar with, but after completing the game I fell in love with it. It just adds so much value to the whole experience. Driving a stage with synthwave blasting, hitting the apex of every corner, the vibrant colors - it just sends you into a trance-like state and I loved every bit about it.All in all, this game is an actual masterpiece filled with humorous references, amazing music and of course - brilliant gameplay. The more you love cars, the history of them and the stories motorsport produced, the more you are going to love this game. This is more than just a game, it's a work of art - The art of rally - an homage to the sport as a whole. A must play for every rally enthusiast.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing game made from a position of love both for rally history but also for the meditation of driving. This is my go to game to de-stress or play during lunch, you can get in quickly do a few stages and get out and back to life. The variety of history of cars shows that someone knew rally and wanted to share the love with the rest of us. The soundtrack is amazing, easily the best part of the game and helps push the overall meditation and zen aspect of the game. While many may find the camera angle a bit disorienting to start with, you easily fall into the rhythm of the stages with some practice.Update: After the Kenya update the game is still awesome.

_childDocuments_.review: takes a short while to get used to, but well worth the journey. I started out thinking I could hurl the 1950s wagons you start with round every corner, pulling the handbrake and trying my best scandinavian flick. I found that the most enjoyment from this game is when you just enter a sort of flow state, and not outdriving your own abilities. this is an excellent game in that regard, the visuals are gorgeous and the general aesthetic is first-rate. I would recommend purchasing this game at full price, something which I don't do very often.

_childDocuments_.review: Almost gave up early but glad I didn't. First starting out, it felt like the controls were wooden and stiff, the cars were unresponsive, and the camera angles were always messing me up. I couldn't control the cars, kept crashing into things, and generally wasn't having any fun.Having stuck with it a bit longer, I came to realize that the game is closer to a sim than an arcade racer and the physics model is heavily focused on vehicle weight transfer. After that, the rest fell into place.Hints:- Control problems? You're probably using too much throttle and not slowing down enough for turns. The physics engine punishes you for constantly flooring it and rewards you for easing into the throttle and using part throttle in a lot of situations. - The brakes are exceptionally strong on all cars on all surfaces. Use them!- You don't need to Fujiwara Takumi every single turn.- Understeering in a slow corner? Lift off the throttle entirely to get the weight back over the front tires.- The game punishes you for crashing. Even the lightest collision almost always results in a 180 spin. Avoiding offs in the first place is the best strategy. - Loss of control and pendulum-ing all over the place? The camera lags behind the car's movements, and amplifies the situation. Lifting off the gas prevents the pendulum effect.- There are no pace notes and sometimes you can't see the hairpin or decreasing radius turn coming up ahead. Discretion is the better part of valor.- Hate the rainy stages? They're the perfect place to practice your throttle control and tons of fun once you get it down.Things I like:- Charming aesthetic- Nice variation in levels and cars- Music selection- Once you get a hang of the physics model and start putting it all together, it becomes super rewarding to chain together an entire stage of perfect corners. Stick with it!Nitpicks:- Camera lag / sometimes you can't see what's coming up ahead- Occasional performance problems / FPS drops- Cuts are allowed but sometimes the game questionably resets your car when you're only a few feet off the road

_childDocuments_.review: - nice artstyle - fun gameplay (relaxing but also challenging)- balancing is fine, can be played just for fun with helps (e.g. traction control) but can also be played without helps against difficult AI which is pretty challenging- nice travel through the ralley history, espacially interesting for people who are interested in racing and the history - cars are not licensed but can be recognized pretty easy ;) - all in all very nice and a good variety to common racing games
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Gorgeous rally-game that feels like doing a blazing sunday-drive (in the best way) where death can be found outside every cornerGreat rally-game for anyone wanting a breather from or a generally less intense game than the AAA driving sims around. The minimalist art-style combined with the vibrant use of colours makes for one of the more beautiful racing-games out there. The physics feel great, and tricks like shifting weight, Scandi flicks and clutch kicking all come into play in order to wrap these iconic cars around the corners. (I'm by no means a rally-veteran, but from what I can tell, this is good enough to be more than simply an arcade-racer)I'd recommend this to just about anyone interested in racing-games and who's willing to learn and get humbled by turn after turn. My only real gripes with the game are the lack of pacenotes and closer camera-options, but their absence are justified by the more laid-back approach to the racing, and the times where you don't see a turn or crest early enough to plan for it, are few and far between.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: This game is something truly special. Whether you take an interest in rally/motorsport or not it is well worth playing. It is inherently relaxing to slide around the beautiful and diverse landscapes while listening to the perfectly selected soundtrack. Besides its incredible presentation, the game features a handling model which is challenging yet easy enough to pick up the basics. Thus you make constant progress which is very rewarding. Moreover, there is an enormous amount of content for a game at this price point.

_childDocuments_.review: Dirt Rally 2 is one of my top 3 favourite games, but playing it I always wished there was a more kind of arcadey, stress-free version of it. art of rally is very much an answer to that in a lot of ways, it's essentially the same game but with a minimalist aesthetic that's really quite pleasing, and the more casual electronic tracks (which are fantastic) that play while you drive help drive home that this is a more relaxed game.With this in mind though, the main criticism I have is that the driving still feels a bit too realistic. With such an aesthetic, very up high default camera, and relaxing soundtrack, I want to be able to slide around the tracks with ease and not feel so frustrated when my car mysteriously understeers and I careen off the edge of the track. Obviously in a game like this challenge is always welcome, just here I feel it struggles to find the middle ground between arcade and realistic style handling and ends up leaning too far towards realistic. All in all though this is a really fun game with a really fun aesthetic and atmosphere, I love all the tracks and the cars and how the career progresses as well as giving a basic history on rally racing. I can really only recommend it despite my one criticism.

_childDocuments_.review: With a unique look, great soundscape, and fantastic car handling, Art Of Rally's been a sleeper hit for me this year. I've loved my time with the game so far (I'm about halfway through the Career mode as I write this), and I can't wait to keep playing more of it. If you're into racing games at all, you owe it to yourself to get the free demo and try it out for yourself.Update: I'm still not tired of this game. It's so great to put on and just mess around in the Free Roam stages stress-free. The Daily and Weekly Rallies are great reasons to keep coming back, and the new environments that have been added for free fit in well.

_childDocuments_.review: I am writing this review for Art of Rally because it is simply one of the best games I have ever played - period. And I am writing such an in-depth review because this game is such a detailed game.This review is divided into some conventional and some unconventional sections due to its nature.The developers are obviously gushing car guys like the rest of us (gushing car guys). You can tell they really are in love with cars & motorsport and what they stand for. They would otherwise not have created such a glowing product. The romance that is a man and his car really shines through here.Attention to detail is the game's biggest strength. Now - at first glance this might not be apparent. But they really have broken their backs to deliver so much in such a small package. Let me list a few points...The sponsor's advertisements: The brand names are just so damned awesome. No brand names to speak of really, just typical logo designs for typical motorsport sponsors. I won't spoil them here but as you play through you'll see them and see why they're easy to fall in love with.The surfaces: The difference in how you drive between different stages really is astonishing for what appears to be such a simple game. You'll see Tarmac, wet tarmac, gravel, wet gravel, snow, surface changes on stage, hydroplaning, slick grass and grass that'll slow you down if you cut (and you should cut, and you shouldn't cut). Elevation changes, jumps, downhill and uphill, pre-turns and tight, tight hay bale chicanes... Really this game is Dirt Rally with cell shading.  It isn't just a simple "turn the stick and nail the throttle" type game. There really is an immense nuance to the handling, physics and surfaces that will have you trying to think faster thoughts constantly to shave milliseconds off your stage time. This game honestly feels like a quality simcade with regards to its physics. You're never going to feel like you're doing anything perfectly... but when you're right on the edge of perfect you'll feel like a million bucks.The cars: The cars are really awesome. The sound differences between different engine layouts, cylinder counts, aspiration types and manufacturers were really well thought out. I am a huge BMW guy and when I get behind something with an BMW motor I am brought back home... The names of the cars are awesome. the little blurbs about them and the liveries especially absolutely hit the right note. The cars are unlicensed and I think this brings a huge amount of charm to the game because the devs were able to name them how they see fit and they did a great job. To reiterate - they really captured the romance.Locations: If you're a rally fan, you'll know the classics and when you're playing Art of Rally the classics really  come to life. The precision required for a pavement rally in Germany, the flight paths of Finland, the curvaceous roads of Japan... All of these tracks are brought to life and feel distinct and awesome to drive on.The little things: The way your brake disks glow and the way they emit sparks under heavy braking. The dirt your car accumulates. The way the gravel and the rain spit from your tires. The crowds the way they feel like true, enthusiastic rally fans and they JUST WANT TO SEE YOU FLYING AT THEM AND AROUND A CORNER... They cheer and honk their air horns. Please do your best to get extra sideways around the fans.Beautiful. Just beautiful and made all the more impressive by, again, more attention to detail. Fog, puddles, trees, blossoms... all in the beautiful, colorful subtle design. Night time is absolutely awesome with a full array of headlights and fog lights. Trees, grass, rocks, animals, houses, shacks... The list goes on.As mentioned before, motor sounds are awesome and distinct but there is a lot of detail to be heard in headphones and the soundtrack is so awesome. I'm the kinda guy that immediately goes and turns off music in 99% of racing games but here the 80's synthwave soundtrack really fits the driving and the art style and there is just no reason to turn it off.Progression is huge. You'll spend 4-5 hours getting to even being able to use an AWD car, but you'll realize by the time you're in the higher end RWD cars that you weren't ready for it anyway. This game does an excellent job of chucking you in the shallow end of a fledgling motorsport and making you really feel like you got in at the ground floor and you're advancing in skill as the technology and the stages become more advanced while the years and seasons go by. You'll never feel entitled to a faster car until the ending races of a particular group. The first 2 groups feel like absolutely helpless little road cars hastily adapted to rallying with their pencil wide tires and low power... But further on the cars start becoming bespoke, faster, more capable, more predictable yet slightly less forgiving in certain situations... Again... Attention to detail.Increase the difficulty when you've gotten used to the physics, the handling and the top down view. Make it a challenge. Like a lot of driving games, you can benefit from having a couple drinks and really letting your inhibitions go. Don't use stability handling or braking assists. Make sure to customize your controls (please use a controller) and find an optimal camera setting.Still a better love story than TwilightA better simcade racer than Project Cars 3A goldmine for inspiration for other games. Other devs, namely AAA devs. Look. At. This. Game. I'm Ricky Bobby and if you don't smoke Righto Cigarettes then F**k Y**

_childDocuments_.review: art of rally is a driving game unlike any other. To begin with, the OST for the game is INCREDIBLE. I believe that almost every song is original to the game and all of them SLAP. The graphics are simple yet inspired - despite the relatively low-poly look of the game, because of the way that lighting is implemented, performance was not fantastic, certainly something to think about if you are looking at this game because you think it looks easy to run on your crappy PC. At its heart, art of rally is based around the idea of creating an incredibly tight, easy to learn, difficult to master driving mechanic. Learning where your skill and the grip of your tires meets is the central goal of art of rally - its not about the graphics or the awesome music, its about the best driving model you will play with outside of Forza or NFS. You constantly feel like you are fighting these historically-inspired rally beasts as you try your best to not spin-out in the corners or blast off the track. The more you play, the better you get at cornering and braking and recovering from mistakes. The first time you successfully drift around a corner without completing pulling the brake or stopping the gas will be when the game suddenly "clicks" for you. All together, art of rally packages cute graphics, an incredible OST, and an enjoyable driving model all into a decidedly pretentious, artsy package that somehow makes the whole thing that much better. If you like racing games, this should be an easy pick-up for you. Forget spinning a wheel for a free car or trying to outrace the cops, this is the game to play if you want the only challenge to be keeping your car on the road!
