_childDocuments_.review: So far, this has been an excellent game to get lost in. Not too difficult of combat, and tons of accessibility options to enable all players. My recommendation is to go in blind, and to read the manual as you find pages. That'll make sense the more you play. The sound design and score are wonderful and really fitting for the ethereal vibe the game puts off. I do wish there was controller button rebindings (as there are keyboard rebindings). That is a minor gripe that I'm sure I could get around messing with Steam's controller support. Also, it's a little too easy to accidentally open the inventory menu and change your weapon loadout during tense combat. Since the game doesn't pause in the inventory menu, this can cause some accidental damage or use of items you do not mean to use. All of these options could have been fixed with controller remapping ;)TL;DR: Pick this one up!Edit: Now further in, this game gets a bit of a FEZ vibe with it's puzzles. Be ready. That's all I'm saying

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is such a neat amalgam of so many other games. It's a cute Zelda game, but with Dark Souls game play+level design and with the Fez/Witness/Outer Wilds undercurrent of discovery. You  something is missing and you slowly unravel pieces as you explore (these 'pieces' are literal pieces to a in-game strategy guide, giving you hints at its secrets.)It's overall a great experience that I'd recommend to any veteran gamer that'll appreciate everything it's borrowing from. The combat is pretty weak, but for a game like this, I'm kind of fine with it being more of 'filler' for all the puzzling.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't care who the IRS sends, I'm not playing The Witness.Probably the best game to take what Zelda (specifically a Link to the Past) and make something more of it. _childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, a beautiful game with some seemingly rich lore marred by its extreme difficulty and pacing issues.  I was not expecting such bulls*** combat from this game.Good: * The art style & graphics are great * Music is great * The store/lore is goodBad: * If you don't pay attention to the "manual" you collect then you may miss crucial game mechanics. * Lots of wandering and trying to figure out where to go * Unmoveable camera is used to obscure paths you need to find * Very difficult.  I liked Hollow Knight but this is harder and the main character just feels slow during later boss fights. * I did not like the stamina system as I feel it contributed to the overall slowdown of combat and punishes you for blocking and dodging.Ugly: * Enemies gang up on you, will notify other nearby enemies, and they will all chase you forever * There are limited ranged weapons so most combat is a slog as you chip away at their health, dash back, wait for an opening, and repeat * There is a "no damage" mode, so the developers acknowledge the BS difficulty, but you still get knocked around if you get hit so it's still a slog trying to get through an area.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll just keep it brief as possible: I liked a lot of the game, but overall grew to dislike other sections of the game more as it went on.The world looks great, sounds great and everything amongst those lines is solid. Early exploration is really fun too. At first I even enjoyed the combat. Plenty of fun mystery to go around too, just generally a really great vibe.But then there's the bosses and the lategame. The former I liked one of, the rest I genuinly despised and simply turned godmode on for. A part of it is me being bad at the game, yes, but the combat also failed to grab me and was generally just boring, also doesn't help that I'm not a huge fan of "souls-like" stuff. The lategame is cool initially and when seeing how all of it clicks together it seems really cool, but I was already tired of just running around the map at that stage to the point where I gave up.Maybe get it on a sale/in a bundle.

_childDocuments_.review: The good- Adorable aesthetics. Nice, minimalistic 3d graphics with vivid colors and atmospheric lighting. The cool day/night system gives it some variation too.- Great world design with multiple height levels, hidden paths and alternative routes that get unlocked gradually as you play. Each region guides you masterfully in order to always be at the right path, but also not limit you from exploring the surroundings.- Awesome core gameplay logic. The way that you unlock secrets and gain small pieces of knowledge through exploration and observation is amazing. Even after a lot of hours you keep discovering things that may related to basic control mechanics. The game is full of well hidden secrets and clever puzzles and always gives you enough hints so it never feels impossible or unfair. It even has its own real language that you can try to translate. So imaginative and well balanced.- Fantastic animations. Soft bodies, particles, physics after each blow, everything seems smooth and natural. Protagonist's walking is so funny.- Fast battles with nice controls and addictive kills. Everything feels fluid and responsive.- It offers a decent variation of abilities, upgrades and tools that introduce new interesting mechanics when you acquire them, so the game never gets boring or repetitive.- Well designed enemies. Each region has its own tribes. Bosses' design seems a little bit generic, but their battles are great and have really good pace.- The story is cool but pretty abstract. The most interesting part though is trying to understand what's going on by collecting all these scattered pieces of information and putting them gradually together.- All those illustrations at the pages you find are simply gorgeous. The bad- It would be an entirely different game if you change this characteristic, but the fact that there are side invisible walls everywhere so you cannot jump down to the lower levels seemed to me odd and I could get used of it till the very end.- Poor sound design with only few environmental sounds. The background music keeps playing almost always, which can be tiring after a while.- Sometimes interacting with some objects like chests and stairs can be unresponsive.- The story is pretty abstract and fragmented which isn't bad at all, but initially it doesn't give you enough clues to understand your purpose, what you are fighting for. So you play half of the game wandering and killing foes without knowing exactly why.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: TUNIC is a cute, absurdly charming souls-like. It doesn't try to be a difficult game in every way like the souls games, but it will have you stressing out a bit pretty often. I feel a little bad calling it a souls-like, because it tries hard to be it's own thing, and honestly, it really is. It's a similar idea to souls, but in a cuter, friendlier package.A lot of your time will be spent exploring, but it's never dull, because there are always enemies to fight or secrets/handy shortcuts to find. I went into this thinking it was more of an ARPG because my sleep-deprived brain wasn't paying enough attention to the details and all that, so when I realized what it is, I was pretty surprised, but very pleasantly. I had no idea what I had gotten myself into, and I've loved games like the souls series for a long time, but sort of fell away from them after I switched to PC. I bought them all on steam, but I haven't played them much, and this game makes me want to jump back into this genre of games and play through them, starting with this one.The gameplay is incredibly smooth, the music is very nice and enjoyable, the atmosphere is great, the art style is very pleasant, and graphically it's gorgeous. The lighting is fantastic and really brings the whole visual package together. It's easier to pick up than others in this genre, you don't lose stamina as you attack, and you can continue to attack just fine without any stamina. The stamina penalties that you really need to pay attention to come in the form of less stability, which makes it easier to be knocked back/down by attacks, and taking extra damage when you're past a certain threshold or have none at all. The story is told through the gameplay and little things, and the way it's all done makes the game feel like a form of art.I'm going to be honest, when I bought this game, i didn't pay too much attention to it, I only bought it because I needed steam points and figured I should get a game that I might play later on so it wouldn't be a waste of money. I don't regret playing it when I should have been working (I work from home atm), and I don't regret buying it. Few games have managed to captivate me as quickly as TUNIC has, and for that alone, I can easily recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The ambient music and cute fox character are just there to lure you into a false sense of security. This game will spank your bouncing booty so hard over and over again. There's something so deliciously sweet about finally figuring out an enemy pattern or a new way to cheese an enemy. This is just about as cryptic as Hyper Light Drifter (which I also totally recommend) and as hard as just about any souls game. It will leave you wanting more, if you're into this masochistic die a million times play style. Like Zelda on Hard Mode.Anyone complaining about the difficulty can either git gud or move on. My advice is play the game in small chunks. After dieing to the same boss 5 times, take a break, grab some water, pet your cat/dog, and come back to it later. Bet you beat it then. Also assume there is a hidden path along every wall. You'll start finding more stuff. And use your damn items. This ain't one of those games where you can just horde items for the "perfect" time. The perfect time is NOW.10/10, can't wait to discover more in this game and get my ass handed to me a few dozen more times.

_childDocuments_.review: Love love love love love this gameIt was well worth the wait, the system runs beautifully and is that puzzle fix while also having adorable gameplay that is actually quite daunting at times but endearing enough to try and try again.  The game help also is amazing if you get to the point where you just... can't anymore and want to just get through it to be able to continue the story.THE STORY - the way its told and shown and you see it play out *chefs kiss* perfection. _childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore TUNIC.While the combat is simple yet challenging at times, the true beauty of TUNIC is discovering the gameplay itself. By collecting pages of an instruction manual scattered around the world the player is slowly drip-feed information which will dramatically change your understanding of the world and gameplay of TUNIC.Never before have I been this invested in deciphering codes and secrets in a game and nothing will ever match the feeling of having one eureka moment after the other. While there are a few secrets that are ambiguous, most of them have logical solutions that are hiding in plain sight and no manual page is ever in the wrong spot.The development team behind TUNIC have created something beautiful and unique: A masterfully crafted experience that oozes with charm, innovation and artistry backed by a great and emotion-evoking soundtrack. The highest praise I can give is that I wished I forgot everything about TUNIC... so I can experience it for the first time again.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Finally came around to trying Tunic after having it sit in my library for years.Was hoping this would be its own unique, contained classic Zelda-inspired adventure from the trailers I'd seen years ago; at least it has decent puzzles, nice music, and a charming art direction.Out of all of the Soulsborne games Tunic was inspired by, the combat and enemy design in Tunic feels straight out of Dark Souls 2 - if you know, you know.Maybe you'll love it - unfortunately, I didn't.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic made me think, "This feels like a spiritual successor to Fez" because creatively nothing has ever been done like this before. No developer drip feeds you how to play the game for 20 hours straight - controls are usually on a splash screen or in the Options Menu. When you learn a new ability 15 hours into playing - that ability was usable from minute 1, you just didn't know you could do it at the time! That type of cleverness made my jaw actually drop in astonishment multiple times throughout my play through. It's funny that I say that nothing has ever been done like that because of course the manual gimmick is a take on the NES games of olde where if you rented a game at Blockbuster and it didn't have the manual, sometimes you would have no idea what you were doing and would have to figure it all out on your own! Still, it Tunic makes it feel like a one of a kind.Tunic does what most puzzle games fail to do in that it gives you all the tools needed, you just have to put in the effort to search and understand. One of the major themes of the game is exactly that - the power was within you all along, you just needed someone to share their wisdom. I recommend to not use any outside guides until the very end of the game because really, you can figure it all out on your own. Take a second to observe your surroundings, review your utility belt, open your instruction manual to this world... something will be there to show the way - hidden in plain sight.The combat is somewhat souls-like in that it's more plodding than other real-time games. Personally I'm not a big fan of the slow / dodge roll / timing / blocking that comes with that territory, but it doesn't detract much from the experience. Eventually you will master it all anyhow. Another minus is that there is a big lull and back step for a time after you gather the 3 gems and experience a major event. Overall, Tunic is a cute but challenging game for the ages. It does what video games were always meant to do but not enough do lately - make you smile.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: I would really recommend this game to people who like explorer games. I've had fun exploring every thing because this game has secrets every where. I would play it again to try to speed run it. It's story is good but some what muddled because you just start off not know anything until you start collecting the manual. Other wise it is a very fun for all the time I have put into it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nope. A box will pop up asking you YES OR NO and the description of what you are choosing is just weird runes.... like.. what? Even if it's just something as simple as picking up a key in first minutes... like, I can infer what it's asking there, but then there's signs and dialogue and a tutorial page thing all with seemingly pertinent information that you just cannot read.

_childDocuments_.review: If this had the combat of Death's Door this game would probably surpass it. I don't feel like using all of my items, my sword, shield and maybe freeze. I would have to agree with another comment on this game, the focusing system is janky, its difficult to switch between enemies especially when you're fighting 3 or more big ones. I also dislike that some items, if you use them, then you die and then spawn at your save - you will not have those items back. There have been occasions where I was lead down a path that didn't go anywhere or a shortcut has been discovered but if you wanted to use it later you would probably miss it because ITS HIDDEN BEHIND A BUILDING OR AN OBSTRUCTION?!? Some of the geography is unintuitive and that was just bugging me as I take a path that leads to a dead end and ask myself "What the hell was this for? Is there a hidden secret here?" only to search and find nothing. The treasures are not very rewarding - upgrades are nice but if you are giving me like 8 different consumables to juggle in between how can you make it so when I open my inventory to switch items mid-combat the GAME DOESN'T PAUSE. And sure, there is an item that helps you  with that issue but it take up 1/3 of your slots (1/3 of which is already taken up by the sword) and so you have one slot left for the consumable of your choice. Again, I think Death's Door is a perfect example of what the combat and items are suppose to look like in these type of explanation games (or at least pause the game upon me opening an inventory)HOWEVER! While the top paragraph does mention the many shortcomings of the game's system  The exploration of the game is great, the fact that alot of secrets can be found by multiple means is great, the game isn't keen on explaining what to do and what to press BUT  I personally like that system more than a tutorial and it keeps you going back and forth through the . Overall, I'm having a good time - its not Ori and the Blind forest (or its DLCs), its not Death's Door, but it is Tunic. Even with its shortcomings it is worth trying out for the good systems it presents.

I really don't like the kind of mechanics that just artificially increase the hours.Pros:- Good graphic- Good gameplay- Nice story- Good musics- A bit challenging sometimeCons:- As i said, at the end, the gameplay is just walking around the map to get collectibles.- We collect bonus through the game, but we have no clue what they are doing, i spent half of the game just ignoring them and then i decided to check online to see there bonuses.- You will get stuck sometimes without any clue where to go, you'll end up checking solution online if you don't want to spent 3h walking the map over and over again.I got it in sale for 20$, it was worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome! At it's core it's a classic Zelda clone, and if that is all you want you can play straight through to get the normal (bad) ending. But if you want the whole Tunic experience you're going to have to do some lateral thinking. I'm talking Metal Gear Solid Merill's Codec kind of outside the box thinking to solve all the hidden puzzles.Simple example without being too spoilery. Throughout the game you collect pages to the games instruction manual. The controls and whatnot are easy enough to figure out, but there are a lot of useful hints and old school scribbled notes in the margins. The main problem is that most of it is in a fictional language you can't translate. What little you can read tends to be vague, but there is repeated mention of a "divine cross" used in a number of puzzles. This cross is nowhere in game... in fact, it's right under your thumb. Your D-pad (or arrow keys for keyboard players).And that is just the tip of the iceberg. Play this game if you want to give that squishy thing between your ears a good workout.

Regaining health requires you to interact with a statue or find a fruit in a chest. You get bombs, yet there's no aiming mechanicA tutorial level with enemies that don't kill you so players can understand how to do combat would be wonderful.

_childDocuments_.review: combat is decent, art and sound design are fantastic, i love the "in-game guide" mechanic and the language of the game, every item and equipment is useful and fun to use, you need to interpret the whole story but i quite liked it, every boss is different and needs a different strategy to be beaten, good enemy variety, perfect map size, the different locations are really unique, could use weapons other than the sword (dagger, comically large greatsword, whip), i played on the keyboard and i can say that there are too many actions that use the 'spacebar', difficulty is medium if you play as intended and borderline impossible without the upgrades (i chose to suffer and played without upgrades and the only enemy i couldn't beat was the), this game is all about the secrets you WILL NOT 100% this game without a guide, the game could inform early that.17h of gameplay doing everthing i could (after ending the game i used a guide to get what i missed) in one playthough.this game was 100% worth my money, imagine if they develop the next game as a online coop, would be perfect.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been excited for this game ever since I heard of it on the Finji discord, and wow I must say it lives up to the hype! Starting with the lovely art style and graphics, absolutely adorable and our little hero is equally as cute. Initially starting the game, there are lots of questions and not a lot of answers regarding what's going on especially with some of the map being inaccessible. I absolutely love how as you continue playing, beating the bosses and gaining more abilities, being able to get to places you once thought were impossible is such a satisfying feelings and a testament to TUNIC's map design. Gameplay and movement are okay on keyboard, but personally I felt its much more suited to controller though still needs a little work, the combat within the game can be extremely punishing and requires a lot of trial and error before you master it. The difficulty as you progress can spike sharply in some areas with certain mechanics and bosses, and can prove very frustrating sometimes. Thankfully there is a no-fail mode setting to enable if it's too difficult!(I didn't realize this was a feature until after I beat the game lol). Now the puzzles/secrets in this game are extremely well done and challenging, I completed a good majority of them before getting stumped at the end and needing a guide. I would strongly recommend trying to figure out all the puzzles/secrets on your own before consulting a guide, its incredibly fun to try and figure it all out! The story for this game, is really really interesting to piece together and I loved every second of trying to figure out what was happening. One more cherry on top for this game is the OST, it's fantastic the ambient tracks and boss fight music each stand on their own and match the environment/action perfectly. Tunic is a fantastic game and should certainly be picked up if you love challenging puzzles, combat, an interesting story, and foxes! An easy 10/10 for me :)
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: I thought the golden era of gaming had passed, but Tunic reminds me of the spirit of adventure in the same way a lot of the RPG's of my younger years did.Absolutely critical that it's played without spoilers, Tunic is the Legend of Zelda/Dark Soulsy hybrid of my dreams, and that's not even considering the fox.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic Zeldalike, Metroidvania, Soulslike, whatever you want to call it. Tunic is fashioned like a Zelda game with a bit of Fez thrown in for good measure. The exploration and sense of discovery is masterful and the craft and artistry put into the worldbuilding is top notch. The combat can feel a bit clunky sometimes but the game gives you plenty of options to deal with foes so it never feels too hard or frustrating. I do wish there were more options for moving around the world though. I actually don't mind backtracking but I think there could have been a more elegant teleport system and the way the levels were designed made me feel like I was running around in circles for way too long. All in all this is a fantastic action/adventure/exploration game and I would put this alongside recent classics like Hyper Light Drifter and Hollow Knight.

_childDocuments_.review: Terrible pacing where you go from easy to frustratingly difficult at the drop of a hat. Early game (first 70% is 9/10 fantastic, then quickly drops to 4/10).Weird mix of puzzles and combat. And again, you quickly go from 'I can handle this' to 'am I in the wrong area' really quick.Early puzzles are easy enough for an adventure game (otherwise too easy, honestly). The final puzzles... if you want to spend the time could be great. I imagine if you were solving them as a community when it first came out it would be a fantastic experience theorizing with others. That doesn't exist now, and then you left with a bunch of tedious and esoteric puzzles.They are "optional", but only really in the sense that the whole game is "optional" because noone is holding a gun to your head. The game you a literal game over screen if you finish the game without the puzzles, and tells you are you lacking X of the thing you need. I don't think of seen such an obvious "bad ending" ever.

_childDocuments_.review: The best Zelda game ever made.The whole world is a puzzle, and not merely a straightforward wysiwyg logic rooms like Zelda dungeons. You have the whole solution to the puzzle already, but you have to decipher it piece by piece to complete it. Unfortunately, there is no cryptography involved. The language is IPA symbols of English existing in a custom glyph set.Also the combat sucks, but not as bad as Zelda combat (both before and after BotW). Enemy hit points and whatnot, however, acts as more of a skill check rather than as a difficulty feature. Hopefully the devs can address this and make the combat more enjoyable as the roll mechanic is cool and all, but there are no active defensive mechanics, and this one passive mechanic is, as one would expect, clumsy and awkward-feeling in execution. When making swings, you expect at least some sort of stun mechanic, but that's only if you do enough damage to a given enemy, and due to the tendency to sort of spam and inability to dodge during attacks, you just get hit which is absolutely trash combat that deserves zero praise whatsoever (there's no skill in waiting for things to happen so I can do what I must, even on the order of milliseconds). This reduces the skill gap check to a monotonous "trudgingly survive" (in certain instances) until you can level up your stats enough to the point where it doesn't matter anymore. Terrible UX. Fix your stupid combat, and definitely don't pretend to fix it and then call it fixed either, or I will fight to the death for a refund for what would be nothing less than an inexcusable compromise no different than contemporary Nintendo!
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: What a crazy ride and I'll try to keep this spoiler lite. This game is very deceptive on the amount of layers that is hiding on this onion of a game. On the surface, it's just another hack and slash with a very cute fox character and the monsters are all much harder than you. As you go through the game, you start picking up cryptic little pieces of paper and there's very little guidance without looking at them to figure out where you're supposed to go next. However, if you find the right pieces and find the pieces of language that you can actually read, you'll eventually find your way to the next location. And the next and so forth.As you get to the middle of the game, you realize there's more. The runes on the pages is an actual phonetic language. Find a translating app... It never fully translates the app, which is a little bit of a shame. Then you realize you had mechanics all along that you didn't know about because the game didn't think you needed to know about it yet. Then you find... the path. If you know, you know.Overall, beautiful game. If you like puzzles, this game is for you. Don't get turned off by the initial difficulty and the weird rune system. This game is DEEP. The final puzzle was too much for me, but I did look it up and even after reading everything, it's still too much for me and I said DONE. Fully recommend for anyone who likes hack and slash, puzzles and a little ARG at the end.

_childDocuments_.review: this one is a fun legend of Zelda inspired game and it's also tough but fair  and some of the puzzles where suprising and 'the holy cross' detail was quite fuun and also explained how they called their 4th wall breakings :).so if you love classic legend of zelda games you  most certainly will want this game but if you hate hard games maybe this one isn't for you.

_childDocuments_.review: "What a great game, it's a masterpiece!"The one who flips: Elden RingThe one they actually call: TunicI tried it on Gamepass and I think it's a gem!! It deserves many sales, so I decided to buy it because it is pure gold! Moreover, the devs put a lot of love on it. It's gorgeous, beautiful, has a great soundtrack. About the combat, very challenging, enemies hit really, really hard. They require to face them with strategy, taking advantage of invulnerability frames and with an eye on the inventory, everything is scarse. About the game mechanics and explanation: believe me, you won't need it because the game is designed so that it encourages you to explore and find out what's going on by yourself. The way to discover new zones, ways to face challenging enemies and find a way to defeat them is a unique experience, and gives you a great feeling of satisfaction. Even the wooden signs are written in a kind of runic language you can't understand, BUT, the game gives you hints as you find illustrated sheets that are a beauty.And best thing is our protagonist, our hero, our little fox friend who steps open facing powerful enemies and emerges victorious anyway.Don't underestimate this game, it deserves at least to be a GOTY nominee in their category, as best Indie.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game thinking it was a Zelda clone, which might have made this game okay. But when the puzzle aspect of the game was revealed, I thought its easily one of the best and most immersive puzzle games I've seen. Its hard to describe without giving away spoilers (And this game HAS to be played without spoilers), but basically even after hours of exploring and mastering the basic Zelda-like mechanics, the game will eventually reveal to the player already implemented mechanics many hours into your gameplay and its so mind-blowing how well these are revealed to you. A lot of the game is hidden but available to the player from the get go but these slow reveals is what truly makes this game fun and immersive. These discoveries really hits you as a player who's already explored a good chunk of the world and realize that there's more areas to discover and more puzzles to solve.I'm writing this review after seeing the Steam Awards nominations and I'm actually surprised that this wasn't even nominated for "Most Innovative Gameplay" as it truly is that: Having a component of the game be the player's tutorial, guide, lore-book and a puzzle itself is a really creative way of merging story-telling and gameplay. What an experience this game was and I look forward to what the developers have in store for their future games.If you love puzzle games, I highly recommend this.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game with a lot of fun ideas especially with its booklet manual. The graphic and music was nice and amazing.I don't like it that much tho and it's probably personal taste seeing how many positive reviews this game has. The exploration and finding more of the booklet was fun and the art style was so cute. The level of challenge of the boss fight juxtaposed too bad with the more relaxed exploration tho and I wasn't as prepared for it. I don't mind this level of challenge if I were to play other games, but I wish it was a bit easier for this game, like, their movement could've been a bit slower or have a tiny bit longer pause (2nd boss was just tedious to deal with). Halfway through the game, I just wish it was done and the only thing kept me going was the mystery of the booklet and the art style.The ending was nicely done. If I'm more invested, I would probably shed some tears of joy too.

_childDocuments_.review: The only games I remember from E3 2018 are Cyberpunk 2077 and Tunic, and this very much lived up to my expectations. Having to gradually find the game manual in order to learn how to play the game is a very interesting mechanic, one that scratches my itch for games like Outer Wilds and other knowledge-based-progression games. A good chunk of the game is fairly linear (even if it feels like you can go wherever you want), so there's rarely a feeling of being lost. There's nuggets of information that will drag you along, and context clues that will make you think and discover solutions on your own.Some of the late game puzzles are very creative, and would only really work in a game like this, and includes one of my favorite puzzles in gaming. That being said, if you're not keen on the idea of these more difficult puzzles, you can beat the game without doing any of the big-brain puzzles

_childDocuments_.review: TUNIC has to be hands-down one of my favorite games ever created. Easily 10/10, one of the best games I've played all year. * Stunning, clean, incredibly well executed isometric 3D art style* Interesting, subdued story that gets deeper and more complex the further you play* Unique, compelling, and rewarding mechanics in the form of the ingame manual and (maybe spoilers) the golden path* Tight, responsive, consistent combat and movement, with enough depth to be interesting and engaging, but nowhere near overwhelming in its complexity* Varied and challenging but not frustrating encounters* Lovely music* Fantastic world building and level design* Chock full of secrets: secret areas, secret mechanics, secret puzzles, and secret shortcutsIf you enjoy classic 2D Zelda, FEZ, FromSoft games, and games that use knowledge as progression (Outer Wilds, Antichamber, The Witness, Return of the Obra Dinn), you'll absolutely love TUNIC. This game has all the best parts from all of those games, and still manages to be greater than their sum.The unique mechanic of TUNIC is the game's manual. The manual itself is a point of game progression, wherein you collect its pages scattered throughout the world in order to reconstruct the knowledge hidden within. Only trouble is, the manual is 70% written in a foreign language you can't understand, with only a few scattered words and phrases legible. You'll use inference and deduction to glean as much information as possible from each manual page you find in order to progress in the game. The game delivers moments of revelation again and again when you find that one page which completes the puzzle in your mind you've been poring over for hours, or reveals a hidden mechanic that had been hiding right under your nose the entire time.All the while acquiring manual pages and discovering the game's hidden mechanics and secrets they reveal, you're also playing a classic Legend of Zelda style open world game about clearing dungeons, collecting their loot, and improving your arsenal with a variety of tools and items, magical and otherwise. The combat is top notch as well, and every encounter with even basic enemies is engaging and never gets monotonous. That's not even mentioning the variety of fantastic boss encounters, offering both dramatic scale, challenge, and satisfaction from beating them. The Librarian and Siege Engine are two of my favorites.Even upon beating the game, if you choose to go back and try to locate all the remaining manual pages (which you definitely should), be ready to break out a pen & paper or your image editing software of choice, as the secrets and puzzles only ramp up in complexity from here. I finished with a veritable collage of all the solving I had to do for many of the puzzles required to follow the golden path.While the intended progression path is well established, the game is incredibly open ended, and can be potentially beaten in any order the player desires with the right knowledge beforehand, much like dark souls.My only critisism with this game is that in some areas, the orthographic camera of the level geometry clashes visually with the perspective camera view of the background, causing some visual inconsistency and a slightly uncomfortable notion of space-warping. It's particularly apparent in a specific late game area, the rooted ziggurat. Other than that, I can't really think of anything else. The game is just that perfect.If you even moderately enjoy any of the games I've referenced thus far, you will not be let down with TUNIC. It delivers in every conceivable way with confidence and unrivaled finesse. Everyone should play this game at least once in their life if they have the opportunity.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this or at least be neutral, but this should be stated. This game Tunic has some really archaic secrets that even if you look them up on a guide are as tedious as pulling out your own teeth with a wrench.Tunic for the most part does a lot right: the adventure feels like classic Zelda, you find a stick, and then a sword, and a shield, and things around you slowly open up with each new item. The sword is stronger than the stick and can cut through trees once barring your path. The shield protects you from strong enemy attacks and projectiles. You gain a mana bar once you find your first magic item. And the bombs become very helpful the more you use them up.For a lot of freedom this gives you, it is also hard to find out exactly where you need to go next. You'll likely be stumbling upon secrets that are obvious in hindsight, but since the manual papers you find use a symbol language more often than English words, it wouldn't be much of a surprise if you look past them until later. Hindsight and all that. It feels like you've uncovered a new gimmick when you do, but it takes a bit of reading comprehension that is lost because, again, the text isn't fully translated. It's like trying to read a foreign language dictionary and trying to guess which words are right based on what you already know. Better to just ignore that and avoid making yourself look like a fool, you know?But what ultimately ruined this for me were the really hard to get secrets. There are a few doors and chests that can be opened or revealed inputting a whole series of buttons either on your directional keypad or controller d-pad. Up, left, right, down, in a series of inputs very fast. You have no prompt or indicator when or how to do just, just so long as you stand in front of the door as you do it. Some door commands are simple, like six inputs. But others, and practically all the chests too, require upwards to ten commands at once.One such secret to open the door in the mountains requires you to look through your manual pages and figure out which directional symbols to draw/input. It was tedious for me to just look those all over back and forth, so I just looked up the solution online... and STILL struggled to get it right. Can you imagine anyone else trying to do this the long way, as shown in the breadcrumb secrets, and still somehow get it wrong because of timing or not realizing they drew the wrong symbol or pressed the wrong button?! There's even a checklist for getting "fairies" in this game but that requires even more head-scratching logic on inputting codes. I gave up at this point because either I'm not sure if the codes were right at all, or if I wasn't pressing them fast enough, or even if I wasn't in the right place to push them. Worse is that they're tied to the second (true) ending so you're likely only going to get stuck with one ending depending on how clever you are finding obscure secrets, much less solving them RIGHT.This doesn't feel rewarding or exciting at all. It feels tedious and frustrating. It's one thing to have hard fights that subtly encourage you to get better with timing or using your items (either bomb throwing or upgrade offerings). It's another thing to have hard puzzles that barely have any sense to them. One you can learn how to do, but you'd have to be smart to figure out the other.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely worth your time. On the surface it looks like a cute Zelda clone. There's an incredible puzzle nature to the gameplay that will leave you with a table full of hastily written notes. There's an in game source of information that hits the nostalgia for NES carts in an artful and deeply clever way. There's a level of clever and intentional game design to everything in this game. What seems trivial at first spirals into layers of interesting gameplay. If you liked Outer Wilds this has some aspects of that idea.

_childDocuments_.review: Damn, this game is beautiful.At face value, it's an isometric Souls/Zelda hybrid with an emphasis on exploration and combat. And an extremely competent one at that.Where this game shines, though, is in its overarching air of mystery. I won't spoil it, but Tunic captures that feeling I, a non-native speaker, had growing up playing games with nary a word of english in my lexicon. It is magical.

_childDocuments_.review: I made it near the endgame, to the gauntlet part in The Cathedral and decided I really don't like the combat in this game, after 9 hours. I-Frames are basically non-existent when rolling. The stamina system (where you take 50% more damage with low stamina) is incredibly inane and frustrating, especially when you have to watch it during frantic combat. Aside from even that, the combat just doesn't feel good, in my opinion. I could probably beat the gauntlet if I spent another 30 tries in frustration, but I decided I just wasn't having fun. This coming from a Souls veteran. I realize you can turn on invincibility mode to beat certain parts, but that's not the type of gamer I am.There are other cons, and also a lot of pros. The music and atmosphere are great. At the end of the day, though, this game tries to be Dark Souls and Zelda, and where it counts, does a crappy job at both.

_childDocuments_.review: I took a break from Elden Ring to play Tunic, and I do not regret that choice.This game is a love letter to both Dark Souls and Link's Awakening, but it very much does its own thing and builds on top of the elements it borrows.Tunics own unique elements are where the design truly shines, and it's impossible to discuss them without completely ruining the experience for anybody else that wants to play the game.Guides and lets plays will destroy the experience, I highly recommend going in as close to blind as possible, the less you know the better the experience will be.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: TUNIC is basically what Fez would be like if it was inspired deeply by Zelda games instead of platformers, and also really liked Dark Souls.The game has simple but gorgeous graphics and introduction that doesn't match the work you'll be doing, either keen puzzle-solving or sometimes punishing combat with a Souls twist on Zelda (saves restore HP/MP and also all enemies, dodges consume limited stamina and attacking prevents it from recharging, and there are a ton of paths forward that you unlock either by dropping down ropes and ladders or learning secret routes so you can skip the enemies next time through).The best conceit of the game is that the manual exists in-game, unlocked by finding pages in-game. The pages are not discovered in-order. As a result, the game keeps game mechanics a mystery until you're finally rewarded with them and can go back and retrieve chests and access new areas. The same manual also provides the lore and story for the game. It's a gorgeous affair that looks exactly like what an original Zelda manual would look like if Link was a cute little fox. The manual gives plenty of hints for the many hidden secrets as well as outright telling you many of the things you'll need to figure out through the game, even if most of the text in it is what I like to call Fox Glyphs.

_childDocuments_.review: The heart of Tunic lies in its gameplay, where players navigate a tiny fox through a world filled with secrets, enemies, and puzzles. The combat system is both challenging and rewarding, requiring precise timing and strategy to defeat foes. As players progress, they uncover new abilities and equipment, adding depth to the gameplay and enabling access to previously inaccessible areas.The puzzle-solving elements in Tunic are cleverly integrated into the environment, often requiring creative thinking and exploration. The interconnected world encourages backtracking and rewards thorough exploration, making each discovery feel significant. However, some puzzles may prove a bit too taxing for casual players, potentially leading to moments of frustration.

_childDocuments_.review: Such a fun game! Just an adorable platformer at face value but it has a deceptively monstrous underbelly of story and game play that made me never want to turn it off. Incredible level of detail put into the level planning and the amount of information given to the player. I was uncovering new secrets until the very end.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, cute game for about 70% of the game, up until you reach the point where you need to gather the last key item (LoZ style, three-count) in order to progress to the last leg of the game. Most of the game is pretty forgiving, with enemies *either* being annoying to fight overall and rarely coming in groups, or being trivial, but often coming in groups, sometimes with the more annoying mobs mixed in to teach you target priority and how to use your kit.The bit that ruins literally the rest of the game up to that point for me is when they decide to suddenly and jarringly pit you against swarths of strong, lithe, and agile enemies, or enemies that two-shot you (with several upgrades to your defense) with frequent, wide-range attacks and no stagger opportunities. That all could be forgiven if the boss guarding the third key item wasn't literally the worst designed boss in the game. Frequent, wide-sweeping attacks with extremely long active frames that make most of even your most perfectly timed dodges pretty much pointless, and only leaving opening for maybe one attack (which with fifth level attacks do maybe the tiniest bit to his huge healthbar), and he basically two shots you with any little thing he does. The gameplay skill requirement skyrockets out of nowhere, starting from baby steps, to okay, gotta be a little competent, to *be a god or you dont get to experience the story.* ♥♥♥♥ design. ♥♥♥♥ boss. Can't even progress the story because just trying to fight this thing is more infuriating than its worth. If you like souls-like games, there are better to play, and if you like story, dont bother, this game won't let you experience it without taking what patience you have with it.

If you love puzzles and that A-HA! feeling when you figure something out, Tunic is for you. If you love immersive music and gameplay, Tunic is for you.If you haven't guessed yet, I love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. The exploration and discovery notions that are in the game are one of the most well-delivered and expansive I've ever seen.After finishing the game, I can say this is one of the most loved projects I've ever played. The combination of Dark Souls with Zelda is perfectly implemented. I didn't live in a time (or country) where physical games with manuals were reasonable, so all games I played as a child were most likely pirated/counterfeit because there were no boxes or anything on them. (NES/Sega/PS1). Even as a foreign to this "manual-driven-tutorials" I was captivated completely and enthralled to do my best to find all secrets.I was not able to find every secret or the main ones on my own due to lack of time, but if you are a gamer with 30 to 40 hours to spare, it should be more than enough to crack everything up. A MUST-HAVE for anyone who likes puzzles/Zelda-like games. Combat can be tuned down for easier approach-ability anyways.

_childDocuments_.review: meets , or  meets . If you think you'll like the game based on the trailer, stop reading these reviews and play the game. Steam has a return window, and the first few minutes will immediately cement if you'll like the game or not.So, I have strange feelings with this game. Don't go in expecting definitive story answers, or a genre-defying experience. When we were presented with the idea that we were collecting items that were visible outside of an in-game "screen", I thought it would have some kind of pay off later. It doesn't. This is a game more centered around "figuring things out". The combat in the game is rather difficult, but mitigated by three factors: frequent checkpoints, the option to give yourself unlimited health, and the fact that the game's boss battles are specifically designed to have a speedrun exploit that nearly instantly kills the boss. I played through the game to the basic ending once blind, and was fairly satisfied with how things went. I got a bad ending, but I didn't get all of the collectibles, and was more focused on trying to survive each encounter. There's a lot of optional backtracking near the end of the game, which I think is weird and unreasonable(?), and doesn't add a lot to the game. This is mitigated/helped by enemies vanishing from most of the world near the end, without explanation*. After getting the bad ending, I reloaded my save and decided to look up a guide to see what I might have missed to get the good ending. And this is where I had issues with the game. There's a tremendous amount of effort put into hidden puzzles scattered across the world, and collectibles the game never properly communicates to you. Even worse in my opinion is that these collectibles don't provide any benefits to your character, at least in terms of combat. It just feels weird seeing how I missed a large chunk of the game's content... only to learn that it's specifically designed to be inconsequential? I used a guide to get the good ending, which amounted to finding a certain number of these optional collectibles. If I would change ANYTHING with this game, it would be the requirements for the good ending. I think it would be better if you got the good ending by either . As it stands, the good ending feels weird and somewhat out of place; you show someone you collected all of the things and they just give up, and everyone lives happily ever after. It contrasts with the rest of the game's world and tone HARD. The lore bothers me because the game can't seem to decide whether or not something weird is happening or not. You're given a map with the in-game manual, and sections of the map are blatantly different from what the world looks like... but the in-game manual also acknowledges the world is falling apart, and has entries for these out-of-place enemies? It feels like the devs weren't sure whether or not they wanted to commit to a 4th-wall breaking gameplay mechanic, but they started to implement it anyways. It irritates me... because the rest of the execution is SO well done. The in-game manual is actual genius as far as game ideas go, and the game consistently goes, "See this door? You could've opened it this entire time if you did X and Y." Replaying the game feels bizarre, as several key doors are locked with pure information; press up against the right walls an you can bypass chunks of the game. Look up speedruns of this game, it's insane.Graphics are smooth and clean. Music is god-tier, I listen to it at work regularly. Boss battles, when fought normally and without intentional exploits, feel extremely rewarding like Dark Souls games; my only issue is the scarcity of them (there's like 4-5 dungeons in the entire game, each with a boss).  There's a lot of accessibility options, too, if you're not here because of the combat. The general experience is very smooth and clean, like the interface implies. If you think you found a bug, I can almost assure you the devs know of it and intentionally left it in (looking at you, ice wand).If you coming off of , you'll like this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Game good, don't spoil it for yourself and just let the game guide you through it. Very enjoyable Zelda-like with fun and unique bosses, an enjoyable progression system, and fun secrets that you can come upon fairly naturally if you're willing to expend some effort being curious. All of that, with out even discussing the beautiful visual style and phenomenal sound design/music, nor the basically bug free gameplay. Overall a wonderful single player game, that I could easily play from start to finish without a second thought, which is something hard to come by now a days. If you know you like this type of game, you should consider this a must have, and if you're interested but uncertain, wait for a decent sale, and it should be more than worth the investment.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is the embodiment of don't judge a book by its cover. When I first saw a trailer for it, I thought it was a cutesy Zelda style adventure action game. But after it released, I heard there was more underneath the cover and I was intrigued enough to pick it up. My playthrough of Tunic reminded me of when I was a kid playing the original NES Zelda. There was no internet back then. You had to figure out things on your own and through word of mouth. The backstory of Zelda was told through the manual. It also had information on how to play, items, enemies, and a map you could reference. In Tunic, you also collect pages of an in-game manual. The major difference is Tunic's manual is mostly in its own language with some english sprinkled in there for important information. This reminded me of what Dark Soul's creator Hidetaka Miyazaki said about how growing up he would often read books he couldn't understand and would have to piece together the meaning. It is pretty clear the Souls games also had some inspiration on the gameplay in Tunic as well.Most of the game plays like you would expect, but near the end there is much more focus on puzzle solving than combat. This didn't bother me much as I love puzzles and the final puzzle of the game was one of the most challenging and satisfying to solve in any game. That said, I would have expected there to be more challenging adversaries near the end game, especially after spending most of the latter quarter of the game powering up.After I finished the game, I discovered there were even more secrets in the game I was unaware of. I won't spoil them here, but it is reminiscent of games like Fez and The Witness. It is clear that the devs put a lot of love into the game and embodied that spirit of putting in content that only the most dedicated players will discover it and I just think that's neat.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the best games I've EVER played in a very long time. It was a refreshing take on players using their brain, both for combat and intuitive purposes that most of all made you actually care to move the story forward. I can't stress enough the frustrations I've had on finding a game that hit so many things right, between the music, the playstyle, the atmosphere, and the outright charm this game has. I could be considered a grumpy person, but this game felt extremely magical to the point where I felt like I was one of those characters from a Pixar film that goes from hard to approach to beaming with sunshine. The level of detail in this game is amazing, the sense of wonderment that I thought was long gone from games because of my age (and even discussed with a few friends not too long ago how when you grow up, games just aren't that magical to you anymore) well, I was wrong! I honestly wish I could wipe the memory of playing this game from my brain, just so I could experience it all over again.That's how I'd describe this game. When you finish it, you'll want more, you'll want to find the end, but when you do, you'll wish there was no end to it. It's witty, it's charming, it's beautiful. I'd give this game an actual 10 out of 10. I didn't even mention the music, one of the most beautiful soundtracks I've ever heard that made me buy it just so I could fully support whoever I could who composed it, and I usually don't care enough to do something like that. Leave here knowing you will truly fall in love with this game if you like a real sense of adventure, you'll WANT to help this fox get through his journey, and that is an accomplishment I find very rare in games, just period, even from years ago.I want to mention something, that this game had me thinking, like, REALLY thinking, both for combat and puzzle solving, and I enjoyed every moment of it. I played this only like a few days or so after it dropped, but I wanted to be absolutely sure I solved every single thing about this game before fully reviewing it. I have to say, even after practically unlocking everything, I'm at my wits end at the very last, LAST secret of the game, so much so that I knew that it was above my scope and I decided to write this review. One day, one day I'll get back to it, try to figure it out, but as frustrated as I am with it, I enjoy it, I'm happy about the level of detail this game puts for you the player to enjoy, and the masterful dedication they put into having you come up with figuring this out. I had no clue how much I enjoyed a genre like this and this is a community I want to be a part of. I want to find more people who enjoy things like this, to befriend them because the energy this game gives off, I can only imagine that the players that figured these kinds of things out are some intuitive people who enjoy adventure!

_childDocuments_.review: An amazingly charming Zelda-like game, with more difficult gameplay and an intriguing world. The visuals are stunning and the music/sound design is fantastic all the way through. I mostly recommend it, but if you do pick up the game: in my humble opinion, . It involves an incredibly obtuse puzzle that took me 4 of the 14 hours I played to figure out, killing the momentum completely for a absolutely unrewarding payoff. I don't know why this was the design decision to gate the true ending, but I didn't feel clever for meandering through an extremely confusing puzzle that no longer engages with the main gameplay loop... and instead left with a sour taste in my mouth.The "bad end" the game gives you is perfectly serviceable, and saves you having to go through probably the worst part of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: One of those games that is more than it says it is on the tin. A very basic art style that complements the very beautiful moments that make you go "Whoa..." and give you that spark of wondrous joy. The rising difficulty of combat was very welcome, and while it does start easy, it does progress into some very difficult fights. The gameplay is a sweet blend of The Legend of Zelda and Dark Souls, integrating aspects of both very well in not only the combat, but the exploration too. There is always another secret waiting for you to find, but the puzzle aspects don't get in the way, and you can enjoy the experience without them (although the puzzle components alone do add a fair bit more to the play time).
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: This game was just what I was looking for! A fun break from reality to fight monsters and solve puzzles. Hard but very rewarding when you beat a boss. Tons of secrets and incredible detail to the clues (fight the urge to google and read the manual, you can do it!). Highly recommend, can't wait for a sequel!

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a brilliant game...that MAY not appeal to EVERYONE. Imagine a more difficult 2D Legend of Zelda with souls-like trappings and Myst-like puzzles. It's not overly punishing...or forgiving. It expects you to figure a lot of things out, but offers one of the greatest 2D action-adventure experiences in years!
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: A fun, clever game with an anticlimactic ending.I enjoyed it a lot for the most part. The exploration is great. Getting treasure, even just money, felt useful, and there's a lot of hidden secrets scattered everywhere. And the experience of trying to piece out hints through context from the manual is something really unique that I loved.Unfortunately there comes a point near the end where there's not really a whole lot left to explore, and that's when you learn about something that's been there under the surface the whole time. I don't dislike the new facet of gameplay that this gives you context for, but at this point it's really the only gameplay left to do since you've already seen everything else. That made it feel like busywork even though I would have probably enjoyed it just fine if it had been mixed in with the main gameplay loop instead of revealed at the end. (If you do want to engage with it from the start, you could ask a friend to look up pages 43 and 44 and show you their images? Unfortunately, this gives you early access to one thing which, while not overpowered, reveals a major endgame spoiler.)I did crack the glyph system as I was going and translate just about everything. This is optional, and honestly I wound up feeling a little let down after putting that much effort in. I have a lot of questions about the plot/setting and it didn't really explain any of them; I just came away feeling like the answers probably don't exist. So...you can translate if you want to;  doing it all blind was a really interesting experience I wish I could do again. But if it doesn't sound fun to you, don't worry, you'll be fine without.Overall, I enjoyed the journey a lot more than the destination, but I really did enjoy the journey a lot, so I'm recommending this.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what can I say?!Almost speechless.This Game and Elden Ring are definitely my GOTY Contender.I can't say too much what other people didn't already say.This is a mix between a Souls Like (can be very difficult at times) and A Link to the Past. Sprinkle in a little of Death's Door and some other similar Games and you got Tunic.But somehow it feels like it's own Game. It is not only the cute Art Style or the great Music.It's the Gameplay and exploration of the world. An example: At first you think that there are not enough Savepoints (Shrines), but later on you realize when you explore more, that there are so many Shortcuts that lead to the "old" Savepoints.Also the thing with the Manual Pages and the Cryptic Language: Genius! (I won't spoil here.)Let me also say: There were some points in the Game where my Head was hurting, I am not used to think that much constantly in a Videogame. There is no handholding whatsoever and I plead to you, if you buy this Game, go in blind.At some points in the Game I was about to look a solution up, happened around 4 times maybe.But I kept on trying and thinking for myself and it felt so good when you finally got the solution. Without spoiling, you can end the Game "early" and when you do like I did, don't worry, there is an option for either "New Game +" or you can select "Retry" and try to go another path (which is what I did, because I want the true (?) ending!This Game is worth every penny!

_childDocuments_.review: One of the biggest gaming disappointments of my life. Incredible atmosphere and aesthetics with some mind blowing puzzles.Unfortunately this game is HEAVILY bogged down by its over reliance on an outdated combat design style that feels very unpolished. Combine that with the games' insistence to be somewhat of a souls-like and it comes out feeling like some sort of bizarre amalgam of ideas rather than a focused project. I definitely think that the 'Majora's Mask' type of combat could work but the lock on mechanic is straight up terrible. Most enemies (including most bosses) can be bullied into oblivion with ease, although some require precise strikes which does not blend with the clunky Zelda-like swordplay. Overall it's an okay game, most of the positive reviews are here however because of the nostalgia factor or the admittedly great vibes.

_childDocuments_.review: "Tunic" has a charming aesthetics and engaging gameplay. The game has a beautiful, hand-drawn art style and vibrant world, which create an enchanting atmosphere that captivates from the start. The music and sound design also receive commendation for enhancing the overall experience.Gameplay-wise, "Tunic" is lauded for its challenging yet rewarding exploration and puzzle-solving elements. I appreciate the homage to classic adventure games, noting the game's clever use of environmental storytelling and cryptic hints that encourage curiosity and discovery. The combat, while described as tough, is generally seen as fair and satisfying, requiring players to think strategically. The lack of explicit guidance maybe a little bit overwhelming, though it is part of the game's charm.Overall, "Tunic" is celebrated for its nostalgic feel, artistic beauty, and deep, explorative gameplay
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fantastic! I have loved isometric games since the days of Knight Lore, Batman, Head Over Heels and many others on the ZX Spectrum, and Tunic feels like a time machine back to that era and, of course, the first Zelda games on NES. Love the art, love the sense of exploration, very clever to incorporate the souls-like mechanics and engaging combat. Also, I think it's really inspirational that this whole game was made (mostly) by one talented guy. Kudos to him and everyone that collaborated!
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Simply astounding game design!In 2022 I passed Tunic off as a mindless Legend of Zelda clone due to the obviously reminiscent design of the sword, tunic, and shield. This year I actually looked into the game and decided to give it a go. It was probably the best life decision I have made in recent memory. The graphics are great, the map design is incredibly clever, and the soundtrack is so well fit and insanely beautiful. It has some similar aspects to a 2D Legend of Zelda game which is great, but Tunic goes so far beyond that. Bosses are really well done. They are equal parts challenging and fair with the various approaches you can take to taking them out. Not to mention there are easier and harder difficulty settings if you desire them.Game progression is brilliant. Sometimes you make progress because you gained an item, and other times you acquire information via the instruction manual that you piece together throughout the length of the game. Sometimes you just find a hidden shortcut that makes getting back to where you were when you died easier. Every aspect of this game is deserving of praise. If you enjoy especially well-made games then this is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Holy crap I loved every minute I've played so far.Tunic is a mixture of modern and retro, combining the exploration and wonder of a classic Zelda game with the brutal combat of your typical modern-day action RPG.As you explore you gain pieces of the game's instruction manual, which will give you information  to progressing. It's a neat touch that I really had fun exploring. The puzzles are interesting, though I will admit to getting stuck on a couple due to being visually impaired. The only downside I could give is that if you don't like cryptic puzzles, you might want to avoid this game. There's a pretty sizable one, and when I talked with a friend about it he decided it wasn't for him. It's in the spoiler below, but I really recommend not looking at that unless you're REALLY on the fence because of the promise of puzzles.Highly, highly recommended. A fantastic 20-hour experience that I'll definitely be revisiting.

_childDocuments_.review: Only 5 hours in, but i'm gonna write a review anyway. I thought I got this game for like 5 dollars, but I got it for 25.97. I was thinking the whole time "what a steal!" I am not unhappy with paying as much as I did for this game. I will beat this game. The game rewards exploration with hidden chests, hidden shops, and hidden areas. Very often i'm just looking for the way forward or a hidden chest and then I stumble upon something rewarding like a shortcut, loot, a new map that I didn't suspect was nearby, etc; it's all good stuff. Combat is easy, you've got your 1, 2, 3 combo, you've got a shield, bombs, pots, and other utilities that are easy to use. The music blends in with the scenery and is easy on the ears. There are various enemy types from slime likes, knights, skeletons, angry birds, and so so.There is no dialogue and the story is up to interpretation. You develop an understanding as you progress and retrieve pages of information that are still not completely spelled out. It's very fun to feel that there is a mystery to be unraveled when it comes to what's happening in the game and "what the heck does this do!?"There is no difficulty setting just like a souls like. It's challenging enough for me. You can swim past some of the fights, other fights mess ya up. I like that variation in difficulty with enemy types just as much as I like the variety of enemy types. I like them good nuff!I like them colors! So vibrant! The look of the game, so simple and eye grabbing! Much wow!Alright cons if any:There's the targeting system which is simple at first. You just hold shift to lock on to enemies. I have not found a convenient way to switch between enemies when there are many of them and so I could be swinging or blocking in the wrong direction and obviously that leaves me vulnerable. I have had another problem with that while traversing the map with a tool for crossing gaps. You have to lock on to points that allow you to traverse gaps. There's an area that spawns enemies on top of the point you need to traverse to. What this does is it causes you to pull in the enemy and in this situation I was on an island of sorts, a minecraft block wide, and as I pulled the enemy they fell below my attack range, dodging my attack. There were two others who proceeded to blast me while I had little space to dodge around on. I was a sitting duck because I could not easily traverse like I wanted. I found that using the directional keys allows me to change my target, but it feels inconvenient to use when you have to use semicolon for blocking along with j, k, and l for attacking and such and so I cannot simply defend myself while switching targets.There is a mechanic in the game, that I'm not sure if I should speak on in detail about so I won't, which you need to know in order to progress in the game. I had not seen an indication for its use in the player book in game. I was stuck in multiple areas and spent time roaming around the large map looking for things that I had missed until I eventually just played around with some things and accidentally found the way to progress. This is me saying that the element of mystery can lead you to become lost or confused. I suggest that if anyone with low patience becomes stuck you should google it.Again, I've only played 5 hours. My feelings on the game may change later, but as for right now I'd say get it if you're looking for a challenging yet relaxing experience. Or maybe it's challenging at times and relaxing at other times. It's up to the player, I reckon.Beaten it at 28 hours. Final notes. The game has so much mystery because you're constantly trying to interpret characters on paper that you cannot understand, which is the intention. I learned about the end game secret mechanic, started doing the secret dance and what not, and the whole time I was so confused. Does it want me to input this or that? Oh, it wanted something else for this one. I felt like some details were missing, which is usually intentional, but I had no idea how to go about doing some other things that I found for the find all the secrets challenge. It has kept me up 'til 5 in the morning. I punched in so many key combos, obviously first doing the ones I was supposed to do, and nothing would work so I just went and had my 35 attempts at killing the boss and got the sad ending. Sad ending didn't make me feel great, but it was still a great game. Maan, that sucks...

_childDocuments_.review: Before getting into the review, I'll say the game has an "Infinite Stamina" mode and "No Fail" mode which is just invincibility if you just want to enjoy the exploration without the challenge from the combat. I played with these modes off but, of course, you should enjoy the game how you want to.Tunic is a top-down Zelda style game with some Dark Souls elements that has a big emphasis on exploration and acquired knowledge through that exploration and inferring what things do.In additional to the exploration elements, the game also has challenging bosses that can be approached a few different ways since there is no one progression sequence in the game and is open-ended shy for a few ability-gated parts that give it a bit of a Metroidvania flavor at times. I wouldn't define it as a Metroidvania but there are hints of that flavoring. I would say the strongest focus and feel is Zelda and Soulslike with probably more Zelda than Souls and a lot of the normal combat can be addressed more with a mind toward Zelda's top-down combat rather than just relying heavily on the dodge roll i-frames. You will want those dodge rolls for the bosses, though. And reflecting a bit more on the bosses, there's also at least a little hint of Gungeon in there, too.It's an amazing game that has an interesting visual style and a lot going for it in the gameplay and design departments. Also the soundtrack is great if you're down for a chill electronic vibe and, if not, mute it and play whatever music you like! :D
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start with the positive.  Neat atmosphere, and the way the game manual sorta steers you forward and reveals mechanics over time is a neat concept.  I just wish there was a way in game to translate it without needing to do the cryptography yourself.Now the negatives.  You move at a pounderous pace, but the game will throw enemies that move faster than you and entire hordes of them.  Your only defensive options rely on a tiny stamina bar, but you are punished double for over using stamina by taking extra damage when you run out.  On top of that, many threats will damage your maximum health until you go to a check point.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Zelda can eat its heart out at this game when it comes to secrets, most of the combat and puzzles.This game has brought a tear to my eye without anything sappy. It expects you to be intelligent and provides hints that are good enough to help you get your head around it. But still make you feel smart for figuring it out!It has been too long since I've seen any dev pull that off in a game.That is a very hard balance to strike without overdoing it, WELL DONE!It rewards you extremely handsomely for exploring, Finding secrets and solving puzzles. It doesn't just expect you to figure it out on your own, it actively encourages you with game breaking magic items that will make you feel very powerful, yet not unkillable. While providing hints and patterns.It will drag that feeling of progression right up to the forefront. reminding you how far you've come, the secrets almost feel metroidvania like with its presentation.“Oh I can get this chest now!!” which also helps you explore towards progression. Small/ slightl spoilery example:  I'll put it this way,without anyone telling people, people are actively trying to keep from doing spoilers in guides and on Reddit.It's one of those games that I would be shocked probably by the development time from how much they crammed into it. Like seriously how small the team is, I expected it would take 10 years. Also worth mentioning its the same team who made night in the woods and helped with Chicory.The True ending is super wholesome and explains the protagonist's motivation very thoroughly!This game is tough, so don't feel too ashamed if you need to dig out the walkthrough for some parts. A few dings in the clear coat though. Specifically combat and I'm not sure if it's a bug or not.Sometimes the enemies have iframes during basic attacks and sometimes they don't. It would be fine if it was consistent. but the inconsistency is rough when you're trying to really pounce on them/beat them down, Before they can even move. Maybe I'm just missing the hint that demonstrates this. There’s also sometimes a bug that pops up that when you're locked onto a target, sometimes you can hold block, sometimes you can't. In order to fix it, you will have to relaunch the game.This next part I don't consider a bad thing but it might bother some people, this game demands that you think about thing/get good. Not in the dark souls sense mind you. Death is not quite that punishing, but figuring out some of these secrets is mind numbing how you would go about figuring it out! They're pretty obvious once it's pointed out to you, so it seems like something that is player orientated to me. You know that box we usually think in? SCREW THAT BOX, You're in tunic's world now!
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is love letter to Zelda like games. It is a isometric action adventure with difficult encounters. However, Tunic is also a puzzle game where you collect the pages of the game manual to solve puzzles. It uses this mechanic very cleverly, as there are notes on the pages left by an unknown brother like figure.Tunic was overall a very delightful experience that made me wonder what was going to happen next. It is a game where you learn more as you play, and each new mechanic you discover feels fresh and rewarding. It isn't very in your face, and it expects some  deductive reasoning from the player part. The puzzles come in varying degree, and the ones that are too difficult are left as side content, which I really appreciated. The puzzles also require no combat capabilities, which give a nice break between fights. The visuals are also pretty and cutesy which create a contrast between the brutal battles.Personally, I would recommend this game to people who like puzzles and also like or don't mind the challenging combat. It has a very nice twist on an already established genre, and overall, a very fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: Myst re-imagined through the lens of The Legend of Zelda.And since it is through The Legend of Zelda, there is combat, it's about as simple as the pre-Breath of the Wild 3d Zelda games, but it can be punishing as early as the second area. Remember that this is a puzzle game first, and if the combat feels too hard, you probably missed something in the manual. Don't ignore anything with button prompts, and you should be fine.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is truly a genuine work of art! I patiently waited quite some time for this title to release only to enjoy a simple little adventure as a charming little fox. However what I did not expect, was a very intriguing journey that seemed to surprise me countless times. I admired everything from the unique use of the manual, to freedoms and convenience of exploration, the beautiful landscapes/settings, and of course the various secrets riddled across the entirety of the game.Personally, the world I was introduced to in this game was rather immersive, and every secret I found made me want wonder what else might be out there. This game has a great mix of both combat and puzzles, some might say that it's difficult, but as far as I've felt the combat was only punishing to the mistakes you made, and most of the more difficult puzzles are pretty much optional, though there are so many that it is likely you may stumble upon one here and there, but when you figure them out for yourself it can be pretty satisfying, and lead you to potential solutions that might work for other things you've come across.Overall, I'd recommend this title to anyone looking to sink some time into a game that feels both modern and retro, if you love hunting easter eggs or games that make you think outside the box, then especially give this game a try!
