_childDocuments_.review: Edit: After some time and watching a few videos  about the game, I had decided to come back to it and give it another go, and it seems that my previous issues about the game were either a bug that was patched or a controller issue I was having that refused to fix itself. Coming back to the game, I didn't experience any issues with controls like the first time, and because of that it allowed me to really deep dive into the game, and I am very happy that I did come back to it. The music is still amazing, and the depth that some of the puzzles portrayed in the guide book and world was great to try and figure out over a number of minutes. The fact that the cypher language is completely translatable and then  as a typing font after you understand it (The Tunic cypher font is downloadable  ) makes it something that I want to implement into a number of different areas and games.I will note, this is very much a game to have a walk through ready on the side just in case as some of the puzzles are  unclear, at least on the first step. but on a personal level, having a guide helping to point me in the right initial direction of what a hint/puzzle is supposed to mean didn't hinder my enjoyment of the game at all, only looking at it when I was full and truly at a complete loss at what something was trying to tell me. Tl;dr Control issues are gone, Game is a blast and the lore/puzzles are very fun to sink your teeth into

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is the most thought provoking and engaging game I have played in a long time. Initially it presents as a solid (but beautifully stylised) third person adventure with your normal attack/dodge/block core mechanics but slowly reveals itself to be much more.The game starts without stifling you with a mandatory hand-holding tutorial segment - instead mechanics and the main quest are explained through interaction with the world and collecting mysterious manual pages for the player to interpret. This may sound daunting but worked seamlessly in practice. I never stalled on where to go and game progression was rewarding because it was entirely driven by the player's desire to explore.Progression through the game comes in the form of upgrading your character, picking up new equipment and techniques and consequently being able to access new areas with new enemies. Normal enemies are typically only challenging in groups but the game operates off a system of checkpoint shrines so it is really a game of how many encounters you can endure while exploring. Game bosses were distinct, challenging, and were satisfyingly spectacular.The game truly shines however on the depths of its puzzles and the evidently large amount of care the devs have put into them. The more you as a player are willing to invest to decode the manual and solve the various puzzles without looking at guides the more you will appreciate the game - I highly recommend playing with pens and paper handy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game perfectly encapsulates the experience of buying a game from a yard sale in a language you can't understand. I can't stress enough how much nostalgia it inspires for games of the 90s, and how much it nails the vibes EXQUISITELY. If you like cute games? This is for you. If you like cryptic mysterious games? This is for you. If you like puzzles that really make you think outside the box and have ASTOUNDINGLY satisfying payoffs, this is the game for you. I will say, if you do decide to try it out (you should), try to avoid looking up solutions, as much of the progress is tied to you the player connecting information, and there are many things you cannot unlearn.

_childDocuments_.review: From the artwork and descriptions, I was really expecting a Zelda-like game, but it’s actually Dark Souls in disguise. Combat is repetitive, unforgiving, uses the campfire / potion mechanic, and resets every time you rest. Maps are confusing, the UI and "manual" are obtuse and deliberately misleading - supposedly as part of a puzzle mechanic, but everything works together to just make the game a frustrating experience. Wouldn't recommend it to anyone. - The isometric view is a key mechanic, but is really annoying walking behind things- The combat is a drag. Endlessly replaying the same 3 battles just to try and get to the next campfire is boring- A manual that doesn’t explain what items do- Hidden paths needed for progression- Spent the first 2 hours trying to leave the area after getting the sword because of weird level design
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a great isometric action-adventure game, it's a bit like a 2D Zelda and Souls-like game combined. I almost think this is better than any 2D Zelda game I've played and I've played them all.5/5 for a 2D action-adventure game.It has more of a a focus on combat and the enemies re-spawn when you rest, sort of like a souls game.The puzzles are a bit different from the Zelda series, most of them don't require an item, none of them are pushblock and you're only forced to defeat a room of enemies a couple times besides bosses.Most of the puzzles in the game can be solved right away, but you won't know how till later after you have learned how to do it.In the game you collect pages to an instruction manual, some pages show you information like: the story, how play the game, maps (with your location), give you hints to secrets, or show where to go.I would REALLY recommend playing this game blind since figuring out how the game works from the instruction manual is one of the best mechanics in the game and the funnest part of the game, almost every page you pick up gives you helpful information or makes you say "oh wait, I could do that?!".
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic deceived me.  I expected a cute isometric dungeon game like The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening and instead I was met with a cute isometric dungeon game like The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening with the difficulty of Dark Souls.  This game will test both your puzzle solving skills as well as your combat skills.  It will do this while playing a beautiful soundtrack with lots of stunning visuals and the most amazing hand-drawn in-game instruction manual that you have to piece together.  I will reiterate that this game is difficult on multiple levels.  If you want a true challenge, you could spend a lot of time with this game trying to uncover all of its secrets.  I will say that at times, the lock-on targeting can be a bit frustrating.  My other major complaint is that the game doesn't always lead you to an unlock directly so it is entirely possible to leave an area without knowing that you missed a key item or hit a switch.  Things are not always immediately obvious that you need to interact with them which is both some of the charm of the game, but also an added frustration at times if you don't feel like retracing your steps a bunch.  Overall, I really enjoyed Tunic and appreciated the risks that they took.

_childDocuments_.review: Summery: Review contains mild spoilers. TUNIC, as some folks in the reviews have said, is a Zelda-Like mixed with Souls combat mechanic game. The game itself is very good and has some very satisfying moments. Especially the adventure and exploration aspects. It’s so much fun to run around and hack and slash stuff on the main area. Our little hero is just too adorable and makes this experience so much fun. The plot unravels like an onion at times and is fluid as it intermixes with the fun of exploration. The pros: Like I said in my summery, the games’ plot intermixes with the discovery and exploration aspects of the game so well. Even the somewhat obscure stuff, like the Golden Path, becomes easy to understand with a little work. The environments and places you will go are also very well designed and rather beautiful. Even some of the more… bleak… areas have a unique charm to them. The overall atmosphere a 10/10 for me. The sound and music design is phenomenal. I like games that reward the player for their curiosity and exploration, and this game delivers in a big way. The cons: The overall difficulty curve really ramps up to a 12 from a solid 8 in the final act. It’s such a climb in difficulty its rather jarring. Specifically, a certain environmental effect you first encounter late in the game, which you have no defense for until later. One of the final boss fights is such a stark difficulty ramp is so stark and jarring it’s borderline impossible. I spent over a week re-playing that fight trying different strategies and things until I managed to win. If they had just nerfed one of his attacks, he’d still be really hard! Overall: I love this game. It’s difficult at times, but very fun and rewarding and aesthetically pleasing other times. 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Few games are like this or this unique and this one has all of the things it's doing going for it, combat, presentation, locations to explore, everything about the music, ambiance and sound effects being very nice and ofc a lot of great puzzles to solve.I initially had my reservations about puzzles and secrets of this game being too esoteric and convoluted, but it was well designed in almost all its parts. There were a few points where it got a bit iffy, some of the 100% parts, but I can accept some of those, even the majority of these were fairly manageable as long as you pay attention to them, including the big puzzle.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a constant stream of dopamine hits as you uncover secrets, learn new puzzle and combat techniques, and piece together a world where little is explained. The world is designed to reward veteran game enjoyers, those who are literate in game design and played many games.While playing, if you dont know what to do or think you went the wrong way, go another direction! Combat too hard? Learn the attack patterns (like a souls game), dont hoard your items (but i know you will anyways), and then get thrive.The flow of dopamine hits really only stops when you hit a difficult boss or sequence, but if you know how to troubleshoot areas and always look for paths that shorten or shortcut through areas (like souls games) then you will be a-okay. Have fun and be curious!

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game on a different platform, but it was so worth purchasing again. I love the art style of this game, the combat is fun, and it is challenging.I feel like this game gives you the experience that older video games had, where you had to try and figure things out and you only had what the game devs give you in their guide book. If you are someone who loves puzzles or figuring things out, this is the game for you. It is beautiful, has an amazing story, and a good challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like some parts of this game, most of it actually. But there are certain elements deliberately placed in it, that are really annoying, such as:-the handbook: you just want to take a quick look at the map? Have fun flipping through dozens of pages every time you are in another location.-the weird language: is it some kind of inside joke I am just to noob to get? Guess I will never find out.-changing items during combat: your bombs are all used up, and you quickly want to equip another item? Take your time doing so, while the game moves on and the boss slaughters you.-the secret chests: the good news, there are about 20 secret shiny chests for you to find. The bad news, you will never find them (if you don't look it up on the internet).-the ability: for most of them I initially had no idea what they are for. And thanks to the cryptic handbook, I still don't have a clue.At first glance, I thought "finally a new gem to enjoy". I guess I will have to wait for Silksong.

_childDocuments_.review: As a big fan of Zelda games and Outer Wilds, Tunic was sadly kinda disappointing.The main draw of this game will be the mystery, how to play and what is happening with the story, which at the start is an incredibly strong hook and makes the sense of discovery very big.There are definitely magical moments where you suddenly realize how to do something or what is going on, which is important for this kind of game.But these moments happen only a few times and the rest of Tunic is just unsatisfying.I think my biggest gripe with Tunic is that most of the "puzzles" aren't really puzzles but rather just something you will eventually be shown within the manual pages you will find, yes technically it isn't an item you use to do the thing, you have to put in a bit of mental work to figure out what the page is telling you, but it's still shown to you through the page you just picked up instead of you applying a known mechanic in a new creative way.Especially the final big puzzles fail horribly, a key to a good puzzle is that it takes a while to figure out what you need to do, but once you realize the solution, executing it should only take a few seconds.In Portal for example, you try to mentally figure out how to place the portals, which can take a good half hour in some of the harder levels. But once you know, you just place them, go through and finish the level.However, in Tunic you know pretty quickly what it is you need to do with the endgame puzzles, but you have go back and forth to note things down (no way that you can mentally keep track of all of it) and be busy for nearly 15 minutes just doing the thing you know will solve it, which makes it drag on way too long and just takes all satisfaction away from solving the puzzle.If you still like the idea of those kind of puzzles, then this game is probably very fun for you, but it just doesn't work for me personally.Besides that, there's some items you need to figure out on your own what they do, but unlike how most games will put you in a situation where you can clearly figure it out, here you can go a while without really figuring out what it does...causing it to not be used at all.And in general the combat just isn't all too interesting, most basic enemies can be dealt with very easily, only the boss battles provide an actual challenge and the difference in difficulty is sometimes a bit too big, since it's not the main draw of the game though that is not a huge problem, if you are struggling too much there's settings to pretty much disable the combat.The story is interesting, but sadly leaves a bit too much open to interpretation in my opinion, there is so much to the world that I would love to be explained just a bit more.Showing instead of telling is good, but showing a bit more would've made it more fulfilling to get the true ending so you can truly understand the impact you are making. It just feels like a cheap wholesome ending at the moment.On the good side, the visuals are honestly really pretty, and the world design is phenomenal.There are countless secret passages that connect different places together, making it feel as interconnected as Dark Souls 1.But sadly it just left a bitter aftertaste in my mouth, it could've been a real gem but just ended up being disappointing, so sadly I can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: While Zelda Souls is a proper description to this game, I think it needs some expanding. The puzzles in this game are brutal, it requires you to think about and analyse every detail you see. Its not that the puzzles are complex, but they are well hidden and so very varied, with many puzzles you see only once and are not repeated.The world is surprisingly big, and exploration is rewarded so well. There are so many ways the game hides its secrets, and many times I leave something for later thinking that I do not have the tools to solve it, only to find out I am not thinking outside the box.I would not call the combat easy, but it is not crazy hardcore either. While combat can be difficult at times, dying is not punished as hard as Souls and recovery is easy. Bosses are very fun and never unfair, with a variety patterns to learn and some can have puzzly aspects to them.The story is very much in tune with Souls and Hyper Light Drifter in that you must force the game to give you a story, it will not give you one if you don't try your best to find it. The story is puzzle in it self and absolutely engaging, I feel so invested emotionally in the world.Also, super cute foxes.Bottom line: 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: There are not many games that nail that sense of "Adventure", But Tunic gets there. Its great fun exploring and unravelling the world around you, that over time you start to find layers upon layers. The game is never too vague to be frustrating, but never too obvious that you feel you are just playing a hack and slash. The combat was good enough and felt pretty well balanced and never slows you for too long.  Some comparisonsI enjoyed playing Deaths Door before this, and the combat is very similar, but Tunic really is on another level with its world and systems. There are more differences to Zelda games then similarities, that said the "feeling" certainly resonates as I has humming ocarina tunes by the end

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a star or scale from 1 to 10 for this, instead of yes or no.  I'd give this game a 6 out of 10.To be blunt, I enjoyed the first half of the game.  Pretty good action adventure, with responsive combat and different combinations which result in higher damage.  Parry, dodge, and stun can all be done, though requires practice to perfect.  The 2.5 design means hidden paths and what not, because that's always apart of a game with a fix camera.  Item combinations and things like that improve your combat and transverse potential.  The instruction manual provides hints, and requires you to pay attention and zoom in on each page to identify things.  An easy to understand combo, for those who like to live dangerously, is the berserk, critical damage, and critical defense combination, where your health is in critical levels at all times, so you deal more damage from the berserk and critical damage buffs, and the critical defense boosts your shield strength (I think).The second half, the line puzzles, I loath.  I don't mind puzzle games, in fact my library has the entire "The Room" series barring the VR game, and other puzzle games.  However, line puzzles, where you have to input a lengthy series of inputs with little feedback of where you went wrong, makes it frustrating.  Hence, I ended up looking up the solutions to most if not all of the puzzles.  The more complex ones requires good old fashion screenshots, and arrangement of images to solve.  Feels punishing to those who have only one monitor as the amount of screen space necessary to solve these things efficiently increases in proportion  the more complex puzzles.Hence, multiple endings, which requires you to know how to solve those puzzles to obtain.  The basic "bad" ending happens if you simply go through the game without doing any of the puzzles.  About the only thing I failed to find, is the ability to translate the language, and instead either intuit or looked up the meaning.I did enjoy the game, and its music.  Just not all of it, and cannot recommend something that has a bit of a niche audience to everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is two different games. On one hand it's a cute lil souls like with a fun aesthetic, awesome sound design, tough bosses, great environmental storytelling, and a very interesting method of progression. You collect pages of the game's instruction manual and most of it is written in this fictional language. However the manual breaks into perfect English on occasion to give you just enough information to nudge you in right direction. For a majority of the game the hints make sense and I feel smart for figuring it out without being explicitly told where to go and what to do.with the exception of a few traversal upgrades you have most of your abilities from the very start of the game but this information is slowly fed to you by the manual pages in a way that, again, feels intuitive!Until you get to the final boss... the last few manual pages inform you in increasingly cryptic ways on how to get the good ending. You are encouraged to take notes on puzzle solutions and take a crack at deciphering the fake language just to get some semblance of how to progress.You get neck deep in this manual rabbit hole and it honestly feels like a completely different game, and it sucks because I want to solve the puzzles as intended, using nothing but the manual and my intuition, like I've done for the rest of the game. But attempting to navigate this this Zelda 1 homage without outside help brings the end game to a screeching halt.So if brain teasing cryptic puzzles really tickle your fancy then well, you have about 6 hours of a souls like to get through just to get to them.This gear shift to what feels like an entirely different genre is what holds back Tunic from being a masterpiece in my eyes.Overall I loved the experience, Just be prepare to whip out a guide for some of the later game puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: It deconstructs the game and lays it wide open on your table, for you to put your own soul in it.It also testifies to video games as "wonder machines". All games try to create wonder to the best of their resources (even  don’t laugh!), but  seems to be more focused on the process than the output, more interested in the "clockwork" behind the magic, the “machinery” that makes the god appear rather than the god himself (shifting the emphasis in the traditional  device). It even has the mechanics and the meta-narration for it. Your main mission will be to piece together and figure out the manual that describes the game, which is also a game guide, a cheat book and your most important resource for puzzle solving. All that because  is essentially a puzzle game, masquerading as a top-down souls-like metroidvania only so that it can push the puzzles into the meta layer of its narrative, hiding them in plan sight, as it were. And they are wonderful, brilliant puzzles! So great they totally overshadow the action mechanics the game relies on in its early stages, to the point that it almost makes them irrelevant by the end game (you can choose a greatly reduced difficulty for enemy encounters and boss fights  if you want to concentrate on the puzzles). And the game will want you concentrated on those. That’s not to say its action mechanics are less accomplished, of course, but the gradual shift from action to puzzles as the game progresses is obvious and a great example of versatile and meaningful game design, that I’ve not seen many games able to attempt so successfully. Therefore, if you want to play it as a slick souls-like metroidvania in a colourful Zelda-like setting, you can totally tackle it like one of those, but its truest nature is closer to the ascetic self-awareness of  and the game manual it has you put together while playing is hands down the most self-referential statement ever made by a video game.LATER EDIT:  is basically two very different games, conjoined at the hip and wrapped in the same fox-shaped package. The greatest thing to ever come out of an identity crisis!

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game for a single playthrough. Not many videogames made me want to use physical notepad and note down all the clues and combinations trying to figure out all the puzzles, but this one managed to succeed in exactly that, and it made the process really fun to boot. Puzzles are very reminiscent of games like "Fez" or - if you want to go REALLY oldschool - Atari "Swordquest". So while on surface level it seems like just a Zelda clone, it's actually a puzzle game deep down in it's core. Despite that it still has some interesting Zelda-like mechanics such as ability to grab most items in any order depending on how good you are with exploring - like in "Ittle Dew" - and there are some devious ways you can combine these items for additional effects.The game biggest flaw would be probably that it's magic is gone after single playthrough, no matter what you do you cannot unlearn the mechanics that are used to solve the puzzles so most likely single playthrough is going to be all of the enjoyment you are going to get out of this game.However that single run is still decently long, the puzzles are top-notch quality and at the end of the day this game is well worth it's asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a great game that reminds me of older games, like zelda 1, where the game doesn't tell you much and you have to figure it out yourself. The game does help and guide you, so it's not as obtuse as zelda 1, but even most of the text in the game is unreadable so you have to interpret what the game is saying instead of being told. For the gameplay Tunic flows well with its movement and combat, the level design is expertly designed and you can see a lot of thought was put into it. It's shocking to me just how many secrets are in this game, your desire to explore is always rewarded with something, and I most likely missed at least half of the secrets.

_childDocuments_.review: Really good game, like a mix of old school Zelda, Dark Souls and Hyper Light Drifter.It doesn't explain anything to you (except kind of, with an ingame instruction booklet), you'll have to figure things out for yourself. The feeling of exploration and discovery is one of the main points of the game, so don't spoil yourself by looking things up in a wiki or reading too much about the game before playing it.The amazing instruction booklet mechanic alone makes the game worth playing, but it's hard to explain without spoiling too much.The combat is simple but satisfying, it's easy to die if you're not careful and there's challenging bossfights.If you like the old 2D Zelda games, souls-like combat, exploration and figuring things out, you will love this.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't be fooled by this cute little fox, Tunic is  clearly not what it looks like !Behind its zelda-like aesthetic, it's a ruthless game that takes its inspiration from the souls games. While I would say it's not at the same level of precision, the gameplay is unforgiving and rewarding.When you progress in the game you'll discover a lot of mysteries and secrets and they clearly are what make this game shine.The "Game Manual" system that helps your progress is  a wonderful idea, it clearly involves the player and contributes a lot to the sensation of reward and progression, I highly suggest that you do not spoil yourself !Played entirely on the steam deck, it runs perfectly.A pleasure to sink hours in, I recommend !

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic was an unexpected gem of a game to me.From trailers it looked like a bit generic rpg game, but in reality it's so much more.What I liked about Tunic:- Beautiful minimalistic art style- Nice non-intrusive music- Suprisingly fun combat system with a lot of tiny details and alternative styles to combat- Pleaseant difficulty curve and nice mix of metroidvania and corridor rpg elementsWhere the Tunic shines the most:- Puzzles are amazing, they are very well-thought and fun to solve, they are different and add so much to gameplay and story- Game Manual! At the first glance it looks like a small nice progress indicator, made as a tribute to old games' paper manuals, but it's so much more. I would say it's a core game mechanic for Tunic - I never felt so much joy and fun finding some in-game writings instead of upgrades and items.What I didn't like:- Most boss fights while not being that bad just feel a bit off, those fights fall out the game flow and fight mechanics.- While most puzzles are amazing and fun, some are a bit twisted and not clear (f* you, chime puzzle) and some leave too large error margin making time to solve artificially longer than it needs (like Mountain Door puzzle, that could be split in parts to make it easier to test solutions)- Small bugs and glitches can be seen here and there - nothing gamebreaking, but they do feel a bit off.Overall, I think Tunic is definitely worth playing, it's very smart about it's complexity - it will let you dive as deep as you wish without forcing you to dig as much as the game goes.

_childDocuments_.review: A charming zelda-like that really captures the classical fantasy adventure RPG while also serving as a masterclass example of knowledge based unlocks with its secrets upon secrets.It's actually tough to talk about the game without spoiling things so all I can really do is comment on how excellently designed it is, providing new twists on old tropes and managing to completely change your perspective on things at several points. The method used is nostalgic and it ends up re-creating experiences that older gamers will appreciate.The art and music are beautiful and really encapsulate the retro feel without actually being retro. The only things I complain about are boss fights having massive difficulty spikes and the souls-like combat feels very out of place.Overall a creative, wholesome, and clever game that takes you on a surprising journey with a lot of unexpected turns.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't get me wrong, this game is amazing. I kind of got slightly lucky that a friend helped me out with a few small pointers, and it is an amazing game, but please note, it is difficult. Not necessarily the combat, but the depth of the entire game, which in part does come down to READ THE MANUAL! It might seem that simple, but, guess what, that one page that tells you when you won't get hit in the middle of the dodge, that page you'll be reading probably over 3 times, just for that information. It in that regard does feel like a nice puzzle game, where, if you don't pay attention to the details will make the entire game a lot harder to finish. In that regard, I would suggest having 20-20 vision, and attention to boot, or be a soulsborne like player, if you want to thoroughly enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic's one of those games you can only truly experience once.At its core, it's a Souls-like Metroidvania. When you die, you respawn at your previously activated checkpoint. You will find numerous items and upgrades, some are permanent, some can be equipped/unequipped. You can't go everywhere, but eventually you will. You'll just have to find the right upgrade/item first.Your only problem is that you don't know anything at all.It "hides" everything from you, leaving you to figure it all out.You do get  help however: a guidebook. But you have to piece it back together, page by page, and you don't understand the language at first. Therein lies the genius of Tunic.If you didn't like Dark Soul, because of its hands off approach where nothing was ever told to you, or because you dislike the progression mechanic, chances are you might not like Tunic. But I still believe there's a chance you might enjoy this.If you like games that hide their cards well, where you are constantly surprised by the little gems they hold, games that draw you in with their impeccable artistic direction, then don't hesitate for a second. Tunic is one of the real ones.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is almost an interesting game within a game riddle that could've succeeded immensely, but I think the pacing undersells that part of the game, in the sense that it leaves most of the interesting parts of the gimmick lingering at the end, probably to lure the majority of the players in first with actual action/adventure gameplay.I still enjoyed it, and would recommend. But I'm not sure from personal experience if they nailed it. The lack of intuitive map traversal and possible backtracking/retracking tedium does have an old school feel to it, but it probably isn't fit for purpose in this day and age. Would've much preferred a warp "between checkpoint" mechanic than the actual hub system in place so I could feel like I was actively solving the overall puzzle than wasting most of my time wondering around aimlessly.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool game, challenging, doesn't hold your hand and has TONS of secrets. This is a unique top down adventure in the same vein as classic Zelda but almost everything taught to the player is through the instruction manual that you find pages of in game. Very unique and interesting way of guiding the player. It's not that simple tho, the manual is in a different language which makes it difficult to read and translate. Very original, high five to the person that thought of this idea. Originally I thought oh I could probably play this with my daughter that's 7, I was very wrong. This is more in line with Dark Souls than Zelda, do not be deceived by the cartoonish presentation, this is challenging exploration, combat, hell even figuring out what all the items do is trial and error, this is very much a throw back to the NES days where you had no explanation only experience, and you share whwt you've learned with your friends from the neighborhood! Such wonderful times, I love it. Of course nowadays you can look something up online, but I highly suggest not doing that. Go in blind and figure it out.This is a fun and challenging experience. Give it a shot if you like classic adventure games with tons of secrets.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a gem! I could describe it as a top down Zelda game with the puzzle mechanics of FEZ, but that would be selling it short. It masterfully unfolds layers upon layers of story and mechanics to you in a way that is both natural and obvious. The manual with its cryptic language just gives you enough info to place the dots in front of you, letting you connect them on your own to immensely satisfying results. Not only did I write down notes while playing, but I went as far as doing crafts with scissors and glue to solve some of the game's most intricate puzzles. Seriously. This game is an utter delight!

_childDocuments_.review: Curator page : TUNIC is an action-adventure game inspired by Zelda and FEZ.You play as a fox who wakes up on a ruined island, with no context and nothing else to do but to explore.You'll quickly find the bare minimum to fight the enemies wandering around, and a few pages of what appears to be the game manual : this manual is the core of TUNIC.The twist is that it is ciphered, written in a language you can't understand. Some words are still readable though, and the game revolves around that : making you guess and guiding you with your senses of observation and deduction. Nothing is directly told to you : everything, whether it is a minor or major thing, is in the manual and you'll have to study it.It has a strong nostalgic vibe, game manuals are not a thing anymore and anyone who grew up with them probably miss them too. I always read them before playing a new game, and I remember I had to put tape on my Super Mario Sunshine and Sonic Adventure 2 manuals due to reading them too much...The world of TUNIC is extremely well crafted, exploring it is very pleasant (the game is beautiful, cute and has a nice soundtrack) and very rewarding, there are TONS of secrets hidden everywhere. Once you get that this is this type of game, you'll start searching any corner you can find... and sure you'll probably get a lot of treasures.But what makes the level design of TUNIC so good and truly genius is not only the secrets you'll find. It's all the things hidden in plain sight that you'll still miss. The game doesn't even try to misdirect you, they are just so cleverly hidden that you won't see or find them.TUNIC has two major sides:- The first one is the adventure, the main game. It strongly reminds of Zelda, but harder. And I'm not just talking about the bosses, common enemies are also threats and some areas can be (very) challenging. The combat is punishing if you just brainlessly rush into the enemies. If you take your time and properly dodge/parry, you won't have much trouble going through the game except for an area near the end. You even have some consumables you can use if you really struggle.The bosses are still the highlights of course, being fun, varied, very strong and usually forcing you to use different items depending on which one you face.- The second one is the FEZ-like side that you'll discover near the end. Full of clever puzzles, including mind-blowing ones that you'll remember for a long time. Some people can find that part too difficult but it's not, it just requires patience and, as always, a thorough study of the holy manual.I unfortunately can't go into details without spoiling anything but if you like puzzles, it's heaven.At this point you probably wonder why I didn't talk about the story at all. Well, like anything else in the game, the story is also cryptic.You'll guess a few things and probably end up understanding what you're doing on the island. But the real story, the context of the game, is locked behind the ciphered language. And you're not supposed to decipher it, at least not until the very end of the game... and you probably won't anyway because it's absurdly hard.That's the only little sad thing I can say about the game, I would've loved more hints about that to really try to decipher myself.Anyway TUNIC is a masterpiece, in case it wasn't clear.And we need more games like that. Games crafted with a lot of love and time put into it. Games that don't hold your hand and recognize players are not devoid of brain. Games that are unique and memorable experiences.I'll just end with a small message to the devs : thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: 5/10 It's hard to recommend the game but it's "probably" worth playing. Most everything about the game is incredible and reminds you of those original Zelda games you played as a kid. The exploration is great when paired with the in game guide manual you piece together over time and the sound track to go along with.The game falls very short in terms of combat. If combat is your main thing, I would not play this. There was very little to no effort put into the combat to make it a worth while experience. It's very disappointing due to the fact the game excels at every other aspect so well. The game itself took me about 10 hours to beat, so it's not a very long game either. As with any game, I'm sure there is replay-ability, but I have little to no desire to replay it with how atrocious the combat is. I do look forward to the idea of a sequel but I hope there was a lot learned in regards to fixing the combat.

But the game offers you an option to turn on "no fail" which means you will not die in battle. This way you can focus on exploring the world and figuring out the puzzles. _childDocuments_.review: I guess the main feeling the TUNIC evokes is nostalgia. Game Manual mechanic is what makes it different from just isometric metroidvania or cute soulslike. I had a great time time leveling up my stats, exploring every nook and cranny, and solving original puzzles. Only a couple of puzzles/secrets were too much to handle, so I had to consult the web. In general, the last third of my playthrough fell too heavy on secret hunting, enemies became only a slightly annoying set dressing. Otherwise, it is an almost perfect gaming experience.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: If you like finding secrets, then there's probably no better game about secrets than this. I would describe the game as being Darksouls but Zelda, or vise versa. It has lots of Darksouls but in a Zelda type of vibe. Combat is pretty basic but still fun imo. The main difference in the gameplay loop is the massive amount of secrets. Almost every screen has a small little corner you can go around and find some loot or a new item or anything, it's really cool and satisfying. The secrets make heavy use of the isometric perspective which might sound annoying but works really well especially when you find a shortcut to an area that you've already been in that was there the whole time.But secrets don't stop at chests obscured from view. The entire game has interesting progression not just in power or exploration but knowledge. There are doors that you literally don't know how to open, not that you don't have the key, or don't have an ability, you just don't know. Items and abilities are figured out through experimentation. A lot of the knowledge based progression is done through the manual so make sure to pay attention to it. It is not required to understand the language. Look at the pictures, diagrams and readable text for information.I should also mention that this game includes THE BEST PUZZLE IN ALL OF VIDEOGAMES.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: The best thing about this game is how little it tells you what to do or where to go. If you prefer a good amount of hand-holding in a videogame, don't buy this. As you play the game, you discover pages filled with 90% codified text and 10% tips and clues which you have to interpret. Finished the game with 18 hours, but I only managed to get the 1st ending. There is a 2nd ending that requires too much work for me, so I don't feel like going for it. Don't really know how many hours that would add to the playtime. There is also a game+ option.- World to explore freely-ish and a myth/history to discover as you play the game- Combat is simple, but engaging- Soundtrack and art is unique and fit together nicely

_childDocuments_.review: visual is an easy 10/10; love the colours, love the low poly aesthetic, love the models, love the animation, everything is just straight on point. soundtrack, also god tier. game mechanics is where i feel split. it intentionally holds some key information back, so far as to not even knowing what kind of item you are getting(you only get visuals and in-game language), and very sparse in giving directions. The first few minutes also lack any kind of tutorial which made me think the game isn't loading correctly or something. if you haven't played a lot of games, it may confuse you too, but it's not too hard to learn as you go.Also a minor gripe as a keyboard player; because of the viewpoint, you have to move diagonally to go "straight". this means you often end up having to press 2 keys simultaneously a lot of times. i wish they had simplified this so that you can control the movement from the character's pov.

_childDocuments_.review: Reluctant recommend but objectively this game is good. My biggest problem is the combat and souls-like nature. Exploring and finding secrets is a hardcore chore when you have an army of respawning trash everywhere. Obviously i can just get good, but therein lies the problem. I don't want to get good at this game, i just wanna discover stuff. Thankfully you can enable god mode in the options otherwise i probably would've stopped playing after getting the first major plot item. Boss fights were pretty fun though, did those normally.If you're like me and are intrigued because it's somewhat commonly mentioned along with Outer Wilds:It's not really anywhere near similar. I went in expecting a similar experience mystery/plot/exploration wise and was hardcore disappointed. In Outer Wilds all rewards for exploration are intrinsic, Here they are the opposite.  Clues are given in the manual you get which CAN be reminiscent of Echoes of the Eye at times but the difference is the secrets you find are largely unrelated to the plot. They dont push you towards closure or a resolution, they all just feel like boxes you tick until you get 100% and are rewarded with the true ending of the game. The secrets dont actually build towards this ending, theyre just secrets for the sake of being secrets. It's not a bad thing, it's just not what I wanted personally. (Note that i didn't actually do most of them, just went and read up on it.)

_childDocuments_.review: First Impression:At the start of the game I was having fun. It was charming and exploration was fun. But it quickly loses all of its charm and fun when you realize how terrible the combat is, which is the main thing you will be doing throughout your playthrough. The combat is very simplistic and gets boring really fast. There is no skill tree or stat tree that you can upgrade to get different moves and the combat items that you find don't tell you what they do, so you literally have to waste one just to see what it does. Its like the developers thought "Hey, you know what would make our game harder. Let's take out item descriptions so that the player will never know what a specific item does or if it would be of any use." And you know it wouldn't be so bad if the game didn't have so many enemies posted everywhere. There is no depth to the combat.Final Thoughts:I really want to like Tunic, but the design decisions just turn me off. Good:The game does exploration and really well. The soundtrack is okay. Very ambient. Nothing very memorable about the soundtrack. The art style looks very good.Bad:I will stand by my statement that the combat is very boring and easy. There isn't any depth to it. Sure you get items that will help remedy with the combat. But mainly, you are just swinging your sword around and dodging. I was expecting more from the combat since that is the main thing you do throughout the game. The game language is honestly stupid. There is really no reason for it other than to be frustrating. Literally every piece of text in the game is written in the language. There is really no point to it since if you take the language out, you lose nothing. The manual could of easily just been made out of pictures and some of the English words they do use in it and it still would say the same thing. No point in it what so ever.Frustrating:Later in the game, when you discover parts of the manual that say something about a golden path. You have finally got to the puzzles in the game. The puzzles range from fun to just plain tedious. The puzzles consist of using your d-pad or arrow keys and sequencing them in the right order. The problem is that some of these sequences are just stupidly long. I don't know I was expecting more from the puzzles from this game. When I heard that the puzzles were hard in this game, I was expecting them to be hard to figure out. But they are not hard to figure out, they are hard to punch in the right sequence, which just makes it tedious. Overall:I had fun playing it for what it is. The game has some really strange design decisions, like the language and the long puzzle input sequences. The combat is boring has no depth or new moves to learn. The exploring is fantastic. The music is alright. Personally, I wouldn't recommend it at the price it is going for. Wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: A cute game where you explore the world, find equipment and fight monsters & bosses. The challenging combat is well made and reminiscent of Dark Souls. This game has a TON of secrets and rewards you for being observant. What makes this game special is the "game manual", a 4th wall breaking nicely illustrated booklet with strong childhood vibes, its pages scattered across the game world. The manual isn't just an 'ol guide that openly reveals all the game's secrets, it's a vital part of the game's progression. The manual is mostly written in an unknown language and has its own secrets you have to uncover. Alternating between gameplay and trying to make sense of the manual is really fun!While you'll spend most of the time figuring out the game's hidden mechanics, fighting, exploring; the (optional) lategame instead transitions into solving ARG-like puzzles across the game world, requiring a lot of backtracking. If you played FEZ, it's kind of like that. Unfortunately, the game never helps you decipher its secret language that you'll see all the time during the game. Deciphering it is possible but probably not worth doing on your own, you need it for the sake of finally understanding the entire manual and the very very optional endgame puzzle.Overall, it's a well made and unique game with challenging combat and I just love the game manual. The lack of language hints and (optional) backtracking towards the end of the game disappointed me a bit but the game is, for the most part, well worth your time!

_childDocuments_.review: I expected this to be a Legend of Zelda knock-off, but it was not at all. It was something _entirely_ different, and was surprisingly smart, fun, and addictive. It has a lot of the same vibe as Fez - it's full of secrets and puzzles that make you feel proud when you've solved them.In my opinion, the only bad choice the game designers made was to make the main character look like Link. My guess is that most people pass the game up thinking it's a Zelda clone. I like Zelda games, but they can be a little grindy and aren't particularly smart. This, on the other hand, is one of my all-time favorite games.

_childDocuments_.review: This is easily my favourite game right now. It has the perfect blend of exploration, combat and puzzle solving all bundled up into a gorgeous souls-like. It's not as punishing as Dark Souls whilst shamelessly borrowing from the game. The gameplay loop contains the right level of confusion mixed with aha moments and all the items you can find gives it a Zelda touch which rounds it out as one of the great video games.The isometric style is new to me but I love how the developers have hidden things in corners the camera can't reach. I've always enjoyed over exploring corners, I like to get into every area of a world the devs let me and this game rewarded me every time whilst keeping frustrating dead-ends to a minimum. Part of me wishes the language was easier to decipher but the result is incredible amounts of replayability. Where Dark Souls started to grow stale as I learnt everything about the game, Tunic feels like it has a lot more "mystery" time.Definitely give this game a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been late to work a few times because I was so engaged with this game. it's a mix-up of Legend of Zelda with Dark souls with an influence of Fez. I mean, come on it's a cute fox game. The story is learned with no narrative and to actually learn the controls and mechanics of the game you have to find pages of the manual scattered about the games or hidden down paths you can't see or ones you stumble onto accidently. I have been having a blast just exploring the map and trying to find all the hidden nooks and crannies for phat l00tz. There isn't levels in the traditional sense either, you get all your stat bonuses by offering tributes in way of items to the fox statues.I thing my only two gripes with this game thus far are 1.) the bosses; they are cool for sure. It's just one of them was BIG and it took me a solid 10 minutes dodging everything trying to run up to it to hit it only to get 2 swings in before it reset. the 2nd one was sort of the same, but it had so much range and engage/disengage that if you tried to hit it you would get 2-shot. 2.) The parry is poo poo and hard to time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a mixed / positive review that aims to clarify what this game is or isn’t without going into spoilers territory. This is what I wished I read before jumping in blind and feeling deceived. Tunic’s trailer led me to think I would be playing a  Tunic quickly evolves into a , which was unexpected but still ok in my book. Then to reach true ending, it evolves into  level.While there are notable missed opportunities, flaws and sources of frustration, this needs to remain a “thumbs up” review because Tunic’s highlights are so fantastic that you’ll be challenged to find many games that can compete. (+) The : it’s a fresh way to give tutorial information about the core mechanics, as well as guidance about what to do next, and being cute & stylish while doing so. The aesthetics of the blurry pages, coffee stains, pen annotations and page turning sounds brought me back to the pre-internet days of voraciously re-reading the paper manual that came with the megadrive and N64 games of my youth anytime I couldn’t actually play. (+) . It’s not unusual to find a treasure chest while you were actually looking for the way to another one. This is nearly on par with the recent and excellent Minishoot’s Adventures in that regard. (+) Some highly . This starts with the warm golden hour sunset lighting, continues with komorebi light flashing through forest leaves, and grandiose camera angles worthy of comparison with Gris and the classics of the artistic games genre. And that fox is so incredibly cute that it must sell a lot of plushies. (-) Some (-) , while it allows for some impressive art style, is a hassle during combat due to its confusing perspective (especially when diagonals or elevation difference are involved, if you’ve played Hades or Transistor you’ll remember what I mean), and downright frustrating during exploration, as you often have to run into invisible paths to progress. This obscures not only bonus chests, but also paths that are essential to progress to next area. (-) , which is annoying as the limited healing charges make taking random hits from trash enemies quite punishing, forcing you to go back home and restart the area. Limited moveset, questionable attack tracking, and awkward locking system.  (-) Some  (max HP reducing mechanics, stripping of upgrades, game over)(-) The level of obtuse “figure it out yourself” was high for my tolerance. While I do appreciate when things are not immediately obvious and require some minutes of reflection and tinkering, leaving you to think “Ahah, that was clever” or "Of course, this was in front of me the entire time!". In this game there are numerous instances that will leave you banging your head against a wall and brute forcing your way, especially if you progress in an order different from the optimal one (where you’re not sure if you’re supposed to struggle that much, or if you missed something 5 hours ago that would have made this easier). After finishing the game and watching other player's reactions over the net, you'll be impressed to see how many people missed at least 1 key mechanic and made their life much harder that it needed to be. Is that what good game design is supposed to be? I no longer have the patience or the free time to hunt for collectibles to unlock a good ending, and still think it’s a game design cardinal sin. Overall I enjoyed this game and can understand how some players can consider it to be one of the best surprises to come out in recent years, although to me it was an imperfect execution of some amazing ideas, which I hope other games will take inspiration from.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game! Fills a old-school Zelda vibe while also being unique to itself with its own gimmicks, the fighting is pretty average, but honestly when it comes to these types of games as long as the fighting isn't bad the adventure carries the load. The environments are varied + fun to discover, but the main feature to this game is finding and deciphering the instruction manual. Very unique element to hide gameplay elements behind discovering pages of the manual, and as you progress the pages get filled out giving you key valuable information that hits you with a feeling of "wait I can do WHAT now?!". Definitely play this game blind without looking anything up about this game, because this is 100% the type of game where if something gets spoiled it'll most likely ruin the experience to a degree. Game is good for about 10 to 15 hours from start to finish (mileage may vary depending on how good you are with puzzles), but this game is absolutely worth the price of admission.

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyable and worth the wait. The game is being frequently described as a "souls-like Link to the Past" which I feel is unfair. While there are very immediate and central connections to LttP, I wouldn't describe souls-like as very apt. There is a death mechanic, a parry, and an upgrade system, but the vibe isn't at all like dark souls and outside of the parry, the other two similarities don't feel all that similar either. The difficulty isn't nearly as high or feel as punishing. I'd describe as slightly more difficult than casual. This game is very responsive, intuitive and holds a incredible amount of character. I had been following this game's development for maybe 6 or 7 years and in that span of time there have been a huge amount of games modeled on the link to the past format. I was worried that my experience would suffer from the market's oversaturation, but this game does an exceptional job of keeping you engaged and interested. The primary storytelling and mechanics-explaining vehicle is based on an in-game instruction manual that you pick up pieces of bit-by-bit and I love everything about it. There is so much attention to detail, a plethora of subtle/enticing hints, and puzzles that are legitimately difficult and frustrating that feel genuinely rewarding.This is probably the best game in the genre that I've played since Hyper Light Drifter. I'd suggest playing blind and really keeping yourself from looking up solutions when you are stuck. There are loads of 'ah-ha' moments that I wouldn't want you to spoil for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: So I don't usually write reviews, but this game is extremely well made and I can't really not give it a review. The game is essentially a mix between a classic Legend of Zelda game and FEZ. The main game involves you being put into a giant open world with no story or tutorial. Instead you find out how to play the game by collecting pages out of the game's manual. There are about 50+ pages to collect which gradually reveal more information about the game. Along with this, the game also has its own language just like FEZ. The main goal of the game is to unlock a temple by ringing two bells and then unlock a secret inside of the temple by collecting three keys. The keys can be collected in any order and you have to figure out where everything is through small hints given throughout the manual. The combat in the game is nothing special but that doesn't change the fact that I think this game is amazing. Along side the classic Zelda style gameplay, the game also has a few FEZ style puzzles that aren't nessecary to get the normal ending. There puzzles can be pretty difficult and they are a nice touch for someone like me who loves games like Baba is You and The Witness. The game can be easilly beaten in about 10 hours but all the hidden rooms, treasures and secret puzzles can let you play the game for a lot lot more. I've already played for 20+ hours and I still have a lot left to explore. Anyways this game is fantastic and if it looks like a game you would enjoy, I highly recommend getting it.

_childDocuments_.review: 2D soulslike with a Zelda skin. At first I thought it was a Zelda-style game with soulslike elements, but it's quite the other way around. It revolves around a stabbing-blocking-dodging combat system with health potions that refill only at rest points. You also lose some of your money and have to go get it back from where you died after respawning at aforementioned rest points. Combat gets brutally hard sometimes, but usually it's very manageable. Overall, it's a fantastic game. Beautiful art, beautiful music, beautiful story told entirely through world building and finding pages of the game's manual, as very little is actually written out for you in English. The items are cool, the dungeons are cool, the enemies are cool (and extremely frustrating sometimes). Throws a myriad of mechanics at you from souls games and Zelda games that fans of either or both will recognize immediately, but it blends them together in a very clever way and absolutely holds its own identity. This one is definitely worth a grab for anyone that likes action-adventure games or indie games in general. Fantastic work from the devs. 8.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game I kept a eye on quietly since its announcement, and I will give you my initial impressions after playing about two hours worth of game time.First of all, I want to say that the game does not hand hold you in the slightest, it is incredibly clear on letting you know that you control where you go, and what you do. This game has done an amazing job at captivating me right from the beginning, with its storytelling through the world, without any use of cutscenes or text of any kind. I've yet to really do anything substantial (I think?), but this game I can honestly say has been the best breath of fresh air in years.It reminds me of how I felt when I hearken back to my first time playing Dark Souls 1. That feeling of being lost, but feeling so awestruck at the environment and the secrets it holds. It also reminds me of Breath of the Wild and its carefree nature, being able to go anywhere and do anything.The musical score and the ambience/tone in the game, from my experience so far, has to be probably the greatest I've had the pleasure of listening to in recent memory. Darker areas, or places like caves have more somber, unsettling sounds, tones and subtle musical notes to boot. As for the brighter areas, it is more impactful, playful, and lighthearted, and noticeably more apparent than the subtlety of the darker areas music/ambience. It is a perfect blend of sound and music, and I personally never really catch this sort of thing, but this game really made this noticeable.The combat is simple, but fun and challenging, even someone who claims to be a avid gamer such as myself, has died a couple times already. I never felt like I was gimped out of sheer difficulty and I made personal errors and died as a result.Overall, even with just the short amount of time I have put into the game, I can already see the labor of love this game has had. It is a blend of Breath of the Wild's environmental storytelling and playful demeanor, with some of the freedoms of Dark Souls 1 exploration, interconnected map, and the subtle soundtrack cues. This is a wonderful game, something I am very happy to have picked up and given a chance, and I think you might feel the same. I would definitely recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: After gaining all achievements, I can say that I really liked this game, to the point that I think it's one of the best games "for me" that I've played in recent years. I found game design elements in it that I already enjoyed in FEZ and The Witness, but handled even better here.All the environmental puzzles and discovery aspects I found extremely satisfying, but there are a couple of points I'd like to address.Of the 36 achievements I managed to get 32 by myself and without any guidance or solution. This to me is extraordinary, since the game has many "metatextual/environmental puzzles" that in other games are generally done in a worse way or that depend more on moon logic. Things that in other games would have me searching on google in no time, here kept me in-game. Tunic is exceptional in giving you "everything you need".Of the other 4 achievements, instead:- One took me almost 3 "empty" hours because I knew "where it was", but a very stupid detail and a red herring (cryptic reference to understand which one I'm referring to: alarmed birds) distracted me.- I found one too "demanding", in the sense that it is the only one that requires understanding of the language that Tunic uses. I reached half of what was needed, but for the last part I looked online for the translation (cryptic reference to understand which one I'm referring to: wet letters).- One I found just free hate on the player. It's something that is extremely missable in the first playthrough, and asked me for an ad-hoc new game just to do it (cryptic reference to understand which one I mean: pew pew).- One is feasible as long as you play "conservative" (cryptic reference to understand which one I'm referring to: piggy bank). The problem I have with this achievement is that I already play conservative in these games by default, but the game at one point pushes you not to, to the point that another achievement is achieved by partially "letting go". It pissed me off that I had to recover it in the ad-hoc run for the previous achievement since I was "almost there" in the main run but reached a point where it wasn't achievable anymore.These last two achievements go so much against what (in my opinion) is the spirit of Tunic, that it would have been a better game without them.Apart from these small negative points imho, as I said above this has been an amazing experience. Without making too many spoilers, the yellow page has been one of the most satisfying videogame things in recent years. The click in my brain when I realized what I had to do was cathartic, I felt invested with otherworldly knowledge.TL;DR: I consider this game an amazing experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a brilliant tribute to the 2D Zelda era without being a cheap copy. The developers added a lot of content and complexity. The only aspect that lost me was the very last puzzles that required some very intense analysis of the clues given, but that did not affect 99% of the experience (and Google is your friend).

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game where you do not need any guide, walkthrough, or anything to play. Because all of it is within the game itself.Tunic is a game that allows you to play it without hand holding. Too many games these days believe that the player needs to be guided first before they can actually play the game. There is nothing wrong with tutorials or linear games, but it came become problematic at times. The whole point of Tunic is you now have the ability to figure out the game yourself. It is all on you.Tunic is a game were it begins and it is up to you to figure it out. It is akin the First Legend of Zelda game and Link to the Past. Picture yourself back in the 80s and 90s and you don't have anything but the game's manual's as guidance. There is no IGN or Gamefacts to aid you. But you still have all the means you need to beat the game. I highly discourage looking this game up anywhere until you beat it yourself as it robs you of the game's true meaning. I do have to warn that this game will be hard and unforgiving. But I believe anyone can beat it as long as they try.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that is not for everyone, but it was absolutely for me. Punishing combat that feels like older Legend of Zelda games, an incredible feeling of exploration that permeates throughout the map and the mechanics, and an optional series of puzzles that felt like playing The Witness for the first time again. If you like souls-likes, classic Zelda, and/or the Witness, this game will be incredible for you. If you don't, then there will be portions of this game that will probably be very frustrating for you. I loved it and I have 4 pages of puzzle notes on my desk to prove it

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think I've ever played a game quite like Tunic. On the surface one can pick obvious inspirations from the gameplay, perspective, and aesthetic, namely Dark Souls and Zelda. One can go throughout the entire game with this mindset and beat it, but in truth there's an entirely different beast lurking underneath, and it's there from the moment you start the game. Going into this game blind is the best thing you can do, because once you realize what's going on underneath the 'Zelda/Dark Souls' hybrid all the people and publications are going on about, it feels amazing. If you grew up in the era of games before the internet was widespread and game manuals were actually a thing, this game will rekindle that magic. I won't spoil the ending of this game, but I will say it resonated with me a lot, and I think it has a lot to say, despite no actual words (aside from the in-universe language) being spoken. And as icing on this delicious cake, the presentation is astounding. Superb visuals, music, and atmosphere make this an amazing package, and definitely one of my top favorite games of all time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough game to review because there's very good parts of the game and some rather unpolished and clunky parts. First the good: The first half of the game is great. There's a real wonder in exploring the world, given only fragments of the game manual, which are mostly not in English. The graphics are simplistic, but work well with the nostalgic game play. The early levels are dense with secret areas and the enemies are engaging, requiring you take full advantage of your move-set. I'm going to dwell a bit on the bad aspects of the game, because there's more to talk about, but you will easily have a good 10-15 hours of enjoyable game to play, which is why I'm giving it a thumbs up. There are a few bugs in the game (i.e. places you can get stuck) and the controls are occasionally a bit laggy (I had to rebind two attacks to the same key to get one combo attack to work consistently on PC), but overall it's very polished.The bad: Too much of this game is a pastiche of other games. Take away the creative manual idea (which is a great idea, mind you) and you will be left with a rehashing of the ideas of other developers. The Zelda influence is obvious, but it doesn't end there.This game steals far too many of the mechanics of the dark souls series. This went beyond being an homage to just plagiarism. Flasks, bonfires, dodge-rolls and a from software stamina bar all make an appearance. The bosses hew to the dark souls style closely. The difficulty is not that high (about like Elden ring, but way shorter and you can't just level yourself up to victory). Only 1-2 bosses will either require you to learn their move set or cheese them. The fights don't quite have the tedium of your typical dark souls boss, where you are forced to wait until just the right moment after a combo before you can attack, but do expect a few to have decent health pools, esp. if you aren't keeping your levels up.But beyond the obvious souls borrowing, you'll find bits of the hollow knight plot line lifted for the default ending with a slight science fiction wrapping and even a dramatic reveal that would be a more dramatic if it wasn't a copy of a shot from The Matrix. Everyone's a battery? Really? This surprise twist was laughably bad.In general, the story is the typical self-serious collection of cliches found in your modern indy games. To the extent that it exists, is told in snippets (as is the default these days) and hinted at through the manual. The basic ending (aka the bad ending) is profoundly unsatisfying. The "best" ending is not much better, though. (Does a crappy ending also count as a dark souls ripoff?) The best thing about this game is its cutesy beginning, but like many games in this genre, the developer's felt the need to make the game turn moody and it doesn't really work.How you feel about these "references"/copying of other games is a matter of taste, but I can mostly look past it to just enjoy the game. However, the last ~1/3 of the game is much weaker than start. The areas become more linear and the items you find are mostly worthless as you seem to stop getting the items you need to level up after a while. You do get one final power-up, but it's so over-the-top it more or less breaks the fun of exploration that was the center of the first part of the game. If you are feeling energetic, you can try to get the good ending, but the final puzzles are tedious and much less clever than the developers must have thought. (One also involves destroying a wall, which has was never possible throughout the rest of the game, as far as I know.) You will find yourself doing variations of the same puzzle over and over. It's not great. My advice is to skip this nonsense and just take the basic ending.With all that said, though, it's an indy game with a small team of developers and the cost isn't that high. You will probably enjoy the opening, from other reviews, it seems most people aren't as bothered by the way it lifts mechanics from other games as I was.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked Tunic. Its not the flashiest of games, but it knows what its doing and does it well. It kind of emulates a feeling of playing a game in a foreign language as a kid, and it works. Its also very obvious where its inspirations lie, with old Zelda games being the most obvious - some of the illustrations in the ingame manual are very, very akin to those of the first Zelda games. And since this is 2022, of course Dark Souls inspired elements are also present - mostly in the checkpoint system being very Dark Soulsy, but a dodge roll is also present. The whole world being mysterious and strange, with the game's lore very well hidden might also count as a Dark Souls-thing, but I think its more because of the "ingame manual is mostly in a fictional language"-thing.There's also some stuff in the very late game I'd like to talk about, but its genuinely best if you experience it blind. I will just say that  a lot.

_childDocuments_.review: As others have said, TUNIC is a Zelda-like, Souls-like, isometric/top-down action adventure, with secrets inspired by both games, as well as   Some of the secrets are references to other games too (FEZ, Celeste, et al.), like any good indie title's secrets.  Also the character design is cute and the sound design is gorgeous!But had it not been for the language (or rather ) seen in the game's old-school "manual" and elsewhere, I would've brushed this title aside as "just another one of those types of games with cuteness and combat."  It's not a mere one-to-one English letter cipher or the like either, like in numerous other games, but something that showcases a deeper linguistic understanding.  This language is everywhere, adding a sense of mysticism to the world until its "Rosetta Stone" is revealed to you.  Say what you will (and many already have :P), but this sort of thing is criminally underrated in all forms of media.Even if you don't understand, the best thing is to   Never be afraid to experiment nor to fail, even a little; and if you are afraid, there are 100% shameless accessibility options in the menu to make things easier.  TUNIC is a harmless singleplayer game after all.Oh, and as you may have surmised, this game is surprisingly spoiler sensitive, so I'mma stop my review here before it becomes a wall of ....All that said, and all things considered, you may want to buy this game on a small sale (15-33% off), as it's nothing particularly groundbreaking (for me, if an indie game is going to charge $30 or more, it had better be absolute top-notch!).If you're unsure of whether to buy the game, the first episode (20-30 min.) of any blind LP video is generally spoiler safe, so maybe watch one before deciding whether the game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Combat is way too shallow to allow for such difficult bosses (You have 1 attack type. That's it. Good luck)Maybe there's a narrative, but you probably need to advance much further in the game. Otherwise you're basically just a fox smashing whatever is ahead of you trying to unlock some doors.And there's absolutely no indication of what to do next. It's mostly guess-work with an in-game language that is made to retain most/all info from the player.I really wanted to like this game, but at this stage, it's not enjoyable at all

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I really liked this game.The story is absolutely amazing 10/10. I was totally captivated by every new mystery that was discovered. The game tells you very little, which is definitely not a bad thing. I also enjoyed every part of the aesthetic. Every area was perfectly drawn and every detail was carefully chosen to add to the mystery. The introduction of each new key item was very well done as well.The actual gameplay I'd only give 6/10. It probably would have been better if I had a controller, but I played keyboard. There were a couple areas which were unintuitive regarding where your character can go and the lock-on enemy targeting could be very frustrating when you want to block an attack from one enemy but it targets the wrong one. The fights are very difficult and they felt a little unbalanced since there were some cases where it felt impossible to not take damage. I turned on no-fail mode halfway through, which I don't regret in the slightest because the rewarding part of the game for me was figuring out the puzzles/areas rather than beating a lot of mobs. Overall, I'd recommend it say its worth the price. If you play on easy mode like me, you basically get an amazing interactive movie with a good chunk of exploring. However, if you're looking for an open world game with good boss fights and combat mechanics then you should probably skip this one.Edit: I replayed the game with controller. The fighting and mechanics are WAY better with controller.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is highly addictive. I've replayed it several times and am still finding new hidden treasures each time I play it. There just seems to be so many secrets in the game waiting to be discovered. I used the no fail mode which allowed me to focus on learning the details, solving the puzzles and treasure hunting in the game. It can get quite frustrating though, when you see some clues that something is hidden in the area but just couldn't find it. Perhaps my most frustrating moment is kicking the skulls around, unlike the rest of the game, that part seem to be depending on luck rather than skills and techniques. Overall, I love this game and would highly recommend it~

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DRThe Good: Absolutely brilliant level design, really good aesthetics, gameplay is simple but tightThe Bad: The lock-on becomes more of a hinderance the moment you face more than 3 enemies, some of the puzzles are... unfairly obtuseThe ?????: FurryThe minimalist and clean aesthetic of Tunic might make you think that is a simple and straight forward game, but, much like the plethora of clerverly designed and hidden pathaways that dismantle the assumed linearity of this adventure, that is just a trick that the game uses to settle you in before bashing you in the head with challange after challange, forcing you to learn, plan ahead, and be crafty if you want to survive long enough to attain your goals. The metanarrative of a hint sistem being the very own game manual - wich must we pieced together from withing the game itself - its the perfect way the game has to tech you it's secrets without being too on the nose about it; they are giving you the answers, you only have to understand it.The game is not without drawbacks, the fights can move from challenging to overly frustrating quite easily, and if you are facing off against more than one enemy, the lock-on might as well be an opponent more. Tunic is filled with secrets, very clever secrets, sometime too clever perhaps, that rather requiring you to think outside the box, they rather ask you to stand a few blocks away, making certain things more of a headache to obtain.All in all, I certainly recomend this game, without a doubt one of the best indie releases of 2022.
