_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a bit like a hybrid of Outer Wilds, Dark Souls, and Hyper Light Drifter, which is to say it's brilliant.  If you like exploration-focused games and don't mind a little challenge, buy this and play it right now.Try to avoid spoilers as much as possible, a bit part of the enjoyment of the game is figuring things out yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Hands down the best game I've played this year, its not often that something comes along and deconstructs an old trope and then builds it back up again with a fresh coat of paint. Forget breath of the wild re-imagining the first Zelda, this absolutely takes that feel from the old NES classic and gives you something new, but with a distinct echo.Combat is challenging but rewarding as you figure the system out, very little is handed to you but as you get father into the game you realize just how much you were being told things in a very subtle way. The unlock-able manual in the game has everything you need in it, every marking on a page is deliberate and meaningful.I won't get into spoiler territory but there were only four puzzles that had bad designs, one is an unnecessary bonus that requires you translate the language in the manual. The other three all revolve around game mechanics that have no use outside of the individual puzzle you're trying to solve and that aren't explained in the manual.While that is getting to be a bit of a nit-pick, this absolutely is a game you should get and not spoil for yourself with any guides or hints if possible.I wish I could truly do a NewGame+ having forgotten everything about this game and play it fresh again.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is the only review of a game I've ever left on Steam. Basically what everyone has said: it's not for everyone- but for the people it is for, one of the hands-down best gaming experiences I've ever had.If you enjoy that moment in a game where you figure out an unexplained mechanic early, you should buy Tunic.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: From my perspective, TUNIC consists of 20% decent and quite enjoyable Zelda/Souls/3D-Metroidvania like experience and 80% of environmental puzzles, ranging from "Demanding" to "Da Vinci Code's Code" difficulty level ("puzzle" on the snowy summit). Provided that at a point you have some kind of divine enlightment, and become aware of their core concept and mechanics.The funny thing is that the only reason for the existence of these environmental puzzles is to unlock a secret ending, that adds nearly zero value to the whole story/plot (if any...).
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is perhaps the most memorable singleplayer game I've ever played. Come for the top-down action blending Zelda games and Dark Souls, stay for the amazing scene-setting and puzzles.As you may have heard, part of this game's challenge is the fact that the manual is presented  and is rendered mostly in a fictional language. This is a major part of what gives the game its unique flair, but it also means that this is a game that requires some measure of patience. In addition to being the most memorable singleplayer game I've completed, Tunic is also the one that had me staring blankly at my ceiling for the longest time. On dozens of occasions I was very, very tempted to just look up solutions to puzzles or guides on what to do next after running in circles -- and in the end I eventually did look at a couple hints just to make sure I wasn't gaslighting myself on a couple of the more elaborate puzzles.If you have the patience to handle the arcane process of learning a game without having any guides, Tunic is sure to be a treat for you. I've never played a game that gave me such a visceral feeling of solving a mystery before.

_childDocuments_.review: I Loved Tunic, and it's probably my Game of the Year. Sort of a Link To The Past meets Dark Souls meets The Witness. The way you build your own NES-styled game manual by collecting pages in order to discover hints about where to go and what to do is ingenious. But I can't recommend this game to anyone. I try to tell my puzzle fan friends about it, and the ass-crushingly difficult bosses will turn them away after they brick wall on the first boss in the Gardens. I try to tell my souls fan friends about it, and the cheery, stylized graphics and poorly tuned combat mechanics will turn them away in less than a half hour. I don't know who this game was made for. Me, obviously. But it makes it very, very hard to recommend to anyone else without an increasingly contrived series of caveats, which is why my score is "negative". I also significantly mark down games for reliance upon color for game mechanics, as an individual with severe color blindness. And Tunic has these by the truckful, mostly regarding the Golden Path and the penultimate series of puzzles absolutely required to get the true ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, it starts so good. The starting of this game, the first few hours, are immaculate. There are no new mechanics to learn, you've seen all the beautiful areas, and there's just a slog of battle after battle. And to add insult to injury, you're locked into a single linear path. The point where I quit is an arena area (mandatory, if that wasn't obvious) where you have to complete 6 battles in a row without dying; all your upgrades have been taken from you, and some of the battles have dozens of enemies at once.I might recommend Tunic to people who already do no-damage runs of their favorite games, or thinks the game looks good enough to give the first few hours a try. _childDocuments_.review: Dark Souls meets Zelda - except not really, as the latter informs only some of the game's aesthetic; I'd argue that Tunic owes much more to FEZ, in almost every regard. Overall, this game's combat isn't notably difficult outside the handful of boss fights (though not trivial either).While it is inevitable that descriptions or even recommendations of Tunic get boiled down to namedropping two existing game series, the real secret sauce, the innovation that sets it apart, is the cryptic scattered in-game manual, which adds a whole other dimension to puzzles and exploration. _childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a game that will have you scratching your head every so often. Its an action-puzzle game with combat that I found quite fun if not a little simplistic and puzzles that were quite the opposite. You can definitely get through this game bashing your head against the wall until you go where you have to go but exploring the world and piecing together information from the Instruction book pages you get has been one of the most rewarding experiences I've had in a puzzle game. Finding the key to a puzzle you've been thinking about for a while after pouring over a new page is exhilarating. I would recommend this game to anyone that's a fan of puzzle games, older Zelda games, and anyone that just loves to explore. _childDocuments_.review: Tunic is an absolute gem of a game that effortlessly captures the essence of the NES era while taking inspiration from timeless classics like Link's Awakening. As a lover of both retro and puzzle-filled adventures, Tunic struck all the right chords and left me grinning from ear to ear throughout my entire playthrough.One of the first things that drew me into Tunic was its captivating art style. The adorable protagonist, a tiny fox exploring a vast and mysterious world, is a perfect embodiment of cuteness. The vibrant colors and attention to detail truly brought the game to life, immersing me in a whimsical experience reminiscent of beloved NES titles.Speaking of which, Tunic successfully channels the spirit of those nostalgic NES games that captured our hearts decades ago. From the tight controls to the challenging puzzles and exploration, it's a joyous trip down memory lane. I couldn't help but feel a rush of nostalgia as I embarked on epic quests, encountered quirky characters, and delved into ancient dungeons.The puzzles in Tunic are both ingenious and satisfying. Each area is cleverly designed, presenting intricate challenges that require keen observation and logical thinking to overcome. Whether it's deciphering cryptic symbols or manipulating objects to unlock secret passages, Tunic keeps you on your toes and rewards your perseverance with a genuine sense of accomplishment.The world of Tunic is a wondrous playground filled with hidden secrets waiting to be discovered. Exploring every nook and cranny feels like embarking on an epic adventure, as the game gradually unfolds its rich lore and presents you with captivating stories. Every encounter and interaction with the charming inhabitants adds another layer of depth to the experience, leaving you hungry for more.What truly sets Tunic apart is its ability to combine nostalgia with modern gameplay elements. While it pays homage to the classics, it also introduces fresh mechanics and surprises that keep the gameplay engaging and exciting. The balance between familiarity and innovation struck a perfect chord, creating an experience that appeals to both seasoned gamers and newcomers alike.In conclusion, Tunic is an enchanting game that effortlessly captures the essence of NES classics and draws inspiration from beloved titles like Link's Awakening. With its delightful art style, challenging puzzles, and heartwarming world, it's a true treasure for anyone seeking a nostalgic and adorable gaming experience. Don't miss out on this delightful adventure—Tunic is an absolute must-play for fans of retro gaming and puzzle-solving enthusiasts alike!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: A Many games, especially in the indie scene, play to nostalgia. They attempt to evoke the style and feeling of games the developers enjoyed growing up and seek modernize established genres to mixed effect. Tunic evokes nostalgia and discovery in a time laden with instant gratification and day-one walkthroughs.  The world resembles the NES Legend of Zelda right down to the green tunic. The resemblance is well understood and the game wants to play into that nostalgia so the game feels familiar. What makes the game unique is how central mechanics are obscured almost completely. Over the course of the game, you will find pages from the instruction manual to the game which help explain key mechanics, maps for areas, and give general guidance. The extra twist comes from most of the game being written in a fictional language meaning deciphering the pages becomes a meta-puzzle to help solve in-world obstacles. It feels like experiencing the joy of video games again for the first time. The, admittedly decipherable, language helps divorce the player from the meta knowledge of games and puts them in the mindset of not fully understanding the references but learning them as you go.  When I was in middle school, I was playing through the original Legend of Zelda on my parents’ old NES. My dad also had a strategy guide where he wrote notes into the margins and, as I played, I made more notes of my own. Seeing the manuals in Tunic feel like putting together those pieces left behind in the guide book and adding to them myself. I even had to grab pen and paper to help make sense of some of the later puzzles. Special praise needs to be given to the developers who expertly dole out information. They constantly showing little pieces at a time, a hidden pathway, an unspoken mechanic, a secret item. It creates so many situations where I feel incredibly clever for figuring out a solution and then seeing how the developers hid all the clues right before my eyes and I simply couldn’t see them without a bit more context. The game simply makes the puzzles just feel like uncovering an adventure. Surprising, charming, and memorable. The game is a masterpiece of puzzle design and should be studied. The world feels deep and meaningful and evolves with the player, not because the landscape has changed much, but because you have changed. The player slowly learns the language of the game and begins to see just how much it has to offer. It is a damn shame it kept crashing on me (though it does save every screen transition).
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: TUNIC's blend of Souls-like combat, FEZ-like puzzles, Zelda-like overworld, and beautiful art style, music and sound design has quickly catapulted it into becoming .From a semi-forced isometric world view, you play as a young fox cub as they stumble around in a world that has fallen from grace, and left worse for wear. What strikes you first time you play it is that the text on signs, the HUD and even the in-game manual is written in a mysterious, indecipherable alphabet, and you have to rely on your own instincts, logical reasoning and curiosity to figure out what most of the things mean. The game does no hand holding. It throws you into the world and goes "You're on your own now!" And that is something you don't see much these days. There's a lot of hand holding in modern games, and TUNIC bucks that trend, which is something I appreciate very much. The game trusts the player to be smart, attentive and inquisitive, and explore every nook and cranny of the world to find all the things hidden just around the corner, out of sight.Depending on how quickly you pick up on the things the game gives you, the  to complete the game can take anywhere between 10 and 30 hours. There's also the case of getting a  ending, which takes up the majority of the time in the second half of the game. And that extra time is well spent for getting the true ending, I will go ahead and say that much.In terms of , it runs excellent on both my PC AND my Steam Deck. Crisp 60 FPS on my Deck with zero dips in framerate and plenty of battery life.So yeah, an absolutely rock solid recommendation from me.

_childDocuments_.review: This might be the saddest Negative review I have ever had to give. This game is fantastic on so many levels. The games visuals are absolutely fantastic. The music is extremely relaxing and nice. There are a lot of clever gimmicks and map design that are a ton of fun to explore. And just the amount of surprises and genuine adventure feel is incredible.My main disappointment with the game comes from 3 problems:- Combat can feel extremely simplistic until the game decides to throw massive HP pools and enemy counts at you, at that point it starts feeling awkward and clunky. Those moments really showcase just how incomplete the combat can be, and some enemy designs as a result feel infuriating to fight against.- Do you want to experience what it is like to go on vacation to a foreign country without barely any guidance at all? Yes? Then this is the game for you. A lot of the game is told in some weird in game language, and the game developers put a ton of trust in the player to find their way through it all. Most of the time this actually works out and its a ton of fun, but like 33 % of my playtime was just spent running around trying to figure out what was the next place I had to go. Not only that but there are so many items that I still have no clue what they do. Those moments are super boring and it feels like a major interesting part of the game is just forever locked behind the gimmick of everything being unreadable.- My last main complaint is related to the ending, some late game spoilers: In the end Tunic is not what I looked for. Its not the 2D Zelda like that I was expecting, and the central gameplay kept pulling me in just to disappoint me right afterwards. It IS a fantastic game, and I think many people will find enjoyment in it, but I also think many players will come out the other side with a sour after taste. It is the type of game where I wish I could give it a neutral review because I absolutely don't believe it deserves a negative review, I just wouldn't actively recommend it either. I think if you go into it expecting a bumpy ride you will find an absolutely adorable, unique and very fun experience. Its just an experience that didn't manage to completely grab me.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't recommend this game, but that doesn't mean I think it is bad. The first half of the game is incredible. _childDocuments_.review: Excellent game, it was worth the wait. Everything is fluid, from combat to progression, the sounds and music are equally immersive, and the sense of freedom and challenge ahead can be felt in the very first minutes of gameplay.EDIT AFTER BEATING THE GAME: I don't recommend it, and you'll understand why. The second half of the game ruins its positive appeal. Anything in life done in an excessive manner is unhealthy. Water is good for our body, working is important, doing exercises is vital, but all that has one thing in common: if done in excess, they can grow unhealthy or harmful. Tunic features puzzles where you are given minimal information to solve them, which requires a bit of thinking that you don't easily find in other games: you've got to figure out things on your own basically. Past the first half, the game does that in an excessive manner: you are given puzzle after puzzle with little to zero information.It is like the game shows you a blank sheet with a single pencil line and expects you to guess you should draw a horse without mentioning anything else. Until you get the horse drawn, you'll be trying to understand over and over what the game means by that single pencil line. After dedicating time to solve that puzzle, you'll find another puzzle that will require the similar amount of effort through the same structure of having basically no info. It doesn't do it once or twice, nor 3 or 4 times, it is honestly 3x that. Isn't it too much of the same thing? I mean, you put a lot of time trying to figure out the game wants you to draw a horse out of a single pencil line, but it never draws a tail or ears in the next puzzle to make it more intuitive for you. That's the keyword: puzzles in Tunic are not intuitive.Now you've understood the analogy with drawing a horse, I will give you a quick preview of what the puzzles are like, in case you are thinking this is similar to Zelda or Tomb Raider puzzles. No, they're not. You've got to go somewhere in the map (say, next to a house) and press a sequence of directions with the D-Pad. Doing so will spawn a treasure chest with a reward. "Bah, doing inputs is easy", indeed, we agree! But such input works only in 1 spot in the WHOLE.OPEN.WORLD. Yes, that's right: you'll have to figure out where in that gigantic world you have to use those inputs. Oh, do you think the game will at least hint you where possibly you could go? Bad news for you: remember I said you are given little to zero information.Besides the excess of literally DIY puzzles, the final boss feels like a buffed version of another boss in the early game and some of the attacks follow the same pattern. There is nothing majestic in the final battle for a game with a pretentious lore. Anyway, the game starts great but the 2nd half is totally the opposite: it's a chore to complete.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a really very exemplary game in many ways. I'd say you have three essential factors on sale here: the atmosphere (visuals, pattery light music, the environments, etc.), the tight, simple (but never simplistic) gameplay, and the meta-textual commentary. That last area I won't flesh out too much here -- suffice it to say, Tunic has a lot to say about the cultural apparatus of gaming itself and the developers work to say those things *through* some very unique gameplay mechanics. Don't be scared away or turned off by the rumblings of "Souls Like" and "Zelda Clone" dissenters; Tunic isn't really either of those things at its core, but rather a charmingly original spin on a fusion of the two. If there is a place the game stumbles, it's maybe in the potentially overwhelming increase in complexity of the final act (and beyond) puzzles -- but for many, this is likely where the game starts to really shine and take on a whole new dimension, something closer to, say, Myst than Zelda or Dark Souls. I'd recommend Tunic as a must-try for virtually anyone interested in any of the aforementioned genres -- certainly a must-try for anyone interested in thinking critically about gaming as a medium.

_childDocuments_.review: If you want a great puzzle and exploration game in the style of a 2D zelda game, Tunic is the game for you. This game world was an absolute blast to explore, and the mystery was thrilling to slowly unravel. Some of the optional secret puzzles I do not regret looking at a guide for as I think they were far too obtuse, but most of the puzzles were wonderfully to try and work out on my own. The combat is good too, but it's certainly not the main focus here.You'll see a lot of people complaining about difficulty spikes but I experienced nothing like that in my playthrough. My theory is they managed to do something out of the intended order, or they didn't fully explore an area and get all the upgrades, which are both totally reasonable but they would make the difficulty curve seem a bit wonky. All in all this was a wonderful game I highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: The meta puzzle is innovative and clever. I wish it was a bit more tightly constrained so you were getting pages as you needed the information. I'm kind of over games being intentionally opaque and thinking that alone is a satisfying puzzle. The camera is awful and almost intentionally so. The way forward is often occluded by level geometry and there is no indication there is a path there that the character would be able to easily see. The zoomed out perspective makes the animations you need to signal when to dodge very difficult to read. There is a reason Souls bosses are generally gigantic. You don't have much choice when it comes to offense, just the same three swing combo. Once you understand the boss patterns, you have to flawlessly hit them 50-100 times to pass them. That's ridiculous. By time I got to the librarian, I just turned on invincible mode and never looked back.If it had just focused on being a good puzzle filled adventure, it probably could have succeeded. It is 90% of the way there. Or if it just wanted to be a Souls-y action game, it could have worked in better combat, controls, and camera. But it doesn't really hit any superlative peaks on either.It is good enough to play for the novelty of the meta-puzzle, but don't expect to be blown away.

_childDocuments_.review: TUNIC is a type of game that feels increasingly less common in this industry, and its dedication to upholding a mystery that it lets the player figure out themselves is commendable. It has an enchanting world that's well worth exploring for yourself, and the way it asks you to use the instruction manual is a breath of fresh air for engaging with a game. While it doesn't fully stick the landing thanks to some later combat sections that sour the experience, it's an undeniable gem of wondrous action-adventure.Original review on

_childDocuments_.review: (game not finished yet)This game is unlike any other I've played. Never have I experienced such mastery of pacing, game design, environmental storytelling and the list goes on.I truly feel like I'm playing alongside the creators, at all times, I can feel them guiding me, subtly nudging me in the right direction yet never making it easy for me, always letting me figure things out for myself, and it feels amazing! _childDocuments_.review: I haven't been playing this game long, but I am already loving it. You find items and weapons to help you continue along the map. The designs are a little too simple with both characters and environment. The game does try to present an old school rpg with instruction manual though, so I think the designs work fine for that. I'm only about 3-4 hours in so I can't speak to the entire game. I did find that so far the map and puzzles are somewhat simple. I mostly got caught up knowing what I had to do but lacking the skill to pull it off.The game play and exploration was addicting. _childDocuments_.review: It's got some fun gameplay, if you like sniffing out secrets and figuring things out.  *Do not spoil yourself for this game*. It really does help.It's beautiful, and the music is quite nice.Most profoundly, though, this game does the thing it does with incredible elegance. You're just constantly discovering things and figuring out how they work by experiencing them in the world or figuring out what the relevant sections of the manual mean. _childDocuments_.review: Tunic is all charm, but little else. Combat is incredibly restrictive and horribly frustrating. Bosses will repeatedly spam the same move, which is exacerbated earlier in a play through when you have low stamina. You have 2 rolls before you're drained, in which you take extra damage, dodge range is reduced and blocking staggers. There is only 1 boss in this game that I would consider fun.The only puzzles that exist in this game are related to extra items and the hidden ending. There are no dungeon puzzles that require problem solving, only roadblocks that need a grapple hook or teleport.The main draw of this game is the player manual that has hints to collectibles and an alternate ending. In concept this is incredibly unique and interesting way to connect the player to the world. The hints, however, are so obscure and confusing that you sometimes need to go online to find a solution, which takes away from the intention having and in-game player manual in the first place. One puzzle requires you to know sheet music and be able to identify the tune of a wind chime by ear, and then use those notes in a corresponding D-Pad input to complete it. This has long been remedied with an accessibility feature, but there are so many other in-game puzzles that most players won't be able to experience without spoiling it with a google search.The developers have put their hearts and souls into this game, and it shows; however, that does not excuse so many flawed and overlooked design decisions that tarnish and sour the overall experience.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr at the end.The game is fun at first, the art style is beautiful, the combat is weighty and fun, but the obtuse level design with poorly hidden pathways that you would never be able to find without a guide, as well as the way the game refuses to tell you any information about any of the items (because 99% of the text is in a fun made up language that you cannot decipher) gets old very quickly and starts to take a tax on your enjoyment on the game. When you can't reach a new area and are stuck because you need an item that is hidden behind an impossible to find cavern it's not fun. When the game fails to let you know that "praying" is a thing that lets you interact with the world in new ways, so you spend hours wondering how many items you're missing since you can't interact with the big metal pillars or the shiny golden platforms. There is no prompt, too. There is no hint, no tips, nothing. The devs just magically expect you to find out that by holding *Lock on + Dodge* you can pray and therefore power the statues (which i did not do because i encountered about 10 of those pillars before finding out -in a guide- that you can actually power them) and use the teleport platforms (because I only found out after looking up a different guide on where to go that teleporting exists, but don't worry, it's not fun either, since there is no way to know where you will be teleporting since all you see is blocks of light). Also, did you know you can run in the game? Because I sure as hell didn't. You have to hold the interact button to run. As well as finding out there's a grappling hook hidden away behind 4 or so caverns.Is that not enough to discourage you? Oh, well in that case the game also has special magical cards you can equip. I obtained about 6 of them. I have no idea what they do after trying every single one of them, healing, dying, fighting, they seem to have no apparent effect on gameplay. As well as the cool upgrades you can spend gold on! There are about 4 of them. Only one of them is useful, which is the one that makes you have a bit more HP, so you can get stunlocked for even longer.The combat is also not fun. It's like the worst aspects of a Kirby game combined with the worst aspects of a Souls game. Some enemies have tells so you can dodge or parry. Most enemies don't. Most enemies simply charge randomly with no way to counterattack or parry (See: large dogs, crows, frogs, large frogs, mages, etc).I wanted to love the game, but it feels like there is no learning curve as the game doesn't give you the tools to improve, it just drops you into the world without letting you know that those tools even exist, and when you get them, gives you no way to find out what they do.tl;dr: the first 30 minutes you'll think "oh man I can't wait for the game to lead me in any way to have fun" until you realize that the game will do nothing to help you have fun with it, and just trips over itself due to its lack of explanation so you know what anything does. Don't buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: My friends keep asking me for my opinion on this game because a common friend of ours has given a "negative" review on this game.So I have to right their error.(Please do not take this serious, people are entitled to their opinion it's just what led me to this review.)Simple Tl:dr, so far the best game I've played in 2022.Now to the actual Review:Tunic's an interesting "Zelda-like" looking exploration heavy action adventure.So despite that, it is not a Zelda game. It resembles Dark Souls more than it resembles a Zelda game.secondly, this game does not hold your hand. It will very much make you figure everything out, make you use your brain and all at some point Information will become a better loot than any weapon, item or whatever the hell you can find.But sadly talking about the puzzles themselves would probably ruin the experience.So let's just keep it simple with a pros and cons list:Pros:-Decent Combat, something you'd somewhat expect from a Soulslike, rolling, getting a few hits in and stuff like that.-Puzzles range from "kind of genius" to literally exploiting the general "gaming" instinct people will have built up.-The Isometric camera and the game's utilization of it is great.-Every single loot item in this game actually feels worthwhile-Good visuals. This game's usage of lighting is kind of stellar.Cons:-The Story, the ending kinda didn't do it for me.-The Target Lock-On, you will probably die once to the wrong thing being targeted.-The Repetition in the second half.Sadly I will not elaborate on my final gripe as that would spoil...... some things but a simple explanation would be.The way to access 100 % completion in this game has something that repeats quite a bunch.They tried a few ways to mix it up but it's just so many that repetition was bound to happen.And one where I am not sure if I should call it a pro OR a con:-The shift from the first half to the second half.I personally loved it, can I see it upsetting people, absolutely.And that's my review, sorry about the bad formatting, just needed to finally stop people from asking me about my opinion on this.This game's great, I don't give scores but i'd give it a recommendation, definitely not perfect but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ great and my favourite game of this year so far.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game.But even just a couple hours in, it had very quickly worn out its welcome. It starts out making you think that it's going to be along the lines of Zelda, but it quickly starts to fall apart at the seams.First off, the game revolves heavily around "hidden" mechanics, which are hinted at, but not explained, by an in-game manual where most of the important "text" is written in illegible runes. Figuring out what these images mean is absolutely essential to progression, but the way the information is presented is more confusing than helpful.Second, the game really badly wants to be a souls-like-- it has a dodge roll, a stamina bar, and a similar death system, but the combat is just... not good. Almost every enemy after the first two or three types has extremely annoying attack patterns that don't really leave you any meaningful window to hit them. A lot of the time you can't even attack once without getting punished, and they can kill you in 3-5 hits.Later areas also introduce enemies that move faster than you and run away whenever you get close, so your only option is to run after them until they go into a corner, but that usually involves chasing them into other packs of enemies so you end up surrounded.The combat ends up being hard without actually feeling skillful or challenging. In a game like Dark Souls, it works because there's a lot of depth and choices involved in how you approach combat, and different styles based on your equipment and build. Tunic has none of this, just repeated encounters with enemies that don't give you any openings and brutalize you if you dare to try to hit them.Areas are also packed full of hidden chests and passageways, but it really just boils down to "run against every single wall and corner until you find the one that you can walk through". There's no puzzle to it, just trial and error, and it gets old very fast.The art looks good (aside from a few later areas which frequently like to desaturate the entire screen and turn it into an eyesore), and there's some neat ideas, but none of it comes together into anything fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked this game as a puzzle game, but I did not like the combat. part of it was that I could not find many upgrades, ended up with most stats being 5 or below, except hp at 7 (these are all out of 8). but when my stats were correct (one fight they tell you to be at 3 attack 3 defense) you can cheese fights by using magic items. but the other problem lies in the healing systems in this game: it basically punishes you for making any mistakes. the heals come out very slow, you can't chain more than 1 for faster heals (just 1 at a time), and it barely ever heals anything, no matter how much you upgrade the potions. it becomes very inefficient to heal, especially against later bosses who attack faster and bigger. also stamina is weird, the recovery rate sucks and the only way to fix it is to use an item you have to purchase. while attacking doesnt reduce stamina, blocking or dodge rolling does. near the end of the game, enemies start getting so aggressive that stamina starts becoming a problem, and when you are low on stamina, you take bonus damage. when you run out, you just have to take damage or freeze the boss, and like I said, mistakes get punished hard because your healing takes too long, so it just compounds. also there's sometimes slowdown cause by an enemy, and it seems like it eats dodge rolls or throws off rhythm. blocking must be very slow, because often it would fail if I tried to use it in response to an attack and not just holding it early at certain enemies in order to counter attack them (birds basically). but any time I tried to block boss attacks, which come out faster and with less warning, shield would fail and I would take full damage, but dodge rolling usually worked fine. also the camera can't be controlled and will sometimes spin around the arena, it gets annoying when I would love the camera to be more static.the puzzles are fine, most of the ones you have to do at least. there's cool revelations of things you can do from the start of the game, if you had the knowledge. it's neat. the main complaints come from how many times you have to go across the same map. at first it's fine, but the more and more you do it, the more draining it gets. eventually there's a different map state and that helps for a second I guess. part of the issue is some areas, killing the enemies is annoying, mostly because you can't run past them: they maintain aggro forever unless you climb a ladder or reach a loading zone, some have very long ranged attacks and can't be ignored if you want to live. sometimes you have to kill a few dozen between you and the next shortcut or where you died, it's frustrating. the other complaint lies with the final puzzles. figuring out the golden path is the real final boss in my opinion; figuring out how to do it, because actually solving it is ludicrous. it requires you to do a very long input, and the method you have to do to solve it (you absolutely need pen and paper and your clues can be a little not clear in some cases if it's a single or double input), it can lead to either little mistakes being made or input errors, so it just adds a bunch of doubt, then you look up a guide and find out, yeah you were right or this one part was wrong, just the one, so glad you clicked those buttons a couple hundred times for no reason. then the reward sucks, not worth the effort, basically just a thumbs up. no lore, no like auto translator, no super item, nothing, it's literally like a pat on the back and a hint to a wonky haiku puzzle.there's a 2nd large input you have to do that's even more optional and even more pointless. you get a mini arg that leads nowhere, not worth the time, do not input that code, just google what it does. also I really do not like the runes. I don't know how one even figures out how they correspond to the correct things with the scant clue provided. the amount of time it would take to translate the whole thing, also not worth it after looking up a translated booklet when I was near finished with the game. don't bother, too much effort.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is framed as a game-within-a-game, complete with a 90's style manual with beautiful illustrations. As you can tell from the cover art, it wears its inspirations on its sleeve, but there's much more here than a basic retro callback. It does have its problems -- the pacing of exploration and puzzles is very wonky, the boss combat is kinda bad, and a few of the puzzles are really dumb -- but there aren't many games where I put in the effort to decode an entire language.The high points of the game are incredibly high. Buy it, go in blind, but don't feel bad if you look up some of the extremely late game puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely leave reviews for games, but holy cow, this game was something else. The way it incorporates the collectible NES-style in-game manual pages into the game's discovery of systems and puzzles is incredible, and something I've never experienced before. When I finally figured out what the Holy Cross was and how to use it, it was... I don't really know how to describe how it made me feel, but I don't think I'll ever forget it. I don't remember the last time I had to grab scratch paper (or cared enough about a game to have the patience for note-taking) to help solve puzzles in a game, but here I am with an insurance company's oversized letter envelope covered in incomprehensible gibberish, arrows, and strange shapes and maze-like constructions of lines. Man, the door in the mountains... I've gotten both(?) endings (I don't know for sure that there's only two) and I know there are puzzles I still haven't solved, like a message you have to stand in water for a minute to reveal. I have no idea what to do with that, and there's hints of plenty of others I still haven't discovered.I still didn't even know what most of the cards did by the time I completed both endings.I wish I could experience this whole game for the first time again.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr: Tunic is an amazing top-down action puzzle game with fun boss fights, satisfying puzzles, exciting exploration, and a fantastic soundtrack. Starts kinda dull but then just keeps getting better until it's become one of the most memorable games you've ever played.Tunic is a surprisingly pricey game considering the store page makes it look like just another cutesy top down indie game. But my god, is this game worth it. I'll start by immediately addressing that this game starts off really dull. The best part of this game is navigating the world and its mysteries, and frankly the start of the game just didn't have enough going on to peak my interest. The world was still simple and very few gripping questions had really been raised. However, this is short lived, as the game quickly opens up by introducing new areas, new goals, and new questions that all serve to keep you invested.The combat of this game is its other weakest point as it's just not that much to it. The combat is very standard top down dodge roll melee combat with the only real mix up here being the different magic weapons you get. On top of this, one of the most basic parts of this combat, the 3 part sword combo that you will basically be doing for the whole game, just doesn't feel very good. In particular, the third attack of the chain just did not consistently work for me, whether in combat or out of it.The boss fights are a bit of an outlier though, as unlike the moment to moment combat, they are actually really fun, and a couple were even quite tough. Bosses had fun move sets to learn, great sound design, and some amazing music tracks that made them truly memorable.Basically everything else in this game is amazing, starting with the absolute best part, the puzzles and the navigation. I don't usually think of these two things as the same, but in Tunic they absolutely are. Navigating the world is the puzzle, and its largely flawless. Using the perspective to hide secrets is genius, and it's extremely satisfying to turn those hidden corners and walk a ways behind a wall to then see yourself appear in some area you thought was unreachable. The way this game likes to give shortcuts by simply showing you that there was a hidden path that could have gotten you there all along is hilariously unique and surprising. This does bring up the only problem I have with this area of the game however. Finding shortcuts that were always there but were hidden form view is fun, but if you take a break from the game you will come back having forgotten where most of these shortcuts were, meaning you may as well not have them as they are not marked on the map. This does make Tunic one of the few games i'd actually suggest people binge rather than playing little bits of over time.There are other puzzles of course that have nothing to do with navigating and they are just as good... sort of. Many of the "puzzles" in this game don't particularly feel like puzzles as you are often given the answer quite directly. This is hardly a problem though because while they may not feel like puzzles, it still feels amazing to finally find out what all the different curiosities in the world are actually for. There is one puzzle though that stands out as king among'st the rest. While I obviously won't spoil, I will say the puzzle is optional but is without a doubt the most hyped up puzzle I have ever solved and my anticipation for solving it still brings me joy thinking about it now. Solving it has become one of my greatest video game memories not because it was hard, but because it was just so much fun. Perfect.Similarly, the world is not all navigation as well. Tunic has a very cartoon art style, but it's cute, and is very often used in tandem with some amazing lighting to create really gorgeous scenes. The variety of locations in this game is really good as well. The variety keeps things fresh, and ensures your eyes stay glued to the scene.The soundtrack in this game is incredible. It's chill vibes rival those of even Minecraft's soundtrack and that doesn't even give credit to the boss themes which all do a grand job of amplifying their respective fights. It's all just so good.Lastly I'll mention the games story which is alright... I guess. For me, the story was largely irrelevant, and I think the game itself tends to feel that way as well. There is a story, and it's got some cool ideas, but the details are so vague as to be non existent for the common player. Fortunately, the story never needs to be a motivator for you to do things, discovering all the secrets strewn about the world does that plenty well.

_childDocuments_.review: The combat of Darksouls meets the exploration of Zelda with no actual puzzles.The combat is dodge roll attacks, attack with your slap-range sword, and spam attack until it dies.Bosses will be constantly moving, so you're trying to reach the boss more often than actually attacking.Alongside that, endgame enemies reduce your max health whenever you get hit by them, and the only way to regain that lost hp is by resting at the game's version of a bonfire.You run around and explore. You can TWO tools good for unlocking new areas to explore in, one mid-game, the other late game.I only played through the main game, no super secret ending or anything of the sort.I saw zero puzzles I can think of. you kill enemies, flip switches, and proceed.Any puzzles would be from figuring out what the hell the guidebook means, translating text, and The art is great, the music is great, the story would be great for someone who actually wanted to translate whatever the ♥♥♥♥ is being said/written. The gameplay has much to be desired. I suggest anyone wanting to experience the gameplay anyway, to enable "no fail mode" after

_childDocuments_.review: 2 hours in and I'm definitely happy with my purchase. Everyone is making Zelda comparisons and they're not wrong. It's absolutely Zelda inspired but by no means a clone. One of my first games on NES was The Legend of Zelda everything in Tunic from the feel of the game to the manual pieces you pick up is giving me little flashes of nostalgia. It's also kind of souls-ish because if you die, you respawn at the last fire and can make your way back to your death spot but the only thing recovered is money and there's money everywhere. Playing Tunic feels like being bored on a lazy Sunday afternoon and your big brother is away so you go digging thru his games. You find a weird one from Japan with a cute fox holding a sword and a tattered manual with notes and scribbles on it. Nothing makes sense but as you play, questions get answered just as more questions get presented. I really appreciate how Tunic just tosses you into the game. No grand, sprawling intro. No explanation. No translating of the language even. I love the feeling of going back to the limited manual pages, pouring over every inch to find just the tiniest scrap of a hint of a clue. Then when you find a new one, delving back in to see what new info/art is shown. Support this developer. This is a good one.

_childDocuments_.review: Entertainment: 30/40 + It was very neat figuring things out as you goDesign: 12/20 + I'm pretty sure you have access to almost every ability in the game, you just don't know you do + It does a VERY good job of teaching the player information without telling you - Combat was miserable to play through in the early game; You move slower then the enemies and many of them prefer to be at a distance. Eventually you can close the gap, but by then there are very few enemies - The parry is by far the slowest parry I have used. When I got a hit with it I felt lucky, not skilled - Enemy attacks, and bosses in particular, have lingering hit boxes to an excessive degreeStory: 13/20 + You have no idea what is happening when you start, so you need to find out on your own + Does a good job of showing not telling + Near the middle of the game you learn something horrifying about the obelisks around the world and it does it in an equally horrifying way - Almost all text is written in a fictional language. I like this, but they went to far by making the dialogue also be in this language except for keywords. It creates a disconnect that lead me to not caring much about the setting very much - The twist was super obvious  - After the 2/3's point there's a dramatic shift in story that is conceptually really cool, but was not implemented as best as it could have been mechanicallyPresentation: 16/20 + The game has a really cute and simple art style + I love the character design for the protagonist + It comes with a unique camara angle that it uses to hide a lot of stuff, though it feels that they might have done so a bit to much - It has one of the worst targeting mechanics I have had the displeasure of usingTotal: 71/100Statement: A great puzzle exploration game plagued with poorly designed combat

_childDocuments_.review: For something that is eeeeereferred to as a Zelda / Dark Souls fusion doesn't come close to describing the charm that this game has.While it does capture the original essence of Zelda 1 with its open world and lack of dialogue, it's puzzles are easier to glean and the hints that they give in the collected pages of the manual are more intuitive. It even does a very amazing job at telling a story without using exposition, dialogue, or spoon-feeding everything to the player.However, some of the late game puzzles are too opaque even if you know the method of how to solve them.It's certainly more simple than a Dark Souls Difficulty, because the enemies won't break logic just to straight up cheat-kill you, but that isn't to say the game isn't without challenge. Although, it seems like sometimes you'll still take damage even during the invulnerable frames of the tumble leading to some really cheap deaths.Overall, I really loved this game, and I'm going back in for second and third playthroughs, and grabbing all those achievements!

_childDocuments_.review: I came into this thinking it was going to be a combat-forward Zelda-like and I got an amazing puzzle game that keeps giving you just enough information to get little AHA moments all throughout every play session. The game doesn't come right out and tell you how to play it, but you pick up manual pages and over time learn how to interact with things and get enough direction to figure out how to make it to the end just by poking around the corners of every area and careful inspection of pages.I do think it can sometimes toe the line on too cryptic, but with the combat and the music washing over me I never felt frustrated. I do not recommend looking up solutions at this time. So many sites lump a lot of later game solutions and secrets in with their regular walkthroughs.I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoyed a puzzle-forward game like Fez or The Witness, but even if you don't enjoy puzzles, the bosses and the exploration are still very enjoyable on their own and you can beat the game without ever touching the deeper secrets.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Zelda, soulslikes, and metroidvanias but this game just didn't do it for me.  It's not terrible, and it's close to being good, but overall I just found it annoying.  Everybody compares it to Zelda and while the visuals and themes are very Zelda-ish there aren't actually any puzzles to solve to progress.  It's very much a souls game level design where you run from checkpoint to checkpoint.  The only puzzles are these weird Dpad input combos that you don't even know about until the end of the game.  Some of them are clever but some are really annoying.That would be fine if it really leaned into the soulslike elements but the combat just isn't good enough to carry the game.  A lot of bosses/enemies are super annoying as they constantly jump back.  Funnily enough you can use that against them and get them up against the wall and just wail on them as they keep trying to jump back.  Combat lacks the finesse and tuning of souls games and the strategy and puzzle element of Zelda games.  Exploration was very meh as well.  90% of the secrets are just things hidden by the camera perspective or darkness.  So you run along the edge of the wall until you fumble through a passage or the interact button appears.  It became very tedious running into every wall obscured by the camera to see if there was anything behind it.These kinds of games don't really need a story or clear directions so the gibberish dialogue isn't a big deal but my god at least tell us what stuff does.  You can figure out what most of the items do easily enough but the cards are often just stat buffs or conditional stat buffs that you usually won't notice.  The gibberish/picture book manual is hit or miss.  I like the overall concept but they took it too far.  It also makes picking the game back up very difficult.  You gotta keep this one fresh in your mind because there is no indication of where you have been or where to go next.  A lot of the shortcuts are obscured by the camera so unless you remember where they're at it will take forever to navigate the world as you gotta run into every obscured area again looking for things hidden by the camera again.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is an ingenious mesh of well-proven inspirations and new ideas. The game is often as much of a tricky puzzle game as it is an enjoyable and familiar-looking action RPG. Tunic undeniably lifts the base of its presentation, top-down camera, tough-yet-fair sword-and-shield combat, and clever interconnected level design from iconic sources (i.e. Link's Awakening and Dark Souls), but the game adds a layer of ‘knowledge-progression’ that’s hidden within a nostalgic, half-translated in-game strategy guide.In a gripping perspective-expanding process akin to the joy of solving Outer Wilds, from the start, you essentially already have everything you need to go anywhere (or at least do some serious sequence breaking before key items get in the way), but you don’t yet know enough about this new land to harness your own potential. Here, knowledge from the game’s scattered manual has the same door-opening/problem-solving power as keys or ‘super missiles’ might. While you go about the intended adventuring route, so many shortcuts and interactions lay just out of reach, merely hiding in plain sight.The value Tunic places on information is quite refreshing. As your tools and stats progress, so does your understanding of the world. You have no idea what subtle details could become relevant later, which bestows this unknown depth and mystery to the whole experience. When new pages of lovely art and inconclusive imagery are revealed to you, deciphering them makes you feel like a real detective. I also love the dramatic irony of knowing that nothing was stopping you from your goals besides a trick that seemed obvious in retrospect.This  concept works so well. That guidebook/exploration dynamic makes for some unforgettable moments. But it’s also worth briefly complimenting how Tunic’s other components elevate the game into something much greater than the sum of its sources. The story is told indirectly and silently. It brings further intrigue into this seemingly friendly animal world. The music, while an initially unexpected tone, evokes waves of synthy nostalgia. Tunic’s soundtrack could’ve been a lot more predictable and I think Lifeformed and Janice Kwan found a great way to add to Tunic’s unique identity. Combat isn’t a major thrill, but it has good moment-to-moment pacing. While parrying is a little slugging, it’s far from necessary to succeed. Most bosses require ample mastery to overcome without having to pull out any hairs.And if it ended there, I wouldn’t be hesitant to rank Tunic among its like-minded masterpieces.Sadly, the game ends on a pretty painful note. I was so into the first two-thirds of this game. Tunic is still certainly worth experiencing for those first ten-ish hours, so don't let my need to discuss my discontent with the final act stain your impressions of the truly brilliant parts. Seeing as fun as Tunic’s learning process was, perhaps it’s fitting that an end to that growth would entail a decline in my interest in it.

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:- The idea of putting together a booklet that explains the game is brilliant and well executed (since you unlock pages of it thoughout the game). Feels like the good old times - playing an N64 game with the companion book for hints and details. You also get a lot of different items and you can try to figure out what they do, but at some point you will find a page that will definitely tell you.-  If you played other exploration games you will recognize where they probably are. The puzzly-hidden things are "unlocked" with the booklet and make you re-visit and re-think parts of the game you already visited to uncover even more things.- The environment is very memorable and easy to navigate.Neutral:- The game is pretty linear, but you can go almost anywhere you want. I know I played a part of the game in an obviously not intended order, but it seems the game is build to allow for that to happen.- You do not need to worry about the camera. It's fixed and the game is built around that specific perspective. That also means a lot of the secrets are hidden with perspective tricks.Negatives:- Combat is not enjoyable and makes the game substantially worse. This is mostly because of the long animations, so it feels like you are swining a longsword while the enemies dance around you in circles. Hitboxes and timing windows are also not that great.- Enemies also do not have a maximum follow distance so you have to fight  you come across. Or run fast enough to avoid them.- The bosses are really bad. They are well designed, but if you crank bad combat to 11 it becomes worse instead of better.- The Dark Souls save system is horrible for this game. I died on the overworld and respawned inside a dungeon all the way on the other side of the map, because f*** you, that's why. Took me ages to walk back. You want to save to set your respawn point, but you also don't want to respawn the enemies while exporing. It's a pain.

_childDocuments_.review: Whilst overall I enjoyed my time with the game, and intend to keep playing after credits, I have two complaints.Firstly the language. I like the aesthetic of a game being in a fictional language. However this only really works if the language is meaningless and is only there for aesthetics. If interesting or useful information is being conveyed in a fake language then taking the time to diagram it out is just annoying. I think an improvement would be for the language to slowly translate over the course of the game. Keeping the aesthetic but also eventually actually giving the mechanic. If I need to put the game down and go looking on the internet for a translation, risking finding spoilers, then that's somewhat of a failing in my eyes. Secondly, my most significant gripe with the game. The parry. (yes, there's a parry). For the most part it's unneeded throughout the game. However for the final fight it feels like a very important tool. Frankly it doesn't really function well. It has a wind-up time and it's time of effect is far too short (even with the buff). It's too difficult to trigger, sharing a button with block. The animation can't be cancelled, so you're left vulnerable whilst it's winding-up. IMO, a parry should be a move you trigger the moment there is a signal of an incoming attack or at the moment an attack hits. More often than not I would get hit because the parry was still winding-up as the attack hit me. Or I would trigger the parry the moment an attack was telegraphed and the parry would be over by the time the attack landed. This is far too wordy now, but I could go on, fuelled by my frustration.Everything else about the game I really liked. The manual pages idea was excellent. The music and visuals are great. Exploration was wonderful, and is often rewarded. There are a ton of puzzles and mysteries that I feel I've hardly scratched the surface of. I'm looking forward to continuing to play until I solve everything or the game wears thin.TL:DR? It's excellent. Really good. But, useful info hidden behind fake language kinda annoying and the parry mechanic is terrible.(played most of this offline on my Steam Deck so recorded hours might be wrong)

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a gem of a game that turned out to be much deeper, captivating, and challenging that I initially thought.The game is full of creative ideas, secrets, cryptic mysteries that all come together at the end if you choose to attempt to solve them. The craziest part of it, is that all of those puzzles are entirely optional, and should you choose not to look into the puzzles, the game is still very solid and worth the time.The use of a map with missing pages, written in an unreadable language is used cleverly and thoroughly during the whole game, you'll often get rewarded for paying close attention to what's in it, especially for puzzles !The music, story, graphics are a joy to experience.Easily one of the best games that I've played in a very long time, can't recommend it enough

_childDocuments_.review: My favourite game of the past 10 years, honestly. It's so cute and every movement, nudge and effect is so satisfying (like when a banana falls perfectly into a trash can, that kind of thing). That's the exterior though and what's underneath is an incredible puzzle game which really expects you to go above and beyond in deductive reasoning and note taking to unlock everything. I'm always pretty disappointed when puzzle games are too easy, too straightforward and puzzles too narrow in scope. For Tunic, I have a whole folder dedicated to sketches, screenshots, decoding cyphers, tentative possible connections between distant parts of the game, etc... That might sound like a chore and maybe it would be, if it weren't so well crafted and fair the whole way through. I've put this game on hold for months at a time and come back to it, only to crack yet another puzzle, which opens up more avenues. I suppose you could finish this game in one day if you refer to a guide online, but everything you need to know is there in the game - looking up answers will probably ruin the whole game. Honestly don't want to say any more, because I stumbled upon this game completely blind and I'm positive the best way to experience it is to go in not knowing anything about it. Whole-heartedly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: At the risk of sounding a bit like that awful copypasta, , you have to have a certain well-roundedness to be able to really appreciate TUNIC.  Without going into actual detail (for this is one of those games which is best appreciated "going in blind"), the potential problem lies in that the game presents a challenge on two fronts which are not really synergistic at all: The result is that there is a very real chance that the game will fall flat for anyone not keen on both aspects; if you find this kind of combat daunting, then the game's action may wear you down before you get the chance to sink your teeth into the puzzles.  And If you are fine with the combat but aren't really tuned-in for the puzzles, you will eventually reach a point where the game appears to have reached a rather unsatisfying conclusion, while further progression, and the true endgame, are locked beyond an activity that holds little appeal to you.No doubt the hope of the game's developers was that, for a certain kind of gamer, TUNIC would hit a sweet spot, becoming one of the best games of all time in the minds of its intended audience.  But, while I absolutely loved TUNIC, my honest feeling is that even the ideal TUNIC player will find the puzzle-solving side of the game to be  more valuable than the combat.  The combat is fine, even enjoyable for the most part, but the puzzles and the general sense of intrigue that arises (again, I have to be frustratingly vague here) are exceptional.  I just don't see anything nearly as special about the action side of the game.So, I would give this conditional recommendation: I wouldn't go into this for the combat alone.  But if you're not fazed by the combat, and you're interested in uncovering secrets and solving puzzles on a grand scale, this could be one of the most rewarding experiences in recent memory.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good. It's astonishingly good. It dropped my jaw a few times. There are a lot of different games that this game is like, but better. However, it is important to know a very select few things going in.1. This game is sparingly, occasionally, rather mechanically difficult. These instances are few and far between, so even if they aren't to your liking, they're still well worth putting up with.2. This game is highly, intensely cognitive. The developers did a very good job making sure that the necessary information to puzzles are always available somewhere accessible (which would be the manual), and ensuring that the information would also involve where to look. However, they did this with the understanding that the player will, by their own accord, keep track of where they've been, what they've done, and where they intend to go. All players should plan to keep a notes system outside of the game. They should also use it.3. This game's progression will depend on accepted gaming standards for things such as control systems, level design, and equipment. This is so that the developers can plainly state as little as possible about the game, no exceptions. It will be the player's job to intuit that "A" on the controller will trigger a dodge roll, and other such things.You must be prepared to be given nothing. You must be prepared to earn your every iota of meaning. You must be prepared to find things insurmountable, and be prepared to simply give up for the moment.If you are prepared, this game will without a doubt be the best game you've played in months. If you are not, then take heart; this game will still be here when you are.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't expect to enjoy this game. I'm not a fan of isometric games, nor do I like the general artstyle of the game. On top of that, I've currently got a bit of Soulslike fatigue. So, I didn't expect to enjoy a game that looks like a mesh together of Legend of Zelda and Dark Souls. Time and time again Tunic would be recommended by someone I respect. I'd consider it, then decide against it. But something about the overwhelmingly positive reviews eventually swayed me to get it. And I don't regret my decision one bit.The exploration in this game is fantastic. The game is in part a metroidvania - with traversal abilities you can unlock that allow you to explore the world. The game is also "metroidbrainia", with abilities you can do from the start, you just don't know how. The world is nicely interconnected with many satisfying shortcuts you can unlock along the way.The game drip feeds you pages of a manual, but unlike pretty much every manual in existence, this one doesn't bore me to death. In fact, it's fantastic! Most of it is encoded in a strange different language, with only key bits of information in English or told via images. The game slowly lets you in on little tips and tricks, but you don't NEED the manual, you can figure these abilities out on your own (and when that happens it is very satisfying).I mentioned earlier that the artstyle was not my favourite. Despite this, the animations, colour scheme, and the sound design are masterfully put together. The environments are far more varied than I would have expected. While I loved the atmosphere of the rustic forest temple-y areas, there were more impressive areas later into the game.The progression in abilities feels great. I love it when games make loot that feels valuable and most loot either contributes directly to a valuable upgrade, gives you an upgrade, or rewards you with information. The combat was good. The final boss was fantastic. The bosses in the runup ranged from decent to great. I had a little trouble with the lock-on system, but all of this could have been mitigated if I'd used the arrow keys to switch lock on targets. Even despite my Soulslike fatigue I still enjoyed the combat. You don't need to solve any  puzzles to get an ending, but if you want to get the  ending there are a lot to solve. The final puzzle required for the good ending is incredible. There are hints hidden right under your nose throughout the game; when you figure out the solution, it feels absolutely amazing. One downside, however, is when executing the puzzle solution, it is very easy to make a tiny error interpreting parts of it - which then unfolds into an unfortunately frustrating experience diagnosing the small error you made. At the end of the day though, I am still very satisfied with my experience figuring it out. This game had me hooked. From ringing the bells to now (having just completed the good ending) I had a burning desire to uncover the secrets around every corner; it takes masterful game design to create that feeling. I was able to recapture similar feelings in this game as when solving puzzles in Outer Wilds. I highly recommend playing this, and I highly recommend playing it blind.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a charming, concise little action RPG that captures the nostalgia of unboxing and playing Zelda 1 for the first time, translated to a modern audience. It borrows elements from ARPGs and puzzle platformers since that era (notably the Dark Souls franchise and Fez) to translate the challenge, mystery, and discovery to a modern audience, while evoking nostalgia for an earlier time through its art style and simplified gameplay.The game itself is not terribly long, but what's there is highly enjoyable and does not overstay its welcome. The combat draws from more modern Souls games while remaining faithful to its Zelda inspiration, allowing for multiple strategies and playstyles to prevail in each encounter. Its secrets and puzzles remain challenging without requiring more than details the game provides and pen and paper to solve (something that Fez notably stumbled with). And the game is very accessible to players with colorblindness, motion sickness, and who prefer to tune the combat to meet their needs. The soundtrack (by the same folks who did Dustforce) is an absolute banger, and hits all the right notes throughout the game.My only complaint with the game is that it's a bit small for the $30 price tag, especially when some of the discovery and mystery does not remain in subsequent playthroughs. That will assuredly improve over time, as DLC, randomizers, and new tricks get added to the game by the developers and community. The experience is also very high quality and respectful to the player's time, something that more padded out 100-hour experiences do not provide. But unless you need this very particular style of nostalgia right now or simply want to support the developers, it may be worth waiting for a sale compared to other options in the ARPG space.Overall though, what's here is very high quality, and when you do pick it up you're sure to have a wonderful adventure. Just don't forget your sword. It's dangerous to go alone. Take this.

_childDocuments_.review: A pinch of Legend of Zelda for the presentation, a yolk of Dark Souls for the combat... That's how I would have described Tunic until I tried to solve the Golden Path. The thing is, Tunic isn't just a Zelda-like game. It is first and foremost a gigantic puzzle. On surface level, Tunic is a simple yet challenging action-adventure game that tests a player's reflexes as much as their deduction abilities. But it is hard to convey how intricate and ubiquitous puzzles are are in this game without facing them first-hand. In fact, every location, each map is packed full with secrets. Most of them can be found quite easily. Others will require to be observant and search every nooks and crannies and, for the most challenging ones, one will need to make extensive use of the clues hidden in the in-game manual. And then, again, there's the Golden Path, a gigantic, incredibly complex puzzle that spans the whole game. A puzzle so intricate, so well hidden that most people will reach the end of the game without even realizing that it exists. And that would be perfectly fine if solving it wasn't mandatory to see the true ending of the game. Thankfully, Tunic is perfectly enjoyable without having to suffer through this perplexing ordeal. I would even advise to skip it entirely because it simply removes the last boss. Unless you're really into over-designed head-scratchers just use Youtube, it'll save you some precious time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels so tailor-made for me so I just have to write a gushing review for it! It's a combination of incredibly smart game design which relies on minimal hand-holding and rewards your curiosity; puzzles that give you that 'AHA!' moment and unlock a whole new way of looking at the world once they click; isometric action combat that feels just challenging enough to keep you on your toes but never making you feel like the task is impossible and you aren't going to progress further; beautiful art direction and compelling world-building through visual storytelling and last but not least, a cute af protagonist. If you are like me and all of that sounds exactly up your alley, then I highly recommend TUNIC! Very quickly into the game, TUNIC teaches you to be observant. You will not be able to progress unless you are curious and are looking for visual clues at all times. The most unique mechanic that TUNIC has is a game manual which can be accessed at any time and contains everything you will need to beat the game and solve even its hardest puzzles. It's very much inspired by actual retro game manuals and the aesthetic of it is *chef's kiss*. The twist is that the manual pages are written in a foreign language with only some english sprinkled around to guide you. You are also able to find only certain pages at a time so you are forced to solve as much as possible with as little as you have. You aren't always sure if you already have the information to engage with what you're finding so that fuels your curiosity even more. One of the smartest parts of TUNIC's design is how both your discoveries in the world and your reading of the manual pages is teaching you to be observant. You will always be rewarded for using your eyes in this game. As you progress the game will also reveal hidden paths & ladders that have been there all along, you just didn't know it but you  seen had you been looking closer. You will find little scribbles on maps in the manual, only to discover secret chests/paths/etc. in the world. It's an extremely smart loop of both secrets in the manual and smart level design that just constantly fuels your sense of wonder, curiosity and gives you a dopamine rush every time you figure out any of its secrets. I never found myself stuck or lost simply by keeping an eye out.Fair bit of advice though, go in as blind as possible (don't even watch the trailer/video on steam as it gives a fair bit away that would otherwise feel more rewarding to discover on your own). I went in knowing very little about the game except that it was a game all about discovery, had a cool retro game manual mechanic and that apparently had one big compelling puzzle (which I'll circle back to), that's about it! This is the type of game where you are doing yourself a huge disservice if you spoil yourself so my biggest advice is:  All I'll say is if you're stuck/lost: "When in doubtie, game manual-ie outie". The game is very smart in the sense that at all times you are given everything you need to progress further, the manual pages are very selectively given to you at certain times to give you all the knowledge you need (). And knowledge really is the biggest "power" you will be given. I was always so excited to receive a new page of the manual and analyze it as much as possible with my current knowledge of the game. Also worth knowing is that you do not need to decipher the manual language to beat the game with the good ending. You also do not need to understand every puzzle/scribbly note in the manual to beat it either. I completed some post-game/side puzzles that I got through using the hints in the manual (that do indeed make you feel like a genius), but there is tons in there just for the pure love of hard af puzzles. There is a whole rabbit hole of secret puzzles and insanity that the community has unearthed online that is worth looking into only  you finish the game. But safe to say, you only need to understand  of the manual puzzles/hints to finish the game and that is always connected to a repeating phrase/word, a whole page spread, etc. The game manual is very clear as to what's important and much more subtle about the extra fun notes/small hints to bonus puzzles. The game also has some awesome boss fights that have the difficulty fine tuned to challenge you but never make you despair and stop playing. I will say though, some of the boss hit boxes could be finicky and your attacks don't always hit despite not being physically possible to get closer to the boss/weak point. Leading up to each of the boss encounters there is so much visual storytelling and world building as you go from zone to zone, each weirder than the last. I was constantly at awe and curious about why this world is the way it is. There are few moments of "revelations" as well that are purely visual/environment storytelling that had me asking so many questions and made me very invested in the lore of the world. As a huge sucker for cryptic visually driven storytelling that doesn't give you all the answers but forces you to theorize, this game scratched just the right itch!Lastly, I want to talk about the "last" puzzle and the ending, but do not spoil yourself if you haven't figured it out yet as it's by far the most satisfying part of the game to figure out on your own.  I will say though, the puzzles/ world secrets in this game definitely lean towards the visual pattern-breaking observation kind of thinking and if that is not how your brain works this game's puzzle hints may not make a whole lot of sense to you. My brain clicks with that type of thinking and puzzle solving very well so it was all immensely satisfying throughout the game!TL;DR Amazing game, fantastic world, joyous game manual, smart puzzles that make brain go brrr, brb going to buy the fox plushie now
