_childDocuments_.review: I will say a lot of things everybody knows already, my criticism lays at the end, in the spoiler part. You can jump ahead if you've played the game.This game, is one of the best thing I've played for some time. It's so well designed, so clever, so challenging, so layered, so referential while being its own thing, so everything I want a game to be. Easely one of my game of the year but let's go deeper:Probably the number one reason you should buy the game. The blend between a very colorful, joyful world with some dark touches behind, The very very assumed Zelda references constantly broke apart, the freaking booklet (the booklet !!) The way everything begins to connect and make sense the more you venture on, The sense of magic "ah-ah" moments the game gives you till the very end. This is very precisely and nicely crafted all along. If you didn't play it, stop here, and play it. You won't regret.The game is a quite well balenced 2d Zelda type game with Dark-Souls-like combat mechanics and difficulty peaks. Add some quite hard puzzles to the mix, sometimes reminescent of the Witness and this is what you got. It's not perfect but it's damn original and fresh and really well done !Controls are perfect, I like the way the stamina bar is used, not used for attacks fore instance, or leaving you escape even if empty (with debuffs).There are some drawbacks, like the very limited equiped items you can carry at once and the fact that changing them is real time, no pausing. I like both ideas but put together it can become a bit hard to manage and make some items totally useless like HP/MP/SP boosts. Since they take a space of your 3 action panel, that you can't equip them during combat withtout taking huge risks and they are lost forever when used... Well you just learn to do it without them. That's how I did.Very reminiscent of the contemporary "Maquette" style, Very Zelda's Awekening remake like. It's surely good without being super original. Some scenery and lightnings are incredible thought, but the magic resides more in the opposition between this very childish look and the way darker themes and challenging combats behind.I have zero knowlege about sounds exceeding "It sounded good" or "it sounded bad". This one sounded good.From there, it will be full of spoilers as I will be talking about end-game content.

_childDocuments_.review: Mix Zelda with the cryptic puzzles of Fez and a drop of Dark Souls and you get Tunic.Tunic is a perfect example of not necessarily doing anything incredibly out of the box, but refining the basics and essence of what makes these type of games fun, it really brings out that feeling of wonder, mystery, and intrigue the first time you booted up your first Zelda game as a little kid. _childDocuments_.review: An isometric Ocarina of Time blemished by unforgiving souls-like combat in the late game. There are some interesting elements at play here that combine to make this a wonderful experience: a puzzle box map riddled with secrets, a story that unfolds itself to the player through pages of game manual found throughout the world, and light combat with all the gadgets you'd expect in a Zelda adventure. However, the game is held back from perfection by the combat which starts off relaxed - offering a slight, but surmountable challenge - only to wallop the player with a brutal mid-game difficulty spike that feels unnecessary and out of place given the Zelda model the game is so heavily drawing from. Luckily, there is a "god mode" toggle in the settings menu for those who prefer to focus on adventure and puzzle solving.

_childDocuments_.review: TUNIC is my nominee for Game of the Year (The Steam Awards), and even though I played only one other game that I felt more affection for this year (Psychonauts 2), as a 2022 game TUNIC is a definite no.1 spot for me.Funny thing is, I couldn't (read: mostly just didn't want to) even finish the game legit.. the Garden Knight bit frustrated me, and I'm not that into "souls-like" approach of boss fights, not because they're hard, but mostly they're just tedium that get in the way of exploration and puzzle solving, which for a game like Tunic are the only aspects I want to deal with honestly. Somewhere before the second major boss I got stuck pretty hard trying to figure stuff out, so I resulted to using guides and a trainer to speed through it to the end - somewhat annoyed with combat, but loving the world, I still decided to see everything for a 100% completion.This is a shallow review, and I'm not gonna parrot what probably thousands have said better already, but TUNIC deserves a spot in most of these Steam Awards categories - it is a Labor of Love just by the fact of how much effort went into making every little detail of its world ; it is visually very appealing (stylistically similar to 'Link's Awakening' remake), with an amazing soothing soundtrack, making it a great choice to sit back and relax (for the exploration bits) on Steam Deck ; it has the same complexity in what at first seems like a simple exploration game (much like 'FEZ' or 'The Witness') having that "oh, wow" effect once you start figuring out just how deep this rabbit hole really goes, and since these types of puzzle games aren't too common, to me that feels innovative still ; and lastly I'd say this is 'the best game I suck at' - being at the top of all of these categories mentioned, making this a pretty easy choice for a Game of the Year in my opinion.P.S. That in-game manual is just the coolest thing ever. Very well done!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game that uses nostalgia to help explain the story and give you hints about what to do / where to go. The combat in this game is top down sort of like the original Legend of Zelda. I enjoyed my time with Tunic, but I quickly realized that getting the alternate ending would be a laborious endeavor. If you really like puzzles and want a challenge to solve on your own, then you'll like the secret ending at the end of this game. However, I had no shame referencing a guide to determine if I was on track with the puzzles since the game doesn't give you a good indication if you're progressing with one or not. In spite of that, I really like Tunic and hope more folks pick it up and like it too.One last thing, the sound track is amazing and I encourage anyone who enjoys video game music to purchase the OST that comes with this game. _childDocuments_.review: Want to go on an adventure? How about exploring a seemingly traditional and gamey world just to discover that there's much more underneath the surface. Don't be fooled by the cover: while clearly being presented as an action-adventure title, the core of the experience is much closer to a puzzle game. Not just because of the puzzles themselves, but because the player is asked to understand rules, uncover truths, figure out how the world works realizing that most of what the player sees actually hides a secret. This is done beautifully with close to no written text, just by virtue of observation and experimentation, with the aid of a "game manual" that ties in a whole new meta dimension into the game. The game manual itself is a brilliant addition that's extremely well executed, managing to drive the player to the next discovery without robbing him of the challenge and joy of actually grasping it.On top of it all, the presentation is top notch featuring one of the best soundtrack in years and great direction at every turn.Tunic is without a doubt a masterpiece: it provides a unique, engaging experience with fresh ideas, both well thought out and well executed, balancing freedom of exploration with a tight and exciting sense of progression. I'd also like to talk about how great, thoughtful and meaningful the story and inspiration behind the game are, and how great of a message it conveys, but that's something I'll have to discover on your own.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not perfect, but  is definitely something special.The easy analogy (and the one a ton of people have already used) is that  is S/NES era  and  in a blender - I think the most surprising thing is that it's more than just a surface-level comparison.This is a game that has been very deliberately and meticulously designed as a callback to the experience of playing videogames in the 80s and 90s   and it achieves it to a degree that I got that experience even though it wasn't really one I can remember having as a kid.  It's because of this that the best experience is to either play it blind, or with someone else who knows what to do on-hand that can push you in the right direction.  As a player there are dozens of little things you'll see that you won't understand immediately, only to have a sudden 'aha!' moment later - after the third or fourth time this happens the entire game becomes positively drenched in a sense of childlike wonderment and mystery, to the point where a good chunk of the thrill comes from finding new secrets and little hidden things that you'd previously written off, and the game does a pretty good job of delivering those with an appropriate atmosphere.There is another side to this, and I think it's where  is a bit less successful: the combat.As a kid, you probably sucked at playing videogames.   recreates this via an iteration of : it's by no means impossible, but the deck is stacked enough against you that you'll die a fair bit before you get to grips with it. The big problem is that the combat stacks things against the player in a frustrating way: once you start a swing, you're committed to the entire animation, which frequently takes longer than it does for an enemy to start flashing and then slap you in the face.  Individual hits aren't exceptionally damaging but the effect is nevertheless frustrating.  The  problem is the lock-on system; it's very bad at prioritizing targets, its range is limited enough that bosses will frequently slip out of it, and if you're playing on keyboard the act of trying to hold shift while moving can get very uncomfortable very  quickly (mercifully Caps Lock gives a toggle-able version).  The camera itself is a bit iffy, as well - it handles exploration and combat encounters quite well, but gets rather panicked and confused in boss encounters.  Half of them will frequently feature moments where you can't see the boss, or moments where you can't see your character, which is a pretty serious problem when the margin for error in these encounters is fairly low.  This isn't a deal-breaker, though: I'm terrible at this type of combat and I managed to get through it with only some frustration, and it's a slightly sour note in a game that has entirely too much good in it to matter.Cannot recommend highly enough if you want something to take you back to less cynical times.

_childDocuments_.review: "And the award for the most interesting gameplay mechanic of the year goes to: THIS FOX!"I read about Tunic in a Penny Arcade webcomic strip, and after a single look at the store page I made the purchase on a whim. Upon starting the game I had some concern that the game was just another cheap Zelda clone and that would be that. Ten minutes later I began to see what Tunic was truly going for, and after a few hours I knew I had a potential Game of the Year on my hands.Tunic is, for the most part, a fairly straightforward isometric adventure game. You navigate a cute fox and fight angry bad guys and monsters that try to stop you. The game is rendered in soft, but vivid colour and style that serves well to both keep the player informed of all the important things there are to see, while doing just enough to hide and obscure the countless secrets embedded in the world. Sound effects provide little to talk about, serving their purpose well without being disruptive, and the music provides a pleasing ambience where appropriate, and a bit of action and thrill when called for.The game draws inspiration not only from games such as Zelda and The Witness, with the former providing general gameplay and the latter inspiring some puzzles, but also from some of the basics of Dark Souls, with how combat revolves around positioning, blocking and dodging. Even things like the Dark Souls bonfire and collecting a recovery after death, though Tunic is far more forgiving and kind with its mechanics.A vague task to ring two bells and free a trapped figure are all you have to go on, but here is where Tunic sets itself apart: the game gives much of its story, exposition and instructions through its manual. But the manual is not some crummy readme.txt file or a PDF document, but rather an interactive and collectible element of the game itself! While it's written in a seemingly indecipherable language, there is just enough to go on here, and the little hints and clues embedded in this intricately crafted and beautifully illustrated document serve to feed one's imagination, curiosity and sense of adventure. This manual is perhaps the most interesting mechanic I've seen in a long time!I could say plenty more of this game, but doing so would risk spoiling too much of the experience.Without the slightest hesitation: I heartily recommend Tunic! It's a wonderful little adventure, and provides plenty of depth even for the completionist player looking to discover all of its secrets.Playtime: 15+ hours (Single playthrough)Ratings (1-10)Visual: 9Audio: 8Story: 9Gameplay: 9Overall: 9

_childDocuments_.review: Edit 2: Months later and I'm still thinking about this game. Really standing the test of timeEdit: Have now finished Tunic, what an excellent game. And I'm just scratching the surface with the puzzles too because there are alternate endings, secrets within secrets, and more. Not sure if I have the time to keep digging, but I want to.Original: Have you ever looked at a puzzle game and though hmm, needs more Dark Souls? Well this game might be for you because it is most definitely for me. If you can go in cold please do, because the joy of discovery here is amazing. I'm 6 hours in, feels like im about halfway through the game, but i wanted to get this review out there for people who are on the fence.Without trying to spoil I'll try to explain what makes this game so good. This game is first and foremost a puzzle adventure game. You don't know whats going on, instructions and signs are in an unknown language, an you have to piece together everything through contextual clues. The world might seem locked away behind abilities like a metroidvania, but you actually have hidden abilities and skills you can do right from the start that unlock parts of the world. It will be interesting to see if / how speedrunners try to exploit these techniques.This adventure puzzle style would be fun on its own but then you have the combat, which is not much more than sword, shield, dodge roll, magic, grapple hook and items, but the enemies design is tough making you truly master the mechanics to beat each boss. Very much like dark souls, but probably closer to Death's Door. It is difficult, so I'm not sure I would recommend it for pure puzzle game fans, but definitely recommend to anyone who loves Souls games and especially the hidden lore aspects of Souls games.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a game that is a blend of classic 2D Zelda mixed with some Dark Souls in the form of minimalist story telling, having bonfire-like checkpoints that you respawn at upon death, having healing flasks that you refill at said checkpoints, and having an interconnected world full of shortcuts that loop back upon itself. The game evokes a feeling of trying to play the original Legend of Zelda game for the NES for the first time and your only guidance is a copy of the Japanese version of the game's manual. This is the game's selling point that makes it stand out from other games in its genre. Throughout the game you collect pages of the game manual that will include game mechanics, controls, uses for items, hints for secrets, maps, and story elements.  However, the challenge comes from the manual being written in the game's fictional language. Furthermore, the pages are often collected out of order, so there may be a 2-page spread where you only have half of the information available. This requires making deductions and inferences in order to "solve" the puzzle with the missing information. This incomplete information is often sufficient enough to progress, but often times when you get the rest of the puzzle the information will help recontextualize the information in some new way that helps further the player's understanding of the world. The game has a wonderful pacing with giving you just enough information to keep you on your toes to solve the puzzle, but not too much to keep you feeling overwhelmed. You will often feel clever by scouring the pages to notice little details for hidden secrets and puzzle solutions. This is how about 90% of the game is, keeping a good pace at drip-feeding you new clues in order to keep you moving forward without keeping you stumped for too long. However, the last 10% or so of the game really falls off, which I will go into more detail later. While you can translate the in-game language, you can certainly complete the game without doing so. Unfortunately, you do not get the crucial clue used to decipher the language until the very end of the game, and even then it seems like translating the individual characters of the language felt like it required making a lot of assumptions and using trial and error to finally get the right answer instead of having a more deductive approach. I looked up a spoiler-free hint guide to try to translate the language on my own with some success, but once I realized how the language was supposed to be translated, it felt like it was going to be more of a chore to not only decipher the symbols, then then also translate the 50+ pages of the manual. I ended up just reading a translated version online. None of the hints/clues were things I couldn't already decipher on my own by using the pictures/context clues in the game's manual. The only real benefit of reading the manual was getting elaboration on the game's story, as well as clearer item descriptions. Had I tried to continue to decipher the the language on my own and try to translate the entire manual, it probably would have taken another 5 hours or so to do this. Considering my total playtime is under 20 hours, spending another 5 hours to solve essentially "one puzzle" the wasn't even necessary to complete the game, did not feel worth my time.I got through the first ending without a guide, but in order to get the "true" ending you have to complete a series a time-consuming, tedious puzzles (e.g. having to input a string of button inputs in a specific order at certain locations). I was able to figure out how to do it on my own and did a few of them on my own, but some of them I knew what I was supposed to do to complete them - but I felt the game did not communicate clearly enough at times what is the "start" point of inputing the commands. And some of these commands could be 10-20+ inputs. So sometimes I could not tell if maybe I double-pressed accidentally or if I made an error in my notes. After a certain point, it became unfun due to it felt it was just wasting my time. At that point, I just looked up a guide to get through those string of puzzles. The "final" puzzle requires you to complete 25 puzzles/clues in order to find 4-5 input commands each, put them all together, and then input those combined total of 110 inputs - in order with no mistakes - in order to unlock the item you need for the true ending. I had the right idea when beginning to solve this puzzle, but looked at a hint guide just to check if my answers were right. Once I verified I did the first 4-5 puzzles/clues correctly by checking a guide, I just found myself looking up the guide for the written command. Because it would probably take another 1 or so hours to get through the rest of the clues to come up with that 110-command solution. But if I tried it on my own without a guide, and - even if I got it all right on the first try - if I found myself making one wrong press in that 110-input code, then I would find myself having to second guess all myself on all those 25 other puzzles to see where I went wrong. Despite my criticisms of the last 10% of the game (really just those last two "end-game" puzzles, I thoroughly enjoyed my time playing Tunic. It was a little slow to start, but once it got its momentum going, I found myself have a hard time putting it down. I was highly engaged and immersed by pulling up the in game map while exploring the game's world. It was always exciting to find a new page of the in game manual in order to learn more about the game, world, puzzles, and where to go next. I loved how the game had tons of puzzles and shortcuts that hid in plan sight. I would definitely recommend this game, even with my reservations with those tedious final puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: A genuinely unique and incredibly creative game, I would recommend you to go in as blind as possible but your reading this so Ill try to keep it simple. it draws heavy inspiration from the classic top down Zelda games but then really steps it up a notch with its puzzles. It's mostly in a made up language and really gives the experience of getting an second hand copy of a game that you can't read so your pouring through images and trying to piece together bits to figure things out, which it really leans into and utilises the fact its not a real manual and is digital while also having perfect looking hand scribbled notes in it.It's hard to talk about what makes the game so special without spoiling the experience, I can however say that so much in this game is hidden in plain sight, a very big part of the game is expanding the players knowledge and regularly challenging what you know. You will run through the early game and think you know everything maybe you found a few secrets, blew up a wall that was neat half way in you will have several realisations about the game and by the end your third eye will be open.The combat is somewhat challenging but honestly after a certain point it felt tedious to me, luckily there is a no fail combat option which normally I wouldn't recommend but I think using it doesn't detract from the main vision/experience of the game so in this instance I would wholeheartedly recommend using it when you feel you've had enough combat, I would recommend to turn it off for the boss fights they all have very quick ways to return to them.All in all, if your looking for a unique game that will stick with you for a long time that is in the vein of The Witness or Fez this game has you covered.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game more than I actually do. If there was a neutral rating between thumbs-up and thumbs-down, I would give it that. But not having that option, I'll go with thumbs-up.I'm not saying it's a bad game, but I feel it has issues that drags it down. I'm not saying I hated it, but I didn't enjoy it as much as I would have liked to.If I had to sum up the game in one word, it is: obtuse. Imagine you've gotten a hold of an NES game and manual, except that they're in Japanese and you can't read Japanese. So you have to interpret, guess, and trail-and-error your way through what the game wants you to do. A lot of info is "in the manual", but since you can't read the majority of the text in the manual, you have to figure out numerous things from pictures and context clues. If you miss an important clue you need at some particular stage in the game, you'll be stuck wasting time. This kind of issue can come up multiple times over the course of the game.I feel like the creator wanted to replicate the experience some of us had of exploring and figuring out a game back in the day, when games didn't force-feed you all the necessary info. But I think that's a goal you can never really reach. Gaming has changed a lot since the 80s when it was expected to beat your head against the wall trying to figure out games. And experiences like figuring out Zelda 1 when I was 8-years-old is not something that can be recreated now that I'm a many decades older adult no longer having endless time to sink into a game.I feel like the creator is also trying to reach a "Nintendo hard" kind of experience. But what was hard for 8-year-old me playing NES games would no longer be hard for adult me. So they've thrown in souls-like mechanics (sparse save points, limited heals, enemies respawn on save, etc). However the combat can be klunky at times, and the souls-like mechanics runs counter to exploring. So it's easy for the game to end up feeling like a tedious slog through enemies rather than a fun adventure.But overall I do think there are many positives to the game. And I appreciate what it attempts to do. However, I could easily see other people having the same experience as me where they find "this isn't as fun as I hoped".

_childDocuments_.review: Atrocious combat completely spoils what is otherwise a gorgeous and actually quite interesting exploration-based puzzler, but even the puzzling elements are made needlessly obtuse by the game's refusal to actually tell you what the things in your inventory are. It puts forward Dark Souls-style 'what if you lost all your money/XP when you die' combat as a key design element, but then doesn't actually let you directly buy stat improvements with it, instead hiding those behind a double-confirm where you can only upgrade if you've found a corresponding coupon to a given stat. Imagine if Legend of Zelda made you spend 200 rupees every time you want another heart container, but also you still have to find the heart container. Combining that with stamina-based rolling and blocking(assuming you even can block; the game actively hides the shield behind several challenges to actually get) and a healing system so obviously inspired by Estus Flasks that it may as well have just called them that results in a player progression that doesn't just feel wonky, it feels actively bent. Boss design feels overly-punitive, with combos that punish you for failing to avoid the first hit by making it impossible to dodge any others, and the gating of upgrades means you can't even grind past a challenging foe. Your own attacks feel unresponsive, difficult to properly range, and there's shockingly little variety to the point the only way the game can make non-boss enemies challenging is throwing big clots of them at you.There's some genuinely good ideas in here, like the main collectible being pages of an actual game manual that give you additional context on the world and mechanics. But it's tied down and ultimately dragged-under by an unnecessary overfocus on combat that isn't rewarding to play and isn't satisfying to beat. It wants to be Zelda Fez Souls, but in trying to serve multiple masters, it ends up serving none of them very well at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely gorgeous visuals which brilliantly update old top down pixel art game-maps. It is very well designed and the controls are excellent, but it's just not a game for me; I don't like the punishingly-difficult willfully unintuitive old-school design philosophy that it is built around.Almost every enemy I encounter in Tunic is likely to kill me, which wouldn't be a problem if I didn't respawn so far way. I spend most of my gameplay sessions racing across the map, dodging enemies to get back to the location I was last exploring. Just figuring out where I am supposed to be going next is very very hard; maybe this area I am killing myself trying to get to isn't even important to explore! Even the mechanics are meant to be obscure, but the game still does a pretty good job at teaching those to you in a smooth intuitive way. Tunic belongs in a genre with the very old Zelda games, where you had to explore and fight through the same area over and over again because the technology didn't have the capability to make a very large map. I don't have the talent or the desire to fight every enemy over and over again, and I don't have the time or desire to canvass the entire map over and over again to figure out how to progress in the game. I kept having to look up walkthroughs and turn the game to no-fail mode in order to progress, and at that point I just wasn't having fun any more, because I didn't feel like I was even playing the game. This game is very well made, and if the genre's what you're into, Tunic is absolutely the best you will find! But despite the cute graphics, it is for a pretty hardcore audience.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely fantastic game! It captures the joy of exploration and discovery that an old school zelda title would hold, while adding tons of modern innovations. The stamina based combat adds a fun layer of challenge to boss battles, and the game gives you plenty of tools to approach bosses in different ways if you don't feel like rolling around so much. The key innovation this game brings to the table is an in game instruction manual that you slowly uncover as you play the game. Without saying too much more, this mechanic elevates this game from just another fun adventure to a unique and treasured memory.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that will make you realise how great some people are at the art of making games. It's a really great experience. Beautiful worlds, controls great, the music is the perfect enabler of the perfect atmosphere for this game... it's a 10/10 kind of game, imo. It's not without a blemish, some of the navigation hinges entirely on the fact it's an isometric view and not a first person view, and the rare enemy attacks have some questionable hitboxes or windups, but that's extremely minor in comparison and you should not let this discourage you even the slightest amount from playing this absolutely excellent game. I think everyone would do well to experience this game. There are a couple of tough bosses toward the end, that you may need to use the 'deal extra damage when on low health' card and stun crystal thing to deplete their health more quickly - like, this shouldn't be the first game you ever play (as beautifully as they nail the joy of exploration and atmosphere in this world) (i mean it would be a great first game to play if not for the fact the latter bosses would destroy you) - but if you've played games for a while, you love the medium, then this game is for you. _childDocuments_.review: A great game. If you fondly recall memories of internet-less age, playing oldschool action adventure games, learning tricks and secrets by reading signs, recognising few words, and analysing pictures within an enclosed intruction book of foreign language, (or you wish to experience such 'thrills'), then Tunic is a game for you. Challenging but not unfair, with subtle environmental story telling, and fantastic, atmospheric soundtrack.It also has those clever moments of "Wait, I could do that since the very beginning?" which makes for an interesting, more varied second playthrough!Btw, the complaints in latest reviews are ridiculous.Especially about combat and exploration - in a game inspired by Souls series and NES Zelda, with metroidvania type world.I do agree the game  seem shallow and simple if you're gonna abandon it after first 20-40 minutes, which goes for most games with this stupid attitude.I never once heard complaints like this in Hollow Knight or straight up Dark Souls.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked Tunic; a lot of work and clever thinking has clearly gone into this game. Aesthetically, it's gorgeous; it plays well and it brings a lot of Metroidvania exploration and replayability. A lot of the puzzles and lore of the game is cleverly weaved together in a way that will gradually unfurl at just the right time for it to make sense, which constantly pulls you along the narrative of the game, almost all of which is not explicitly stated.But I recommend Tunic with some caveats. The combat system is lacking - a lot of the bosses use difficult, sophisticated and punishing attacks, but you lack a moveset or maneuvers that allows you to deal with them. In many cases, I had to rely on good luck and RNG, waiting for bosses not spamming their most unavoidable attacks to get by, because although the game gives a dodge mechanic, it can only be used so many times and what the game lacks is a way of manuevering around the monsters you need to fight with.As well, towards the end of the game, the action takes a backseat to puzzles and lore, unless you're happy with a straightforward, unsatisfying and 'bad' end. These puzzles are obtuse; you absolutely WILL need to go to the Internet; these are not puzzles that can be realistically solved on your own. Even understanding the meaning behind the puzzles requires a significant investment of time - the game comes with its own language and alphabet; it English ultimately, but with its own alphabet, and not just one based on a straightforward substitution of characters. You don't not need to understand it to get through the basics of the game, but you will if you want to commit.As a minor ♥♥♥♥♥♥, a lot of the end-game puzzles require use of the directional pad keys; I play on a PC, with a mouse and keyboard. This is the Only time in the game those keys are used, and if you're not aware of that you'll never stumble on the solution. The controls and positioning of the environments also lends better to a controller, so that's recommended if you have one.Overall, recommended. Tunic is a clever game, enjoyable and doesn't quite outstay its welcome. It's worth the play.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Whilst I can see why people like this game, given my own experience of the game so far, I can't help but feel that 92% positive almost seems like those 9/10 or 10/10 reviews often seen from games journalists. So far, I'm a 4 bosses in and there's not much I can think of that lends to an overall positive experience. To me it seems like a lot of people just like that this game is going back to how old games used to do things. Lots of reviews detail why they think the game is great, so I'm going to go through my gripes with the game. This is really one of those games where I feel like it deserves something in-between a positive and a negative review. If I were to put a number to it, it would probably be something like a 7/10 (on an actual scale out of 10, not a the games journalist scale which only uses the top third). I'd only recommend it if you're looking for this specific kind of game or you can take the gamble when it's on sale for a lower price than it is currently (30% off, £17.49). Jump to the last paragraph for a TLDR.The exploration isn't particularly fun. Nothing that other games haven't already done but with some overdone aspects. Lots of things are hidden from view of the camera, so you just end up sticking to walls all the time to find all the hidden alleys and rooms. Having to do this everywhere isn't particularly fun and dulls down most "aha" moments due to the many things that are hidden this way. To me, this kinda of exploration isn't all that fun. It's exploration turned into busywork, especially when a lot of the rewards for doing it are just money and the occasional consumable. The mystique and intrigue that Zelda dungeons create is quite absent from this game and the bosses don't really do anything to balance that out.The puzzle element is mysteriously absent from this game, despite being tagged as so, unless the dev's idea of a puzzle is trawling through an area just to flip a switch. This game is as much a puzzle game as dark souls is if you consider opening doors from the other side or knocking down a ladder is a puzzle element. I haven't played through the whole game, so maybe all the actual puzzles are later, which is a failing of a game aiming to be and is lauded as a puzzle game.Of the bosses I've encountered, only 1 really felt all that well designed with the others having major issues with the camera that make focusing or moving accurately far more difficult than it should be. Imagine trying to beat a group of enemies whilst your camera is spinning just so it can keep the boss on the same place in view. You have no control of the camera throughout the game and it's just for the cinematic aesthetic and  hiding things out of sight. I'd also recommend turning off depth of field for at least the boss fights. The effect is way overdone and often leaved the boss and the environment blurry unless you're up in its face.The combat overall doesn't feel particularly great. It's relatively basic and of a similar vein to that of Zelda but they've tried to make it more challenging. Personally, I don't find it all that interesting or challenging after you get to grips with the general feel. There's not anything fundamentally flawed about it, just nothing that makes it something I actively want to do more of. Most encounters practically can be attempted the same way with a handful of enemies needing something other than your sword and shield to initiate. I've enjoyed a number of Zelda games, but so far, this game has too much of an emphasis on combat without making it interesting. The game forces you to do things different very infrequently. It's only when you get to boss fights do you actually have to use your brain in a meaningful way. Where in many other games, the encounters you have leading up to a boss will teach you things that are useful when facing the boss. In this game, every boss (of the ones I've faced) have been completely blind and will be the first time you actually need to use core mechanics. To me, this means a significant portion of the real challenge in the boss fights is in learning the mechanics in the middle of a boss fight (or relearning them because you haven't had to use them in a long time). This only creates needless frustration and means the devs could make simpler bosses with the illusion of difficulty.The game takes an old school approach to tutorials in this game, relying on a manual to communicate mechanics, objectives and the like, but the manual is built into the game and you have to collect the pages as you play. The execution of this is mostly well done. You get more pages as you explore. It's one of the few actually meaningful rewards you get for exploring outside of upgrades and equipment. That's not to say it's flawless. At the start of the game, you're given very little direction, aside from a few pages in the manual. This manual is mostly written using pictures and a cryptic unreadable language with the occasional interpretable thing or english word. There's a lot of guesswork that goes into understanding what the manual is going on about and on a number of occasions, I only understood the actual point until I had already done the thing, practically making portions of the manual redundant.The game is also specifically advertises its soundtrack as a point to buy the game. I love a good soundtrack. A good soundtrack can be the cherry on top in a truly awesome game or can save an average game from too many bad reviews. Hollow Knight, Vermintide 1 and 2, Link's Awakening, and Octopath Traveler are a few games that come to mind with great soundtracks. This game's soundtrack is a bit of a let down without even considering those prior mentioned games. It's just okay. It's a bit of background music. It doesn't do all that much to set and maintain the atmosphere. It is truly just an accessory to accompany the rest of the game. It is not a soundtrack that is worth my money.All of this is to say that in my experience, there isn't much to cry home about. It relies on an old school way of designing games which is absent from modern game design and that alone seems to be one of the major features that people love about the game. I think it has plenty of flaws and is far from a perfect game, but people are willing to overlook that because of the different design philosophy used in this game. There's very little hand holding. All the gameplay is reliant on exploration and using your brain when you're stuck. With all that said, I am mostly enjoying the game. It's not amazing but I am entertained and I don't feel like I'm wasting my time most of the time. If what I've said above doesn't sound all that bad to you and you want an exploration/combat game with very little hand holding and some occasional difficulty, then it's probably the game for you. I'd still recommend waiting for a sale though (larger than the 30% at the time of this review).

_childDocuments_.review: At first glace I thought Tunic was just a souls-like Isometric side scroller which sounded fantastic to me. But  I was amazed at how well the game progresses. You start off barely touching any of the controls aside from moving, attacking and dodging. But the game never gives you a controls tutorial. Instead, the world is littered with pages of a retro-like game manual that's written in a weird runic language, save a few words in English. The manual gives you little hints to controls that you didn't know existed, which then lets you progress further.As the game goes on, you find out that you aren't actually playing a side stroller. It turns out the whole world is littered with puzzles that rival The Witness in design, and then you find yourself pulling out a notebook to try and take notes on things you think might be a puzzle.The game is super immersive, the soundtrack is fantastic, puzzles are challenging and make you think, I love the cryptic hint style progression with the manual, and there are so many secrets to discover. I strongly recommend buying this game, and if you can help it don't google the puzzles. There are answers out there, but it's so much more satisfying to take your own notes and figure it out on your own. I really hope to see more like this from Finji, well done!
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, I cannot recommend this game enough. It is a wild ride--as many other reviewers note, it is best to go in blind, so I'll keep things general in this review to avoid spoilers. This game is stuffed full of puzzles and secrets, layers and layers of them. Both the story and the puzzles truly blew my mind at multiple points. As you pick up pages of the "instruction manual" throughout your adventure, more puzzles become clear. Enough hints are eventually dropped that I was able to solve all the puzzles without resorting to looking things up online--other than some of the hidden treasures that are optional and much more difficult than the puzzles you need to solve the game and move forward. This game makes you work for it, to think things through, but still provided enough guidance that I rarely felt frustrated or stuck. It is a truly masterful puzzle experience and I'm not sure what will fill the puzzle void I will have in my life after I finish the post-main storyline extra secret things, because I've never played another game quite like this. On its surface it's a combo of Zelda and Dark Souls. I haven't played much dark souls but I would say this experience is less punishing, as you only lose a small amount of currency if you die, but does have the element of enemies respawning every time you heal/rest. Additionally, in the accessibility menu you can turn on infinite stamina and/or "no fail" mode where you can't die, in case you'd rather focus on the puzzles rather than the combat. Combat is probably the weakest part of this game, and the thing I got most frustrated with at some points. I did have fun with it for a while, but it did get old to me after a bit and can be a little clunky. There is a part in particular where combat gets a bit rough and I did use the "no fail" mode briefly to get past the annoying bits of it so I could continue with my puzzling. There are a few magic items that are fun, but mana is unfortunately quite limited.Overall, this game is truly an experience and you will feel very rewarded for exploration, creativity, and problem solving. Enjoy your adventure!
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: On top of looking and sounding gorgeous, Tunic stands out for its approach to revealing gameplay through manual pages and its layers of secrets in plain sight. Though you often progress by finding an item that opens up new paths, much of what you can do is hidden only by your knowledge of what your character is already capable of and how to look at the game world. It manages to borrow concepts from Zelda, Fez and Outer Wilds without feeling like a re-tread of those games. In some ways it's like someone made the original NES Zelda but was working only off of a description of what it was like.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: When this game was first announced, I remember seeing that it was made by a guy in Halifax (the city I'm from) and I got really excited. The aesthetics really stood out back then and I wanted to throw some support to Andrew and his game. Throughout the years preceding the release, I forgot about the game, but I got into game development myself. I worked in a local game studio and heard about this guy through a bunch of random pipelines of my life. He was still at it.I never met Andrew but I couldn't believe he was still getting funding. I ran into his roommate one time at a bar and he said he was working day and night to bring this thing to life. My coworkers knew him, and I have a friend who is friends with his wife and my god, he was just putting his all into this.By the time the game was getting close to release, Death's Door came out right before it. I remember thinking to myself how I really was itching for a top down action RPG. I wanted to wait for TUNIC but Death's Door just looked so charming so I bit the bullet.It was fine.I left that game thinking, "maybe I just don't like the genre anymore?", It all felt so done already.After years and years of waiting for TUNIC, I just lost all hope. This game was so over-hyped in my life throughout the years of murmurs on the streets and console generations that went by. After Death's Door, I just didn't care anymore.I bought the game around release to support the scene but I let it sit...and boy was that a bad idea.This game is everything.The amount of times my jaw went to the floor. It is charming. It is inventive. It is a passion project where you can feel the amount of time that has gone into it. This is one of the best games I've ever played.You've heard it before, but the way TUNIC hides its secrets is just something that makes me happy.It is a puzzle game, inside a puzzle game, inside another puzzle game. I don't suggest this game if you're not interested in sitting there with a pen and paper sometimes, but that ♥♥♥♥ is for me.So thank you, Drew. Thank you so so much
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: I've been really uninterested in trying new games as of late, but with the cute nature and charm I saw in the previews on steam, I decided to try it out. I was not disappointed. This game had me playing for hours before I took a break each time. Every monster has an appealing design while still holding a respectable tone despite being cartoony.           This game is in every sense a "zelda game." However it feels more punchy and fast paced while still holding onto those key elements of game play by having all those fancy gadgets you get along the way. What I admire about this game is the story. Everything is not a handheld "this is what happened" story telling. You practically piece it all together by finding fragments of an adorable game manual that tells you little hints at just the right time as you progress the game while the world itself tells you what happened. Something that the dark souls series (as this game does adopt mechanics and gets the silly "souls like" tag) did not really do "Here's an item that barely explains anything."          I'm learning what's going on AS I explore each new location, and the next location shows me why the last location is in the condition that it was. i'm around 10 hours in and what I think is the last boss might not even be that. I'm enthralled with this game, and if you're into exploration with a bit of challenge you would be too.      My only real pet peeve about this game though is the perspective i'm sad to say. There's no way to change your camera angle (playing it you can understand why) and it only changes in specific areas as you're walking. With the lighting in certain areas it also makes it hard to determine what's accessible or even where you are exactly.   Overall, however, even with this game not being beaten yet, I can see me playing this game again in the future when I do beat it.

_childDocuments_.review: Everything is amazing!The music, the world, the interactions, the secrets, the way everything just flows together is soooooo nicely done. Tunic just makes you want to explore everything after you find your first secret shortcut and it just feels so good.This is the one time I skip saying "I'm going to wait until this is on sale and buy it". _childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic, I loved the mystery/intrigue of the world and was hooked until I completed it. Honestly one of the better, more compelling games I've played in recent years. And definitely amongst the most clever and creative.(++) Awesome world filled with many, many secrets. It's an absolute joy to discover stuff, and was an even greater joy to see all the layers I missed after I completed it. I got addicted to coming back to it to see what was next(+) Music is excellent. Gets stuck in your head(+) "guidebook" is really cool, and adds to the nostalgia for an earlier era of gaming. No real tutorial, and it works great (mostly)(=) A lot of the gameplay is typical zelda/metroidvania stuff. Not terrible, but a bit rote as a core gameplay loop (i.e. you see heavy bushes, you know you need to unlock some item and come back later to go down that path).(-) I did not enjoy the combat all that much, and its a major part of the game. I think they either needed to reduce the importance of combat (and focus on the puzzle/discovery side); OR make combat feel a lot better. Even having a longer sword might go a long way. A few of the bosses were of particular difficulty for me (which works better in games like Elden Ring or Hades, where the combat is actually decently fun)

I highly recommend it if you like to go through the same areas several times but with new abilities, shortcuts and objects that allow you to find new things. It is not boring at any time.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like an old school Legend of Zelda game (NES, A Link to the Past, Link's Awakening), but with Souls-like dodge, revive and flask mechanics. Combat can be challenging, but difficulty is adjustable for an easier experience. The real meat of the game comes in its willingness to let the player figure everything out for themselves. There are dozens of secrets for you to figure out on your own, with little to no guidance directly given to you (unless you know where to look, that is). And, best of all, the game is a joy to look at. Cute. Adorable even.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: People often compare it to The Legend of Zelda (particularly Link's Awakening, Link to the Past, etc.), combined with the combat difficulty of Dark Souls, and Fez-like puzzles; but while all that is true, it must be emphasised that the game has oodles of unique spins, features, and charms all of its own.Rarely have I played a game as enrapturing as this one. The wanderlust the game instils in you is addictive, the combat is challenging but highly, highly rewarding; the puzzles are tough, but make you feel like Sherlock Holmes when you finally do solve them.It's best played with an XBox controller, and going in as blind as possible. It's very easy to be spoiled on the game! There's secrets and hidden things everywhere, all over the place.The care and attention to detail in this game is astounding, and is truly a tour de force from the sole developer behind it. As someone who's been waiting for the game for all seven years of its development—someone who signed up for the mailing list back when it was still called "Secret Legend," someone who played the demo of TUNIC all the way back at TwitchCon 2017—I can say that the wait was worth it.The soundtrack is fantastic, the art is beautiful, the gameplay is refined.Side note: if you're a Vtuber, this is an excellent game to use dynamic Vtube lighting on! The beautiful lighting of various areas lends itself very well to that effect.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: 9.8/10 Game. Wonderful game for puzzles, combat, open world and story. I enjoyed using the manual as much as it was necessary. Very cool concept as i'd never seen necessary to accomplish puzzles before. :) The style is beautiful and cute. I like the combat mechanics even though i use keyboard.I'm not a fan of back and foreth-ing but i understand that it is like a Legend of Zelda game in that aspect which it took inspiration from. Apart from that layout, the main things it made in similarities are the main charters clothes, some items and the main "triforce". I like that this was chosen to be done as it gives an immediate sense of familiarity and set of expectations to completely destroy once you get into it for its true mechanics. Again 9.8/10 game :D I found it amazingly enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended – 9/10I decided to pick up this game due to the unique graphics and the impression I got that this was some kind of old school Zelda with an updated look.  And at first, it was just that, however I then realized that there was much more to this game.Since there was nothing telling me what the story was, I began coming up with my own narrative on who my character was and what was my goal.  As I continued to play, pieces of the story were revealed in different ways that started filling in gaps and kept driving me to continue.  This eventually led me to discover many more secrets and puzzles within the game that would further flush out the story and help me beat the game.The game’s combat is pretty simple and was easy to get used to.  I do think there quite a bit of a difficulty curve once you get to a boss.  I feel like the bosses almost force you to learn to do certain technique that help you do better in combat.  However, I could never get how to perform a parry.  I got it to work a few times, but it was highly unreliable and sometimes I felt like not being able to parry was making bosses more difficult than they needed to be.  Another thing I found cumbersome about combat was trying to combine powers into new attacks.  I would struggle a lot trying to get these combination attacks to work and wish it was simpler as these would probably have made boss fights easier as well.Some of the puzzles in TUNIC can be tedious to solve and I can’t see this being something everyone would enjoy.  I myself didn’t even realize that the in-game manual could be translated until I read about it online…then I saw the work involved and I was like…NOPE, I don’t have that kind of time.  I do hope there is some effort to make a sequel though as I found this game to be pretty unique and would like to play more.This game also has a new game+ mode that lets you go from the beginning of the game with most of your items and abilities from your previous playthrough.  However, you can’t complete everything from the first playthrough in new game+.Overall, I would recommend this game and I would suggest going into it blind as it is more fun that way.

_childDocuments_.review: I had no idea what I would get myself into by playing this game. I expected a fairly standard Metroidvania experience with lots of difficult combat, backtracking and cute graphics. That's definitely what I got, but this game also delivered in way more fronts than that. Puzzle solving that was executed in a way I haven't seen in any other game yet so far, it got me incredibly hooked all the way through. Amazing soundtrack and a very interesting and surprisingly deep story.Don't expect much replay value out of it, but by the end of it, you'll definitely be craving for more like it.An absolute masterpiece of a game. Unbelievable to think this was for the most part conceptualized and realized by a single developer. Can't wait to see what comes next.

_childDocuments_.review: The gimmick of this game is that you know nothing about it at the start (so don't look it up!), except the movement controls. But you're controlling a cute fox who's ready for an adventure, so you go on one anyway and decide you'll learn as you go.This game is phenomenal - I had so many jaw-drop moments as I discovered something new, and it goes through so many different genres! _childDocuments_.review: I have never in my 3 years of playing games from steam have i EVER written a review on a game, yet i feel strongly that this game deserves one. Prepare to die and rage a lot. You can improve your stats but only up to a certain point.If you are not good at that type of quick reflex game and pattern recognition, in the late game you will have no choice but to activate the "no fail option" in the menu. Unfortunately doing so takes away all the interest of the progression system.I recommand the first part of the game (it was wonderful).I don't recommand the last part of the game (it is a nightmare if you don't have the skills).

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool game, it was about what I expected it to be. I had a few issues with it but I'll start with the pros first.Pros:Exploration is really cool. My favorite thing about this game by far is how the game introduces the mechanics to you... or rather you introduce them to yourself. Finding a new page of instructions is like finding money on the floor. You can't help but wonder what new possibilities are in store.This is more of a loor heavy rather than story heavy game. One of those games like hollow knight where you could beat the entire game and still have no idea what's going on. I think it gives it a nice charmThe game does not hold your hand unless you want it to be held. For the main story at the very least, you can easily complete it without help or guides, and every time you discover something for yourself, it feels really good.ConsIt feels like combat was sacrificed a little bit to fit the art style. It feels clunky and the 2.5D aspects of the game makes it difficult with the way the camera will move in a boss fight. Attack tells are pretty lacking, and blocking just doesn't work unless you're a second earlyThis may be personal, but I did not like the stamina mechanic much at all. I understand that many souls likes have some sort of poise bar that drops so you can't block everything, but this bar also takes away your ability to dodge, sprint, and evade too. I think personally this game would benefit to have dodge rolling and sprinting separate from block stamina.End game exploration for me was really boring really fast. Some of the puzzles in the game are really satisfying and really fun, and I can't think of much if any puzzles that were just down right bad. But by the end of the game even before I finished the main story I found myself just wanting to watch guides or shortcuts to get it over with. Once everything had been explored, I wasn't intrigued enough to keep finding all of the in depth secrets on my own.Basically, I really did enjoy the game. I do highly recommend it. Really fun exploration, decent combat, good story. For those who are wondering about the difficulty of puzzles, main story stuff is easy. If you're like me and you want to 100% the game, don't get discouraged if you can't do it all by yourself. It's a lot like FEZ, in the sense that the community worked together until all of the peaces were in place. I doubt anyone could find the solutions to every puzzle by themselves without at least a little bit of help. I would recommend looking up hints first and then look up answers as a last resort, unless you just want the achievements with the least amount of effort.One more tip for my 100% people out there: look up missable achievements before playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Depending on whether or not the controls sit well with you, it can be a very frustrating game.Controls/Movement doesn't feel good. It doesn't feel very responsive. I don't think it's any technical issue, more of a design choice that doesn't sit well with me. A lot of things don't feel very intuitive. You run to a ladder or some other intractable object and press A but nothing happens because you have wait for the popup to come up. You don't roll when it feels like you should've have. You have I-frames on roll but sometimes it seems like it doesn't matter if the attack goes through you then you get hit. The camera moves around constantly in boss fights, making it very difficult to control your character. The bosses' attack connects if the attack animation moves over your character even if in the 3D space you feel like you were behind it. It is very difficult to judge the reach of your weapon and most of the time you miss and then move painfully slowly to catch up as the dodge and run button are the same and happen in sequence.Overall very frustrating. I know many would just jump with the phrase "Git gud" but I don't particularly care, and I have seen others having similar issues. I guess it's just not very well suited to me, even though I like soulslikes, metroidvania, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is cute, the soundtrack is from lifeformed (dustforce), the in-game guide idea, the nostalgia and recipe are good.However :- The combat is poorly designed, with slow animations, a single 3 hits combo, a slow and unresponsive dodgeroll (which doesn't animation cancel), a ineffective block, and a parry with a 2 second delay. - Enemies' AI is annoying and dumb as hell, enemies (bosses mostly), will backdash repeatedly until cornered. Note that your reach is ridiculously low, which will ensure you won't be able to hit any monster that behave like this. - The mana system is plain bad, there are only three way to replenish mana : use a consumable which are limited in supply, kill some specific enemies that drop small amount of mana, or rest at a statue and reset all enemies. Which make it so you won't use spells for most of the game.- I found navigating the world frustrating with dead ends and blocked paths all over the place, often requiring one or more items, so be prepared to constantly backtrack. - The devs decided to use the dumbest way to hide secrets : abuse the camera angle. There are countless shortcut or hidden passages exploiting the camera's dead angle. This is annoying and cheap as hell. You will have to hug every walls if you want to find everything.- The puzzle are either trivial or a complete pain in the ass. - Almost everything is written in giberrish, including NPC interaction, which I found more lazy than interesting. I honestly wouldn't recommend this game. The cons far outweigh the pros.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't particularly know what I can say about TUNIC that doesn't feel like an inherent spoiler of some sort. What I will say is simply this. _childDocuments_.review: This game is worthy of much praise. It is very much like a Zelda game but has much more to offer in the ways of both action and puzzles. You will be required to identify attack patterns in combat and be able to quickly react in order to succeed. In some cases the bosses can be tough, but once you pick up on their pattern nothing is too frustrating. It never explicitly tells you where to go and at times only exploration and a good memory will help you continue in the right direction. There is a lot to collect making the game like a treasure hunt in more ways that normal.Where the game shines is the mystery behind many of the concepts and features of the game as well as most of the puzzles. The items you find in game will put together a cryptic notebook of vague hints to game features, clues to puzzles, as well as the game lore. Many of these puzzles are like decoding ciphers and secret code. Half of which are simple while the other half will make you feel dumb. While I praise this aspect of the game, i was left stumped and wasted a few hours trying to figure out some of the puzzles on my own. Some of these answers are extremely cryptic and nearly impossible to figure out without outside help. I could say some of the solutions were so far out there it makes completing the game in a traditional sense impossible, but I would also argue they are also some of the most clever I have ever seen.The graphics in the beginning are quite simple and the game isn't too flashy. Before long you are seeing a much more detailed world like some very nice visual effects. The cute polygonal style of the game is very fitting for the setting. The music was very mellow and tame for most of the game. The music does not distract from gameplay or get annoying being in the same area for long periods. I highly recommend this game is you enjoy action adventure games, lots of brain teasing puzzles, and a cute game with lore that keeps the story simple but solid. The best part is if the game is too physically challenging, there are in-game options that will turn off the difficulty. If you hate puzzles know that most of them aren't even required to beat the basic portion of the game, and there are so many guides that will answer every question and give a location to every item so completing the game 100% isn't a chore.I give this game a 9.5 out of 10 because of everything it does right. While some might think the price is steep, I could argue that it rivals competing name brand AAA game titles or the same genre/style.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: This game is something else.Tunic has learned from and built upon it's predecessors. It's hard to say Tunic is "inspired" by Zelda or Dark Souls, because at this point those games are just a part of its DNA. Really, Tunic was created from the lessons learned by games like Hyper Light Drifter and Death's Door.Tunic is best experienced blind, it shares a quality with Outer Wilds, where learning the game is part of the experience. With that in mind, a rundown of what to expect is: The start of the game is *very* Souls-like, with a slow transition to a more Zelda feel as you progress. Then puzzles start to become more crucial, and the game feels very much like Fez.Tunic is an easy recommendation. It's clever, beautiful, and fun to play. It's a celebration of games and the people who play them.

_childDocuments_.review: This game goes WAY deeper than I thought it would. At first I thought it was a cute top down adventure tribute to Zelda, but Tunic evolves into so much more than that.
