_childDocuments_.review: Ahhh, this one could have been something special. Could have been the one that brought balance to the force and finally give us some front mission goodness dressed in tasty looking combat system. But alas, it's just a mirage.The game will trick you (it certainly tricked me to play it for almost 20 hours) into thinking it has more to offer than it really has. Nice intro cut-scene, voice-overs in the tutorial sections, mission structure the works, and then...just one of the most bland sandbox territory conquest I've ever seen.The  robots are good looking I guess (at least some models) but they offer pathetically little in terms of customization, essentially trying to find balance between heat generation, armor and speed suitable for that role, which is essentially simplified into literally what weapon you're wielding. Guys, the idea was already there, you could have just taken it for ♥♥♥♥ sake. Either go hard points like battle tech or allow shoulder carried missiles, shields etc that front mission sported. Why the ♥♥♥♥ would you miss opportunity to allow pilots to gain experience? To have skills. For ♥♥♥♥ sake front mission did 3 decades ago.It's so ridiculous it's not part of the package as the game begs for it. there's more things to be said, unpolished UI, inconsistent AI etc etc, but in all honesty not worth going into too much detail.The bottom line is simple, this one needed A LOT of more work, and I mean A LOT. But it could have been the one.maybe it still can if they provide some crazy level of DLC goodness, or at least modding support. But I doubt it. I feel the way prologue is designed is purposefully misleading and a little bit scummy. To developers, I cannot believe you blew something that had this much potential. Hire some people who can actually put some meat on this thing and go back to work.

_childDocuments_.review: The base tactical game is solid and it's a really cool spin-off for the tactical RPGs, but lacks polish, balance, performance optimization and most importantly meaningful strategic progression. After some time you see all the game has to offer and you're going through the same motion over and over again, it gets repetitive really quickly, as the strategic mode doesn't evolve or provide any interesting context from one fight to the next. Needless to say the campaign has not replayability.The coolest part of the combat - the melee weapons are extremely limited in diversity and janky to play, it's a coin toss between missing the enemy, colliding with the enemy, which could stun your mech or doing a one shot kill of one or several opponents.The base upgrade tree is extremely boring - most of it is increase speed by 15%, increase visibility range by 15%, increase energy by 10... No pilot progression or XP. The mechs are completely customizable, which however means that there's zero identity to them. Creativity comes from limitations, if there are no limitations to how a mech could be built such as different classes of mechs they loose meaning. I don't care, if I loose a mech, it's just a bundle of parts that I can easily put on another frame. Given the history of the devs and how slow they're releasing content I don't see them fixing even a fraction of all the issues in the game. I guess they're too busy figuring out their pronounces. I can't really recommend the game at this price point.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite games of the year so far. This has been on my radar for the last 5 years as a massive mech fan, and although development looked rough for a while, they took a ton of player feedback and the game has launched in an incredible state. Little to no bugs, incredibly high quality animations, a nice soundtrack, and event text bursting with emotion, Phantom Brigade's only flaw is its almost non-existent story, which only serves as a basic rationale for why you're playing the game. But you're a mech fan. You know what you're here for.The game's super innovative turn-based/real-time time rewind gameplay system is one of the coolest takes on turn based games I've ever played, and it makes you feel like you're creating your own Pacific Rim action scene in every turn. Couple with a customization system that is a cross between Armored Core and Battletech, and you have an incredibly robust mech experience. In a time where mech games are few and far between more than ever, Phantom Brigade stands tall as one of hallmarks of how fresh the genre can still be even after all these years.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not all that far in, but in the few hours I have played the game has been very promising.At its core, Phantom Brigade is a mech combat game pitting you against AI controlled mechs. It has an overworld map with enemy patrols and sectors you can move around to liberate, while replenishing your forces and upgrading your units (as well as you main mobile base). Mechs are customizeable and can be upgraded with parts you salvage from your battles to fulfill various roles, and parts themselves can have a wide variety of effects and upgrades applied to them to keep builds unique. The meat of the game is in the combat aspect, and I find it quite enjoyable. You effectively play in five second rounds, with you and the AI moving simultaneously. However - the important part of this is that you can see what your enemies are planning to do in that time, and this allows you to effectively read the future and micromanage your units for maximum efficiency. You can see when an enemy with a missile launcher is going to fire, so plan a move to have your unit being targeted dash behind a tall building right before they hit. You can see when an enemy will come around a corner and into range, so plan to hit them with your sniper rifle right as they do. This leads to some really tense moments and really good gameplay, and while you are frequently outnumbered and outgunned you always have a chance due to this system.Mechs can be damaged in combat, limiting their effectiveness, such as losing their arms/weapons or being slowed to a limp by leg damage. This applies to both the enemy and to your own mechs, and while you cannot target specific parts of enemy units you can still utilize their weaknesses in a strategic manner. For example - enemies are weak to impact attacks from behind, shields can only be held up for so long in one go, and you can circle around to the weak side of enemies to get extra damage on them.In 7.7 hours, I have done the little tutorial area, and fought quite a few battles in the zone after that but am nowhere near conquering it. The game has about 20 or so more zones at least after this one, and I have managed to build up four mech units (you only start with two) by this point. I have a sniper with an augmented rifle and close quarters precision SMG if needed, who can jump into position to hide. I have a marksman unit with a burst shotgun secondary attack for enemies that get too close, with its very high mobility allowing it that option. I have a unit with a burst shotgun primary and a shield that dashes in and out of close quarters combat, usually running down pesky enemy snipers. I have a missile launcher extremely heavy mech that can provide constant firepower upon the enemies, with a heavy shield that can be utilized if it ever is in danger.All in all, I recommend it if you are into this kind of game. It is very well presented and has a very good core gameplay loop.Edit: After a few more hours, my review still stands. However, I will say that this game does have a few minor annoyance. The UI can sometimes be a bit rough to navigate - it lacks granular controls for certain things like telling your mechs to "Wait," so you sometimes will need to fiddle with things to get what you want. The writing sometimes comes across as a bit amateurish, but the game is clearly crafted with love. I also lament the fact that there doesn't seem to be much in the way of progression for your pilots - they have traits and such but they don't see to actually develop in any way, and this is a huge missed opportunity I hope they improve upon in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Specifically due to the unique concept, I give it a thumbs up. The main highlight of the game, synchronous tactical battles, looks very fresh and intriguing. It appears quite spectacular and dynamic, considering each turn lasts for only 5 seconds. It's a pity that the developers didn't include a feature to review the entire successful battle. Nevertheless, observing the battles here is quite interesting!However, during the cleanup of the third location, I realized how much grinding here. Out of 5 hours of gameplay, about 1.5 hours are retries. There are a bit too many attributes, which makes the game's balance somewhat fragile, requiring careful study of each characteristic. After each battle, you acquire new items and start everything anew. Also, I couldn't quite get used to the controls; even though the editor seems simple, what you intend to do doesn't always get realized immediately, which adds frustration to the experience.Apparently, I wasn't in the right mood to play it.I don't regret purchasing and trying it. Perhaps I'll return here in a year. But I would like to see more projects like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: Aight, lets start with the bad first:- Weapon balance is wonky, you will find weapons that are fantastic (missile launchers) and weapons that suck (canons). They will dominate your choices for mech design and make some AI encounters feel terrible.- Melee is... to call it a learning curve isn't accurate, it's a cliff. Suddenly it works and you feel like a god.- While I ran into the last map about 30 hours in, 90% of them I had seen and replayed endlessly by hour 20.- Some spawns can feel unfair, imo this is balanced by the fact some spawns are downright unfair to the AI.- There's not really any curveballs in combat, no differences from hour 5 to hour 45 of combat.the TL;DR here is if any of these issues look like deal breakers, its probably not for you. This game relies on the "15 seconds of fun" concept far more than most and if that 15 seconds is not fun for you at hour 2 it won't be any more fun at hour 20 or hour 45.That said, for the love of god it grabbed me. That 15 seconds had me enraptured for all 51 hours of my first play-through, one that cleared the map and did basically everything you could do in the game on the standard difficulty. Hence why I still recommend it, if you enjoy every time you get into combat even if it seems repetitive on the surface this game will grab you and you will have an absolute blast.Said combat is challenging at first, but once you understand the gimmick and start to learn to use cover and attack intervals to your advantage you'll begin walking your way through enemies. Discovering good squad design is key, knowing which mechs pair well together and what sets you up to absolutely dominate the AI regardless of the engagement. The loop of raiding, getting more supplies, slowly upgrading your mechs, trying out new parts, and going at it again is fantastic. I was jumping from province to province excitedly looking forward to the next fight wondering what I could get at the end of it.The music is good. I won't say its amazing, you're going to be listening to the same tracks a lot but they're all really fitting for when they play and act as wonderful indicators of how you're doing in combat, but thats not the only thing you'll encounter in the overworld.If you want a game that fleshes out a world with the tiny things, this is it. I won't speak much on them so as to not spoil them but the little events you have a chance of running into add a flavor to the game that I genuinely don't recall running into anywhere else. It's refreshing, but also helps enrapture you in the world, making the nation and its people something you care about despite rarely actually interacting with them.As I said before, if the bad is a deal breaker, then thats understandable. The game isn't perfect by any means. But if by chance you do want to give it a shot, you have the chance to find gold here. (I know I did)

_childDocuments_.review: Phantom BrigadeA fun, but slightly shallow turn-based tactics, mech-combat game with a pre-planning style combat system.Also, what's up with games set in an occupied Sweden-like nation that's been taken over by high-tech machines? Swear this is the third game I've played that's like this.The game has you follow a resistance group of mech-piloting Swedes hell-bent on taking their home back from The Evil Swedes (or something, fifteen hours in and I still don't really have any idea 'who' the invaders are). You'll slowly push into occupied territory, fighting enemy patrols and raiding enemy patrols and bases while you slowly liberate your home back using your prototype tech and the local resistance Home Guard, who're actively fighting alongside you (though don't actually make any progress unless you step in and save their ass every single time they get into a fight).Gameplay boils down to two 'loops'. The metagame/overworld map, where you control your little squad of mechs around, using the radar to discover new targets and patrols, with some minor crafting and decent mech-customization, along with a few little bits of gameplay elements. Then, when you engage an enemy patrol or base, you'll swap into the actual turn-based combat mode, in which you will pre-plan five-second intervals of your actions. Movement, firing, taking cover, boosting, blocking, etc, while also being shown the enemy's next five seconds of movement, letting you pick the best angles or pre-fire certain angles, or force enemies to friendly-fire themselves by knowing which of them are targetting which of your mechs, or where they'll be walking, and so on. It's a neat system, if a little cumbersome to get used to at the beginning. It's really, really grown on me. I've thoroughly enjoyed the system, since it lets me do some cinematic, perfectly-timed coordinated moves that'd be ♥♥♥♥ you'd see on a high-budget mecha anime or movie.Now, where the game is a little 'shallow' in my opinion, is in regards to it's progression systems and customization. The painting is alright. Could certainly be improved, but it's serviceable. There is no pilot progression. I've been deploying the same four pilots for fifteen hours, and I've yet to see them 'upgrade' or skill-up, or otherwise improve. Despite the game saying to the contrary, as far as I can tell- there's basically no real pain in losing a pilot beyond purely sentimental "Oh, well, I've had him for sooo long", along with the cost of buying a new pilot. Mech customization is the biggest pain, though. You have three tiers of parts: Light, medium, and heavy. Along with three rarities: Common, uncommon, rare. Both legs are considered one part, each arm is its own part, and the torso is its own part. That's a total of four parts. Then, you can pick between a primary, and secondary weapon, such as a shotgun primary, and a missile rack secondary. Or a machine gun primary, and a mini-shotgun secondary, and so on. The weapon selection is actually pretty decent, but... That's all you get... Unless you're using Uncommon or Rare parts, which allow you to add additional little bonus parts ONTO each part. For example, a rare leg lets you choose whether you use heavy armor, light armor, completely strip out some of its armor, or some other thing. Torso pieces let you choose which generator and thruster to use- but the differences aren't very noticeable, especially on torsos that don't naturally have good heat management. Most of these mods/attachments mostly have a benefit or downside of 5-20%, and don't really radically change how a weapon can be used. And most of them are kinda ♥♥♥♥.While all the mech customization is important- what has the largest affect on gameplay is weight, and weapon choice. Weight affects speed (Which, obviously, lets you move more or less per turn depending on how high or low it is). Weapon choice affects how often you're able to attack, at what ranges, with how much accuracy, and how much damage you inflict. Some weapons are better than others, for sure. The game definitely needs a decent bit of balancing done to it. Assault rifles are hilariously weak. Shotguns are middlingly alright. Sniper rifles kick ass, but rely on other friendly mechs to draw aggro, as sniper rifles have a minimum effective range- meaning if anything is within it, your rifle suffers a massive accuracy penalty, forcing you to use your secondary, or reposition. Machine guns are very powerful- provided you're willing to tank, or nothing's targetting you. For a rather long burst, you get a fairly heat-efficient attack that deals plenty of damage. The various missile launchers are pretty alright, especially since they're one of the few weapons (early game, atleast), that don't require direct LoS to fire. The various melee weapons... Are heavily map-dependent, but generally on the weaker side. The ones I've found take the primary slot, and kinda require you to play a light-armor mech in order to close the distance quickly enough to start dealing damage soon enough to be worthwhile, especially since many missions have timers before reinforcements can potentially arrive. Generally, the mix of weapons I've seen so far are pretty interesting and varied.Also, one thing that sucks, but isn't gamebreaking, is that there's no real 'replay' mode. You can replay the five seconds of the turn you just finished- but you can't replay the entire mission in real-time, which sucks. It's not going to kill the game for me, but it'd certainly be nice to review an entire mission in real time. Whether to see where you could've improved- or just for the sake of spectacle- since the game DOES look good.Despite my complaints- the game is still solid fun even at release. If given a round of updates, content additions, and rebalancing, I can definitely see it becoming one of the better tactics games we've had in a long while.

name: Robonauts
detailed_description: The beloved game that was originally released only for the Nintendo Switch console is coming to PC gamers now! Learn the story of Robo and help him save the galaxy, alone or together with family and friends. Welcome interplanetary traveler! In a nutshell, Robonauts is that arcade game which includes 12 levels. Each level will challenge you. You will explore a universe which consists nearly 50 planets, facing Bosses and creatures and meeting powerful opponents bent on universal destruction. Who will you be (literally)? Robo is a little robot whose curiosity got the better of him and led to his sudden exit from the confines of his safe environment. Now little Robo is far from home, fighting for his life against a constant barrage of enemies. When developing Robonauts, we chose to give Robo human traits based on our own emotional experience. Robo acts like you and I, and we sense his emotions when has to choose between sides in a battle, trying to figure out who the good guys are. Once you get to know him, it’s hard not to love Robo. Universe! While the game is very dynamic, you get to choose your tempo of gameplay. A lot of troubles await you on every planet. We have tried to fill Robo’s universe with enough graphically various worlds that everyone who plays can find a unique favorite to which they can return. The graphics in this game are truly spellbinding. And the color scheme makes the game enjoyable for both kids and the kid inside every adult who remembers what it was like to spend a day in the arcade. We really wanted to recreate the experience of the best arcade games from our childhood, so to pass a level, you have to jump between mesmerizing planets and destroy every opponent that stands in your way. Really, there are no words to adequately describe the Robonaut universe. Music - the best for last Game soundtrack composer, Simon Viklund. Yes the same Simon Viklund who worked on PAYDAY series and Bionic Commando Rearmed!!! His music exemplifies the very essence of Robonauts – dynamic, retro, arcade-style, energizing. What Simon has created is not only music for our game, but also the perfect soundtrack to your life - if you're just like us, that is. FEATURES: - great for the whole family, - solo and local co-op - local versus mode - 12 unique planetary systems, - large variety of weapons and enemies, - explosive art style and graphics, - epic music composed by Simon Viklund, - easy-to-learn yet challenging gameplay, - 2 difficulty settings: casual and hard.

name: Necromunda: Underhive Wars
detailed_description: Deep below the nightmarish, polluted hive cities of Necromunda, in the twisted, vertiginous, dark tunnels of the Underhive, rival gangs fight to the bitter end for personal power, wealth, survival and the honour of their Houses. Only the strongest survive. Lead, customize, and grow your gangs of Escher, Goliath, and Orlock. Specialize each member and send them to battle in hazardous dystopian environments. Exploit the terrain in tactical gunfights: climb raised walkways to take advantage, set traps, and ambush foes to force them into bloody melee engagements. Learn new skills, loot equipment and bring your evolved gang to 4-player online gang fights. Lead and evolve your gangs in this compelling tactical-RPG Follow a rich narrative campaign in the Underhive Engage in immersive and persistent game modes First video game adaptation from mythical tabletop game Necromunda, the most famous Hive World of Warhammer 40,000 Play solo or join thrilling 4-way online gang fights

_childDocuments_.review: Look, let's be honest.  This is not X-Com or Phoenix Point, it's not what you call a traditional tactical game. It's a digital adaptation of a tabletop miniature game that has been played by hobbyists for 3 decades. Critic reviews are already not liking the game but that's because you can tell they never played the tabletop game. It's a niche game for a niche group.  One review writes:"The gang customization and sandbox mode/operations will be a treat if you’re into that content. However, since it doesn’t tie into the story and knowing that the campaign itself is forgettable, you’re looking at two disconnected modes that could’ve been combined to make the progression and narrative more entertaining. "That's everything that makes Necromunda the game it is! The single player story is fine enough, it serves as a small introduction to a vast wealth of underhive lore and game mechanics.  THE game is the sandbox mode with operations, missions with 2-4 AI/Humans, seeing your team level up, getting new gear from the missions, losing people, getting injuries that give your team members personality, having those crazy stories where your juvie takes out a heavy and steals his gun against all odds.  This game is the mordheim engine with some benefits but it oozes Necromunda.  Do I recommend it to non tabletop Necromunda players?  Probably not, it's not an X-Com game, it's a digital Necromunda for good or bad and I'm loving it.

Despite being an older and abandoned product, it's much better than this one in SO many ways...

_childDocuments_.review: Currently after not quite 4 hours I cannot recommend this game. If you want something more engaging in story and mechanics I´d suggest the predecessor Mordheim: City of the Damned.At this point the only praise I have for this game is that the AI seems to be better than inMordheim, but that´s it.I´ll revisit this review and build upon it if something more comes to mind and I remember.Not worth the money,.UPDATE:Not quite six hours in and I´d really would like to refund this game.It´s pretty to look at but then I could just take out my minis instead.Main souces of salt:You have to see all the actions the characters take. It´s like looking at someones vacation video of a walk in some unpictoresque town. And everytime someone does a buff there is an animation. I´d wager that more than half of the game time is taken up by animations that are mindnumbingly annoying after the second time they do them.As in Mordheim, against AI, Never split the group and high ground is key. There is no kind of defensive stance, which is odd for a game that´s built to have both melee and ranged. For ranged you can crouch and try and hide.In the story mode the arena fight against the champion can just go and ♥♥♥♥ off.Stay tuned for my next rage induced outpouring of distain.

_childDocuments_.review: Mordheim with less rats, more guns, and better voice acting.This is an improvement over Mordheim in every way, and there is a lot more polish than I thought there would be at launch. I played and loved classic Necromunda on the tabletop, and I enjoyed Mordheim by this same studio (warts and all), but to be honest I was skeptical that this would be any good. My expectations have been exceeded.I haven't experienced any of the crashes that others have reported. Other than that, there are the usual basic launch day problems/bugs, and there are the usual balance and AI issues you see with games like this. The developer has been super responsive to complaints and feedback on Discord, so it seems like it's getting the support it needs.I truly do not think this game deserves the level of vitriol it's getting here. "Not even beta" and "early access at best"? Get real, get the heck out of here with that. Some people are absolutely raging mad because they have to watch AI turns and plasma doesn't melt a dude's face clean off his skull and House Cawdor isn't flooding the map with cheap units and etc and blah.  I don't want to invalidate anyone's frustration, but maybe put down the friggin' gasoline can for a minute. Yeah, there are some balancing issues and some UI problems, but this is already more than any reasonable Necromunda/40k fan would expect at this price, and it's just going to get better with updates.Cut scenes are incredible, the synthcore bgm is fantastic, movement and combat make so much more sense than in Mordheim, the scenarios are great. It has that same punishing flavor as Mordheim. Necromunda steps up acting like it's gonna hold your hand through a nice long tutorial, but instead it just shoves you into a burning building and runs away laughing. It's got no bugs or balance problems that can't be patched, and the issues that do exist are fully livable until then. If you kinda liked Mordheim but you thought it was a little clunky and wish it had more flamers and boltguns, pick this up and give it a spin.
_childDocuments_.name: Necromunda: Underhive Wars

_childDocuments_.review: Long ramble below, the TL;DR is: If you enjoy the setting and liked Mordheim, you should enjoy this and it will only improve with some patches and future DLC.Long ramble in 3...2...1...So, elephant in the room: The AI. It is derpy and makes mistakes often at the starting operation and then after if you are playing low difficulties. The highest 2 difficulties are MUCH closer to Mordheim level of aggression and play.Something odd about the early difficulties AI isn't even how they derp about the map, ignore what seem prime targets or accidentally gas themselves and co-workers. It is outside of the battles - if you get a strong start, wipe the whole team and ensure you pillage EVERY weapon they are holding then most likely, they will not buy replacements and you will be fighting what equates to a fist-toting scavenger party for the rest of that operation - they will just go to grab the items and Extract! I felt bad enough when the objective was to kill each other and/or extraction was banned (even more so when I raided their HQ) and they could only thump their puny fists and feet against my armour-clad murder-machines as I wiped them by the end of round 2.Other complaints I have seen have been about the long time-to-kill and seemingly wet-noodle attacks. This is ONLY in the beginning when you are using the beginner (Tier1) items and armours. Time To Kill will be much closer to table-top by the time you are using/facing Tier3 across the board and every play/mistake will result in someone dying (unless a tanky Brawler) when Tier5 is the majority.The maps are cool and have plenty of opportunity for playing different styles - especially if you play to the House strengths.The gang development, levelling and ranking up is superior to Mordheim, it has evolved and improved. The visuals are a massive step-up too.♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that could benefit from patching:No dodging animation - you can avoid the damage but the visual will still have you taking a heavy/bladed/cutty thing to the face and a blood-splatter.Glitches for collecting items for objectives - it is infrequent and tends to only affect 1 of your gang at a time. Annoying but not enough to make me spew bile and shoot fire from my fingers.Disconnects - I have had one disconnect, but have spoken with a lot of people playing that have not been so fortunate. I logged back in and it had autosaved the turn before, no great loss.Ambush/Overwatch tuning - Ambush is terribly unreliable in current iteration - overwatch triggers when they move more than a few steps within your engagement bubble, works better.Final thoughts - once your gang is established (Tier4 with some Tier5s and at least rank 8 on everyone) then this game really starts to shine and require planning, forethought and a little luck. I personally enjoy the early stages when building a gang, but can see why some enjoy it less whilst they are impatient for the 'true' sense of the game. I just hope we don't have to wait too long for the next gangs - I imagine I will do 2-3 iterations of each House gang we have now before I start feeling desperate for new stuff :)

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is nice, a little balancing here and there might be required, but else good.There's quite a lot of bugs, but lets just hope they get fixed asap.HOWEVER, the story is boring, you get fixed characters to play with, meaning there's no way to specialise, and there's no difficulty option, in case you're having a hard time, and you swap between the gangs too much (I've only reached story mission 5, but have already swapped gang once and get's fustrated with the lack of abilities, after having played operations).OPERATIONS and MULTIPLAYER is where the games strengths are, you customise your own gang, train them up, give them the abilities YOU want, and see them grow and get hurt, and maybe even see your hard work disapear, because they can also die, making it feel much MUCH more personal.I would've personally prefered if the story was instead done with YOUR OWN gangs, so you could train and prepare between missions (to balance it, you could simply not get any rewards, but in return, you should not lose anything if failing).While operations are the better part, it still needs working, more diffrent types of missions, more options here and there, and more different gear would be more than welcome.So in short, story missions sucks (can't speak for the story STORY, yet)Oerations and multiplayer is the best partSome gameplay needs to be balanced a bitBugs needs to be fixedAnd more content is not just welcome, but needed.At the moment, it's not worth full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really enjoying this game. It suffers from a lot of the jankiness that Mordheim (dev's previous title) had and it is obvious they didn't learn enough lessons from that game's shortcomings this time around. But I was having fun nether-the-less. It is addictive to theory-craft the different possible gang builds and having fond memories of the tabletop version from ages past doesn't hurt either.However, there are a lot of bugs. Some make the SP campaign pretty much unplayable. But it's levelling up your own gang and building something formidable to troll your friends with that appeals, so i could look past them mostly. But then I was hit with the reset infamy bug. _childDocuments_.review: So lets start with the good.This is not a bad stab at bringing the new table top version of Necromunda to the PC - however that is part of the origin of some of its short comings.Graphically it looks ok, with some well thought through arenas and solid character work and some good environmental, lighting and effects work.The mehIts slow, this is very much not a fast play!Progression mechanics don't 'feel' that meaningful especially in terms of equipment.The world feels empty - if the various cut scene's didn't point out that a hive world is meant to be teaming with humanity you'd be forgiven for thinking that the gangs are few and sparse. There are some level design touches that try to give the impression of some level of inhabitedness (and some concept art in loading screens) but it dosn't really got that far and dosn't sell that the place is anything but abandoned.Weapons are  mostly flavour with little to pick between them.Gang size being limited to 5 is probably due to the way the new tabletop game works, in the original one of the choices that you had was to go tall or wide in terms of gang composition. In this iteration you take 5 gangers, due to the action economy if you -do not- have 5 gangers you will get squished easily as there isn't reeeeallly the ability to go Tall with abilities or kit. Every gang is basically a box. The gang hide out / operations mechanic is meh - its a real shame. The bad:As others have commented the AI is as thick as a plank making really dumb choices - but not in a dumb person way, in an inexplicable broken way. For example you will see Brawlers ignore opponents -right next to them- in favour of running around the map and spamming various other abilities (other than strike). It is cripplingly dumb. TBH its probably trying to do something complicated but this is not working in terms of gameplay. It would be signficantly better to acctually have a much simpler set of AI routines that at least would not be so painfully thick. Or if the developer wanted to do something interesting open it up to the community?Its buggy, mostly with crashes back to desktop, There are some weird graphical glitches (vibrating camera due to environment intersections) and wacky physics. Its a real shame as the IP is interesting and the developers obviously are talented, as it is -ok- . But it could have been something special.If you liked their previous titles and/or the new table top game you'll probably get on with this, if not maybe avoid for the moment or pickup in a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: How to review a game without being a fanboy? well let's try to consider the facts, this game wants to be a turn based strategy game with HQ and Teams progression system based on loot, skills, stats and scavenging.As a strategy game turn based it uses a fluid movement system ,that means you move freely by X meters depending on how proficient the character you're moving is, and you have a pool of 2 different meters to perform actions and tactical skills.So far so good yes? Well the problem is that, despite the depth in every single aspect of the system on paper, the gameplay is atrociously bad.Why is that? Well because they made a dumbed version of a TT game, that doesn't even feel like a PC strategy game because everything has to be dumbed down to a point it makes every system absolutely irrelevant.You see in Mordheim you had a way to perform zone control and crowd control, and this thanks to the fact that characters moving in an influence area of an enemy would get stuck in melee combat, if they were to disengage their offensive and movement capabilities would have been debuffed if not totally removed in favour of a retreat (same thing as in TT BT♥♥♥♥INGWAY) and so on. Here? Here not so much, you can retreat, do whatever you want, creating a mess on the battlefield that AI makes a great job in highlighting. There's no unit coesion as everyone runs freely with no sense of positioning, that is caused also by the IDIOTIC decision to field 5 characters at a time in a game that, being insipired from the TT, requires at least a minimum of 10 per team to have a decent strategy, tactic, and overall experience. This decision also insanely increases the health of every character making it more like a deathmatch style of game were cahracters run here and there and take 3000 shots or nades or whatever to die. The game features a campaign that has the sole purpose to be a tutorial for the totally unexperienced, you might dig it Idk, but all these features of management and customization of your crew are obviously absent, it's just a chain of standard mission and overpriced cinematics that could have been scrapped entirely with a good basic tutorial, saving time and avoiding paying somebody to write you a lame story. But HEY! This game has to come out on consoles too, so it NEEDS a dumb tutorial disguised as a story.Fights have no impact, so little care has been put in the audio samples or even graphic effects, considering it's UE4 we could see gore, blood splatters, amputations etc...but no, nothing, just a phew phew airsoft version of 40k Necromunda.Also it's spectating simulator, they said "WE'LL PUT 5 MEN EACH TEAM TO MAKE IT MORE ACTION PACKEEED" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ slow also because you have to spectate every move of the opponent and everybody knows exactly what the other players are doing, what buffs they are using, where they use ambush stance, where they are etc... great strategy right?One might say, "In the TT everybody knows what they are doingggg!!!"" Yes too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bad the TT has rules that balance that kind of game that are completely disregarded in this videogame, resulting in something skinned as NM but has nothing to do with it. Ambush stance and overwatch stances are completely useless (even if the CPU pretend not to see what you are doing and gets in there no matter what, but it's not gonna happen in PvP, so yea, the AI is stupid as ♥♥♥♥, but really stupid and underdeveloped to the point that they waste action and movement point in useless skills because they are just programmed so naively that they are scripted to waste all their points before turn end).You'll see stuff that should never happen in a fight or nowhere near even to the TT version of this game that, in comparison, is like comparing Jesus Christ (the TT set of rules and gameplay) to a piece of ♥♥♥♥ (Necromunda Underhive Wars).Gameplay aside (that is absolute trash) everything else is good. The customization is good, the management is good, the graphics are I'd say good enough, very nice in some corners, a little less in others but absolutely acceptable overall.Mordheim was a game with flaws yes...wasn't like TT yes, but was balanced and dared to be complex and (considering the period) was a good starting point to get a next game better. What they did is completely scrap complexity and create a dumb turn based game with a very decent ideas in terms of PvE procedural campaign (boring after a while since you keep doing the same ♥♥♥♥ over and over, not like the REAL ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ TT NECROMUNDA), a PvP aspect of the game they castrated the whole SP experience for that will be totally BARREN forever, where every house has the same classes and plays the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ waaaaaay. It's a insult to fans and an insult to Necromunda TT.IF they had the guts to really listen to fans when they had the time (because it's absolutely obvious those people enver even touched Necromunda TT or world save for maybe couple of introductory games) MAYBE this game could have been waaaaaaay better. And it's not a matter of how much money it would cost more, NO it would actually cost ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ less! Or equal but at a 100 times more value.But who am I to judge, the never listen, there's a bounch of ppl in the forums defending the game even when community was very concerned about very alarming red flags...we were the toxic ppl. Now you get the game you deserve then, a massive pile of ♥♥♥♥ probably worth 5$ that even a kid 10 years old would find shallow after 5 hours.Oh btw the decision to make each player field 5 characters in the spawns at mission start but actually spawning them 1 at a time every action round and keeping the rest as "ghosts" is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stupid and gets bugged if enemies rush in your spawn while you characters hasnt' spawned yet. Learn how to make videogames first, then ask people for money.Your art guys are good, it's gameplay design that is an idiot, or whatever chimp at Focus is telling you how to do stuff.As it stands for now the User plays 5/10 minutes TOPS every 1 hour he is spectating others or the CPU doing sh1t. And this count came up from a guy that was naively trying to defend the game. Yes you play actively 5/10 minutes every ♥♥♥♥♥♥ HOUR you're spectating being braindead. You guys judge for yourself. Go see streams and have a blast falling asleep.

_childDocuments_.review: I will give this a precarious thumbs up.With not much experience in the War Hammer franchise I cannot really comment on the lore or be an authority of judgement on that matter.What i can say is its fairly neat.One of the slowest turn based games I've played but the fidelity of the graphics and scenery holds it together and sometimes can feel cinematic.With that being said, its ruined by a rough handled AI that enjoys colliding with what ever is in its way for a bit leading to very long play sessions. This happens often enough to be an issue.Atop this the camera will jut around scenery, instead of through it, making it a rather jarring experience.The minute to minute game play is dragged on by a lot of this.But you can customize your crew, which is also a very slow process. I would not call it deep, however, there are tons of character builds to play with. There is noticeable progression in perks and weapons and it flows rather well from a design a game play point of view. There is also limited character customization. You can paint your gear and change your outfits and what the crew looks like. There's just not a whole lot of it.I do not have the DLC and cannot comment on it. Other than its already in the game, you are paying to unlock it...There are interesting dynamics to the combat system itself. I personally love the grappling hook abilities that add nice mobility to the game. Though its big dumb you cant drag people off ledges. The gang perks are unique from each other and the stats are varied enough to feel dynamic.The combat is also a slow process because of the statement above. For the most part its good, just slow.There are strategics that often play out the same because of a crippled AI. So you wind up running through the processes after a while, even with the varied stats and abilities.The controls seem to be designed for a controller and the keys used can change or overlap with other things leading to to attack to target the wrong thing. Its frustrating and generally just wastes time.No notable bugs, but i did have a CTD. I dont remember what i was doing, but the beer and pizza was fantastic.....Overall, its fine.If you enjoy slow paced systems and like the world of Necromunda its pretty neato.

_childDocuments_.review: Thanks for the game, I'm sorry it didnt do better. Recommend.Back to my first 5 hours review:Infinite Vertical Movement: I get it. I still disagree with it. However, the movement system creates new tactical dilemmas: force your opponent to expose themselves to get a clean shot etc. If youre higher than your opponent, advantage is huge. And there are options to control  movement, sabotage the lifts or zip wires and you can have very firm control of the high ground.Indistinct Abilities:The abilities are small bonuses who's benefits arent immediately apparent, but persevere: they are better than they appear. Unfortunately there are also simply trash skills.Which brings me to consumables...oh my what a sh*t show. 1: Sort option? Please? After a few hours your stash is packed with crap with no way to sort them.2: Levelled items, you can have each item in 5 different levels, that dont stack, and do nearly the exact same thing. And I get it 5HP can make the difference...but there are better ways to handle it. Have them scale to gang rating, have the med facility upgrade them?  3: Random. Theres a gang focused on consumables (Escher)and acquiring consumables  is random? Orlocks arent randomly out of ammo, Goliaths dont have random moments of weakness. So..?Awful Campaign:No change. Its a travesty that the game was released with this terrible excuse of an introduction to the game.Bugs:99% squashed!Good:See 5 hour review, all unchanged: I cant wait for the first expansion. (slated for December..? :fingers crossed:)- The game's mechanics have some lovely synergies, Anoint Armaments and Plasma weapons, Iron Will and the Gravely wounded skill that gives even more hit resistance, etc The depth is really confusing at first but really worth thinking over and is a true highlight...spoiled only slightly by the fact that the good skills completely eclypse the bad ones, limiting your choices, although there are still excellent choices!Finally I have to mention the AI. Its not great. BUT.With the level design and scope of abilities and options I am not surpri the AI is lacking, its choices are vast, and making a system able to comprehend them and evaluate them property is a momentous task. Other games have managed but I have some sympathy here: in creating an environment in which two players can play against each other with the maximum of options they have stuffed up their AI. A choice I would have made also. I  hope this gets fixed and more solo and coop options are added. Id love to see Operations with/against other players.Probably my last update here, the game is excellent, buy it, even full price is a bargain. The scope means you'll need patience, or enjoy it with friends where the AI plays no role. Because the core of the game is astoundingly good. Recommend.I started playing hesitantly, on a family library, because of the mixed reviews.I followed the game's guidance: campaign first "to learn the game".What a horrible mistake! Its supposed to teach you the game, what it does instead is cut out every fun element of Necromunda: gang development, controlling the growth of your gang, learning how best to use abilities, acquiring gear, and being able to be proud of your heavy plasma gun that you stole from some scum-sucking Orlock.Instead the tutorial is a random series of spiritless encounters with gangs that change so often that you cant possibly give a monkeys about because you could well be trying to kill them next match. You have no control of their development or the abilities they have, and you cant get used to using any abilities as next game you wont have them any longer.Once you get into the campaign mode its a delight, everything you would expect from a modern AAA and from Necromunda, developing your gangs and kitting them out with armour pieces and weapons to be proud of, the right Stims to make them monsters of combat, and learning how best to use their abilities you chose.At this point the true drawbacks to the game are pretty much exclusive to the AI. Which can have moments of genius: laying mines in choke-points, and then setting overwatch over that point. But it can also have moment of chronic stupidity: walking into boxes, throwing grenades at walls or just failure to path. Most heinously it has no idea how to deal with destructible walls. I hesitantly recommend. - Infinite vertical movement. This makes it movement wildly unintuitive and the AI has a natural advantage in using it due to superior 3D comprehension. It means the AI can move seemingly infinitely far, eliminating most strategy in placing your people, because the AI can just get above your cover anyway and knows exactly how to do it. Cover :is: strategy in TT Necromunda, not only should it have a greater effect it should be harder to bypass, which isn't achievable with infinite vertical movement. It also makes the AP cost for using zip lines redundant in some maps as walking around to get up there is free, it just takes longer. Which is dull, and unrewarding when you could be zipping about, which is cool!- Abilities are numerous and not individual enough. eg I don't want 8 healing variations with slightly varied other spam on them. 1 is fine, maybe 2 if you can make them distinctive enough. - The campaign is awful. Not because of the story or because of game-play but because it fails heinously as a tutorial. See Above.- Zero control over progression in campaign. Because you cant shape your gang(s) you have zero pride in your them, and even less understanding of abilities that change often. See Above.- No rewards. Collect some gear in a mission? Its gone when you end the mission. Turn based without rewards is not a winning formula. At least have loot carry over!- The map is a work of art! Understanding your position is simply pressing M. Mouse wheel to scroll through layers. Excellently done.- Bugs & Devs. Largely cleared up, (tho some obscure conflicts remain) so prompt work by the devs gives huge kudos in my mind. The AI needs work, but isn't nearly as bad as some claim.- Combat is good. It feels gritty, damage is certain, teamwork is core. You feel the need to plan and the excellent map enables it nicely, there are clear objectives. And rewards for completing them (whilst on the map) such as no more reinforcements or valuable healing items.- Great level design. The maps are intricate but easy to navigate, the multiple levels add a great deal of interest, combined with destructible bridges, and zip-lines, placeable terrain and traps, simply outstanding!- Beautiful. Graphics are great, awesome atmosphere, really does the maps justice. Gangs and weapons are distinctive detailed.- I found difficulty well balanced, always peril without feeling overwhelmed all of the time. You can loose at times. I am still in the campaign, so I hope it continues into building my gang. - The potential. DLC gangs would be amazing, new tiles sets? Possibilities are huge.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, as I am a huge fan of all things 40k, however there are some issues in dire need of fixing. I am honestly not sure how these kinds of issues get through testing, because quite frankly, they're annoying and no one likes to be annoyed by something thats suppose to be fun. My biggest gripe with this is the rather bad ai pathfinding. I played a single mission for nearly an hour due to the ai fighters walking into junk piles or walls and just ending their turn there after trying to walk through the object for a minute straight. That or they'll walk their full move range and then backtrack to go somewhere else and you get to watch this all for each enemy character. Another thing I felt needed work and maybe this is just me, but I feel like the ai gangs prioritize the player even when there is a third gang on the field. I often get to watch as an enemy gang walks right through another enemy gang just to repeatedly attack my characters. During one operation, which is a series of missions, I managed to strip one enemy gang of weapons so they'd show up with just fists as weapons. Kinda funny to watch at first until you realize they get 3-5 attacks that deal 4-15 damage, which can end up being about the same damage as one swing from a 2 handed weapon. Personally I don't feel like that its logical to be able to beat a character who has a big ol axe with bare fists but that's just me. One final problem I've noticed, slightly less annoying than the others, is the seeming lack of penalties for disengaging. I have managed to get an enemy to low health only for them to disengage, turn their back on my fighter, and proceed to use the med station to heal most of their health back, with no real penalty for having done so.While it does have its issues, overall I am enjoying Necromunda. There is a fair bit of variety in weaponry and colors to customize your gang. While some additional clothing and hairstyles would be nice I feel there is a decent amount of visual customization for a game of this type. Map design is great, with multiple floors and an atmosphere that really goes well with what I'd expect from a gang heavy environment. After nearly 12 hours playtime I haven't noticed any real repetitiveness in map design. I have a fair bit of playtime in Mordheim and one thing that always bugged me was how easy it was to have characters die or be injured to near uselessness. I felt it was difficult to easily replace a veteran in the later game, (Although i was never very good at mordheim) however with Necromunda it seems more forgiving with the injuries and I haven't had a character die at all. Although not sure if they can actually die, but I try to keep my characters alive as much as possible because I'm sentimental or something.TLDR: Good game for 40k fans, with some issues needing fixed but nothing overly game breaking, that I have seen, with nearly 12 hours play time.

_childDocuments_.review: Before you even consider buying this game, you need to realize that it is NOT based on Necromunda: The Game, it is based on Necromunda: The Books. This game does not play anything like the cult classic miniatures game, and instead plays like their previous game Mordhiem with sci fi skins. Besides the name for weapons and gangs, there's pretty much nothing actually from Necromunda in here, not even the gangs themselves; every gang behaves exactly the same, but has six unique traits only they can equip. This of course is a far cry from how Necromunda actually works, where every gang is supposed to have strengths and weaknesses. In this game, you have have an active team of four not-leaders and a leader; each of which has an arbitrary class that locks specific weapons to them. Brawlers can use the good melee weapons, heavies get big guns, etc and it's just screams of laziness. While brawlers kind of automatically win melee combat, there is a problem in that division to: This game runs off of percentile, and only borrows mechanics from Necromunda rather than actually implement the Necromunda rules. So if you try to play this game as a Necromunda fan, you are going to just be pulling your hair out screaming "How could they screw this up!?" So gangs don't have agency, gangers have arbitrary classes, and the only game mode is stealing carried objects. There are several creatures and factions depicted in the games art, none of which actually shows up in this game. The Palantine Enforcers are in several artworks, and don't seem to actually appear in game. And this kind of moves onto my big, final point about this game: It's clearly meant to invite Necromunda players, but is a total bait and switch. Entertain me on this thought experiment, okay? Every now and then one or two people go into the forums and defend this game, saying that this is not meant to be sold to Necromunda players, but is actually intended to get new people into Necromunda. We, as fans of the series, are the ones to blame for expecting a licensed game to be true to it's license. Here's the big problem with that, this game outright disobeys how the actual game works. If I tried to show people this game, and then get them to play the real Necromunda, they would be thrown for a total loop. It's kind of like how somebody tried to tell me once that Warhammer games are not marketed towards Warhammer players (they are)I bought this game when it was 60% off in order to really figure out how bad this trashfire is, and it's bad.... if you approach it while judging it as a Warhammer game. If this was just some generic Sci Fi punk game, it honestly would not be that half bad. BUT, sorry, the geniuses that made this game used a Warhammer license so if it's nothing like the licensed game, it's just not worth playing. For some reason, developers keep buying Warhammer licenses and making generic strategy games in the hopes that another total Warhammer will happen.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't normally review games but I thought Necromunda deserved a thumbs up from me after the hours of fun I've had with it. I've been a Necromunda fan since the first TT edition came out back in 1995, and I picked it back up again when it was re-made in 2017. This game is a fine representation of three of the six great houses engaging in turn-based objective-centric skirmishes. Please note that I haven't tried the multiplayer yet, so this is from the perspective of single player content only.This is not a 1:1 digitisation of the TT game, but rather has it's own ruleset. I see the wisdom in this, because the digital format allows for more complex abilities and background calculations to occur. There are many more skills and abilities and lots of factors weighed in to every shot. However, until you understand these systems the game can feel a little arbitrary or off balance at times, and I think there is still work to be done to perfect these new systems.Plus points:- Graphics are great- Lots of customisation- Sound is good (although the Lascannon could do with a little more oomph)- Level design and traversal is great- Turn based battles- Good stability, I've only had one CTD (ymmv - some forum users and reviewers claim the game is broken beyond repair)Negative points:- AI behaviour can be very odd/broken at times, making many scenarios easier than intended- Weapons feel too homogeneous. A plasma gun should be a substantial upgrade from a lasgun, but there is little apparent difference in damage output- Poor voice acting in the single player campaign. The guilder does a good job but the gang leaders leave something to be desiredOverall, if you're a fan of Necromunda or turn based games, I would recommend this, particularly since it is at a budget price point. It is far from perfect and needs work to balance the different classes and weapons. I'd also like to see some DLC support for the missing three great houses.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm so sad not to be able to recommend this, as were it not for the ridiculously silly AI the game could be *fantastic*.  The graphics are great, gang customisation extensive enough that they really feel like *your* gang, maps and missions are interesting (they do run out after a while, but that's true of almost every base game of this type), and the gameplay is satisfying, with even that touch of silliness that brings memorable moments I recall from playing tabletop Necromunda (e.g. skilling characters so they can do crazy movement around the map and take out a 'safe' opponent from behind).  But the AI is so awful that there is no challenge to the game, and it really hurts the immersive, role-playing experience.  I get that no AI will be truly like a human opponent, and tend to be predictable, but many games still manage to make them act broadly sensibly.  In Underhive Wars, they regularly use their movement to jump off a platform then action points to zip-line back to their starting point, for no apparent reason.  They move close to a target and then throw a grenade so they hit themselves/their allies rather than simply doing it from further back.  It's neither a fun contest nor a thematic, role-playing experience, which the game could otherwise offer so well.  Yes, you can ramp up the difficulty to give them skewed advantages to try and present a challenge, but it then becomes about gaming the system and exploiting the stupidity.  Like fighting an idiotic giant who swings around randomly and occasionally clubs themself in the face, rather than a balanced battle between rival gangs.  Or like playing tabletop with my 6yo who wants to randomly run around then make things go "boom".  In other games you can make it an interesting contest by giving the AI some minor advantages to make up for the limitations of programming, but in this game the AI is just too silly for this to work.Sadly, I reached a stage fairly quickly where the AI's craziness outweighed the fun immersion of playing and developing my gang.  If the AI gets improved I'd jump at playing this again, and I'd happily buy whatever DLC was required if it truly fixed it, as I love tabletop Necromunda and the rest of the experience is so well done.  But every time I get drawn in by this to give it another go, I quickly realise why I stopped playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Before buying and playing this title, I have to admit that I was really put off by the negative reviews - here on Steam. Then I got it dirt cheap on a sale and still had a bit of anxiety trying it.While I've waited for the download to complete, I dug deeper in the reviews and I have to say this: many people complain about the bad UI and difficulty/stability (yes, it has a bad UI, something that feels to be ported directly from consoles - but still pretty functional). The difficulty doesn't feel neither too hard, nor too easy. At least in the Story mode. Ofc, this may come and bite me in the ass along the way - but so far (having played 4 missions) - it seems pretty reasonable. Yes - there is no way of choosing the difficulty mode, but that is not an issue.I've seen reports of having bad AI. Well, what can I say: I wasn't expecting much - but so far, I haven't seen enemies running in front of a wall and hanging there. You shoot them, they shoot back or run and shoot back. Pretty standard AI for this type of game. The ranged classes seem that always try too keep their distance. At least in the Story mode.Stability wise, I had no real issues. Sure, there is the occasional camera glitch here and there - and sometimes the reflections/textures glitch while moving the camera fast (in the tactical mode), but nothing to really bother you. I've played Gothic 1 back in the day and this is nothing to that glitchiness. No crashes so far as well. I'll update this review if that happens. And c'mon - this is not a AAA game. Remember Cyberpunk at release? This is nowhere near that.Lore wise, you ask? I have no idea. I'm a fan of the 40k universe, but my interest was more along the lines of the Black Library books and DoW games. Probably the 5 factions available (3 default and 2 DLC gangs - all playable in the Operations/Skirmish mode) are not exactly 100% accurate, but honestly? It doesn't bother me that much. The mechanics are fun and there seems to be a decent learning curve - as long as you play the Story first. Even the game tells you that: "play the story first".Mechanics are plenty. And even though the UI is not the most uncluttered out there - it's still serviceable. With a bit of practice, you'll learn what you need by playing it, mostly. The rest is flavor.Sadly, the MP is dead. I guess the bad press took care of that. I would have loved playing vs. some human opponents.From what I've seen around the web - the launch was a mess. Might have been. But this was years ago. While not really updated since 2021 - One more thing: I've seen people comparing it to Mordheim. This is not that either. It's an entirely different game, made by the same company - using a bit of a similar gameplay. But don't get this if you are expecting a game like their first title.PS: It also has cool cinematics that really give flavor to the action. This is definitely an uncut gem for the 40k fans out there ;) .

_childDocuments_.review: I'll get this out of the way right now. Necromunda: Underhive Wars is the type of game which will be great in two years. Does this mean that I think the game isn't worth playing now? No, it is worth playing! Just be aware that Necromunda: Underhive Wars captures the Your Dudes aspect of GW's Specialist Games about as well as one can expect of a video game. If you're going into this game and not taking the time to come up with a little story for your guys, then you're missing the point of Necromunda.Yes, Necromunda: Underhive Wars is full of jank, moreso than one would expect on a game at launch. Yes, there are only three gangs out of the eight in the newest edition of Necromunda.No, that isn't the point. The point is watching Queen, my Orlock Lay-Tech showing the Esher gang leader who I've fought shift after shift exactly what happens when someone steps onto my turf. It's watching my merry bomb throwing Juvie Tiffany Trio hock three of her homemade grenades at two Goliath thugs, teaching them the meaning of spacing. It's watching Ace pick off enemies after crossing the entirety of the map by jumping down and leaping up from building to building like it's Assassin's Creed.If you want to suspend your disbelief and enjoy watching Your Dudes grow through success and failure, then enjoy. If not, then check this again in a year or two.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid 4/10The worst AI I've ever seen in a published game.  Makes the AI from Mordheim look like Einstein.  Eg. one of the five classes, the Saboteur, only ever runs around like a headless chicken throwing grenades at itself.  WTF.  It makes you watch ridiculous "YOUR TURN" "ENEMY TURN" animations every time you switch characters.  Every single action, including crouching, has lengthy animations, effects, and cinematic pauses baked in.  95% of my playtime is spent tabbed out while the AI circles the map, gets stuck on every corner and object, while randomly spamming all its abilities, only to go right back to where it started.The mechanics, skills, unit variety have all been dumbed down.  It's a leap backwards from Mordheim in every aspect.  Especially the movement system.  How do you go from a sensible, logical pathing method, to this trainwreck that gives unlimited vertical movement, that lets units run unlimited circles around terrain, that lets you run into your opponent's spawn in the first or second turn?  Why have all the classes transformed into Usain Bolts, with no movement differences between them?Building gangs is fun.  The art department is on point. But this has no business being a full release.  It's an early-access pre-alpha demo at best.

_childDocuments_.review: Overview: A fun but flawed game. Quite a few rough edges that need to be fixed, and a lot of content I'd like to see added, but Necromunda is a solid gang-builder with enough customization, skills, and satisfying gameplay to keep me playing. I'll absolutely pick it up again when there are some improvements and DLC.Reasons why you should play this game:- You enjoy building a team, upgrading them, finding fun skill and weapon combos, and then unleashing them on your enemies.- You really like the 40k universe and enjoy seeing the weapons, environments, and characters brought to life.- You don't mind repetitive gameplay.Reasons why you should not play this game:- Bugs, glitches, and exploits are dealbreakers.- You require competent AI to feel challenged.- You really, really, really liked XCOM and this looks similar.- You hate repetitive gameplay.The good:- Graphics are solid.- Level design is pretty good, with a lot of vertical movement and fun ways to get around the map.- A variety of weapons, with enough differences that you might build a character and a team specifically around different types. - Advancement actually feels really solid, with stat upgrades giving you an excellent overview of *precisely* how they will help, and many skills being a lot of fun to use.- The interface is pretty quick and intuitive, with your movement and action points feeling pretty sensible in terms of how they're used to interact with the world around you.- In Operations, it's an absurd amount of fun to loot all the weapons off your dead enemies, and watch as the gang becomes more and more impoverished over the course of an "arc." Eventually, they'll be coming at you with little more than fists and whatever they could buy off a trader, while you brandish all their old gear. And laugh maniacally.- Autosave is magnificent, allowing me to get right back into the action even with CTDs.The bad:- There are some serious bugs at the moment. I've had more than a few CTDs, and part of the advancement system for your custom gangs is broken.- For some reason, you need to complete the story mode before you can unlock all the customization options for your custom gangs.- The aforementioned story mode isn't great. It's not bad, but it's not great, with widely-varying difficulty and a pretty uninspired plot. It also goes on for way too long.- Weapons are not all created equal. Deadeye, for example, gets access to a perk that grants Action Points for scoring a critical hit. Critical hits are on a per-round basis, so weapons that fire more rounds (the autogun) are much, much easier to score crits with than a single-fire weapon (the lasgun, plasma rifle, etc). The amount of bonus action points is enough that you can fire again. Firing twice, even with a slightly inferior weapon, is the significantly better option. Hence, even with many fun options, I have never used anything but the autogun on my Deadeye.- Some skills are very underwhelming. Charge, which ostensibly allows you to melee attack an enemy without triggering Overwatch, has an oddly specific range of 8-20 meters. This means that if someone goes into overwatch too close to you, you can't use it. Too far away, and you can't use it. If they have a ranged weapon, they shoot you as soon as they can see you move, but charge requires a VERY clear path to hit them. I tried to love charge. It does not love me. The ugly:- The AI is broken. Period. It works okay when you're just fighting each other, but throw in objectives and it has no idea what to do. I've watched six gangers from two different gangs share a tiny platform, caught in a loop of buffing their teammate and raising a flag, without ever actually attacking. I've watched melee fighters run up, take overwatch, then change their mind and run away. They put a huge priority on buffs and item use, and actually fighting is secondary.- Movement Points make zero sense with the vertical layout, as movement is calculated by drawing a big circle around your character, as opposed to how many STEPS you've taken. This may seem like a small thing, but it's very frustrating to watch the AI run up 10 flights of stairs, zipline over to an objective, grab it, jump down, and then run halfway across the map to an extraction point. - There isn't much mission variety. The custom gang Operations are all centered around simple objective grabbers, which typically turns into whether you can set yourself up in such a way as to pulp the enemy before they use said terrible movement system to steal the objectives out from under your noise and run to the extraction point, laughing and pushing each other into the bushes.- Once all the enemy gangers are dead, you immediately enter the "looting round." This is your only opportunity to grab both loot from the enemy, and any objectives left on the map. So what if you killed all 15 opponents in 2 out of 6 rounds and control the field of battle? You gotta be HOLDING those batteries, missy, otherwise it's no points for you.That's all I got. For me, the positives outweighed the negatives - building up my own gang, turning them into broken killing machines, and slowly stripping all my competitors of their weapons while moving up in the world kept me going for a good long time. It's not a great game, but it's a fun one.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR I expected Mordheim in future - I got DisappointmentWot I liked- Well made GUI: you can get most information which you need. It has its own quite unique stylisation and control scheme, but once you get used to it, it's quite friendly;- You can use space in character names! For some reason most games don't allow you to do it;- Operation seems to be the main game mode (skirmish is a random combat arena): you're set out at a part of Necromunda and has to carry out several missions to vie for resources with 2 competitor houses - all missions are eliminate or extract with the cargo;- Infamy points system provides your current operation with 2 facilities (chosen from 4) and 12 buffs (chosen from about 30). In order to increase your Infamy you need to complete various tasks in-game;- There are 6 classes with slightly different roles. The leader variant of the class provides access to leader skills;- There are 8(9) items slots: 3 implants, body armour, arms, legs, weapons. Each class has its own version of equipment;- You can choose 5 passive skills (chosen from about 24) and 5 active skills (chosen from about 24). Each House has some unique(ish) skills;- Enjoy crawling in the biggest city in the universe's underbelly;- Third person tactical turn based game;- Very impressive and useful 3d map;- An interesting Mordheim redux;- Pretty loading screens.Wot I disliked- Very few of everything;- Maps are dead. The textures look fine (just fine, definitely no eye-candies for 2020), however there are but none interactive elements: ziplines, lifts, trap spots, barricades, gangplanks, healing stations and chests. Of course there are no destructible environments;- Environmental hazards, pick-ups, traps or barricades are ineffective and are never used by AI (or you) and are largely unimportant and affect nothing;- The game’s visuals are very PG-13: no gore, no wounds, no gory finishers, hardly any blood (hardly any animations to be honest);- Houses are basically the same with very minor difference in visuals, weapons and skills. Two houses are given as paid DLCs — you’re paying for dozen skills and skins;- Campaign (I think 90% of players will start and end Necromunda experience with it) is hot garbage:  you cannot change the composition of your team, you cannot change the loadout of your team, you cannot back one house and have to play for all of them, the list goes on and on;- Operations are quite grindy: it would take you quite some time to get your team to max level. Party members can get injured, which can make them basically useless, meaning that you have to start over;- Crashes, bugs, glitches i.e. some skills and mechanics not working (melee cannot destroy barricades, ambushes failing), dumb AI, etc...To sum it all up, I expected Mordheim in future but got a severely limited and handicap copycat. The campaign is so awful I could not finish it and dropped after mission 6. Operations is a much better and fun mode yet still a limited game.

_childDocuments_.review: The only thing this game has got going for it is its visuals which perfectly captured the aesthetic of 40k and Necromunda. As a game itself, it is a buggy, feature starved, poorly written/voice acted mess of a game that should have remained in development for at least another year. It was a barely functional alpha when officially "released" and had horrendous AI. The game was in such a bad state that the multiplayer was dead on arrival after just one week. The singleplayer "story" revolves around the three core gangs rushing to be the first to uncover a powerful relic - which is never revealed or explained why it is so important. It's just a macguffin to tie the three gangs to the same location. The story jumps every couple of missions between gangs and serves more as a tutorial than an actual narrative campaign. Worst of all is that you cannot level up, customize, or even edit the loadout of your gangers. Combined with the point of view switching every few missions to a different gang leaves the player completely detached and unable to identify or care about their warband.All in all there is not much here. The singleplayer is a glorified tutorial, the multiplayer is dead. The only thing worth playing is Operations mode - a kind of repeatable string of missions where you can play against the AI. It was supposed to be like an endless campaign you could play but it was poorly done and is boring and repetitive. Combined with the terrible AI Operations mode sounds great on paper but is dull and very shallow much like the rest of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I was put off from picking this game up even though the concept intrigued me by the negative reviews, but I haven't seen anything during my playing to make my opinion negative. There's a lot of personality in the storymode and you can play individual gangs you can customize after you're done with the story so there's a lot of gameplay here. _childDocuments_.review: Rogue Factor returns with an ambitious Necromunda: Under hive Wars. I finally got a first look at this follow up to the cult classic Mordheim. Some things I was impressed with and boy some work needs to be done. I will keep it short and sweet.What I liked:Cinema-tics: The Real Engine was a nice choice for the animated sequences and story mode. This table top translation has some passion to its scope and presentation that bring it to life.  So far so good.Tactical Warfare: Whether console, keyboard or controller. There is a lot of little nuances you like. Its clear and precise to the attributes and skill choices.Third Person: Still the best presentation of table tops and turn base mechanics instead of the old isometric that forces you up close and into the action. Still love it.Improving Modeling: An improvement in the customization and models from the Unity Mordheim that made the looks of the character more aesthetically pleasing.Music: Not a bad sound track that fits Necromunda's universe.What needs to get better:AI issues: The same stuck characters, coding and bug issues that plagued Mordheim, are even more profound in Necro, which was disappointing. Incomplete: Despite the great setting. Barely any of its needed as you play within a very confine space. Do not ask me to go up and down an elevator again. Tedious: Unlike Mordheim where you had large warbands to control that made tactical play more enticing. Here it is slow and redundant.  Small parties just don't have the same power as watching one character surrounded by 4 in Mordheim. PVP: Tables tops are pvp, but in game its disregarded because of the solo game play. If this was 1 v 1 clan leader pvp. I still would not do it. That tells you something. Choices: This plays like battle chess table top with guns and knives. Then an under hive massive war band war. Each character has limited animation sequences that become mundane. ShameMode: This franchise may have been better served in a different format than turn base even if it is a table top game. DLC clans: A practice of models w skins to me. Then true story mode additions. A mistakeFirst impressions. They matter and I applaud their ambition. It has some wondrous scenes in Necromunda. However, I felt even with 20 clans. The game felt limited in its scope of game play with small parties that hurt tactical game play. Mordheim, to me is a better table top game translation despite its flaws where Necro feels incomplete and small in comparison. I never played Necromunda's Table top, but I found this to be less about story and more about moving and shooting. The Necromunda world was reduced here. Please see the game play in Video above discussion before deciding. Is it worth the price of admission? I would wait for a sale. I wish Rogue Factor the best because I did enjoy Mordheim so much. They get a marginal thumbs up simply for the passion and effort. However, despite its beauty, it has some issues it needs to fix that take away from it. Execution of ideas is everything. I do reserve judgment when development is fully completed, but for now. My Score 2.2 out of 5.
