_childDocuments_.review: I backed this game back in 2015 and I'm honestly disapointed. I liked the combat moves and the dynamic music. Even though I'm not used to fighting games I can appreciate how good it feels to rack up combos. But, the game falls short in pretty much every other way.First, let me address the missing story line. I might not be a game developer, but you don't need to be a chef to tell if the food is burnt. How exactly do they have an error in the story so large that it causes you to delay it's release? This should've been figured out months ago through beta testing. Regardless of how "busy" the progammers are.Another major gripe of the game is how there is no quick play. This has nothing to do the story so why is this missing from the game? Another thing missing is the pixel lobbies that were present in the trailer. Unless I'm looking in the wrong place, there is only one pixel lobby and it's very small. There's nothing to do in it either. Unless you count collecting "salt" which only purpose is to gain access to the salt mine which just allows you to collect more salt.Could there possibly be more missing content? Yes, there is. There is still place holder art present all over the game. The salt mine exits are black squares and some attack animations for the characters are just cardboard drawings. How could they have originally planned to release the full game while still using placeholder art?Theres a lot more I could nitpick like how I have no idea which skins are the backer only ones or how the voice lines don't match the lips of the characters (often times the the right character isn't even talking). But there really is no point in talking about the flaws in a game that wasn't even finished. Come on guys, did it really take you $600,000 and 3 years to reskin that my little pony fighting game that got taken down?

_childDocuments_.review: It's funny, it's cute, the music is phenomenal, the fighting is fun and easy to get into. The character roster may be a tad small, but the current six characters are each unique and have different playstyles, not to mention the pallette references, oh the pallette references. Also, I don't care what you've heard, you don't have to be a fan of any cartoon show to appreciate this game. The game also uses the Z-Engine, which you may have heard of from Lab Zero and their game, Skullgirls, who helped the devs of Them's Fightin Herds, Mane6, by letting them use the Z-Engine here. Currently it includes a single player arcade mode, training and target mode, with story mode currently being worked on to be released soon in episodic format for free. Multiplayer modes include a lobby play function, and the pixel lobby, which is essentially a lobby with avatars from which you can challenge other players to 1v1 fights, and get cosmetic hats in the pve salt mines. The Game's lore is also fairly interesting (the lore info is on Mane6's website) as well as the overall aesthetic of both the characters and world. The world and characters are somewhat adorable, but that doesn't detract from the fighting by no means. For those of you out there who are fans of a certain TV Show.....y'all might be interested to know that Lauren Faust helped to design the characters and world as well. As for gameplay. I normally suck at fighting games typically. This wasn't that hard for me to learn, it helps that theres only 4 attack buttons (Light, medium, heavy, and Special), whereas other games have things like kicks and such to add onto that. Also, specials and combos aren't that hard. Each character plays differently, you have Arizona, a brawler/grappler, Pom, a pet user / summoner, Tianhuo, an aerial attacker who can string combos very fast, Velvet, who excels at controlling the field and playing keep-away with attacks that block or push you back, and finally Oleander, who is basically Houdouken-Horse. As for community, there is a small following which will likely grow as the game reaches the end of Early Access. Also, while I hate to say it, fighting games on PC are by definition, a bit of a niche, even with big titles like FighterZ and arguably Blazblue, you don't have that many PC users as compared to the console versions. That being said, the game is still fun, both in singleplayer and when you get a MP match. The real thing that I'm looking foward to though is the singleplayer, as it's supposed to have an RPG mechanic and overworld to it, which is something no other fighting game has done, in addition to the fact the game already has a ton of lore. Now, to end this review on a high note, allow me to just ask you a simple questionWhat other game allows you to play as a headbanging cow or sorceress with a necronomicon on the same engine as Skullgirls for ONLY 15 dollars? None? I thought so. AlsoOleander is best Po-I mean Ungulate 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I'm the type of person that buys a bunch of fighting games (because they all look so cool) and never seems to get good at any of them. This is usually because those other titles are overcomplicated, have poor (or nonexistent) tutorials, or just end up not being fun to play. On the contrary, TFH is the definition of "easy to learn, hard to master" and at only 14 hours logged (as of the writing of this review) I feel like I have a firm understanding of my two mains (Arizona and Oleander) and can hold my own online. My friend and I run matches on weekends and its the most fun I've had with a fighter in a while; not to mention that the GGPO netcode makes those online matches run smoother than butter.My only complaint is that the game sometimes starts running at a low frame rate on my laptop and then randomly shifts back to 60 fps mid-match despite my laptop being more than powerful enough to run it (i7 CPU and Geforce GTX 1050 GPU). I play on desktop most of the time though so it doesn't bother me too much.If TFH has peaked your interest I wholeheartedly recommend it (unless you plan on maining Velvet. Keep that icicle deer away from me)

_childDocuments_.review: What you're paying for isn't some huge budget fighter such as Dragon Ball FighterZ, but what you ARE paying for is a passion project built from what used to be an already amazing My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic fighting game (before Hasbro shut it down for obvious legal reasons).The game was built from the ground up with help from the creator of MLP:FiM Lauren Faust to make a completely original, yet simple, fighting game based around the 6 character simplistic fighting game that the old MLP game was.Like I said before, this wasn't just a game, it was a passion project from Kickstarter that took a few years to make, and I can personally say that I like the outcome so far, even without the story (which is coming soon as of this review). The fighting isn't hard to learn but maintains the heart of a fighting game without becoming a jugglefest (due to a juggle cap, which is an incredible feature).The pixel lobby is a great idea. Like in Dragon Ball FighterZ, there's a lobby of 20 players where you can choose your favorite character, put a hat or neckless on them for fun, and chat in the lobby. You start multiplayer fights there, make friends, or be silly with random people! It's my favorite addition to the game.From a DMCA take-down to a Steam release, I'm glad to finally be a part of the process of a kickstarted game, watching it grow over the years into what it is, and look forward to seeing where it goes now.

All made by a small indie team.In short this game is a good package made by a dedicated indie team that has a clear respect and passion for the genre and what its players want.While I can easily recommend this game on its own merits and the small teams efforts I would think it is better to get this game on a sale given the recent news of content coming to a halt for the future, especially the story mode which wont be completed due to having to end future support.All in all, I think with what content is currently here the game deserves a chance and doubly so if you can snag this on a decent sale and can enjoy with friends and/or a small local community.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great lesson in how not to develop a fighting game. The reason you don't typically see indie fighting games is because they are extremely difficult to develop. But, I figured since the developers were able to license the Skullgirls engine and had the blessing of Lauren Faust, that it would at least be a good start. It also helps that I hate Hasbro as much as any (ex)Brony.The first major issue is that half of the animations are missing. I get its early access, but all that is hinted at in the information box is that the story mode is being developed and maybe some balancing needs to be done. Not the fact that half of the art needs to be developed. Secondly, the AI, while not a major role in these kinds of games, is absolute bottom of the barrel trash. Seriously. Normal / competent mode left me dead from a 38 hit combo on the first fight. Easier difficulties just made the characters guard and run away constantly. If I'm supposed to use AI as a practice point, then the developers have certainly failed. You think since they licensed an engine, enemy AI (which is one of the more difficult parts to develop) would be included. I played Skullgirls. That game had great AI. Actually, calling it "intelligence" is an insult.Thirdly, the game's gimmicks and controls are by far the most confusing thing I have ever seen. Magic is nearly useless. Only a few moves use it and they are barely effective. They either do minimal damage (Paprika) or have absurdly limited range (Arizona). It appears you also can't regain magic (or regain it easily), so instead of focusing a few good moves for a combo, you just barely hit the enemy sometimes maybe who knows. Also, the move execution is the dumbest thing ever. All the inputs are mostly the same. This is fine and good for beginners and veterans alike. However, the inputs that are standardized are bizzare and don't come from any fighting game I've played. The supers require you to hold 2 attack buttons. Not press it twice, but hold both at the same time. It's not quarter circle + punch, it's not a direction + magic, but quarter circle + two buttons at once. Confusing in both practice and when communicating the moves to the player. I legit thought half the moves were broken.The fourth and most glaring issue is that the 6 characters are obviously carbon copies of the ponies from My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic. They all have the same personalities and move styles (when they aren't ripping off King of Fighters character's move sets). I get a response would be "that's not an important part of the game"! But characters are actually important. They draw you into the game more easily. Imagine Mario was a red rectangle or a guy named "Jim". Would the games still be remembered as icons? They would probably still get favorable reviews, but would be criticized as bland or lazy. And that's just what this game is. This is honestly the first Steam game I've refunded. It's sad as unique fighting games are a rarity outside of foreign arcade machines. Yet, to be candid, I honestly feel this game is doomed. The pony basis, despite it no longer existing, has greatly polarized the game already. The fanboys will defend the game uncritically, while the game itself suffers to the curious. Maybe it will improve, but I m honestly doubtful it will.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't bring myself to downvote this because it's made well and it seems to be developing since I bought it earlier in the year. But the thing is I bought this as a present for a little girl who likes a tv series, and it's so difficult she can't even really watch daddy playing it unless I invest the necessary days or weeks to "get good". I have been bad at fighting games since at least SF2, but sometimes one succeeds in teaching enough of its basic mechanics to a complete beginner for it to start to be fun. Like maybe Mortal Kombat, Golden Axe, or One Must Fall: grown-ups can play those with kids because they still work at a sort of "rock-paper-scissors" level even if neither player can do any of the combos or special moves (let alone knowing what "juggle decay" is). And I believe little girls should be able to derive as much enjoyment from a fighting game as a bearded middle-aged hipster, so for my purchase the "serious mechanical depth" of this game is actually a disappointment. I've up-voted because of the game's obvious quality for those who want that depth, and I haven't refunded it because I want to support the devs even though I don't care much for the game they made.I probably don't understand enough about fighting game mechanics to even articulate the problem or what could be changed. But I don't think it's anything to do with the "difficulty" characteristic on an Easy/Normal/Hard/Nightmare type scale. It's not about an option to "make it easier". A child to start with might only move and press one attack button - it's not that the game should let them win by mashing one button, it's that it should give that enough reinforcing feedback to teach them to start also dodging and blocking. And then gradually build on that. This game's seriousness-of-design kind of stops it providing the simple feedback - so the child can't tell why pressing one button doesn't work and that's frustrating for them.I have a version of the same problem but I can live with that ok ^^Could they develop a game mode where the AI spots the child's favourite move in the first few seconds of the match, and adopts a simple counter-strategy - to make them start doing more than one thing?Another thing I guess is that young children don't anticipate balance, like with different characters having different strengths and weaknesses. So they won't adjust their tactics to the opponent - at all. I guess a lot of the painstaking balancing between the characters has to be muted back out. It might not even be possible if things like hitboxes and animations are too finely set up. But kids have low standards and they learn quickly so even if it was a bit rougher than the main game they probably wouldn't care. It would just be so good to have a mode where they could be an animated character, protecting itself, and be able to tell what the heck was going on. Currently it's beyond overwhelming.And do it for the kids: because for some of them one day the friendship problem will be that their violent ex-partner is going to batter them with a table leg, and they won't have 22 minutes.

_childDocuments_.review: It has the potential to become a fantastic fighting game if it's given the right support.Them's fightin' herds is a 2D fighter that works with a four button scheme. And to make it better, the movesets themselves are as simplistic as UMVC3. despite the fact there's not a 2v2 or 3v3 mode, that makes picking one of these characters to main even easier as opposed to being forced to pick 3 members, then an assist move for each.Right now the arcade mode, target mode, and practice mode are the only things you can do locally, but then there's online. Is the netcode for online good? YES. I most framerate drop I ever experiecned was maybe 2-3 frames during online fight. To give you some perspective, Street fighter 5...it has moments it drops 7+ frames making awkward skips in the battle to catch up. So for the most of the game, you'll be playing in lobbies online.The lobbies themselves are these cute pixel area's to walk around in. As far as finsing items or cosmetics, i have no clue. haven't spent enough time out there. But its more entertaining than looking at a menu screen to say the least.Since the game is only a day old, running into other people is always there. And until the game progresses enough and the community surrounding it grows, there won't be many them's fightin herds tourney's or locals of any kind.Its clear that competition is in mind from the devs. there is just yet to be enough time for things to be worked into the game. If your so worried, keep in mind, its an indie game in early access. it'll get there someday.The game is in early access as in, WOW you can be reminded of that easily with some drops in framerate, the occasional crash, or lip syncing not working.For the most part, the only bugs I encountered were those, and with one I hope is only a visual hit box not aapearing in training mode. It also supports the use of fight sticks, which came at some surprise. I expected it to require me to go into a menu and switch controllers and remap the controls along with dealing input lag, but no. I put it in, click. and its good.For those who want to take it seriously, just play online for awhile and lets work to build a community around this game. Thats the healthiest thing for any fighter.until the game gets fleshed out some more, to later be a full release, I give Them's fightin herds7/10

_childDocuments_.review: I've been following this game's progress since the Fighting is Magic days, though I've hesitated for quite a long time to buy it, simply for the fact that I do not particularly enjoy fighting games. I finally decided to pick it up a week ago and I am happy for the most part! Let me state what I did and did not enjoy:Pros: - This game has so much personality and each character has their own unique fighting style that fits them perfectly. It's not everyday that you see a fighting game with cute animals!- The tutorial is great at teaching you how to play the game, even if you're a beginner like me. - Pixel lobbies are not only fun to hang out in, but contain particular activities to do together (ex: salt mines run, fighting for chests)- Story mode is a diamond in the rough, expands the lore and story of each character.- Music dynamic! According to whoever is winning a round, the game will play a variant of the track that includes that particular character's main instrument (ex: Pom is winning, you will hear a flute variant). Cons:- Due to its fairly small playerbase, you'll have a hard time finding players around your same skill level. Not entirely a bad thing, but it can be tiring to get repeatedly beaten up by players that have spent hundreds of hours into the game.- The roster is small, it only has 7 characters at the moment. New characters will eventually arrive, but via a season pass which you'll have to pay for.- Lack of content in general. This game has been released in 2020, yet 2 years later there has been hardly any new content. I understand that the team does not have many members, yet you'd think they'd focus more on completing the game first before releasing it on consoles (for a higher price might I add). Story mode is unfortunately still at chapter 1, as well as other things that have been listed as coming soon for a while now.Final thoughts:Even though I have put a thumbs up for this review, I would much rather say that it depends. This game has an equal list of pros and cons. Most cons will be fixed with time, but it is up to you if you wish to play a game for some hours and then keep it on a shelf to collect dust until new content is released. This game has a lot of potential and is crazy fun, I hope to see it grow in the future so I can 100% recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: After having kept an eye on the development of this game for a long while, I was interested to see how it would be when it finally hit a wider public release. Fortunately, the hype seems to be vindicated, since the game oozes a personality that it inherits from the fiction it's descended from. Though the character's animations are unfinished, they move beautifully and the attack animations have a lot of charm. The pixel lobby is pretty neat, too, and contains a "hidden" adventure mode that puts a new flavor inside what would otherwise be a typical fighting game.The online mode is neat, with the aforementioned pixel lobby functioning as a "hub" for players in the lobby to chat, dress up their pixel avatars, and start fights. It's all fairly seamless and the lag isn't terrible, which is good, since, as an Australian, lag is a constant concern in a fast paced fighting game.I'm not particularly proficient in fighting games, though, and my only method of play is with the keyboard, and this seems more appropriately played with a fightstick. In addition, some character's moves have wonky hitboxes and too often I find myself being bodied by things that I was certain I was avoiding. The CPU difficulty is also bizzarely balanced, with "normal" difficulty being on par with the worst kinds of input reading CPUs I've ever seen. The game is still in beta, so while it can be changed, it does pose a significant obstacle to someone new to the game.All in all, the game is a fine addition to the fighting game genre, but I doubt it will change the minds of those prejudiced against it because of where it came from. If you can get over that, you'll find a solid fighter with some growing pains that the devs will hopefully address in the coming months. If you're in the mood for a new fighting game and Dragonball isn't your thing, and you loved Skullgirls, I would gladly reccommend you pick this up and give it a go.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun, little game that was inspired by FiM, and is a cute, humorous title. The music is well-done, and the fighting animations are clean.That's where my praise ends. Despite over a year of development, there is still no new story since last year, no new characters, and the DLC is comprised of skins and a soundtrack. Shanty was released well over a year ago, and I popped back on after noticing the game had a 1GB update. "New story!" I told myself, hoping that there would be SOMETHING different, something improved. It's the exact same game as a year ago, and I'm getting to the point of dropping the project altogether due to a lack of updates on story. Improvements are fine and dandy, but neglecting the game as a whole to focus solely on 'improvements' is not a good idea. As it is, I don't even notice any of the 'improvements' that have apparently been added over the year. I supported this team all the way back when they were trying to make their MLP fighting game, one of the first to play the demo. This game's story is a diamond in the rough, but seeing it sit on a shelf and collect dust is just depressing.Great concept, the dev team seems to have grown bored with it though. I recommend this to anyone who doesn't mind their story being stopped mid-way and don't mind a small cast of characters (seven, to be exact) to play as. For the average fighting game enthusiast, I would have to give this a hard pass for a recommendation as it is.EDIT: Frankly, I'll probably wind up changing this to a recommend once the story is done and the cast expands a bit. A whole year with no changes is a tad frustrating, regardless.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I wanna preface this by saying that I WANTED and would've given this a thumbs up, but there's a lot of smaller add-up problems paired with fewer-but-huge, serious issues with this game that I can't and won't overlook. There's a lot to like about this game, but the major problems, some others have already written about, are so big that I can't give this game a pass in good faith. If you're absolutely set on getting this game I strongly reccommend waiting on if the community and story mode is actually completed -it's at barely 20% and that's being generous, and getting something else in the meantime. But honestly just get something else period.Like with my first review i'ma list things in pros+cons point format for the most part for sake of ease. And this review's gonna be in several parts because it got too big for the character limit. Click for full review. --- There's a lot to love about this game and where it might be going potentially.- Loveable characters who have a lot of potential for some meaningful arcs. (I'm lookin at you especially Pom, Velvet and Paprika) and cool, colourful and sketchy art style that I wish I saw more of (another example I love for anyone who also likes this style and similar, is Super Mario Strikers.)- Worldbuilding's interesting, humourous and draws me in. Though there are some questionable spots, there's lots of room for some amazing stuff if done well. - The story mode structure has you getting to see some of the world of Foena, top-down rpg style.- The lobby makes for a neat little hub, and if you play certain areas in Story Mode you might gain more appreciation for the connections and worldbuilding.I wish I could add more on pros compared to cons but that's all I can put.--- Conversly there's a lot to hate about this game and it's intended direction and current excecution, mechanically. And there's also other major issues.- So that worldbuilding? y'know where I said questionable spots? Yeah let's talk about that consitution in the Reine Museum cause uhhhh-- The Alpace Region. To be fair the storymode's extremely unfinished, but right now without spoiling too much, the current setup of the Alpace people is: being characterized as a native and traditional, but EXTREMELY long-suffering people whose hardship, suffering and dedication to tradition is deliberately played up to illogical degrees for laughs. I have extreme and seriously doubtful apprehension about this, because in terms of joke and plot setup this is a big gamble and can either be a well-done tearjerker+underdog plot (especially because it's clear from jump they have MASSIVE ties to the main plot and worldbuilding), or wind up a ♥♥♥♥♥♥-up punch down. It already is starting from a punchdown perspective with the whole played for laughs thing. We'll see. And the part about it being illogical is hard to explain without spoiling anything so i'll put it this way: There's every last piece of evidence thier region was more than liveable, it was thriveable. And so in thier current situation, it literally makes no sense for them to be living they way they are with such hardship. Wouldn't they have retained something? What happened?All that being said given the previous location, I have some theories about how that arc might wind up being handled, why they're in thier current state, and I hope i'm proven right. But i'll stop there -this is a review.--- You know how I just said the story mode's unfinished? I lied. It's WOEFULLY unfinished -This is gonna be another subsection so expect a long read. - Arizona is the only playable character, the current amount of content is very, very much padded out with more fights than needs to be necessary imo -even for a fighting game, and worst of all those fights wind up stressful by horrendously unbalanced AI. So much that I skipped entire sections of areas and sacrificed full completion JUST to avoid dealing with them.- Going into that, the story's tutorials don't teach you how to deal with said CPUs. They teach you competitive techniques which isn't in-itself bad, Problem is they try to cover it up as being needed for the story... namely to cross over needlessly hard terrain. This comes with later predators thrown in that your techniques don't help with dealing with AT ALL, because they weren't built around that or even with that in mind, and the commands I found were very analog-stick unfriendly as I had consistantly, only slightly, less trouble on the dpad.. Until I had to fight an opponent. which meant switching between the two and often. _childDocuments_.review: As an almost total newcomer to fighting games, I can't recommend this game enough just from the quality of its tutorial alone.I've always been curious about fighters and have bounced off more than a few of them, and never really understood any of the terminology or mechanics, but TFH taught me so much, and most importantly how to put it into practice as well. Beyond just the basics on combos, juggles, how to control your character etc, advanced concepts like hitstun, blockstun, negative edge, frame advantage, push blocks, armor, techs, cancels, resets, what '-2 On Block' means and so on are all explained in real, practical terms, with visual and playable examples that teach you how to actually use that information. In just a short time with the game, I've gone from knowing nothing about fighters to what feels like a really solid set of information, and in a way I don't think I could have gotten from just a guide, and definitely not from just bashing my head against CPU matches.It even encompasses character specific tutorials for each member of the cast, how to get the most out of training modes or understanding frame data, with the icing on the cake of being wrapped in a charming and approachable format. It feels strange having so much praise for a tutorial, but it was the most effective and thorough one I've seen in any game, ever.In my experience, as a newcomer to the genre you won't be immediately ready to jump right into online,CPU matches, or the story mode. This game does require patience and a willingness to learn, but I found it more than earned it, and the learning experience itself has been really compelling. It's a great feeling putting what I've learnt into practice against friends in online matches after going through its tutorial systems, and actually even being able to win matches faster than I ever thought I was going to during my time with the game.Netcode is absolute perfection, I'm an Australian playing with friends mostly in America, and I've never had such a smooth experience in any game with them, even at pings of over 200. Part of why I never played fighters was struggling with a lack of local community for them both on and offline, and the online experience being ruined by the quality of netcode across higher pings, but this game was such a pleasant surprise in that regard. I've seen GGPO praised a lot, but it has never been more apparent to me how much it earns it.As for the actual game itself, I'm so completely charmed by it, both aesthetically and mechanically. The world is unique and compelling, and I'm a huge fan of the character design and art style. Gameplay feels fluid and intuitive, the characters have a great combination of some universal inputs for basics like launchers or anti air, but beyond that could not be more different to each other. Even with a small cast size, it feels offset by just how varied and unique each character feels to play. Likewise, there is only a small set of stages, but each one has dynamic musical themes for each character, blending their own theme with the stage theme, and every matchup of characters has unique back and forth dialogue at the start of the fight. In general, the game gets a lot out of what seems like a little, and the level of polish on each element of it is incredible. The online lobby system stands out as wonderfully executed.I've never written a review on Steam before, but I really want people to give this game a chance, especially if you are new to fighters like me. It doesn't feel like a simplified version of the genre, but instead puts in the work to teach you how to play it for real. I don't want to see the developers work on this game overlooked, because I really think its doing something special. Also hey, it's only fifteen bucks.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: At the time of writing this review, it was in the early stage before Shanty came out. I'll not change the "recommendation" due to Mane6 deserving better... but I would suggest you hold off from purchasing this game until it is given back to the original development team.I did pick the game on Humble Bundle. Spoiler alert: awesome work from Mane6!After playing a couple matches online, taking a look at the Tutorial and practicing the different characters, I can honestly say that Them's Fightin' Herds is worthy of attention.Let's start with the odds: the characters all look comically absurd because they are animals fighting each other. You have a cow, a sheep, a reindeer, a flame horse, a unicorn and an alpaca. Much like Skullgirls, they are female (and yes, Skullgirls now has two male characters but that's not the point) and are fully-voiced with pre-fight taunts. Lauren Faust has also contributed to the design of these characters so if you're a My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic fan, you'll be at home.This game feels extremely fluid and responsive yet like every fighting game, Fightin' Herds will take a lot of time to understand if you're a newcomer. Thankfully, Mane6 has come up with an incredible tutorial that will allow you to go through the basics and, if you're wise and take your time to read and get past the comedy, you'll eventually learn the concepts of the fighting game genre allowing you to understand the basics and apply them in other games of the genre.The training mode is Skullgirls level of genius (it's the same engine) with frame data, attack data, hitboxes and input display which, in a modern fighting game, is required and most welcome. Each character has a Magic button for different mechanics with Supers to be spent over the match. You have three buttons like in Injustice with Light, Medium and Heavy Attacks and an universal launcher for Juggle Combos. Of course, you have defensive options like blockpush, perfect blocking (more daunting than it sounds) and different ways to get your character up post-knockdown. There's a level of depth that is explained and worth practicing.While this game does compete with Skullgirls for the value proposition, Fightin' Herds is a passion project worth supporting thanks to its odd and funny characters but the crowning achievement is the implementation of the excellent GGPO netcode in the same style as Skullgirls (now featuring GGPO) and the incredible rollback system featured in Killer Instinct. The online matches have been quick, fluid and soul-crushing because I've yet to figure out my own combos, parts of the system for me to fully grasp and the craziness that is happening on screen.If you are a fighting game fan and you wanna send a message to the editors, Fightin' Herds is that message! And it's an excellent product. Yes, you can criticize the amount of characters but even Killer Instinct and Skullgirls started with less characters. Fightin' Herds is on par with Skullgirls and Killer Instinct as the best fighting games you can play online with friends or simply for learning the basics of the genre without feeling intimidated by poor explanation.

_childDocuments_.review: First, this needs to be said: the reason this game is in early access is because of major complications with the story mode, which includes the "how to play a fighting game" tutorials, and there are still a (very) few unfinished animations. If you prefer learning from tutorials, your best bet for maximum enjoyment is to wait until full release.HOWEVER...If you want to play a fast-paced, 1 v 1 fighting game with oodles of training mode features, the best available netcode (granted, not perfect, but still better than the rest), and characters with personality, there's no reason not to pick it up now. Players coming from a Marvel \ anime background should feel at home quickly after adjusting to particular character quirks (for example, every character's movement options are a little bit different). Feeling a little lost? The friendly community has your back, regardless of whether you prefer Discord, Reddit, or forums. The pixel lobby system is great, especially if you're a fan of the 8 & 16-bit eras, though I do wish you could fit, say, 32 people in a single lobby instead of the current limit of 20.  My only real complaints are mostly personal taste: some of the stage music feels too low-energy for fight music (seems more like music for a story scene), especially compared to the main menu theme, and chip damage (damage taken from blocking certain attacks, usually specials and supers) seems a bit high for a game that allows chip-outs to win rounds (though this is probably just my bias, since I typically play games with no chip-outs, and of course will likely change as they continue to balance the game before full release).

_childDocuments_.review: Currently quite divided on this one. On one side, the game looks great, runs great on just about any rig and has some pretty great characters.The actual combat however.. it's not bad, but it needs some *serious* polishing. Some attacks, most notably heavy attacks have hitboxes larger than their animations, Tianhuo's slide attack hits the target the moment the animation of it begins *even if you're out of range* and then there's the special move system, which works by pressing a combination of keys in a certain sequence, this however often either does not work, or performs a special move when you wanted to do a normal attack, something that happened a lot to me when I wanted to perform a dash and immedeatly attack afterwards.Another issue are the combo's, in many an occasion once you get knocked up, or knock your opponent up and start hitting them with combo's, the target can just as well leave the computer, quietly make themselves some tea and come back without their character's control actually returning.Sure, the game's not pricey, at 15 bucks, but if I pay for it I'd very much like to actually be able to play the game, and I did not pay to see my character being flung through the air and I'm sure neither did my opponents.Besides all that there really isn't anything that makes this game stand out amongst other fighting games of its kind, other than that the characters are all 4 legged animals.In its current state I rate it a 6/10, I hope the developers will polish up their gameplay before the full release so I can improve this rating.EDIT:It's been a long time now. Still no campaign mode, which was promised to come "soon" and the game itself still has tons of issues.You know those sweet fighting games with that hitbox porn? This isn't one of them. Half of the time you're hitting opponents by hitting the air around them.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great 4 button fighter. I never watched MLP, so I am looking at this game as its own thing. It got a pretty good entry range when it comes to mechanics, tho the story can be quite frustrating.Story mode asks allot from the player. And has some weird difficulty spikes. Even at casual the boss/character battles can combo half your health bar down on the first round. I hope the devs looks into the difficuilty so its isn't as frustrating or at the very least make it easier to jump back in, instead of dealing with a short cutscenes and game over screen each failure. Cause how it is currently it feels very unfair with 3 rounds without health recovery. Regular PvP battles gives you a new set each round like any fighter. But in story they expect the player to go through 3 rounds with only one health bar and learn new boss exclusive moves on top of that.Certain fight even does some nasty tricks that feels incredibly cheap (Paprika on Round 2 is a good example on that). So it can feel very trail and error. Which is not fun when they are already so difficult. Tho maybe I just me needing to*git gud*  which I can admit to, if no one else has a hard time with it.Still tho, if you are more interested in the PvP elements I can recommend this one to any fan of 2D fighters. Don't let the MLP skin discourage you if you think it looks fun.

_childDocuments_.review: The Brony fandom left a scar on my life that I'd prefer to forget.But the passion to make a deep and engaging fighting game really shows with the amount of polish in this game. Companies like Capcom could learn a thing or two about bringing engaging features and detailed tutorials into their games.The gameplay is a bit "anime" as the FGC calls it. This means, faster pace, mechanices like air-blocking, instant-airdashes, pushblock, just guard, etc. are all present. If you're looking for a more footsie based fighter with a slower pace, this is not the game for you.No fighting game could every teach you how to play for real, so I expect a lot of salt, but I think this game does a good job of trying to engage players at every step of their fighting game journey. The netcode is great and I've had nothing but solid matches online.My only complaint is that the roster is very small right now. 6 characters means a lot of matches feel the same. My other complaint is that lobbies can be fairly empty at times.If you're willing to accept the game for what it is and look past its design, it's a truly amazing fighting game.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start off by saying that I am not a brony and I really dont care for the idea of playing as an animal like a llama or a cow or a deer. That just really doesnt appeal to me. However, as a fighting game player, I have been really enjoying this game and I certinally recommend it for those of you who disagree with the reasons I gave, or if you like fighting games, specifically skullgirls (you'll fit right in as it runs on the same engine.)This is a satusfying fighting game that offers a lot to learn for fighting game fans, and plenty for more casual players even at its current early access state. That being said, the target mode is pretty useless and just some kind of speedrun mode. If that is what you're into, godbless, but I dont find any value in it. The training mode has a helpful combo trial mode that can teach you the basics of combos for each characters and what you should think about landing in a match. as far as online, there are basic lobbies, but the highlight of online is the pixle lobby. If you dont find yourself privvy with the fighting game crowd, you'll really enjoy walking around here and chatting with other players and discussing strats or going into the salt caves, a pretty entertaining mode that could use some more fleshing out, but is still very interesting.Currently this game is in early access. It is missing animations, sounds, and has some balance issues. However, it is very much a playable and enjoyable game. Even now, i can recommend this game for nearly anybody. That being said, you may not get the most enjoyment out of the game if you are unwilling to learn even a bit of fighting game basics. Plenty of fun ways to play with friends, but expect killers online and ready yourself.This is a fun, enjoyable game that if even if the subject matter and history this game bothers you, if you can swallow your pride and give this game a fair chance, I think there is plenty to enjoy. Give it a chance before you judge it.Update: Recently there was a new mode added in the salt mines that is one of the most creative and interesting features in a fighting game i have seen in a long time. It truly gives you a new way to play the game. Players race to get the most salt from mining it from rocks and beating opponents. At the end of the round, the player with the most salt becomes the Bear, a super over powered boss character and has to hunt the other players down in the mine. It is a ton of fun. try it out.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an easy game to start learning with and has great tutorials and mechanics. _childDocuments_.review: I have been following this team's work since their inception of a 2D fighter fangame. When I heard that they were finally moving on to instead work on something of their own creation, I was nothing short of ecstatic. This team has always aimed to please, and has a great grasp of what makes a modern 2D fighter great -- from the visuals, to the sound design, to the juggle mechanics... _childDocuments_.review: There was a time I could say I highly recommend this game as a fantastic, fun 2D fighter with unique character designs, great music, and great mechanics. That time is no longer. And it has nothing to do with Mane6's development team, they're very talented people and did their best to make a great game. They succeeded, in a sense, but seem to have made a deal with the devil in the process. That devil is Modus Games, now rebranded as Maximum Entertainment, a publisher that handles indies like this.The long story short is Mane6 signed on with Modus to be their publisher. It worked for a time, and the game and community along with it flourished. However, it was announced a few months ago that after the final two characters (Nidra and Baihe) were released, major development would cease. Twelve of the fifteen members of the Mane6 staff were fired unceremoniously by Modus Games, and it was announced that the much-anticipated story mode chapters due to be released in the future would no longer be coming. Nor would any more characters, nor any major balance patches, nor anything other than maybe some minor fixes here and there if we were lucky. Soon after, Modus Games fired two more of the developers, stripping Mane6's original team of fifteen down to just one.Maybe these problems could've been overcome. But just a couple of days ago, patch version 6.0, which releases the final two characters I mentioned, was released. Baihe in particular, conceived as a zoner character, was given some of the most oppressive tools of any character in the game at any and all ranges, a thoroughly overpowered character, but more than that, she was broken. I don't mean "broken" in the "OP" sense, I mean "broken" in the "doesn't work" sense. She had easy-to-execute throw loops that could easily lead into effortless infinite combos. A single mistake is a round loss on the spot. And even worse, Baihe shipped with game-breaking crashes and bugs to boot. Inputting the right buttons with this character could (and would) cause bugs that broke the game or just made it crash entirely. It's a nightmare, and community organizers for tournaments are already debating whether to ban the character entirely or roll back to the previous patch version in the future. Even in those cases, Baihe's still totally playable online in casual matches, available for anyone to completely ruin the experience of other players.And then it gets worse. The game doesn't work on consoles anymore if you've got a digital release (which you almost certainly do), and I hear it doesn't work on Steam Deck either. As in, you actually just can't play it. It doesn't work.Even this could be overcome, perhaps, with a lot of community effort.. But now, at the time of writing, Mane6's own website seems to have been purged from the internet. It cannot be accessed, and therefore the art books, patch notes, and forum posts from the community are erased from time. Probably forever.Modus Games/Maximum Entertainment saw a game that wasn't turning the profits they wanted, and regardless of how good it was or how much the fanbase appreciated it, how loyal its grassroots fandom was, they didn't see enough dollar signs. They cut development, liquidated damn near the entire staff, released a game-destroying patch, and expunged a bastion of the community that cataloged the game's history. And then they rebranded from Modus Games to Maximum Entertainment to dodge the deserved backlash, duck the anger from the community they screwed over so thoroughly.I can't recommend this game at $20. I'm not sure I could recommend it at $5. Even if it were free, in its current state, I might tell you not to waste your time anymore. I legitimately don't know how much longer this game has left, and my guess is "not very."You'll hear people say that Them's Fightin' Herds died. It didn't.TFH didn't die.It was murdered.P.S. The upcoming Avatar: The Last Airbender fighting game is being published by Maximum Entertainment. Food for thought.EDIT: Mane6's website is back up as of Feb 27, but large parts of it are still gone and parts of it still don't work, like the News section. As far as I'm concerned this isn't really any better.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like fighting games, give TFH a shot! The characters are fun and the systems are deep. Lots of technical stuff to explore and lab, but a foundation with mechanics that should be familiar and intuitive for any experienced fan of the genre.I'm at about 40 hrs, so I'm still pretty green, but I love the combo training features. You can track your combo success rate, mirror the combo trials, and easily record and share combo recipes with others. The Discord community makes good use of this to help you ramp up on new tech, BnBs and pressure strings the devs didn't include (at least, this was my experience with what's available in the #shanty pins).The game works nicely (and natively!) on Linux, which is a plus for me and anyone who might hope to grind out combos on a Steam Deck.The online pixel lobbies are well done. If you're intimidated by online play, you can spectate, train or play some NPCs in the salt mines and unlock gear and accessories for your avatar.Only 7 characters with an 8th on the way. That might be a detriment for some, but I don't mind only having a handful of matchups to learn for the moment :PIn any case, play this game it's dope.

However, playing it really taught me that I can't just keep mashing through everything. I started off with the story on the easiest difficulty. It was plenty easy to fight through the basic enemies on the map. Couple that with the generous health drops and I was cruising through. That is, until I hit the first boss. I had no idea what I was doing, so after the movement section, I finally was able to throw hooves at the lad. Then he hit me with some attacks and I realized something: I had no idea how to block. Or combo. Or... anything mechanical. Needless to say, I lost quickly.This is where the tutorial came into play. I wish every game had a tutorial like this. Not only did it explain the basic movements, it also led right into tutorials centered around each character. Since I started as Arizona in the story, I stuck with her. At the time of writing this review, I've played 3 hours. I think the story only took up a half an hour of that. While progressing through, I could see myself getting better. I started unable to build a combo. I ended able to......sometimes build a combo. I think the tutorial taught me 4 or 5 combos directly, but I was able to figure out some more along the way. Coupled with the game teaching advanced mechanics and systems, I was finally able to feel halfway competent with one character.I'm excited to keep playing. Don't let the aesthetic put you off, this is a solid game that I can see myself playing for a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: I was not meant to like this game. I've dabbled into more than my share of fighters but, on a mechanical level, I will always be held back by poor execution skills, a reason why I tend to stay away from combo-heavy brawlers. Cute critters isn't what I'm usually seeking in my games and, moreover, I'm certainly no MLP enthusiast (sorry Ms. Faust). Yet...What Mane6 managed to do here is absolutely bluffing. Those guys get what it takes to make a good fighting game.Built on the same engine than Skullgirls, the animations are slick, the combo system competent with universal safeguards implemented to prevent being chained to death without any opportunity to reset. The duels are tense and with its implementation of the GGPO rollback netcode, the game runs pretty smoothly online even with 100+ ping.Those things are to be expected in a modern fighter but Fighting Herds goes far beyond the basics by offering some excellent tutorials, certainly amongst the best on the market; very didactic they don’t shy away from more advanced notions like hitboxes and frame data, things that are central to the genre but usually hidden from the public eye. Even better, very complete training options allow the player to lab extensively. All in all very good things that make for a very accessible and beginner-friendly fighter.All of this would already be great but the game totally took me by surprise with a rather ambitious story mode at the crossroads of an early 16-bit era RPG (lite) and a fighting game, not unlike what we’ve seen in recent years with the Smash Bros series.So yeah, those devs made me a believer. There’s one big downside that prevents the game from reaching true greatness though : the core roster is very, very, small by today’s standard, with only six playable characters (seven very soon!). That’s even smaller than the original Street Fighter 2! Really not enough when most games in the genre won’t launch under 12 characters. Hopefully this will be addressed with future updates.

_childDocuments_.review: These days, if a fighter doesn't have over twenty fighters, people complain that it's pretty limited in terms of content. I'm generally one of those people - I threw a lot of shade at Blazblue CTB when it first came out, and it was primarily for that reason. A fighter generally needs a decently sized roster to allow people to mix up their options a bit so the game can keep feeling fresh.That's not the case here.How does a fighting game with only six characters (so far) lend itself to so much replayability? Because the devs put their heart and soul into making sure every move, every option that you could possibly take at any given time, was dead solid perfect. I've had this game for a decent amount of time, since I got the early access version off of Humble. Let me tell you - it was tight back then. But now? It's AMAZING. The framerate is extra smooth no matter what I run it on (I've played the game on both a 1080 Ti monster desktop and a Vista-era laptop!), and the responsiveness of the characters goes beyond framerate - it was CODED tight, and it remains tight at all times. Even the few times it did lag for me in early development, it always seemed like ONLY the graphics hanged, but the gameplay itself went on unimpeded. That shows you their priorities, and I'm beginning to think that every fighting game should be coded with that kind of mentality.Another reason it keeps so fresh is that it really mastered the "four-legged battle" concept that other games didn't dare to tread for so long. Remember the uproar that came when MvC3 launched and people raved about how unique Amaterasu felt? It's like that, but times six (again, so far). Movements that you wouldn't think would feel natural, even COULD feel natural, DO feel natural. I'm almost beginning to suspect that the dev team members all have four legs themselves.And, of course, the style of the game is superb. Looks great, sounds great, the character designs and dialogues are great, the whole shebang. I REALLY appreciate the option to choose between 2D and 3D backgrounds, that helps a TON with keeping the game hardware-accessible (something that many "AAA" teams should take some cues from).Overall, the game is great! It packs a heap of content in despite what seems initially to be a very small roster, and I know you'll have a blast with it!

Not only that, there is a platforming section too, which is neat!Some people may find the game's lacks of characters is bad, but fret notWhile the game currently has only 6 playable characters on its roster, each character plays differently.The tutorial in this game teach you the basic of both the fundamental of fighting game and your character of chosen.The training mode is where the gem really lies. It has complete aspects that you need to improve your play, ranging from record-replay opponent inputs to frame data. Which is a great job from the dev because there is other developer with more big budget that outright selling you frame data for additional prices.The online pixel lobby system is similar to Blazblue Lobby, which you can find your opponent, and customize your avatar visual (this is the most important aspect of the game). _childDocuments_.review: Before you ask: Yes, this is that (ex) My Little Pony fighting game you've probably heard about. And no, it doesn't matter, because this game rocks and is a lot of fun regardless of your feelings on MLP.I'm the first to say I'm usually a little hesitant towards combo-heavy fighters because my execution isn't the best, but in TFH I actually didn't find this an issue since the input timing is generous and the combo paths are pretty simple. If you've played Marvel vs Capcom 3 or DBFZ and know what a "magic series" is, you can pick this up right away. If you don't, good news! The tutorial is very in-depth and explains things in a way that anyone can get into. Visually the hand-drawn sprites look great, and while there's only six characters, they all feel unique and there's a balance between rushdown (Arizona, Tiaunho), keepaway (Velvet, Oleander), and, uh, miscellaneous (Pom, Paprika). There's a good variety of modes (though part of me wonders if they got a little *too* ambitious with the story stuff - right now only chapter 1 of 6 is done and they're working on other stuff like a new character before going back to it) and the training options have everything you want, including combo trials and visual hitboxes.And also - holy crap, I did not expect the music to be so good! The fact that each characters respective themes "overlap" the stage theme as one character begins to dominate the match is genius. I absolutely love dynamic music stuff like this.Well worth the asking price. Don't let the long combos or cutesy visuals dissuade you if you want a solid fighting game.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't normally like Fighting Games, but Them's Fightin' Herds is so creative, endearing, and fun that it's on my top ten favorite games list of all time. Many people will write this game off because it's a "furry game" or whatever, but the characters are all really unique and charming. Once you get rid of your internalized fear of furries because of societal norms, you'll see that the characters are super awesome and were written really well. Though even if you ignore all that, this game is functionally better then most fighting games because it *actually explains how to play the game.* Games like Marvel Versus Capcom or even Dragonball Fighterz have really boring tutorials that bore the player and don't teach effectively. Marvel Versus Capcom in particular doesn't even explain that "B" doesn't mean the same "B" that's on your controller. Fighting Games expect you to already know all of this. However TFH does the exact opposite. Oleander leads the tutorial with her fourth wall breaking jokes, you can skip parts you already know or can't quite complete yet, and it's accompanied by the games amazing soundtrack. Well the whole game has that soundtrack but you know what I mean.Currently the game does suffer from a lack of characters though. A season pass has been announced where we will be getting four new characters, but there still should be more by now since it's been almost like 2 years since the game came out. Additionally, there aren't many players right now as well, though when this game comes to consoles with crossplay soon, that problem will be solved immediately. I know a toonn of friends on Discord who want to play but don't have PC's.And lastly the community is just super duper wholesome especially for a fighting game. And don't worry about people being weird, all the bronies and furries on the game are really nice and awesome.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: 3/5 Okay under the circumstancesA game that will never be finished and was never professional.The primary reason not to buy TFH is because its production has been canceled and all further proceeds will go to the publisher Modus instead of the individual developers. I picked it up for ulterior motives and am not likely to play it indepth. I am not in any rush to provide more money to either party.The other reason is that nobody plays it.The game was cancelled as the ultimate consequence of its unhealthy development, leading to reliance on third-party support such as Modus. Like many other Kickstarter projects, it is too ambitious of a title for its means, due to underestimating the budget needed, inefficient planning, and unknown other demands on the developers' time and energy (i.e. "we got jobs and families".) Because of all of this, it isn't an especially contentful or particularly polished fighting game compared to other modern offers. There are nine characters that work right and two that at time of writing do not. The character select screen looks depressing due to the massive amount of empty space, which could be mitigated just by larger icons but would ideally contain the other half of the character cast, a pipe dream which is no longer on the table.I've seen other players say TFH is most similar to Blazblue. I've never played Blazblue. The most similar game I'm familiar with is Skullgirls, whose engine was licensed to produce TFH, and which is based on Darkstalkers (which I played.) The primary inheritance of this is the combo system, which generally goes "up the ladder" of weaks to mediums to strongs to specials to supers with a few special cases. TFH gradually nerfs combos the longer they go on.TFH cannot make up its mind what image it wants to present, partially because it is held back by its fundamentally derivative origins.Much like Freedom Planet and Sonic, TFH is terrified of openly admitting its powerful and blatant creative influences from My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic and the fandom thereof, especially as it was in 2013. This is likely in part due to Hasbro's C&D against Fighting is Magic, which makes any perception of TFH as derivative in any way a dangerous concept.The initial six characters, whose redesigns are provided by initial FiM showrunner Lauren Faust, are directly based upon the main six characters of Fighting is Magic. As these characters were in different states of completion their gameplay similarities are stronger for some than others - e.g. Arizona plays almost identically to Applejack, while Velvet plays only vaguely like Rarity.Their personalities, however, are consistently derivative and recognizable to the pony fandom with one exception, and these personalities are extrapolated to form the civilizations of the game world. Oleander is a prim snob like Twilight in early seasons while collectively every other unicorn is Celestia seemingly ignoring Twilight's concerns, Velvet is Rarity if she thought being Swedish was in and every single deer is Rarity if she never realized what a PoS she is, Arizona is Rainbow Dash pretending to be Applejack and the biggest difference is her parents are around, Paprika is Pinkie under Poison Joke (while all other alpacas have no personality), and Pom is Fluttershy in constant "I guess I have to do something" mode while all other sheep are Fluttershy outside of that mode. Tianhuo is the exception: maybe if Rainbow Dash ever grew up she'd be more like Tianhuo, who is a bit showboaty but is very mature and responsible. The longma nation is typical wuxia fantasy stuff - not Rainbow Dash-y stuff.The voice acting varies dramatically in quality. Tara Strong with a goofy country accent gives Arizona easily the best vocal performance of the first seven characters, Paprika does not actually talk and just makes weird noises. The other five are quite frankly terrible, and out of them only Oleander remembers what her accent is (horrendously British.) Now, Velvet is supposed to be faking her accent, but she sounds bad regardless. Chris Sabat performs a fantastic booming superhero voice for Stronghoof and the other DLC characters are just kind of tolerable.The story mode is the most visible casualty as it was going to have a chapter each for at least the initial six characters but will never be finished beyond Ch. 1 (Arizona). The writing of story mode portrays the initial six with much heavier accents than the voice acting does except for Oleander who is English so her text is just English, Paprika who does not talk and whose text is wingdings, and Arizona who is properly accented in both. Shanty does not appear in Arizona's chapter to take a crack at Jamaican, which is unfortunate as that accent is endearingly incomprehensible both spoken and written.Reine City, home of the Rarity-deer, is hornier than Bangkok and loaded with unsubtle sexual references on just about every street corner. It's bizarre, and in context of its known pony influences and its preoccupation with shipping, a bit cloppy and uncomfortable.Online play features a Pixel Lobby with a Salt Mines PvE mode that is good for learning the basics of playing the game or developing a new character. Story Mode and the Pixel Lobby feature collectible cosmetics whose descriptions are absolutely all referential humor that further damages the game's dignity.All in all, the game is okay, but it never seized a hold in the fighting game market, no longer has a chance to, and was never going to escape its image as a My Little Pony fangame in any event.

_childDocuments_.review: Before i start this review i wanna say that this is my first fighting Game ever and in general im really suck at those kind of games. But even If i suck at this game i still had the fun of my life.The first thing i have to say is that the tutorial in this game is absolutely fantastic and perfect for beginners like me, because it don't just give you a list of combos, it explains the basic stuff of fighting games and much more. Besides of that it even explains the basic and special moves of each character individually. There are even some jokes here and there to make the tutorial more fun which i think is a really cool touch. A thing that i also like is the story mode. For now only the first chapter is available but the other chapters will be added to the game later for free so personally i don't mind. Normanly the story mode in fighting games is mostly nothing special and kind of lazy. Luckily i can't say the same thing about this game. The story mode in this game is amazing: the story is great, you can move freely around the map, the characters are fun and have good dialog, the music is amazing, there are jump and run section here and there, the pixelart is beautiful and it has a lot of attention to detail and is in general a really fun and charming experience. The online mode is really good too, because you don't just get connected to a player and fight, you get a little overworld where you can walk around with other players and challenge them to fight. You also can buy cosmetics with the ingame currency salt. To get salt you can go to the salt mines with other players and collect salt, fight enemies and find chests with cosmtics in it. There is also the function that a chest with a lot of salt will drop and two players can fight for it, wich is a cool idea. As a whole the online mode is a lot of fun and i really like that the online mode is more then just fight with other Players. The only negative stuff i could think of is there are only 7 characters to play, but each character is so well thought, its not that big of a problem, and there will also be 4 characters added to the game with the season pass. The other thing that catched my eye was that there was not a lot of people in the online lobbys. I mean most of the time there will be enough players to play with, but mostly there is one lobby full and the rest empty, but hopefully the issue will be fixed when the game lauches on consoles with crossplay. In conclusion this game is a hidden gem, it has fun combat, it is beginner friendly, its well animated, the music slaps and it has a lot of attention detail. You can really tell that the devs put there hearts and souls into this game. I would recommend this game to everyone, especially for people who never played a fighting game. I know the whole pony aspect is a little meh, but if you look through that you will find a game who has a lot of charm and soul. So please give this game a try.

_childDocuments_.review: The controls are such a mess on controller, and without a controller, the game is unpleasant to play (at least for me). I literally couldn't activate some specials because of how hit-or-miss the controller sensitivity is. You have to do quickly an up and down movement? 50% chance it'll work as intended, 90% chance you will go into another completely different direction because the stick was moved 000.1mm too much to the left. Blocking is also incredibly hard to do right because of this. It's so frustrating.You also have 0.1 second time to continue your attack movement else it will be cancelled. You literally need an inhumane reaction time, and especially as you start playing this game it is impossible to do. You need to have the button/stick combinations so much nailed into your head that you are able to recite it at a more serious level than by heart.This fighting game is absolutely not for beginners and not even for more experienced players. It is for the extreme hardcore players - you have to put 100% of your time into this game else you won't get even moderately good at it or even learn it. _childDocuments_.review: Designed for the fighters hardcore base, need to be deeply mastered to enjoy the extra content.The story mode is absolutely not a tool for learning the game or enjoying it (but it should be),Even the tutorials do not prepare you for being wrecked over and over, eventhough they are quite well done.Only long training and practice can help you.Game mechanics feel incomplete (air dashes ? in-air combo breaking ?) and poorly balanced.All characters needs a wider range of normal attacks.Contact feedback feels super smooth instead of chunky like actually hitting something...These are the two great dark in my opinion :First one, the AI is basically reading all your moves even in the first half of difficulties choices.It responds in a far too robotic fashion, virtually never making mistakes and giving the most optimized reaction all the time.That's a long time i've not had such a bad feeling against a CPU opponent in a VS...A more concilient AI is the key to open the game to new player who just want to enjoy the game without particularly cumbersome training.The second point is a combination of animations timings and H-boxes not enough polished to expect players proper call & response.Imagine :* a character being able to fireball in any direction in the blink of an eye...* having a protection of a dozen frames of invicibilty for each (wiff ? no problem i'm covered!)...* the projectile translation covers all the the screen width within 10 frames @ 60...* the projectile hitbox being larger than the visual...* ...and call this character "Velvet" (at least its not an Alpaca!)This makes the player unable to discover instinctively through random practice (Story mode anyone ?) the priorities.Nothing which would visually be coherent works (hugh....these unprobable overheads...)Only long training sessions with H-boxes activated can help you there for VS.Some of the story mode predators are particularly unreadable and hard to decipher and too frequent die and retry is not helping to understand how to properly handle their fights.The game falls into the bad extreme of allowing "very long" combos.They are frustrating to endure (as every juggle) and frustrating to miss the tools to escape with.Others fighting games have since a long time implemented combo-breaking mechanics and smoother air recover, which feel missing here.The story mode (playing in hard mode) could serve both the narrative and as progressive tutorial.Instead and to repesent its real nature, it should have been titled : "Have you practiced 100 hours Arizona ? No ? Expect to vomit blood."What's more frustrating than wasting players interest and engagement, with a cute universe, if it is to have them suffer through :* poor checkpoints* nausea-inducing cameras (Flappies...)* harsh bashing at each boss if not to completly regular enemies* very slow retry pacing (and slow loading ???)* being unable to tweak the difficulty (at least toning it down)In multiplayer the game is fun a for a couple of hours and that's it.If you want a cartoony VS game, prefer it Skullgirls, BlazBlue, or any old doujin fighter.

_childDocuments_.review: TFH is a gem among the many online-focused arcade-mode-only fighting games in today’s market and it’s admirably fulfilling for a casual who has tried and failed to get excited about participating in this genre.Each character in the game’s smaller, more precise roster is immediately distinguishable and comes equipped with their own distinct moveset, mechanics, personality, and catchy music. Seven doesn’t sound like a lot of characters, but to someone who constantly feels like a complete fighting game noob, it’s a perfect number. After all, it’s overwhelming to be expected to eventually understand the mechanics of 26, 45, or 89 opponents or even pick a main from an oversized cast that’s all instantly available to you.Even with all the fighting games that I’ve sampled, this was my first four-button fighter and I instantly found this layout to be more appealing than the traditional six-button one. It’s a massive relief to have less options to constantly consider as well as a single logical hierarchy of attacks. It also requires less right-hand movement on a fightstick, further reducing the unnecessary mental strain and physical fatigue that comes with playing with two additional buttons.There’s a universal character sheet that describes the basics that every character shares. So, once you know the straightforward fundamentals, you can pick up any character and not be completely stranded. It just goes to show that depth and fun can be achieved without forcing the player to wrap their head around the exact location of every finger on whatever button-covered device they’re using.TFH’s story mode is exactly what this genre needs and I desperately wish other games would adopt this standard. Rather than simply being a mix of cutscenes and default AI matches, story mode pits you against ‘shadow creatures’ that all act differently in predictable ways. Each one is there to teach and reinforce important concepts. Unlike scripted tutorials that tell you to block, grab, or anti-air on queue, these enemies punish and reward specific behavior in a free-form context. Since lost health carries over between fights and healing isn’t too common, it’s in your best interests to slow down and think carefully about the AI’s strengths and weaknesses. It’s more akin to genuine practice and scaffolding than the dull memorization that’s employed in the lab. After just a few hours of the story mode, I actually felt like I understood how TFH works. By the end, I may have not mastered performing any eccentric combos, but I felt as if I knew how to react to various common moves and how to position myself against different enemies. That’s why it’s all the more disappointing that I couldn’t find any human players to test my newfound confidence against.I’ve never been as motivated to lonesomely play a 2D fighter, but I can't seem to find any online matches. Thank goodness you can play other modes while you queue for casual matchmaking because I’ve spent hours doing so and have never found a single human opponent. Unless I go as far as to join the discord and  communicate with strangers, it looks like all I've got left to do is get destroyed by the vicious high-level AI or maybe grind out the combo tutorials. TFH may shortly end up on the shelf since the few internet strangers I know would be unlikely to look past the game’s premise and visuals (that I adore by the way). Regardless, I'll most definitely be back when the next chapter of the story mode is released!

_childDocuments_.review: Well, the game is finished. Time for me to review this game... 4 years later.Gameplay is some of the best I've experienced out of any game I've ever played. Its fun, energetic, fast paced, its all I could ever want. Its a dopamine rush that would get me sitting and playing for HOURS. I'm happy they fixed the gameplay in the last patch, because that was what made me call it my favorite video game before the Shanty release. Also seeing the characters move around the screen and beat each other up is so satisfying and fun to watch. The characters are all fun and designed in each of their own ways that make them special depending on player preference. I find Velvet and Baihe the most fun, and fit my playstyle and pacing well. The music is also soooo amazing. I hum it to myself a few times every other week and it plays in my head sometimes. Its so fun and memorable. Tian and Paprika's themes mostly. Same with Oli's forest and Shanty's themes. The dynamic music adds to the experience in so many ways, its hard how much I can describe how amazing it is.The artstyle is really nice. Better than MLP which Lauren Faust helped design the game's style and characters, and I think this is the best she's done so far. They all have cute and sharp character designs that make them stand out. They may not fit a fighting game aesthetic, but they're fun to watch on screen. That is what's important. Now to the part everyone has been upset about... the story mode is canned.  I was personally not very happy to hear that news. Part of what drew me to want to play more was the more casual oriented story mode. I get it was cut due to the devs lack of motivation and a company buy-out, but I jsut wished they gave us the whole thing. It was even promised during the kickstarter. However it doesn't matter because most of Mane6 has been totally canned from this new company. Alright, to give a final rating, its a 9.5/10. TLDR===========PROS + - Some of my favorite perfected gameplay a game has ever had PERIOD.- Good character designs all with unique personalities and relatable based on who you main- Awesome worthwhile OST with DYNAMIC MUSIC- Cool stages to fight in- Easy to learn but hard to master difficultyCONS - - Updates would change gameplay and make it worse for a time but its good once again (thanks)- Story mode is not finished and it never will be- Just enough characters but could've used some more (non-DLC)
