_childDocuments_.review: The Outer Worlds is effectively the Fallout 3/New Vegas formula, scaled down exponentially in size, and sillier. While both The Outer Worlds and the Fallout games have dark comedy, The Outer Worlds is a bit more whimsical and over-the-top on a more frequent basis than the Fallout games. There were definitely a lot of dark events I read about and a couple of dark story beats throughout the game, but Fallout is the more serious setting. That said, by the time the credits rolled in The Outer Worlds, I had certainly gotten thoroughly invested in the fates of quite a few of the characters and the colonies. This game basically very similarly to a Fallout 3/New Vegas game, complete with mountains of items to steal and pickpocket from people. The setting/tone and size of the game are the big differences here.Although my play time shows as 67.5 hours, I don't know how many hours of that were me being AFK. However, this game is markedly shorter than a game like Fallout 3/New Vegas (I'm not bringing up Fallout 4 because I think The Outer Worlds' dialog systems were MUCH better than Fallout 4, in my opinion). If the selling point for you in Fallout games is that they take dozens and dozens of hours to finish, then you might not like The Outer Worlds. If you don't like space-faring settings or comical shenanigans, then you might not like The Outer Worlds.The only things I can really complain about with the game are that while the main storyline is present/active throughout the length of the game, it felt like it was absent in most of the middle of the game. On the one hand, it's cleverly subtle and doesn't feel like the main quest is a separate "thing" from the rest of what's going on in such a way that it's jarring. On the other hand, though, you may feel like the main storyline "stopped" a little ways into the game and doesn't really pick up again until you're in the final hours of the game. Other than the storyline, the companion characters were rather hit or miss. One annoyed me to no end, one has no personality, and one was a fellow who just didn't interest me. I adored the engineer girl, Parvati, however. I don't think I ever removed her from my party unless I had to. Oh! Last complaint: jumping feels weird in this game. There are no quests I can recall that require "platforming," thankfully, but there are a few boxes you leap to or shortcuts you might try to take which would have you jump on things. The jumping is clunky and did not satisfy me at all in this game, but these are minor gripes.Without spoiling what happens in the ending, I will say that it consists entirely of a slideshow and narration, much like Fallout 3/New Vegas. However, I LOVED it. I was shocked at how many different characters/factions were given ending narration, and the conclusions for them were generally really fulfilling. Now, if I had been a violent psycho-killer and ruined everything, the ending may have been a lot less satisfying (or more? =p), but I was left smiling and pleased with the ending of the game. It's nothing artsy or shocking, but I was not left disappointed. It's financially cheap to make an ending like this when compared to animated endings, but honestly, if they have as much screen time and decent writing as we see in The Outer Worlds' ending, then I would love to see other games adopt this sort of ending. Far too often, there isn't enough in the budget and a crappy 30-second movie plays that doesn't give you any closure. This ending is one that delighted me as a fan of closure. I'm not saying it's amazing, but it's the kind of thing I'd like to see more of in games, since endings tend to be some of the worst things in games, in my opinion.In closing, it's my opinion that if the gameplay loop of Fallout 3/New Vegas, space-faring sci-fi settings, and dark/silly comedy are things you would enjoy in a game, that there's a good possibility you may like The Outer Worlds. Unlike some who place a large amount of value on a game going out of its way to take a long time to complete, The Outer Worlds takes that Fallout 3/New Vegas gameplay and compacts it down into something that doesn't waste as much of players' time. There are a handful of locations that aren't related to quests, but not a lot, and I love that. The Outer Worlds respects your time compared to Fallout 3/New Vegas, and for that, it has *my* respect.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: The game feels like they tried to cut costs at every possible corner. No cutscenes, no voice acting for your character, "cities" containing only six buildings—three of which can be entered, every second home looks exactly the same inside, a low variety of weapons, and the "epic fight to decide the fate of a conflict between two factions" is actually just walking a few meters, killing three enemies, and then repeating the same thing about six times. I also can't say anything positive about the story other than the fact that it exists. The game is too easy, even on the hardest difficulty level. It's also quite short, especially if you don't engage in any side activities.I probably found only one aspect of the game that could be considered positive: a pretty good RPG-feeling (excluding how the equipment system works). I had a constant sense of my character getting better and better with each level, both in terms of combat and in non-combat situations. It made leveling up somewhat enjoyable.Overall, if you liked New Vegas, there's a decent chance you'll like this one too. For me personally, I couldn't find almost anything I look for in an RPG, so I wouldn't recommend it to my friends.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: you get to become a freelancer in space completing odd jobs and stuff trying to discover who you are, its pretty fun so far, there is a fairly big skill tree and you can specialize in something, like sneaking around or focus on your gunplay. there are also crafting type skills you can specialize in as well. wide variety on what you can make your character be. If you dont like s certain build you can always reset it with a price. story is good and choice driven.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. A great new shiny product from a studio who's games I've enjoyed for decades? Yes, please! But it loses so much momentum so early. Much of the quest text and the majority of flavor text you get from notes and other records is bland and pointless. The combat was passable, but the bad A.I. really ruins it. The weapon variety is extremely disappointing. You start getting re-statted and not even re-skinned weapons as early as the 2nd quest hub/location. Companions are a huge part of a game like this, and they all fell very flat expect for the first couple. Weak characters that are also very shallow and poorly written. Good voice acting overall though. Worth it if it's on sale. Otherwise wait it out, because this game is not worth full asking price.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: A decent-to-good game that's always going to get negative reviews because Obsidian made New Vegas and this isn't New Vegas.   It doesn't claim, at any point, that it is or wants to be New Vegas, but these people saw a youtube video saying it was by Obsidian and thus decided it must be exactly like New Vegas. It isn't.  The Outer Worlds is an FPS with RPG elements, closer to the original Mass Effect than any Fallout game.  The only similarity to the latter is that the plot and characters are supposed to be satirical and whatever, but go miles past the mark with no subtlety whatsoever, because the modern gamer is expected to have the mental analytical capacity of a bottle of tomato ketchup.  Let's be honest - they aren't wrong.  The Outer Worlds is a fun game, not too challenging mentally nor mechanically, just a pleasure to sit down and play. That's what we're here to do, after all, right?  It looks pretty good too.  Don't believe the edgelords saying it looks like its from 2008.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: Big fan of RPGs like Fallout, so I was very excited to play through The Outer Worlds. For the first in the (what I imagine will become a) series, it was great. Very impressive what they pulled off and just how similar it felt to a Fallout game. It's very rough around the edges like a FO game, not the best animations and movement, but the real star of the show is the freedom of the world and the feeling that it's a real futuristic setting. I love Firefly and Serenity, so I was hoping for that from the characters and setting, and that's exactly what I got. Combat was solid and character attributes are plentiful to really pick your own playstyle. I didn't get too obsessed with side-quests and after a little while I ended up committing to just push full force into the main quest. Took a little less than 20 hours to complete. Can't wait to play through their next title.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: When I first started playing this game I thought it looked great. The run through Emerald Vale was fun, interesting and the combat and crafting system felt well balanced - playing on normal setting did feel a bit easier than it should be but that kinda fit the vibe of the game and I could live with it... or so I thought.Being fair, The Outer Worlds is very well written, excellently voice acted and wonderfully beautiful to look at. there are other details I like too: like the representation of Parvati as an asexual character was very well done among a good few other things but first off, I've got to ask: why completely copy Fallout's theme's - they obviously have good writers so why not try to write something original?Then there is the combat system, it's unbalanced. As I said, it feels okay in Emerald Vale but once I reached Monarch it was beginning to show flaws. Okay, i'm playing on normal difficult but it is far too easy. I just used guns, I could have a beast attack me in melee but all I need to do his hold down the left mouse button while it claws away at me and fire - I might need to reload while its hitting me but it's not like I'm going to die or even need to use an inhaler. Combat at this level starts to get dull. Sure there are a few instance that have a modicum of risk on normal difficulty but they are few and far between. Gorgon was an exception to this, I did need to use the inhaler a few times there but that was it, Eriadnos was just back to normal. Tactical Time Dilation? Great idea for a game mechanic (not original but a potentially fun addition to game play) but only if there is any need for it. There isn't, combat is simply too easy. Melee is another obsolete addition (admittedly, I don't like 1st person melee so I am biased here) - guns do the job fine, why waste skill points on melee skills and why learn an intricate button combo combat system when you enemies are so fragile they pose no threat? Of course I am aware there is a harder difficulty but I didn't feel comfortable with that either. I like to play a normal difficulty game, not hard. This game has easy and hard, there's nothing inbetween.To be honest though, I could have lived with the combat/gameplay flaws - the plot and its presentation is good enough, what broke it for me was the level cap. I'm not exactly sure when I reached the level cap (36 if you didn't know), in the central plotline I was ready to travel to Byzantium for Wells but I had decided to do both DLC before I moved on to that. I hit the cap either towards the end of Gorgon or early in Eriadnos. Shortly after I hit level cap and before I complete Eriadnos a number of things became apparent: there are no new items to be found aside from a couple of uniques, everything in every box, corpse or case is something you have seen before - furthermore, I've got the best equipment I need for every character and on top of that I've tinkered everything to the max. This means there is no point collecting money or items anymore, so why explore beyond plot nav points when there is literally nothing to find. Yes, there is the need for ammunition, weapon/armour parts but I have so many of these I guessed I wouldn't run out of any of them before I reached the end of the game. I was right. So, no point in exploring or looking for stuff anymore and on top of that the crafting system is obsolete now as well given that all equipment is modded and maxed out and there is nothing new to find.For me, removing the exploration, the search for new interesting 'stuff' or building my character removes the main factors I find interesting about this sort of game - mix that in with a sub par combat/gameplay experience and they've lost me. Sure, there's still the plot but I didn't pay for a visual novel, I paid for a GAME.Anyway, I powered from plot nav point to plot nav point to get the game over and done with once I realized the games strangling limitations. I've completed it now. I can uninstall it and forget about it. My advice to you, if you haven't been put off is don't pay full price for it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I recommend it. A solid first person RPG with a story that keep me in. The writing is clever, and funny at times, and the choices you need to make end up being up to your own morals (which is great, no "wrong" answers). Definitely a game to playMy only complaint, and its not anything that would ever deter me from playing the game, but I feel like I was too powerful too quick. I went all in on "Long Guns", and ended up keeping the first Assault Rifle i found the entire game. I used a total of 2 weapons (the AR and a sniper) because I literally had no need to use anything else. Pop everything in the head and it died. So for that the combat is decent. Also you level up a lot, to the point where I didn't have anywhere to put skill points that I cared about because everything else was maxed, or as high as I wanted it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: Great semi-open world RPG with top-notch storytelling and quest design, set in a masterfully written and designed world that easily competes with Obsidian's Fallout NV, although at a much smaller scale. This game doesn't get half the acknowledgement it deserves. If you are looking for a modern, yet genuine role playing experience, and craving for new worlds/IPs to get into, this is a no-brainer. Be sure to grab the season pass as well, as it grants you access to at least one solid expansion pack.My only blame would be, do yourself a favor and play in highest difficulty mode right off the bat to face some decent challenge.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: I bought The Outer Worlds: Non-Mandatory Corporate-Sponsored Bundle for about $42 since it was on sale. Good god was it worth it! One of my hobbies is watching YouTube video essays that can be as long as 2+ hours on video games, even if I've never played those games before. I did that with pretty much all of the Fallout games even though I've never played a single one. The way people (including those who make video essays) talk about New Vegas and the fact that it was made by the same people who made The Outer Worlds are half the reason I bought it. The other half is that it's a brand new franchise! No need to sit through 100 lore videos or play 10 games some of which are older than sin just to not feel like you're missing out on references. Just install it and play, you've got this! I don't feel like I know enough about the other games in the genre that came along before The Outer Worlds to recommend it to veterans twice my age, but if you wanted to get started on playing this kind of game but didn't want to start some place like Elder Scrolls 50 or Fallout 10 billion or Deus Ex (released 200 BC) this is the game for you!
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: *Be aware of spoilers*As far as the first impression goes, the step-up from Fallout franchise is obvious immediately, as many of the design choices revel around the post-second world war era, just like Fallout does. This game however, takes to whole another level, as you are not wandering an empty wasteland, but a whole new solar system. Reminded me of Mass Effect: Andromeda and No Man's sky in terms of the environment designs. Would I recommend it? Hell yeah. Those seven hours I've poured into the game today, worth it. Every damn minute. However, from the standpoint of repetitive game play, I know it might turn into standard RPG model we've seen in Fallout 3 and those that came afterwards. Only time will tell. But, for a half the prize I've got the game for, still worth it. Characters are funny, they have you empathise with them and their little stories. Even a damn guard at the door of the first settlement has more story to him than the carboard filler characters we see in triple A games. Gun play is your standard 1st person shooter. Guns can be modified. There's quick-melee as well. Rifles can be a bit inprecise at range. Nothing too surprising, had the same issues in Fallout games.One bug I keep running into is when there happens to play more sounds at once, there's a chance the sound engines gets stuck and no sounds, or music are played. Returning to main menu fixes the issue. Usually happens after 3-4 hours of game play.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: As far as Obsidian games go this one is different. It's an FPS with limited RPG and tactical elements. The game is packed with eye-candy from being able to watch Jupiter-like and Saturn-like planets from your space ship or the surface of the moon you're on to being able to walk around on their moons' luscious landscapes. It's set in a charming, wacky, satirical universe overrun with overbearing corporations and you're a freelancer who makes his living doing odd-jobs for clients. Combat feels finely tuned and time dilation is an interesting feature which gives you a pause for you to figure out what you want to do in an encounter. You can command your team mates to execute their special abilities on enemy forces. There's an inventory where you can outfit your character's gear and weapons, as well as your team mates'. You gain levels and distribute points to different skills and perks, as well as your team mates'. You shape the world based on the choices you make in the story. You can modify weapons and armor with 'mods' that you pick up. You break weapons and armor down at a push of button that you can use to repair your gear at workbenches or you can sell it to vendors. Team members offer interesting diversions and some back story as well. It's one of those games that makes you want to know what's gonna happen next.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: I was hoping to get Fallout in space but this game tries to be both that and Borderlands and fails either way. While admittedly I only have a few hours playing the game I realized this wasn't the new RPG experience I was looking for. Character progression seems pretty shallow (Take this perk to do 10% more damage with _) and weapons are generated in the same way as Borderlands, which works well in their game but in this single player experience I'm not really sold on (it was a little annoying in the first Mass Effect). Quests as well seem to be pretty standard fetch stuff that doesn't seem to have much of an effect on the world. Combat was pretty lack luster although their version of V.A.T.S. was interesting. Enemies were not super interesting to fight and found myself turning up the difficulty to get some sort of challenge because I wasn't having fun as it was.It doesn't feel good writing this review because I loved the concept and was excited for an RPG from Obsidian again but this really fails to live up to some of their previous works in terms of character development and story building. I will try playing again in the future and hope to find more fun to have than I did the first time.Quick Pros:Decent writing to where I chuckled a few times.Combat while not perfect is fast paced.I was excited to receive my own space ship but haven't used it as of yet.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: Although a very well structured game, it is very short. I completed the game in 36 hours on normal difficulty and that was not achievement chasing. The other difficulties will be more challenging and i look forward to. Overall very story rich. It doesn't really have the open world type feeling to it as places are so small, Enemies have a respawn timer. loot boxes do not respawn loot etc..visually stunning of course. I expected a-lot more from the game if i am honest, but overall satisfied, hoping more dlc to come in the Future.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: Aggressively mediocre. If you are desperate to play a first person RPG, this will do. But I can't actively recommend it. Replaying New Vegas for the 10th time will likely be more fun.Loot and gear in particular are some of the most boring you'll find anywhere. It's similar to Fallout 3, but with even less variety, and a silly level-based gear system. Replacing a generic level 25 pistol with a generic level 30 pistol is so fun!
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing the main story and a couple side quests,I think what a lot of people say about if you like NV you will like this is not true. There is a big change you notice when playing this came compared to any other fallout game. Its that the map feels significantly more closed off and in some cases it is. This was probably done to improve performance but nonetheless is still more restrictive. I personally enjoyed the setting very much and looking up and seeing a different sky depending on the planet you are on was pretty cool. The planets themselves seem small and the map in general will as you have to move to your ship every time to switch planets. My only other gripe with the game is that yes, it indeed feels quite short at least compared to fallout. Otherwise awesome game with fantastic charcters with tons of soul. Great gun play , I thought it was better than fallouts. Weaker on the custimization side with not too many outfit possibilities but it did not feel to impactful as there is no third person anyway.  A solid 8/10 , I would buy it if it is less than 30$
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: I originally played this on the Epic store, but repurchased it on Steam to try it again as I didn't want to keep playing on Epic; is The Outer Worlds this better an Starfield? Sure. Is it a good game? Absolutely not.I haven't even put an hour into it since repurchasing it on Steam, but this may have one of the worst introductory areas I've ever seen in a video game. I was hoping that perhaps I was misremembering something, but no, it's just an embarrassment.I'm going to put a bit more time into this to push through the beginning in order to see if I can find anything redeeming, but if I remember correctly, there is nothing; spurts of mediocrity followed by bouts of boredom and cringing at the terrible writing.I am heart broken this is what we got from the people who made Fallout: New Vegas, one of the best and smartly written games I have ever played despite it's flaws.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: The game is not bad, it`s just not great and I lost interest in finishing itThe Story is kind of Ok. The critc of corporate cultrure gone rampant is alright, but the cheesy humor deflates any tension and at the end undermines the story since you do not take anything too serious. I.e. you are not invested into what happensThe items are not that great,  it´s mostly numbers, not varietyLeveling is not that great. the perks in Fallout made me invested into the leveling system, but here I`m kind of:"Meh, guess I`ll take this generic % bonus."The design is not that great, I did not enjoy the planets but I cannot pinpoint whyThe characters that you encounter are meh i.e. not that great, there was not a single character that I liked in this game and I have to say, I kind of lost interest and I don`t think I`ll finish this gameAlso there`s nothing difficult about enemies other than being bulletsponges, with pretty much zero AI. Borderlands kind of introduced this comic like UI with numbers popping up above bulletsponge enemies and now everyone seems to do that and I am not a fan of that, although that`s just me.I remember the AI from RAGE was amazing with enemies flanking, retreating, regrouping calling for help if pinned downed. Don`t get me wrong RAGE had many other problems and I remember it being a quite flawed game. But I have never encountered an AI that good before or after. Which I don`t get why.This game is kind of stale for me, due to things like there are only 3 types of armor basically just with different numbers attached to it and different colors.Overall it`s an ok game, but I would not buy it again, don`t get it at full price is my recommendation. I`ll try to get a refund on the expansion pass, since I have not touched that contentHope this was helpful for you
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: Its just..so mediocre. For the company that made Fallout: New Vegas this is just atrocious, The game play, mechanics, character creation are just not engaging/boring as sin. The Story is just terrible, legitimately bad. I honestly don't know how you create something this bad after making as deep and immersive as New Vegas. The villains are so incompetantly and cartoonishly evil that its no real choice to try to work for them. Bioware released that 96% of people who played Mass Effect played Paragon, this is shocking to no one when the only difference between the two is that instead of saving the day, you save the day and you nuke the galactic government in the process... that's not a real choice. Outer Worlds is a whole bunch of not real choices. The humor is also way over the top, to the point where its annoying and entirely screws with the emotional tone of the story.Buy it on sale if you really want it give it a whirl, but it plays like vanilla Fallout 3 or 4 so just reload New Vegas
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: The very definition of generic.Is generic "bad" in the scope of things? Not at all. Generic cereal is fine. Generic pop is fine. Generic products, in general, are fine. That's kind of the point: you want a specific, generic thing and you don't care that it's not exactly perfect because the thing you wanted wasn't perfect or close to perfect to begin with. Have you played Fallout: New Vegas? Skyrim? Fallout 4? Well, this is the generic version of those games. The only thing this game has over them, in general, is graphics.Open world? No, not really. You have several places to choose from, but you'll have to unlock the content as you go. You're not "locked in" like most linear adventures, but you might as well pretend you are for the first several hours of the game.Interesting conversations with a useful dialog system? I mean, I guess, but it's nothing you haven't seen before. The NPCs are even more generic then usual. If I pretend to be someone I'm not, and you call me out on that, and it just so happens I'm impersonating one of your friends, you'd think there would be some character behind that interaction. You'd be wrong.Do you like Role Playing Games? Don't expect innovation here. It really is mostly "Hey, let me strangely explain to you an ENTIRE situation in which strangely you can solve by going from here to a map marker, killing some things, and then picking an item up."Ultimately this is a game Obsidian put a lot of time and love into, in an attempt to create the kind of game they think we're looking for. The problem? We found those games, we played those games for thousands of hours, and we really, really needed something new.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really nice RPG. Combat isn't anything to write home about, but that's okay, because the quests are fantastic and the number of ways you can solve them make you feel more like you are playing as an explorer rather than a one-man army. The game has its flaws, you can see some repetition in house layouts, faces, things like that. Something that could be addressed in a sequel, which this game deserves to have, because it's a labour of love. And it shows.I forgot to mention, the art style is also pretty vibrant. Byzantium has GOAT-tier interiors.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: This game is mediocre. The story is boring. The companions are boring. The weapon play and selections are boring.  The dialogue is boring. The quests are boring.This game has no depth or style. Its a New Vegas light. Side quests take about 10 to 15 minutes to complete and they all feel like chores. I've put a few hours into the game but it doesn't get any better. I'm just bored. I won't be finishing it. If you want to play a generic sci fi shooter with perks and mediocre game play, this is the one for you. Otherwise save your money.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: I basically murdered the whole solar system but made a good choice in the end so I was somehow redeemed and seen as a savior/legend.For a game that pushes the whole faction-reputation mixed with moral choice and consequence thing, there are little to no downsides to just turning whole towns and major planets into graveyards.. and that kinda sucks. So many strange dialogue options that don't line up with how your character is playing/what they've done.I did have a lot of fun just running around and soaking the atmosphere in. Great environment design, well optimized game, pretty fun weapons and skills to take...but it isnt enough to recommend this game to me. especially if you're looking for a decent RPG where choices matter.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: The Outer Worlds is visually stunning. The story is gripping, compelling, and well thought out. The voice acting is very good. Overall, the developers have done an outstanding job of making a great game that is extremely enjoyable to play. I look forward to playing the expansions and hope that they continue to amaze. One thing that I would like to have seen done differently is utilizing the thirst, hunger, and sleep aspects in other modes than supernova. Although you are able to sleep on any bed in all modes other than supernova, there is no need to do so. Consumables buff/debuff your character in all modes, but you will only suffer hunger and thirst in supernova. I think having to utilize these things in easier modes would give more depth to the game in all levels besides supernova. However, these are trivial things that others may not even notice. If your looking for a story rich game, with a good amount of fighting and lots of choices that affect the outcome, then The Outer Worlds is definitely worth the play time. Enjoy!
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: Found myself losing interest part way through the campaign and after a year or two I came back to it. The last 5 or so hours of the game really pick up and its apparent that every decision you make can dramatically change the ending. And since its an Obsidian RPG, the ending is very thorough and satisfying (think New Vegas). The combat and perks aren't super exciting but the other roleplaying mechanics are very fleshed out and deep.  8/10!
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: its... good. to some people thats a good thing or a bad thing. so to make a tl;dr, its a good game and you should get it and explore what they halcyon has to offer. there just wasnt anything to leap from a good game to a great game to me. story is good but there were no real teeth that really grabbed me and throw me in for a loop. the story ends almost exactly its been set up to you. the gameplay is good, but its just there. companions feel lopsided. some are fleshed out and have very long personal quests, while some are just feel like an afterthought. game has good visuals, sometimes gorgeous, but most of the time its fine. overall its a good game, but felt like i just stomped my way through the game by just pumping persuade/lie and long guns. really wish those aliens were real.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game.  It ranks in the top 30% of about 500 games I've played over the course of my life.  A lot of people say, "IT'S NOT AS GOOD AS FALLOUT, BRO." I disagree.  If you like Fallout, you'll love Outer Worlds.  Outer Worlds is the result of the development team putting Fallout through a sieve as to distill what worked best in Fallout while abandoning what didn't work in Fallout.  Outer Worlds is also a more hopeful version of Fallout.  Ostensibly the only difference between these retro-future universes is that in Outer Worlds, there's no nuclear holocaust, and humanity's able to expand into the stars.  I don't know.  That made it a little different for me. The marksmanship is fun, the stealth is straightforward, and paying attention to the narrative will reward you with experience points, gear, and extra missions.  I had a good time.  A few caveats:  The character level cap is 36, so choosing strengths and weaknesses is tough.  This also kills replayability.  There's no new game plus, and there's no postgame.  The DLC will skyrocket you to 36, and you'll chill there for the latter fourth of the game.  Hard mode feels unbalanced, and if you're torn between hard mode and normal mode, do normal mode.  If you kick ass in normal mode, good for you.  Enemy behavior doesn't change.  Enemies only have more health and deal more damage.  I've seen some complaints that the game's "funny," like Borderlands.  I sort of disagree.  The dialogue isn't any less insufferable than that of another adventure game, and there's a bit of a saturation in "humor," but ultimately it's not so bad, and you'll chuckle a bit.  Not a lot, but a bit.Not the best game you'll ever play.  Neither is Fallout.  But good!  About 35 hours, including DLC.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Mass Effect™ 1 in first person with no psi abilities set in a world where you get advertised to 24/7 and companies own everything. I don't know why they thought that would be a fun universe to set it in, but I guess it worked somewhat because the advertisements are the only remotely notable parts of this game. Everything else is trying to be Bioshock™.Anyways, it's trying to be a Bethesda™ game, so you have the obvious ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. It Just Works™, lag spikes when you get near towns because the game can't handle NPCs, gratuitous gore except ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ than Fallout™, the same side quests you've played in every single 3D Fallout™ game so far (And no, that's not an exaggeration). _childDocuments_.review: My name is Hush. I used to be a game design person. I have too many games.So I've started a mission to clean out my entire Steam library! I'll do this by beating all of my games and reviewing them. TLDR at the Bottom of Each Section.6/10/2021The Outer WorldsOverview:I'm way late to this party. I probably will be for most of my games! The Outer Worlds is the worst type of game. A game that was on the brink of being something REALLY amazing, but just falls short. The Story:The story of The Outer Worlds is really engaging. You can really sink your teeth into it, and if you take the time, read a lot of the  journal entries about the company employees, you will find an interesting plot that will suck you in. The problem? They Never really get around to introducing big plot points. I spent most of this game wandering around planet to planet, not really knowing anybody on “The Board” ( The Outer Worlds big villain). I didn't know who Chairman Rockwell was, what he looked like, or really what he was doing for a good 90% of the game. I NEVER knew who Sophia Akande was, until I put a bullet in her because she was shooting at me. I spent most of the game walking around and wondering, “What is the point?” and having several existential crisis’s. I feel like the villain of this game should have been a big overarching crippling character in most of Halcyon's colonies. For as much damage as They had done, I sure didn't see much of a representation of them anywhere in the game at all. The game just keeps assuring you that they are bad, tells you some info about them, and moves on. Even when you eventually get to the main city of Byzantium the place is almost completely empty. Sure, it's filled with a couple pompous idiots, but where are the resources that are being drained from everyone? Why is the city so ran down? Why is everything broken? Then they hit you with a right hook: THE WHOLE COLONY IS ACTUALLY FAILING! The game becomes accelerated to a million miles an hour. Lots and lots of plot points are happening really quickly. Almost as if they forgot to put the rest of the story in the early part of the game where it was very slow. Before you know it, it's over. Somehow by killing two people I eliminated the whole Board. There never was a big boss battle. It just... Ends…Strange.5/10 - “What just happened?”TLDR: Story is pretty blah. It has the makings of being a good story, but they executed in the most wild and silly way ever. It ends pretty unremarkably.  A good message in bad packaging..Characters:I felt no emotional connection to anybody in this entire video game other than Parvati. No one else was believable. I really wish I had more to put in here, but I really don't remember anybody That I met along the way that I would say is a standout character. Maybe SAM the cleaning unit. He had some funny moments. 5/10- “Remarkably average.”TLDR: Parvati is the only good one. Gun Play:The Gunplay was pretty cool until you realized that the whole gun Market is controlled by certain companies in this game. Whether this was by Design or not, there was a very limited amount of weapons. Each company brought to the table a pistol, rifle, heavy weapon, and possibly a sniper. I opted for the heavy weapons because I think big guns are “sweet as ♥♥♥♥”.Now I may have had a weird experience in this game, but somewhere around halfway through the game I found this minigun made by Spacers Choice that was just WILDLY overpowered for some reason. Then I started to find more, and figured it was pretty normal so I started to give them to my companions. The game after this became boringly easy. I was already playing  the Hard difficulty setting and found myself just casually walking through places. In an effort to make it harder, I had to use different guns. But it seems like what I was mostly encountering was either now weapons that were woefully underpowered or capable of creating a crater the size of Texas. I'm really surprised that in a game that is controlled by a giant corporate Overlord there isn't some sort of underground Gunrunner movement or black-market weapons? You can have all sorts of very fun exciting things there but instead they often stick with the boring and call that reality.Let's talk about science weapons. I didn't use these for about 75% of the game because I didn't know they existed. Again, I have no idea how I was supposed to be introduced to these, but I found one by accident and then was prompted by a series of missions where I can go get more! “Ohhh, ok.  This is why the guns have been so boring this game! It’s because I didn't even know there was a whole other half!” I was wrong. There are about four of these.   Each one of them is pretty fun in their own right, but two of them are completely useless. The Gloop Gun is my far the best. The Shrink Ray and the Mind Control Ray are both very fun to play around with in concept, but don't make really any sense. Using them was kind of a hassle and didn't render many benefits. Modding feels pretty boring and doesn't really change much about the weapon unless you're changing the energy type or ammo type. Tinkering with weapons for some reason costs money and not components and you don't really grow attached to any weapons because they all look the same and act the same.5/10-  “I want my black market guns.”TLDR: Gets really oldGraphics:The graphics feel pretty crisp! I will say that they did do a pretty good job at making you feel like you're on a different planet. Unfortunately The Outer Worlds likes to reuse a lot of the same creatures which is really a bummer. I don't know why raptadons would be on multiple planets, but they find a way to explain that away in the game. To me it seemed like laziness in order to avoid making tons and tons of different creatures. Outside of the city it seemed harsh and dangerous and you can walk around and really enjoy the sights. I think my only complaint is that everything felt so damn empty.7/10 - “They do the job!”TLDR: Too many raptadons. IN CONCLUSION: The Outer Worlds promises a lot and unfortunately just doesn't deliver. Although I am happy to see this type of genre getting a little bit more attention lately, I'm sad to say that this one just didn't meet the standard in my book. Much like space, The Outer Worlds provides a few interesting bits, but the rest is lost in a vacuum. Overall Score: 5/10   “Finished it.”

_childDocuments_.review: There will always be comparisons to other games when playing a new game; that's just how the human mind works.  Outer Worlds sort of finds itself in a weird spot, because which game you compare it to will likely factor heavily in whether or not you enjoy it.  If you want Fallout 5, this will disappoint you.  If you want Mass Effect 4, you might scratch that itch here.Truth be told, I found this game highly enjoyable but I'm a bit shocked at how highly rated it is.  As others have said, it's very short.  I estimate 20 hours would get the average player through to the end.  It's also not very deep, which is probably my only complaint.  I never felt like leveling up my character made much difference, nor did my party selection.  In the whole game, I probably got into a 'difficult' fight twice and I'm not a pro gamer.  The loot you find isn't usually exciting.  All this adds up to what I call lack of depth from an RPG perspective.  As a shooter, it's also not super deep but at least there are some good elements there. So, why do I recommend it?  The real reason is your strategy does matter.  The way you get through conversations, the way you manage your reputation, if you choose to fight through an encounter or sneak through WILL make a difference later.  If you want to kill some NPC because you don't like their face, you can!  If you want to choose sides and help one faction gain an edge, you can!  It won't make you a stronger character, per se, but you can do it and that is why it's a roleplaying game.  Not because of leveling up or character customization or open world exploration, but because of the story-driven gameplay and choices that matter (even when outside of dialog).

_childDocuments_.review: Games like this would not exist if the consumer culture was a little savvier. Well, they might exist, but in a better form. As it is, you market a game as a redefining of the genre from experts in the field and you'll get a million bored people with disposable income dropping cash on it before it even comes out. With the way gaming journalism works, you have 'reviewers' lining up to give it 9 or 10 outta 10 immediately, so they can farm those clicks and make their money off the surrounding hype. The game itself doesn't need to be good by that point - everybody who stands to make money has made it, and if you're left with a half-baked RPG, who cares? Certainly not the people who made it.This is not a revolutionary RPG. This is Bioshock-Borderlands-Fallout, and each of those games did a 'corporations are the enemy' storyline more compellingly, discussing issues of trust, responsibility and consequence. This game abandons nuanced ideological investigation in favour of patting you on the head for supporting the poor. Gunplay is adequate. Environments are ugly and shallow. Take a few things out of the Fallout character building system and add a few gimmicks from other FPS games and you're good, right? Who cares if the gameplay is a disjointed, hollow mess? Insulting.At some point, the consumer has to start exercising some discretion, or we're going to see every beloved developer milked for tripe like this based on pre-order cash alone. Also, what is it with games about evil corporations being made by evil corporations? This should never have been an Epic exclusive. Would not recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Great VisuallyEasy to Use Combat SystemSolid Nav Point Quest SystemEngaging StoryCons:Several issues with certain graphics settings cause crashesLevel cap is far too lowWeapon choices are limitedTerrible Companion Combat AISummary:This game is like a combination of Firefly and Fallout New Vegas. It's a somewhat open world sci-fi RPG, with a slight low-tech/retro tech look to it, somewhat reminiscent of the old 1940s styled Flash Gordon or Buck Rogers. Graphically, it is an extremely visually appealing game, the only complaint I have is that on the highest settings, many graphics cards seem to have issues causing start up crashes and random crashes during game play. However, with some careful adjustments in the graphics settings you can easily get a good balance of visual appeal and game play performance, though it may take a couple of tries before getting it just right for your system.The main story is engaging and entertaining. One the things I really enjoyed are the "no win" scenarios, where no matter what path you take, someone is going to get the short end of the stick, makes it more realistic. The combat started to get a little repetitive towards the end, especially at higher levels where enemies don't offer the same threat they did in the beginning. The lack of weapon/armor diversity was a little disappointing. You would think with plasma weapons available, laser weapons would be as well, but sadly no. There are only about 20 different weapons and armor in the game, with only two or three variants. The mod system definitely helped, but like the weapons and armor there are only about 20 different mods in all, making it very limited. I also noticed that helmets almost never take damage at all, very rarely does one ever take head shots.The companion AI is absolutely garbage, any combat setting other than "Aggressive" will result in your companion standing around doing nothing in combat while all enemies target you. Even with a "Ranged" and "Far" setting with "Aggressive" often results in companions charging headlong into any enemy group, even enemies not in visual range, making using stealth when hostile forces are near almost completely pointless, forcing you to often deal with missions completely solo.Overall, it is a fun game to play, solid storyline, good script. It looks beautiful when graphics are set at the highest settings. Anyone who is a fan of Fallout New Vegas, BioShock, or the show Firefly will probably love this game. Despite it seeming kind of short, it was still enjoyable.

If I had to give it a rating its probably 7/10. Solidly good, and solidly worth playing, but likely not something I would come back to.  Certainly, worth it on sale. Otherwise maybe not. Don't get me wrong, there are a couple and its far better than your average new tagged on "rpg" cough cough, but it feels like some offer a lot more than others. E.g having below average intelligence gives you very frequent "dumb" options, which are hilarious, but having some for other extrems like "very strong" or "super wimpy" etc. would have been great too. I saw some perception checks, but thats about it for attributes. Skills on the other hand can be used a lot in dialogue, so its mainly attributes that are lacking imo. Combat is solid, not great, but thats not the reason for playing this so I am okay with that.

_childDocuments_.review: Straight up- if you like Obsidian's fallout games, you'll love this one.The story's pretty good, nice and long. But the ending leaves me wanting more.The ending is similar to the Fallout: New Vegas ending, and it seems this game is trying its hardest to emulate FNV without ultimately being it. The 2 DLC are pretty good, I did have hopes they would be better, especially Gorgon.Murder on Eridanos was a really good DLC, straight up. One thing Obsidian definitely does well is write detective mysteries.Don't buy this game for its combat, because you're going to be disappointed. Though the rare and elusive science weapons do spice it up a bit, especially when you give them to companions. _childDocuments_.review: Worth it - for half price.  The game suffers from feeling shallow.  Some examples would be the large number of inconsequential items, limited inter-party dialogue (I think that each set of companions has maybe 3 different interactions), potential side plots that only play out in the weakest of ways, extensive map and building reuse, limited enemies (even Peril on Gorgon pretty much just took existing enemies and slapped 'cold' or 'corrosive' on them), minor graphic and pronoun bugs, maps that felt like recycled FPS maps rather than something designed for this game, side quests that felt straight out of an early MMO (go fetch 10 pieces of leather from creature X), the special items in the game were uninspired, the crafting an afterthought with a fatal flaw, etc. etc. etc.  I don't know if Obsidian ran out of time, money or just the will to put out something truly special.   That being said, there are some good bones of a game here.  The voice acting ranges from decent to spectacular.  Having two full quest paths is always nice to see, along with multiple ways to solve a good portion of the game (stealth, conversation, combat etc) and the end credits were rewarding to see.  It's just a shame that this didn't get the time and attention it needed to truly be stellar.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: "Outer Worlds is not the best choice! It's the spacers choice!"After spending much more time than I expected into this game to fully finish the main game and both of its DLCs completely,i must say i really enjoyed it, at least for the most parts.The game looks gorgeous! The rather retro-futuristic design of everything in this game really stands out and the gameplay is decent,such as running and walking animations,shooting,etc.The dialogues and writing is good for the most part, but it sometimes falls short.Specially since they flexed so hard on this game being the devs of the classic Fallout games and Fallout NV's next big game, well the absence of Chris Avellone's godlike writing is horribly clear throughout the whole game.Soundtracks are decent, hit-and-miss IMO.The RPG elements and perk system are as good as you'd expect from an open world action RPG, not too complicated like some hardcore RPGs but also not too simplified the game feel empty.As for the story and plot of the game, i have to talk about the base game and its 2 DLCs separately.First the base game : The story is engaging enough for the most parts, and the plot is rather simple and does its best to show you the horrors of a world fully under the control of cruel corporations.However, it is too short and leaves you like : Ok, that was it?! Even for me who spent actually much more time than the intended time to finish the game, the game felt lacking in the end. That's actually a reason I really look forward to the second game tho! 7/10Now, The Peril on Gorgon : This DLC really feels like the pre Wastelanders update fallout 76, except for a few interactions with certain people, most of the story is told trough terminals, robots and audio tapes you find all around the map. I REALLY liked the atmosphere and the overall feeling of Gorgon, and the main plot was  interesting, but it has its own problems when it comes to the ending and the logic of many things happening throughout the story, i avoid going deeper into it to avoid spoilers. 7/10 And finally, the best piece of The Outer Worlds for me ,the Murder on Eridanos DLC! This DLC is just awesome! The story is so interesting from the beginning, and it's filled with mind-blowing plot twists (at least for me) The cast of characters you meet in this DLC are much more interesting than the rest of the game, and the choices you make feels much more satisfying and meaningful. I also love the sense of mystery that covers the whole DLC and how you as the inspector are the one to settle everything.9/10 P.S : The game had more than its fair share of technical issues and game breaking bugs for me, one of them made a whole area of the game hostile despite not having any enemies around, so I wasn't able to finish a side quest since I couldn't interact with a terminal.And the latter totally avoided me from continuing peril on gorgon from a certain point, I contacted Private Division's support regarding the issue, and they couldn't be any help, hence I had to make an entire new save only to finish that DLC.To wrap this up, The Outer Worlds is a very good game, which could be great if it didn't fall short in some important areas, I keep my fingers crossed for the second game!

_childDocuments_.review: The first few hours of this game seem OK. The problem is that despite taking 55GB of disk space there is very little variety in scenery, fauna or flora. The towns/stations all look alike, the NPC's seem to have about the same  amount of dialog/chatter than  the guards in Skyrim. and the companions soon become very, very tiresome and annoying.Add to this that the enemies strength seems to level with your character so combat feels the same throughout and this starts to drag on. I played far too many hours hoping for some change of pace.At least I got this on sale, but even at about £15 it was still too much in my opinion.Since I stopped playing this game I went back to The Witcher III: A game where the characters are varied and memorable, the dialog is delivered well and most importantly, the story is actually interesting, It is also true that the "fetch quests" are much the same and can be a grind, But! While your at it you make well find yourself trying to battle a beast way above your current ability and the fact that when you 'level up' it means parts of the game that were too difficult before are playable.I have also recently decided to re-install "Fallout New Vegas"; the graphics may be very basic by modern standards, but like TW3 it is much more fun and challenging the play than this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Tell me if you've heard this one before. You have a quest to go find some guy. You follow the quest marker out into the wilderness, fighting through an assortment of monsters and bandits, until you come across a strangely wholesome family of four. The husband gives you the whole Southern Hospitality schtick, while the wife talks about how the stew is going to be ready soon. The kids are vaguely creepy. There's no mention of the guy you're looking for and when you mention it the family keeps going on about dinner being ready soon. Hmmm what could be going on? HMMM! It was maybe surprising when this story happened in the Witcher 3, the Walking Dead or Red Dead Redemption 2,  but by the time the Outer Worlds comes around to it, you know the story immediately before it starts, so I just went ahead and pulled out my gun, killed everyone in the building and then looted the place. And this is the problem with Outer Wilds. It just doesn't really have a soul of its own, you know? It's just doing the same things that other better games have done a lot better. This would be a lot more forgivable if the game had a decent modding scene. I generally hated Fallout 4, but still got a lot of hours into it because I was having fun modding my character to be a Japanese schoolgirl with a samurai sword beating up Super Mutants. But for whatever reason, this game doesn't support modding and thus has a real NO FUN ALLOWED feel to it when compared to other games of the same type. Maybe I'll give this thing more time. I don't know. I keep meaning to but now I find that two weeks have passed before I last was able to bother, which is a review in and of itself. Ranking of the Open World Bethesda-type games:1) Morrowind2) Skyrim3) Fallout NV4) Fallout 3 5) Oblivion6) Outer Worlds 7 ) Fallout 4

_childDocuments_.review: I'd recommend The Outer Worlds to scratch a new WRPG itch for no more than $15. You'd enjoy this game if you appreciate WRPGs enough to notice what TOW does with crew storylines. I wouldn't gloss over them as "like Fallout."In TOW, you are a lost colonist and the captain of a space ship you unwittingly earn as a drop, and no one seems to care. You address complex social issues as an external observer in a oligarchy's blind spot. After 50 hours, I think that "complex" means that yes, there are consequences to being hostile to kind people, but being a good person normally means padding play time. You quickly gain appointment-free access to every officer, executive, relative, spirit guide, and fugitive you meet. You are  the fate of entire factions, often in the form of optional work. "Work," as in, completing quests does not feel rewarding. NPCs show little awareness to others outside of their conflict. To be fair, TOW depicts emphatically evil corporate cultures that spread only learned helplessness. That might explain the callousness of bystanders and organizations in the colonies, but not the crew's. Your crew judges your emotional reasoning on decisions they care about, but will unquestioningly fire radioactive explosives at pedestrians any other time. It's hard to feel invested with distractions.If you care about gunplay, then you *might* appreciate the simplicity of the upgrade system, but the actual firefights require little to no prep work on Normal difficulty. If you care about challenge, there's not much variety in the challenges themselves. If you care about story, some of the cutscenes and dialogue choices are worth paying to see. But none of them are worth navigating in-between moments on a replay, because then the game feels like a more labor-intensive DVD menu.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: It's a neutral-positive. If you like RPGs and Sci-fi - you probably going to like that one. The main strength is story, everything else is "ok" and even the story is somewhat set back by rather uncreative/by the book narrative designThis game is best described by the word "average" or the game's titular corporation slogan "you tried the best, now try the rest". This game isn't trying to be the best, instead it's very clearly trying to be "an ordinary rpg"Narrative we have a classical theme park rpg with N mostly independent stories in the same theme, each within it's own distinct set. Within each set there are M sub-stories that again mostly independent from each other and have loose connection to the main area story. Each area story is extremely patterish - you have faction A and B, they have some conflict, you have to make a "hard moral choice" (although the game mostly very clear about which choice is the best) or do some more exploration (usually revolves around doing those sub-stories) and achieve a compromiseMain story is exactly the same pattern, and much like area stories, it doesn't really depend on the area stories, except for the final solution flag (which side you choose) and some other abstract parameters. Sub-stories sometimes have bits of information regarding the parent story, but that's just for the player exposition - it doesn't affect anything. That's especially clear in DLCs both of which are about mysteries and if you explore things good, then you sort of know the main twists way before they are coming, but the characters act clueless, you can't refer to things you understand/saw in dialogs, unless it's a proper story-sanctioned piece of information that triggers that knowledge. Anything optional is simply ignored by the worldExecution-wise it's also average - I can't say it has some terrible problems, but there are lots of small annoying things here and there. Both from technical and gameplay perspective. Like all the decision making is very ham-fisted - if you said character X that you are going to do something (accepted some quest), then it means you are going to do it and that's it. All other characters instantly know that and refer to that (sometimes complaining) and you don't even have an option to say "hey, no, we aren't actually going to do that". Same with certain quest outcomes - those "compromise" options usually require very careful order of what you say and to whom. If you are going to say anything definitive to any character, then you may not have required dialog options in other dialogs, simply because apparently you already made a decision.Gameplay and combat wise is, as usual, decent - not bad, not terrible, but many of things feel unnecessary and added just "because an rpg needs it". Like you have stats with points and whatnot. Those points are pretty limited, so you can't be a super-charismatic leader, thief and hacker that is also proficient in combat. Except that "in combat" part mostly doesn't matter and you'll do just fine without investing points into offensive skills and you NEED to invest points into dialog and hacking skills to get outcomes you want. Lockpick seriously simplifies your life, but realistically there is almost always is another way. Leadership is only needed to boost your companion bonuses to your stats (to get through the dialog checks). Tech skills are useful for dialog checks, but there almost always is another way - that's probably the most "RP" part of the game.Oh, but none of that actually matters, because you can always just respec your character at any point and the only dialogs that matter are at the end of area stories where you need to pass dialog checks to get the ending you want. But it's annoying to get through 5 loading screens each time you want to respec, so in most cases you'll be running as charisma-focused character and have little problem with fights (gotta be a bit careful though)Art and overall presentation is nice, it's a bit on a comical/humorous side, but there are some technical issues, including tons of loading screens everywhere, slow streaming, invisible walls in places you don't expect, etc. But not very much to really annoy youI liked the story though - it's a nice departure from your usual saving the galaxy heroic epic stories that are common for RPGs - it's still heroic, if you want to (or not, if you don't), but a lot more grounded in reality and a lot more "sober" so to say. And I like the overall theme, although due to patternized nature of the stories, it feels a bit overused as you basically hear the same story 4 times.The characters are also quite good, I liked most of them - and while their stores are not integrated into the main story (besides the binary outcome), the characters themselves are rather fitting and, again, grounded in reality. And Obsidian mostly evaded the boon of modern RPGs and didn't turn it into a dating sim, so interactions with most characters also make sense. You also almost don't need to kiss your companion asses - the difference between endings if you do and don't is minimal

_childDocuments_.review: All of its strengths and none of its weaknesses they saidOuter World is fun little rpg, like something mixed together from Borderlands/Bioshock/Fallout. It looks nice, runs well(didn't have any bug/glitch whatsoever in the 27h playthrough) and frame rate stayed consistent almost all time( loading  into new area or starting game up had some few sec drop, but after that it was smooth 60fps onward). Also the game world is patched together from smaller open ended areas rather than one huge open world and i'm okay with that. However for the supposed “Bethesda killer” and coming from  “master mind rpg makers” it falls rather short. Main story is weak and blends in with overall game settings. Npc looks awfully samish, like most female npc have the same face with the same hairstyle, sometimes i wonder did i see that character before. Music is meh, loot is boring and while the game has a nice art style it is samish.. Basically after you explore the first area you have seen 90% of what the game has to offer. While the main plot is somewhat meh, smaller side quests tend to be more interesting, even if they are the same old fetch and go kill this quests. Dialogs are one of the best part of this game, having different options based on your character build, they also tend to be funny. I love how companions chip in with whatever they have to say.  However i'm not so happy about their flaw system. When I make a character, I already make it somewhat flawed. And when a game offers flaws and in return gives the same perk point that one can get when he levels up, it is lame. And most of those perks are somewhat boring to start with carry more/move faster ect.. After my first flaw was taken, there was no reason to take more, since they don't bring anything new to the game, if only make you weaker, if that's your thing.Overall not a bad choice if you hate to put hundreds of hours into a game, if you don't like games filled with content that you don't know where to start or games with endless busy work. Looks nice, pew pew works great and there is fun to have.However if you are looking for a good story, open world where you can sink hundreds of hours, this may not be for you.Honestly I was waiting for something more of this game. At release this game get overhyped to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ heaven. However now i wonder, was this just for pure hatred of Bethesda, since its fallout 4 with all its flaws and bugs feels just better rpg than outer worlds. Since OW feels more first person shooter then rpg, as I played on normal, the only challenge I got was the very last mission and even as I made melee character, guns worked surprisingly well, with a lot higher dps, weird huh?
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic RPG. It's a Sci Fi game that doesn't take itself seriously and contains an absolute ton of dialogue options. Felt like Fallout with some Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy if I had to put words to it! Appreciate that there were several ways to go about solving problems and that there was real weight to the decisions! The combat felt smooth albeit simple. If you just want action it may not be the game for you (I suppose you could just shoot everyone and everything), but if you enjoy lots of options and some hilarious dialogue you'll probably enjoy Outer Worlds, I certainly did!
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard one to review as it does have redeeming qualities. It isn't an awful game, it just isn't that good either. The worlds look good I guess but I didn't find them interesting to explore and they didn't make me want to look deeper than I had to. Though it looks good, it doesn't look so good to justify the really bad FPS drops at times and the performance that tanked in cities when first loading into them and loading into the game. I like how the devs clearly have a sense of humour with some ridiculous parts of the story and the dialogue. Shame it is just not that interesting overall. The feel of the game gave me Borderlands/Fallout 4 vibes and I did not enjoy either of those games, so it is no surprise this has missed the mark with me I suppose. Though I could forgive all of that if the combat was good but sadly it just isn't. The enemies are all pretty much the same regardless of what location you travel to (at least as far into the game as I have got) and I don't find shooting robots and alien bullet sponges to make for satisfying gun play. I played through both Rage 2 and Far Cry 5 (again for the latter) in the last few weeks and after playing them the gun play in this game really is exposed for how un-fun and lacklustre it is. I also found small things annoying such as the fact that if I run it will cancel reloading my weapon rather than just preventing me from running until the reload animation is finished. I am not saying this game is awful but for me personally it has been a let down and I decided after 8 hours I feel I am just not enjoying it enough to keep putting my time into it. If you can get it for very cheap it may be worth a try to someone who enjoys Borderlands etc but for me this one is a purchase I regret as it wasn't cheap
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: The Outer Worlds is a new single-player first-person sci-fi RPG from Obsidian Entertainment and Private Division. Lost in transit while on a colonist ship bound for the furthest edge of the galaxy, you awake decades later only to find yourself in the midst of a deep conspiracy threatening to destroy the Halcyon colony. As you explore the furthest reaches of space and encounter various factions, all vying for power, the character you decide to become will determine how this player-driven story unfolds. In the corporate equation for the colony, you are the unplanned variable.

name: Super Meat Boy Forever
detailed_description: The challenge of Super Meat Boy returns in Super Meat Boy Forever! This time around Meat Boy is always running, like literally...it's an auto-runner . He can't stop and he won't stop. Levels are brutal, death is inevitable, and players will get that sweet feeling of accomplishment after beating a level. Players will run, jump, punch and kick their way through familiar settings and totally new worlds. What’s better than playing through Super Meat Boy Forever once? The answer is simple: Playing through Super Meat Boy Forever several times and having new levels to play each time. We created over 6000 level chunks and smash them together to create new unique levels and each time the game is completed the option to replay the game appears and generates a whole new experience by presenting different levels with their own unique secret locations. We’ve handcrafted literally thousands of levels for players to enjoy and conquer. You can replay Super Meat Boy Forever from start to finish several times before ever seeing a duplicate level. It is truly a remarkable feat of engineering and a monumental example of ignoring the limits of rational game design and production. Super Meat Boy Forever takes place a few years after the events of Super Meat Boy. Meat Boy and Bandage Girl have been living a happy life free of Dr. Fetus for several years and they now have a wonderful little baby named Nugget. Nugget is joy personified and she is everything to Meat Boy and Bandage Girl. One day while our heroes were on a picnic, Dr. Fetus snuck up on them, beat Meat Boy and Bandage Girl unconscious with a shovel and kidnapped Nugget! When our heroes came to and found that Nugget was missing, they knew who to go after. They cracked their knuckles and decided to never stop until they got Nugget back and taught Dr. Fetus a very important lesson. A lesson that can only be taught with punches and kicks.

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing for people to mouth often is "autorunner??????" with 0.2 hrs of playtime, and whilst it's fair for people to be upset it isn't just more meat boy, I feel it's a bit unfair to only talk about that design decision. There's a bit to like, but a lot to complain about too. It's not just a disappointing sequel, it's pretty poorly designed gameplay wise.Before I get there, let's go over the positives. For one, it has a great artstyle and the animations are quite smooth, I liked the small touches with idle animations and the cutscenes are very charming. For two, the warp zones were pretty cool concepts, kinda harsh sometimes, but fine. And finally, a fair few gimmicks are actually quite cool but underused (like pipes in world 3, which only appeared once). Now, let's get into why I think this is simply not a good game, nevermind a sequel.I've tried to give this game justice, so I played through the 5 base light worlds and at least attempted every regular dark level, so here we go. First off, why the hell is this game proceduraly generated? Whenever a new save is created, the game chooses a seed and randomises most level's structures. For a endless runner precision platformer, why would you do this? Platformers should be recognised for their level design, nevermind a precise one like smb, so it being semi-random is so obviously dumb it baffles me. Second, a weird design choice was making the levels in a more traditional format, being longer but with checkpoints. There's a reason original smb used short levels, being it's a tough game, so being able to take a break between short yet quite difficult levels levels was quite nice. Worse yet, A+ levels in this game is just AWFUL, nevermind the new frame-perfect S ranks. The game shows how much time you saved from an A+ after each checkpoint, problem being, if you mess up a section, guess it's time for a full restart or find a way to die before next checkpoint since there's no restart from last checkpoint option. I had a level once where there was no way to die between checkpoints, so I had to do THE WHOLE THING without more than one mistake to A+ it. The fact dark worlds are much harder contributes a lot to the new level system's issues, speaking of, the difficulty curve is very dumb, often spiking and then dropping back to piss easy, again, doubly true for dark worlds. And lastly, the elephant in the room, it's an autorunner, but worst part, it feels like a damn mobile game. The jump and punch button are the same button (or buttons) so often you'll end screwing up thanks to a precise use of, say, a teleport.TL;DR: Great visually, but quite lacking in gameplay. Only buy on a heavy sale if you're curious to see what it's like or for visuals.

_childDocuments_.review: is an auto-runner "sequel" to beloved hardcore platformer, Super Meat Boy. The game originally started development back in 2014 as a mobile spin-off of the original and that's fine if not for the fact that after Ed left Team Meat the game became a full on sequel. One of the main selling points of the game is that the levels are procedurally generated off of level chunks (over 6000 of them) based on your seed, but that's about all that the game has going for it.Buying this game on Steam I knew exactly what I was getting myself into. I played the game a year ago and after doing 100% on the first world and beating the second, I did not like it. It felt clunky and had no soul. So why did I decide to buy it again? I decided to give the game another chance. Maybe I just got a bad seed, maybe the collectibles had a bad spawn, maybe I just played it at a wrong time. Sadly, after giving it that second chance I can confirm that the game is simply just not that great. the game has no reason to struggle to push 60FPS (mostly running at low 30s) on a PC with i7 and RTX2060, especially when games that are actually graphically tasking like DiRT5, Destiny 2 or Halo Infinite have no trouble running at 60FPS on high settings. This just should not be the case. like mentioned before, the game has no soul. It's not about turning Meat Boy into an auto-runner. Well, maybe partly, but the game lacks any sort of indie cameos or depth that Super Meat Boy, or even the original flash Meat Boy had for that manner. The fact that it's an auto-runner just makes it more frustrating, as all the mistakes that happen feel less like lack of skill and more like the game just not working how it should (and believe me, this can happen a lot considering that the game had trouble reading inputs).The game is incredibly short, each world having only 6 levels (12 counting Dark World) and a boss + a single warp zone. If you plan on just beating the game without thinking about perfecting the game, or even just getting collectibles for that matter, it can take anywhere from an hour to 4 to complete the entire game depending on how good you are at reacting to the environment. To make the matters worse, some levels can take over a "minute" to beat, and by that minute I'm talking about a perfect run, which seems like an attempt to make the game feel longer.Looking past the 1 year exclusivity deal with Epic, the game just really lacks potential of what it could've truly been. Lack of diversity in characters, short gameplay time and massive optimisation issues just really ruin for me. I'd really want to like this game, especially since I put over 200 hours into Super Meat Boy, but I just can't. The game really is just painfully mediocre. It's sucks as a platformer and is just okay as an auto-runner. Soundtrack is okay, not the OG SMB level, but it's okay. The art style is very pleasing to look at so that's one of the redeeming values of the game. I'm really happy that there are people who found enjoyment in this game but sadly I didn't. Alongside Super Meat Boy Rival Rush, it feels to me more like a "nostalgia cashgrab" than something that someone tried putting their heart into, though I doubt that was actually the case. If you're looking for good platformers check out , , or , and if you're looking for a good auto-runner, the best I can offer you on steam is ,  and . If you want to buy this game I guess I can recommend it for $10 but you shouldn't bother with anything more.

_childDocuments_.review: Lacks any and all charm of the original. It feels like a very cheap imitation. The original had hand-crafted levels, a responsive control system and gorgeous music. I'd rather have 50 levels that were made by a person, than 5000+ procedurally generated levels designed purely to pad out the game time. Don't be tricked into playing this "sequel". Play the original game and let this one fade into obscurity.
