_childDocuments_.review: (Note: Played this on Switch when it first came out, now replaying it on PC.)If you're only playing the main campaign itself, this game is a fantastic follow-up to the original SMB. The autorun is weird at first but I genuinely think it helps this game and allows for a lot of interesting level design that takes advantage of the limitations of always running. The visuals and music are stellar; I want to specifically note how brilliant the cutscenes are, and how well they animate and inject personality into the game's characters. Dr. Fetus in particular is excellently animated; he has a very well-done presence and aura to him in this game that elevates him to one of my favorite cartoon video game villains. Very entertaining to look at.Once you get into 100%ing the game and doing the Dark World though, this game becomes a miserable slog, and I say this as someone who 106%ed the original Super Meat Boy. The original game's difficulty worked because of how short and sweet the levels were; here, levels are very long and separated into 8 chunks. Why the game developers chose to have the player beat every level without dying to 100% the game is beyond me; these levels are huge. It simply is not fun or engaging to do the same 7/8ths of a level over and over again just because the last 8th is particularly challenging. SMB found its difficulty through precision platforming and momentum... not through the tedium of making the player redo long levels over and over because of a mistake near the end.TL;DR: The game is fantastic and a worthy successor to Super Meat Boy if you don't plan on 100%ing it. Once you do though, be ready for a genuinely boring and tedious time. I would recommend this game - hesitantly.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this for 50% off on the day it released on steam. I genuinely enjoy the game very much. The visuals are a nice upgrade from the original, and the autoscrolling and new punching mechanics add a run and gun feeling to the game which I appreciate. The boss fights are also very fun and well made. Both of my kids, ages 5 and 11, enjoy the game as well. My 5 year old and I play together; she will try a section as many times as she wants, then asks for help if it isn't working out. My 11 year old has essentially played through the whole game in two days and is now going back to A+ the levels. The speedrunning aspect (going for the A+es) makes each level feel entirely different, and the added difficulty makes the game enjoyable for me as well. The "level chunking" seems interesting, and I'm looking forward to giving the game a few playthroughs.

_childDocuments_.review: So I bought Super Meat Boy Forever now that it was finally released on Steam... And holy ♥♥♥♥. I don't think I've ever played a less fun game than this in my entire lifetime.The concept is cool on paper - turn Super Meat Boy into an infinite runner - but the execution falls flat on *so many levels*. The end result is a borderline unfair experience that's rightfully alienated many Super Meat Boy fans, me included. The sheer precision the game asks of you becomes way too much way too quickly, and the complete lack of mercy that it shows only ends in insurmountable degrees of frustration. You make the slightest wrong move and it's bound to end in disaster. Not to mention that because you only see so far ahead, you'll almost inevitably run into trial-and-error ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. And that's in the first world alone.Nearly all of those problems are epitomized by the first world's boss fight, Big Slugger. A simple boss fight conceptually, but it too becomes frustrating when you die to one of its blades suddenly slamming down on you when you're mid-air and essentially defenseless.There's just way too many fundamental flaws in the game's design that become painfully apparent 20 minutes in for me to enjoy it. Let alone see myself finishing it. Which is a shame because I did quite like the art style and what little I got to hear of the soundtrack.Your suffering is not worth $20.

_childDocuments_.review: and now onto the short review//intro//Hyper Space Brawl is a fast paced, arena style brawler sports game. You take the role of an intergalactic HyperForce hero & battle against others to be the greatest one in the universe. Did Milky Tea Studios create a potential eSports contender or is it a dud? Let's find out.//Graphics, Sound & Artstyle//The whole aesthetic of Hyper Space Brawl is reminiscent of an 80s Tron feel with the glowing arenas and synthwave music, & I'm here for it. It looks good, it sounds good and overall this is a game that will pull you in. I'm gonna knock the sound down for a bit just because the announcer needs either, more lines or to be just muted. It's nice for him to remind you when your weapons are recharged but the line about him ordering food and not paying attention when someone scores was only half funny the first time, nevermind the 30th time in a match.//Gameplay//A lot of flashy terms are thrown around to describe Hyper Brawl Tournament- but honestly, it does it justice. Each match is 2 teams of 2 in a PvP arena style match where the objective is to win more rounds by scoring the ball on your opponents net all while being able to punch/fight each other and having weapons you can select on the character screen. I've been enjoying the hell out of campaign mode as it's sort of works like a franchise mode, setting you up in weeks of battles vs other opponents (CPU) and even has a point system with a W-L-T standings table. There is also a "domestic cup" competition in the midst of the campaign. Online is bland, only because not a lot of people are playing this game but as hinted out in my intro, I truly believe this game could have potential to be a competitive game that people can really sink their time into.//Price//19.99 USD//How many hours estimated//It's all dependent on whether or not you are the type of person who likes to play vs real people or if you don't care, personally I'm the latter and when I'm done with this- I'm gonna go ahead and try playing a campaign or two, until I can unlock more characters. I'm 6 hours in, and this is the type of game I'm coming back to for at least another 15-20 hours //Final Thoughts//Lots of great execution in this game, good amount of content and it plays spectacularly but the biggest flaw of Hyper Brawl Tournament is the lack of popularity of this game. I'm currently sitting in second place in the League Standings with 2 wins, 1 draw and 1 Loss and I love the difficulty curve it has, everything feels balanced- so if someone like me is having a blast with this game, why haven't i heard more talk of it?? Maybe the entry price might be too much for some people that aren't completely sold on the game, and I understand the devs might not want to go the F2P way to support this game as it can "cheapen" the experience for the playerbase. But I ask you- what playerbase? according to SteamCharts the current 30-day average is 0.6 players. The 30-Day Gain is -0.1 and the percentage is -18.74% (all data as of December 8th 2020). The lack of Steam Remote Play also hurts this otherwise amazing game. I love the characters, I love the gameplay- plain and simple Hyper Brawl Tournament feels like my Shadowrun (2007), an amazing game with potential to be one of the best online multiplayer games but no audience. I am still recommending the game but under a Wait for Sale because a game can only go so far with only single player components for what could be an iconic party game.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: Game seems abandoned and sadly the majority of issues listed still persist.TL;DR: If you're expecting the same gameplay fluidity as Mario Strikers then sadly the game isn't there yet. A few minor but very important gameplay issues have to be ironed out before that happens. But that really is it and despite that, if you have friends to play with the game is still a ton of fun.The game feel and pace mimics that of Mario Strikers very heavily while at the sametime delivering on its own twists like:While the game currently only supports 1v1s which consists of two choosen characters for each side, the game really does shine once you have a friend or a party of 4 to play with. A lot of issues outside of some minor gameplay clunkyness mostly boils down to the fact that the game is 1v1 when its made for 2v2s.The gameplay suffers from a few clunky mechanics like the pass which feels counterintuitive and unreliable. It has a wind up, slow ball speed and its very easily intercepted.Once you start charging a shot you're committed to it and can for no reason stop or initiate a different action unless you're hit, making it similar to tic-tac-toe that once you figure out the timing for catching fast balls, the game essentially gets "solved" and causes the gameplay to slow down significantly.Tackles are extremely fun to use while punching feels underwhelming and unreliable. Mainly because the reach and speed is slow contrary to tackles which are instant and fast which also makes it a great tool for moving around the field.I honestly can't say that I recommend the game unless you have a group of friends to play with, as a solo experience the game is lacking but as a group activity its extremely fun despite its current short comings.

You can join the Discord server of the game to get updates.The leaderboard basically only counts the number of wins, goals and KOs you've made. _childDocuments_.review: For a game that flew under my radar for about a month.... a ton of fun. I mean, big huge heaping pile of fun.I mean really spectacular, the sort that will make you shout when you score. HOW IT PLAYSIt's a 2v2 exercise - players can be human or AI, in whatever combo. (some mode limits do  apply)The object of the game is to achieve the highest score.Fundamentally, the game plays a lot like speedball - you grab the ball, run it, pass it back and forth, and shoot it into the opponent's goal/net; the opponents try to stop you, recapture the ball, do the same in your net; result is constant scramble.  Shooting feels really good - you have full directional control; you can charge and bank your shots, and additionally have the ability to curve the ball. As you move across the field, you have the ability to fight and KO opponents  - you can punch, kick, and use weapons.  There are a series of interesting fields - they introduce variables to play (shifting floors, moving walls, obstacles that must be dodged, etc.)You work as a team - opportunity for lots of teamwork, passing ball back and forth, shifting into different roles at different times, applying different strategies and tactics.There are some pretty cool maneuvers at your disposal - the characters can do dramatic dives to catch the ball, and you can even use ball like a weapon, charging it and throwing it at opponents to clear the way.There is a power up dynamic - you gradually  charge up as you get pounded by the opponent, and then you eventually enter a "hyper" state, where for a brief burst of time, you hit harder, run faster, etc.Games are fast - best of three rounds, plus sudden death where needed; each around is about a minute and a half. All of this combines into a rock solid competitive game experience that really shines.PLUS:It has characters with attributes - each character has strengths and weaknesses (strength, speed, ability to curve ball, and health)At the start of the game, you can pick a weapon of your choice (grapple hook, ball magnet, homing mine, booster pack, shield wall, etc.).  WHAT IT FEEL LIKE:I mean, my goodness... Speedball, meets Brawlhalla, meets League of Legends, meets Rocket League, meets Mutant League, meets Bloodbowl, meets Powerball, meets Pitball... WOWSA. CONSA tiny bit of menu wonk, but you get used to it; not miserable, and only effects menu experience. It does take about an hour to get comfy with all the controls, abilities, etc.; But once you practice for a bit. it become quite fluid and natural. No cross play yet, but it is on every platform.SUMMARYIt's great and promising, quite accessible, something very special.Play is fast, smooth, fun and dramatic.I could definitely see this game catching on if it gets sufficient exposure. There is enough here to like a lot.It is definitely filling a niche.It is fantasy sports the way it was meant to be done, and there is plenty of room for this one to keep growing.Find a friend and play... Rare game that is honestly worth every penny.I'm hooked.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those rare cases where I wish I could add an asterisk to the "Recommended/Not Recommended" tag. Ultimately, I went with Not Recommended for a couple of reasons.On the one hand, this game with friends is a good bit of chaotic fun, in the same way that playing Smash Bros. with 8 players, when no one knows what even is going on and the result of the match doesn't even matter because the chaos is its own reward. I can also say that when the game works with you, pulling some moves off can feel incredibly satisfying and rewarding.On the other hand, the game is clearly not optimised to play with keyboard + mouse. When punching or kicking, the character would randomly decide between punching where I'm looking with the mouse or kicking in the direction where I'm moving, even if I'm walking backwards.The menus show incredible polish, but the UI itself is a bit clunky to use. When adding bots, you must manually select the character and weapon you want them to use, there's no option for the CPU to pick randomly. The button to start the match shows up on the bot's character portrait itself. Some buttons have a slight delay, and a friend kept running into the problem where he'd press on his controller again thinking the input didn't go through and he'd quit the match, as his cursor was automatically placed on the "Quit match" button once the game caught up.Leaving those issues behind, which are easy(ish) to fix and can even be nitpicks, the game feels unbalanced. Characters fall into 2 archetypes: Big slow brawlers and fast nimble strikers. There's no reason to play as the faster characters since the kick has no delay, can be spammed endlessly, and you dash when you kick, making you just as fast as the faster characters. The hammer weapon has standard delay and is a one-hit kill AoE on any character. Since the arenas are so small, these two problems are amplified.Lastly, during the match itself, you can lose track of plenty of things. Who has the ball? Where is the ball? Where is my character? Is my character even alive? Is my weapon ready? These things are indicated on the top of the screen, requiring you to take your eyes off the match, or are indicated by tiny arrows above each character, which can blend with all the visual noise of the match.Now, I can't say that I didn't have fun, but if I planned to play this game seriously, I can see myself ragequitting less than 10 hours in. At the current pricepoint, I think it is not worth it, but I want nothing more than to see these issues fixed or at least worked on. If you have some friends to play with and this goes on sale, I'd say it can be fun for a while, but beware as it is a niche genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Got the game as part of a key giveaway.Honestly though, the game is a lot of fun, getting in a trickshot just feels super satisfying as does using different weapons (turbo boost is definitely for me!)The announcer is actually really fun, a lot of games like this tend to make the announcer too annoying/cringey but I'd say in this case the announcer is really well done (and a great voice on top of that!)However I'd say the game is missing some...juice, visually its stunning but this isn't show enough, it could look great to get some goal replays perhaps with a different camera angle, just to show off the visuals of this game more. _childDocuments_.review: There's no better feeling than curving a shot after you throw it and scoring a goal.If you want to see my first impressions as they happened, watch my video above. If you're looking for a great time with a friend, HyperBrawl Tournament will be a great time of beat-em-up, dodgeballs aimed at the head, whiffed throws, and the rare time where you score on yourself. The lack of remote play is the real killer here, so you'll either need your friend to be sitting next to you on your couch or you'll both have to shell out the money to go against each other online.The biggest fault is that keeping track of which character you have selected is difficult at best. There were times where I had completely lost track of my character, other times where I smacked my bot teammate (yes, friendly fire is enabled, and it's glorious), and other times where, worst of all, I thought I was my opponent's character.This is a rare title where words can't do a game justice: you'll want to experience this one for yourself. Watch some videos, play with a friend if you can, or play it safe and wait for a sale. HyperBrawl Tournament is at its best when played with a friend.
_childDocuments_.name: HyperBrawl Tournament

_childDocuments_.review: A great game that allows for a lot of epic Rocket-League-esque moments. Spent a fair amount of time with it on Apple Arcade, but I also had to give it a go with a controller on PC. Personally can't pick a favorite between the two control options, which says a lot about how much care was put into this game for it to not matter. A very coherent visual language and easy to grasp gameplay rules. Once past the tutorial you only get better with every single match. The amount of satisfaction you get from scoring goals by purposely throwing the ball at maximum speed in walls or other environmental obstacles at calculated angles is what will make people addicted to this game. The game features a plethora of offline and online modes, progression opportunities, customization options — a sea of content! Totally worth checking out and supporting!

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr - HyperBrawl Tournament is a very fun game reminiscent of mario strikers that comes with a singleplayer campaign and surprisingly local co-op, something rarely done on PC games.Graphics:Very pretty, the game is quite easy to run even when upscaling it to 4k. i've had no major issues. a few fps drops here or there on max settings, but for the most part the game achieves and maintains 144hz on my system. The maps all have a unique aesthetic and feel to them and the characters can be differentiated quite easily. Sound:The sound design is great, the electronic music suits the game quite well. The punch and kick audio cues give a very heavy and powerful feel to the attacks. my only issue is that some of the announcer lines can be a bit cringeworthy.Gameplay:it's feels a bit like mario strikers if everyone started beating the hell out of each other. Some weapons are definitely more useful than others and might do with a bit of balancing. the only issue i have is that you only know if your weapon is ready via an audio cue from the announcer, it would be a bit better to have a UI element indicate you can use your weapon. I like the map design, having small elements like barriers etc make the maps feel different from each other. I think if new maps are to be added, i'd definitely suggest a larger map. the maps are of a good size, but i feel like a larger level would help spruce up the variety a little more.Controls:There's nothing particularly unusual to be said about the controls. They work just great, i tried the game with both M+KB and a controller, both work well. However the precision aiming with the ball is a lot easier on mouse, as you'd expect. The ability to rebind keys etc is nice too, but the base controls really don't need to be changed.Multiplayer:Multiplayer is definitely where this game shines, as a singleplayer experience it's fun if you're a fan of the genre, but playing with friends is way more entertaining. the ability to do couch co-op as well as online via steam is a very nice feature indeed given how multiplayer on a single machine is not something most PC games readily have. All in all this is a really solid title and i recommend it to anyone who's looking for a fantastic couch co-op experience. there's a few minor adjustments i'd make, but i'd give it an 8/10

_childDocuments_.review:
The universe's greatest heroes have gathered to compete in a showdown for the ages; the legendary HyperBrawl Tournament! Armed with unique weapons and a thirst for glory, take to battle-tested arenas in this 1-4 player arcade-style sport played locally or online.

Only the universe's elite champions can summon this incredible skill. The HyperCurve lets you seize control of the ball mid-flight to 'magically' manoeuvre it around the opposition and obstacles to score legendary goals that could only happen in HyperBrawl. The fabled HyperForce runs through your very DNA, channel it to launch game changing attacks that can literally see your enemies shot out of the arena with its devastating power.

Already fabled heroes of their own worlds, competitors are drawn across the furthest realms to compete in the HyperBrawl Tournament. Choose from 12 heroes in three classes and load them out with lethal weaponry combos and paint their armour for victory.

Travel the vast expanse of time and space to HyperBrawl arenas from the home planets of the heroes themselves. Take in Chrome City's elevated stadium with its Cyberpunk stylings, the ancient stadium of Steelhenge or the demonic Court of Azdritch. Each arena is laden with perilous obstacles and traps that layer more challenge and unpredictability into every game.

name: Squishies
detailed_description: Get lost in the Squishy-verse! Squishies is a head-scratching, puzzle focused VR platformer where you guide courageous and cute creatures through a series of increasingly hazardous, challenging mazes. Use unique motion controls, custom designed for VR, to push and pull the Squishies through their adventures in a colorful universe full of strange flora and fauna. Keep those little rascals safe while they climb, jump, fly and teleport-by-fish through 100 levels in five alien worlds.! You push and pull the Squishies from one side of the maze to the other, all while earning medals, gathering crystals, climbing slopes, and avoiding pitfalls. Explore a huge universe, across 100 levels in five different worlds. A game truly made for VR - the controls and design were specifically designed for this dimension. Challenge yourself - gather all the crystals, beat the clock or find the hidden egg in each level. Level Editor - Squishies really comes into its own with its innovative, fully featured creation tools. The same tools we used to build the game! The Squishies are in need of a hero! A long time ago, aliens invaded the Squishy-verse after discovering that it harbours a huge number of crystals which can be used as energy sources. Now long gone, they have left the Squishies stranded all over the five worlds of their universe. Fortunately the aliens also left behind one of their crystal collectors. This is where you come in - take control, operate the alien fish and save your friends by finally rolling them home! Valve Index Support Although the game is playable with Valve Index, we ask for your understanding that we have not yet mapped the control scheme. Therefore some buttons might do different things than you expect them to - but just try them out and you'll get it! Servers inactivei Unfortunately our service provider for sharing levels has ceased operations, sharing levels with the community is currently not possible. Due to limited resource we were unable to migrate to a new service, we'll keep you posted on our progress.

name: Ooblets
detailed_description: Ooblets is a relaxing yet deeply-weird farming, creature collection, town life, and dance-battle game with a lot of heart and character. It's a game for people who want something cozy, eccentric, expressive, and full of things to do. Make It Your Own Convert your rundown shack into a cozy homestead, spooky sanctuary, retro-futuristic retreat, or just keep it as a rundown shack. There’s plenty of furniture and decor to collect. For your character, there are a bunch of hairs, hats, clothes, costumes, accessories, and more throughout the game. Grow Your Friends Collect ooblet seeds and grow your own lil followbabies on your farm. Each ooblet has a couple variants to nab, including the lauded and rare GLEAMY type. You can also make non-ooblet friends by talking, gift-giving, quest-fetching, and whatnot. Get to know a bunch of offbeat townsfolk, like Mayor Tinstle, Rugnolia, Outgrid, Videon, Millew, and even Taffy. Familiar Farm Functions Grow stuff, put things in machines, cook treabies, stuff your gob, or sell your produce in town. Oh also your ooblets can help out on your farm using oobcoops that can be upgraded to expand what kind of farming they can do. Settle It On the Dance Floor Instead of combat, handle challenges and disagreements via the art of dance. Each ooblet has its own unlockable moves, so put together a team that works well together (or doesn’t and just looks cute—you don’t get anything for beating the game faster). So Many Things to Do! There are daily challenges, tasks from the mayor, dance tournaments, quests from townsfolk, lost ooblets to find, sea-dangling to dangle, as well as plenty of badges, gleamies, clothes, furniture, decor, and friendship stickers to collect. Events and Limited-time Stuff There are a few realtime events, each with their own collectables, activities, and unique ooblets. So far, we’ve added events for Springtime, Halloween, and Winter—and we’re hoping to add more in future updates. Run Your Own Lil Shop Unlock the player shop, where you can sell the stuff you’ve grown and crafted to the people of Oob. You can decorate, negotiate prices via a minigame, restock shelves, and unlock shop upgrades. Maxed-out Minigames We spent way too long making some pretty serious minigames, most of which are in arcade cabinets in Port Forward. There may even be some sneaky ways to beat the arcade games if you get stuck. Themey Regions Explore a bunch of regions, like the arcade-filled boardwalk in Port Forward, the spooky swamps of Nullwhere, the deserts of Mamoonia, and the frozen peaks of Tippytop. Also, there’s a dirigible. Maybe a mystery island, too. Is there A story? Oh Yeah! Badgetown needs your help! There’s plenty to fix up and unlock, as well as a major threat that only a series of contrived dance battles and mini-games can resolve. The overarching story/mystery will take you through all the regions of Oob where you’ll meet a lot of interesting folks, new types of ooblets, recipes, and crops to plant back at your farm. The game even has a discrete ending… but there’s always more to do in Ooblets, even after the main story is complete.

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen a lot of (valid) criticism surrounding what people call "cozy games." Games that you play at your own pace, often involve entirely low-stress encounters, and piggyback off of the 'cozy' aesthetic. I'd say that Ooblets fits under this category, but as a glowing example of what I WANT with this experience. Since I'm super autistic, I'm not skimping on the details. Here are the multiple factors that drive me to recommend this game to ANYONE:1. The "cozy" aesthetic. Let me get one think clear, this game doesn't simply come off as 'cozy.' Describing it simply by that one term isn't fair to the energy the developers created. The game is weird, silly, charming, and much more. Of course any game with farming as a primary mechanic is going to feel cozy, but when little creatures sprout from seeds you planted, of course "cozy" isn't all you're getting.2. Ooblets. The game is CALLED Ooblets, and for good reason. The creatures that you will encounter are called Ooblets, and let me tell you.. these little guys are so varied and charming. The creature design here is so charming, as they feel like if something you doodled on the side of your math notes was fleshed out and fully rendered. The ones here are already great, and judgeing by the consistent updates, I imagine more will be available. I am OBSESSED with these little guys, and I can guarentee you will be too!3. Dance battles. This mechanic is one of my favorites. Are you ever playing Pokemon and feel bad that you have to hurt yours and another Pokemon to progress? Not here. If you encounter Ooblets out and about, you get them by making your ooblets DANCE OFF with them. I won't go into details with how the mechanics work since you'll figure it out when you play, but its FUN. And when you beat an ooblet, instead of catching it and taking it away from its pals, it gives you a seed that you can GROW ON YOUR FARM, and raise to be your very own. Basically mechanic good.There's more I COULD say, but I'd rather people just get the game and explore. I'm not quite finished as I'm trying not to rush through the game, but it gives you a LOT to do, and all of it feels incredibly fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: I've often looked for my "holy grail" casual game - ie. a game I can pick up when I only have time to play for an hour and still feel satisfied, a game that I can put down for 3 months and come back to later without feeling lost and unsure of what I had been doing, a game that is relaxing and lets me set my own goals. Ooblets, more than any other cozy game I've played, is exactly that for me.While there is a day-night cycle, I don't feel the same time pressure in Ooblets to complete  in one day that I do when playing Stardew Valley and I'm not trying to constantly min-max my profits; I generally have goals in mind (make money, collect all the furniture and clothes, maybe someday fill out the almanac with every ooblet) but within each game day, I do whatever I feel like doing! This makes it very low stress to put the game down for a while - I know when I pick it up again, all I have to do is toodle around and I'll start vibing with the game again.Ooblets has a  of (well-designed) systems and little mini-games that integrate well together. Farming is in service of making currency, but is also necessary for catching a good amount of ooblets, and for cooking food that boosts your energy or used as gifts for the villager friends. Catching ooblets fills out your collection, provides you with helpers for your farm, and adds some strategy to your card selection for dance battles. Making printed models of ooblets might sound like a little throw-away mechanic, but maybe you want to fill out the museum displays in the town hall, or sell them in your player shop when they're in demand for extra cash. Sea dangling (aka fishing) is probably the mechanic I've engaged least in, but it provides useful resources and items to sell in your player shop. There's also mini-games, like a slider puzzle mini-game and actual arcade games, that are fun diversions. All of these various systems and the collection-oriented nature of Ooblets means that even when only playing for a short time, there's plenty of satisfaction in moving goals forward.In thinking about what makes Ooblets engaging for me, I also have to highlight the wonderful character writing. While the villagers you can make friends with don't exactly  their nature over time, they'll reveal more of their thoughts, emotions, and backstory the higher friendship you get. Even better, the  of dialogue is so much greater than Stardew Valley, much less Animal Crossing - I've maxed out a character's friendships stickers and started worrying I'd start getting the same daily dialogue, but instead one day they casually dropped a piece of backstory I hadn't heard before and made me go "ohhhh" about their character. I can't emphasize how much hearing new dialogue lines from characters even so many hours into the game sets Ooblets apart from other games where chatting with villagers becomes a chore because of the repetitive dialogue.My biggest (and basically only?) critique of the game is that there's roughly 3 music tracks that play in Badgetown and they get super repetitive, super quick. I'd love some kind of "town audio" vs "battle music audio" slider so that I could mute the town music but still enjoy the dance battle music (but also being on PC I'll probably just go mute the Badgetown audio tracks in Audacity so I can still enjoy the other areas' music).

_childDocuments_.review: Really cute game! I think the best parts for me were the graphics and the concept. This will mostly be a negative review but please read it to the end to understand where I'm coming from.Unfortunately, didn't really turn out to be my cup of tea. For one, the gameplay (imo) is pretty shallow and not very well designed and balanced. For a few reasons:1) In the early s†ages of the game, my time was spent wandering around the pretty small map waiting for resources to respond, because I had nothing else to do. After watering your crops and talking to the 10ish NPCs around the map, your choices are between picking up garbage, fishing, and dancing against wild ooblets. Picking up garbage takes about 5 minutes tops. You can't actually fish up any fish (you fish up resources instead), and ooblets don't want to dance against you if you don't offer an adequate tribute, which is often a crop you have to spend days growing, or some kind of dish that requires a crop you have to spend days growing.2) Ok, easy then. I'll just sleep to pass the time, so that I can grow my crops faster to get to all the fun stuff. Not so fast - in ooblets instead of the day being separated by day, it is separated into sections of the day. I don't think I actually counted how many there are because they aren't clearly defined but I think it's split into 4 or 5. So you try to sleep, but you don't actually wake up the next day, you wake up in the "next section". And you cannot go back to sleep if you have too much energy. So what ends up happening is I'm taking 2 naps and then going back to wandering around the town trying to find things to do to burn my energy so I can go back to sleep to pass the time.3) All the quests are mostly fetch quests and not that interesting. This would not normally be an issue for me, but because of the above reason it becomes really grating to wait for the crops to grow.4) Instead of having in game seasons, the seasons, similar to animal crossing, are gated by REAL TIME. There is actually no good reason for this other than the devs being able to have real time events (for example: a halloween or christmas event), compared to animal crossing where the different bugs and fish were gated to our real months and seasons.5) Some of the balancing is very bad. It's actually possible to LOSE MONEY growing a crop in this game, which I didn't even conceive was possible until I noticed the sell price for the crop and the buy price of the seeds. In ooblet dance battles (specifically 1 on 1s) it is possible to stunlock your opponent and BE STUNLOCKED by your opponent until the whole thing is over - in any kind of game, its really bad design to be able to have a situation where your player is just locked out of playing the game for a solid 5 minutes. I have also had a dance battle where both me and the opponent were doing nothing the whole battle and both ended on 0 points (he brought a support type, I brought the one that can steal points). I think that this can be solved by limiting 1 on 1 battles to a selection of  specific Ooblets.Despite all of this, I pretty much went on a Ooblet fever for 4 or 5 days before I eventually got tired of grinding so much.  I have gotten up to restoring the oobnet, but not pass that - I think I was pretty burnt out from everything. I went into this game thinking that it was a cross between Stardew Valley and Pokemon, rather it is a cross between Animal Crossing and Pokemon. This is an important distinction because Stardew Valley is a farming sim, and Animal Crossing is a life sim with farming elements. Despite ooblets being a farming sim, I found that farming was probably the smallest part of my day, unfortunately. They also ported the mechanic of a daily cycling shop from animal crossing, which is one that I particularly hate (importantly, you get a catalogue of all possible items later, after you restore the oobnet, which is good).HOWEVER, reading the reviews, there are a lot of positive impressions that Ooblets has left in other players, and I believe it. The game is really charming, the ooblets are cute, and I'm a sucker for growing pets out of plants. I think if you don't really mind the mechanics that make the game grindy as listed above, then you will really enjoy this game. Same if you played both animal crossing and stardew valley, and liked animal crossing more because it was more relaxing and slower pace, and it was fun to decorate your house and farm :). However, if you're like me and preferred stardew valley because you liked managing your farm, progressing technology, making money, and building relationships with the villagers, I would recommend maybe watching gameplay footage instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Yo wtf is an Ooblets?!?!……..…only the cutest game your future wife’s boyfriend should be playing!!I still have no idea what an Ooblet is, but now I want to take one home and call it George.So… it’s Pokemon… if you grew your own Pokemon on your farm, had them help with the farming (use them instead of sprinklers etc), and instead of battling to catch them you had a dance battle to earn new seeds. So it’s nonviolent Pokemon and yes, I wanna catch 'em all.I have a hard time sleeping at night due to anxiety, and I would play this in bed after washing up and it helped me sleep. Best cozy and comfort game! Everything in Ooblets is downright adorable, from the cheeky dialogue to the unique dance battles to the well-designed creatures themselves. That charm was enough to draw me in from the get go and keep a gleeful smile on my face for most of the story. It just feels like something I'd have liked to play as a kid. Really weird stuff all around but so always like the game equivalent of hugging a baby Panda. I don't like games where cards are the gameplay but this one just felt so right. I don't know why it did to me what it did to me. But I'm glad it was done. This game is crack.I absolutely adored Ooblets. At first the dialog threw me off but I grew to absolutely love it and love the charm of the game. The story is hilarious, the card game is very fun, and even post main story I still play because I want to catch all the Ooblets. It has farming and decorating and fashion, which I love. Honestly it’s an absolute blast. It's like if Stardew had less stress inducing timetables on things, for one, and two everything is friendly and fun. At most a character might be a bit of a butt, but that's life. I loved making all the recipes to befriend Ooblets, trying to collect them all so I could have them all over my farm. It’s the loop of growing things and gaining progress without the threat of idk, dying in the  mines or forgetting to water something and it dying at the end of the season. Here I can focus on full forward momentum, with the only backslide possible being me selling or eating something without thinking.I loved the silly quirky vibe of the game. The art style and characters and music is all just so goofy and fun! Ooblets feels a lot less like you’re trying to make super efficient use of each day, it’s a lot more chill and wishy washy but it has it’s little routines and you have to think a bit about how you want to use your energy each day. Everything in it does have a purpose, from gardening (which is how you grow your Ooblets from seed too!) to cooking and crafting/improving your farm etc. You also make friends with the locals and help improve the town. You even get to run your own shop eventually! Also there's a mystery on the island that needs to be solved. It’s not ridiculously big on customisation, it’s much more like old school Animal Crossing where you’d go about your tasks, not designing a whole island, but it can be super fun and has hidden depth through all the stuff you can work towards collecting and unlocking.I honestly think the story alone is worth a play through! It’s definitely silly but that’s kind of the whole point and is definitely part of the charm! The storyline is engaging, but there's no pressure to progress any faster than you want. If sounds / music are important to you, it's great. It's like a more modern Animal Crossing: Population Growing! Vibe. Upbeat and cute, with satisfying popping noises when you pick things etc. I adored the NPCs and their dialogue. The dialogue is also super funny. It’s got so much personality, very upbeat and silly and cute and just a good positive time. I’m always in a good mood when I’m playing Ooblets, it’s hard not to be. It's supposed to be a silly fun little game to collect things and bop along to. There’s a ton of stuff to complete, like collecting and scanning every Ooblet, displaying all the figures in town hall, collecting all the recipes and unlocking the wildlands upgrades. Collecting all the friendship stickers (the first time around you get a few unique items!) I also think the player shop that is eventually unlocked is so much fun, and you can purchase upgrades for that too!! There’s also the house upgrades and the decorating, not the mention the wishy well which has loads of upgrades and things to buy/unlock. There’s just so much to do! This game is lowkey a completionist’s wet dream. Finally, and many reviews have said this, but I’ll go a bit further, the game has so much heart. The silliness is just that, but the amount of character this game has is just incredible. I struggle to think of another collection/farming game with as much personality as Ooblets. It’s hard to pin it to one genre and I think going in with a very open mind and seeing what you can grow or collect or who your favourite NPCs are or how the little story grows, is your best bet. I think overall I just loved the cute creatures and cute silly feel of the game. I think it is an interesting hybrid of game types (farming, card battle, collecting creatures) and it’s very much worth it, even at full price. It’s so quirky and lighthearted, and you can take it at your own pace. Sometimes with cozy games it can feel like you're playing the same game over and over, with a few differences, but Ooblets feels fresh and creative. I think its totally fair if you play it and find its not your thing. Not everything is for everyone-- but it’s a great game if you want a super low stakes game to relax to. I’d say if you like collecting things and the card game aspect, plus really strange humor, give it a chance!10/10

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful, extremely polished and has a visual style that is incomparable to other games. It also has a sense of humour that I also just really dig. Definitely a fun one that I am looking forward to enjoying for many, many hours. It's cozy, delightful and shows a lot of love and constant updates.People thinking about buying this shouldn't get dragged into the controversy. I've read through the entire thing, done my research, and everyone acted badly. I am not going to blame an indie dev for taking money to help make their product in order to be able to see their dream realised. I am not going to blame a dev who is self-aware that he acted badly and admitted they could have done better.I do blame a horrible, toxic fanbase who brigaded someone three years ago for entitlement, and went so far as to fabricate fake evidence against the dev just to drum up more hate, and I do blame the same people for not being levelheaded about certain situations and cherrypicking things to attack others with due to personal grievances.In my personal opinion, it was a bad situation all over and there are no heroes here, but the dev was the only one of the two parties who has moved on and has learned from it.And the game is a great show of what people can do through adversity.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really wanted to like this game. I really did. I like farming games like Harvest Moon and Stardew Valley and i also really like creature collector games, so the concept of combining them was interesting and appealed to me in a fundamental level. But there are just too many things that kinda stopped me from enjoying it.First let me start with the things i DID like. As i mentioned, i like the concept of combining the farming game with the creature collector and i think that, if done correctly, this would be an amazing concept. I liked the little community we have at Badgetown and all the little quirky things about the game. It has a charm about it that you just don't see in many games.The concept of the dance battle was an interesting twist to the creature collector battle mechanic that throws away the somewhat troublesome idea of making animals fight each other, though i do have my problems with how it's done here that i'll talk about in a bit.I also liked exploring the different locales and the excitement of what kinds of ooblets i could find there and what seeds they have. Nullwood in particular was really cool. I like the shear number of things there is to do as well, it was hard to run out of things to do.Now for the things i didn't really care for or thought could have been better implemented.First off, i mentioned the idea of the dance battle was cool, the problem though was how it was done. It felt really lackluster. There are no explanations on what anything actually does until you try it and find out. Hype for example has zero in game explanation, i just had to do it and see what it did and then hope that it was good. It was, but i prefer to be able to plan out my battles in turn based systems like this. You could say that after you figure it out then that's not an issue, and you'd be right, but the lack of clarity initially was a bit of a turnoff for me.Additionally, the card deck. OH the card deck. NO WAY of modifying it? REALLY? Considering how much your strategy relies on pulling the right card at the right time, not being able to modify your deck was irksome at best and devastating at worst. The basic deck has so many cards and your ooblets have so few special moves to add to it that it almost didn't matter what ooblets you used and trying to make synergies between them was a nightmare because you couldn't pick when you would get that signature move you want over something useless to you in that moment. You also lose all your beats and cards you have in your hand if you don't use them all up. You should be able to save them and use them in subsequent turns. Doing so would add A LOT more strategy to the battles.Another thing that got on my nerves, you find an ooblet you want to battle so that you can add it to your collection. It WANTS to battle you. But you can't just battle it, no. You have to give it some kind of VERY SPECIFIC thing as an offering first. Now you could argue that it makes you diversify and have to farm and make things you otherwise wouldn't in order to get that ooblet. That's a fair point and i would concede that isn't a bad thing. However, the fact that they want things that you have to get recipes for that you can't just get the recipe for and have to rely on RNG to get is stupid and very contrived and demoralizing. I found a cat ghost looking thing that i wanted VERY BADLY in Nullwood. But required a specific dish i had to cook to let me battle it. Ok, how do i get that recipe? I can only earn it as a reward from the dance barn, which i can only participate in once a day to get things. And the recipe was apparently super rare to pop up in there and i never saw it even come up once. Even if i could get it to come up in the dance barn, the dance barn was painfully RNG based on if you can win or not. Due to the nature of the nonadjustable deck and other factors involving the dance barn, i would often find myself losing in the dance barn due to completely unavoidable RNG bullcrap that i had no way of avoiding. Welp, i guess i can't get that one probably ever.I mentioned that there was plenty of things to do, and this is true and great. However, all the things you do are incredibly shallow and skin deep. It's like playing in a very large kiddie pool that the water only goes up to your ankles. Lots of places to go and things to do but nothing deep or satisfying and it just feels like that trying to advance on anything is artificially locked behind a contrived in game paywall, like the things you have to offer for dance battles for example. Almost all of the main story quests revolve around glorified fetch quests. There was one part of the game where in order to progress, i had to bring some entitled idiot 10 freaking cups of expensive coffee. Could i have technically farmed the stuff i needed to make it myself? Conceivably, but at the time i had no way of getting the springbeans needed, i didn't have a recipe to grind them, and i didn't have the recipe to brew the coffee either, so i had to go and buy them all which was extremely expensive for me at that stage of the game and i could only buy 3 a day, which means it took me 4 in game days to do this idiotic quest.The thing that killed the game for me entirely though was when i got to Port Forward. It was explained that in order to progress i had to beat some uppity moron's high scores on every single one of the arcade games in town. Minigames are cool and fun as an option, but not when they are mandatory. Forcing you to have to do ALL of them was so dumb that i just couldn't take it anymore. They are all super shallow reflex based games too, which i find incredibly annoying and do not enjoy playing in the slightest. So locking my progress behind gameplay that i find to be just irritating and infuriating at best is just going to make me quit playing the game.If i had any input on how to improve this game, there are only a few things that would have to change.1. Make the deck modifiable. This is the most important thing. Add in a card shop that you can buy different cards to change out your deck with and give the ooblets more special signature moves they can do that you can ALSO toggle on and off when you use them with your deck. Even without adding new card mechanics, this would be a huge upgrade, though more interesting card mechanics would be welcome as well.2. Lower the requirements to be able to battle ooblets. I'm not saying that you should be able to battle them for free because the idea behind the concept is not lost on me. But maybe you have to make an offering that meets a certain amount of points and different things you can offer will give different amounts of points based on that ooblet's preferences. Like if you make it the certain dish that it likes then it'll fill up the offering points you need a great amount.3. Have more things you can do to open up places besides fetch more planklets and nurneys! Maybe you have to have a certain ooblet to help build the place, or perhaps there is a group of ooblets in the place you have to battle out like at the very beginning of the game with Mayor Tinsel's office.4. For the love of all you hold sacred, don't force me to have to beat the high score on all these stupid, shallow reflex based arcade games that are just knockoffs of mindless, idiotic mobile games! It's explained in the story that in order to have claim on the tower, that you have to have the high score on ALL of them. If you beat his high score on 1-2 of the games, wouldn't that void HIS claim on it? Or how about this, you have the option to do a side quest with the mayor of that town to have them declare that tower as public domain that no one person can have claim to and kick his stupid butt out of the tower? Add an additional reward for people who WANT to beat all the high scores.

_childDocuments_.review: I've had this game on my wishlist for a while, so when it launched on Steam, I got notified and decided to buy it on a whim.As others have noted, there may be some balancing issues with the game, but that may also be a matter of play style and taste, so I'll leave those out (I'll say that I am frustrated that it feels like my progress is halted by my inability to do what the game wants me to do and I just don't know what it wants me to do).The biggest issues I have with the game have to do with controls and menus. I play with keyboard and mouse, and the game is very inconsistent on when it allows you to use the keyboard and when you have no choice but to click a button with your mouse instead. There are also a lot of simple but annoying UX issues with the menus. For example if you've clicked on an ooblet, you can't click on another ooblet without going through deselecting the current ooblet. Sometimes just tapping space will get you out of menus, but sometimes you have to reach for escape. I've tried rebinding esc to control, but every time I restart the game it will forget my rebinding. You can't rebind keys to mouse buttons. Disabled buttons in menus are sometimes selected by default, so you have to manually switch to a non-disabled button to leave a menu. Other times you actually can not leave a menu using escape, but instead have to do something else to get out. I could go on.This, combined with the balancing issues and flat out bugs, like getting out of bounds just by walking through a door (which was fun to be honest, but still a bug), at first made me think "ah, that's fine, these are just launch issues, I'm sure they'll be ironed out".But of course I had forgotten that this game has been out for a year already as an Epic Games exclusive.While I didn't know and don't care about the drama, the fact that the game has been out for a year does make me less hopeful that the gameplay will improve much from the current state.Either way, I try to justify not refunding by supporting indies and more calm games in general. So with that, I hope the best for the devs as well.

_childDocuments_.review: unfortunately I cannot recommend this game.  It is a fun quirky game but the amount of fetch quests ruined it for me. Along with that you have an insane amount of resource usage for these quests and with the price for seeds and how long it takes to grow some crops you never have enough cash. The one thing that really gets me is that this game does not have you water your crops first thing in the morning. It goes by whenever you last watered each individual crop. So let’s say you watered and planted some seeds at night and some in the day (because after selling somethings you were able to get more seeds), well at night is when the soil will dry out again for those crops that you watered at night, then during the day the other set of crops will dry out. Now imagine you have planted a variety of plants all through out the day. This creates chaos. Especially when you have used your stamina away from the farm because everything looked watered before you left, but when you return every other plant pops up dry and you have zero stamina to water them.some people may not care but it just got boring after a while.

_childDocuments_.review: My initial encounter with “Ooblets” dates back to 2020, the year in which it was primarily launched as an early-access farming simulator. Originally, I stumbled upon the game on Epic Games inasmuch as it hadn't been released on Steam; which, much to the fandom disappointment—myself included—, so remained for three more years. I am far from being impartial, since I am quite keen on the genre in question and have had rather pleasant previous experiences playing Ooblets. It had an indisputable positive, soothing and heart-warming impact on my personal life, and I dare to say that this reverberated to countless other players, notably so during such an astoundingly obscure and somber period—if not the most of all over the last two decades—for humanity.I, for one, had been highly anticipating the arrival of this game on this platform and I am much content with all the further improvements the developers brought into play. The storyline is now much richer and cemented compared to the its first version. The side quests and regions to explore have been expanded, matured and polished. All in all, I am satisfied with how the game turned out to be in these more or less three years of development. A true labour of love, as you surely will witness yourself if you join the game's Discord server. Just bear in mind that Ooblets never aimed at being profound or story-rich. It is what it promotes itself to be: simple, cute, casual and relaxing.  This piece holds a special place in my heart (≧◡≦) ♡ As of now, mine is the gleamy version of Dooziedug.

I've finished the story and am still playing because I'm enjoying it.Ooblet variety is good, I find cooking fun, and the silliness of crop types is delightful.My one complaint for this game is the organization of the Ooblet page in your journal: I wish it it either grouped all the same oob together, or all the same types (common/unusual/gleamy or point-of-origin), so that finding the oobs you're trying to add to your team was a little less of a hassle, but alasI have played this title exclusively on the steam deck and have been very happy with the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun but it's feeling like its kind of lacking in a way. If you're looking for a super story based game this game isn't it. There's really no connections with the characters or the ooblets and it's not as engaging as I had expected it to be. I feel as though it's more based on mainly collecting and farming and kind of accessorizing your character and your ooblets. The map starts out super small and it threw me off and also the fact that farming is what you rely on the most but it's difficult to make a good earning in the game. There needs to be more ways to earn money rather than having to sell things or do quests that still require you to collect crops or materials. The ways you can collect materials is also very limited as you run out of wood and rocks eventually and have no other way to obtain them as far as I can see from the amount of time I've played other than buying them. The drawing and ooblets are fun and the dancing is interesting but it's always the same thing and it slowly starts to be less engaging since it starts to feel more like a grind instead of having any strategic way of winning. I wouldn't say I hated the game completely but It was lacking more than it was entertaining and I would not say it would be worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: I was expecting to like this game, but not as much as I did. It came at just the right time, I've been going through a rough time and I just needed something cute and simple to take my mind off things. Ooblets scratched that itch.The game is a cute mix of farming, creature collecting, daily quests, friendship building, and dance battles.Farming can end up being fully automated so long as you provide seeds once you have enough ooblets and ooblet houses, so you can move on and explore.I enjoyed all the different islands you go to. They change it up too so it's not always just dance battles you need to do to accomplish thing (though I think I liked the dance battles the most).Eventually you can even open your own shop and sell your items to the townsfolk. I never really ran out of things to do as the game progressed, if anything I always wished I had more energy and time in the day so I could do more. Which isn't a bad thing at all.I'm glad I started playing during the Hallowe'en event. There were lots of cool spooky items to get for my house and with all the leftover candy I was able to recycle to make lots of bait for fishing which helped a lot with supplies I needed towards the end of the game.Oh and I really like their take on shinies (gleamies) in this game. If they spawn, you'll know. There's shooting starts and fireworks around the town so you can't miss them, you just need to look around a bit. So while it's still down to change that they'll spawn any given day it's not down to chance per encounter.Anyway this game has a lot to love. I've already gotten all the achievements but haven't finished the main story yet. I'm at the very end though, and I'm glad I played this game.There isn't much commitment needed either, you can play as much or as little as you like without feeling the pressure to get to the next save or the next big thing like in other games. It's just good casual fun for as long as you want or need.Pick up Ooblets and have a splenda time ;)Update: Wow after all these hours on the game I only just got the joke that is Outgrids name >_<

_childDocuments_.review: I might return to this review for revisions as I continue the game, but I feel like I need to express my thoughts on this game as is. This is going to completely disregard the entire EGS fiasco.Ooblets is a casual farm-sim, creature collector, deck building game. The game-play cycle revolves around you challenging ooblets to dance battles, which are basically simplified versions of typical card-battle games like hearthstone. Winning a battle nets you a seed that you can take to your farm to grow a new Ooblet. That's the core game play. I think the largest issue the game faces is how unbelievably slow the beginning of the game is. You're going to find yourself spending all of your money on seeds for your farm, and making back just enough to buy more seeds and maybe something else, if you're lucky. Everything you grow has some sort of in-game use, which typically is to feed to an ooblet to challenge them to a dance battle. You NEED the resources you grow in order to get more Ooblets or open new things in town, but, these plants are also supposed to be one of your main sources of income, either from the mission board or just selling them directly. It is a slog to get everything in Badgetown open, or expanding to new areas. The sense of progression is minimal, and it makes the game feel a lot more like busy work rather than a fun game. This game takes heavy inspiration from other life-sims like Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing. It doesn't try to hide that fact. it borrows many of its core elements from those games. However, those elements are watered down from their source material. There's a day/night system, but there isn't a season system or any sort of change in day-to-day life. You grow the same crops all the time, with the same ooblets, and any events are tied to the real-world calendar rather than an in-game one. Instead, the change in the daily-life comes through a level-up system, where new crops and ooblets appear as you gain XP. Leveling up is a slow process, meaning you're stuck with the same old same old for extended periods of time. It causes the game to feel very stagnate, rather than a living changing world like other life-sims. Characters. The characters in ooblets are completely unremarkable. Remember-able and unique NPCs are one of the foundational elements of a life-sim, and the characters in Ooblets are all too similar. There's a lack in dialogue variation, so many of the NPCs talk in the same way, and don't have much remarkable about their personalities. Even when doing introductions, I found myself unable to remember who it was I had just talked to. Many of these NPCs sort of just wander aimlessly around all day, lacking any sort of schedule aside from those who are also shopkeepers. With Badgetown also being very small, you'll wind up seeing them walking in circles or stuck on the geometry somewhere. The Ooblets themselves are the same. The player character is also a bit strange, as the character creator is barebones. Your character also has a voice, with the game already having quite a lot of dialogue for the player character, often breaking the immersion of you being a resident of this town. The game's art style is... okay. The biggest hindrance to it is that it's sort of generic. Everything looks so similar to one another, especially in regards to locations. I found myself trying to find a specific building in Badgetown, and going in 2-3 wrong ones every time. Ooblets themselves also look very same-y. There's not much interesting happening with the vast majority of them aside from trying to look cute and marketable. They all have the exact same animations that look like they were pulled from the unity store. Many of them are just an animal or a plant with silly eyes. The NPCs also have this issue with sharing too many animations. That and the game's programming often doesn't account for the outfits, environment, or anything the characters can hold, so these animations clip right through. The style of animation doesn't match the art style, really emphasizing  the "store-bought" feeling behind charcater movements. Especially when dance battles happen, which is what you're going to see the most of.The elephant in the room is the game's writing. I mean the literal writing in the game. It tries so hard to be weird and quirky that it comes off as forced. None of the characters speak in a natural way, instead, talking like 2012 tumblr posts. The slang and abrupt attempts at humor just feel so commercial. There's no thought behind it. No attempt to craft an interesting world or even a fun story. it's just bland. I don't know how an indie studio managed to make all of their dialogue feel like a corporate attempt at being quirky. It makes me feel cynical, but it's just not cute or charming. The excessive use of vowels and baby-talk feels like they're trying to replicate Adventure Time slang but didn't understand how to. Others may feel differently, but seeing "Ok cool." at the top of the screen any time i pick up something new just makes me feel upset. It's bad.

Farming is a thing you do so you can make recipes to unlock new ooblets; it works well, but it's a background system. _childDocuments_.review: Firstly, I'm being very critical of this game, and you may enjoy this game despite the things I find lacking about it.This game mixes the excitement of creature-collecting and creature-battling a la Pokemon with the coziness of a farming sim, and honestly, it works. The game is very charming. Each day I always find myself excited about what new ooblet I may be able to recruit into my ever-growing menagerie, and I get particularly excited when a shiny ooblet shows up in town.To recruit an ooblet, you must win a dance battle against it so it gives you a seed of its kind. To challenge an ooblet to a dance battle, you must give it a certain set of materials. Some ooblets ask for forage, others ask for crops, and others ask for crafted foods.This is where the negatives begin to pile up.See, for ooblets that ask for forage, you probably already have them on hand as long as you're not neglecting to pick up stuff while walking around town. But for the other two, it causes a dilemma. In a normal farming sim, the primary (if not the Only) purpose of crops is to make money, this makes sense. On occasion, you may need to keep a few crops on hand for quests or gifts, but still you want to sell the majority of your crops to earn money for the next batch of seeds or upgrades. Not the case in Ooblets, because now crops are equally important for money AND for recruiting new ooblets, which creates the two-pronged problem of wanting to hoard crops "in case i need it" and being constantly low on money because you're not selling your crops. It's even worse when the ooblet is asking for cooked foods. Many cooked foods require at least two steps to make (for example, Quib Tart for recruiting Unnyhunny requires you to process Sweetiebeetie into Froobtose, then Cook that that with Quibs to make the tart), while others are even more complicated (for example, Soggy Bread requires you to first process Sweetiebeetie and Muz into Froobtose and Muz Flour, then Unlock Bread Sammy recipe in the wishing well, cook that, then Unlock Soggy Bread recipe in the wishing well, and finally use the bread sammy to cook the soggy bread.)This, combined with how there's no clear linear way to progress in the game, makes it very overwhelming in my opinion. I'm always stuck trying to decide what I should be growing in my limited farm space, and what to do with whatever I grow from it. Do I sell it so I  can buy stuff? Do I keep it to recruit ooblets? Do I keep it for the 500 other quests that tend to just randomly require these crops? Am I suddenly developing a self-destructive hoarding habit? (the answer to that last one is yes)Anyway, cute game. Very overwhelming. 15 hours was enough for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Ooblets is a very special game to me. Special in the fact that after a 1 year wait to get it on steam, Glumberland is still hard at work making a fantastic game even better. Is it good though? Well this is a tough question to answer but the reason is with all the fun activities, where do I start with?I guess at its base it's a farming sim, the meat of the fruit and veggies is that you will be planting and watering a lot, kinda like other farming sims such as Stardew. The twist is that the second biggest aspect of your new farm life is that you must dance battle other plant/animal/robot monster things to get seeds to grow your own allies to get in even more dance battles! Shake it Followbabies!Other notable aspects are doing tasks for the mayor to help develop Badgetown, the town you live in, and progress the game's story line. Travelling to lots of different locations. Talking to people all over the world and giving gifts to help develop friendships. Raising crops to sell and cook into tasty dishes. Daily dance tournaments that give exclusive rewards. And my favourite task of all, tracking down beautiful colourful "gleamys" (they are effectively shiny pokémon folks) and really taking to the dance floor with tracers and sparkles as I dance the night away! There's also fishing that has no mini game! You just put bait on the line, cast it away and you're always guaranteed to get something, wow!If I haven't sold you on the ridiculous zany fun that is Ooblets by now, perhaps this is not the game for you. It is kinda a niché music card battler farming sim dance battle extravaganza. But if any of this sounds like it would appeal to you, I would heavily encourage you pick it up today and start your new life with your new Ooblet friends! <3

_childDocuments_.review: I will be honest. I read a lot about this game. It is highly suggested on different forums when looking for something cozy. I was expecting a great game.But... I was really disappointed. IN THE BEGINNING.This game at first, for the first several hours, was super confusing. I had no idea what to do. There's barely any handholding. I don't like when games treat you like an inefficient toddler but I also don't like it when they leave you alone to figure EVERYTHING out. But if I had to pick the lesser of 2 evils, I'd choose the former.This game at first is confusing af. I had to keep googling how to do things. I didn't understand how anything worked. The game gives you less than the basics when you start.However, now that I am 20+ hours in, everything is so much better. Don't get me wrong, I still have to look up certain recipes and how to do things but the game is SO much fun. And it IS relaxing. You can do everything at your own pace. Yes, there is a clock but nothing is constrained by time restrictions.This game is highly addictive in the farming Sim category. You need to grow various amounts of crops in order to make money. Some of these crops need to be further broken down into ingredients to use to battle ooblets in hopes to get a seed. This seed, once planted and cared for, will grow another ooblet and further grow your little army.I haven't played many card based battle games but once you get the flow of this, it's highly addictive and cute.I really recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a fun farming sim that allows you to take it easy. Be patient (more than me!!), explore, and enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: I've put in a few hours and can say that I genuinely love the game! It has its own appeal to farm sim and creature collector fans, and I can see that it takes inspiration from a few other games. I was not aware of any community drama until after I got it so I don't care to comment on it tbh.The progress is much slower than Stardew Valley. In fact, it's just slow in general. The main campaign tasks are tied to your level, so you can actually complete them at a lower level and then only have side quest options. However, I never felt like I had nothing to do since I would spend my downtime foraging, micro-managing my farm, fishing, crafting, cooking, and decorating/accessorizing. Hot take, but I feel like Ooblets does the farming part better than SV. It's easier to gain momentum when harvesting/planting, and the crops are actually useful for completing the main campaign. They are also much easier to profit from, as you can process them into food with ease or you can use the Plenny export shack to earn massive profits for set amounts of crops. The creature part is very unique! The dance battles are executed via deck battles like Slay the Spire. When you win, you get an Ooblet seed which then can grow into a new friend! Your Ooblets follow you around like in Heartgold/Soulsilver, but you can also leave a few at the farm to help you take care of your crops. One of the cons is that the game doesn't let you talk with your following Ooblets or let you feed them treats, which I would've liked to see. There is an incentive to collect many different types to allow for synergy with your chosen dance troupe; some Ooblet dance moves work best with others. The game does allow for adventuring to other areas to collect new crops and Ooblets. The game also lets you put accessories on all your Ooblets! :DAll in all, I really do recommend it if you're interested!

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent experience of videogaming. Ooblets scratches a lot of itches at once. It's a little bit monster collector, a little bit farming sim, a little bit town life, but it's not too deep in any area. Although there are some ways the game could be fleshed out in perhaps a sequel or big content expansion (I'll get into a few ideas about this later), overall I think the balance is actually just right for me.I have a lot of games that ask a lot of me and I also have some games which are relaxing but in some ways ask *too little* of me. It's tough to find a game that hits a sweet spot between too much and too little sometimes. Ooblets is, for me, in an ideal point where there's just enough to engage with to keep me motivated but not so much that I ever feel overwhelmed or like I just need to slog through a bunch of grinding etc.The style and theme are unique and quirky in a way I overall liked. I'm not saying every joke lands or anything but such is the nature of comedy. Overall I liked the light-hearted interactions with townsfolk as a contrast from too many games which try to do Grand Storytelling when sometimes I just wanna buy a new jacket and didn't actually need to get a whole lore dump about how the shopkeeper was sad a lot as a kid.At just over 40 hours I've completed the main storyline and I'm now I'm mostly winding down and collecting gleamy ooblets, perfecting my farm, etc. I'm not sure if I'll get a ton more out of the game but I wouldn't be surprised if I play for at least 10 more hours and that's a pretty good value overall.There are a few areas I'd like to see fleshed out. Vacation spots are a little underwhelming. Having the Dance Barn as my only reliable source for battles with other trainers at the end of the game is a little disappointing it would be cool to maybe have Dance Barn type locations in other places like Nullwhere and Port Forward that maybe hold events less often but would give you another excuse to travel. Lastly, without major spoilers, the endgame feels like it could use some kind of epilogue focused on tearing out some unnecessary facilities and doing restoration perhaps.None of these criticisms are major detractors though and the game still stands up as a fantastic experience. My best hope is for an Ooblets 2 where I can dance battle my friends as so many of my buddies are playing this game and we all talk team composition/strategy and how we we wish we could battle each other!

_childDocuments_.review: I've put several hundred hours into this game on another platform before it came to Steam, and I look forward to playing it more here as well.Ooblets is a very cute and charming game with memorable characters and silly dialogue. There are lots of adorable creatures to befriend and collect, as well as a farm, home, and shop for you to expand, improve, and decorate however you want. You can travel to different regions of the world, each with their own unique setting and theme. There are also seasonal events that inject some fresh and exciting activities that will keep you coming back every few months, even if you haven't played in a while.Ooblets appeals to casual players and dedicated spreadsheet optimization folks alike. You can play at your own pace, and there are no consequences for doing anything "too slowly."This game is one that you can play for hours on end, but it is also easy to pick up and put down if you only have brief windows of time -- making it an excellent game to play on the go if you happen to have a Steam Deck.The community surrounding this game has been very friendly, positive, and rewarding to be a part of. The devs have been releasing free content updates several times per year since the game launched, and there are even more new features on the way.I have found it to be worth every penny at full price, and if you can get this game on sale, I consider it a no-brainer.Lastly, Nuppo is the best boy; may you all receive the blessing of many Nuppo spawns!
