_childDocuments_.review: Freedom Planet 1 is a game that is near and dear to my heart, so I'm going to be reviewing this primarily as a comparison to the first game. I've played 5 stages with Carol and tested out all the other characters within the tutorial and first level. 👎 The artstyle is very distinct from the first game. I can't really say that I appreciate it after playing the FP1 so much and associating all the characters and whatnot with the old artstyle. It doesn't feel like a natural progression for the series's artstyle in the same way that something like 2D Sonic games have evolved. I do think all of the new assets look great in a vacuum, but the first game's artstyle was so striking that this feels like a downgrade. It doesn't help that the higher pixel count sprites end up making the game blend in with other indie games going for a similar look. I get the impression that whoever made the decision on the new artstyle wanted to distance themselves from the Sonic and Megaman X inspired artstyle of the first game. I feel like it's kind of too late to do that though. 👎 The music is very much a mixed bag. Some of the songs sound really great like the new Dragon Valley remix and Shade Armory. Other songs though are either unmemorable or feel unfinished. The boss themes I heard in particular were quite a disappointment. Even with the songs that I like though they don't really have the same appeal as the FP1 OST. They end up feeling overly busy and not as cleanly mixed as the songs from the first game. It seems like some of the songs from the beta/alpha have remained unchanged in the final game as well like Bakunawa 3, which is still just a 46 second loop. The end result of all of this is that the music quality feels very inconsistent throughout the game.  compared to FP1, which I felt maintained a very consistent level of quality throughout its OST. 👎For the most part the entire cast controls really well. There's just a few mechanics that I personally disagree with. The game has a guard button. This was something that was in the demo I played a few years back and I hoped it was a placeholder mechanic but I'm sad to see that it's still here. I'm not a fan of "press button to negate damage" mechanics as I find them to be unengaging and promote a passive playstyle. And that's exactly what they do in this game. The timing for the block is  (despite NPCs dialogue's attempts to convince you otherwise). You can pretty much just stand in one spot and keep negating damage as long as your timing is half decent. I wouldn't have an issue with this so much if I could just ignore it like the bullet time in Katana ZERO, but it is ingrained into the game and so you will need to use it. FP1 did not have a block button (unless you were Milla, but that's a different kind of block), so all bosses were designed for you to avoid damage by moving out of the way or using invincibility frames. Not the case here. Boss design in this game is far more loose and cheap as a result of the guard mechanic existing. Pretty easy to design bosses that you can call fair when you give the player a get out of jail free button. I could harp on this mechanic for another paragraph, but I'll just say that I don't find it very interesting or engaging and leave it at that. 👎The levels don't feel as tight as the ones from FP1 from what I played, and you can feel it from the very outset of the game. They feel kind of empty and bloated sometimes, and convoluted and mazelike some other times. I think there was another review on here that echoed a similar sentiment. I do think the level design picks up after the first 3 levels, but I never really felt like it got as good as the first game's levels. The end level bosses also were pretty underwhelming from what I played. Apart from the boss of the 5th stage they all felt more like minibosses from the first game. Speaking of which this game doesn't have those. The structure from the first game of Act 1 --> Minor Boss --> Act 2 --> Major Boss is gone. You just have level and then boss here, and the bosses are generally just random big robot, while the bosses and minibosses from the first game often had a story reason for existing. Overall levels are shorter and more bite sized in this game, but they have a lot of empty space and glorified hallways. 👎I like the idea of FP2's camera as a proof of concept. FP1 had a single viewframe for the whole game that never zoomed in or out. It could be kind of claustrophobic in a few places, but I didn't find myself minding it too much. FP2 attempts to fix this issue by implementing a camera that zooms out depending on how fast you're going, allowing you to see more of what's ahead. You can adjust how far the camera zooms out in the settings or turn off the feature completely. The downside of this is that it makes those pretty hi-pixel sprites look like total garbage, and you often can't hardly tell what something even is supposed to be because the pixels are so crunched when it's zoomed out. I really don't think it's a good idea to put control over the camera in the player's hands in a game like this. A better solution would have been to handcraft the camera according to the level design: zoom in during the slow and complicated sections and zoom out during the high speed sections where the player is expected to go fast. Instead what they've done is implemented is a clunky system that tries to automate the hard work of proper level and camera design away and fails at it. 👎It's quite buggy. Within the first two hours I found more bad geometry that I was getting stuck on than in the entirety of FP1. There was also someone complaining about the controller glyphs, and yeah those are screwed up as of writing this. Game feels rushed despite taking so long to come out, and honestly that's what I was expecting. I'm not going to say it's Duke Nukem Forever levels of bad or anything but it feels like it's within that territory. 👍From what I played it seems like they got almost all of the original cast from FP1 back to work on this project. There are some replacements like Gong and Syntax, all of the major VAs still seem to be there. The VAs for the new characters sound good as well. I really liked the amateur VA cast from the first game and I'm very happy they've returned to work for this project. I think they do a pretty good job in their delivery for the most part. However I can't really say that the spritework always does the voiceovers justice. The original game had that problem from time to time as well, but I feel like it's exacerbated here because of the more zoomed out camera in most scenes. This segues into my next complaint which is... 👎👎👎The presentation in this game is a wreck when you compare it to FP1, and I think it mainly is due to the overambition of FP2. There are text only dialogue boxes now, which weren't a thing in the first game. In FP1 whenever a character opened their mouth you got voice acting, and they were able to pull that off because of the smaller scope. In FP1 you would go through a level and get a cutscene. Rinse and repeat until the credits. Here you also have towns segments (that feel completely pointless) and have NPCs to talk to. When major characters show up as NPCs to talk to they don't get voice acting either. You don't always get a cutscene after each level like in the first game, and some levels seem to have no place within the story of the game either (Tiger Falls is just a level you go through to get to another city). I can't make myself expect less when the first game set the bar for my expectations.Would you look at that, I’m out of space. Can’t fit anymore. No conclusion segment, sorry. I’m going to try and refund this.tl;dr go play Freedom Planet 1 if you didn't

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this is kind of a hot take, but I think the only reason this game series didn't get more attention is mainly due to being perceived as "furry" on the outside, but trust me is pretty good. But yeah, this sequel is amazing, it does distance itself a lot from being a 'Sonic fangame' even if the first game had already lots of influence from other Sega Genesis/Megadrive vidya. This game pushes a bit more the beat'em'up feel, adding even a dodge button, and slowing just a tiny bit the gameplay sometimes. Speaking of it, many stages are way larger, sometimes levels not being as straightforward as in the first game, but I think this is actually a right step (one of many) in comparison to the first game, giving room for more complex elements and enemies. Overall this game has so much more content and the OST is amazing even if you'll miss a couple of the iconic songs from FP1. You're likely to finish your first playthrough in around 15-20 hours or so (including beating every level, battle-sphere, boss rematch, etc... but not 100% completion) and it does not feel draggy at all. If you played the first game, basically you'll be missing our lil' alien guy, Torque, and a continuation to the previous villain's whereabouts, which (spoilers from FP2)  , but to be honest, I think they did good with changing the subject of an otherwise predictable sequel, and giving us in exchange a pretty deep story and lore about almost anything that was rather unanswered in the first game and tons of new characters, including a new antagonist.TLDR; buy it, it's sooo worth and I love this game, there are very minor caveats but nothing is really stopping the fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Great sequel that manages to surpass the original.It has the same good gameplay and setting of the first Freedom Planet (albeit with a few design changes in the characters), topped with some more goodies.First, the addition of Neera Li as a playable character (who was a quite a challenging midboss in the first entry of the series) in which she functions as a power-type character.While not as a fast in movement and combat as the other characters, Neera possesses a variety of moves that can pack a punch to enemies; ideal if you're into a more aggressive, battle-focused style of gameplay.Also, the addition of the guard action for all characters adds more depth to the gameplay by providing you with a very fast and short protection for those moments when you get yourself into a bind (a bit comparable towards the insta-shield for those who have played either  or ).Furthermore, the game's difficulty is more customisable than its predecessor due to addition of items that can be held before entering a stage and either give passive postive or negative effects depending on the held item in question.The items are grouped into "boosters", "potions", "charms" and "brave stones".Boosters, charms and potions makes the game easier by granting passive bonuses when held, but at the cost of a penalty on your ranking and crystal shard bonus that gets granted by completing a stage (crystal shards are used here as a currency to buy items in the hub-stages of the game or to exchange into another currency to buy other certain items that are being sold in the hub-areas).You can also fiddle with the assistance settings in the options menu if you really want to play in easy mode.On the other hand, brave stones makes the game harder by granting negative effects on your character, but rewards you with a boost on both ranking and crystal shard bonus; if you play really well with brave stones, you may even get the highest ranking possible for clearing a stage: a rainbow S.The story is just as enjoyable as it was on the previous title and there is even some lore to be found in this entry.The only small downside is the lack of character-exclusive stages and that the difference in dialogue in most cutscenes can be minimal when playing with different characters.One thing of note: the game will reference certain elements, events and a certain character of the previous title, but I don't think it won't have too much impact if you haven't played the first .In overall: a great sequel to an already great sonic-like indie platformer with its own identity that also manages to succesfully expand upon it.Definitely worth recommending!

_childDocuments_.review: I had a very high opinion of the first Freedom Planet game so I was a little afraid that the sequel might not deliver. However it ended up winning me over to the point of not wanting to stop playing and getting all achievements.I wasn't the biggest fan of the artstyle change (specially Lilac's concept art. Sorry but I really like her OG design. She looks better in her sprite form though!). However comparing it to the first one I definetly see the technical improvements. Not to take credit away from the more primitive, cutesy style of the first one, it's just a different vibe. Also I'm really sorry to say but the OST is not as well recieved as the first one and I agree with that take. It's definitely not bad, it's just not as good. No offense!Some of the new gameplay elements such as guarding, items, revivals and boss HP bars made me want to try only a couple stages; however after taking a break and understanding how they worked it made the gameplay really flow (even though it made it feel easier compared to the first one). There's some fun rewards for completing the Gallery and getting the "True Ending" so look forward to that!I've seen some people not really satisfied with the story and I suppose I see their point, but I wouldn't call it a bad narrative, there's interesting worldbuilding and plenty of room to expand on it with other games. What really sells me on the game is the wonderfully responsive controls and the character's different platforming/battling styles. Not to mention the incredibly appealing pixel art.All I can really tell you is that I highly recommend this game. If you're expecting "Sonic but better" or a carbon copy of Freedom Planet 1 it is not going to happen. This game has its own identity and if you learn to play it you're not going to want to stop (well, that's my personal experience at least).

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Oh, and well, if you haven't played FP1, and are wondering if you should buy this, you don't need to play the first one, and most people will enjoy this one more, since there's less chance of getting stuck on a boss and there's more content. You should probably try at least one of the games either way.I was sceptical about a positive review, because I felt like I enjoyed and remembered FP1 more by a bit. But it's still a good game, I've given positive reviews to worse, and will probably replay it eventually for other characters, so here you go.Despite being a better game in QoL, mechanics, content, voice acting etc, as a lot of other people mentioned, I'll just focus on my complaints:- the music wasn't as memorable as FP1.- the game has a lot more of speed sections compared to the slower platforming of FP1, and it felt like the stages were more empty as a result. Totally subjective though, most people seem to like this more.- I think I actually missed the FP1 bosses, because these ones were easy, probably because of the extra tools you're given - guarding (which might be overkill, since a lot of attacks seem dodgable normally) and Lilac's Dragon Boost being cancellable now. Maybe I should've used more difficulty raising items (especially since I think the game lets you switch items if you game over, and continue at a gem cost, so you don't need to reset the whole stage), and other characters don't have as much i-frame attacks (I think...), but I remember needing to learn patterns more in FP1. The arenas being smaller in that game might help it too, there's more safe spaces here.In particular, I preferred the final boss of 1 compared to this.

_childDocuments_.review: Liked:- Incredible gameplay, reminiscent of Sonic Advance games. There's also quite a few super-levels that feel a bit like a traversing through a Zelda dungeon that gave a nice amount of variety to the stages. Ancestral Forge was a pleasant change of pace from the high-speed stages from prior. Despite their size, these levels were designed very well, and I never felt lost. Certain levels are very memorable due to their length, like Globe Opera, Ancestral Forge, Lightning Tower, and Clockwork Arboretum. There's like one new gimmick per stage and you'll never know what'll be in the next one, which is exciting.- Guarding feels satisfying and you'll definitely be using it against the souped up bosses. A lot of attacks will track you and test your ability to guard, which I feel adds some extra complexity to the boss fights.- Plenty of replay value. It took 8 hours for me to beat the game on one character, and there's four characters, each of which have their own special cutscenes that get teased on other characters to encourage you to play them: I was playing Lilac and Carol's disappearance and what Milla promised to Serpentine were practically begging me to play their characters to find out what happened.- Story is great and the villain is multidimensional unlike from the previous game. You can really see their point of view and understand why they do what they do.- Characters, interactions, and dialogue is interesting (and hilarious). I think there's a perfect mix of old-school corniness, seriousness, and humor. I remember when FP2 was originally going to have VN-style cutscenes, but they decided to go for the more standard in-game cutscenes, which I feel was a great decision. This probably was one of the reasons why the game took so long to release.- Overworld and hub areas add a lot of lore and coziness to the game. Just walking around the different maps and interacting with things adds a lot of worldbuilding that the action-packed stages can't do.- Music is excellent and I bought it instantly after finishing the game.Disliked:- Choosing one of three stories to play for each act doesn't feel like a very exciting player choice. I recall they got rid of it at some point in development, and then brought it back. I feel the story could've felt more connected if they just forced a certain order on us. Players will naturally do the easier stories before the more difficult ones, so it feels a bit like an illusion of choice that isn't necessary.- It would be nice if long levels allowed saving at certain checkpoints, or if they were broken up into sections (but still preserving the togetherness). Something came up while I was playing Ancestral Forge and all I could do was leave my computer on and the game paused.- There should've been a hint at the existence of a true ending and how to get it, maybe a post-credit message for the player. I only found this out by looking it up outside of the game. Instead of Time Capsules I feel a better requirement would've been to complete the game with every character.Things I wish were in the game that the developers probably also wanted in the game but had to drop to avoid even more scope creep:- Another 3-storyline act between acts 2 and 3: It feels sudden that the villain's evil plan is happening and we're immediately going into space to stop her. Catching Dail, maybe gathering materials for the trip, and something else would've added a nice rest stop before the intense final act of the game. I was a bit disappointed when Dail's capture happened off screen and when Serpentine instantly built his ship to get us to Bakunawa.- More content for the secret ending: I feel there could've been at least 3 additional stages dedicated to building up the final, final boss, kind of like how Sonic games have a final story.- Character-specific stages, which would add even more replay value beyond just different dialogue and slightly different boss fights.- A post-game act given how the ending is so open-ended and there's plenty of unanswered questions. I wouldn't be surprised if this ended up as DLC.Would I recommend it to others?- Yes, you'll probably like this game. You can definitely tell why it took so long for this game to release when you're playing it.Hopefully, Freedom Planet 3 doesn't take as long to release once the developers start working on it. Maybe they can pull a Wizard of Legend 2 and have another studio helping them with it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a great sequel, improving so much from the original. It's an amazing game and might be in my top 5 favorite indie games. The smash bros x Sonic and other 16-bit inspired gameplay feels so much better with all of the tweaks and extra moves. The stage design has also improved, or at least changed with it now focusing more on speed instead of platforming like the first game did. There's more of an even mix between large stages with multiple routes and more linear or confined ones. I can definitely see myself coming back now and then to play a stage just to have some fun.The game offers a lot of content. There are like 30 stages and 4 characters to beat them with. The added hubs, npcs and world map also makes it feel so much more like an adventure and spending time interacting with the hubworlds' npcs is quite charming. Some may not care about the story or extra content however and just want to play through the stages. There is a classic mode where it's just the stages but you have to beat the game once while in adventure mode. I don't see the problem with that honestly as you should at least experience and understand the story. Unlike the first game, you don't have to worry about being stopped from playing the game because you're having trouble with a difficult boss. I myself never needed them outside the final boss, but you can buy gear and items via shops to make the bosses easier. With other extra help settings you can toggle, you can really tailor this game to your skill level if you so desire to.The amount of replayability is great. You are encouraged to explore levels to optimize your speedruns. You get a goal to beat the "par time" of a stage and also get achievements for getting less than half the par time. There is also a ranking system but it isn't tied to your speed. It is based on the combat of the game, and to get a perfect rank, you have to beat the level, defeat boss and also not get hit. It can be pretty brutal for some bossfights, but you can still get shields to avoid the instadeath, so it makes you have to optimize a route through stages in order to get as many shields as you can. The story of this game is honestly weaker than the original, I won't deny it. The main problem is that the game no longer has separate campaigns for each character unlike the first. Combined with a lot of extra villains, it makes it harder for them to shine. The main antagonist themself really suffers from this, as unlike Lord Brevon from the first game, they aren't nearly as intimidating or involved with the conflicts. They're supposed to be overpowered, but outside of the lore/backstory, there's only a single time in the story where that's shown besides from the final boss. I really wish they had divided the villains across multiple of the character's campaigns, along with making some stages more tailored to certain characters and their abilities. The dialogue itself suffers from them not doing this in some cases. Characters have unique dialogue or conversations you don't see in other campaigns, but then there are times where other characters who speak to your player character don't have unique dialogue to say to them. This creates some weird flowing conversations and is also disappointing if you wanted to see what is different ( Especially to me, someone who really likes a lot of these characters ).The music of this game will go down as being one of my favorite osts. The only complaint I have is that due to the amount of stages, some of them are less unique to others. This in turn makes some music themes less memorable or distinct. The ones that do stand out however I really do love. I also started to like some of the themes that didn't stand out to me at first the more I played the game across multiple campaigns. It is really down to your preferences whether some will stick out to you. If it weren't for the non-distinct campaigns and for the weaker story and characters, I would say this game is a perfect 10/10 platformer. Right now though, I'd say it's a very very solid 8-8.5. Even if you're not such a sonic fan, you should really try this game out. It's easier to get into than the first I'd say and is overall quite the polished game.

_childDocuments_.review: Freedom Planet 2 is a huge improvement over the first game.you have a few characters to choose from which all have different ability that reflect the different kind of archetypes you would expect from a sonic game , the soundtrack is fine even if It's not highly memorable and the story is good enough while being delivered by some decent voice acting.the controls are tight and the game mix platforming and fighting pretty well , the level design is well done and offer a good ammount of variety and the game is very fast paced. The boss fights are also much more enganging then in the first game too.visually this game look impressive , very colorful art style and detailed animations bring a lot's of life in the universe of Freedom planet 2.if you like platformers , especially 2D Sonic games , this is a must play game.

_childDocuments_.review: Having really enjoyed the first Freedom Planet and played at least enough to complete every character's path, I feel confident in saying this game is better by leaps and bounds. That's not something typically said about sequels, but it's true here. The main thing that really makes it, is that the developers took all the character abilities and dialed them up to 11, making all of them really and truly enjoyable to play. To a point that I don't really have a favorite or one I consider "the most fun." It's almost a miraculous thing, most single-player games don't do well with multiple characters and abilities that are too different, but Galaxy Trail pulled it off. The first game, while fun, was mainly made for Lilac-- unless you're one of those crazy speed runners. Seriously, check out Milla speed runs in FP1, you'll be blown away. Maybe even a little scared. o-o; I was.Speaking of Milla, she absolutely takes the cake for cute mascot characters, her idle sequences will make you go "awww!" I guarantee it. Sooo effing cute! ^-^ But overall the character designs I say, were vastly improved over originals. So much more detail, better movements, and I'm in the camp that strongly dislikes the over-sized head/hands/feet. It's a real turn-off, so I'm glad the sequel did away with it. Between this and the prior point, I just about can't play the original game anymore. Not to say it's a bad game, certainly not. And if you're new to the series I think you should buy it and at least play Lilac's route. But for me, it lives as a cherished memory and that's about the extent of it.One thing I would have liked to see carry over from the first game: Dedicated character levels. There were a handful of these mini-arcs across the game, each was 3 levels you could do in any order. Out of 32 levels, I think it would have been really cool, to have one mini-arc specially tailored to each playable character. Truly differentiate everybody's play-through, as well as flesh out more of their individual stories-- just a little. Cuz that is one thing too, the story was still largely centered on Lilac. There was some personal stuff with the others, ranging from "quite interesting" to "downright spicy," but none so poignant as "last of the water dragons business." I'm not set to complain about that in earnest, because in a game like this, the mechanics and "fun factor" are so much more important than the story. But there is very clearly an intentional emphasis on SOMETHING narrative-driven, which is fine-- great even. The cherry on top of a fantastic and fun game sundae. Not worth mention if the goal was "focus on Lilac" anyway. Usually nobody cares about sidekicks anyway, I get it.Lilac's final rant though. Gave me chills. I'll say this much: It's a bit too meta for real life social discourse right now, and I don't appreciate that. But it was handled well so, have a pass. And be more mindful in the future. I play games to ESCAPE reality, not be dragged through more of it, kthx.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been over 6 years since I played the original Freedom Planet, and since then, I've been waiting for what seemed like forever for Freedom Planet 2. Now, here we are. I've beaten the game for the first time, and I have to say, the wait was worth it--and then some.Freedom Planet 2 is something that I like in a sequel: one that is bigger and better than what came before it. The game took everything from the first game--from gameplay, to story, to bosses, to outright spectacle--and gave them a massive upgrade that is welcome to see.The world of Avalice is expanded upon with a brand new country. A fourth playable character joins the three from the first game. The story is bigger as it is darker. Nearly everyone from the first game returns, alongside some new faces. New revelations shake up what we know about our favorite characters, and set up what's to come in the franchise's future. There is a LOT that I enjoy about this game.As for who I began the game with, I chose Carol as my first character. She was my favorite character in the first game, due to her tomboyish charm, hilarious personality, adorable appearance, cool ride, and the fact that she's a cat (I am admittedly a cat person myself). And yep--Freedom Planet 2 made me love her even more. Her comedic charm is put on full display during her story, and the ending of Avian Museum reminded me why I love her in the first place.That being said, the fact that I played as Carol first instead of Lilac may not have been the intended path, in hindsight. Some story elements were clearly meant to be shown if you were playing as Lilac as your first character; because of that, some twists either don't have that wham to it or just come out of left-field unless you were playing as Lilac. Of course, this could be chalked up to my love for Carol; if I played as Lilac first, then these hidden plot points could have that same gravitas they were meant to have.But even with that in mind, it was still worth it playing as Carol and enjoying her hilarious antics. And as of this writing, I am indeed playing as Lilac, meaning that I'll see the plot twists the way they were meant to be shown soon enough.Regardless, Freedom Planet 2 is a game that makes the eight years of waiting worth it. And I want to tell GalaxyTrail, and in particular Sabrina DiDuro, something. You stated your intentions to make Freedom Planet a franchise with the release of this game. And I think--I hope--I bet you've succeeded. As long as people want to see the further adventures of Lilac and her friends, the Freedom Planet series should never end.I encourage you to create countless more games in this wonderful series, each one even bigger than the last in all facets. And it make take years for the next game to come out (I hope not), but remember: we've waited 8 years for Freedom Planet 2 (6 for me), so we're used to it.Which is to say, here's to Freedom Planet 3. Here's to more adventures in Avalice and beyond. Here's to the future of this incredible series: Freedom Planet!Weh.

_childDocuments_.review: In some ways, this game is better than the first; in others, it's honestly not as good.A lot of what I enjoyed about the first game is brought back here. The story takes place 3 years later and focuses on a new threat named Merga, the last of the Water Dragons who wants to destroy Avalice and wipe out the Earth Dragons. It's a much deeper story, one that focuses on political intrigue and social prejudices throughout the 3 Kingdoms of Avalice and its many species. There's also more backstory given to the characters, such as Lilac being the other remaining Water Dragon, and her origins with the Red Scarves. Carol has a sister, Corazon, who's working with Merga, and her main conflict is convincing Cory to defeat Merga instead. Milla's backstory is further elaborated, revealing who and where her parents are, but I won't give it away here. Neera Li joins Team Lilac, and is shown to have a hard time trusting people as she's constantly being betrayed; she has a black-and-white view of the world, calling everyone either an ally or an enemy; her loyalty to Shang Tu is sometimes taken to the extreme; but over the course of the game, Lilac and Milla help her to open up and have faith in their group. And, of course, the writing once again balances out with plenty of charming character interactions, which is the main source of comedy again.However, this game's plot falls into the same trap as the first game: some of the cutscenes still go on WAY too long and slow the pacing down; the only way they're sped up here is that dialogue plays out automatically, moving from one line to the next, unlike the first game where you had to keep pushing one button after every textbox. There are also instances where the game diverges from the main plot, and has the player go through 3 episodes in any order they want; the episodes have their own subplots that do connect to the main plot, but still make it go on longer than necessary.Otherwise, it's a great continuation of the plot that fleshes out Avalice and sets the stakes for the next game.I should also bring attention to the presentation. The pixel art is more detailed and expressive than the first game, leading to a wider range of emotions and more fluent movements from each character. The environments have a bigger color scheme, which makes many of the stages look gorgeous! And they take it a step further by making some objects 3D polygonal models that are well integrated into the 2D setting.The audio is a slight downgrade, but only slightly. The music has a few REALLY good tracks, but it's not as memorable or energized as the first game. The voice actors are just slightly less convincing than they were in the first game, and the sound mixing has the same issue, where the music can sometimes be louder than the dialogue; but they still give good performances that sell the characters pretty well.As for the gameplay, there's a LOT of improvement.Lilac can use her double jump without draining her blue meter and go straight into a dragon boost without waiting for the meter to fill back up. THANK YOU. She's easily the fastest character in the game, at the cost of having weaker attacks than the rest of the characters, something I found more noticeable during boss fights.Carol still has her motorbike which can ride up walls, but she also has the Jump Disc, a projectile to throw at enemies and even magnetize to them for a few seconds, dealing more damage; the Disc also lets her teleport, making it easier to jump across large gaps or travel up to high ledges.Milla's shield can now block almost anything; in fact, it can bounce most projectiles back at enemies, causing them to take damage, which is useful defense AND offense. She can also summon her big green gelatin blocks a lot faster, which she can either fire as a laser, like before, or she can shoot out tiny green bullets until the cube is depleted. And of course, she still has her floating ability, which is still fun to use.Neera is the powerhouse character, who can freeze enemies for a short time, and use her "Focus" ability to make her attacks faster and stronger. If you feel she moves too slow, you can speed her up by mashing the attack button, which forms an ice trail underneath her to slide across the ground like she's ice skating; this can make her sometimes move faster than Lilac!But beyond individual differences, each character has basic moves and abilities that they all share.They can all perform basic melee attacks, which vary in damage, status effects, and targeting based on which direction you tilt the control stick. As for defenses, the items in this game act similar to the elemental shields from Sonic 3 & Knuckles; letting you breath underwater, protecting you from fire or electricity, magnetizing collectibles towards you, or just providing basic protection like the shields from Sonic 1 and 2. And each character has a guard maneuver, which blocks enemy attacks and prevents you from taking too much damage, which is essential for the boss fights. Speaking of which, the bosses all have visible health bars, which also determines when the player reaches the next phase of the fight.And, I should mention that, as a game inspired by 2D Sonic, the high-speed platforming is expanded. If Freedom Planet was a combination of Sonic Advance 1 and 2, Freedom Planet 2 is closer to Sonic Advance 2; once again, acceleration goes from zero to sixty, and they've introduced boost rings and grind rails, both of which keep your character ZOOMING across terrain. It's still the best thing about the gameplay!But then there are the downsides of the gameplay; for one thing, the main campaign is TWICE as long as the first and ends up overstaying its welcome again. In fact, some stages here go on for 20 to 30 minutes at a time! Never mind Sonic, that's way too long for ANY 2D platformer. I've already mentioned the episodic structure that makes the campaign go on longer, but there's also exploration in between stages. The world maps are one thing, and they mark your next destination with red exclamation points; but then they have you going through HUBWORLDS in a 2D game! You have to go talk to certain characters in this or that building to watch the next cutscene, you have side missions to complete by talking to townsfolk, and there's NPC's in each area, some of whom offer their own perspectives on the events of the main plot. It's not terrible, but it still comes off as padding.Finally, on top of all this, Freedom Planet 2 has a true ending that you unlock by finding 13 time capsules! You do this by finding one in a HUBWORLD (the top of the tall building in the beach area), and then the other 12 are rewarded to you for completing Battlesphere Challenges. To give this game SOME credit, they made it super easy to find and collect these time capsules, just like collecting Chaos Emeralds in a Sonic game. It's better than other games where you go FAR out of your way to complete cryptic nonsense you'd only know about by using a guide. Here, it's just a small diversion that adds a little more time to your playthrough and involves the same content as regular stages. In that regard, the game is fair, but it still adds more extra steps to a campaign that's already bloated with content. I only went after the true ending with Lilac, because I just wanted to finish the game with the other characters and move on. I will say that the true ending has one more stage, and a cool final boss that gets me excited for Team Lilac's next adventure!Freedom Planet 2 makes improvements to the first game, and it's still a fun 2D platformer that took me for a WILD ride. Whether you're a Sonic fan, or you've played the first Freedom Planet, or both in my case, you owe it to yourself to play this game. But make sure you have enough free time and enough patience, because it's also a much heftier time sink, and you may be worn out by the end.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best 2D platformers around, honestly.At its core, it's a lot like Sonic, but with tighter movement and quick, satisfying combat, both melee and ranged.Stages are a great blend of Sonic-like rollercoaster sections with fast paced platforming and combat, and take place across a huge variety of environments, all fleshed out with fantastic pixel art and catchy music. To top it off, there's a massive amount of bosses, many of which are considerably challenging, and are quite satisfying to beat.As a sequel to FP1, it improves almost everything. It adds a world map, with towns and shops to buy items that can either ease the difficulty or make it much harder, if you want to chase those perfect scores. There's even arena challenges on top of all the regular levels, and a museum, for viewing the fantastic boss models you've faced along the way. It really built up the world as a whole and it feels like they went the extra mile.It's pretty great. Definitely pick this one up if you want some retro style platforming fun.

The first game felt a bit bland to me, but the setting feels much more engaging this time around. The antagonists in particular. - I feel I need to give a special shoutout to the absurd number of unique NPCs running around. A lot of the designs are great and fill out the world a lot. _childDocuments_.review: What is Freedom Planet 2?Freedom Planet 2 is the sequel to Freedom Planet 1, and tried to take steps to differentiate itself from being game in the similar style to Sonic the Hedgehog, which it'll naturally be compared to. As a 2D, pixel art, side scrolling platformer. Freedom Planet 2 was released on September 13th, 2022 across Windows, Linux, Switch, Playstation, and Xbox. With the Dev and Publisher being GalaxyTrail. It's quite the substantial development since Freedom Planet 1, which was largely a single person accomplishment growing into a fairly size-able indie team. Especially since the first game was a Kickstarter Project and the sequel was entirely funded by that success. -=-=- Art -=-=-The Art, and Character Design has taken a significant change of pace due to the inclusion of Tyson Tan, who did fan art of the various characters after the first game and was brought on to design the characters for the sequel. As a result, the design of the game has taken a notable change from the previous game's design limitations.Lilac has had a huge overhaul in terms of her design, while the rest of the cast has remained largely the same. With some small changes here and there to accentuate their various quirks. -=-=-Gameplay-=-=-Gameplay and Story is broken into a four character narrative with points where the story breaks off and the characters perform individual tasks related to their individual goals while beginning and ending at the same point. Each Character does play differently enough from each other, but I felt like Lilac, whose the series protagonist (and the frontliner, in Purple) at times feels like this game was designed around the other characters rather than her. Lilac (Purple Dragon) is defined as a "Speed" character, Carol (Green Cat) a "Brawler", Milla (A Dog that I keep thinking is a Rabbit) as an "Explorer" and Neera (Panda) with "Power."Each Character has their own quirks, Lilac is quite mobile, Carol is designed more around the combat changes since the first game, Milla is geared towards exploring environments, and Neera is a hybrid of the three with her own unique quirks. Freedom Planet 2 has a much stronger emphasis on combat this time round, and I don't know how I feel about it. Each boss encounter involves breaking through a bosses defenses before hitting the boss again to remove a hit point. I NEVER figured out how to use the Guard  or Parry mechanic. There is nothing that explains how that works beyond a bit of tutorial text (without demonstration.) This makes boss fights potentially drag on quite a bit. As you get used to the nature of how the fight goes, and then you have to make sure to capitalize on opportunities as they come.I didn't mind it, but I can see where people can get frustrated by it. So be aware. Beyond that, there was at least three bosses of note that felt like unnecessary difficulty spikes. As a change from the first game, there's a continue mechanic that involves spending the crystal currency you pick up during a given level to revive yourself either on the spot (with significantly less health) or at a check point for full health. I'd rather respawn at the point where I died then replay through a cutscene (even if you can skip it) to restart a fight. This felt like a feature that wasn't really thought out. Most levels consist of moving right, with the occasional left segment while trying to get to checkpoints. The levels are large and varied with some unique element to break them up. I found some of the ideas behind these levels to be rather enjoyable and they broke up what I expected from a 2D sidescroller. The levels can stretch into being rather long. These are not short 5 minute romps. Some can get upwards to 10-12 minutes from my experience. While they are rather large, I didn't have too many instances where I didn't know where to go or what to do. There is equipment this time round and it took a bit for me to get used to it. There are various potions that you can buy from Milla during the game that allot a small bonus to your game-play, such as increasing run speed, jump height, damage, defense, etc. They don't really explain how this mechanic works, so I had to figure out that you need to go to the bottle icon, then move over to the particular potion I wanted to add, then press "up" to add it to the bottle. This feels like an oversight.There are also equipment you can find in chests, but these are rather well hidden. So I can't really comment on them as I found one that made the aforementioned Defense/Parry Mechanic worthless and nothing else. I beat the game as Lilac and started two alternative runs as Milla and Neera. Both of whom start out with the same starting mission and have the same cutscenes, but from different perspectives: which is a nice touch. There are moments where Carol and Milla leave the team, so I'm interested to see if those come with wholly unique levels. -=-=-Story-=-=-There are two modes available, the intended "Adventure" mode which includes moving around an isometric map and checking in on non-combat and zones.There is also a Classic Mode which skips the plot and goes from area to area with the non-combat areas linked together into one large (growing) shop to make various purchases. You do not need to have played the First Game to enjoy the sequel. As I didn't. I had watched a play-through of the First Game, but hadn't had the opportunity to pick it up. You will miss out on some context, some jokes, and references to the first game, but I don't feel it's totally necessary. Following from the Steam Page: The story consists of Merga, a Water Dragon freeing herself from a prison and her ambitions for the world at large. With the four aforementioned heroines getting wrapped up in trying to stop her from her goals. Freedom Planet 2 expands on the world around the three Kingdoms from the first game and continues from where it left off.I can't really talk about the story without spoiling it, and I enjoyed my time with it. I didn't feel my time was wasted. -=-=-Final Thoughts-=-=-I completed the game, as Lilac, at about 8 hours and started two separate runs as Milla and Neera. While there was initial interest in continuing to see how the other characters go through the plot, I don't know if I'll actually play through the game (at least right now anyway) with the others. If you're looking for a 2D Sidescroller that is evocative of (2D) Sonic, while trying to become it's own thing: then I'd recommend Freedom Planet 2. There's some growing pains, but the sequel builds on the original and is one of those cases where the second game IS better than the original.

_childDocuments_.review: They are speed.New Entry: Fast Opportunity.When the first game came out, we all have this proportionate expectation of the product coming out good or bad. While it isn't too good, it also wasn't that bad. This game is a huge step up from what they've put into, with simple controls (mostly) and high momentum potential. There can still be a few bugs, but it doesn't stop players who play this game casually, competitively or for completion.Each character has their own unique dialogue in certain scenarios, including their own combat style. Much like the first, each scene is replicated in true action; by any means it isn't a still picture. Their personalities and purposes are deeply noticeable, but they hit hard (in a good way) in the heart and mind. The flow of the writing and levels, no matter which order it is chosen, makes sense and doesn't force you to go from a low difficulty to a higher one. The landscape is polished to visually appeal each level, map and hub. I certainly got stuck on the eye candy no doubt about it. Then again, those four aren't going to stop fighting chaos.I would highly recommend this game to people who crave adrenaline, action and quirky characters.End Entry.

_childDocuments_.review: If you played the first, you'll almost certainly love this. If you haven't, I still think you'll love this.The original was a brilliant throwback to Sonic and Gunstar Heroes, and this neatly distills the formula into an even better experience. The characters are all charming and play very unique and distinct from each other, so playing the game from one to another feels like an entirely different experience. The storyline is simple but entertaining, and if you don't care about that, there's a Classic Mode that just gives you the gameplay. It even has a few branching paths and a "secret" ending you can get under certain conditions. And for FP1 fans, you'll be happy to know the story pacing is much better here: you'll never be stuck in cutscenes for  long before it's back to gameplay.On a technical level, the levels are technically brilliant. (Eh? Ehhhh? Oh never mind...) They're huge with numerous pathways, and taking the time to explore can yield some nice bonuses, though nothing is stopping you from trying to speed through them. They're also a visual treat with excellent pixel art and gorgeous backgrounds. And just about every single one has some unique gimmick or mechanic that shows up just for that level and then may never come back again... no surprise to fans of FP1, which similarly featured unique one-and-done level mechanics: a testament to the love and dedication that went into the game at a fundamental level. And of course, each level is capped off with a highly unique boss battle.It also helps that the controls are responsive and very easy to get the hang of, so if you're getting in trouble, it's not because the game is cheap, it's because you screwed up.A big change to the game is the new Items and Potions that let you customize and modify your experience. Some of them can make the game easier, while others are designed to make it much harder. More health, more lives, more speed? Not a problem. You'd rather play the game as a one-hit KO? Also not a problem!In terms of criticism, I don't have much, but here goes:-The music is still great, but I don't think it has quite as many earworms as FP1. None of it is ever annoying or uninspired, but I don't find myself humming it quite like I did the first game. And that's the meanest thing I can say about an OST that is still stellar.-The game is also significantly harder than FP1, which might be a plus for some folks. Admittedly, that's partly because the game really expects you to get good and use the new Guard mechanic and the Items and Potions, but, on the other hand, those aspects aren't taught as well as they could be either, even in the optional tutorial.Those minor gripes aside, this game is well worth your time and money. If you're a fan of retro throwbacks or just excellent gameplay in general, I highly recommend this one. Hopefully we get a Freedom Planet 3 within the next decade!
_childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: The first Freedom Planet was a game that held a very special place in my heart, not only for being a solid Sonic-esqe action platformer, but also for being incredibly inspiring to me as it initially started life as a Sonic fan project and it starred characters that I remember from browsing DeviantArt in the mid 2000s, since I have my own passion project I have had in the works that started out as a fan project.And now after waiting almost 7 years, listening to the Alpha OST religiously, seeing awesome fan art and watching the community grow, Freedom Planet 2 is finally here. And it's bigger and better than before!The gameplay is greatly expanded upon with the characters feeling a lot more versatile thanks to some new moves such as Lilac's Boost Breaker, Carol's Jump Disc and Milla's Cube Blaster. And the new playable character, Neera can be very satisfying once you get the hang of her powerhouse-like playstyle. The addition of a dodge button, the various hub worlds, the ability to revive yourself at the cost of a stock Smash-Bros style and ways to customise your play experience with the Potions, Brave Stones and various other difficulty options are very welcome.And the stages are still as fun, creative and action packed as ever, with big shout outs to Airship Sigwada, Globe Opera and Tidal Gate to name a few.One of my only real gripes with the first game as fun the story was, there were things that the game either forget to tell about or weren't properly explained such as the character's backstories. Not only does this game "mostly" address them, but greatly expands on the lore and world-building with it's more in-depth story and characters. There are a lot of fun and heartfelt moments along with some interesting themes,  twists and stuff left open for a potential sequel.The visuals, character designs and sprite work for this game are genuinely gorgeous and are some of best I have seen for a game of this type. And the music absolutely slaps!It has been quite the journey to see the evolution of this series from it's humble beginnings to now. After waiting a long time for this game, it didn't disappoint! I had a blast with this treasure of a game that deserves to be up there with the other indie greats such as Shovel Knight & Shantae!

_childDocuments_.review: I don't have a beefy PC, so 2D indie games are my main guilty pleasure, especially 2D side scrolling platformers. More levels (more than double the size of the first game), more soundtracks, a longer storyline, more characters, more pixels! The stages also all have something setting themselves apart from each other, each stage has its own theme / gimmick. The plus side is, the devs are quick to try and fix/patch most bugs.If a 3rd game is planned, count me in as one of those excited for it. Freedom Planet was originally inspired by Sonic the Hedgehog games, but I think I had more fun with just FP1 + FP2, compared to playing Sonic(s) 1,2 CD, 3 and Mania combined.

_childDocuments_.review: After 7 years of development, GalaxyTrail released the sequel to Freedom Planet, a Sonic fangame turned full-fledged indie with cues from Sonic, Treasure, Mega Man, and more. The first game was already stellar, but with the hype that built up over the game's development cycle, the new eager fans (myself included) who got caught up in the wave from the console ports of the first game, and a highly passionate team with high ambitions, how did this sequel fare? I'll cut to the chase: it did Picking up three years after the end of the previous game, although Brevon's been long gone since his invasion of Avalice, a lasting peace has been difficult, what with a recent string of mysterious attacks. As such, Lilac, Carol, and Milla, our heroines, are summoned by the Royal Magister of Shang Tu to help investigate the matter and figure out what exactly is going on, with Lieutenant Neera Li accompanying them on their mission. What starts out as some seemingly disconnected incidents, however, lead back to a phantom from Avalice's past, one who has spent the past three years plotting her revenge...Summary aside, this game's story is absolutely stellar, helped by there being an actual writing team this time. The main cast's gotten older and wiser, the new characters, heroic and antagonistic alike, are incredibly written, making their arcs and character dynamics very compelling, and had me appreciate those I already did  even more than before. What also helps is the strong VA work by everybody on the cast, be it the returning faces such as Dawn M. Bennett (Lilac), Edwyn Tiong (The Magister), and Alejandro Saab (Zao), or the new additions to the cast, such as Christopher Sabat (Askal), Morgan Berry (Merga), and Lindsay Jones (Corazon). Even better, the voice acting quality is consistent by virtue of Christopher Sabat allowing the cast to record in his studio, Okratron 5000. I admit, my earlier summary of the story is only scratching the surface, but given how it's so impactful in its writing and handles really well heavy subjects in its back half,I do hope you forgive me for not elaborating much more on that matter. Trust me, it's well worth it.On the gameplay side, the returning playable cast feel amazing in motion, having picked up new tools that extend their already solid moveset (Lilac's Boost Breaker and Blink Dash), address their old moveset's key shortcomings (Carol's new melee options, Jump Disc, and bike reworks), or both (Milla's revamped Phantom Cube gameplay and her new melee attacks). Neera, an NPC and boss turned playable, also feels quite solid in motion, being lacking in a solid airgame but compensating with a strong combat-oriented movepool that can melt bosses when used right. This great feel, supplanted with the incredibly versatile new guard technique, works in tandem amazing well with the stage design, covering all kinds of fun challenges, from the pipe networks in Sherlin Park to the amusement park feel that is Zaoland. The strong stage design is complimented with some incredible bosses that are tough, but all manageable and satisfying to defeat, even if some of them, during endgame especially, ask players to have a strong understanding of all their tools to overcome them.The sound design is as strong as ever, with the stage themes covering all kinds of great moods that match their stages, the map themes suiting the overall feel of their areas, and the new hub areas having great songs to accompany their more downtime-oriented design. Leila Wilson (otherwise known as Woofle) and Falk Au Yeong have created some incredible compositions that help make the game incredibly memorable.Visually...it's sprite art. Need I say any more? The art shift away from the chibi style to a more proportioned design, beyond acting as a great look at how the cast's matured, also manages to make them look just as adorable as they were before, or even moreso  with all the great animation that game has to compliment its sprites. On top of that, the various locations, stages, maps, and hubs alike, are incredibly beautiful and make them an even bigger joy to run through. Just be mindful of some latergame stages, the shaders they use for their 3D elements isn't exactly the nicest on older systems, although it's nothing unplayable.Overall, this game is an indie masterpiece that has had so much love put into it, I could go on and on about what I enjoyed,  I wholeheartedly recommend this game to fans of the first game, Treasure fans, Sonic fans, or just anyone in general looking for a really good indie platformer.Verdict: Worth your time!Final remarks: Seriously, please play this game, I adore it so much~

_childDocuments_.review: Just like the first game, this is a criminally overlooked modern classic that blows the series that inspired it out of the water. Freedom Planet might have started out as a love letter to Sonic, but it improves on and surpasses it in almost every way. The tight gameplay, the flow of the levels, the incredible bosses, the lovely art, and the 10/10 soundtrack easily make this one of my games of the year. If there's any part of you that likes 2D action games, you owe it to yourself to play this.By and large Freedom Planet 2 is very reminiscent of the first game, though you don't have to have played FP1 to enjoy it. It's a bigger, slicker, tighter, and better paced experience than the original, hitting all of the same highs while offering more than twice as much game this time around. The gameplay has seen numerous small improvements like the addition of one or two extra moves for each character, along with a parry button that really helps take some of the boss fights to the next level. It's amazing to maintain your speed and momentum mid-fight by parrying your way through an attack rather than having to slow down and carefully dodge.The storytelling, as well, is probably the most notably improved area compared to the prequel. The FP games are bubbly and enthusiastic, but they do read like Sonic fanfiction at times. This is part of their charm for me, but regardless of whether the cheesy blend of silly humour and high drama works for you, it's delivered in a far more digestible manner this time around. FP1 suffered from trying to cram a world full of political factions, side characters, and interplanetary war into a linear action game, with cutscenes sometimes just as long as the levels they followed. FP2 carries all of this over, but with more stages and hub areas full of optional dialogue to dilute the cutscenes, resulting in much better pacing overall. The script also feels tighter, with the humour hitting the mark more often and the world building feeling natural rather than bloated.The addition of a fourth playable character and a bunch of optional challenges also helps to flesh out the playtime. If you want hours and hours of Freedom Planet, this game has it for you. This does lead into my one criticism of the game, though; while I'd say the overall quality of the experience is easily on par with FP1, it feels a bit more stretched. I found the gimmicky stages to be more conspicuous in FP2, and some of them felt like misfires. While it does modulate the pacing to intersperse fast actiony levels with slower puzzley and exploration-based ones, the action stages are universally better suited to the game's mechanics. I found the dedicated boss stages a lot more enjoyable than the ones that had me backtracking in multiple directions or hunting down keys to progress. I wouldn't have minded if the game had fewer, but more tightly designed levels.I could gush for a long time about how awesome some of the boss fights are, how many bangers the soundtrack has, or how the game pulls off a finale that's both similar and different enough from FP1 to stand toe-to-toe with it, but it's easier to just say that this game is incredible. Galaxy Trail have succeeded in putting out a fantastic sequel to Freedom Planet that I hope garners all the recognition it deserves some day. They've taken this subgenre and made it their own.

_childDocuments_.review: Freedom planet 2 is an incredible experience and is easily a must buy if you enjoyed the first game. Everything has been improved and expanded upon: from the absolutely gorgeous pixel art, to the infectiously catchy soundtrack and the overall much better pacing. The background lore for lilac, the squad and Avalice as a whole has also been expanded upon, presented very nicely through a well written narrative that actually features quite a sympathetic antagonist. On the gameplay side of things, each character handles well and can take advantage of weaving their way through the multiple pathways of each stage in their own unique fashion. Some characters are better suited fr specific purposes however: Lilac is great for speed and would generally be considered the easy mode, whereas Neera is a boss killer whom lacks mobility in comparison to the other heroins. Speaking of bosses, they're all a treat to fight, having well telegraphed attack patterns and make good use of the games' new dodge mechanic, but some less experienced players may have trouble with the insane speeds of later ones. To compensate for players of all skill levels, the settings menu has a plethora of accessibility options including free revives, auto guarding, reducing the cost of continues and increasing the sensitivity of the screen zoom out, among others. In addition to these options, if they weren't enough the game itself includes a shop system, accessed from vendors in hubs. As a side note these hubs all have their own atmosphere and incredibly charming NPCs that add to the feeling of this world being alive. Most of them have unique dialogue linking to different story events, some dialogue being character specific. Anyways, the shop system acts as a way for players to spend their currency rewarded by exploring stages on a multitude of items that either assist players, or hinder them in exchange for a higher rank and crystal bonus at the end of stages. If you want to be an absolute powerhouse then you can equip yourself with a full attack potion if you really want to, but if you want to go for those elusive rainbow S ranks, try using on hit KO and get through a stage without being damaged at all. Thankfully the ranking system has no in game effects outside of achievements and a higher bonus, so going after high ranks isn't necessary if it's not comfortable. Freedom planet 2 takes you on a tour of Avalice, with stunning visuals, amazing level design, a banging soundtrack, endearing characters, a smooth difficulty curve and bosses with so much spectacle. it's one of the most fun and well crafted experiences I've had in a video game and if you couldn't already tell, I love it to death. Wonderful 2D platformer, would highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: The short summary: 11/10Much like its predecessor, Freedom Planet 2 is a side-scrolling, platforming adventure along the same vein as classic Sonic the Hedgehog games.  But Freedom Planet 2 has improved upon the original in almost every way, having grown from its Sonic-inspired roots into something more distinctive and unique.  Freedom Planet 2 feels much more fleshed out with a lot more story, which is just what I was craving most from the original; I wanted to learn more about these characters and this universe, and Freedom Planet 2 scratched that itch; though having played through all four characters' campaigns with the "true ending," questions around the history of Avalice remain,  which I hope to see answered in future Freedom Planet games, DLC, or other media.  Even if you haven't played the original (which you absolutely should), Freedom Planet 2 is well worth a playthrough.  The full review:Much like the original Freedom Planet, this is a side-scrolling platformer featuring four playable heroines, each one with their own style and characteristics.  Your first play through will be in Adventure Mode, which in my opinion is the best way to experience the game, because one thing FP2 does way better than the original is story.Cutscenes and dialogue flow better than they did in the original, with quality voice acting and funny moments throughout.  Many of these scenes are the same regardless of which character you play, but some are exclusive to each character, so to get the full story you'll have to play through as all four characters, but in my opinion that is just part of the fun!Gameplay is pretty simialr to FP1, except now we have more fine-tuned controls and returning characters have had their move-sets reworked. The biggest feature is the introduction of Guarding, allowing you to completely evade damage if well timed.  Traversing levels and battling bosses feels much more fluid and is super satisfying. The art style has been greatly improved upon from the FP1 style, and the levels themselves sport unique themes and charm, complete with amazing background music, much like the levels of FP1 did.  While FP2 dropped the collectible Cards of FP1, there are still secrets to be found within the levels, primarily Vinyls to unlock music and a few Brave Stones.Speaking of which, Brave Stones and Potions are a new feature added to enhance the gameplay.  Throughout your adventure you will collect Gems and Orbs, both of which can be exchanged into Gold Gems. Gold Gems are rarely found within levels too.  You can mix and match Potions to give yourself different buffs, such as increasing attack damage or making your attacks heal you a little bit.  Brave Stones can also offer buffs, but many act as difficulty multipliers, and you are rewarded with extra Gems for completing levels with detrimental Brave Stones equipped. I love this system because it allows players to tailor the difficultly to their liking, and gives them options if they find themselves struggling at a particular area.Additionally, if you're the completionist type, there's a Gallery in Adventure Mode that you can donate resources to in order to complete exhibits.  They're neat to look at, but in my opinion the main treat here is that you get access to a special gallery upon completing all the exhibits.  This special gallery shows off some behind-the-scenes stuff from the development of FP2, including early concept art and scrapped assets, so if you're into that kind of stuff, completing the Gallery is a worthwhile endeavor!As a final point, I've noticed some comments about issues playing the game (crashes, softlocks, etc.) so if you experienced problems before, I'd recommend giving the game another try.  The Developers have already released several updates to fix bugs and even add a few new features; it's obvious to me that this game was a labor of love for them and that they want this to be the best experience it can be after all this time since FP1. :)All in all, I've thoroughly enjoyed my time with Freedom Planet 2.  At the time of my writing this, I've completed all four characters' stories in Adventure Mode and unlocked all but two secret achievements.  I love the characters, I love the gameplay, I love the game world, and I don't plan to stop playing until I've done everything this game has to offer!

_childDocuments_.review: Freedom planet 2 exceeds the first game in every aspect. From charterer control, adjustments, level design, art and everything else. (But maybe except the story) The four different playable characters you play as have their own unique set of powers that vastly different from one another. Depending on who you play as, it may change the way you play the stage and how you interact with foes and bosses along the way. It creates great replay value and experimentation in each play-trough you do. From Lilac ability to speed trough the stage, or Milla's exploration and ranged kit. (My personal favorite is the newcomer, Neera. With her double jump and power moves, you can defeat foes and move around quickly if you know the stage well.)The stages in this game are wonderful design from art, to level layout. Each level having their own set of gimmicks as well to keep the pacing consistently fresh every time. Whenever it's climbing up an tower needed power throughout or a gauntlet of challenge rooms of tricks. The levels in this game are awesome! This also applies to the hub worlds throughout the game. Each having their own neat details and lore of that part of the world. You can also buy items from these hub worlds to help you out in the main adventure if things get tough.The story of this game is the only thing I kinda don't like about it. Compared to the first game, it doesn't have the same impact, from story beats, to the characters , it's watered down. It still has it's moments in the middle and all, but most of the time it remains flat and never evolves the new heights. ( If that made sense) Though I do very like the additions of the new side characters and the expanded world building. They are fun, cool to the world, and bounce of the main ones very well. If you want to see more of the same characters you like in the first one, you will probably like the story just okay. Overall, if you are looking for a platformer with plenty of  speed and awesome level design, and or liked the first game, this one is for you in my opinion. It has beautiful art design, music that suits the mood of each moment, and plenty of replay value as well. _childDocuments_.review: FINAL REVIEW, 50 Hours In - Ive completed ALL FOUR STORY ARCS. GET THIS GAME!!FANTASTIC!!  Most games have a very, very difficult time being on par with their predecessor. NOT FP2! This game smashes almost all expectations! Let's go through it --STORY - 12/10  Holy Sh... Hoooollyyyy HellsBells! They HAMMERED this one out of the park! Lilac's story? Daaaammnnn. Absolutely stunningly done. And when you unlock her secret level? Thats where the bonus marks come in. You Will NOT Regret It!  ALL FOUR Stories, while much more related to each other than FP1, Do a fantastic job expanding on each character; Poor Neela has a hell of a hard go but at the end earns her place.  Each of the four Story arcs had me stunned.Graphics - 10/10  They pulled off stuff with the medium that no way in hell even a Saturn could do. The love and lavish they poured into this is very clear. Perfection!Audio - 8.5/10 For the most part, the music is glorious.  Sound effects are clear, VA is Dead On. Level tracks are GORGEOUS!  My only real complaint is the boss battle tracks - some are remixes, but most with maybe two exceptions - thankfully the final bosses - tend to fall rather flat, IMHO. The boss battle tracks could of hit harder; but thats subjective. The explosions also need a bass boost, but again, extremely minor.Gameplay - 8.5/10 NOW THAT IVE DONE ALL FOUR ARCS - Lilac's combat capabilities are only slightly improved over the original. At times, it doesnt feel improved at all. I even went and did a boss rush back to back vs FP1, and while her charge attack DOES charge faster, it still feels damn slow, especially for someone thats supposed to be fast. If you are a dedicated old school Rocket Knight Adventures fan, Lilac is still going to be frustrating to play, but a bit of a slight improvement from FP1.   Carol's attack, once you master it? MUCH better than it initially seems. A step up.  Milla? ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ she got buffed!  Neela? She IS the hardest to get the hang of, but once you do, she's a solid fighter; and im pretty sure they buffed her guarding. Im certain it wasnt working in the previous patch; now it works just as well as the rest of the crew.ALL IN ALL? ABSOLUTELY WORTH EVERY PENNY.  Quite frankly My complaints are more subjective, most certainly not game breaking.  Most people wont notice the issues with Lilac, and all the gals gameplay is master-able. Hopefully, after the team rests for a bit, they go for a Trilogy.  They did drop the hints that a trilogy is on the table. GO FOR IT GALAXY QUEST! This game is worth DOUBLE what they are charging for it! Im dead serious; I virtually never say something like this, but this time? They absolutely EARNED it. BRAVO! This game is a MASTERPIECE!  Not only is it a Masterpiece? IT absolutely SHATTERS all expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok I'm gonna start with one sentence:Freedom Planet 2 is the best game I've played this year and I could easily give it a 10/10Could end the review with that, but if you're thinking I'm joking or something or you're not convinced, well sit down, relax and let me explain why this game is so important to me:INTRODUCTION:Let's start with this: there is just no compareson with the first Freedom Planet, yes it's still a good game, but the sequel just overshadowed it completly in every feature. I need to remind you that the firts game was after all a solid Sonic fan game that gained his own identity and you can't deny that. This formula of taking inspirations from bigger franchises or creating spiritual sucsessors of our favourite games when the original creators are not willing to, as been used now more than ever to preserve good game design and artistic freedom and (when done well) can create true masterpieces and fix the hissues of the original proprietys.What FP2 did was cleaning up the dust from it's firts game and rebuild a totally new and original experience, detatching itself from the Sonic series wile still mantaining what made the game so good in the first place and did so much more.GAMEPLAY:The gameplay is fast, clean and fun! Every stage has it's own mechanics and all the 4 playable characters can provide new game experiences and the replay value is at his core!First thing they did was cleaning up the annoying parts of the firts game. The movement for Lilac for example feels much more fun, now the spin attack does not cost power so you can use it in combo with the charge attack and the collectibles are no longer like... 10 per level?! But just 1 or 2, because the devs understand that in a game where you need to go fast, the SLOW exploration can feel lame at some point. But don't get me wrong you still have a lot to collect in other fun ways.The first game was linear, a simple experience, this game have an overworld map, towns, NPCs, minigames, challenge modes and FINALLY a ranching sistem so you can have fun getting rank S for every stage in game. There are also items to equip, but I rarely use them cuz they take a way a bit of the final reward, but you can equip an hourglass to race against time and hearn extra cash for finishing the level before the timer runs out, super fun to play.STORY:Will be short to avoid spoilers, the first game got an average story that tryed to get cool at the end, but was nothing more than... the power of friendship against evil alien dude, that was good for a game like that, but the sequel got REAL!!You got world bulding, drama, relationships, betrayal, fun shenes, very sad shenes and jsut something that will make you feel so fulfilled at the end of it, plus a secret ending if you can get it (it's worth it).ART:Yeah the art in the first game was good, but a bit silly and I wasn't really convinced about any character that wasn't Lilac or Carol and yeah was still too similar to Sonic...This game owever changed the art completly and it's one of the amin reason why it feels so original. Every character EVEN THE NPC are fully animated and every stage filled with detail. Really nailed it this tme!MUSIC:The music is just great, not much to say about it, not an expert in music, but it fit the stages very well soooo yeah!DUBBING:Now the cherry on the top, the first game was already dubbed and that was impressive for an indie game like that, but with this? GOD! It is so well done! Every characters they played at was perfectly delivered expecially Lilac, Merga and Cordelia.I can say in some shenes I was at the edge of crying for that and you guys get all my respect for it.IN CONCLUSION:FP2 is how you make a good sequel, and I mean sequel! Not like we call it XXXXX 2 and then is a prequel or some kind of AU or whatever, I mean sequel sequel and all game devs big and small should take example. Can't wait for FP3, IF there's gonna be one (I hope so).wait... I should add some cons as well or people will think I'm just being a fanboy...
