_childDocuments_.review: As a Civilization veteran, I find many of the concepts in this game refreshing.  I'm enjoying it so much and am concerned by some of the feedback coming from the "20 hour" crowd.  So here is my War and Peace novel on the first 4X game to really suck me in since Civ6.Characters:Its just fun to have to think about your heirs and your spouses and what their attitudes are towards you.  The shock I felt my first game when my daughter assasinated me after several slights was genuine and enjoyable.  I've seen others complain about their characters constantly dying off but I find lifespans to be reasonable and flavorful.  The fact that the attributes of your family and court drive global values is also cool as it gives you a lot of focus and control on what you're doing as your characters level.  Succession planning can actually matter as having high value characters die can have significant impact.  Make sure your heirs are doing something productive, even if they're psychos!Movement/Orders:My workers aren't working because I didn't order them to!  Freaking slackers.  What an adjustment to have a cap on the amount of movement/action (orders) across all your units.  In Civ you could dominate by building a few productive cities and spam units.  Don't try that here.  Having a ♥♥♥♥ ton of warriors doesn't matter if you can only move half of them.  It feels restrictive at first but it really isn't.  It forces you to plan ahead and manage your priorities based on what is happening around you.  As your civilization grows, your legitimacy as a ruler rises and your capacity to multi-task grows as well.  Don't be a zerg.Combat:I've seen some complaints about combat and I think it could be better, but it isn't bad once you understand it.  The ability to move several units across the map quickly means isolated units can get ganged up on and if you don't have sufficient force to punish with a counter attack, you can fall behind very quickly.  This is compounded by the fact that when two melee units clash, the defending unit does relatively little damage compared to the offensive unit.  Because of this, in an offensive war, you can't just sally off attacking the first city you see because the counter-attack can crush you.  On defense, you must balance between barbarian attacks on the edges while still maintaining a sufficient central force that can deploy to a threat.  There is a definite "Battle Brothers" feel to it.  That said, I do wish promotions and generals mattered a bit more.  It definitely feels bad to have the unit you poured resources into get wiped by 3 or 4 scrub archers and a chariot.Winning:4x struggles in the late game.  This is no secret.  Knowing you're going to win but having to complete thousands of meaningless tasks over 2 to 3 hours of game play to get over the finish line can wear you down.  Every Civilization game I've ever played suffers from this.  My general approach is to focus on my win-con, use multi-queuing as much as possible, and try to avoid late game military combat.  So how does this game stack up?  Well, the late game is tedious.  There's a lot to do.  Your court size increases exponentially, worker spam is back, and the more cities you have, the more queues need to be managed.  Multi-queue and automating workers helps a lot once you're comfortably ahead.  But as others have said, waiting for your next turn on larger maps can get pretty tedious as well.  I honestly think that with some optimization and a better balanced set of win conditions, the late game could improve dramatically.  They definitely have some creative ideas in the win condition realm.  Here are my thoughts on where they stand currently:Domination Victory: If you try to do this, good luck.  Even if you manage it, you'll probably trigger another victory condition first.  If you don't, call me in 2 months when you finish.Double Points: This one is actually a bit frustrating on lower levels because it can trigger suddenly.  Basically you earn victory points throughout the game (think Settlers of Catan).  If you double the next highest civ total, the game ends... just when you were starting to have fun.  On higher levels, I doubt this win condition is all that feasible unless you have a God start or do some serious domination.Complete 10 ambitions:  These are random missions that show-up from time-to-time throughout the game.  The AI doesn't have access to this victory condition so its up to you.  There's an element of chance here because Ambitions vary wildly and they're not always compatible with what you're up to.  In addition, if you select one and don't complete it within a certain amount of time, you get a penalty.  I've won this way but its hard to plan it out.  Usually I just happen to get it finished before I reach a points victory that I probably would have gotten anyway.Victory Points: There is a victory point number assigned based on the Map you're on.  First person to get to that total wins.  If 200 years pass and no one reaches the total, highest points win (God help you if you have to go 200 turns).  Most efficient way to do this is typically power as many wonders as possible while pouring culture into your cities.  You get points for cities anyway and as their culture increases, the point values become exponential.  This favors highly expansionist play style.  I've had some fun games carving at AI borders and incorporating enough cities to get over the finish line and I definitely like this win condition as a variety of gameplay can contribute to the total.  In a weird sense, it can almost be THE victory condition as you can use numerous play styles to get to it.Final Thoughts:There are a lot of things going on in this game that are fun and enjoyable to explore.  Not everything is intuitive and it can take some work to figure things out.  But it is very rewarding and the experience is more personal because of the character element.  You also don't have those jarring moments that you have in Civ where you're just starting to enjoy having knights and now you're moving into the industrial era.  You can really relish the experience and flavor of a full game in one era.  I highly recommend it and am hopeful that new features, world events, balancing, and optimization continue coming from the developers.If you made it this far, thanks for reading!
_childDocuments_.name: Old World

_childDocuments_.review: I like Civilization V and VI, but Old World surpasses them both. The reasons for that are threefold:1. In Civ, I enjoy the first turns in the pre-modern times such as Stone Age, Classical Antiquity and Middle Ages the most. Fighting wars with Cleopatra or Tokugawa with tanks and robots simply feels weird. In comparison, Old World stays in the Ancient Times!2. I love the Crusader King inspired system of characters, families and dynasties. It is awesome to build your own dynasty, so you're not only managing your cities and units, but are also taking care of character and family relationships respectively. Also diplomacy and your leader's reputation both play a major role. Your leader eventually dies and your heir takes over, so this feels more realistic and natural.3. Events! Events shape your whole game and change how you play. There are a lot of interesting things happening and it feels like you actually play your dynasty's story. It's a lot of fun if you like role-playing even in strategy games.To me, Old World is the perfect 4X game and adds what I felt Civilization has always been missing.
_childDocuments_.name: Old World

_childDocuments_.review: I love the music in this game.  I love the "undo/ redo" option.  I like how many resources there are in the game.  I like the family system (though I keep wanting it to be more in-depth like Crusader Kings is).  I even like the Orders resource in this game.But the thing that really pulls me away from loving this game is the combat system.  It might be the worst combat in any 4X/ Civ-like game I have ever played.  It actually makes Victoria 3's combat seem reasonably passable.  All they needed to do was allow players to stack units into actual armies (similar to Civ 4 or Humankind or Age of Wonders, etc). Then have characters command ARMIES instead of just single units.  That way you are spending your orders moving entire stacks of units instead of having to micromanage hordes of little units all over the damned place.  It's just... tedious... and also it doesn't make sense because the scale of everything just seems so off.  Slingers throw rocks over the Acropolis and hit people on a hill on the other side.  The Acropolis is ~350m long.  That's quite an arm on those Slingers!  Who needs Trebuchets when Slinger bois can just throw rocks several hundred metres farther!

The 4X part is well developed, eg clever family system, city optimization is a minigame in itself, .... Lots of different tactics and ways to play. _childDocuments_.name: Old World

_childDocuments_.review: A very good mix between Civ and Crusader Kings 2/3.  The interesting mechanic that separates it is the order mechanic.  You do not get to move each unit every turn.  Unit improvement and leveling is reminiscent of the old Alpha Centauri game.  Characters are important, but not quite to the level of CK2/3.  However, you make better use of the talent in assigning them to manage cities or as generals of units which convey abilities and stats to them.  The civilizations are differentiated and certainly feel different at the beginning of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Old World

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent historical grand strategy game. The role playing aspects are really well envisioned and integrated. The devs are supporting the game with various updates, improvements, and additional content. The attention to detail in this game is amazing. The individual characters feel unique. In my first game, Queen Dido married someone with the "Romantic" character trait and with each of the events in the first few years and options for how to respond it felt like a romantic movie playing out in the game between the two (mostly based on the decisions I made for the ruler). There were three back-to-back decisions I had to make for the queen in how she responded. There were lots of options, intentional decisions, and also guesses, but also random events that prompt you to make decisions that sometimes you do not have much control over (which made the game more realistic, to an extent). It's  fun to see how each of the characters interact with each other and you have just enough influence on the ruler's decisions that you can steer things in a certain direction but sometimes things don't turn out the way you hoped (maybe another character starts trouble, for example, you weren't expecting or you lost track of a random minor noble who starting talking with another nation's courtier that then affects your standing in their court) and sometimes they do any number of other things that affect your ruler and nation or individual characters for better or worse. It's detailed, rich content, not always predictable, though characters' opinion of your leader is a good indicator of which characters to keep an eye on and maybe have a courtier send them a gift or intercede on your ruler's behalf to put in a good word. This game is very dynamic and throws in lots of different events that can completely shift your strategy. My second and third games were very different. For one thing, I had different starting characters (I played with a different nation each of my first three games) with a different inheritance law enacted (e.g., seniority primogeniture, or absolute cognatic primogeniture, for example). But even if I didn't, there are so many different ways the games would have been different (leader character traits, for example, random at the start of each game). In one of the games, there was an event that gave me several decisions, one of which was to change the inheritance law (which I decided to do) so this changed things in that game quickly. There are a lot of other examples, but that gets the idea across that no two games are the same.The ruler, their spouse(s), heir(s), the court, appointing ministers, influencing individual characters (the rulers, house leaders, governors, generals, diplomats, chancellor, courtiers, etc., your ruler's children growing up and all the decisions that go into that, who the nobles marry, random events that affect character's traits (there are a lot!), health, wisdom, courage, and on and on the details go. It's got a lot of depth, dynamics, and complexity. The diplomacy feels really well integrated into everything; again, each character is unique and the way they interact is great to interact with in the details. I'm looking forward to seeing what additional DLC there might be from the devs for this game. They do a great job of supporting this game with updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Old World

_childDocuments_.review: The most innovative take on the 4X Turn Based Strategy genre I have seen. It's familiar to Civilization but with family character elements from games like Crusader Kings, it's an event based, narrative driven game and while it has similarities to other titles it's an entirely unique game where every playthrough feels different.

_childDocuments_.review: 5/10 so-so.I took the plunge because some reviews raved about it being "better" than Civilisation and that the game was a mix of Civ with Crusader Kings.In reality, it's a fairly narrowly focused 4x game, think of Civilisation but with just the one 'era', and a handful of nations to play with. There are some unique mechanics; Cities can only be settled on pre-defined city sites for example, you also don't benefit from 'tiles' unless you build an economic action (i.e. a farm, mine) on them, and you also can't get luxury resources until you build the economic action PLUS a specialist unit on them.The mechanics make it different, a little flavour to the whole thing, but it's still at its heart a civilisation building game, with the same tricks as always - expand, exploit massively, and carry a bigger stick than your rivals.The other 'unique' spin on the game is a bit of Crusader Kings, you have to settle cities with 'families', who all bring different things to the table; A military family will make a city a military powerhouse, whilst landowners classes make ideal farming cities etc. You get to pick 3 from 4 families, and these families dictate your overall build of cities (ideally), so everytime you find nice farmland areas, out come the landowning classes, and anytime you find a nice seafaring spot, you might pick a family that offers strong naval bonuses.Thrown into this mix, are a fairly watered down family and character setting, with various events to go through ~ you marry people off, have children, educate them for when your leader dies, and so on. Keeping everyone happy is another cog in the machine, but it seldom feels unique and interesting in the grand scheme of things, for me anyway.Overall, it's a decent, average attempt at the genre. Worth the full price? Nope. Worth the sale price? Probably not, unless you get it under £20 personally, unless you're a massive Civ style fan, in which case you probably already own the damn thing.I think it's worth a try, but whether you'll stick to it, is up in the air, it just doesn't really feel that compelling to hang around in tbh.

It should be approx 90%!

_childDocuments_.review: I strongly disagree with the combat system.1. Enemy units move over your entire vision range in one turn. I've seen elephants from their capital embark go 7 tiles on boat disembark walk 4 tiles and attack. In a single round. Building fronts is just madness.2. Units that attack take no damage. This is even more absurd. What is this simulating? Game play wise this leads to insane optimal strategies. Since if you are attacked by your western neighbor you should have all you units as far from the front as possible, that you can let them enter deep into your territory and then just kill them with the counterattack taking no damage. What?This also makes combat incredibly one sided. You either just mop the floor with them or vice versa. Edit: After more time i maintain my criticism. The infinite movement is really insane. The enemy is breaking through at the center? Just teleport in 6 units to kill them. Need a unit to finish off an enemy unit? Just teleport a cavalry unit 20 tiles(for three orders over boats btw) and finish off not one but three enemies. On the opponents turn you get to watch this from the other side. Fresh spawned Units just walk from Assur to Babylon(500km in rl) in one round and attack. The effect is that you essentially just trade off units and combat devolves to a drunken bar fight in a chaos dimension. It also devalues a lot of decision making, because mistakes in unit distribution are easily mitigated by just teleporting. There is no possibility to perfectly position your units so you lose nothing in the counterattack because you will be attacked from newly produced units halfway around the world that you obviously could not know about/plan for. Yes if you are inefficient with your orders you pay in the long run. In the context of the war i never ran out of orders for my units (just for everything else at times). If you have a slight advantage you just snowball because defensive positions do not exist. (Not even a city wall(and subsequent defensive buildings)/stronghold/citadel building keeps enemies from entering your urban areas)For me the conclusion is: Tactical combat in old world feels like stepping into a insanity dimension of teleporting bronze-iron age units. If you can accept this it might be worth trying, since it is overall very innovative in every system. I will just mention one and otherwise refer to other reviews: The order mechanic makes alliances incredibly important. If you can get another civ to declare war on a common target and you have 80 orders of your alliance against 40 orders for the target they will loose even if their military would be strong enough to fight both, they just can’t order their troops to fight both. So the setup before the war, the posturing at the border can be genuinely interesting, once the war starts the dice are cast and it gets boring to me. For this reason Multiplayer might be very interesting/stressful. (Though i have not and probably will not try.)

_childDocuments_.review: Old World is a complex, interdependent game. Everything is related to everything else. The systems all interlock with each other in a deep, satisfying way. The game design is pretty damn incredible in the way that everything works together.That said, because of everything being interrelated, it's going to take some time to learn the game. It is most assuredly not just another version of Civilization. It is its own thing that needs learning on its own terms. Characters in particular add a whole new dimension to the 4x experience that is refreshing, fun, and makes for some epic stories.I still remember some moments from games I've played now months ago -- For example, when I ventured out with some chariots to attack a tribal camp and got surprised by my opponent ambushing with me with a horde of Camel Archers that blocked off my path to retreat. Or when I had my Schemer leader abdicate so his Hero heir could assume the throne and then immediately launch a surprise Launch Offensive against my opponent to beat back their onslaught. Or when I was playing an FFA and, through creative diplomacy, managed to convince a distant Rome to march to my assistance against an aggressive Assyria ... and then 50 turns later, managed to win the game without ever breaking peace with Rome.The developer team has been incredibly responsive to feedback through the early access and post-Epic release period, and I'd expect that same high level of responsiveness to continue now that the game is on Steam. The team clearly loves this game and are dedicated to making it an epic game that will stand the test of time, if you will ;)I've played hundreds of hours of Old World, primarily in multiplayer play-by-cloud games against other human opponents (using the Epic client, before the Steam release).
_childDocuments_.name: Old World

_childDocuments_.review: I thought I'd like this game being as it is Civilization in the classical era. I don't. I don't enjoy this game at all. It's how the units and cities are managed and controlled. The tutorials do a terrible job explaining what their attributes mean and how they are used. The influence and use of characters is terrible. Again, not explained well in the tutorial. This makes the game mechanics more complex. Almost like the designers had to do this so it wouldn't be a Civilization copy. Anyhow, I don't like the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Old World

_childDocuments_.review: Three reasons why this game is amazing:1. Innovation. Old World has a multitude of design decisions which don't follow established conventions of 4X genre. It is also clear that these design decisions weren't just made for the sake of innovation, but following lead designer's overall vision of how to make a 4X game which plays very differently from Civ franchise. You may disagree with certain decisions (and it's clear from browsing the reviews that there are people who do disagree), but they make sense, and are part of what makes the game such a step forward for the genre2. AI. This is the first 4X game I experienced where AI is competent in controlling it units. Of course a human player can still outsmart AI, but it does present a challenge, and a war against AI will never be a walkover. For the first time since Civ5 adopted the 1-unit-per-tile system, we have a game where AI can properly utilise it, and solving tactical puzzles presented by Old World warfare is one of the most satisfying parts of the game3. Multiplayer. Recent Civ titles clearly focusing on single player experience and including abilities which are fun to use in SP but completely break MP. Old World is designed with multiplayer as a cornerstone. In addition to the common online MP, there's play-by-cloud mode, where the save is passed between players by uploading it to the cloud, similarly to how it would be passed by email back in the day. It's a great option for those who like to take their time thinking about a turn, and can't commit several hours to play out an online game
_childDocuments_.name: Old World

_childDocuments_.review: Conquer the Old World in this historical, epic strategy game from Soren Johnson, Lead Designer of Civilization IV and Offworld Trading Company. Every year is a turn, and each leader is a mere mortal, so your lasting legacy will be the dynasty you leave behind.

name: BIOMUTANT
detailed_description: BIOMUTANT® is an open-world, post-apocalyptic Kung-Fu fable RPG, with a unique martial arts styled combat system allowing you to mix melee, shooting and mutant ability action. A plague is ruining the land and the Tree-of-Life is bleeding death from its roots. The Tribes stand divided. Explore a world in turmoil and define its fate – will you be its saviour or lead it to an even darker destiny? Key Features: A NEW TAKE ON 3rd PERSON COMBAT The martial arts style combat system allows you maximum freedom of movement and agility while mixing shooting, melee and powers from your mutations. Learning new Wung-Fu combat forms through progression and learning from masters you’ll meet, will constantly add to your choices and make sure combat never gets old. EVOLVE YOUR GAME-PLAY You’ll be able to re-code your genetic structure to change the way you look and play. This will of course affect your attributes and in addition to this, exposure to bio-contamination in the world will lead to mutations like the Turtleform and Mucus Bubble, while exposure to radioactivity found in bunkers from the old world will affect your mind and unlock psi-mutations like telekinesis, levitation and more. NEXT LEVEL OF CRAFTING You are totally free when crafting weapons. Mix and match parts to create your own unique 1H or 2H slash and crush weapons. Revolvers, rifles and shotguns and add modifications like cork-screws and battery-powered chainsaw modules to bio-contaminated sludge vials adding to your combat arsenal. There are even characters you’ll meet that’ll craft cool stuff for you, like bionic wings, a jump-pack and even let you modify your Automaton - the scrap-toy sidekick! GEAR UP FOR ADVENTURE You are totally free when equipping your character. Not only when it comes to choosing weapons you created, but what type of gear you wear. Equip a gas-mask and an oxygen tank for exploring the Dead Zones, thermos-resistant clothes for venturing into cryonic areas or protective gear for taking on bio-contaminated creatures, the choice is up to you. SURVIVE IN A VIBRANT OPEN WORLD You are free to explore the world and what lies beneath its surface, by foot, mech, jet-ski, air-balloon or area unique mounts. Explore the dying wildland, the tunnels and bunker networks of the underworld, and find your way up the mountains or out in the archipelago. There are lots of discoveries to be made, mysteries to unravel, creatures to confront and weird characters to meet in this vibrant and colorful world. AN UNUSUAL STORY WITH AN UNUSUAL END Your actions play a major part in the unfolding of a story where End is coming to the New World. A plague is ruining the land and the Tree-of-Life is bleeding death from its roots. The Tribes stand divided, in need of someone strong enough to unite them or bring them all down... You are guided through the world by a Storyteller that narrates every step of your journey, but it’s your actions and choices that’ll decide how your story of survival ends.

_childDocuments_.review: Biomutant : By Triple FIn a world where open-world games often tread familiar paths, "Biomutant" emerges as a breath of fresh air, a colorful tapestry woven with creativity, charm, and adventure. Experiment 101's ambitious debut is an ode to the unconventional, a captivating journey that marries vibrant visuals, a unique combat system, and a plethora of choices that mold the fate of a post-apocalyptic world.Set in a post-apocalyptic universe where mutated animals roam and nature reclaims civilization's ruins, "Biomutant's" standout feature is its unabashed originality. The landscape feels like a painting in motion, a seamless blend of mutated flora, diverse biomes, and stunning day-night cycles that breathe life into the environment. This picturesque world begs to be explored, rewarding intrepid wanderers with hidden stories and awe-inspiring vistas around every corner.Beneath the surface, "Biomutant's" combat system proves to be a double-edged sword. At first glance, the kung-fu-inspired martial arts mixed with firearm skirmishes offer a refreshing take on action game-play. The ability to customize your character's genetic code, leading to mutations that grant both combat and traversal powers, is an exhilarating touch. However, the controls occasionally falter, and the camera angles can become unwieldy, momentarily disrupting the fluidity the game strives to achieve.A symphony of narrator-led storytelling adds a layer of distinctiveness to "Biomutant". The narrator, with a voice that feels like a fireside bard recounting a fantastical epic, guides players through the tale, often interjecting with cheeky remarks and insightful commentary. This storytelling approach is a double-edged sword, as it amplifies the immersion but occasionally clashes with the desire for player agency in shaping the narrative.The true essence of "Biomutant" lies in its moral choices and their palpable consequences. From aligning with various tribes to deciding the fate of rivaling characters, the game presents a web of ethical dilemmas that force players to evaluate the consequences of their actions. Each choice, big or small, becomes a brushstroke on the canvas of the protagonist's journey, leading to multiple endings that beckon replay-ability.Yet, "Biomutant's" beauty is not without blemishes. Some may find the game's pacing a tad inconsistent, with certain segments feeling like a sprint while others a leisurely stroll. Quests, though abundant, occasionally succumb to repetitiveness, dampening the otherwise engrossing experience.In the grand tapestry of gaming, "Biomutant" stands as a testament to the importance of innovation and risk-taking. Its world is a living, breathing work of art, its combat system an amalgamation of styles both fresh and flawed, and its narrative a choose-your-own-adventure with immense consequence. While not devoid of imperfections, Biomutant paints an unforgettable odyssey that rewards those who dare to venture into its vibrant universe.So, is "Biomutant" worth the journey? Absolutely. It might not be flawless, but it's a testament to the magic that can emerge when developers dare to break the mold. With its rich lore, stunning visuals, and a willingness to embrace the unconventional, Biomutant stands tall as an amazing and original gaming experience that deserves a spot in the libraries of adventurers seeking something truly different.
_childDocuments_.name: BIOMUTANT

_childDocuments_.review: So, Biomutant... hyped, then forgotten, then hyped again... and this is what we got.Have you played Breath of the Wild? Biomutant is like that. As long as you remove 95% of the exploration capability, because, unlike that game, everything blocks your way, even what you should be easily capable of climbing or jumping over. Remember how you were pretty much always 30 seconds away from something, be it an encounter or a collectible or a secret, something to explore? Forget about that. Empty spaces is what awaits you for most of the "open world."Have you played any Arkham series game? Biomutant is like that. As long as you remove 99% of the responsiveness and fluidity of the combat. Locking on? Who needs that, let the game randomly decides who it wants to make you attack based on some obscure code that picks who you're "looking at." Timed dodges? Sure, just don't expect them to move you to another enemy to continue a combo. Or for it to make you evade any attack beyond the basic. Blocking and countering? Sure! Well, kinda. You see, when you're a furry, lifting your arm consumes "chi," and without "chi" your muscles just can't receive the orders from your brain. You want to block really bad, but it just won't happen, because you're out of "chi." And you don't lose "chi" only on a successful block, no! Furry limbs work in mysterious ways, you'll lose "chi" even if your half-second arm lifting does nothing. Oh by the way, dodging also consumes "chi." So yeah, you'll feel like Batman - if all the fun in the combat was sucked out of it and you were left with a fur-covered floppy skin rag.Have you played Mass Effect? Awesome voice acting, right? Everything is voiced, and with quality, with emotion. Biomutant is like that. As long as you remove 99.9999999% of the voice actors, leaving just one. One ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ "narrator" who "translates" everything your character should be able to understand. "Lazy VA" will be divided in Before Biomutant and After Biomutant, because this laziness was just that groundbreaking. Small studio, they did it to save expenses? Well, what they got was an example for the ages of how half-assing something is worse than not doing it in the first place. It would have been better to just have the animal noises and subtitles, no voice acting. All you will get from this is the shared desire that the Narrator is someone you can meet and murder to finally have silence.It's a pity, the game looked like it had a lot of potential, but it made an unfortunate choice when leveling up: their pick of Mutation was "Disappoint."
_childDocuments_.name: BIOMUTANT

_childDocuments_.review: 10 hours in and I love this game. Yes it is repetitive and there are no ground breaking idea`s but for exploring, loot collecting, interesting fights and quite alot of freedom, this is a fun game.You can make a pretty unique character that can mix play styles to be as fun or boring as you like. Mixing melee, ranged weapon attacks with your other abilities during fights is very fluid so every fight can be so different from the last that for me at least makes me want to go hunting for more battles.Quests are pretty basic and the little puzzles are easy but do add to the general feel of exploration.Have I played better games? Yeah.Is this a bad game?  No, not even close.The best way to play this game is to forget the hype and just play it for fun, the way games are supposed to be played, then you will see it shine.I really hope there will be lots of dlc added in the future and another Biomutant game to follow on from this one.In my opinion I think too many people expected Biomutant to be more than it is and they ended up being overly harsh in the negative reviews.With such a small team the game turned out better than soooooo many AAA games of late and Im glad I bought this game rather than wasting my money on the AAA fails.
_childDocuments_.name: BIOMUTANT

_childDocuments_.review: I've had Biomutant since launch - 25/5/21. I have only just got to it on my backlog of games. I had a bad PC back then so I could hardly run it. I can remember the hype behind it. "OMG, It's and open world fighting game with a martial arts combat system and cool furry creatures!". It looked amazing! But, what we got was an absolute disappointment. Below I will explain why and I'll also give my opinion too! So, let's get to it but first a small disclaimer.  ⚫The "narrator" is clearly a robot. Not only is he DULL and BORING, he just drags everything out and ruins the entire experience. If you removed the Narrator, the game would be a bit better.⚫BIOMUTANT offers you "morality" choices. In reality, you just save or kill everyone. To me, this was very misleading as consequences did not really matter.⚫Loot in this game is in abundance. 90% of the time you will be looting just garbage over and over again with no actual reward.⚫All the puzzles are copy-pasted "mach the colours" and they feel like they are made in 2007.⚫No boss or enemy in the game offered me a challenge which was really disappointing. ⚫The start of the game is so stupidly slow. It takes about 2-3 hours before you can freely explore.⚫It throws about 20 different game mechanics at you within the first 2-3 hours for you to remember rather than teaching you as time goes on.⚫This will be in PROS too - The combat was initially fun at the start of the game but as time went on, it got so stale, boring and repetitive.⚫All the voice acting is done via the narrator. He ruins the immersion and the "creatures" the developers made for this world as they felt FAKE due to this reason. Budget reasons probably. ⚫The character "Creation/picker" is pretty cool. I can make my OWN "BIOMUTANT" look and feel unique to how I tailor It.⚫The world is filled with truly fantastic character designs and many different types of enemies, rival creatures and mutants to battle.⚫The Open-World was gorgeous. Very vibrant and "alive" despite the games setting.⚫The game supports an impressive range of weaponry, skills, abilities that YOU can choose to use/learn to help fight the many dangers in the world. I quote "No 2 friends will have the EXACT same play-style" and it really shows with BIOMUTANT.⚫Another thing about the Open-World was that I felt FREE to explore how I wanted. Go where I wanted to go. It felt fun to just explore, at least for the first half of the game.⚫This will be in CONS too - The combat was initially fun at the start of the game but as time went on, it got so stale, boring and repetitive. If they toned down the narrator, or gave us the option to just TURN HIM OFF COMPLETELY, maybe the game would not be so.... tedious. I mean, the narrators cheap interjections about your character fighting just made me want to mute the entire game... after all... it's basically hamster VS hamster, right? We get the point narrator, just stop talking.If they also made the mechanics more spread out rather than forced upon the player within the first opening hours of the game it would not have been so repetitive, would it? Like, if you learned WUNG-FU after you cleared your first MAJOR boss or you earned your first "powerful" weapon from a morality choice, different being on good or bad. All in all, the fantastic enemy design, gorgeous open-world and being spoiled of choice on how to "build" your character is ruined/spoiled by a NPC like annoying Narrator, who sounds like a cheap David Attenborough,  boring puzzles which are YEARS behind compared to other open-world games and the early repetition on quests leaves a sour taste in your mouth.It's not a bad game, nor is it good. It is VERY, VERY selective. Niche almost. You will either like it or not. Personally... I hated almost every minute of the narrator and every minute of "late game" combat  because of EARLY game.I would not recommend Biomutant full price. You might have more mental stamina than me to be able to put up with the Narrator but honestly, the game is not worth it full price anyway. Grab it on a HEAVY discount.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is nothing new to the open world gamer, it functions like breath of the wild meets skyrim meets fallout. I have had so much enjoyment tracking down toilets to fix and broken washing machines. The battle is difficult for me since i do not do shooters well but i am coping. _childDocuments_.review: Reminded me of all the great experiences I had playing The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, but with a fresh coat of paint in an equally beautiful and expansive world.Covering the game from an unbiased perspective while limiting opinions (no spoilers):~This game is an expansive map of 64 beautiful square kilometers with so much to explore I haven't found everything even with just over 40 hours of gameplay~Even with computer hardware that is at this point two or more generations old I had no issues running this game with everything cranked to max settings, and rarely encountered any stuttering if any~The story is really nothing super special but the game's focus is more using the story to push exploration instead of trying to be something remarkably riveting~Combat is very fun and my only complaint is it's easier to just run away and shoot instead of using melee weapons but that may just be my experience as a player~Some small glitches like UI in the menu and especially in crafting, but it's nothing more than a minor annoyance that resolves itself with a quick exit and re-entering of the menuOpinion time (still no spoilers):~A $60 price tag for a triple A title with a map this large and with so much built-in content (main quests, side quests etc) is not an unreasonable price by any stretch of the imagination. Why some are complaining about it in other reviews or recommending to wait for something as massive as a 50% sale is beyond me.~The crafting system is really cool, being able to upgrade the material of weapons and clothes to keep it relevant as you progress if you like the look of it is a nice little touch. My main complaint is that holy cow it costs a lot of resources for some items for a very minuscule improvement in specs.~Stop complaining about the narrator reviewers, you can turn him off completely if you like.~Unlimited ammo is....nice but a little immersion breaking because it doesn't really line up with the rest of the game's outlook on resources and using them to upgrade and craft.~The "overly fast progression" is not something I'd complain about, as you really shouldn't have to sweep the entirety of a map this large to get the best gear you can. The rest of the map that waits after the main story and getting top-end gear is there to be explored at the player's leisure.~This game does copy-paste many assets, but in an effort to keep things more interesting the devs added different puzzles and paths in areas that re-used assets.~Yes, dialogue and naming-schemes are childish and playful but when "comic book effects" are an option in the settings menu what else are you expecting? It's okay for a game to be childish and fun, not everything needs to be The Last of Us II.TLDR:~Is this a $60 game? Yes of course it is. A map this expansive with the ability to craft, customize, and explore and whatever pace you want with massive potential for replay-ability as each path and tribe chosen changes the outcome of the game. People complaining this is maybe a $20-30 game need to sit down and enjoy the world a bit more. It isn't DOOM. Some of the gameplay is slow because it's meant to have such a heavy emphasis on exploration.~Again yes, this game is $60 and it's the same price as any other triple A title, but offers more replay-ability than many other triple A games I've played that cost the same amount and got nothing but raves of positive reviews. Give the game time, it's a big world out there, and it's meant to be enjoyed at pace.

_childDocuments_.review: I have 30 minutes in this game before I refunded it, which might be a new record. By all means, I have a very small experience of what this game truly provides, but I already feel comfortable in sitting this game out.The combat was the largest offender. It's floaty, visually confusing, and mechanically dull. These problems are predominantly found in the melee combat, and it's problems goes to the core. Ranged combat felt at least somewhat promising, but was still more than disappointing. Plenty of other fundamental issues exist, like the rolling, but these were the major ones.The skills and character creator were also wildly disappointing. I'd typically take up to an hour in the character creator alone, it's one of my favorite parts of a game, but this game had next to nothing for me to do. Even though there were many options, the options just weren't that good, and I couldn't bother spending much time on them.Then there's the story, cutscenes, and narrator. Those were problems, but nothing I could comment too strongly on. Narrator was a bit annoying and the cutscenes were rampant, but those could totally be the tutorial's fault and improve with time. However, the story was already building up to be concerning. At best, it's inoffensive, I can't even really remember much of it. Very straight forwards "good or bad" decisions and it had the most generic sweeping music that covered the scenes to make them seem less awkward than they truly were.In short, I just can't safely drop 60 dollars on this game. It's been a long time since a game has been so polarizing in the first 30 minutes, and I played Cyberpunk. Hell, I enjoyed Cyberpunk. That game was obviously a mess, and I went in expecting it, but still got a good story and alright combat. This game is below the bar that Cyberpunk was still able to pass. _childDocuments_.review: is a third-person Action RPG set in a post-apocalyptic future Earth, where mankind has gone extinct due to a massive ecological catastrophe. Sentient life however continues to exist, thanks to a new species of mutated animals that now populates the land. As one of them, the protagonist has to choose his own path across the world, destined to change the balance of things forever.Visually, this game is extraordinary, and not only because of the cutting-edge technologies used. The art direction itself manages to depict an original post-apocalyptic setting that is colorful and vibrant, instead of faded-out and depressing. Rich in detail and nuances for the attentive observer, the vast world is consistent in design and offers solid location variety.Disassembling, reinforcing and mix-matching gear parts is fun and interesting throughout the game. The overall not-so-great diversity of arms types is compensated decently by the possible combinations, which eventually enable creating the perfect weapon roster for any playstyle.Each starting class has several unique passive perks that can define a build. Some of them are more tank-oriented, others best suited for raw DPS. The combination of attributes, passive perks and gear opens up to a good number of play-styles, such as fragile but powerful Psi "mages", agile sharpshooters or durable melee fighters.The overly-used "bad guy killed my family so now I become a warrior" trope is used yet again, to lead a forgettable story that desperately wants to emphasize player choice without succeeding, with a contour of anonymous, bland characters as  cast. The choice of ALWAYS using the same third-person narrator for everything, demolishes any flair characters may have had.Initially, questing and exploring while battling various abominations and fellow (bio)mutants is interesting enough - after some hours however bosses, dungeons, puzzles and quest types start to be always the same, just re-skinned or outright copy-pasted. A wonderful world... filled with utterly repetitive, boring tasks over and over again.The lack of proper enemy-lock on, in favor of a weird "auto-lock" system that in many cases ends up making players attack the wrong enemy, is very frustrating. Unlimited ammo paired with plentiful stamina, mean ANY fight can be won by spamming ranged weapons while dodging in a circle - YES, really! Hitboxes and collisions are floaty, while the general feel of "eurojank" permeates most fights.At around 20 hours in, top-tier gear, weapons and equipment will generally be acquired. Unfortunately, the entirety of the world takes quite a lot more than that to be cleared. This translates into players already having unlocked most abilities and the best gear relatively early, having nothing to look forward to anymore in terms of progression - still huge amounts of filler and quests to clear.Except for the main quest itself, most side-missions have very little to no choice at all in most cases. For example, an evil character cannot choose to kill a secondary character to steal something he needs from him - he will still have to do a "helping quest" just in the same way as if he actually offered to help. On top of that, there can be major inconsistencies between the lore and what actually happens in some situations.Is performed on foot, on mounts when available and also by using several vehicles in specific biomes (such as a jet-ski to traverse watery areas). Fast-travel is available between discovered and "tagged" banners outside of combat, although not while in enclosed spaces. The world is vast, and has many optional areas, secret loot containers and places to discover. Attentively scouting every ruin in search of containers is recommended, to acquire vital consumables and better loot.Plays out in a fast-paced manner, either in melee or using ranged abilities such as various gun types, psi skills or organic mutations, which all need "Ki Energy" (Stamina) to be activated. Melee on the other hand, doesn't consume stamina whatsoever. Depending on character attributes such as strength, intelligence and so on, the damage dealt with a specific offensive means can greatly improve - passive class-specific perks can also greatly help with this, in turn "forcing" specific classes to a certain combat style. Perfect dodges, parries and combos are all present, however none of these mechanics has ulterior depth onto itself, with simplistic combinations and underwhelming risk-reward on most counters. Status effects can be inflicted with elemental weapons or abilities, however their effects are barely noticeable, while the weakness / resistance systems are just an afterthought, never really used in any meaningful way.Is done in a standard inventory menu where one can choose the protagonist's gear loadout. Equipment has a color-coded rarity system, where found loot quality is mainly influenced by the luck statistic, fundamental to get good gear. The mutations panel allows spending three different "currencies" to unlock Wung-Fu combos, mutation-related abilities and perks, other than increase passive elemental resistances. Leveling up and finding specific containers awards such point types. Each level awards 1 (+10) attribute point to spend in one of the six main statistic, and a passive perk point.Is performed in a dedicated menu that allows dismantling, scrapping and creating new weapons. Any melee or ranged arm can be upgraded or changed in type to best suit one's current build and style. The same can't be done with armor, which only can be upgraded with "Addons" but never created from scratch. Eventually the "meta" is taking the best pieces from all the greatest weapons one has, to create the ultimate tool of destruction.

_childDocuments_.review: The short of it: I don't really understand why the developers said this is supposed to be a post-apocalyptic kung fu journey when in reality the best option is to just shoot your way through the world. It ironically makes a statement that guns are just the way and Kung Fu movies died to action gun bro movies for a reason. This rating is not a final decision but as it stands this is a jank game that needs a lot of work to be good and re-balancing. This is at most a 15-20 dollar game and lands in 5/10 territory thus far. Also it has the Fortnite UI and is so out of place and terrible looking.Gonna flat out say it, the best class in the game by miles is the dead-eye. They get the best perk in the game, the rest of the classes are laughable at best but let's go over them here.Dead eye – Gets a perk at level 15 that doubles their damage with all two handed guns. If that gun is also not automatic they gain an additional 20% boost further and lots of crit. They absolutely dominate  in terms of power over all other classes and as an added bonus because guns do not benefit directly from any stats you can gain at character creation you can make your little gremlin look how ever you want. Pick this if you want to be powerful.EDIT: This perk has has been nerfed since this review. Guess what though? Guns are still the best, and Dead-eye is still the strongest pick by a country mile. Nothing they do can balance guns in this game short of throwing the entire system out and starting over which these devs will not do.Commando – Worse version of the dead eye, the only reason to play them is to duel wield pistols as they have perks that will actually benefit you for doing so. Again as an added bonus they can look however they want because guns do not effect appearance at character creation unless you want to hybrid into melee, then you get to look like the hulk at random.Psi-Freak – Somehow the tankiest class in the game. They do ability damage and the only way to increase that is to level INT, any points spent elsewhere will be wasted unless you really want a piece of armor that increases something else and needs a different stat. The reason they are so tanky is they get a perk that gives damage done with abilities back to them in the form of health. So long as you are attacking you aren't dying. Mercenary – The best melee class in the game, by a lot. Just better in every way than the saboteur and sentinel.  Has the best perks of all the classes focused on melee, not much more to be said other than still fails to out damage and survive the Dead eye.Saboteur – worse version of Mercenary. That's really it.Sentinel – REALLY worse version of Mercenary with slightly more tank, which is what the class is all about save for one thing; they are paper compared to Psi-Freaks due to no additional healing and melee is generally super floaty and dangerous in this game.The fact that you cannot separate your starting stats from your appearance is a big no from me, with the only option you control that won't effect your stats and appearance being fur pattern and color. It seems neat to some, I don't like it. The only class you can get away with playing and do well on default stats is the dead-eye and maybe the commando due to guns not increasing from any stat other than luck (which you can only level via level up). If you like the default look of any species and want to play anything other than range, forget about it.The shapes your creature's head and body take are random every time you select a bread by the way, so let's say you pick the dip bread (good spell caster), then drag your stats towards INT, sometimes they will get a normal sized head, sometimes a really elongated head, other times it will just be a massive bulb shape because we big brained now. Either way the moment I realized this I spent about 10 minutes just clicking back and forth between the stat sliders and the spices to try and get a RNG look that wasn't terrible with the stat spread I wanted.Why is this bad? The devs give you the ability to randomly make a look you want, but instead of just letting you do it they put morphs on an RNG rotation. The character creator wastes your time, the intro wastes your time, and the animal's speech wastes your time. This game is all about wasting your time and throwing RNG at you in ways that are frustrating, not rewarding., floaty, and generally a worse option than Ranged of any kind. Feels like kingdom hearts floaty levels of melee but more jank. Not much more to say about it. The only good thing about it thus far is how well it stun locks some enemies. feels okayish, sounds bad, and is also floaty but less so compared to melee. You also get to do a bullet time sort of jump whenever you want which can help slow things down to let you access the combat situation more. This game also heaily auto-aims so this is less about accuracy and more about timing your shots and where they go, it's odd. There's like a total of eight spells in the game and half of those are locked off depending on if you're good or evil, spoilers being evil grants you the better spells! Several do no damage and are just utility, meaning there are about 5 actual damaging spells total.INT is the only way to raise spell damage, which means you're going to be bad at everything but surviving (bad barter prices, bad luck so no crits, bad loot drops). At least they get a perk that lets them (assuming you picked Psi-Freak) gain health for damaging enemies. Lastly, I do not understand how you could be a spell caster without chosing Psi-Freak. You have to be super evil and wait until around level 6 at the earliest to get your first Psi-freak damaging spell and it takes all of your psi points to get it while psi-freak just starts with it out of the gate. Melee magic just isn't viable at all past utility spells, gun ranged works a bit better (because gun damage is not tied to stats save for luck for crit) but you'll have to get reallllly lucky to find gun parts at a decent clip without any luck stat.You have three characters you hear. The dark spirit, the light spirit, and the narrator. I personally did not find the spirits voice acting grating but my friends watching my stream of the game thought they were terrible, so take that with what you will.This game has no real voice acting past a narration. All of the characters speak gibberish and the narrator translates for you. This sucks absolutely all the life out of the game and any quaky fun characters are from appearance only.  It's much easier to pay one guy to voice everything than to pay a whole cast to voice things, it cheapens the experience.This could be an amazing game if the devs reworked... Well most of it. From balancing to sound design there are problems. This game isn't No Man's Sky levels of “it needs to be fixed” but it is kinda' close. _childDocuments_.review: I saw a trailer for this game and it looked pretty cool. Didn't research the game at all, only found out about it maybe a month ago. I was expecting a complete game with engaging gameplay that made an overall positive experience. The tribe war seemed cool, with the impending doom of the world tree. So I bought the game day one. And boy, what a terrible mistake that was.As you can see from my time played, I didn't just play this game for a few hours then say it's dog feces and wrote a review about it. I explored the world, sat through 30+ hours of that annoying narrator... narrating things, and dove into the game's mechanics. I grinded XP and leveled up my character into the upgrade system. I chose to take over each enemy tribe instead of opting to quit the game after just TWO TRIBES. I put in the work, I ate up every hour of gameplay this game had to offer. And it sucked. Don't get me wrong, the game looks beautiful. Nobody will argue that. The world is massive and has several different biomes that you have to prepare for with resistance boosts, there are many cool looking structures and broken down buildings due to the apocalypse. But it's just so empty. There are zero enemies out in the wild other than scripted fights of a grand total of 5 NPC's fighting outside outposts. And don't get me STARTED on the outposts. It's basically every Far Cry game in existence. Go to the enemy outpost. Do a mini mission there like blow up a gun, or hack into a door or whatever, or just kill a bunch of people, and then your "faction" takes over that outpost. It's all BS we've seen before, and they did it worse. The devs took a look at that outpost mechanic and made a WHOLE GAME just on that.This game is nothing but literal repetition. Doing the same thing over and over again for hours until eventually you beat the biggest bad guy and beat the game. There's nothing new or special here, and it's clearly unfinished. The world is empty. For a bunch of warring factions, there isn't a whole lot of WAR going on. Do not buy this game. It isn't even CLOSE to being worth $60. Not even $30. Literal free mobile games have more content than this. Rant over.

_childDocuments_.review: BIOMUTANT is a game that benefits from having some expectations before playing it. I had an excellent time with it after following it for a few months before it's release, gleaning a sense of what the creators wanted to accomplish with this release. It's exactly what I expected, though, inevitably lacking some polish as the team was of moderate size (~20 people). Anyway, the negatives are already ubiquitous within every review posted thus far, so I'll focus on the major positives.Ultimately, I think gamers with a proclivity for investigating every nook and cranny of an open world and a penchant for whimsy will really enjoy this game. The beautiful world of BIOMUTANT is filled with an abundance of life and charm if you care to look for it. It really scratched by exploration itches while still providing a rewarding and malleable combat system. But malleable, I mean that any way that you prefer to play the game, it will allow you to, with a real RPG feel to creating your character and specializing in the combat aspect that most interest you. I loved the Wung-Fu combo system. It takes some time to find your rhythm with the combat, as I believe everyone will feel there own subjective inclination to combine particular moves together. If you take that small time to play around with each type of weapon and ability I promise you will find a harmony, otherwise, you will likely just spam the ranged attacks which will get mundane fast, and is, unfortunately, effective. I had a ton of fun with the combat myself, mixing a number of ranged, melee, and psi powers into my arsenal. I felt the combat was far more rewarding than other exploration focused open-world games, like Breath of the Wild.Again, the world is lively if you allow yourself to embrace it. Although you'll reach a point (~20 hrs in if you are going out of your way to stop at every destination) that the areas will appear redundant, you will still encounter unique mini-bosses and spectacular loot; the loot and the crafting is truly one of the best facets of the game. I have spent an inordinate amount of time with the crafting system. Every weapon you create feels so unique and you have a personal connection to it, since you built it piece-by-piece. The armor, too, (especially the interminable list of hats you will collect) is so diverse. There is a menu where you can easily swap between 5 outfits you've put together, injecting a mutable personality to your character. The side characters are quirky and charismatic, though, your interactions with them are almost always fetch quests that will at least result in a cool reward. The lore, while superficially intriguing, does not have much depth and the main story is relatively short. However, the main bosses (the four world eaters and Lupa-Lupin) do offer some challenge and unique fights. Every world-eater requires a new, fun vehicle to defeat. I slowly progressed through the story, focusing more on the exploration and letting the excellent foundation of the lore breathe life and meaning to the world and its different biomes, tribes, and creatures. It's a charming game. One I had a ton of fun with. I'm not sure how it fares on a second play-through, and expect the games cracks to be accentuated then. But I'm very happy with what I got out of it, with just under 50 hrs at the moment. Objectively, the game is good -- slightly above average, probably a 6/10; that is, when including all of the negatives, which was not a focus of this review, as I'm sure you've heard them all already. There is a lot of potential here and I personally had a blast. That's why I'm giving BIOMUTANT, based on my experience and love for exploration heavy and zen gamer friendly games, an...8/10

_childDocuments_.review: This game claims to be an open world, but in reality it's a game on rails that gives you very little freedom OR reason to explore the open world. Every. Thing. Is. A Cutscene. Why? I found myself just wanting to skip most of this and just get into the game. I thought that this was a problem with just the tutorial part of the game, which is expansive, but it even persists into the main portions. Perhaps it would have been better if the characters weren't just inanimate objects looping the same idle animation over and over (again, saw this in Ocarina of Time, a game literally 30 years old).I feel like the combat is all over the place, but ultimately boring. _childDocuments_.review: Biomutant is a game that has been in its own development hell for a long time. And it shows.Compare it to titles put out by the big studios and its a janky mess. But this is not a game made in the USA by a big money games studio or a studio sponsored/owned by a gigantic US publisher. It's a game made by a small studio in Europe comprised of about twenty people supported by a mid tier publisher with a much tighter budget.So long as you don't go into this expecting a highly polished tightly knit game that is the product of the copious quantities of human misery that anything involving Americans tends to require, then you'll find a game with a lot of crazy ideas, a lot of heart and a charm of its very own.The melee combat is very floaty and inspired more by Devil May Cry but without that series large number of highly complex movesets. The gunplay is basic and borrows a bit from the melee elements in its combos.The "magic" is highly inconsistent ranging from absolutely broken if done right to absolutely worthless if done wrong.But the combat system doesn't want you to just stick to one of these. It expects you to mix it up. Blending melee and gunplay can be extremely satisfying with a surprisingly high skill ceiling. Figuring out the most optimal power combos can also be delightful if more repetitive. The world is beautiful and has a charm you rarely find in modern titles. While the devs do copypaste assets everywhere they do so in a manner that makes sense and doesn't create a jarring impression. In my opinion the best areas are those that stick to the whole "dumpsterpunk" aesthetic the game is built around. Unfortunately the villages and tribes often don't stick to this which is disappointing. The menus are hideous and often miss important details that aren't explicitly mentioned. The tutorials are a mess that range from very explanatory to nonexistent.The soundtrack can get a touch repetitive. The narrator is an idea that I personally consider to be a bold and inspired move. But as is often the case with such moves it is either a hit or a miss. This time its mostly a miss whose novelty wears off and detracts from the game.The story is a bit of a mess that is clearly a product of the development hell the game was in with there being basically three main stories running together jostling each other for screentime to the detriment of them all.Overall the game is a product of the mess that was its development and its developers lack of experience or strong leadership (but then what does one expect of Swedes?)But it oozes heart and soul in a world of soulless games. And has the bonus of being a genuinely fun game if you're willing to overlook the jank. If you've a habit of playing of Eurojank games? Then grab it.

You can only see the map in an menu and can't zoom. Furthermore, there's only confusing waypoints that can often lead you into a deadend.(Preface: I'm using a PS5 controller) Control wise, the game feels pretty good and I don't have a problem with getting around. Graphics: I can easily play this game on the highest graphics and it seems that some details do no look as good as the gameplay trailers, mostly things like fur.Combat: The combat was by far the most disappointing thing in this game. It does not feel balanced and it's almost not worth doing anything other than deadeye and ranged attacks with dots. However, the most egregious thing about this game is the fact that the actual combat is so floaty. There's zero impact on the hits.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a little more than 3 hours on this game. I don't find it boring at all, however, I'm a different kind of gamer. _childDocuments_.review: First time I write a review but I was so bummed about this game that I have to warn people about what could have been an amazing game and is finally a bad joke.Let's delve into the three components of this Action-RPG in an openworld. Fights are boring. There is no technicity, no challenge and animation are not even entertaining. So much that as soon as you'll get a good range weapon (so very quickly since the loot system is broken), you will stop to fight and just shoot enemies from afar. : This is the worst part. The game will drop you in the main quest with the poorest introduction I have ever seen, "Go left or go right, this will pretty much change all your alignment in the game but who cares ?". This situation won't improve during the game, the four big parts of the main quest are copypasted (talk to this guy, get a piece to build a vehicle, gather little animals, underwhelming boss fight). The second main quest "Tribes War" is so useless that even the devs knew it and you get the option to end it after defeating 2 out of 5 tribes. Side quest and dialogs are boring as hell (especially since there is only one voice actor during the whole game), I won't develop this part, you get where I am going : The fact that you can craft stuff, manage your gear and change your stats is a poor excuse to call this an RPG. The world looks great. And that's it. There is no point to discover anything since every spot is just a copypasted version of another place (you'll have an amazing time discovering "shop 10C" after your last exploration of "shop 6E" - yeah most places do not even have unique names -) and there is nothing to do except for looting stuff ...After 17 hours, I finally finished the game - just because I always try to complete my games but it was a chore - and I can say that it was one of my worst gaming experience (the ending makes no sense btw). This could have been an amazing tale about karma, environment and balance but not even one aspect of this game is entertaining.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay.  I'm 17 hours in.  BioMutant:  Game of Cute Hats and Awesome Art.  I normally don't write reviews, but I felt like I could on this one.  Am I having fun?  Yes.  GOTY?  Maybe not, but it's a fun game.  I wish it had a bit more to the underlying character system including perks and what your skills did, but it's Cute-Fallout: Lite, Now with: HATS!.  Watch any gameplay videos on YouTube.  They're fairly accurate.  If you think that gameplay is fun, play.  If  you don't, definitely don't.  It's a very black and white game.  You will like it, or you won't.  No Meh.My Take Aways:- The crafting is very cool.  They've created something interesting there.- The Art is very well done.- Combat is very Soul Caliber-lite.  Dance around, dodge, swing.  Repeat.  Use a few combo inputs.- The Story is going to beat you over the head for drinking a disposable water bottle.  Come prepared.The world flow / level design is all over the place.  If you wander, prepare to get lost side trekking.  Not a bad thing, but it does make certain systems become less obvious because you didn't go from A->B.- Enemies aren't crowding every zone. _childDocuments_.review: Being a older gamer i felt as though this game was created for a intended audience of gamers from 12-16 years old. The visuals were great with a cartoonish/watercolor style for the environment. The story was not bad however lacks a hook that it  really needed to set a well immersed story. Dialogue in Biomutant is done through a narrator translating the languages of the other NPCs in the game. This was not really a problem for me however it did end up making my choices feel less and less impactful. The longer I played the more I felt a lack of investment in the NPC characters and what happened to them. The puzzles are so easy that they probably shouldn't be called puzzles. On to the biggest problem with Biomutant, the combat. Wow does this need some major improvement. From the lock on to enemies even if i don't want to, to the recycled animations/fighting style of the bigger foes in the game, and the desperate need for the combo system to be something other than a 1-2-3-4 rotation. I felt like the tools were there to create awsome combos but it was just so repetitive that i did not find myself enjoying the melee combat I normally do in most games. Most of the flashy powers you can get are the same way, cool to finally play with and experiment with but for almost no payoff. The powers needed to evolve like getting stronger pending on your karma alignment, Light or Dark. Or the powers needed to have branching pathways to alter them to the players fighting style. With all this said to a younger gamer this would be a fun button masher and slight puzzle solving game however to a average+ gamer this will fall short. Overall 4/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not bad at all. It's not the next greatest RPG of all time either. It feels like a true video game though. I feel like a kid again playing on my dad's ps1. Not caring about whats going on except the pure fun I'm having. The world is vibrant and beautiful. The combat is different and I find to be fun to learn. The game is so easy to explore because you will always find another thingamajig to add to your weapon or armor. The customization is insane and goofy. _childDocuments_.review: Biomutant is a game unlike any other I have played before, and I mean that in a good way. Biomutant is a beautiful and charming post apocalyptic and mutated open world action RPG. The world has a spirit and pulse which embodies Kung Fu, magic, crazy weapons and other unique game play elements. These elements all add up to be an enjoyable game albeit some setbacks such as repetition in questing, lacking a deep meaningful story, and mediocre at best narration. The open world is a good sized map with colorfully diverse terrain and plenty of locations to explore and loot. The graphics are amazing, the world is detailed and characters pop into life with vibrant colors and textures. There are many character models in this game. NPC's and enemies are diverse and have their own distinct look and feel to them. The combat is fast, fun, and you have a wide array of weapons, magic, mutant abilities, and combinations to defeat the enemy. It's hard not to smile while you are flying around  swashbuckling enemies with cool Kung Fu combos blending chaos and elegance in combat. There are plenty of magic abilities and fighting combinations to be utilized, and a ridiculous amount of customization when it comes to melee/ranged weapons and armor. The world is filled with loot which helps you craft your arsenal and armor. The playful design of the game gives you a sense of place in this odd but magical world. There are a lot of quests and side quests however they do become repetitive after time and are not the most impactful. The story is light hearted and easy to follow however the narration feels not genuine. Also the dialogue between the NPC seems unnecessary at times and drawn out. Overall I enjoyed Biomutant despite some setbacks. You wont find a game similar out there and for what the games does do well its worth checking out at a discounted price. Score: 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. I didn't watch anything about this game because I didn't want any spoilers or to get overhyped for it. When I started to play it, I couldn't decide if I liked it or not so I kept on playing and then I realized that feeling of worry I was getting was because the game is very repetitive. One of the first parts I noticed was the lack of voice acting with the exception of the narrator. Now this could have been fine if they executed right but the problem is even the narrator has very few voice lines. Resulting in the feeling of annoyance every time you repeat a similar action and get the same dialog every time. The second thing I noticed is the tribe mechanics are very very repetitive. There are 6 tribes and you can take control of their outposts for your allied tribe. The problem is each of the five tribes has 3 outposts and each outpost has its own mechanic. You'd think that means there are outposts with 15 different or somewhat different mechanics to take it over. But no there are literally 3 mechanics. So you take over the first tribes set of outposts and after that they are all the same. Nothing new. After the 3 outposts you take control of their main fort and fight their leader. Even these are very boring. You get a "tribe weapon" Which in my case I never used because my weapons were always better. There are also 4 other bosses you have to fight which are the World Eaters. They are all way too easy and pretty much all have the same mechanics just basically with a re-skin. 1. Get vehicle 2. shoot at the boss till it dies. The final world eater was literally the exact same difficulty as the first. So have fun with that. After all of that being said the one thing I enjoyed with this game is the loot you get to make your character look cool and have more armor and damage but even that fades because I was no longer getting any loot that was better so I just continually passed things up. So even the one good thing gets taken away really. I wouldn't recommend buying this game. Like I said I really wanted to like it so I beat the game. But my opinion of it only got worse with time.

_childDocuments_.review: I have 2 hours played so far and I must say that this game looks amazing and the game play is really smooth! The game has a lot of dialog at the start, but once you get past it, it's open world exploration with looting and lots of combat. I currently play the game on hard difficulty and it gives me a challenge. It has that dark souls feeling when it comes to combat since I can die within 4-6 hits without healing. The combat feels great whether it's ranged, melee or sorcery. People who complain that the combat sucks either doesn't know what they are doing or don't know how to use the combos and just spams buttons. There are a lot of abilities to choose from, combos to unlock and buffs to select when you level up. You can find loot from killing enemy's or looting the environment as well. The music is also not bad. The music is not childish at all like some people say. The story teller is not as bad as people say he is either. The story teller has a nice and warming voice that is nice to listen to. He explains the story very well and in a way where keeps me wanting to know more. You can turn the story teller off in the settings by turning the volume all the way down for him. I also have not ran into any weird bugs or crashes as well. The only bad thing I can say so far is that some cutscenes end way to quickly and cut off.Overall, the game is awesome. Don't listen to people who down vote and have less then 2 hours played because they most likely have not gotten far in the game to experience what Biomutant really is and has to offer.I rate the game a 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game for the right sort of person. If you enjoy exploration, crafting, and dressing up cute/ugly anthropomorphic critters, this game provides 10s of hours of fun. The world is actually very large, with a seemingly endless number of areas to explore that all feel nominally unique, aside from certain individual buildings. Some things that you need to appreciate in order to fully enjoy the game would be: side quests, easy puzzles, child-like naming conventions and philosophizing, a single voice actor narrating the entire game, and a relatively simple combat system.The combat is a very important aspect of the game, but once you get the hang of the super wung-fu system and unlock certain perks or psi-powers, the combat becomes somewhat trivial. The same combination will allow you to dominate most encounters, as either a gun or psi-power build. Melee is a bit harder because you end up in the middle of the enemy constantly, they will attack you from off screen, you have to distribute your points a tad more evenly than the other builds, thereby lowering your damage, and you don't get an overpowered perk/psi-power like the other builds. The guns build is particularly strong because your primary stat, luck, is also the one that gets you the best loot. Deep challenging combat shouldn't be your primary consideration when choosing to buy this game, even though enemies level with you, and you occasionally find an encounter that comes close to killing you.Here are a couple personal tips that I don't see mentioned:1. Play as either a melee or ranged build on your first run--melee if you want a challenge, or guns if you want to blast everything to smithereens. Even on hard, the ranged build will defeat the majority of encounters easily. Both builds engage heavily with the crafting system, and you'll get more out of them. The psi-powers build doesn't rely on equipment as much, and is probably best left for a second playthrough, when you aren't interested in the loot and crafting as much.2. If you play as either guns or psi-powers, don't put more than 30 total points into strength or agility (from character creation and leveling). Not putting points into your primary stat, luck or intellect respectively, will indirectly lower your damage. Strength and agility are mainly useful for meeting gear requirements, and the last 30 points can be gained from workout equipment throughout the world.3. Wood is precious! Get every single wood resource totem you see!
