_childDocuments_.review: It's like a cross between Metal Slug and Streets of Rage. I always loved the side-scrolling beat 'em up genre of the 80s/90s, but those games often felt unfairly punishing (e.g. Battle Toads, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles for NES). Huntdown doesn't suffer from that problem. Instead it strikes a balance of difficulty through infinite lives. The game does demand to be played in a particular way, but once you get the hang of the flow it's very satisfying to run and gun down the enemy. Huntdown wants you to play and enjoy everything it has to offer.  The game leans into its 90s origins, with cyberpunk sprites and references straight out of classic action movies from the Schwarzenneger era. Each level feels carefully crafted, with a unique and fun boss fight at the end of every stage. My only gripe about the game is that it is short. It feels like an arcade game that you can sit down and beat from start to finish. I liked it enough that upon Normal mode completion, I immediately started up a Hard mode run and made it more than half way through the whole thing. The game is quite fun. It remains to be seen what this studio will put out next, but I look forward to seeing it. Fully endorse.
_childDocuments_.name: HUNTDOWN

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent old-school run n' gun arcade shooter. It's fast, simple, and most importantly, feels fair while still being difficult. It has a fun story, solid voice acting and excellent music. I'm hopeful East Trigger Games does a sequel.I did get occasional framedrops, on both my steam deck and my high-end PC, which was a little surprising, but overall a really great game for fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game loop! A little short but far exceeded my expectations. Each level was full of surprises. Fun game to play casually as there are many check points and levels usually take around 10-15  minutes to complete. Bosses are imaginative and memorable and each had a unique movelist that made them very satisfying to beat. Game has around 25 levels. One play through took me about 5 hours. I think the ride was pretty reasonable for the ticket price. Wish there were more awesome gangs to fight; Free DLC would make this a no brainer!
_childDocuments_.name: HUNTDOWN

_childDocuments_.review: The 'Member Berries showed us that our nostalgia and memory aren't always one and the same. Huntdown seems to be aware of this to provide us an abundance of nostalgia and gameplay we 'think' we remember and it comes out as a terrifically fun game.I love the difficulty pacing, allowing me to adjust (somewhat) to gameplay by the end of a level and then throwing something new at me. I feel the sting of losing without the anger towards the game being "unfair".Levels are short; much shorter than Classic Era 2D platformers, but the way I can keep approaching the game makes the levels feel so good for being shorter.Multiple characters to try with slightly different weaponry and Arcade Mode, combined with the already brilliant level designs, have me replaying like a madman to Git Gud.Huntdown incentives learning to be more aggressive in areas. You can snag a number of combo attacks, pull off eye-pleasing explosions and get a lot of one-liners.This is one of the most fun 2D Platformers I've played in a very long time.
_childDocuments_.name: HUNTDOWN

_childDocuments_.review: An awesome 2D action shooter that takes on an 80s theme and is chock-full of references dedicated to the decade, Escape From New York seemed to be a big influence in particular.  is beautifully detailed and colourful, which compliments all the explosive carnage throughout the campaign and Arcade Mode.You have a choice of three protagonists to take on the gangs of the criminal underworld. The gangs have their own themes and are composed of lieutenants and leaders who serve as mini bosses at the end of each stage. The protagonists and gang leaders are voice acted and feature unique personalities which really helps elevate the game's cheesy humour and charm.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is a template for what run-and-gun games should look like. Great 80's aesthetic with varying gangs and decent amount of differing levels. There are a good deal of guns and grenades that do add some variety, but the only knock would be it is short and does feel pretty repetitive as their isn't much variety at all to the gameplay loop, and adding abilities or things to unlock or some form of progression, or even levels with a vehicle or something would have made the game better, as even though it is short since its so repetitive it makes it feel longer which isn't necessarily great. The bosses are the best part, as they all have different feels, different design, and even on normal difficulty some of the later ones are pretty tough and required multiple tries to lean patterns and perfect dodging. 8/10.
_childDocuments_.name: HUNTDOWN

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely game. Awesome action. A lot of guns to choose from. Great replayability, which is needed because the game is short - you can finish it in maybe 3h? But you WILL certainly want to play it at least 2-3 times to completion. We need more levels! More brilliantly balanced bosses! More 80s/90s action movies references! Get this game, enjoy it, and support the devs so they can provide us with more content!
_childDocuments_.name: HUNTDOWN

_childDocuments_.review: Huntdown is stylized as an 80s contra shooter with 4 worlds with multiple bosses each. You choose from three agents that each have a different default gun and voicelines, and traverse through a story mode or arcade mode with varying difficulties available. Other guns, melee items, and projectiles can be acquired for time limited by ammo before defaulting back to your agent's main gun. You can even tap a partner in for local co-op play.I do recommend the game if the above sounds appealing. Huntdown brings some modern aspects to the genre by splashing in very unique bosses that could not have been achieved years ago on older systems. What stands out to me that might make this a regrettable purpose is the game is relatively short (unless you intend to replay levels for points and achievements), the gameplay outside the boss fights is not super novel, and there are many modern aspects not applied that feel like a lost opportunity--only three agents? No permanent upgrades? Nothing procedural or lengthy? It seems like the game would greatly benefit switching to a rogue like style, but as it is is still worth it on sale.If you enjoy this developer, I highly recommend Deep Rock Galactic, which has some design and music similarities.
_childDocuments_.name: HUNTDOWN

_childDocuments_.review: Huntdown is a pretty fun run and gun 2D shooter. Gorgeous 2D pixel art with a surprising variety of levels and bosses. No boss seems to rehash anything from a previous boss and each encounter definitely feels unique. This is the kind of game that you play purely for gameplay, but if you MUST know, the Shimamoto corporation has hired the three playable characters, John Sawyer, Anna Conda, and Mow Man, to take back the city from 4 notorious gangs. I’m sure you may have realized that the corporation we’re working for is using us to take down the rival gangs so it can have an easier time making their word law but like I said, this isn’t the kind of game you play for the story.Not really much else to say. My only issue with the game is that though you are mobile, it doesn’t feel as responsive as other Run and Gun games like Cuphead, and though you aren’t hampered significantly it’s a shame that you can’t aim in whatever direction you want like you can in Cuphead and metal Slug, but that may be intentional. One thing I can knock the game though is though the difficulty is tolerable, a lot of things can come out of left field and kill you quite unfairly, like the hoverboard enemies in the last area who fly at you while they are off the screen or enemies shooting at you literally as soon as they appear as you move right. In future titles, I’d hope that there would be better tells, and one good one I’d note is making it so maybe minor enemies can’t shoot while off screen or as soon as they appear.Anyway, took my brother and I about 4 hours, and I found it well worth it. This is definitely something I see myself replaying, so I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: HUNTDOWN

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a nostalgic game that will take you back to the days of the SNES with a more updated feel in controls you will like this one. This game places an emphasis on cover shooting but in a old-school 2D environment. There are fun hidden areas to find. A variety of weapon pick-ups.The downside is if you are a casual player (like myself) you might get frustrated at the difficulty. If you are not afraid of dying you will eventually figure out a pattern and the best way to get through the level. You might just get a little angry at the game before that happens.The music and aesthetic of the game has a very fun low-budget 80's feel. The characters each have unique weapons and strengths. 2 player remote play is available but no additional players. The game is worth checking out for the price tag.
_childDocuments_.name: HUNTDOWN

_childDocuments_.review: If you don't like this you need a bounty on your head.Brilliant game. One of the first times in years I've played a game & just thoroughly enjoyed every aspect of it.If this game had been released in the 90s, it'd be revered as a classic. It does everything the classics do but does it better. The pixel artwork is stunning. The weapons satisfying. The sound effects and voices on point. The levels feel alive. It can be unforgiving but never feels impossible. There's replayability. The enemies are full of character.I'm not sure what the negative reviews are on about to be honest.

_childDocuments_.name: HUNTDOWN

_childDocuments_.review: Huntdown is a tribute to the old action and sci-fi movies and classic "run and gun" games. It's full of crude humor (when i heard for the first the enemy from the gang "hoodlum dolls" shouting "dolls with the balls!", I was laughing outloud). Huntdown takes a lot from pop culture. Sometimes it fells like a merge of movies: Robocop (distopia, gangs, corporations), Mad Max ("motorized" gangs) and Bladerunner (cars and china town) and the like. But the game merges it into a new experience. You can see lots of references (i've noticed a movie poster of "The Thing" and a poster with Rachael Rosen) but at the same time the vibe feels unique. The gameplay gets really more tactical on hard difficulty level, where you understand that any weapon type you choose and a box you can cover behind really matter.
_childDocuments_.name: HUNTDOWN

_childDocuments_.review: Brings me back to my Yoof, playing games in the 80s and early 90s. Love the retro graphics, feels like an old Sega game. It's definitely fun, but possibly too much of a challenge at times. It's one of those games where you'll need lightening fingers, especially with some boss battles. If you like an arcade sideways scrolling shooter, that's obviously been designed by people with passion for old skool gaming, then you'll love it. It will stress you out though, be warned!
_childDocuments_.name: HUNTDOWN

_childDocuments_.review: Just about everything about this game is enjoyable and satisfying.  The whole game nails the kind of dystopic futuristic RoboCop vibe.  The look of it is perfect.  The scenarios and levels are fun and interesting.  The weapons are fun and the gibs are chunky.  It all goes for a theme and pulls it off really well.And I love the way the game spices of the basics of platforming.  It may not sound like much, but the game has a slide move you can do.  It's not like other games' slides, where it's more of a dodge.  This is a way to get just a tiny tiny boost of speed across a short distance while minimizing your exposure.  Add in the cover mechanic, which is sort of a mix of sticking to certain terrain and the "step into the background" approach of Blackthorne.  It makes the fact that bullets are flying around survivable and fun.  You could always run for cover, but why do that when you can slide?A very fun game.  At this point, I'm at the last set of levels, which will probably be another hour of gameplay.  I just wish there was more of the game - would love to see a Huntdown II build on this one some day.

_childDocuments_.review: Having been playing twin stick shooters with menacing bosses for quite a long time, I would recommend this game. The story in this game is nonexistent with you being a bounty hunter tasked with mowing down loads of enemies and miscreants down the street. Further, there are 3 characters for you to choose and to be frank, all 3 of them play just the same . The only big difference between them is the weapon loadout. Speaking of weapons, this game shines in that department with the groovy music added to the feeling. The enemies drop health packs and important weapon loot as you kill each one of them with shotguns, missile launchers, heavy machine guns and sniper rifles. Ooooffff.... the gameplay is just simply amazing.  The retro 8 bit graphics really suits well for this twin stick shooter as the setting reminds you of an old 80s vibe. Moving on , be ready to face tough bosses during the levels. The worst of them being the final boss which was getting on my nerves ( I did beat him eventually :)   ). Therefore, I would recommend you to play it on Easy Difficulty in your first sitting. The game isn't that long and can be completed within 2 hours minimum If you were to add in the arcade mode you would add in an extra hour making it 3 hours at best.  Pick this game on a deep 75 pct sale as the game is a bit short . Overall, I would give it a 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Huntdown is a fundamentally solid throwback run-‘n-gun action platformer which should make for a mostly fun time, but which may be outpaced by the bevy of alternatives within the genre. It’s a harder sell with all the strong competition out there, but it is worth playing in its own right.	You play as a bounty hunter with no moral code, killing riotous gangs for a payout – an eyebrow-raising premise for a game released in 2021, and one which the game seems to have no qualms with leaving unchallenged. Of course, story is hardly crucial to a game like this, and it mostly makes for a backdrop to the action. You do get to meet plenty of quirky characters in the boss encounters; they’re one-note, but they have memorable personalities. The protagonists, meanwhile, mostly exist to spout one-liners and action movie references, which has its own charm but leaves them somewhat shallow.	The combat is solid. There’s a decent cover system which isn’t too intrusive if you want to be more aggressive. If attacking up close, the attack button triggers a melee attack which shoves foes away. I wish this had its own button. There were some frustratingly finnicky instances where I found the melee attack unreliable, or where said melee attack interrupted my gunfire, and these scenarios each cost me more than a few lives. However, melee into gunfire is a satisfying one-two kill method that never gets old. At times, the combat really clicks and I’m disposing of enemies at a lightning clip; aggression can be unexpectedly rewarded too. At other times, the pitifully scant invincibility frames leave me dead in the blink of an eye.	Much like many a classic Mega Man game, Huntdown got better on replay, as I could more skillfully maneuver the stage, razing through foes and weaving through the bosses’ attack patterns. The first playthrough was perhaps the most frustrating part of my time with the game. Arcade mode can be more satisfying than Story mode, thanks to added positive feedback for skillful play and kill combos. It also provides a more stimulating gameplay loop, with the added pressure of limited lives, keeping combos going, and the larger droves of mooks. But Arcade mode can be frustrating in its own right, especially on later levels; I often found myself slammed with enemies approaching from all over, and the annoyingly sparse invincibility frames saw me dropping dead before I could even respond.	The name of the game is to keep moving forward, mowing down every foe between you and the level’s boss. Each character has their own default weapon and subweapon, with more options available to pick up throughout the stage. The weapon selection is varied, but the moment-to-moment gameplay is less so. The level design is fairly flat too, leaving it to the enemy types to spice up the action. In this way, I feel the flow and stage progression more closely resemble a beat-‘em-up game than an action platformer. In that same vein, positioning can prove crucial to survival, as you’ll be in a much better spot if you can keep enemies on one side of you.	The boss battles are clearly meant to be the standout encounters here, with more involved fights and patterns than when facing off against droves of mooks. They certainly managed to make the twenty boss fights creative and distinct, though they aren’t without faults. In particular, bosses can be absolute bullet sponges, and fights can drag. This also only makes it more exhausting to die, as you’ll be starting from the beginning of the fight, whittling down that daunting health bar all over again.	The presentation really stands out here. The soundtrack is nice and punchy, and I appreciate how each gang gets its own themes, instilling them with that little bit of extra identity. However, it’s the visuals that really steal the show. From the gorgeous title screen to the lovingly detailed environments, it’s clear Huntdown pulled no punches. Even the little animation flourishes elevate this beyond the game’s retro roots, such as how you can see visible damage on the environment, from destructible setpieces to bullet holes in the walls. Huntdown uses its many presentation components to paint a particularly moody atmosphere, enhanced further by the surprising amount of voice acting. Its style specifically harkens back to the FPS games of old, especially given how its main cultural point of reference seems to be 70s and 80s action flicks, from one-liners to pixelated recreations of film posters.	Huntdown may dissuade some with a tepid first impression. Its repetitious design and frustrating elements are genuinely disappointing, but I referenced the beat-‘em-up genre for a reason. Despite its shortcomings, if the combat clicks, I think it makes for a good, easy title to pick up. There are definitely better choices out there, but I do think Huntdown stands as a flawed but fun entry into the action platformer pantheon.

_childDocuments_.review: Highly Recommended!I love almost everything about this game, except a few unbalanced boss fights which essentially turn into dice rolls on hard. Also, this is nothing like Contra, May be a bit of Metal Slug, but not Contra.Very few games have managed to catch the retro cyberpunk theme as well as Huntdown, and I did nor feel bored for a single minute, even after 35 hours of playtime!Also, I am not a fan of "pixel art," but this game does it so well that I have to mark this one as an exception. Everything looks really good and detailed, despite the intentional and beautifully executed pixel style.Controls are buttery smooth, animations are slick and audio is decent enough (could have been much better!).I do hope the developers add more DLC though, because there is massive potential here.
_childDocuments_.name: HUNTDOWN

_childDocuments_.review: I don't need that many hours into the game to tell you this is a very good game. Simply put, if, like me, you grew up among the cigarettes fumes in an arcade, lost many quarters to the machines, and moved on to Genesis and Super Nintendo, and can't get over the fact that this era, with all its shortcomings, is still over, then Huntdown is for you.The pixel artstyle is great, the game is tough-but-fair, with very little luck involved but not too much die'n retry either. The devlopers listen to the players, as far as I'm concerned (they included a QoL change I suggested super fast), and the game's cheap yet I can tell there's some meat left on that bone.Also it doesn't beat around the bush with bullsh*t challenges and rewards everywhere, or daily quests or what-do-I-know: it gives you honest challenges and a medal for each on each level (killcount, 3 hidden collectibles, one life). That's it. And that's good. No mental load with side quest or in-game shop. As an old gamer, I appreciate it a lot.Seriously, just buy it.
_childDocuments_.name: HUNTDOWN

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful Amiga-era pixel art mixed with rock, freestyle, and synthwave provides the candy coating to complement Huntdown's challenging, intensely rewarding, and incredibly satisfying gameplay -- the creamy caramel center.But it's not enough for a video game to merely play well and also look and sound great, oh no. Huntdown, luckily elevates itself above the rest through its aesthetic -- a Verhoeven-esque cyberpunk world that pays homage to the juggernauts of vulgar cinema: Robocop, Escape From New York, Death Wish, and many others.Huntdown's own cast of characters is expertly voice-acted and written, blessing the game with the hilarious and attention-grabbing feel of a punchy action schlock movie you got on VHS at the video rental store next to the pizzeria you stopped at for dinner. I no-♥♥♥♥ guffawed out loud at some of the lines, even the simple ones like Anna Conda's "burn, baby, burn!" after setting several creeps alight with a flamethrower. It's all delivered so well that even the corny stuff feels good. (There's an early boss fight that had me exclaim "Oh, my god!" in complete shock when I first heard him speak. I won't spoil it but anyone who's gotten this far will know what I'm talking about.)Huntdown's platforming and gameplay feels so *right* in a way that can only be adequately attributed to extremely careful attention to its design. Streets of Rage-style weapon pickups along with a Castlevania-esque subweapon that can be changed out for tools like grenades or molotovs give your bounty hunters the edge they need to slaughter criminals wholesale and mop up the streets. Movement isn't quite as methodical or precarious as Castlevania, but your jumps and dashes have a momentum and weight to them that must be considered.I cannot recommend this game enough if you're a fan of action games, action movies, action one-liners, action music, or if you still need their thirst for cyberpunk slaked after last year's debacle left them high and dry. Don't sleep on Huntdown.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the best of this type. It's a must buy if you are into this kind of art style (early to mid 90s arcade/console pixel art), gameplay (co-op run n gun), and setting (80s/early 90s dystopian cyberpunk).One thing I miss about console games back in the day is that there were so many radical couch co-op games. Yeah they are out there for PC, I know but the majority are pretty subpar in quality. Modern retro style games in this genre that are actually solid experiences as both single player and multiplayer, don't come around as often as they should. Kinda reminds me of Duke Nukem aesthetic meets Broforce meets Metal Slug. It has excellent support for controllers and for people who like using arcade sticks (I use a modded Mayflash F500 V2), it works great with those as well. regarding remote play:It has worked flawlessly for me when I have played 2-player co-op (with remote play) with at least 5 different people on separate occasions since the time I purchased this game when it was released on Steam. It has also worked very well for the people I have played with. I do however realise that remote play still has a long ways to go, and often doesn't work as intended with many different games. Your experience may vary. I also agree that official online play support is most ideal, but I'm glad they put their efforts towards making the game better rather than putting energy into official online support. Still, would be nice to have something that can work for most people. Perhaps they could talk to Ghost Ship Games (who is distributed through the same independent publishing company, Coffee Stain) about getting P2P servers like they have in Deep Rock Galactic set up for Huntdown. It's unrealistic to expect dedicated servers for a game like this, but P2P under the right circumstances is plausible (I think?).Ultimately, it is the developers call whether or not they are able to allocate time and resources for this, based on their budget and where they want to take the game. It's lovely if they do, but sometimes these things aren't as logistically possible as they seem from the outside.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece in the 2D shooter genre. It nails EVERYTHING right. Don't let the aesthetic fool you into thinking that's why this game is so good. That's the icing on what's already a delicious cake. 1st of all, it is very aware of a lot of pitfalls in this genre.  Think of how Contra games gave you that bummed out feeling when you died while having the spreadshot gun. That's not a thing in this game. Weapons are constantly available in all the levels, so they aren't rare to get. Melee weapons have they distance disadvantage, but they make up for it with big damage. They all have limited ammo though so you can't keep any of them for long. All weapons you pick up feel powerful and do real damage, but your standard weapon also tows the line very well as it doesn't do puny damage (again, a far cry from Contra's pea shooters). Each character also has a distinct throwing item that does great damage and has a very short cooldown. It doesn't feel so bad when you run out of ammo for a weapon you picked up because your standard gear does a good job. 2nd, the actual combat is well thought out too. Enemies don't feel cheap like in a lot of other games. They don't jump around constantly like some dumb fodder enemies in most games of this kind. They are indeed fodder enemies, but most of them utilize the game's smartly designed cover system, or surprise you with numbers. Melee based enemies have their own unique challenge as they can damage you while in cover, giving you that pressure to move, but not in an unbalanced way. 3rd, each level has it's own thing going on with just enough difference for each level, and they're just the right length. They will vary quite a bit along the campaign. None of the levels are overly long, and the checkpoint system is placed at good intervals as you proceed through levels. You never feel like you have a long way to go in order to get back to where you died. Health pickups are common, but not in a way that makes the game super easy. Even boss battles have weapons and health available at the right time. Just when you feel like the next phase of a boss fight is too much, health becomes available. They really designed all this thoughtfully. 4th, the bosses are AMAZING in Huntdown. There's a lot of variety between all of them. No fight is really the same, and considering the fact that each stage has a boss, it's quite the achievement that no fight feels like the other. There's always some kind of little mechanic or element that differentiates them between one another. Despite the 2D shooter constraints these fights are all varied in great ways and hilarious too.5th, despite the 80's action aesthetic and the humor, this game is surprisingly and artfully written. A ton of games try to get by with crappy writing by making everything a joke. This game masterfully does what Ubisoft's attempts at 80's humor don't do: It's not overdone. Huntdown is a funny game, but it's thoughtfully funny. Jokes and quotes are not used to death. They're all in the appropriate spots to not make it stale, unpleasantly predictable or corny. It uses movie quotes, references, and is even self-conscience at times...when it's actually right to do so. I've laughed so much when the game wants to be funny, and they just stop when they should. It's strange to see this kind of balance. As far as video game love letters to action films of yesteryear go, this one takes the crown in the 2D side-scrolling shooter genre, hands down. 6th, it's the aesthetic. It's attempt to look like a Sega Genesis game from the 90's is beautifully executed. Honestly though, a ton of games do that well these days. There is an X-factor with this one though: Between you and me, I'm real tired of developers using cyberpunk styling as a lure to what are ultimately disappointing games (LOOKING AT YOU, CYBERPUNK 2077). Let me be clear. They are two separate genres. One of them is a small game with a small budget and a small team. Yes, the other is a enormous game with an enormous budget and an enormous team. But you know what? The truth is this Easy Trigger Games is more successful at utilizing the cyberpunk theme in a satisfying way. How? They did not over-promise and under-deliver. The game itself is absolutely what the trailers imply.  You're getting a cyberpunk 80's themed 2D side-scrolling shooter with humor and it's executed flawlessly, unlike the legion of cyberpunk themed games out there. That means a lot to me, and I'm sure it does to you. If you are even remotely interested in what this game offers, please buy it. Devs that do what they say deserve every penny, and this small team deserves all the credit they can get for making a game with this incredible degree of quality.   10 out of 10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent 90s inspired Run n Gun shooter - very tight and responsive controls, great sound design, good level design, and a lot of character to the enemies and bosses. Can feel slightly unfair at times, but pattern recognition will always have you kick everyone's butt quite easily (if annoyingly): see the Nadja and Murdoch boss fights as an example. The characters are more like playstyles: Anna is 'balanced', John is 'power', and Mow Man is 'speed'. I stuck to Mow Man because of his lines and his spammy pistol - rip my fingers.Only minor gripe: the music could be better than the 'ha ha 80s retro vaporwave' trend, but otherwise extremely solid game overall. Almost wrote it off at the beginning because it was easy, but difficulty picked up soon enough to keep me happy.

name: Unto The End
detailed_description: Coverage 'An experience that doesn't quite fit inside a specific genre... From beginning to end Unto the End is immensely rewarding and captivating' Screen Rant – 9/10 'Unto The End is not an easy game, but it is only as hard as you make it for yourself... Easy to recommend to those who enjoy tough fighting challenges' TheSixthAxis – 9/10 'Unlike anything that I’ve had the opportunity to play before... Despite existing only on a two-dimensional plane, 2 Ton Studios has somehow managed to cram the heart of a 'Souls' game into this diminutive package' PC Invasion – 8/10 'If you're a fan of tough but rewarding games that aren't unfair or constantly cheap, this one is certainly worth a look' Finger Guns – 8/10 About the Game You play an average warrior trying to get home to their family. Kill everything you see or look for ways to avoid bloodshed. Sword fighting is challenging and unforgiving. It demands practice and recognition of subtle tells. Likewise, finding peaceful resolutions requires keen observation of your opponents and their surroundings. The choice is yours. Defense-first Sword fighting One of a kind defense-first sword fighting system focused on skill and mastery, designed and built from the ground up specifically for 2D. Fight intelligently and strike tactically with your sword and range weapons in fierce one-on-one and group battles. Opponents not enemies Each creature you meet is unique. They are scared, territorial and have families, just like you. They learn during fights, better defending against your attacks. And every one of them can be passed without bloodshed if you correctly read their tells and the environment around them. Minimal handholding A challenging single-player experience with minimal handholding. All the father's abilities are available from the outset and mastery of those skills, as well as keen observation of your surroundings, are key to survival and success.

_childDocuments_.review: Feels harsh to vote this down, as this game is clearly a labour of love, and there's a lot that should be liked about its intentions.But good grief, the combat mechanics are absolutely grade A broken and imbalanced, full of issues that balk at the idea of fairness, and side with just plain pot luck.Now, the complaint of the combat in general is obviously ripe for the "git gud" response, and I can accept that. But I just can't get my head around the general attack+parry mechanic here, which constitutes for 90% of the gameplay. Things like rolling and charging serve limited purposes due to the jankiness of hit detection, and AI cheating, which we'll come onto in a bit. But, just in general... enemy attacks are way too fast and visually inconsistent to block half a dozen times in a row to succeed. There should have been far more lenience in not just the timing of attacks, but how they're visually represented. Certain enemies, like the spear enemies, will do an overhead attack, which is clearly a High Attack, and a low reaching attack for Low Attack. But they can also do a thrust, which counts as high. But it really is too difficult to define between Low and High within a milisecond. It's just a really disingenuous system designed to confuse, and it feels like it betrays the whole point of having a Rhythmic combat system. It somewhat reminds of the vagaries of Sekiro's Perilous Attack system, where distinguishing between sweeps and thrusts was kinda obtuse. But the difference is there were far more options to adapt, and far more forgiveness for failing one input.My main problem is the AI itself, which, for want of better terminology, cheats. Or at the very least, has a very stringent set of behaviour checks that betrays a combat system which should be adaptive. This can be seen most with how enemies will instantly roll/sidestep out of your shoulder charges, in a very consistent manner. I tried and tested a very specific combo, and the process just kept repeating itself. I would block an attack and then use shoulder charge, for it to be instantly avoided, again and again and again, when visually and mechanically it doesn't make any sense that the enemy could achieve such an instantaneous dodge. We're talking Psycho Mantis levels of reading inputs here. It didn't matter how many times I repeated the process, the enemy would keep doing this over and over, almost as if there is some kind of RNG in play, that will not allow an enemy to succumb to a specific action, until certain other paramaters are met. This seems evident with other actions, too, like the fakeouts. At certain times in a fight, an enemy will be vulnerable to reacting to a fakeout, then at other times, they completely ignore it in a predetermined fashion. In fact, this seems true with almost any action. If you roll into a charge and succeed with it, it likely won't work again. Perhaps that's the enemy learning from a mistake? Maybe. But why would they potentially insta dodge this action the first time, and let it occur afterwards. It just makes little sense, and the fakeouts are worse in this regards, because it's never really apparent when the enemy may or may not succumb to a fakeout. It's just an RNG state you gamble with. And that's why you will just revert to engaging with the parry system for a lot of enemies.Which brings us to the viable way for most people to play the game - Assist mode. It's good the game has this, but it doesn't really approach the previously stated issues, and only adds further tedium, because it slows the entirety of the combat down. What needed to be addressed was simply the speed and visual representation of attacks in the game.

With Swordplay.You move very slow, and rolling  is your last, desperate action because its most likely the last Thing you do before getting stabbed.Each Encounter has its own ways to be solved, more than once in a peaceful way, for example by sheeting your sword, running past, waiting or friendly offerings. Sometimes tho you have to take the fight:PRO:-different attack options (throw, feint, tackle, heavy light attack-interesting health system, you become slower the more wounded you are-combat system seems like it wants you to"git good"...CON:-...but you cant "git good", because the majority of the Combat Encounters confronts you with very distinct and different Types of Enemys. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR — This game offers the opportunity to retrain habits and find rest.I'm not gonna regurgitate things already said in other reviews. Anyone can tell you "this game is hard", whether that's why they recommend it or not. They've also done a decent job of explaining  it's hard. But no one mentions what I love most about Unto The End and why I stuck with it even though I got reeeal salty.So, without further ado, here we go . . .You and I learn a lot without realizing it. We have habits, and often aren't even aware of them. Games are no exception. While  (the link is to youtube), returning gamers face a different issue: What happens when your habits backfire?Those can be simple enough to resolve, like when Mirror's Edge forced me to jump with the left bumper rather than A.But what happens when the habits are broader than merely button mappings?The modern world is busy. Work, school, and media—we're often pressured to work as fast and efficient as possible. This creates a habit of "busy-ness" and "speedy pacing" within us. The thing is, this pace can be fun! The rise of movement shooters (Titanfall, Apex Legends) and the plethora of movement-focused platformers and bullet-hell games prove that. We like action movies  they're full of explosions and dynamic combat. (And if you study media over the past 50 years, you'll notice a trend towards faster pacing and shorter attention spans.). . . but this pace is also exhausting. Professional burnout, mental breakdowns, domestic PTSD, depression, addictions, and other such issues are strongly linked to this frenetic life-pace without rest. This speed isn't unhealthy by itself, but when we never rest, that's when it starts to destroy us.Unto The End intentionally bucks the popular trend of meeting the average players where they're at, and instead opts for a system that forces players to slow down. (Each individual strike may be too fast to react to at first; but the overall pacing of a fight is much slower than we're used to.)This. Is. Frustrating.Popular games have forgiving mechanics that allow players to play at their own pace. But that's one reason why they're so popular: they don't require players to change such a deeply ingrained habit. Unto The End doesn't only require precision in gameplay in order to win. It requires players to take a breath . . . slow down . . . let go of their frustration . . . take a break . . . and dive back in.The entire identity of the game is wrapped around this concept. It's not merely the combat mechanics, but the visuals, the sound design, the environmental storytelling, and specific in-game moments. Unto The End whispers, "Stop for a moment. Look, and take it all in. Then you'll find what you're looking for." I myself am recovering from childhood trauma, and I yelled at the screen a few times because of it. But I also recognize therapy when it's offered to me. Now, after playing Unto The End, I can breathe a little bit deeper . . . I can pause a little bit longer . . . I can go to work, and I don't feel as overwhelmed or pressured by life. It reminds me of when Jesus said, "Come to me all who are weary, and I will give you rest." Yet, to be a follower of Christ also means metaphorically "taking up our cross" and "dying daily". It means facing things about myself that I don't want to see, being provoked, angered, terrified . . . and still enduring. But I've endured for 9+ years now, and I've experienced the peace and joy which comes only from remaining faithful through horrible circumstances. The only way to find peace and rest and healing is to endure the pain and frustration of retraining the habits we never knew we learned. And the ability to rest in the midst of hell is itself a skill (a habit) we only gain by training.What I'm saying is, the only way back home is to endure unto the end.That's where the game gets it's name.
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: (UTE) is a single-player fantasy adventure focused on melee combat, exploration and interaction diversity. Players impersonate "The Father", that chooses to depart for a perilous journey across the ice-encrusted mountains, snowy valleys and dark caverns of the region. The protagonist's travels will be harsh: local inhabitants don't react kindly to visitors, with treacherous terrain and scarcity of resources on top of that. In an untamed land full of different cultures and opportunities, Father's journey will prove to be more than mere survival as his actions will determine the fate of many, including himself.🟩 🟥 🎮 Gameplay is divided into Exploration, Combat and Character Management.Is performed on foot, through the hazardous terrain of the mountainous region where UTE is set. Ranging from caverns to icy cliffs and snowy paths, the environments proposed are not that varied but well done. While exploring, Father can loot resources from certain scene elements such as piles of twigs, corpses or dead animals - this is very important to keep the protagonist stocked at all times, as running out of supplies (especially Herbs) often proves lethal. There are many secret areas and divergent paths in each location, often hidden or less obvious to reach. These places may contain more resources, easier shortcuts, or even unique items that can impact Father's combat proficiency or allow hidden interactions. Most characters encountered are at first neutral, and depending on the player's past and current actions they may turn hostile or leave peacefully. Level design is linear as several places have one-way drops, autosaves happen often but can be overridden by sitting at campfires, found sparingly, to also heal and craft better equipment if possible.Is highly skill-based, and uses an original system comprising Dodge rolls in a souls style, Feints to mislead the enemy, Directional Blocks (High and Low) to counter enemy attacks, Bashing to knock enemies down, and Throwing a single dagger to stun and damage the opponent. Enemies are often fast, highly lethal (most 1-2 shot) and even appear in multiple numbers in some occasions. Using the right tactic at the right moment is essential, as each enemy is never the same so the strategy that carried Father up to a certain progress may not be successful with the next foe.Even victory sometimes doesn't end the struggle. Bleeding wounds can still kill players if they happen to not have the necessary healing supplies to hold on until the next Bonfire is found: this results in losing progress all the way back before the last fight, and is a way to tell players "you won, but didn't do well enough and were unprepared".Is performed via an inventory menu holding resources and unique items alike. Some of such items can be used in specific occasions (for the player to understand) in order to gain an advantage or avoid conflict. The quick crafting menu allows igniting and making Torches to light the way, while also a single Dagger to throw if the previous one was lost. At Bonfires, players have extended crafting options, as a Tonic Flask can be brewed to heal all wounds on the go, while existing ones can be healed for free there. Armor can be improved with materials, however it will degrade and break over time, requiring more maintenance but also making Father more resilient.

_childDocuments_.review: ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ (UTE) is a cinematic platformer that like several other indies rakes in uniqueness and originality. The main focus is the challenging combat that has excellent nuance. It doesn’t have much of a setup nor does it try and hold your hand at all. I should also address the storyline or rather, lack thereof. All that is shown is a Father leaves his family to presumably go on a hunting expedition. Of course, it isn’t long before he gets into trouble and players must aid him through an unrelenting frozen wasteland to return to his home.▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬UTE sets a high bar for itself right at the start by saying this game is different. And it delivers. Combat is brutal and most fights will end with just a few hits. You can’t spam buttons to cut through monsters, as that will make you vulnerable. Instead, observation and perseverance are vital. Opponents come in a variety of shapes and sizes, and they each have differing battle tactics that help keep things fresh. Fighting also has a steep learning curve as players can do light and heavy attacks, feint at an enemy, bash them with their shoulder, dodge roll, and even throw their dagger or spear.Most fights will only involve one or two enemies but keeping an eye on each one and learning when to strike is the key. It’s not numbers that will overwhelm you here, but rather that they don't have set pattern attacks. You must learn how they will strike depending on their poses. Even then in some cases, you need to be quick to change how you are blocking, or duck and roll out of the fray. As you get used to the system, some fights will feel easier but the game is never without challenge for long. Some fights can be even unfair but the game does have an assist setting that slows enemy attacks down so you have more time to read and react.With the punishing combat into account, dying is commonplace. However, UTE offers frequent checkpoints under one condition and that is if you're uninjured. If not so, there are multiple ways to heal. Crafting a potion from collected herbs and tending to Father's wounds at a campfire will bring him back to full health. Although, there will be stretches where he has already used a potion and there is no access to a campfire. Eating herbs will slow the bleeding, but it won't open checkpoints back up.  Other items such as leather, sticks, and bones can be gathered as well to make torches or armor improvements.There will be times when he can avoid conflict altogether. When he comes across these creatures, something as simple as sheathing your sword and offering up the correct item can grant him a brief friendship, whereas the wrong item can end in a fight. He can’t avoid every fight like this but it’s nice that the world isn’t against him all the time.If I was to describe the overall visuals of UTE in a single word, the first that comes to mind is minimalistic. The minimalism has been merged with a wide range of locations and weather conditions. Another strong point is the lightning which helps to set an ominous mood throughout this death march.The sound design does a solid job of creating the atmosphere. Everything from the sounds of water dripping from the ceiling to snow crunching underfoot and the breath of Father works well at drawing you in. The music is subtle but builds up in the right places to create a catchy atmosphere.🔹🔹The game uses about 60% of VRAM at 1680x1050 60 FPS.🔹🔹▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬UTE is wonderfully minimalist with nuanced combat. While I enjoyed mastering the fights, it's unforgiving and can get frustrating to some folks. Each failure teaches the player more about the mechanics and the result is a satisfying experience, even though it finishes before you put what you've learned to more use.▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: Unto the end is a cinematic platformer which pushes the player through a minimalist story of violence and perseverance. The main content is the battle system, which is punishingly hard.  While there are many options for combat, those options are fairly under-utilized. Ultimately each encounter comes down to understanding the enemy tells and countering them accurately. Room for different tactics is very limited. I can appreciate that the combat system is meant to emphasize the deadliness of the game world and to make the fights seem like desperate battles for survival. At its best the game delivers on that vision perfectly. Ultimately the game failed to motivate me to push through the difficult battles - the story did not grab me, nor was the exploration particularly engaging. It wasn't that I was dying much, it was that I didn't care to spend time bashing my head against an enemy over and over again just for the sake of being able to spend more time doing that on the next enemy.While I would not recommend this game to most, it might just be the game for some cinematic platformer enthusiasts out there.

_childDocuments_.review: , even though it has a heavy price tag for how short it is (beaten in 4 hours) and the combat is decorated with frustrating imperfections, I found myself accepting the faults of the game since it was an impressionable experience.Unto The End is a 2D action platformer and is the debut release by 2 Ton Studios. You play as a nameless faceless father who goes out to hunt for food, only to have the land crumble below him, dropping him into a cavern full of enemies and characters alike that may help or hurt him on his journey home. The game features clean, high quality visuals, incredible sound design, and enough worldbuilding details to put the devil to bed.The game will take you through a couple of different regions including forests, villages, and mountaintops where you’ll face both generic and unique enemies that would resemble bosses. All beatable, but with all their own patterns that need to be picked up in order to overcome them. However, you won’t have to fight  as there are some NPCs that are neutral and would rather have a gesture of peace, sometimes leading to an item that can help you on your quest.When it comes to combat, the game operates in highs and lows in both strikes and blocking. In addition to those, there’s dodging, jumping, ducking, shoulder bashes, a throwing/stabbing dagger, and feints. Combined, these should allow you to overcome every foe with time, experience, and a dozen deaths at least. If you successfully block enough of an opponent's hits you’ll have a chance to hit them back with a specific type of strike called a riposte. You’ll also learn as the game goes on that your opponents don’t always follow the combat rules. If you find yourself having trouble, you can turn on  in the options menu which will slow down the combat a little bit so you have more opportunity.In addition to combat, there’s some self-management via the knapsack - you’ll pick up items in trade as well as items off of corpses and piles of supplies and trash. Also in the knapsack, you’ll be able to drink a crafted healing potion, light a torch which consumes a stick, and craft a bone dagger in case you lost the original one you had. You’re also able to eat herbs if you decide not to craft a potion out of them, which just slows your bleeding.Speaking of damage, this game also features a minimalistic UI which is only visible in the Start Menu or the knapsack. There’s no health bar or stamina meter or anything of the sort - you’ll only be able to tell how you’re doing based on the amount of blood on your character, which is also featured on your enemies. While you can heal these with the healing potions, you can only craft these at the uncommon campfires. While also at campfires, you can repair, craft, or upgrade armor and heal your wounds at the cost of no resources. There’s also the ability to spar with a memory of your partner if you need help warming up.I think I’ve covered the foundation, so let’s move into the things I enjoyed.The thing I enjoyed the most was the game’s art direction, both visually and audibly. The landscapes, characters, and objects are all well designed. The effects that they give off compliment them well; the sparks from striking a hard object, or the embers from a torch as you walk through the dark cave. To compliment the visuals, the sound design is just as great; I originally thought it to be strange that music wasn’t predominant, but I began to appreciate that as I picked up on all the other sounds the game produced. The game has features a small handful of sound cues that help you, but there’s a lot of flavor to some of the others like the labored breathing of the character, or the cue of an upcoming riposte.Another thing I enjoyed is the progression or the reward of defeating formidable foes. Not to be confused with combat, since I have my own separate thoughts on that, but the achievement of overcoming your foes feels great. It has its own sound cue which is incredibly satisfying after getting your face kicked in for the last twenty minutes. In addition, there’s also plenty of opportunities to trick enemies into hurting each other if you’ve found yourself in an uneven battle which feels great to pull off.Lastly, I appreciate the details when it comes to interacting with neutral and peaceful NPCs. While you can trade and offer things to NPCs, there are some other characters who’re in some life-or-death situations. In most games, you would have absolutely no capability in helping them, but in Unto the End, you have small windows of opportunities to make a difference. While I’m unsure if this actually brings anything to the overall ending, I appreciate the ability to make an impact in the little fictional storyline.Now that I’ve covered the good, let’s talk about the things I liked a little less.So I have two main topics that end up touching some of the others by relation. The first is the knapsack - I played on a PS4 controller on DS4 Windows software. Every once in awhile, my knapsack would no longer respond (to the “Share” button on the controller). If this happened, I had to close and re-open the game. While this isn’t  it can be highly convenient, and it even exposed a problem with the save system.While the save system is pretty linear -- one slot with auto-saving only it seems, there was a part where I had picked up a spear and went to a nearby campfire that had some NPCs. I wanted to try and trade something to the NPCs but my knapsack wouldn’t open, and after reloading the game the NPCs and the spear were gone. Unfortunately since there’s only one save slot, I had to just press on, but it was disappointing to see that happen.Like many others, combat had some frustrating parts to it. My main gripe was particularly with feigning attacks -- it never worked for me. I tried it several times but always ended up just getting hit by the enemy. I realized that even if I was feigning, I’d rather just try and do a shoulder bash for the knockdown effect which made me question feigning’s overall use. Speaking of the shoulder bash, that leads me to my next point.There is a shoulder-bash combo exploit for regular-sized opponents. Essentially, you can chain together a knockdown with a hit until they randomly block from prone  you push them into a wall. Now, you don’t  to take advantage of this, but if you’re upset with your current obstacle maybe it’s a solution for you until it gets patched. I only did this to three enemies to test for consistency before stopping since it detracted from the experience.All-in-all, combat has its own problems like enemies perfectly blocking or dodging almost all of your shoulder bashes which just seems unordinary. It’s unfortunate that it seems like even you throwing a mixup has nearly zero chance of hitting because it shoe horns combat into going into relying on riposting for success.That’s all the character count I’ve got room for - if you're wary of the content, at least wait for a sale. I think the game is worth experiencing if you are a fan of the things I thought were great in this review.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start of by saying that I have now beat this game 3 times. This game is truly a 9/10 for me as a standalone game. Does this mean this game is perfect? No. Does it mean it's for everyone? No. First: the not so good of this game. Initially, the combat in the game feels clunky. It's quite difficult to learn early on, and the first play through can be VERY frustrating at times. Once the combat is learned well, it feels very satisfying though, but it never gets easier. There are no tutorials in game except for the "sparing area" which can be accessed from any fire. Though this helps with the basics, I wish there were a few more advanced techniques gone over. Another con for the game is the apparent random damage amount a player takes from enemies. It feels like sometimes you're really hardy, and other times you're a piece of over ripe fruit. Initially this can be frustrating, and apparently illogical, but after DM'ing 2TON about this in the game, I was told that damage variance comes from the current position of vulnerability the character is in. For example: if you are rolling when you are hit, you take 2 or 3 times the damage than if you are in a guarded position. As a design decision, I think that this makes sense for the type of game this is, but I would like to have maybe seen at least a mention of this in the "sparing area". Last con for this game is that in some areas visibility of the character is frustratingly difficult where you need to interact with something because of placement of a rock or something.Now let's get to the good part: the pros. I would be doing a disservice to this game by not starting my PRO's list with the story. (NO SPOILERS). The story of this game is gripping, subtle and incredibly told. There is no pomp and circumstance ever with the story, meaning every part of the story is either organically uncovered, or gently set in front of the player but never shoved in the players face. What this means, is that it feels like as you play the game YOU are living the story, not being told it. I would be lying if I said that parts of this game did not make me emotional. Second pro for me: the characters ability, or lack there of. This directly connects to the story, and is consistent with the plot, but your character is NOT a super human in any ways. I heard Stephen, one of the creators of this game, describe the main character as a "farmer with a sword", which is exactly what it feels like. At no time are you over powered, or even any better than any of the enemies at all. Your character doesn't get more powerful, you just have to get better at the game. What this means is that combat in this game feels extremely realistic. Every encounter feels desperate, and that it takes everything in you to do, making the game feel immersive and purposeful. Never boring. Even though the combat in this game definitely has it's cons (as listed above), overall I very much enjoyed it. Even though the character isn't particularly good with a sword, the way that combat is structured feels visceral and bad ass. (Pro tip: use spears whenever you can. They are awesome). To conclude I want to acknowledge that this game is not for everyone. It is punishing and brutal, and definitely has some quirks. That being said the world building, art, and feel of the game is addicting. The only other  game that I have played that has given me similar vibe is Rain World. So if you are up to the challenge and want to live through an incredible story: definitely play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very nice, entertaining game, but it is too short and costs too much for the experience. There is no story, the game is solely battle-based and the battles are not many. You could easily finish the game in 1 - 2 hours and there is no real replay value. _childDocuments_.review: I decided to write this review after finishing the game twice, and reading users' reviews, as the negative ones pissed me off. Yes, the game is rather short, but the adventure it offers is worth it. Yes, the fighting system is unfairly balanced. BUT THAT's THE IDEA!As a fencer, i'm always on the lookout for good swordplay games with smart systems that offer the joy of attack and parry play. And this one delivers. It's tough, it's fast, but IT'S DOABLE as long as you stay calm and observant.THIS GAME IS WHAT IT PROMISES TO BE on its intro screen. And the contract is there, respected. Think Rain World, but with a dynamic sword play system, and you'll get it.I just wish it was as long as Rain World, my only regret.But i happily return to it, just for the sword fights.

_childDocuments_.review: Really charming art style, good sound design. I want to like it, but I don't. I think it's too hard, and not in a good way. My character moves like he's got molasses in his veins, the timing on parries and dodges feels inconsistent, etc.One fight in particular a couple of hours into the game involving an enemy with throwable spears and another enemy without them took me probably 30+ tries to beat. I have beaten Dark Souls 3, Bloodborne and Sekiro each multiple times, so I certainly understand and can appreciate the idea that a game like this intends me to learn lessons from losing. I did so. I adjusted my tactics to this fight and within a small handful of failed attempts understood that I should do things like (1) let him throw his spear into the other guy (2) dodge his spears until he is out of them (3) watch for the jump attack and dodge instead of trying to block it (4) block attacks until I hear the "parry sound" indicating I can strike. Even knowing all these things I failed the fight more times than seemed justified due to what felt like inconsistent iframes, block times, etc. I eventually beat this fight and felt slightly rewarded by it and continued to play on only to end up shortly after in another weird fight between two enemies, this time in a cramped place with no way for me to back track and look for a camp fire to heal at, etc. After about 15 failed attempts at this I just didn't have the energy or desire to give a sh*t what happens afterward. Gonna try the game again in a few months, see if they figure any of these issues out.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the idea of the game and the art style, i love idea of the combat.. lets give it a buy... I played for about an hour, messing about with the combat trainer and trying to see if i preferred the pad of the keyboard (i preferred the keyboard), after which i started my journey. i spent another hour working my way through the caves, found a helm, made some makeshift armour and i really loved everything up to now.. i sent messages to all my mates telling them to have a look at this little gem of a game.. i killed a troll, i killed another after being beaten to death by a dear.. i killed some more "boss" type enemies and i exited a cave.. i walked... i walked some more.. the end! what! the end! not even 3 hours in the actual game and i find myself starting it all over.. _childDocuments_.review: A polished cinematic platformer with excellent melee combat.You are a father gone hunting who finds himself trapped in the caves below, where cold and darkness reign. Yet there are those who claimed this place to live in. Outlandish inhabitants of the caves have their own motives in the world and are wary of you. How will you, strange creature from above, choose to interact with them, and find a way back home?Unto the End does two things remarkably well. First is environmental design which is very deliberate and will provide you with all the clues you need through visual presentation: observe, consider what you see and act accordingly. Second are combat mechanics, with detailed animation and complex, responsive read-react melee system providing many options, which means it might present a longer learning curve to truly master but is very enjoyable once you do and cannot be experienced elsewhere.If for any reason you don’t like combat, you can play through the game without engaging in battle at all. Additionally, combat isn’t commonly an appropriate solution to a situation. Experience is evidently intended to be realistic and best way to play is to act as you would if you were really there, in the skin of lost father.A lot of negativity in reviews comes from people begruding the game its length. It’s true that game is relatively short. It was also made by a small, very dedicated team and if it comes down to a choice between quality or quantity, i would choose quality any time.A suggestion for delevopers: You’ve succeeded in making both remarkable and distinctive melee system; consider releasing an arena DLC or an altogether new game primarily focused on combat encounters. It has reasonable potential to become a hit in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: Combat feels unfair, not hard. Most encounters with enemies or traps seem designed to kill you at least once, with no way of knowing what's about to happen. Game feels repetitive and tedious. Very short game. Very simple and basic story with no depth. I don't think it's worth the money, I highly advise against buying this game.Longer version:--Boring Combat--At first, the combat seems good, with various possible actions to take. Enemies telegraph most of their attacks enough to be able to defend, even when it's only a short window. But you quickly  realize that most moves are pointless and ineffective outside of the tutorial and sparring, and that having to defend using an analog stick (I used a controller as the game recommends), can feel pretty awkward at times. Both feinting and shoulder bumps seemed useless against most enemies I tried it with, and I quickly gave up on using them. I just ended up sticking with basic defending and attacking. The game also leads to believe in the tutorial/sparring that if an enemy attacks high, you can defend and then attack low since in order to attack high they have to expose themselves to low attacks, and vice versa. Good luck trying to pull that off against enemies though, as a lot of them will just effortlessly block it before they keep attacking. I ended up just having to parry enough attacks for them to get stunned and then attack them... in pretty much every single fight.--Unfair Combat--Not only do you have the classic trope where an enemy only needs a couple of attacks to kill you while you need several, this game, unlike something such as dark souls (which a lot of people seem to compare it to), is mostly based on reaction time. The intervals are so so small, that even if you know exactly what the enemy is about to do, you can still miss it. This is even harder when you play with a controller and try to block using the analog stick. At the beginning of the game, most enemies will make it fairly obvious if they are attacking low or high, but at a certain point you not only get enemies with attacks that are pretty much impossible to predict whether it's high or low until after the fact, but you have enemies with an attack for which the movement starts low, and all of a sudden hits you high, which again is impossible to know before you get hit by it. Finally, the devs seem to mention how every encounter is hand crafted, but a necessary footnote would be that they are designed not only to be unfair, but to kill you on your first try. Take three different examples:1) In some encounters, there will be parts of the map that will block your vision, making an already hard combat system even harder by not allowing you to see what your enemy is doing unless you stand in a very specific spot.2) At one point, you start a fight with what seems to be only one enemy, and suddenly a spear will fly at you off screen taking most of your health. There's no clue that he's there, and there's basically no way to dodge the spear unless you already know it's coming.3) At one point you cross a large gap by walking across 2 boulders. At this point in the game, you would assume that these would fall off when you walk on them so you must be quick. And you would be right. What you don't know, is that the other bigger boulder standing on the other side that can be easily be mistaken for part of the background scenery (especially in such a dark cave) is actually about to fall backwards into the gap to replace the other boulders, and if you try to go forwards you actually can't and it will fall on you. Even if you don't go forwards, there's basically no time to react to the boulder falling since it falls so fast the only way to dodge is if you know it's about to happen and you are ready before it even happens.--Trading and avoiding fights--When you are walking around the world you will often find non hostile NPCs that you can trade with, that you can give stuff too, and those that you need to give something in order for them to grant you passage or offer another valuable item. The problem with this, is that with the exception of NPCs that are clearly bleeding and injured and need medicine, there are no clues what so ever for what an NPC might want. And you if give them the wrong thing, they will immediately turn hostile and attack you. Another thing is at several points in the game, in order to interact with an enemy you can click LB and it will open up the bag for you to decide what to offer. Other times, LB does nothing, leading you to assume you cannot trade or interact with them. This is not true as with some NPCs, even if LB does nothing, you can still open you menu and offer them things, and they will react.--Edit: Story and Other Stuff--After writing this review I decided to give another try, since I already paid for it. And some how it only got worse. Found a guy that is basically the epitome of unfairness. He kills you in one hit, he has unblock-able attacks that you won't know are unblock-able until you try to block them, he will start to wind up an attack and if you try to shoulder charge him he will just stop in the middle of the attack to dodge you, and he takes more than 5 hits to kill. I don't know how many exactly because I couldn't kill him. I ended up searching for the ending online and turns out that's pretty much the final fight, and I'm only 3 and half hours into the game. And I'm not exactly breezing through the game if you couldn't tell.As for the story and ending, the whole game is just you trying to find a way back home, and the ending is you seeing the house in the distance and the credits rolling. That's it. It's up to you if you think this game deserves your money.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I want to recommend this game, I can't.I like the art style and I adore games where the story is told through visuals and the environment.But the reason why I do not recommend the game is because of the combat, which is a huge part of this game.The combat is pretty much trial and error..You first have to die 20 times against the same enemy to figure out what attacks of them are upper or lower attacks because sometimes they are not what they appear, you have to block upward or downward in order to do an effective block, failing this could be fatal to you..Then you have to be lucky that there is no foreground blocking your view which can be very frustrating. And you have to be lucky to be fighting near a light source if you are in a dark area..You basically have to 'train' yourself against literally every enemy (dying and reloading over and over again), so that you can react within a millisecond to their attacks because some attacks happen so fast that you barely have any time to process what is happening..At that point is becomes tiring and frustrating and it takes all the fun away..The only way to play the game at that time, is with assist mode - Where time will slow down when you engage in combat but even then the slightest mistake can screw you over..Yay fun..

_childDocuments_.review: Greetings! Here is a true depiction for UTE (Unto The End)1. Game is NOT a dark-souls clone. Arcade style sword/board with barrel rolling isn't here at all and THANKFULLY2. Combat is Punch-Out style where your reactions and clever adaptation will rule the day3. Beautiful somber environments kept me fully immersed, incredible sfx and OST Difficult as it may be, i've seen alot of "reviews" being negative, for that I am not surprised. Not because it is true but since the game is not holding your hand, it give you the freedom to explore however you wish, interact how you like with creatures, sometimes NOT even having to fight. I won't spoil it but you are not invincible Kratos from God of War here. You must truly plan each interaction and make sure that you have all you wits. These elements are so rewarding when the challenge also just as intended. I do wish for more of the game, the ending left me wanting more! _childDocuments_.review: I would call Unto the End a harsh game. From the moment you set out, leaving your wife and daughter and home behind for some unknown mission amid the frigid winter winds and snow, you feel it. That stark, unforgiving isolation. Your breath is shivery and turns to frost. The only warmth you will know in the wilderness and beneath it are the sparse fires and the memories you carry.There is a tutorial, an optional one, and it far from explains the rules to you. This is intentional. You will fall, you will bleed. Your torch and dagger may become lost, and those lucky enough to have the means to craft armor will see it splintered. Never once did I have the supplies for more than simple bone bracers. But as you stumble, you will learn -- what you are allowed to do, how not all is as it seems...that to survive, a man must be observant and understanding of the world he dares to cross, and above all resourceful. (Trying not to spoil anything here :P)The combat is unforgiving. I'm not Sonicfox or anything, but I say this as someone who cut their teeth on early 2000s FPSes and used to play For Honor pretty seriously. There is an option to turn down the enemy attack speed, but I felt it would betray the character of the game to do so. As someone who hates repeating boss battles and failing often, I didn't care a damn that I died twenty times to a single foe. I felt compelled to rise to the challenge. Most enemies feel very unique, not necessarily because of their attack patterns, but in the ways you meet them, the ways they present themselves and challenge you. So often I felt remorse for the foes I ended. So much was left unsaid.I will admit of the combat that a couple mechanics shown in the tutorial are totally unnecessary. There is not a single enemy, for example, you will need to feint attacks on. It's far too slow to do so, and foes have too much attack priority to risk wasting a window. As such, the combat is ultimately pretty rudimentary: learn the enemy attack patterns through trial and error, be quick on your blocks, be prepared to duck or roll, and stab when they're tired or leave an opening. I still enjoyed it considerably, but I can imagine some folks might want something more complex.Unto the End is an experience. It's beautiful. It's endearing. It's cruel. I loved it, and I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Correction. I didn't realize it, but this game has 3 endings I won't spoil and a very difficult Old Warrior Mode unlocked after two playthroughs. There's definitely some replay value in that regard then. I'll keep my original review below. I still mostly stand by what I say. Looking at the other endings, it's not something I'd replay the whole game over for, but again, I still enjoyed it. I just think it's too pricey as is.I really wanted to like this more than I actually do. I enjoyed the short time I had with Unto The End, but for $25, there's much better out there. I love cinematic platformers and this one stood out for its emphasis on brutal combat. The combat is the highlight here. Many players didn't gel with it, but I really liked it a lot. It's got a lot of depth and it's very challenging. The adaptive AI made each encounter feel like a legit brawl. You gotta mix high/low attacks and blocks and time them accordingly. Mix in feints, throwable weapons, dodging, shoulder checks and you got a pretty intense combat system. You can adjust the combat speed in the options menu if it's a little too fast for your reflexes. The main issue I have is the extremely short length. You can beat this in less than 3 hours. Take out all the deaths and multitasking I was doing while playing and it probably would've been over in 2 hours. For a supposed cinematic puzzle platformer, there are few challenging platforming sections and even fewer puzzles. There's also a lack of variety in levels. You spend way too much time inside of samey looking caves with 90% of the screen being completely black and the little you can see obscured by rocks in the foreground making hard to determine if you're actually moving forward at all. Cave levels aren't fun at all. I'll never like them. The presentation and sound are quite good, but I wouldn't call it amazing. Very simplistic art style with stock sound effects I've heard before in other indie games. The atmosphere is very strong for sure, but it's not enough in my opinion. They would have benefited by having an arena mode so we could enjoy the combat more and give some more bang for our buck cause for a survival game, I rarely needed to worry about supplies at all. I literally upgraded my armor right after the final "boss?" fight and didn't have anymore combat encounters. It's an immersive experience, but something that needed more meat on the bone cause there is no replay value here. If you're looking for another cinematic platformer that's cheaper, longer, bigger, more immersive, very difficult, with an arena mode, multiplayer, and mod support, give Rain World a try. If you can get this for no more than $10, I say give it a try. I hope they take this foundation and use it for a bigger better game.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting story, cool animation and art. Combat, however, is a mixed bag.
