_childDocuments_.review: I've paid much more for much worse games. All and all if you like deck building games at all this offers a really fun and challenging system. Theres a rougelike element to it, where you're playing the same story over and over but with subtle differences, especially depending on your choices. The story is fairly interesting, though with only limited voice acting it becomes a chore reading all the dialog that has no bearing on your run, and I find myself skipping through quite a bit of it. But its easy enough to scroll back up and see any important detail you skipped if you're confused about whats happening. As far as I'm concerned the real fun is in the cards and just deciding how to deal with situations as they arise. The rest is just cute sci fi set dressing, but i'm not here for the lore and world building tbh. Though if you're more into just reading a sci-fi graphic novel theres also a story emphasized difficulty where you can immerse yourself in the world and not worry about getting good at the card game. All told, 3 hours in and I see myself playing much much more. I assume it'll get a bit boring and tedious doing at some point, but it seems there'll be enough variation in each run to keep it interesting, albeit with maybe some breaks between runs. Not to mention theres a daily challenge mode I unlocked but haven't touched yet. Griftlands is plenty of fun for the price and its a perfect game to relax and unwind with. Even the challenging parts, and times where I got my ass handed to me didn't feel frustrating or necessarily unfair. This is my new go to for now when I need a break from more competitive online games that sometimes get me a little too worked up. I found this game exactly when I needed it. Wonderful!

_childDocuments_.review: Turns out what Slay the Spire was always missing was a greater story focus! The story generally has one clear end goal for each character but everything that happens in between is random or a choice of 2 opposing factions making it unique each time. Some of the random quests are also great. Like I was going for a prisoner exchange and then on the way my team mate says: hold up there is a criminal we should arrest. So I do that and then when we deliver the half dead woman to the prison they are like: that's no criminal that's the admirals second mate! Combat is pretty much the same as sts but you can also hire mercenaries or pets to fight for you. New is the negotiation which is another card battle but with different mechanics and cards. It's really refreshing. Great card game with heavy story focus.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game for its campaign, but I think there are too many negatives to really recommend it as a roguelite deckbuilder.- The campaigns are fun. The latter ones are well-written.- The dual deck system creates some variety of play within a run and theoretically provides some balance decisions (using a deck more makes it better ... but neglecting one can make you lose)- The negotiation format is unique in my experience of deckbuilders and I think it's a neat conceptualization.- Managing relationships with NPCs is simple, intuitive and additive.- Linking upgrades to card use is satisfying.- Artwork and sound design is great.- Run variety is too limited. - Each character has unique elements, but the majority of the mechanics are functionally similar between them.- The starting decks feel a little too thick. This makes it hard to quickly specialize into a build.- The starting cards have too many upgrade options. It's great that they give you two choices, but 90% of the time you want one of those options to be the option where the card is destroyed after a single use so that you can replace it with specialized cards.- The previous points are mainly a problem because .- Mettle progression is super slow relative to the other meta-currencies. And apparently the highest difficulty removes this progress anyway.- For the sheer number of potential friends/enemies, there really isn't much variety. In negotiations, you'll only fight ~10 different enemies. In Battles, most characters are indistinguishable.- And run pacing doesn't feel good in Brawl (roguelite) mode. Part of why Slay the Spire works is that individual battles are fast and you get to update your deck rapidly. Monster Train takes the opposite approach -- fewer battles that take longer, but you make big changes between each. Griftlands has lots of medium-length battles with mostly small upgrades in between. Maybe my decision-making would get faster if I played more, but after 50 hours it's still taking me 2.5 hours per brawl. I was attempting 20-minute runs by that point in Slay the Spire.Ultimately, I think the achievement completion rates are telling. The achievements actually reward doing cool things in the game and I wanted to attempt them ... but the lack of replayability means it's not fun enough to stick around for that. Considering the most-completed achievement is 4.3%, it seems like others agree.

_childDocuments_.review: A good card game of the flavor of Slay the Spire (one of my favorites), but adds an engaging story on top that gives some depth to the characters and battles you are playing. Each of the 3 characters has 2 decks (battle and negotiation) which have different feels to them. Within each deck is 2 clear overarching strategies that play very different and of course can be mixed for extra versatility. Lots of variety packed into 3 story lines that makes me want to keep playing. It was extremely satisfying the first time I won a run, much more so than other games in this genre.

_childDocuments_.review: One word: Mind-blowing.Initially, I suspected this would be a replica of Slay the Spire. But I was proven wrong immediately.First impression of the game - insane. I was blown away the moment I launched the game. I'm someone that takes graphics really seriously so the main menu itself was enough to make an impression. It was so well made. Not just the menu, the game graphics and sounds are amazing. The narration of the story wasn't annoying either. It felt like it was supposed to be there. Everything just gel-ed together.Then there's the gameplay. Sure, it's about playing your cards right, like Slay the Spire and any other card battlers. But there's so much more to  this game than just that. There's 2 types of fights that I am aware of thus far - flat out beating your opponent or negotiating. And both of them are 2 different systems. You get to be more adventurous in how you would like to experience your run.NPCs will also react to you differently based on your choice of actions. Kill their friend? They'll hate you. Give them money? They'll love you. You can even bribe them or buy them drinks to improve your relationship. This just adds a whole new level of depth and immersion to the game because it seems like you have control over your character's fate! Also, befriending different NPCs can provide you different perks, which further contributes diversifies the 'blocks' you can use to build your play style.Oh and did I mention you can get PETS? PETS. Sign me the freak up. I'm more than just in love with this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands borrows the best gameplay mechanics from Slay the Spire (Deck Building) and FTL (Desicion Making) while also adding some unique twists to this genre. You're playing with two decks. One for fighting one for negotiating.At times the dialogues feels lackluster but seeing that this game's still in Early Access there's still room for improvement on that front. Otherwise the game feels really refreshing when you played your share of Slay the Spire and that's due to the story, the setting and it's characters.And it looks nice as well. You can tell it's made by the creators of Shank and Mark of the Ninja.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has never played virtual card games before, I wasn't expecting much from Griftlands. But man this game provides so much fun replayability. You have three characters with their own unique stories and encounters. Each of them have their own play styles that can be customised to suit your preferred playstyle. My favourite way to play, so far, is having a mix of (over)charge and burn effects for the character Rook. Oh and you get two decks, one for battle and one for diplomacy. Characters also have different playstyles for diplomacy too, which makes every run feel somewhat new. However, battle decks do take precedence as most bosses will end with a battle (diplomacy can weaken them sometimes). The artstyle and writing is solid. NPCs are quite memorable thanks to the great artwork. Overall, this is a great game with a lot of replayability and it is something I can easily recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly can't believe this game is only $15. I liked Slay The Spire and this will naturally get lots of comparisons made to that. However, this game is a fully functioning RPG and not nearly as simple. This is definitely the next step-up in the card battle genre. Even in Early Access It's a masterpiece. I love the artwork, I really enjoy the story to it, and I absolutely adore the characters. The best part is just how different each character is and that they each have their own unique traits when handling negotiations or combat.This is the type of game where time just melts away so be prepared to clear an entire afternoon as you get engrossed. There's just so much to do, so many choices to make, AND THIS ISN'T EVEN THE FULL RELEASE! Absolutely insane.Now if you would excuse me... I have to get back to negotiating. Just one more strategic card battle and I'm done I swear.Just one more before I go to bed. Wait hold on, nah man, just one more.Seriously I have a problem.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the world. I love the art. I love the dry wit writing. I love the music. I love everything EXCEPT the actual game.Griftlands is a roguelite, but very little actually complements that design. Each of the three campaigns takes roughly 5 hours to complete on average, which is too long for the pick-up-and-play appeal of typical roguelites, but also too short for the kind of multi-layered stories this game wants to tell. I think part of the problem is that the card games, both for fighting and negotiations, take a very long time to play out compared to other games of this type.The main draw of the game is the way the world dynamically reacts to your actions. You make a friend? That friend will help you out when they can, but they might also have enemies. Kill someone? Their friends will be out for your head, but their enemies will like what you're doing. And it gets a lot more nuanced than that. But since the campaigns reset either at the end or if you die, nothing ever sticks. So this system never reaches its full potential.Basically, I'm fascinated by the world this game created, but the roguelite format prevents me from exploring it as much as I would like to. If it were up to me, this game would probably have been better as a D&D-type experience, with procedurally-generated characters existing in this world within the various factions, and a player that can interact with and influence everything for a seamless, evolving story.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know. It's an okay deckbuilder with an okay sci-fi plot, where you have to manage two decks (one for combat and one for negotiation). _childDocuments_.review: I wanted to wait until I experienced the game out of early access before writing up my review. Griftlands is the hermit on the desert island in the sea of roguelike deckbuilders. Not satisfied with having one deck, the game tasks you with the challenge of constructing two different decks for a run that independently need to be proficient in order to have success. In addition to the deck you use for combat, you also have the deck that lets you negotiate, which can help avoid fighting or make combat easier. Combat and negotiation each have their own encounter system and strategies, providing a nice batch of gameplay variety to keep things from getting stale. Your game over only occurs when losing in combat, but it's quite probable for a lost negotiation to be the determining factor. Make sure you don't neglect one in favor of the other.The game is quite polished, both visually and mechanically. The animations are fluid and captivating, with combat animations being downright impressive. If you're looking for a deckbuilder with style, look no further. Of course, if we're talking about the roguelike deckbuilder genre, there are three very important questions that need to be answered: how long is a run, what's the difficulty, and how much variety is there between runs?First off, Griftlands runs are some of the longest I've ever played, second only to Dungeon of the Endless. A single run can take about 3-5 hours, compared to a 1-hour run you might get from Slay the Spire or FTL. A major part of this is because Griftlands is a story-based roguelike, telling a narrative alongside the deckbuilding. You can basically skip all the dialogue once you've seen the story, but it doesn't really reduce playtime. You go through 3-4 days of story to get to the end, and each day can take upwards of an hour. Suffice it to say, losing toward the end hurts after so much investment, which can damage one's desire to start up a new run. Fortunately, this game very intelligently employs a highly intricate progression system, one of the best I've ever seen. It's both a completionist's dream and nightmare. Between characters, grafts, perks, and the mettle system, it's actually very difficult to go a run without making some progress. That forward momentum helps you feel like you're still getting somewhere even when you lose, which I very much appreciate.So then, how often are we going to be losing? If you're worried about things being too hard, the game has a "story mode" which basically puts the question of winning/losing aside to let you just play out the story. It doesn't let you progress, but if you're not itching for difficulty, you're probably not gunning much for progression either. If your concern is that the game will be a cakewalk, have no fear. This game employs the standard "new game plus" that most roguelikes do, as yet another means of progression. If you want a challenge, this game can acquiesce. There are only about 6 difficulty levels compared to Slay the Spire's 20, but that just means they scale faster. Given the game's length, I think this was the wise decision.Of course, even a difficult game will lose the player's interest if the game isn't compelling. Roguelikes are known for their replay value, so surely this game must have some as well? Griftlands definitely manages to change things up between runs. While the overarching story is identical, the non-story missions you encounter, as well as the NPCs you meet, the grafts you can find, the cards you can draft, and all bosses except the final one vary between runs. The way Griftlands treats NPCs is novel in itself. Each character has an "opinion" of you, ranging from love to like to neutral to dislike to hate. Higher opinion makes negotiation against them easier, while lower opinion does the opposite. If they love you, they will give you a special passive ability that applies for the rest of the game, unless that NPC dies or stops loving you. If they hate you, you'll get a negative passive with the same rules. This "love/hate" mechanic can make for some interesting scenarios where someone is in trouble, and you can choose to let them die because they hate you or risk your life to save them and potentially make them a friend. The love/hate mechanic also offers another sense of progression, as while the specific boons and banes are tied to the character, you won't be able to see what they are until you've unlocked them. This means intentionally making people love or hate you in certain runs to work towards 100% completion.Also, in regards to variety, I should briefly mention the "brawl" mode, as an alternative to the story and regular modes. For those who aren't interested in the story and just want to experience the deckbuilding roguelike aspect, this mode offers players the same ability to make progress without dealing with the story. Everything you accomplish in brawl applies to your overall progression, so you don't have to worry about needing to 100% both modes to reach perfect completion. Switching between the two modes can add more variety, though you'll find that they both can still take around 3-5 hours to complete.After playing dozens of runs, totaling over 100 hours, I would describe the experience as "addicting but exhausting." If you've never heard of choice fatigue, you can play this game to experience it firsthand. Every run gives you so many options that can make or break your run, and it just keeps going on like that for 3-4 hours. This game was not made to be played in one sitting, but the game really does have that "one more turn" factor that can turn one more encounter into taking on the rest of the day. Then after you lose, you may feel compelled to start up the new run and make those initial decisions, starting the process over again. I definitely recommend this one to any deckbuilder fans. It's hiding out on its desert island with its treasure trove of interesting ideas, both familiar and new. Just be cautious if you're the sort to really get into completing every little task the game has to offer. This game may be your best friend or worst enemy.

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful art, three very unique MC choices and a slew of interesting characters make Griftlands a unique experience. The choices you make have a major effect on the path you'll take and the ending of each character's story (should you survive that long). While the upgrades that can carry over between runs are spendy, it doesn't bother me much as I imagine I'll be spending a considerable amount of time in the Griftlands.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: While being beautifully designed in Klei's unique graphic art the story is average at its best. It offers nothing spectacular and has cliche character origin stories.To put it simply. If you are someone who likes to get a good ending and wants the best possible outcome, then you know that you will have to endure quest grinding. This is a problem in many games, endings based on honor should be affected by player's choices and not by how many times you grinded the same quest gameplay structure for 100 times. This game has the exact problem, I was so exhausted when I saw another negotiation gameplay but I had to do it anyway for the good honor/gameplay advantage.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal game. Extremely enjoyable. The world building and atmosphere is engaging and nuanced. The dialogue and plot is fun to read and bite your teeth into. It gets you wondering and imagining what unseen parts there are. The game play is extremely fun. If you like deck builders and rogue-lites, you will love this game. It has plenty of new mechanics that set it apart from other similar deck building/rogue-lites like Slay the Spire, Monster Train, etc. Overall, it's a blast, and I can see myself playing it quite a bit more. $20 is more more more than worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a fun deckbuilder with great art and interesting mechanics.  There is a huge amount of content and replay value for the price.  Each run has various narrative things that can happen, and you can choose who to side with which keeps things fresh.  It scratches the itch of creating a completely OP deck with careful planning and a little luck.

The card system is rather simple and yet it has some depth. You can either battle or negotiate with NPCs and get different responses/behaviour from them. _childDocuments_.review: I just finished my first run with . It took me 7 hours, because I played very slowly, trying to learn all the cards, grafts and mechanics, and making every possible conversation. Having played Slay the Spire for a while now, it was nice to see a game that is so familiar yet so novel at the same time. For reference, my battle deck came out as a Bleed-focused, fast and aggressive deck (which made me skip a ton of Combo-based cards), a bit familiar with Silent's Poison decks in StS, but with more front-loaded (burst) damage.- The fact that you can choose to fight or negotiate in basically 90% of your decisions.- The story, the writing, the diversity and personality of the characters.- The fact that you can make friends or enemies with basically any person you encounter, and the buffs or debuffs they give.- Familiar, mostly straightforward card mechanics and an easily understandable UI.- The card upgrade system.- I am by no means an experienced player of deck-building games, and my first try did seem a bit too easy. I once got close to being defeated in battle, and once get beaten in a negotiation, but that's it. I blazed through the final boss with only a pet on my side, and . Hopefully the Prestige levels (what Ascensions are in StS) will make the game a bit more difficult.- Replayability in vanilla seems a bit iffy, with the story being the same for each character, but there are different paths you can go down on, different decisions to make, characters to befriend or anger. Also with the new mod compatibility, I'm sure that tons of community-made content will be available, including new stories and PCs.Overall I feel like I found a new favorite, and I'm very much looking forward to the final product and all the additions the developers will implement in the game in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Never played a deck builder before, so initially I was put off by the card system and just generally lost and frustrated. _childDocuments_.review: It's sort of split for me.   I think the game is innovative and polished enough to give a solid recommendation to try it. But for me the experiment never yields a good enough addicting loop that I want to keep coming back for more for hundreds of hours.   That might be just fine, though, and others might have a better experience.I think one of the things that puts me off is the fact that the game is actually a time management strategy game without much feedback or information.   Since time is one of your most important resources, the only way to deal with it is to repeatedly play the same scenario until you uncover and memorize enough that you can manage the resource well enough to progress.   That just isn't for me.

To my surprise, I could not get into this game and refunded it because it was so bad. The first game I've ever refunded on Steam.It felt like a chore more than a game. I was being prompted to make decisions while the game provided vague information about what the consequences of each decision may be.The terminology used for the game mechanics is horrible. It is like someone was dead-set on making a deck builder within a certain setting, and tried to piece together a bunch of random ideas to make that happen.The tactical aspect was almost non-existent. It was dull. Not exciting by any means. Bad sound effects contributed to the problems. It just wasn't engaging.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome. For an early access game it is incredibly polished. From the artstyle to the gameplay to the setting, everything is phenomenally done. This game takes an ingenious move with making a card based dialogue system AND combat system. I've loved my time with the game. My only gripe would be asking what the point of the rogue like element is to the game. It's such a dialogue and story based game that making it a rogue like seems out of place. I would love for a developer to explain what the purpose of the rogue like mechanics are of multiple runs so I could better understand. Overall, as a person who is slowly losing hope for new games in the industry, this game is a shining example of a game that was made with passion and skill. A+ Would strongly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, I'm pretty sure you're all comparing this to other relevant games, so here's my recipe:2 parts Slay the Spire (but with 3x better art)1 part Hades (art and music are clutch)The individual runs aren't quite as fast as either, and the run-over-run gains are more like StS than Hades (as far as what you gain between runs--this assumes you're "restarting" the timeline, in a more traditional rogue-like sense).  I'd say a run is 45-60 minutes, at my pace.The art is almost as good as Hades, and miles ahead of StS (love the game, though I do, it looks like stuff I did in highschool).  Music is solid, too.  Plot is fairly fixed, so the rogue-like elements are a BIT light, but the deck strategy keeps things interesting for several full play-throughs. The comparison to StS is especially accurate on the difference between character play styles.  I've only played the first two, so far, and it's definitely as diverse and interesting as the different styles in StS.I guess more than StS or Hades, the closest comparison might be Monster Hunters, but with better art and music.  Worth it all the time, a steal on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Remember when everyone thought  was going to be the new hotness? No? Can’t say I blame you. For just a moment, it looked fantastic! A super cool world, solid art, and  innovative gameplay. Unfortunately, I found replayability to be low, and it’s too short to be very memorable. But if you are just looking for a something that’s good for 15-30 hours,  is a solid choice.Let’s start at the top. Brought to us by ,  shining star is it’s truly innovative gameplay. This is the same studio that made the surprisingly captivating side-scrolling stealth game , the very non-traditional survival game , and of course, the rougelike rhythm game . Good, innovative games is what  does. combines the deckbuilding rougelike genre with solid RPG elements to make you feel like your choices are much deeper than just, “what’s the best card I can pick.” It also adds . You have two completely separate decks/stats to develop. A traditional combat deck, and a deck built around resolving your conflict via negotiation. Sure, in the grand scheme of things, they are both “card-based combat,” but approaching it as a negotiation means you have to think about the cards and the underlying system completely differently. Do you want to be Intimidating? Or Diplomatic? If you do both, your deck could get watered down. If you don’t have some diversity, you might run into someone who counters you hard. How you chose to approach the Negotiation part of the game has a big impact on how the game plays out as well (people may not like you if you are Intimidating).You also have to be careful to work on both your Negotiation and Combat decks. Negotiation can get you past a lot of encounters, or make some things a lot easier. But your deck gets stronger the more you use it…and by the end of a run you will have some very tough negotiations and combats that you cannot avoid.There are three main characters, each with their own unique story. They all play out very differently, with different combat and negotiation specialties. Skills you learned playing the 1st character, do not translate well when playing the 2nd or 3rd. The story is very well written, and helps you stay tuned into the game. Lastly, the world felt a bit like…(if I can exaggerate a bit)…like watching  for the first time. A deep, well thought out world that has immense potential…and you know you are only seeing a tiny piece of what is possible.My biggest problem with the game revolves around the replayability. Each run consists of 4 days. Within each day, there will be a lot of procedurally generated encounters and events. Even when you are given a “story quest,” more than half the time it is picked from a short list of possible quests. The quests are balanced well for the level that you encounter them, but…What isn’t balanced are the rewards. You might get a rare reward that already plays into your strengths (or you get it early so you can build on it)…or you might get trash that works against the deck you are building. Get that awesome rare late in the game…too bad you didn’t know it was coming because you built your deck wrong. I was on a serious struggle-bus with the 3rd character…I was building him so he had a lot of people love him. I had failed probably 4 or 5 runs in a row. Then I landed a rare (that I didn’t know existed) that turned my “loved” stat into a negotiation buff…WHAT?!  I breezed through that run. I want to think that the skills I was learning had something to do with it, but if I’m honest I think the card combined with my build turned the game into easy mode.Now, I enjoy games that let you try to “break the system,” but they can’t be based around what you randomly get. I don’t want to increase the difficulty because RNG might deal me a pile of crap I can’t win with…or it might deal me a hand that I can win with while I’m passed out drunk on the computer room floor.Sadly, the RPG/story elements make the game a lot of fun to play once…but they make it tedious to play after you have won. The story takes a lot of time, and you find your self trying to frantically click away the dialog because you’ve already read through this part of the story 3 times. I find it sad that the really good story turned into something annoying at the end.As a rougelike, you also expect to lose sometimes as you figure out how to win. Runs take a good bit of time (3-4 hours if you read all the dialog, 2 if you don’t), so failing and starting over starts to become a slog. Buy the time I finally completed a run for a character, I was done with the slog.  I had zero interest in replaying the story on a slightly higher difficulty.The game does offer a “combat arena” if you just want to play the card game without re-slogging (did I just make up a word?) the story. But I never tried it…I felt like too much of the magic was in the narrative and story. Plus, I couldn’t wrap my brain around a “Negotiation” combat arena…where you are negotiating for…what, exactly?So, if you only want/need a game to putz around with for 20-30 hours, there is a whole lot of good in . If you want a serious game that you can sink your teeth into for hundreds of hours, you should probably look somewhere else.

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands ReviewGriftlands is (yet again) another Klei game, but this time, it's a deck-builder. You play as 3 different 'grifters', traversing the lands to try and complete a goal. These set of grifters will make friends and enemies, they could and probably will use either their silver tongue or their silver bullets (occasionally both) to get out of tricky situations. You make several decisions, but be warned, every single one counts, and can be the difference between life and death.As you play, you get new cards, each with certain abilities that can come into play. Everytime you play a card a certain amount of times, they can be upgraded into 2 alternatives. Some are straight upgrades and some are amazing but have severe downsides, but just remember that you can only pick one.The two different modes of battle are 'Fight' and 'Debate' (not actual names, mind you). 'Fight' is generally considered to be the easier path, but you have to potential to DIE, losing the game, not to mention that you can make enemies, so I generally stay on the 'Debate' path. 'Debate'-ing helps solve problems with words (and occasionally money). Not that it won't make enemies, it'll just make less. However, it is often harder to predict enemy actions and argue. But just remember: some situations you can't solve with your fists, and some situations, you just have to let your inner warrior come out.Each grifter has a story to tell. Each grifter has their own personalities and abilities. Heck, even the NPCs are more like people than just extras, even the minor ones, the insignificant ones, and actual extras.It's an amazing game with extremely compelling stories to tell. I really absorbed myself into it. Each play-style can make different options come into play. For example, an aggressive player would try to sink in as much damage whilst caring little about their own health. After all, your opponents can't dream of hurting you, if they're not there. Each grifter has their own backstories, personalities, quirks, and abilities in combat. Klei has, yet again, outdone themselves.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. At first I was skeptical of the combination of inspirations of Slay the Spire and choose-your-own-adventure games: the deckbuilding aspect seemed a bit forced. Moreover, I specifically say Slay the Spire because the first character, Sal, in particular feels like a Frankenstein of various different Slay the Spire mechanics. However, as I continued to play, I adjusted, and I began to feel how natural the swirl of genres could be. The first campaign felt strange, and in many ways it is: 4-5 hours is kinda an odd duration of a story and gameplay, the first character is very cliche as is her surroundings, and I felt like I was stumbling through familiar yet disorienting mechanics but still finished the first campaign with very little challenge, only coming close to failure in the final boss fight. Yet I think this is just because I had not yet adjusted how the game worked, and was still working towards higher difficulties. The thing about Griftlands is that there are a lot of subtle, moving parts. There are a lot of different incentives pulling you different ways. There's a lot of outcomes difficult to predict. There's lots of mechanics you will only learn through repetition. However, I did find that I learned, and it continuously made me excited to keep playing. I felt like I was mastering the game, and yet there was still always more to learn as it got more and more challenging. It felt so rewarding to adapt to a game that feels so odd, and yet still would encourage me to at times abandon "optimal" strategy to help characters and follow plot threads I was more endeared by.The real pull of Griftlands that brings this all together is polish. The game's logic feels consistent and dynamic. The music is fantastic. The art is varied and beautiful. The interface is straight-forward and does well to navigate the many moving parts. The writing is, for the most part, good. Sal and her story is by far the most disappointing: she herself is a stereotypical downtrodden and sarcastic bounty hunter, her setting is classic sci-fi fair of violent insurgent bandits vs corrupt and cruel government police and a plan of vengeance. The other stories are considerably better. Rook is a bit more fun, as both a bit of an old fart but also a genius spy moving through a recognizable spy drama of class warfare and conspiracy, but I felt like it never really payed off because it always feels like you are never in control of the larger conspiracy. Smith's story is by far the best, as Smith is a wonderfully depicted ne'er do well who can be played either as a lovable ruffian with a chaotic heart of gold or as a cruel, selfish, entitled rich kid. His dialogue is consistently hilarious, and his supporting cast is endearing, dynamic, and often perfect straight-mans against Smith's absurdity. The larger story as well feels compelling and driving, and I found his mechanics the most fun to boot, albeit the most complicated. Kind of a bummer it feels like one story got so much more care than the other two.My one real critique is that the meta progression feels a little tacked on. It doesn't feel particularly rewarding or monumental, just small bonuses that eventually add up to greater power/ease. Some of the perks were fun to combine, but for the most part I barely thought about them and didn't really look forward to unlocking new ones much. The huge variety of new unlockable cards and increased difficulty were enough to motivate me.Anyway, great game. Worth many play-throughs. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun deck builder.  Just finished the first character's storyline.  Took about 5.5 hours, taking my time and then I started the second character's.  There is a lot of meta progression in the form of upgrades, flourishes (ultimate moves kind of), perks, and card unlocks that definitely has me excited to keep playing and then replaying.  You go through a day and night cycle and each day seems to end with a boss fight.  You get branching choices throughout the day on a map that also has random events sprinkled in so it is like slay the spire's branching choices except you don't see the entirety of what is available before the boss and it just feels really dynamic and fun.  The split between battle and interrogation card battles is just another great way that it builds upon slay the spire's legacy and sets itself above being just a clone.  The story aspect is nice to have, well animated, with nice voiced gibberish and a decent amount of branching decisions.  The card mechanics are excellent.  I haven't played and unlocked enough to know if there are any bad imbalances but all of the build possibilities are enticing and make you want to give them a shot.  You can also get grafts (relics I think they were called in spire) that can define a run and a pet that will fight alongside you.  I bought this full price because I like the developer and I am not disappointed.  This is a nicely polished game well worth the full price and a definite buy if it goes on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Through an interesting combination of style and innovation, Klei has nailed what makes deckbuilder games so damn fun to play. Though there are only three characters compared to other builders having a variety of choices, each one is dramatically unique in both styles of card driven combat. How you play one will not be how you play another. And it's not always obvious until you've given it another run or several. However, whether you experience all the game has to offer you (which is a lot) is entirely based on how deeply this game can grab you for each of its extended sessions. At 20 hours, I feel that I'm about at a point where I'm ready to call it enough.So first off, negotiations. Griftlands is all about risk, reward, and relationships - most of them bitter and hateful to some degree. Negotiations hit this the best by being a straightforward source of conflict. If you succeed, something great will happen for you, but if you fail, then you risk failing an objective, or making the following battle harder, or even creating a battle where there wasn't going to be one. Plus it uses its own unique health pool so you're pushed to use it as your first line of defense compared to your "die if exhausted" health pool. If you do really well with it then you can spend a good chunk of your game with health preserved for the really bitter fights - such as the unavoidable boss fights at the end of every day. Following that you have battles, which play more like a traditional deckbuilder in execution - play cards, defeat enemies. Griftlands personalizes it a little more through its complicated sense of morality. You can kill enemies to get more precious limited money and special powerful items - but risk upsetting their friends whom will hate you and inflict potentially crippling debuffs to you. Or you can let them go - often leading to them hating you and inflicting you with crippling debuffs anyways - not that you're aware of these outcomes, it's all in the game.Where I feel Griftlands stumbles is a weird thing to discuss. Past Prestige 0, running out of health means game over which is a loss of your entire run. In Griftlands, a run is about 3 to 5 hours. A lot happens and the game is generous in how it eases up the difficulty so it's rare to actually die, but it is a constant risk to suddenly find that you're back at the start again. Plus every time you gain a level from post-game exp, you gain more interesting cards that can greatly mix up how you play each character in exciting new ways. But I hesitate to go back in knowing that if I don't take breaks (not something I do often with roguelike games) then I'm dedicating a lot of time to a run. Like, a lot of time. Most games have runs that last around an hour and a half at most. It's hard to imagine Griftlands as being a shorter game in its current state. Some of the excitement is in building a monster deck that shreds through foes, decks you spend a lot of time building and perfecting. Even the streamlined Griftlands experience that is Brawl mode will be three hours, and the deck I build feels like one that I wouldn't want to spend less time working on. All these resources to improve, and it's difficult to say that shortening the game in some way would make it better.Ultimately I feel my time with Griftlands is coming to an end, not due to lack of content, interest, enjoyment, or otherwise - but because other roguelike experiences fit in a cleaner time frame. I feel motivated to do run after run in shorter "popcorn run" games. Failure doesn't hit as hard (though, again, terminal failure thankfully doesn't come often in Griftlands). There's a lot still here to experience and it's all very interesting, but I don't think it's for me. Then again I struggled with Slay the Spire and everyone loves that game, so maybe I just am not a big deckbuilder roguelike person. Griftlands gets an easy recommendation at full price, though as of writing Smith (the third character and a personal favorite for getting into fights with) doesn't have a full campaign yet. That doesn't mark against it in the slightest. Klei knows how to make solid beautiful games and continues to demonstrate it with Griftlands.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good deck building game with an interesting setting and nice art style. There are plenty of builds to try out (I advise against just taking every card you can get), and different ways to tackle most problems. It's a lot more than just hoping you draw so-and-so card; you can really influence how things go with abilities and special cards.I'd say the difficulty is just right for the first couple of days in any given run: challenging enough to be engaging, but with a solid chance of victory. There was a *huge* difficulty spike on the last day of my first Sal playthrough. I'd suggest playing through each character on the Story difficulty (no permadeath, easier battles and negotiations) once first to get your bearings, then seeing where you want to go from there. I just wish we had an option to keep the usual difficulty, but disable permadeath; I dislike wasting my time and attachment to story choices on death, but the Story setting greatly reduced the other elements of risk as well, making things less interesting.Anyway, now that I've beaten all three stories on that setting, I'll move on from this for a bit, but I can definitely see myself coming back to do a run or two once in a while.

_childDocuments_.review: 142 hours. The amount of time played so far on the highest prestige level on one character. The actual length of the game can be played in half an hour. In fact, its a common past time during lunch. Yet there is a maddening quality to the game that feels addictive. A nagging feeling of I could do that better or if I could make this combination it would be amazing. Griftlands is a deck based game with three characters using slightly different mechanics for their combat and negotiation decks. Their currency for efficiency differs to a degree. In battles and verbal challenges. This creates a sense of familiarity with the core mechanics while offering a modified challenge with individual mastery. An interesting mechanic is the social effects of hate and love from other characters than provide boons or bane to the player in different situations. Boons may be persistent such as bonus health or intermittent such as a boost to the first turn of combat or negotiation. Banes operate the same way. This can affect choice in combat as to whether you wish to comply with quest objectives or skirt around it and attempt to deflect using social challenges.Friends that you make during one mission may become enemies in another.Some of the challenges can be mitigated over time with perks or mettle awards and flourish unlocks. The perk system allows customization on your desired game play. Do you focus on pet enhancement and creating a pet horde or do you focus on social advantages like forgiveness that removes hate and charm that increases like to beloved state. Overall its an experience that you can customize to suit your play style. The stories and objectives aren't complex but they are entertaining and can take up the length of a couple of movies. It's not quite the quick play you might expect but neither is it a time sink of an epic adventure. It's a comfortable game for a casual player looking to whittle away a few hours without going over a few days unless you choose to do so. As you progress in winning the difficulty meter can be adjusted to more brutal endeavors. Options to reduce healing over night, decrease starting health and resolve, stronger bosses and minions give it a nice replay option. I've managed to play over 60 hours on a game that can be finished in 4 hours on a single play through.Stem deck verified with a play time of a little over 4 hours. Controls are generally fine with some mouse over during map transit or in starting conversations. Its somewhat unnecessary since way points are preset and npcs are set in place so it could have been scripted to toggle through with button presses rather than requiring stick movement. A minor inconvenience in an otherwise decent game.

_childDocuments_.review: I like it. A lot. _childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend. _childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: "Visionary" is a word that gets thrown about a lot, but that's what Griftlands is. What Klei have done with Griftlands is fundamentally new and innovative for both RPGs and Deckbuilders.As someone who loves playing social characters in RPGs, I always lament that it is never as interesting as the combat. Often you are relegated to one extra option in dialogue, if you're lucky. With the Negotiation Deck, social gameplay is as core to Griftlands as combat. Negotiation decks have their own cards and mechanics that feel distinct from combat. Even better, because this is a rogue-like you are encouraged to talk you way out of situations wherever possible (you don't die if you lose an argument, but you do if you lose a fight).The relationships are another amazing feature that bring social roleplay to an equal footing to combat. You can clearly see at a glance which characters in a scene Like or Dislike you, and getting someone to Love you has huge benefits, while having someone left alive to Hate you has a huge negative.  this is made central to  quests and scenes because they always involve named characters you have probably met and have a relationship with. Who you side with matters, and your relationships with others will impact your missions. Rarely is a bounty you are hunting a random one-off character you have never met, if it is, there is usually a good reason for that.For an Early Access game this is incredibly polished. I haven't had any crashes or bugs. The only cleanup is a little bit of UI improvements IMHO - .My only grievance is that I was surprised I completed the first act of the 2 available characters after just 2 runs. I expected more of an FTL experience where it would a lot of runs to even make it to the final boss, let alone beat it. Right now its more of a Diablo III experience, where the gameplay really gets going on the 3rd run, but you're starting to rush through the story which is sad. Hopefully this will balance out with more story chapters and more characters (and there is so much room for them to do that!), but for once I wouldn't mind if a Rogue-like was a little harder. Top Deckbuilder. An inventive and truly rare game that balances combat with social roleplay, along with story and gameplay. Basically a finished game, and there is plenty of room for more content. Not a bug in sight.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game takes some really great concepts from Slay the Spire and other games in this genre and packages them into a very unique roguelike. Instead of choosing a clearly drawn path and going from point A to B, you spend days building (or destroying) relationships and deciding between various mutually exclusive encounters. When you get under the hood, the way the game progresses is largely similar to it's brother and sisters in the same genre, but the presentation makes it feel entirely different. This game feels like a larger, more classic RPG in comparison to something like Slay the Spire, and Slay the Spire in turn feels like the streamlined action/arcade version of this.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very good game that is still a work in progress, and there are some things I would like to see improved. That being said, the general game is very fun. If you've played Slay The Spire, this is a similar concept.• Interesting story and fun characters.• Unique deckbuilding for (currently) 3 protagonists.• Diplomacy and social interactions are just as important as combat.• Lots of options and plenty of challenges.My main worry is that the game currently doesn't do the best job introducing decks and playstyles to new players, and I find myself getting a bit lost while trying to play the second or third protagonist. Hopefully some more tutorials or other help will be provided in time.Great game, would recommend, but beware it has a learning curve.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first booted up Griftlands, I was slightly anxious about its busy UI and constant decision making. It was extremely reminiscent of old-school CRPGs, games like classic Fallout or Baldur's Gate, where you're given a lot of freedom and a lot of information right from the beginning, and you have to figure things out for yourself. In theory, I really like games with complex systems where 'your choices matter,' but in practice, they tend to exhaust me, and I rarely finish them. As I kept playing, I got a taste for the mechanics and found them enjoyable. Then I died, restarted, and realized the genius of the game.Griftlands is a Roguelite, so it is intended to be replayed many, many times. This means that you get to screw around in the story, experimenting not just with different playstyles but with different versions of your main character. The game always offers you more than one way to progress, and are given a lot of freedom both in a single run and in between runs to choose the playstyle you want. Want to be a silver-tongued slick talker, avoiding conflicts through wits and negotiation? Give it a try, and then whether you win or die, you can start over and try a more combat-focused approach. Either way, the game rewards you after every run with a bit of progress towards unlocking permanent perks and difficulty modifiers to help you hone any chosen playstyle.And there are a lot of playstyles. Griftlands is also not just one but two very well designed deckbuilder card games. Negotiation and combat each have a dedicated deck with its own set of rules and a handful of different approaches available. Choosing to fight or talk through a problem means choosing which of your two decks to use, and using a deck gives both experience to upgrade your cards and a chance to add new cards to the deck. The more you use one strategy, the better you get at it. Building and playing with a well honed deck can feel really satisfying, and figuring out how to make a good deck is made accessible by the game's replayability. Failing doesn't feel punishing, because you're always moving forwards in something, unlocking some new content or learning something that helps you strategize for your next run.The game is also surprisingly well written. Intriguing moral choices pop up naturally throughout the game, and your responses to them aren't tacked on in cutscenes - they're a natural part of the existing mechanics. There's always two sides to a story, and you are always given the chance to choose sides. A lot of quests have little twists in them, where the person hiring you didn't tell you the whole story or where things just get out of hand and you find yourself with more than one valid way of 'completing' the quest, up to and including failing it on purpose, forfeiting the reward and putting you at odds with the person who hired you. There are no throwaway characters - every NPC is unique, with something to offer if you befriend them and a complication they can toss your way if you get on their bad side. Also, all of them can die - any character you beat in combat gives you the choice to kill or spare them, and there are often compelling reasons on both sides of that coin. Killing opponents can give immediate rewards and remove the ability for that character to complicate things for you later. However, gaining a reputation for murder might affect other aspects of the game, making enemies of your victim's allies and changing how other characters see you. It also removes those characters from the run, while sparing them might open up new options and oppurtunities.Replaying the game and finding out all the different ways things can play out is made rewarding both in gameplay and in the story. This makes roleplaying accessible and interesting, but also makes it fun and engaging to actually learn the ins and outs of the game. The game's difficulty is highly modular, with different characters, modes, and builds that all have an oppurtunity to utterly change the experience. It's not a game you get tired of easily. There's just so much content, and all of it is good.

_childDocuments_.review: Klei is very good at making games. I'm stating the obvious, but it's true - between the art, gameplay, branching story (and multiple MCs), and replay value, I can't recommend this game enough. I've played 150+ hours of StS and 25+ hours of Monster Train (probably the closest comparable things), I LOVE rogue-likes and deckbuilders. I love the 2 deck system as a fresh take of needing to balance what type of encounters you choose (spoiler: there will ALWAYS be encounters where you have to fight, so always negotiating, like I did initially, can leave your deck woefully unprepared for certain encounters). I like that USING the card is what gains experience for upgrades, so you don't have to wait for certain events. The "relic" system ("grafts") are interesting and pretty well balanced, and they level up based on encounters like your cards. The art is breathtaking and there's a great deal of environmental storytelling. And speaking of storytelling, yes there are some cliches, but overall it provides two (soon to be three) solid MC characters with backgrounds that are fun to explore and branching paths that allow you to craft multiple permutations on the story. Very satisfying, and so much fun to replay.One thing I will say is that this game is still in development, so expect some bugs from time to time. Balance between certain cards, relics, and abilities can be skewed. I've also noticed some balance issues in the "Brawl" modes (i.e. snowballing can be really easy later on in a brawl run), but story gameplay is rather balanced. Overall, these are small observations that don't lessen my enjoyment.Overall, 9.5/10, and that's as a DEVELOPMENTAL build - I can only imagine it will keep getting better and better all the time.

_childDocuments_.review: Engaging mechanics. This is the first roguelike game I've played with an actual in-depth story I fully engaged in while playing the game. Most games like these are purely in it for the gameplay, and while that clearly works, Klei went above and beyond that.The "negotiation battle" aspect will be a bit intimidating at first since the "tutorial" is barely any help and there doesn't seem to be any glossary. Fortunately, if you stick with it and give it a chance, if you're an experienced deckbuilder, you'll get it within perhaps 30 minutes. The things to note here that I had to painstakingly figure out.- "Resolve" is hitpoints/life.- "Composure" is shield.- "Arguments" are just status effects that appear as "objects" in the screen that can be attacked and destroyed.USE YOUR MOUSE and hover all over the place. Klei did the right thing here where almost everything has tooltips.One last thing. Once the negotiating battle starts, ALWAYS check the main "icon" of the opponent to see what his innate abilities are. That will save you a lot of pain and a lot of moments where you have little idea what's going on.

_childDocuments_.review: In the modern day sea of early access games or fully completed games being unpolished and poorly executed, Griftlands is a game that restores some faith in the gaming community.It is tagged as Early Access, however that's not accurate. There are 3 characters to play through. 2 of them are completed with their stories while the third is about half way done. And even as they continue to work on the 3rd character content is added that affects all of the characters (like no gameplay mechanics and cards).It's a deck builder rogue-like (I think its rogue like. Can never remember difference between like and lite). Cards you choose from throughout a run are randomized. Encounters are randomized, etc. Standard stuff for anyone who's played StS or Monster Train.Yet, I don't play Griftlands for that bit. I play it for the stories and characters. It's an anthology game. You get three characters and their stories take place in the same world. However, each one plays differently, with different gimmicks, and have their tale set in a different locale then the others. There's references and other things that connect the stories in terms of lore, and there's even a chance of bumping into the other playable characters as NPCs. There's a special touch added to the game that doesn't just make it feel like 'Another run, another deck to build', Every run I do I am curious as to what characters and encounters I'll have to work my way through.And for the gameplay. Look at the reviews. There is So Much to this game, so many layers, when it comes to playing it. I do enjoy my runs of Monster Train. Yet at the end of the day, it's just another Monster Train run. With Griftlands, there are so many perks and modifiers you can add to your run before even starting the damn thing. Then while in the middle of a character's story there is so many things to add to them that isn't just another card for your deck (of which there are two for each character).If you are looking for something in depth. Something fresh and new. Something with a captivating story even though you can play through one in a few hours (or 30 min if you want that achievement). Just buy Griftlands. It is a game that will not disappoint.

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is an excellent game.It is a Rogue-lite, story-based, deck-building game, so certainly targeted towards a fairly specific niche, but it does it's job excellently. The story is fairly short, so casual players could easily get some enjoyment out of it, but they added a lot of replay-ability, with everything from scaling difficulty levels (prestige), mutators (for custom challenges), daily challenges (for global competition), multiple characters, slightly branching story paths, brawl mode (less story more rogue-lite), etc. The best thing I can say about Griftlands is that it makes your deck building feel creative. While some successful run decks end up essentially being every card with the same keyword on it, many feel like an interesting creation/set of synergies that you've come up with (whether or not that's an illusion). I already have a few pet decks after only 20 hours. Because of the replay-ability, I can assure you I will be putting many more hours into this game. The biggest criticism I can give is the amount of similarities it has to Slay the Spire (which speaks to developer originality rather than quality of the game). While the two deck system and individual mechanics are different, the core gameplay loop- seeing enemies' actions ahead of time, having about 3 action points, not healing between battles, discarding your hand at the end of your turn, even mechanics like expend or removing cards from shop keepers are all there. These mechanics suit rogue-like deck builders perfectly- that's why they were in Slay the Spire. That being said, while fans of Slay the Spire will likely love Griftlands (in the same way they would love Slay the Spire 2), I wouldn't call it an original masterpiece. Griftlands has enough to distinguish itself (especially the story and two decks, but individual mechanics being vastly different help as well) and stand firmly on the idea that it built on the ideas of others in the same genre (just like most video games we play), it is still not as original as it could be. Nonetheless, mostly nothing but praise for the game- it is fast becoming one of my favorites from one of my favorite developers.

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is, in its current form, a good game. The early access build is stable and has a lot of content, so I wouldn't be afraid to check it out because of that. Klei has a good track record for early access.The game itself is built on a roguelike deckbuilding formula that has become exceptionally popular the last year or two. It brings with it some unique ideas, a unique and well-done art style, and Klei's track record of solid games.Unlike many of the heavy hitters in the genre (Slay the Spire, Monster Train), the main mode of Griftlands is story based. You lead one of two (eventually three) characters through their story. I've only played with one of the characters thus far, but the writing in her story is good. The dialogue is interesting and often funny, and I like the world they've put together.The thing is, in a game like this, the 'fail forward' formula of a roguelike doesn't mesh super well with a narrative heavy game. As a result, on my Xth run, I'm skipping most of the dialogue because I've seen it all before. It's a bit of a shame, but I suppose if it did start to bug me I could play the newly introduced Brawl mode, which, to my understanding, is a series of escalating challenges without story.Apart from the narrative, it has what you'd expect from a game like this. You get new cards, upgrade your existing cards, have multiple difficulty tiers that you unlock by winning, unlock new cards into the available pool by finishing a run (win or lose), artifacts-but-not, etc. It does have a few unique ideas, namely that you have two decks per character (one for combat and one for negotiation), and the negotiation half of the game plays quite a bit differently than the combat (which would be similar to Slay the Spire and the like). They also recently added Perks you can unlock through gameplay, and you can take a handful with you per run.For now, I'd say Griftlands is good. It doesn't quite have that spark that makes me want to keep going back to it and back to it and back to it, but it's possible that those hooks will come in a later update. Griftlands has a lot going for it, and while I may be done with it for a while, I look forward to checking out the 1.0 release.
