The visuals are the signature Klei GORGEOUS, fluid motions, interesting attacks and very suitable attack sounds. The gameplay is much more forgiving and flexible than sly the spire. Most decks are salvageable and thus randomness more like a novelty than a hindrance most times. Haven’t met any bugs so far and the game is truly worth investing in its current early access state.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun game with good replayability. Lots of cards to unlock, permanent upgrades that carry over in future runs, diffferent sides to pick and multiple characters with their own stories to explore. Pets suck though, as you'll end up training them just to get oneshot by a boss. Save your money, drill another graft slot into your head instead. It hurts less than losing your ravenous flea companion.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's in early access but it's already a great game.  Weaving a slay-the-spire-like deckbuilding game around an RPG core was a smart move, as the little tidbits of story you get do help change the pace a bit.  Every run feels unique because of the different relationships you build.In this game you build a negotiation deck and a battle deck.  Both have sufficiently different mechanics to make them compelling.  It's interesting to have to balance the development of the two decks, as leaving one of them weak might put you in dangerous situations or close off opportunities.All in all, if you liked Slay the Spire, this could be a great game for you, one that might just feel a bit less repetitive.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game!What is better than a rogue like deckbuilder in the style of Slay the Spire? Two deck builders like Slay the Spire in one.Balancing your social and battle decks really adds a lot to the game, with the developers doing that alone would be great, but they did not stop there. On top of it there is also an interresting character story with a dynamic NPC social systems.Still playing the game, far from done just like the developers
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A great exploration of what a narrative-driven rogue-like can be. Great story and characters, tight combat, novel system for negotiation battles. The deck-building is balanced differently from Slay the Spire. StS is more about elaborate instant-win combos, where Griftlands is more about leaning into themes in your deck to get small efficiencies.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The worst thing about this game is that it (or should I say "I") suffer from the classic "One More Turn Syndrome".The game is great. The world (and the stories built within it) are interesting and fun. The combat/arguments are fun.Really the only reasons I would not suggest this game is either a) you don't like card based games b) you have something you should be doing because this game will suck up all your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I think you really need to be a card game fan to get into this. I've played little of card games, didn't enjoy Slay the Spire and I found this okay. The gameplay can be addictive, but it's really meant to be played over and over again from sheer enjoyment of mechanics. I enjoyed it enough to complete each character's campaign, but after that I put it down. The art style is pretty ugly, the story is only enough for passing interest.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game! Its early access, but really doesn't feel like it at all. Its very polished, I've yet to discover any bugs (which is saying a lot for an early access game these days), it has a lot of content to discover and enjoy, also holding many in depth mechanics to master, but yet are not difficult to grasp. This game puts a lot to emphasis on managing character relationships, and totally nails it. Many other games don't incur much of a draw back (if any) for making your character act like a trash human being. This game is not like that. You do have consequences to your actions. That being said, the Devs don't alienate players that want to play their character that way. It is completely possible to make it through the game as an aggressive criminal, a diplomat, or anything in between, all the while giving the player satisfying feedback to their choices through out the story. The character design, art work, sound track, and sound design are all great features to the game. You can really tell the team put a lot of work and love into this creation, all the way down to muffled voices that come from masked characters. Wonderful attention to detail.So far there are 3 different characters to play. Each with their own unique story to play through and unique mechanics to enjoy. Griftlands also offers A lot of replay value, with content unlocks every time you finish the campaign. and being a part of different parts of the story, depending on your choices
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Meh.... a pretty mediocre game in term of the mechanism after playing through the first campaign. The gameplay is not challenging enough to keep me engaged and only took me 2 runs to complete the first campaign which suggests that the game emphasizes more on exploration (exploring new cards, new relationships, trying out different strategies) rather than offering a brain-burning challenge that pushes the limits.I dont think this will hit home if you are here after playing slay the spire.Not really motivated to continue exploring the rest.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: recently replayed some and man they have really improved this game.8/10 if you haven't played a card battler before and you might want to try this is a fine place to start.9/10 card battler/rpg (slay the spire ish) The game has improved quite a bit. They have greatly improved on many of my earlier issues. the game is super fun now, i think it still sits slightly behind my absolute favorites in the genre but im mighty glad now that i got it in early access. exp your cards as fast as you can. They added some interesting meta progression. They made it a lot more reasonable for survival into a few nights of play. the bosses definitely have a smoother ramp than they used to, and they added much better advantages for getting allies.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Another great game from Klei. It's aspects are similar to slay to spire however it is more narrative and lively. Plus you have two deck to manage which seperately used on event (negotiation and combat). Negotiation events feel unique and has different battle system that we do not see commonly. I do love how negotiation mechanics, battle is more straightforward. It isnt a clone and i am sure it will hold it's ground in market. If you do love StS or similar game, it is suit you well. Strongly recommended and keep it up Klei :)
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: extremely fun deckbuilding roguelite. i'd put it up there with the greats of the genre in terms of entertainment value.pros:- enjoyable, well-balanced card play for all six different card sets (three characters, combat/negotiation deck for each)- interesting balancing act between improving both of your decks to make sure neither of them are too weak, while still making sure to fight/argue at the right times- the faction and friendship system makes you think about what you're doing more than in other roguelites, killing everybody thoughtlessly will usually end badly if you don't prepare for the large consequences- well-written story and frequently fantastically written and humorous dialogue-surprisingly high replay value for a story-oriented game. there are multiple paths on each campaign, multiple choices to make on those paths, and a large variety of random quests that are pulled from for the random quest sections.grey areas:- you're very likely to make big mistakes if you don't pay attention to the story at all and don't know what's going on. however, if you skip a section of dialogue, you do get a short summary of it in its place. i don't know how effective these summaries are, since i always read the dialogue even whenever i play now, but they're there if you don't want to read the dialogue (i recommend reading it at least the first time though).-runs are quite long. i think the game is well-balanced around its runs being as long as they are, but they're quite long. probably looking at around ~3 hours for a first playthrough of each campaign. which can be somewhat painful if you die. cons:- high ascension levels are pretty poorly balanced in my opinion. some story paths become pointless because the bosses you fight on them are too strong, some builds aren't viable, et cetera.highly recommended. it's on sale at the time of this review. if you're considering it, buy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: While a big draw of this game is the "talk or fight" mechanic. Since you have 2 different decks for both and you generally can only do one or the other.  You generally get a much more powerful deck of one type and while the encounters are new. I'm not sure I'd call them very fun. They get extremely reptitive. Very fast.  I put in a good 66 hours and finished each campaign at least once. Looking back tho, I wish I had refunded.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the first deckbuilding game I ever played. First I was highly sceptical about it simply because of the epic store exclusivity.  I guess Griftlands lost a lot of audience because of it. Years of development without steam hurts. But speaking about the end product I cannot express how good it is. It is quite forgiving and noob friendly. It has a lot of replayability and a lot of fun mechanics to explore. Also, it has an awesome soundtrack!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Bought it last evening and already clocked in eight hours. If you like roguelite deckbuilders like Slay the Spire this is right up your alley. The deck building is easy to understand with highlighted keywords you can mouse over for explanations. It's fast, snappy and the art style is gorgeous.The feeling of choice with the two decks (negotation and battle) adds another dimension as you can attempt to convince the characters to help you instead of killing them. The surrender mechanic is also a lot of fun, as you have to weigh the value of someones life over upgrades for your character. Choose wrong and it may come back to haunt you down the road.A great game that stands on its own. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best roguelikes. I've had my fair share of time playing games similar to this, chiefly Slay the Spire, and for a game to come out that eclipses it like this is just so good! The combat is very similar to any other deck builder but what really draws me in is the Negotiation option. Having the option to solve things with words instead of violence is super cool and engaging for me and for it to have it's own "combat" mechanics is super fun and makes me wanna silver-tongue my way through the entire game! And you ALMOST can but damn those boss fights are tough!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I was a bit reluctant to buy this game when it came out because I was not a big fan of its art style, though I do like card game and RPG. After watching reviews and recommendations from a couple of Youtubers, I finally decided to give it a try. And Griftlands does not disappoint. It not only has very high quality of production with all the animations and voice acting and beautiful sceneries, they are reinforced by a tons of interesting mechanics such as the negotiation and battle system, character relationship and related unique perks, recruitable companions, quests and random encounters and emergency events, upgrade choices for cards, equipment, etc. etc.In a market filled with Slay the Spire clones, Driftlands stands out as something that looks similar at first but in the end feels quite different and unique to earn a place of its own. My only regret is that I didn't buy the game earlier. 10 out of 10.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the first two hours, you'll like the rest. If you don't like the first two hours, you won't like the rest. For me this is a swing and a miss from Klei Entertainment. First of all, the gameplay experience feels very "faux" rogue-like. Meaning, while there are obviously randomized events you are also very clearly hand-held through the story. You are given 2-3 choices of what to do next, and about every 1/2 or 1/3 times you pick a choice, you get pushed alongside the main storyline with handcrafted story quests. So instead of choosing between playing the main story line or doing sidequests, you end up in a loop where you HAVE to do 1-2 sidequests before you are permitted to continue the main storyline. The main questgivers will tell you as much - "go do something else until tomorrow or until I trust you more".Second, they've broadened the scope of a deckbuilder game by introducing the concept of two separate types of decks. One is used in combat, one is used in diplomacy or trying to persuade people. As you progress through the game, you can choose which of the two to specialize in - do you want to be the combat expert or the talky guy? This division between the two is actually extremely well implemented, up until the point where it isn't. Because the main storyline always has unskippable combat/persuasion events. And what one chooses to specialize in, and thus depend on, isn't balanced for these events. Meaning - you can focus primarily on being a talky guy and end up in a super difficult fight that you can't complete. The idea is that if you're super-persuasive, you can convince people to fight with you, or make the enemy fight weaker. The balance of that just doesn't work out. You can spend an hour building up a strong team of people to fight with you, and run into a boss fight that wipes them out in two turns because you didn't choose combat skills.Third, the meta progression is atrocious. By meta progression I mean how you improve between different games. The progression is almost universally "+3 health" or "15 coins at start of game". It is extremely boring. It does not unlock new ways to play the game, or new content for the game such as alternate endings or more events. You know how some games feel like they needed to pad the game length by making you depend on meta progression, literally forcing you to play the same game several times over? This game does that.The deckbuilder design is flawless. The animations/graphics are decent. The storylines and immersion feels pretty good.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: While I was not a big fan of Klei's previous games, I knew that they were a quality developer and this game proves it beyond all doubt. They tell you exactly when each new update is going to be, and they give you a way to directly send feedback through the game itself.While being a huge departure from the survival and base-building games they made, it manages to knock it out of the park with an experience that has the depth and complexity of Slay the Spire while also adding an interesting dialogue and story-based experience that makes it a very unique offering in the single-player card game genre.The main strength of the gameplay is the dual dialogue and combat system, which means in most situations you can choose whether to talk or fight your way through a situation (or both, at times -some enemies will fight you either way,  but softening them up with words beforehand can always be useful).The combat and dialogue systems are both card-based, although quite different from each other. The combat part is basically exactly like Slay The Spire (which is fine, if it ain't broke, don't fix it), the dialogue part is, in my opinion, much more interesting and nuanced. It's hard to explain, you basically target either the enemy's resolve (akin to HP) or their arguments and counterpoints while building up your own verbal skillset. Of course eventually it does boil down to numbers, but there's many skill-based decisions you will have to make in both systems, with just the right amount of randomness to keep things interesting.I also have to point out how flavorful the effects are, which is a staple of good card game design. As for the game's overworld, you travel along a map to many different locations and you meet/fight many different characters. There's a lot of randomly generated mini-events and rewards that make each run unique without breaking the main storyline.Everything is well-drawn and appropriately grimy given the game's dystopian sci-fi setting (think Mass Effect+Fallout), the dialogue is good, the music is good and the progression system is definitely enough to keep you interested for a while.It's basically a completed title despite being in Early Access, for 10 euros it's an absolute STEAL.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game! Gameplay similar to Slay the Spire but with a story attached this time. Fantastic writing, too. While the stories are not world shattering innovations, they are excellently delivered with good characterization and humorous dialogue and events. I do wish, however, that they let you share difficulty levels between the characters. As it stands you have to clear all 7 difficulty levels with each character independently. So if you reach level 5 on one character and want to play another.. back to level 1 with you. Similarly each character has their own meta-progression that you have to grind out. I think they made these choices to give people more "things to do".. but I really would have preferred if they hadn't. I'd be more likely to play the game more if I could at least share the difficulty levels and play whichever character I wanted without having to go spend hours grinding easier content.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I am absolute garbage at deck building games. Despite this minor flaw I still enjoy them thoroughly. Griftlands is absolutely a deck builder, but it contains a lot more story than I am used to in these games. At some point, after a lot of hour, I assume that it will boil down to a more mechanics focused game for the player, but for me, that is still not the case after 15 hours.To my understanding the setting is unique to this game, and the story, and the main characters in them, are vastly different, allowing for different kinds of decks to be built. The storys can be played through at an increased difficulty as well, giving you potentially lots of hours of gameplay, figuring out what kind of broken combos that can be assembled.Unfortunately, from what I have been able to see, there are no plans for expansions or similar additions to the game. Potentially due to lackluster sales or player activity (looking at steamcharts) which is incredibly sad, since I really enjoyed my experience. There are still some kind of daily challenges available for those that want more in the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Oddly enough, I always hated Deckbuilders prior to playing this game.I consider both Hearthstone and Magic The Gathering pay to win as you can pay to have access to more cards. So I never bothered with either of those. I tried Slay the Spire, but it really lacked in depth during combat, choosing which card to play didn't require much thought at all. The only strategy that game required was building your deck then just relying on the RNG to give you the cards you want.Griftlands on the other hand has a lot of strategy involved while also being an RPG. There's permanent buffs/debuffs you can unlock by choosing different outcomes of Quests and becoming friends/enemies with NPCs, you can level up the cards you play most choosing from multiple upgrade paths for each one. The RPG elements really enhance the gameplay as there's even random events that occur while you're on your quests. I'd highly recommend this game to anyone interested in Deck Builders or even just RPGs as this one combines them really well. Sadly, there's not much voice acting just weird noises made by the characters when talking, but honestly you can probably skip most of the dialogue and just choose what you want to do to each person when the options are given to you lol.There's even 2 main modes to the card combat. Negotiation and regular Combat, both having different decks that you build throughout the campaign. Each playing fairly differently. Negotiation focuses on creating buffs and debuffs while trying to destroy the enemy's buffs, where as regular combat is all about creating combo attacks.It also has a lot of replay value as there's different characters to play as with different starting decks and multiple quests you can do during a playthrough as well as multiple outcomes to each quest.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Shortest way I can describe Griftlands is Slay the Spire meets Fallout. Conflicts are resolved with words or weapons (and sometimes both). The upgrade system means cards are improved with XP, gained by playing them, which is probably my personal favorite upgrade system for card battlers. Each character has a distinct negotiation and battle style, often having two or more distinct specializations of each. Grafts grant further bonuses, and a character's opinion of you can modify the game even further. Just don't expect each run to result in success.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really fun deckbuilding, story-heavy roguelike with one of the unique features being that you have two different decks you use depending on what encounters you get in: either your negotiation deck to talk people over to your point of view or the battle deck for when things come to blows. The negotiations and battles follow similar rules but still play very differently from eachother and the differing playstyles even within the same genre help keep the game feeling more fresh than either of these two styles could do on their own. The consequence-heavy approach to storytelling and the varied random elements ensure that no two playthroughs will be the same, especially since there are multiple paths you can take to your goal even before adding those random elements. One word of warning though, while you can take a break and pick up where you left off without losing much (if any) progress, a single run will be SIGNIFICANTLY longer than your average rougelike. If you're looking to finish a run in 30 minutes to an hour, that won't be possible here. I could talk all day about the nuances to both negotiations and combat, but that'd make this review longer than I feel like typing at the moment.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I played through Sal's campaign in one sitting, I was glued to my computer. There is an endless mode like other roguelike card games (ex: Slay the Spire) It has a narrative, there are interesting characters and a relationship system that I really enjoy. It feels like a fully fleshed out game and its still in early access.  I have probably put 30 hours into Slay The Spire but this might take the spot because I really enjoy the RPG elements this game has. The card leveling mechanic is also really neat, you level cards by using them, so it is possible to upgrade multiple cards in a fight.8/10Its not perfect, the story mode is on the shorter side and that's what I felt really shined most but this is a roguelike so you can't really have long campaigns.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredible. Not one but TWO different card games with really great mechanics. With RPG elements. With Rouge-like mechanics. With great story-telling, world building, art style. Everything about this game is a hit and it's a blend of ideas I've never seen in a game before. Super impressed.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: If you’re a fan of deck-building games with a strong narrative twist, Griftlands is a gem you won’t want to miss. Klei Entertainment has crafted a truly engaging experience that combines strategic deck-building with rich storytelling and decision-making.Griftlands places you in a gritty, dystopian world where every decision can have far-reaching consequences. The game’s standout feature is its dual-layered gameplay: a deck-building system that’s as deep as it is satisfying, and a narrative-driven choice system that keeps the story evolving based on your actions. Each playthrough feels fresh, thanks to the multiple characters you can choose from, each with their own unique storylines and abilities.The deck-building aspect is brilliantly executed. You’ll find yourself constantly tweaking your deck, weighing the pros and cons of various cards, and strategizing how to tackle the diverse challenges that come your way. The combat is engaging and requires tactical thinking, and the blend of negotiation and combat adds a unique layer of depth to the gameplay.Visually, the game is a delight with its distinctive art style that perfectly complements its narrative and thematic elements. The character designs and animations are full of personality and bring the world to life.However, the game’s complexity might be a hurdle for newcomers. There’s a learning curve that can be a bit steep at first, and the sheer amount of mechanics and choices can be overwhelming. But once you get past the initial adjustment period, the rewards are well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Great combination of roguelike and CRPG with excellent draft deck building. Worth picking up if any of those things are of interest to you. I loved getting my teeth into this game and have been enjoying the unique gameplay and campaigns of all three characters. Smith is my favourite purely for the drunken master vibe of the combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10Pros:- nice graphics, great music and sounds- interesting stories (for a indie card game)- multiple ways during the runCons:- Deck building too slow and too random (I see it is a problem with most deck building games). You buy/trash couple of cards here and there, get some free and thats it.- Especialy combat is too simplified. No sophisticated play. You have too little time during the run to really focus your deck on combos. Cheapest cards + bonuses from implants and other sources are usualy enough. Even if you invest in something stronger, it usualy works similar - just better.- Negotiation on the other hand is much more interesting to play, but sci-fi cyberpunk game based on talking, talking and talking - when combat looks so cool - is "meh". Unfortunately the game pressures you to negotiate most of the time (with only exception of boss fights) as it is usualy gives you more options/bonuses/rewards.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best early access games I've ever purchased. The devs are very active and consistent, which is the most important marker of a worthwhile EA purchase in my opinion. They are devoted to making the game as good as it can be, delivering updates and bug fixes week after week. As of this review, there are two main characters to choose from (with a third in development). Both of their play styles feel fresh and unique. Choices really matter; who you choose to befriend, betray, kill, or save helps and/or hinders your run and shapes which options and events are available to you. The recurring, core choice of the game is between negotiation or combat. As you progress, you build decks to tackle both situations. This dual deck approach is well-executed and refreshing; the negotiation mechanics in particular are so satisfying and original. I could wax poetic about this wonderful game for ages. It truly is a labor of love. Buy it and see for yourself!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I was hesitant to try out Griftlands, because I had previously tried out Slay the Spire, another Roguelite Card Battler, and I did not like it.In these games, you have a starting deck of cards that you do battle with, and throughout your adventure you can add new, more powerful cards, as well as get rid of some of your old, weaker cards. The new cards can have synergies with one another, and there were dozens of synergies you could build your deck around in Slay the Spire. My problem with that game, is that 90% of these synergies didn't stand a snowball's chance in hell of making it through the game's 3rd and final level; there's only a couple of builds per character that scaled well enough to actually beat the game with, and everything else felt like a trap. Slay the Spire presents you with a wide range of false choices that will inevitably fail, with a couple of real builds hidden in between; I don't find that enjoyable.By contrast, Griftlands offers you a range of synergistic cards that actually work. Mind-blowing, I know. Griftlands has a far superior art style, it offers different locales with their own distinct atmospheres and circumstances as the adventure's stomping grounds, it has two parallel combat systems in its combat and its diplomacy system, and does a good job of portraying how as you gain notoriety, you gain new friends, but also make new enemies. It's a pretty challenging game, I've had runs where I've lost when my build didn't come together, and other runs where I was a hair's breadth away from losing.So, as someone who didn't like Slay the Spire at all, I would describe Griftlands as: "Like Slay the Spire, but good"
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: By far one of the best deck-building rogue-likes I've ever played. I wouldn't have expected a genre like this to be as good at storytelling as this game is (similar to Hades in that regard)There's a wealth of key-words and mechanics that I expected I would just bounce right off of, but it's shockingly intuitive and I found myself getting the hang of everything way faster than I expected. I love this game. If you like Slay the Spire, you'll love this game too.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I picked up the game because I liked Slay the Spire and it was suggested. By adding a second deck during your run and more story-driven choices, the game becomes more interesting (and complex). I really enjoy this addition to the game so far, but I'm not sure if it will continue to be interesting after a few runs.I'm glad I bought the game so far, and I plan to play it through, but since the story is such an important part of the experience, I doubt it will be as replayable as other games.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I had this game since I loved Mark of the Ninja and this one didn't disappoint. I'm no stranger with Deckbuilding Roguelite like Slay the Spire and Monster Train and although this game is often criticized for it's lack of replayability but I actually disagree. This game has tons of replayability with how : - alternate endings from the choices you make - various cards you could get and explore - friends and enemies you could make down the line . - various dialogues you can exploit -  decisions that might haunt you or help you down the road There are twerks that i wish the game could resolve such as : - the ability to see post-ending cutscenes. - Read more lore during your spare time like the Bog underground and more info on certain races and background stories with the main character. - Saving specific parts of the days ( which of course defeats the purpose but would make the game less punishing ) Overall, this didn't let down my overal enjoyment with its animation , fantastic writing and world- building .
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This is a solid game, though a little too forgiving for having too many cards in your deck, at lower difficulty levels. It does not give many options to remove cards from your deck so be careful. campaign is long compared to Slay the Spire and most card games of this type. Game is easier than Slay the Spire as well, so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game as always from Klei. I don't usually play early-access games because, in my perspective, what's the point of playing something that's incomplete? This was worth it.I was invited by a good friend to try it out. The most charming point of the game is that no two playthroughs are exactly the same. I like how each card seems to tell your story as you play along. During my first few playthroughs, I essentially went on a murder-spree against any of the Admirality faction since it seemed like something that Sal, the first character you play as, would do. Because of that, I earned Battle cards that became more and more geared towards psychopathic tendencies, and my Negotiation cards started to build an interesting mix of overaggressive Hostility with "shuffle"-Diplomacy. In my most recent playthrough, I decided to try a "peaceful route" and focused on making everyone love me instead, which made a cool Negotiation deck based on Arguments, and a Battle deck with Combo-Finishers. There's something addicting about one-hundred percenting these decks.I encourage you to try out the Demo, at least, to support Griftlands and Klei's team. There's a lot of potential for growth through community efforts and feedback. I don't think there's going to be a bigger discount than what we have right now because of how new the game is - it seems like there's already a huge pool of players early-gaming it, so I don't expect any bigger discounts on this game until it's done.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: When I last played, thematically and story-wise, this did a very good job of assembling an interesting and coherent narrative, so if you are interested in that, i would check this game out. The actual gameplay is a little weaker - while it's a deck-builder in style, it doesn't mechanically scratch the great itch of putting together a coherent deck. The upgrade system is interesting, but the requirement to have multiple characters can make combats unbalanced, and negotiation can be a little difficult to parse at times. I do hope those improve while the game is in early access, and the price is a little high as is. However, it's at least worth a look.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome deck builder, each character gets their own story, cards, map and overall playstyle, can't wait to get the rest of Smith's story arc. There's even a brawl mode for a quick playthrough without all the dialogue, challenge mode with draft boss rush... this early release is very promising, give it a try if you're the deck builder type.

_childDocuments_.review: A game that is almost less than the sum of its parts manages to make for an engaging (if overwhelming) deckbuilding game.I almost didn't want to recommend this game. What it took was biting the bullet and just playing through the story on easy so I could unlock the Brawl Mode where you just play "a roguelite deckbuilding game." The art is gorgeous, but you won't be looking at much besides the cards and effects. The writing for the story parts is stellar, but you'll be skipping it to get to the card games. I feel this game fundamentally missed what I wanted from a deckbuilding game.To explain, to start, you have one character unlocked, and you must *attempt* her story before the second character unlocks. The story mode is interesting, as you travel a zone in almost in a Fallout 1 style map screen (, meaning it's not based on a grid). You make decisions of where to go and what to do from there, but unless you have an active quest giver or shop at a location, you can't specifically navigate there. This feels like an interesting design for a roguelite scenario, and it serves the game well enough.From the map, the infinite permutations of RNG arise. A major factor in these chances seems to be how various characters feel about you. Living characters fall on a scale of Love/Like/Neutral/Dislike/Hate, which can be modified by beginning of the game perks, as well as your interactions with them in game. Additionally, Characters that Love or Hate you will give you Buffs or Debuffs respectively, which are fixed to those given characters.Character design is largely Fixed. While some characters are explicitly the same from run to run, many names will still be out and about, and may even come up in the different settings for different characters. Their bonuses are tied to their job, and are fixed and remembered by the system if you acquire them. You can largely tell by their visual design which different powers and abilities they'll have in Negotiation and Combat, as well as what they'll reward.Which brings me to the actual game where you play cards. There are two fundamental decks each character has: a negotiation deck and a battle deck. Additionally cards gain experience as you use them, meaning if you pick one thing to do more often then you'll often end up leveling up only that side of your abilities. This system ironically balances really well in the Brawl mode, as you can typically do both or neither, but it lacks a lot more in the story modes where those actions are tied to morality and other systems in the game.Speaking of systems that get in each others' way, in a review ostensibly about a deckbuilding game, it took me 3-4 paragraphs to get to the actual deckbuilding talk. The major issue with  is that it has  it constantly feels as though one or the other is actively getting in your way when you're looking around. I mentioned perks briefly, but perks are purchased with points that can also be spent in game to get flourishes for characters, while playing characters in general gets you Mettle. To give an example of how obtuse the language can get, I really enjoy playing Smith as a Moxie-based brawler who relies on Gain effects, as well as running a Quip-based to orchestrate my bravado so my bullies deal maximum damage. I don't have enough Mettle to Flourish quickly based on my builds, but I'm building up. Not that confusing? Well I don't know which card packs I'm keeping in the mix, but the fact that I'm basically in love with a few cards seems the exception to the rule. Each character has what seems to be at least 3 "themes" for Negotiation and Battle each, and that's on top of their inherent mechanic. The reason the Brawl mode works so well (but you can't brawl with a character without having completed their story at least once, even in easy mode) is that you're just constantly immersed in those systems as they swirl around you. In the story itself, I'm distracted by becoming either a triple agent, or by whether I want to be a murderer, or by the fact that I  don't know how to (and this is a keyword) 'train' a pet. Additionally, the story mode just kinda ends. Even if you find that to be a suitable conclusion, I actually enjoy the more Fallout-style going around and making friends and enemies gameplay of moral choices through dialogue and card games. If you're not careful, this game can be so much less than the sum of its parts, and that's a shame.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this on switch awhile ago, in fact it was my first switch game from the nintendo online game store. Loved it, finally bought it on sale here just to have with my steam deck on the go games. At first I was put off by the less roguelike more narrative style of this game but it quickly grew on me and really love the world the developers created here, its the little things, the language that each person speaks, the way you can have npcs love and hate you, kinda makes you feel like a han solo type figure in their world. Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Very challenging and very satisfying. Both the negotiation deck and the combat decks for each character are fun and it's neat to work with each character's gimmickEdit: now that the game's full campaign is out, I can easily say I loved each and every one of them. Each had their own style to them, and building decks around each play style was a satisfying challenge
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10A Spire-like with enough uniqueness to stand out. Adds a story, RPG elements, parties, and great art to the Spire formula. I had fun and it's challenging in a good way.Pros:The mechanics are very good. The card-specific XP system forces you into interesting decisions constantly. The character and animation design is really beautiful, top notch work. Having two different decks makes the game more interesting and this mechanic is thematically worked in very nicely.Cons:The card design falls a bit flat. Cards lack the personality / flavour you see in Magic, Hearthstone, or even Spire. Everything from the naming, to the art, to the way the cards are laid out, the mechanics... When you upgrade a card it changes the name. Afterward, I would often be unable to recognize the new card at a glance. I think that speaks for itself.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty nice. Nice mix of strategies, with many card types and upgrades (some per run, some permanent). The option in many cases to negotiate or battle adds a nice element, although negotiations can be a bit long.Graphics are nice enough, story is ok. I like the different play styles/card decks for the characters.Price seems quite reasonable.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a charming deckbuilder roguelite where you play as a variety of characters and manage two distinct decks, a combat deck, and a negotiation deck. You play out a story that evolves as you make decisions, allowing you to recruit allies, make enemies, and gain powerful items to help you in your fights or negotiations. It's generally not a good idea to invest heavily into only one of your two decks, but it can work depending on your foreknowledge of how the run works. I've been impressed by the mechanics, but it's not exactly the most thinking-heavy game. All-in-all it's just good fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely YES! I was just waiting for this game to leave EA to start playing it.It has really all what's needed to make it a true masterpiece, and could be played from every kind of player.- Absoltely original and innovative mechanics- Great feeling of progression and challange- Every run new surprises (bad and good)- Unique approach of having both a battle deck and a diplomacy deck, to face situations- Very well written story, sfx, background soundtrack- Every choice got consequences (Characters love/like/dislike/hate) giving you semi-permanent buff or debuff- Very addictive, especially for completionist!- Regular Updates from Devs, new features, daily challanges and much moreJust go for it, worth the full price definitely.This game definitely won a place on the podium together with slay the spyre and monster train, but it adds as well a story and lore, making it even more valuable!Excellent job, devs!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's an interesting take on a roguelike deckbuilder game - it has much more of a focus on a story. The combat is more interesting and deep than many similar games, and the split between physical combat and negotiation gives it a very different feel than many games these days. That said, it's still in development and the more "pure" non-story roguelike aspect of the game needs more work.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I couldn't care less about the story, and the fact that there IS a story is basically the only thing Griftlands brings to the rouge-like deck builder genre. That and the fact that you can often choose if you want to fight in a more traditional card battle setup  or if you want to have a "negotiation" where you use a second deck that is overall much less fun and with much more convoluted mechanics. The worst part of the game is the relationship system, how the game tracks who loves, like, dislikes, or hates you. Did some random Chewbacca ripoff attack you? Did you kill this thing? Well now two random dudes you've never met hate you, and this means you get a random debuff like losing a certain amount of currency daily or a ton of other stupid things that a persons hate for me couldn't control. I bought this game because I like the genre and I like Klei, but Griftlands is easily the worst game in their catalog.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's still in progress, but it's already a fun deck builder. The story modes are enjoyable and it's easy to get into the RPG aspects of it (do I want to play a more ruthless or cunning character this time?) both in deck choices and non-deck choices.The game is based around managing two decks in a run, one for negotiation encounters and one for combat encounters. These decks have different base play styles and each character has a specific different style of play for both, and there are plenty of choices to make for each. In general though, negotiation encounters make you work back and forth because you can 'attack' the opponents core argument or you can attack their various negotiation buffs, while combat works more like straight forward deck builder RPG combat.I'm not sure if this is just something that has changed or not, but the description of the game as being more about non-deck based game play don't ring true to me. The majority of my enjoyment of this game definitely comes from the combat and negotiations.I don't think the combat flow is as smooth as some other games. Making a really focused deck is tougher in this game because there aren't as many opportunities to gain or lose cards, and card upgrades appear to be random options. Because of this, you often have to balance the decisions you're making in any given turn a little more, even into the end of a run. This is a pro and a con, but it's also balanced out a bit by other things in the run which affect your gameplay, such as bonuses from grafts - items which give a boon for the rest of the run - or nerfs given to you cause an NPC to hate you.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a well executed game. At first glance it seemed like a Slay the Spire clone, but the Griftlands team delivered a game that is much more interesting to me.  I loved the separate Negotiation vs Battle mechanics and how negotiations can influence battles. I also like how the story elements are built for replayability. I pick up new nuggets of either character or world story with each playthrough. Good stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very fun game. The story sections can get old after a while but that's why the game gives you brawl mode eventually. This mode simplifies the game down to just the basic gameplay loop, which is almost endlessly fun. Griftlands isn't the absolute best card game I've ever played, nor is it the greatest story ever told, but I'd really struggle to find anything about it to criticize. It's just really solid.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Very polished for early access. Been following this project for a while before I purchased.Does not mislead you on the difficulty- expect to lose quite often at first, as you get a proper handle on things.Story telling work is excellent. At points I laughed, and at points I actually had to sit and debate myself on the best course of action. It's a 3 energy Card System, like almost every other card system. That's not a complaint, the system works.With two kinds of health pools and two separate decks, which can be developed into very different styles, there's a LOT to explore in this.Small qualms- very rarely, text may be misleading (Gold for friendship bribe and not paying off the debt they hold... which is less than the bribe). This is not a savescumming game. The autosave makes you commit to your mistakes. While never intended, visual glitches tend to be rapid flickering. These will eventually be resolved but worth mentioning if you're photosensitive. I love this game. I'm going to pump a dozen more hours into it, and probably fall back into it once a month for a weekend at a time. I hope most of my friends pick this up, because it's a great time sink for solo play.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I remember not giving this game a shot because I thought it was just another deck building kind of game. Much like how Klei knocked it out of the park in the survival game genre with "Don't Starve", they've done it once again with the rouge-lite, deck building genre with Griftlands. This game manages to make each card you have in your desk tell a story with how your character interacts with the world around them. Although the destination for each character arc remains the same throughout very long, possibly multiple-day runs, how you arrive at that situation is up to you and the types of decks you build- if you can even make it to the end. Really good stuff. Excited to see how they end the third character's arc.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This Rogue-lite RPG has great style and offers two forms of combat, verbal and physical. Both systems are card based but deck progression is not persistent. Runs vary greatly besides the story beats making each run unique. NPCs speak a gibberish language, which is hilarious to make fun of. (Sounds like Huttese.)
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Overall just an awesome game. It's a Rogue-Lite Deck Building Game that has a story for each of the characters as well as a repeatable "brawl" that skips the dialogue and gets right into the gameplay. They have a daily "challenge" that is a run with some funky interaction. Biggest difference in this game (gameplay wise) than most other Roguelites is that you can see enemies "intents" prior to them going. I, personally, love this, but it warrants being noticed for those who dislike this kind of interaction.That mechanics are a blast, the stories are immersive, the character differences are drastic, and the gameplay loop is addicting. Can't recommend this game enough. :)
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: As most people have, I found this after playing Slay the Spire. Since then, it has become one of the best games that I have played—and it's not even in it's release version yet.The strategy doesn't stop with the cards, as any decision you make throughout the day can change your experience for the following days, or dictate your survival of the current day. There are lots of interesting mechanics in the game that I haven't seen anywhere else.Highly recommend to people who like deck-building and roguelite games, though I also recommend anyone else to try it out as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Slay the spire was delicious T-Bone Steak perfectly medium rare and cooked to perfectionGriftlands Is the T-Bone Steak with oven cooked chips seasoned with herbs and garlic With a fried tomatoes and mushrooms with finally Bearnaise sauce on the side.Its not only more of what you love but many things on the side that accompany it well i could go on into detail about the good story that this game has or how well the negotiation mini-game fits into the game but all i can say is that its well worth the money i've already spent on it and it hasn't even exited early access.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely feel like writing a review for a game, even if I loved it, but seeing the recent mixed reviews angered me enough to write one.This is a deep and highly polished deckbuilder with loads of different builds thanks to the two deck system.Comparing it to Slay the Spire or Monster Train is absolutely ridiculous.Sure, these are also deckbuilders, but they are focused solely on gameplay with just enough plot to justify their existence.This is a story driven game with dialogue and branching scenarios while still being a damn solid deck building game.Claiming the game is not replayable is wild - it has two game modes with the option to apply various rule modifiers, daily challenges and mod support with many mods expanding the gameplay readily available.There isn't any less content here than in other big deckbuilders, but even if there was it would easily make up for it with polish.If you're tired of story mode you can play brawl and focus on battling, but I still keep coming back to story mode because of each scenario having two branches, all quests having at least two solutions and the emergent gameplay based on the relationships you have with characters.I've spent thousands of hours playing deckbuilders, be it big names like StS or less known (and less good) ones like Roguebook, and Griftlands is up there with the best of the best.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a boring, slow-paced, overly simplified knock-off of Slay the Spire with too much pointless reading of cookie-cutter copy-pasted RPG sidequest dialogue. Boggles the mind how people can actually play this. Not going into an in-depth critique of the mechanics because it's not worth it - this game is so bad that I lost interest before my first run ended.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I was skeptical of a deckbuilder focused around negotiation. However, I've found that the negotiation and battle mechanics complement each other nicely. Negotiations make battles easier with allies or intimidation. However, you CAN'T play through the whole game without fighting. There is no pacifist run possible and it ensures even if your negotiation deck is flawless, you have to develop your battle deck.Outside of the gameplay, the characters and setting are unique and fun to explore. I really enjoy the relationship mechanic which can make your game a lot easier or a lot harder depending how many people you help/screw over. This puts some weight to your interactions with the people you meet.Overall, because I was skeptical about the game. So, I feel it's necessary to tell other people the game is certainly worth trying. Even if you're not into deck-builders normally, this is a very user-friendly game and everyone will find some enjoyment out of it
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Truth be told I logged over 60 hours in the *demo* for this game. (It was because of an agreement I had at the time with my wife to not spend money on new games.) The demo was amazing, and the full version is even more so. I keep coming back to it and it never gets old. A masterpiece, in my opinion.10/10 would recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. Never really captured my attention, but it's fun enough to play. I kinda wish it was easier to put together more varied builds, though. It started to feel very samey a few runs in - So many of your options rely entirely on rng, and I don't think the overall slowish speed of gameplay and long run length helped that feeling. That aside, there are tons of cool systems in the game - maybe even too many, considering how many I just ignored most runs. Feels like they made 60% of a whole-ass rpg and then tried to fold it into a roguelite. Plenty of pros to that, but a few cons too.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A great combat/negotiation system that encourages many strategies and experimentation.The missions are vast and varied. The Smith Campaign especially has some very interesting mission where you can choose many ways to accomplish the same task.This game is simply fantastic.Also, it can even run on a crappy laptop
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Brand new update came out. Changed mutators. Now you can't gain any progress for using them. If I can't play a game the way I want to play and gain meaningful progress for it, then I'm not interested. Also, beat this game about 10 times so far and got zero carry over progress for perks. So, in order gain anything from this update, I have to beat it another 10 times with zero mutators or any way to customize my experience. Quite possibly one of the most disappointing updates for a game I've had for a while.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: While lacking in long campaign content, but peppered with a respectable variety of events and interactions, the mechanics are such that I think with a more ambitious, in terms of duration, campaign, this is shaping up to be a genre defining deckbuilder. Also I am always pleased when amorality or immorality are made central to the workings of a game world, without manichaeistic guardrails, and you are truly a creature of that world and operate within it's reality. Love it and can't wait for more content to dive into
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: For what I have played so far the game looks really interesting, dying doesn't cost much because we get some benfits out of every runs. BUT I think the combat system is really hard and that the bosses start with a lot of health compared to our character, which is quite stupid. I also wanted to know if achievements or cards (badges) will be added in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Fantasticly addicting, and a lot of fun.Going into the game after playing a lot of similar games - but it's fresh.The first hour was very confusing, but you quickly learn the ropes.I wish there were more minigames here. The brawl can get a bit intense to sit through it all.Definitely better to play story version with quicker scenes for a good replay experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is another kind of Deckbuilder Roguelike.And that isn't meant negative, not at all.Just after I thought Monster Train was a fresh take on the Deckbuilder genre and would be my go-to Deckbuilder when I felt like playing one, this gem here came out of nowhere and hooked me.In Griftlands you see, you essentially pick a Character at first (There's currently two, out of which I only played one by this point). This Character has a set goal/story which you play out.Gain friends and make enemies along the story, earn weapons, skills and boons to create your own build.When you manage to beat the story, you unlock Prestige 1, and as you might guess from that, when beating the story at Prestige 1, you unlock Prestige 2 and so on. Even if you lose, you get XP and unlock Cosmetic skins and/or new cards for future runs.The two things that really seperate this Deckbuilder from others, in my opinion are;1. The "rounds" are way longer. In Monster Train, my longer rounds take somewhere from 30-45 minutes. In Slay the Spire I'm anywhere from 45-60. In Griftlands my average is inbetween 2.5 and 3.5 hours.That can be a good thing, with more time on your hand, you get more invested into your current situation.And from a developer standpoint, if you make the rounds have a longer time, you can pack more events and different encounters in those, and they'll never feel repetitive.Of course, sometimes I'll also just want a quick round, but that's not much of a problem, I'll get to why it isn't problematic later in the Review.2. You are building actually 2 decks, not only 1 per run.While in any other Deckbuilder you build only your Combat deck, in Griftlands you also create a Negotiation deck, next to your Combat deck. That way you get a lot of freedom in character-building. You can make a character with a silver-tongue, that doesn't really excel at fighting. A character that mows over people, but has the verbal skills of a speech impaired monkey. Or a well balanced out character that can do both pretty good, or neither, the choice (and as with all Deckbuilders, luck) is yours.To get back to the thing with wanting quicker rounds sometimes.For that, I like to have Monster Train, which I then play, but Griftlands also offers another mode aside from regular Story mode, in which you play it more in a linear fashion, as with most Deckbuilders. In that mode the runs are way shorter and allow for a quick run when you just feel like getting that Deckbuilder fix satisfied.Overall, I can just say; The game released only a little while ago, and is already a lot richer on content than most Deckbuilders out there. Can only recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredibly fun. I love the rpg elements and the negotiating mechanic especially seems unique. I really enjoy that the quests can be a range of negotiate or battle and most of all i love getting the battle pets. Also excited to get more outfits for Sal. I hope to see more story added or "campaigns" for sal. As well as looking forward to playing the other characters. Definitely the funnest card game i've played since it doesn't require me to battle douchebags online and has an actual interesting story and characters in it.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a game I would recommend.To be clear,yes,its a card game along the lines of Slay the Spire  or Monster Train.While not quite offering the same level  of deck combo power surge some players might enjoy from those games,its nevertheless an exceptional card game.What makes is unique is its emphasis on story rich campaign for every character,as well as the choice between dialogue or combat for most encounters.+)Pros:+ Beautiful art style and animations+ Variety of decks and playstyles+ 3 characters with their very own story,decks and feel+ Great mix of story and gameplay+ Made by Klei-)Cons:-Some systems,like the perk system,feel a bit bare bones.However,I am hopeful this will change until this game is released.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I think I bought this game for the wrong reason. It's not a bad game. I was intrigued by the idea of a story-driven rogueliite. I enjoy roguelites pick up and play nature, their good for when I am too busy for bigger games. I find deck builders more engaging than traditional turn-based RPGS. And the artstyle is awesome. So I was excited about this game. I tried it once for about 5 hours, and then stopped playing for months without even realizing. I kept looking at it in my library and being like, "Huh, why did I stop playing that game? I thought it was good." I then picked it up again and realized why I stopped played. The story feels like it may as well not even be there. All the bits are chopped up into ways that you end up just feeling like quickly clicking through because nothing anyone says has any consequences, merit, or weight to you or whats happening. It's all flavor text. And the main plot and characters on their own don't offer enough for me to come back.Also there is an imbalance in getting to "choose" to be passive or aggressive ends up being fake as you end up needing both to progress. So yeah, all the elements I was excited for ended up being not quite there. It's not a bad game, clearly as many people have pointed out, but I got bored as I generally need a story to carry me through these types of games.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot more to it than any other roguelike I've played from a story perspective (although that's not to say it's story-driven), and difficulty-wise it's not so bad you'll be restarting every ten minutes, which is what turns me off about others in the genre. Add the great art that Klei always has and in the end it's definitely my favorite game of theirs.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Not really great as a deck builder. For each character, there are really only two different metas you can use for your battle and negotiation decks; so you can't really get creative with your builds. It's probably fine though if you don't actually care about the deck building aspect, but to me that's really the whole point of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I've been enjoying this gem since the beginning it seems.  Huge fan of Klei Entertainment.Seems to be much more balanced than before, though perhaps a bit too easy.  I cakewalked through all 3 characters main quest.  But luckily, there are harder difficulty levels available as well, plus the RNG to keep things fresh.  Always finding new things every run.Great job Klei!  Another wonderful success that I will be enjoying and sharing with others for years to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay of Griftlands isn't as tight, original, or replayable as something like Slay the Spire.  But what it lacks in those departments, it makes up for with to-notch writing, art, and lore.   The stories are delightful.  And the negotiation battles are truly inspired.  If you like deckbuilders and  are willing to overlook some mechanical shaginess in exchange for the opportunity to luxuriate in an exquisitely-drawn world inhabited with charming dirtbags, this game is a great option.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Super fun Deck Building game that allows you to bargain your way out of trouble or if bargaining fails, try and murder your opponents instead. I truly love the art and design of every character in this game, it kept reminding of something like Treasure Planet.Klei Entertainment knows how to create a engaging universe and they've done so very well with Griftlands.Can't wait for further updates and for a full release soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I did not expect a card-based roguelike to inspire me to write an entire setting for the Genesys RPG system, but it did. The world and lore is just that interesting.Also, this is not a Slay the Spire clone like so, so many others. The limited use items you get in your deck, deciding who to befriend for their bonus and who to kill for their equipment (angering their friends for a penalty), and the card EXP system all create something that feels very, very different - more methodical and calculated.It's still in Early Access, so not all of the story content is present quite yet, but the three characters, each with unique and varied mechanics, present more than enough variety to enjoy the endless "brawl" mode over and over again.Quite simply, Klei knocks it out of the park, again.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Very very fun. If you're a fan of Slay the Spire or Monster Train, you HAVE to try Griftlands. Because the RPG-like story of each roguelite run is so satisfying, it really feels deep. Superb design and writing from the people at Klei as well. Plus the prestige system and multiple characters keeps it very replayable. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, just wow! It has been awhile since I have played a game so polished to the brim. Griftlands is an immersive, extremely well-made, and wondrous deck-building experience — combining the best elements of card game-play, world-building, narrative storytelling, and social-links into a cohesive and awesome deck-building experience.PROS:+A great deck-building engine that makes sense, creating a seamless card-drafting mechanic from choices made within the game via its branching story, card upgrade options, and social-links (NPC's can love and hate you, providing boons or negative side effects).+The game is extremely optimized with beautiful and creative world-building, characters, animations, and special effects.+The User-Interface, icon placements, and description of status effects or card abilities is displayed in a very convenient and helpful manner. Everything is very well thought out and just clicks!+Replay value is extremely high here with Flourish (Limit Break Unlocks), Mettle (Carrying over perks), and Prestige (Difficulty) mechanics. Bonus points for having varied Character Skins when you progress through these unlocks.+The Daily Challenges with unique modifiers is very well made and works as a quick run to the joyous game-play that is Griftlands!CONS:-Griftlands is extremely ambitious and sets out to do a lot of things at once. However, if you are looking for a complex and in-depth card game with meta deck-building, you might find Griftlands wanting. This can of course be improved by adding more builds and content into the game. over time!NEUTRAL:-I would say that the voice over that is being spoken in gibberish might not appeal to some but this method also allows the creation of more scenarios in the game to be created (without the need for narrated voice-over). It is actually pretty ingenious how the overall design of this game offers a captivating semi-sandbox content packed world-building galore that will only get better in time.The Developers did a phenomenal job and I really hope Griftlands will continue to receive the tender love and care it rightfully deserves with DLC content as the fundamentals for this game is amazingly poised to be one of the best and most polished single-player card games out there.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this and another early access title on the same day. I'm not going to tell you the name of the other game, but it rhymes with Morchfight Tree.I don't know how long both games were in development, and I know they're totally different genres, but Griftlands is Early Access done right.This game is amazing, if you're into Deckbuilder type games. So far, Sal and Rook play totally different, and like other roguelite games, even if you fail your game, you'll unlock cards/items/cosmetics for future runs.Griftlands is really fun stuff, and unlike Morchfight Tree, I don't have to worry about the servers being up or not being able to zone, or why do all my characters share the same quests!? _childDocuments_.review: Early Access review: If you've played Slay the Spire (amazing deck builder if you haven't played it) you'll understand a lot of the underlying concepts straight up. However Griftlands is different. You're not just dealing with combat, negotiating is a completely different beast (still deck based), and while different, honestly no less enjoyable and cool because it mixes things up. Not only is combat and negotiation different, the narrative is a lot more compelling. A Slay the Spire run when it's going well draws me in pretty hard core, but my desire to go back after playing each character is fairly minimal, although done several times. Griftlands gives you the same journey, but with more journey. Making a decision isn't a split path that you can see ahead of time making the most informed decision, it's a path including the unknown. Going from A to B may mean you run into C, and now you must deal with the consequences of encounter C, which was not planned. And that's why I'd really recommend it.

Yeah that's Griftlands for me. I'm blown away by the amount of polish this game has for an early access title, and how deep this game is for a deck builder. _childDocuments_.review: I've played for 3 hours in early access and I can already tell it's another KLEI masterpiece. Don't think they've made a bad game yet.if Oxygen Not Included is any indication it will probably be in early access for some time, but you wouldn't know because it's probably entirely bug-free and already feels like you're playing a complete game. So the coming months won't be feeling like waiting for Klei to complete it, but it's going to feel like a monthly free DLC when they keep adding stuff. _childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This is just a fantastic game, and well worth buying even though its not a "full release".  You get two complete characters with two copmletely different playstyles and stories.  The only thing you're waiting on is a third character.  The stories for each characters are entirely isolated to themselves, so the only thing you're missing is just one more short story.The art style is fantastic.  The music is perfect for the mood.  The writing is clear, fun, and has great world building.  Humor is just right, not over the top.  It is a deck builder combined with a choose your own adventure.  Even then, dialog is not too long, and easily skipped on repeat playthroughs.  Combat is quick, has depth, but feels very fair on the beginning difficulties.  Like most deck builders, each "complete" playthrough will unlock more abilities, and make the game more difficult the next time around.I can safely say this is an outstanding game, and likely a masterpiece of this genre.  It is rare to see all the moving parts of a game come together like this, and I am honestly shocked and overjoyed at the quality.  If you have even a passing interest in deck builders, choices, and a decent story, you would be remiss to not grab this gem.Get it.  You won't regret it.  And if you actually do?  Steam refund time is enough to get a feel for the game.  I have a feeling though that time is going to fly right by because you'll be enjoying yourself too much.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel comfortable recommending Griftlands to literally anyone who is interested in any deck-builder game.Mechanically, Griftlands is exceptionally well put together. The three main scenarios are challenging and varied. The story is well put together and actually has some pretty good writing with some interesting moral dilemmas. Different choices yield different upgrades and challenges, so story choices are impactful and immersing at first, and still engaging when you're playing as a pure psychopath on your hundredth run.The story is also completely unobtrusive for people looking to skip it. We're talking an average of 3-5 seconds between actual decisions when you're skipping stuff. The dialogue/combat battle system is also very compelling. Decisions to fight or talk can have huge impacts for your entire run with the Loved/Hated system that gives you potentially powerful buffs/debuffs.Many simple systems intersect in very complicated ways giving the game an insane amount of depth while still being very approachable. All in all, Griftlands is a great game that you can enjoy in many different ways, making it an easy recommend. I don't really enjoy deck-builders but even I found this game really fun. It's truly under-rated.

It's negligible and easily guessed as you play along, but some people not used to the game might be put off by that. _childDocuments_.review: If you want a longer, more in-depth video review you can watch it here: Griftlands is one of the most revolutionary roguelites I have ever played.It takes inspiration from games like Slay the Spire but completely innovates in a huge amount of ways.The first big thing in the game is the fact that instead of just building one deck you actually are building two. You have your combat deck and then you have a negotiation deck which you use when you try to convince someone of something.The next huge thing is that this is an extremely narrative based game where the runs take around 5 hours to complete.  In these campaigns you can work for different sides and you can make friends or enemies with every npc in the game. You can kill some people and completely remove them from the story and it is all really dynamic. It feels like a big choose your own adventure roguelite which is really cool.The last big thing is just the sheer amount of unique cards, passive grafts, and events. Every game really feels different.I would highly recommend this game as it is one of the most innovative and revolutionary roguelites I have ever played.
