_childDocuments_.review: So I have put a TON of hours of gameplay into this game already so it's easy to say I really enjoy this game. That being said, I see a ton of reviews saying it is like STS and that's a fairly decent comparison (I've put plenty of time into both games), although not a completely accurate representation. I would say STS is much more straight forward to pick up, but is more difficult to master at higher ascension levels through the interactions of it's game mechanics such as a higher emphasis of artifact implementation for the deck and the broader card "themes" than you would see in GL. For Griftlands, the learning curve is definitely more steep due to a higher integration of rpg elements. Often you will be looking at the game and wondering if the decisions you could make would benefit you and give you an edge in the story, and it may have nothing to do with the actual deckbuilding elements of the game. There is also the fact there are two decks you're actually building at once, a battle and a negotiation, both of which are used in completely different ways. This may seem overwhelming at first, especially for the negotiation portion because there aren't too many battle systems like it, but it comes together quickly with the unique themes each character provides. The cards make it pretty easy to determine what type of deck you can do early on since they can be extremely useful in one archetype and complete garbage in another with a few exceptions (Rook's Headbang Rare Negotiation card for instance works in a wide variety of decks and I've never felt any dissatisfaction picking it up). After you finish the story for each character, you do unlock a brawl mode which definitely has the familiarity to the Rogue-Type game mode you see in STS. My last dictation for the game is the most recent update, which I admit, I need to spend more time checking out. These are just intitial impressions of what I've seen so far. It has changed it's prestige mode dramatically, which is surprising since there really wasn't a problem with it. It's not better or worse, it's just interesting to change. I do like the perk system which rewards the grind even more with your playthroughs. The mutators are not gone but they are utilized differently, but that's no big deal since most people don't use those game modes until they feel they've reached a limit to the standard play and just want to mess around. The last and -if I had to choose- most irritating change is the interface. It's much more cluttered than it was from previous patches, trying to give all the information on one screen. If I hadn't been playing as much as I already have, I would be completely overwhelmed looking at all the icons. I feel the devs were looking for a look somewhat like STS but there are too many mechanics in GL to do that so it seems more simple to stick with menus which can be opened and closed with quick keys. Overall, Griftlands does not seem to take as long to master as STS but the amount of content this game has is frankly astounding and it is a very rewarding experience to grind, especially since it's in early access. Granted, this could change depending on the state of the game in the future, but as long as they stick with the "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" mentality, keep the game's identity, and focus on creating a more playable experience (A more interactive tutorial for both types of combat for instance), then KLEI Entertainment will have a great title on their hands.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A fairly early assessment but this might become my all time favourite rogue-lite. It manages to pull off an incredible balancing act between making the story fun and interactive while at the same preserving the core gameplay loop of a deck-building rogue-lite. Being the first of your kind and and starting out with such a hit is quite an impressive feat. The soundtrack is phenomenal and I catch myself humming the battle and negotiation theme all the time now.The tutorials could be a bit more extensive and include an optional training match since a few of the concepts introduced are not exactly intuitive to understand and hovering over 15 icons each battle for the first few runs to understand what they do can probably be annoying for some newcomers.I can't recommend it highly enough right now. It's an exceptionally unique combination of genre's and works beautifully as such.

This game has been rewarding but still difficult, and I’m still curious what the game has for me. Each fight has me attempting to think one step ahead, although I’m not great at that. _childDocuments_.review: wonderful story-driven deck building roguelikebe prepared for many deaths as the main mode has permadeaththe way you improve is through death - similar to other roguelikesi feel like a lot of the complaints are for people who either havent experienced this genre of game before or werent expecting the difficultythe multiple options for optimising your character makes for different gameplay every time, as well as the procedurally generated quests and storylinesbalancing the political mechanics and social aspects with the battles is an interesting dynamic - do you keep people alive and let them hate you (which affects gameplay giving you debuffs), and possibly face them again, or do you kill them and create more issues with other people hating you or seeing you as a killer which affects relationships down the linewith the choice of negotiation and combat, and within the choice for a more peaceful or violent / threatening approach, i find my character is different every time and there are multiple ways to playoverall enjoyable game for both the story and gameplaynot to mention the soundtrack, sound effects and visual design which are also impressive and engaging as well as creating a unique world

_childDocuments_.review: Solid content and replayability for rogue-light fans. Mechanics are easy to learn, but there's a learning curve on how damage gets distributed/mitigated. Been playing since EA release off-and-on, and the end product is much more effectively balanced across all the play styles so when RNG pushes you in a build direction you can sustain and win instead of railroaded to failure by "bad" RNG. Each player feels unique. There's some repetition in buffs from relationships, but its usually limited to their background type so keep that in mind when investing. _childDocuments_.review: What a huge breath of fresh air! I haven't played a game quite like Griftlands, though I've played several games that share facets of the game. It takes bits and pieces from titles like Darkest Dungeon and Slay the Spire, along with nearly other roguelike/lite and deckbuilder from the past decade. And yet Griftlands has an aesthetic that feels like a Sci-Fi version of The Banner Saga; a story filled with intrigue, and several characters to play as through various tales.The combat works much like a traditional RPG, attacking and using abilities in a turn based fashion, but all the while you're performing those actions by using cards, and various mechanics included on them. It gives a bit of randomization to combat, but in deck building lies your consistency, as any TCG Player will tell you. This is standard fair for games that utilize cards as the primary engine for combat. Where Griftlands sets itself apart is by having an entirely separate deck used for diplomacy (or the lack there of). Most encounters will allow you to choose between traditional combat and negotiation. Negotiation is essentially a battle, but it's represented on screen differently, and honestly it's difficult to describe with out seeing it, but essentially your intents are arguments fight against each other until someone's core argument is defeated. Just as pets and temporary allies will help you in normal fights, they will also add arguments to your side of the field as dialogue begins. There's a wealth to do here. I've put in runs as all three characters but have yet to complete a run (Sal's end boss has killed me a few times), but you still earn account wide progression some of which is shared between characters, so eventually you'll gain an easier advantage through the game. Since gear and cards are randomized each game, you never know if you'll get the best deck or be forced to build in another direction, so some runs will be easier than others. I could go on and on, but I'll leave you with this. If you enjoyed any of the games I've mentioned in this review, you'll probably like this game. For bite sized RPG goodness with some TCG flavor, you can't go wrong, and it's CHEAP right now. 10/10. Would graft ♥♥♥♥ to my skull again.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I was intrigued on how there will be two different types of approaches in the game and I love how it was implemented into the game. You can approach things through negotiations or just be a barbarian and kill/fight everyone. I tried to balance both of my decks during my first run and it was a success. I tried improving only one of my deck in the following run and it was hard because there are some scenarios that forced you to follow a certain approach . If you love deckbuilding games, I highly recommend this game.  In terms of art, music and dialogue, I love everything and it shows how much effort they put into Griftlands. Note: I spent around 10-20 hours of gameplay on my epic account. Kudos to klei for giving everyone who bought from epic an option to get a copy on steam.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR This game is hard to comprehend mechanically and doesn't reward understanding itI understand why people like this game, but it doesn't click for me and I think there is good reason for that. Most times people view a game having a lot of content as a great thing but for me there is a meaningful differentiation with this game. This game has a lot more complexity than it has depth. Each character has a dozen different one word keywords on their cards, some of them do pretty much the same thing but have different names, like defense/composure or adrenaline/temporary power; a lot of the fights have unique passive effects that you only understand if you hover over the opponent and read it and all the little things floating around them; Each encounter has convoluted dialogue that gets thrown at you with little impact. It is hard to engage with everything if I have to memorize a paragraph to know the difference between wound/bleed/burn/poison and all the other debuffs you can apply.Compare this to slay the spire you can see a stark difference. Slay the Spire has low complexity and high depth, Griftlands has high complexity and low depth. If you read a card in Slay the Spire you instantly know what it does if you were to play it in any fight, but each decision you make while drafting or playing matters and is interesting. In Griftlands runs are so inundated with information, I just block it out and just try my best to throw things together.I enjoy the game type and appreciate the hard work that obviously was put in but it feels like there so many mechanics that are in the game for their own sake and do not improve the game.

_childDocuments_.review: These are my thoughts after 8 hours of play. I have fun playing this game, but for some reason the art for the females makes them sort of masculine looking. The game mechanics are solid and the game feels fair and balanced. The story is so-so and not really my favorite aspect of the game. I want to be the good guy, a traditional hero, not an antihero who only has options of being the misunderstood bad guy or a deliberate bad guy. If the writers wanted to offer a path that allows for villainous behavior then that's fine, but only allowing immoral choices makes the story rather dull. The music and sounds are perfect. _childDocuments_.review: A beautifully animated and in-depth variation on the mechanics that Slay the Spire first made popular. The use of separate decks for negotiation and combat means that you can choose to specialize heavily in one area, and even on just the first play through I can see a number of different synergies and strategies that could be used in both. The limitation of the number of grafts (what would be relics in Slay the Spire) makes it interesting to figure out what items best pair up with a given combat or negotiation deck.The one potential downside is that runs in this take much longer than those in Slay the Spire - that much story and dialogue can only be condensed so much, after all. A run in Slay the Spire would normally take about an hour, but I've only gotten about 60% through my first run of Griftlands after 4 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Feels like card roguelikes are increasingly common these days but this is a great addition to the genre, it has to be said. The mechanics are well smart, deep and varied often enough to keep things interesting whilst the script is actually sharp enough in places that you aren't always just racing through the dialogue. The quests are naturally generated randomly (or seemingly so) for each run-through but it always makes sense and never feels overly repetitive.Each character has a unique play style and backstory that keeps each of them compelling. _childDocuments_.review: It's not the worst deckbuilder in the world, but now that I finished 2 campaigns out of three, I can say that it didn't provide a lot of enjoyment. It has a lot of qualities (Art, world building, some gameplay ideas), but I will only remember how disappointing and how draining the whole experience was.The runs are so long, at least 4 hours if you make the effort to read half of the dialogues. The difficulty curve is strange. Everything will seem relatively easy for hours and hours, then you'll enter a fight with surprise mechanics and suddenly lose. This feels bad. What's also funny about it is that they implemented a star system to indicate the mission's difficulty but it's totally useless because you have no real alternative (contrary to most RPGs). During a run, you can only make a choice between two missions of the same difficulty (3-star, for instance). Every single time. And that's when you're not doing a main quest on the rails.The deckbuilding is weirdly implemented. There is quite a decent amount of cards, but it's hard to build synergies and make those decks feel personal. They become bloated very quickly, more than in any other deckbuilder, and there are really not enough opportunities to strim them.The story is ultimately uninteresting. The characters can be interesting, the very short relationships are nice (but they are way too short to have an impact), but the overall plot plays with the classic scheme of the rich/dominant class vs the rebels/proletarians, with some good and bad persons in each camp to create few moral dilemmas. The endings are anticlimatic in my opinion. I sadly didn't care, because it's too short as a story, because is too long as a deckbuilder, because it's way too cliché to my taste.It could have been a better game if it wasn't a scripted story. It could have been a true roguelike. They could have kept the world building, the factions, but all the dialogues and relationships, outcomes, would have been influenced by your choices and generated by a complex algorithm. Because right now I have no desire to replay the same characters and the same stories barely modified by the fact that this time I sided with the bad guy... Wow... I'm already bored to death just by thinking about it.

_childDocuments_.review: I spent a ton of time on this game and have really enjoyed it, but I've disliked nearly every EA change in the last several updates. Their attempt to add rogue-lite meta-progression systems, of which there are now three, have all been increasingly unsatisfying. Compressing the prestige tiers was a good idea, except now they're drastically unbalanced because of card and NPC changes made in light of the meta-progression systems, causing the difficulty to arbitrarily spike because you rolled into a promoted NPC rather than a normal one, for example. Their idea of a daily challenge is one of the least fun of its type I've seen, focusing on an aggressive challenge and score-based model but basically forcing you to play the run twice if you actually want to be competitive- once to see the seed, and then again to actually play your run- otherwise you run into situations like where you intend to use no status ailments, but the card draft hands you nothing but, and your early draft choices are useless because you never found the other pieces. The Mettle and Flourish update also seem to come from a really strange place, offering some of the similar bonuses from the Perks engine, but incremental, and I just don't understand the point of aiming to complete Grifts but also push money into Mettle at the same time, and I definitely have no interest in more grinding. I love Klei's games and their design sensibility is great, and I've recommended Griftlands in the past, but I have no faith in it going forward, since I no longer understand what their design aims are. I don't know if I'll install 1.0 to see the rest of Smith but for the time being, I'm out.

As other reviews have said, the mechanics of the fights & negotiations is easy to pick up but hard to master, but the game does a great job of making you want to master it. _childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I was getting burnt out of Slay the Spire and wanted to find a game within the same genre to breathe some life back into it for me, and then I was recommended Griftlands. The game has 2 different "combat" systems, fighting and negotiating, with most scenarios letting you pick which to use. You follow a main storyline for each character, but the game has slightly different paths and choices you can do that's really helpful in keeping you hooked. There is also random encounters and little pop up events you can choose to do, which I also really like. I did mention the branching pathing, and while it did help hold my attention, I do wish there was more choices you made that actually influenced the story. Each of the character's stories only really has 2 endings it can have, along with a couple other minor things that get tacked on along the way. For being mainly a story-driven game, I do feel it needs a bit more juice into it to make it worth the price. I finished all 3 of the storylines within 7 hours.The leveling system is also painfully slow. Similar to StS, the more runs you do on a character (and how well you do) levels them up to unlock new cards. You also earn mettle in-game which can very slightly increase that character's base stats for all future runs. However, the leveling is painfully slow. At 11 hours in with many successful (or good attempt) runs, none of my characters have even reached the halfway mark yet. This just feels like a cheap way to keep players playing, if I'm being honest.That being said, I really enjoyed this game. I look forward to seeing what future content updates they make to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands feels exactly like what all Roguelike Deckbuilders should strive to be, in my opinion. It feels like a classic RPG in that it is story-driven with quests and unique characters to meet and build (or break) relationships with. On top of that, the world feels incredibly alive, with events happening and your character being a part of them, not always being the hero that swoops in to drive the plot entirely. You have to make hard decisions sometimes, even outside of the strategic deckbuilding choices. Maybe it's building one relationship at the expense of tearing another down. Whatever gets you to your desired goal is up to you to decide on each run.Even with all of this, Griftlands doesn't leave out the combat complexity, with 2 independent decks per run to build simultaneously. Both systems (Negotiations and Combat) are deep and rewarding in their own right as well, neither feeling like it completely overshadows the other in importance or depth.I bought it on sale, but I can safely say that this would be worth the purchase at full price if you like anything about the idea of a Story-driven Roguelike Deckbuilder.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's a solid game in a lot of ways. The core gameplay is engaging, the artwork is nice, and they clearly put a lot of thought into the world they created. The glaring problem it has in my mind is that they made a rouge-like game with an expectation that the player will fail multiple times before getting a good run, and also included a deeper storyline that gets reset every time the player fails. I found it very annoying to have to click through the same long dialog exchanges between characters every time I started a new run. It prevented me from getting immersed in the storyline and felt like a waste of time. Which is a shame, because it looks like it could have been a good story  if it didn't keep forcing the player to start back at page one over and over again.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll add my voice to the chorus: Slay the Spire's bare bones plus Klei's expert fleshing-out leads to this budding masterpiece of a game.Deckbuilder roguelikes are an intensely fun genre for the kind of mind that likes to mini-max on the fly, and in addition to an expert and interesting story and 'persuasion' element that you'll see detailed with many other reviews on here, the deckbuilder framework itself is excellent in Griftlands, not just being a Slay-the-Spire clone but streamlining it.  The most noticeable mechanic is how card upgrades work: instead of relying on special events to upgrade, cards upgrade naturally with use and give you choices in how to upgrade them.  Imagine in Slay the Spire that you were trying to build a card draw deck, and instead of having to lean into card removal the whole game to clear out your strikes and defends, you could choose an upgrade on your strikes and defends that also gave them card draw.Klei games come with sky high expectations for those familiar with the company, and Griftlands delivers.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a lot of Slay the Spire and a little bit of Monster Train, but Griftlands is the one I keep coming back to because of how inventive it is. I love the negotiation vs combat decks, the meta progression, the sound + music design - and above all, the world. Griftlands has a more fleshed out world (with consistent factions and characters) than most games - completely unexpected for a card battler but wow does it appeal to me.For some people, the length of a run seems to be a con - but I don't really mind it. There's enough story variety that I feel like I'm getting something different each time - even if it's only in small ways.Keep bringing freshness to games, Klei - you rock.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start off by saying that I'm a sucker for card-battlers, I probably have over a 1000 hours combined over games like Hearthstone, Slay the Spire, Artifact, Monster Train, etc. I MUST say that this game is deep. If you like card games like me, don't skip this one.

_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Too tired to post a proper review, so you probably want to read the next few lines and scroll on.What I can tell you is that this game is amazing. I just did my first run, started some time in the afternoon, looked at the time and it's 1:19 AM. Only other game that's done that to me was Civ 5. Excellent writing really makes the world come to life in all its dark splendor, with just enough humor to keep it in a good spot.The different characters' cards use different mechanics, similarly to Slay The Spire - which on that note, I would absolutely rate this game as well as I would STS which is saying something, seeing how I have hundreds of hours on it (on Switch) and I've never found any other deck builder to come close. The changes are interesting and meaningful (by the looks of it - only done a run with the first character), and there seems to be plenty of variety across the different game facets (cards, interactions, quests, ways to approach just about anything, etc) to warrant multiple runs with each character, providing dozens if not hundreds of hours of gameplay. EDIT: I was too curious and started a new run before heading to bed, and the first 3 quests I could choose from were completely different from the first time, meaning that there's even more variety than I originally thought! This may very well be my new favorite game.Combat is a similar formula to STS, and so is the deck building component, though here cards get upgraded through using them. You can also have a pet or companions which is fun - I think you could also have multiple pets if you worked toward that. There are also prestige levels - 7, at least for the first character, the others may have more / less. The art is unique, and I wasn't sure I'd be into it at first, but it works well with the rest of the game and I found myself enjoying it quite a bit as I explored Murder Bay.A decent amount of unlockables also contribute to the replayability, but because there are so many ways to do things I feel like a lot of them will get unlocked just by playing the game in different ways, making different choices, etc. though there's still something there for those looking for new ways to challenge themselves or something new to aim for. Maybe you just never managed to get that one resident to like you...So anyway, if you're still here, hopefully you'll buy this - it's frankly an amazingly good game. It's extremely immersive in my opinion and they devs built a really interesting world with fitting characters. I hope that we'll be getting either a sequel or some DLC in the years to come, just because I already want to see & know more about this world and its inhabitants!!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so cool. I love deck-builders (Slay the Spire, Monster Train, Dominion, Ascension, Fights in Tight Spaces, etc...), and this is one of the ones doing something different without feeling like its giving up the simple core. Usually I will start someone off with Slay the Spire, and put them on to Monster Train if they want something with a little more meat: Griftlands is now my recommendation if they really like the Slay the Spire system but just want more variety.  Its not really more complex, just has a bit more flavor.

The second character's set feels underwhelming - but that could just be my play quality.Games in the deckbuilding rogue-rpg genre can't help but be compared to STS: the graphics are crisper, the sound design is great, the pacing/flow is a bit worse.  I appreciate the world and story building, but would definitely like separation from needing to follow it sometimes (especially in a high replay game) - but that says more about me than it does about the game. Like the merchants only sell special cards that disappear after using it, which doesn't help me build my deck at all, I'm actually shocked by this design like what's the point bruh.Plus, I could have done so much more in one day with my HP and money. _childDocuments_.review: So after two hours I can already say that this is a great game.  Once you get over the rather obtuse wording that accompanies the battle and negotiation vocabulary the game is a joy to play.  The negotiation battles are a particularly interesting take on traditional battle mechanics ... the way it is set up is just fantastic ... intentions and arguments of the adversaries is pure fun and somehow draw you into a psychological battle that I have never seen anywhere before ... great work from the developers!  It is well worth the money .. will most likely be the best example of a great deck building game, maybe the best one available for the PC ... it might even turn out to be better than most board game deck builders, thinking here of Dominion.  I mostly do not like the story telling in PC games because the writing is just substandard crap ... but this one is an exception ... I really have nothing bad to say about this game.  Go get it ... 9/10 and its in Early Access .. I'm pretty sure it will be a 10/10 when its all done.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game! Each Main char you get to play feels very different while the core game functions remain the same each run. You level up after each run so you don't even need to survive to the end of a run to unlock more cards to play and different upgrades to unlock. The game is very hard but when fortune finds you it can become much easier and the game slowly gets harder with different prestige tiers as you play to keep things fresh. My favorite thing about the game is that choices matter and your not just fighting fighting non-stop like in other games with a negotiating side that a bit tricky to master at first but once you get it down you'll be talking your way out of sticky situations in no time. The game crashes a bit more than I would like BUT the game auto saves at the start of each conversation so if you crash mid run or need to leave while playing you can pick up right back where you started. Protip b4 I go. If you see if graphical bugs(dark screen, text missing ect.) just close the game and restart. That's fixed those issues every time for me. This is one of my most favorite card battle games I've played. Def pick this one up if you like card battle games like me : )
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Even though the story focus of the game conflicts with the rogue-lite gameplay, theres enough variety to have about 5 unique playthroughs for each character and even after that the small changes add enough new stuff so the game doesnt get boring on repeat runs. They also recently added mod support and even though the current list is small, the possiblity of modding is a really good way to add new things to the game. If you're a fan of rogue-lite turn based card games, this one is a definite grab.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best deckbuilders I've ever played. Every aspect of it, from the negotiation deck to the way you can make other people like or hate you, works together to provide a cohesive and enjoyable experience. The game is difficult, but despite the existing RNG no loss ever feels unavoidable due to the number of options you have at any given time.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a beautifully-crafted, single player deck-building game. I must admit, when Slay the Spire was announced I was not attracted to this kind of games at all. I just brushed past it, never tried it and never even considered playing one. Last month I bought and downloaded Pirate Outlaws for mobile and it is fantastic, play it up to this day on lazy morning.That was up until last week, when I (re)discovered (I totally forgot about this title until it popped up in my wishlist) Griftlands. First things first, the choice of which deck to use (combat or diplomacy) is a great addition. Having to manage one deck in other DBGs (deck building games) can be challenging and rewarding, but having two of them is just that complicated, but when you finally master both decks: nirvana.If you've played any other Klei Entertainment games, you will know the Artwork. Sharp, comic-like and well defined. It serves the purpose of this gritty story like Shank and Mark of the Ninja were, and it is superb comparing it to other DBG. Suffice to say, I was completely blown away when The storyline aspect is the new selling point for this genre. Having to balance how you reach to your objective is made a lot more stressing when you are faced with the choice of going against your previous friend or making someone actually hate you. Oh, right, the friendship system! Just like in any RPG, you will have to do missions for different factions and people. Doing so will antagonize the opposing faction and person, whatever the case may be, but do not despair! You can always buy them a drink previous to any combat or diplomacy to try and reduce their hatred towards you. That is, of course, if you can actually find them in the map at the exact moment they are in a bar and you can buy them a drink because you find them, provided you have the money (maybe there should be a way to find people you are looking for on the map)Overall I recommend Griftlands, even at this point in Early Access. Even if you don't like this kind of games but you are a fan of Klei Entertainment games you should try it. It changed my perspective about the future of this genre and what kind of games Klei can actually do. Klei, you slippery b******, never delivered a bad game yet. Kudos to you!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like Roguelikes?If yes: Play itDo you like a story rich campaign with good writing and where your choices matter?If yes: Play it.Did you like the concept of charisma in Fallout, and how it could get you out of trouble if your stat was high enough?This game turns that into a secondary battle system that's just as fleshed out as the normal one and has its own deckDoes that sound interesting? PLAY IT.Do you like deckbuilding and crafting your perfect build?There's tons of cards, and you unlock more as you progress.  You can craft builds for both negotiations AND battles.If you're that kind of person: PLAY IT.Do you actually hate card-based games?If Yes: So did I.  Play it anyway, it'll make you love them.Have you played Slay The Spire?This game is very similar to that, but way deeper, and with a story campaign that slightly changes every time you play, and 3 of them at that, one for each character that's completely unique from the last.  Slay the Spire isn't bad, but Griftlands outdoes it in basically every way.I'll say it one more time.PLAY THIS GAME.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely my favorite deck-building game since Slay the Spire! I played this since Early Access times, and I'd say it was one of the best EA games out there; there was a lot of content, constant updates, and pretty much no bugs. Now I finally finished the final campaign (there are three different campaigns, one for each character), and I can't recommend it enough. If you liked StS, you'd definitely enjoy this one as well. In addition to pretty addictive gameplay, there are also great stories, characters, and some branching paths. I rarely came back to games after beating them for the first time, but I could already imagine playing this one more time to see some other outcomes and simply try new cards. Again, if you like the genre, you'll not be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't liked a game this much in a while -- if I have one complaint, it's that after 70+ hours of play, I've seen the dialogue screens a zillion times and having to click-click-click through them is aggravating. That's minor -- I love it! The dual fight/negotiate mechanism, the ability to scale difficulty up and down, and the amazingly built out and lived in world -- the art -- the music -- this is just the pinnacle of all the deck-building strategy games I've played to date, and I've played a lot of 'em. I keep choosing Griftlands over Slay the Spire, Against the Moon, and Monster Train... it's just more _fun_ to me, for aesthetic, play, and world reasons.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Wasn't sure if I was going to like this game at first, but I enjoyed it.There's 2 combat systems, negotiation and battling, and you make choices to advance through the story. You can unlock perks to make the game easier. Additionally you get bonuses/negative effects from your decisions. Oh, and your cards upgrade as you use them, which is another thing I really liked about this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a complete package. Some games are minimalist, they strive for mechanical perfection, to do one thing really well, the core mechanics. This game takes that fine tuned system from a game like Slay the spire and also build a whole world as setting, a plot, re-occurring cast of characters, introduces multiple ally options and more.While games like Dicey Dungeons can be oppressive with its constant drain of resources, Griftlands gives multiple strategic options on how to cope with that challenge. Lots of tactical considerations at every single step. It's great. And it's in a fuller experience than when it was launched on epic games store. It is the best game in this rogue-like-card-based-tactics subgenre.

_childDocuments_.review: I would very much like to recommend this game, but there is one reason I simply cannot.There are many good things to be said about the wonderful atmosphere, the interesting characters, the great music and a story that's been decent enough so far. However, if there is one thing I simply can't get over is the fact that even if you steamroll all encounters, the final boss will have some overpowered items/abilities at their disposal which provides a massive jump in difficulty that you weren't exactly waiting for. I absolutely hate such unexpected changes when everything else is ridiculously easy. I was very much immersed in the game until that point.Sure, you get a chance to remove one or two of the boss's items if you play well, but there is no reason the first character's final boss should even have those items to begin with and that honestly breaks all immersion for me. Especially since you can't know which items are the worst unless you look it up outside of the game. Not only that, I enjoy the negotiation mechanic but if you want to have a decent enough deck you'll have to do quite a bit of battling and that kinda goes against the way I played this game. Negotiation is useless when you're at the end boss, so just focus on your battle deck throughout the run.Oh, and don't bother asking people on the Steam forums for help. You'll only get to hear 'git gud' and that's about it. I don't play games for their difficulty. I play them to enjoy my free time. This sudden and unnecessary jump to an overpowered end boss that Griftlands did really messed up all enjoyment I had with the game up till that point. I'm not sure if I'll ever come back to the game. The story and choice system was fun, but this boss business looks like a dealbreaker for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game so much. It's a really good blend of story and deck-builder, while also throwing in yet another wrinkle, of having two separate decks to manage. It's a rich world, seen from three campaigns, with plenty of variety and interactions with characters from run to run. There are a ton of unlocks to work towards, such as getting every character to hate you or love you, along with upgrading every single graft, and so much more. The nice part too, is that if you don't want to follow the story, it's very simple to skip through all the flavor and just get from battle to battle. Highly recommend if you like deckbuilders at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is just absolutely wonderful. I am usually not really interested in deck-building card games but this one has a really fresh and ambitious take on the genre. The sci-fi world of Griftlands hearkens back strongly to the Gilded Age of the late 1800s (most overtly so in the Bog Job), which presented a unique setting that I really enjoyed seeing in an indirect fashion in this game. The writing is terrific. Not only is the prose striking with many great quips and intriguing world-building, but the information you're told and the decisions you choose to make with them are genuinely meaningful. Even something so little as choosing to ask for clarification from a stranger who's dodgily telling you to quickly do as they say can result in you being caught speaking to a wanted fugitive by a patrolling officer. You have to really think about the options presented to you as they're presented to you. You're not going to have the ludo-narrative dissonance of being told you must act quickly and then you ask numerous questions anyway to receive a lengthy exposition dump before proceeding to successfully act in time as you would in another game. The choices you make can burn you hard enough that sometimes you have to scrutinize the opportunities presented to determine if intervening in a situation and helping either side is even worth the potential trouble. I could gush over how much I love the gameplay of Griftlands all day.Even though I don't have a whole lot of experience with the first character Sal yet (I couldn't get the hang of her in combat). Rook is unbelievably wild in both negotiations and combat. The gamble mechanic allows you to snowball in a super satisfying way if you play your cards right (forgive me), and his pistol charge mechanic gave him good depth in battle, as you're encouraged to flip-flop between low-charge and high-charge for defense and offensive respectively.  Defeating bosses is so unbelievably thrilling in this game, because they're all pretty challenging and I usually only beat them by a hair. All in all, this game is an absolute steal for only 15 USD, and it's only going to get even better as it receives more content.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game could be so good...The main issue I have with this game is the lack of engaging stories in the provided campaigns (excluding one, which is still average at best).  There's some story driven decisions to be made, but they feel somewhat predictable and lacking of weight.  The deck building provides some unique twists and gameplay loops, even providing additional ways of play outside of combat, but compared to counterparts like Monster Train and Slay the Spire still feels uncharted and lackluster.  One aspect that balances the scales in favor of Griftlands is the art direction (which Klei never seems to miss) and tight, hypnotic sound effects.Although overall there's still a mediocre experience to be had, it's surprisingly and disappointingly cut short with a lack of variety in deck building content, player-driven decisions that warrant additional playthroughs, and un-engaging short stories that made me wanting more, but having nothing left to play with.

_childDocuments_.review: Deck builder. Story line. Choices on each run are varied by random one-shot events to choose from.Best art in the genre. Voice acting is appealing. Theme is consistent.UI is elegant though it takes time to get used to (the concentric rings take some time to understand instinctively).and PETS that help in battle and in negotiations.If you enjoy the other titles mentioned in the other reviews, then this is the most polished contender in the field. _childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a wonderful blend of genres. I had been excited for this game when it was first revealed, and despite the fact the game has been on a strange journey, what the team have produced in the end is a really fun and characterful game. An RPG with card battling and some unique systems, all with a gorgeous art style and that one thing we all love: consequences.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It seems to me that this game was made by people who really loved Slay the Spire, and wanted to double-down on the elements that that awesome, fun-as-hell deck-builder lacked--and not only did Klei double-down, but they then proceeded nail a hard 21... in spades! (how's that for a strangled metaphor, ey? lol) There's a sly joyfulness to this game--it's a celebration of the genre that will satisfy deck-builder afecionados and entice noobs with its combination of elements. The dialog is witty, the plotlines are engaging, the characters are relatable, and their choices meaningful. As for replicating the things that StS nailed: the combos/synergistic decks you can assemble are pretty much just as addicting, the balance of difficulty and run-length is there, and the additional mechanics (as well as all those other bells and whistles) are integrated perfectly... and, most importantly of all, the sum total is motherheshin' FUN!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Card games aren't really my thing, but Klei has a knack for taking a genre that I find boring and making it into an amazingly fun experience.Wow. Klei has done it again. The card mechanics are great. They make it easy to understand how the card's affects work. The rogue-like elements allow them to introduce new cards as you play the game. In no time flat, you will understand how the cards are meant to work together, so that you can build decks that capitalize on particular mechanics, and find a strategy that works for you.On top of that, the negotiation game is super interesting. It works out much in the same way that battles do, just with a different set of cards and mechanics. It allows the game to make for diplomatic encounters that are just as fun to play as the combat.In between the card games, you are set loose on a world map that is constantly changing, and giving you fresh options for where you want to go, next. At each story beat, you will encounter a myriad of lovable, charming characters and will have to make the hard choices as to who you want to help, or harm. The dialogue is masterfully written, giving the characters a ton of personality, and describing scenes like an overly dramatic storyteller in a Dungeons & Dragons game.So, satisfying game mechanics that keep me coming back for more. A narrative that makes the context for the gameplay deeply interesting and memorable. Art style/animation that makes me wish it was an animated series. Soundtrack that never gets old. I don't know what else I can say to convince you.Griftlands is a masterwork.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing the game for a couple of hours.For an early access game, it already seems quite polished.The split between negotiation and battle is quite interesting and allows for different solutions to the same quest.I hope the diversity of playstyles is high enough to keep the game interesting for a long time, but so far it's looking good.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I grabbed the game last week (?  Maybe the week before?)  Anyway, I lost track because I couldn't put it down.  I think my second playthrough was even more fun than the first.  I thought card balance, flavor, and gameplay were all great.  I have to get back to Griftlands now; enough talk. _childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Quite honestly the best deck builder I have ever played. Having two decks one for combat the other for nogotiation is genius, letting you for the first time I've seen go for two unique builds in every run to make for a amazingly fun thing to wrap your head around. that and each of the three playable charicters each have their own mechanics, passives and cards for each of their decks with more making replaying each of them fun as all hell. Plus the writing and the art are both masterful making this game fun as all hell oh my god.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Similar to Slay the Spire, but a bit more going on with characters who have random appearances and personalities; compared to the gameplay of Spire, there's a lot more freedom and leeway on your deck rather than having to optimize your deck completely like you have to do in Spire. My only complaint is that the second character, Rook, is a bit lacking in powerful cards besides the specialized card he gets at the beginning of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible deck-building game, which reminds me of Slay the Spire or Monster Train, but with a lot more diversity in deck-building, and many other fun mechanics which affect the gameplay. The game's relationship system which gives perks, alongside many grafts and card types/deck types, in addition to the negotiation/battle system makes the game very replayable. Lovely Game, 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Really excellent game. The setting and everything is awesome, and the plotlines variability is lots of fun. _childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A kickass card building/roguelite game. Has two core mechanics: one is a traditional turn based battle mechanic and a negotiation mechanic which is a bit different but still combat-like. Likable characters, great dialogue, and an accessible story. Honestly, a must buy and an entry fee of $15 is extremely kind. The main menu has a prompt that says when the next update is coming, which is pretty awesome and not something I really have seen before. Also from the creators of Don't Stave, so the quality is certainly there. This really doesn't feel like an early access game, so I cant wait to see what they add.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a very unique experience. The deck-building is similar to 'Slay the Spire', but the world building is more like a tabletop RPG. The cast of characters is quirky, the dialogue is fun and creates an atmosphere of weird late night sci-fi cartoons. The names of the cards is very expressive, building your decks also feels like building your characters attitudes and style. If you like deck-builders and sci-fi, you have to check out GRIFTLANDS!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Great rogue-like deck builder! Having two different decks adds a nice amount of variety and flexibility, along with having three different playable characters each with their own narrative and setting keeps this game fresh for hours. Deck building isn't too complicated, its fairly easy to build up a reliable combo or game-plan with either of your decks. I would recommend this game to any fan of the genre, those trying it for the first time, or if you've had difficulties with other deck building games in the past and want to try again.

_childDocuments_.review: Narrative card collecting rogue-like. Having a narrative plus rogue-like can be a bit tricky, but since there are three characters to switch between, some randomness plus some light choice and consequence you are unlikely to get tired of seeing the same events play out over and over. Has that great Klei animation too.After clearing all three campaigns I don't feel the same drive to instantly start over on a higher difficulty level that I had in Slay the Spire or Monster Train, but that's alright, not every game needs to be terribly addictive. _childDocuments_.review: So many games now are "It's a deckbuilder, but with this cool new twist!" and it usually ends up just a worse version of Slay the Spire, where the 'new twist' doesn't actually make the game any more fun.This is NOT the case with Griftlands.Here are the things that make Griftlands special among deckbuilders:    Using a card enough can let you upgrade it (from a random set of upgrades), this brings not only extra customization towards a deck strategy, but can sometimes upgrade it to a 'destroy' option, so sometimes you can get rid of a card that doesn't fit your strategy by playing it enough to upgrade it.    There is a plot, and you can raise or lower your relationship with various NPCs for discounts or even passive bonuses for gameplay.    You have two decks, one for combat encounters, one for social encounters.  They both play VERY differently mechanically, but both feel fully fleshed out as game styles (helps keep things from getting repetitive).Honestly it's a fun, fresh take on deckbuilders with enough depth to play over and over.The one flaw is that the plot gets boring fast, there are currently only 2 characters with 1 plot apiece.  And while there is some variability in their plots, based on who you side with and who you kill, it gets repetitive.  There is a 'brawl' mode that just jumps from battle to battle, but that loses some of its charm.The framework is there though; and if they open this up to modding, where people can customize their own plots and characters, this game could go from clever to HUGE.

_childDocuments_.review: Card Rogue-like games have really been extending their boundaries recently. This is one of the newest twist with a large emphasise with story. A risky choice, considering rogue-likes charm is the fast in-and-out replayability. But they really managed to stick the landing. The deck building aspect is simple enough, and if you came here you already know how they work. The interesting part of this game is that you can focus on combat or negotiation and you have two different decks that you build to accommodate that. If you want to be a mass murdering psychopath who everyone hates, you can be that. If you want to be friends and talk your way out of almost every situation you can do that as well. Or maybe somewhere in between is fine as well.Theres a bit of learning you have to go through, but thats part of the fun for starting any new card rogue-like.The only problem I have is that the replayability does seem to get hurt by the huge amount of story it wants you to read. You can skip it, but it just feels odd to do so. Still fun , but its hard to play for long periods of time compared to others in the genre.tldr : A fun new story driven card rogue-like, but is missing the addiction feel that others in the genre have.8.0/10

_childDocuments_.review: Klei! I love Klei. Klei games are the best. Here's another best game; this time a roguelike card battler set out in the backwater badlands of space. You'll meet lots of NPCs who want you to do things for them in exchange for money and favours. Take sides and follow a main quest as one of three playable characters, all with different card decks. Fight battles, but also negotiate; each character has both a battle deck and a negotiation deck, with each type using different mechanics. There's a great number of builds to experiment with, the writing is excellent and it's beautiful to look at. All round super polished and memorable.- Unlike most roguelike card battlers I've played, this actually has a story to follow for each character. It plays as a series of quests and relationships instead of a simple 'walk across the landscape killing things'- Once you've played the main campaign as each character, you can either play at higher prestige levels which make it more difficult (there are perks to unlock), or you can play a sort of "day in the life" where you play as that character just doing normal mercenary jobs.- Gorgeous artwork- It's not just shooty combat. Each character has a deck for combat, and a deck for negotiations. Both of these have different mechanics. In battle you have damage, health and armor. In negotiations you have manipulation, hostility and diplomacy. On top of that, each character not only has their own decks, but their own mechanics. The second character has a coin he flips sometimes, which gives some cards extra effects.- You get a preview of what the enemy is going to do (like Slay the Spire) so you can prepare for it. No randomness.- You can enlist and train pets to fight with you.- One of the first quests had me uncover a theft. I confronted the thief in a bar, but chose to buy them a drink first. Not only did this get them drunk, giving them a disadvantage in combat, but it also made them like me, which reduced their resolve in the following negotiation- Cards gain XP by being used, and you get a choice how to upgrade them. You get a choice between 2 upgrades for each card, with lots of potential different upgrades- In one encounter, I was able to negotiate with them first to demoralise them in the fight afterwards- You earn a permanent currency for every fight, which makes you stronger over time (There are character-specific buffs, character-wide buffs, and perks to unlock)- You have a relationship status with every NPC in the game. Based on that, there are random events. A thug who likes you might share a target for a robbery, or someone who hates you might track you down on the trail and try to murder you when you're in the middle of a job. Relationship statuses also give you passive bonuses or penalties- You can provoke someone who hates you, which causes a negotiation. If you win the negotiation, they'll attack you, which means you're acting in self defense, so you can kill them with no penalty and remove the debuff from having someone hate you- The battle segments are fairly similar to other games; play cards which deal damage to the enemy. The negotiation battles have unique mechanics, and revolve around deploying arguments, manipulating the enemy and protecting yourself with composure- If you play the same story twice but take different sides of the main quests, you can see both sides of each NPC's version of the story- The game says 'progress will be saved at the end of the last conversation', but it seems to be the conversation BEFORE that one because I sometimes had to re-do the latest encounter when loading a game- There's no combat log to see what happened if you didn't understand something or missed it- If you take too long to win a negotiation, the NPC starts getting passive buffs every round called "impatience" which basically makes them do more damage. It's annoying because it stops you from playing a slow build-up/control deck- I feel like I missed something important at the beginning about the story. I know I'm going after Kashio, but everyone keeps talking about an auction that isn't in the introduction video

_childDocuments_.review: What's so different about yet another deckbuilder? Let me give you a quick run-down:You can play Story Mode or a quicker Brawl (series of 5*5 battles).You've got 2 Characters who each have 2 decks - 1 for Battle (max 4 vs 4, NPCs are AI controlled, play a card on a foe or self) and 1 for Negotiation (you fight against opponent's "core argument", negotiation gets harder the longer it takes). Characters have unique options for both decks, eg Battle focus on Bleed, Discard, or Draw effects. Negotiation on Green Cards (diplomatic) vs Red Cards (aggression).After every conflict you get to pick 1 of 3 cards for the deck you just used.Instead of hoping for an event, you can upgrade your cards when they gain enough XP (1 XP per card play). You can choose between two upgrade versions per card.You have the option to kill or spare an opponent after battle. This influences your relationship with them.Relationships can grant you Boons (eg merchants discount) or Banes (+1 Dmg received).Of course you got also some evergreens like if you beat the story, you can start to modify your game experience with Mutators (eg start with draft decks) or Prestige (more difficulty).

_childDocuments_.review: 1)map feels cramped. At one point you will have to choose to support 1 of 2 merchants from the night market. whoever you dont choose will now hate you and will raise their prices by 50%. 3)combat is split between battles and negotiations but battles are magnitudes more important as the game will force you into boss fights that you must fight to survive. impatience mechanic means after 5 or so turns enemies gain +1 damage in negotiations a turn then one more every turn afterwards. a very lazy way to make sure talks more difficult. On the final day it is impossible to out to defend and it becomes a dps race4) unless you watch a guide you will not be able to beat the boss your 1st, 2nd, or 3rd try. _childDocuments_.review: I played this game for 8 hours and gave it a good review (read that as fun + minimal bugs).  But after playing for another 15 hours, the mechanics I thought were interesting, I now find as distracting from the experience.Griftlands styles itself as a rogue-like deck-builder, and currently, I consider Slay the Spire to be the Gold Standard for that genre.  Griftlands has some interesting ideas that help it strive for excellence, but in my opinion, it comes up short.  Perhaps Griftlands can close the gap between good and great while it's still in Early Access, but I think some of the core mechanics will prevent it from doing so, but you can decide for yourself:1. Two decks.  Griftlands approaches the idea that if you're buying a deck-builder, then perhaps it can double-the-fun by building 2 decks at the same time.  While this idea has some merit and fits well with the theme of Griftlands and how you approach problems, I think it ultimately detracts from the deck-building experience.  It gives you the illusion of choice that you can focus on negotiations instead of battles, or focus on battles instead of negotiations, but in the end, you focus on both.  And to make matters even less interesting, the decks have nothing to do with each other.  You might as well be playing two different games at the same time bundled together.  The only interaction that I could find between the two was at the end of a battle encounter, if you kept killing people, you would get reputation cards added to your negotiation deck, but even the choice of killing had very little to do with the battle deck itself and was an 'after the battle' decision, and falls more into a choices matter category.2. Actual deck-building.  While there were a lot of cards, I found the actual differences between the cards underwhelming.2a. Battle deck-building.  To understand the problem in the battle cards, you first need to consider these three cards:  Card A is 1 action for 2-5 dmg.  Card B is 1 action for 3 dmg.  Card C is 2 action for 6-12 dmg.  To me, these 3 cards are basically the same card but with slight variations on cost vs output.  Imagine getting +3 minimum dmg, and Card A and B are identical, and imagine getting a +10 received dmg debuff on your target, and Card C is less impressive if action points are scarce.  The cards still have their place, and while I enjoyed the debuff mechanics in Griftlands, each debuff seemed to have the same template of cards to it... such as debuff, dmg+debuff, improvised debuff, discarded debuff, ability related to debuff, etc.  There was nothing that gave each mechanic a life of its own with its own unique cards.  The available battle cards tended to be variations of template vs mechanics to fluff out a large card set.  In a word, disappointing, especially when you consider how varied the lore behind the game is.2b. Negotiation deck-building.  Negotiation cards suffer from the illusion of choice even worse once you realize how negotiations work best.  There are 3 types of cards in negotations: Diplomacy, Hostility, and Manipulation.  Diplomacy cards tend to do lower amounts of damage but synergize with a mechanic called Influence that ensures Diplomacy cards will always do max damage.  Hostility cards synergize with a mechanic call Dominance, which adds +dmg to each hostility card.  What you find quickly is if you focus the deck on one track or the other, it works way better than trying to play both sides of the fence, which means when it comes time to pick a card to add to your deck, there isn't much choice once you've picked the path you want to take.3. Grafts.  This is one part of the game I think Griftlands did really well on.  The variety is a little scarce but unsurprising given the illusion of card choice (imo).  Think of them like relics from Slay the Spire, and they can be leveled up once, like cards.4. Card upgrades.  Cards have an xp bar, and once it's full, the card can be leveled up.  This is an interesting idea, but most my runs ended with 80%-90% of my cards leveled up and I quickly became desensitized to the mechanic, especially when I realized that there were at least 3 options that a card could level up into so even if I got a card leveled up, I might not get the level up I want.  Perhaps if upgraded cards could be merged together or cards could be leveled up multiple times, it might offer some strategic component for leveling cards, but I found this as a noise mechanic that had little impact on my actual deck-building strategy... with one exception.  Any time I could level a card up into something with the Destroy mechanic (to remove the card from the game), it was a guarantee that was the upgrade option I would take to avoid deck-bloat since so few cards had this option.5. Choices matters and NPCs and dialogue.  One of the first impressions I got from Griftlands is the abundance of dialogue it had in the game.  More than you'd expect in a rogue-like, but a great repository for a lot of Griftlands lore.  I was entertained and didn't mind the abundance. In encounter required me to remember a password too, but it was the only time it seemed important that I pay attention  The initial play-thru supported a choices matter feel in the decisions you make when picking encounters and the choices made during the encounter (prior to play the relevant deck).  It also seemed to matter about people liking/disliking you.  Once I started working thru the speed runs (prestige levels) though, I suddenly wondered what game I was playing.  There were no real choices., just encounter after encounter, and I found myself throwing all my money at NPCs to buy them off and get their social boons.  And if I did something that caused an NPC to hate me, resulting in a social bane, odds were that I'd run into that NPC in the tavern and could provoke them so I could kill them too without consequence.  In the end, my choices did not matter during the speed runs, resulting in a drastically different game-style than the initial play-thrus, leaving me wondering which game mode was the intended game-mode and the work that was put into the other game-mode when focusing resources on only one mode may have propelled the game from good to great.6. Allies.  The game offers allies you can take with you on your encounters.  I really like how Griftlands used allies in the negotiation encounters, where allies offer a buff/debuff during the start but leaves the emphasis on the deck once the encounter is running.  Unfortunately in battle encounters, the emphasis shifts away from the battle deck and leans towards a numbers game of dps vs dmg mitigation based on how many allies you have.  The battle deck is still important, but didn't feel as important as the negotiations   Allies is an interesting idea.  I found that battle encounters in the speed run were a lot more balanced than the initial play-thru, but I wish they'd find some other way to balance the battle encounters that contain allies.In conclusion, the game is in Early Access.  While I don't think Griftlands is a great game, it's still a good game, and I don't think it was a waste of money.  However, after 20+ hours in the game, I doubt I'll play it anymore except to explore the Early Access features.

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a nice departure from the deck building rogue-likes we're used to. (Slay the Spire, cough cough) While it maintains many similarities, Griftlands specializes in it's role-playing aspects, but also rewards players who pay attention to the finer detail and patterns.You choose between three Grifters, one of which was just fully released, acting as a sort of sci-fi bounty hunter. Any Boba Fett fans? Cause you can live the dream now. Decide who you're working for, and discover creative ways to tilt odd jobs in your favor or completely muck them up. Will you be a rough and tough street thug, a greedy grifter, or a kind smile in an unforgiving universe? Well you get to decide each job who you're going to be, but remember, actions have consequences.Each character has 5 days to reach their goal. You'll do odd jobs for the most part until scripted story events will further their plot. But each day will be a test of survival, cunning, and luck. Not to mention some subtle influence. ;) But seriously, the card play is familiar if you've played other games like it. You control two decks, one for diplomacy and one for battle. After battles or jobs you'll get to pick a card to add to your deck(s) until you find a synergy that works for you. There is a steep learning curve, even after 80 hours I still find new situations, dialogue, or routes I haven't taken. Try being the good guy, then the bad guy, then bad at being good and good at being bad, pretending to be bad at being good, but really you're good at being bad. That's confusing I bet, but each day gives you options to become something new, or double cross old friends from yesterday, allowing for a LOT of replay value.Each Grifter has unique cards, a unique map, story, and characters, The universe feels very defined and fleshed out, everyone fits in and you have to navigate the faction wars with grace or deception. Another thing worth mentioning are the smaller mechanics, first of all, you can have a cute lil' death trap for a pet! So you never feel alone. Another is that the game will offer you extra gold for picking cards you never pick, rewarding players who step out of their comfort zone. You can also pay a body guard to look the other way, or get people drunk so they love you. Did I mention you can choose 3 perks(or modifiers) each playthrough out of like 20? Again, replay value. Oh and there are prestige modes similar to ascension in StS.So much charm and finesse goes into this great title by Klei. If you're a fan of rogue-likes, deckbuilding, and a bit of roleplay, you'll feel right at home in the Griftlands.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game... as someone that dislikes permadeath and card games this is actually enjoyableThe moment i saw KLEI i thought BUY and i dont regret it, at allId like to see more ''afterdeath'' mechanics and stuff involved, better buffs and just more stuff to it. Currently theres stuff that keeps you playing but not a whole lot like Hades for example. In Hades you objectively get, idk, 50% - 75% stronger. Here in Griftlands its like 12% - 20% stronger which isnt a whole lot and the fact that you can only pick 3 perks feels kinda bad for how interesting more than ''strong'' every perk isOverall i hope development keeps going towards more random generation or even procedural regarding missions and stuff. _childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: While the cardplay will likely not live up to the expectations of a Slay the Spire veteran, this game offers its unique storytelling style, the masterful inclusion of many RPG elements, and dual deck gameplay to make itself stand out against its predecessor. The real highlight of this game is the variety of its gameplay. On top of the inherent variety provided by a typical deckbuilder roguelike, there are 3 different fleshed out campaigns with their own branching stories filled with consequences and variations of stories to tell. And, if for some weird reason you aren't a fan of the storytelling aspect of the game, you can always play the Brawl gamemode, which is more traditional for roguelike veterans. Highly recommended if you are at all interested in the blending of the Roguelike-deckbuilder and RPG genres.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a level of polish that most finished games don't have. _childDocuments_.review: For a fan of card games and tactical games AND turn based games, this was a very good surprise! Solid gameplay, varied play modes, and pretty strong replayability makes this a very good investment if you like this type of games. And the fact that it is easy on the eyes doesn't hurt one bit.PROS- Visuals and art is spot on, well done and immersive- Big card variety- Serious amount of unlockables - Multiple characters and game modes give this some very nice longevity - The story is surprisingly engaging for a small indie card game- Personally, i really like the humor. It's subtle, original, and not corny or forced like most games that try to be funnyCONS- The amount of clever decks are limited (but they exist). It's more about having a balanced deck with strengths, rather than going with very few cards and one super optimized way of dealing with everything. This is not slay the spire or other games that let you run super thin decks. But it's a minor downside, the game is fine once you adjust your expectations to its special flavor.- Having a lot of unlockables is nice, but i felt like most of the cards you add to the pool are very weak and just "pollute" the pool rather than truly unlock new strategic possibilities. Thankfully you can disable the packs that you unlock, a very good idea.- As with all card games, the RNG component can be frustrating when you are trying to build a deck around an idea and you just can't find the cards to make it work. You get cards randomly at the end of fights (choice of 3) or can buy from a very small selection at shops, that only change every day. Keep in mind a single run lasts 4-5 days only. You basically lack options to pick cards that you want, which makes sens because they built this as a rogue like and you're meant to do the best with what you find. That being said, alternative game mods and mutators (think of them as ingame mods) are better for building focused decks than the default mode.WORTH IT?Yes! Very much so. It's well built, well designed, and it's not even done yet. With most games i feel loss of motivation to play past the few first hours, but with this one the pacing, combat, and interactions come together nicely to keep you going.Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is difficult to explain. It's a sci-fi deck-building card battle roguelite  with open world RPG elements and a faction/relationship system where taking missions for certain characters will either make them friendly/antagonistic towards you with two battle systems where you can either attempt to fight or talk your way out of encounters. It's an ambitious idea, and I'm happy to say it works.However, the thing that concerns me is that while Griftlands attempts to be a melting pot of all these ambitious things, it spreads itself thin in some points. For my first run I'm attempting to choose to fight instead of talk my way out of encounters, and while combat is fun it lacks the depth something like Slay The Spire has where you can build some crazy and powerful combos that make you feel like a galaxy brain when you execute them. Hopefully Klei will keep adding onto this in the future, but it's something to note.Overall, it's a fantastic game that is IMO very reasonably priced. It's worth picking up if you a fan of deckbuilding/card battlers and worth at least putting on your wishlist and picking up during a sale even if you aren't a fan of card battlers.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I've tried, I've never managed to get into computer deck-builders, which is odd because I love them IRL. This is the single exception. While it says 32 hours of play on Steam, I generally play this on my offline laptop on public transport, and would have clocked up several times that.The difference for me between this game and other digital deckbuilders is that Griftlands works overtime to give context to the gameplay. The game is played on several levels, which includes an overmap and dialogue level between battles. This can be surprisingly fun as you interact with other characters, making friends and enemies, and contributing to an emergent sense of story. How you interact with characters can have surprising effects later on in a campaign.The card component of the game itself is quite engaging, and includes elements that would be extremely difficult to incorporate in a physical card game, such as cards having 'experience'. Each campaign features slightly different mechanics, and there are multiple potential build pathways for each character which allow you to both minmax your deck AND roleplay simultaneously.On top of this, the art style is beautiful, the world is intriguing and feels well-realised, and while the stories are straightforward enough, the writing is quite good.Altogether, a highly recommended game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a fan of card crawlers for a while now (Roguebook, Spire, Monster Train) The bar was set high by these previous games, but I've been totally impressed by this game. It seems to have carved out a very specific, unique niche in this class of game... The visual style is great, and animated constantly, which keeps the relatively still screens feeling 'alive' - Combine that with the choose-your-path adventure story, and this feels like an interactive graphic novel, which kept me engaged in the overall journey.  Fun writing and characters with personality.The negotiation game is a whole different beast from standard-style battles, with its own deck, and is a solidly engaging sequence I never got bored of being in. Negotiation isn't a tack-on minigame, it's a well designed and intricate thing of its own. Almost every single situation allows you to choose Battle or Negociate, so it's totally integrated in the design. So in a nutshell, you're actually getting 2 different card battlers in this one game, and you get to choose how much of each one you spend your time in - beautiful. The way card rewards and upgrades are based on usage, this also builds your character to be strongest in your preferred play-style. All these pieces work together beautifully, I found.I've got very few cons on this one. The biggest 'down' is kind of a compliment too: The character campaigns were too short. When you got me interested in the progress of my character and this world, I was hoping to grow a lot more and see a lot more of my choices ripple forward in time. I was actually kind of stunned when I finished the first run when I thought we were just getting started - This is more of a "one week in a life" tale  rather than the winding RPG adventure I was ready for.So it sits a little uncomfortably for me. The short cycle to complete a run seems to want to be in the "Quick runs" category like Spire. But the heavy emphasis on storytelling, dialog, characters with love/hate meters - All of this seems more about long-term investment in much longer runs. It's too bad, I think this will make it get old faster for me because I'll get sick of going through the same story beats over and over. For a quick run, I'll keep leaning more to Monster Train for its 'disposable' level of attention investment. But maybe Griftlands 2 will see their potential, and lean more towards longer, more complex narratives with rippling choices - to really take advantage of what they got going here. I want to see more games like this one, now that they've set a standard. There's a lot of potential to take this model and push it into something bigger!Overall, if you like the other games referenced at the start, I say you can't go wrong giving this very solid and unique entry a play. It's not just another clone of the genre, and I can feel the care and passion the makers had for this vision.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a breath of fresh air in a sea of remakes , reskins and just poorly executed ideas.Griftlands is a Card game at its core with rogue lite elements that allow you to save one thing from the previous game or once a day your character which i love.
