_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of Slay the Spire, but find that the overall story side of the game is lacking then this is the game for you. Griftlands takes a genre, and makes it a work of art. Each mechanic in the game is well thought out and integrated making nothing feel clunky. I'm shocked that this is still in early access with how polished the game is right now. Yes, we're still missing days of campaigns on the third character, but with a nicely detailed roadmap and how well executed this game is so far, I'm confident that it will be delivered... and even if it isn't there's already more than enough of a game here to put away a hell of a lot of hours.Mechanics that i personally enjoyed:Decisions feels like they matter - Everything you do has some form of consequence. You can make friends and enemies, the people you help (or backstab) respond to the actions you take; these give you boons or nerfs when it comes to negotiations and combat, you may also find situations are easier / harder if those people are around. Go on a murderous rampage, friends of the people you kill will start to hate you and make your game harder, and you'll start to get a reputation that inserts cards into your deck.Brawl mode; sometimes i just can't be bothered with the story side of the game and i just want to play a more linear playstyle. Brawl mode allows you to ditch all the fluff and play a game more similar to Slay the Spire. Changing the game - the use of perks and game modes allows you to play in different ways; want to own a pack of dogs to fight at your side, you can do it. want to instead draft your entire starting negotiation deck rather than use the base deck, thats an option. THERE. IS. SO. MUCH. HERE.This game honestly has it all when it comes to this genre of game. I'm trying to think of a negative; you have the ability to change the appearance of your character, this is purely aesthetic, which is fine, and im nitpicking, but if this had some kind of passive depending on the outfit you choose (pick a certain type for a change of picking cards of a certain type, or something) then it would make the game more interesting and give you a reason to try on the different outfits.its safe to say i love this game and its quickly become one of my favourite games of this year.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a deck building rogue-like that borrows its core elements from Slay the Spire wholesale. However, Klei has added several enjoyable twists:-World-building and role-playing elements added to quests-Separate "battle" and "negotiation" decks, which increase strategic options in addition to adding role-playing flavor-A relationship system which offers minor or major buffs/debuffs; also lethal/non-lethal playstyles are supported and tie strategically into these systemsThe game in this state feels essentially like a complete experience, though a new character + campaign is yet to be released. Right now it's much easier to complete a run than in Slay the Spire, but thankfully prestige difficulty and mutator options for campaigns increase replayability. Right now the game is easily worth the full purchase price, even without a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: IMO a more fun version of slay the spire or at least has the potential to be with a few more updates (although I havent played STS in a while so maybe that game has improved over time). Rougelike card builder with two decks, one for negotiations and one for physical combat. Story mode is much more interesting than more linear rougelikes. On the other hand, I'm about 26 hours in and don't feel like starting up another run. This game just got released for early access, so I think I'll be coming back later down the road once more cards have been released.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game, and all the other games from this developer, are a great example for how early access should be used. The game offers a lower price in early access because it wants to reward people that trust the developer. They make clear progress and they keep you up to date. But now, the game itself...It is just a piece of art, the art style is so well done and it really gives the right atmosphere to the game. If you are a person that hates losing / starting over again, don't buy this game. It is a rogue game which means you will start over multiple times and you will have to repeat certain dialogues again. When you die you will receive some perks which will increase your chances of winning for when you try again so that will keep you going for sure.The story is very well done with a nice lore to it. Skipping through dialogues you already had in a previous run is fairly quick so you are not stuck being bored. The music could be better for sure though, it is a little bit annoying at times and very repetitive.The game is not hard on new players, everything is explained thoroughly but it will take you some time to figure out the combat and negotiation system but there is a lot of fun in doing so!There are also no lies told on the store page so if you like what you read on there you should buy it because you'll most certainly like the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game. Obvious comparison is to Slay the Spire which I think is fair enough to entice people - though after playing for a few hours its quick to see they're far apart beyond genre. Griftlands' strongest point is the story telling for me. I appreciate when games make morality choices just that. You might make an enemy murdering this person, you might have to deal with the consequences of showing mercy if not. While I'm sure you can find ways to min-max the rogue like aspect you at least get a great introduction to the world, story, and characters before the full rogue like side takes over. My only complain is I wish Rook was the starting character. Even though you unlock all characters very quickly he would have been a better first impression in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I've had this game since it was first made available during early access. The developers took into feedback into account and came out with a perfect game for those who like deckbuilders and roguelite genres. The game has an immense amount of replayability due to the number of paths you can choose and the number of NPC interactions. If you like roguelite and deckbuilding games this is the perfect game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr It's fantastic and you should buy itI really love this game! It goes beyond the simple ladder climb of Slay the Spire or Monster Train and fleshes out the deck building experience with an interesting campaign story, which includes some player choices that add variety. I love that there are two different types of combat as that means you're not playing the same deck every single encounter. The characters are fun and the writing is great! I've had a lot of laughs both from onscreen writing and from details I've imagined because of the scenarios the game creates!There's just one slight draw back in my opinion. The cards themselves feel like they lack the depth of some other games, and I've found my decks end up kinda similar each run. The story building is where most of the replayability comes from in this game. This has meant I got bored of it quicker than other, similar games. It doesn't help that games in this take me a lot longer to complete so it feels like more of a commitment to start up. That said, I still put 50 hours on it very quickly, while having a lot of fun, and feel like my money was well spent!I really hope a modding community pops up around this game because that could keep me interested for a very long time!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A fun card battler that I got more than my money's worth out of.The graphics are great, the idea of having two completely different decks is new to me and works well. My only issue, and it is fairly minor, is that the difficulty is a bit on the easy side. I completed two of the three different characters on my first attempt. But that is okay for me, because given the story nature of the game, each run takes quite a few hours to complete. So having the traditional rogue-like "many attempts required" would have made the necessary play time too great.Of course there are many difficulty levels. After playing through the three stories I didn't feel motivated to try the higher difficulty levels, the story wasn't that interesting to me. But there is still lots more to discover.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is an amazingly fun deckbuilder, don't let the Early Access state worry you, its got *plenty of content* to offer already!Its an RPG/Deckbuilder game with rougelike elements where you select a character and play through their story, if you fail you get to keep some of what you earned and try again, gaining experience for how well you did. Experience unlocks more cards and even neat outfits to wear.The game can be challenging but never really feels unfair and its easy to learn after a couple of matches, the two characters are both pretty different, and each one can even have several kinds of builds for even more variation. Rook, for example, can build up charges, each one granting more damage (and overcharges which can be spent by certain cards) or the charges can be spent to gain defense. This allows him to build decks around managing his charge/overcharge, but he also has the option of having a deck built around Burn status ailments and doing damage over time.The story is neat, there's a lot of lore and vibrant characters.As well as fun system that rewards you for befriending or infuriating the various character with boons/banes which are like passives.I can see myself putting well over 100 hours, if not more into this game with its charming artstyle, lovely characters and above all fun deck building gameplay!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: great pick up on the steam sale would pay full price its a game with actual new combat mechanics for a card game. While there is fear for me that this game would get boring if i played it too much, there is no boredom yet after 13 hours. I would give this game a solid 8.5/10 with room to become a 10/10 in the near future
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A cleverly done deckbuilder-RPG-roguelike in the spirit of Slay the Spire. Very well executed with a lot of pretty Klei polish on it. It has a lot more flavour and charm for those interested in more than just the challenge of Spire but does not lose sight of presenting a fair and balanced challenge.I'd very much recommend Griftlands, well worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's Klei, so I bought it. They've never disappointed me.This one is different than your usual Klei game though. It doesn't feel yet like much of a sandbox experience, but it's also not a railroaded RPG either. It's ... different. I've never played anything like it.Is it fun? Oh yeah. Absolutely. Different dialogue trees, a lot of different missions and randomness makes for fun on multiple playthroughs. It's hard and you can't restore a saved game so it's very rogue. But it's not frustratingly difficult and I don't feel like the game cheats. All the numbers are there and displayed. I'm going to recommend this one, even so early in early access. Klei sticks to good release schedules and certainly improves things along the way. And the price is good right now too.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful art style, fun world and characters. I wish there was a bit more variety to the alien species, but only because I love the art so much and want to see more character designs.The actual "Roguelike" game play is solid and challenging. Assembling two complete decks, one for combat and one for diplomacy, is fun and rewarding when you feel things coming together.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Easy to understand, decently deep gameplay/replayability with different classes, unlocks and the usual roguelike elements presented in a different format. The combat both conversationally and physically happens separately  andis very well done. The story is interesting due to how much agency you have on it.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: There is too much talking in the story and too little playing.Also, the explanation of the game mechanics is rather poor. Battle is probably a bit easier, but I have been mostly choosing negotiation and despite playing it over 10 times I am still struggling to grasp basic concepts and what some of the keywords mean.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A very solid and fulfilling rogue-like deck-builder with a cool world, engaging characters/relationship system, and the unique aspect of having 2 separate decks for combat and negotiation! Playing from the beta and seeing where the game has come from, it's been an absolute treat to experience all of the care and additional content the developers have put into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Upgrade your cards - you have two separate customizable decks to upgrade.  Do they summon extra cards?  Upgrade those!  Get upgrades to yourself, and upgrade those too!  Finish a game, and you get upgrades to the game!This game ♥♥♥♥♥♥' slaps.  Its dry sense of humour is just a dollop of whipped cream on top of an itch-scratchingly great upgrade-fest.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I've fallen in love with this game so fast with literally no complaints so far. I think with this game giving a lot more card offers and the experience of building two different decks at the same time majorly offset my initial dislike of cards' damage ranges (coming from slay the spire with little to no randomness in card functionality). Now I also appreciate the steps it takes to offer solutions to these rng factors, appreciating this newfound randomness too.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Game is very repetitive in a bad way. The way the story works is very shallow. Choices never make even the slightest of impact both roguelike and story wise. `Decks` are shallow. Each deck has no more than a couple of mechanics going for it while one is superior. `Deck building` can not even be considered that, it is more like just picking cards that you know works.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Turns out I'm keen on deck-building games, after all!So, the game proper, even in its early stages of development has a lot to offer.What I liked most about it is the familiar style and 'feel' of a Klei game.The graphics are neat and sharp. The sounds simple, yet polished. I did find the soundtrack a bit boring and repetitive, however.That being said, the game has a lot of promise and potential.I must add, it's got quite decent replayability value as is, with more to come.Definitely grab it on sale, if you're a fan of Klei games or card collection per se!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: GRIFTLANDS Mini Review:Deckbuilding Roguelike by the creators of Don't Starve, that tries to push the Deckbuilding genre forward in similar ways Hades did the same for roguelikes overall last year. And for the most part, Griftlands succeeds.Balancing 2 decks, one for battle (think Slay the Spire) and one for Negotiation (pretty unique gameplay) is great. Constructing it all around a narrative with a sprawling cast of interconneted characters and factions, with a TON of options for customizing your playstyle is too.One run takes way more time than in most roguelikes (my first full clear took me around 5 hours, but can definitely be done way faster), but is even more engaging for that reason and rarely ever feels "unfair". You are allowed to play it very safe at all times if you choose to do so, yet run risk of running out of ressources fast if you never take risks.There are 3 different characters with unique decks and a unique storyline. There is a LOT bang for your buck in here. The only issue I've had so far comes with the narrative aspect, which while great, can repeat itself a bit too much after multiple runs with the same character.For: Fans of Deckbuilders and RoguelikesFans of Narrative-Driven games with a lot of personal choices that matterNot For:People who just wanna do "one quick run"People who don't wanna think about narrative consequences in their deckbuilder gameOverall: Great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Oh man, this game is great. This is a very clear case of "Standing on the shoulders of giants", as you can see many of the tried and true mechanics from other games such as Slay the Spire displayed. But this game is by no means a rip-off and improves on the genre in, imho, almost every way. The sound design is great, I love the art, the theme is wonderful, and the story is interesting enough to add to the game without being so cumbersome as to keep you from card-battler fun that you're here for.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely thought I hated this game in the first two hours, I wanted a fun fast Slay the Spire clone but instead I got some weird pseudo-RPG with two types of decks and waaaay too much dialogue. But somehow you dig past all that, die a few times then you figure out what the hell is actually going on during negotiation fights and suddenly you've found a complete gem. A steal, especially on sale for any fans of the genre. Just give it a little time and everything will suddenly start to come together and you've got a game that's just as fun as the best of them out there.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is okay - too much story focus for me personally and I don't like the idea of the two decks, one for combat and one for negotiation. Also many cards feel underwhelming when using them, too many crappy consumable cards as rewards and consequences for each action (for example you kill a guy and another random guy you didn't even know exists hates you, which gives you a debuff).Also the game regulary crashes so hard that my pc restarts itself. Can't recommend, play monster train / slay the spire instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands give a refreshing twist on the usual deck building genre. The character stories are entertaining though leave little room for replaying again, though this is a minor setback from the incredibly re-playable gameplay loop that always gives you a different way to approach each situation. Unique gadgets and pets can give you the edge you need in a bad situation and cybernetic enhancements can completely shift how you play.Another must try from Klei, particularly if you are a fan of Slay the Spire or other deck building games.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Currently have 32 hours, and I really like this game.  Haven't even played the other two characters yet.  Seems like Klei is committed to frequently updating with good content.  I would give the game an 8/10 in current state, but it has the potential to be higher still.  Maybe it's just my play style, but negotiations seem super easy, and battles are way hard.  very few cards, abilities, or grafts seem like I would ever dream of using them.  Regardless, the rpg integration of the card base roguelite genre is quite fun
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Did you know that Klei Entertainment makes good games? After 12 hours, there's some criticism to be made here, but it's surface level to the point of it not really needing to be brought up in full. It's got three characters, each with an assortment of styles to play with. It one-ups the likes of Slay the Spire and Monster Train by having actual worldbuilding, and there's a branching story for each character that you can just straight up ignore if you want -- or soak it in with a "story mode" difficulty. Griftlands is really great.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The way Klei mixed story with game mechanics makes this feel more like an RPG than a deckbuilding strategy game, and I mean this in the best way possible.  The choices you make in how you build your deck directly affect how your character plays and interacts with story decisions.  Great game that I highly recommend for any RPG/Strategy enthusiast.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I love, love, love the direction of this game. The art style, the music, the worldbuilding. Unfortunately, as someone who has gotten a bit bored of Slay the Spire, this doesn't replace it for me. This suffers from having too much stuff stuffed into it. Your deck starts with a lot of variety to begin with, and then the amount of choices you are constantly presented with is daunting. The sheer amount of things in your deck(s) you have to keep track of, and all of the various battle/negotiation effects, complete with flashy animations make this game fairly hard to grock. To counter this, the game itself is fairly easy. I never felt like I had to understand much about the various combos, but I could still win regardless. It was on my second or third playthrough that I finally understood every faction has their own traits.It would be nice if this game had a stronger "vanilla" flavor - a more boring starter deck? Make the concepts introduce themselves slower? Make me do multiple playthroughs to unlock factions/card abilities, etc?Obviously, the game may reveal itself on more playthroughs, and maybe I can up the difficulty in turn. But it's hard to pick this up over something that's a truer roguelike. The "runs" are pretty long, maybe a few hours? Definitely feels too long to be a roguelike, but too short for an adventure game. The story mode loses it's replayability a few times through. The game gives some other play modes, like an onslaught mode that just slams random encounters together, which loses a lot of the charm of the story.All that to say, I certainly enjoyed the game! And I will find it easy to get my money's worth! But it's hard to say I needed this game in my collection. And it's really close to something great.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the first play through very much, though some of the mechanics felt a little bit overdone. I have major respect for Klei taking on such an absolute behemoth of a design project. Different playable characters with completely different playstyles. Two completely different types of combat. A ton of NPCs each with their very own unique in-game effects and dialogue.However, I couldn't really get in to a second run after completing the game once. If I was Klei, I would have focused on making the game longer rather than making new characters, but I guess that's just my opinion.Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The combination of all these story and quest elements in a roguelike deckbuilder might seem like a nice idea, but it doesn't work. All those extra elements just add too much length to runs.Giving each character 2 decks means that you only really have enough stuff in a run to customize each deck half as much or less as in Slay the Spire. This makes each run very similar to other runs.The difficulty is weird in this game. I got to the final boss in my first game easily, then it totally crushed me. I thought this was cool, essentially this would have meant the first part of the game is more about setting up that final fight, rather than actually being difficult to survive (similar to FTL). But, that didn't turn out to be the case. I aborted my second run early on because I was unhappy with my choices. My third run I crushed everything in my path including the final boss without any feeling of difficulty. For my fourth run I played the second character for the first time (Rook) and it was the same thing, way too easy.Not sure how the higher prestige levels are, but I don't want to grind for hours just to get to a difficulty I actually enjoy. Compared to Inscryption, the story and atmosphere are dull and repetitive and overstay their welcome.The music is forgettable. The art style is too busy, annoying, and nonsensical. I guess it looks nicer than Slay the Spire, but that's a very low bar.Compared with Slay the Spire, there is a lot more breadth (doing a lot of things at the same time) but this does not make the game better. Slay the Spire has more depth of strategy and is a lot more focused on the most important thing: gameplay. TL;DR: Fun for a bit, but got too repetitive for me after only 4 games.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's basically Spire with a face lift. I was a little disappointed by that. But that's only because I've played a ton of Spire. It's kind of the same card system, and even the same mechanics for the first two characters I've seen so far. The map screen, though it doesn't look like it, is still a progression based over 5 days. It's a clever way of rejigging the mechanic of Spiral but that's what I mean, it is the same mechanics. It does look a ton better though.The characters are better, the story is better, the art is great, the argument system is a nice touch. There is a lot of depth here. If I was going to play this type of game, I'd probably play this over spire now. Having team mates is cool.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a deck-building rogue-like where you fight and negotiate your way through a broken-down sci-fi world.

name: Empire of Sin
detailed_description: Pick Your Empire of Sin Edition Empire of Sin - Deluxe Edition Upgrade to the Deluxe Edition and receive access to the Mobster Pack which includes four recruitable and playable gangsters, the Golden Weapon Set that comes with three exclusive weapon skins plus “Romero” gun sound effects, and unique execution animation for your boss character - the Curb Stomp Execution. Empire of Sin - Premium Edition The Premium Edition grants access to all Deluxe Edition content - the mobster pack, Golden Weapon set and Curb Stomp Execution kill - plus two post-launch expansions and the stylish Al Capone’s Fur Coat costume. About the Game Empire of Sin is a new strategy game brought to you by Romero Games and Paradox Interactive that puts you at the heart of the ruthless criminal underworld of 1920s Prohibition-era Chicago. Slip into the shoes of one of the fourteen real and historically inspired mob bosses such as Al Capone, Stephanie St. Clair, or Goldie Garneau and assemble a rag-tag gang, build and manage your criminal empire, and defend your turf from rival gangs. It’s up to you to hustle, charm, and intimidate your way to the top and do whatever it takes to stay there - break a leg! Roleplay: Choose one of fourteen unique bosses based on fictional and real-world gangsters, then set out to build and manage your criminal empire in Chicago’s infamous Prohibition era. Empire Management: Build your Empire of Sin and run Chicago’s underworld economy with business savvy, brutality or city-wide notoriety. Strategically manage your establishments such as speakeasies, supply chains, casinos and more. Turn-Based Combat: Assemble your gang and slug it out in turn-based combat to defend and expand your territory – or send a message to opposing gangs.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited for the update/DLC to play this, but it still ended up in disappointment. The premise of the game is great and there's so much historical source material to pull from, so it's really confusing how this was botched this badly. All you had to do was copy the Crusader Kings diplomacy/relationship formula, throw some X-COM in there, and put it in a Prohibition era. I agree with most of the reviews on here: visually, the game is decent, but the gameplay is a an absolute slog. Your territorial expansions and combat wins don't feel rewarding so there's no incentive to keep pushing forward. All the rackets feel the same and the upgrades are still pretty worthless after the update. There's no customization options for anything so everything looks bland as hell. Not to mention the atrocious UI and character movement jankiness. Albeit, there are a ton of different systems and game mechanics scattered throughout the game. However, they either 1) barely have any impact on the gameplay, like the police system and character backstories, or 2) the different systems don't work well together, like the relationship mechanics with the hiring system. Also, this game lacks some serious quality of life upgrades. I cannot believe there's still no way to speed up and/or skip time, which makes the game feel like some weird FTP-mobile-Clash-of-Clans nonsense. TL;DR: great concept, terrible execution.

This means I have replayed the game from the start 3 times. Sigh.....This game wants to be 3 things.Strategy game, management sim, and tactical shooter. TACTICS: 3/10Terrible wouldnt pay 20$ for this game. Perhaps it will be good in the future but I doubt it. I will be playing this game to get my money out of it. _childDocuments_.review: I don't think I have ever written a review for a game, but this game was so terrible that I felt it necessary.I regret my purchase and I am actually disappointed in Paradox Games, a company that I trust, because this game was not ready to be released. Why not put it out as an Alpha and get some feedback and work out some issues and concept? The game is hollow and not fun. The concept is good and it has some good ideas, but it is not challenging and gets quite boring. I completed it just because I kept hoping that it was going to get interesting...but when it was over I felt completely underwhelmed.Also, what is up with all of the female gang members? This is the 1920s and women weren't getting involved in organized crime at the level that this game portrays. Also, every "romance" that sprung up for my gangsters was homosexual. That wouldn't have happened openly back in that area. It honestly was just really cringey seeing the lengths that were made to have this game be inclusive or whatever they were going for. _childDocuments_.review: (UPDATED)"Tropico" + "X-Com" + "Mafia". Developed by John Romero (Doom, Quake) and Brenda Romero (Wizardry) Pretty addicting Turn Based Strategy Game with RPG elements. No idea what all the negative reviews are about. The game is much better than expected. The first Empire Builder I've played where I didn't immediately crash the economy. You run around, take over peoples rackets and replace them with your own. You can build breweries, speakeasies, brothels, casinos or hotels. If you have enough gang members, you can build a safehouse and assign a lieutenant to it. There are 14 gang leaders to choose from. Some are real like Dean O'Bannon, Stephanie St Clair and Al Capone, but others are fictional characters created for the game. There is a pretty even mix of male and female bosses, which doesn't seem too forced as there were plenty of real women bootleggers in real life. Some of the gangs are themed around particular rackets and will excel best with that kind of business. Alot of the negative reviews come from people who don't understand how the economy works. You are bootleggers. That means, you have to bootleg. Build breweries and sell top grade liquor to minor factions and rival gangs. Use the funds you earn to crush them. This is what Al Capone did. This is what Arnold Rothstein did. I don't understand how people could get this wrong. If you just keep buying rackets, you'll tank the economy. The best way to expand is to kill the boss of a rival gang. You earn all of their rackets for the cost of one safehouse. There are some issues that I have, but nothing major. When you attack a building, your guys just scramble to their nearest "cover", even if it puts them in a worse position than if they did nothing. This is very annoying sometimes. There's no diplomatic way to play the game. You can't really absorb other gangs.  I also wish you could run legitimate businesses too, like Butcher shops or pizza parlours. Could use more customisation for the gang members (What clothes they can wear, ect). I would like to see these things added in the expansion. UPDATE:The Precinct Update and the Make It Count DLC greatly expand the gameplay and improve many of the features of the game. Gang Turfs now have supply lines that must exist in order for you to invade. Diplomacy is now a valid option with the ability to peacefully buy out a rival's empire. Police response and presence is greatly improved. This update is free and includes mod support. Make It Count adds "Not Meyer Lensky" due to some legal issues with Hollywood and Loansharking. Easily the best boss in the game, Maxim Zelnick, as he is called, has the ability to spawn 2 random expendable henchmen and sic them onto his enemies. He also makes for a good diplomatic playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played about forty hours so far of Empire of Sin and have finished the game six times.  It's not a perfect game, but I have a lot of fun when I am playing it and it does keep me coming back.The setting is great, and I love the different feels to each of the neighborhoods in Chicago.  I really like the dynamic zoom mechanic that the developers made for this game, where you can smooth-scroll from inside a building to outside the building, to a view of the street, to a tactical view of the neighborhood, to a tactical view of all neighborhoods, all in real-time.  This feature is great and is not getting nearly enough credit in the reviews.The game has quite a bit going on with it.  You've got a light economic management thing going on, which mostly consists of producing and setting the correct types of booze, and buying or taking over buildings.   You can also upgrade establishments, but with the current build of the game (Dec 2020), upgrades are usually not worth it, as they are expensive and take a long time to build after you pay for them.  The game rewards going as wide as possible as quickly as possible, so my go-to strategy is basically to start to clear out and take over the neutral casinos and speakeasies as soon as a new game starts.Meanwhile, you've got a bunch of other mob bosses running around setting up their own empires.  When you meet one, you can either tell them to go pound sand or you can sit down with them to cut a deal.  The deals that you cut with the mob bosses are so incremental that they are barely noticeable, but I think the sit-downs themselves are quite fun, if a tad repetitive.  After your initial meeting, there are a range of diplomacy options available.  These are generally pretty useless, except for the trading, which is currently rigged in the player's favor.  It does not take much to convince bosses to sell your their unique weapons in exchange for some garbage ones and have them walk away thinking they got the better of you.While it is currently very easy to complete the game without diplomacy at all, diplomacy can be used to win, in a manner of speaking.  I did play a game where I quietly took over unoccupied neighborhoods and made nice with all mob bosses and stepped on no toes.  Then, I sold them all weapons for peanuts, and they all trusted me.  Then, I kept calling in favors and repeatedly called in a hit on every boss with every other boss, and watched them wipe each other out.  Then, when there was one left, I just went in with a small team and took that person out.You've also got an RPG-like quest system in this game.  There's a few generic quests available to every mob boss; these were fun in my first playthrough but the rewards were pretty crappy so I have more or less ignored most of them since.  Each boss also has a main questline, this can be a nice diversion.Finally, you've got the gangster system and the tactical battles.The gangster system is a neat idea and does a lot of things right, but needs a bit of work.  There is a roster of henchmen that both you and the CPU opponents can hire.  While theoretically you can assign your henchmen as neighborhood managers or as protectors of one of your buildings, in reality you and your henchmen will all fight together as a roving squad of death, as that is by far the most effective use for them.  Gangsters have different classes, but the doctor and demolitionist classes are far superior to any of the other three, as doctors get free healing and can also use rifles, the best weapon in the game, and demolitionists get a free grenade that does massive AOE damage and causes bleeding. As you increase in notoriety, you can hire more expensive and more skilled henchmen.  Currently, there is not much difference between the cheapest goons and the most elite killers; I would love to see the lower tiers of henchmen nerfed quite a bit, and the higher tiers buffed.The tactical battles are the best part of the game and are the reason I keep coming back.  The difficulty is generally pretty easy, except when you are up against a group of enemies who all decide to lob grenades on the same turn.  The safehouse raids are so much fun!  (they need to be harder, though, and a greater variety of safehouses would be sweet).Empire of Sin also has a great score by Crimson Diamond composer Dan Policar and team; I would pay extra for a soundtrack if Paradox decides to sell one (please, Paradox!).All in all, this game is a lot of fun right now, but also has a lot of room for improvement.  I am optimistic about the future of Empire of Sin.

_childDocuments_.review: Empire of Sin is a mildly-RPG, pauseable RTS of the Prohibition era beginning in 1920--it covers a range of activities and a timeframe that is hard to find anywhere else. The tactical combat is early Xcom style, designed well, top down, with a small range of actions available to each actor. The real joy of this game, IMHO, is the wonderful variety of quirky bad guys--first, a wonderfully broad variety of bosses you can start with, and then dozens of widely differing henchmen which you can select as your tools. The henchmen are categorized by how much they cost you on the regular vis a vis their level of skills, and sometimes, special weaponry. It is important to pay careful attention to your selections for a couple of reasons. First, if you take more than one or two from the top two categories, you will end up spending so much on them you can hardly make your rackets profitable--they run 20% and 16% of your overall take respectively. Second, the relationship between cost and skill lever is less than perfect. One of my most consistent performers is a bottom row doctor named Nora who shoots like a Marine Corps sniper and can heal guys on the fly without meds in the middle of a firefight. Also, some characters are listed as "Giants" with special bonuses in melee, but for some reason their supposed prowess is not reflected either in Hit Points or in melee skill. So pay attention to what you're getting.The music does a wonderful job setting the mood. The dynamics of the social relating with other bosses is great for setting power balances. But, eventually, the game does begin to drag. As you grow in power, and you manage to eliminate a boss or two, the game seems to automatically queue some other organization to declare war on you. Funny thing is, if you take a squad of 4-8 guys with you into a few of their rackets in a row, they will quickly come begging for a truce and may give you 200 barrels of swill or rack to accept. The fights are fun, but they are endless, and even someone who enjoys it as much as I do can tire of the constant need for small skirmishes. There's no targeted assassinations, no blowing up of supply chains, no exploding of rackets. The "missions" available along the way are primarily a means to thrust some additional $$$ at you--this isn't Cyberpunk. Finally, the core management aspect of the game has to do with spending your hard-earned capital on improving your businesses, adding much-needed security, ambiance, protection from the police, and word of mouth reputation. For your breweries, you can raise the quality of your alcohol. For casinos, the quality of your games. But, eventually, it feels like mass tweaking of minor elements of your fortune, repetitive, and without enough engagement of the immersion aspect of those businesses.So, in the final analysis, I give this game a thumbs up. I will start a new boss soon and enjoy a different atmosphere of play... for a while. But from what I can see so far, I will eventually wear the newness and immersion of this one off, and may not go back to it again. It is a slightly better than average implementation of a very rare game focus. I love, love, lover the characters. But it would be nice if you could do more with them.

_childDocuments_.review: Empire of Sin is a turn-based tactical/empire building “gabagool” simulator developed by Romero Games, a studio created by DOOM creator John Romero. Originally coming from the mind of John Romero’s wife Brenda Romero, whose hobbies included creating her own historical board games. This desire to create the game had lasted for around twenty years, and after the studio was formed the two then decided to approach Paradox Interactive, whose history of publishing strategy titles led to a partnership formed for the development of this game. It’s debut started I believe in 2019 E3 during the Nintendo Showcase (according to sources, as though I probably watched this showcase I don’t remember this moment) and was later released December of 2020. My personal history with this game is limited, I honestly don’t remember if I watched the Nintendo Showcase but I do remember hearing “Mafia strategy game” and wishlisting it immediately. I was cautiously excited for the game, hoping that it would be an updated version of Gangsters: Organized Crime. It was not, and debuted with Mixed reviews (almost negative on Steam). However, I picked it up after waiting for it to go on sale I believe at some point and gave it a playthrough (with cheats activated of course, thanks WeMod) to just relax, having replayed it twice or so over the past two years. My opinion on the game is that the mixed reviews are correct, but here’s how I specifically feel.As the most important part of any tactical empire builder game, it’s important to note that the strategy aspect of the game has to be both fun and technically competent. I’ll start with the technically competent one: ehhhh kinda. Sometimes it runs perfectly fine and I can’t complain! Other times, like when I was playing Al Capone’s game, I would be told to, for example, go find Frankie Yale inside of some bar. However, I can’t do that because “the guards” won’t let me do that. I try to talk to the guards, sometimes the guards will attack and sometimes I’ll be able to talk to the guards, who will say “sure come in” and then I still won’t be able to go in. I kill them, still won’t be able to come in. The only way I’ve been able to move past this was if I were to view the inside of the building and then right click to move my guys inside but that’s kind of a hit or miss depending on the objective. Another time I would do a protection treaty with another group, and if another group was bought out but had bad relations and had declared war then the group you’re protecting would ask for your help. Click on the notification and not only does it say that this group is still alive and needs your help, but you won’t be able to close this pop up which requires a full game reset. Stuff like this didn’t occur too much but occurred enough to where after a while of playing it that I need to take a break after a bit. As for if the gameplay is fun, I’ll go through a general description of what the game is like. First when you start up, you start as your boss and go through the tutorials of hiring specific goons (the limit is 16), from there you go to certain buildings which have random thugs and wipe them out in X-COM styled combat in order to take over the building and turn it into a racket. From there you choose between your four (or five depending on if you have DLC) rackets which vary in price depending on district conditions, and from there you grow your money in order to upgrade your rackets. Once you upgrade your main district hideout enough, you can choose between multiple different buildings for bonuses to those districts (ex. Boxing Gloves for an extra guard in that district only, a Mob Lawyer to lower police presence, etc). You can gain more of these by obtaining certain quest awards or using certain bosses (like Malting will boost your booze but can only be unlocked from a side quest outcome, or Al Capone’s Suit Shop which will boost the chances of police bribes being successful that’s unique to him only). You’ll get quests which offer semi open ended pathways which lead to different rewards sometimes (mostly money) while also dealing with a giant contention of other rival gangsters. Your specific gangsters (as well as your boss) form their own relationships with each other (off-screen) and can get perks and traits. For example, one thing I didn’t notice is that when I went AFK one time, I left all my people inside of a pub, where a whole bunch of them became alcoholics and gained negative traits. You can also gain traits and perks due to combat actions, and using perk points can upgrade their skill tree when you level them up.In between dealing with rival gangsters, you’ll also have to deal with the game’s most important currency other than money: booze. Being the Prohibition Era and all, it’s important to establish a consistent stream of booze and supply. Different types of booze lead to different payouts and outcomes, but also lead to rival bosses trying to ride your s h i t. What I’ll say about the bosses aspect is that the way the game limits you, while it may be realistic can also be really annoying. At one point I found out the location of a rival boss's hideout, and I wanted to send a bunch of goons to go in and kill them, but I couldn’t because none of my territory surrounds them and “supply lines are cut off”. Like that hasn’t stopped people from sending in hitmen to kill  bosses, and truth is I’d rather have the option to fail then get restricted like that because it’s really annoying. The only other things I can think of for the gameplay is that you’ll get certain weapons either as loot or through the black market/police contacts. It’s important to get the best hardware that you can possibly get as not only does it help with combat but also rival named goons could have really heavy firepower and could wipe you out quickly. Being a strategy game, there’s so much stuff involved with this game, between police attention/bureau raids as well as balancing diplomacy, random world events, there’s a lot of stuff in there that I know I’m probably missing.The gameplay itself for the most part is fine, and I’ve gotten myself lost in the game’s mechanics multiple times. I personally had fun with the game, though I also messed about using WeMod Dev cheats because I wanted to have a game to chill and vibe too. However, even with the cheat codes, I can still sit there and respect certain aspects and vibes even if I’m not experiencing them due to my mod use. This game feels like a strange mix of complex and painfully simple, which depending on the type of player can be really frustrating or okay. Overall, it’s a decent time as well as a time sink, just have patience with how buggy it can be on the gameplay front at times. Also there's a very small Steam Workshop community that I Hope eventually gets expanded one day because that could add for some variation! _childDocuments_.review: Alright, First review here we go!i absolutely love this game, the aesthetic, the music, the concept is all in place and match the time period, while giving it a great X-COM feel. however, at this time, it is VERY unpolished. in the span of 22 hours i have come across 3 bugs, with one being a game crashing one. the gameplay at the standard rule-set of lieutenent difficulty and 10 factions is easy to handle. gang fights get easy to handle and Joseph Saltis +speakeasy spam is win. the game is easy to comprehend and easy to figure out.here is my issues with the current form of the game:the diplomacy needs work, and plenty of it. the A.I is intransigent and the moment you do something mildly rude to them they decide that you and your extended family will be murdered, burned and dragged through Chicago. there is very few options to get them to like you or to interact with them overall, the business agreements are rarely worth using due to the bonuses being so small (but that may be the bosses needing a Buff), as far as iv'e seen there is no way to lower the A.I's threat of you, the Chicago police bribe function does too little to matter and ultimately, you get to the point that the most viable option is to just kill them all, which i did in my first play-through. after i bumped it up to the under-boss difficulty, most of these issues were fixed, money got harder to come by, the A.I is alot more aggressive, diplomacy is very much more viable and you cant just kill them all, but that comes back to the big issue of there not being alot of diplomacy.Overall, this game is great and has tons of potential, what i'd like to see later on is:a Multiplayer added, either turn based or real time, make it stable and make it WORK.more options for diplomacy and to make diplomacy more viable, tune the A.I to be more agreeable depending on who they are, add more options like proper alliances, gang merging/vassalization, favors: loaning out guards or giving a temporary upgrade to rackets, promising to stay out of your neighborhood, demanding a racket or to allow me to sell a racket to a potential friend over just selling it and removing it from the map.Slight tweaks to abilities and combat, kill chain and the perk that lets you move after killing a enemy is essentially Big Joe Saltis clearing huge warehouses full of thugs with a tommy gun and one turn, allow you to place your gangsters in designated places of buildings you want to take over, instead of breaking into a brothel and your starting spot is some room with a couple getting it on. expand the arsenal of thugs and guards so its not just 80% shotguns and 15% pistols.Ultimately, i love this game and would recommend it to anyone who loves the 1920's gangster theme, anyone who loves X-COM or the style of combat, or "up close and personal" strategy over the disconnect of the standard paradox map game (still love those as well). as far as recently released games go, i give this a 7/10 with a potential 9/10 further down the line.

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't bad but it isn't good like I expect most Paradox published titles to be like.First of the starting leaders all have a unique storyline, voice, and special abilities with their own ability tree which makes them unique to your standard mobster type. The mobsters you can pick are all different but have a set class, their voicelines become a bit boring after around 4 hours, their isn't really anything unique about them since you can't customise them to give them your own feel or sense of attachment to a character, but as the developers pretty much said in this regard on their ep 1 livestream "OH we added modding tools so you guys can do it yourself!"... They do help you play to a certain play style however which kind of makes it similar to XCOM but very poorly similar since you have to wait a stupid amount of days to make one of your characters have a certain ability instead of it going of experience per say, but I feel that might be because you don't really have counters to certain enemy types because they all pretty much act the same, melee characters are the only ones that have a unique way of attacking you which is pretty much just sprint at you and try and do damage. The combat seems to be something that is getting a lot of hate to be fair, but honestly? It really isn't that bad, It got a little more difficult for me when I was fighting my second mob boss just because their businesses were more upgraded compared to the previous mob boss I took over, but you can just hire another mobster to make it easy again really, the real challenge comes from attacking safehouses, like attacking and taking over places is usually easy as anything, but safehouses actually put you against mobsters with high health meaning you have to play strategically, but that really just means using full cover more so your squad don't take loads of hits, as for people saying"the enemies just run in." well, the THUGS DO, THE ACTUAL GANGSTERS YOU FIGHT LATER ON IN THE GAME DON'T. The world is incredibly dry, you go to point A, quest progressed! Then go to point B, read some absolutely pointless dialogue, IF YOU'RE LUCKY YOU GET TO HEAR SOME POOR VOICE ACTING! But thats pretty much every side quest.. The diplomacy is quite frankly absolute garbage compared to any other paradox game, I shouldn't really compare but when they said that diplomacy would play a big factor in this game, well they lied, non-aggression okay fair enough it makes sense for later on when other factions have more then one district but early on its just a pointless mechanic, you can make a business agreements but you honestly could just rush the starting district and basically get the same benefits, you can ask for money, and booze, you can sell booze, and the war mechanic is incredibly basic, like why in the world would you make a mob game where you can't just straight up blow up a business to start said war, why do I have to go into the diplomacy tab and select "start war" like no, even the old godfather games on ps2 had more depth to them in this regard, there is other options sure but they really aren't even worth going into because they're quite frankly disappointing in comparison to other games with diplomacy, why is there no option to rob stores and banks? I do reckon they will become more fleshed out as months go by but it should be done from day one.Business types are pretty boring; casinos which is RNG cash, brothels which is just a set amount of cash, brewerys (tbf i do like the idea of choosing which alcohol you want to make because MANAGEMENT), but they produce alcohol, speakeasys again, set amount of cash depending on which alcohol type is being sold, and then a hotel which increases customers but you can only build one in each district. Its actually baffling why they didn't add businesses like loan sharks, protection rackets, ponzi schemes, chopshops, and gun/weapon racketing, sure its the prohibition era but really!? These type of businesses played a big role as well.The only bug I've come across is one of my mobsters literally taking 10-15 secs to fire their gun which would take like 1 second with any other of my mobsters i use, it ain't that annoying but you can't help but think HAS THE GAME CRASHED?!?! but no it hasn't its just you have to wait 15 secs for this stupid mobster to fire his damn weapon off every single damn time its his go and you make him target someone.To be honest, its not awful but its not a gem like major reviewers made it out to be, I'm enjoying it at the minute, but after about 5 hours i felt like I'd pretty much done everything already. I really think in a few to several months time that the game will be either decent, good or amazing, but until then, just wait until they add more to it because its honestly not worth the £34.99 price tag, its basically a £20 game at its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to say this. Where to start... I fell for the hype on this one. I am a huge fan of anything Paradox publishes because I am a huge fan of there genre of games. I went into this wondering a few things, Why haven't they shown any management and empire ruling gameplay building up to the release. Simple, its very lacking and barley exists. I had half expected this to be like City of gangsters especialy in the management sense and it didn't even come close. The combat is well ok at best. Nothing feels new or original. Trying to make money in this game is a joke and dosen't feel good at all. Your only resource is booze and its boring management concept. Make booze build rackets that use the booze, 3 to be exact. The intro into the game is laughable.... "Welp welcome to sins, here's 3 buildings for you, here's a gun, trigger is right here and safety is over here on this side and yeah have fun, Oh by the way here's a map of all the bosses in your area just waltz right in and shoot them in the face... don't worry no one will care or come looking for you! _childDocuments_.review: I paid £41.99 for the Deluxe Edition of the game and so far I have 31hrs on the clock, so the question is, do I recommend the game? I have to say YES.That said the game for me currently sits at a sold 6/10, which does not seem to be high after spending £41.99, but there is enough to take away from this game that is good. Having read some of the negative reviews, I can't say that I totally agree with their points of view, although there are one or two things that do ring true.The good bits.1: The game feels authentic to the period, the environment feels authentic to the period, so yea well done to the devs in bringing the 1920s to life. Graphics are good and sound too.2: The story starts at the beginning of the notorious lives of the characters such as Al Capone. Some have argued that its boring all the running around and does not feel authentic. well what people fail to realise is that in the 1920s (just watch Boardwalk Empire) people like Al Capone were nobodies, it took years for them to build up their reputations and power. People like Capone did a lot of the grunt work until such time he could get people to do the work for him.3: The game at the moment provide an average challenge and there is some reasonable character development.The bad bits:1: The game is fun, but very repetitive. There does not seem to be a right or wrong way to play the game and as such if you bypass some of the set missions, all you seem to do is go from A to B, raid a building, and then develop the establishment. And that's it. That's £41.99 right there.2: There are annoying quirks in the game that really serve no purpose, like when gangsters in your team fall out over who they fall in love with. Its a distraction that's not required, but I can probably get into it more if the Devs developed it a bit better such as being able to create multiple teams and you have to choose carefully who to put in that group.3: I have yet to come across any game killing bugs but I have found some annoying mechanics that need to be fixed, such as anomolies of enemy henchmen stuck in walls, or were their movement matrix fails so they can't exit a room. With the first issue I left the area and re-entered, the problem seemed to fix itself. The second issue fixed itself but I had to wait a few mins, I went to make myself a brew, when I came back it was fixed.Although I have ticked yes to recommending the game, in its current state, its not good value for money. I would suggest waiting till it goes on sale and getting it, hopefully by that point we might see a DLC and some mechanics improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: Hello. I recently acquired Empire of Sin on the Steam sale. I bought the base game not the bundle. I am glad I did because I felt there was a lot wrong with the game... To a point where I think $22 is not worth it. I was expecting better from Paradox. Here is a small list of what I think is wrong:An independent launcher should not be present for a Steam game. If it is on Steam, it should launch from there so you can take advantage of Proton or the other services Steam hasThe recruitment process of the game makes this game RNG heavy. When you have the same recruitment page as all other players, it makes it so that it doesn't reward you for using tactics. Meaning if I chose to not follow a main quest for notoriety simply because I am not ready to go to war, then I shouldn't be punished for that. Punished in the sense it gives the other players time to get ahead of me on notoriety while I upgradeI think the recruitment page is overall an interesting idea.. Relationships, connections and the likes are very unique but it should of been treated as a hero type of thing. Not a "main force". I should be allowed to recruit custom gangsters kind of like how I recruit soldiers in other games like XcomI could keep going but in short.. I can't recommend this game. If people want to buy it as a game to sink time in to, then by all means do it IF it is on sale for $10. This game is not worth more than that in my opinion

_childDocuments_.review: UPD: Having put more time in it, the game at least got easy enough to steamroll the enemy gangs. I'll finish this one playthrough eventually, and move on.But it is still mundane and repetitive. - Grinding combat until you discover the boss hideout, capture, repeat for the entire city. No shortcuts there.- Abandon hopes of building a full-size all-Italian or all-Irish gang. It's a side effect of VERY diverse, but small roster of unique gangsters. And many of them hate each other, or are hired by another gang, further limiting your options. At 8 gangsters, it looks more like a jRPG party or a troupe of Cosplayers, than a gang of made men from Sicily.- Feels like interior has less than 10 maps total. And most are not fun, either.So I still would not recommend.There are better tactical games out there, and better Mafia-themed games.---Clunky, repetitive, lacking polish.But the worst, it's just not fun. Combat is boring, it's just same gang of thugs, over and over. Empire management is boring - it does not feel rewarding.Any randomized events, odds and rolls that ever happen, seem to only bring misery and bad things. I tried to like the game, but it fights back and makes sure I'm not having any fun there.How you can take a classic power fantasy, with existing videogame examples to look up to (Gangsters 1/2, Mafia 1-3 etc), and mess it up this much, is a mystery.Don't bother, save your lifetime for something more worthy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was on my wishlist for a long time and I almost counted the hours today before the release. But now I will try to get a refund.These are the reasons why I will try to get a refund;-Cutscenes; seems and sounds like a cheap indie game, would have been much better with stylized static drawings and a better voice acting. I obviously didn't see much of it in 70smthg minutes I played but it didn't promise much.-No campaign; although it seems like all the bosses have their own stories the game doesn't play like a campaign but a sandbox. I would have loved a storyteller telling the stories of these important mafia bosses.-No Auto-Resolve on defense fights! Why? No one would want to pass hours controlling basic characters defending a speakeasy. -Although I didn't experience it fully, the business side seemed a bit light.-And the biggest no no no THE AI; I have been in fight a few times after the tutorial, and to tell it gently, the AI is bad. On most of the fights the computer chose to move between 2 positions back and forth, without attacking. I was playing on normal difficulty and was expecting a minimum of challenge from the beginning. This game is marketed as a turn-based strategy game, if you failed the AI sorry but you failed the game.These are good though;-Music; sounded good.-City/Neighborhood/Map Graphics; looks pretty although it feels like char animations requires a little more work.-Item and char speciality mechanics seemed good, shame that the negatives are so strong.Notes;I didn't get to meet the game destroying bugs but people who played it longer seems to suffer from them.Although the game is maybe 4/10 I wouldn't have try to refund it if you had put one feature in the game; multiplayer. When I quit the game and started to think if I was going to ask for a refund or not there is one question that made me decide; after I finish the game once what will make me play it again? Well the answer seemed to be "nothing" for me. Why would I play the same neighborhoods, the same city and the same fights again and again? It seemed to be that it was going to be a one time finish and uninstall. I think whoever took the decision that both the multi and the campaign were not needed, at the same time, should play more games.As a gamer who played and loved both Gangsters and Omerta I hope they will fix the negatives and add much more to make me buy it again, then I would happily edit this review and change it to positive. For now, this is disappointing.

_childDocuments_.review: In it's current state, this is definitely a do not buy from me. Let me clarify that statement:First, the positives: the passion that was clearly put into this projects seeps out of every pore. It is a true love letter to the era. There are also some very good ideas like the sitdowns, the gang wars etc.Now for the negatives: it gets extremely repetitive, even after the short while I've been playing the game. Getting drawn into combat, especially during gang wars with redshirt guards, is a chore. The missions add a good sense of urgency and structure, but of the seven I have tried to complete, 2 of them have a gamebreaking glitch at the end which means they can't be finished.There are at least two animations that fail to load, one of them being an early-game skill allowing one of your henchmen to take revenge upon receiving melee damage, one of them entering buildings (size 2 buildings, most of the time).I hold out hope that the glitches will be fixed and the combat will be enhanced, but at this time, it feels like a game in very early access. What a pity.

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly a very bad game. Its not easy saying what is wrong with this game because about everything is. The game massively lacks content and flavour of all sorts. Even with the first DLC there are like 4 kinds of buissnesses you can build each can have 4 repeated upgrades. That is the entire Economy of an empire builder... With some statistics it makes the impression of a complex System but it is really straightforward and boring. The city of Chicago has like 10 different buildings so if you have seen one neighbourhood you have seen them all. The game is so bad the entire time i playerd it i have been anxious a pop up would tell me i ran out of energy and need to purchase some in an online store. Seriously i have played better "free" games.Some Gangsters look fine but the political correct distribution of races and genders will make your gang look less like a mob and more like a depicion of one in a silly 80´s Musical. The implementation of relationships between Gangsters is as half baked as the rest of the game being boring and bringing obscure effects like having alot of gay gangsters in your mob. The more i think about it it feels like some sort of political statement. Now what is the game then you ask? Well you have your weird looking gang and capture the same looking buildings over and over again to establish the same 3-4 buissnesses. The fights are always the same because the enemys are always the same and the locations are always the same. Interactions with Characters can be boiled down to: go somewhere, talk to someone, kill someone. The worts part of the game is the storytelling. I dont think i have ever played a game that does it worse. There are boring storys accompanied by bad animations that are repeated every 4 seconds and often have nothing to do with the content of the conversation. I really struggle in understanding how anyone in romeo games and paradox was okay with this :DThe game is a front or a concept. Made to be expanded into a real game with dlcs. That has become a normal paradox strategy but as a consequenz they publish unfinished games like this.The game is often compared to Omerta: City of Gangsters and that makes sense because both games have much in common. The sad truth being that a ten year old mediocore game that has been critizised for lack of content has way more content and is much more polished, immersive and has better storytelling than this new paradox. I payed "only" ten bucks for the game and still dont think it is worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: I know, I have 300+ hours on a game I don't recommend. It's cause I'm a sucker for steam achievements.PROS: - I like the combat itself. I think I may just like tactical RPGs, though, since I haven't played a lot of them. - The period details are nice, they definitely did their research on the storefronts, weapons, etc (not so much on the factions, as half of them are fictional). - The equipment system is very RPG-like and works well.- The boss fights are satisfying, fun, and challenging. CONS: oh boy, I've thought about these for a while. Essentially, Empire of Sin doesn't know what it wants to be. - It seems to be leaning towards a tactical RPG since that's what the combat is, but once you play you realize you have to employ 4X tactics to actually win. Maybe 4X is a bit inaccurate, since you can't really "expand" peacefully; somebody has to die, but when it's thug rackets that don't pose any actual danger to you it might as well be. The problem with this isn't that it's mixing genres, but combining lots of combat with how granular squad-based combat is makes the game extremely tedious. You're going to be taking over about 30 or so thug rackets, none of them are going to be remotely challenging, and it's going to be boring once you've seen the handful of building designs they have for each size racket, if not before.- The 4X nature of the gameplay gets worse when you realize there's only one way to win: the equivalent of a domination victory. Even the original Civilization in '91 let you win the space race if you didn't want to nuke everyone. Sure, you can buy factions out if you're protecting them, but this leads to a lot of thumb-twiddling while you save up the cash and have to do dumb stuff to get them to like you. You also won't be considered enough of a threat to get protection from until you've killed at least three bosses in vanilla (I only had to kill one when I played with Make It Count).- So in other words, you are going to be fighting a lot of barbarians (thugs) and other factions. And it's going to get boring. Really boring, really fast. I get that any kind of strategy game is going to have a degree of repetition when you've got multiple factions to play as, and that's not necessarily an issue. But in Empire of Sin there's really no reason I should be fighting this many battles where no one is taking damage, it's just a waste of time. I believe they foresaw this and added the "auto-battle" feature, which would be nice if it didn't massively underrate how likely you are to win a fight and required saving before/after to avoid a game over.- The game plays out almost exactly the same every time. Sure, the bosses have different abilities that are mostly pointless (we'll get to that later), but what you're doing is the same every time. You're killing a few bosses (or all of them), you're buying the Golden Tommy Gun, you're hiring Norah Quinn because you have to have a doctor, etc. Nothing changes but the layout of the neighborhoods, which may be of minor tactical importance but is ultimately nbd. Let's look at some other strategy games: In Civilization and EU4 (New World), you can randomize the map so resources and strategic points are different every time. You can't do this in Crusader Kings, but the game world is so vast that playing in sub-Saharan Africa is completely different from playing in the Mediterranean which is completely different from playing in Siberia. There's also different eras you can start in. Something like this is BADLY needed to preserve replay value.- The side quests are way, way, way too easy. Talk to your crew member, kill a guy in a completely pointless, one-sided battle (sometimes you don't even have to do this), collect a few thousand bucks. Probably takes less than five minutes even if you read all the dialogue. The only ones that are a little better are the boss quest lines, which are both more challenging and more interesting story-wise, but there's still maybe on the level of a randomly generated Skyrim fetch-quest.- There are probably dozens of mechanics that just do. not. matter. at. all. I almost feel bad saying this because I'm sure some poor Irishmxn or two probably spent months coding these but here's a short list: honor, hunkering down, brothels, BOP raids, Chicago PD raids, alcohol storage, morale, loyalty, gangster roles, neighborhood lieutenants, the gangster rating system, any of the gangsters that cost more than $3-4K to hire (about half), gangsters hating/loving each other, the "worried" status effect, and temporary business arrangements. A lot of these things feel sophisticated until you realize they don't matter at all; it almost feels like the team that came up with them had a different vision entirely and thought this was more of a sandbox strategy than what it was.Conclusion: not worth it in its current state. There's definitely some solid potential here, and I think a fun sequel could be made if they ditched all the higher-level strategy (neighborhoods, weekly income, rackets, precincts) focused on boss fights and actually doing something challenging in the quests, but I think you'd also have to ditch the whole multiple playable factions thing. Make it more like GTA or Mafia but a tactical RPG, and make it absolutely nothing like Civ.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, so for anyone who is a sucker for Mafia themed games in any format, its just downright sort of a dream come true. You manage a specific crew with an amazing wide range of bosses to choose at starting point. _childDocuments_.review: I do not feel that this game deserves most of its negative reviews...Yes it feels a little bit janky at times, and the combat camera can at times be an annoyance, but this is a pretty solid grand strategy/turn based RPG.The only real negatives I have stumbled across so far are small UI glitches and occasional awkward camera issues.As for the gameplay, i have found the combat to be up to par with XCOM....it doesn't set the world on fire or bring anything new to the genre, but it is solid and enjoyable, however I do feel that the different classes do not really feel unique enough and there could be tweaks to make each class stand out, but as a counter to that, every character in the game has a set of personality traits (similar to crusader kings) which does add a lot of strategic elements to building a team of mobsters that can not only bash skulls but also run your businesses whilst managing to get along with each other...its a nice touch and, for me at least, it made the world feel a lot more alive. If you are looking at this game because you were a fan of the old Omerta or Gangsters series, just buy it, this game will scratch the itch for a modern Organised crime empire building sim!I will conclude by saying that, if you are looking for the "next gen" groundbreaking, game changing turn based strategy game...this isn't it, but if you are like me, an old dude whos into strategy games looking to kill a few hours while scratching the nostalgia itch (this game feels like the Gangsters 3 we never got) then theres easily 20-40 hours of fun to be had here before it gets old.

_childDocuments_.review: Very much a game that tries to do way to much at once, and as such it is unquestionably shallow. The management part lacks any strategy, and mostly consists of waiting for money, buying a few upgrades and then more waiting. The turn-based combat is the now standard XCOM-style. The RPG-elements and relationship-system also feels undercooked The AI barely seems to do anything and is rarely a threat. So with all that why the hell do i like this game. Well, the theme does alot of heavy-lifting, they nail the feel and look perfectly, everything about this has that wonderfully cliche gangster-film feel. And while the combat is basic, i still did enjoy it. It has a ton of weapons and they are fun to use. I also enjoyed recruiting and trying out the diffrent gangsters you can hire, and that does have a real feeling of them getting more powerful. I do like the fact that it does actually have a story, each mobster you can play as i think has a diffrent main one. It's just kinda cool for a game like this to have that, and does add alongside the opening conversiation a more character and story-focused approach which games like this never really does. Yeah, there aren't really that many of those missions and it doesn't really matter that much to the overall gameplay, but it still is pretty cool. I can't fault the game for it's ambition, even if it falls short. I hope that with time and expansions they are able to really add depth and fix the problems it has. Because i did enjoy what i have played. For now i recommend this for people who really love the gangster setting and enjoy fun, but basic, XCOM-like turn-based combat.
