_childDocuments_.review: Ambitious game developed to late-2000s standards that did not live up to the marketing or pre-release reviews.  First Steam refund.  Hoping the dev team or modders make it live up to its potential, but not worth full price for a game that is at best early release.The game has basic elements for an interesting concept, but execution misses the mark across the board.  The business management component is simplistic with little variation across rackets.  The turn-based combat is poorly developed, with AI behavior, combat mechanics, and one-line comments from characters that make it a frustrating process to click through.  The neighborhood/empire component of the game is also simplistic, with nothing required other than brute force expansion across the city, ignoring the largely unnecessary boss meetings that simply result in a classic boss fight with no opportunity for diplomacy or other outcomes long-term.  Character development, moral decision-making, and skill progression are also limited compared to modern standards.There are also numerous bugs still in place, particularly in the combat interface, including characters not moving to squares, AI characters abruptly shifting clothing when animations are stitched together, and a clunky interface that borders on defective.Some of the graphics are very well designed and developed, including building interiors and the city street view (although, again, several bugs observed for building interiors).  The dialogue and animations are also stylized to match what you might have seen in the late 2000s, which was off-putting given modern design standards.
_childDocuments_.name: Empire of Sin

_childDocuments_.review: An ambitious game that doesn't excel at anything it tries.For what it’s worth, Empire of Sin really embraces the Roaring ‘20s style, showing off Chicago streets that are initially fun to navigate and a roaring soundtrack of jazz mixed with some more modern pieces. The writing and weird cast of characters, both fictional and fictionalized alike, have a lot of charm. There's even really delightfully over-the-top voice acting for nearly every character, littered with standout performances like gangster boss Frankie Donovan, aged Western sharpshooter Grover Monks, or the hammy duo performance of a gambling bookie and a button man. (They're in love.) The charm wore off a lot quicker than I’d have liked, though.Fights quickly become rote due to mindlessly repetitive maps and poor, buggy combat AI.The challenge here is to run a complex illegal empire while also balancing the chaotic personalities of criminals both in your gang and outside it. Like many of Empire of Sin’s ideas, it's a brilliant concept: You have to keep a lot of violent people with poor impulse control both happy and alive in turn-based tactical RPG combat in the vein of XCOM. You direct your chosen gang boss around the city, doing missions with bits of flavorful dialogue to enjoy and controlling a crew of hired guns in battles against other gangsters. Those might be fights with rival gangs, groups of independent thugs, and very occasionally even the police or the Bureau of Prohibition's agents. Interacting with the characters of the '20s is where Empire of Sin shines, but the fights you're doing to earn those stories quickly become rote due to mindlessly repetitive maps and poor, buggy combat AI.The tactical battles are built on good bones: Gangsters have a to-hit stat, hit points, and you find weapons with varied stats. Basic combat numbers are pretty granular, with health in the 50-150 range, so a thug might take two to four pistol shots to go down. It's just enough randomness to make the weapon stats and upgraded rarities really matter. There's also a half-or-full-cover system you'll recognize from every tactics game since 2012, well implemented here, with angle of attack and distance mattering depending on what weapon you're using: a shotgun does best from within two tiles, a rifle from seven or more, and a submachine gun is happiest somewhere in the middle. There are balance issues, like one-hit kills from sniper rifles and surprise damage from unavoidable dynamite attacks, but there's fun at the tactical core.It's the maps that really kill the combat. They're pretty, at least, thanks to locations like dim speakeasy interiors and luxurious gambling houses, but they’re chokepointed, poorly laid out, and offer very little tactical variety. Most fights end up revolving around a single corner or doorway as you set up a kill zone and watch enemies swarm into it – and many of the maps only have one or two of those chokepoints to fight over. The terrain is static as well: there’s no destruction, and no interesting ways for characters to get around. It's an honest crime that you can't vault over the bar counters into cover like in every gangster movie ever.The dominance of some strategies over others undermines what should otherwise be a wide-open sandbox game.All of that goes on as you build up your network of illegal breweries, casinos, speakeasies, and brothels to get rich on the management side. To do that you have to  stay out of the police force's sight and try to one-up rival bosses in both business and territory control. The way it’s all executed, though, makes it little more than surface-level fun with no balance or depth: Alcohol out, money in, but you never make enough money to really feel like Scarface because upgrades and gang members are absurdly expensive. Of course, that rarely matters because the dominance of some strategies over others undermines what should otherwise be a wide-open sandbox game.You can, in theory, play many ways, such as diplomatically catering to allies and placating opponents as you build up your empire, but those are never the best idea. Why would you wait for your cash reserves to build – and I mean literally wait, since the management layer is real-time and has a single speed – in order to wage a full-scale gang war when you can just directly attack enemies and take everything they have in one fight?Part of the issue with the strategy layer is that while the city is nice to look at, getting your characters to where you need them to be becomes a major chore. Your characters control in real time on the streets, and you order them around like units in an RTS until combat starts. They're slow to react, slow to move, and frustratingly bad at pathfinding, requiring constant hand-holding. This makes attacking enemies building-by-building frustrating and boring: You move from place to place and attack, fight the same three or four guards on the same three or four maps, then take over the building.While the city is nice to look at, getting your characters where they need to be becomes a major chore.While you’re doing this, enemy crews are attacking your rackets, subjecting you to an endless stream of boring defensive matchups between your hopelessly outgunned guards and big swarms of enemies. You, meanwhile, can really only afford to field one effective combat team. I have no idea where the other side gets their large bands of roving, well-armed, disposable muscle, but you're limited to a few precious and expensive gangsters.Fights might be more fun if you could afford more gangsters and more security upgrades for your rackets, but you really can't. The economics are so poorly balanced that amassing any large amount of cash is really only possible once you’ve already built a huge empire of rackets, and even then you burn through it buying just a handful of incremental upgrades. Think spending $3,000 dollars for… +7% on a building's income of $500. Woohoo, only 85 in-game weeks before I break even! That's just a mere... hour and a half of my life. (One game speed, remember?)The interface, by the way, is truly terrible for managing a huge empire. You can own dozens of businesses but there's no single screen to manage them all at once. Instead, you get to sort through them neighborhood-by-neighborhood on screens that also have all your competitors' businesses. To upgrade them, you must open a new screen for each business, one at a time. I eventually resorted to simply building new businesses, ignoring all upgrades, and hoping that quantity had a quality all its own. Thankfully, that worked.Just drive over to the other boss' house and shoot them in the face.So how do you win a gang war, then? How do you get rich? Simple: You just drive over to the other boss' house and shoot them in the face. See, your units can teleport around the city by "driving" instantly to any discovered place. So you just declare war, teleport to the front door of the enemy's safehouse, and assault it, bypassing any defense their armies of soldiers would have provided. Defeating the enemy boss in their HQ means you instantly take over all their buildings: Congratulations, your empire has now doubled in size and you got a really overpowered bit of unique gear to boot.It's a shame, because the glimmers of a great game are here. Take your crew: The network of thugs-for-hire in your black book all have morale and loyalty scores, their own specific background traits, personalities, and relationships to the other gangsters. They get mad or worried when their lover is injured, and they won't shoot a friend on the other side of a fight. They can gain new relationships in play, become alcoholics, or get syphilis. Gangsters can die permanently, too, which is fun to avoid once someone becomes integral to your crew. Push them far enough and they'll leave your gang. But even with all of that promise, Empire of Sin’s many faults have pushed me too far.

_childDocuments_.review: Honest Opinion. I purchased this game hoping it would be somewhat similar to the 1998 classic 'Gangsters Organized Crime', which I still play. I am a big fan of Paradox also, so I always pay attention to games released by Paradox and have done so for over ten years. My first pre-game play impression was that of a somewhat in depth game with interesting mechanics however the biggest turn off was the turn based combat, which I was never a fan of. If anything, at one point i decided I wasn't going to buy this game due to the turn based mechanics but my love of gangsters organised crime, the whole genre in general and my faith that paradox always releases games with great play ability and depth, made me purchase this game. To help give an honest and structured opinion I will address each of the main points below. 1) Turn based combatTo me surprise, I enjoyed the turn based combat and felt it went fluently. Some of those up close attacks that would keep missing at points is a little annoying. If the target is right in front of you, but behind a table, you should at least be hitting them with some damage each time. My only complaint is that it gets very repetitive , especially when your constantly having turn based battles. Also, your basic goons seem to have the worse aim ever, so when you go through the motions of using your 2-3 guards against an attack of 4-5, you will miss A LOT and it feels like the outcome is a forgone conclusion. The enemy can be right in front of you, and in a lot of cases you won't even nip them with the spray of a sawn off... surly it can be tweeked to work better, but it makes grunt battles very tedious. This has opened my mind to other turn based combat games so that's also a plus!2) Strategy & management I hate to admit it, but the strategy and management aspect is lacking greatly. Sure, you find yourself planning on building more breweries if needed, choosing which one to upgrade so you can produce swill / whiskey or the needed beverage. Maybe your drawing too much heat, or your expecting a war and beef up security at interfaces so you can fight off attacks. But you will find yourself running through the motions making very basic decisions when it comes to management. Other than trading goods, diplomacy is shallow, feels pointless, and the game ends up turning into a free for all of repeating  turn based battles. After taking 2-3 rackets the enemy wants to give up and there's no personality behind the AI, all other factions simply send squads to your rackets. It would have been much better if each gang had their own methods or preferences when going to war. It seems the other real difference is the enemies colour and location. The types of rackets you can have are extremely limited also. A speakeasy, a brewery, a casino and a brothel....... why not take a leaf from Omerta (the only leaf anyone should take from that god awful game) and add other options such as protection rackets, food joints, have celebrity areas, politicians and so on, it would have added so much more to the game in terms of strategy, rpg elements, missions and so on.Another thing, it is also very easy to attack an enemy safe house, kill the leader and take all of their rackets. I was a half hour into one game and asked the North side mob to wack the head of the Genna family. It was promptly done and the genna empire suddenly become the northside mob. This is a bad idea... There should be a mechanic whereby the rackets in that part of the city get taken over, but the gang remains in a weakened state in the hands of the underboss. I have also played on easy and normal, it seems each gang expands very slowly and their income is always quite low. The AI needs to be a bit more aggressive and active. I am going to try it on hard next, but there was not change between easy and normal so I'm doubtful it will make much of a difference. I found I was easily able to accumalate thousands, build up my gang and just attack a bunch of rackets if the other gangs became annoying. That's all the other gangs are in this game, irritating....As your mob gets larger, the game feels like its about turning the map into whatever color your faction is. There is very little you can do to feel like a rich, powerful mob boss. NO flashy cars, flashy homes you can customize, no clothing for characters, no personality or image you can give to your gang to make them stand out... it just feels pointless...it doesn't even feel like there is any challenge... you just rinse and repeat 1) Ransack vacant properties 2) trade the weapons for cash 3) build up rackets 4) Do it again and again. 5) If a gang attacks, then attack some of their rackets forcing them to surrender. Again and again and again..... Yes, there are missions, but they fall far far short of what is needed. If your looking for a minimum of CK3 immersion then forget about it. Why would I still recommend this game you may wonder?1) I love the genre2) There's a complete lack of any game like this (other than gangsters organised crime).3) It looks good and is somewhat enjoyable. 4) While its hugely lacking in areas, its still okay... 5) I had a good time playing this. But more than anything, the more i played this game and the more i enjoyed it, the greater i felt it could have been so much better. I believe tweeks can fix some of the above (and a few bugs i came across), and I hope some DLC's come out which add more possibilities , abilities, depth, options and mission branches. As well as the chance to reflect your progress within the game in a cool manner which will motivate you. That's my honest opinion....

_childDocuments_.review: It's a mess, but at heart it's a fun tactical X-Comish game with a management layer thrown on top.Let's start with the "mess" part, just in case you're looking for a reason to skip it:* The UI lacks a lot of standard quality-of-life features, like being able to select people by clicking on their names, being able to jump to a location by clicking on its direction icon, being able to center the map on your character* The combat UI is *finicky* about selecting enemies to hit, and you'll often set up a long combo attack hitting multiple people and then accidentally click on scenery while trying to click on a target and have it reset so you have to set it all up again* The gangsters you can build into a team are the exact same ones, game to game, so there's not as much replayability here as you'd like* The voice acting is mixed (some voice actors are so focused on the accent that they bring no emotion to the line itself, for example) and the character animations are poor* Some of the game is written in a dark, serious, gritty, Godfather-esque tone, and some of it is written in a zany "it's just a game, why so serious" tone and obviously they don't work together well* There's a huge selection of randomized-effect weapons ala Borderlands included to power up your people, but there's not an easy way to compare their stats against each other - you have to mouse over, scroll to the specific stat, and then go to the other weapon, mouse over, and scroll to the specific statBut if you can get past that, there's some good tactical and management fun to be had here. Not sure that without fixing some of these things that it's really worth the full $40, though.

_childDocuments_.review: I dont write many reviews but I felt obligated in this case. This game does not deserve the hate that it gets. Its probably the best modern empire building gangster game. Its an X-com (combat) -Jagged Alliance (crew management) - 4X sort of hybrid game. I can see why it gets negative reviews but it depends how you look at it. If you are on the fence (like I was) then maybe consider;PRO- You WILL have fun. Its got the X factor. - You WILL get your monies worth. There are 100's of hours in here. - The devs are interested in building on the game. - Its got a good prohibition era feel about it. - Chicago is nice and big and I like how it is split into smaller zones.- The gangsters all have nice flair about them. - The CIV style sit downs with rival gangsters give personality to your rivals. CON- Yeah its buggy. But not deal breaking. Some animations are a bit off. - The AI is prone to idiocy at times. - It can get grindy. But there are always events or wars going on. - Sometimes during a war there is seems to be unnecessary combat. For example if someone attacks your racket you take over the your guards and fight it out. You can skip it but you really shouldnt - unless you want to lose your business. BOTTOM LINE Yes this game has a few problems. Going by all the negative reviews, I thought it was going to be hot garbage...I was quite happy when it wasnt. Its one of those games that you can zone out while playing. There are so many rackets to take over that it will satisfy the compulsive. This is the sort of game that will get better with time. I suggest if you are looking for a nice bit of turn-based...this will do nicely.

_childDocuments_.review: I will begin saying that I do enjoy this game, but I would not recommend buying for its current cost.  The game is entertaining but should not have been released in its current state.  It is difficult to invest in any playthrough because of how many bugs are present.  For a game with Paradox's name on it, the economy is not very in depth.  It's a simple balance of brothels, breweries, speakeasies, and casinos.  Each building has four or five components to upgrade, up to a maximum of five times.  The more they're upgraded, the better they perform. Combat is fun.  It's your typical XCOM turn-based combat with some special abilities between characters.  But it's sloppy.  Animations will either not play or be super jank.  Other bugs that make the game difficult to see through is dialogue prompts locking on screen, preventing you from continuing play.  Sometimes quest rewards don't trigger even though you perform the action and see the progress icon.  Other tooltips that inform you of the condition of a neighborhood sometimes get stuck on repeat, constantly flashing at you and not really changing anything that it should related to that part of the game.This game can certainly be fun, and shooting up a street mobster style with a Tommy-gun just activates certain neurons that nothing else can. But wait for a sale until these bugs are fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: Score 6 (could also be a NO)Played as the Genna family and finished the game (took about 5 years).Positives- Atmosphere is really excellent. The streets are alive with people, transport and their sounds. The inside of the buildings look also great although there are not many variations.- Nice story line(s) for the main characters. Voice overs are ok.- The turn based fighting and the customization of your mob members.Neutral- Business simulation has not a lot of depth in it. There is no downside in over building and over producing. Prices are always stable. So a lot of building will result in a runaway winner.- Communication between families is too random and illogical. e.g the moment they want to ask for your protection, while you haven't the means to do so. Or every minor faction asking for extra products all at the same time.- UX good use some improvement: better viewing of the entire map, direct jump to characters, zoom in to cursor and more. Negatives-  Pathing during fights and on the map view. On the map view this will result being stuck. In fights wrong choices are being made by the AI, e.g. cover is more valued than distance, which could result in having some cover but they stop next to you.- When at war you don't have a good enough overview to handle threats. Attacks just start out of the blue, which are mostly boring fights.- Most of the time you are not the boss of the family. The balance between running the family and doing footwork is wrong. Most of the game you get the feeling you play as an associate or a made man instead of handling the strategic part of running the family.About the last point. My personal preference would be to add more roleplaying elements with a growth in character in stead of in rackets. You can have to first half of the game working up the ranks and doing a lot of footwork and in the later part you direct the footwork. In the first half you learn the trade of one of the four rackets to have specialization bonuses later in the game. In the first half of the game interaction with the police is more prevalent. In the later game politics will be more important. Almost all elements are available in the game to some extent.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a third recommendation option besides "yes" or "no".  Something like "eventually" or "when it gets fixed", whatever.I am optimistic that this game will eventually be a "Yes" recommendation for me.  It's fun.  I'm still playing it.  Will probably play it more in the future.  The design is fine.  The mechanics are fine.  It's not the greatest game ever, but it's enjoyable for what it is.But right now, I just can't give it an unqualified "Yes".  Reason:  the BUGS.  A playthrough starts pretty smooth, but the longer you play, the more bugs start appearing.  Weapon & attack animations stop working.  Stats change on items (mainly protective clothing).  Worst of all, eventually, buildings become un-attackable.  On my most recent playthrough, it reached the point where I had to reload a save every time I wanted to attack another building.  I soldiered on for a while because I like the game and I'd grown somewhat attached to the characters in my crew, but finally just had to abandon before completing.This sort of thing happens a lot in the gaming industry these days, and it's rather sad.  But it seems particularly rampant in Empire of Sin.(EDIT)  I came back to this game after over a year.  Pro:  There's been some improvements.  The game doesn't seem quite as buggy as before.  One major update apparently added a "precinct" system which I like.  That said, multiple quests are still poorly designed and non-completeable.  I've tried two different bosses this time around, was not able to continue their main questline; it simply "failed" without explanation (both of them).  Apparently these questlines are on some sort of timer, which the quest information doesn't tell you.  There is also some sort of politics quest which is explicitly on a timer, and one of the conditions is to upgrade a building. This upgrade takes longer than the quest timer, so this quest is also non-completeable.  So the game *has* improved since release, and is more enjoyable.  But I'm rather annoyed at these poorly-designed quests, and having "failed" quests littering the quest log.I'm not changing my non-recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: Listen, I really wanna keep liking this game but.. It get's pretty painfully boring after awhile. If the game is on a big sale try it out but, I wouldn't even say it's worth the 40 bucks.The game at first is shiny, distracts you, you wanna do stuff and get into it. After a few hours you'll realize the tutorial was basically the entire game. Sure there are other mechanics to it, but it's shocking shallow for a game with Paradox' fingers in it. Resource management is trivial, and while I'm a sucker for Xcom like combat it's also incredibly easy to abuse with the trading system(Sell a bunch of junk weapons for one End game weapon and you're set for that character, hell you're set for half the game). Dealing with other gangsters and wars becomes easy when you realize you could just... not fight anyone and just other ♥♥♥♥♥♥ booze in every situation. Not to mention the developers make a lot of empty promises, which you can tell they care but, they're investing too much on hype and teasing. People lost interest. Fast. I really wanted to like this game, and I do but.. overall it's not as much of a time consumer as you'd think and if you're a fan of tough strategy games, be it Xcoms or the usually Paradox resource style. It's not tough at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Empire of Sin stands as a testament to what could have been, yet feels somewhat neglected by both its developers and the modding community. It's reminiscent of a game left to languish, yearning for the vibrant support seen in the old Paradox model – where DLCs introduced game-changing features and multiplayer support flourished.Imagine a DLC offering the ability to craft custom characters, coupled with a deeper economic system, all bundled with new characters and win conditions. Perhaps even expanding the game's scope to include different cities like Montreal or New York would have breathed new life into the experience.It's disappointing to note that ambitious mods, such as the proposed integration of the Vampire: The Masquerade IP, now seem abandoned. Despite this, Empire of Sin remains enjoyable, albeit not quite justifying its full price in its current state. However, on sale, it may be worth considering, in hopes that future expansions will capitalse on its promising foundation and enrich the overall experience.

_childDocuments_.review: 2 main reasons why this is not the game quality we expected from this game.1. Terrible AI. Will run from cover using all their actionpoints (not shooting, just running) and leave the cover to end their turn in the middle of a room.2. Bad UI design. The management tabs are a hassle since they dont do what you expect them to do. No simple menus for upgrading your rackets. The tab named "gangster promotion screen" is not where you promote your gangsters, it is a place to admire your maffia tree, with no interactions possible at all. No button to find your gangsters in the world, dubble-clicking on a character portrait is usually standard for centering the camera on that character in the world, but nope does nothing. These small things shows that the game simply is not tested enough by actual players, probably only the developer themselves and it is very easy to be blind for these things when you are the developer of the game and know how to find everything.I am still enjoying this game because I have paid for it (I feel forced to enjoying it because otherway the money is lost for nothing). I even bought the deluxe version because I love XCOM-series and thought this would be a "modern" take on it, and there is some cool stuff, like the abilities of the bosses etc. But would I recommend it to someone else, definately not. Keep your money and buy XCOM 2 instead, it's sadly a better game in every game mechanic. This is the 2020-version of XCOM, I'm hoping Paradox gives them time to make this right by bringing it to new light next year.

_childDocuments_.review: Frankly, I was waiting for this Dec 1 date to finally try the game. The teaser was so nice and atmospheric. I love the topic of Great Depression, so everything was set to meet the game.And this drove me even to a bigger disappointment when actually playing the game.There are still so many nice things:- Many game with different features- Atmospheric dialogues exposing the personalities- The items and weapons are done so much with love and preciseness- Tons of statistics and dashboards to overview your empireBut it's gameplay and its routine that are annoying:- The other fractions are continuously calling you for a sitdown with short lead-time and long dialogues which unfortunately lead to a super minor outcome, like casino maintenance decreased by 4% (!) Well, maybe you can ignore them and reject the sitdowns.? Yes, you can. But the other fraction will immediately decrease their perception of you. At the end you find yourself running continuously from sitdown to sitdown.- The other fractions can ask you to supply 0.234587154896423 (!) items of alcohol.- The alcohol is shown by somewhat similar icons but in dialogues it called by name so you need to remember what is what. Same with fractions: you are in business agreement with "orange fraction". Then another fraction comes and invites you to fight vs Ragen. Will you agree? What if orange fraction is Ragen? This you cannot check during the dialogue, you need to answer blindly.- The alcohol preferences are strange: a city (all together!) switches to some type of alcohol ignoring the price ups and downs. How can it be?! This drives you to switch production at your breweries every time it happens or try to produce a lot to the stock to simply avoid this irritative action in the game.- You can rename the people but not your casinos! (you can only give a name at acquisition) Strange, right? This makes very difficult to remember the buildings. Later, when one of the buildings is being attacked you can only imagine where it was.- Battle targeting system is very unsustainable. You sometimes need many attempts to finally confirm the aim.- Battle locations are always the same.- Weapon system is misbalanced. Any moment you can find a super gun that will solve easily any battle. Why to buy them from the black market for x10 price then?- A relation overview is strongly needed. You can only review it fraction by fraction for the time being.So for the time being I would wait to buy the game. Though I really see a great work done and hope the developers can add some more interesting features to the game. I wish they do.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, I have to agree: something went terribly wrong with this game. Similar to fellow players, I went from excited and pre-order to utter disappointment and astonishment.Paradox - how could you let this happen? To us and to your reputation.Maybe there is still hope to fix this mess. Here are some points that might help.1. Bring more differentiation to the bosses in terms of gameplay To be fair, their special combat abilities create some kind of uniqueness. But the empire traits/bonuses like a +20% here and a -5% there have no tangible influence whatsoever.2. Reduce the businesses and make them actually meaningful Ten neighbourhoods with somewhere around 30 rackets each is way too much. Soon, you own so many business that you don’t care about any of them. They are just numbers on an Excel list.3. Enable visible and meaninful customization for the businesses/rackets You basically level up the same 4 traits for every business you have. There is no meaningful decision or differentiation. And the gap between earnings and costs for one upgrade look rather steep, especially if you consider that all you get is the next segment on a donut chart being colored.4. Enable us to understand the economy system It seems there are different aspects to be considered, but it doesn’t become clear what they actually mean and how I should react to them. Also, how come I got two speakeasy places with different upgrade levels, but both making the same profit. 5, Make combat meaningful Right now, it feels just like grinding. Too many of them, too similar. Most annoying is when somebody attacks one of your places you don’t care about and you have to defend it in a combat that looks and feels just like the other 10 fights you had before.6. Bring strategy to combat Once you enter and attack a place, your team and your enemies are placed quite randomly and mixed together. Taking cover is often useless because everything is so cramped and mixed up that there’s always someone near whose at your flank or back. Then, you start shooting, often missing even though the enemy is like 2 meters right in front of you. It’s just total chaos.These are just the most disappointing findings after 3 hours of gameplay - likely, there are other aspect that need an overhaul. This went really so wrong - still can't believe it.After all, the mechanics EoS is using are existing ideas that have been established successfully in other games already. There’s no need for innovation. The answers are out there. All that needs to be done is transferring them into a different setting. Go for it and bring us the game we want.

_childDocuments_.review: Empire of Sin is a combination of a grand campaign game such as Total War, and turn based strategy like XCOM. It might sound like a lot of game, but the amount of each element is not enough to present the player with a satisfying amount of content. That does not mean however that the amount of content here is not well put together, as little as it might be. Curator page:+Music+Ambiance+Empire upgradeability+Great gameplay combinations-Missions are lacklustre-Amount of content is lacklustre-Combat is uninspiring-Action points in combat are unintuitive-No fast forward-Bugs that should not be present over a year laterIn a nutshell, you are a mobster in Chicago trying to take over the city by claiming various neighbourhoods for yourself. You must eliminate enemy presence by defeating them in their rackets, and finally revealing their safehouse. Once you take over the safehouse, you have successfully eliminated the enemy presence. Just like in the Total War games, you have the option of razing, taking over, looting, or demolishing the property you have successfully attacked. Unlike TW however,  while in the "grand campaign" mode, there are no turns or limitations of how you move. All factions, including yours, are free to walk about the world map and perform various actions. The lack of a fast forward option however means you will find yourself sitting and waiting for the day cycle to progress in order to receive your weekly funds and progress through claiming the city. You do have the option of destroying the enemy rackets you attack, but that would mean you are robbing yourself of higher potential earnings. The weakest part of the game by far is the combat. Once combat is initiated, all units on the map move randomly, mostly towards cover. A lot of the time however those moves prove to be nonsensical and makes the player question the intelligence of the AI. On lower difficulties the combat does not present the player with a lot of challenge, but the enemies do get progressively tougher to face.What is questionable at best, is the AI behaviour during combat. Instead of seeking to progressively move towards the player strategically, they instead tend to rush the player and put themselves in less than favourable situations for themselves. I have a lot of fun upgrading my rackets to higher levels and see how they change in appearance in their interior design, looking more upper class and attracting more customers which in turn brings in more money. But I do not enjoy waiting for that to happen. Without a skip to a certain day feature, I am stuck simply wandering around looking for things to do while the day cycle completes.  Having a combat that is not quite as intuitive as a game such as Xcom really adds to the injury's insult.With all that having been said, I do enjoy the game, for now. I am not certain how I will about it after I take over a second neighbourhood, as it really seems like it is the same thing over and over again. If you prefer a challenge, I would suggest you up the difficulty from the easiest. Enemy AI is not very keen on attacking your rackets or waging war at you in the easiest level.Overall, this is a tough one. What the developers have put together here is certainly of high quality. From the audio design, to the layout of the city, to the attention to detail with the factions and the character creation. The upgradeability of your rackets, and also the visual changes that come with every upgrade are very respectable for sure. All these nice things come very close to being overshadowed by the boring and unintuitive combat, and the lack of content to be presented to the player overall. And also, the lack of a MUCH needed fast forward option. More detail can be found in the video.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow... Just, wow. Even if next week a certain game about cybernetically enhanced punks turned out a lemon, this would still be the disappointment of the game year. I really expected to like this one even though at 30 mins in it was glaringly obvious that it wasn't perfect and quite what was promised, but it just kept on going downhill from there.The pond is wide but oh so shallow. On the surface, it seems like there's a lot to do. Management, diplomacy, economy, missions, conversations, character development. Most of it ends up being horribly unwieldy and/or completely pointless and you just run around in the city from one overly easy (on difficulty 4/5), buggy, clunky and just way too simplistic a fight to the next. Went to war with a faction. After some one-sided bloody slaughter, they offered me a laughable 1000 $ to stop attacking. I scoffed and ran over their HQ with my 3 starting characters and took over the whole empire instead. Why bother waiting for money to slowly trickle in so you can purchase an arbitrary +5 % upgrade for one of your buildings at a time? That's enough of this sin of a game for me, thanks. Wish I'd stopped trying to give it a chance before the 2 hr mark.I also wonder why so many say that the visuals are beautiful. As a representation of its setting sure, maybe, but from a purely technical point of view, its quite the ugly duckling. Struggling to find positives. The musical score is good.Consider buying maybe at a considerably lower price point or after a lot of extra work and polish.

An expansive world inhabited by quirky, charming and sometimes deadly inhabitants of the afterlife, the Underworld includes Aftervale, a happy hub where the dead come to spend eternity. Instead of seeking gold or other treasure, they kidnap Aftervale's elder skeleton Elzedon and then go after the magic that kindles the spirits of the dead: the Blue Flame. Visually rich art style. Fight the Humans before they plunder your un-life! Extensive check point system of Blue Flames to practice your jumps!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun, but it's about double the price than it should be for what you get. Lacking achievements and I completed the game in just under 4 hours. Despite some other misleading reviews, this is nowhere near like a roguelike game. It's also not a Metroidvania game. It's a platforming game through and through.The story is relatively generic and predictable. There are a few "challenging" platforming sections, but given the proximity of the save points to those sections, they shouldn't take any experienced gamer that long at all.Avoid unless on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Skelattack

_childDocuments_.review: Skelattack is a game I had a lot of fun with. The art and animation convey a wonderful world full of vibrant characters each with unique personalities. This is only backed up by its music. Skelattack has a jazzy(?) soundtrack that is full of charm.The gameplay, while difficult, is VERY fun once you master it, though I think the development team went a little overboard with the instadeath spikes. This is balanced out by the generous amount of checkpoints, but it doesn't stop you from getting angry when you lose some of your money when you die and THEN lose even more trying to get it back. It makes the first two non-tutorial sections (which I feel had the largest amount of instadeath spikes) immensely frustrating. Keep on trucking. I PROMISE it gets better.I guess the other criticism I would have is that it's a bit short. I have 7 hours on it, but the average playtime seems to be around 4 hours. I wonder what that says about my skill level. I wouldn't blame you for waiting on a sale before buying.As for the story...the game doesn't take itself very seriously. It's not one of those story-driven games. Most of the dialogue consists of banter between the two main characters, but it's mostly entertaining and makes you grow fond of the main duo. This gets you invested in the story when it decides to stop fooling around and get serious towards the end.All in all, I think this game is worth playing. It's difficult and a bit short, but also gorgeous and really fun once you get the hang of it. I give this game a solid 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: While this game is quality over quantity, something i respect, the price is truly ridiculous. I'm already on the final boss with 2.7 hours.  It also tried to be hard, but isn't and ends up spamming obstacles in some places. Look at cuphead, hollow knight, and celeste. Cuphead is deserving of it's price, it's around 25 hours long (depending on how good you are) AND hand drawn. It was also made by a small studio, both hollow knight and celeste are 70-100 hours if you do all their content, all for the price of around 15-20. This game is extremely short and not worth the money. It's 10 dollars at best, and that's pushing it, avoid unless on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has gotten a lot of hours from me; I originally got it for Switch before grabbing it on PC to try some speedruns.The freedom of movement is my favorite thing about the game, as you can often choose your path through a level, even avoiding what the devs intended entirely. For example there are sections where you need to be carried through deadly areas by your bat friend (with spikes covering the floors, walls and ceiling), but many of those sections can be done on foot if you're careful. The tutorial is very short, which could be good or bad. The game doesn't spoonfeed you all of your movement tech, but play around with it and you'll be rewarded for your effort.The story is very heartfelt and takes some turns that I don't think I've seen before. The dialogue can often run long, but if you're into a bit of reading it's fine. Otherwise just hold the button to skip past.The game is often brutally difficult, but there are lots of checkpoints so you never really lose progress, and your many deaths actually play into the story of dungeon life. There's some replayability, but it's mostly gonna be in the form of speedruns or other self-imposed challenges outside the limitations of the game. The game is only a few hours long, worth it for the low price.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game. I really do. The art is excellent, the sound is good (Not really any obnoxious noises), some of the mechanics are neat, the music is pretty decent, the story is kinda fun, and the characters are endearing enough. This should be a no brainer for a great combination to make an excellent game. Why is this review negative then? The absolute garbage movement and handling."Sounds like a dumb thing to give a negative review on", well buckle up fabricated strawman I made up, because I'll tell you why on this very thing alone this game gets a negative review:There are two jumping systems. One is your normal jump and double tap on the same button for a double jump... Cool beans. Standard stuff.The other jumping system is the wall jump which is used by the direction pad only. Meaning you have to press the direction against the wall to "slide" or stay on the wall and then move the opposite direction on the joystick or keyboard to perform a successful wall jump. It's a bunch of going back and forth on the keyboard or joystick to wall jump. The "normal" jump mechanic can actually hinder you if you try to use it during wall jumping. On top of that you cannot just jump straight across since the wall jump gives you a fixed jump height upwards when performing it, meaning you'll likely die many times by trying to use the regular jump out of a wall jump in very tight areas that require you to use both. It is beyond frustrating to control and it is one of the main core mechanics of the game. You will be doing a LOT of it. This is more or less "artificial" difficulty that spawns from this...Whoever's crackpot idea it was for this dogsh!t mechanic that is so counter intuitive it's ridiculous for wall jumping, deserves to be flogged in the streets with a barbed d!ildo by some douche in gimp suit for some added humiliation.Before any Stans come to defend this with a "git gud scub" mindset, I beat the stupid game and got all of the secret goodies in under 135 deaths (Most all of them caused by this sh!t jump mechanic). If there were achievements you'd be able to see that. Another poor decision. This isn't some mechanic that's just hated because it's "new" and I'm scared of change. I'm not your boomer parents. This is genuinely frustrating and you never really "get used to it". Sometimes while using the regular jump mechanic and trying to control the direction of that, you'll be too close to a wall and end up wall jumping and the fixed upward jump height will kill you. If there weren't so many "insta-death if you touch it" things in the game it wouldn't be so bad, but there's a lot of them. If you can get over this and don't think it'll bug you, go for it, buy it. Me personally? I despise a singular mechanic that's core to the game so much I can't, in good conscience, give this game a positive review. I wish it weren't like this because it's a pretty good game otherwise.EDIT: I have now beaten the game twice and under 80 deaths for another 100% completion run. I can safely say that I still stand by what I said. The jumping alone makes this game a negative review from me despite all the other praises I have for it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is right in between recommend/don't recommend. Its a platformer that has a cool old-timey aesthetic in a similar vein to cuphead. The problem is in the design decisions. While the jumping is precise, the wall jumping/climbing aspect is horrible. You cant press jump to jump off a wall, instead for some reason you have to hold your directional button away fromt the wall and it jumps. This is unintuitive and finnicky, and add in the fact that the wall jump makes you jump not just across but up and you constantly bump into hazards around you because it isn't precise. Add in the fact that wall climbing involved pressing jump and spamming direction toward and away to go up a single wall. This isn't ever explained and once again is super unintuitive and finnicky. The next main part is nearly every single platforming section is fill with all instant death traps. And not traps on the ground, but lining the air, the walls, etc. Combine this with the shoddy hitboxes/detection and you constantly die. This isn't much of a problem since there are generous checkpoints, but you lose money when you die. For some reason that money stays where your body dies which is usually right inside of the instant kill trap, leading to you dying a bunch of times trying to get it and usually just giving up since its almost un-gettable. Why they wouldn't put the loot in a place you could ACTUALLY GET TO is beyond me. Then theres the story which is pretty bare bones and uninteresting. The combat is meh because all you can do is just spam 1 attack with no evasion besides jumping away which is slow and delayed especially since they don't signpost attacks. This mean you usually just spam attack and tank the damage. On the opposite side the boss fights are great and well designed. The game is pretty short, although you can get lost because theres no waypoints and it can be regularly confusing where you're supposed to go or what you're supposed to do. Theres a few powers you get but besides that there isn't much to the game. You could do worse but there are a lot of games that do combat and platforming better than this, even if the visual design is pretty cool. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Skelattack is an action platformer with a unique retro art style. With that said, the generous checkpoints and upgrade system helps prevent any of the flaws from getting in the way of the game's fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I almost quit the game within the first hour due to how they handle wall jumping and the sheer number of insta-death spikes; but once I got a handle of the controls it really didn't get in the way too much.  One really annoying aspect of the game is that if you die on spikes you will lose some game currency that you can recollect if you make it back to that spot before dying, similar to Shovel Knight. The annoying issue here is that the dropped currency will be sitting practically on what killed you making it impossible to pick back up.  Overall it doesn't necessarily matter because upgrades don't impact gameplay much; but it was really annoying.Overall, I'd recommend if you can pick it up on discount.  There's just not enough content for 20 dollars; but what is here is enjoyable if your in the mood for a moderately challenging platformer that isn't all that frustrating due to the frequent checkpoints.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: 8/10If you like Metroidvania's then you'll like this game. I'd best describe it as a cross between Shovel Knight and Hollow Knight. You're given a vast world to explore and platform your way though along with enemies.Positives: The formula is implemented well, and has all of the supporting characteristics we like to see in these titles (e.g., world building and art direction).Negatives: The biggest negative is the price. It's not too bad, especially when on sale, but with just a bit more polish on the mechanics it could justify that price tag. The other notable flaw is the fine tuning on some of the platforming and recovery. For the most part, the platforming feels pretty responsive, and the reattempt cycle is relatively short. The major issue I have with it is that it uses Shovel Knight rules, where you drop money when you die. Not so bad, you can always pick it up again, but it's so hard to earn the money in the first place that I find it deterred me from exploring out of fear that I'd lose all of my money. Lastly, I feel that there should have been more health and mana recovery throughout the map, but that's less important if the reattempt economy gets fixed..

_childDocuments_.review: A Konami game in 2020!?Skelattack is an example of a game that I liked, but didn't love, yet I would still recommend it (if you are buying on a sale). I LOVE hand drawn graphics, and will buy just about any game that has that style of graphics. Skelattack is a charming 2D platformer, with some Metroidvania-lite elements. It suffers from some stiff combat and wall-climbing mechanics, and some of the animations are hit-and-miss (some look absolutely gorgeous, others look a bit rough). The biggest issue is simply that the game is too short, and too easy. I finished the entire thing in a little over three hours, and there isn't a new-game+ or even achievements to encourage playing again. Still, if you can buy it on sale, it's fun and charming, but don't expect it to be something like Hollow Knight.

_childDocuments_.review: Great art for the creatures and skeletons, but everything else here is amateur to downright bad.The game runs at a locked 35FPS, with seemingly no way to change it, as the developers confirmed this was done as an artistic choice because the game is hand drawn. Which I don't know if I fully buy that response considering plenty of other hand drawn games have higher framerates and still maintained their artistic integrity. Like what part of background scenery blurring/ghosting as you move was like...a positive artistic choice???This is NOT a roguelike game by any means of the word. The "review" quote from Red Bull Games on this game's store is not from a review, but an interview with the developer. The interview clarifies that the roguelike element is "The enemies themselves are the random element, because although there are a set number of enemy types, how you send them to their doom will change. Take a knight, for example, perhaps you hit him twice to beat him, but next time he takes four hits."  I don't know about you, but roguelike to me isn't 'sometimes this enemy takes less or more hits, randomly' or is what I'd call good game design. Games teach players rules of the game so they can play it.The combat is simplistic to the point of being boring. Enemies telegraph their attacks slowly, and feel lifeless, so you end up sidestepping the same attack over and over and swiping at them until they die. Also, sometimes they block. It's like The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's combat, in that it is also bad in the same ways.This is also not a Metroidvania, but more so a rather linear platformer with Metroidvania-like maps. You meet characters, talk for way too long, then get sent on a fetch quest which unlocks the path forward (at least in the first level, and from what I could see skimming a 3 1/2 hour play through on YouTube). The platforming functions, but things like wall jumping just feels clunky compared to other games. Here you jump to stick to and slide down the wall and simply press left and right to jump off the wall, no jump button needed which feels like a swing and a miss. You can essentially climb walls by doing this then air jumping, then sticking to the wall again, but it just doesn't feel good, especially after having played so many platforming bangers that get it right.I feel bad being so harsh, to be honest. I realize this was made by a solo developer, and honestly the art is fantastic, and the soundtrack is fitting cartoony Halloween vibes. I think with more time in the oven, play testing, and an overhaul of the AI, combat, movement, and allowing players to unlock the framerate (unless the engine requires the framerate be tied to the animations, in which case RIP) I could see this being a pretty good little game. Like, I'd play a remaster should one ever exist, but I'd encourage the dev to make something new and fresh, or at the very least make art for other games because it really is great.

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say about this game that hasn't already been posted by other people. Is it expensive for what you get? Yes - they definately didn't pick the right price point for this game, wait and get it onsale. Is the wall-jump mechanic really how people say it is? Yes - you wall jump, not by pressing the jump button, but by moving the analog stick in the direction away from the wall you are currently on. It is a weird way to do a wall jump, but you do get used it it throughout the game. Do they have Steam Achievements? No - they do not have Steam Achievements which contribute to why it feels incomplete. Is it like they took the time to develop this game, and then at the last minute, rushed to put it out without thinking about some of these details (proper price point, gameplay mechanics, achievements/extras). In the end, I know I am sounding critical of the game, but I have to say that I did enjoy it very much. It is a challenging platformer with some basic combat elements and in those respects, it was an enjoyable game. The graphics are cool as it looks like a hand-drawn cartoon. Aside from the weird wall-jumping, the controls feel responsive. I used an Xbox1 controller and it worked well and I completed the game in about 5 hours. In the end, I have recommended this game because I enjoyed it and feel like these developers should get another shot, as long as they can address some of these issues in their next project.

_childDocuments_.review: The main complaints I've seen of this game (wall-jumping being a single directional press without the jump button and the game FPS cap being roughly 35 or so) were annoying at first, but about ten minutes later I accepted it as part of the game and rarely had any issues with them.  The platforming felt pretty satisfying once I adapted to it.  You can scale walls by just alternating left and right rather quickly which kind of made some sections a bit too easy.  There are a slightly absurd amount of instant deaths here and there and it makes it very difficult to retrieve the gems you leave after you die.  However, I left behind quite a few gems and still had enough left over to buy all the upgrades required as killing every enemy you see and doing a bit of exploring gives more than enough gems.  You also respawn quickly when you die so I never really felt like I was being punished.My biggest complaint is that every single boss fight could be won just by attacking and healing with no dodging required.  The final fight  but it was still an easy fight with minimal dodging.  I got nearly 4 hours of gameplay and I think I found everything there was to find, so I don't feel any urge to return.  I bought this game while it was on sale and I would recommend others do that as well.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game only if you know what to expect.  The game took me only 5 hours in a casual run (and another reviewer 4 hours).  The game costs $20.  I compare that other games at that price range that last a lot longer and have great replay value.  This game doesn't have much replay value after it's done, except for lore I guess.  The platforming is solid.  All the reviews and YouTube videos about how it is solid are true.  I do REALLY wish I could turn off the auto jumping off of walls by pressing the other direction.  I got used to it mostly, but I can count many times where I would've survived if I could turn that off and instead use the jump button (like in the flash game N).  It is much easier and faster to repeatedly tap the jump button than to constantly rock the dpad or analog stick back and forth.  Another gripe I had was the sword attack because it seemed a little slow.  But instead of it feeling like the Castlevania NES whip where you had to be methodical and think ahead, it just felt like it should've been faster.  I will also note that the music was fun and neat but sometimes was too repetitive or inappropriate for the mood.  The story was okay, maybe somewhat predictable, but I still found myself disinterested and skipping dialogue boxes that lasted too long because I just wanted to play the game.  Other than those problems, I don't have much to complain about.  Also, this might just be a new game problem, but I cannot figure out how to transfer my saves from one computer to another.  There is no Steam Cloud for this game right now.  I started the game on my laptop and I wanted to finish it on my desktop, but I couldn't figure out how to move saves around.  Google is empty when I searched.  I had to finish on my laptop.Personally I wish I didn't buy this game because it was so short and quite expensive.  But, if you know what you are getting, you won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Play Skelattack and save the Underworld in this  action platformer. Being dead is not so bad when you have the Underworld to live in. An expansive world inhabited by quirky, charming and sometimes deadly inhabitants of the afterlife, the Underworld includes Aftervale, a happy hub where the dead come to spend eternity. You are Skully, member of the newly deceased and just when you start to get the hang of being dead, your newfound home and friends are attacked by humans. Instead of seeking gold or other treasure, they kidnap Aftervale's elder skeleton Elzedon and then go after the magic that kindles the spirits of the dead: the Blue Flame. Together with your best bat friend Imber, you have to jump, slash, and flap your way though the Underworld and stop the human threat.

name: Psychonauts 2
detailed_description: Simplified Chinese This game only supports Simplified Chinese interface and subtitles for users on Windows operating system. Photosensitivity Notice Certain visual content, including flashing lights or patterns, may affect photosensitive players and viewers. Please visit for additional information. About the Game Razputin “Raz” Aquato, trained acrobat and powerful young psychic, has realized his lifelong dream of joining the international psychic espionage organization known as the Psychonauts! But these psychic super spies are in trouble. Their leader hasn't been the same since he was rescued from a kidnapping, and what's worse, there's a mole hiding in headquarters. Combining quirky missions and mysterious conspiracies, Psychonauts 2 is a platform-adventure game with cinematic style and tons of customizable psychic powers. Psychonauts 2 serves up danger, excitement and laughs in equal measure as players guide Raz on a journey through the minds of friends and foes on a quest to defeat a murderous psychic villain. Experience an imaginative, cinematic story that mixes humor and intrigue, brought to you by legendary game designer Tim Schafer (Grim Fandango, Brütal Legend, Broken Age). Explore unique environments using Raz’s ability to dive into people’s brains to battle their inner demons, unlock hidden memories, and resolve their emotional baggage. Leap acrobatically through the air, traversing tightropes and trapezes in a varied, challenging, and joyful platforming experience. Wield a powerful array of psychic powers to blast, burn and levitate things, or even slow down time itself to solve environmental puzzles and battle strange enemies.

_childDocuments_.review: This is, hands down, my new favorite game ever made. It is expertly crafted and made with an utterly absurd amount of love and care. Each and every moment of playing this game felt like a gift I waited a decade to receive with every moment being entirely worth it. Never before have I played a game that made me feel like this game does. To start this review, I'll go over changes from the original:Raz is much snappier to control and almost all of the awkwardness with his Levitation ball, pole/swing bar interaction, and camera issues have been eradicated in this game. Whereas the original Psychonauts controls as you'd expect (a semi-early 3D platformer), this one absolutely crushes it in the control department. The only changes I can think of from the original I truly dislike are Raz's double jump and the Levitation float.Double jump has been drastically changed to be more in line with platformer expectations whereas the original had a floaty double jump that had Raz dip down before rising back up. It was bouncier, and felt somewhat defining to that title. The Levitation float has been eviscerated. No longer can you float forever nor fly with the speedrun exploit. While I expected the exploit to be removed (sadly) I did not anticipate the forever float being taken away as well.Figments are easier to grab, are more visible, and are less hidden on average. Collectibles in this game tend to not be hidden behind stationary objects but rather out in the open, behind a puzzle, or near some sort of interactive object. This makes finding everything relatively easy for those scouring about and makes full completion more of a time-based endeavor rather than one based on scrutiny/attention to detail. The Scavenger Hunt items do not require the quick puzzle-solving of the originals and feel like a bit of a downgrade on that front. Almost all of these are either out in the open or behind an ability gate and is slightly disappointing as someone who was a fan of the original's mini puzzles. The new collectibles are top notch.New enemies! Psychonauts had an EXTREME lack in enemy diversity which has been remedied almost entirely here. Each enemy functions differently and is many times more interesting than just the standard Censors. Many function essentially as mini-bosses if there's enough support surrounding them though are easy to beat on their own. It's well worth experimenting with abilities on them as the devs made sure to include multiple ways to fight and interact simultaneously.Level-ups function much differently. Rather than periodically getting enhancements to powers or new powers altogether periodically Psychonauts 2 gives four upgrades per ability you can buy with your levels. Powers unlock at set intervals in the story now and are not level-related. There are some powers missing from Psychonauts but there was a distinct effort to make the new ones feel just as, if not more interesting and even an attempt to combine older powers together in the new title.Now, onto the new stuff:The game leaves an incredibly strong first impression with its stylized opening that does a serviceable job of catching new players up and a nostalgia trip for existing fans. I'm going to be entirely honest here. I cried. I cried during the opening cinematic because I was **actually playing Psychonauts 2** and I couldn't believe this game was real. The score at the beginning (and throughout) is fantastic and is littered with leitmotifs and themes from the first game that pull me back into the world with ease and elicit old memories. It felt like coming back to an old friend anew. I can't think of any other way to describe it.Each and every level has a wonderful theming and is delightful to play... barring one. But, I will fully admit that one level is more than likely going to be enjoyable for the majority of players and it just didn't tickle my fancy. The mental issues presented are still very welcome choices even when the first Psychonauts took the lion's share of the big, well-known illnesses. The levels twist and turn on themselves with frequent use of impossible architecture, world-bending pathing, and straight up impossible changes to an incredibly impressive degree. I remember circling around in one of the late game levels and immediately realizing I was curling in on myself and I started giggling like an absolute idiot. It was bliss.The new characters are overall very well-designed aside from one of the interns whose name I consistently have to look up as he's just that forgettable. The writing is pretty great all things considered. I actually had to look up if Erik Wolpaw worked on this title as well and apparently he did but was not credited for it so I'm not entirely sure how much of the game he contributed to. In any case, if your game's writing makes me look up if one of the main Portal 2 writers was involved you've done something very, very right.The story is sublime and dives into the heart of the beginning of it all. I won't say more so as to remain spoiler free but if you pay attention and collect the Memory Vaults you will walk away with a pretty comprehensive history of the Psychonauts, their world, and how they fit into it. All of which is ridiculously satisfying for someone who had questions about all that subject matter after/during the first game. I, again, cried multiple times throughout the story both due to plot points and from joy that I was **STILL** playing the sequel I had waited so long for.Visually the game is certainly up to snuff. It's not groundbreaking or anything but it doesn't need to be. The world design, concepts, and how the devs play with the idea of being inside a mind was always the main draw to Psychonauts and it's here in spades. It's beautiful to look at with many areas/enemies having detailed flourishes. I should clarify that when I say "groundbreaking" I mean "this title's visuals will shake the industry or entirely revitalize a style of graphics". That word comes with revolutionary standards that Psychonauts 2 doesn't meet, even though it still excels.All in all, Psychonauts 2 is an enthralling experience through and through. Nothing quite measures up to it and it is wholly unique to the point of standing in its own field. I sincerely hope the success and popularity of this game motivates Double Fine to add to this franchise every 4-5 years rather than leaving us all high and dry for so long.I highly recommend it to literally anybody. There is not a soul on this planet who should not play this game.The original is a cult classic, and this one is a modern masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright. I know a lot of folks are very happy with how this game turned out, but I feel it's not as good as the first. That said, still give it roughly a 6.5/10. If you enjoyed the first one, you'll likely have fun here.Negative opinion:That said, there are a few differences. Brains tend to be more about going straight from point A to point B, with either a bit of platforming, people talking to you as you walk down something, or combat breaks that you Burn your way through as quick as you can against enemies that feel like they take too long. There is nothing like the Asylum levels from the first game, and most 'puzzles' are just more basic platforming. Except for one level, but that one is more about time management than a thinking puzzle.Have a few personal gripes too. Certain puzzle elements are introduced for a couple of levels then never used again. A particular power is withheld until it can not be used in any of the 'real world' areas as you are locked into a zone, and you will need to beat the game to go back an use it.  A lot of characters have names in the main hub, but do little more than have different lines from the unnamed characters that share the space. Combat seems to take too long with spongy foes that make Raz feel extremely weak. Boss fights are mostly just story, without any elements to make them stand out mechanics-wise from each other(throw thing at enemy with telekinesis, hit until reset). The story has too many characters that it acts like are important but uses them sparingly, and felt kind of off. Levitation got nerfed and serves as little more than a way to run on flat surfaces slightly faster, while things like the confusion bombs, stealth, and shield are simply gone without a replacement. Instead, you get one slightly interesting new skill, and two that only really get used in regards to moving forwards in a level that accepts no other solution. Raz won't shut up that he's able to do task X and should go on to do task X in the real world. Over-world feels a bit empty at times. The boss fights are extremely straightforward and are nowhere near as interesting as the originals. Heck, my main complaint could be that, other than the storyline, Psychonauts 2 feels like a simpler version of the first one.Positive opinion:First off, you may notice several of my negative opinions are comparing the original game to this one. The game is still fun, I just did not find it as good as the first, and do not want people to assume that it ever hits similar beats as the first in terms of level design. I kept waiting for a fight similar to those with the luchadores in the first, or bosses with different mechanics like the Critic vs the Lungfish and so on. If you go into this expecting *gameplay* that is on par with the first, you will be disappointed. Writing-wise, it does alright. Background conversations are funny, interactions between Raz and anyone who is not an intern tends to be amusing, and the story was pretty darn interesting. Music is good, platforming is responsive, and it is nice to get an ending for the first's cliffhanger. There are a lot of new mental enemies to fight, each with a better way to take them out, though they are usually just lumped together with a small horde of other foes that come in waves.I had fun. The story gave me some emotions, and at no point did I ever really feel stuck or bored for long.Is it worth $60? I kind of regret paying that amount for it, but it's definitely worth getting if on sale, or if you really enjoyed the writing and general platforming of the first.Edit: Yeah, after going back to play the first one a bit, this game is one sixth the value at six times the cost. If you want a Psychonauts game, play the first. Only get this one if it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game very much. The story line is absolutely the best part of the game with twists and turns that even if you can predict some of them somehow find a way to subvert the expectation through the ride along the way. The Game play has many great elements and features that are modern and feel like a proper sequel. The introductions of new thematic enemies is really well received, and is a fun premise. Now this is the part where I mention the games biggest flaws. The gameplay is good, but I'd honestly say I prefer the first game much more. Several mechanics are introduced in interesting ways only to seemingly be ineffective or outright meaningless later on. Along the same line, some advancements seem to have no flavor to them asides from being #Different. Several Abilities were scrapped from the first game to this one as well, including the ability to use and cycle through items. Dialogue feels almost entirely optional, the fighting takes a lot longer and doesn't seem as effective, and you're left constantly switching abilities in the middle of battle or tanking damage.The Supporting Cast is very Very flat, but tries very hard to convince you they're interesting and memorable to the point I'd literally entirely forgotten one of them existed until the showed up at the end of the game. The Map layout is REALLY GOOD, but the collectible placement leaves much to be desired being very difficult to find without google, but absolutely not impossible. Speaking of Collectibles! The Pins, and Other things available through the Otto-matic (the in-game shop) are entirely flavor text. They don't feel like something you'd have any real desire to try out unless you're like me and 100% the game, Even then I only bought them all for the achievement, ESPECIALLY THE CAMERA! Which has no other use than to take screenshots!Everything being said, I would play this game through again. The Main characters are absolutely lively, relatable, and so very interesting (though perhaps suffering a little sequelitis). The Story is top notch. The Art is true to the original, and I had fun playing and Streaming this game.

_childDocuments_.review: What a delightful game. A+ all around.I LOVED the original Psychonauts game, and I actually replayed it right before moving on to this one. This game has the same creative flair, the same whimsy and cheek as the first--but my goodness it is so clean and crisp and intuitive and expansive too!! Hats off to you, Unreal Engine 4 & Double Fine.It's not too difficult to 100%, either, especially compared to the first one. I found myself only looking up 1-5 missing objects per level. Someone more stubborn than me, with more free time, could 100% it without a guide.While the last level of the first Psychonauts drove me insane (it needed way more checkpoints), I don't really have similar complaints about the sequel. It was a little annoying, at first, that I couldn't gather all the collectibles until *after* beating the game, but I changed my mind after I got there. I like how you can run around and talk to everyone when it's over, like reading the epilogue of a novel.Here's to Psychonauts 3!

_childDocuments_.review: A great return to a more classic era of gaming.I'm a big fan of older-styled 3D platformers and collectathons, so having a game like this in recent years was a breath of fresh air. And as someone who also recently played the original Psychonauts for my first time, playing a sequel to a game I quickly fell in love with just made the experience better.Overall, I can say with certainty that Psychonauts 2 really improves upon the aspects of platforming, and more useful Psychic abilities overall. Both of which could be hit-or-miss in the original game. Reworks to powers like Telekinesis and Pyrokinesis were a godsend, and the new powers like Mental Connection and Time Bubble were really neat additions, in the process replacing somewhat useless abilities like Invisibility and Confusion that were present in the original Psychonauts.As far as content goes, Psychonauts 2 also has more than the original Psychonauts. The hub areas in combination may be just as large as the combination of Whispering Rock and Thorny Towers in the original Psychonauts, but the areas in 2 feel much more diverse, and have more engagement when it comes to platforming, and using various powers to navigate.As for the mind levels themselves, Psychonauts 2 also has more than the original. Perhaps even double what the original had. However, this is one aspect that kinda a hit-or-miss aspect to the game for me. Some levels I absolutely loved, due to their concept, level design, use of platforming, or narrative. (Levels like Hollis' Hot Streak and Cassie's Collection being highlights for me.)While others I just couldn't get myself to like as much. Be it level layout, visual theme, or narrative. Overall, I felt like the original Psychonauts was better in its level consistency than the second, but Psychonauts 2 has some really big highlights, with some...average entries sprinkled in.Another aspect I think I like about the original Psychonauts more is the story overall. Don't get me wrong; Psychonauts 2 has some really good highlights here and there, and even some fun twists. Call it nostalgia, but there's just something I like better about the original Psychonauts' story. I think the aspect of the Thorny Towers Asylum had a big part in that. Especially with how different and varied the mind levels in that section could be. While in Psychonauts 2 most of the mind levels felt...connected? I guess? More like it was multiple viewpoints of the same plotline, instead of something unique and varied with each level. ...But that could just be my personal opinion.As for some other random notes, I kinda miss the item system the original Psychonauts game had, feeling like it was a sort of callback to the developers' original roots with adventure games at the time. However, Psychonauts 2 still has great writing just like the first game, and the addition of choosing responses to dialogue is a really nice addition to character engagement as well. (Also, I absolutely love Raz's facial animations to many of the responses he gets to the questions they ask. Props to the animation team.)In summary: Psychonauts 2 is definitely a worthy sequel to the cult classic original. And while there were some aspects I wasn't a big fan of in 2, the pros severly outweighed the cons to me, and that's a win in my book.
