_childDocuments_.review: I was a bit skeptical when I heard risk of rain was going 3D, but this game has proven how very wrong I was.  The combat feels fluid and fair, and the devs took verticality into account as an actual mechanic, and a nice world.  Overall, there are only 2 real problems I have with the game right now:1) Only 1 character on startup for a multiplayer game is risky.  Having at least 2 means that players can look at eachother and think "wow, he's better than me at X, but at least I do Y. We both do our own thing."  While I expect this to resolve itself over time, as the average unlock number rises, it's still a bit rough starting out.2) Navigation in the world can be awkward.  While I don't expect a full minimap with pointers to everywhere you want to go, it takes much longer in this game to explore an area than it did in the first game.  Since the timers are still relatively similar, this means that if it takes a while to find the teleporter, it can be much more punishing in the first game.  I'd like if teleporters had a space ray that grew as the level progressed, becoming easier and easier to see.  That way, it sets a soft limit on how long the player can go without finding it, while still keeping that element of luck/skill in tracking it down early.  Additionally, boxes should be a bit easier to see.  This could either be through making the colors pop a bit more, or even just letting pings be permanent, so you can always see them through walls.  Overall, I've been having a lot of fun with this game, and really look forward to where it goes in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: In case you are reading the current reviews and deciding if you should purchase the new DLC then let this be a median as to why the reviews are mixed. To start, the base game and Survivors of the Void DLC are amazing. Absolutely worth the purchase. The Survivors of the Void adds new item mechanics and characters that make the game fundamentally play different, however you can't really say the same about the Seekers of the Storm. The main reason the DLC is getting negative reviews is because of the lack of polish it seems to have. The latest update introduced a TON of bugs that make the game feel more "clunky" than it ever has before. As for the DLC content itself, it's not bad, but it's not spectacular in any way. A lot of people like to blame Gearbox publishing because they have no frontal lobe control, but in reality there are less than three developers working on this game and just a year prior, they released a remaster of their first game. While it's possible Gearbox may have rushed them to release this DLC, one way or another, it's not polished or ready for publishing at all.The new items are "bleh" at most. The new boss is fun, as well as the three new survivors but overall it feels less innovative than Survivors of the Void. Is it worth it? Well yes if you are a die hard fan of Risk of Rain and no if you are just a casual player. Overall the update shouldn't deter you from trying the game out (despite the newly added bugs) and I believe the devs have a lot of work cut out for them; but for now it could be a lot worse than it is and the game is still one of the best Rogue-Likes out there.

As I write this, I am having to scour mod sites for potential, community-driven fixes to the plethora of issues Gearbox's poor conduct, culture, and mismanagement have caused and cannot be trusted to resolve.In a word, practically everything surrounding this update is simply shameful.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting till I got all the achievements to write this review, and well today is the day. Long story short, this game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing. Buy it, get some friends to buy it and you will have a wonderful time. This game is a 10/10 in every category and everyone needs to experience it. But, personally I feel this game isn't deserving of such a short review so here we go.-Gameplay and CharactersThe initial gameplay is just amazing and borderline addicting. It, of course, is a roguelike so you will be trying and dying and trying again but that death is almost never frustrating, especially in the early game. This is because you will be getting item after item, working to unlock everything you can and every run feels like you are making progress even if you didn't get much further than the last run. And the main gameplay elements feel amazing because of the great cast of characters. They all feel unique with their own advantages and disadvantages and the feeling of finally unlocking a new character is unmatched by any other roguelike. In other games, you may unlock another character but many times they just feel like a reskin of the first character with a different weapons but here each character plays so vastly different from one another it is incredible. The cast of characters range from a gunslinging dude in a space suit, to a lizard dog thing that shoots acid at people. Some of my favorites include Mercenary - a samurai who while very tough is just fun to play - Captain - who has an amazing primary shotgun but is bogged down by lack of mobility - and Loader - who is basically spiderman mixed with the prawn suit from subnautica. The best part is that no character feels really bad. Some are worse than others to me but it allows everyone to find someone they enjoy playing and stick with them. Plus they all have more unlockable skins and abilities which makes you want to play them all. -Atmosphere music and GraphicsThe atmosphere in this game is top ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ notch. Each area is distinct with a certain style that is only helped by the amazing score. When I first heard it, I likened it to a mix of celeste and subnautica. An oddly calming and alien blend that I know see and distinctly risk of rain. The music in the final level is downright a masterpiece,  and after playing the first game, I can say that the music is some of my favorite rivaled only by celeste and the doom games. The graphics likewise, are amazing. Compared to the low res pixel art of the first game, the models here looks so damn nice. The characters and items fit perfectly in these truly breathtaking levels. Scorched Acres, Titanic Plains and Sundered Grove are just beautiful and a joy to explore and look at. Then you have the more alien worlds like Gilded Coast and the Bulwark Ambry which give you such a good sense of atmosphere and make me wish I could just teleport there and listen to the soundtrack while reflecting on life as a whole. -Level design The interesting part about this game is that while it is a rogulike the levels aren't completely random. They are always pretty much the same with some areas not being available sometimes with bridges being out or tunnels being blocked. This does wonders to the gameplay because you can become familer with the stages while also having variety from run to run. Plus there is the fact that there are an average of 2 different locals you can visit for each of the 5 stages. This does lead to some flaws with some being better than others but on the whole it is very nice and I hope to see more stages added to each level. As for each level, They are all very good but have a few flaws. Some are much harder to navigate if you character doesn't have any mobility and some are harder to find the teleporter, but on the whole they are all quite good. -Enemies and BossesThe enemies in this game are just great. You have certain enemies like beetles and hermit crabs that pose no threat but on the opposite side of the spectrum you have the most terrifying enemies like parents, greater wisps and elder lemurians who I still have nightmares about to this day. These enemies all spawn in different ratios and certain enemies only spawn on certain levels which adds to the variety and uniqueness of each stage. Having different types of enemies makes the player think but there aren't too many overall types as to overwhelm the player. The extra variety comes in the form of elites which can make even the most trivial enemies forces to be reckoned with. Then there are the bosses which come in 10 forms and spawn as teleporter bosses or as regular enemies in later stages. They are all unique and pose different challenges. There are also more formal bosses like the Alloy Worship Unit, Aurelionite and the Final boss. The first 2 are just reskins of other bosses but the Final boss is something special. I would say he might be the weakest part of the game but that is only because I have only fought him a few times. When the 1.0 update first came out, he was almost impossible on monsoon but now I feel like he is a little more balanced. Again I would have to fight him more to develop a final opinion but as for a final boss, he fits quite well.-DifficultyThe challenge this game poses can be quite daunting at first but I feel like on the whole it is perfect. To start there are 3 difficulties to choose which affect enemies, regen and other factors which lets players choose how they want to play but there is also the time mechanic. The longer you take on a stage the harder the game gets. This means that you have to balance your time between looking for items and beating the stages and progressing. This makes for a great difficulty curve and I would say the only spike in difficulty is on stage 5. It is insanely hard and will be one of the biggest roadblocks in any run. But there is also more choice in difficulty, because you can end the run by beating the final boss or looping which sends you through earlier stages with much much harder enemies. I prefer to loop because it allows for crazier god runs but overall it is amazing to have so much choice.-Fun with friendsBefore I wrap this up I want to touch on how amazing this game is with friends. Most of my playtime was with my friend who had most of the stuff unlocked already and it made the game easier to get into. Now playing with 2 or 3 other people is just great. Failing over and over again is much better with friends, and it works just great here. The only issue is that it is much much harder in multiplayer but I would prefer that to it being a complete cakewalk. -Final ThoughtsOverall this game has been a joy, and though I have most things completed I still want to keep playing. I may try it with mods or might just stick to vanilla and see how good of a run I can get. I would also like to point out artifacts which I am very mixed on. They can make the game hectic and amazing but sometimes command just breaks the game to a point where is gets stale. That is to no ones fault but my own but I can't help but feel like I'm cheating. Hell, I didn't even beat the final boss on monsoon without artifacts till the time I'm writing this review. Anyways, I am extremely excited about the future of this game with more updates and DLC and I hope the next one will be able to rekindle that magic of unlocking a new character for a first time. And if you made down here without buying the game, what is wrong with you?!

_childDocuments_.review: (Not Recommended) I feel like I'm missing something with this game. There is not one thing in this game that makes me want to play it for longer than half an hour. Sure, this is a fine game but I feel like the gameplay is just the same thing that I experienced from the last run that I played. But with all of these positive reviews of this game, I feel like I might be giving this game a rough time, so I'll probably keep playing the game to see if my opinion on it changes. But for now, This game is fine. There are little to no bugs, I can tell that the devs put a TON of work into this. But this game is not for everyone. Even if I'm the only person who doesn't thoroughly enjoy the game. Edit (Not Recommended): I think I have finally cracked the code on why I don't 100% enjoy this game. I don't feel like this is my kind of "Cooperative game." I always feel that when I am playing this game with my friends, It's not usually about the team, it's about the individual players. I also don't generally like games that are based on some sort of luck. I like a uniform game where I can control it, but maybe that's the thrill of this game. Also, I feel like I am the third wheel when I am playing this game. It always seems that I never do enough damage, I can't kill bosses quick enough, but when I see my friends play the game, ON STAGE 4 OR 5 THEY KILL THE BOSS WITHIN 10 SECONDS. LIKE HOW????!?! I can see why this game is so appealing to some audiences, but the randomness and just my utter inability to understand what I am doing wrong makes it impossible for me to enjoy. Edit #2 (Recommended): Ok, I have played 37 more hours since my previous review, and my views on this games have completely flipped. This game is still well-made, but I really want to talk to the importance of learning the game's mechanics and it's items. I got this game because my friends wanted me to play with them, and for the first fifty hours of this game, I really didn't make any effort to learn the game at all. With about four hours of playing by myself, and playing more with my friends, I think that this game is really solid. While I don't think there is much more to say in this review, If you are not enjoying this game and not giving an effort to try to learn the game, I implore you to try to learn the game, its items, and the mechanics of all of your character. Try to learn, and the game will come to you naturally.Edit #3 (Not Recommended): This game was great, now there are a substantial amount of bugs in need of fixing. Do not buy this game until they iron them out.Edit #4 (Recommended): They fixed a good portion of the bugsThis is a 100% biased review and this should not be used as a tipping point on whether or not you should purchase the game. I say try it out (with friends), and if you don't like it, refund it.

_childDocuments_.review: OK, this thing didn't need another positive review since the day one due to the hype, so I didn't recommend it at first, just for the sake of lowering the expectations. Now, for the first time ever, I decided to delete my first review and replace it with a big thumbs up, even though I'm usually too lazy to write something, let alone re-writing.Basically, two things work for me here: diversity and exploration.While you usually have one playable hero and a bunch of items in a typical roguelike, Risk of Rain 2 already has eight characters to provide you with different playstyles (and that's an Early Access!). Moreover, they also got alternative skills to choose from in the latest update, so you have even more options now. Literally everything in the game tries to work towards variety: weapons, abilities, carriable items (including game-changing ones), achievements that unlock them, altars, monsters and bosses of different types, and what I love the most about this game is the obscurity of everything around. Sure, you get some general idea, like the characters being called survivors, all wearing the same kind of helmet and trying to escape from aggressive monsters. However, the rest is largely a mystery, and you only get slight hints about the purpose of things and what's going on. This allows developers to unleash their imagination at its full potential, and having a chamber pot with legs as one of the most dangerous bosses is the thing that I truly admire, loving and hating it at the same time.It's all drawn in single style, however, and doesn't look too absurd, which is a good thing. It's just mysterious, and fun. Besides, being in a full 3D makes it perfectly fit for exploration, despite the levels being hand-drawn instead of procedurally generated. In fact, remembering them and learning their well-hidden secrets provides the sense of progression, yet there are so many randomly placed objects and monsters that you do not tend to get bored for a long time. In addition, the game already has a number of mods around, if you wish to make your experience even more diverse.My first complaints were about the somewhat ascetic level design combined with too challenging geometry in a number of places. However, as the game keeps getting filled with various content, this is getting fixed by itself, and right at this moment there's basically nothing left for me to whine about.Still, I should also add a couple of words about the soundtrack. That main theme is great, but... to be honest, the overall quality is far below the bar set by the prequel (which is an awesome game, too). So, let's just believe in Chris and remember that it's an Early Access. The game is already a masterpiece in its current state, and having some friends to play this in co-op makes me love it even more than I could imagine.

_childDocuments_.review: As of writing this review, Risk of Rain 2 is still in effectively an Early Access period, with its planned June update on the near horizon. Despite being someone who abhors pre-orders and shies away from early access titles, as a huge fan of the first game I couldn’t help but see if the stellar game that was Risk of Rain 1 survived the shift to 3D. And I can happily say the series has not survived…it’s absolutely thrived. Risk of Rain 2 is a gorgeous love letter to the first game, with gameplay arguably better than its predecessor thanks to the third dimension, visuals and music that are a joy to indulge in, and an insane amount of potential and promise that I have no doubt the tiny team of Hopoo recognizes and will capitalize on, if the sampling we already have is anything to go off of.Risk of Rain 2 is a class-based, third-person, action rogue-like. In most ways, it is exactly like its predecessor. There are different characters with unique abilities that emphasize different playstyles, a variety of interesting enemies and bosses, chests randomly stocked with a plethora of different items (many of which unlocked through performing different tasks on your runs) that enhance you in various ways, and perma-death. Just as in the last game, you spawn in different lands scattered with chests, shrines, enemies, and the teleporter. Activating it starts an event where a big boss and lots of enemies rapidly spawn while you stand nearby, ‘charging’ the teleporter. Complete the event, hop through the teleporter, and go to the next area—rinse and repeat as you get more powerful to match the increasingly-strong enemies and bosses.However, the third dimension introduced in Risk of Rain 2 adds an incredible amount of depth (pun intended) to the combat of the game. Whereas I-frames and tanking were your only real options for evasion in the 2D predecessor, in RoR2 evasion and mobility are shining stars. You can run around enemies, leap over them, dive out of the way of projectiles; the movement of RoR2 feels satisfying and works perfectly with the re-designed enemies and mechanics for the 3D space.The rogue-like aspects of the series are also fantastic. This was largely to be expected—Hopoo really nailed that satisfying feeling of growing in power with random items providing tons of unique effects, and fighting powerful monstrosities. Item selection is still sparse compared to the finished first game, but I have no doubts we’ll be getting a ton of fun new additions to add to the already-passable arsenal. I’ve got over 100 hours in the game and can assure you, there’s already enough variety now! Bosses and enemies are very unique and interesting; again, more would be much appreciated, but with that promised already I have no real worries there—I’m already enjoying fighting what we have.Balancing issues aren’t too prevalent, though hopefully as development continues a few small gripes I have will be addressed. Damage does get a little absurd late into runs, to the point where only one-shots are realistic threats—the addition of armor mechanics from the first game would be great. Fire damage is also still over-tuned in my opinion, and some enemies need slight reworks. But overall, the game is in a great state balance-wise.Sadly the weakest aspect of Risk of Rain 2 thus far. As it’s in Early Access, most of the item and enemy descriptions are blank, and it lacks the final stage that Risk of Rain delivered. These all are promised to be finished by the end of the year or so, but it is definitely a problem at the moment. However, I will note the few things that do have descriptions paint an arguably more interesting story than even the first game had, so I’m extremely excited to see how this aspect will grow and development—what we have hints at an incredibly strong aspect of the game to come.Just like its predecessor, Risk of Rain 2 boasts incredible replay-ability. The RNG nature of the game means no two runs will be alike, and combined with the unique playstyles of the several different characters we already have (with more to come!), there’s a ton to see and try out. Maybe one run you’ll blast everything away instantly with a crit build with Commando, the next you’ll develop an obsession for fungus as Engineer, and another you’ll be zipping around the map swinging a samurai sword like a madman. The Red and Lunar items especially contribute to this, as their rarity means each one will change up the run substantially with their unique and powerful effects (Except for H3AD-ST v.2, they need a massive buff ASAP!). I will admit, I was skeptical of how good the visuals of Risk of Rain 2 would be. After all, I had fallen in love with the gorgeous pixel art of the original, how could that possibly translate to 3D? Well, I can happily say Hopoo absolutely blew me away with what they came up with. The game’s cell-shaded style looks positively amazing, with stark and vivid colors being a feast for the eyes. I especially enjoy the slightly dark nature of the lands themselves, which make your colorful-item-covered character seem all the more ‘wrong’, in a good way! Enemy designs translated fantastically as well, especially the Magma Worm, a classic staple from the first game. There are few games that have genuinely taken me aback with a particular visual; some games have certainly wowed me with their overall design, but very few have ever made me pause and just say…woah. This is one of those games—standing at the mouth of a frosty whitish-blue cave and staring out towards a frozen beach in the distance, and staring as a blinding white-orange enormous Magma Worm erupted from the ground and soared high into the air with a deafening roar, spewing firey rocks around it—yeah, it’s safe to say the visuals are better than they’ve ever been in the series.This of course goes hand-in-hand with the visuals, but the stages we have so far are absolutely beautiful. Each has their own unique design, and the later levels perfectly emphasize the growing hostility of the land itself towards our character’s continued journey (and slaughter). There are some problems with the gameplay design thus far however—the Roost feels a little boring and uninspired compared to the other levels, the Abysmal Depths have a lot of empty space and just get way too dark when enemies start messing with the lighting (Looking at you, Overloading Worm!), and the Gilded Coast is just a absolute pain in its current design for basically no real reward. There’s definitely some room for improvement on this point, and more stages are definitely needed, but what we have right now is by no means bad gameplay-wise.Just like the first game, the muted music of Risk of Rain 2 is fantastically chill. No one track is very special in my opinion, but they all perfectly set the tone for each level and menu, often without you even explicitly noticing them. In addition, enemies sounds notably great and in some places even improved—wisps and especially lesser wisps are not nearly as annoying-sounding as they were in the first game, for example.Overall Risk of Rain 2, even in its current very incomplete state is an absolute blast. Every aspect of it that’s complete is, in my opinion, a improvement over its predecessor—visuals are gorgeous, sound design is a bit more polished, gameplay is undoubtedly more nuanced and interesting—and the aspects that aren’t yet complete—item/stage/character/enemy variety, storytelling—already show incredible promise. Even if Hopoo were to announce this is actually the complete game, I would still be able to recommend it, and given I have absolute faith in them to flesh out the game further I am unable to recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Risk of Rain was a great game. It had an excellent soundtrack, enjoyable gameplay, and was able to appeal to several audiences (as long as they were fond of difficulty). I enjoy the game so much, I speedrun it. So when I heard they were making a sequel, and it was in 3D, I was very excited and only slightly anxious that it wouldn't work as a 3D game.It followed the path of Super Mario 64 and Metroid Prime. It worked really well.This game improves on the original in every way. The soundtrack is even cooler, the graphics are very stylish, and the gameplay is super fun. It's the first game I ever bought on early-access launch day, and I have absolutely no regrets. In early access, the game was already very solid and enjoyable. Now that it's been fully released and updated, I can say for certain that it's one of if not the best game this year.Of course, it's not perfect. It took some doing to get used to the graphics having absolutely no anti-aliasing, and some of the artifact codes are annoying to find. Plus, there can be infuriating moments where you're having a really good run and then get obliterated by a Clay Dunestrider because you were playing a melee character.But I firmly recommend this game. It's an amazing experience alone, and even better with friends. Plus, check out the original, which is still good and different enough from 2 that it has a unique experience.

_childDocuments_.review: before i start the review, i want to say this: DO NOT BUY THIS GAME. ITS OWNED BY GEARBOX NOW. BUY RORR, OR ROR1, BUT GEARBOX DOES NOT DESERVE YOUR MONEY. now, to the review:Despite being riddled with a lot of questionable, if not bad design choices, this game is incredibly fun and will make your brain rot. (DLC is not necessary for the best experience, btw. I would instead say that in its current state, its clearly too buggy and rushed. Maybe pick it up while its on sale.)The music is as usual great, the characters all feel pretty diverse and have their quirks, the gameplay is overall very enjoyable although i think that hopoo should really try to add features that the players have been asking for YEARS- a restart button, ways for dead players to keep up with the others, the ability to drop items in multiplayer, as well as small reworks of older survivors like commando and huntress, that really need some sort of buff. They are both fun in their own way but are completely outclassed by every other survivor in the game.Changing the final bossfight a little would also be welcome as it can be cheesed with enough mobility and i guess a bit of experience. Funny moon man literally cannot touch you if you are in the air, and i believe that he should have a (reasonable) attack that can inflict pressure on high mobility players as well.Maybe remove the final countdown before leaving the moon and make the ending cutscene trigger once you have reached the spaceship? Having to run from void reavers and moon explosions(?) is already pretty exciting by itself, i dont think that having to do ANOTHER useless "teleporter event" is very fitting, besides, the reavers cannot get within spaceship range, and if you dont attack them, you have no way to die. So, what is the point of the timer? Maybe make it shorter or make the players do something else instead of just waiting.Some lunar items would also definitely benefit from a rework, for example gesture and brittle crown have NO drawbacks and can be picked up whenever, it really doesnt matter. I would mention the autoplay issue, which is a big one, but honestly as this point its useless because the devs would have to spend ages to completely rebalance the game from the start in order for its gameplay to feel more skill based than rng based. And i dont think they have the time, or the motivation for that. I just wish lategame was fun and didnt break completely with you killing all enemies on the screen just by looking at them.Aaaaand many more problems.I have to mention a last thing; one of the main selling points of this game is its multiplayer element. Yeah, a multiplayer that is only enjoyable with friends, because random lobbies are not fun. Please do consider adding the changes i mentioned at the start of the review, as the multiplayer experience really needs some extra polish.Though, to be fair, you will only start to notice the games design issues once you have several hours into it, and at that point you will most likely be too addicted to care. Its still a fun game that i enjoy very much, so i still recommend it, despite probably sounding very judgemental in the above paragraph.

_childDocuments_.review: There's always at least one game each year that comes completely out of nowhere and cements itself as one of the most memorable experiences said year had to offer. Risk of Rain 1 was one of my favorite roguelikes when I was younger, so seeing a sequel I thought would never exist pop up on the steam store got me very excited to see what Hopoo had come up with. Then I saw it had switched dimensions to 3D, bringing me even more excitement, but alongside a fear that the first games original charm would be lost in the transition. Regardless, it was pretty much an instant purchase, and I have no regrets.Risk of Rain makes one of the most seamless shifts to 3D that I've seen in years. I'm surprised just how little was lost in bringing the game to this new perspective. Almost everything that made me put 50 hours into the original is here, and I suspect everything and more will be integrated by the time this game comes out of early access.+ Port-Forwardless Co-op, even though pretty much no game in 2019 still requires portforwarding i'm still very thankful that its so easy now. Having to portforward just pushed my friends and I toward choosing a different game, and I never got to experience what the original co-op mode was like. That probably doesn't matter much anymore though, because I'm 99% sure RoR2's co-op completely outdoes the original's. I'm having a blast playing this game online finally, and I don't expect to drop this game anytime soon. Plus you can queue with randoms online.+ Some of the most unique characters out of any roguelike I've played. By that I mean that even though there are only 6 characters, each one feels so radically different that they completely change the way you play the game, and I wish I could say the same for games like Binding of Isaac or Enter the Gungeon.+ Fluid, exhilarating, fast paced combat, backed by solid controls. While the game is lacking some content right now, the core gameplay is already amazing.+ Lots of ingame achievements and unlockable items for earning said achievements, probably adding the most replay value out of anything in the game currently.+ Another great soundtrack. If you loved RoR1's music like I did, then you'll love RoR2's just the same. + This game excels at making every run feel different. Not only can you select different characters to mix things up, but in you'll be able to jump 4 times and run across the map in mere seconds, another you might have an army of phantom daggers homing in on enemies and multiplying as they rip apart anything in your path.+ Daily runs/challenges. They feel unique, shorter than a regular game, and challenge you to go as fast as possible. There is no reward for getting a good time currently unfortunately, but the addition is still appreciated.+ Pretty great performance for day 1 of early access. Not perfect, but more than acceptable.+ No game breaking bugs, at least none that I have found so far. No crashes either.+ Much more content, improvements, etc. to come.-Pretty unfair to call this a flaw in the game, but just be aware that the game is, as you probably already know, in early access. This means that there is no final boss or ending yet, not all of the characters or items are finished yet, the artifacts from the first game aren't implemented yet, there are some frame drops (especially when there are tons of late-game enemies or you are fighting a boss like the Magma Worm) etc. - Sometimes it will take a while to find the teleporter and that might be annoying. The teleporter can also spawn under shallow water sometimes, making it hard to see. Overall I think they should make the teleporter easier to see when you find where it is.- no rain, misleading titleOverall this sequel is looking up to be everything I wanted and more, especially considering I never thought Hopoo would even make one. _childDocuments_.review: There's probably nothing I can say about Risk of Rain 2 that hasn't already been said by a lot of other people, but it's one of my favorites and a genuine stand-out from all kinds of other offerings out there. Killer aesthetics and art direction that oozes vibrant color and design at every turn, medium-fast-paced PvE shooter gameplay that's both approachable and rich with a ton of fun items that give interesting effects, worldbuilding that - while piecemeal and revealed mainly through bits of lore text you unlock in your logbook - invokes a sense of weirdness and wonder that few other sci-fi and fantasy titles out there manage to, even when it leans on common tropes. That goes for the game's predecessor RoR1 as well, but Risk of Rain 2 improves on the gameplay of its forebear while implementing the base concept masterfully in 3D, both mechanically and aesthetically, and if you liked the RoR aesthetic in 2D then it is truly a sight to behold in 3 dimensions. I will say though that if you're coming in from RoR1, the "normal" difficulty has been significantly increased, and final boss is even harder. However, he's also pretty easy to cheese.One of my few complaints about the game is the little "you died, hahaha" messages you're sometimes given at the end of a run; it would be nice to be able to turn these off. All in all, I highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Risk of Rain 2 is largely an improvement to the first game, which was already very fun.I think Risk of Rain 2 is worth the purchase at full price ($20 at time of writing) if you think you'll get at least 20 hours out of it.What might be an indicator of this?First, you should be generally interested in the main mechanics of the game. It's focused around killing enemies to obtain loot while finding and activating a teleporter to go to the next stage. When the teleporter is activated, a boss is spawned, and you have to beat the boss and some more enemies to go to the next stage. At this point in development, there are 4 types of stages you visit in order, each type of stage has two possible maps that you can go to. You can keep going through the loop of stages indefinitely, or you can end your run when a celestial portal spawns after you activate certain teleporters.The game is played as a third person shooter, and you can choose one of nine survivors who all play differently from each other.If you are generally interested in the mechanics of Risk of Rain 2, then I would say it's worth a buy if any of the following describe you:1. You liked Risk of Rain.2. You like rogue-likes or rogue-lites.3. You enjoy grinding to beat specific challenges in order to unlock gear (this will certainly get you 20 hours in the game).4. You enjoy games that you can play for 30 to 60 minutes.5. You are enthused about this game and are looking for confirmation that it's good for some definition of "good".Risk of Rain 2 is in early access, but even in its current state I think it's a good enough successor to the original game. The devs are actively tweaking and adding content, so hopefully it only gets better. I would not let the early access tag push you away from buying.One great improvement over the first game is dedicated multiplayer support (you no longer have to go through the trouble of hosting your own servers). The game is good solo, but even better with friends.The main difference between the two is movement and scale. RoR 2 is 2D instead of 3D, which makes dodging enemies and traversing the map more complicated. It also allows for some characters (e.g. Loader, Mercenary) to have even crazier movement options than they did in the first game. It's very satisfying to swing around the map as Loader. Maps are much larger and take longer to traverse. You need to be much more focused on your surroundings, both enemies and chests are harder to visually keep tabs on than in the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is hard for me to write.After four long years being quite possibly my favorite game of all time, Risk of Rain 2 has been disgraced in it's most recent update.If you're a fan of this game and have been following it even half as much as I have, you understand why I have to make this review negative, but for those out of the loop:The original owners of the Risk of Rain IP, Hopoo Games, sold their IP to Gearbox Software after the release of Survivors of the Void in 2022.Ever since then, we have been patient and optimistic; waiting for them to fix the broken state of console, bring the Survivors of the Void DLC we already had on PC to them, and finally, release new content and streamline the experience to be equal on all platforms. All of these things were promised and eagerly awaited by the absolutely incredible community this game has fostered over the years.The monkey's paw curls.We now have a downgraded, buggy, mess of a game (with a subpar paid content drop, Seekers of the Storm, yeah its kinda mid) with a new codebase (that's ♥♥♥♥) on PC that is on par with what the console experience has been for years.Let that sink in. Knock Knock, open the door, its the sink:The PC version was DOWNGRADED to match console, not the other way around.But wait there's more! Now we have some shiny new critters! Such as but not limited to:Tons of collision issues, clipping, visual and audio issues all of which were not present before. (this is a LOT in one line)Physics and GAME DIFFICULTY being tied to FRAMERATE.Broken survivors that previously had absolutely no issue.A singular common item that makes the final boss unkillable.One tiny, innocent little bug where connecting a second input device will delete your entire save file.An ENTIRE CONSOLE edition that is UNPLAYABLE. Xbox players cannot even navigate the menu.And on top of all of this, we have a team of people behind the scenes at Gearbox Software and Take-Two Interactive that are not acknowledging the problems and the upset they have caused.I do not simply wish to be atop a pile of hate that this game does not deserve, but I feel like this is one of the only ways I can help. And I feel this way because this game DOES have:A brilliant and loving fanbase that has been collectively enjoying the ♥♥♥♥ out of this game for years.Incredibly talented people that have made the game what it is already, such as the GOAT Composer, Chris Christodoulou who's music does not deserve this treatment. (seriously the new SOTS DLC stages and tracks are incredible, credit where it's due)And people, like me, that only want our game back. The 10/10 better than sex rogue like experience that we all were enjoying just a week ago.I pray that I am able to change this review to positive as soon as humanly possible, but I can't do that in good conscience until progress, back to where we were, is made.I want to play Risk of Rain 2 again.

_childDocuments_.review: In Risk of Rain 2 you start as your chosen survivor, landing on a bizarre planet. For the entirety of your run, you will be fighting for your life. As with other roguelikes, there's a number of commonalities you can expect to see: upgrades to pick up, a horde of enemies to fight, a boss to cap off each level. However, unlike many other roguelikes, the levels aren't procedurally generated (but the sequence of the levels do vary somewhat). As you complete achievements, new items and artifacts become unlocked and useable for future runs.You can spend hours playing a run, or beat the game in under 1.5 hours. You are largely playing the same 20 levels over and over, but the way in which you play within each run varies. This variability and versatility is what gives it such a strong replay value.RoR2 is not an easy game. Sometimes you find a good combination of items; sometimes you don't. Sometimes, you juke left when you should have juked right, and you're dead. RNG hits pretty hard and regularly crushes you. Despite this seemingly frustrating description of the difficulty, I implore you to stick with it. Play on easy mode for a while. Learn how the items interact with each other. As you start unlocking new items, characters, and artifacts, your possibilities branch out, and the enjoyment goes up. Default RoR2 will always be hard (and darn near impossible on the hardest difficulty, "Monsoon"), but after the first several runs, I almost never played it "default" from that point forward. I always played it with some combination of artifacts, most importantly the "" artifact. This single artifact changed the game for me, as it gives you much greater control over how you upgrade your character.Besides the base difficulty you set for the run, there's an enemy difficulty scale within the run, which slowly increases over time. It creates quite the interesting dilemma: Complete the levels quicker to ensure the enemies you fight don't get too hard, or spend more time collecting items to make your character more powerful. It's a delicate balance you must continuously maintain, because if you swing too far in one direction or the other, you're dead. Keep in mind this a general rule. As you experiment with other artifacts and game modes, you'll notice that some rules go out the window. It's a design that broadens the more you play it.One drawback to the continuously scaling difficulty, is that you don't get much time to plan. You're always on the run. You can't view your inventory when paused, and in multiplayer, you can't even pause the game! The only exception is when you choose to go to the shop between levels. This will be a drawback for those that like to do a little more planning with their roguelikes. Better take a bathroom break before starting a run with your buddies!Throughout each stage you'll pick up items to boost your character during a run. Duplicate items can be stacked (e.g. each additional 'boiler plate' you pick up gives you +5 more damage reduction). Items often synergize with other items (e.g. an item that gives you extra crit hit chance + an item that gives you some benefit every time you crit hit). This is the foundation of much of the versatility of RoR2. When you're playing "default" RoR2, it is possible to get bad loadouts. Some items are lame and almost completely useless. But most items are at least useful in certain combinations or contexts.There are over 100 different items and equipment. It will take a while to learn what they all are, and how they help (or even hurt you). To make it harder, the items are sometimes nonsensical in their effects. A ukulele?  Well, that zaps adjacent enemies with electricity, of course!  A slug? That increases your heal rate, naturally!I was pleasantly surprised that in certain modes, this game doesn't hold you back. Your character can be grossly overpowered. I even pushed it so insanely far as to cause my PC to crash. I love that it lets me do this without limits. It's a refreshing contrast to the thousands of games out there that throttle you back just as you feel like you're gaining some momentum. Sometimes it's fun to simply annihilate boatloads of enemies with little effort. However, in most other modes, there's a great deal of balancing mechanisms, where if you are getting too overpowered, it can come back to haunt you.It's really hard to sum up all the different angles and strategies for such a seemingly straightforward design. Even 100 hours into the game, I was still discovering new ways to do things, and new ways to combine items for specific effects. You'll frequently be referring to the very extensive wiki to refine your understanding of every item and character.Despite being known as a co-op game, I didn't find the co-op portion to be that strong. It was ok, but I mostly preferred solo mode.Some downsides to co-op:Having said that, there are some benefits for playing co-op:The soundtrack is absolutely amazing. I would even say it contributed significantly to how much I enjoy the game. I bought the OST at full price.It took me 174 hours to get all achievements. There are some challenges that you can do that aren't related to achievements. For example the "logbook" which requires you to basically encounter every possible item and enemy. I completed logbook entries after my 200th hour of game time.As mentioned earlier, the achievements are all tied to unlocking items, which I think is a great way to add significance to achievements. You not only earn the achievement, but get a new character/weapon/item for doing so.The goals for every achievement are quite different, and will require you to pursue various combinations of items to get there. Some goals will mean you have to forgo getting  normally helpful items that you typically want to use every run. The achievements often require such radically different approaches that the 118 achievements don't feel that grindy. Difficult yes, but not grindy.

_childDocuments_.review: I typically don't write reviews, so bear with me here.Risk of Rain 2 is a phenomenal experience. From the art style, the music composed by the wonderful Chris Christodoulou, the gameplay, and even the complex lore, there's not much I can complain about in this game. I'm not a huge fan of rogue-like games, but Risk of Rain 2 has always stood high at the list of my favorite games of all time. The gameplay consists of you dropping into one of various stages, and battling monsters to get experience and money. You can spend money on things spawned with you in the stage, always changing location every run or visit to the stage. This will be spent on chests which will give you a random item, terminals which allow you to choose a certain item out of 3, and various drones and turrets. Alongside these, you can use items on certain interactables like 3D printers, which exchanges an item for another. Each item comes with its own unique and interesting lore, and each one is iconic in its own right, even ones as simple as "Gasoline".The monsters that you'll encounter are all also quite unique, and all have different things you need to watch out for. Even after learning about monsters and their attack patterns, an "elite" version of them could spawn which switches how you need to play around them. At the end of every stage, there will be a teleporter which you need to charge to reach the next, and charging that will spawn a boss, or multiple bosses. All bosses can be very deadly, especially in the late stages of the game. You could be having a run which you felt invincible in for the entirety of, and then make one false mistake near a boss and die instantly saying "What?". Progression in the game feels seamless, and being able to see the scaling difficulty in the top right definitely feels nice. At the start of the run you won't encounter many monsters, and you won't be gaining that much experience or money. As the game goes on, you can see in the top right a difficulty meter that goes up the longer you stay in a run, starting from Easy, to the game becoming sentient and laughing at you for the hell you're going to endure. The enemies will continuously become harder as this meter  goes up, dealing more damage and taking more hits, with items helping you scale alongside the monsters. More elites will spawn, and even harder variants will show up further into the game. You could even encounter a teleporter boss as a normal enemy on a stage. During each run, it's likely you'll unlock something new, such as an item, which could be found in your next run. Each unlockable has its own unique challenge that is required before you unlock it, some being easier than others, and some being incredibly difficult and requiring some effort to obtain. Alongside item unlocks, you can unlock new survivors, and even new abilities and skins for those survivors. Most of these unlocks you'll naturally obtain simply by playing the game, and rarely will you ever need to focus on that one unlock just to get it in a run.Risk of Rain 2 has no definite story to follow that's easily found just by playing the game, and requires some looking into if you want to learn about it. Each item comes with its own unique lore, and secrets found in game help build the world. Additionally, monsters can drop logs which detail things about them, explaining what they do and some behaviors of them. If you don't like worrying about lore and having to constantly remember it, this game would be perfect for you! But, if you do enjoy lore and story, you also have the option of looking into it and having a pleasant time doing so. Each entry has a unique feel, and doesn't just feel like a wikipedia entry, as most of the time it's written by a survivor or some other entity. The music. The entire soundtrack was composed by Chris Christodoulou, and there is not one song that I dislike. Of course, music is quite a subjective topic, but I feel most will find the soundtrack to be stellar. Each song that's placed in a stage or a boss fight fits seamlessly, each song managing to fit that alien-like feel that they're supposed to be giving. The song that plays can go from beautiful to intense in seconds, my favorite of this showing during the battle against the final boss. I myself can easily listen to the soundtrack on my own time outside of the game, and while some may not be able to do that, I'm sure  they'll enjoy listening to the soundtrack in game.I'm sure I missed quite a lot of key points, but this is what I could come up with. Risk of Rain 2 is in my top 3 games of all time, and I highly recommend it for everyone. Even if you aren't a big fan of rogue-likes, I recommend you give it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: As a newcomer to the Risk of Rain series, I was attracted to Risk of Rain 2 because of its co-op online, horde-like shooter structure with a fresh 3D perspective compared to its predecessor's 2D format. Just like other horde-like games, it follows the "loop" design of kill mobs, collect loot, defeat the boss, and rinse-repeat.The gameplay is simple, intuitive, yet challenging all at the same time. The gameplay is brutal, but fair. It is challenging but not in a frustrating way. I just want to play more. It is the kind of challenge you can appreciate and learn from your mistakes. I'm new to rogue-likes-lites and I was able to solo for more than an hour. As far as unlockables, there are six characters to unlock, four zones, and 99 items with more on the way. Items that you collect along the way are adorned on your character like trophies. Despite all the unique passive abilities you get from each item, I want to see more items with cool powers and abilities that I can summon. For top-tier players, they may feel content-starved. Personally, I feel there is enough content here in Early Access to keep you coming back for more. Playing with keyboard and mouse and the controls feel slick, snappy, precise. Items and abilities complement one another, making for a perfect formula for mayhem. Aiming and gunplay are precise and accurate. Enemy hit box is fine-tuned. Using terrain adds another layer of dimension to combating enemies.  Discovering new items and experimenting with them is extremely fun. And using them on enemies is even better. One of my favorite items is the black hole. Needless to say, it speaks for itself. Visually, Risk of Rain 2 sticks to what its good at, and just like the original it sports a very similar coat of aesthetic that is hauntingly beautiful and minimaliistic. The game runs extremely well @ 3440x1440 on my ultrawide and doesn't miss a beat. As you well know by now, Risk of Rain 2 is in 3D. Unlike its 2D predecessor, the third-person perspective and added dimension does not take away from what makes RoR great. Enemy attacks and projectiles now come from every direction instead of a lined approach, which changes things up for the series.The soundtrack is superb. If you like listening to soundtracks from "Deep Rock Galactic", "Blade Runner" or the movie "Drive", your ears will be pleased. The soundtrack is calm and soothing to the ears against all the chaos on the screen. There's also some rock, too, that goes well with some intense play sessions.Online multi-player consists of co-op online featuring quick play or simply hosting a game and inviting your friends. It has a  Some of the issues I experienced were some rubberbanding and the "Unknown Lobby ID" or "Invalid Lobby ID" when trying to use QuickPlay. Other than that, it has been pretty smooth for an Early Access game. Another feature that I really liked was the option for players to vote on difficulty level in the lobby. In the past, I have found too many games fall into the trap of map selection based on difficulty, which can really split the community. On the other hand, this may cause some players to quit because the difficulty level is too hard. One draw back is that it runs on peer-to-peer online connection. I had a few great "monsoon" difficulty runs end because the host quit. My one caveat with the online portion is that any player in co-op is able to click on teleport prematurely which transfers the entire group to the next area before looting everything. This causes some players to miss out on collecting the remaining items on the map. On easy difficulty, this isn't much of a problem. But on harder difficulties this can present an issue. Some players have complained about the visibility of the teleporter. I do not think it is all that bad. The teleporter visibility and randomization varies. Sometimes, I would go rounds finding it rather too easily. Once in a while, it feels like it doesn't even exist on the map.Another issue are how boss drops are distributed. The boss will drop at least one item per player. Sometimes, the boss will drop more items than there are players. In my experience, some players would grab more than one item or all of them, possibly to troll others in the group or they just do not want to share. Also, because the items drop very close to each other, it is easy to grab more than one boss drop item by mistake. The levels are hand-crafted like the original. While they are designed well, there is not enough randomness. The teleporter is randomized, but you can expect the rest of the levels to be the same.It was not until recently that I got into rogue-likes, thanks to some Steam friends. Usually, I would play co-op, horde-like games such as Deep Rock Galactic (excellent game btw), Vermintide 2, Helldivers, and so forth. If you like any of those games and you like some rogue-likes, or you are at least open to them, I think you will probably like Risk of Rain 2. I was not too fond of the original RoR, but I felt right at home with RoR2. It is like a love letter to co-op, horde-like gamers.Risk of Rain 2 was a pleasant surprise. Rarely do I instantly like a game this much within the first hour. Its simplistic and elegant design has a mild complexity when it comes to its challenging gameplay. It consists of smart design that allows any type of player to jump right in, so long as you have the patience for it. In the future, I would like to see more rogue-like-lite titles become 3D games. As long as it makes sense and works well with the gameplay style. Hopoo Games has shown that indie titles such as RoR can be a 3D title and still retain all the aspects that made the original a great, fun game.RoR2 is in Early Access and kicking with overwhelmingly positive reviews and it is well earned. The developers plan on adding more characters, bosses, items, a true endgame boss, and a true ending when the final product releases. Game modifiers that can be found in the world will be coming soon as well. Furthermore, I want to commend Hopoo Games for doing the "Buy One, Get One Free until 3/30" promotion. That was a very cool thing to do. Ultrawide 21:9 Support: Yes.i5-8600K @ 4.6 GHzGTX 1070 Founder's Edition (stock)16GB DDR4 RAMSamsung 850 EVO SSDLG Ultra-wide 34UM69G @ 2560x1080

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for June 2024, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before July 2nd, 2024, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle. A strange sequel. Risk of Rain was a sidescrolling rogue-lite with tiny graphics that was amazing, Risk of Rain 2 is a third-person rogue-lite and while it’s a similar game, and I can see the original here, thus doesn’t feel like a sequel… This is so much better.  In Risk of Rain 2, you’re running through multiple vibrant worlds, hunting treasure chests, finding the damnable teleporter that will take you to the next world, and fighting a boss while it charges up.  All of this was in the original.But if you ever played the original, you probably know this is different.  There are so many beautiful worlds, multiple fleshed-out classes, interesting enemies, tons of combat here, and a freedom of movement that feels like a massive upgrade.   There’s multiplayer that works very well, though I think it is harder than single-player.  There are also tons of items to find. Which is also one issue I have.  The game doesn’t tell you what an item does, so quite often you’ll have to use a mod to show that or look online for info.   I also got stuck twice while playing for over ten minutes in two different levels hunting for the teleporter that I couldn’t find.  Even knowing what to look for didn’t help.   Also, I struggled with the multiplayer but devastated the single-player, and maybe that’s a mod issue, but it did seem easier in a single-player. Pick this up if you like rogue-lites, if you are going to play with friends, I can tell you this is a lot of fun, and I’ve had a group of four that I’ve played with multiple times.  While playing this solo on stream this is the first time I remember winning so… yeah maybe it’s easier solo. _childDocuments_.review: Don't get me wrong, I love RoR1 and I love RoR2, however, I very much disagree with the rushed move to leave Early Access. Please be aware that this game should still be in Early Access, it is in many ways not finished.I'm certain Hopoo or the modding community will address many of the reported problems in the coming months or years (as they have in the past).The game has many smaller weaknesses, bugs and valid criticisms, too many to list here, but it can still be an enjoyable experience for many hours. In my opinion it really shines when played on easiest difficulty with one or more friends in the same room or with voice chat.Multiplayer with strangers is mostly not enjoyable, due to various big technical and design problems:- Missing host migration (game exits if the host leaves the match)- No tools for meaningful communication (game is often too unforgiving to chat for even a second, pinging items and locations is absolute barebones)- Quickplay was completely removed in 1.0.0- Teamplay and item sharing is not encouraged, as almost all items purely give benefits and most players only look out for themselves- There is no way to pick up and drop an item for your team member, worst case they have to run across the whole map. The only exception to this are 3D printers and item transformers, which come with other downsides- The game rewards splitting your team up, to more quickly scout the map for items. Not splitting up exaggerates the problem of item sharing even more, as items will be found more slowly, making the game generally harder for everyone. This can partially be avoided with unlockable modifiers, which remove the need for scouting the map for anything but the teleporter to the next map.- No way to vote pause the game (with a single run often taking between 1-2 hours), you have to be lucky to find a portal to the shop area, which stops the game loop until exited- Rushed and unbalanced final level and boss that should have never made it into the game like this. It is an absolute disappointment compared to the amazing boss level of RoR1- Many unlockable abilities for characters do not exist yet, "Work in progress" icons have simple been removed for 1.0.0- Missing local co-op, due to technical difficulty in implementing split screen. Splitscreen can already be enabled via mods, but it is still buggy and reportedly not a priority. There is no way to run or hack together multiple game instances on the same PC for a local co-op experience.For me these are the most pressing issues. Until most of them are fixed, I can only recommend this game if you have at least one actual friend to play it with.

_childDocuments_.review: RoR2 is a great game. It definitely scratches the Rogue-like dungeon crawler itch for me. However, it's not a traditional dungeon crawler in the sense that the maps are procedurally generated; the stages are always going to be the same. What's different in RoR2 is that location of the teleporter is always randomized, so along with random item drops, each run is always a fresh and new experience. There are also plenty of characters to choose from - each featuring a different play style, which brings a lot of variety to the experience. The initial learning curve is a little steep, as you're just thrown into the world and you don't know what the items do, and haven't memorized the layouts of the different stages, but that is largely mitigated by the Drizzle difficulty as well as the Artifact of Command, which helps one acclimate to the gameplay quicker. A thing that I appreciate about RoR2 is that your earlier runs never influence the outcome of your later ones. While you do unlock different items that can influence your future games, they're never handed to you for free. What you do get, however, is better at the game, and that's a good time!The game can get a little intense or sweaty, as there can be lot to know, but at the end it's also just pretty casual, and you can just hop in!

_childDocuments_.review: "Just One More Run" Syndrome: You'll say you'll play for 20 minutes, but suddenly it's 3 AM, and you're still battling waves of monsters. Time flies when you're trying not to die!Picture this: you've been fighting your way through hordes of enemies, barely surviving, when suddenly a giant, monstrous...thing appears out of nowhere. Your heart races as you realize you're about to face the ultimate test of skill and teamwork. Or, more likely, panic and chaos. Ever wanted to experience what it's like to be a hamster trapped in a wheel of death? Well, look no further, because Risk of Rain 2 has you covered! The game throws waves of enemies at you faster than you can say "I regret my life choices." And just when you think you've cleared the horde, the game laughs in your face and spawns an even bigger, angrier boss. It's like a never-ending cycle of pain and suffering, with a sprinkle of hopelessness for good measure.The vibrant colors, the detailed environments, and the way my character flails around while getting pummeled by enemies... it's all a visual feast for the eyes. I particularly enjoy how my character's expressions perfectly match my own when facing a horde of alien monstrosities: sheer panic. My partner and I had a lot of fun going through the game. My best advice is: Just be prepared to die. A lot.I understand that games are supposed to be challenging, but Risk of Rain 2 takes it to a whole new level. I also struggled a little bit with the controls, but nothing we can't overcome. We had issues with the multiplayer aspects, 2 or 3 times. The respawn system is not my favorite. You basically respawn at the same place you die... to be killed again a second after respawning.Risk of Rain 2 is like a rollercoaster ride through a hurricane—it's chaotic, it's unpredictable, and there's a good chance you'll end up soaking wet and questioning your life choices. But hey, at least you'll have a good laugh along the way. I recommend this game and I want to play more with my partner in the future. :-)

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: Newest update broke many aspects of the game, even if you don't own the dlc.Pros of the new update:+ Artificer hover can be set to be a toggle instead of a hold+ The logbook can now be looked at mid run+ Option for scaling teleporter particles when further away+ Option to mark teleporter when discovered+ Directional damage indicators, with a slider for intensity+ Loader's Thunderslam audio is no longer deafeningly loud (introduced with the Devotion update, which was in May)I think these are all good changes/additions on their own, but most of them have issues/questionable implementations along with the plethora of other bugs that were introduced:- Artificer hover is now set to toggle as default, instead of leaving hold as the default- Opening the logbook mid run messes up the audio (everything was a lot louder and directionally incorrect)- The regular damage indicator no longer exists (?), and the directional damage indicator intensity is set to 0 by default (at least for me)- Changing UI scaling now makes certain text (ex. numbers on your health bar) hard to read, even at 75% scaling (scaling options are fixed, there is no in-between for 75% and 100%)- Things are now tied to FPS, either completely breaking them or changing how they work (ex. Loader grapple at 60 FPS feels normal, but will send you flying at higher frame rates)- Rarity outlines on items in multi-item terminals and adaptive chests don't exist, and the items in them are shadowed, making it hard to tell what they are even at semi-close distances- Enemies can easily clip through walls and other solid objects, sometimes even without player interaction- Certain enemy behavior is just strange (ex. Parents walking back and forth in the same spot until aggro'd)- Sometimes you can see a frame of an enemy before it spawns (seemed to mostly happen with beetles/other small ground enemies)- The animation on health bars for losing/gaining health is far too slow- Audio now gets crunchy/choppy if a lot is going on at once (happened by stage 6/7 on a normal difficulty run)- This is nitpicking, but most, if not all, of my settings (besides keybinds) got reset- And more that I either haven't encountered or can't remember at the moment.I cannot genuinely recommend this game in the state that it's in, either stick to the Devotion update or wait for ♥♥♥♥ to get fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember a lot of apprehension when Risk of Rain 2 was announced. It wasn’t unwarranted, either, as the jump from 2D to 3D has been dire for more than a few franchises. I wasn’t super hot on the original Risk of Rain either, owing to how sloggy the combat could be if your build didn’t keep up with the hordes. But all those concerns melted away in my first few minutes with the game. Risk of Rain 2 benefits so much from the move to 3D that it’s almost hard to believe it started as a side-scroller, with free movement and open arenas allowing you so much more control over encounters. And I can only assume it’s going to get better from the handful of foes and levels it has now.The story in these games is always a pretty big question mark, but the premise at least is simple enough. You’re some kind of space badass, landing on a bizarre alien world full of things eager to teleport all the way over to kill you. The only way to progress through these realms of slaughter is to find and power up a teleporter, which of course will attract the attention of things far worse during the charging phase. On a happier note, the planet is dotted with mystical shrines, drones in need of masters, and cases full of suspiciously powerful items, all of which can enhance your survivability if you can wrest enough coins from your foes to pay for them.At this precise moment, Risk of Rain 2 is a loop of six levels, each a wide-open space of fields, cliffs, walkways, ruins, and other features to explore. The map itself is always the same, save for minor differences like some doors and caves being open, but the layout of loot and the location of the exit teleporter is always different. You are free to explore to your heart’s content as enemies teleport themselves into your vicinity to murder you, but just as in the first game the difficulty rises as time passes. The main challenge of the game, then, is balancing your exploration for more powerful gear against the need to press on as your foes become stronger and more numerous. Once again, this is a balance that will take time to learn, and may end with you dead in the very first stage a few times as you seek to find it.The big difference between the first and second games now is the pace of the action. In Risk of Rain you often found yourself corralling foes into a stack to whittle down, boxing in enemies and chewing through them gradually. Part of the reason for this was your low movement speed and lack of mobility options in platforming. All that is out the window now, and not just because of the addition of a third dimension. Relative movement feels so much faster here, with a dedicated sprint button and more dramatic movement abilities for the different classes. Items that add additional jumps are also pretty common drops, but more importantly enemies can no longer box you in. You’re free to circle around foes, weave through crowds, and retreat in any direction if things get too intense. You have to stay in the vicinity of the teleporter to charge it but that’s still a sizable arena to work with.For the most part, the grinds against enemy health bars are gone as well. There are certainly some enemies that need further adjusting but the overall experience feels balanced more for cutting down big groups in a hurry. This is facilitated by the builds you can get going, featuring powerful pickups that conditionally enhance your damage or add leaping electrical attacks or explosive effects, all of which can be stacked with themselves. They say it right on the store page, they want you to exploit these items, creating builds that will tear through your foes like some kind of super-science reaper. These items will be familiar to fans of the first but it’s easier to get a build rolling in this one, possibly due to your greater relative power compared to your foes.There are six classes to unlock and use in the game now, from the familiar shootyman Commando to the nimble Huntress with her homing bow to the absolutely mad techno-magician Artificer. More levels and classes are coming prior to the full launch early next year, as well as the game-altering Artifact system from the first. Right now you can enjoy some wonderfully chaotic drop-in multiplayer (which works like a dream compared to the first game) and daily challenges, the staple of modern roguelikes. All you really need is that core loop of looting and shooting, though, because it’s absolutely sublime here. I never expected Risk of Rain 2 to outperform the original so completely, but the move to 3D has treated it incredibly well. For wild arena combat and fast-paced adventuring, this one is hard to beat.Did you enjoy this review? I certainly hope so, and I certainly hope you'll check out more of them at  or on my !

_childDocuments_.review: Yo, so, I've been waiting till the game came out of E.A. to write down my general opinion on it and on some of the characters you'll unlock in your play through.The games got a huge curve in pace when it comes to how you play it from start to end.Kind of as a "Calm before the storm" sort of deal. You start your game on a ship that seems to be having some sort of malfunction, as items in the background of the character select screen are kinda thrown around like as if the ship had taken some sort of random impact to it's hull. You only have one survivor to pick from at the start, that being commando. Let me just say he's a pretty reliable character to pick from. With his primary attack dual pistol burst fire allowing the player to handle enemies from close to mid range with ease. He also has a decent chance to proc the items you pick up as you go along. His secondary skills also good for dealing with a small stream of enemies as well, being as you fire a single phasic shot that punches through enemies and wallsHe has a dodge roll that works really smoothly at first but can be sorta buggy once you get in late game for reasons that make sense.and he has a decent stun weapon that sorta is useful early to mid run, but becomes more or less weaker later on when you start dealing with routine big monsters that are immune to stun procs.The game itself runs on a sort of snowball ideal. Where you know how your game's going to go based on how fast you get through the first 3 teleporters. Because your character gets stronger and stronger the more items they accrue throughout the run. It's kind of like playing DOOM, but you're managing the time spent at each zone you complete.The items themselves are all unique and actually have a decent sorting system when it comes to items and how powerful they are. With a unique tier that offers powerful bonus at the cost of having equally major debuffs. White items: These are items that get stronger the more of them you have. Starting off small like +10% attack speed from soldier syringe that gives an extra 10% per soldier syringe you have in that "Stack".Green items: These items are more or less rare, but don't always affect the player directly. usually having an effect on the world around the player, rather than directly affecting the player themselves. Red items: These items are super duper rare, but just having one of these items can majorly affect how you play the game. With anything from major buffs to healing from all sources, to making swarms of voodoo enemy seeking knives that appear when ever you kill an enemy. Blue items: These are called "Lunar items", they're very mysterious artifacts that give the survivor a major edge in battle while also trading something in return, like being able to deal damage to  in the area around them for a period of time, to dramatically increasing health gained from sources but making it act as healing over time.Yellow items: These items are boss drops. not all bosses drop yellow items but they're usually useful regardless, from giving you bonuses to max health and health regeneration, to giving you an allied bug boi to help tank damage.Orange items: These are equipment items. they provide useful effects that can be used reliably for a short period of time that stay with the player as a side ability, like being able to call down a lightning strike on a enemy for massive damage, or giving yourself +100% critical chance for decent amount of time.A lot of these items harmonize with one another. And all are useful for any kind of play style, from nuking the map with all out damage, or just healing faster than the enemy can deal damage. The games meant to be fast paced and addictive, and there's nothing in the game that, in my opinion, really slows it down. Each character is also super unique and doesn't feel like an upgrade from one another. I really like all of them, but the one that interests me the most is the Artificer. She's essentially built around the use of her abilities as all of her skills have cool downs. Even her primary attack has a limited amount of charges that regenerate over time. As much as you'd expect it to slow the game down, it really doesn't. it forces the player to take into account the cool down periods of their abilities to maximize their damage output in a really unique way that makes the character fun to play. It's a deceptively game that becomes ever more intrinsic the more you play, as you unlock more items to expand your game play with each run you do. I really enjoy it, and I hope you do too. Overall, 10/10, will obliterate myself again.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played Risk of Rain 1 for too long, as a party game with local coop up to 4 players, as an online game, as a singleplayer game, as soon as Risk of Rain 2 came out, I got almost as many hours instantly, you could see this on my profile... probably.This game is awesome to pass the time or just have a good laugh with friends, you're sent to an unknown, hostile planet, and you have to scavenge and fight your way through anything you see, this rogue-like game is all about survival.Difficulty increases as time passes by, you can see this on the top right screen, there's a slider that will tell you how long have you been here, and what difficulty are you in, there's a point in which this game is just  because of how insane things get if you survive long enough.In the current state of the game, even if some might say it lacks content, it has a lot of replayability, you can play solo for a long while, and play multiplayer even more, at this point if I got burnt at some point I haven't noticed because I still play it, just maybe not as often, and even with the sales here we recently just got our first content update and it's a great moment for new players to come into the game, and absorb players who were waiting for new content, right now the game might not really be in the "most difficult" phase, and it lacks a final stage and final boss, but
