_childDocuments_.review: I really feel like i should give this game a review, because many people are talking nonsense about it.So, Naruto to Boruto: Shinobi Strike. Or, if you'd prefer, the Naruto Xenoverse game.It's the first multiplayer Naruto game, or even the first Naruto game ever, to let you create your own ninja, and that alone is really awesome, and something i was really looking forward as both a gamer and a long time Naruto fan. The customization of the game is really good, many people will say it's not, but you'll see the same people making cosplay characters of Naruto or Sasuke, or terrible mashups like Madara + Kakashi, and not really putting some thought into their OC.But the aspect of character creation goes much beyond cosmetics. You are able to freely combine jutsus, or at least your class's jutsus, and make creative and fun combinations. And, again, most people will just use the skills that everyone thinks are OP, and the same people will, again, complain about the customization.The graphics are ok, but what really catches me is the movement. The movement is so fun and fluid, it makes the game really fast paced, and you WILL FEEL LIKE A NINJA.But nothing is perfect, and this game is no exception. It lacks a custom match lobby, a story mode, the aim lock system is pretty bad, PVE really sucks, and the hub world is kindda small. Yet, keep in mind that this game was released not even a month ago, so i'm sure we can expect both fixes and content updates.All in all, i've played about 15 hours so far, and i'm far from getting bored.It's really fun to learn all the jutsus and try different combinations against different opponents, and i'm looking forward for what the devs are planning on the updates, especially when it comes to new weapons.Is the game worth it? YESIt's a really fun game, it still feels like a beta, but so what?People give up on great games too early, and that's why good games die.Don't let this game die.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought the game a few days ago because I likes the trailers and the announced DLC. At first I was happy with the game and then I was really annoyed.So, this game has a lot of positive things: -You can personnalize your character entirely and add stats to your character.-You can play with your friends (4 players maximum)-There is a large choice of jutsus (in game attacks)-The fact that there is 4 possible classes of gameplay (Attack, Ranged, Defense, Healer) is good.These things are why I bought the game and I was really happy about those.But, there is a lot of things that you can't do and it wouldn't be very hard to implement in the game, or things that are just really annoying: -The servers are REALLY laggy. (I had 40ms ping and still lagged in game. It's probably because the game is pair to pair when online gaming.)-You can't do a private party to play against your friends. You can play with them online against stranger or doing PVE.-Some of the jutsus are really buggy. I'm talking about the "Rasengan" for example, sometimes the ennemy would fly away and I would still continue to hit him (considering it's a close range attack, it's weird). Or sometimes the ennemy would still be in range of it and I would not hit him for whatever reason.-The game modes are really repetitive. I don't quite understand why but the developper team thought it would be a good idea to lock two of the four game modes available in ranked mode. So half of the season (which is usually 3 weeks long), you can only play 2 of the 4 game modes. _childDocuments_.review: To be fair, this game honestly has one of the best combat mechanics in any game I've ever played thus far, and I'd wanna see more games with similar mechanics to it. The game also features some neat character customization and give some cool rewards for events which are completely achievable for anyone. So with those said, the problems lie elsewhere.1. There is a jarring amount of bugs - although you cannot expect a game to be completely bug-free, this game has jarring amount of it. Examples include but are not limited to a) Screen dimming after a cut scene b) Ability indicators would display cooldown when inflicted by certain skills despite being entirely unaffected and c) Severe latency issues with the host.2. There is a severe lack of PvE contents -  PvE contents are only significant in early game, for unlocking some of the more generic gears and for accomplishing some weekly objectives. Otherwise there would be no reason for putting too much effort on doing PvE unless you don't mind doing extremely repetitive stuff.3. The game is pay-to-win - you can purchase the base game at up to 90% sale but you also need to buy enough DLCs to at least be competitive enough not to burden your team. While the game allows you to customize your costume to a wide extent, the best gears can only be obtained through gacha mechanics and would force your character's appearance to look more from a Wuxia or Scifi game than a Naruto character instead.4. The connectivity is terrible - the matches employ peer-to-peer connection and can be horribly laggy and can be very prone to disconnections depending on how bad your connection with the host is. You would expect an esteemed publisher to provide a good server for their matches than to trust their players to have good hosting capabilities. The game cannot and should not even afford to punish players for disconnection due to how bad their match connectivity is.5. The matchmaking is imbalanced - The solo matchmaking is horrible as it is- putting players with high deviation of experience and performance in the same team just to balance it out with the opponents (if the game even actually try to balance out solo matches), then pre-made teams breaks all the balance. A full stack of elite players will often be matched with a random group of players that just happened to queue at the same time with them. This game basically heavily encourages you to play with a pre-made team and will punish you for trying to queue solo.6. The recap screen is very unhelpful -  What's up with the 15 second match recap? The game should let the players scrutinize the match stats so they can contemplate on player performance, including finding suspicious activities. If the game thinks that allowing the team leader to queue quickly outweighs the importance of a good recap, then they have their priorities wrong.7. An abundant population of cheaters and hackers - while it is not the game's fault that hackers exist, the game features give hackers some good level of opportunity. The game doesn't even have an in-game report function for suspicious and disruptive activities, and the game does not check for suspicious codes upon boot up (but will continuously bother you about the anti-cheat failing to properly load itself). The reporting system would give you much more of a hassle than just swallowing the bitter pill that hackers have an unfair advantage.So to recap, the publisher and devs should:1. Fix annoying bugs.2. Give more incentives for playing PvE or playing solo in general3. I think pay-to-win is tolerable for a premium game, just maybe lower the skill floor, give more f2p options, and/or give some premium-level incentives that doesn't include gacha mechanics.4. Stop being so stingy and give players some proper match servers.5. Balance the matchmaking process. Make it less traumatizing for new and/or solo players.6. If the game cannot provide a more meaningful game recap, at least remove the ridiculous recap timer.7. Developing a PvP intensive game should come hand-in-hand with a good and accessible reporting system, otherwise the game would be a good breeding ground for abusers and pave way to a more toxic community.Personally I'd want the devs to be more "in-touch" with the game and experience it a bit more, but maybe that's asking for too much.

_childDocuments_.review: - Great concept, poor execution. Unpolished.- Pay to win (lootboxes and pay to unlock best abilities)- Lobby is terrible. It is small, completely void of purpose (all the things you do on the lobby, on a any other game, would be in a simple menu for quick access. Lobby is there to give an illusion of an open world and to make players waste time traveling just to change one combat ability)- Chatting with other players is impossible, besides a few non-customizable pre-defined sentences- Combat is fun, but the camera is really clunky.- Impossible do fight a 1 on 1 match- I know the game is destined for multi-player, nevertheless the lack of single player content is just sad. The bare minimum would be to be able to play in normal matches (ie. CTF, combat, etc) with bots if you want to, but this is not an option. All the single player content comes down to a few boring and repetitive missions. The argument that this is a MP game and doesn't need any SP features really seems dumb to me. Many MP exclusive games give you the ability to play alone with bots if you want to (Counter Strike, League of Legends, etc). This does not hinder MP gameplay whatsoever and more features in a game is always good IMO. - The game looks like a poor man's Xenoverse and it would be that much better if it had drawn more inspiration from it. It has many of the same concepts, except poorly implemented and a lot less content- This is the only Naruto game with a decent CAC system, and the devs know it and take advantage of it by selling a game for 50€ with a handful of characters and making you pay 4€ for each extra character (which unlocks not only abilities, but customization options). The main problem with this game is that there is no competition for it and that's the only reason why people play it, not because the devs did a good job in creating a game for the fans.- In summary the game really feels like an early access game, but at full price and with microtransactions (then again, this seems to be the norm nowadays). Another game with huge potential that was screwed by greedy devs/publishers.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really cool at first, but always leaves much to be desired. A desire that is never filled GRAPHICS:Similar to any other Naruto game you have played. The render distance on pickups is awful. Even in the circular arena of the Ninja World Tournament where items only drop 1 at a time, you won't see the item unless you are close enough to it. Everything else is totally fine.AUDIO:I was impressed there was so much English voice acting here. Not all dialogue is voiced but there is a decent amount here from the anime voice actors. Music is decent. If I played much more though, I would probably have muted it from hearing it over and over. UNLOCKABLES:This is the thing that got me to play as long as i did. You can train under different characters to unlock their abilities, costumes, and random scrolls. There is lots to unlock and its probably the best part of the game. COMBAT:The amount of things you can unlock means little if you aren't able to provide compelling gameplay.Your dash is awful. Pressing the button once jumps towards the target. Pressing it again before you hit the ground, sends out a sort-of fishing line. If your line hits an enemy, you will dash towards them. The problem is you are already in the air and you only throw the line straight ahead of you. So more often than not, you will miss your line. That, or you will teleport away because the dodging just is mapped to the same button. You can also waste your dodging jutsu AFTER you get hit. So maybe you just got knocked away, and you want to get back into the fight so you press the button to dash, only for you to waste your dodging jutsu to dodge an attack you were already hit with.The slowness of the guarding doesn't compete with the enemy attacks. You must stand still to block and you cannot attack immediately before blocking. Large enemies have attacks that usually effect the entire area around them. If an enemy starts swinging its arms at its sides, you will not be safe by simply attacking the legs. You will get hit most of the time, unless you want to use your limited dodge to move a short distance away. However, now you are far away and must get closer again to deal meaningful damage. Ranged attacks to negligible damage to enemies so are usually useless unless dealing with the exploding ones. You are limited to 4 on a recharging cooldown but they could be unlimited and you would not be overpowered in the slightest.Along with your ranged attack, you have light and heavy attacks. I could not tell the difference between the 2 besides a different animation. Heavy attacks are supposed to be slower and break guards easier, but unleashing a full heavy combo at an enemy seems to be just as effective at breaking a guard as a light one. So let's just say you have 1 standard attack. They also swapped the ranged, and heavy attack buttons from Ninja Storm Revolution for some reason.unleashingYou also get 2 standard jutsus. Only 2 at a time. That's it. Certain Justus are only usable by certain classes. Same with weapons. You can switch your class anytime outside a mission, and when you die within missions. The only class worth anything is the attack class. The game doesn't have many players so the attack class is the single one that is well rounded enough to do single-player content. You also have an ultimate Jutsu but they, along with many other jutsus, have a hitbox smaller than you would expect. This leaves them feeling unsatifying. These ultimate Justus also require you to fill a meter before use but all other abilities simply have a cooldown. You can pickup scrolls during missions but im not sure what they do. Scrolls are supposed to be kinda like loot boxes. However scrolls I pickup in a mission does NOT translate to how many scrolls I can open after a mission. On the note of things I don't understand, if an ability is on cool-down, you can stand still and channel the ability anyway. Doing this . . . . Might make the cool-down reduce faster but if it does I cant tell a difference.MULTIPLAYER:On the subject of multiplayer, everyone who is still playing, is better than you as a beginner. You will not win. Co-op is no easier or harder than single player but you have to wait for matchmaking. If you are trying to matchmake for a specific mission you may as well quit. Matchmake by rank and you may get a match after 2 minutes of waiting. Even when doing single player content, there is still an arbitrary waiting period between each quest AFTER you select it, exit the menu you are in, and press X to start the mission. Only then will you be able to wait 5 seconds (on a timer) to start your mission. You can also only talk to other players through canned responses. That never works in anything ever.MICROTRANSCTIONS:This game has loot boxes and the best ones can only be bought. Even opening the best scroll that you can get for free, I managed to receive 4 of the exact same item. You can sell these for Ryo but not for enough. At least it's just cosmetics.CONCLUSION: This game is bad with a few good bits sprinkled in to make you think "if I just keep playing it will get better." But it doesn't. It's the same. And with the online community dwindling, its better to get one of the ninja storm games.

When this is done, the flag will fly and land in a random location, which can quite literally decide if you win or lose a ranked game. It is super inconsistent and flags can land 50m away from where the carrier originally dropped them. It is extremely frustrating in maps where there is large death pits with no bottom, so the nearest ground you can stand on is where the flag will leave, and even worse in the Cloud Village where the entire map is floating rocks. The main joy of this game is the fighting, which is really fun and satisfying to do, there is a lot of cheesy moves that are locked behind DLC's but they are very well priced for what they offer at $3.99 and even lower for some. I would much rather them add King of the Hill over Flag Battle, KOTH promotes playing what makes the game fun rather than making corny speed zoom boys so you can cap the flag in under 30 seconds, it is not fun to do and it is not fun to stop.I would normally not have such an issue with a single mode but sadly this is one of the two gamemodes in Ranked PvP, so yeah, it will end up taking up half your time in what is most likely your main activity when playing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: The coop mode is working for random players only. If you want to play this game together with a friend or your daughter, it will end up in disappointment and despair.There seem to be community workarounds for this, which unfortunately work very unreliable. We played the start sequence three times now but the published strategy always failed. In two out of the three cases, there wasn't even anybody playing together with us. _childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: This is, without exception, one of the most pretentious games I have ever played, to the point where I thought Kojima was involved in some way, but there is actual "gameplay," so that rules him out. And you know what? I hesitate to call it "gameplay" because it isn't anything special; it is a very boring walking simulator. Truly one of the worst genres in all of gaming. Sure, the graphics are pretty, but when that's all there is, then it's not really worth it, is it? The game also fails to leave an impression in any meaningful way; there's no gameplay segment that I can point to and say, "That was cool." The levels are bland and forgettable on account of their little to no interactivity; isn't that the whole reason why we play games? People say the soundtrack is good, but nothing really sticks in the mind. The "story" is so lame and appeals to the lowest common denominator because "iT'S A MetAPhoR FoR LifE HuRR dUrr."  You gotta love how pompous and condescending some of the reviews of this game are, calling it "aN exPeRIeNCe" rather than a game. I hope I never get to that point where I think my farts smell good. Another thing I found funny is that there is an achievement for not playing the game for a week. Yeah! They literally reward you for not playing the game, as if I needed a reason not to play this game. Also, the complete game time comes right up to 2 hours, so I can't get a refund.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: Possibly one of the best games I ever played. A masterpiece!I played it on PS3 before (so many times) and there seems to be a few minor changes on the PC version. (New secrets? Probably not but if there are I will find them!) Still most likely a game that I'm gonna keep playing over and over again for years!
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: To describe this game shortly, Journey makes you feel a connection with a faceless, voiceless, and nameless stranger who you met less than an hour ago. It makes you wish the game was longer to experience more of the world and more of the friends you made along the way. I bought this game not knowing anything of it and finished it wishing more knew about it. Great game all around.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: As an avid, long time enjoyer of Sky: CotL, I was ecstatic when its predecessor went on sale last year for Black Friday. Mind you, I had just set up a PC for the first time, and was completely unfamiliar with any PC games than HER interactive’s Nancy Drew mysteries from the early 2000’s, and a childhood spent playing Animal Jam on my parent’s ancient dell laptop- most of my gaming experience had been acquired from the comfort of my iPhone’s App Store- and to be honest, I really do think that Sky is quite an improvement on this game.  Don’t get me wrong, I loved Journey. The character designs, the scenery- and nothing gets me better than a sand sliding mechanic. However, it lacks the sense of joy and freedom that Sky has. Journey has an altogether more melancholy feel, a very lonely and lost vibe that made me very emotional toward the end- which is certainly not a bad thing, especially if that’s your cup of tea- but there is something so tragic about the loneliness of never being able to find a traveller you spent time with in game after having gotten used to the ability to add friends and communicate through emotes in its more recent counterpart.  Aside from these very obvious personal preferences, I also found that the ending left me with a distinct sense of “that’s it?” I was able to complete the game in less than a day, and was surprised that it wasn’t longer. I likely won’t replay it soon, as I wouldn’t want it to get old too quickly- but I’ll certainly pull it out again someday if I feel the need to kick back and play something atmospheric and calming.  To put it simply, this game is comfort food, but don’t expect it to keep you occupied as an open world forever. There are definitely defined levels in this game. I would, however, recommend playing this, and then downloading Sky on your phone (It’s free!), especially if you are looking for something with a more open world that constantly changes and updates seasons and cosmetics. I love both, but I think playing Sky first spoiled me.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: I can't even begin to describe the magic of this game. You never know who your companion is - only their symbol. You form attachments to these players without even knowing who they are, and I just find that amazing. The story, the co-op and the little teaching moments between you and your companion just add to the joy of playing through this Journey. It brought me to tears when I first played, and coming back after a year just deepened my love for this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: This review might contain what some may consider spoilers. It's hard to truly spoil a game like this but consider playing the game blind.Journey is a one of a kind game.The first maybe half hour I was wowed by the visuals, and meeting others along the way was very cool, but a small corner of my mind was thinking about if this was all it was blown up to be.Then, I got to the surfing sequence and decided that yes, this game ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rules. It was a joy and awe that's extremely rare to find, I was smiling like an idiot the whole time. This and the viscerally terrifying section right after that would alone be enough for me to recommend this game to anyone with no notes.I got to the final mountain not long after. It was past midnight, and I considered leaving it for the night to finish tomorrow, but I'm so glad I didn't. I decided to finish it in one sitting since this is a short game and I thought the end wouldn't be too far.Eventually I reached a windy area where someone else was trying to push through. I slowly but surely caught up to them and from that moment, for about half an hour, we stuck together to the very end. They almost got killed at one point, and I was so worried when the wind pushed them off a ledge before I saw the other ledge underneath. The relief I felt for meeting back up with a bunch of polygons controlled by a stranger in the safety of their own home was incredible.I don't know who this stranger was. I don't know if the list of companions met at the end is in any particular order, and either way both the first and last names were series of random numbers, but I know I'll never forget them. I've played plenty of co-op and multiplayer games but none have made me so attached to a complete stranger before, and I don't think this is something you can get in any other game.Thank you, friend. I hope we meet again.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: This game is quite short. Finish it in just over an hour. It doesn't explain anything at all to you, but it's not difficult how to grow your scarf, power up your scarf, or anything. Other than that, there is not much you can honestly say about it. It's called "Journey" and that's pretty much all it is.It apparently has a story line, though I had no idea what it really was, as it just shows it to you in cut scenes between each "zone". And they really don't make that much sense.It looks as though the developers wanted to do something "artsy",  and this is what was produced. Personally, I find "art", the way is applied to today's "styles" pretty pretentious, and completely full of ♥♥♥♥. To me, these so called artists, painting a blue square in the middle of a canvass and then just splashing red or some other color across it, and then giving it a name like "Swan's in Flight"... it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and a way from the pretentious elite to display how much better they are than anyone else.To me, art is a painting with a subject you can actually see and not just paint smeared around on a canvass. And frankly, I don't really get this "game" as "art". I just don't buy it. A personal taste. To me, this was just a boring walk across a desert.

It was a delight to share this unusual and artistic game with you all, whoever you are.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was...something else! Like sure you can call it a game, but it's more an "experience" than a game. _childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolutely perfect example of why the debate around whether video games are an art form is ridiculous. I don't ever want to see it, think about it, or let alone play it again, but I can't recommend it enough. It is a classic that demands no more than a single afternoon.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; A pleasant engaging experience that is brief yet immersiveThis game took just under two hours and for ten dollars (the sale price) it was satisfying enough. The best way I can describe this is like going out for a show or movie, perhaps a ballet or a play. I think a ballet is most accurate.This Journey is just that - a journey following the protagonist through an elegant world with simple controls and a lovely soundtrack. You will neither hear nor read a single word as you travel through this world to your destination and journey's end. You will see small clips and markings as your story unfolds. It is very reminiscent in style for me - in that sense at least - to games like Limbo and Inside. After two hours you will have quietly, through music and movement, taken a journey.If you are looking for a simple, pleasant, and peaceful way to spend a couple hours and clear your head, save this for that moment. It will do your mental health wonders.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: The game started off reminding me of Rime - I think it was the music and the ability to 'call' to communicate with things. It is quite different from Rime though. At first I wasn't sure about it because there didn't seem a lot to 'do' and I was expecting more puzzles etc. But I've played it through twice now and it has a real charm. I think I enjoyed it a lot more when I started playing with someone who stuck with me for the rest of the journey. Thanks JORDY for guiding me through and showing me some of the secrets, and drawing a touching little heart in the sand! I'm sure I will be returning to this game again quite soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: Every single grain of sand and speck of snow is a symbol. When you see it for the first time it's awe-inducing. It gets me to cry every single time I finish, the music is beautiful and finding your companions every playthrough is always unique. Every time you play, you are assigned a new symbol and hold it dear the whole way through. Gets you thinking, gets you looking for every little thing you can find and gets you some really great friends. Always check up on your companions you met after credits and message them if you really enjoyed their company. It's gotten me a few friends on steam, here! Wonderful game with a wonderful community <3

_childDocuments_.review: when journey first dropped on the playstation network in 2012, it instantly became my favorite game, and remains so to this dayim of the opinion that video games can be art, but while im hesitant to call any "masterpieces", journey is the exceptionpick journey up when its on sale, pick it up when its not, just pick it upyou owe it to yourself to play this game

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game. There is something special about travelling the unknown world, trying to piece together the story. And then you meet another traveller. And you continue together. Maybe they can help you when you don't know where to go, maybe they show you a secret, maybe you'll do the same for them. It captivated me.10/10 you wouldn't regret buying it.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr: Though I am an uncoordinated ogre, this game made me feel like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ballerina.Journey is a walking simulator with plenty of platforming elements. It has fantastic visual design, great level design and a fabulous musical score. The mechanics are minimalist. The game is short - about two hours. I strongly recommend playing the entire game in one sitting, ideally with headphones.The controls are simple and progressing through the game poses little challenge even for hopelessly uncoordinated players like me who constantly end up pressing the wrong button. Despite my lack of skill I was treated to fluid, responsive movement that allowed me a level of immersion and control I very rarely get to experience in games. It's a rare treat.The only negative thing I can think to mention is that the camera struggled occasionally - I had one instance of clipping though a rock face that I found surprisingly jarring. This was most noticeable in the beginning of the game and caused little issue.I can see how one may balk at the cost knowing the game is only two hours long, but in this case quality far outweighs quantity. Not to mention that I find Journey to have excellent replayability value. For me, the game costs about the same as a cinema ticket, which made the choice very easy.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen articles written about this game before, and I must agree: This game is a masterpiece. If not for the gameplay mechanics, for the intuitive story that transcends language. I thoroughly enjoyed playing with a companion when I did have one. (I also always had a longer scarf hehe.) Even though it is a mostly peaceful game, there are some moments that actually excited and scared me, and deepened the immersion for me. Will definitely return to the game again in a week for the achievement. :)

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, so I'm not sure where to even start with this so I think I'll start from the beginning. I'm someone who really doesn't review games in general, but this game has made me want to share my experience with it. So this will not be very focused in the gameplay, graphics or any of those aspects, but mostly how this game has... impacted me, as cringy as it may sound.The first time I knew of this game was many years ago, my father had installed the demo for the PS3 and he was enamored with the visual style, the simplicity and the vast world that made his imagination go wild. I found certain charm within the game as well, but nothing that made me too invested in it. Fast forward to this year I was dumped by my girlfriend (I know, I know, drama queen yadda yadda) and I had a void in me. I saw the game again in steam and since it was pretty accesible to me I decided to give it a shot.Long story short, I loved it. The simple but charming visuals, the scope of the world that while not completely explorable it gives that feeling of sheer magnitude that makes you feel small in comparassion. Those sliding moments in the desert felt like rejuvenating joy from childhood paired with fantastic music that simply got you rushing.I am someone who likes rpg lite focused games like Dark Souls and Mount and Blade. Levels, dungeons, quests, combat, conquest. But Journey is nothing about that. It is as its name suggests a journey. No grand bosses, no powers beyond gods, no urgency, just you going from point A to point B. And I wouldn't want it any other way. Journey really makes you feel like going from one place to the other as a beautiful and impactful story either solo or with the people you meet in the way.The first time I finished this game was a couple months ago while encountering other players throughout the journey, it was a marvelous experience. But today... Today I started another journey after feeling blue because of life. And I finished it alone this time. I think I can count in one hand the times a game has made me bawl my eyes out, even more strangely for those tears to be of joy. The final segment made me feel happy, hopeful and left me with the sensation that life is beautiful. Art is beautiful. And everything will be ok. It may sound like I put this game on a pedestal, but honestly I kinda do. I wish to make my own games one day and the sensation this game gave me is one I wish to be able to recreate for other people and myself. As short and relatively simple as this game might be, it is a beautiful and soothing experience that I will hold close to my soul.I look forward to sitting on the couch and watch my father play this game from beginning to end. I know he'll love it probably even more than I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: I've known of this game and yearned to play it for as long as it has existed, but unfortunately for me it never seemed to get published on platforms available to me... Until recently. It's not every game that makes you confidently say that the ten whole years of waiting for getting to experience it were absolutely worth it, but Journey definitely does! It's just breathtakingly gorgeous in every way. In the beginning I was a bit unsure of the multiplayer aspect of it, but even those fears were unfounded: after meeting many travelers along several journeys, I can safely say that this is likely the most wholesome online multiplayer in existence and it might've restored my faith in humanity a little bit. All in all I can't think of a single thing I would've disliked in this amazing game.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: This was aimed more as art than a game. As art, I can understand how others appreciate the style, form, and ensemble. However, as a game, it misses some crucial marks.Repeatability/Length: I only have 2.1 hours because that's all there is to the game. I'm sure if I spent more time trudging through sand to find more of the golden symbols then I would have more time, but I didn't want to go achievement hunting for an artistic emotional experience. It's too long to replay as it's a very slow 2 hours, but there's not enough content to justify any amount of $$$.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: I fell in love with Abzu a bit ago and this game has been sitting in my to-play list ever since. Glad I finally spared the time for it.Journey is a journey of observation, (stress-free) puzzle-solving, and apparently companionship, but also a game of being completely immersed in the atmosphere, the sounds and the music, the lovely graphics, the nuance of a story.The gameplay "is there", it covers the platforming and exploration rather well. It isn't a game about how amazing it is to jump or fly though, it is a game about exploring around, trying things, checking places, which is also how the puzzles worked. Camera behaved suuuper well for a 3d plat/puzzle, steering you ever so slightly on the right direction here and there while not getting in the way of your freedom to explore, real nice.If you're looking for an atmosphere of mystique and mysteriousness, for ruins and sand to explore your way through, for a good relaxed time in a forgiving game, this will be a nice journey for you.Thank you RossettiMay16

_childDocuments_.review: As beautiful, stunning and moving now as it was when I first played it many years. Journey dives into existential concerns about life, purpose, and the ties that bind us all, just as Dune does with themes of power, destiny, and the human spirit. There are no words to describe my excitement for Journey. Every time I listen to this gem, I become happy. Playing Journey is something you're really missing out on if you haven't done it already.

_childDocuments_.review: I was astonished to discover that the fellow travelers encountered along the journey were all real players. This realization transformed the experience into something truly remarkable. Encountering fear in the darkness, overcoming obstacles on snow-covered mountains, and witnessing players disappear midway through the adventure were all part of this unique experience. There were moments I wanted to give up, especially after being attacked by monsters or feeling overwhelmed by the stress of navigating through the snow. Yet, when my character finally succumbed to the elements, collapsing into the snow and the screen fading to white, my thoughts weren't of defeat or sorrow, but a serene acceptance: "now you may rest in peace."This game is a profound journey that evokes the full spectrum of human emotions: curiosity, happiness, fear, and joy, akin to being part of a movie where you're both an observer and a participant. Although I had heard about this game years ago, completing it in just a few hours marked my first foray into its depths. It's not a game for everyone, nor is it something I'd recommend universally. Instead, it feels destined for those who find it, offering an experience that is as unique as it is memorable.

_childDocuments_.review: *This review contains spoilers*Journey was released 10 years ago for the PlayStation 3, and with the traction received by both outer wilds and stray also published by Annapurna Interactive, I think its time to see how this game holds up. Initially, Journey feels very slow, and that's largely due to the very slow movement speed of the player. Luckily, a power mechanic is later introduced where interactive objects, made up what seems to be the same fabric as the players clothing, allows you to glide, albeit a limited number of times. Compared to the slow moving nature of the game on foot, the flying mechanic feels almost liberating once you get to it. In terms of mechanics, there is very little other than this, although the game does find interesting ways to use them. The level design is very linear, and there is no way to fail a level. Holding the W key throughout the game is enough to get through most of the levels, but some problem solving is required here and there. The most interesting part of this game is the way you can meet other players while travelling. This is pretty much hidden, so most players don't know they are playing with other people until its actually revealed at the end of the game. In terms of game mechanics, this is probably the most interesting one, as not only is it cool to see who you've interacted with, but it also ties into the theme of the story.The story itself is kind of interesting. Although its may seem very cryptic and odd at first, slowly as you play the mystery of the game starts to reveal itself. While the story isn't the best thing in the world, it does fit the style and game play nicely and is interesting to think about. The nice looking graphics, while being low poly, do make the game interesting to look at. The story is, while relatively simple, very nice to experience. While there is definitely very much to read into, the simple and short nature of it does leave much to be desired. The soundtrack is an absolute delight and enhances every single part.The biggest downfall of the game (at least in my opinion) has to be the price. The game is very short, maybe spanning 2-4 hours of content depending on how much you're willing to play the game over again. It shouldn't take more than 2 hours to complete, and should be done so in one sitting. The problem is, this game costs 20 dollars, and barely has enough content to warrant that price. If you're looking for a simple and short interactive story, then the game might be for you, however even then I don't recommend buying it at full price. Journey, despite its downsides, will never not be an at least somewhat pleasant experience for anyone with an attention span and 2 spare hours. The game is very immersive, but the length and cost do make me feel like this story would work better as a movie than a game, if it weren't for the unique multiplayer aspect. Still, anyone looking for a decent yet short interactive story game would not be disappointed, just wait for a sale.Thanks for reading.7/10

Be gone!…Ok, so Journey is a kick ass lil game (maybe like 3 hrs top per go thru) about a thing in a robe going on trip to a big ole’ light on top of a mountain. Why? Who cares, just get up there. Because as it should be pretty obvious by the title itself, it doesn’t matter where you end up. What matters is the... Naw, I’m not doing it. But along the way of this adventure, you’ll be treated to beautiful music, gorgeous visuals & brief but authentic moments of interpersonal connection. And while it’s not a mechanically complex experience by any means, it’s one that evokes raw feelings of joy, fear, wonder and sadness. But let’s talk about how huh?So to start, the game’s aesthetic leans toward the simplistic side of the spectrum, but not without letting some flecks of detail shine through. Yourself & the beings you encounter are mostly depicted in ways that emphasize shape & movement, through lots of flowing fabric-like appendages. In fact the only time when something doesn’t move in a wave-like way is when it violently attacks, sending a message that rigidity isn't a friendly attribute in this world. These hostile beings are interestingly made of hard surfaces, seeking to literally destroy those who don’t conform into their solid shapes. This diametric theming also extends to the environment, most of which consists of malleable materials like sand & snow, leaving hard surfaces to make up long abandoned structures or obstacles that are slowly being swallowed by the environment. But plastered onto these surfaces are intricate textures that highlight important areas & effectively add to the feeling of forgotten history. And even though the large majority of each section is dominated by sand, their colors differ fantastically to fit the desired mood. The folds & waves of grains can be tan, pink, blue or bronze and are a sight to behold in the context of their respective parts of the trip. Each almost forces you to accept the feeling the developers want to impart on you. The lighting setups in each of these sections also work towards accomplishing this goal. Sometimes the sun will beat down on you from directly overhead, making you feel dominated by the desert. Other times it'll set itself just below the horizon, silhouetting you & emphasizing the beauty & elegance of your movements. But then in rarer times, in the darkest moments, you’ll only be treated to a few slivers of light scattered through the space, or even have them disappear completely, leaving you feeling abandoned & lost. It’s just all-in-all, a real treat for your eyes.So now that we’ve received the delivery to those eyes, in what’s best described as a left-hand jab, we’ve gotta prep for the strike to our ears. And that’s gonna come at us in the form of a right-hand cross that if we’re not ready for, is gonna hit hard & dampen the effect of the music & the sound design. Now, it's pretty well known by now that Austin Wintory’s score has been universally praised & even earned itself a Grammy nomination. But what’s more important is how that score & EQUALLY (& I’m stressing that so hard b/c I really don’t want the sound devs to be overlooked), the sound design is so complimentary to the aforementioned intensely moody areas & your own movements. In the areas where the tone is light & easy, the music is full of light stringed instruments that flow from bridge to chorus in an airy way, motivating you to move forward with at a brisk pace, punctuated by the sounds of your own dainty steps & smooth sliding action. On the opposite side of things though, when you’re in a tough spot, there’ll be loud & long blows from bassy horns that'll try to make their way through the windy and/or combative sounds echoing from the environment. But, even though they’re in competition, they’re really just working together chaotically to give you as much anxiety as possible. And then finally, there’s the moments where little bits of the good & bad are mixed together. When the game decides it’s time to smack you in the face, real quick, just to stun you for a sec. This is where the set piece moments happen. Where everyone involved in the making of this game is doing their absolute best to make you sit up & feel all the things they want you to. Where the light of the strings meet the dark of the horns, but instead of clashing, they swap sides to make your brain scramble for a moment. And that’s the exact moment when your thing in the scarf starts to travel across the screen with such strange artistry that you didn’t think anything on two legs could move like that. And that’s obviously because it couldn’t in real life but because the sound of its steps, spins & slides sound so damn good, you can’t help but accept the possibility for a little while. And that’s why the sound of Journey is so important.Ok, so we’ve now survived the one-two punch of the boxing metaphor that I created & now deeply regret. But it’s too late to stop now, and that’s because the final challenge is here: the surprise roundhouse kick, the gameplay loop itself. And I actually like how me from 5 seconds ago chose the word “loop”. Because that’s exactly what this game is, a circular experience which is meant to be “journeyed’ through multiple times, preferably with a stranger for you to share the whole experience with. Because the world you get to travel through is a lonely one full of world-building elements that prefer to prompt more questions than answer them. And so it feels good to have someone by your side to help anchor you and share in the amazement with, even if you can only communicate through chimes. And as for the loop itself, I’d describe it best as an adventure gamesque experience, with the majority of gameplay being of the puzzle, stealth, and platforming varieties. And while none of them provide much of a challenge, they’re really just meant to enhance the mystery of the world by encouraging exploration and, more importantly, to strengthen the theming for each section of the adventure. The dark and oppressive segments lean more into restricted stealth gameplay, while the ones that are light and jubilant only consist of some of the easiest platforming ever seen. But because these actions are so well matched to the respective sights and sounds you’re taking in by doing them, they fade into the back of your mind and become instinct, allowing you to engage almost seamlessly with the whole experience.So, all-in-all, Journey is really just an adventure game centered around LOTS of complimentary aesthetics which try, with fine-tuned details and techniques, to make you feel feelings. And I think through the combination of those beautifully crafted visual & audio touches, it easily accomplishes that. But once again, I think it's very important to approach this game openly, with as little skepticism to its reputation as possible. Otherwise, you’re just gonna scrutinize all the details to death & lose the magic. Because while there are dozens of games that have done what Journey did, it was a truly remarkable piece of art for its time & still can be today if you approach it with the right mindset.

_childDocuments_.review: If you’ve spent any time in the indie scene, you’ve surely spent part of it wandering through some beautiful, thoughtful landscapes. Narrative adventures that let their environments do the storytelling have indeed become quite popular over the years. Their origins can be traced to several sources, but a cornerstone of the genre has to be Journey. Originally released in 2012 and only recently freed from exclusivity on the PS3, Journey set the style and the tone for so many games that came afterwards. It suffers a little, then, in the comparison if you happened to play its successors first, but even so it’s not hard to see what makes this such a magical… well, journey.You awaken in a vast desert, clad in crimson robes and driven by a vision of a distant peak. Setting out towards your mysterious goal takes you across a land of ancient ruins, strange machines, and breathtaking vistas. Towering gates and cliffs may stand in your way, but you can do more than simply walk, slide, and hop. Tattered tapestries found along your path can boost you high into the air, and some will join with your own robes to let you jump higher and glide further. They’ve got a mind of their own as well, which will become more apparent as the other inhabitants of this land return to life. And even when these beings are out of the picture, this is not a journey you’ll need to make alone.It’s easy to use a lot of grand language to describe the places and scenery in Journey, because grandeur is easily its most striking feature. The desert you start in seems to roll on forever, with massive structures poking up from the ruddy sands. You can venture far afield from points of interest, farther than I expected, giving the place an enormous sense of scale. This sense only grows as you move on to new areas, with even larger landmarks and bigger spaces to explore. The graphics are simple but purposefully so, focusing on bold shapes and contrasts to draw the eye towards the most impressive forms. It’s a style that’s been widely adopted in Journey’s wake, so much so that I’m sure you’ll be immediately familiar and comfortable with it from the start.As a founding member of this genre, you can expect to spend most of your time wandering these beautiful places. Your character moves at a decent clip, and the features and landmarks you find tell an interesting, subtle story about the world you’re travelling through. You can jump and glide as well, and both of these are enhanced by finding special scraps of cloth that join with your scarf to make it longer and lovelier. Other banners and tapestries of similar material recharge your floatiness, as well as exhibit some interesting behavior of their own. Your one other ability is to speak a sort of tone, which can be charged up to make it louder and interact with fabrics and other objects in different ways. There are some minor puzzles that make use of this, but mostly this is a game about making it from point A to point B, and enjoying the scenery along the way.I mentioned before that this is not a journey you have to make alone, and that’s probably the most unique aspect of Journey. There’s a silent multiplayer system running in the background that pairs you with other players, providing you with a real-life partner for each leg of your trip. They’ll wander around the world the same as you, interact with the same things, and fade out if you stray too far from them only to be replaced by another later on. With no chat of any kind, the emergent communication that springs from the simple gameplay mechanics are a real treat, and I felt an actual kinship with some of the folks I traveled with. You can even boost each other using your voice which can make some sections easier or get you to new places, or simply help you move around faster with long glides.I wouldn’t want to play Journey without this system, but it does have its drawbacks. There’s one puzzle sequence in a tower where my partner at the time ran ahead and did everything for us, which prevented me from exploring or interacting with the mechanics there. I feel like it’s probably the only place in the game where that could happen due to how the puzzle works, but it still dampened the mood. It’s also worth noting that, as strong as the game’s aesthetic is, it’s still a game from 2012 and this is not a remaster. This means there’s a fair bit of outdated design like invisible walls and poor collision in places, as well as some graphical roughness and blurriness in places. My graphics card didn’t seem to get along real well with it either, leaving a few areas blacked out when there was supposed to be some sort of environmental effect.Journey is a landmark game, make no mistake, and a major reason we have so many great games like it now. It naturally doesn’t hold up quite so well when compared to more modern titles, and for my part it isn’t really the religious experience some people seemed to feel it was. I had the same experience with Abzu honestly, which is fitting since it was made by some of the same folks. Journey is beautiful and woven full of meaning, but I enjoy it more for the atmosphere and the relaxing gameplay than any sort of revelatory experience. Definitely check it out if you’re a fan of the genre and missed it before, and then join me in hoping that its clever multiplayer scheme makes a comeback someday.Did you enjoy this review? I certainly hope so, and I certainly hope you'll check out more of them at  or on my !

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game. The whole experience was very nice, but there was a stretch while playing the game that felt like it was exactly what the designers intended. During that shared experience, you can't really communicate other than through sounds, but you can follow each other or show each other around.I went through several levels near the middle game, including one of the creepier ones (no spoilers), and we stuck together and helped each other along in a way that was genuinely moving. Eventually I had to leave to go help my kids with something, and I legitimately felt bad to leave him after 3 levels of dedicated cooperation. _childDocuments_.review: This game was truly an experience; I don't recall the last time a game hit home on such a genuine emotional level.  I cared when the other person struggled or got hurt; finding secrets or successfully making it past the more difficult bits resulted in elated chirping from both the stranger and I that felt truly joyful or that we were happy for one another. We were invested in finishing the journey together, making sure not to leave the other behind.  The first person I met logged out and I was genuinely sad they left; the game paints the feeling of isolation and connection, The 2nd person was clearly someone that played before, but they were very patient and made a point of showing me things or what to do if I didn't see it myself.  The end stage evokes a joyful feeling and I honestly regretted that my partner and I were soon going to part ways. I don't know about them, but I felt a genuine connection during this experience. I think that since they're lost in the shuffle of anonymity it adds to it in a way, keeping the memory distilled to the pure and evocative experience.

The depth of the bondage with players differs every time. In my first playthrough I met somebody who just rushed and didn't take time to explore. I now aspire to be like my previous partner and made it my task to guide lost travelers  when I meet them.Overall, I can only recommend this game. _childDocuments_.review: Quality time.Quite often a thing hard to come by.It's elusive, even planning for it may fail.Journey gave me just that - while it may be short, it felt like quality time.It has a simple beauty to it, both graphically and 'story'-wise. The sand, in particular, has a dreamlike reality to it that I haven't seen very often. The simple character-models, both player and other, are strangely expressive, especially since they have neither faces nor arms with witch  to convey expression"Life is a journey, not a destination" - has never been more true. Especially when what little 'story' there is is somehow turns accomplishment on its head and transforms it into a Sisyphean task. (Ok, choosing between rolling a boulder and playing Journey may seem a no-brainer - but eternity is a mighty long time.)In the final moments of the game - final as in after it, in the credits, came the revelation that elevated Journey from 'good', 'beautiful' and 'zen-like' to something lightly touched by Awesome. Also, the more you play the game, the faster it goes in a way. I now understand why it got so much praise.A first playthrough is about 2 hours, but there's reasons to play it again :)+ Supports 21:9 natively!+ Keyboard, Keyboard & Mouse or Controller, do what you want.+ Beautiful graphics and music+ Implied storyline+ Exploration and replaying is rewarded with subtle upgrades and understanding.- If another player exits the level you move on too :( (this happened once, maybe a glitch?)It's something I will come back to again! Definitely recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: A story of drawing symbols of love and peace with a stranger on a mountain. _childDocuments_.review: At 3 am, curiosity led me to try a new game. Initially, it felt slow and uninspiring at first. Then, unexpectedly, another player appeared. I assumed it was an NPC, moving alongside me. But there was something different. This "NPC" wasn't behaving predictably.Puzzled, I wondered if it could be a real player. Yet, I hadn't logged into any account, nor chosen a multiplayer mode. Perplexed, I continued. Unfortunately , in an underground level, we lost contact, making me question if it was just an NPC after all.Emerging from the tunnel, a player greeted me and it surprised me. This time the signs were clear: I was not alone.Overjoyed by seeing each other , we sang for a few seconds together and continued our journey. We journeyed together, sharing the path and its wonders, reaching the end side by side.Having been without friends for years, this unexpected companionship brought a warmth I hadn't felt in a long time. The beautiful scenery of our final journey, experienced with another soul, moved me to tears of joy.After i finished the game i searched online, and confirmed this game is indeed multiplayer, but unlike any other. It's a rare gem, a beautiful blend of solitude and connection, bringing strangers together in an unforgettable way.
_childDocuments_.name: Journey

_childDocuments_.review: I think there are two slightly different games here. I had the luck to meet someone on the first level and we journeyed together. That took an hour, partly due to not wanting to hold the other person up. It was sweet and nice. The slightly different game would be a solo play-through when one seeks out the hidden things and explores a bit more - that'll probably take ~2 hours.How people went on about it when it first came out about being the new gold was a bit much - but it is nice.I'm a bit of a tight wad - so half price was a bit much: 2/3s off would be better. I suggest getting it on a steep sale - as then other people will be getting it too and the chances of having a play-through with someone will increase (playing at peak times will help too).

_childDocuments_.review: The story line is left intentionally vague, but if you really think about your "journey," you'll realize how much meaning it actually has. _childDocuments_.review: Lovely, short-ish, and oh so scenic game that lives up to its name perfectly. Beautiful visuals and audio combine to make for a very evocative experience, rich in atmosphere and discovery. This is a good job as there's not really that much to do besides an inevitable push towards the mystery mountain, peppered with some light platforming and stealth-like moments. Like the winds that can sometimes engulf you, you can easily get swept up in it, thanks to a wonderful realisation of a world after the fall, with the mysterious history of the civilisation revealed by progressively finding and activating murals. If you enjoyed a game like Gris, then I think this should also appeal on a similar level. Thay have similar vibes, especially in the music, and Journey focuses very much on an experience over a multitude of game mechanics.There's a good chance you won't journey alone as you can meet other travellers along the way, communicating to each other by way of chirps, and abstract vocalisations. Whilst it is nice to meet fellow wanderers, I'd recommend taking Steam into offline mode for your first journey so you can experience it in your own personal way without another dictating the pace by doing and/or activating things in the levels that you should probably discover by yourself initially. I think it's best suited that subsequent journeys can then be partly or fully enjoyed with others if you wish to before going separate ways (world's apart).It doesn't offer much of a challenge but that's not the point. I think this will be a lovely, cozy one to just return to with open arms every now and again purely to soak up the world and get wrapped up in its magical tapestry all over again.And if you doubt you can make it to the end, just, er, don't stop believin',

_childDocuments_.review: WOW.First of all, I want to deeply thank my friend for gifting this to me. I didn't even know it was on Steam 'till it was gifted to me...Again, WOW. This game is... truly an experience. There's no dialogue, no words, no nameplates, no chat, no emotes. A story told through imagery and nameless companion(s) that accompanies you along the way. It was tense, beautiful and an absolute joy to play. When I buy games, I normally buy it based on the amount of enjoyment I'll get out of it. (I like to follow the $1 per 1 hour rule as a guideline). This is absolutely worth it on any type of sale and even full price if you want to. It's short, but like another reviewer said, it's replayability is pretty good. Different companions can change the way you play the game. Slowly, fast, frustrating, and sometimes even alone. The levels and flying around never gets old. tl;dr: get it. I'm so glad it got ported to PC so I was able to experience it.

_childDocuments_.review: Journey feels almost literary in a sense, like immersing yourself in a hieroglyphic script. I found the controls to be slightly frustrating, but I can forgive that for its wholly unique style and emphasis on intelligent, minimalist storytelling.

_childDocuments_.review: I first played Journey on its initial release on the PS3 way back in 2012, and immediately fell in love with the quiet, solemn gorgeousness of it. I remember putting many hours into my travels with companions, some frustrating and some fantastic, but always peaceful in the end. Journey became something of a means of meditation for me, I think. It was a soothing ritual to set out time and again on the familiar road to reincarnation; a small sort of comfort in crossing paths with another traveler and finding immediate connection in the wordless communication of chirps and hops. I played Journey again and again until I no longer had the console to play it on.So it was a surprise and an absolute delight to find it re-released onto Steam some 8 odd years later, completely by accident. Playing again felt like returning to an old friend. Warm, nostalgic, joyful. The simplicity of controls and stylized art give the game a feeling of timelessness. An experience I know I can return to whenever I'd like, still finding the same sense of heartfelt wonder with each pilgrimage to the mountaintop. Thatgamecompany will always stand as my champion for showing just how artful the experience of video games can be.

_childDocuments_.review: Journey is one of the greatest games i have ever played.The game in itself is quite simple, just go towards the shining mountain,but as the saying goes: It's not about the destination, it's about the Journey.During your travel you will meet other players that will accompany you throughout the journey.You are not able to talk to them, hell, you don't even know their name (Although, you CAN get their name after beating the game)The game shows that despite our differences, despite the language barriers, you can still get together and understand eachother, learn about one another, without a single word.For me, THIS is the best thing about Journey!Without companions, this game would not be the same, it wouldn't make me feel as much without them.I have managed to grow such a bond with some travelers and it was always so heartbreaking having to leave them behind.Some of them left early, and some stayed until the very end and I will never forget my first few playthroughs of this game. Actually, I don't think I could really call this a "game", it's more of an interactive art piece!If you do end up playing Journey and want a similar experiance, albeit with up to 8 people, I strongly recommend you play another TGC's game, Sky: Children of The Light! _childDocuments_.review: It's just a chill adventure.I've been told so many times how it's some sort of a unique meditation on the nature of human connection, a milestone in non-verbal storytelling, a deeply original experience, but... it's just a chill adventure. It has puzzles, enemies, little comics, and everything. It doesn't do anything unique.I guess you had to be there and play  when it was just released. It was original back then... except it wasn't. It was released in 2012;  did great non-verbal storytelling in 2005.  did great meditative non-verbal multiplayer in 2005 as well.I can't give  a thumbs down because it's a well-crafted and pleasant game, but it seems like my expectations were completely off the mark. Recommended to people who just want a chill adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: (Attention, the review may contain spoilers)The way was always the goal ...You begin your journey in a desert and explore the surroundings, which are peppered with ruins, perhaps of a long-dead civilisation, a mountain in the distance probably indicating the destination of the journey. Graphically alone, it's an incredible experience. The music is also excellent and the end credits in particular are musically very special and touched my heart so much. On your journey you can randomly meet other travellers, which are other players. Sometimes for a shorter, sometimes for a longer time. You can't chat with them or anything like that, you don't know anything about your fellow player. However, you can emit melodic whistles and communicate with each other in this way. You wear a scarf that can be "charged" on the way, with pieces of cloth that fly around in some places. You can then fly a bit yourself and reach higher places. If you are accompanied by a fellow traveller, you can "recharge" each other and thus reach unreachable places alone. In this game, you dive down into questions of meaning, where does the journey lead to, is the summit really the goal, what lies beyond it. And even after the end of the game, I felt that the game continued to have an effect for a long time, because the summit was never the goal, the path, what you experience and with whom, alone or together, was always the goal. The second time I played the game, I was only alone for the first few minutes, the whole rest of the journey I was with a fellow traveller. You don't know anything about the other person, gender, skin colour, age, but none of that matters. You experienced this wonderful journey together and that's what counts. I was shown places I had never seen before. You could communicate with each other through the melodic whistling, towards the end of the game even in the same beat. When we reached the top, we knew it was the end of our journey together and we would never see each other again ... we both didn't want to go any further, running around each other and whistling and flying a bit at a time. We both drew a heart in the snow almost at the same time ... then walked through the mountain together ... I never had such a beautiful and at the same time sad ending as in this game. In the end, all I had left of my fellow traveller was a rune with letters and numbers ... Thank you for this journey.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an utterly stunning game that evokes a wide range of emotions without even using a single word. Either written or spoken. That a lone is a great marker for how well this game was designed and made. While I am sure there will be a slight difference for everyone who may play this in terms of events due to the nature of how it works. I still think at the core of it people will genuinely have felt a lot of things during it and be left with a great impression of their time in the game.It's an incredibly simple game. With practically only a basic movement system, you can jump and glide and ring a bell while also pinging in an area. It has a beautiful artistic style and really works simplistic pallets to their best without having to overload every area or moment with too much visible clutter. It doesn't lack for beauty and really works the camera and the environments to great effect. Small touches to signal things like health, or being under the effects of something is so intuitive the game basically just leads you with no real interruption to the gameplay nor story.I highly recommend playing this game at least once. It may well be an experience you remember fondly and at worst you'll waste very little time completing it. But you'll support a great game and potentially have a great unique experience that you'll not find in many other games.

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is alright. Nothing life-changing or incredibly emotional as so many have put it in the past. But having gotten it on sale, it's good value, and I finally got to experience a game I had wanted to play for a long time, precisely because of the high praise it had received. I'm sure those high expectations did not help.However, the port itself is terrible. Strangely, I get great performance with graphical settings cranked up to the max, but after suffering several crashes during the Underground Passage section, I dropped everything to the lowest.  After this, the game runs terribly, but at least I managed to get past that section. Having so many frame stutters muddles the experience.And now that I'm trying to get all achievements, still running with lowest settings, I'm again crashing during that section. Unfortunately, the game is not interesting or fun enough to put up with this or look up a patch. In conclusion: get it on sale, temper your expectations, and hope you don't crash constantly. Hopefully you get more fun out of it than I did.

_childDocuments_.review: First things first, lets talk about what makes this game so great.Journey is one of the most beautiful game ever, by it's art style and it's story. It will take you on a unique experience that you will never forget if you like this kind of game.The game is gorgeous, and will get to you without using any words or text.However, I cannot ignore how poorly it was ported.Performance is really not where it should be for a game released on a PS3.A lot of users reported high CPU usage, crippling performance, where there should be almost none for a game like this.When turning the MSAA to max, black halos form around the menu text and performance drop to unplayable levels. Trying to reverse it causes the menu to glitch and the game crashing when clicking apply (using a 7700HQ and a GTX 1070).Releasing a game with this kind of obvious bug is unacceptable and they should at least remove the option if they can't fix it.Lapotps users beware, the game launches on integrated graphics, be sure to switch it to your dedicated graphics card.To wrap it up, Journey is one of the best game out there, who will take you on a chort, but unforgettable adventure.It's just a shame to not be able to enjoy it as it should be because of a rushed poor pc port.
