_childDocuments_.review: Scarf is a game that some might consider beautiful but short, and they will be right to some degree. This game is reeeeaaally beautiful and it's story combined with some very well thought gameplay mechanics makes every second of gameplay enough to recomend it. But in case you need to know more about the game before buying it I've prepared a short "Good" and "Bad" list with some of the most important aspects of the game that you might want to know.-The visuals are outstanding, it doesn't matter if you play in high or low, the game looks awesome always, and it's art direction is really good.-The sound design is quite good during all the game.-The story it's a little bit cryptic at first but as you get more into the game it becomes more and more interesting and clear.-The gameplay mechanics are really good, and the puzzles aren't placed as obstacles, they feel really well implemented with the level design and they give sense to the rest of gameplay mechanics most of the times.-Some might say the game is short (2/3h.), but I'll say that they nailed it in that aspect as they game ends right when it needs to end without getting extended artificially.-I played the game in the 1.0.0 version and I saw some strange performance issues, that sometimes affected not the game itself as they affected OBS while I was recording. I could be playing sometimes at 60fps and for some reason the game would start getting recorded at 20 or something like that during a few seconds (it happened even being static at the same place, I've done some testing on it)-The game sometimes felt really straight forward, but that's my personal opinion as I got into it thinking it would be more like and "open world" game.-Some animations of the chracter are a little bit rough as they feel robotic, especially those times where the camera it's pointing right at you during a cutscene.-The level design is quite good overall, but sometimes I manage to find some bugs or get stuck into some elements of it.-For some reason I've experienced at the desert level some performance issues that translated into some input lag issues.I hope this was useful to you, thanks for reading ^^In case you need to look for a walkthrough of the game or a gameplay of it here you have mine:

_childDocuments_.review: I'm rather torn about this game. There are certain things that I really did like, and there certain things that I just cannot overlooked no matter what. The art design, graphics, level design, the narrative is really good. The music and puzzle has high potential with one major flaw at the end. The performance though is really bad. Really really bad. It might only be Linux, but the game was cooking my GPU, with temperature reaching 87 degrees celcius but performing at sub 20 frames per second at times. Controls is also janked and is only saved by the considerate platform design. If this was an action game, the controls would've failed miserably. If you're on Windows, you might consider it but if you're on Linux skip this entirely or it'll cook your machine. The game looks good with simple and clean graphics but with vibrant colors and contrast. The story and plot is also very interesting where you get a choice of listening to both sides of the story. This is something that I wish more western game developers try. The level design is also very good with the map winding in on itself, good use of terrain and an interesting water mechanic. The platform is likewise well crafted if not a little unsophisticated. The puzzles though very simple but not mindless nor are they lazy puzzles, rather you actually have to put some thought and consideration. The puzzles and level design show the highest potential of what Uprising Studios could do with a little more experience. My only gripe is the last puzzle on the Forest level, a.k.a the hide and seek puzzle is simply very annoying and the last part where you have to hide, the game doesn’t actually tell you what to do and so I’d imagine a lot of people are going to get stuck. Every platforming game whether 2D or 3D must – MUST – get their controls feeling good. No exceptions. Bad controls on a platformer means a bad experience from start to finish. The controls on Scarf is not bad, but not very good. The hit collision is off when interacting with switches or environment and when traversing elevation and jumping as well as input delay when using your move set. The only thing that saves the controls is the considerate platform design that gives a lot of leeway to the controls. The game is also very short; you can finish it in under 6 hours but for the price (at least in my region) the value is okay. The worse thing about this game though is the terrible performance. I haven’t checked on Windows, but this game performs terribly on Linux. On an AMD Ryzen 3700x with Nvidia RTX 3070 gpu, the frame rate is often sub 20 fps and temperatures often reaching 87 degrees celsius even on 1080p resolution on low settings. This is just unacceptable in my opinion, but since it may only be a Linux thing and not a Windows thing, I won’t hold the game against it. This game is okay though it’s nothing great. If you’re on windows, you may want to check it out however, if you’re on Linux or Steam Deck, do not buy this game or it will cook your machine.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start off by saying the game isn't necessarily bad, just the concept isn't very enticing anymore and it doesn't have much of anything else to offer. Sure, the graphics are nice and none of the puzzles are too difficult so you don't need to scratch your head all that much yet feel fun to solve for at least a while but that about sums it up when it comes to the good parts.Then there are the meh and bad parts. The story is here, however it's quite boring and forgetable. Although the puzzles are fun to solve at first, they get repetitive fairly quickly. Also the game is janky and buggy, I managed to make my way across to sections of the map where I wasn't supposed to be, that especially holds true when I randomly walked up to a wall and found myself on the other side without being able to come back so I had to go to the main menu and start from the checkpoint where I left. It's those little things that really ruin the experience for me. On top of that, the game fails to distinguish itself from the competition, since as I previously mentioned, it doesn't have many innovative features (if any). Even the abilities your character has aren't new or done better.You can collect stuff along the journey as well but basically every single game in this category has it so who cares really.The optimization could've been better too, there are parts where the FPS drops a lot for some reason. the game is definitely a mixed bag for me. Even though I like these type of games, I just can't push myself and give this game a positive review. The game appears to me unfinished and rather tedious with nothing significant that sets it apart from other games in this given genre. If the game wasn't broken and had something interesting for the player, I would give it a better rating, still a solid 4/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Upon writing this review, I have played through the game once, getting the "Truth" ending and started a second run to get the other ending along rest of the achievements.I just finished the ocean world, and realized that you do need to collect the "truths" to get the worlds "all secret's" achievements... Due to the poor wording at the re-entry of a level, I restarted the whole game instead of continuing on the already finished timeline to get couple achievements I missed, and now realize I have to play through the levels a third time to go after the truth's again. (Upon first play/read through, I had gotten the image that everything would disappear from my file and reset the whole area, not that it simply hides the things I had already collected.)SO HERE'S A USEFUL HINT: ON YOUR FIRST PLAY-THROUGH DON'T OPEN THE PYRAMID TO LEARN THE TRUTH. Which triggers said ending since you'll need to replay everything to get the achievements! And for the love of God don't restart the whole game unless you want to re-hear the whole story.To the review:Tutorial is easy enough, but funneling the player felt jarring immediately as you meet your scarf.I really wish your "carrying speed" (when ever you're holding an item) would be your actual walking speed permanently or that you wouldn't even have a need to press anything and just automatically run. The character's weight is SO HEAVY it doesn't feel right with their design.The hub-area feels small, but it divides the game nicely. The "spark"-hints in front of the door though can be misleading, as usually the requirements to getting into levels, and not what you'd actually find in there. (Also the fact that the spark that opens up the first portal is not counted in any way throws off the math in general of the whole hub area.)Ocean was a wondrous first experience with how the levels actually could function with it's puzzles. The collectibles though, were a nightmare and truthfully spoken; unfair. (Dev's know what they did.)The desert was fun but felt drawn out due to it's vast size. The collectibles felt too much out of the way for someone to actually realize they could go in certain places. Yes, I understand that they're rewards for exploration, but when things look like you're gonna hit an invisible wall immediately after bonking into one just earlier that looked similar to the other place, you really don't find them with ease as you should.For me, the Forest was the best area to find the collectibles. They felt well earned, and were in area's that weren't too much off the beaten path and HAD path's to follow in the first place if you paid any attention. It almost felt like the forest was the most thought out of area's compared to everything else, but, again, it felt drawn out in certain places, were it not for the lore implications. Except at the "5 puzzle pieces" location, there was some major rendering issues and tanking going on due to the area being too large and too many components having moving parts near the upper are'as waterfall. Oh- and "Hide and Seek" had me confused the longest since, despite the indicator, said indicator wasn't as clearly seen due to the lighting of the area for you to realize what it was you actually needed to do. (Also if the main dev was actually one commenting spitefully on the Steam conversations due to this problem: SHAME ON YOU. THAT WAS BAD DESIGN, OWN UP TO IT, and if possible, fix it in a patch! There was NO indication on what you were actually supposed to do when it was your turn to hide nor that the rules of the game had CHANGED.)I didn't have trouble finding the truths in every level, getting all of them immediately upon first play-through.The environmental storytelling is amazing. The mural's are beautiful and slowly reveal the story to to you as you go on along how the area's have been "decorated". The storytelling through truths felt horrible though. I would've preferred you'd get the whole cutscene per level when you'd found all 3 truths, rather than get a piece of a cutscene that ends suddenly mid sentence. Seriously, that was annoying as I'd need to re-watch the earlier cutscenes again to get a fresher on what was being said before the sentence cut off mid way.In all and all, the game can be janky with it's movements, story gets predictable if you pay attention to the environment (which is actually good storytelling in my opinion, as long as it's not plastered onto your face immediately or in rapid success), and music can be charming! So despite my gripes, I'd still recommend the game to be experienced by others! (Just buy it on sale!)

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes you just want a relaxing game to unwind after another stressful day in the current world, and scarf will offer just that. This game is very light on mechanics both in terms of platforming and puzzles but that really works in its advantage as it allows you to better soak in the absolutely gorgeous graphics and entrancing soundtrack. I really did feel relaxed in my 4 hours with this game and it was suprisingly hard to put down. Some people may find the lenght to be a downside but this gave the game the perfect pacing gameplay wise and narratively. And even though the story and writing could've been executed much better, the animated images and voice over are very well made. The game also telegraphs very well how much content it has, as pretty early you'll be able to estimate how much more you have to go through till the end. Speaking of the end there's two different endings which was unexpected but a welcome addition. This depends on how much collectibles you discovered while exploring the 3 diverse worlds. Unfortunately some of the achievements pertaining to these collectibles are bugged and didn't unlock for me at the end, i still felt satisfied finding all of these. I also encountered one crash and some lag in the final level, which felt like a slight drop in quality at least in terms of polish and technicality. It looks and sounds incredible and works most of the time, so other than a few slight blemishes the game was a worthwhile experience that doesn't seek to challenge you but instead offers a captivating journey away from earth for a little while.

_childDocuments_.review: It's somewhat similar to . It's got parts obviously inspired by . The indie game it's most like is . But if you liked those games you'll probably like this too. It's that kind of "atmospheric experience with light puzzle action where you can't really die but get to explore interesting worlds" game.The controls are a little bit fussy, this is one of those games where there's an unnecessary number of buttons to accomplish simple tasks rather than a single "action" button that intelligently changes what it does depending on circumstance. "Glide" and "swing" with the scarf both use different buttons when it could easily be context-dependent. "Pick up" and "use" both use the same button, but inexplicably there's a different button for "drop/let go", which can make puzzles where you have to drag blocks around unnecessarily frustrating. You will find yourself getting snagged on plants, pebbles, corners, edges and the like. But the graphics are nice with a smooth cartoony style, and the soundtrack is ambient and atmospheric. Despite the game's innocent appearance the story is surprisingly dark, with eldritch elements and hints of Lovecraftian horror creeping into the gameplay. It should be longer though, three worlds only is very stingy, and if you know what you're doing you can get through the entire game on a replay in just a couple of hours.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like what you see in the trailer, then play it. If the trailer looks a little boring to you, or you expect more out of it than what appears in the trailer, it doesn't get more complicated than that. As a platformer, it falls short. The character moves too slowly for the environment and and levels are massive, taking 30 seconds to a minute just to walk from one part of one of the smaller puzzles to another. Its rather unpolished all things considered, most animations and character movements aside, and the mechanics never get more complicated than 5 variants of jumping (Jump, double jump, glide, grapple, etc) used to cross increasingly longer gaps. You push some blocks around that dont like sticking to your character, and when you go to let them go, your character doesnt want to unstick. You walk into a flight of birds, and they shriek at you for a minute before your controller is given back the ability to move. You can't re enter old levels to get one missing collectable you know the location of, you must literally restart the entire thing. (despite the levels having unlockable shortcuts!???) The little idiosyncrasies and lack of polish add up overall to make the game an absolute mire. There are fun bits in here, and the game is beautiful. But while the story starts interesting for a brief moment you suddenly realize that it has exactly one plot point and nothing else happens. You walk into the final boss knowing exactly what is going to happen, 3 hours early. Note; that's the entire game's runtime. If what you want is a cutesy world with a the barest smidge of puzzle solving and the barest smidge of platforming, Scarf will deliver.

_childDocuments_.review: Since the early 2010's, we've been seeing a much welcome influx of indie games with beautiful visuals, minimalistic storytelling and profound themes. "Rime", "Stray", "Inside", "Layers of Fear" and "Aporia" are some examples. And in this category goes "Scarf", developed by the aptly named Uprising Studios in their inaugural project, and published by THQ Nordic's subsidiary HandyGames."Scarf" is an economic project, but it packs quite a punch in its considerably short duration (it took me little more than five hours to complete it, with all collectables). It's a game that fascinated me at each setting it brought me. And with all the puzzles and platforming it tossed at me, I would hardly classify it as a casual game. It may indeed be very lenient with players: there are no enemies, no fall damage, and drowning makes you respawn at the nearest shore. But in the end, it demands too much of players to be considered casual. It is a game with personality, that shows confidence at every challenge it presents us.Let's start with character movement. Following the tradition of platformers like "Banjo-Kazooie", your character will gradually gain new powers as you move forward, from the classic double-jump to gliding. You'll encounter these areas that require certain powers to be traversed, and the way to acquire them is usually by taking another path. The levels are not so open-ended; they're more like these corridors that lead to larger areas in which you'll need to collect certain items or perform certain actions in no particular order. Curiously, if you feel like wanting to return to a level to collect things that you missed, you'll start it all over again, losing the powers that you gained from that level onward, meaning that you won't be able to cut corners. Fortunately, the game has no Metroidvania-like backtracking: there are no areas that can only be reached with powers you would gain in future levels, meaning that all levels are pretty self-contained. But unfortunately, I don't know of any way to quit a level and to return to the hub area, which is a massive lack of insight from the developers."Scarf" has a lot of platforming going on, with moving blocks, jump pads and small rings meant for swinging. I guess that's a central aspect of the game, but sometimes you'll need to carry something in your hands and you won't be able to jump, meaning you have to follow certain paths carefully. Other times, you'll come across this glowing orb that has the power to repel water from around you, allowing you to walk underwater - I should mention that you can't swim in this game (in fact, water is the only thing that can "defeat" you). And, as it's common to such platformers, you'll sometimes drag large objects to activate floor buttons or to reach new areas. Strangely, in the control scheme, you grab items with a key, and let go of them with another. I saw no point in it and it was so counter-intuitive at first: if there was a point, I would have noticed and understood.The game is divided into three levels: an ocean level, a desert level and a forest level, in this order. Once you gain a level's main prize - these runes in possession of little creatures - you'll open the path to the next level. A way of the game to point players into points of interest is by having the dragon/scarf leave the character and go to a certain area, and without it, you'll be powerless. So you might as well see what your buddy wants you to see. At larger areas, you may have to find these light threads that, when all collected, will open a path moving forward. At other moments, your dragon/scarf will be powerless, so you'll have to go across an area - without your powers - to collect light orbs for it. And then, there will be moments when you'll come across puzzles with critters, as packs of rabbits need to be lured away from objects of interest with apples, and crows need to be scared off with a mask or by a gust of wind.The levels are seamless... for most part: at a moment in the desert level, after I collected a key, I had to backtrack all the way to its door (but there may have been a shorter path I missed). And there was this ultra-obnoxious moment when I played hide-and-seek with one of the creatures: seeking it was already a bore as it was, and when it was my turn to hide, I didn't know what to do, since the game didn't communicate to me my objective. So I kept on thinking I had to lure the creature to the dragon/scarf, when what I was really meant to do was to interact with its spot while it was gone looking for me. But those were small sore points from what was otherwise a game with very well designed levels.The game is a moderate collectathon. It does have its collectables in the form of paintings, toys and "inks", which are these dark orbs. When you collect such orbs, your character will slowly get visually darker, and you'll see these cutscenes telling this story about... well, I'm not going to spoil anything, but to be fair, you can see the ending coming from a mile. The curious thing however is that, once you collect at least six orbs, you can open a pyramid in the hub area and have a different ending.Now, everything you saw in the stills is true: this game looks magnificent. It's a feast for sore eyes, and a carefully crafted work of art that focuses on lighting and colours rather than graphic fidelity. The desert level really made me feel like I was in this oasis temple in the middle of an arid hot desert, and every time I saw a body of water, I just felt like taking a dip on it, like refreshing in the cool, nice pool... but once again, you seriously can't swim in this game. The forest level brought me memories of "Rime", feeling like this ancient temple from a long gone civilisation. The game represents the Unreal engine being used right."Scarf" is a wonderful little game that is fun, satisfying and hits the spot, if also imperfect. If you're in the mood for what it is offering - a quasi-casual platformer - then you should take it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game looks and sounds beautiful, I won't deny that, but beyond that it has... not much of quality.The platforming is rare and slippery when it does occur, the puzzles mostly consist of lugging objects back and forth or memorizing a picture (or waiting!! yay!) and the collection aspect is butchered by the game's need to reset -everything- should you fail to 100% complete a level. So, yes, I ended up using a walkthrough to play through the second and third stages because playing them a second time would be more trouble than it's worth. Oh, and, get used to tons of repetitive cutscenes - every time you have to put the scarf back on is another 10 seconds down the drain. And this is a minor gripe, but... you basically have to play through the entire game twice to see both endings, and consequently get every achievement. That sucks. Don't do that. The game is not remotely replayable and definitely not good enough to warrant that.More importantly, the game's performance is crap. I don't even think it's just a graphics issue either - it almost feels like this game doesn't have the good grace to only render what's on-screen at any given time, because some specific rooms caused the biggest FPS drops (down to single-digits in the desert and forest at times!) and checking my memory as the game was running I saw absurd, unreasonable numbers. The game definitely doesn't look good enough to warrant the extreme level of performance issues I faced. I also noticed it doesn't load your graphics settings on startup so have fun resetting them every time you boot up the game.Even the performance issues aside, which definitely impacted my enjoyment of the game, the game itself is at its core not good enough to recommend beyond that - it's just very tedious to play without being particularly clever or feeling particularly good to move around in. Beautiful aesthetics and nothing else, really.

_childDocuments_.review: This game wants to be somewhat like journey, at least that's what it reminded me of. _childDocuments_.review: Scarf is a little, relaxing game that offers a little bit of everything. Its three worlds are packed with exploration, platforming, some puzzling and a nice story that starts in one way, but then evolves in a different truth.If you're looking for a challenge, keep looking: Scarf is very easy, there's no getting stuck. I'm not saying this as a negative thing, it's just a statement, I guess it was the developers' choice to keep the game more entertaining than challenging and that's ok. Despite being short, Scarf offers a great variety of mechanics and situations, staying interesting and fresh throughout the whole adventure.The only two real cons I found in Scarf:- the character feels a bit "heavy", especially while jumping. You almost never die, but I feel when it happens it's mostly because of miscalculation in leaving the platforms. The experience could have benefit from some more refinement in the controls. However, the game is very generous when it comes to checkpoints and savings, so you never end up repeating large chunks of world because of an error.- replaying a world erase all the progresses in that world, forcing you to retrieve all the collectibles. There's a warning telling you so before re-entering, and that's fine, but saving what you already found would have been much, much better for replayability. My suggestion is to deeply explore the levels the first time already, because the collectible are hidden, but not hard to find if you check every corner.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun and worth a play. The platforming mechanics are solid and the scarf/dragon is used to turn some traditional platforming features into a companion. Overall I recommend a playthrough.There are some gripes for achievement hunters/completionists. The game forces you to replay levels in their entirety when going back to hunt collectibles, including unskippable cutscenes. Then there is no "return to hub" option so even after you're finished collecting, you have to complete the level again to get back out.In addition, there are two achievements that you can't get without intentionally missing certain collectibles (collectibles which present themselves as very important to the story). You wouldn't know this without reading a guide before playing. This essentially forces you into a full second playthrough of the game. In my opinion the game just doesn't have the replay value to warrant that and it's not worth it to me to go back and get those last two achievements.

_childDocuments_.review: So far, it's a LOVELY game!If you like Journey or Abzu, you'll like this one!It has a lot of similarities, but a lot of things are different/unique for it to be its own thing.Pros:- LOVELY art direction. You could probably already tell that from the store's screenshots and trailers, but this game has great artistic direction in both its colors and environmental design.- Lots of variety in gameplay! So far in my playthrough, you can double-jump, slingshot, swing, and glide. Which helps keep movement around these levels very enjoyable. Puzzles also keep things fresh with new mechanics very frequently.- Great story-telling! Outside of the lovely painted-like story cutscenes, there's a lot of visual story-telling in the paintings and architecture. You can even collect drawings about their culture.Cons:- Meh optimization. The stability is very solid, but the framerate switches between good and poor. Nothing too bad, but that depends on if you are okay with it hitting 30 fps at times. name: No Longer Home
detailed_description: Bo and Ao are graduating university and preparing to leave the flat they’ve lived in together for a year. Thanks to visa limitations, Ao is forced to return to Japan, leaving Bo in England. Disillusioned by post-educational life and shoved aside by a government who doesn’t want them there, both are trying to come to terms with their uncertain futures. And deep under their South London flat, something grows... Wander through an intimate flat and examine the everyday belongings of Bo and Ao. Have BBQs, play video games, and stay up late just talking in bed. Follow the day to day activities and conversations of two queer, non-binary students and their friends. Get to know Lu, the multi-eyed, animal-like new flatmate. No Longer Home was born when the developers were similarly forced apart after university, and decided to stay in touch by working on a game together. Development duo Hana and Cel chose this project as a way to explore and express the emotions that came with saying goodbye.

short_description: No Longer Home is a game about letting go of the life you've built due to circumstances beyond your control. Immerse yourself in the lives of Bo and Ao and learn about their dreams, frustrations and fears. Welcome the magic of the everyday and somewhat extraordinary.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to preface this by saying I play a lot of visual novels so I am the ideal audience for games that are very text heavy and don't have much in the way of actions. I don't dislike this game because it lacks shooty-bang-bang. I dislike it because... it fails at everything it's trying to accomplish. To it's credit, it at least has the decency to be a short game with a two hour run time as it's problems run so deep they can't be fixed by adding more story. The premise of No Longer Home concerns Bo and Ao, two college students in a relationship who are living in a cheap flat in London. They are about to graduate university and faced with the life changes that accompany that: feeling like you at a total loss as to what to do next, friend groups slowly drifting apart as paths take you to different places, that anxious feeling that you made a mistake and will end up working a minimum wage job forever while buried until student debt. Bo and Ao have to come to terms that their relationship may be over since Ao, as an international student, will be forced to return to Japan and there is no guarantee of returning to London.This sense of everything coming to an end is something I remember strongly from my college days and was excited to see it represented in game form. Unfortunately, No Longer Home is one of the driest, most meandering stories I've ever read. There are two inter-related things that the game needed to pull off to work: a) characterization through dialogue and b) characterization through environment. The way the game plays is that you walk around the house interacting with things that will advance the plot forward, and the plot is composed of dialogue scenes. Just the characters talking until the game ends without a real resolution -- which honestly is to be expected when the story's about a couple hitting an intractable impass, so I'm not dinging it for that. What I am dinging it for is Bo and Ao are about as interesting as paint drying. I don't care about their relationship because I never got a sense of who they are as individuals, and if either of them was my placeholder boyfriend I would not be fighting for this relationship either. The dialogue between them is dry and boring. They feel a lot less like lovers enjoying their last few days together and more like two acquaintances trying to make awkward small talk. Their heart to hearts tend to suddenly swerve into socially conscious lectures - like a conversation late at night where they discuss their fears about the future suddenly turning into a TED Talk about gentrification.There are a few awkward and weird attempts to flesh the characters out, but nothing really sounds sincere. By this I mean, one of the characters is hinted at having depression, but the way they talk about it sounds less like it was written by someone with depression and more like it written by someone very familiar with depression posting on social media. And there is a bizarre moment where Ao goes into a room that previously was blocked off and meets a monster who is supposed to represent his poor self-esteem. It was not relevant to the story in anyway and we never see it again after that one brief appearance. Environmental detail should have been important in carrying that wistful sense that you are leaving something important behind but I found it vexing that the descriptions did not match the appearance of the diorama-like town house. The visuals say cluttered but not filthy, but the written descriptions give the vibe that the place is a pig-sty. Like the bathroom looks clean but the towels are so nasty they are growing fungus. The music works very hard to establish the mood. It's twangy slow guitar, and it's really the only thing that feels contemplative and nostalgic. Any atmosphere would disappear completely if you muted the soundtrack. The long and short is that the writing is really bad. It is not up to the task of telling a story like this, which I hate to say since the game makes it very clear that this is based on the developers' real-life experiences. I guess sometimes lived experience doesn't automatically come with the ability to express it in an engaging way.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly, my review is unlikely to count towards the review score, as I was a Kickstarter backer, and my licence for the game and the OSTs was provided as a CD key redemption.That said- I do recommend the game.The opening chapter Friary Road is not a true representation of the complete game. It gives background to the story and the 2 main characters. It is skippable only after completing it fully one time. After that you start the main story.Not really a "Visual novel" in the way most people think of them these days- it is not anime, no physical battling, etc.This is an Interactive Story, point-and-click, where you wander through the home shared by the main protagonists and their flatmates.The art is colorful and minimalist. The way the scenes merge from one to another is quite interesting, and quite pleasant. The music is unique, and suits the game very well. Relaxing, with small points of tension at the right times.The narrative choices are interesting, and I am not yet sure if making different choices results in different dialogue being shared- 2.3 hours was my first playthrough, and I will test this on my second playthrough when I look to unlock the last 2 achievements that I missed the first time.Not completely fictional- the story contains some obviously fictional elements (the creatures you meet and talk with- the inner monsters we all carry with us in our heads?), but the story is based on the real-life experiences, feelings, and emotions of the 2 main developers. It is not a "for everyone" game. If LGBTQ+ bothers you, you aren't likely to understand the emotional side of the story, but then again, you may learn something if you are open-minded.For me, the game ran well on both my laptop (MI GS 75 2018 model) and my desktop (i9 9900K/NVIDIA 2070 RTX Super/32 GB DDR4 RAM @3000 MHz) and I suspect it will run well on my old Windows 7 Quad-core toaster (though at lower settings, I imagine. I'll run it on the old girl for my next playthrough to test it).The game is a short experience, and you may need 2 or more playthroughs to unlock all achievements. The OSTs are quite good- relaxing, escapist music good for chilling out when you need to or want to. Yes, as a Kickstarter backer I paid a bit more than you will if you buy the game alone, but I knew that going into it, and the OSTs were included in my backing pledge. Price/hour is a bit high for some people, but games are not cheap to make these days. I feel it was worth it- YMMV and you may want to wait for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Graphically and stylistically too derivative of Kentucky Route Zero, and as such I had a difficult time investing in the extremely short and, unfortunately, boring story; two characters have finished University and now must move on with their lives. It seemed a bit.... self important and indulgent. It felt weightless. The conversation around privilege due to finances felt extremely disingenuous. These characters clearly are not poor, yet speak as though the have it rough. Indeed it is a beautiful designed game, as it is based almost exclusively off of KRZ. A nice touch here is the ability to rotate the scene and the added sound effect when done so. Unfortunately, some of the icons that denote interaction didn't interact and I had to click more than once. Occasionally when attempting to open a door nothing happened and appeared to freeze. Having only one location to explore made the whole experience too insular.I don't recommend primarily due to how short the experience is. I bought it because I wanted to support the developers and honestly, that might be the main reason one should buy it. Here is an expensive first project, but maybe with money they will make something more substantial at some later date if this small team doesn't disband. Just don't expect much from this experience.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: A short game about the shared anxiety among newer generations regarding adulthood and the future.  As a millennial, I can certainly relate. My parents' generation told us all that if we went to college/university, that we'd, more or less, be guaranteed a decent life, but that was a combination of illusion and wishful thinking. I thought this issue was more American, considering the late-stage capitalist hellscape the US is, but this story takes place in England, where it would seem gen Y and/or Z is having similar issues. It even discusses the gentrification of parts of London. I guess any country infected with capitalism is prone to failing new generations. What are we to do with our lives? What is the future going to be like? ... We all get to worry about that together, I guess. The game has a lot of abstract symbolism, which seems fitting. There are also several accessibility options; there's even a link to a free screen reader. I recommend it to those who feel quite the same way about life.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Home is a 2 hour story about two non-binary art students anticipating their long distance relationship. The art style is clean and comforting, the music is soothing (if not mezmerizing), and the writing is pretty decent. I've had to let out a smile or a chuckle here and there, and by the end of the game I noticed myself caring a tiny little bit about the characters. It feels like a game developed entirely by artists, for where the artsy aspects shine, the design falls short.Movement and interactions feel sluggish and non-responsive, often trapping you while the camera is slowly zooming out. And for a game with such an emphasis on reading, a small italic font on a transparent background might not have been the best choice. But my main point of criticism is the apparent meaninglessness of interactions and dialogue choices. features dialogue sections in which you can answer as any of the people involved in the conversation. This abruptly breaks the connection between the player and the player character, and removes the whole point of the conversation. These sections made me feel like a 4 year old playing with a couple of dolls, doing the voices for each one of them as I made them talk to each other, and it made me question why I was even playing this game in the first place. At some point talking to the second protagonist turned them into the player character, which emphasized the unity of their relationship through gameplay quite nicely, but I wish the game would have leaned into this mechanic a bit more instead.On top of that, the choices within these dialogues held no real value. Sometimes you're only presented with a choice between which character to speak as, which felt completely arbitrary (as discussed above). And the rest of the time the two dialogue options don't differ enough for my brian to register it as a choice. All this results in sometihng that's more akin to a silent movie than a game.The art, music, and prose were good, but in the end they could't offset the poor design.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to enjoy this game, I really really did. However, it's two hours of slow-motion camera panning, object clicking (there are begonias growing from the cabinets, but the cabinets don't change in appearance?), and it's hard to follow the overarching plot long-term.I'm prone to migraines and ended up with a headache and nausea from the camera angles and wall flipping. Maybe someone would enjoy this, but I'm not sure I'm that person.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: A two hour walking and commenting upon objects simulator. A lot of object commentary regards peeling paint, dead plants, and mold growing through cracks; it sets the tone, but it's overly played. Players simply progresses to the next stage with an illusion of choice. That's part of the theme, but it's not quite compelling content for a game.Anxiety, angst, and ennui unnecessarily pepper dialog. There is no resolution to be had for any issues the leading characters face. Character growth does not exist, and there's not any plot to be had from it.Well written dialog, shame it never goes anywhere.Great shoegaze soundtrack though.

_childDocuments_.review: Finding good games with well-developed LGBTQ+ characters can be challenging. While there are certainly games that have included those characters, and even developed them well, those games are sadly few and far between. It’s even rarer to find an LGBTQ+ character represented as a main rather than a supporting character.  is one of those rare quality finds. follows Bo and Ao, two students just graduating from university in London. While both Bo and Ao are non-binary and use they/them pronouns, in many other respects they are very different from each other. Bo is a native Londoner, while Ao is from Japan; Bo is funding their education with student loans, while Ao’s schooling is being paid for by their parents. The game takes an introspective tone as the characters navigate the major life event of transitioning from university to post-university life. While they pack up their flat to move out, the game explores themes surrounding adulthood, such as student loan debt, job applications, taxes, and affording rent, as well as gender identity, such as dysphoria. Hints of magical realism are also incorporated. is semi-autobiographical, based on the lives of the two main developers Cel Davison and Hana Lee, also both they/them pronouns. The story may resonate differently depending on the age of the player. Players who are more similar to Bo and Ao in age (early 20s) or stage of life (university or recent graduate) may find the game more personally relatable and immediately relevant, while someone who is in their 30s or older and several years past that part of their life may find the game more reminiscent of their past experience.Included in the game is a 10-minute prelude called , which takes place a couple of years before the start of  and before Bo and Ao move in together. There is an option to skip the prelude if desired, but Friary Road is mentioned by several of the characters throughout .Since  is interactive fiction, the mechanics are fairly simple, but still more robust than many visual novels I’ve played. The player alternates between playing as Bo or Ao and can make dialogue choices for them as well as other characters in the story. The playable character can be moved around the environment, which can be fully rotated in 90 degree increments in order to get a different perspective of the space and open up different options for interactions. Icons pop up for looking, talking, or touching depending on which part of the room or place is being viewed.The game has an interesting way of giving instructions regarding how to play, such as saying that the function of your actions may seem abstract and try not to worry about it, or saying that going through doors will help you gather a sense of place. The game autosaves, although players can also choose to manually save. However, there is only one save slot per playthrough (although you can have three playthroughs on file total).The art style for  is minimalist, with characters having no eyes or mouths, yet each character is still visually distinct. The environment is represented in a visually interesting way, with a two-point perspective that can be rotated 360 degrees to, for example, see all four walls of the room and the spatial relationships. Since the game is taking place over a span of time where the characters are moving out of their flat, as the game progresses you can see the effects of slowly packing as objects disappear from walls and boxes appear instead. The animation style is also distinctive, showing the walls floating or sliding in and out from the sides, top, and bottom of the screen to construct or deconstruct the rooms or yard of the flat or widen the view when entering a more mental space.The music for  uses piano and other instruments with synth in the musical tradition of video game composer greats such as Nobuo Uemastu of  fame. The main composer and sound artist, Eli Rainsberry, is also non-binary, and they have crafted tracks that dovetail perfectly with the story. The included ambient sounds also enhance the overall experience, both the sounds that are evident to the characters (such as ambulance sirens or the cat purring) as well as the sounds that are for the player only (such as the apt sounds that play while rotating the environment or while the dialogue text is being typed on screen). While the sounds and music are excellent in and of themselves, I also really enjoyed that the game provided audio descriptions - text describing the music and sounds. I found this text added an interesting extra component in interpreting the game. I imagine that the audio experience would be even further augmented by the recommended use of headphones, but I was able to fully enjoy and immerse myself in the experience with my speaker setup.  has 12 possible Steam achievements. It may be possible to unlock them all in one playthrough, but I at least will have to do a second playthrough to pick them all up. is a brilliant example of LGBTQ+ characters and stories done right. At $14.99 at the time of review and approximately 2-2.5 hours for first playthrough, the game is technically a little expensive in terms of time/content for price when compared to a movie ticket, but I think it’s still worth buying at full price for its treatment of subject matter that is so often handled poorly.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is a simple game about letting go of the life you've built due to circumstances beyond your control. You get a close look at the lives of Bo and Ao and you learn about their dreams, frustrations and fears. This is an Interactive Story, point-and-click, where you wander through the home shared by the main protagonists and their flatmates.No Longer Home is fine for what it is, but feels like it could have been so much more. The writing is really well done and the characters feel real and well thought out, and the game really hits that "life in your early 20s" vibe that's a crossroads of frustration and uncertainty, but at most times it feels like its dragging on in conversations that are not interesting and not contributing to the story at all.Overall, I did really find the characters and storyline interesting. I genuinely wanted to know more about them and where their story would lead. You know, how the situation between them would change or if it would stay the same, how would the characters evolve and improve themselves, but then the game was over, without any further progress on the story or characters. No finalization of anything. I also find it sad that all those metaphorical symbolisms remained unexplained and vague.In the end, No Longer Home is a decent story based interactive game with LGBTQ+ main characters and relatable story, but it falls short with the storytelling and the story progression finding it's end. I would recommend the game, if you find it on a really good sale, but at full price, the game is not worth it, therefore I will not recommend this game. I wish there was a neutral option for steam, but sadly no.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Mixed feelings about this one. I say I recommend it just to push up the avg review score, but honestly, I wouldn't recommend it to most people. I enjoyed my time here. It is less of a game and more of a time capsule, both specific to the protagonists and yet relatable to most. 20-somethings who have experienced the sudden thrust into society and been a bit lost. Pressure from family or society pushes against your own desire to do something different. Frustration at yourself and the world for going through the whole academic system and still coming out rather unprepared on the other side. And some rather newer struggles many younger people feel these days about sexuality and gender norms.I never finished uni myself but still had a lot of the same feelings and worries depicted in this. To be honest, I had mostly forgotten them. Having sort've relived them through this game, through the lens of a 30 something year old, I realise that it was a bubble that seemed like a mountain at the time.Any piece of media that can remind me of feelings and times long forgotten, and allow me to reflect on it with a different perspective, is something quite special.I will refrain from giving this a mark out of 10 as it just doesn't feel right for this particular game, but I will recommend this game to anyone going through any of the struggles I have mentioned, or anyone who did years ago and wants to relive it a little.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home had a great deal of inspiration from Kentucky Route Zero, it is a short game which can be completed first time round in under two hours. The game itself is an enjoyable point and click narrative if you are prepared for reading dialogue and the mundane reality of university, figuring out what to do next, I empathised with this aspect as I went through this myself after graduating. It can be hard to figure out a path in life when you are unsure of what career you want. The developers did state it was semi-autobiographical game and I could relate to the themes portrayed.The game itself does not have the eloquence of KRZ in terms of its writing or the length. I do think the price point should be cheaper because of its length and factoring in its price point, however, I did enjoy my time with this game so I will recommend it and suggest buying when it is cheaper.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: €15,- for an incredibly slow, short game?? Definitely overpriced, and I'm glad I got it as part of a Humble bundle with games I'm actually interested in. I can see why this game has mixed reviews. There are some good points (soundtrack, art style, LGBT+ representation), but overall... the experience was just a snore fest. The animations are slow, the camera motions are slow, EVERYTHING is just... so slow... Personally, I cannot recommend this game, but if it feels like something you would enjoy, you can be your own judge and decide for yourself
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: I finished this game in less than 90 minutes my first playthrough, and that was even taking time to explore the environment and reading all the dialogue. I played the first 1/3 of it a second time to get a couple of achievements I'd missed in my first run. About a quarter of that time wasn't time that I could spend interacting with the game - it was time that the game locked my character in place and made the camera zoom in, or out, or pan around, really slowly. It was frustrating at times.I was excited for this game, which is why I was a little let down that I didn't really find it enjoyable. It feels less like a narrative, which goes somewhere and includes some growth or at least change, and more like somebody venting for an hour and a half. The characters begin the story facing both emotional and real-world problems and by the end they've made progress on...none of them. The problems they're facing also don't take place during the game. It's just a little snapshot of life as two twenty-somethings who are unhappy and don't ever do anything to change that. I'm currently somebody who is in their age range and is facing the same uncertainty of graduating from a university soon, and I found both the story and the characters unrelatable and difficult to want to spend time with.This game is also obviously hugely inspired by Kentucky Route Zero, taking a lot of design elements straight from it and even having an easter egg reference KRZ directly in one instance. I've now played both games, and if you're looking for a narrative based game in the magical realism genre and are torn between these two games, I cannot recommend KRZ enough. If you're dead set on this game, pick it up while it's on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: *no spoilers contained* At first I really enjoyed the game, even though the screen rotation system, which won't work until the previous turn is over, and the interaction icons not appearing unless I approach close enough were kinda disturbing. I really found it interesting about the characters and storyline. I genuinely wanted to know more about them. You know, curiosity of where this would lead to and how everything would change or stay. But then the game was over, without any further progress to solve my desire as a player. I'd say I'm very disappointed to not have the opportunity unless they give this game a sequel. I also find it sad that all those metaphorical symbolisms remained unexplained. I kinda get a grip of how it is standing for the situation and mental status of the protagonists, but I wish it could be more clear as the story continues.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: After reading the review that this game is about LGBTQ+ characters and after watching the trailer where you can see some mystical creatures you definitely be curious and after a while buy this game.So, you get a story about two students who live together in a big house. Ao and Bo are not in the relationship but they respect each other and as a player you learn about their problems (adulthood, society acceptance of their gender, etc.) and after a while they are going to move out...The main problem is how could you write a story about student's life SO BORING? It's says that it's a semi-autobiographical story but the story is... just plain.The graphics is not the strong point in indie game though the visual idea where the environment is represented with a two-point perspective that can be rotated 360 degrees looks fascinating. Autosave here is quite annoying. You need to replay the whole game just to know what leads after choosing the second/third reply and you can't skip the dialogues.The game wouldn't be unmemorable if developers had written more lore about Ao, Bo, their friends and neighbours.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: This a really moving story of two non-binary final year students where one is having to move back to Japan forcing the couple to go long distance. Some really emotional scenes about not feeling like you belong and some mental health discussions as it is clear both characters are struggling mentally. Perfect game to try out this pride month!
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Although the art style and narrative focus are unique, it feels like paying for someone's prototype student project. It doesn't really have any concept of pacing, and although the story is relatable for many, relatability isn't enough to carry a story - it needs to be impactful.It could also do with a clearer description of the length of the game and what the gameplay is like.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home takes you on a journey of finding stability and navigating life post-education. The good: - the game boasts a truly unique art style with beautiful visuals that reflect a clear and well-executed vision. - the audio work is impressive, immersing you in the ambiance of terraced houses on the outskirts of London's first zone (was kind of waiting for the sound of screaming foxes in the background, ngl).The bad: - gameplay tends to be on the dull side, mainly involves walking around the house, pointing, clicking. - the writing feels like a direct transcription of real-life conversations, but unfortunately, it falls short in creating a meaningful connection with the characters... it leaves you feeling more like a spectator at a puppet show. It's not a bad game per se, but grabbing it on sale makes more sense, imo the full price does not justify the ~2-4 hour experience it offers. Despite my hopes for an emotional pull and connection, it unfortunately fell short. There are a lot of similar games that do this better, e.g. Unpacking or Night in the Woods.Overall rating: 2.5/5.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: I liked and disliked this game... but I'll lean towards liking it because I liked what it aspired to do.  How the game went about achieving it though, I disliked.  I'm a big fan of emotional games like this, but this one was rather boring to me.  There's so many different dialogue choices and none of them really feel like they matter.  There's hardly any cutscenes or events that make  you feel like something important and should be remembered is happening.  it's kind of like a dull... end of time kind of feeling, but I suppose that's what you're supposed to feel.  An end is coming, and you're supposed to take everything in and brace for what's coming.  The art style is interesting, reminds me of Untitled Goose Game and Donut County.  I suppose this can be a great experience if you're really trying to take a break from other traditional games, but it just didn't quite hit any marks for me that would make me remember it or even really want to mention it to others.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Games like these all come down to how well the story is told, and how you as a player connect with the narrative and characters. I didn't mind the slow pace (at first), I thought the minimalist graphics were fine, and I quite enjoyed the music. However the way in which this story was told did not grab me. Everything felt a bit too... hazy? Like all the dialogue was written to evoke an emotional response of nostalgia, but for me it did not, so it just felt meandering for meandering's sake. I did actually enjoy the characters and sympathised with their plight, but the slow pace of the game wore me down over time and I stopped caring after the main point of the story had been reiterated for the hundredth time.The main mechanic of flipping the world around also felt a bit superfluous. It just served to slow the pace down further, for me it didn't enhance my experience at all. I'd also agree that it's overpriced for its runtime of <2hrs. All that said, I admire the developers for making the game that best represented this period of their life, and commend them on being vulnerable enough to make it.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Having been a long time follower of Humble Grove's work, it's been a delight to finally get to play , which is a project that I know went through many iterations before crystallising into the game it is today. It was well worth the wait.If you’re into weird, deeply human, slow-paced point and click games that will haunt you forever and probably make you cry a bit, then you’re in for a real treat. is a game that wears its heart on its sleeves. It’s extremely confident in its writing, and its ability to convey emotions and small fleeting moments, and the game doesn’t shy away from its influences either. It’s always nice to see such earnest work out in the world.The art style is gorgeous. Every detail in the environment is lovingly rendered, making the small flat feel lived-in and all the more heartbreaking to leave. The soundtrack is also incredible, there’s a moment in the game that pretty much brought me to tears and the music is what really brought it all together. Magical experience.I can see myself coming back to the game whenever I feel a bit lost and need to ground myself and be reminded that in time, things will be OK.Yes the game is short. Yes it costs money to play it. Personally, I think it’s worth it, but I’m also a short games goblin so... *shrugs*
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this game was an interesting experience, but it had its ups and downs.One of the first things I noticed was the camera movement. Turning around and moving back and forth through the rooms could get pretty dizzying at times, mostly at the start. On the other side, I really liked the animation and art style, it wasn't the kind you are use to which gave the game a distinct look, although it could be improved. However, the game is very slow-paced. The characters walk slowly, and changing rooms takes a while, when talking with other characters there is always this silence waiting to be able to continue playing, so don't expect any fast-paced action here. Another thing that was kinda annoying were the dialogue options. The choices you make don't really affect the conversation, which feels pointless except for getting certain achievements.It was interesting to dive into the characters' lives and choose answers for different characters tho, which I haven't see in many games. A problem i noticed is that, sometimes, if you interact with a specific object, you might lose the chance to interact with another one later, which was frustrating.Personally, I didn't feel very connected to the characters. Even though we get an idea of their thoughts and worries, it wasn't enough to make me want to explore the different dialogue options deeply and therefore get to know them more.Overall, it's not a bad game, but it's not amazing either. It's nice to chill with if you are looking for something low-key.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: This game felt like a chore to play. Writing is good, dialogue feels very authentic, story is interesting if a bit mundane (but it's not really about the plot, it's about the characters, so that's fine). But overall, the game isn't engaging. This would have been far better as a graphic novel than as a game. It's barely interactive, and the interactivity feels like work.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: no longer home captures the hazy, ethereal nature of lying around with your friends hopping from topic to topic of discussion, losing track of time, having your poignant thoughts tumble out unexpectedly. the backgrounds drift in and out of focus along with your own. one second you're talking about a painting in the hallway and the next you're interrogating the nature of yourself.i've written before about how i think games that get in and get out within two hours are the Exact Right length for narrative games, and this is no exception. i love the pacing and length of the game, but somehow i almost wish that there was just liiiittle bit more to sink into.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is an authentic and often unsettling story about the process of moving out and moving on. Of course, every player will take something different away from their experience playing, but it is an experience that I highly recommend. With beautiful designs, excellent characters, and a great soundtrack, No Longer Home is well worth picking up.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: I had a tough time getting through this game and pretty much just ended up barely registering all of the dialogue early on and only completed it to get it off of my list. It was hard to connect with or care about Ao/Bo even when I had faced similar feelings of apprehension, lost, trying to self-identify, and the like. A lot of the dialogue seemed disingenuous or sort of faux deep especially when trying to touch on depression. The way they communicated with each other and their friends felt like just acquaintances and I was being put through minutes of empty small talk. Aside from that, it was difficult to get actions to register and many times I'd end up across the room because I somehow clicked the action of something across the room even though I was trying to click on a microwave in front of me. It started feeling slow and tedious with the panning in and out that you could not skip and the character movement somehow felt how I felt dealing with how much panning in/out there was. The dialogue choices were inconsequential and some of the choices seem kind of silly to be saying. This game just was not it for me.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Thankfully I got this game on sale through a certain website, and if I had gotten this game at full price I would've been beyond disappointed. There just isn't enough content to justify a 15$ price tag. The game is incredibly SLOW paced- it took me 2 and a half hours to complete something that should have been an hour tops.  It is so slow that i found myself disengaged during the last chapter and just clicking trying to get the game to finish. Oh and there's no way to skip dialogue that you've already read, so if you're trying to 100% the game, you'll have to sit and click (slowly) through it all again.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game a lot. The art is impeccable, the music is a masterpiece (it's my favourite kind of music), and the way the level 'pieces' float and construct themselves is truly astonishing (it really adds this element of atmosphere and reality breaking down). Thoroughly enjoyed the games minimalist, soft art-style and the camera movements are delicious too.I think there is something to be said with just telling a story. Having a story be told is enough (imo). I really connected with subject parts of the narrative, specially Bo (me being from England and being LGBTQ too did help - thats not to say non Brits, or non-LGBTQ's wont, there is something here for you). It is a lovely and thought provoking snippet of two people's lives and their emotions at that time. I think it does handle the subjects discussed goodly, however while in the game, I did find myself needing a minute or two, to process and understand what was being said - which was absolutely fine, since I could take a minute by not progressing the dialogue to reread and grasp the subjects being discussed. I found myself wanting to know more about Ao's and Bo's flatmates Controls are simple and easy to grasp. They worked perfectly fine for me, when I clicked on icons and the ground to move the game did just that. I enjoyed exploring the home, which being so small, enabled the game to be more intimate.I enjoy short, emotional, art games - of course everyone wants more (who doesn't). I would love to see how this story progressed, to see how they both ended up emotionally (but perhaps again, that was too painful or too personal), but hey, short game-play time is not a downside to me :) extending from this, the dev team is fairly small and creating a game like this was no easy task. Adding or extending game-play would have added huge amounts of time onto the dev process - so congrats devs, i see you!To summarise, for me, the art and music of No Longer Home is the best thing about this game. I do hope there is a sequel, if not, I'm excited for the next game!8/10

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely short story about change, uncertainty and all the feelings that come with it. No Longer Home tells its story through a mixture of writing and exploration with a beautiful use of audio and visuals. Its story focuses on the very grounded idea of graduating and moving out of your house but sprinkles in elements of the surreal to reflect the various emotions of the characters.While the game may be too short, or lack enough interaction for some players, it’s overall aesthetic and presentation is worth checking out for anyone with a love for narrative.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful, chill game. There isn't much of a plot beyond what the synopsis already tells you. This game is rather about reminiscing, regrets, anxieties about the future... _childDocuments_.review: Beautifully crafted game that explores themes of transition, friendship, and the bittersweet nature of moving on. The heartfelt dialogue and relatable characters resonate deeply with anyone who has faced significant life changes.The game's vibrant visuals create a warm atmosphere, while the soothing soundtrack enhances the emotional experience. However, the character movement can feel a bit unpolished, as they sometimes continue walking when obstructed by game objects, disrupting the flow of exploration.Overall, No Longer Home is a touching and introspective journey that captures the complexities of change. I highly recommend it for those seeking a narrative-driven adventure that lingers in your thoughts.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR - Only tentatively recommend- Interesting art style- Great soundtrack that sets the tone well - Potentially relatable content for post-uni city dwellers- Love the representation from the protagonists- Not a lot of player agency in enacting change in the world; feels like a long, drawn-out conversation- Choosing responses in a conversation from different characters feels a little unsatisfyingIn all honesty I felt like the game's dialogue went on too long in places, and became tedious to go through as the key concepts were rattled out. While the themes came through clearly, I didn't feel comforted or empowered by the journey of the characters throughout the game. Felt like I was witnessing my generation experiencing a crisis, with little in the way of resolution. Feels like it could have been covered in a graphic novel, rather than a game, as the interactivity with the world itself is so minimal, taking away player agency. I also became a little frustrated by being able to just choose responses from different characters throughout, rather than pick a response for the protagonist I was playing as, and receive one in return based on my choice. Additionally, the relationship between Bo and Ao could have been explored more deeply;Overall interesting concept, but I don't immediately want to replay it. Tentatively recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has surreal interpretation of scenes and elements and the surrounding ambient music coupled with chill guitar tunes to set the mood, text adventure game within a game, simple polygonic graphics with UI that is from primitive early age of computer graphics, straight lifted from the Kentucky Route Zero from 2013. When you borrow things from creation of others you must draw a line. It's one thing to say that they were 'inspired' by KRZ but this level of copying is shameless in my book.But how is this game really? Dialogues are boring and have a repetitive theme of what they could've done and how it was in the good times. In short, self pitying. I am often referred as a very pessimistic person by the others but even to me reading through all that was pretty exhausting and depressing. As a result, whole game feels like eavesdropping your not-so-special neighbors over a fence or a wall, which might be interesting for a while, but gets annoying after some time. The game's length is also very short, some talking, one BBQ party and following gaming session, some more talking and you're done.A very shallow experience, especially for the price. Hard to recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually buy narrative games but I saw this nominated for the game awards and gave it a shot. The game is short and details the time a lot of young people go through at the end of university/college where you have no job and have to reluctantly go back home to live with your parents for a bit. The prospects you thought you were getting in university haven't materialised yet. You thought you were an adult but you are going back to being a kid again. The city around you won't stop changing. You lived in a dump. You love your friends but know that you might not see them again for a long time ...or ever. Everything is changing but it hasn't sunk in yet. The place you lived wasn't perfect but it was home. Your hobbies are incredibly dorky. Narrative wise, the game is good. You get a sense of two people orbiting each other and then having some final goodbyes with friends. Meeting their anxieties manifested as spirits. Having a final talk where the two realise this might be the end for them and blaming circumstance, their identity, themselves, etc. The ending is slightly more hopeful. Gameplay wise, it's slow. Moving around the apartment is a bit of a chore. A few of the superfluous details that you can look at could have been removed (e.g. saying the building is falling apart too much). It does the job but little else. The game art is simple and effective. Music is full of spacey drones and noodling. It fits the setting.All in all it was good and relatable. You get a real sense of the two people who made it had/have a deep affection for each other. I wasn't surprised that the in the credits was a message from one wishing that they could live together again one day (and good luck to them!) I guess the game wants to say something akin to 'change is a lot like loss' or 'we can't control the things that control us'.  It's a bit sad but that is how these things go.

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is a deep audio-visual experience, with a bonus of maybe petting cats. And the beautiful narrative content and themes that follow along with it. The visuals are stunning, the story is great. And damn it. As much as I love deep dialogue, the content here really resonated with me. Being queer, and a just graduated art student. And down to the details of owning a borrowed record player from my parents, and wanting to quit school foundation year. I love how the game builds up simple choices and a sense of direction. Being able to influence how the narrative is told, and feeling like my choices really followed through on the next sentence. That's not always a given in games, that the dialogue resonates as well as it did in No Longer Home!I have to say the most impressive feature- is being able to rotate the room. The simple 3D environment and shading works great, with a sort of abstract feel. Which further emphasizes the characters' feelings. The interactions and accompaning audio really drew my focus into the game. Music, audio design and simple effects works great as a part of the experience, and playing with headphones (as said in the game) is a must-have.Subtle environmental animations are great, with lighting and shading doing most of the work- Good move! And the objects of the environment perfectly conveys the lived in space, down to details of crooked cabinet. The london townhouse seems perfectly sized for this 2h little adventure. Best enjoyed in one sitting (I really stretched it out to 3h + a little break). My advice would be- don't rush through it. If you play this game, I invite you to stand still for a minute. sometime you're a bit into the game. When the audio-landscape is a bit bigger. And just notice the details in the environment. Close your eye for a second. And maybe you hear the neighburs, a cat purring, or city traffic.And a bit of nitpicking- simple ui, symbols and fonts fit nicely to the otherwise minimalistic and abstract styled game. During dialogue option it would however be nice to have a bit more visual difference between the selected text choice. As for animations, character walking isn't completely smoothless and was noticeable a couple of time, but with interesting dialogue I didn't focus too much on it. Also after seemingly stealing the mop and bucket- and putting it in the kitchen. It was still visible on the stairs the day after sleeping? Confused. And my last question I was left with- what happens to the cats when they move out?Thank you developers- for making this game. And delivering a great narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: This game is deeply personal to its creators, but it also turned out to be personal to me. I, too, spent several months in London uncertain about my and my family future, trying to figure out life. Thus, the imagery, the struggle, and the themes felt familiar, dear, and nostalgic. This is not as much as a puzzle or an adventure game as it is a story that you somewhat control or rather follow. Don't expect much of a challenge, just flow with it and feel it. I am, certainly, biased, but I think that the authors achieved their goal with this game, even if none of us, or especially because none of us, knows what the goal was.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is fine for what it is, but feels like it could have been so much more. The writing is really well done and the characters feel real and well thought out, and the game really hits that "life in your early 20s" vibe that's a crossroads of frustration and uncertainty. However, I really feel like it cuts itself off in its first act. What's here is great, but I was really interested to see how the relationships of these people developed or didn't develop post leaving the place they considered home. I don't think it's bad to leave your audience wanting more, but you have to balance it correctly so that people can fill in the gaps themselves or have been with the characters long enough to mentally piece together the next steps in their own head.If a year or two down the line the game received an update and there was even just another hour added as a sort of epilogue to what's presented, I'd say the game is definitely worth trying out, but in its current state it just leaves me wanting more.
