_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the game, it left a bittersweet feeling in my heart. I enjoyed the experience to switch between the perspectives of Bo and Ao. It added depth to the story, as you see the shared apartment and their life together, as well as their own individual story and struggles through both sets of eyes. The whole atmosphere of the game was subtle but effective in the way of emphasizing themes of disorientation, belonging, and change or...well the end of something. One of the aspects I like most about the game is how the environment constantly shifts, almost like a dynamic theater stage. The transitions between locations and perspectives might be disorienting (maybe even unpleasant) for some, but I found it perfectly suited to the story's tone.The music/sound complements the atmosphere perfectly. It adds to the overall experience without overpowering the narrative. In this case less really is more. My first impulse was to write that this is a "cozy" game, but I would describe No Longer Home as more melancholic and contemplative. It’s a quiet, very slow and short reflective experience that might not be for everyone, but if you’re in the mood for something that speaks to the quieter, more introspective parts of life, this game is definitely worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: My recommendation comes with some caveats. If you don't like slow games that are all about walking around and reading a bunch of text, this isn't for you. If you aren't nonbinary, depressed, anxious, poor, or a part of some minority, this isn't for you. That being said, I think this game does well at what it sets out to do, which is tell a deeply personal story and be relatable to certain kinds of people. As a nonbinary, depressed, anxious, poor person myself, I certainly related to Ao and Bo's struggles.

_childDocuments_.review: It made my breath falter and my heart wail. The game is way, way too pricey for what they have got to offer. The scene transition was smooth enough, yet the character movement animation was sloppy. There wasn't much to do. It's more of an interactive fiction than a game, and it's not that interactive, if you ask me.But, yes... the game made my breath falter and my heart wail. Perhaps the feelings the two protagonists went through were universal, or a cliché, you choose. Their doubt, uncertainty, and fear expressed through their dialogues were mutual among people of common experience in life transition. If you are a freshly graduated who are lost, then perhaps this game might give you a pause. Or a reflection. It won't guide you in any way. Yet, all in all, this game is a great reminder to you all who are lost that you are not lost alone, and in the right time, for some people, something like this is most needed. Please note that this alone outweighs my decision to rate this game down. Purchase with caution. P.S. personally, the ending was inexplicably impactful and perfectly encapsulated--or concluded, or accentuated?... words elude me--the whole  of the two. But I really wouldn't want to recommend a game just because of some favorite ending. So, really, purchase (or not) with caution.

_childDocuments_.review: is a semi-autobiographical narrative point-and-click adventure game features an incredibly compelling story about the process of letting go of the past and moving on.The game follows two non-binary roommates named Bo and Ao, who share a flat in London. They are both preparing to leave university after graduation and are struggling to find a job and find meaning in post-education life. The setting perfectly illustrates what life is like at the age of university, with the mess and clutter that kept me extremely nostalgic.The low poly art style is a wise fitting style for . Each character feels distinct, even if all of the people are faceless. The way colors and lighting are used is perfect, and each location feels incredibly unique. The way the rooms change when you rotate them is also a fascinating design choice to watch in action.Overall‚  is an authentic and offer unsettling story about the process of moving out and moving on. Of course, every player will take something different away from their experience playing, but it is an experience that I highly recommend. With beautiful designs, excellent characters, and a great soundtrack,  is well worth picking up.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: NLH is a game made with a great deal of care by very talented people. There’s a lot to explore in it but that’s really on you, the player, to engage with. I’ve played through it three times now (only once on steam) and every time I discover something different I never noticed before, or find a different path to go down. I do think it trusts the player to want to engage with it and think about it and do the legwork. I think it’s probably easy to rush through and that’s where people get short playtimes but it’s a game worth relaxing into and making the effort to explore,For people that have struggled with depression or mental health issues NLH feels very familiar, it’s a story, snapshot, of these characters lives, in a small isolated area. It takes place mainly in one small flat and even when the setting changes during the ‘Between the Leaves’ section it’s not going outwards, it’s shifting inwards. Deeper. During the BBQ you can see the shadows of the clouds shift across the garden and you know that there must be a sun to cast them, but you can’t see it. The way you, the player, see the world is very fixed. Ths isometric view makes me feel like I'm observing the characters in a studious, detached way. For some reason that makes me feel closer to them though, we’re all our own voyeurs, and the sections where the camera sweeps in and gets really close feels all the more intimate for it. Almost frighteningly so. It happens when characters are talking about their feelings and fears and they feel vulnerable at that point. They were safer in that isometric view.Ultimately though, for all the things it makes me feel it’s a game about hope. A good one at that. The mental health issues hit closest to home for me but there’s a lot tied up in there about the violence of capitalism and borders, it’s not navel gazing. It’s in fact a very special journey, one that’s worth engaging with.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is an absolute amazement!It's a deeply melancholic exploration of loss and uncertainty. The game follows Ao and Bo for a day or two at a turning point in their lives, right after uni, before they know what is coming next. Set in South-West London, Ao is being forced to go back to Japan due to visa regulations, and Bo also needs to leave the apartment and thus their other flatmates due to rising cost of living and not having transitioned into the job world, yet. The game takes place in their flat and the backyard, as they reminisce about the time they have spent there, about the lives they have led, about their perceived failings; personally and as part of a demanding society with very unclear guidelines on how to successfully navigate one's life. Both are at an impasse, without any directions for their future, and struggling with their identity.If you've been in any kind of similar situation, this game hits home way too close. It plays out as a point-and-click exploration with lengthy choice-based conversations, leaving a lot of things unsaid and lingering as unspoken truths and ways the characters see themselves and the world around them. There are many other things that make this game excellent and hauntingly beautiful. The conversations and repeated exploration of the space of the flat itself are dispersed with stage-theatre and dream-like scene transitions that make this game truly shine. The immediate surrounding walls of their flat-and, one can imagine, their everyday boxed-in mindspaces-often fall away and dissociate to give way to their lingering and hauntingly beautiful melancholic imaginary worlds.Dissolvement of boundaries of identity is also a core part of the game in another way: instead of following and "playing" as one character throughout the game, the narrative dialogue choices and perspectives are frequently transgressed from one character to the next. You can often choose not what is said next, but who says it, which enables a symphonic arrangement of voices, but also let's you silence out entire characters if you choose to not engage with what they have to say. This multi-perspective narration reaches one of its heights when we're given the voice and perspective of a neighboring couple that the main characters only ever surmise about. This is also one of the moments where the stage-theatre qualities of the game are executed so flawlessly, literally shining the spotlight on these side characters, giving them their own moment in time and space to be filled with life, instead of just being an idea in the main characters's heads. These kind of techniques are rarely found in video games but are a testament to the maturity of the medium and art form that they are today.Last, but not least-at all-is the music and sound design. The game suggests upfront to use headphones while playing, and I absolutely have to agree with that. The meandering conversations, the exploration of space, the scene transitions are heightened to an immersive experience I had not expected with a point-and-click exploration game. Getting into these characters's heads and imaginary spaces is an experience you want to shut out your own surroundings for. The intimacy and imaginary worlds that are opened up through that are just astounding.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a strange case. I moved multiple times, watched flat shares break apart, said goodbye to people I lived with for years, experienced anxiety about what to become in life, uncertainty about choices I had made, felt the pressure of parental expectations, had periods of existential doubt, consider Kentucky Route Zero one of the best games of all time, in short, I've made many experiences that should make me resonate with this game.But I didn't resonate with it. Not at all.I played it through one evening and found nothing: No memorable characters, no relatable writing, no emotions that mirrored my own. It's just puppets rambling that passes by, with you a spectator watching from outside and finding nothing to latch onto. Normally I'd be the first to defend this kind of game against people demanding conflict, involving gameplay, pacing and character arcs, but I won't do so, because I feel like the game simply failed at what it set out to do: Make a phase of growing-up with all its turmoil and uncertainty relatable.

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is a semi-autobiographical game by the Humble grove team. The game is about two recent graduates Ao and Bo saying goodbye to the home they shared throughout their studies.Felt I could relate to a lot of the themes explored from being a recent graduate myself and also nonbinary, having difficulty finding a place in the world. It’s one of those stories that you need to hear, to be reminded that you are not alone in your experiences or situation. The art style uses a lot of geometric shapes, scenes tend to unravel then disperse with many shapes to make up the building blocks of the world. We are given an aerial view of the house, as if it were a doll house and we the player are moving the characters around, looking through the house from different perspectives. Despite there being a lot of motion in the way the player can rotate the house, move the two characters and interact with objects or other characters. There is a stillness to the game, this sensation that time stops when you are alone as the character, moving through each room and discovering secrets in the house. And time only starts moving again when you interact with other characters or move onto the next sequence. It reminds me of what it is like to dissociate and to lose perception of time. You get so caught up in your own isolation that you forget about your environment and the world around you. We don’t really see the world outside of the house apart from a brief section of the street. The only instance is the sequence where the characters are playing a choose-your-own-adventure game and it takes them through a forest. I guess to create this impression that this place is the most familiar to them and what feels like home out of the rest of this world. It feels more like a memory in a sense to capture that autobiographical image, that this location is the scope of the memory and we are unable to leave it as we will be met with an endless void that exists outside the house.The music as recommended goes in par with the game, it is very dreamy and suits the atmosphere created. It can feel both soothing and isolating, lurking in the background while you explore. Instead of voice acting, there is a sort of “du-du” sound, to mimic the typing sound when pressing keys on a keyboard. As if someone is typing up a journal entry while reflecting back on these memories, you can notice this in how the text in the speech bubbles gradually appears with “du-du” sound for every section of text. Also there is a click sound every time the player clicks on a particular object to continue this effect. Every time the player rotates the room there is a sort of “sifting through boxes” sound, as if the narrator (or us) is trying to remember specific details in the room. I really enjoyed this game, I played through it in the one sitting after I came back from holiday. It was a nice change of pace from the fast-paced action heavy games I was playing at the time. Definitely would recommend to anyone going through similar experiences with their identity or currently dealing with burnout. It was nice to have nonbinary protagonists for a change, I feel it has been long overdue. I hope to see more games of this genre, you don’t really see too many semi-autobiographical games on the market.

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is a small-scale indie point-and-click game, where you switch roles between two students who will soon be graduating from university and are faced with employment and relocation issues, as well as relationship struggles.It's also grossly overpriced for the quality and length of the game.Additionally, it's loaded with insufferable, angst-ridden twaddle masquerading as deep, meaningful dialogue.Positives: It didn't take too long to complete it....but given how generally slow the game felt and how irritated I became with the navel gazing, head-up-arse dialogue, it felt twice as long.  Oh and the graphics are moderately decent to look at in a low-poly way.Meh:  The controls are clunky and the camera doesn't always let you see what you want, resulting in some obscured environments and difficulty getting the right view of clickable objects.  The movement of the characters is also glacially slow.....almost as slow as the pace of the game/dialogue.Negatives:  Did you ever find the character of Holden Caulfield a bit of an annoying, whinging prat?  Did you think that maybe, just maybe, the play Hamlet should have been shortened by at least an act and two or three soliloquies because of how the character just constantly goes on and on about the futility of his existence and whether he should end it all (over and over and over)?  Well, then don't even dream of getting this “game” which is filled to the miserable brim with two characters who do nothing but bemoan their academic existence, and whether they've made the right choices at university, and what they'll do afterwards, and whether they've wasted their time and their parents' time by taking these courses, and on and on and on and on, and NONE of it is interesting or compelling, it's just wank!Totally not recommended, and at 15 USD for this boring, glacially paced excuse for woe-is-me existential ennui, it is not reasonably priced (I got it in a bundle for about three or four bucks, and at that price, if you are someone with a stronger stomach for characters with no emotional spine whatsoever, then it might, MIGHT be worth it).

_childDocuments_.review: It's simple: this is Cultural Marxism disguised as a video game. For reference, I gave this a chance, and finished the game with several achievements. Let's start with the good, because credit is due where credit is due:- the moving geometry designs are really well executed.- the music and sound effect are spot on. Little details here and there give the game its charm.- the game won't make use of it, but supports ultra wide screen (ie, it will boot and run at 21:9 on a 32:9 screen).Now for the bad.- None of the characters in the game are engaging if you are the kind of person who works for a living. You know, if you're part of the working class, or god forbid, if you are 'priviledged like a doctor or a nurse' (both of whom receive scathing commentary from the protagonists). Literally hunchbacked, walking as if they were 80, they spend their time whining about how their (actually privileged) life of drinking and playing video games is boring, aimless. They have no dreams whatsoever. Going to uni in Japan (I wish I ever had the money to do that) paid by mum and dad feels to them like a death sentence. - You can control their dialog but nothing can exit the themes of 'gentrification', 'capitalism' and noting that 'there was a marxist era (??) but that led to "some bickering". Let me help you out honey,  has a list of the millions dead as what you describe as 'bickering'. - Everyone in the game is 'non binary' and visually represented as such. Pronouns are strictly VERBOTEN. In fact, one of the characters laments 'how their Korean parents don't know how to use their pronouns'. Yeah the same Korean parents who paid for your fancy Japanese university and travels to the UK so you can pursue education in 'music' and 'arts' ??? Oh boy do I pitty the parents to have created such offspring.- Finally, as an ultimate affront to common sense, the very same characters benefiting from open borders and lax visa policies forewarn the players of seemingly dreadful immigration laws. Thing is, I AM a first generation immigrant to the UK. My kids are brown and 2nd generation immigrants. I did research if at the time of the game release there were any rumors of such laws. There was none. There are none today, in fact, immigration to the UK is at an all time high, and my family benefited from this directly, complete with a life saving intervention from the NHS to my (foreign) grandfather which cost him nothing. That's the system they hate. Finally, and quite hilariously, the way the character speak in this game is as if it had been written by Americans - no slang such as 'quid' instead of 'pound' is used. I never said this about a video game but it's utterly tone deaf, self pitying, self-loathing, divisive and probably the only video game sanctioned by ANTIFA. The only 'good guys' in the game are the workers briefly depicted building crossrail from under these lazy pseudo-intellectuals too busy to enjoy the smell of each other farts to have ONE decent idea of what to do with their miserable lifes. Absolutely pathetic. And if you hate capitalism so much, please tell me why you charge for this game? I'd like my 7.51 pound back please, I guess I can't, can't I? Also, why release it on STEAM? Surely by your standards STEAM is evil. Funny how that works hey? Pathetic - 0/10.

_childDocuments_.review: The same day I played through most of this I also played through another short narrative game about being a twenty something insecure about the future and nostalgic about the recent past-and this was a much smoother and better designed experience.  Obviously influenced by Kentucky Route Zero, no bad thing thing since that is a great game, you play as two protagonists as they have conversations, get lost in their own thoughts, have surreal encounters, and wander through their apartment that they will be forced to vacate soon. The only downside to the game is that in two hours it did get repetitive (when you aren't having longer conversations with someone, you basically trudge through the same six rooms looking for flavor text).  The upside is that I did feel like I knew the characters as distinct people by the end of the game, not just generic genderqueer narcissistic art students which they could have easily come off as if the writing wasn't as good. I don't know how often this particular moment of life needs to be gamified, but I am glad these developers used their life experiences as inspiration for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home wears its inspiration on its sleeve, having a scene from the opening of Kentucky Route Zero on its protagonist's computer screen at one point. It bears some resemblance to KRZ in its dialogue system and set design, but taking place over a much shorter time-span and much smaller space. This is a nice little slice of life game about a couple of recent college grads about to move onto the next stage of their lives. Taking place the day before the big move, it deals with a lot of the stresses and anxieties that come with not knowing what comes next in life, how your relationships might change, what personal and societal expectations there are for your future, and how the market forces of capitalism muddy the waters even further. While the visual elements are steeped in magical realism, the semi-auto-biographical nature of its writing gives the story a very personal feeling that lets you really linger in this moment of the characters lives. It would have been nice if it had more time to really delve deeper into some of the topics it brings up, but for an exploration of a small moment in life, I enjoyed the brief time I spent here.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Playing out like a stage play amid a floating, cosmic backdrop, No Longer Home elegantly wrestles with one’s place in the world, or indeed the universe, asking to what extent any of it might matter at all. From Cel Davison and Hana Lee, No Longer Home is a semi-autobiographical point and click story title that charts the anxiety of stepping out of university and into the uncertain wildland beyond where many of us are doomed to be lost. Their character surrogates, Ao and Bo, are in the very last days of university life with the past 4 years of their life seeming a fleeting breeze gone by, and leaving them now directionless and without opportunity. You take partial control over their story, choosing their conversation pieces, but ultimately this story is one that is doomed to slide away from you as it does the characters. With wonderful art direction and deft writing No Longer Home manages to pack itself full with questions and ideas in a little over 2 hours. On the face of it this point and click game in the vein of Kentucky Route Zero might seem straightforward, but there is plenty to be gleaned from this uncomfortable, often otherworldly, journey. _childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is such a beautiful game. I love the art style and a lot of the game dialog really resonated with me. It's a beautiful experience with queer representation. It's a nice slice of life story that allows you to explore in multiple ways. I was provided a code to check out this game, but I would have bought it and streamed it for my community and I regardless. I highly recommend checking it out.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: I was one of the Kickstart Backers and immediately saw potential in the game. I wasn't disappointed. It was a short but intense experience and certainly very hearfelt. It reminded me a lot on Kentucky Route Zero, a game that has inspired so many marvellous indie games. I certainly enjoyed the small reference to that.The feeling of being lost, of the uncertainty of future, of leaving a place that so long has been a home is very relateble. I wrote many of the dialogues in my diary, which usually speaks for a good game. I wish it could've been longer as many concepts seems only been brushed upon and kinda rushed. There  is certainly so much more potential in the themes and the directions the game goes.The only criticism I can say is that sometimes the movement of the rooms was a bit awkward and I didn't have the feeling that I got all the things to interact simply because I didn't move a room into a certain direction. It also disrupted the interactions if you accidentally moved the room around, which sometimes was annoying.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: I appreciated the opportunity to play No Longer Home it was a bittersweet story of having to tackle saying goodbye and getting through those sometimes paralyzing moments before that moment comes. I appreciated all the relatable talks of the worries of trying to decide what to do with your life while struggling with the idea of /why are we saddled with the pressure of having to pick one thing to do with the rest of our life?/ as it is in my opinion a lot of what people in our generation struggle to think through. No Longer Home was sweet and worth a playthrough, thank you to the devs for your hard work with the game.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Not gonna lie, some parts were slow but I liked the whole idea of discovering a character. My favourite parts about the game: the fact that you start off with only seeing one view before you transition into flippable geometry, the fact that you play as both Ao and Bo, the fact that they're non-binary, tiny little things like how the bathroom haunts them, cats that you can pet, hahas and all these snide little remarks about railing against the forces of capitalism as an artist but also being restrained by those very forces (arts student sedness).The other concern I see being raised is the abrupt ending. Not sure if there'll be a follow-up chapter because a previous developer post mentioned this being a 3-part piece? Crossing my fingers for a follow up! Although I can see how it'd be interesting if the follow-up is also delivered only much later when the development team themselves have aged a bit since this release.It's a splendid game (and reading list I love it), looking forward to seeing more from the team ~

_childDocuments_.review: No longer home is a visual novel, semi-autobiographical narrative point-and-click adventure game. Developed by Humble Grove and published by Fellow TravelerIt follows the history of two non-binary roommates, Bo and Ao, who share a flat in London. We control both, hearing their thoughts and struggles while we explore the rooms and click things around.In conversations, you select the dialogue. Many times, there are multiple character options. I don't know how this affects the story but, it makes you more immerse.It is a short and little sad story about growing up, saying goodbye and moving on with life. It has a beautiful art and music that fits really well with the narrative.Maybe this is a not a game for everyone but, I felt some of my own personal struggles and, it is nice to see that you are not the only one who went through them.I recommend it if you are looking to experience the move-in process and move on.7/10🧁

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home has a compelling story about two individuals moving on from university and starting their own life. The writing is so natural, and it will make you emotional as you relive how it felt to graduate and the pressure of getting a "real job." I related to this so much and I think you would too.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: "It feels like it's all rigged against us."Quarter life crises, post-graduation ennui, being non-binary, art students, the melancholy of moving out, expectations, depression, guilt, self-doubt, South London, and a pinch of magical realism are bundled in just 2 hours by Humble Grove (Cel Davison, Hana Lee, Adrienne Lombardo), backed by a nostalgic bittersweet score by Eli Rainsberry and Derek Daley. The game starts with a prelude at Friary Road in Peckham, before they move to Camberwell. Two characters sitting in chairs, silhouetted, then are lit up (much like a stage play) as the camera descends from the stars to the ground. The camera then rotates and objects materialise into existence, which is a cool visual trick that never stops getting old and fits with the magical realism. Ao and Bo, sitting in chairs reflecting on university, describing non-binary identity, parental expectations, debt, and figuring out what things you want to do. The camera pans up to the stars as they discuss extraterrestrial life and parallel universes. Then we come back down and the building comes into view, with an effect much like when stagehands assemble a set in real-time. You as the player can choose Ao and Bo's dialogue in a similar manner to Kentucky Route Zero, along with all the aesthetic choices that pay homage to it (and the developers openly acknowledge and reference throughout). This freewheeling, longshot conversation goes for ten minutes until the second game-length No Longer Home chapter starts.No Longer Home plays like a traditional point-and-click adventure with an isometric perspective where you point to somewhere and your character moves. There are no puzzles here other than the mental puzzle of how to deal with moving on and drifting apart. You can rotate the environment around and much like Fez, some things become more visible and can be interacted with. One neat little quality-of-life addition for this genre is the game automatically knows if you click an area of the screen close enough to the playable character, they will walk (the pointer becomes a plant sprouting up which is very cute) and if you click further away they will automatically know to jog. Before in games like these, you’d have to double click to make them run or press another button. Like mentioned before, there is branching dialogue but it’s not to give you different endings, it’s just to add flavour to the characters and give players some agency in how they define the protagonists (again much like KR0). Unlike other adventure games where you’re travelling to different locations, the story is specifically based in and outside the apartment up to a backyard, so these are intimate spaces being explored. Nonetheless, things and layouts change even in the same rooms such as one tiny room opposite the bedrooms, which lends to the magical realism. There is even a game within a game when all the protagonists’ friends hang out one last time to sit down and play Among The Leaves, a text adventure game where the branching dialogue options are the different characters’ dialogues you can choose from. There are some missable scenes here based on the choices, like I visited a weird underground school but I didn’t come across a Japanese style temple with a lanky creature hanging around. The relationship between Bo and Ao is quite deep and relevant, especially to anyone who’s been through moving house, not sure what they want to do after education, career and financial anxiety, or how to deal with their gender expression (“existing as praxis”) and things in their head. They started off as hesitant to talk to each other, making assumptions one was cooler than the other or not knowing how to be social, but then eventually developed to be able to talk about their own issues. The discussions are often socially relevant and regularly humorous, such as gentrification in London, but never didactic and the dialogue feels authentic to two progressive characters trying to make it out in a capitalist reality. Bo is the more pragmatic of the two but there’s a lot of self-doubt there, and Ao is the more depressed one who can’t handle the expectations of being from a creative family and themselves not amounting to be a very productive artist. There is an initial blame towards others, such as them talking about how parental expectations and the traditional life model messing them up (study->work->family), but they are later able to take responsibility for their own lack of motivation and career aimlessness. However, they both are able to pick each other up when the other one is down on themselves, which goes to show it’s easier to support others more than ourselves. Just as both characters had a long conversation at the start of the game, so does the game beautifully bookend with a 15-minute vulnerable and emotional conversation in bed, and it’s the first time we get to see Ao with their hair down literally and figuratively. For Humble Grove’s first game, the storytelling on display is exceptional. There is an existential, dreamlike mundanity to the game’s atmosphere where these real-life worries about saying goodbye to others and moving out are made extraordinary. The length of scenes being quite short and divergents with other characters goes along with the theme of transient moments, much like in a Richard Linklater film. Self-doubt and self-loathing can manifest as supernatural creatures that you confront in the tiny room. In general, there is an empathic air to the mental health issues explored even with magical realist aspects on top, and that’s quite hard to pull off especially in a videogame without feeling like it’s trivialising. Neglect of the house is represented by the dying plants everywhere and the regret the protagonists have for not taking care of them enough, but as mentioned before, there is hope with the pointer becoming a growing plant animation wherever you click on the screen and Ao and Bo wanting to do better. The cinematography is excellent. A friend leaving the party early helps drift the camera from the BBQ party conversation to the underground train and discussions happen about a possible underground society. There are some cool quirks to the sound design, which is phenomenal overall, such as one scene where Bo talks to a goat-like creature, Lu, about past jam sessions and music (Lu refers to Bo as Edith which confuses them) whose dialogue sound effects are of a bass guitar and if the environment is rotated, it’s a record scratch. The magical and social realism in particular, calls to my mind the work of Apichatpong Weeresethakul. Easily one of my 2021 GOTY contenders for its reflective, dreamlike, and punk quality and depth of storytelling with quite resonant themes and contemporary concerns. For any fans of Kentucky Route Zero, arthouse filmmakers, or just people who appreciate art about mental health issues and quarter life crises in a post-recession world of uncertainty, this is a must play.

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is a pretty and short game. The art is pleasant and cool, the writing is human, and the music is engaging. It's melancholy, but it never goes for a gut punch.  I very much enjoyed the time I spent with it.I could mention minor nitpicks, like the walking animations being a bit stiff or the camera sometimes being a bit slow, but I don't think those are relevant points for a game of this length. If the game wanted 40 hours from me, maybe, but it doesn't. If you're the type of person who needs to get a ton of hours from each dollar you spend a game, this isn't for you. But if you enjoy quiet and story driven games, I think this is worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Such a good looking game, the details are important because the setting is really one house. The dialogue fits well, realist and not too flowery (? idk how to word particularly well) but fantastic enough, where it matters. Take it slow and enjoy the sound design and music, the fact the door opening noise sounds specifically plastic has stuck with me haha.You can stroke the cats!! always a plusI kind of like how a playthrough is like the length of a film, obviously there were a load of cinematic influences.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Gentle, sad, and deeply introspective. This is a bittersweet piece of semi-autobiography, and honestly if that doesn't sound your bag then it almost certainly won't be for you. For me, though, spending 90 minutes exploring the relationship and inner thoughts of two people (Ao and Bo) as they come to the end of sharing a home was an affecting experience. A simple, sweet look into the minds of two people going through an everyday, but life-impacting upheaval, No Longer Home offers a rare approach to interactive fiction: no bombast, no excitement, just quiet drama and emotion. It helped me reflect on myself and my own life; seeing aspects of my personality brought to the surface in both Ao and Bo was actually a little startling; it's relatively rare to see myself — particularly the more 'internal' aspects of my personality — reflected in any media, let alone interactive fiction. All in all, this was a moving experience, and I'm glad to have played it.PS - a shout out to the game's aesthetic, as well. The simple, affecting writing is amply supported by a beautiful art style and perfectly matched minimalist soundtrack; the whole thing is just a pleasure to experience.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

name: Star Renegades
detailed_description: RESIST. RECLAIM. REVIVE. REPEAT. A service robot named J5T-1N has arrived in your dimension to warn of impending doom from an overwhelming force known as the Imperium. Fight for survival across a procedurally generated and emergent mission-based campaign through reactive, tactical turn-based battle system that emphasizes interrupts and counters. Standing in your way is an intelligent Adversary system with enemy officers that evolve and move up in the ranks. As your band of heroes fall in the fight against invading Imperium and hope is all but lost, J5T-1N must be sent to the next dimension with everything you’ve learned to give the next group of heroes a chance to prevail. Each dimension, and each playthrough is unique, challenging, and never the same. Outwit your foes with interrupts, counters, and combos in our fast-paced Reactive Time Battle System Survive the relentless onslaught of an Intelligent Adversary system that generates unique enemies and bosses that evolve as you play Unlock dozens of alternate characters as your surviving squad members form bonds and create progeny Battle your way into the heart of the Empire as our Rebellion Engine creates a unique experience with each playthrough via emergent gameplay and events, procedurally generated missions, shifting priorities, evolving enemies, and tons of equipment/upgrades for your squad

_childDocuments_.review: Basically, this game starts off feeling like a kinda mean RPG that will kill you, and eventually evolves into its true form as a rpg-inspired puzzle game.  The basic puzzle is to combine all your characters moves to stagger enemies off the timeline and/or kill them before they do damage beyond your shields and start taking chunks out of your much harder to heal health pools.  There are a large number of different characters, and every single one of them is capable of contributing a meaningful way - the balance is great.  There are different strategies that work - tanking/redirecting, healing, and pure stagger, as long as you have enough damage on top of the rest of the build to actually finish off the enemies before you run out of shields.there's a little exploration game, where you decide your specific encounters, and a camping minigame to heal/buff/bond, but the vast majority of the time you are fighting very challenging combats.  The reason the game feels so mean when you just start playing is that there aren't trash mobs.  There's no grinding.  Every enemy has the capability of doing some real damage or even defeating your entire team, ending that run.  The common roguelike expectation of endless trash then some randomly generated elite that 1-shots you is not enforced here.  Every fight feels like you have a chance and if you're careful enough, you could win (well, maaybe not the final boss sometimes if it gets the extra round of summons off.  ugh).  Take the fights slowly and carefully, and never dismiss a fight just because it doesn't seem like that big of a deal, and you can get some real fun out of it.  I did have to use a wiki for the progeny unlocks, though.Anyway, thumbs up.  Great puzzley/tactical gameplay that gives a good thoughtful challenge.  Just dig in and have some fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Star Renegades

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game as a turn based RPG Rouge Lite is exactly the type of game I've been wanting to play. The time line mechanic is cool, I like the games loot system, item slots etc, and the camp fire mechanic is cool. The Art is fine, becomes an issue later in the game when you are fighting a lot of enemies everything starts to blend together, and that brings us to the biggest issue with the game, the UI and controls. Navigating menus is a chore it's a pain to find the information you're looking for when you want it. The tool tips when they exist aren't great. It can be difficult to click on the enemy you want to attack sometimes, and if you miss click with your final hero it's locked in... feels pretty bad.All in all the game just isn't enjoyable to play due to the UI and controls
_childDocuments_.name: Star Renegades

_childDocuments_.review: Star Renegades is even better than I thought it'd be.Don't let the pixelated graphics (which I'm sure was a deliberate style choice) fool you. The animations are emphatic, the portraits are emotional and the sprites capture the energy of every character you can unlock.You read that right.  are abundant. You can unlock alternate versions of characters, discover new characters on your adventure, or raise the influence of two companions up enough that they create a progeny. There are so many different ways to get new characters, I'm still discovering them, so this review might not even list them all. It's fantastic.And let's get down to the gameplay, shall we? This scratches my  itch. I was thinking of picking up Final Fantasy X/X-2 on Steam and was just waiting for a Steam sale. Timeless classic, right? Well, one day, I restarted my computer, saw this Steam ad pop up for some RPG-ish thing that had some sort of weird "Star Wars" knock-off name, and hoo-boy! Did it deliver! I am more than 20 hours deep in this game and see no signs of stopping.You can have 5-6 team members altogether (you start off with 3), and you have this nifty meter at the top of your screen that basically allows you to manipulate time. Well, not really, it allows you to manipulate the enemy, but you're pushing them "back" in time whenever you attack them (with most attacks, not all do), allowing members of your team to go first, and sometimes delaying an enemy's turn all the way into the next round. It's a neat mechanic that often reminds me of the aforementioned Final Fantasy X's turn-timer, except as you learn to play the game, you'll find that manipulating your enemies on each turn is actually way more important here in Star Renegades.Which brings us to the difficulty. Star Renegades can be punishing, it can be frustrating, and if you screw up your manipulation of your foes (the manipulation is in the preceding paragraph, if you're skipping around) then that can cost you an unrecoverable amount of health. This game is not for pushovers. On a scale of Telltale to Dark Souls, I'd rate this game about 6-7 out of 10 in terms of difficulty. It's not likely to make you rage-quit, as you'll probably keep getting farther and farther as you replay the game, but it's not afraid of giving you the stick, either. It's also a rogue-like, so you're not likely to have the same exact run twice in a row, which of course subsequently increases or decreases your difficulty per run. You will find repeating maps, if you make enough runs, but the rewards, enemies, bosses and other secrets will often vary.There are apparently some bugs in the game, but I have yet to encounter or recognize any. After 25 hours of gameplay, I'd say that's pretty decent.Star Renegades, truly, is one of the best games I've ever played. Easily a top 10 game for me. This game is well worth the full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Star Renegades

_childDocuments_.review: Has many positive aspects, awesome art, engaging battle systems and really funny quips, however is let down by its overly complex battle system and clunky, unintuitive UI. There are just so many stats, keywords, status effects, abilities, modifiers and hidden conditions on many moves and although they affect the battle somewhat, most of it is just fluff. It's complexity for complexities sake, which would be fine if the UI was good but...The main killer is how the UI just doesn't show enough at a glance, you have to fiddle with turn order, double check enemies over and over with too many button presses to ever really get into a flow state. There are also instant attacks that cannot be revoked, why they decided to include this is baffling, why plan out your turns if some actions are instant and cannot be revoked, what if you made a mistake? This means you have to memorize staggers sometimes and really feels like an oversight. Overall it feels like you are constantly fighting the UI to survey the battle field effectively, this leads to the long runs being really mentally exhausting because even fodder enemies means wrestling with the UI to double check everything.The menu problems extend to the equipment as well, It tells you who equips what when picking things up, but as to what slot it goes on, I'm not sure, its hard to make out what goes in what slot and whether it would take up a currently equipped item or even how it compares without memorizing each characters slot types.Runs are also far too long with too much filler in the beginning and little variety, you just mow down your first 2 scenarios without a care in the world, maybe this is fixed by harder difficulties but I'll never get there. My first run took 8+ hours, and characters are largely the same through each run, so it feels more like a JRPG battle gauntlet than a true rogue-like.Its such a shame because that first run was really magical, but these design decisions don't encourage repeat playthroughs. Simplicity that hides depth, an easy flow state, smooth UI, variety and clarity in systems in mechanics makes for a good roguelike, for a good example just look at Slay the Spire, it nails all those aspects.
_childDocuments_.name: Star Renegades

_childDocuments_.review: I have over 200 hours on the game as of posting this, mostly played on switch.(I got this game for free on steam but bought on switch)This is an excellent game, undoubtedly one of the best that I've ever played. It has an amazing visual style, far beyond many and perhaps every popular game. True, it is 2D, but the amount of detail dedicated to every single frame is astounding, no wonder it is hard to run on switch.Truly, problems do exist, many bugs, none of them make the game unplayable on steam, but they do interfere somewhat with gameplay. They are nothing to worry about, really.Some lunatic a while ago posted a review that I considered utterly unacceptable and biased. This game is a rouguelite, which implies that you will repeat the problem in a slightly different but always challenging way. Saying that the game is redundant or repetitive is attacking the whole point of the game and genre of 'rogues'. There is no completion, the fight always continues. The point is to play the process, the construction and development. This game tests your skills in several ways, as difficulty increases, it is necessary to know more of it. Some dude complained about 'difficulty spikes' on bosses. It is true, you have time to prepare and generate a COMPETENT strategy. After some playthroughs, you will know exactly who you will fight where, sometimes you can even determine how and when, since you can adjust your strategies in several ways: The pick-a-path fixes the pain of linearity of Slay the Spire and improves on the map selection/reward acquisition of Into the Breach and the burden of sacrificing rewards and tough fights that Hades introduces.This game is about knowledge, uncertainty management, and complex team building. It is quite intellectually demanding on higher difficulties, one must prepare carefully for the challenges presented, enemies have Strengths, abilities, immunities and weaknesses. An adaptation process is important every step of the way.  I would say the main weakness of the game is its LONG campaign, commonly rouguelikes and roguelites distinguish themselves by lasting about an hour, one and a half hours if you really decided to think through and also take the long way. This game needs 4 hours per campaign, which is titanic compared to the average of the genre. For a gamer like me, who likes to finish what he starts ASAP, means that whenever I play I require the full 4 hours on it. It is a really enjoyable time I must say, but the time consumption is a weakness that cannot be emphasized enough.  This is* considering fast animations during fights on my average gameplay, so its hard to summon that kind of space in anyone's life. Should you buy it?if you like to think and truly conquer foes (not taking damage is not a measurement of an easy game, it is a measurement of a challenge conquered).if you like to plan and create harmonic teamsif you like visuals, audio, and constant high quality updatesThen this game is for you.However, if you like cheap and easy, you should try candy crush instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Star Renegades

_childDocuments_.review: Everything that happens in your first playthrough will keep happening in the ones to come. Yes, that's the gimmick with the story but why does it have to be exactly the same everytime? Besides unlocking heroes, gameplay does not evolve in any way, no matter the difficulty.Small pool of enemies and attacks to deal with.Maps, always the same, are just branches you'd see in Slay The Spire made to look presentable and waste time on movement animation. Maybe you haven't played enough? I sure have played more than I wanted to... So I checked out a run on the hardest difficulty and it's no different.Whomever designed characters, Cantina and the dumb corgi. I salute you for being unoriginal. Wars Trek galore.
_childDocuments_.name: Star Renegades

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun turn based strategy rogue-lite that is also just a bit of a puzzle game as every fight you are trying to delay/break enemy actions.  The pixel art is great and the combat is enjoyable.  The only real downsides to the game is that each run is very long so you don't feel like much progress is being made for your time and that unlocking characters is a difficult thing to achieve as failure restarts progress in this regard.As a side note, while the game lists its nemesis system as an important part of the gameplay it is not like LOTR Shadow of war and ends up being wasted. and inconsequential.
_childDocuments_.name: Star Renegades

_childDocuments_.review: If I was to conjure up my own game out of thin air, it would be described as "it's kind of like Star Renegades"Star Renegades make things work together that conflict in nature:Elements of RNG are applied slowly and either sparingly or minorly with the calculated tactical decisions you have to make.Another way of putting it: "Prepare for everything, because you'll have to face everything"Long RPG games and rogue-lite together is a recipe for disaster.Could a longer version of this game exist without the rogue-lite elements?Oh yes, I also think it would've been better if it did.One of, if not THE biggest advantage of the rogue-lite style is the different party combinations that the player can pick from.Conclusion: Good job Devs!
_childDocuments_.name: Star Renegades

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game because it comes from the same devs as Halcyon 6, which I remember liking. It's got an interesting "queue" turn-based combat system where you build up the whole round at the beginning, and multiple abilities can push an enemy's turn to the very end. I wanted to like this game.Unfortunately, it suffers *badly* from Joss Whedon Syndrome. Characters refuse to take anything seriously, they undermine the tension of a scene with corny jokes--there is a villain who literally introduces himself by saying that he is a villain because he has unresolved family issues. It's kinda *hard* to play this game with my eyes rolled all the way to the back of my skull. Firefly was cancelled 20 years ago, can we please move on now?And thinking back, I'll bet I'd have the same complaints about Halcyon 6 if I played it now.
_childDocuments_.name: Star Renegades

_childDocuments_.review: I'm torn between recommending this game.  One the one hand it's gorgeous, and fun but it's also really very punishing.  I feel like, what it really needs is a story mode with a different kind of progression loop.  The current rogue-like state of the game feels more like a proof of concept, or the endgame mode you should unlock by playing and completing the story.  I feel like most players going in blind are going to either blitz through the game on their first try, or they'll get stuck on the third planet over and over again (Like me).So guess that's a yes?  I want to adore this game, but it will never adore me back.  I want to see more and play alternate modes.

_childDocuments_.review: Although it gets somewhat repetitive for a roguelike after a couple of runs, it's honestly a really really fun game overall. Absolutely gorgeous pixel art, smooth animations, a pretty in depth battle system and probably has my favorite battle mechanic in a turn based game. Using different characters each run will help alleviate the repetitiveness as each character feels and plays uniquely, really solid game

_childDocuments_.review: A game I keep coming back too. Fun the first time and good progression and balance in later runs. Not perfect but the tactical choices are varied enough that its fun to come back and reply every once in a while. Also, the relationship dialogues have often made me laugh out loud. Like all my favorite games that have huge potential I wish this had mod support, but the core game is solid and definitely worth getting.

_childDocuments_.review: Mostly excellent Roguelike with great gameplay, visual style and sound and solid writing.Sadly it has some pretty puzzling issues like awkward pathfinding on the worldmap, an often confusing combat prediction system and unclear figures, perspective issues where it can be hard to click the right character, and one of the weirdest overcomplicated party menus with way too many screens for just a few functions. All of this should be easy to fix, yet isn't.But in the grand scheme of things these are just minor nuisances while the overall game is more than solid.

_childDocuments_.review: What does a star renegade against?---Overall it's a great game, but it has some hiccups, The art, music and combat are all great, story is ok with some silly banter from your team and enemy. The main problem though is that the rougelite elements need some tuning with some character progression or something for using character in a run. _childDocuments_.review: Played it for 60hours+ through XBOX PC Pass and when my subscription expired I bought it on Steam again because the game is just the perfect blend of turn based tactics and roguelikes (and a sniff of puzzlesolving).  There is a learning curve to understand what is happening and how the statuses, staggers, armor and shields work but runs will be more and more enjoyable the further you comprehend these things. Devs are doing terrific work with support and updates, it shows that there has been put alot of love and work into this project.
_childDocuments_.name: Star Renegades

_childDocuments_.review: Visually the game is absolutely gorgeous to look at. Not only the characters/enemies but even the backgrounds and world maps area are just a joy to watch.The music is great and fits the game very well. Being a rougelike though the music will get stuck in your head which can be a good or bad thing.Gameplay wise it can be a either challenging or a cakewalk depending on the characters you choose(there is a difficulty option after your first win/defeat). Some characters are definitely WAY stronger than others since the combat revolves around a time line system and you can basically negate an enemy or group of enemies from ever attacking with the right team but I wouldn't say there's a weak or OP character. The behemoths (bosses) can be weird in the sense that the 1st behemoth can be the hardest and the 3rd behemoth the easiest because of the team members you unlock on the way(2 + your starting 3)Also there's this nemesis system which I guess can be annoying if you keep dieing to the same lieutenants and elites, but since you want to kill all of them anyways to gain the most exp per planet this systems doesn't really matter IMO?I think most will say that the narrative/lore is very 50/50.You'll either love it or hate it. It's very jokey and it has alot of charm which I enjoy, but there's alot of lore we don't really get to experience unfortunately. Overall I think the game is very enjoyable and has good replay value if you want to unlock everything it has to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Star Renegades

_childDocuments_.review: + nice looking game+ fun combat, it can be unbalanced sometimes but in a fun way (you can create insane combos) + good permanent upgrades after each runs+ good number of characters with different styles- the runs are long, it can take easily 6 hours and it turns you off after dying- after you finish it once the game doesn't have enough things to try to lure you in again, especially knowing that you have to spend a number of hours in each run, everything you can unlock is not attractive enough to repeat it.-\+ I wish there were bigger variety of music\environment in the gameit took me 12 hours and I finished the game from my second run, it was enjoyable 2 runs and worth my time but I will not comeback for another one

_childDocuments_.review: My full review is apparently too long for Steam's character counter, therefore, here is a link to the Turn Based Lovers website which contains the entirety of it, I am only including a couple portions below: A title that has enjoyable gameplay that’s hooked my attention for sustained periods of time, which is a rarity for my taste. That being said, like most games, whether someone “likes” or “dislikes” it, mainly revolves around what you as a player enjoy. Hopefully this review can answer some of your questions about this game instead of making assumptions based on the store page description; which, while not bad or something, doesn’t necessarily tell you everything you need to know to make an informed decision.Star Renegades uses a roguelite formula with JRPG-type combat. For well-known games you can use as conceptual references, I would include things such as Darkest Dungeon and Battlechasers, but mixed with common rogue elements as seen in Into the Breach, Chrono Ark, and Dead Cells. Each run takes approximately 6-8 hours (depending on how quickly you play, and how familiar you become with the game) to beat the final boss. You’ll venture through an intro section, 3 planets, and the enemy’s main ship for essentially 3 main zones with a finale on the ship which is much more abbreviated compared to the planets.  Between each zone, you’ll have the opportunity to buy equipment at vendors using a temporary credits currency and recruit one more hero for your crew. Therefore, this means that for each of the planets, you’ll have a team of 3 / 4 / 5 for planets 1 / 2 / 3, with a VIP that you have to protect who joins for the final ship zone. If you’re familiar with the game Chrono Ark (another roguelite), it’s similar in nature to that, where you’ll get your choice from 2 heroes to add to your team that run (or choice of 3 with a certain optional upgrade). Whenever your run ends (whether victorious or defeated), you’ll have the opportunity to spend your two different meta-currencies on various kinds of unlocks.Meta progression takes three main forms in this game, and are unlocked using two currencies:Like most roguelites, this game does offer difficulty options (I’ve seen only 3 levels), for an increase of challenge for an increase in meta-currency gains. Merely beat the game on a given difficulty to unlock the following one.The robot upgrades (little flying thing that goes with you everywhere) are a “choice of one” situation with some pretty cool stuff, including things like some free armor repair when camping, more vendor options between planets, and more flexibility in adding heroes during your run (choice of 3 instead of choice of 2).Equipment unlocks work in a similar fashion to something like Dead Cells, where once you’ve unlocked certain pieces, they’ll potentially show up in future runs.: There is one really good and one really annoying aspect to this system:: You can choose one piece of equipment to start with on every run. It will just be the level 1 version of it, but, this can help things go a lot smoother from the get-go. I really like this, as it gives you “one more little significant choice on your starting loadout”, especially as the early parts of a run can be a little more difficult before your crew develops that much.: Unfortunately, Massive Damage didn’t learn the lesson about equipment unlocks that Dead Cells eventually did: you can unlock “subpar equipment” which just dilutes the item pools with stuff which is clearly inferior to others. This therefore incentivizes the player to “skip over” unlocks for pieces of equipment which they deem “not as worth it”. I can feel hopeful that perhaps Massive Damage will reconsider the way that item pools work in a similar fashion to how Dead Cells allowed the player to remove things from the possible item pools. Otherwise, players can end up going “oh no, I’ve made things worse for myself by unlocking X item, and I can’t do anything about it unless I start a fresh file”.Hero unlocks tie in mainly with the relational system which I made mention of in the camping description. Most heroes will only have relational levels up to tier 3, but some will have up to tier 4. Tier 1 gives a small passive bonus to each hero, tier 2 unlocks their fury combo ability (kind of like a duo-limit break), tier 3 unlocks another small passive bonus, but tier 4 unlocks the ability to purchase “Progeny Heroes”, to give you more options for your crew in the future. Note that the relational system and its bonuses (save for the meta-unlock of progeny) is on a per-run basis, and not permanent.:There are only (number spoiler)  “new heroes” to unlock through this system. All of the other progeny heroes are merely variants of the (number spoiler)  heroes in total. This is not to say that “this sounds lame compared to what the store page made it sound like”, but moreso to temper players’ expectations about the game. These variants on the heroes are actually pretty neat, as they’ll have adjusted base stats and small differences on their active abilities, such as swapping out A ability for B, and/or learning certain abilities at differing levels than their other progeny variants.The second kind of hero unlock you get are class perks for the various heroes. As you gain the blue currency during your runs, it will go into a meta-counter which you level-up in. When you reach certain thresholds of this, it will unlock a second / third / etc class perk for each hero. This therefore gives you starting loadout options of either “Rookie” (which makes relationships improve faster) / class perk 1 / class perk 2 / etc for your three starting heroes. Along with the various cool bonuses these can offer, it also changes the color scheme on your hero for a nice effect.For the various flaws that Star Renegades has, I am optimistic that Massive Damage will smoothen things out with post-launch support. They’ve been quite receptive to the playerbase’s bug reports, and have announced plans for more content development.I love the game’s battle system and how it makes me think a lot with every turn. Every situation I’m faced with is a puzzle on “ok, how am I going to deal with this?” Executing those perfect turns and combos feels satisfying, and when you take casualties, it’s a learning experience on “ahh, yeah, I should watch out for those kinds of issues next time”.Some may not be too thrilled with how each run takes “so long” (6-8 hrs) for a roguelite, but personally, I’ve been fine with that, as I can comfortably save and exit whenever I need to and continue next time.I’m not super into story / thematics on games, so my opinion on them on Star Renegades is that it’s not a game you play for the story. I’ve heard both praise and complaints for its non-serious and comedic tone, with plenty of dialogue interactions which honestly don’t make sense. Such things don’t bother me as there’s just “thematic fluff” on the game’s actual mechanics. Basically, the story isn’t something incredibly deep or long to keep you motivated to play -- you’re playing this run after run cause you like the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Star Renegades takes a good idea and squanders it. It isn't worth the full price. At $5-6 maybe. $25 is a hard pass.On the surface, the game seems like it should be quite good.The basic gameplay, Grandia-style combat with a heavy puzzle element is quite fun.The sprite work is quite pretty.But everything else ranges from mediocre to awful.Almost all of the game's problems can boil down to one thing: Star Renegades does not feel like it was playtested for user-friendly design.The map system by which you navigate levels wastes your time, obfuscates paths, and is generally pointless.The game does not explain any of its icons and has too many statuses and effects to easily keep track of.The preview does not accurately preview all effects. The game points this out. Not accurately previewing everything is a huge, huge problem for planning purposes. The preview system breaks with: healing, defending, putting moves earlier on the timeline than what is already on, guarding, and status effects. It is extremely unreliable.Any move that occurs at the beginning of the timeline happens immediately after you click it. This is unlike all timeline moves, which only occur once combat starts. When planning, this can accidentally screw you over big time.You cannot see the stats, formation, moves or any information about the enemies you are facing. For first time through, this can be really, really bad for the player. In a game about preparation, it decidedly refuses to give you the information you need.The status screens are a complete disaster. The information about any character's moveset and passives are displayed in a very clunky way. You can only see 3 at a time, you have to click and drag to see what they are, and they are only shown by icon (you have to hover over an ability to see what it does).The camping is poorly implemented. You build bonds between characters by using their camp cards to interact. When they hit breakpoints, the characters unlock either strong passives or a combo move. These are very powerful and the need to balance them with the buffs you need to be effective in combat (massive shield buffs or +25-33% dmg are camping buffs you can use). Balancing them could be cool, but new characters come in with 0 bonds on anyone. So in reality, you just get your original 3-4 chars super beefy on friendship while the later ones languish because they are down 2-3 levels worth of camping. You can't see what the friendship unlocks will be either, which also greatly hinders planning. You can't even use higher tier camp buffs on characters on others unless they reach a high enough bond, so latecomers just get screwed.The puzzle element of combat also falls off fairly hard, as characters generally have 1-2 moves that are head and shoulders above the rest. It becomes use each char's strong move, which is effectively their role, with all their other stuff being fluff for niche cases.You are given the option to recruit one of two characters after each planet. The game does not let you see their stats, abilities, or anything. You choose based off a little discussion they have. This is not the information you need when making party composition choices.The game does not feel good to play. It feels less like you are fighting enemies and solving combat puzzles and more like you are fighting the game's poorly designed, implemented, and presented systems.

_childDocuments_.review: First impressions after one run (3 hour playtime)? Great. Big fan of the mix of camping skills, deep JRPG combat, the gorgeous pixel art style, and different party compositions. The only points of feedback I'd like to see in the game are: an easier UI to use, and the ability to mouse over different stats and symbols. The learning curve of so much front-loaded information (which attacks can target front only, have the reticle symbol to permit targeting anywhere, etc.) makes the first hours tricky to get ahold of, though there's plenty of system depth once you get to grips with it.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic turn-based roguelite RPG with a novel stagger system for manipulating when enemies go. Very unfortunate that this one didn't take off as this developer did great work and supported it with myriad free DLC. If you are on the fence, I am very confident you will enjoy this should you take the plunge.

_childDocuments_.review: FIgured I would beat it at least once before reviewing since I got almost to the end on my first run. It took me just a second run to get there, so I would say difficulty isn't insanely impossible once you grasp the system.The turn system is pretty solid. Reminiscent of ATB with its own shake-ups and choices that help it stand out in a sea of turn-based games. Gameplay loop is fairly straightforward as far as levelling and exploring go. Levelling provides no options outside of which characters to level and when, but that's made up for more in the choices you have as far as squad makeup and gear selection. It can feel a little limiting at times, especially later in the game when you have five characters to outfit but only get so much gear and experience, but that factors into the difficulty so it's definitely an acceptable limit.All things considered, this is a pretty enjoyable experience, and I could definitely see myself spending a decent bit more time doing runs in the future. Great graphics, cool designs, fun combat. Quality stuff.Also, a bit of a side-note: I saw in some other reviews that people had issues with the turn previews being inaccurate, but honestly I can only think of one time this happened the entire 14 hours I was playing. It can be a bit confusing once you start trying to keep track of all of the turns at once since you choose your actions before anything happens most of the time. My recommendation is to choose your actions based on who you want to act first in the timeline rather than the prescribed order and it'll make everything far more manageable.
