_childDocuments_.review: I'm not normally a huge fan of roguelites, but UnderMine caught my eye (thanks to DangerouslyFunny's videos). I've played about 16 hours of it so far (version 0.3.3.8), and I must say that it shows amazing promise. The game already feels like a fully released title, despite still being in early access.The aim of the game is simple - progress through (currently) 12 levels of the mines, fighting creatures and hoarding gold. Along the way you'll find NPCs who return to your hub and offer their services, secret areas that reward you, artifacts to power you up, and curses which have various negative effects, but offer some reward in return.The permanent unlocks are one of the things that caught my eye. Once you have enough gold and have the correct NPCs unlocked, you can upgrade your character for every subsequent run. This can be more health or damage, the ability to carry more potions, or even an upgraded sack to lose less gold on death. This means that no matter how poorly a run goes, you still feel like you've achieved something.The runs themselves can last up to about 30 minutes - so they're well suited to shorter play sessions. There always seems to be something new to find, and in 16 hours, I definitely haven't seen all the game has to offer.The graphics and audio are also well polished, and I haven't noticed any bugs so far. Once you've finished the current content, you get an item which respawns the bosses and ups the difficulty slightly (while improving the rewards). In the recent update, you also have the ability to toggle the level of this item, so you can return to non-NG+ if you prefer.UnderMine is an excellent game, and the developer deserves to sell a lot of copies. It's definitely worth the current asking price of €12.50, and I hope the community around the game grows. I can't wait to see what's in store for future updates as well.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a simple and fun game, deceptively addictive, you will die often in typical rogue-like fashion, but the gameplay is smooth and in-game items and buffs add complication to otherwise simple combat mechanics. Some things are pretty RNG-heavy and that can be frustrating, but you have to accept that some runs are simply not going to go as well as others due to luck. _childDocuments_.review: UnderMine has good music/art/characters and it feels polished. But the core gameplay loop is just repetitive and tedious. Randomization (maps, artifacts, potions) barely changes anything. Combat is roughly limited to two attacks (close & long-range) which never change. And combat movement isn't precise. There is also a horribly slow 2 seconds transition between combat zones and monsters that try to steal your gold as if you had too much of it. So you're left with repeating the same levels over and over again with almost no differences in gameplay to come back fighting whatever you died on until you learn the mechanic. With enough grind, you might get enough upgrades to see a noticeable impact. It's lightyears away from titles like Hades or Dead Cells.

_childDocuments_.review: Swiftcast Review9/10 - A roguelite game with constant action that becomes enjoyably chaotic the further you descend to the floors below -Classic Zelda feel with use of bombs, boomerangs (pickaxe in this game because, mines), and all the loot to collect-Curses, blessings, and potions massively change the way you play especially in the late game.-Grab that treasure before the pesky slimes try to get away with them! _childDocuments_.review: Pros: - New NPCs / Game mechanics get introduced at a good pace and unlocking them feels satisfying- Polished graphics- Bosses have interesting mechanicsCons:- Gameplay is not very interesting and feels repetitive. Almost all relics and blessings are just stat buffs, so the runs feel all the same- Jump mechanic feels very awkward. It is very hard to estimate where you are going to land and hard to steer mid-air. Platforming feels terrible. A dash-mechanic (which most other roguelikes go for) would probably have been better.- Bosses don't respawn. This is especially disappointing since the bosses are the main strength of this game. Not being able to replay them feels like a poor design decision.- Difficulty of rooms varies widely. Sometimes your run will just end because of a room full of mines with moving sawblades, several holes in the ground and a ton of enemies shooting at you. This kind of rng would not really be a problem if not for the next point.- I don't like that the in-run and out-of-run currencies are identical. This leads to me never buying any expensive items in-run since the run may be over anytime because of a very difficult room and i would rather save the gold for permanent upgrades. I understand that this is a deliberate design decision but i personally don't like it.Conclusion:I am especially disappointed in this game because the core idea is really good (of course a lot is copied from Binding of Isaac), boss design is really cool and the game feels very polished (except the wonky jump mechanic). But the main point of a roguelike is having great replayability through different playstiles in different runs. Unfortunately, Undermine does not deliver this at all. If you are new to roguelikes, this game may be for you. Otherwise, i would rather play Hades, Dead Cells or Binding of Isaac.

_childDocuments_.review: Hello Everyone, Presenting to you my first review on this gem of a game.  Reminiscent of commonly known dungeon crawling roguelike games such as Rogue Legacy, one of my favorites on both PC and PS4.  The game is currently in Early Access, however, a planned 1.0 release is scheduled for August of this year.  The price tag during the summer sale is more than fair.  I like to calculate a game's worth based on a 1 for 1 cost-benefit ratio.  1 dollar/euro per 1 hour of playtime.  I have already logged 11.5 hours on this game and anticipate many more even though I have only paid 9 Euros.  So, in premature conclusion, I give this game a definite buy, whether it is to pass time when bored or because you want to dive in, punish yourself, and conquer the extensive achievement list.  It also allows for +++ games and no run is ever the same as the last!WARNING:  MAY CONTAIN MINOR SPOILERS..............................General information about the game:- Randomly generated levels.  - Each dungeon contains 4 levels.- Lose a certain amount of gold upon death.- Can upgrade items and equipment only after returning to the start of the game.- Full of secret chambers.- Forces you to utilize your equipment sparingly and make tough decisions as resources may become scarce.- Bosses can be brutal or a piece of cake depending on how you play/your skill level.- You are a peasant, enjoy that, peasant!Pros:- Game is in early access but, runs as a full release.- You can join the Discord for the game and easily discuss development with the developers and other like-minded    individuals.- You can get lost for hours in this game.- Very  a good way.Cons:- After long time playing - 4hrs + - it may begin to consume an increased amount of RAM and you may see character stutters.  It all depends on your machine capabilities. - Nothing other than that so far.  Decision:Buy this game and support the developers.  It is a great game for its class with an exorbitant amount of content.  ENJOY!Respectfully, AcoKnight

_childDocuments_.review: If i could put a review as "meh", i'd put it as so. If you haven't played any roguelikes (which this game isn't, more below), or really few roguelites (which the game isn't... either), you might find this enjoyable. If, like me, you have, you quickly notice it has zero originality. You know that time you forgot to name your game in that game dev sim and it came out as "Game #27"? This is that game.If you don't want to read the detailed description, there is a summary at the end.Gameplay - General: It's a slog. Enemy attack patterns either aren't a thing at all (rats), only exist to slow you down (slimes, yetis), or just get random free hits on you when they shouldn't (any enemy that fires projectiles). Your hitbox is gigantic, and you often fall down pits for the sole reason that your pinky toe happened to brush the edge. Bosses are nothing but gigantic health bars with mechanics that often have zero windup, so either you spend an absurd amount of time playing it safe and getting 1 hit in every minute, or you grind for money. There are no other options.Gameplay - Character: I don't know if the peasant class is intentionally garbage, or is it even the only class in the game. However, it feels like it is intentionally garbage. Your attack has extremely short range, and stops you dead in your tracks. Your melee attack is entirely worthless except for disposing of enemies that can't hit you when hitting them in melee (smaller rats), every other enemy is better fought with the weaker ranged attack that doesn't completely stop you. You have a jump, which makes you seemingly completely immune to damage, but it doesn't work as a dodging mechanic when they're trying to pull off attack patterns like ones seen in Enter the Gungeon and Binding of Isaac, both games you should be playing instead of this.Gameplay - Items: There's 2 kinds of items in this game, most of them in the latter category: useful, and useless. Most treasures/relics/whatever you have are completely worthless. Gold explodes as it drops? Wow, it could deal a tiny amount of damage to an enemy if you hit a rock twice instead of hitting an enemy. Gold arcs lightning to an enemy when picked up? You could just hit the enemy instead for the same reason as above. There are no items that stand out, and the only even slightly useful relic i found throughout the entire gameplay (and i found more than 20) was one that let the thrown weapon ricochet to 3 enemies. On that note, the descriptions of the relics are awful. There's boots that state "they allow walking and jumping in oil", what do they actually do? While they do allow you to jump in oil, they also drop a splatter of oil at your feet after any jump. There are a lot of items that say "increases damage", but none of them say how much. Details. They're important.Graphic Design: Here lie more or less the only good parts of the game at its current stage. The pause menu fade is genius, the enemies are well animated and have a lot of love poured on them. While the maps themselves are pretty bland, the graphic design still feels tight and unique.Sound Design: I already forgot how anything in the game sounds, and i shut it down 10 minutes ago. "Generic" is literally the only thing that comes to mind.Polish levels: Really, really low amount of gameplay testing, the core gameplay loop is not only really slow, but it gets repetitive within 2 hours. The bosses as mentioned before are just giant slabs of meat that take hundreds of hits. It is not fun to play at this stage and it was put out on early access far too early.Game Design: Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V. There is nothing even close to original here, and despite that, the level of quality is as if they're trodding on completely uncharted territory and making it up as they go along. There exists countless of examples of exact replicas of what this game has in other games, all of them doing it better. Binding of Isaac and Enter the Gungeon are the obvious comparisons, but it even muddles down those so much that it only becomes an action RPG with kind-of-but-not-really permadeath mechanics. And even that "RPG" part of action RPG is missing. There are so many examples they could've drawn and iterated from and try to do better."Roguelike": No. Not even close. Nethack is a roguelike. Dungeon Crawl: Stone soup is a roguelike. Dwarf Fortress (adventure mode) is a roguelike. The genre's name already explains itself "a game that is like Rogue". There is nothing comparable to Rogue here. For that matter, it isn't Roguelite either. The items you get in the dungeon itself are so powerless, and the bosses have such absurd levels of health, the entire game hinges on you spending thousands and thousands of gold after you've died so you can have at least feasible chance of taking the bosses on.Difficulty: Healing is expensive gold-wise, and heal-item drops are very rare. While the average character dies in 10-15 hits, there are a lot of cases where there is legitimately unavoidable damage in the game, particularly with bosses if you ever wish to damage them even slightly. Unavoidable damage should only really appear as a dilemma in these types of games, but here it's rampant. As previously stated, the bosses are the worst offendee in the difficulty department. They don't have difficult attack patterns or complex, varied mechanics, so they just have an absolute assload of health, and guaranteed hits on you.Summary: As stated in the prologue, meh. It's original only in how unoriginal it is. The graphics design is great and lively, but apart from that it seems to fail at every single hurdle there is. It copies mechanics from already existing (and in some cases cheaper) games that have come before it and instead of trying to do better, it does worse and makes things clumsy. Its lack of difficulty is compensated by bosses having unavoidable attacks and absurdly high amount of health that practically forces you to grind if you don't wish to spend the better part of an hour on the first "real" boss even if you happen to chance a good item drop. The item drops in most cases are not even worth picking up, and they aren't inventive or clever. It's not a roguelike or a roguelite, and calling it even an action RPG would be an insult to games like Secret of Mana that did this style of combat well nearly 3 decades ago.

_childDocuments_.review: Undermine is an incredibly fun roguelike that I think anyone who enjoys there genre will enjoy, there's a few reason for this. At its core the roguelike mechanics work well with randomly generated floor that follow a theme and death is sometimes more of an opportunity than that of a hassle. Personally I am a big fan of seeing where even though death is permanent, you can still see yourself getting stronger and improving one way or another. Not to mention the different cute familiars you can get that can fit whatever playstyle you prefer.But whats great is that while the base game of undermine is a bit easier than many other roguelike, the game provides plenty of ways to give more of a challenge should you request it. There's the summoning stones the can make subsequent runs harder, the hexes from the crone that can give you permanent difficult curses, and of course, the Othermine which lets truly has no progress and you have a random start to challenge the Othermine. The gameplay mechanics and the sound absolutely slaps, and there's plenty of variety in types of rooms, enemies, relics, and curses that its takes a while for it to feel repetitive.Speaking of those things, Undermine also has does something that I think all great roguelike (e.g. binding of Isaac) should do. The relics and blessings that you receive can inadvertently combine into incredible combinations that are powerful and fun. Probably the most infamous example would be getting the right relics to essentially drop a nuke whenver you place a bomb that can wipe out the entire room (and maybe you in the process). Another thing in that regard which I consider a plus is that curses you receive can also combine in such terrible ways that you feel like you're getting screwed other and wonder which god you anger to deserve such karma.Lastly, the more QoL things, the different interactions and the story you see unfolding with the characters in the nexus is rather charming. It doesn't have the detail of games like Hades by any means but its nice to see you slowly bringing more and more people and as a result life to the nexus by saving people or completing quests in the mines that make you feel like you've truly contributed to the mines. However, no game is without flaw and I think undermines biggest flaw is the pacing of unlocking things. There are many different relics, potions, and familiars to unlock in Undermine and many of them require finding the blueprints for them. This isn't too bad because you can get a lot of recipes from the Othermine but the thorium needed to unlock all of these recipes can feel rather slow. Sometimes it can feel like it takes a while to unlock all of the upgrades but this is mostly post endgame content.Overall, Undermine is a great game that is definitely worth the price. I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys roguelikes or has an interest in them. Its a fantastic game for beginners and veterans alike to play and I'm sure you'll enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has 3 problems I can see after playing for a few hours.1. Basic combat is not that enjoyable, no variety of attacks available.2. Gold pickup. It's a chore to have to run around and pick up 4-6 gold pieces every time you hit a rock. That alone is a waste of time. On top of that, you have their mascot (Pilfers) coming to steal the gold if you're not fast enough. How is this an enjoyable gameplay loop? It's like if you bought french fries at the beach, someone knocked it out of your hands, and said "Better go pick it up before the seagulls get it." In Wizard of Legend you just have gold magnet to you if you're close at all.3. Gold integrity. It's fine to lose a percentage of your gold before the next run. But consider Rogue Legacy. In that game, you get to spend from your total earned gold, then you lose a percentage of the unspent gold right before the run starts. In this game, you lose a percentage of all earned gold right when you die. You know for a fact that 50% (starting value) of your gold is going to waste.So my experience was farming for increased gold integrity (50%->70%) since I don't want any gold to go to waste. When farming for gold I have to rush to pick it up or lose it to the Pilfers. Then even when I get it, it's reduced no matter what. Also the whole game is brown apart from the dungeon, which is grey. Maybe different floors could have different themes.It's not a terrible game, but it is tedious. You have to question what the devs are thinking with some of these decisions. They could learn from previously released roguelikes.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. The music, art style, and setting are really well done. Let highlight a few things the developer(s) absolutely need to spend some time on.1. Losing gold mechanic - Starting with a blanket 50% loss of gold when you die is really bad mechanic. This isn't a problem starting out as the upgrades are relatively cheap and you can quickly reduce this to 65-70%. HOWEVER, little monsters in the dungeon ALSO steal gold if you don't get to it quick enough, making it probably closer to an extra -5-10% per run loss depending on your skill and luck. Please, for the love of god, implement a floor with the sack upgrades, ie (Level 1, 500 minimum, then 50% loss) or something. The way it works currently makes saving for upgrades extremely risky, even just with two separate runs.  If you happen to be unlucky with your 20 grand starting off, welp, sucks that you now have 14 grand. Also, for please re-evaluate the monsters stealing gold - either in intensity or in having them literally be worth SOMETHING for killing. 2. Unavoidable Damage - what I mean by this is it's entirely possible to get hit by a monster that deals damage, which then pushes you into spikes dealing more damage, which then knocks you into a hole, for some more damage. For god sake, implement a small invulnerability timer. This exemplifies point #1 for some real deep frustration on gold loss, taking 50-60% of your heath in damage in one go.3. Power Loss - It might be because of #1 again but skipping dungeon floors seems extremely hard to do because getting upgrades is also really hard to do. You need the relics you get in order to actually progress.4. Relic Tooltips - Some of the artifact tooltips almost seem intentionally vague. Kurtz' Statche for example (description: "A mysterious box that invites calamity"). Look, the secret rooms in the game are already obscured, and some rooms themselves having puzzles are sometimes impossible to figure out what to do from the environment - the last thing you need to do is make the items the players' have already EARNED puzzles too. Also, some of the relics are just really bad by themselves (Catalyst) unless paired with another relic. Make the relics be able to stand alone by themselves at least. The chances of getting the correct combo with ~100 relics is mathematically unlikely, especially when skipping dungeon rooms.

_childDocuments_.review: In short: After playing 8 hours into the game I cannot recommend it. It is too repetative with too little progression.Spoilers ahead:The good part: -I've seen no bugs, It runs smoothly.-The absensce of an (interesting) story is in this case actually a good thing. I don't miss anything, If I have to do the stuff over and over again.The bad ones:I've compared with lets play and goodled, if I simply was mistaken. But there is barely some progression. You will fight the same areas and the same enimies with barely rising stats over and over. Only to -maybe- buy a new item that barely changes anything.On top of feeling no progress the death penalty of loosing gold is another downer. It is somewhat the designing boni and mali. because what if instead of losing gold just pick up less gold in the first place? to me this was mostly a "awww ♥♥♥♥ again" moment I didn't need.On top I really don't like, that the game forces you to 1: enter a room 2: kill everything 3: loot everything 4: enter next room. The enemies never give you anything. the only reason to kill them is to open the doors the the adjacent screens. There is no "nope , I'll come back later' and no 'nope I just loot and run past the bad guys'. It's like the devs force you to aproach a room in this manner.The mechanics of fighting almost never change. You're stuck with Axe swing/ throw and jump. Most upgrades consist of +x to some stat. Sometimes you find a temporary relic for a run, that makes you perhaps use the throw more often than just hitting the thing. In my 8 hours I just got better with using the basic moveset. On that note I even wondered why there are 3 saveslots. Because doing different builds is unlikely to happen.After the first exitements of purple chests I started to avoid everything of that color. They give you a small benefit, most likely not relevant, and a curse, most likely to increase the chances of death. In a game all about avoiding death as long as possible it is reasonable to ignore the shiny violet chests(and flames). I know that the curses can be lifted, but this is a rare happening. So actively ignoring content is the strategy.When I discovered a NPC that can teleport me, I was not convinced as well. This "Hoodie" guy just teleports you down in the mines. First: Why do you want to teleport into dangerous levels, when you need the items of the lower and easy levels?Second: I asked myself several times, If he can teleport you again up to the village. This is of cours only motivated by the Idea of avoiding the death money loss. So in the end I ignored him.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a huge wasted potential. It would be alright if this was alpha stage where balancing is still very janky and there is no content, but this game is sold as a fully completed product, it boggles my mind.It is hard to sort out pros and cons because nothing is finished.Kinda pros:- """Progression system""" which is just a time waster, plain grinding in order to raise attack and hp, no special features, no nothing. Just attack and hp.- 100+ "different" relics or so, 85% of which are just attack and hp. Other 15% can influence your gameplay style in very minor ways.- Animation is good when talking about the characters.- This game has a very short, very meaningless story. Yay..?- Blessing/curse system which gives more variation to your playthroughs. Blessings can raise and curses can lower your attack or hp.... Cool. Oh and there are major curses, you can get some bombs or keys in exchange for a major curse which can completely ruin your run. There are amazing curses like all key doors require 50 hp. With maxed out character, you have around 400 hp and there are ~2-3 doors per floor and about 15 floors in total.Cons:- You have two attack moves all game and there are no real attack modifiers like brimstone in binding of isaac. One is a very short range melee hit during which you stand for a second and the other is a very slow and tedious pickaxe throw, maxing out pickaxe increases throw range which makes attacking ultra slow due to very long path and same velocity for some reason.- ONLY DODGE MOVE IS A WONKY JUMP.- NO REAL ATTACK MODIFIERS. Only +atk, +def, +hp.- Background animation is quite bad. A hole, a wall and an oil puddle look exactly the same.- Enemies swarm you or start a bullet hell while you are a mister - every attack is stationary blergh. It is super tedious if you can't one shot everyone and 95% of the time you will be able only to five-shot and so on. - During aforementioned swarms you can't see jack cause all the explosions and enemies overlap and you can't see yourself.- Super repetitive.- Terrible hitboxes - yours and enemies.- Crazy damage scaling, in the last stages you can get one-shot or two-shot especially if enemies start to juggle you.- Enemies cannot be stunned, they attack while getting hit in the face.In summary, don't buy this game unless it will be very very cheap or free. This game requires complete overhaul in order to be good.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game, exactly. It's kind of fun. But it's not great. It's like dollar slice pizza. I've played a lot of Binding of Isaac so the comparisons are easy to make, and this game isn't quite as good as it. Some key points:- The items you find don't spice up the gameplay that much.  There doesn't seem to be anything like Brimstone or Ipecac like you'd find in Isaac that really change things up. There don't seem to be (m)any interactions, either.- Running the early levels repeatedly gets boring. That's tied to the above, I think. In Isaac you can find some weird ♥♥♥♥ in the basement and it gets fun right away.  Also each area in Isaac is two floors, and there's four here.  Twice as long, but not twice as fun. Isaac also gives you at least two items per floor (room + boss), but you only get one here. This game seems to only have you fight bosses once instead of every run. Boss fights can be more interesting than just trash. - Metagame progression feels like a grind. I had the same problem with Rogue Legacy and to a lesser extent Dead Cells. You can upgrade your stats for gold. You always get gold for a run. If I spent a day grinding gold runs while watching youtube, I could max out my stats. Knowing that is irritating to me. I prefer how in Isaac all the unlocks are tied to accomplishments (win with this character, take no damage, do this thing, etc) or even just luck. You can't really grind to change your stats there.  Here, you can, and it kind of feels like a time gate for some of the later levels. I'm sure someone has beat the whole thing without any upgrades, but I'm not that good. I don't like the grinding the difficulty down like this, though.I could also compare it to Dead Cells. Dead Cells has some of the same problems (namely, the metagame grind). But Dead Cells is also a much *faster* game, and encourages you to go fast. By comparison, replaying undermine's early levels feels glacial.Overall it's not *bad*, it's just not as good as the nearest competitors.

_childDocuments_.review: UnderMine is an action-adventure roguelike where you play as miners who should delve deeper in the mine/dungeon to farm gold and occasionally discover secrets. A roguelite progression system is also available - you spend gold on permanent upgrades for your gear/shops/vendors/blessings etc.There's a lot of aspects that would be familiar for The Binding of Isaac players but at the same time UnderMine succeeds at delivering its own unique experience. I totally enjoyed my first 6-7 hours in the game:+ A really good first Early Access build. A lot of content, no bugs (at least from my experience).+ The game is actually fun to play.+ There's some characters you can interact with and each of them has some cool dialogues/jokes.+ Nice visuals and music.+ Decently balanced progression via unlocks/upgrades. It's not perfect but it's good enough to entertain you while providing challenging gameplay.+- When playing this game I compare it mostly to Isaac and some of UnderMine aspects (jumps and combat mechanics in general) are just not my cup of tea. Maybe I'd like those more at later stages of the game. Variety of axe attacks/improvements (and character development in general in terms of combat) is quite poor.- You can attack only in 4 directions with melee attacks (up, down, left, right) and this could and will lead to stupid misses. Why not to make it possible to attack diagonally?- Falling down is not really fun and player hitbox makes it even worse. "Airwalking shoes" is the best item in the game by far. is one of the best roguelikes in a long time with a good potential to enhance during Early Access period. Highly recommended for fans of the genre. 8/10

That being said, I really grooved on the game for over 30 hours and it was absolutely worth the $10 I spent on it.  I do highly recommend this if you are a fan of roguelikes and top-down action.

_childDocuments_.review: It has been a long time since a game captured my heart enough to write a review. Its been a long time since a game devastated my sleep, but oh did I welcome this endlessly sweet sin with Undermine. Roguelike's comprise a massive part of my steam library, they are most likely my favorite genre of game. As of late, I haven't found one that's captured that "ONE MORE RUN" feeling they used to. I've been in pursuit of something desperately fresh from the genre, but I was wrong. Undermine takes all that you know about Roguelites and roguelikes and packages them in an incredibly smooth and delicious game. So far, I've experienced what is seemingly ENDLESS progression. IN ALL ASPECTS. BOSS PROGRESSION. DEEP STORY PROGRESSION. GLORIOUS ITEM PROGRESSION. NPC CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT. DELVING INTO A MULTI LEVEL UNDERMINE FULL OF SECRETS AND BEAUTY ( and plenty of horrors). IT JUST KEEPS GOING. And I'm talking directly to a scope that feels nearly unobtainable at the moment, and I LOVE IT.But if that wasn't enough, it boasts possibly the most aesthetically pleasing art in the genre, a soundtrack of BANGERS, a cast of varied characters you actually want to learn more about... (HUFFS). I just can't get enough. And I won't. I must keep digging deeper into The Undermine. I recommend that you do too.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fantastic game for what it is so far, but there's not enough content to binge this game like other, more established roguelikes.It needs more mobs/bosses/stages; and the bosses in the later stages are made artificially difficult by overtuning their HP. The last fight is probably the easiest mechanically.Also, as it stands there is only swing and throw- and and item that makes your throw hover in place. Which is a good baseline for most playthroughs but the game would have a lot more replayabilty if there were more items that changed how the player fights- not just changing numbers like range, damage, speed, etc.Overall I'm reluctant to recommend this at it's current state for it's price tag.If rogue's are your favorite genre of games than I'd say pick it up- it's not the best but it's also a lot better than others that are out there.If you're not really a fan of rogue's I can't really recommend until it gets more content.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: 8/10 will recommend.Pro’s:- Not that hard, but slightly unforgiving as well.- Funny at times, especially in dialog with NPCs.- Surprising sometimes.- It contains hidden things, like entrances to extra rooms, but also in what you (accidentally) can do.- The developers did listen to the players and made the game way better during early access.Con’s:- A bit of a grind at start (for upgrades).- A bit repetitive, but not really boring due to random generated maps. And when you get better and upgraded, you can access more difficult areas with more ease.Tips: - Play with controller, but mouse also works. You can switch anytime you like.- Use the mirror in the room left of the starting hub to change your gender.I enjoy this game as an easy way to set off my mind after a hard day's work or something else that I need to calm down after. It is definitely not frustrating. Defeat is not that big of an impact, but it does come with a minor setback (losing some gold to buy upgrades mostly). Just enough to keep me going without stress. I love that idea!It is a bit of a grind at start though, especially when you lack the skills of mastering a controller like I do/did. It may take a while you get enough gold to get good upgrades (gear, bag, abilities) and enough currency to get potions and gear crafted by the NPCs, but for me just when it started to get repetitive and boring, I finally managed to kill the first real boss and it opened up a way to skip the starting zone (Goldmine) to the next part where the scenery does change enough to keep my interest again. Explanation: when you die, your pet tries to bring your gold back to the starting hub, but it does not contain all your gold anymore. Upgraded bags loose (slightly) less gold on death.Also the hidden things keeps me interested. Not only for entrances to hidden side rooms, but also for things you can do. Throwing your pickaxe on fire through a brazier and cooking some food while doing that, as for an example.And the way you do your “quests” (no quest list, just something asked by an NPC) for unlocking the NPCs and meeting some other NPCs in the dungeons was also nicely done.The game is quite not a graphical masterpiece, but still appealing to the eye. Also goes for the sound.I played since the end of early access and I can confirm the developers really did listen to the players and improved the game with their feedback. Bonus points for that!

_childDocuments_.review: No time for a detailed review so I give this game a rank A.Great game - you should definitely do it!!See my profile for more details about my reviews.Additional notes: my goodness, this game was a complete surprise! I bought it a few years ago, never thought about it, and when I installed and tried it, I was completely hooked for dozens of hours! That little game here is HUGE in content, replayability, attention to details, combos, addictive gameplay. Imagine a bit of a mix between Isaac, Spelunky, and Rogue Legacy. Of course it does not reach the heights of a narrative masterpiece like Hades, but it is still a GREAT game in terms of gameplay. The infinite possibilities you can have between your combos of powers, skills, blessings, curses, enemies, is insanely huge, and has nothing to envy from Hades. I can not believe this little game did not make more buzz than that! It got out in August 2020, and last updated in November 2021... after that nothing. If you ask me, that game did not get the attention it deserves. The addiction this game creates is totally fair, as you WANT to go deeper, you WANT to finish it.Sure, the visuals are fine, they are cute, almost a bit casual, and maybe that did not help for the hype around this game... but in terms of game design? My god, Thorium did a real goldsmith work here. I will follow these guys! It has a nostalgic feel in its exploration and level system, but it is completely up to date in terms of rogue like gameplay and features. Why didn't this game go more successful!? Such a shame, a REALLY great game.

_childDocuments_.review: An awesome rogue-lite game with a lot of replayability. Had a blast (pun intended) discovering the different items and unlocking the new levels.It's a dungeon crawler where your primary goal is finding Relics that change a bit of how you play during each run. These can also be paired with blessings and curses to create unique builds each playthrough. You have both melee and ranged attacks (personally I like range attacking), and there are builds/items that help both of them so whichever you enjoy you can build upon. There are even permanent choices and upgrades in the Town hub to make it a bit easier as you progress over time.  As you beat the current final boss you get a 'ng+' type of mode where the enemies get more difficult and the bosses seem to unlock some new mechanics. Each death feels worth while as you return to town with gold for another upgrade and you can upgrade your 'return' amount of gold fairly steadily. Overall a very fun game, and the devs are quite active giving constant updates to their progress and what's coming next. I just heard about the December update for the new level and I'm super excited! I already have 45 hours in but I think i'll get plenty more.WELL worth the money in my opinion!Great job devs, keep up the amazing work!!

_childDocuments_.review: If you like games with permanent upgrades, roguelike runs through randomly generated dungeons and items, and unlocking stuff as you play I highly suggest trying this. I think this game is at a good place for where it is in development.The game is ultimately unfinished as stated when you "finish" the content that they have, which took me roughly 12 hours to complete.  The game makes a statement that there is further content on the way.I definitely would like to see a bit more content for the game.  It felt like a full game, but I think it would thrive with a couple major updates.The devs also sound super exicted and passionate about the game from posts they've made in game and on the update logs, so I get a good feeling that they're not going to abandon the game.The concept is similar to The Binding of Isaac- each level is a floor where you can find a treasure room items, shops, bombs, keys, health ups, secret rooms, and you jump down a shaft to get to the next level. However, it does not feel like Isaac, to me at least.  I feel like it's a neutral aspect. I really liked:-The game felt overall fun.  I have a positive experience with the game and looked forward to coming back to it to play more.-The upgrade system.  You go dig for gold and use it for permanent upgrades and unlocking things around the base.-The game felt decently challenging.  Some of the rooms felt a little unfair, but I feel like it had the correct difficulty when it comes to an item dependent type of run.-The bosses were unique enough for me-While there are a few bugs I encountered, none of them were anywhere near game breaking, the game felt decently polished.  I saw a lot of people complaining about the movements and combat but I never had any issues with it.There are a few things I would like to see improved.-A lot of the items feel a bit under powered.-The blessing/curse system is a bit unbalanced as the curses are way more detrimental than the blessings are helpful.  Every time you get a blessing you receive a curse as well, while it's not too hard to get rid of the curses, some of them are just brutal.  I eventually just started ignoring the entire system and played without it as it felt too unbalanced towards failure.-The progress is a little bit slow, even for me.  It starts off decent but noticeably tapers off.  The higher upgrades get really expensive but the money is hard to gather as you lose a decent percentage of it when you die, and the only option is in the run is to die... as you find out after the first run or two.  There are upgrades to reduce the percent loss but it becomes expensive to upgrade it.-The prices of the shop start to scale up and become pretty pricey as the game goes on.-The game in its current state does not seem like it has much replayability once you "finish" the content they have.None of those were major killers for me,  just something I would like to see improved on.I'd say the price should be more around $10, but I'm glad I got it, and I feel like future update will justify its cost.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Game improved enough for me to recommend. More variety, combat is..better, and now has enough content to make it enjoyable. (Old review)It's not quite there, but with a few tweaks it certainly can be.My main issues lie with the combat: Your throwing attack needs to be painfully precise. Hit boxes on smaller mobs are, not surprisingly, small, and your pickaxe never feels like it's covering enough area to hit what you're aiming for.The speed in which some enemies move doesn't really dance well with your attacks either. You are often clunky, while enemies are much more agile (and abundant. I'll get to that). Put it all together, and it makes you feel like you're threading a needle that's moving around like a hummingbird. Enemies: Their movements are okay in theory, but I don't know if they thought about all the different variables when packing these rooms full of different enemies. Some enemy attacks require you to move and do things a certain way, while others require you to do something wildly different. That's okay on paper, I mean, it's a game.. but if you get a variety of these mobs in a room, and they do wildly different things, you end up with a conflict. One mob will make you suffer for doing whatever it is you did to dodge the other, with no solution but to take a hit. So..what do you do if you have many things coming in at every direction, beating on you? Well, you jump around in circles like a madman, dodging everything you can! That's where the holes and spikes come in. Again, too many variables, and not enough thought as to how they work with one another. I shouldn't have to jump around in circles. There should be options and a way to "dodge" this, while I "attack" that. Before I go on, I have to say I'm a huge Isaac fan. I have over 2k hours in the game. Since the games are so similar, I have to be honest and say that it also suffers from the above conflict. The difference here is that Isaac has a multitude of options and choices that takes the edge off. Sometimes the game is unfair to you, but sometimes you are unfair to the game..if that makes any sense. Undermine either feels fair enough, or not fair at all.Bosses: Boss difficulty is controversial in games, but I find it really hard to believe that anyone thinks the final boss (for now) is harder than Selt (the first boss not counting that rock guy you fight literally once and never see again). It actually feels like the difficulty decreases boss-wise. I beat the final boss the first time, and every time after that, and I'm still dying to Selt. I think a lot of it has to do with the small area you have to hit on him, so it suffers from the combat issues I explained above.Build variety: There isn't any. Well, not much. You either A: Go for a gold-seeker build, getting relics, blessings, and potions that maximize your gold collecting. B: Increase your throw stats with speed and damage or  C: Increase stats for the regular swing attackEven those build don't end up different from one another. You'll find yourself mostly mixing because, to make your gold collecting worth it, you'll need to be strong to get through it all. So all variety in builds end up narrowing down to about the same thing every time.There are very few item combinations that do anything together uniquely. But I'm not gonna hold it against the game too much. It is still early days. I feel like the game needs a musket or something. I dunno. All that said, I do think the game can be really great instead of mostly frustrating with just a few changes. They really did put a lot of work into it, and it shows. Hopefully they take feedback well, and if they do, I see this being a solid entry into the rouge-lite genre once it comes out of EA.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a great introduction to the rogue-like genre, with charm and great art to boot, but also offers plenty to keep veterans coming back for more. Undermine walks that fine line between "sense of progression" and "just one more try". I'm someone who's generally wary of rogue-likes. While I almost always love the aesthetic and those 'OMG-long-runs' that happen every once in awhile, I often find the lack of progression and/or the constant restarting to be highly frustrating.That said, I've spent my fair share of time in the genre. Of course like anyone else, I praise instant classics like Dead Cells and Binding of Isaac; I was a fan of Hero Siege and Rogue Legacy. In that same vein, Undermine might just be another standard for the rogue-like genre; Undermine deserves to be held in that same regard.There's plenty to enjoy here as well. Beyond the great art and music, it has a nice collection of tile sets (five+ iirc) and a spectacular risk/reward item system. Like most rogue-likes, there are trinkets to collect that give the standard benefits you've expect. Where the game gets really interesting is in its "blessing"/"curse" system. There are blessings that bestow incremental buffs (e.g. swing damage, throw distance, max hp, etc.), but they are almost always combined with a curse. A curse can decrease your stats (e.g. swing damage, throw distance, max hp. etc.). The end result is a sort of min/max system whereby if you really want to push your character to the highest strength levels and delve into the mine as deep as possible you will have to give something up to get something in return. The net result is the ability to craft your character for that run. Have you gotten two throw buffs and a swing debuff? I guess it's a throw run. Did you get a really interesting bomb trinket? Time to play with bombs. Etc.And it's in that trinket and blessing/curse system that the game begins to shine. Granted it's not necessarily as deep or varied as Binding of Isaac for example, but considering how much more Undermine has to offer beyond just those two systems, it's not noticeable.I'd rather not explain more about how the game works or what you'll discover, because that's part of the joy of Undermine. Rest assured, the game has a lot to offer and for those seeking more replayability and harder/longer challenges, you will be very satisfied.

_childDocuments_.review: UnderMine is a really fun game and is probably my favorite of the roguelite genre.  It's a good challenge and there is a bit of grind to it, but I really didn't mind at all.  I've seen other players complain that the game is "broken" because of what they felt were undue amounts of grinding.  You could crush the game in about 4-5 hours if everything was handed to you and it would kill the challenge in my opinion.  The mechanics are good and I did not encounter a single bug in the 35 + hours of game play so far. Plus, it really scratches that Legend of Zelda itch.  I do wish there were a greater variety of foes as opposed to making the same ones stronger as you progress through the mine. I bought the game on sale and it's a really great value at that price. _childDocuments_.review: Undermine makes sense in the context of being in mines without actually mining and using more and more items, good or bad, to meet enemies and friends. The pickaxe flies loops and can also be swung, the deeper you fight your way. You collect gold in a sack on the way to reduce inflation. When you die, regardless of your sex, you start over again without any gold. Cave number one starts in mountains with lots of slime and bees that do not mine honey. You should avoid bee droppings and go deeper into the mine as soon as possible to find more oxygen, which does not get less the deeper you go. Among the mines are corridors that are decorated with gold like palaces. Here you have to pause and soak up the atmosphere before the sack of gold implodes and the player realizes that this is just a pc game. After the palace-like regions you travel through other biotopes, which differ in consistency and are relevant in terms of construction compared to the mining mine. In the end, everyone has to feel for himself if he wants something like this. In the bible death is infinitely long and for most people too short, because that is exactly what Undermine is based on.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: They've fixed a lot of the issues I've had. Risky gameplay isn't punished so harshly now and most of the curses are fair, ie, they do the exact same thing as the blessings but in reverse. Curses are also easier to get rid of now. There are still plenty of relics that don't do much, but many were buffed up a bit so that you can feel an impact. The spider room was actually fixed (the spiders are more spread around the room and they don't aggro you all at once) but I've not had a chance to face the boss again since one match and you're done. All in all, they did a good job and I'm glad to see the active development.Pros-Good sprites, good animations.-fun gameplay loop of slowly powering up your characterCons-punishes risky gameplay, rewards boring tactics. If the game offers you a cursed chest, 9 times out of 10 the curse is going to be way more debilitating than whatever treasure might be inside. By which I mean, it will reward you with something like 50g and maybe a key, but punish you with buffing all enemies with poison attacks that double their effective damage or empty out every chest you find for the rest of that run or make you lose max health every time you kill an enemy...even though killing every enemy in a room is mandatory to progress.-It's not just that you should ignore cursed chests either. You'll also come across levers which you can pay 15 health to pull with a chance of a reward. Testing them out, I pulled them as much as I could in three separate runs, knocking my health all the way to 0. In that time, 80% of the time they dropped worthless skulls, and the other 17% of the time they dropped 5 gold, and 3% of the time they dropped a food item to heal me for 20 health. Basically ever RNG mechanic in the game is rigged against the player, making the optimal play to IGNORE ALL NOVEL ENCOUNTERS.-The curses are super debilitating, but the vast majority of the relics you can find in a run are almost always mediocre at best. There's a lot of variance, with the best one I've encountered being "your ranged attack autohits two extra times after a successful hit", but most are middling like "you don't take damage from spike traps" or "gold does a tiny bit of damage when you mine and throw it around the room uncontrollably", down to incredibly useless stuff like "increased defense at critical health, ie you might be able to take an one extra hit at low health, unless that attack killed you outright" or "the shop stocks an extra item, feel free to buy it, though that will gimp your longterm progress"-some of the rooms can be unfair. In particular, sometimes you'll be put in a room filled with spiders that all immediately jump on you and hit you with a ton of poison damage, and since they stagger their jumps, avoiding all of them while fighting back is nearly impossible.-the 2nd boss is a giant headache. I'm not much of an expert at gaming, but I can at least handle the final boss of Dead Cells with 2 boss cells activated, the final boss of Hades with 50 skulls active, and cleared some runs of binding of isaac. The second boss is more difficult than most of those because it's constantly spawning minions, it's invincible everywhere aside from its butt, it moves around unpredictably with only a few chances for you to land attacks, and when you do attack it, it has a ton of health, all the while hoping it doesn't change direction to immediately hit you and lop off a fifth of your health twice in a row because the cooldown on taking damage from enemy attacks is basically nonexistent. The game has potential, but it's very Early Access and rough right now.

_childDocuments_.review: For an early access title, Undermine is very polished. If you've been trying to find something that scratches Binding of Issac itch, but Enter the Gungeon is way too hard for you, this is a great game. It's like if Binding of Issac had a baby with Rogue Legacy.My only complaints are that:1. Hitboxes are inconsistent. I feel like I'm hit with projectiles I dodge, and occasionally not hit with projectiles I don't. 2. Sometimes gold can appear in walls in the corridors between rooms, if you accidentally enter the room while trying to pick up gold, any you've left behind will be gone.3. Cursed chests/torches are usually not worth whatever is inside of them. Some curses are basically benign (shop cost inflation), and others make boss fights impossible (swing speed -). There may be some tweaking there for these to feel balanced.4. The pilfers are really annoying. I get that they add some urgency to grabbing gold, but they just annoy me since they make clearing an empty room more tedious.Quick tip: Play with a controller, or at least try it. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Overall the music and the graphics of this game is great and i had a whole lot of fun.  However there are stuff that separate this from an amazing roguelite game like hades. Played for a solid 13 hours and it is quite fun.  it draws on a lot of mechanics from old school zelda games which i love,  however there are a few issues i find which separates this game from an amazing rouguelite.1) I still recommend it as i had some fun but this is not hades.  it takes a while to build up the equivalence of a boon in hades and there are a lot more trashy ones which makes you feel like you wasted your time.  2) unlike hades, you know when you stumble upon an amazing build and the game really makes you feel satisfied.  you feel powerful and it makes you want to keep playing.  Undermine just lacked that little rewarding feeling.  I got 5x relics (boon equivalence) that boosted my throw damage but i didn't feel strong, the relics didn't have amazing visual/audio effects to feel different.  Overall you just feel like you're stacking numbers. 3) hit boxes doesn't feel very clean, sometimes you miss a mob even though it feels like you hit them.4) quite similarly there is a few times i walked near a hole, totally still on the edge and my guy just fell in.5) progression seems a bit unbalance.  I get that they want to make gold easily obtainable so that it reduces the grind.  however i feel like those upgrades makes it so that you are very strong which makes the game easier (make you tankier, do more damage, more range).  In comparison to hades (again, i am using this example cos that was a rouguelite that just blew my mind) which the permanent unlocks are a completely different playstyle, something that is more challenging/higher learning curve with higher potential to get you further each run. So i feel like the permanent progression mechanic of undermine just shortens the re-playability of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Updating my December 2019 review to reflect my views now the game has been further updated.The Othermine update truly makes this a solid Roguelite, and is truly the mode the game should be played. It addresses my previous gripes of the game - runs are now shorted, relics are fewer and transmuting/rerolling them is much harder to do, and your gold actually matters. By limiting the choice you have, it makes your decisions more impactful and your run play out in its own isolated way - no more is the game "transmute until you get Key Blade or a similarly broken item" and instead you play each run through the Undermine in a unique way. My first Othermine victory was a throwing build, a build I never used in regular ascensions 1-15 because why would I bother? But my Othermine run strengthened that area of my play and limited what other options were available. It was fun, it was unique and it made me appreciate more of the items in the game and regularly made my decisions more impactful.Previously, I'd have given this a 6/10, now this is easily an 8/10 with more room for improvements if they lean into Othermine as the "true" mode of the game with further updates.

_childDocuments_.review: Skip. This is inherently a frustrating classic isometric roguelike.Play Binding of Isaac, Risk of Rain, Dead Cells, or FTL if you like Roguelikes.Play Rogue Legacy or Hades if you like Rogue-RPGs.If you like difficult games, this is more just frustrating.Play anything else if these are not your thing.The bombs are highly limited but key to gameplay. Bombs are used for both damage (see trite 'RPG upgrades') and for finding secret rooms, often on accident as there's no indicator except sparkles, which don't always appear. The special abilities don't make you feel special and are often either a plain stat increase, side-grade, or self-harming playstyle. You'll get bounced around by enemies and bombs and control taken from you, fall down a hole, take damage, and bounced again; the only means of dodging is to jump, which takes away control. Controls aren't very responsive. There's no just-in-time response to pits or dodging. Art is good but animation feels repetitive and unfeeling (get hit, bounce, anything, same walking animation). The addition of upgrades bought with gold is just a crap unlocking schema which feels more like an added reason to grind. I wanted to like this. I love Rogue Legacy and Hades. I'm not big into arcade games (which is what a roguelike is after finishing grindy item unlocks), but I know a good one when I see it, and this isn't.

_childDocuments_.review: After some playtime I decided to give this game a negative review. It started out promising with a beautiful art style, a fun combat system (with a mix of melee and range attacks) and much stuff to discover (items, NPCs, new levels).Unfortunately, the game becomes one thing after said playtime: tedious. Mining for gold becomes a boring grind, and the upgrades you get for it don't feel powerful or effective at all. The game offers a variety of items - buffs, companions, potions and such - but you won't see 80 percent of them. Because they never appear (nor their recipes). Some buffs offer synergies, so they evolve into a more powerful version - I've only managed to get one of those...Another thing is the control of your runs. Or the lack thereof. You can't really influence, which buffs you get, some of them are utterly useless, some of them have the same effect as another buff. Your success is greatly depending on luck. Which adds to the grind factor.There are 5 bosses, after that the game is supposed to offer new challenge modes and a new dungeon. I never got that far. I think I could handle boss no. 4, but after some fruitless attempts with nearly the same useless buffs/items I asked myself: Why continue playing?

_childDocuments_.review: Exceptionally good roguelike with a huge supply of persistent upgrades to improve your spelunking.  In UnderMine, you play the role of a 'Peasant' miner under the direction of a wizard to go into the mine and look for a lost Blacksmith.  Before long you're on a quest to explore the depths of the mine and beyond--seeking out various ancient bosses and completing quests.  Along the way you'll unlock new NPCs in town from which you can permanently enhance yourself and unlock new items which will drop randomly in the labyrinth below.I've played through this game to the current "end-boss", though this is in EA so there are at least 2 more planned.  Upon each game completion, you can further increase game difficulty and respawn all the dead bosses.  This can be a *very* difficult game, and I can break down the mechanics into a few key areas, though there are a handful of other mechanics I won't go into.  You'll find this in pretty much  room in the dungeon.  You mine it, and these little things called Pilfers immediately spawn and try to steal it from you.  They don't do any damage and are pretty fun to smack away, but it keeps you on your toes and makes you be a little careful when using potions or blowing up multiple gold nodes at once, due to the likelihood that you'll be Pilfered.You lose a % of your gold when you die--but you can purchase persistent upgrades to your gold bag which will let you take more back to town with you, up to a max of (I believe) 95%.You'll find a shop on just about every floor which is randomly stocked (you can upgrade the size).  A core part of the game is balancing how much you need to spend on items here (especially bombs and keys) vs how much you want to save for going back to town.These are your core resources for opening locked doors and chests as well as blowing up walls to secret rooms, rocks, etc.  Maintaining a constant supply of bombs and keys is core to exploration and finding upgrades.  You'll rarely have more than 3-4 of each and often will be scouring a floor for a bomb or key to let you into a treasure room.You probably won't be using bombs in combat too often unless it's a boss or one of a few special enemies that will wreck you if you don't deal with them pronto.  That said, you have a pickaxe which you can throw or swing.  Throw does less damage, and the pickaxe is unavailable while it's boomeranging out-and-back to you, but it's a safe option which will probably be your bread and butter damage option.  The swing does more damage but it has some dead frames which will leave you totally open.  You can jump around to dodge (I think you have invincibility frames for the entire duration of the jump), but you can't control yourself while in the air, so you have to be careful you didn't panic jump towards a pit/fire/spikes/electricity/etc.The game starts out easy enough, but you'll soon discover how nasty some rooms can be.  When you walk into a room with enemies, the doors lock until they're all dead.  In true roguelike fashion you can be having the best run ever--tons of upgrades, gold, bombs, keys and no curses--and then wander into a room where there's oil and spikes everywhere, tons of projectile-spewing mobs, things that teleport, and if you aren't ready to react you can kiss most of your healthbar goodbye.  And you won't be replenishing that easily (or cheaply).You can find upgrades in the dungeon in the form of relics and blessings.  These are typically things like faster swing speed, faster throw speed, more damage, more health, poison-on-hit, etc.  Some of them are pretty unique, like heal every time you pick up gold, or modify how your bomb explodes.Generally you find one guaranteed upgrade per floor, and (eventually) one blessing--which always comes with a random curse.  More on that later.  You can definitely find more than 1 upgrade per floor, it's just not  and you'll have to solve some puzzles or spend some bombs/keys.  Which you'll typically want to.  You can also find/buy potions, which have a wide range of effects like any of the other upgrades., you'll find blueprints/recipes/formulas/scrolls/books, etc. which you can give to people in town to let you spend a rare resource called 'Thorium' to unlock.  You can immediately take one of these into the dungeon with you, losing it after you die, but that upgrade can henceforth be found in the dungeon at random like any other upgrade (think Dead Cells).The last thing I'll talk about is curses.  I think this is the one area in the game that could use some balancing, since it's extremely random and there are some  curses out there.  You can remove curses, but it's random whether or not you'll be given the opportunity.  It's also random which curse is removed, and it can be prohibitively expensive--sometimes costing progressively more life for each curse removed.  You can sometimes find potions/talismans which can remove curses for free (provided you didn't buy it at the shop).Curses are (generally) a risk vs reward mechanic--you willingly do one of a few actions, knowing it will give you an item or two  apply one random curse.  I won't detail  these actions are since it's a little spoilerish.I've found that it's just not worth it to take a cursed item unless you know  that there's a shrine, talisman, potion, etc. available on the floor to dispel it .  This is due to the chance of receiving a severe curse--like reducing your max health when you kill an enemy (you can't skip enemies due to the doors locking in each room).  There are curses that destroy your upgrades, cause all chests to be opened, make you lose more gold on death, make  cost double (like 2 keys to open a door), and a whole bunch that just make you take damage for various reasons.While I like the concept and the general effects that the curses have--I just think their frequency should be toned down.  It should be a small chance to get cursed when you do some actions and maybe a reduced  of curses for one of the major events.  As it stands I never play the risk reward mechanic because it's screwed me too many times without any appreciable benefit--I  take curses if I  I can immediately purge it.  This is honestly my only gripe with the game--everything else is fantastic!I can't recommend this game enough for fans of the genre.  It's challenging, there's a ton of upgrades, and there's a lot of content on the horizon.  Don't skip it!

You can drink potions, or jump, place bombs, also you can move don't forget that. The difference much like BoI is you get relics that change effects of your attacks and things in the world. It is very much an endurance run but it's quite enjoyable with some cuteness. If you aren't set on this genre for this price just wait for the sale, it's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: "Delving into Delightful Depths"Rating: ★★★★☆Introduction:"Undermine" is a hidden gem that shines brightly in the ever-expanding world of indie roguelike games. As a dedicated fan of the genre, I found myself pleasantly surprised by the depths this game explores and the fun it consistently delivers.Gameplay (★★★★☆):The core gameplay loop in "Undermine" is addictive and satisfying. You play as a lowly peasant armed with a pickaxe, delving deeper into a procedurally generated mine. Each run offers a unique experience, with a variety of enemies, traps, and treasures to discover. The blend of real-time combat and resource management keeps you engaged and challenged. The frequent upgrades and power-ups add an element of strategy, making each decision count.Graphics and Audio (★★★★☆):Visually, "Undermine" has a charming pixel art style that feels nostalgic yet polished. The environments are filled with detail and personality, from the bustling hub area to the eerie depths of the mine. The audio design complements the game perfectly, with a catchy soundtrack and satisfying sound effects that immerse you further into the experience.Story and Narrative (★★★☆☆):While "Undermine" isn't primarily a story-driven game, it manages to infuse its world with subtle lore and amusing character interactions. The witty banter with NPCs and the occasional surprises hidden within the mine add an extra layer of enjoyment to the journey.Replayability (★★★★★):One of the standout features of "Undermine" is its exceptional replayability. The game encourages multiple playthroughs by offering an array of unlockable characters, relics, and secrets. The constant sense of progression, even in the face of defeat, keeps you coming back for more.Cons (★★☆☆☆):While "Undermine" excels in many areas, it's not without its flaws. Some may find the difficulty curve to be a bit steep, especially in the early levels. Additionally, occasional technical hiccups and minor bugs can be a slight annoyance.Conclusion:"Undermine" is a delightful roguelike that manages to strike a harmonious balance between accessibility and challenge. It's a testament to the potential of indie game development, offering an engaging experience filled with surprises and moments of triumph. If you have a penchant for roguelikes or are simply looking for a game with substantial replay value, "Undermine" is a worthy addition to your library.Overall Rating: ★★★★☆

_childDocuments_.review: I've really enjoyed my time with this game, and I'm still looking forward to new content and release. Runs are long enough to feel satisfying, and you start to get attached to your build/character before dying or finishing the bottom level. This game is much like Isaac but with a lot of progression overarching each run. Initially, the runs feel pretty varied based on the items and upgrades that are found in randomized levels. Eventually, after buying a good amount of upgrades and finding a lot of the items (and there are a lot), it starts to feel much more consistent, making it easier to put together certain types of builds. Some rooms continue to feel challenging in late game (of current content). The latest update adding familiars adds another layer of gameplay as well. Highly recommended for an early access buy, and it's well worth the purchase price.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun gold-grind roguelite with RPG elements. Interesting curse/blessing system for buffs and debuffs that can be managed throughout a run. It's kinda like gambling on your run every time you come across an alter or a cursed chest/room, seeing if you can come out ahead by potentially removing really bad curses along the way and reaping the benefits of the extra blessings and relics you get by potentially nuking your run with a nasty amount of curses. Challenging in the short term with big payoffs and rewards for those willing to put their nose to the grindstone and dig into this thing. Cool cast of characters for the small amount of lore available right now. Would love to see it keep expanding somehow and get a little deeper (pun intended) on that aspect of the game. Overall a solid game and it's still Early Access.

_childDocuments_.review: Most times, nostalgia is a mistake.Most of the difficulty in this game is due to poor control and annoying/clumsy design choices. Besides an unfortunate desire of the designers to restrict you to old school zelda controls, you get a wonky jump with no air control. They'd likely try to pawn this off as "plan your inputs carefully," but that's a mentality better reserved for games that have tight player interaction like enter the gungeon, where your tools are useful and varied, not so loose that you can get shoved into pits by hard to see bottles dropped with gold. Most fights involve running around, swinging and then mashing jump to avoid incoming armored punish from your spongy foes. Unlike other roguelikes, it's rather difficult to find relics and blessings that fit together, and those that you do generally fall under three camps. 1. Generally good, flat bonuses that are useful but don't really affect your playstyle for a run. 2. Mediocre build changing items that force you to play suboptimally and can't be removed. 3. Useless chaff. There are maybe 2-3 relics that are great and unfortunately game breaking - having them means I'm beating the next boss, until then grind gold again to get past the next gear check, but they're also boring (like the soul aegis).There's a misvaluation of opportunity costs everywhere because most choices you have terrible returns for the risk. Everything costs too much, and gold is unreliable so the cost of a run is prohibitive - this leads to runs where you get as much gold as you can and die, and then true runs where you try to beat content. That's inherently boring game design.Blessings are trash due to the lack of predictability of curses, and are so weak that it's almost always a waste of time to get them even if you can double back for an omori to cleanse them. The other trade you'll often find yourself making is whether to carry keys or bombs, but besides a few relics, keys = gold and meat, and bombs = gold  meat and damage. The bomb relics are all "bombastic" and unfortunately risky and stupid. In most cases you don't want to upgrade your bombs because the bomb upgrades hurt you and are less predictable. 1-2 of them are better for bossing but destroy items you want. Also, there are several "dead" rooms that spawn with nothing in them, or rooms that take lots of resources to provide you with a trapped box. The latter is par for the course with Roguelikes, but Roguelikes also rarely give you rooms that have immense rewards to counteract this. I have pretty much never found a room or item in this game that made me feel a sense of satisfaction.You're better off with Enter the Gungeon, Hades, Dead Cells, hell even Rogue Legacy is more entertaining.

_childDocuments_.review: I gave my best shot but I cannot find enjoyment playing this game. Combat is barebones yet it is also slow & repetitive at the same time. Floors are filled with traps and pitfalls to the point you have to actively focus at looking around the room while multitasking fighting enemies, which gets tiring & annoying very fast. Jumping is clunky and you have no air control. You aren't even allowed to relax and feel rewarded for collecting Gold, because Pilfers constantly try to steal it as soon as it drops on the ground. Most relics (at least during my playtime) fail at making a major impact or making runs feel different from each other. Upgrading/progression also feels like it moves at a glacial pace, you spend something like 20 minutes on a decent run and after losing half of your gold on death you spend the rest of it on only being slightly (if not barely) stronger, making the game feel unrewarding for how much time you're spending on it. If anything, I feel WEAKER because it seemed like as I kept doing runs, the game would spawn stronger new enemies on the first floors, so instead of doing better & progressing, I'd die at around the same points and get stuck. Making the player feel like they are becoming weaker in a game about upgrading & strengthening the character, is bizarre. That was when I ran out of patience with the game.

_childDocuments_.review: To preface, I have 2265 (afk or playing) hours in Enter the Gungeon.Undermine is REAL good. It's a roguelike where a basic function of the game is gathering as much gold as possible during your runs, and using it to DRAMATICALLY increase your power in the next run. Instead of something minor like Hades or ETG would give, this game will do something like give you a new relic that does something insane like give you double attack. Another area where this game plays way different than most Roguelikes, is that relics are rarely bad. There's not many rare relics, and all common ones can be overpowered in their own way, or especially if combined with another. (like getting popcorn to cause gold to duplicate when it hits the ground, and the pilfer ring to teleport gold to yourself, and the relic that makes you damage enemies when you pick up gold causes you to kill everyone in the room by farming)Because most powerups are equally strong, you can have a good run, every run. Beating the game allows optional additions to difficulty in various ways, so the game takes very mundane tasks and makes them meaningful, and that's nice :)The music is good, albeit could use some variety, the sound effects are great, the graphics are great, the gameplay is great, the story... haha you aren't playing a roguelike for story. 10/10 buy this game

_childDocuments_.review: Movement feels sluggish. Combat is pretty simplistic. You have two attacks: swinging your pickax, or tossing it to have it return like a boomerang. The former animation locks you until you finish the swing - which hampers combat flow imo. Enemies get really annoying late game - doesn't help that healing is somewhat sparse. Most relics - items that give you abilities during each run - are pretty anemic. The ones I encountered hardly altered my current run, although I did run into a flat "Increase Damage" relic a few times. But yet, the game requires you to use keys to unlock relic rooms after a certain floor. Ugh.Oh, but I forgot the STUPIDEST thing about UnderMine: .In UnderMine, gold is a very important resource. It's used for purchasing items from shops during a run, AND is used to permanently upgrade your character's stats (max health, ranged/melee damage, etc.) from the game's hubworld. When you die, a portion of your current gold is kept - and you use this to buy upgrades to your health, swing damage, throw range, etc. gold is dropped in a room, a bunch of NPCs called pilfers spawn and try to snag it. If they grab a gold piece and get to the edge of the room's screen, they get away with your hard-earned gold. You have to hit them with your clunky swing attack, or aim just right and throw your pickax. Either way, you can end up missing a few pilfers because of the clunky attack animations, and be short of whatever gold dropped in a room.Now, making a resource/"XP" for a character a time-limited pick-up is not a new mechanic at all; Nuclear Throne's rads (XP) disappear in a few seconds, and Voidigo's shards (currency) de-value over time the moment they drop.But UnderMine's pilfers are non-damaging enemies that sometimes move faster than your character, and can swarm over gold easily if a room contains active hazards like sawblades or fire-orb firing turrets. One time I walked over a pit to reach a treasure chest, on a spindly-pair of minecart tracks that had a sawblade running on them. I got to a chest that spewed a bunch of gold on the tracks. At least half of the gold was either snagged by pilfers or knocked off into the pit by the moving sawblade - lost forever. Real fun.  I believe you can purchase a pass to prevent pilfers from spawning during a run, but it costs a ludicrous amount of gold. Wow!Did I mention sometimes, a pilfer that drops an active bomb upon death spawns when gold drops? Who even thought this was a good mechanic?

It may not be super innovative on the roguelite-metaprogression formula itself, but it's gorgeous, very well polished, and very slick.And so, so, so many  moments of "OH FOR F--- SAKE THAT WAS A BS DEATH ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! ok ok ok chill out... one more run... this is my last one i promise I've got this down I'm gunna do it this time" *6 hours laters its 3AM* "ok just one more run i really gotta sleep since i have work tomorrow.... totally got it this time i swear....."
