_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax is a weird game that exceeds expectation in both gameplay and story. You start off as a journalist heading off to a mysterious island to interview a renowned explorer. When arriving you find everything in shambles- and it is up to you to solve both the mystery of bugsnax, and the villager’s problems. The gameplay is what 3D pokemon should have been; you have these adorable silly creatures called bugsnax wandering around in these biomes doing their own thing. They have different behaviours that make them unique- and the objective is to catch them all. Villagers are hungry, and they crave the bugsnax. You have a variety of traps at your disposal to catch the, so each scenario might involve planning. There are puzzles, secrets, and criteria required to progress and discover more. That being said, the game isn’t much difficult; there is no health, nor can you really die- or lose. Some of the bugsnax requires moderate critical thinking skills, but for the most part things are simple tasks. This shouldn’t discourage you though; the game makes up for it by pulling you into the story and compelling you to solve the mystery. The difficulty isn’t important; fun is. A lot of the fun comes from the story itself. Each villager has their own brand of issues and quirks that you have to deal with. They fight with each other, argue, and over all just don’t get along. Most have a partner with them, which brings a lot more nuance to each relationship and what is required to solve it. Each has their own little storyline you follow, and through it you discover what their problems are, and resolve them as the plot progresses. This all becomes apparent in the end, however it might end. There is a lot more to the bugsnax than what you see on surface level. Everyone might all be goofy creatures in colourful environments, but there’s more too it than just that.The art direction is that of a silly generic children’s cartoon; everything is playful and absurd- and it all sets a comfortable safe tone. The bugsnax itself are a great example of terrifying body horror; every time a villager eats a bugsnax, part of their body is transformed to resemble that bugsnax. Despite that being unsettling, the villagers are seemingly unphased by it, and instead are optimistic and delighted by the sight of the arm becoming a pickle. This is the contrast; the fun carefree appearance is offset by the uncanny nature of the bugsnax- and how the villagers are handling it. They are completely enamoured by the result of them. You get use to it, as it just becomes normalized as you hop around each area catching creatures to the music.I cannot really say anything too special about the music; in a way it has its charm, but it’s honestly long and drawn out- it’s like a modern 1950s grocery store music that just becomes a part of the ambiance. It is something you will just stop noticing, as it doesn’t really add much to the environments- aside from complimenting them slightly. The absolute most positive thing I can say about it is that it’s almost hypnotic; it’s this zen sort of melody that keeps things calm enough that you lose track of time.Overall, I would consider this a great game that is worth playing. It’s a game that you should get comfy for and chill. Grab a controller, kick back, and go catch some snax.

_childDocuments_.review: + Does a good job of blending a silly/weird concept with serious undertones. In general a really bizarre concept but the world and story are really well done.+ Memorable characters who all go through their own personal development and feature good voice acting.+ Loads of types of bugsnax with inventive designs, their own behaviours, and which amusingly repeat their name over and over in silly voices. There's some repetition, e.g. the same model but with a different colour, but overall a lot of variety.+ Core gameplay of finding and capturing bugsnax is good and lets you problem-solve with a variety of fun tools.+ Fun finding new biomes and new bugsnax critters to discover.+ Interesting to see what will happen to your Grumpus friends when you feed them different bugsnax.+ The boss fights are pretty fun.+ The graphics aren’t technically powerful, but they’re charming and simple and fit the theme well.+ The journal you get is really good - you can flick through it and see everything you've discovered (as well as what you haven't discovered). There’s some nice extras as well, such as each quest having their own drawing depicting the quest.+ Over the course of the game you get a hut to yourself which you can customise. It’s simple but sweet.+ Great theme song which is fun and light-hearted on the surface but with hidden meaning that makes sense once you’ve beaten the game.- The animations are simple and are generally decent, but in parts they can be quite stilted / disconnected, primarily concerning the characters.I had lots of fun with Bugsnax. It’s a unique, if very strange, premise that’s surprisingly fleshed out - both the characters you'll meet and the titular isle of Bugsnax itself. It's downright good fun to discover new biomes and go hunting for all the new bugsnax, seeing what they do, what they're called, how they work and thinking of ways in which you might trap them and feed them to your Grumpus buddies. If you’re someone who sees a game like Katamari Damacy and is interested because both the art style and gameplay appear to break the mould and offer something different, this is a confident recommend. Alternatively, if you’re into Pokemon you’re likely to really enjoy discovering all the bugsnax, documenting them, and figuring out how to catch them (although not battle them unfortunately!)

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax has quite a bit in common with Slime Rancher, IMO: - Gameplay focus on exploring biomes to catch weird but cute creatures. The main thing players are meant to do with these creatures, is kinda gross in both cases, but also kinda addictive (at least to me)- The story and NPCs start off seeming like they'll be just be cute, funny and simplistic, and at first there's only hints about how they'll not be entirely happy. And then the games start sucker punching you with assorted existential crises. And the NPCs and story turn out to be deeper and sadder than what might've been initially expected (though in Bugsnax the NPCs get more fleshed out than in Slime Rancher, and unlike Bugsnax, I doubt that anyone could really call anything about Slime Rancher horror). Both games give a lot of bittersweet vibes. - They both have some quite a bit of diversity in their cast of characters, in different ways, and as far as I can tell, they both do pretty well with their main diversity focus? While Slime Rancher has some POC characters and just a few hints of LGBT+, Bugsnax has some very clearly LGBT+ characters, and a bit of racial coding. - They both have some pretty scenery, and very nice soundtracks, and it's fun decorating your placeDespite it's child-friendly look, Bugsnax has some adult themes sprinkled throughout it, but I think it's about the same level as an average Spongebob episode. Other than the level of tragedy that Bugsnax can reach. I guess if you're thinking of letting a little kid play this, you might want to watch a playthrough first - or maybe even do a quick playthrough of it yourself - including checking the possible bad endings, by leaving side quests incomplete. Then decide based on that. You could get through the game a lot faster than I did, there's just a lot of optional content.

_childDocuments_.review: I watched two full playthroughs of this game a year ago and still decided I wanted to buy it on Steam (I did not buy it on Epic Game Store because I do not want to touch Epic Game Store).It appeals to me in many ways. I enjoy food. I enjoy wasting time repeating tasks such as capturing bugs in a video game as long as it is enjoyable to do so. Bugsnax makes this very enjoyable with the voice acting for the Snaks, the bright and vibrant artstyle, and the excellent tropical BGM. I spent actual hours just catching Bungers so I could fully turn the resident villagers into Bunger form despite knowing full well that I could easily do it later through other means just because I wanted to turn them into hamburgers as soon as possible and I enjoyed the process of capturing the Bungers so much. As for the villagers themselves, they are all fun characters. Even if I like some less than others, I could never say I hated anyone. And, as someone who doesn't really care for this kind of stuff, I feel that the ones that fall within LGBT-etc character types are the least-obnoxious and intrusive implementations of such types within a Western game that I've seen, so good job on that.The DLC content, which I had not seen prior to my purchase, is a nice addition to the game. I liked the house customization and the challenges that allowed me to use the Lunchpad to propel me to places I never thought that I'd be able to reach. Even if the Bigsnax are just regular Bugsnax with an extra step of throwing the shrinky powder at them, they're still enjoyable to catch. Also, spaghetti is my favorite food so I'm happy to see Spaghider as part of the DLC Bugsnak roster. My only complaint is that it didn't add anything new for my favorite character Cromdo outside of his mail challenges.The game's story, while not the best I've ever seen in a game, is memorable enough that it'll probably stick with me for the rest of my life. Decades down the line I'll look back on the games that I've enjoyed and I'll remember Bugsnax and think "Yeah, that was a good game. I like the funny hambunger. I like the Danny Devito Guy. I like the . Good times". I'm glad that the more lore-centric bits of the game got some expansion upon them in the DLC, a welcome addition. The few complaints I have about the game are the various bugs such as the DLC boss not being able to be defeated with uncapped framerate, and FPS tanking whenever I cover a trap with sauce. Nothing game-breaking but a bit of a minor annoyance. I also didn't like the year-long Epic Game Store exclusivity, but I understand that the team needed the money from it in order to make the game as good as they could.All in all, Bugsnax is a game that, while not perfect for everyone, is perfect for me. I'll probably replay it once a year and enjoy the hunt again and again. I'll also need to purchase that plush Bunger one of these days when I have a stable cash flow. Thank you for the pleasant experience, Wild Horses. I wonder what you'll make next.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid thumbs up.Why? The graphics aren't the best. The music seems a bit out of place. The gameplay loop can get old after a while. It was a novelty launch title for a console. etc etcAnd yet it stays good. It's hard to really compress why it's good into a review without spoilers, but let's just say that the flavour hits you in waves. Initially you have this cutesy game with muppety creatures called Grumpus that are searching for their two lost friends, and you're there to help them because you want to get a career-saving interview. You have the mysterious Bugsnax that are like food-based pokemon in that they can only vocalise their own names, and have weaknesses you have to exploit to catch them, with each zone being a little playground of sorts where you learn how to exploit their interactions to be able to catch them to tick off your roster and meet one of the many fetch-quests.But just as that gets old, the next layer kicks in. These happy-go-lucky Grumpus muppets and their soft cartoon peril start to reveal that actually they have a bit of depth, and that they aren't purely one-tone tropes even if they stay true to the parts they play. Sub-themes start to appear. Before you know it, you're not playing because you just want to catch that one adorably dumb flying tree-banana creature, but because you want to see what happens next, or how the interactions will develop.It sounds odd, but go into this game as blind as you can, and try not to google anything. If you get really stuck then maybe ask a buddy who has played it before. Also don't sweat the small stuff, because while there is a "point of no return", you can load the game and go back to tie up any sidequests or extra missions you didn't do later on.Also, those dumb little Bungers are stupidly adorable. I bought a friend a plush one for christmas. :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the definition of a good game. I can not think of any aspect that would be a negative in the minds of it's core audience... In the minds of it's core audience. I suggest before you buy this to watch through the trailer, and pay attention to the graphics and to the and humour. If you have no problem with that, this game well suit you perfectly. However, for some I can see things coming off as kiddish. The game play is fun and relaxing. It is puzzle based in nature, though not horridly difficult. New mechanics are introduced on occasion and they remain simplistic. The challenge rather comes in finding combinations of them to achieve a goal. Don't allow the notion of this to overwhelm you, because this game is a perfect experience for someone seeking an ephemeral & pleasant encounter. Bugsnax necessitates about 10 to 25 hours to reach completion, with the second figure representing 100%. While you're helping out the community that arrived here prior to you, you'll be well-qualified to form bonds with distinctly dissimilar characters, absorb data concerning their unique personalities, & assist them with their individual troubles. Commit crimes with Cromdo Face, the pragmatic businessman with a laser-eye focus on his monetary gain; scrutinize Snaxburg's residents with Beffica Winklesnoot; mediate the marriage disputes of Wambus Troubleham (the farmer desperately trying to provide sustenance for civilization) & Triffany Lottablog (an aloof archaeologist with a nihilistic streak), or witness the queer romance between Chandlo Funkbun (the town's resident himbo gym bro) & Snorpy Fizzlebean (a scientific conspiracy theorist that frequently goes off the rails). Regardless of who you converse with, it's possible to locate one's self in an array of admiration, irritability, and melancholy. In your possession, there will be a journal that drastically reduces time spent on logistics, rendering it feasible to track your progress. This includes a section for side quests, lore involving new companions, a bestiary that even lists caloric intake, & the rest will be discovered during your run.Sift through the remnants of your tools at your discretion, uncovering animalistic traps, a springboard that's known as the "Lunchpad," a puzzling apparatus referred to as the "Snaktivator" (which was designed by Flooty Fizzlebean, Snorpy's sibling and a stereotypically unethical scientist), the Buggy Ball (a clear hamster ball with a trained Strabby called Sprout encased inside), amongst many others. _childDocuments_.review: I first learned about Bugsnax from a teaser trailer shown off at Sony's Summer 2020 Presentation, in which my first reaction was a mixture of confusion and amusement, the game struck me as a complete joke, to the point that I even wondered whether it was a real game or just part of some viral marketing campaign for another game that was making a satire of other games on the market in which you capture/collect/raise small creatures such as the Pokémon series. In fact, right up until its release I used to joke around with other folks online about how it was going to be Game of the Year 2020 (tongue-in-cheek) because it just seemed like a nonsensical mishmash of different concepts that couldn't possibly work together.However, upon watching streams of the game, I found myself growing increasingly interested in playing the game because for as strange of a game as it is, it has a lot of undeniable charm and character which really drew me in. So, with that out of the way, let's stumble on through the rest of this haphazard review in which I struggle to collect my thoughts. With any luck, hopefully it will turn out as good as the game itself.Bugsnax features surprisingly good visuals with rich colors, models, and even textures which I didn't expect from such a cartoony-looking game. Everything stands out in Bugsnax, which is good because obviously if everything blended together then it would be completely impossible to spot certain Bugsnax amidst the environment, thus making them all the more difficult to find, catch, and, well...feed to the other characters. (Yeah, we'll get to that later...)Not to be out done by the visuals, Bugsnax features a remarkably diverse assortment of music, voice acting, and sound effects. Much like everything else in Bugsnax, the audio is a mixture of weirdness and wonder.Bugsnax places you in the role of a formerly famous Journalist whose reputation was recently tarnished by a report on an unspecified story which turned out to be a hoax, faced with one last chance to reclaim your credibility by taking on a risky report which could make or break your career. You've been invited to Snaktooth Island by the world-famous explorer Elizabert Megafig who claims to have made the scientific discovery of a lifetime which must be seen to be believed. Snaktooth Island is said to be a very dangerous place with an active volcano among other unknown dangers, but with your career on the line and no better options to fall back on, you ultimately accept the invitation and make the trip.You arrive on Snaktooth Island only to have your airship knocked out of the sky by a mysterious creature of massive size, but fortunately you survive the crash, along with your camera and trusty tape recorder. You embark only to discover that Elizabert has gone missing without a trace and that the rest of her motley crew has deserted the basecamp and split up in the absence of her leadership. What's more, the island is inhabited by strange creatures known as Bugsnax, who as their name implies, are a bizarre combination of insect and snack food, which for the most part make up the only edible substance on Snaktooth Island. Problem is, they're tricky to catch, most of the inhabitants lack the necessary skill to catch them, and are going hungry as a result. Fortunately, it just so happens that in addition to your skills as a journalist, you also have a knack for catching Bugsnax. And so, you must use all of your skills to investigate the disappearance of Elizabert Megafig, feed the starving, scattered visitors of Snaktooth Island, bring them back to basecamp, and interview them to gain clues, follow the trail of Lizbert, get the scoop, unravel the mystery of Bugsnax, and escape Snaktooth Island before the volcano erupts...or worse.The story of Bugsnax is surprisingly more complex than it appears on the surface, and even has some shocking twists along the way, with a lot more depth and character development than you would typically expect from a game that looks the way that it does. In other words, in spite of its bright, colorful, cartoony appearance, the game has a lot more to offer than it would appear.In Bugsnax, you traverse Snaktooth Island on foot, catching the eponymous critters. Along the way you'll gain access to various gadgets to help you solve puzzles and catch a wider variety of Bugsnax.Fortunately, Bugsnax is a rather simple game which controls well, so none of the puzzles are especially difficult, nor are the various methods of catching Bugsnax once you've gotten the hang of them. However, the game doesn't especially hold your hand, and there are plenty of interesting methods of catching Bugsnax using combinations of gadgets which the game itself doesn't directly tell you about, leaving the player to discover them on their own through experimentation. Catching certain Bugsnax can still be challenging though, which can be somewhat frustrating before you've learned everything, so it's best to take it slow. Bugsnax is best enjoyed at a relaxed pace, so players who like to speedrun through games on their first try may find themselves frustrated because the game really doesn't let you go everywhere or do everything all at once, but if you take it slow and go with the flow of the game, then it's a lot of fun.Bugsnax is a very enjoyable game with a lot more to offer than it would appear on the surface. I highly recommend it to anyone who is seeking a fun, relaxing, yet still somewhat challenging game with a unique setting, story, and characters. The game managed to exceed all of my expectations and became one of my favorite games of the year. I really hope that there will be a sequel someday too, as there are many ways that the gameplay could be expanded upon without overcomplicating it or making it less accessible.

_childDocuments_.review: Another game that I bought about a year ago and became a hidden gem in my library.Bugsnax really blew me away, and I totally underestimated how good it was going to be. I figured it was just capturing Bugsnax and feeding people, and that was it. I was surprised though to see how interesting and engaging the story and characters can be. The characters are probably the one part of the game that surprised me the most. They each have their own side quests, and relationships with the other characters and the player. As the game progresses, so does the characters relationships. The Bugsnax are obviously the crowning feature though. Each of them has a wide set of voice lines, some of which can be super funny. They also have some unique quirks, like one turning into multiple others, or having various elemental effects. Capturing them can take some thought sometimes because some of them require you to use unique strategies or even other Bugsnax to capture. There are over 100 Bugsnax in total so you will definitely be busy and there is always something new to see, and when you think you're rounding out the last of the Bugsnax, there always seems to be more you didn't know you were even missing.Even towards the end of the game I continued to underestimate it. I put off the final story mission until I got 100% on everything else, and I went into the final mission thinking I had seen it all, and the game just kept giving. I was blown away by the overall depth of the story compared to my expectations and overall it is an amazing game in every aspect applicable and I look forward to Bugsnax 2.

_childDocuments_.review: Kinda bug and kinda snack Bugsnax is what I personally want from gaming; just devs having a great time making something fun, with a lot of heart. You can tell a lot of effort went into crafting the Grumpuses (Grumpus’?) personalities and the Snax. Each character brings a lot of, well, character, each bringing a different personality to the table and maintaining good (or intentionally bad!) chemistry with the other characters. (I personally believe in Snorpy and Chandlo supremacy :D)THE SNAX:The best part of the game. Goofy lil dudes with goofy little designs. I caught myself smiling many times upon seeing new snax for the first time. Also, shout out to the voice actors for the snax, because they sold those lines. Very goofy, and obscenely silly. I often think fondly of the sounds Bopsicle and Scoopy Banoopy make.THE STORY:You play as an investigative journalist who’s on a last ditch effort to save their job after receiving an invitation from Elizabert Megafig on Snacktooth Island. A bit of mystery, a bit of seriousness, a lot of fun ensues. Your job is to find out what is going on on the island, as well as finding out what happened to Elizabert. Without spoiling anything, do all the loyalty missions for your buds in snaxburg (why wouldn’t you? They’re your buds!) for the best and happiest ending. Overall, this game is fantastic and if you’re looking for something short, sweet, with a lot of heart, buy it. I was not disappointed, and would gladly pay full price again.

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax is a monster catching game where you catch... food. The games allows you to explore an island full of creatures to capture and characters to befriend. With  compelling story and characters, a lot of tasks to complete, and cosy graphics and music Bugsnax is quite an amazing game to experience. If some aspects of the gameplay can be a bit repetitive or frustrating, the game still manage to offer an Amazing experience. When Bugsnax was revealed years ago I was a bit sceptic about what it could offer as it seemed to be a monster catching game with a simple twist, the monsters are food-like creatures. Still a bit curious about it, I booted the game only to discover that this twist was more than it first seemed. The game has a cartoonish and colourful look that only gives more reason to explore each of the map the game offers. Although simple, the game has a cosy vibe, and the design of the game is definitely a strong point. If anything, they contribute to reenforce the serious moments of the story by contrasting so much with them. The music goes quite well with the cute graphics as it showcases fun synth music but also some other elements such as acoustic guitar played by one of the game’s characters.  Some notable tracks are:  If you’re going to spend that much time hunting creatures, their designs have to be good to keep you interested. In Bugsnax you can find 112 Bugsnax. They are typically a mix of a bug and a snack (hence the name). Of course like in many of those games, some of the Bugsnax you will encounter are recoloured versions of previous ones but overall they are quite inventive and interesting. Each creature has a different label like “spicy” or “cholate filled” which allow them to be notable during side quests where you have to collect snacks with particular tastes. A lot of them are simply a pair of googly eye on top of a fruit and although it could seem bad, it is enough. None of the creature look bad and they fit well in the environment they are found in.  Another nice touch is that the names of the creatures are often puns like Tacroach or Crapple.You’re exploring an island divided into 8 zones and a resting area. Each zone is filled with different types of Bugsnax that you’ll have to catch to complete various quests. The nice thing about it is that each snax asks you to use a different method to get them. You start with two tools but then unlock more throughout the game. It can feel like each zone is a tutorial for each tool at times, but it’s never totally the case. Some tools are definitely better than others and some can be a bit frustrating until you discover some hidden usage by experimenting (or going through the game but I was taking my time to do everything before moving on). I mentioned the completion of quests which are almost entirely fetch quests. You have story quests, secondary quests and also mail quests which are little challenges such as “catch three snax with one trap” etc. A particularity of Snax is that they transform the body of the person eating it, meaning that some quests ask you to transform characters in particular ways too. Something I appreciate a lot was that the game gives you a house in the village and that you receive furniture by completing the mail quests. It’s simple but it such a nice thing to have in a game and they do it less and less. You play as a journalist that goes to the Island to investigate the discovery of Bugsnax by a famous explorer. When they were there, they build a whole community and a village and each of them contributed to the life on the island. However, something happened before you arrived, and the leader of the community disappeared and consequently all the inhabitants scattered around the island and abandoned the community. You will have to bring them back but also discover the mystery of the island and the disappearance of the community leader.A good thing is that the characters are very likeable and although they are often representing one stereotypical type of character (jock, scientist...) they have still nice back stories and elements that make them compelling. The game also present different couples and even place two gay couples in the centre of its storyline which is quite nice! Well, to be fair once you discovered the end of the story and catch all the bugsnax, there isn’t much else to do. Maybe if you got stuck with a bad ending then you can retry and have the right one but I got the best ending directly and did everything the games had to offer in about 20 hours.  Bugsnax has 30 achievements and none of them are missable. A lot of them are story related but you also unlock some of them by trying new things within the game. Quite easy to get all of them too.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished but not completed.Bugsnax is an all-around good game, it offers a blend of adventure and puzzle-solving gameplay mechanics. The vibrant, cartoonish graphics and entertaining characters immediately draw you in. The gameplay mechanics are simple, centered around using the various tools you are provided with to capture Bugsnax, each with their own unique behaviours, capture methods, and interactions with each other.The mail challenges, though engaging at first, became quite tedious near the end. I completed about 85% of them before I felt myself no longer enjoying the game as much.The story of Bugsnax is fairly good. It doesn’t try to be anything more than it is – a funny and enjoyable game to spend about 12 hours in with a satisfying ending. The writing is straightforward yet engaging, filled with humour and emotion. The characters are well-developed, each with their quirks and backstories that add depth to the game.The sound design and music are also notable, with catchy tunes and fitting sound effects that enhance the overall experience. The voice acting is particularly strong, especially Bunger, love that silly little Bugsnax.I got this game when it was on sale for CDN$8.69 which for the 12 hours of gameplay I got was well worth the price.In summary, Bugsnax is a great little game with a charming aesthetic, creative gameplay, and a lighthearted story. While the mail challenges get repetitive, the overall experience is fun and worth the play through. It’s a great choice for anyone looking for a humorous and engaging adventure. I would recommend getting this game if you like casual adventure puzzle solving, and you are okay with spending CDN$28.99 on a 21-hour experience, if not, then maybe wait until it is on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay: 9/10Visual Design: 10/10Sound/Music/Voice: 8/10Story/Writing: 8/10Fun factor: 9/10Overall: 8.8The gameplay loop is very satisfying, exploring and scanning new biomes to see which bugsnax you can catch now and which you'll have to come back for later. Figuring out strategies to catch bugsnax is satisfying, because some of them are actually pretty challenging and require planning and patience.I was drawn in by the cute food creatures, but got much more than I was expecting. The character design in this game is great, each of the bugsnax feel unique (with reskins between regions, which I thought was perfectly fine to do). All of the grumps have clear personalities even before you hear them talk. The voice acting is great. Paired with the great character design, the voice actors bring even more life to each character. The story has more depth than I was expecting. I saw the trailer years ago when the game first came out, but totally forgot it and thought this was just going to be a whimsical monster catching game.The game is just pure fun and there's always something to do: exploring regions, scanning bugsnax, figuring out how to catch them, and getting to know each of the grump villagers. I never felt like I had to slog through a portion to get back to the good stuff. Everything is the good stuff. I got this on sale, but I think it would be well worth it at full price.Replayability: I don't think I'd play this game again, but I could see someone wanting to go through at least one more playthrough if they didn't catch all the bugsnax on the first run.

_childDocuments_.review: Interested and intrigued to play Bugsnax? GOOD.Bugsnax is a seemingly cozy and fun creature collector but it is secretly a psychological horror LGBTQ+ story title. I felt so cool catching the harder bugsnax like the Scoopy Banoopy. All the bugsnax have such cute and playful names such as Sandopede which is a kind of 4-part centipede made out of sandwiches. My favorite bugsnak, Rootle is a carrot worm that burrows itself into the ground if you scare it. I love the sound it makes when you catch it, the sound it makes sounds so cute and I can't stop petting it in the barn, YES, YOU CAN CATCH BUGSNAX AND DONATE THEM TO GRAMBLE'S BARN AND PET THEM!!! (and eventually dress them with hats!!!). ROoOoOotle...Don't be fooled by the bugsnak's cute nature, the story behind Snaktooth Island and Bugsnax as a whole is terrifying and DEFINITELY not fit for a children's game. Eating bugsnax has a severe side effect of body disfigurement which turns body parts into the thus eaten bugsnax. _childDocuments_.review: Great story, amazing voice actors, fantastic gameBugsnax is a fun game where you collect bugs that look like snacks. You play as a journalist reporter who was invited to Snaktooth island by world renown explorer, Elizabert Megafig, to come interview and report on Snaktooth island. Making it to the island you find out that Snaxburg, the settlement Lizabert set up, is abandoned and Elizabert is nowhere to be found. The last remaining resident and only mayor, Filbo, asks for your help to bring everyone back to town and help find Elizabert, while collecting bugsnax for the hungry townsfolk.The game at first glance is very silly and childlike. The game is very bright and vibrant, you have walking food creatures with googly eyes saying their names like Pokemon do and with names like Filbo Fiddlepie, Wambus Troubleham, and Gramble Gigglefunny, you'd probably assume this is a baby game made for small babies. Well you aren't entirely wrong... but you are still wrong. Bugsnax is a game that can be enjoyed by all ages where you collect and and document bugsnax. Yes there are silly names with silly food bugs running around, but the characters are incredibly well written with amazing voice actors that brush over mature themes that even us big kids are more than familiar with. I can't emphasize enough how fantastic the voice work is for this game. The contrast of what the characters are talking and the vibrant carefree world they live in makes it even funnier. The further along in the story you get the more serious the tone of the game is, with an intense and horrifying twist near the end.If you have the money, buy this game. It's fun to play and is easy to pick back up again after a long break. The story good, the characters are endearing, it scratches the completionist itch, and it's just a fun game to sit down and unwind to.

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't shy about the fact that it's heavily inspired by Pokemon. (One of the achievements is even called "gotta catch em all".) But at the same time, it's not remotely a rip-off of Pokemon; the gameplay style is completely different.So here's how the game plays out: You go out into one of several gorgeous biomes in search of Bugsnax. You employ a variety of tools, bait, environmental elements, and other Bugsnax to help you incapacitate the Bugsnak you want so you can capture it. Then you take your Bugsnax back to town and decide what to do with it – whether to have someone eat it, or just have it be a pet. You check in with people to get new requests for specific Bugsnax. And then it's back out to the wilds for your next hunt!If your favorite thing to do in Pokemon is catch new Pokemon and fill out the Pokedex, I think you'll like this game. There are no RPG elements in this game, which leaves room to flesh out the catching experience for all it's worth.I won't say anything about the story other than that it has layers. It's an iceberg - how far down the iceberg you delve is up to you.

The game has some of the most brutally honest dialogue, its amazing writing and delivery. Cute, silly, great voice acting and a surprisingly kid-friendly introduction to the wholesome world of body horror. I tried it out for its premise, but I stayed for the surprisingly deep characters.Once the characters start getting into their discussions, you learn it is in fact a decently mature story with elements of mental health problems, relationship dynamics and complications, as well as introspective analysis of the main characters and how they behave/respond to those around them.The whole vibe is also just amazing. Super eerie which I was very surprised about with the whole mystery feel going on which I loved. From the very beginning of the game you start to speculate and realize things are not what they seem and you start to understand there’s a lot more depth to it. There’s just such a sense of mystery and a slight unease that I hadn't felt from a game in a very long time. Amazing soundtrack as well.The game may look very simple, but they did a lot with it, from fully physics-based creature states to fire and ice gameplay mechanics as well as top-tier quest-tracking/management UI.  Each bugsnax is such a treat to discover and learn about and every single one is voice-acted, and though they can only say their name, they didn't just settle on 1 recording of it, all Bugsnax have 3 or so variations of saying their name so it never really gets monotonous or annoying, and each actor is bringing something unique to their performance which keeps it fun and adds a lot of personality to each creature.Also, the ending may be on of the biggest reveals and best endings in recent memory. I’m not spoiling but it is definitely something I believe everyone should experience for themselves. I seriously was moved to tears when it ended. You just can't even imagine how well the game gets to its end. Seeing how some your actions have consequences for the ending is great and offers some replayability to see how characters change and react differently depending on your choices. Game is literally the definition of not judging a book by its cover.People laugh at it but I would recommend it to anyone. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing game. I'm usually pretty picky when it comes to games that focus so much on story telling and heavy dialogue, but more often than not I had a smile on my face even during admittedly cringey dialogue. I think this is in large part due to how well everything is broken up by the unique gameplay. It may appear like a pokemon clone at first, but it's far more than that. Even the large pool of fetch quests were fair more bearable than most games thanks to the variant each biome and Bugsnax adds to the world. I think a large portion of the fun I had was thanks to the friends I streamed for while playing this, but that in no way discredits how great this game is. My only complaint is the DLC content. Even though you can only reach it by the end of the game, it becomes strangely hand-holdy with new mechanics more obvious than previous ones. The DLC boss was also my least favorite out of the entire game, being way too clunky with the massive models inside of a space that felt too small for what was going on. On top of this, bugs were fair more apparent in this area of the game. Besides that, I highly recommend Bugsnax to anyone and hope that there's more DLC content or a sequel in the near future.

_childDocuments_.review: Bunger?!Ok but seriously, I love this game so much! I'm currently almost finished with my second playthrough. I initially discovered Bugsnax through RTGame, and I just had to try it myself. Everyone likes to talk about the twist at the end, and although it certainly threw me through a loop, very few seem to acknowledge just how great the core gameplay mechanics are. It was really fun trying out different combos of tools to try to catch different kinds of Bugsnax. I also liked that there were multiple ways to catch most Bugsnax, further encouraging creativity. Even the most ridiculous of strategies can work. The Bugsnax are also very cute, especially Hunnabee and Our Lord and Savior Bunger.The Grumpuses and their relationships between each other are surprisingly fleshed out as well. Sure, some had better character arcs than others, but each one has a distinct personality that makes them iconic in their own way. My favorite Grumpus has to be Chandlo because he's an absolute chad and a nice deviation from the typical jock stereotype. Snorpy's a close second because he's silly, gay, and mentally ill, he just like me fr fr.Overall, don't let the cutesy graphics fool you from thinking this is a simple children's game. It's so much more than that. I'm excited to see what the devs are cooking up next

_childDocuments_.review: The first game ever i bought because of the discovery queue here on steam. The art style looked interesting, the reviews here on steam as well as on youtube etc were looking promising, therefore i gave the game a try.And oh boy, it was such a fun ride. For about 21 hours to get all achievements i enjoyed almost every minute (except the times you get pushed around by the Bungers :D ). Not only is the art style fantastic, the gameplay, writing and sound design is amazing as well. Never boring, punishing or too difficult. The gameplay mechanics are perfect and nothing was just a gimmick. Missions never became obsolete, because the storytelling made every mission interesting. And the whole game ran without any issues or bugs (well there a bugsnax in the game). It's definitely not a game for kids. The topics which the game touches ranging from relation ship issues, mental health to climate related topics. At the start of the game it's pretty delightful, but the story is becoming more and more darker and sinner towards the end. That doesn't mean though, that from time to time you laugh about the jokes the grumpus are making or the wonderful design of the bugsnax. Or let's say: If your kid under a certain age want to play this game, then make sure to watch your kid every now and then.I suck in writing reviews, but i want to add my two extremely positive cents to this game, so maybe you are more willing to give this game a chance. It's definitely worth the full price (even though i got it while on sale) and i really hope for a sequel! The cliffhanger at the end let it look like that at least.Bunga Bunga!

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax is a game about collecting little creatures and feeding them to your neighbors. It's a simple premise, but the game completely blew away every expectation I had for it. The creatures are adorable, and learning about all of them and solving the puzzle of how to catch them was sometimes challenging but always rewarding. The characters are unique and interesting; the voice acting is some of the best I've heard in gaming, and the diversity in the case (even though they're all monster people) was such a pleasant shock. The world is vibrant and alive, and unlocking new areas felt exciting. The story took so many sharp turns that I was always guessing at what would happen next--and I was never right. But I was never disappointed, either. This game was great fun, and I'd easily recommend it to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to enjoy this game, but the amount of tedious troubleshooting I've had to do just to get it to function has left a very, very bad taste in my mouth. I have never in my 10+ years of gaming been pushed away from a game due to technical difficulties, but I don't think I'll be returning to this game any time soon.The first hurdle I hit was that the game wouldn't utilize my GPU if I looked around at all. It worked fine as long as I didn't touch my mouse, but as soon as I looked in any direction the frames plummeted.  After about an hour of troubleshooting, changing to directx9, updating drivers, etc etc, it finally starts working and I begin to make my way through the game.The next hitch was just a hard crash to desktop without a warning, which was just weird but since it autosaved I wasn't really too bothered by it. The next time it happened, however, it decided to really screw up my audio. I use voicemeeter to split my audio tracks for streaming, so I don't know if it had to do with that or not, but it scrambled up my sounds so that discord/chrome worked fine, but the discord and windows notifications were going through a channel that by all means should have been audible, but wasn't. Same with the game, on the next launch I couldn't hear a thing, even though it was in the same track as audio from other applications that I could hear.. At this point, I'm through with it, maybe I'll give it another try in a little while but this has taken entirely too much troubleshooting for me to want to continue.That being said, I did enjoy the few hours it was functioning properly. And, for the record, I have a mid-end rig, so maybe I'm not up to the Bugsnax™ standard, but again, this is the first game I've had problems with in years.

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax is very easy, lacks satisfying depth, and has some really strange thematic flip-flopping. The characters fight and antagonize each other, some are genuinely unlikable and do not grow or change, and while certain moments threaten that the game might open up and reveal that it was actually deeper and more mature, that depth remains an implication. The ending tries to pay off a dark secret that the rest of the game never really suggests, leaving the whole experience mystifyingly hollow. The game isn't actively unpleasant or bad to play so this is a worthwhile cheap on-sale pickup, just to mess around in the sandbox and to rocket through the very short, very straightforward story. Though, I will say that the DLC island that is unlocked by completing a couple side stories was very refreshing, delivering the feeling of exploration, environmental puzzle solving, and character/writing that the rest of the game should have really had to begin with.

_childDocuments_.review: This has gotta be one of the most underrated indie games ever. Think of it as Legend of Zelda meets Pokemon meets Veggie Tales with an undertone of body horror throughout. The writing and voice acting are fantastic and there's a surprising amount of depth to the gameplay in terms of figuring out how to combine mechanics in order to catch the more unwieldy bugsnax. Regarding difficulty, it's "easy" in the sense that you don't have health/there's no real consequences for failure, however, there's a lot of optional content that offers a moderate challenge to your puzzle-solving skills and timing ability if you're up for that.  I won't spoil the story, but tonally it manages to be funny (I legitimately lol'd a few times), wholesome (the characters are fully fleshed out and you actually care about their fate), and delightfully bizarre (I wondered at several moments what kind of person would come up with a concept like this and somehow convince others to help them execute it fully) all at once. Anyway, that's all to say that Bugsnax is definitely a new fave of mine and I could totally see it becoming a cult classic in the future.Btw, if you're worried about price, there's at least 25 hrs. of content here if you do most of the optional quests/areas, so imo at $25 you're definitely getting your money's worth. Notice how high the completion rates are on the achievements, most of which aren't main story-related. That should be proof enough that you won't want to stop playing this game until you've finished all the silly little side quests and captured every goofy-a$$ looking bugsnack there is.

_childDocuments_.review: I won't talk a lot about what you'll be doing, but most of the time you'll be capturing bugsnax and feeding them to the npcs. Basically speaking, the majority of them are captured by setting a trap and waiting for them to come near it without having to do a lot of work. Throughout the game you'll find new tools to help you capture some bugsnax, some of them will need patience and strategies to get.There is a day/night cycle which is really nice it makes you feel more immersed in the game. There is also a mechanic that changes the moon phases which is important because some bugsnax only appears in certain ones. You can also skip the time by sleeping.There are a lot of quests, most of them are side quests and "requests". Completing requests will get you  rewarded with a decoration for your house.And yes, you can have a house and customize it in some ways. There are some areas available for you to change the furniture to another one, you can also change the painting of the walls etc. It's pleasant and satisfying to get a nice decoration to put in your home. are really unique, each one of them has their own personality, which is reflected by their colors, expressions, thoughts and actions. They really show that to the player and to the other npcs. For example, you'll often see them talking to each other about themselves/ sharing their own thoughts. This is also really good because it makes the Snaxburg (Camp - the place where they live) alive, which also contributes to immersion. The bugsnax are the peak of creativity in this game. they often represent food. You are going to find a lot of food types in each one of them and It's really interesting, they also make funny and cute sounds, It's hard not to like them and hard to describe them. Beautiful! Very pleasant views with nice colors that represents the biomes in a very charming way. On top of that we also have an amazing soundtrack which consists in electronic music, synthesizers in a very ethereal sounding while representing the biome in which the player is located. Very relaxing and memorable songs. Really gooood. I love the island itself (Broken tooth). I didn't feel tired to be there, and spoilers ahead . I won't talk a lot about this dlc (you really should discover it by yourself), but It's very worth it. It introduces a new mechanic to get the bugsnax in there, and there is some secrets there too + it also has a nice plot and dialogues between the characters. I really recommend playing the dlc before finishing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax has always been a comfort game to me. You play as a journalist grump (yep, grump) who has set off to find the missing explorer Elizabert Batternugget who tells us to meet her at Snaktooth Island, the location of the illusive "bugsnax". Once you arrive, or rather, crash land, you meet all the grumps who traveled to Snaktooth Island with Lizbert and help them find out what happened to their mysterious leader.The overall premise of the game being catching bugs that are shaped and taste like snacks and bringing them to your new friends to consume is such a goofy and unique concept. I love how colorful each snak is and how vibrant the surrounding areas are - the island shares a beach, a desert, a lucious forrest, and a frozen mountainous terrain. Each of the grumps have their own personalities and insecurities that you learn about and they can feel pretty heavy at times. Perhaps being on an island that defies reality doesn't mean you left all your emotional baggage at home. Bugsnax takes a wonderful approach of how to deal with your past, emotions, and insecurities to better yourself as a person (grump?).While searching and finding unique ways to catch bugsnax can be fun, that's basically... all you're really doing in order to advance the story. It can feel pretty repetitive at times and some of the ways you capture bugsnax are not very intuitive (I'm looking at YOU Flamin' Cheepoof!!). I wish they had integrated other elements into the story missions, but honestly, I really love running around and catching all the bugsnax and supporting my new friends with everything going on in their intertwined lives. It's very heartwarming to see everyone come together over time and rekindle relationships.Obviously every game will have at least one flaw, even the best of the best have at least unlikable trait to them - but I have such an easy time looking past these small issues that it's an easy 10/10 for me. It's such a colorful and beautiful game with a very interesting premise that no sane person would have come up with on their own, and I completely mean that. Part of me really hopes to see a sequel at some point because I just can't get enough of these wonderful Bugsnax!

_childDocuments_.review: Didn't expect to enjoy it as much as I did, but honestly the gameplay is a great break from your usual story shooter. Has the same sorta draw as something like Stardew Valley does for me, just relaxing and fun.Gameplay is very simple but very enjoyable tbh, gives you that satisfaction of completing your collection but doesn't make it impossible to 100%, just challenging enough to be fun without being super frustrating.The "horror" element that I've seen a few people mention is a bit of a stretch. So don't go into it expecting things to take a turn towards lovecraft or anything.Regardless, very fun little game, gave me a good amount of enjoyment for 3 or 4 days. _childDocuments_.review: I had this game on my wishlist for years, in my mind marked as merely 'maybe interesting'. On my wishlist it remained through numerous sales because I had other priorities. A friend gifted me Bugsnax for Christmas this year and I finally had to try it. I wasn't disappointed.Bugsnax has a bit of everything.- Your thirst to collect will be quenched.- Challenges, both easy and medium ones (none are hard, I struggled a bit with one of the letter quests because I was unlucky, but that's it)- Characters with exaggerated personalities- Possibilities to be creative through customizing both the grumpuses and your house- Achievements, all doable and not too trying- Amazing design choices in a lot of places- Fun tools and weapons to aid youBugsnax is in many ways a beautiful game. I wasn't too big a fan of the grumpuses design, and I actually found their faces a bit distracting when the story unfolded. I had a hard time taking the story seriously with the grumpuses looking like they do. On the other hand, the environment and the bugsnax themselves are beatifully designed. A LOT of fantasy went into making this game and it's hard not to appreciate that.It does feel that the game tries very hard to be PC, which annoyed me a bit. It just didn't feel natural, but again, with all the fantasy maybe that wasn't even the point.Overall I had a very good experience. It took me about 20 hours to finish, including doing all the side quests and letter quests. I also spent a good amount of time just screwing around looking for hats, customizing my house and shooting hoops. Bugsnax is casual if you want it to be, and not if you don't. You decide.I warmly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Goofy, sweet, and fun.Most of the game is about collecting adorable and hilarious—and weird—critters. They start easy, but as the game progresses you'll have to use your tools, and wits, and patience creatively. It's not very hard but it's not a casual game either. I was challenged.There's actually a story and characters and they're fairly fleshed out and elaborated, at least within the ridiculous logic of 's ridiculous world. Do you gay? Yes. There is gay. The kind of gay that is just taken for granted: portrayals of same-sex love and non-gender conforming folk. And those are just inconsequential details in the story, as they should be in real life. Do you therapy? It normalizes that, too.Most surprising is how many hours of fun you will have. Or will you? Beyond the main quest there are a few optional quests and also a great many optional challenges. My one criticism of the game is that there are just too many of them. More than 100! Optional does mean optional, but the game unfortunately doesn't warn you or tell you how many you have left. Once you start going down that road you might stubbornly decide to see it through, and ... well, there are really too many. As much as I enjoyed the game, it felt very repetitive and tedious getting to that "100% achievements" finish line. I don't regret it, but, yeah, 50 instead of 100 would also have been great.But don't you worry your fruity, chocolatey, crispy little head over a minor flaw.  is not just a surprisingly good game, it's a good game, period. I had fun, laughed, and learned a valuable lesson about getting along with people with difficult personalities. Oh, and to avoid eating foods that turn you into themselves.Bugsnax!

_childDocuments_.review: I've waited for exclusivity deals to expire and dodged spoilers for two years to play this game.Was it worth it?Yes. Yes it was.Young Horses delivers again with a wildly creative and engaging monster collecting game featuring an expertly written cast of characters I grew fond for over the course of my playthrough. While I was drawn in by the cute bugsnax designs and the planning process behind catching them, learning about the residents of Snaktooth Island and breaking down their personalities, strengths, weaknesses, and so on while unraveling the mystery behind Lizbert's disappearance kept me hooked right up to the end.Besides the story, Bugsnax is a game that encourages creative use of your tools and the environment when going about catching snax, and I was often finding very creative methods for using what i had on hand. While the game isn't incredibly punishing (you cannot get hurt or die in any way) it can still provide a unique challenge to new and seasoned players alike.Overall, I found Bugsnax a wonderfully charming and engaging experience and would encourage giving it a try if it seems even remotely interesting to you.

_childDocuments_.review: A cute-looking creature collector with far more depth than it first lets on. Catching the titular Bugsnax is mostly fun, though some can be rather annoying; but the writing is definitely the highlight of the game for me, with surprisingly engaging character development that will have you hooked on each one's personal stories. Plenty of fun to play, but attempting 100% completion will try your patience, namely due to the optional challenges added in a post-launch update. A journalist on the verge of losing their job and in need of a breakout story receives a video tape from an explorer named Elizabert Megafig, delivered to you from her camp on the fabled Snaktooth Island. The tape reveals that she went there alongside a ragtag team to study a species of bug-like creatures that inexplicably resemble different kinds of food; and she invites you to come to the island so its mysteries can be revealed to the world. However, after a sudden crash-landing, you learn that Elizabert has gone missing and the other residents of her established settlement of Snaxburg have scattered across the island. In a pursuit for knowledge much grander than they bargained for, the journalist must track down the rest of the group, piece together the events that split them apart, track down the missing Elizabert, and find out all there is to know about the curious creatures known as .The core gameplay revolves around catching Bugsnax to fulfill various resident requests, but you can't just run up to them and pick them up off the ground. You're given an assortment of traps and lures as you progress, and you need to observe a Bugsnak's behavior to figure out which of these tools can catch it. Some are pretty straightforward, while others require careful setup or a bit of ingenuity; and the physics engine that drives the game can lead to some really funny moments whether or not you succeed at catching something. There are eight biomes outside of Snaxburg, each one with their own unique assortment of Bugsnax to catch, for a total of over 100 to find. , especially when the game introduces fire/ice mechanics that prevent you and your tools from interacting with certain Bugsnax directly. That being said, these are few and far between, so it shouldn't become any more than a mild inconvenience during your playthrough.Once you catch some Bugsnax, you can feed them to the residents of Snaxburg, and doing so will transform their body parts to resemble what they ate--whether you consider this to be "funny" or "a weird new form of body horror" is up to you. Most of your quests throughout the game require you to feed specific Bugsnax to people and/or change specific parts of their body, but you can still feed them whatever, whenever, if you're running out of inventory space or just want to make the residents look as silly as possible. If you'd rather take a kinder approach to clearing your inventory, you can donate Bugsnax to the camp's ranch in exchange for upgrades to your bag space, allowing you to hold more Bugsnax and reduce the need to return to camp as often. This also initiates a second unofficial collection quest to not just catch one of everything, but also donate one of everything; however, this isn't needed to max out your bag space and doesn't provide an extra achievement if that's your main metric for "completion".. Starting out, every resident of Snaxburg feels like a one-dimensional trope--the grumpy old man, the diva, the shady businessman, etc.--but work on their side quests and they'll start to display a surprising amount of emotional depth. Most characters meet for the first time when they arrive at Snaktooth, but some have extensive histories with one another (typically through romantic relationships) that generally influence their character arcs. Each resident claims to have come to the island for simple reasons, but over time you learn that each one did so in a failed attempt to deal with an underlying problem; and your ultimate goal during their respective side quests is to help them work through these problems. I won't give away specifics, but things get a lot more serious than you'd expect, and  There's no violence or overt sexual themes--though there is some suggestive dialogue--but character arcs are focused on subjects that were definitely written with an adult audience in mind: deep-seated insecurities, complications in romantic relationships, and the search to find one's place in the world, among other things. The writing can get a bit dark at times, and while it doesn't warrant an M rating or anything, I wouldn't go giving this game to a little kid without digging further into the specifics first. was originally a PlayStation/Epic Games Store exclusive that launched in late 2020, before finally moving to Xbox, Switch, and Steam in early 2022. Before it was ported over, it was announced that it would come with a free update called "The Isle of BIGsnax", which includes two key additions: a new biome with more quests to beat and Bugsnax to catch, and over 100 challenges that would reward you with furniture to decorate your own personal hut in Snaxburg., which included catching/donating every Bugsnak, completing the main story, all side quests, all DLC quests, and maybe 50 or so challenges. My attempt to beat all the challenges wore on my patience until I ultimately gave up on that venture; but take that out of the equation and you're still left with something unique and fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I give this game a rank D+ (50-55%)Forgettable game - sadly nothing really good here..See my profile for more details about my reviews.I should have refunded this game, then I would not have felt bad to give it a thumbs down. Thank you no thank you Steam for your stupid system I disapprove with (I still believe a rating like on BGG is better). I give Bugsnax about 52% in rating, and in my notation, it means that no, I would not particularly recommend it. I should have stopped before the 2 hours mark and refunded it, then I would not have had to review it negatively. At least I am just glad it won't hurt its standing on Steam at all (what is one little negative review with 94% positive reviews!). And who knows, maybe my kids will enjoy this game?I wanted meaningful depth and emotional sense from this game, and I got neither. As soon as the game started, the cartooney art, the funny voices (an hilarious spider squeaking and running away from you) and the quirky mechanisms of the game made me think "could it be an Outer Wilds-ish game?!". Which meant HIGH level for me. And that is what I kept hoping all throughout the game. But after 10 hours, I finished it, and NEVER got what I expected. My bad! I am not the target for this.The silly outlook of it felt like a pretend to me, some kind of appearance to hide something more meaningful, and so I was waiting for the depth at every corner... but in the end it was silly and non-sensical all the way through. Despite a very interesting take on some recent genres such as Outer Wilds, Subnautica, Slime Rancher or even Stardew Valley and a Short Hike (very, very light influence for some, mind you), this game was just silly, awkward and cringey all the way. And if it was just for the bad style that I did not like... but the problem is, I also disapprove with the content: this is NOT a good, worthy of narrative fictional content in my opinion. The bugsnax (pokemon-ish creatures) and story (stranded on a weird island) are quirky but secondary in content, the primary content here seems to be relationships? emotional feelings of awkward people towards others, as awkward, in a broken society? Practically all the characters work as a couple (either of friends, hetero, gay, enemies, bromance, what have you), and they all try to live with that. And all the dialogues and story revolve around that.And that might be why the game is not for me: I don't care! I don't give a damn about that. Some people will wrongly use the tag LGBT to promote this game, while some others will dumbly use it to condemn the game: who cares! I don't like to be shoved in the face with relational stuff, private stuff, emotional-baggage-issue-stuff ("I am worthless!" "no you aren't!" "yes I am!" "no you are beautiful as you are!" "oh thank you come here let's kiss" "smoochie smoochie"), I never enjoyed that in any piece of art whether it is a movie, a painting, a video game, maybe it is my autism and lack of empathy, but I just can't relate and get into it. It has NOTHING to do with emotions, as I can definitely cry in a game like Outer Wilds. It is just private stuff RUBBED in your face, and I could not care less. AND it is shown here in a quirky, silly, nickelodeon style, which I truthfully abhor.Also, half a joke but let me give an additional thumbs down to the bugsnax representation: I don't mind Pokemon (who cares) but what a WEIRD look on food, what a broken, sick relationship to gastronomy, what a weird depiction of ingredients and meals... only a US studio could imagine such a thing I guess.Is it a generation thing? Maybe if you are 15 and love this content? I am a simple man who doesn't like intellectualism from Jonathan Blow, but I also am a grumpy old man who can't suffer this silly non sense. Note however that I don't give this game a 20 or 30% in rating: I do not think it is BADLY made. I just think there is nothing worth people's time here, there are better things out there. Sad, because the voice over is remarkable, the dialogues are very well written despite all the characters being insufferable, and the mechanisms of catching bugs are clever. Oh well! is  on  on  on

_childDocuments_.review: Never have I ever been so compelled to give a thorough review for such a game. The last review I made was nothing more than a half-assed attempt to be "funny" 3 years ago. On the surface level, Bugsnax is not an entirely complex game - the description follows suit.Just as the description seems simple, so is the game at it's core. What ended up being an impulse buy to play a casual game, ended up becoming a (perhaps) unhealthy obsession over the world, the characters, the environment, the setting. Everything was wonderful, and wonderfully goofy. The Bunger and it's glory is but one of the many Bugsnax that can be seen in game. It's a game that runs with it's concept, utilizing simple concepts to solve different puzzles, and though I can't tell you that this game offers an extremely varied way to solve everything, I can tell you that it gets close enough.The development of characters - both physically and mentally - create a solid foundation of characters that you can love, and grow to love (or ultimately just hate). Those same characters are not as they first appear, nor are they static. They change as you help them change, offering to solve their problems - and by extension, help them grow through it. My addiction to side quests, whether attributed to my ADHD or not, was enhanced by the characters offering them, those likable and real people that are vibrant and exuberant, just like the scenery itself.Speaking of which, this world isn't that huge once you've explored everything. Quite honestly, this isn't a particularly big game, taking around 10 hours to really push through the story. I find that it's the side characters and the missions you can do for them that makes this game much more huger. Though I have 100% on the achievements in Bugsnax, it doesn't mean that I've unlocked everything in the game. There isn't much merit for it other than personal, and I already feel achieved enough throughout this game.A wonderful story, setting, character cast, and charming premise for a game that I assumed would be something I'd put down after an hour or 2. I can't believe that I spent so long on this game, but I know it was worth the time spent. Hell, a majority of the time was me streaming this game to my girlfriend, even the side-quests and letters that are arguably much better spent playing than watching. She played Bunger voice clips while a very dramatic scene was playing towards the end, so that was pretty lit.Buy the game if you at least want something entertaining for a couple hours. It'll be worth the money, I guarantee it.

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax is a wonderful combination of cute artwork, fun quests, exploration, creative tools, and real sh*t. I'm telling you, dude, there are some pretty constructive social themes in the dialogue here, and it's awesome.You learn a lot about every character, and their relationships with other Grumpuses. Some more than others, ofc - and they still have little cartoon personalities - but even with the veil of "cute colorful kids game," it's got great interpersonal development. It's structured like a cartoon, but there are plenty of mature conversations around how to navigate your relationships, communication, finding courage, seeing value in your capabilities, and accepting your limitations as a person - all in a digestible format, contextualized for the setting this game exists in. Like I said: This game contains real sh*t, if you ask me.What surprised me the most was how absolutely marvelously this game normalizes identities of all kinds, from personality to gender to orientation. Every Grumpus' identity is totally diverse and presented as normal. It's refreshing to see a game in which characters are able to exist in many different forms without those forms being subject to criticism from within the writing, or even to harmful stereotypes. Granted, I couldn't give you an example of a game that does either of those things, but this was a pleasant surprise nevertheless. You don't see a nonchalantly non-binary character with everyone being totally chill with their pronouns like it's an average Tuesday every day, do you? Nope! Not even on Tuesdays!The story of the island revealed itself very suddenly, but there were always hints at what was to come. I really enjoyed this story, and I especially liked the dark theme underneath the cute and colorful mask.Overall, absolutely recommend. Great game, great characters, great writing. I hope other games can live up to this gem. Thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: Trying to be as objective as I possibly can; Bugsnax is a fun, quirky, charming, extremely charismatic experience. It's style is well defined, the gameplay is massively entertaining, the silly-yet-real dialogue is backed up by a surprisingly strong voice acting cast, and there's a clearly good staff putting it all together seamlessly. In short words: Bugsnax good, play Bugsnax.However, I will allow myself to embrace a bigger level of subjectivity here. Bugsnax is downright one of the best games I've ever played, and it has consumed me whole like a Bunger in the maw of a hungry Grumpus. This is the only game in Steam I have all achievements on. I've actually 100%'ed my first playthrough, not just all the snax and junk, I mean ACTUAL 100%, as in: Literally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ everything. I scanned everything that's scannable, got all mail, discovered the secret area, caught all snax, did all the sidequests, got all 112 Snax on Gramble's farm and got all the tapes. I ain't an achievement hunter or a completionist type, it was all out of genuine, raw, unadulterated love for the game. Charm is definitely the word I would use to TLDR the experience. Is easy to get hooked when everything is clearly filled with an astonishing level of love and care. The tiny additions of dark humor and messed up subjects played completely straight in spite of it stark contrast with the colorful, bubblegum pop of the visuals and designs is handled wonderfully; None of the elements fight between each other, they hold hands and dance around, creating a perfect balance between honesty and self awareess.Its utterly ridiculous, it knows its ridiculous and yet it is so emotionally earnest it loops around and becomes endearing.

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax was quite fun. A remix of Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs 2 where the bugsnaxs have to be caught to be eaten by the starving villagers of Snaxburg. It took me 24 hours to complete (it may take less time if you aren't interested in all the side quests and the mail quests).Story: You are a journalist and want to investigate the new discovery from Elizabert, an island with bugsnaxs. When you arrive on the island, Filbo is the only Grumpus in Snaxburg. You have to convince the others to come back, catching bugsnaxs with new equipment along the way. There are four bigger bugsnaxs that are part of side quests, and a big showdown at the end requiring a new variant of the equipment you've used so far. You do find Lizbert eventually, but she (and Eggabelle) won't be coming back with you to the city.After the credits (with pictures as a sort of epilogue), a conversation can be heard which might points to a sequel? Maybe? Pretty-please?

_childDocuments_.review: So, I really was contemplating if it was a thumbs up or down for me, because this is a middle of the road game.5 or 6/10 I can't really decide.So Bugsnax in the first 6 hours or so was quite enjoyable. A typical chill/cozy Game where you can't die, you explore relatively small regions and scan/collect/hunt bugs and feed them to Grumpuses (which become your friends over the course of the game).But after a certain point this Game became extremely tedious.Some Bugs were very frustrating to catch and what the Game basically became was a fetch quest simulator.There were just soooooooooooooooo many fetch quests.The Main Story was kinda interesting and this was the only thing that kept me hooked enough to finish the Game.But the Sidequests were a) uninteresting and b) they didn't stop. Also there were Sidequests and there were "Mini Challenges".A big part of the "Mini Challenges": Fetch Quests. And they also didn't stop. You finish 3, you get 6 more. I did so many of them and it wouldn't stop and I just had no interest in backtracking the same areas again and again and again.Voicework was excellent though, only in the Credits I saw that they got Yuri Lowenthal and Fred Tatasciore. Music was alright also.Graphically it is highly stylized and it was fitting quite nicely.So yeah, the Game has some positives to it, definitely. I even started out, thinking that I might 100% it. But when a Game starts to bore me after a while because it's just fetch quest after fetch quest, I can't really recommend it.Still, as I mentioned before, it is also not the worst Game, just middle of the road. Still a very close thumbs down from me...
